## Complete Course of Patrology

—or universal library—complete, uniform, convenient, economical, of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprint of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition throughout the first twelve centuries of the Church, prepared from the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with numerous manuscript codices, and corrected with the utmost care; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched by two general indexes: the one, of subjects, by consulting which whatever any one of the Fathers wrote on any topic may be viewed at a glance; the other, of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily learn which Fathers commented on the individual books of Scripture and in which passages of their works they did so.

A most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others, if the following are taken into consideration: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the exceedingly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

# Preface to Volume Ten

After the Donatists had been utterly defeated and overthrown in that famous victory of the Catholics at the Conference of Carthage, the Church immediately had a new enemy rising against her to defeat. This enemy attacked no longer, like the Donatists, the body of Christian society, but its very soul—namely, the grace of the Savior by which we are Christians. We consider it our responsibility to present here the history of this exceedingly pernicious heresy, known as Pelagian and Coelestian from the names of its authors, reconstructed from the earliest writers. Nor could anything more suitably take the place of a preface than to prepare the minds of diligent readers, by means of a brief account of Pelagian affairs, for reading Augustine, who in this final volume fought against that heresy.

## I. The Homeland, Way of Life, and Character of Pelagius the Heresiarch

Pelagius, the leader of the heresy, was commonly called “the Briton.” Augustine believed that this surname had been given to him in order to distinguish him from another of the same name, whom they called Pelagius of Tarentum (*Letter* 186.1). Prosper likewise calls him by this name in his *Chronicle* under the year 413, as does Gennadius, whose text has been corrected against the older manuscripts (below, Appendix, part 2). Orosius also calls him “our Briton” (*Apology*); Mercator calls him “a Briton by race” (below, Appendix, part 2). Finally, Prosper, in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*, identifies the author of the Pelagian heresy in these words:

> The doctrine which the serpent of Britain,  
> sated with the poison of the ancient dragon,  
> vomited forth in a pestilential speech.

Much farther below, speaking against Semi-Pelagian impiety, he says:

> Following the rejected Briton, its author.

And in an epigram against a certain detractor of Augustine:

> Or this man, he says, the watery Britons fed with their own produce.

Moreover, in his work *Against the Collator*, where he mentions certain enemies of grace discovered in Britain, he writes that these alone occupied the land of their own origin (ibid.). And if this was indeed the Pelagius whom Jerome calls “weighed down by Scottish porridge,” Jerome attributes to him precisely what suited men neighboring his native land. Thus, in another passage, he says of him: “He has the ancestry of the Scottish people, from the neighborhood of the Britons” (ibid.). By these words he signifies nothing other than that Pelagius appeared to be a Scot, or Irishman: for he possessed the innate vices of the Scottish—that is, Irish—region, and had come from neighboring Britain.

Orosius indicates that he was born of humble parents (*Apology*, ch. 26); for he says that his birth did not provide him with the means of being educated in more respectable disciplines, and that for this reason, in composing his books, he needed assistants who would lend him their labor and supply him with their manner of expression.

Pelagius is regularly called “the Monk” both by Augustine (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, below, §36; and volume 8, *On Heresies*, ch. 88) and by others who mention him (below, Appendix, part 2). From this one may infer that he not only professed this way of life, but also possessed no more distinguished title by which he might be called, and was in no way honored with clerical rank. Hence Augustine asserts that his heresy was introduced not by bishops, priests, or any other clerics, but by certain pseudomonks (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, below, §61).

Orosius expressly calls him a layman (below, Appendix, part 2), and complains that a place was given to him among the priests at the assembly in Jerusalem. Pope Zosimus, initially favoring the same Pelagius, whom he believed to be falsely accused of error, called him “a layman striving toward worthy conduct through a long life of service to God” (ibid.).

Whether Pelagius became a monk in England among the Bangor community or in Italy is not important to determine here; nor is it worthwhile to review the other conjectures of English writers about him that may be found in Ussher. Almost everyone, however, was convinced that, at the time when John Chrysostom was being harassed by his adversaries, Pelagius was living as a monk in the East. They also believed him to be the same man of whom the holy bishop wrote to Olympias in a letter apparently sent in 405, while he was in exile at Arabissus in Armenia, in these words:

> I have been deeply distressed by Pelagius the monk. Consider, I ask you, how many and how great crowns those deserve who have stood firm with courage, when we see men living with such care, zeal, and endurance being led away.

Without doubt, that Pelagius had deserted those who defended John’s innocence; the holy Bishop had no other reason to mourn his fall. As for the Pelagian heresy, it does not seem credible that Chrysostom—who died in 407—had ever heard anything about it, even though its parent may perhaps already have been gradually insinuating it at that time.

Indeed, it is readily believed that Pelagius the heresiarch was in Rome in this same year 405, when John was lamenting the defection of Pelagius the monk, once it has been noted from Mercator that Pelagius absorbed his heresy at Rome, when a certain Syrian named Rufinus was disseminating it, during the pontificate of Pope Anastasius (ibid.). For he did not withdraw from that city, where Augustine testifies that he lived for a very long time (*On Original Sin*, below, §24), until approximately the year 410. The letter which Pelagius recalled having written to Bishop Paulinus nearly twelve years earlier, in letters addressed to the already deceased Pope Innocent, must likewise be assigned to this period (*On the Grace of Christ*, below, §38).

[Column 0011]

Having spent a very long time in Rome, Pelagius had made himself known to many people and had first won for himself in that city a reputation far from ordinary. Augustine also began to know him there (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, below, §46), so that, although many approved of Pelagius’s life, in his earliest works against his errors Augustine almost always mentioned him with honor and praise.

Thus, in one passage, Augustine testifies that Pelagius was called by those who knew him “a good and praiseworthy man”; elsewhere he says that, as he had heard, Pelagius was “a holy man and a Christian of no small advancement” (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 3, §§5, 1).

Elsewhere he praises the opponents of grace in general as follows:

> Although they live chaste lives and are praiseworthy in conduct, they do not hesitate to do what the Lord commanded the rich man who asked for advice about attaining eternal life. When he replied that he had already fulfilled all the commandments of the Law, the Lord instructed him, if he wished to be perfect, to sell everything he had, give it to the poor, and transfer his treasure to heaven.

(*Ibid.*, book 2, §25.)

Again he writes to Honoratus:

> Nor are they such people as you can easily despise; rather, they live continently and are praiseworthy in good works.

(*Letter* 140.83.)

Bishop Paulinus of Nola certainly held Pelagius very dear, considering him an outstanding servant of God. At Pelagius’s urging, two young men, Timasius and Jacobus, rejected what the world promised them and devoted themselves, together with all their hope, to God.

For this reason Pelagius later produced letters from many bishops, intending by the exceptional praises with which they honored him to remove from himself the stigma of the heresy charged against him. “As though,” Augustine says, “all who heard his vehement and, in a certain sense, fiery exhortations to a good life could easily have known that he held these perverse opinions” (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, below, §50). He also boasted that he counted many holy men among his friends (ibid., §53).

But after he once abandoned the true faith, whatever piety had seemed to exist in him diminished day by day or vanished altogether. In the *Apology* written by Orosius in 415 or 416, he is called “the new master and servant of tables.” Orosius then calls him “Ἀναμάρτητος” (*Anamártētos*, “sinless”), one who assures us that perfection of an immaculate life can be attained while eating, drinking, and sleeping.

He is also mocked below as though because of drunkenness, in these words:

> Finally awakened after a great debauch.

And after Orosius had described him in the form of a giant as follows:

> There stands Goliath, most monstrous in his pride, swollen with carnal power, confident that he can do everything by himself—his head, hands, and entire body clothed in an elaborate display—

so that he might portray with all his colors the appearance and form of a man whom he had even known by sight, he subsequently added new lines to this rough sketch. In one place he says:

> But perhaps you have a special confidence that you can carry this burden because, nourished by baths and banquets, you carry broad shoulders and a powerful neck, displaying even fatness on your forehead.

We do not know, however, whether he also intended to portray him as both a eunuch and one-eyed when he says:

> This mutilated fellow of ours, smooth on the forehead, “μονόφθαλμος” (*monóphthalmos*, “one-eyed”).

Finally, he asserts that no one is ignorant of the manner in which Pelagius orders his life. Nor would we consider it implausible that Jerome refers to this same man when he calls him “the white dog, large and corpulent, who can rage more with his heels than with his teeth” (below, Appendix, part 2).

A letter of Isidore of Pelusium survives addressed to the monk Pelagius, from a man who did not know how to praise or flatter a sinner in the desires of his soul. It reads as follows:

> Gray hairs are scattered upon Ephraim, and he did not know it; that is, he was growing young again through vicious affections. In the same way, the great multitude of years has brought gray hairs upon you, yet you have a rigid and unbending mind, continually moving from one monastery to another and examining and searching out everyone’s tables. Therefore, if the smell of meat and the seasoning of dishes concern you, flatter those who hold public office instead, and seek out the kitchens of cities. For hermits do not possess the resources to receive you as agreeably as you desire.

(*Book 1, Letter 314.*)

If this short letter was sent to Pelagius the heresiarch, it must have been written before his heresy became publicly known, and therefore not long after he departed from Africa in 411, as we shall say later. Certainly, the moral corruption which Isidore observed in Pelagius supplies a significant argument for believing that it had not yet occurred before his stay in Rome, where he lived in high esteem among all reputable people.

## II. Pelagius’s Earliest Writings Already Imbued with the Poison of Heresy

Gennadius has left it on record that, before Pelagius incurred the reputation of heresy, he published several good writings: namely, three books on the Trinity, very useful for students who wished to learn the Church’s teaching on that subject, and one book of *Eulogies*, especially suited to forming the conduct of a Christian man (below, Appendix, part 2).

In it he presented various testimonies from Scripture distributed under different headings, evidently following the method and practice of Cyprian. He declared that he wished to imitate—or even complete—Cyprian’s work addressed to Quirinus in his own book addressed to a Roman (ibid.), while always commemorating that blessed martyr with the honor due to him (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 4, §21).

This book, like Pelagius’s other works, was written in Latin (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, below, §4). Augustine calls it not the book of *Eulogies* but the book of *Chapters* (ibid., §§7, 54), and elsewhere the book of *Testimonies* (*Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 4, §21). Orosius asserts that this latter title had been written above it by the author himself (*Apology*).

There is no doubt that when Pelagius composed this book he had not yet fallen under suspicion of error; Gennadius explicitly says so. But he was certainly already a heretic, since the bishops at the Synod of Diospolis brought forward various passages from the same book against him (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, §§2, 5, and elsewhere).

Jerome does the same, and charges him especially with this: in a book in which he professes to be an imitator, or even a completer, of the work of the blessed martyr Cyprian, he sets forth opinions contrary to the teaching of that holy bishop. Above all, he asserts under heading 100 that a human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes, whereas Cyprian, in heading 54 of the third book of his own work, states:

> No one is without defilement and without sin.

(Below, Appendix, part 2.)

In the profession of faith which he addressed to Pope Innocent in 417, in order to prove himself Catholic, Pelagius cites a lengthy letter which he says he had sent nearly twelve years earlier—thus around 405—to Paulinus, bishop of Nola, who at that time was especially devoted to him (*On the Grace of Christ*, §38). He argues that almost nothing else was commended in this letter besides the grace and aid of God, and that it was also declared there that we can do absolutely no good without God.

Augustine, however, who had read the letter, asserts that the powers and capability of nature are praised throughout it, and that Pelagius virtually makes that alone the grace of God. Augustine says that scarcely any mention of Christian grace occurs except perfunctorily, lest Pelagius seem to have omitted it altogether; indeed, it is not at all apparent whether by that grace he wished anything other than the forgiveness of sins and the teaching of Christ to be understood.

Augustine reports to Paulinus that letters of Pelagius written to that same Paulinus exist, in which Pelagius says:

> He ought not to be thought to defend free will without the grace of God, since he said that the power of willing and acting, without which we could neither will nor do anything good, had been implanted in us by the Creator.

(*Letter* 186.1.)

Thus the grace of God taught by Pelagius is understood to be something common to pagans and Christians, the impious and the pious, believers and unbelievers. We shall readily agree that these letters are not different from those mentioned above.

In addition, for the purpose of clearing himself, Pelagius produced a letter addressed to a certain Bishop Constantius (*On the Grace of Christ*, §39). Although brief, he claimed that in it he had plainly joined the grace and aid of God to human free will. Augustine had been unable to find this letter. But if it was not unlike the author’s other writings, it too did not contain the true confession of Christian grace which Catholics demanded from him.

Furthermore, Augustine says that he had been informed by certain holy men in 416 that he possessed exhortatory or consolatory books written to a certain widow, whose name was missing there. They stated that nearly four years earlier they had begun to regard these books as Pelagius’s, and that they had never heard anyone express doubt as to whether they were his (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, §19).

Jerome mentions the same works, from which he produces two statements: one displaying Pharisaic pride, the other shameful flattery (below, Appendix, part 2). Both were included among the charges which the bishops brought against Pelagius in the Palestinian synod (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, §16). Pelagius evaded and avoided their objection by denying that the passages could be found in his writings and condemning them as absurdities.

He had also made a practice of disowning these two passages even among his disciples (below, Appendix, part 2), and Augustine did not think it necessary to press him on the matter. Nevertheless, Jerome insists that they truly belonged to Pelagius and that this could be clearly detected from the style (ibid.).

We suspect that the booklet of Pelagius which Marius Mercator testified that he had in his hands, containing an exhortation addressed to the widow Livania, belonged to this same work (ibid.).

Furthermore, in various places in his works Augustine cites a certain commentary by Pelagius on the Pauline epistles, although he is uncertain about it (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, §§1, 5; *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, §39).

Pelagius composed this commentary at Rome before the devastation of the city by Alaric, king of the Goths, in 410, and published it for the benefit of those whose friendship he presumed upon (below, Appendix, part 2). He had gathered into it many arguments against original sin. Yet, lest he appear to rise up in such open rebellion against the faith of the Church, he presented them not in his own person but in that of another, as objections raised by an opponent (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, §5; *On Original Sin*, §§19, 24).

They reasonably believe that this commentary of Pelagius is the very one that still exists among Jerome’s works, actually filled with Pelagian errors. As for the principal passage cited by Augustine but missing from the commentary in our time, either Pelagius later removed it himself, or—more likely—this was done by Cassiodorus.

Cassiodorus, who mentions a certain exposition of the Epistles of Saint Paul under the title *Annotations*, excepting only the Epistle to the Hebrews, says that these works were held in such high esteem that they were attributed to Pope Gelasius. Yet although they were remarkably penetrating and especially pleasing because of their brevity, they were infected by the poison of Pelagian error spread through them. Cassiodorus says that he had done what lay within his power to cleanse the exposition of the Epistle to the Romans, so that it might serve as an example for doing the same in the other epistles (*On the Institution of Divine Literature*, ch. 8).

Nevertheless, the work still presents Pelagian doctrines in many places, and it is surprising that Cassiodorus passed them over. Indeed, at Romans 9:16 one reads the very annotation which Augustine cites elsewhere (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, §39). Learned men have observed that Primasius borrowed no small number of passages from this commentary, although he did not identify the source from which he derived them.

## III. The Origin of the Pelagian Heresy: Pelagius Begins to Proclaim It at Rome, and It Soon Spreads Far and Wide

[Column 0015]

The Pelagian heresy first drew its origin from the East, sown, as they maintain, by Origen Adamantius, but especially by Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia (below, Appendix, part 2).

A certain Rufinus, a Syrian by birth, first brought it to Rome under Anastasius, Roman pontiff—that is, around the year 400 of Christ. “Being clever,” says Mercator, “and shielding himself from the odium it incurred, he did not dare to put it forward himself; instead, he deceived Pelagius, a Briton by race and a monk, and thoroughly imbued and trained him in the impious vanity mentioned above” (ibid.).

This is relevant to the claim made by Coelestius at the Council of Carthage: that the holy priest Rufinus, who stayed at Rome with Saint Pammachius, denied original sin in his presence and hearing (*On Original Sin*, §3).

Some understand this Rufinus to be the famous Aquileian Rufinus, celebrated throughout the Christian world. Yet it can be asserted that Rufinus of Aquileia was never a member of Pammachius’s household at Rome, nor did he reside in the city during the time of Pope Anastasius.

Others therefore maintain that another Rufinus should be understood, one known from Jerome (*Jerome, Letter* 66), who came to the West around 399, sent by Jerome to Milan to Venerius. Nevertheless, Jerome clearly counts Rufinus of Aquileia among those whom he names as the first authors of the Pelagian heresy. He also unambiguously declares that this heresy had already been crushed in Grunnius, a disciple of Origen—a name with which he sometimes mockingly refers to the same Rufinus (below, Appendix, part 2).

Most also think that Pelagius is the man whose precursor, at least in attacking his writings, Grunnius was said to be; and against whom Jerome rises elsewhere as against the heir of Rufinus’s hatred toward him (ibid.).

There is, however, an easy answer to these objections: Jerome did not hesitate to call all who did not openly oppose Origen together with him teachers of Pelagian error. Moreover, after the Pelagian heresy had arisen, Augustine cited the *Ecclesiastical History* of that same Rufinus of Aquileia, without ever marking it with approval or disapproval.

But, lest we wander farther from our subject, we have already observed from Pelagius’s own writings that from as early as 405 he held corrupt opinions and that his mind was already entirely perverted while he was living in Rome.

Augustine also testifies that Pelagius became very well known there for the discussions and arguments against grace in which he habitually engaged (*On Original Sin*, §24). Thus the Romans, among whom he had lived for so long, were not unaware of his opinions and doctrines, although he communicated them cautiously and secretly (ibid., §9). They also knew Coelestius, whose impiety was more evident, to be his disciple, and could therefore offer the most faithful and firm testimony on the matter.

At that time an opportunity arose for him to disclose his heresy at Rome in a conversation. A bishop who was present had quoted from Augustine’s *Confessions* the words:

> Give what you command, and command what you will.

(*Confessions*, book 10, chs. 19, 31, 37.)

Augustine says that Pelagius could not endure this. He contradicted the bishop with some agitation and almost quarreled with the man who had quoted the words (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, §53).

Thus, God willing, he exposed himself through certain occasions. Otherwise he was a remarkable master of concealment and thoroughly skilled at wrapping his errors in Catholic language. He sent out his disciples, who spoke more openly, so that, after observing how their statements were received, he could then approve or reject them according as it seemed more advantageous to him (below, Appendix, part 2).

His error spread so far and wide within a short time that Augustine, in one of his earliest writings directed against it, asserted that there were already more followers of Pelagius than he himself could have believed. Others too were being drawn into his sect wherever the followers were not refuted. Finally, the heresy was gaining such daily growth that no one could easily foresee where the matter would eventually break out (*Letter* 157, to Hilary, §22).

Pelagius was still at Rome when Augustine was informed that he was arguing against the grace of God. He learned this from men whose faithfulness was entirely trustworthy. The holy Doctor was deeply troubled; yet, lest he be accused of imposing something upon Pelagius, he did not wish to write against him until he had either addressed Pelagius himself in person or discovered in some one of his writings evidence of such an error.

Pelagius actually came to Africa and landed on the very coast of Hippo. It happened, however, that Augustine was then absent from the city (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, §46). This arrival of Pelagius in Africa is placed around the year 410, when Rome was captured. Augustine does not conceal that at that time he had been absent from Hippo somewhat longer than usual, and that this had provoked complaints from the people (*Letter* 124.2).

Nor is it unlikely that Pelagius left Rome together with Coelestius, whose departure from the city Mercator assigns to approximately 409. They may first have withdrawn together with this disciple of his to Sicily, which openly produced certain shoots of their heresy around 413 (*Letters* 156, 157), and then crossed from there together into Africa (below, Appendix, part 2).

In any case, Pelagius did not disclose his heresy at Hippo, because he departed from there sooner than expected. He later went to Carthage, where Augustine saw him once or twice in 411, but was then extremely occupied with matters relating to the conference with the Donatists (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, §46).

We believe the following words of Augustine refer to this same period:

> A short time ago, when we were at Carthage, my ears were casually struck by certain people speaking in passing, who said that infants are not baptized in order to receive forgiveness of sins, but in order to be sanctified in Christ.

> Troubled by this novelty, and because it was not appropriate for me to say anything in opposition, and because these were not people whose authority caused me concern, I readily regarded the matter as past and forgotten. And behold, now it is being defended with burning zeal; behold, it is even being committed to memory by being written down; behold, the matter is brought to such a crisis that we are now consulted about it even by our brothers; behold, we are compelled to argue and write against it.

(*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 3, §12.)

[Column 0017]

Leaving Carthage, Pelagius hurried to cross the sea (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, §46), perhaps intending to go to Egypt, if the letter which Isidore of Pelusium wrote to him is to be assigned to this period.

Shortly afterward he is believed to have gone to Palestine, where he remained for a long time and aroused Jerome’s hostility. This may explain why Jerome, in the preface to the sixth book of his commentary on Ezekiel, composed, as we believe, in 412, complained that he was being harassed by the successors of Rufinus’s error and hatred.

## IV. Coelestius, a Disciple of Pelagius, Is Accused by Paulinus and Condemned by the Council of Carthage in 412

That pestilential doctrine which Pelagius had begun to teach at Rome was carried into Africa. Although it did not occupy and penetrate that province so broadly and deeply (*On Original Sin*, §24), it immediately found there certain followers who scattered the new seeds of their error wherever they could (*Letter* 157.22).

There, through the mouths of those who were regarded as disciples of Pelagius, these doctrines were seething. Thus one of them, Coelestius, was brought from Carthage before an ecclesiastical tribunal and received a sentence worthy of his perversity (*On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, §46).

He was easily the chief among Pelagius’s disciples, both in chronological precedence and in fame of name. He followed his master’s footsteps so diligently that the adherents of their heresy were called equally Pelagians or Coelestians (*On Heresies*, ch. 88).

Indeed, Coelestius seems to have attained in the East a reputation more widely known and more broadly propagated than Pelagius himself. His homeland is not recorded. Nevertheless, we consider it somewhat more likely that he was the very man whom, as we said above, Jerome called “the white dog.”

A learned man conjectures that he came from Campania (Garnerius, in Mercator), on the basis of this line of Prosper, which he interprets not of Julian but of Coelestius:

> Or, for this Campanian, hearts swell with grass.

(Below, Appendix, part 3.)

He was noble by birth, but by a defect of nature he was born a eunuch from his mother’s womb (ibid.). Perhaps this is why Vincent of Lérins calls him “monstrous” (*Commonitory*, ch. 34).

For some time he practiced in the forum and, unless we are mistaken, for this reason Mercator called him an “auditorial scholar” (below, Appendix, part 2).

Later he served in a monastery. Then, according to Gennadius, before he joined Pelagius and while he was still a young man, he wrote three letters in the form of booklets to his parents. These were useful to all who pursued divine charity, since they kindled such devotion to virtue and contained nothing of that perverse doctrine which he later openly professed (ibid.).

Hieronymus, who was accustomed to humble his opponents with his words, greatly exalts the style and talent both of Coelestius and of his teacher Pelagius. Of Coelestius he speaks in this way:

> One of his disciples—or rather, already his teacher and the leader of the whole army, and, against the Apostle, a vessel of destruction—running through thickets of solecisms, and not, as his followers boast, of syllogisms (ibid.).

Yet the few remnants that survive from his writings [below, *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, nos. 1, 2 ff.] show that he possessed a subtle intellect and was practiced in philosophical quibbles and sophistries. Augustine calls him “a man of the sharpest intellect, who, if he had certainly been corrected, would have benefited very many” [below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 2, no. 5]. Pelagius too is called by the same holy bishop “extremely acute” [below, *On Nature and Grace*, no. 41]. What he thought of their abilities is also clearly demonstrated by the following statements, among others:

> Who, he says, could believe that such intellects did not see this absurdity? [below, *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, no. 41]

Again, elsewhere:

> Lest we be thought to wrong our friends, whose very strong and swift intellects we wish to run not perversely but straight onward [below, *On Nature and Grace*, no. 6].

And again, elsewhere:

> Those intellects, although perverted by a wicked error, are nevertheless not contemptible [below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, no. 5].

Moreover, concerning teacher and disciple he gives this judgment:

> What difference will there be in this question between this Pelagius and Coelestius, except that the former—that is, Coelestius—was more open, while the latter was more concealed; the former more stubborn, the latter more deceitful; or certainly, the former more free-spoken, the latter more crafty? [below, *On Original Sin*, no. 13]

Coelestius, then, being both ready in spirit to undertake bold things and endowed with a prompt and keen intellect, was, it is said, the first to write against the transmission of sin, perhaps in the year 402. “And he made many,” says Mercator, “through incredible loquacity, participants in and accomplices of his madness, daring openly and publicly to disseminate Pelagius’ errors everywhere among the peoples” [below, Appendix, part 2].

In the year 412 he was living at Carthage, where he had already begun to insinuate himself into the dignity of the presbyterate. But because he preached his heresy without concealment, he was detected and accused before Bishop Aurelius [*Letter* 57, no. 22]. Soon, therefore, when a council was held at Carthage—Aurelius attended it with many other bishops, while Augustine was absent [below, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 23]—Coelestius was summoned, and two documents containing the heads of the accusation brought against him were presented to the judges; one of them is called the shorter document.

Opposing Coelestius from the other side was a certain Paulinus, undoubtedly the man who wrote the life of Ambrose at Augustine’s request. He himself testifies that he wrote it in Africa while John was prefect of the praetorium—a dignity John held in the years 412, 413, and 422. In a certain book *On Heresies* [Col. 0019] this man is called a deacon, defender, and procurator of the Church of Milan. Mercator expressly reports that Coelestius was accused by a certain Paulinus, deacon of the holy Ambrose, bishop of Milan, on the ground that he not only taught certain heretical propositions himself, but had also sent various persons throughout the provinces who were allied with him, so that they might disseminate these propositions among the peoples [below, Appendix, part 2].

The following propositions from Coelestius’ teaching were set out in the document:

1. Adam was created mortal, and whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.

2. Adam’s sin injured Adam himself alone, and not the human race.

3. Infants who are born are in the condition in which Adam was before his transgression.

4. Neither does the whole human race die through Adam’s death or transgression, nor does the whole human race rise again through Christ’s resurrection.

5. The Law leads to the kingdom of heaven in the same way as the Gospel.

6. Even before the Lord’s coming there were human beings without sin, that is, free from sin [ibid.].

Mercator drew these propositions from the records of the council, copies of which he had in his possession. Yet we suspect that the seventh proposition of Coelestius, which he presents elsewhere, was omitted by the copyists of Mercator: namely, that Coelestius taught that infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life [ibid., at the beginning]. For the same author indicates that seven propositions were brought against Coelestius by Paulinus when he says that, concerning the propositions written above, the fathers of the synod stood against Coelestius with seven corresponding objections—that is, that seven propositions had been formulated against him in response to Coelestius’ seven propositions.

At this point there is also lacking the corollary to the sixth proposition. Although the African synod, according to Orosius, had already condemned it in Coelestius, Pelagius nevertheless continued stubbornly to assert the same thing at the assembly at Jerusalem: namely, that a human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes [below, Appendix, part 2].

In answer to the second and third propositions at the Council of Carthage, Coelestius neither dared to confess these errors nor wished to deny them. Instead, he said that such questions could be debated on both sides, since, as he claimed, he knew many men from the order of presbyters—and especially Rufinus, the companion of the holy Pammachius—who denied original sin. He nevertheless added that he had always said that infants need Baptism and ought to be baptized [below, *On Original Sin*, no. 3].

Indeed, in a very brief document he conceded that even infants themselves need redemption and that for this reason Baptism is necessary for them [below, *On the Merits of Sins*, nos. 62, 58; *On Original Sin*, no. 21; *Against Julian*, book 3, no. 9; and volume 2, *Letter* 157, no. 22]. He evidently feared to deny this Catholic doctrine openly before Christians. Yet he did not wish to state more clearly that sin had passed from Adam into infants, or to express openly that some sin in them was remitted.

Zosimus undoubtedly speaks of this in his document when he writes that an earlier document given by Coelestius in Africa provided evidence of his faith, and that this should have prevented the judges from condemning him. At that time, however, Zosimus had not yet understood the deceits of these heretics. Nor had he evidently seen the actual records of the synod, since he also says that nothing was clearly decided there [below, Appendix, part 2]. For those same records showed that Coelestius had been heard repeatedly, had confessed, had been convicted, and, since at last he persisted with an obstinate mind in the heretical doctrines of which he had been accused, had rightly been condemned and deprived of ecclesiastical communion [ibid.; volume 2, *Letter* 157, no. 22; volume 1, *Revisions*, book 2, chapter 33].

Coelestius appealed from the synod’s judgment to the Apostolic See. Apart from Zosimus, in his letter to the African bishops where he recalls Coelestius’ earlier appeal, witnesses to this appeal are Paulinus, Mercator, and Facundus [below, Appendix, part 2; Facundus, book 7, chapter 3]. Mercator adds that the same man, soon abandoning his appeal, went to Ephesus, a city of Asia, and there dared to seek the office of presbyter by underhanded means.

The followers of Coelestius’ errors at Carthage were deterred by his condemnation from daring to attack the Church’s faith, which they recognized as firmly established, except only in speeches—or rather, in complaints—which they secretly and mutteringly spread among the common people [*Letter* 157, no. 22]. Therefore the Fathers of the council held at Carthage in 416 rightly affirm that this wound alone had been cut out of the Church by episcopal judgment: namely, the Pelagian heresy. They also affirm that this judgment concerning the name of Coelestius had been debated at Carthage nearly five years earlier, and thus around the beginning of the year 412 [below, Appendix, part 2].

Augustine also places this after the conference held with the Donatists, or at least makes it sufficiently clear that it did not occur before that conference was undertaken [below, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 46]. Perhaps the history of the Pelagian heresy that seemed to Photius also referred to the same council, when it reports that these heretics were expelled from the Church during the time of Theophilus of Alexandria and Innocent, bishop of Rome [below, Appendix, part 2]—unless perhaps, instead of Theophilus, one should read Theodore of Antioch. For Theophilus died in the year 412, before the other councils at which they were condemned had yet been held.

## V. Augustine first attacks the Pelagians in sermons, and afterward in written works. He writes two short works against them to Marcellinus, one on the Baptism of Infants and the other on the Spirit and the Letter; and during the same period he also writes a letter to Honoratus on the grace of the New Testament.

As we saw above, Augustine was not present at the council convened against Coelestius. But when he later came to Carthage, he reviewed its proceedings. He did not immediately begin to write on the subject, however. Both he himself and other Catholic bishops attempted, each according to his own ability, to tear down the Pelagian errors both in public sermons and in private conversations [*Revisions*, book 2, chapter 33].

Augustine’s sermons 170, 174, 175, and others delivered either at this time or somewhat later clearly belong here [below, at the end of the volume, see the Index of Augustine’s Short Works against the Pelagians]. In them he completely overturns the Pelagians’ positions, although he does not name them explicitly.

In sermon 176, arguing against them, he says:

> Let no one whisper foreign doctrines to you. The Church has always possessed this; it has always held it. It received this from the faith of its ancestors, and it preserves it steadfastly to the end . . . . Therefore, brothers, let each person speak as he can on behalf of him who cannot speak for himself. The patrimonies of orphans are commended to bishops as a great trust; how much more the grace of infants? The bishop protects the orphan, lest, after his parents’ death, he be oppressed by strangers. Let him cry out all the more for the infant whom he fears may be killed by his parents (*Sermon* 176, no. 2).

After he had attacked the Pelagian heresy for some time by word of mouth, he was also compelled to fight against it with his pen. For that same Marcellinus, who had been appointed by the emperor Honorius to preside over the conference at Carthage, was daily forced to endure extremely troublesome disputants from that heresy. He therefore wrote to the holy Teacher, proposing their questions and difficulties and begging him to communicate their solution [below, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 25].

These questions were directed chiefly toward the Baptism of infants. Concerning this matter Marcellinus also reported a new absurdity of some of the Pelagians: they admitted that even in infants the remission of sins takes place through Baptism, but said that infants did not possess sin originally and had begun to have sin in their own life only after they had been born [below, *On the Merits of Sins*, no. 62].

Marcellinus also warned Augustine that they were assigning a completely new and unheard-of meaning to the Apostle’s words, “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin, death.” He pressed Augustine to refute those who preached that Adam, even if he had not sinned, would have died; that nothing had been transmitted from his sin to his descendants; and that the human beings who are, have been, and will be in this life possess absolutely no sin [ibid., nos. 8, 9 ff.].

When Augustine saw that the minds of many weak people were being disturbed everywhere by questions of this kind, he composed the books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, moved not only by the request of his most intimate friend but also by concern arising from his own love for the Church. This is how he calls them in the *Revisions* [*Revisions*, book 2, chapter 33]. Elsewhere, however, he calls them *On the Baptism of Infants*; Hieronymus also praises the same books under this title [below, Appendix, part 2].

Indeed, this was the principal question proposed by Marcellinus; nor could any stronger argument be drawn from anywhere else than from the Baptism of infants to demonstrate the original sin that Augustine defended against the Pelagians. He dedicated the work to Marcellinus. Hence, at times he calls these books “my books to Marcellinus,” without adding any other title.

In the first book he proves that human death did not follow from the necessity of nature but from the merit of sin. He also binds Adam’s entire stock to Adam’s sin and teaches that infants are baptized so that they may receive remission of original sin. He had read a book by one of the Pelagians containing the arguments that he refutes from the beginning of this work through chapter thirty-four of the first book [below, *On the Merits of Sins*, no. 63].

In the second book he first teaches that, in this life, a human being can be without sin through God’s grace and the free choice of that human being. He then shows that nevertheless no one in this life is entirely without any sin. Third, he explains that this is so because no one wills as much as the situation requires, either because what is just remains hidden or because doing it does not delight him. Finally, he demonstrates that no one, except the one Mediator, Christ, is or was or will be in this life immune from every sin.

A few days after completing the two preceding books, Augustine obtained Pelagius’ commentaries on Paul. In them he found a new argument against original sin, one that had not occurred to him as something anyone could invent. Pelagius presented it not in his own person but as though it belonged to someone else. Since the first two books had been brought to their proper length and already concluded with a definite ending, Augustine judged that nothing should be added to them. He therefore thought it better to write a separate letter on this matter to the same Marcellinus and attach it to the first two books as though it were a third book.

He refers rather clearly to the document presented by Coelestius to the Council of Carthage in the second book. Elsewhere, however, he states more explicitly [*Revisions*, book 2, chapter 33] that he wrote this work after the episcopal judgment by which Coelestius had deserved excommunication—in other words, in the year 412. In the first books he does not name Pelagius, Coelestius, or any other opponent, evidently hoping by this moderation to bring them back to sound faith. Even in the third book, when he refutes what Pelagius had put forward in his commentaries against original sin, he does not hesitate to address him in more honorable terms.

Hieronymus praises Augustine’s two books to Marcellinus on the baptism of infants—Marcellinus, who, as Hieronymus says, was later innocently killed by the heretics, that is, by the Donatists, in 413, amid the odium of the tyranny of Heraclianus—and a third book to the same man against those who say that a human being can be without sin if he wishes, without God’s grace [below, Appendix, part 2]. Julianus attempted to turn certain statements from the first book back against Augustine himself [below, *Against Julian*, book 5, no. 54; book 6, no. 68; and *The Unfinished Work against the Same Man*, book 1, chapter 68].

While the holy Teacher was writing that letter to Marcellinus to be joined to the two books on the Baptism of Infants [*Letter* 139, no. 3], he also had in hand a book, or letter, to Honoratus [*Letter* 140] concerning five questions proposed by Honoratus. Augustine himself added a sixth question, on the Grace of the New Testament, in order to attack the new heretics who were enemies of God’s grace [Col. 0023]. He examined this question there with particular care and diligence and brought all the others back to it.

Augustine joins to this letter another work against the Pelagians, likewise dedicated to Marcellinus [*Revisions*, book 2, chapter 37]. In the second book *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins* he had said that it was possible for a human being to be without sin if his will did not fail, with divine assistance aiding him. Yet he had also said that one could not rightly infer from this that any human being, except Christ, either had been, was, or would be in this life of such perfect righteousness.

Marcellinus therefore wrote back that this seemed strange to him, and that he could not sufficiently understand how something for which there was no example could nevertheless be proclaimed possible. This moved Augustine to send him a new work, which he called *On the Spirit and the Letter*.

At the beginning he demonstrates that countless things which have neither existed nor ever will exist are nevertheless supremely possible. Marcellinus could have replied that such examples should be counted among miracles and divine works, whereas the perfection of righteousness in a human being belongs to the work of the human being himself. Augustine acknowledges the distinction but at the same time insists that this perfection is a divine work.

Taking this as his occasion, he continues to discuss the assistance of God’s grace. Explaining the Apostle’s words, “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6), he shows that Paul does not understand the killing letter to mean only figurative expressions, or the ceremonies of the Law that were made obsolete by Christ’s coming. Rather, he means even the holiest commandments, and those most worthy to be observed piously and inviolate, if we possess only knowledge of them from the Law and do not possess the power and love for carrying them out—those qualities that are infused into us through God’s Spirit and grace.

This was why he gave the book the title *On the Spirit and the Letter*. In that book, he said, he had argued vigorously against the enemies of the divine grace by which the impious person is justified [ibid.].

## VI. In 413 Augustine preaches against the Pelagians at Carthage. He writes back to Pelagius. He confirms the doctrine of God’s grace in letters to Anastasius and Paulinus.

After Augustine had published his books to Marcellinus against the new heresy, he traveled at some point to Carthage and celebrated the birthday feast of John the Baptist in that city. It therefore cannot have been in 412, for in that year he was present at Cirta—a city roughly one hundred and more leagues from Carthage—at a council held there on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July [*Letter* 141].

Accordingly, at Carthage he delivered a sermon to the people on the feast of the blessed Forerunner [*Sermon* 293]. He says:

> Among the other matters that seemed to require discussion, the sermon came to the Baptism of infants. Since it had already become lengthy and it was being considered how to bring it to an end, as much was not said about so great a question as anxious people ought to have said in so great a danger (*Sermon* 294, no. 1).

For those who had allowed themselves to be persuaded by Pelagius’ errors concerning original sin were attempting day by day to spread those same doctrines more widely and to attach as many people as possible to themselves by every means [below, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 25]. They even threatened the Eastern Churches, saying that unless those Churches held these doctrines, they could be condemned by their judgment.

It was not enough for them to discuss and debate certain impious novelties. They also tried to accuse the Catholic teachers of saying something new. They did not hesitate not only recklessly to resist the defenders of the ancient faith but also to call those defenders heretics [*Sermon* 294, nos. 18, 19].

Therefore the holy Teacher, wishing to uproot completely the errors from the hearts of those who had offered themselves to be deceived by them, decided, at the urging of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, to preach on the matter again on the fifth day before the Kalends of July. It happened that the commemoration of the martyr Gudden was celebrated on that day. But Augustine judged it better to devote the day to instructing the faithful than to praising the martyr.

After the reading of the Lord Christ’s conversation with Nicodemus, therefore, he undertook to treat the question of the Baptism of infants in the Basilica of the Majores, or, as others read it, the Basilica Major or Majorinus. First he refuted that Pelagian invention by which they said that infants, even if they were not baptized, would obtain salvation and eternal life by the merit of their innocence, since they possessed no sin at all, neither their own nor original sin. They said that they were baptized for the reason that they might also enter the kingdom of God.

He then attacked the evasion of those who, when confronted with the apostolic statement, “Through one man sin entered into the world” (Romans 5:12), replied that this had been said because Adam was the first to sin and those who afterward sinned did so by imitating him.

He went on to refute their quibbles. One they posed in this way:

> If sinners were born from a sinner, why are righteous people not born from one who has already been baptized and is faithful, to whom all sins have been forgiven?

They posed another as follows:

> If Adam harms those who have not sinned, they said, then Christ ought also to benefit those who have not believed.

Finally, in support of the Church’s perpetual agreement on this question, he read out the notable testimony of the martyr Cyprian, whom he calls the ancient bishop of this see, taking the codex containing Cyprian’s letter to Fidus into his hands.

He later concluded the sermon by commending the patience that the Church had shown toward the new heretics in those early times, using these words:

> Let us therefore obtain from our brothers, if we can, that they not also call us heretics. We could perhaps call them that, if we wished, when they debate such matters, and yet we do not call them so. Let the mother endure them with devoted affection, so that they may be healed; let her carry them while they are being taught, lest she mourn the dead.
>
> They are advancing too far; it is much—indeed, scarcely bearable—that such things should still be endured by such great patience. Let them not abuse the Church’s patience; let them be corrected. It is good. We exhort them as friends; we do not quarrel as enemies.
>
> They disparage us, and we endure it. Let them not disparage the canon; let them not disparage the truth. Let them not contradict the holy Church, which labors daily for the remission of the original sin of infants. This matter is firmly established.
>
> A disputant who errs in other questions that have not been carefully arranged and have not yet been confirmed by the full authority of the Church must be endured; error may be endured there. But he must not advance so far as to attempt to shake the very foundation of the Church.
>
> It is not expedient—perhaps our patience should not yet be reproved—but we must fear lest even negligence be blamed. Let your Charity be satisfied with this. Since you know who they are, deal with them as you should: in friendship, brotherhood, peace, love, and sorrow. Let piety do whatever it can, because afterward impiety is not to be loved (*Sermon* 294, no. 20).

To this same period, when the pious Bishop judged that the Pelagians’ minds should be treated in this friendly and brotherly way, one may reasonably assign a letter from Pelagius to Augustine himself. The following reply is recorded:

> I give you very great thanks because you have deigned to gladden me by your letter and to assure me of your well-being. May the Lord repay you with good things, so that you may always be good and live with him forever in eternity, my most beloved and most greatly desired lord and brother (*Letter* 146), etc.

At that time Augustine was possessed by a great desire to converse with Pelagius in person, for he had already heard that Pelagius used every opportunity to strive openly against the grace by which we are made righteous.

Although Pelagius had lavishly praised him in his letters, Augustine nevertheless wrote back with as much courtesy as was appropriate and restrained his praise of Pelagius in such a way that, insofar as he could do so without offending him or stirring up any controversy, he also admonished him to think rightly concerning God’s grace [below, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 51]. Augustine himself preserved this reply by inserting it into another of his short works, where he explains each of its words and shows that Pelagius had no reason to read it aloud on his own behalf at the Council of Diospolis.

It is surprising, however, that Augustine did not wish there to mention Pelagius’ position on the question concerning God’s grace, lest he seem to have injured him even slightly. At that time he was very willing, even without being asked, to discuss this matter against the rising heresy in letters sent to his friends.

Thus, in writing to a certain Anastasius, he took care to persuade him that righteousness is fulfilled not through the Law but through grace, and not through slavish fear but through free love. He indicates that he enjoyed discussing this matter with him, saying that he did so because of certain people who were excessively presumptuous about human will. They thought that, once the Law had been given, human will could suffice to fulfill it, without any grace of holy inspiration assisting the teaching of the Law [*Letter* 145, no. 8]. Here, as in his earliest writings against them, he thought that the name of the Pelagians should still be spared.

In a letter also sent around that time to Paulinus, bishop of Nola, when Augustine came to the questions Paulinus had proposed from the Apostle, he took the opportunity to explain the doctrine of predestination [*Letter* 149, no. 18 ff.]. He then expressed himself about it so clearly and so seriously that one could readily persuade oneself that this was the very letter over which the Semi-Pelagians later caused an uproar—unless Augustine remembered that they had contradicted not just any letter to Paulinus but specifically the one that had been published against the Pelagians [below, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 55]. That is undoubtedly the letter written to the same man in the year 417 [*Letter* 186].

## VII. In 413 or 414 Pelagius serves the poison of his heresy to the virgin Demetrias. He attacks Hieronymus with slanders, being deeply offended that Hieronymus refutes his errors. Augustine refutes the Sicilian Pelagians.

The veiling of Demetrias, which had filled everyone with admiration, stirred the tongues and pens of all the men who at that time excelled in the Church. They were rightly persuaded that whatever ability had been divinely granted them could not be put to more useful service than by instructing her through precepts and strengthening her in so noble a purpose.

What the letters of the others, which have perished, were like may be judged from the letter of Hieronymus that still survives, written to the same virgin [Hieronymus, *Letter* 8]. He wrote it in 413 or 414, having temporarily interrupted his commentary on Ezekiel, which had by then reached chapter 43.

Among the many instructions that Hieronymus gives Demetrias, he strongly impresses upon her the importance of adhering to the faith of Pope Innocent and avoiding the snares of those who, having already been defeated by the authority of Pope Anastasius, were attempting to rise again and secretly spread the poison of their doctrine throughout the East.

There is much that leads us to acknowledge that he was referring to the Pelagians, although he touches there on no heresy other than the one concerning the existence of souls before bodies, which belonged to the Origenists. On the same occasion Augustine congratulated Demetrias’ grandmother Proba and her mother Juliana in his letters [Augustine, *Letter* 150].

Pelagius decided to add his own voice to the words of these distinguished men and to gain glory for himself by treating so noble a subject. Yet he did not put his own name on his composition—or at least it was absent from the copy later brought to Augustine, from which the work is also known by its title [*Letter* 188, nos. 4, 14].

Pelagius himself acknowledges that in 417 he had written a letter in the East to the virgin Demetrias [below, *On the Grace of Christ*, no. 38]. Orosius, writing about it in 415, already attributes the letter to Pelagius [Orosius, *Apology*]. He also quotes several words from it, which can be read in the letter beginning, “If with the highest intelligence,” and so forth.

This letter survives in the Appendix after Augustine’s works. There one may likewise find whatever Augustine quotes from Pelagius’ letter to Demetrias. It is both ornamented and elegantly written and contains excellent rules of piety. Yet they are infected with that pride which was Pelagius’ distinctive characteristic and which brings certain destruction upon piety.

Orosius indicates clearly enough that Pelagians held the letter in high esteem when he says, “In that most laboriously written letter of yours” [ibid.]. Augustine, when complaining about this very work, testified that many people read the writings of the Pelagians because of their sharpness and eloquence [*Letter* 188, no. 13].

Orosius adds that, in composing it, Pelagius used the style and language of others, perhaps of Julianus or of Anianus, the pseudo-deacon of Celeda. According to Hieronymus, the latter was therefore lavishly fed by his companions in error, so that he might supply frivolous words for another person’s blasphemy [*Letter* 202, no. 2, among Augustine’s letters]. This may perhaps have given rise to the fact that Beda attributed the letter to Julianus.

Augustine did not see this letter before 416. For he indicates that he was uncertain whether it had been written before the Council of Diospolis, which was held toward the end of 415, or afterward [below, *On the Grace of Christ*, no. 23].

Pelagius’ purpose in publishing this work can easily be understood from these words of its preface:

> Whenever I have to speak about the formation of character and the conduct of a holy life, I customarily first show the power and quality of human nature and demonstrate what it can accomplish. From there I stimulate the listener’s mind toward the forms of the virtues, and so forth.

Pelagius nevertheless also used his letter to Demetrias as testimony to show—as he himself claimed—how far he was from denying Christ’s grace. Augustine admits that reading it almost persuaded him that Pelagius acknowledged the true grace of God, although it appeared to him that the author contradicted himself in many passages.

But after Augustine had read other writings by Pelagius, in which Pelagius revealed his mind more clearly, he readily detected that Pelagius used the word “grace” merely to lessen the odium against him. In Pelagius’ mouth, Augustine found that the word meant nothing other than nature established by God, or doctrine, or at most the forgiveness of sins or the example of Christ [ibid., no. 40].

Once Augustine and Alypius had discovered this—and since they had brought Demetrias, through their exhortation, to profess a life of virginal holiness [*Letter* 188, nos. 1, 2]—they judged that it especially concerned them to warn her also to avoid doctrines contrary to God’s grace.

They did so in a letter sent to her mother Juliana around the end of 417. From Pelagius’ writing they quoted this passage in particular, as plainly contrary to Christian humility and grace:

> “Physical nobility and wealth are understood to belong to your family, not to you; but no one except yourself can bestow spiritual riches upon you. In these, therefore, you are rightly to be praised and deservedly preferred to others—qualities which can exist only from you and in you” [ibid., no. 4].

Augustine and Alypius continue:

> We believe this about the discipline of the holy virgin and her Christian humility, in which she was nourished and educated: when she read those words—if indeed she read them—she groaned, struck her breast humbly, and perhaps even wept. She confidently prayed to the Lord, to whom she has been dedicated and by whom she has been sanctified, that just as those words are not her own but another’s, so her faith too might not be such as they express.
>
> Therefore, tell us by your reply whether we are mistaken about this feeling of hers, or make us more certain concerning it [ibid., no. 9].

Beda also points out the hidden poison concealed in various passages of this same Pelagian letter. For example, the letter says that many philosophers were chaste, patient, modest, and so forth, and that these good qualities of soul, which please God, were present in people alien from God only because of the goodness of nature.

It also says that such men demonstrated by their example to one another that, since everyone possesses one and the same nature, all these ornaments of virtue can exist in everyone—either all of them in all people or individually in individuals.

It further says that if people show, even without God, what they have been made by God to be, then from this one may understand what Christians are capable of, since their nature has been restored for the better through Christ and they are also assisted by the help of divine grace.

It adds that Job, by opening the hidden riches of nature and bringing them into the light, showed from himself what we are all capable of.

It says that nature must be vindicated from this injury, lest we appear to be driven toward evil through its fault; for we do neither good nor evil without the will, and we are free always to perform one of two alternatives, since we are always capable of either.

It says that some will judge and others will be judged because, although we are all capable of the same things, we do different things.

It says that, unless both men had been capable of either alternative, the just God would not have deservedly punished the one or chosen the other; and that the same must be understood of the twins Esau and Jacob. One must recognize that the cause lies solely in the will when merits differ although nature is the same.

It says that no other cause makes it difficult for us to live well than the long habit of vices.

Finally, it says that the just God could not command anything impossible, nor could the merciful God condemn a person for what that person could not avoid.

Centuries later Beda extracted these points for the purpose of exposing them [Beda, book 1 on the *Song of Songs*].

Moreover, at the time when Pelagius was mixing that poisonous draught for Demetrias, he was also taking pains to spread his errors in Palestine. They suppose that he was carried there in the year 411, when, as stated above, he sailed from Africa. At first, since he wished to appear bound by friendship with every distinguished and holy man, he had perhaps entered into some intimacy with Jerome. This is indeed indicated by these words of the holy man: “Lest we should seem to injure an old relationship” (Below, Appendix, part 2). But when Jerome omitted nothing in order to restrain that heresy, which was already spreading more widely, the Pelagians tried to avenge his generosity by those slanders with which, as he often complains, he was attacked by them.

Since it is beyond doubt that Pelagius was active in Palestine in 415, no one should find it strange that Jerome had designated him, together with someone else, when about the year 416 he spoke as follows: “This man is silent here, but elsewhere he brings accusations; he sends throughout the whole world letters that were formerly golden, but are now abusive, and interprets our patience, which proceeds from Christ’s humility, as a sign of a bad conscience. He himself barks mutely through Albinus, a large and corpulent dog, who can rage more with his heels than with his teeth; for he is of Scottish stock, from the neighborhood of the Britons” [Col. 0029] (Below, Appendix, part 2).

These words fit Pelagius well, since he was a Briton; and elsewhere Jerome seems to intend to call him a Scot (ibid.). Yet we see no one whom Pelagius could have regarded as his superior, so that he might be called that man’s dog—unless someone wishes those words, “This man is silent,” and so forth, to be referred to John, bishop of Jerusalem, who had in fact deserved so ill of Jerome that Jerome was justified in addressing him so reproachfully.

Nor did Jerome always confine himself to these limits, so as merely to condemn in spoken words the errors that Pelagius’ disciples were privately taught there. Moved by the pleas of certain Catholics, he first wrote his letter to Ctesiphon, in which he promised a fuller discussion of the matter, perhaps in 414; for Orosius testified at the Jerusalem assembly that Jerome had recently published it (ibid.). Nor did he delay long in fulfilling his promise: indeed, by the end of July 415 he had already begun the three books against the Pelagians that he composed in the form of dialogues.

The letter to Ctesiphon reproaches Pelagius for reviving the opinions of earlier heretics and philosophers concerning *apatheia* (ἀπάθεια, freedom from passion) and *anamartēsia* (ἀναμαρτησία, freedom from sin). It attacks especially these propositions of his: “A human being can be without sin, if he wishes,” although, in order to deceive people, he added to this proposition “not without the grace of God”—while understanding God’s grace in such a way as to refer it to free will and to the commandments of the Law.

Moreover, he said that those who lacked knowledge of the Law could not avoid sins. Next, he maintained that free will was destroyed if it needed another’s assistance and if God’s help were always necessary for it; therefore, “each person is governed by his own will.” Finally, he held that God’s commandments were easy.

Jerome urges him to proclaim publicly what he says privately to his disciples: “For,” he says, “it is the Church’s victory for you to say openly what you think” (ibid.).

Apparently in that same year, 414, Augustine wrote his letter against the Sicilian Pelagians. In 415, Jerome affirmed that Augustine’s three books addressed to Marcellinus had already been published some time before, but that his book addressed to Hilary had only recently been completed; Orosius spoke similarly about the matter in the same year (ibid.). There Augustine states that he had already written various works concerning grace. The questions being raised by the Pelagians in Sicily gave rise to this letter.

Certainly, about the year 416 Jerome testified that the Pelagian plague was growing not only in the West but also in the East, especially on the islands of Sicily and Rhodes; that it was corrupting many people; and that it was spreading daily more widely because, although its authors publicly disavowed its doctrines, they nevertheless transmitted them secretly (ibid.).

What happened in Rhodes is unknown. From Augustine, however, we learn that many people in Sicily were in error and were leading others into error; and that a certain book of Caelestius himself, as it was said, had been found there, which the holy bishop undertook to refute (Below, *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, no. 1).

This poison particularly afflicted Syracuse. In that city the same doctrines that had been condemned in Caelestius at Carthage were being taught. But the Syracusans also added certain other teachings which, although they may seem unrelated to the errors of the Pelagians, nevertheless arose from the same source of pride, from which their pretended display of holiness also flowed. For they held that a rich man, while remaining in his wealth, could not enter the kingdom of God unless he sold all that he possessed; and that no one ought to swear at all (Letters 156, 157).

Accordingly, Hilary took advantage of the opportunity presented by certain people from Hippo who were returning from Syracuse to their own country and gave them a short letter for Augustine. In it he had written out the points of doctrine that were causing disturbance, and he also asked Augustine to inform him by letter what should be believed concerning them.

In his reply Augustine greets him as a son and declares that he was glad to have been informed of his good health. By this he plainly indicates that Hilary had already been known to him. Thus it will not seem at all rash if we identify him with that same Hilary who later sent the holy bishop a letter against the Semi-Pelagians, in which he professes that he had at some time enjoyed the delights of Augustine’s presence and had been nourished by his life-giving breasts.

Augustine answered the difficulties Hilary had proposed point by point, as each matter required, in a lengthy letter, which he sometimes also calls a book (Below, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 23). There he testifies that those who followed the Pelagian errors were more numerous than people supposed, and that he did not know whether necessity itself would eventually compel them to be cut off from the body of the Church, in which they had until then been tolerated in hope of correction.

He also mentions Caelestius there and recalls his condemnation by the Council of Carthage, because the holy Doctor feared that such disturbances might perhaps be stirred up by Caelestius himself in Sicily (Letter 157, no. 22). Yet he seems later to have learned that Caelestius was not the author of those disturbances, since in the following year he states, according to common opinion, that Caelestius was not active in Sicily.

When Orosius brought this letter of Augustine with him to Palestine, he presented it at the Jerusalem assembly and, with the approval of John, who presided, read it aloud (Below, Appendix, part 2). It was again praised at the Synod of Diospolis (Below, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 23).

## VIII. In 415 Augustine recalls Timasius and James from the errors of Pelagius and refutes, in his work *On Nature and Grace*, the book of Pelagius that they had handed over to him. He writes another work against the propositions attributed to Caelestius, entitled *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*.

Among Pelagius’ disciples, Timasius and James were especially devoted to him. They were young men born of highly honorable families and educated in the liberal disciplines. At Pelagius’ urging, they had cast aside every secular hope and devoted themselves wholly to the service of God (Letter 179, no. 2).

Following his perverse doctrines with the greatest zeal, they had advanced so far that they openly argued against the grace by which we are Christians (Letter 186, no. 1). But God freed them from this destruction through Augustine’s efforts and admonitions. They had already, as they themselves say, been taught by the spirit of illumination that was in Augustine (Letter 168, among Augustine’s letters; and below, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 48), and had rejected their error, when they handed the holy Doctor a certain book that they claimed was by Pelagius, earnestly imploring him to answer it (Letter 179, no. 10).

Accordingly, setting aside his other occupations, Augustine read the book with great concentration. In one of his letters he quotes a passage from it and shows from the passage that this was its author’s opinion—an opinion which, however, Pelagius later refused to acknowledge at the Synod of Diospolis: that there is someone, specifically Abel, who lived here in such a way that he committed absolutely no sin (ibid., no. 9).

Pelagius employed in this work every capacity and strength that he possessed in reasoning, in order to defend human nature against God’s grace. When he raised the objection that certain people say that some lesser sins, because they occur so frequently, cannot all be avoided, he denied that anyone ought to be reproved, even with a mild correction, if such sins cannot be avoided altogether (Below, *On Nature and Grace*, no. 13).

He also argued that nature had not been weakened or changed by sin. Otherwise, he said, punishment would itself become the material of sin, if the sinner had been weakened for the purpose of committing more sins. Indeed, Adam’s descendants were not only no weaker than Adam; they had even fulfilled more commandments, whereas he had neglected to fulfill one (ibid., nos. 21–24).

He further maintained that it was impossible for the flesh to be opposed to anyone who had already been baptized (ibid., no. 60). Yet he himself raised the celebrated question whether he excluded the grace of God when he said, “A human being can be without sin in this life”; and he agreed that this could happen only through the grace of God (ibid., no. 10).

This very open confession by Pelagius gave Augustine considerable pleasure. Not long afterward, however, he detected that some ambiguity lay hidden beneath the word “grace.” Finally, from what followed, he learned that by “grace” Pelagius understood nothing other than nature possessing its own rights, or nature created with free will; to this he occasionally added, as though incidentally and rather obscurely, the help of the Law and the remission of sins (Below, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 47).

As for the true grace of Christ, Pelagius not only failed to acknowledge it, but also advanced many propositions wholly opposed to it and directed toward nothing other than removing faith in Christ from the minds of Christians (Letter 186, no. 1).

He tried to support his perverse opinions with testimonies from certain ecclesiastical writers and even from Augustine himself. Pope Innocent testifies that he had examined that book and found in it many blasphemies, nothing pleasing, and scarcely anything that did not utterly displease him—things to be condemned and trampled underfoot; no one other than the man who wrote them would entertain or hold such views (Letter 183, no. 5, among Augustine’s letters).

The distinguished historian of the Pelagian controversy, Henricus Noris, judges that Pelagius attempted in this work to answer Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon (Noris, *Pelagian History*, book 1, chapter 6).

Augustine therefore considered it his duty to refute this work, since Timasius and James were also appealing to him about it. For this reason he composed a substantial book against Pelagius’ heresy—for he uses these very words in that year, 415 (Letter 169, no. 13). He dedicated it to the young men from whom he had received Pelagius’ writing, so that, if any remnant of the perverse doctrine still clung to their minds, he might tear it out by the roots.

Yet he refrained from using Pelagius’ name, fearing that Pelagius, taking this as an insult to himself, would make himself less amenable to treatment by medicinal hands (Letter 186, no. 1). The holy Doctor also says that he thought he would be more likely to help Pelagius if, while preserving their friendship, he still spared the man’s modesty, though he could no longer spare his writings (Below, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 47).

Later, however, he regretted this. Although he had feared causing pain, his moderation had accomplished nothing except to increase Pelagius’ swelling pride (ibid., no. 50).

He entitled the work *On Nature and Grace*, because in it he defends grace not against nature, but as that through which nature is both liberated and governed (*Retractions*, book 2, chapter 42).

In that work Augustine condemned Pelagius’ declaration that “a human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments, if he wishes”; Orosius bears witness to this (Below, Appendix, part 2).

The testimonies of the ancient authorities cited by Pelagius are examined, including those that he had quoted under the name of Sixtus, Roman pontiff and martyr. The holy Doctor had not yet discovered that these sayings belonged to a certain pagan philosopher; as we suppose, he learned this later from reading Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon.

Finally, Augustine is said to have examined Pelagius’ book with such diligence that he gave an answer to every single point (Below, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 48). Elsewhere we observe that in that same year, 415, Jerome and Orosius mention this work of Augustine as begun but not yet completed (Below, Introduction to the book *On Nature and Grace*).

Augustine immediately granted Evodius permission to have it copied (Letter 169, no. 13).
