The following year he sent the work, together with Pelagius’ own book, to John, bishop of Jerusalem, so that John might discern the mind of that arch-heretic from it; he also asked him to forward both works to Pelagius (Letter 179, nos. 5, 10). Similarly, in 416 he sent the same discussions to be delivered to Pope Innocent (Letter 177, no. 6).

Although Augustine could not doubt that the writing handed to him by Timasius and James was Pelagius’ work, he nevertheless never mentions it without qualification. He knew, of course, that Pelagius was the kind of man who, if he could not extricate himself by any other means, would not hesitate to deny it.

Thus Augustine does not cite it in his book *On Grace and Original Sin*. In that book he shows that Pelagius’ opinions must be condemned on the basis of works that Pelagius acknowledged in his letter to the Roman bishop, not on the basis of writings which, he complained, had either been secretly slipped to Augustine before they could be authenticated or had been entirely and falsely fabricated.

Similarly, when Pope Zosimus received the same letter, he says that faith had been placed too rashly in certain writings on the testimony of Timasius and James (Below, Appendix, part 2).

Julianus was hostile toward these two men and abusively called them dissolute monks, despite their being young men (Below, *Against Julian*, book 2, no. 37).

It has seemed appropriate to assign to this year another work by Augustine against certain Pelagian arguments contained in a short document headed as follows: “The Definitions, as they are called, of Caelestius” (Below, *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, no. 1).

Some brothers—that is, Catholics—had brought this document from Sicily. Bishops Eutropius and Paulus handed it to Augustine. These were the same men who, not long after Orosius’ arrival in Africa, that is, before the middle of the year 415, presented the holy Doctor with a memorandum concerning various heresies (Below, Introduction to the book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*).

This little book contained various arguments, brief and compressed, intended to establish that “a human being can be without sin in this life.” To these arguments had been added testimonies from Scripture: some which, as the author said, proved that human beings had been commanded to be without sin; others intended to show that God’s commandments were not only not impossible but not even burdensome; and finally others that seemed contrary to the testimonies commonly brought forward by Catholics against the Pelagians.

Augustine states that, judging from another writing of which Caelestius was certainly the author, these very brief arguments were not at all alien to Caelestius’ manner of thinking. He himself dissolves them with equally brief answers, teaching that the perfection and fullness of righteousness by which a human being is entirely without any sin is neither possible without grace through the powers of nature—especially nature already corrupted—nor ever attainable in the present life.

Nevertheless, he thinks that one should not strongly oppose those who affirm that certain people, through the help of divine grace, have lived entirely blameless lives and wholly free from sin. Certainly he would not have said this after the canons against that opinion had been enacted at the Council of Carthage in 418.

## IX. The assembly held at Jerusalem in 415 by John the bishop, at which Orosius disputes publicly with Pelagius. John, excessively favorable to Pelagius, shortly afterward accuses Orosius of blasphemy; Orosius repels the charge in a written apology. Jerome’s dialogues against the Pelagians.

When the presbyter Paulus Orosius set sail from Africa that year, he arrived in Palestine about the middle of the same year. Having heard of Augustine’s reputation, he had come to him from the farthest parts of Spain, eager to learn. Augustine sent him on to Jerome so that Orosius might consult him about the origin of the soul (Letter 169, no. 13).

Just as Orosius had left Augustine occupied in defeating the Pelagians, so he found Jerome also engaged in the same struggle. Once it became known that Pelagius had made such great and celebrated men in the Church his adversaries, no one could doubt that his doctrine had caused considerable disturbance in Palestine. Indeed, the Jerusalem colloquy that we must discuss here arose from no other cause. The presbyters of the Jerusalem Church appear to have taken the initiative and pressed for it to be held.

It took place forty-seven days before the solemnity of the Encaenia, that is, on July 29 or 30 (Below, Appendix, part 2). Everything points to the conclusion that this festival was none other than the dedication of the Church of the Resurrection, celebrated every year with great ceremony on September 13 or 14 (Nicephorus, book 8, chapter 50, and the Greek *Menologion*).

The discussion took place in the presence of John, bishop of Jerusalem, who, as can be understood from Orosius’ account, was the only bishop present. It was an assembly of presbyters only, among whom were Orosius, Avitus, Vitalis, and Passerius.

A certain unknown interpreter was also present. He must doubtless be counted among those false brothers who, according to Orosius, sat on the opposite side. Besides all these, a former commander named Dominus is also mentioned.

This Dominus, like the presbyter Passerius, had acquired considerable renown through his faith and experience, both in matters pertaining to God and in secular affairs. Since they knew both Greek and Latin, the priests of Jerusalem had invited them to attend the assembly as interpreters, and had brought them there themselves, with John agreeing.

At the urging of the presbyters, Orosius left his retreat at Bethlehem and went to Jerusalem. When he entered the place of assembly, he sat down at the bishop’s command.

Yet one fault was committed in that assembly: they appointed no notary to record what took place. Everyone immediately asked Orosius to state faithfully and plainly whether he knew of anything that had happened in Africa concerning the heresy that Pelagius and Caelestius were spreading against the grace of God.

Orosius therefore declared that Caelestius had been condemned by the Council of Carthage. He also mentioned the book *On Nature and Grace*, which Augustine was composing at that time. From this we understand that Orosius had left Augustine only a few days before.

He added that he had in his hands a letter that the holy bishop had recently sent to Sicily (Letter 157). When Orosius was ordered to read it aloud, he complied.

After these proceedings, John requested that Pelagius be brought in. The members of the assembly agreed, both out of reverence for the bishop and because they hoped that the refutation of Pelagius would thereby be fuller and more useful.

When Pelagius entered, everyone with one voice asked him whether he had taught the opinions that Bishop Augustine had refuted. He immediately replied in these words: “And who is Augustine to me?” (Below, Appendix, part 2).

This response was so insulting to that holy bishop—through whose mouth the Lord had granted all Africa the health of unity by extinguishing the Donatist schism—that everyone present was offended and shouted that Pelagius should be expelled not only from the assembly but from the entire Church.

John, however, whom he ought to have expelled, ordered him to sit among the presbyters, although he was a layman and had moreover been discovered in the crime of heresy. Furthermore, so that he might more freely forgive Pelagius for the insult offered to Augustine, John professed that he himself accepted the same insult: “I am Augustine,” he said.

Orosius immediately replied: “If you assume Augustine’s person, follow Augustine’s judgment” (Below, Appendix, part 2).

After this, John asked whether the matters being read from Augustine’s letter applied to Pelagius or to someone else. He added that, if Pelagius was being attacked, they could explain what they found objectionable in him.

When the others assented, Orosius spoke as follows: “Pelagius told me that he says that a human being can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments, if he wishes.”

In the hearing of everyone, Pelagius replied: “I cannot deny that I both said this and say it.”

Then Orosius said: “The African council condemned this doctrine in Caelestius. Bishop Augustine recoiled from it in his writings, as you have heard. He now condemns it in Pelagius’ own writings by his reply—that is, in the book *On Nature and Grace*. The blessed Jerome has also condemned it in his letter recently published to Ctesiphon. All the West awaits his eloquence as one waits for dew upon a fleece, and many heretics have already been crushed, together with their doctrines, by his opposition. He also refutes it in the book that he is now writing, in which he conducts the dispute in the form of a dialogue.”

John, however, stopping his ears to all this, tried to induce them to undertake before him, as the bishop of Jerusalem and their judge, the formal prosecution of Pelagius.

Everyone repeatedly answered him: “We are not his accusers. We are informing you what your brothers and our fathers thought and decreed concerning this heresy, which a layman is now preaching publicly, lest it disturb your Church—especially the Church to whose bosom we have fled—without your knowledge.”

Meanwhile John continued trying to entice them into taking the role of accusers. Under the pretense of instruction, he brought forward various arguments, and many of those present noticed that some of them had been borrowed from Origen.

But he received only this answer from them: “We are sons of the Catholic Church. Do not demand of us, Father, that we dare to become teachers over teachers or judges over judges. The fathers whom the universal Church throughout the world approves, whose communion we rejoice to share, have decreed that these doctrines are damnable. It is fitting for us to obey their approval.”

John continued arguing at length. Orosius does not report what he said in the course of the debate. Clearly, he wished to attack Orosius as though Orosius were saying that human nature had been created by God evil and subject to the necessity of sinning.

When that same bishop was later questioned at the Synod of Diospolis about what had recently taken place before him in the Jerusalem assembly, he reported, among other things, that Pelagius had been vigorously charged with heresy because he said that a human being could be without sin if he wished.

“And when we questioned him about this,” John continued, “he replied: ‘I did not say that human nature had received the condition of being impeccable. I said that whoever wishes to labor and struggle for his own salvation, so as not to sin and to walk in God’s commandments, has this possibility from God.’

“Then, when certain people whispered and said that Pelagius was asserting that a human being could be perfected without the grace of God—that is, that a human being could be without sin—I rebuked him on this point also,” John said, “and cited the Apostle Paul, who labored greatly, not according to his own strength but according to God’s grace: ‘I labored more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God with me’ (1 Cor. 15:10), and so forth. We also cited many other similar passages from the holy Scriptures” (Below, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 54).

When the others, by their objections, indicated that they were still not satisfied with what John had said, Pelagius declared: “I too believe this: let him be anathema who says that a human being can attain the progress of every virtue without God’s help.”

Orosius himself acknowledges that Pelagius said that a human being could be without sin, but not without God’s help. He then reports that the bishop added: “If he had said that a human being could do this without God’s help, it would have been utterly wicked and damnable.”

Afterward John asked what else they were bringing against Pelagius, and whether they denied God’s help. Orosius immediately answered: “Anathema to him who denies God’s help. I certainly do not deny it, especially since I have refuted the heretics on the contrary point” (Below, Appendix, part 2).

Orosius spoke Latin, while John spoke Greek, so that neither understood the other and each needed an interpreter. The man who had undertaken this duty, unknown to Orosius, performed his office very poorly.

Indeed, he rendered some statements with a meaning different from what had been said; he changed others into different statements; and finally he omitted certain things altogether. In this way he either distorted or suppressed almost all of Orosius’ replies. In this matter, however, Orosius criticizes his skill more than his good faith.

The presbyters Passerius and Avitus, as well as Dominus the former commander, noticed the interpreter’s distortions. Therefore, when Orosius realized that he was being forced to use an interpreter who was so incompetent and a judge so little impartial, he openly declared that the accused was a Latin, that he himself was likewise a Latin, and that the heresy was finally more familiar to Latin judges. John, he said, appeared to be a less suitable judge because, although no one was acting as accuser, John himself was thrusting himself forward as judge.

Several people openly supported Orosius and testified that the same person could not be both advocate and judge. Finally, after much had been said on both sides, John himself pronounced that certain men should be sent to Pope Innocent of Rome with letters, so that everyone would follow whatever decision he made.

In the meantime, Pelagius was to observe the silence imposed upon him, while his opponents, as men already convicted and confounded, were to refrain from attacking him [Col. 0037].

Everyone agreed to this decision. After giving thanks to God and exchanging the kiss of peace, they devoted themselves to prayer in order to confirm the agreement by a more certain testimony. At last the entire assembly was dismissed.

After forty-seven days had passed, on the first day of the Encaenia, Orosius came, as usual, to escort John. Instead of receiving a friendly greeting, he was addressed by John in these words: “Why have you come to me, you who have blasphemed?”

Struck by this and conscious of no crime, Orosius asked what blasphemy John was attributing to him, and when and before what witness he claimed that Orosius had uttered it.

“I heard you say,” the bishop replied, “that a human being cannot be without sin even with God’s help.”

Orosius then called upon the consciences of the presbyters and all the others who were present as witnesses and categorically denied that he had ever said anything of the kind.

Certainly, if he had used those words in the Jerusalem assembly, John would never have allowed himself not to rebuke him immediately and at the same time admonish him as a father not to let such a dangerous statement escape him in the future.

Nor could John in any way be heard when, after forty-seven full days had passed, he accused Orosius of a blasphemy that no one else had noticed Orosius uttering. Thus John was both accuser and judge of a crime for which he could claim to be its only witness. Yet, being ignorant of Latin, he could not properly serve as a witness to a statement made in Latin; he could affirm no more than that he had learned it from the interpreter’s mouth.

The interpreter appears later to have said this after being corrupted, and to have asked that witnesses be provided who would make his lie credible. Pelagius also appears to have confirmed the accusation by his testimony. Orosius’ words clearly refer to him: “I shall try to discover how those who assert that we answered in this way appear themselves to have asked their questions,” and so forth. For Pelagius says that “the answer was given by us” (Below, Appendix, part 2), and so forth.

It was not enough for Orosius to protest verbally against John’s accusation. He also considered it necessary to defend his innocence in writing. He rejoiced that an opportunity had been offered to bring Pelagius’ impiety into the light. He thought that it had not happened without divine providence that he was compelled, through the insolence of the heretics, to expose an evil that had already been tolerated with excessive patience.

At the same time, he would not merely attack the error, as Aurelius Augustine and Jerome had until then considered sufficient, but would attack the heretics themselves as well (ibid.).

For he saw Pelagius and Caelestius openly spreading the poison of their heresy everywhere. He also saw that they had occupied the holy see of the Jerusalem Church, into which they had insinuated themselves, so completely that they trusted that the terror of their power could prevent true believers from appealing to it.

As for Orosius himself, who fought against them, he was being expelled from the Church, in whose bosom the heretic was fed and cherished—a heretic who, like Goliath, had long been challenging the servants of God to battle and reproaching them for cowardly timidity.

Accordingly, Orosius published a writing in the form of an apology and addressed it to the priests. He never fails to call them by this title, “most blessed priests.” We should have no doubt that he means the presbyters of the Jerusalem Church, especially those who had taken part in the colloquy.

At the beginning he gives a brief account of the entire order of the colloquy and dissolves John’s accusation. Then, taking the opportunity to explain his own opinion more fully and to attack Pelagius’ error—he mentions Pelagius very frequently—he undertakes a fairly lengthy discussion of impeccability and the help of grace.

This discussion is highly consistent with the mind and writings of Jerome, with whom we have no doubt that Orosius had conferred on the matter.

Orosius admits that a human being, aided by divine grace, can live a life entirely pure from every sin. He nevertheless argues that this has never happened and never will happen, for such is not the condition of human beings in this present life, amid the corruption in which they live.

Augustine does not remain silent about the disagreement that arose between John and Orosius. He records that at the Synod of Diospolis he reproached that bishop, both for his treatment of Orosius and for that of certain others (Below, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 39).

Since the Synod of Diospolis itself was approaching, we must learn what the situation of the Pelagians in Palestine then was not only from Orosius’ *Apology* but also from Jerome’s dialogues against them. In those dialogues Jerome answered all their various little questions at precisely this time (Jerome, Preface to the *Dialogues against the Pelagians*).

In the first dialogue Jerome therefore dealt with what he had heard Pelagius write: “A human being can be without sin, if he wishes, and God’s commandments are easy.”

Pelagius intended this to be understood as meaning “with the grace of God.” But he referred God’s grace to the benefit of our created condition, since we were created with free will. Nor did he agree that God’s help was present in the individual things we do in any other way than that the grace of free will, once given to us, is preserved.

Moreover, he maintained that some people had actually existed without sin, such as Job, Zechariah, and Elizabeth.

From the passages of Scripture in which human beings are commanded not to sin and to be perfect, he argued in this way: “Either God gave possible commandments or impossible ones. If they are possible, it lies within our power to perform them if we wish. If they are impossible, we are not guilty for failing to do what we cannot fulfill.”

Finally, he held that human beings, even while existing in this body, could possess every virtue.

After refuting these arguments, Jerome brings forward for examination several propositions from Pelagius’ book, which Pelagius had entitled *The Chapters*. Some of these propositions are likewise touched upon in Orosius’ *Apology*, and most of them were later presented to the judges at Diospolis.

In the second dialogue, the character who speaks for the Pelagians objects that blame is being referred to God if he created human beings in such a way that they cannot be free from forgetfulness, ignorance, and sin. He argues that no testimony can be found in the New Testament in which error, ignorance, and the impossibility of the commandment are treated as guilt.

As for the passage commonly brought forward from the Apostle—“I see another law in my members” (Rom. 7:23), and so forth—and similar passages, he says that Paul does not speak these words in his own person, but in the person of the human race, which is subject to vices because of the frailty of the flesh—in the person, that is, of a sinner.

Those words of Daniel also—“We have sinned; we have acted wickedly” (Dan. 3:29), and so forth—must be understood in such a way that Daniel and all the prophets spoke not on their own behalf, since they were holy, but in the person of the people.

In the third dialogue the Pelagianist argues once again that nature is being accused, that guilt is being referred back to God, and that free will is being taken away unless we admit that a human being, once justified through Christ’s Baptism, can preserve righteousness forever and thereby avoid every sin. Jerome complains that the already-condemned error of Jovinian is being revived here. In the preface he also warned that this was Origen’s doctrine: that it is impossible for human nature, from the beginning to death, not to sin; and, conversely, that it is possible, once someone has turned toward better things, to attain such strength that he can no longer sin. Finally, two chapters from Pelagius’s writings to a widow, expressing the swelling of Pharisaical pride, are briefly examined. From this point the discussion gradually descends to the question of original sin. Jerome recalls that Augustine had treated it splendidly, and he closes the dialogue with these words:

“Some time ago the holy and eloquent bishop Augustine wrote to Marcellinus—who was later killed by heretics, though innocent, under suspicion of Heraclian tyranny—two books on the baptism of infants, against your heresy, and so forth. I therefore think that this labor should be left aside, lest Horace’s words be said to me: ‘Do not carry wood into the forest.’ For either we shall say the same things unnecessarily, or, if we wish to say something new, the better arguments have already been occupied by a most distinguished intellect.” (Below, Appendix, part 2.)

Here he did not wish to name his opponents, so that by this means he might show everyone that he hated not human beings but errors, and that he was not seeking anyone’s disgrace, but grieving over the plight of those who had gone astray (Jerome, Preface to the Dialogues against the Pelagians). Accordingly, Pelagius’s name should be removed entirely from the preface of the work, where it now appears in printed editions, since our old Corbie manuscript never contained it in that place. The work preceded the Council of Diospolis by a short time; for at the gathering held at Jerusalem at the end of July 415, Orosius testified that Jerome was then engaged in composing it.

## X. Pelagius, accused by Heros and Lazarus, is brought before the judgment of the Council of Diospolis: at that judgment the Pelagian heresy is condemned, while Pelagius himself, the heresiarch, is acquitted.

John of Jerusalem’s accusation against Orosius, together with Orosius’s own Apology—in which he addressed that bishop in rather harsh terms and declared that he did not wish to maintain fellowship with Pelagius unless Pelagius repented (Orosius, at the end of the Apology)—could hardly fail to provoke disturbances by which everything agreed and decreed at the Jerusalem gathering, namely that both sides should observe silence and a truce until the Roman pontiff had judged the case, would be overturned.

It is therefore not surprising that, not long afterward, we find Pelagius denounced to the Palestinian bishops under the name of heresy. His accusers were Heros and Lazarus, Gallic bishops: Heros was from Arles, Lazarus from Aix, though at that time both had been driven from their sees. Pope Zosimus treated them with extreme harshness, at the time when he allowed himself to be deceived by Pelagius’s and Caelestius’s calumnies against them. Prosper, however, in his Chronicle under the year 412, calls Heros a holy man and a disciple of Blessed Martin. He says that, when Heros was presiding as bishop over the town of Arles, he was driven out by the people of that city, although innocent and subject to no accusation.

Baronius says that we should learn about his companion Lazarus, whose memory has remained more obscure, from Heros himself; for those whom a common calumny has entangled should be thought to have been adorned by equal virtue, since the wicked have customarily hated only the good, and heretics have harassed only Catholics (Baronius, under the year 417). Augustine certainly calls the same men “holy brothers and fellow bishops,” and elsewhere “good brothers.” He admits that John of Jerusalem had brought some complaint against them before the Council of Diospolis, but maintains that it had no force against them and seemed to the council fathers to possess no weight whatever (Below, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, nos. 2, 53, 39). The bishops of the Council of Carthage likewise call them “holy brothers and fellow priests” (Letter 175, no. 1, among Augustine’s letters).

We do not know what circumstances led those two Gallic bishops to be in Palestine in 415, or why they rose against Pelagius with such vehemence, except that Augustine writes that they had been offended by the perverse doctrine which they had detected in his disputations (Below, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, no. 53). They placed in a written memorandum the errors collected from the books of Pelagius and Caelestius, though, as they admitted, they had reduced them to a summary because they had not been able to excerpt entire passages (ibid., no. 29). They added both the articles on account of which Caelestius had been condemned by the Council of Carthage and those which Hilary had sent from Sicily to Augustine. They presented this memorandum, written in Latin (ibid., no. 2), to Eulogius (ibid., no. 9). Augustine always places Eulogius before the other thirteen bishops of the Council of Diospolis, and even before John of Jerusalem himself. Hence he is rightly thought to have been bishop of Caesarea and metropolitan of the whole province of Palestine.

The matter was brought before the Palestinian council, as Augustine calls it. No one doubts that this was the same council which, as Jerome writes, was held at Diospolis, a city of Palestine known in Scripture by the name Lydda (Acts 9:32) (Jerome, Letter 202, no. 2, among Augustine’s letters). The account of the discovery of the relics of the martyr Stephen teaches us that, when those relics were found—around December 20, 415—John received the news at Lydda, or Diospolis, where he was attending the council (Lucian, Letter on the Discovery of the Body of the Martyr Stephen, in the Appendix to volume 7). On December 18 he had not yet departed for the council and was still at Jerusalem, where on December 25 or 26—manuscript readings vary—he transferred the bones of the blessed Protomartyr. Accordingly, no date more suitable than December 20, or approximately that date, can be assigned to the council.

Fourteen bishops were present: Eulogius, John, Ammonianus, Porphyrius, Eutonius, another Porphyrius, Fidus, Zoninus, Zoboennus, Nymphidius, Chromatius, Jovinus, Eleutherius, and Clematius (Below, Against Julian, book 1, nos. 19, 32). It is certain that Eulogius and John presided, the former at Caesarea and the latter at Jerusalem. It is similarly believed that one of the two Porphyrii was the famous bishop of Gaza, who died only in 420. In the history of the translation mentioned above, we read that John took with him to carry out that undertaking two other bishops: Eutonius, or Hestonius, of Sebaste, and Eleutherius of Jericho. Fidus, bishop of Joppa, attended the Council of Ephesus. It may perhaps be permissible to identify Jovinus with the man whom Palladius reports to have been appointed bishop of Ascalon before 420. Nor, perhaps, was Zoboennus someone other than the Zoboennus whom Sozomen calls bishop of Eleutheropolis, and who may have succeeded Turbon, who held that see around 386.

Pelagius appeared before the council; Heros and Lazarus, however, could not come because of the grave illness of one of them (Below, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, no. 2). Orosius was likewise absent. No one at all was present to act as prosecutor against Pelagius, to expose the perversity of his meaning, compel him to explain his position, and finally distinguish any ambiguity that might exist in his teaching.

This may indeed seem strange, and it appears not to have happened without some hidden conspiracy. Although Augustine could not have been unaware of it, he nevertheless did not think it should be committed to memory. We have certainly seen how hostile the bishop of Jerusalem had shown himself toward Pelagius’s opponents. As we shall see, this produced disastrous consequences and also broke out within the council itself. John was asked by the bishops to explain what had taken place in his presence at the Jerusalem gathering. He delivered a speech, part of which Augustine reports, in which he maintained not only that Pelagius accepted Christ’s grace, but also attacked Heros and Lazarus, Orosius, and certain others (ibid., no. 37).

Pelagius, however, was not content with John’s protection and favor. To magnify his reputation before the judges, he boasted that many exceptionally holy men were joined to him in friendship, and produced numerous letters from bishops who praised him highly. He had some of these read aloud at the council, including one from Augustine (ibid., no. 51).

At last it became necessary to read the memorandum in which Heros and Lazarus had written out Pelagius’s statements. The judges, who did not know Latin, used an interpreter; Pelagius, however, gave his answers to the charges in Greek (ibid., nos. 3, 2).

Among the passages read from the memorandum and brought against Pelagius was this first statement, which he had written in one of his books (Book of Chapters; see Appendix, part 2): “No one can be without sin unless he has knowledge of the law” (Below, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, no. 4).

After it had been read, the council said: “Did you publish this, Pelagius?”

He replied: “I did say it, but not as they understand it. I did not say that one who has knowledge of the law cannot sin, but that knowledge of the law helps one not to sin, as it is written: ‘He gave them the law for their assistance.’”

When the council heard this, it said: “What Pelagius has said is not foreign to the Church.”

The episcopal council added: “Let another chapter be read.”

It was read that Pelagius had written in the same book: “All are governed by their own will.”

After it had been read, Pelagius replied: “I said this on account of free will, for God is the helper of the person who chooses what is good. But when a person sins, he himself is at fault, as one possessing free will.”

When the bishops heard this, they said: “This too is not foreign to ecclesiastical teaching” (ibid., no. 5).

It was likewise read that Pelagius had written in his book: “On the day of judgment the wicked and sinners are not to be spared, but are to be consumed in eternal fires.”

Pelagius replied: “I said this according to the Gospel, where it is said of sinners: ‘They will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.’ Anyone who believes otherwise is an Origenist.”

The council said: “This is not foreign to the Church” (ibid., nos. 9, 10).

Pelagius was also charged with having written in his book: “Evil does not even enter into thought.”

He replied: “We did not write it in that form, but said that a Christian ought to strive not to think evil.”

The bishops approved this (ibid., no. 12).

Another passage was read, in which he had written in his memorandum: “The kingdom of heaven was also promised in the Old Testament.”

Pelagius replied: “This can also be proved from the Scriptures. Heretics deny it in order to insult the Old Testament. I, however, followed the authority of Scripture when I said it, since it is written in the prophet Daniel: ‘And the saints shall receive the kingdom of the Most High.’”

When his answer had been accepted, the council said: “This too is not foreign to the ecclesiastical faith” (ibid., no. 13).

After this Pelagius was charged with having written in the same book that, “if he wishes, a person can be without sin,” and with having flatteringly said in a letter to a widow:

“May piety find a place with you, though it has found one nowhere else; may righteousness, a stranger everywhere, find a home in you; may the truth, which no one now knows, become domestic and friendly to you; and may the law of God, which is almost universally despised, be honored by you alone.”

And again to the same woman:

“O happy and blessed are you, if the righteousness which is believed to exist only in heaven is found on earth in you alone!”

And in another book addressed to her, after the prayer of our Lord and Savior, while teaching how the saints ought to pray, he says:

“He worthily lifts his hands to God; he pours out his prayer with a good conscience who can say: ‘You know, Lord, how holy, innocent, and clean from every trouble, iniquity, and robbery are the hands which I extend to you; how righteous and pure, and free from every lie, are the lips with which I offer you my supplication, that you may have mercy on me’” [Col. 0043].

In response Pelagius said:

“We did say that a person can be without sin and keep God’s commandments, if he wishes, for God gave him this possibility. But we did not say that anyone can be found who has never sinned from infancy to old age. Rather, after turning away from sins, a person can, through his own labor and God’s grace, be without sin; yet this does not make him incapable of turning back in the future. As for the other statements they have added, they are neither in our books nor have we ever said such things.”

When the council heard this, it said: “Since you deny having written such things, do you anathematize those who hold them?”

Pelagius replied: “I anathematize them as foolish, not as heretics, since this is not a doctrine.”

Then the bishops judged as follows:

“Since Pelagius has now anathematized in his own voice this uncertain foolish speech, and has rightly replied that a person can be without sin with God’s help and grace, let him answer the other chapters as well” (Below, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, no. 16).

Pelagius was then charged with statements said to have been found in the teaching of Caelestius, his disciple:

- that Adam was made mortal and would have died whether he sinned or did not sin;
- that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race;
- that the Law leads to the kingdom in the same way as the Gospel;
- that before Christ’s coming there were people without sin;
- that newly born infants are in the same condition in which Adam was before his transgression;
- that neither through Adam’s death or transgression does the whole human race die, nor through Christ’s resurrection does the whole human race rise again.

These statements were brought forward in such a way that it was also said that they had been heard and condemned at Carthage by Aurelius and the other bishops with him.

Other chapters were then brought forward, with Augustine’s name mentioned among them. These had been sent to him from Sicily, when the Catholic brothers there were being troubled by such questions, to which Augustine himself had responded in a book written to Hilary. They were as follows:

- that a person can be without sin, if he wishes;
- that infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life;
- that baptized rich people, unless they renounce everything, are not credited with whatever good they may appear to do, and cannot possess the kingdom of God.

To these charges Pelagius replied:

“As for the statement that a person can be without sin, it has already been explained above. As for the statement that before the Lord’s coming there were people without sin, we too say that, according to the tradition of the holy Scriptures, certain people lived holy and righteous lives before Christ’s coming. But the remaining statements, according to their own testimony, were not said by me. I therefore do not owe satisfaction for them. Nevertheless, to satisfy the holy council, I anathematize those who hold or have ever held such views.”

After this answer the council said:

“The present Pelagius has given a sufficient and proper answer to the chapters mentioned above, anathematizing statements that were not his” (ibid., nos. 23, 24).

Pelagius was charged with saying that the Church here on earth is “without spot or wrinkle.”

He replied:

“We said this, but in the sense that the Church is cleansed from every spot and wrinkle through the washing of Baptism, and that the Lord wishes it to remain in this condition.”

The council said:

“This also pleases us” (ibid., nos. 27, 28).

Next, statements from the book of Caelestius were brought forward, with the contents of each chapter given more according to their meaning than their exact wording. The accusers explained that Caelestius had treated the matters at greater length, but said that they had not been able to include everything in the memorandum which they had presented against Pelagius.

Thus, in the first chapter of Caelestius’s book, they said that this had been written:

“We do more than is commanded in the Law and the Gospel.”

Pelagius replied:

“They presented this as though it were our statement. But we said it according to the Apostle concerning virginity, about which Paul says: ‘I have no command from the Lord.’”

The council said:

“The Church accepts this as well” (ibid., no. 29).

Other capital charges from Caelestius were then brought against Pelagius.

In the third chapter, Caelestius was said to have written that God’s grace and assistance are not given for individual acts, but consist in free will, or in the Law and teaching. He was also said to have written that God’s grace is given according to our merits, because if God gives it to sinners, he appears to be unjust. He then added these words:

“Therefore grace itself has also been placed in my will, whether I am worthy or unworthy. For if we do everything through grace, then, when we are overcome by sin, it is not we who are overcome but God’s grace, which wished to help us in every way and could not.”

Again he says:

“If it is God’s grace when we conquer sins, then it is itself at fault when we are conquered by sin, because it either could not or would not preserve us at all.”

Pelagius replied:

“Whether these statements belong to Caelestius must be decided by those who say that they are Caelestius’s. I have never held such views, and I anathematize anyone who holds them.”

The council said:

“The holy council accepts you, since you condemn these reprehensible statements in this way” (ibid., no. 30).

When Pelagius was charged with the statement in the fifth chapter of Caelestius’s book that “each person can possess all virtues and graces,” and that it removed the diversity of graces taught by the Apostle, Pelagius replied:

“We did say this, but they have criticized it maliciously and incompetently. We do not remove the diversity of graces; rather, we say that God grants to one who is worthy to receive them all the graces, just as he granted them to the Apostle Paul.”

The council said:

“In accordance with ecclesiastical understanding, you too have understood the gift of the graces contained in the holy Apostle” (ibid., no. 32).

In the sixth chapter of Caelestius’s book, the following was charged against Pelagius: “The children of God cannot be called such unless they have been made entirely without sin.” Accordingly, Caelestius was said to have implied that the Apostle Paul was not a son of God, since he said: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect.”

In the seventh chapter: “Forgetfulness and ignorance are not subject to sin, because they occur not according to the will but according to necessity.”

In the tenth chapter: “There is no free will if it needs God’s assistance, since each person possesses in his own will the power either to do something or not to do it.”

In the twelfth chapter: “Our victory does not come from God’s assistance but from free will.” This was said to be expressed in these words:

“Our victory is ours, because we took up arms by our own will. Conversely, it is ours when we are defeated, because we refused to arm ourselves by our own will.”

He also cited the Apostle Peter as testimony that “we are partakers of the divine nature.”

He was said to have constructed the following syllogism:

“If the soul cannot be without sin, then God too is subject to sin, since a part of him—that is, the soul—is subject to sin.”

In the thirteenth chapter he says:

“Forgiveness is not granted to penitents according to God’s grace and mercy, but according to the merits and labor of those who, through repentance, have become worthy of mercy.”

After these statements had been read, the council said:

“What does the present monk Pelagius say concerning these chapters that have been read? For the holy council and the holy Catholic Church of God condemn them.”

Pelagius replied:

“I say again that these statements, according to their own testimony, are not mine. As I have said, I do not owe satisfaction for them. But the statements which I have confessed to be mine I affirm to be correct. Those which I said were not mine I reject according to the judgment of the holy Church, anathematizing anyone who opposes and contradicts the teachings of the holy Catholic Church.

“For I believe in the Trinity of one substance, and in all things according to the teaching of the holy Catholic Church. But if anyone thinks anything contrary to this, let him be anathema” (Below, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, nos. 42, 43).

The council said:

“Now that we have been satisfied by the statements of the present monk Pelagius, who agrees with pious teachings and rejects and anathematizes what is contrary to the faith of the Church, we confess him to belong to ecclesiastical and Catholic communion” (ibid., no. 44).

In this way the gathering ended. Jerome calls it the “miserable Council of Diospolis” (Letter 202, no. 2, among Augustine’s letters), undoubtedly considering nothing other than the offense that would be given to many of the less informed, who, since they could not penetrate the matter itself thoroughly, would observe only this: that the man accused of heresy had been received as a Catholic by the Eastern bishops.

Pelagius did not fail to exploit the result for the advantage and authority of his party. He proclaimed that his opinions had been approved by fourteen bishops and boasted that his opponents had been covered with shame (Below, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, no. 54).

Nevertheless, this did not prevent Augustine from consistently judging the council in the most favorable light. He calls its fathers pious and Catholic judges, who would never have declared Pelagius innocent unless he had condemned his errors (ibid., no. 4; Against Julian, book 1, no. 19). Accordingly, although Pelagius had been, so far as human appearances were concerned, acquitted as a heresiarch, Augustine maintains that all those doctrines from which the heresy had spread had nevertheless been publicly condemned (Below, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, no. 58; Against Julian, book 2, no. 34). Hence he cites those fourteen bishops against Julian as witnesses to Catholic doctrine (Below, Against Julian, book 1, no. 19).

He further adds that, at that time, the Pelagian heresy had been completely overthrown—its head severed, as it were, by Pelagius’s own tongue—when Pelagius condemned it through fear of his own condemnation (Against the Same, book 3, no. 4). Pelagius had stolen his acquittal by deceiving the judges (Below, On Original Sin, no. 15), or, more accurately, Pelagius had not been acquitted at all; only the position which he professed with his mouth had been acquitted (ibid., no. 17; and in volume 5, fragment 1, no. 5). Pope Innocent declared that he could neither censure the judgment of that council nor approve it in turn (Below, Appendix, part 2). Prosper speaks of it in no other way than Augustine does, though he acknowledges that an indulgence was granted to Pelagius which seemed to exceed proper limits somewhat (ibid.).

## XI. Pelagius, remaining firmly attached to his heresy after the Council of Diospolis, widely publishes various writings in 416. Theodore of Mopsuestia defends the same heresy against the treatises of Augustine and Jerome. The blasphemy of a certain Pelagian at Rome.

Although Pelagius hoped that the judgment at Diospolis would bring him every possible advantage, he did not hasten to publish the proceedings of that council—which it was in his interest to make public (Letter 183, no. 3, among Augustine’s letters)—and send them to the Roman pontiff and the other leading bishops, as he would surely have done if he had truly been cleared. Indeed, as long as he could, he delayed their circulation (Below, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, no. 55).

Their publication was preceded by a letter full of vanity, which he took every care to disseminate widely. Among other things, he boasted that what he had said—namely, that a person could be without sin and easily keep God’s commandments if he wished—had been approved by the judgment of fourteen bishops:

“This judgment,” he said, “has covered the mouth of contradiction with confusion and separated from one another the whole association conspiring toward evil” (ibid., no. 54).

Thus he passed over in silence the divine grace which he had been forced to confess at the council, leaving only human pride to boast as the victor. He also added the word “easily,” which is nowhere mentioned in the council’s proceedings. We do not know how it happened that Heros and Lazarus entirely omitted it from their memorandum, even though it was especially characteristic of Pelagius. Certainly, whatever had been said about this question at the council was wholly opposed to this alleged ease; indeed, it expressly excluded it.

In this letter Pelagius wrote back to a certain presbyter among his friends, who had kindly warned him to take care lest anyone, because of him, separate himself from the body of the Church.

At that time he also widely circulated an apologetic pamphlet, in which he used the authority of the Palestinian proceedings in his defense against his opponents (ibid., nos. 1, 57). There he boasted that he had answered the charges of the Gallic bishops and had been completely cleared (Letter 179, no. 7). Augustine, however, demonstrates that Pelagius had obscured and corrupted the truth of the proceedings in certain respects (Below, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, no. 57).

Pelagius sent the aforementioned pamphlet defending himself to Augustine through a certain Charus, a citizen of Hippo but an Eastern deacon, without enclosing any letter to Augustine himself (Below, On the Proceedings of Pelagius, no. 1). Accordingly, the most prudent bishop, who greatly wished to explain in writing what he thought about Pelagius’s exculpation—for he immediately judged that Pelagius had been acquitted by the Palestinian council merely because his answers had presented orthodox opinions—did not dare to carry this out on the authority of a writing, since the document could either be denied or found to differ from the original.

Augustine also mentions this writing of Pelagius in letters sent to Pope Innocent in 416 (Letter 177, no. 15), and at the same time mentions a letter to Pelagius, now lost, which he himself had written on this occasion.

At this same time Pelagius published his books on free will. He composed them after the Council of Diospolis (Letter 186, no. 34), whose proceedings he boasted about in those books, and not long before the letter which he wrote to Pope Innocent at the beginning of 417. In that letter he praised the work as a certain testimony to his faith:

“Let them also read,” he said, “my recent little work, which we have lately been compelled to publish on free will. They will recognize how unjustly those who have eagerly sought to disgrace us by denying grace have acted, since throughout almost the entire text of the work we confess both free will and grace completely and intact” (Below, On the Grace of Christ, no. 45).

Nevertheless, it clearly appeared that he understood the assistance of grace as nothing other than what he seemed to have condemned at the Palestinian council. Augustine demonstrates this by citing various passages from the same work, one of which contains a particularly careful and complete expression of the whole Pelagian doctrine (ibid., no. 6).

Whatever he appeared to say there in favor of grace could easily be referred entirely to nature and the Law. Thus he believed that prayers themselves were useful for no other purpose than that divine teaching might be disclosed to us by revelation, not that the human mind might be assisted, so that what it had learned ought to be done could also be accomplished through love and action (ibid., no. 45). It could also be thought that he wished to grant the assistance of grace as something added over and above, since he said that grace was given to human beings so that they might more easily accomplish through grace what they had been commanded to do by free will (Letter 186, no. 35).

Pelagius had divided this work into four books, whose publication served as a response to Jerome’s dialogues (Below, On the Grace of Christ, no. 45). Julian said of these dialogues to Augustine:

“Of this work you say that Pelagius, crushed beneath the weight of the Scriptures, cannot defend free will. But a Catholic man who had been attacked answered that work” (Below, Unfinished Work against Julian, book 4, chapter 88).

Jerome, however, says that Pelagius attacked his letter—perhaps the letter addressed to Ctesiphon—in those same books:

“Nevertheless, I did a great deal to ensure that, while he was attempting to answer my letter, he would expose himself more openly and reveal his blasphemies to everyone.”

He adds:

“For whatever he denies having said in that miserable Council of Diospolis, he professes in this work” (Letter 202, no. 2, among Augustine’s letters).

Although Jerome had earlier identified Anianus as the author of the books together with Pelagius, he rightly assigns them more to the man who contributed his blasphemous ideas and plans to their composition than to the one who contributed his style and verbal nonsense.

It is certain that Augustine knew nothing of these books until after he had received the proceedings of the Council of Diospolis (Below, On Original Sin, no. 15). Nevertheless, it is clear that the same books reached Augustine first and Jerome later (Letter 202, no. 2).

Not long afterward, Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia in Cilicia, saw the treatises of these holy Doctors against the Pelagian heresy. The Pelagians, as the collapse of their affairs was beginning, had doubtless hastened to report the situation to him as the principal progenitor or teacher of their heresy (Below, Appendix, part 2).

Accordingly, to come to the aid of the struggling heresy, he composed five books against those who defended original sin (Photius, Bibliotheca, codex 177). In them he says that the author of this teaching, originally from the West but then living in the East, had published books composed concerning a heresy recently devised by him—such is Theodore’s own expression—and that he had imbued entire Churches with those opinions.

We read in Photius that Theodore called this man “Haram,” evidently a corrupt form of the name Jerome. The accusations added there against the supposed author of that heresy can refer only to Jerome: one concerns his fabrication of a fifth Gospel (Below, Unfinished Work against Julian, book 4, chapter 88), because in his work of dialogues Jerome had mentioned a certain Gospel used by the Nazarenes; another concerns his rejection of the Septuagint translation of the Old Testament by a man who, having been scarcely accustomed from childhood to the Hebrew language and having used no teachers for learning the meaning of Scripture except certain Hebrews of low status, had undertaken to fabricate an edition of his own.

According to Photius, who is drawing on Theodore, the principal doctrines of that sect were approximately these:

“Human beings sin by nature, not by will. By ‘nature,’ I mean not that nature with which Adam was endowed when he was created at the beginning; for they assert that this nature was good and was God’s good work. Rather, they mean the nature which Adam acquired after sin, when, through transgression and sin, he exchanged the bad for the good and the mortal for the immortal. In this way, they say, human beings too were made wicked by nature,” and so forth.

A second doctrine derived from this was that infants, although newly born, are not free from sin, since, because of Adam’s transgression, nature was established in sins and is propagated to all his descendants as a sinful nature, to use their own expression [lacuna].

They further taught that holy Baptism and participation in the sacred Body, granted even to infants for the remission of sins, provide this benefit, and so forth.

They also held that no mortal is righteous.

The fourth doctrine was that not even Christ, having assumed a nature infected by sins, was free from guilt, and so forth.

Fifth, they asserted that marriage—or at least the desire for intercourse—and the emission of semen, together with everything of the same kind through which the human race is propagated by succession, are works of a perverse nature. Adam had fallen into this nature through sin and, through the defect of nature, had thereafter taken upon himself the seed of all evils [Col. 0049].

We could hardly say whether Theodore himself was the first to devise the calumny contained in this fifth chapter. When Augustine later heard that the Pelagians were directing it against Catholics, he undertook to repel it in his work On Marriage and Concupiscence. He was likewise compelled more than once to dissolve the charge contained in the fourth chapter in his books against Julian (Below, Against Julian, book 5, no. 51; Unfinished Work against the Same, book 4, chapters 76, 87).

When Mercator produced excerpts from several of Theodore’s books, he prefaced them with this title:

“From the fourth book of the second codex of Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia, on folio ten, against Saint Augustine defending original sin and arguing in the Catholic manner that Adam was made mortal through transgression.”

Not long after news of the Council of Diospolis had become public, Augustine delivered a sermon in which, in the fragment that still survives, he discusses Pelagius’s acquittal in these words:

“Let no one say that he was acquitted by the bishops. The confession was acquitted, as though the correction itself had been acquitted. For what he said before the bishops appeared Catholic, whereas what he wrote in his books was unknown to the bishops who acquitted him; and perhaps he was corrected. We must not despair of a human being, who perhaps preferred to join himself to the Catholic faith and flee for refuge to its grace and assistance. Perhaps this is what happened. Nevertheless, it was not the heresy that was acquitted, but the man who denied the heresy” (Sermon Fragments, fragment 1, no. 5, in volume 5).

These words make it sufficiently clear that Augustine had not yet seen Pelagius’s books on free will, and that nothing had yet been written by Zosimus either in Pelagius’s favor or for his condemnation. Indeed, it is also clear that Innocent himself had not yet pronounced anything on the matter.

The holy Doctor relates in the same place that Urban, who had perhaps been ordained bishop of Sicca after serving as a presbyter of that church in which Augustine was then speaking—possibly the church of Hippo—had disputed at Rome with a certain Pelagian. When Urban pressed him by the force of the Lord’s Prayer, demonstrating that we would pray in vain, “Do not bring us into temptation,” if it were indeed within our power not to sin and to overcome every temptation to sin by the strength of our own will alone, the Pelagian replied: “We ask God not to bring us into temptation, lest we suffer some evil that is not within our power: lest I fall from a horse, break my leg, or a robber kill me, and so forth. For these things are not within my power. But to conquer the temptations of my sins, if I wish, I both can—and can do so without God’s help” (*ibid.*, no. 1). Augustine admits that this reply struck him with no ordinary horror; and the entire congregation, too, was no less horrified at these Pelagian utterances.

## XII. Several writings of Jerome are brought into Africa by Orosius, together with letters from Heros and Lazarus concerning Pelagius. The Carthaginian synod writes to Innocent against the Pelagian heresy. The Council of Milevis does the same, as do five bishops jointly. On Augustine’s letters to Hilary and John.

Paul Orosius, whom Augustine had sent to Jerome in the preceding year, returned to the West at this time and was the first of all to bring back some relics of the martyr Stephen (Marcellinus, *Chronicle*). This is not the proper place to describe the ceremony with which they were received or the number of miracles God performed on their account. Orosius certainly departed from Palestine at the very beginning of spring, since he was already preparing for his return when the bones of the blessed Protomartyr were discovered; such was his longing for his homeland (Avitus, *Letter to Palchonius, on the Relics of Saint Stephen*, in Appendix to volume 7).

There can be no doubt that Jerome sent Augustine a letter by this same bearer (*Letter* 172, among the Augustinian letters), which begins as follows: “I received my honorable brother, your son Orosius the presbyter, both for his own merits and at your command.” He excuses himself for not having replied to Orosius’s two books, namely *On the Soul* and *On the Epistle of James*, on account of the misfortunes of the times. He expresses his attitude toward Augustine in these words:

> “For my part, I have resolved to love you, receive you, honor you, admire you, and defend your words as though they were my own. Certainly, in the *Dialogue* that I recently published (*Dialogue* 3, *Against the Pelagians*), I remembered Your Beatitude, as was fitting. Let us rather devote ourselves to removing from the churches this most destructive heresy, which always pretends to repent so that it may obtain the opportunity to teach in the churches; for if it reveals itself in the open light, it will be driven out and perish.”

Augustine cites this same dialogue not long afterward (*Letter* 180, no. 5); hence one may reasonably believe that Orosius brought the work itself to him.

Orosius also carried letters from Heros and Lazarus, which accused Pelagius and Coelestius of having devised a wicked and detestable doctrine (*Letter* 175, no. 1). They reported that Pelagius was active in Jerusalem and deceiving some there, although all the most perceptive men, by whom his meaning could be investigated—and Jerome above all—were vigorously resisting him (*Letter* 176, no. 4). Nor, as one may judge, did they disregard the history of the Council of Diospolis, since they were openly examining Pelagius’s case (*Letter* 186, no. 2).

Orosius presented their letters to the bishops of the province of Proconsular Africa (*Letter* 175, no. 1), who at that time were holding their customary and solemn synod in the city of Carthage, convened for various reasons, perhaps around the month of June. Provincial synods in Africa appear generally to have been celebrated either at this season of the year or around autumn. As for the year of Orosius’s return, there is no reason to doubt that it was 416. The reply of Innocent to the aforementioned synod, dated in January of the year 417, will also be demonstrated below.

Sixty-eight bishops had assembled at this synod, and the names of all of them have been recorded [Col. 0051]. It will not be difficult to identify nearly all their sees from the *Conference with the Donatists*, held in the same place in 411. The most distinguished among these bishops were Aurelius of Carthage, Vincentius, perhaps of Culusa, and Theasius of Membressa.

After the letters of Heros and Lazarus had been read there, the bishops judged it right to employ whatever authority they possessed in defending the cause of the Church, which had already been attacked (*Letter* 186, no. 2). Accordingly, they ordered the acts by which Coelestius had been judged nearly five years earlier to be read (*Letter* 175, no. 1). Although it was plainly established that his condemnation had been pronounced at that time, they nevertheless judged that he—and likewise Pelagius with him—ought again to be anathematized unless they most explicitly anathematized the heresy of which they were the authors, even though Coelestius had reportedly already insinuated himself into the honor of the presbyterate in Asia. They considered such severity necessary to heal the minds of many whom those men had either already corrupted or might corrupt in the future.

Indeed, everything was already full of contentious men who, by disputing incessantly against God’s grace, were both carrying away weak and poorly instructed minds and exhausting even those who were firmer in the faith through endless controversies (*Letter* 177, no. 3). To oppose this evil on every side, the Council of Carthage also judged that the matter ought to be referred to Pope Innocent, so that the authority of the Apostolic See might be added to their decrees (*Letter* 175, no. 2). They desired this all the more eagerly because some were asserting that Pelagius had not only been cleared by the Palestinian acts but that the Roman bishop had also yielded to his arguments (*Letter* 177, no. 2).

Possidius, certainly, testifies that the Pelagians had tried to persuade the Apostolic See of their perfidy, and that for this reason the African synods had acted with the greatest urgency to demonstrate first to Innocent and afterward to Zosimus how detestable that faction was and how deserving of condemnation by all Catholics (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chap. 18). Since the African bishops therefore hoped that the heretics would more readily submit to the authority of the Roman pontiff when it was drawn from the authority of the holy Scriptures (*Letter* 176, no. 5), and since, amid so grave a temptation, they wished to learn from the Pontiff’s replies whether he found their own judgment consonant with his, and thus whether it was evident that both judgments had been drawn from the same source (*Letter* 177, no. 19), the synod sent Innocent the letter of Heros and Lazarus together with the acts of another Council of Carthage, at which Coelestius had been condemned in 412.

They also added a letter of their own, authenticated by the names of all the bishops. In it they implored Innocent to have compassion on them with pastoral affection and to consider how pestilential and destructive the Pelagian doctrine was to Christ’s sheep. Finally, they pronounced the sentence of condemnation in these words:

> “Even if Pelagius and Coelestius have been corrected, or say that they have never held these views, and deny that any writings produced against them are theirs, and even if there is no way to convict them of lying, nevertheless, whoever teaches and asserts in general that human nature is sufficient for itself to avoid sins and fulfill God’s commandments, and is thereby found to be opposed to the grace of God, which is more clearly revealed through the prayers of the saints; and whoever denies that infants are delivered from perdition through Christ’s Baptism and receive eternal salvation—let him be anathema.”

As for the other charges brought against Pelagius and Coelestius, they leave the matter to the Pontiff’s judgment, so that, after reading the acts of the Council of Diospolis, he himself may decide whatever seems expedient (*Letter* 175, no. 6).

A provincial synod of the bishops of Numidia assembled in the city of Milevis. When it learned what had been done by the bishops of the province of Carthage, it resolved, following their example, to write to Innocent. After placing before him how destructive was the heresy that removed from adults the necessity of prayer and from infants the necessity of Baptism, it begged and entreated him that, if he could not provide for the salvation of Pelagius and Coelestius by turning them away from their wicked opinions, he should at least protect others by condemning them.

A considerable number of bishops signed the letter; their names, sixty-one in all, are listed at its beginning. The more distinguished among them were Silvanus of Zama, then primate of Numidia; Aurelius of Macomades; Alypius of Thagaste; Augustine of Hippo; Severus of Milevis; Fortunatus of Cirta; and Possidius of Calama (*Letter* 176).

The letters of both synods were carried to Rome by a certain Bishop Julius. We may infer that his diocese was in Africa from the fact that Innocent replied through him (*Letter* 183, no. 1), and that, in a special letter to Aurelius, Innocent said he was restoring Julius to him.

Baronius attributes to this same Council of Milevis eight or nine canons against the Pelagians. As we shall say below, however, these canons were composed only in 418 at the Council of Carthage. In this matter Baronius followed what may be called either the acts of the Council of Milevis or a confusion of its acts. Their beginning belongs to the first Council of Milevis, held in 402, and therefore to a long period before the Pelagians arose. The material that follows is attributed in the African collection to various other councils, except for the twenty-third canon, which is found nowhere else.

Besides the synodical letters of the Councils of Carthage and Milevis, five African bishops—Aurelius, Alypius, Augustine, Evodius, and Possidius—wrote another letter jointly to Innocent (*Letter* 177), as to a friend and intimate (*Letter* 186, no. 2). In it they explained the entire case of Pelagius more fully and clearly, and they discussed how Pelagius could have been absolved by the Easterners, if that had indeed happened; for they had not yet received the acts of the Council of Diospolis.

They also explained that it was especially Innocent’s responsibility to remedy so great an evil, because there were many followers of the Pelagian doctrine in Rome. “If they learn,” the bishops said, “that the very book which they either think or know to be his has been anathematized and condemned by the authority of Catholic bishops, and especially by Your Holiness, whose judgment we have no doubt carries greater weight with him, we do not think that they will thereafter dare to disturb faithful and simply Christian hearts by speaking against the grace of God, which has been revealed through the passion and resurrection of Christ” (*Letter* 177, no. 15).

They added that Pelagius himself ought to be summoned to Rome, so that he might be carefully questioned whether he acknowledged the true grace of Christ; or, if that was not possible, that the matter should at least be pursued with him by letter. Thus, once absolved in the future without any scruple on the part of the Church and without any hiding place for ambiguity, he might provide the faithful with an occasion to rejoice in his own correction.

They also sent Innocent the book just mentioned, which Augustine had received from Timasius and James, together with Augustine’s refutation of it, marking in Pelagius’s book all the worst passages so that the Pontiff might attend to them. They likewise sent him Augustine’s letter to Pelagius, in which Augustine replied to the writings Pelagius had sent him after the Council of Diospolis in defense of himself. They therefore asked Innocent to arrange for the letter to be delivered to Pelagius, believing that Pelagius would be induced to read it with the reverence due to Augustine’s dignity.

In the meantime, they declared that they did not wish to define whether perfect completion could be attained in the present life or only in the future; provided that this remained entirely certain: whoever might at any time attain this perfection could attain it only through the gift of grace.

At that time a certain Palladius, about to cross the sea, was at Hippo Regius preparing to board a ship. He asked Augustine for a letter of recommendation to a bishop named Hilary. Taking this opportunity, Augustine wished to inform that bishop about the matters recently undertaken in Africa against the Pelagian heresy. He briefly disclosed to him its principal points, so that Hilary, too, might, according to his office, protect those who might perhaps have been infected with this poison (*Letter* 178).

We have explained elsewhere why we think this Hilary was none other than the bishop of Narbonne, to whom Zosimus wrote in 417 (*Note on Letter* 178).

It is also quite plausible that Augustine’s letter to John of Jerusalem belongs to this same period (*Letter* 179). When Augustine wrote it, he had already received from Pelagius a document written by Pelagius in his own defense, sent as a substitute for the Palestinian acts; but he had not yet seen the acts themselves.

Thus, although the holy Bishop had previously written to John and had received no reply, he encountered a servant of God named Luke, who was traveling to Palestine and would shortly return from there, and he wrote to John again through him. The sole subject of the letter is Pelagius. Augustine admonishes John to show him affection in such a way that John may not meanwhile appear to have been deceived by him.

Augustine also sent John Pelagius’s book on the powers of nature and his own book *On Nature and Grace*, which he had composed to refute the former, so that John might recognize how perverse and dangerous the heresiarch’s opinions were. Augustine demonstrates that Pelagius had taught in his book doctrines entirely different from those that, according to Pelagius’s defense document, he claimed to have professed at the Council of Diospolis.

Finally, Augustine asked John to send him the genuine acts of that council, thereby obliging not only Augustine but also many other bishops from whom the acts were likewise being requested.

## XIII. At the beginning of 417, Innocent replies to the African bishops and anathematizes Pelagius and Coelestius together with their condemned doctrine. Augustine publishes a book on the acts of the Council of Diospolis, in the final part of which he recounts the Pelagians’ attack upon Jerome. He also writes a letter against the Pelagians to Paulinus.

To the three aforementioned letters—the letters of the Council of Carthage, the Council of Milevis, and the five bishops—Pope Innocent replied with three others in the year 417, all dated on the same day, January 27. They were all carried to Africa by Bishop Julius (*Letters* 181, 182, and 183, among the Augustinian letters).

Some believe that Innocent did not write them until after he had convened a synod, since at that time the Roman pontiffs were not accustomed to writing about matters of such importance unless they had first summoned to a council not only their own clergy but also neighboring bishops, including those who were then residing at Rome (Garnerius, *On Mercator*, vol. 1, p. 194, no. 1).

In various passages Innocent praises the learning, zeal, and vigilance of the African bishops, since they cared not only for the churches entrusted to them but also embraced all the others with pious concern. He praises both councils in the most honorable terms chiefly because they had consulted the Apostolic See, whose dignity and authority he greatly extols (*Letters* 181, no. 1; 182, nos. 1–2).

He had already received the acts of the Council of Diospolis through the efforts of certain laymen, but he attached scarcely any weight to them. This was partly because he desired sincerity in Pelagius’s replies, and partly because the acts had been delivered to him without any letters from Pelagius or from the bishops by whom Pelagius had been absolved. For this reason, Innocent partly doubted the truth of the acts and partly judged that Pelagius had very little confidence in the absolution he advertised (*Letter* 183, no. 3).

Accordingly, without considering this judgment, and following the reports of the African bishops, he declared Pelagius and Coelestius excluded from communion with the Church, as unworthy of fellowship with that holy body and, indeed, of any association with Catholics (*Letter* 183, nos. 6, 3). He condemned under the same penalty those who, with equal obstinacy, presumed to defend their errors.

In his letter to the five bishops, he expressed the hope that the condemnation of Pelagius would recall to sound faith all those who might be in Rome—if indeed there were any, for he did not dare either to assert this, since no one professed it about himself, or to deny it, on account of the multitude of the citizens—or who might be in Jerusalem or in any other region of the world [Col. 0055].

Augustine frequently cites this judgment of Innocent against Julian:

> “What could that holy man have replied to the African councils except what the Apostolic See and the Roman Church, together with the rest of the Church, have steadfastly maintained from ancient times?”

As Augustine immediately adds, Innocent held nothing different on this matter from Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, and the other renowned bishops of the Church—men later in time than these, but earlier in place (*below, Against Julian*, book 1, no. 13).

Elsewhere Augustine writes again:

> “He replied to all our questions in the manner that was right and necessary for a bishop of the Apostolic See.”

When Augustine was preaching to the people of Carthage on Sunday, September 29, in the year 417, he ordered those who contradicted and resisted to be rebuked and brought before him:

> “For two councils have already sent their letters concerning this matter to the Apostolic See; replies have also come from there. The case is finished—would that the error might at last be finished as well!” (*Sermon* 131, no. 10).

Gennadius relates that Innocent issued a decree addressed to the Western and Eastern Churches against the Pelagians, which his successor, Pope Zosimus, subsequently promulgated more widely (Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chap. 43, corrected against the Corbie manuscript).

We ourselves cannot determine what Gennadius means by these words. The historian of the Pelagian controversy holds that, however the words are interpreted, one must not say that Innocent issued any decree other than the three letters mentioned above. Zosimus, he maintains, composed a decree in the form of those letters and promulgated it throughout the Church (Henry Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book 1, chap. 11).

Nor do we know whether Possidius joins together the decrees of both pontiffs when he says that both of them, by letters sent to the African churches of the West and to the churches of the East, judged that the Pelagians were to be anathematized and avoided by all Catholics (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chap. 18).

When Augustine wrote to Innocent in the name of the five bishops, the acts of the Council of Diospolis had not yet come into his hands, as we have observed. He therefore entreated John of Jerusalem to send them to him. Whether he received them from John, from Innocent, or from someone else is uncertain. This alone is clear: toward the end of 416 or at the beginning of 417, not long after the trouble stirred up by the Pelagians against Jerome, the acts came into Augustine’s hands.

In them he found, not without the greatest pleasure, what he had always been convinced of: that Pelagius had been absolved solely because he had made a profession ostensibly consistent with the Catholic faith. This led the holy Doctor to write on the subject, in order to make it clear that those by whose judgment Pelagius had been released had in no way approved his opinions and doctrine.

After completing a book on this matter—although he sometimes calls it *The Book on the Palestinian Acts* (*below, On Original Sin*, no. 15)—he entitled it *On the Acts of Pelagius*. He may have done so either because it had already become customary to call those proceedings “the acts of Pelagius and of his acquittal,” which Pelagius claimed had cleared him (*below, On the Acts of Pelagius*, no. 53; and vol. 2, *Letter* 177, no. 15), or because the book dealt with the very acts that Pelagius had previously issued in abbreviated and corrupted form—namely, his defense document, which he had arranged to have circulated publicly in place of the acts, as a kind of abridgment of them (*below, On the Acts of Pelagius*, no. 57). For this reason Possidius rightly called the same book *Against the Acts of Pelagius*.

Augustine dedicated this work to Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. In it he examines in detail each of the charges of error brought against Pelagius before the Palestinian synod, together with Pelagius’s replies to them. He then investigates whether any doubt remains concerning Pelagius’s conversion or innocence, showing that this is not an easy matter to believe. Finally, he proves that Pelagius was absolved by the synod’s judgment in such a way that the heresy itself, on account of which he had been brought to trial, was nevertheless unequivocally condemned.

In the work *On Nature and Grace* Augustine had avoided naming Pelagius; here he names him openly:

> “But now, if Pelagius is mindful of God, if he is not ungrateful for God’s mercy … he will receive our letters with greater gratitude, since by naming him explicitly we open the sore in order to heal it, rather than, as we regret having done when we feared causing pain, increasing the swelling” (*ibid.*, no. 50).

He nowhere uses the letters that Innocent wrote to the African bishops. One might therefore perhaps conjecture that those letters had not yet been delivered to him. Nor does he mention there the letters that the Africans had sent to Innocent.

At the end of the same work Augustine recalls the injuries inflicted upon the blessed Jerome by a band of wicked men who favored Pelagius. During this revolt one deacon was killed, the monastery buildings were burned, and Jerome himself was barely shielded from their violence by the protection of a very strong tower (*ibid.*, no. 66).
