They also attempted every extreme act of violence, by sword and fire, against the holy virgin Eustochium and her niece Paula, while their household servants were slaughtered before their eyes (*below, Appendix*, part 2). By so atrocious a crime, the minds of all who learned of it as the report spread everywhere were gravely wounded.

Jerome, in a letter sent through Bishop Aurelius—whom some believe to have been Aurelius of Carthage (Baronius, under the year 416)—complained to Innocent about these events. From Innocent he received a reply by the same channel. The Pontiff also replied that the complaints of the virgin Eustochium, when brought before him, had caused him grief and distress. He wrote a very severe letter to John of Jerusalem, in which he indicated clearly enough that John did not seem to him free from blame.

Although neither Jerome nor Eustochium named anyone explicitly, Innocent nevertheless testified that he knew the author from whom these things had originated (*below, Appendix* [Col. 0057], part 2); he clearly intended Pelagius.

It is not doubtful that the bishops of Numidia, if the report had reached them, would not have passed that event over in silence when they informed Innocent of Jerome’s conflict with Pelagius in the East (*below, Appendix*, part 2). Nor is it easy to believe that Innocent, if the rumor had already spread throughout Rome and Africa, would have remained silent about it in his replies. Thus the event cannot more conveniently be assigned than to the end of 416.

It is sufficiently credible that the letters Innocent wrote on this matter reached Palestine after John had already died. For Zosimus, writing to the Africans on September 21, 417, indicates that Praylius had long before been appointed in place of the deceased John (*ibid.*).

Innocent himself, after conferring those benefits upon the Church, departed to the heavenly realm. It is clear that his death occurred on March 12 of this year (*Preface to volume 2*, on *Letter* 186).

That holy pontiff had departed this life, already adorned with the title “of blessed memory” (*Letter* 186, no. 2). Yet Zosimus had still done nothing in favor of the Pelagians when Augustine sent, through Januarius, a lengthy letter against the Pelagians to Bishop Paulinus.

The whole letter is occupied with a discussion of the grace of Christ. Augustine was drawn to this subject not only by the pleasure he took in mentioning it frequently, but above all because he had heard that among the clergy or citizens of Nola there were some who opposed it. They attacked original sin in such a way that, with the utmost madness, they attributed to infants still enclosed in the maternal womb the exercise of free choice, together with the selection of good or evil, and therefore personal merits and sins.

Some of them had so hardened their minds in error that they said they would sooner abandon Pelagius—who had anathematized those denying original sin—than allow themselves to be called away from their own position. Augustine promises that Januarius will explain to Paulinus what had been reported to him about these men and who they were. He himself indicates no more than by calling them men of great and penetrating intelligence (*Letter* 186). Julian may perhaps have been one of their number. Although it is not established that he was at Nola at that time, he was staying not far from that city; and he had already fallen into the snares of the Pelagians (*below, On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 55).

Augustine sent Paulinus the letters of the African bishops to Innocent, together with Innocent’s replies, so that Paulinus, who was devoted to proclaiming the grace of God, as his writings sufficiently demonstrate, might also be equipped with weapons and defenses with which to protect it from the assaults of its adversaries.

Augustine also transcribed for him a considerable portion of the proceedings of the Council of Diospolis, and mentioned the books that Pelagius had most recently published on free will (*Letter* 186, nos. 27, 34). Later, the Semipelagians criticized certain statements in this letter, and for no other reason than that they overthrew their errors concerning predestination and perseverance (*below, On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 55).

During the summer of this same year, Augustine wrote a book to Dardanus in which he remained intensely focused on combating the Pelagian heresy, although he refrained from naming it (*Retractions*, book 2, chap. 49).

## XIV. Coelestius comes to Rome and presents a statement of his faith to Zosimus. Zosimus considers him innocent and writes to the African bishops concerning his case, although he does not meanwhile absolve him.

When Pelagius and Coelestius heard that they had been condemned by the Apostolic See and by the entire African Church, they readily understood that their reputation was ruined if that condemnation were to have force. This was undoubtedly why Pelagius wrote to Innocent for the purpose of clearing himself, while Coelestius went personally to Rome.

Although they were deeply conscious of their own guilt, they nevertheless thought that they were not so deprived of deceit and fraud—or perhaps not so entirely abandoned by their friends at Rome—that they could not deceive the Roman Church (*below, On Original Sin*, no. 9; and *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, no. 5). They hoped also to draw not a few Roman clergy into their party and into their wicked opinions.

It had first been widely reported that the adversaries of grace were receiving considerable assistance from the Roman presbyter Sixtus (*Letter* 191, no. 1), who was later elected to the pontificate. Julian, bishop of Eclanum in Campania, was already fostering their opinions at that time.

After Coelestius had been excommunicated by the Council of Carthage in 412, he departed from Africa and hastened to Ephesus. There, according to Mercator, he even dared to seek the office of presbyter by stealth (*below, Appendix*, part 2). The African bishops certainly wrote in 416 that they had learned that he had been elevated to the dignity of presbyter in Asia (*Letter* 176, no. 4, among the Augustinian letters). Zosimus also calls him a presbyter, as does Nestorius on this point (*below, Appendix*, part 2).

Several years later Coelestius left Ephesus and went to Constantinople. In that city, as he had once done in Africa, he began disseminating the doctrines of his impiety (*ibid.*). When Atticus, the bishop of that city, first discovered this, he expelled him with great zeal and diligence. Atticus also sent letters concerning him to the bishops of Asia, Thessalonica, and Carthage.

We do not read that he wrote to Rome at that time, undoubtedly for no other reason than that, since the affair of John Chrysostom had alienated him from the Roman pontiff, he had not yet been reconciled with him. Some maintain that Atticus did this on the authority of a council convened for the matter, since according to the discipline and custom of the Church only councils were permitted to send public letters to provinces such as Asia.

But what if we say that Atticus wrote only to the bishop of Ephesus? Nothing prevents us from referring to this what Augustine recorded in a letter in 420 or 421 [Col. 0059], namely, that Coelestius had been routed from Constantinople by the army of Christ (*below, Against Julian*, book 3, no. 4). We do not, however, think that the events said to have occurred there against the Pelagian legates (*below, Appendix*, part 2) took place until several years later.

Coelestius, therefore, expelled from Constantinople, immediately hastened to Rome, where Zosimus had succeeded Innocent. He approached the Pontiff, claiming that he wished to clear away the false suspicions that, as he complained, had been brought against him before the Apostolic See.

He charged that the judgment issued against him in Africa was obscure. He called his accuser, Paulinus, before the Apostolic tribunal. Or perhaps the words mean that he challenged his accuser: he declared that he was prepared to defend his case against anyone’s accusation.

Paulinus himself testifies that Coelestius had appealed to the Apostolic See. He says that there he was accused of flight and of abandoning his bail, and that at Carthage, on November 2, Basiliscus, a subdeacon of the Roman Church, had notified him that he was required to appear before Zosimus. Zosimus likewise asserts that Coelestius had come to him in order to undergo judgment on the basis of his former appeal (*ibid.*).

Coelestius then presented a statement of his faith and cited it in the ecclesiastical proceedings (*below, On the Grace of Christ*, nos. 32, 36; and *On Original Sin*, no. 5). In it he proceeded, as fully as he wished, through each article of the Creed, beginning with the one divinity of the Trinity and continuing to the resurrection of the dead. No one found fault with him on these points, and he explained his faith in detail.

When he reached the matters that had been called into dispute, he said:

> “But if questions have arisen apart from the faith, concerning which there is disagreement among many, I have not, as the author of any doctrine, established them by a definitive authority. Rather, the things that I have received from the source of the Prophets and Apostles we offer for approval by the judgment of your apostolate, so that, if perhaps some error of ignorance has crept in among human beings, it may be corrected by your decision” (*below, On Original Sin*, no. 26).

How he explained his view concerning the assistance of grace is unknown. As for original sin, however, he did acknowledge that infants ought to be baptized for the remission of sins; yet he denied that guilt is transmitted through generation. He argued that this opinion was contrary to the Catholic faith and did injury to the Creator.

For his words were these:

> “We confess that infants ought to be baptized for the remission of sins, according to the rule of the universal Church and according to the declaration of the Gospel, because the Lord established that the kingdom of heaven can be bestowed only upon the baptized. Since the powers of nature do not possess this, it must necessarily be bestowed through the freedom of grace.
>
> “We did not say that infants are to be baptized for the remission of sins in order to appear to affirm sin transmitted through descent, for this is far removed from the Catholic understanding. Sin is not born with a human being; rather, it is subsequently committed by the human being. It is shown to belong not to nature but to the will.
>
> “We therefore rightly confess the former, lest we seem to create different kinds of Baptism; and it is necessary to guard against the latter, lest, under cover of the mystery, something evil that has not yet been committed by a human being be said to be transmitted through nature to a human being, to the injury of the Creator” (*ibid.*, nos. 5–6).

At that time Zosimus was occupied with many and weightier affairs. Nevertheless, he did not wish to postpone deciding this matter, lest he keep Africa suspended for too long in expectation, since Africa was anxiously awaiting the outcome of Coelestius’s journey to Rome and the judgment that would be rendered there. (Thus, reports that Coelestius was in Rome had spread throughout Africa.)

On the day appointed for this purpose, Zosimus chose the basilica of the blessed Clement as the place where he would hold the session. In this way, the authority of so great a pontiff—who had consecrated his faith by martyrdom—might demonstrate by his example the reverence with which the case ought to be judged (*below, Appendix*, part 2).

It is established that, besides the clergy of the Roman Church (*below, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, no. 5), various presbyters or bishops from different regions were also present at the session. Zosimus embraces them all under the single designation “priests” (*below, Appendix*, part 2).

Whatever had been done in Caelestius’s case up to that day was examined there. Caelestius himself was also brought in, and the written statement by which he testified to his faith was read. Concerning this statement the Pelagians later boasted that not a few of the Roman clergy had not been averse to his views; they claimed that, by their own judgment recorded in the proceedings, they had supported Catholic doctrine (below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, no. 5). In fact, this profession appeared Catholic to Zosimus—not because he himself approved the doctrines contained in Caelestius’s statement, but because Caelestius declared himself entirely ready to embrace the judgment of the Apostolic See. “In a man,” says Augustine, “of exceptionally keen intelligence, whose reform would certainly have benefited very many, it was the willingness to amend, not the falsity of his doctrine, that was approved.” For this reason his statement was called Catholic: “because it is also characteristic of a Catholic mind, if it happens to think in some way contrary to what truth requires, not to define that position with absolute certainty, but to reject it once it has been exposed and demonstrated” (ibid.).

Since Caelestius had thus presented his faith, Zosimus nevertheless did not consider his written statement sufficient. Rather, through various questions he repeatedly tested the man’s mind, to determine whether he inwardly believed what he had expressed in writing, leaving the sincerity of his answers to be judged by God, who alone sees into the secrets of minds. Caelestius, for his part, repeatedly reinforced with spoken professions what he had set out in the statement that had been submitted (below, Appendix, part 2). Zosimus indeed saw that the man was swollen with the poison of corrupt doctrine, but thought that gentler remedies should be applied to him, as to a delirious person, so that he might be made more composed (below, *On Original Sin*, nos. 7, 8). Paulinus reports some of the questions with which Zosimus thought Caelestius should be pressed; among them he records the question whether Caelestius condemned all the errors that common rumor attributed to him (below, Appendix, part 2). “Do you condemn all those things that have been circulated under your name?” To this Caelestius gave the following answer [Col. 0061]: “I condemn them according to the judgment of your predecessor, the blessed Innocent” (below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, no. 6). He even promised that he would condemn everything condemned by that See (below, *On Original Sin*, no. 8). Yet when Zosimus pressed him to condemn the charges brought against him by the deacon Paulinus, he refused to condemn them. He was also questioned about the matters charged against him in the letters of Heros and Lazarus, which had been sent from the Council of Carthage to Rome. He replied that he had scarcely seen one of the two, and then only in passing; and that the other—Heros, namely—had sufficiently satisfied him by having held a different opinion of him (below, Appendix, part 2).

Although Caelestius’s display of obedience toward the Holy See induced Zosimus to deal more mildly with him, Zosimus nevertheless did not think that he should be released from the bonds of excommunication with which he was bound. Instead, as a precaution, he extended his judgment for two months, so that during that interval Caelestius might return to sound judgment and the Africans, who were more fully acquainted with his case, might write back (below, *On Original Sin*, no. 8). In the case of Heros and Lazarus, however, he acted more precipitously: although they were absent, he deprived them both of their episcopates and of communion, moved either by Caelestius’s accusations or by the complaints of Patroclus, who at that time occupied the see of Arles in place of Heros.

Once matters concerning Caelestius had been settled in this way, Zosimus informed Aurelius and the other African bishops by letter. In those letters he reproached the holy bishops with an irritated tone for their hasty judgment of Caelestius. Zosimus’s letter to the Africans on this subject bears the consular date, but neither month nor day. Since Caelestius’s case is later found joined with Pelagius’s, it seems sufficiently credible that this occurred not long before the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, when Zosimus wrote to the same men concerning Pelagius. It is not at all necessary, however, to infer from the date of that letter that Caelestius’s case had already been completed in June or July, and therefore that the two appointed months had already elapsed before that day. For the letter dated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October was sent only because of a newly arising circumstance. If the allotted period had already expired, Zosimus would undoubtedly either have restored Caelestius to communion—something he would certainly not have omitted to mention in his letter—or, at least, after explaining why he had not yet restored him, would reasonably have asked that this be added to the record.

When Zosimus says, “Where are Heros? Where is Lazarus? Where are those young men?” and so forth (below, Appendix, part 2), he did not mean by these words that they ought to have come from Palestine to Rome within two months, since neither they, nor Timasius and James, had anything to do with Caelestius’s case. Rather, as he explains sufficiently in the sequence of his letter, he means that they ought to have foreseen that Pelagius’s case would be brought before the Roman tribunal; and thus that they were at fault for not having come there to pursue the accusation they had initiated.

The instruction should also apparently be attached to Zosimus’s letter by which he ordered Paulinus to be summoned to plead his case before him. This order was not verbally announced to Paulinus at Carthage until the fourth day before the Nones of November, by Basiliscus, a subdeacon whom the same pontiff had sent with the records of the proceedings held at Rome concerning Caelestius. Zosimus himself indicates in his letter that these records were being sent by him to Africa (ibid.).

### XV. Pelagius’s letter and profession of faith, addressed indeed to Innocent but delivered to Zosimus. Here Zosimus too allows himself to be deceived by Pelagius’s ambiguous language and writes to Africa on his behalf.

After Zosimus had written to Africa in support of Caelestius, he received a letter from Praylius, the bishop of Jerusalem after John, who was most earnestly commending Pelagius’s case. Pelagius himself had added a letter in which he sought to repel the charge of heresy against him, together with a profession of faith in which he claimed to state sincerely what he believed and what he rejected. He addressed both documents to Innocent, since he had written them before hearing of that pontiff’s death (below, *On the Grace of Christ*, no. 32; and *On Original Sin*, no. 19). But since Zosimus had already been appointed in his place, the documents were delivered to him.

This Pelagian letter has perished. From the various passages Augustine quotes from it, however, it can be understood that Pelagius explained to the pontiff that there were two matters concerning which people were trying to defame him. The first was that he denied the sacrament of Baptism to infants and promised some of them the kingdom of heaven without Christ’s redemption. The second was that he said a person could avoid sin in such a way as to exclude God’s assistance, and relied so completely on free will that he rejected the help of grace (below, *On the Grace of Christ*, no. 32).

After saying that he had never heard even an impious heretic say such things about infants, he went on to add: “For who is so ignorant of evangelical teaching that he would not only attempt to affirm this, but could even lightly say or think it? Again, who is so impious as to wish infants to be excluded from the kingdom of heaven, while forbidding them to be baptized and reborn in Christ?” Then, after inserting a testimony from the Gospel, he added: “Who is so impious as to deny to an infant of any age the common redemption of the human race, and to forbid one who was born for an uncertain life to be reborn into perpetual and certain life?” (below, *On Original Sin*, nos. 20, 21).

Although by these words he seemed clearly and explicitly to profess original sin, he nevertheless did not lack certain evasions by which he adapted those words to his heresy. For when questioned about this matter, he was accustomed to answer: “I know where infants who die without Baptism do not go; where they go, I do not know” (ibid., no. 23). He also distorted by twisted interpretations the Catholic response he had given at the Synod of Diospolis to the charges brought against him (ibid., no. 16).

As for the charge of denying grace, after many complaints against his accusers he tried to dismiss it in this way: “Behold,” he said, “let this letter, which I submit to Your Beatitude, clear me, for in it we say plainly and simply that we possess an unimpaired free will for sinning and for not sinning, and that in every good work it is always assisted by divine help.” Then, after inserting certain remarks about natural power for sinning and not sinning, he added: “We affirm this power of free will to exist generally in everyone—in Christians, Jews, and Gentiles. In all alike there is free will by nature, but only among Christians is it assisted by grace. In the others the good belonging to their condition is naked and unarmed; but in those who belong to Christ it is fortified by Christ’s help. The former are to be judged and condemned because, although they possess free will by which they could come to faith and merit God’s grace, they misuse the freedom granted to them. The latter, however, are to be rewarded, because by using free will well they merit the Lord’s grace and keep his commandments” (below, *On the Grace of Christ*, nos. 32–34).

By this profession of grace Pelagius still did not satisfy his adversaries: first, because by “grace” he could understand, as he usually did, the law and teaching; and second, because whatever grace he understood, he nevertheless plainly said that it was given according to merits. He then referred his readers to his statement of faith and to various commentaries that he had issued at different times. These are the passages Augustine preserved for us from that letter of his (ibid., nos. 35–38).

In his statement of faith Pelagius, following Caelestius’s example, discussed at length those points about which no one was questioning him. He treated all the articles of faith, from the unity of the Trinity all the way to the resurrection of the flesh. When he came to the question of Baptism, he said: “We hold one Baptism, which we affirm is celebrated with the same words of the sacrament for infants as for adults.” Yet these words did not bind him to confess original sin. Nor did he explain what sort of grace he acknowledged as necessary, when shortly afterward he said: “We confess free will in such a way that we say we always need God’s help; and that both those who say with the Manichaeans that a person cannot avoid sin and those who assert with Jovinian that a person cannot sin are in error,” and so forth.

Indeed, from what Augustine reports concerning the frauds and paralogisms of the Pelagians, we understand that this exposition of faith, in which nothing at all seems to appear except orthodoxy, opened the door to all their errors. He closed it with a very Catholic conclusion, if only that conclusion had been sincere: “This is the faith, most blessed Pope,” he said, “which we have learned in the Catholic Church, and which we have always held and do hold. If anything has perhaps been set down in it with insufficient skill or caution, we desire to have it corrected by you, who hold both Peter’s faith and his see” (below, Appendix, part 2).

Whenever Pelagius wished to be regarded as a Catholic, he vaunted this profession of faith. We do not know whether Jerome should be understood as referring to this very profession when, in the preface to his fourth book on Jeremiah—written, it seems, in the year 416, before he had experienced the violence of the Pelagians—he complains only of their calumnies and asserts that those heretics, in order to deceive the uneducated, publicly proclaimed an exposition of their faith everywhere, but nevertheless did not produce it.

When Zosimus received Pelagius’s writings, he ordered them to be read in a public session and approved them in a remarkable manner. From them he judged that Pelagius had plainly cleared himself and expressed his faith with such clarity that he left no room for malicious interpretations. The same impression was produced on everyone who heard them. “What joy,” says Zosimus, “was there among the holy men who were present! Some could scarcely restrain themselves from weeping and tears that men of such unblemished faith could have been defamed” (ibid.).

In this style he wrote to Aurelius and the other African bishops about the matter on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October, enclosing Pelagius’s writings. Here he attacks Heros and Lazarus with even greater indignation than in his earlier letter. He likewise complains at length that the Africans had placed confidence both in the letters of these two bishops and in the testimony of Timasius and James.

Baronius published both of Zosimus’s letters concerning Pelagius and Caelestius, drawing them from a manuscript of the Vatican Library. Some have thought that they should be counted among spurious writings, as though they agreed insufficiently with Augustine; yet in reality nothing agrees more closely with him. It must nevertheless be admitted that these letters do little to protect Zosimus’s reputation, since they make it perfectly clear that he placed the fullest confidence in Caelestius’s words, as he himself declares when he lodges a complaint against the African bishops (ibid.).

For this reason, after the Pelagians had been condemned by Zosimus, they accused him of betrayal (below, *Against Julian*, book 6, no. 37). They brought the same charge against all the Roman clergy, whom they loudly accused of shamefully abandoning the Catholic doctrine that they had defended in the sessions mentioned above (below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, no. 5).

When the same pontiff later corrected the fault that he had imprudently committed, Augustine wished to cover it with a modest silence. Whatever he thought worthy of some praise in the man whom he regarded as the first bishop, he placed openly before the public; the rest he excused as far as he could. Yet he does not deny that at the beginning Zosimus was deceived by the fraudulent words of the Pelagian professions and especially by Caelestius’s simulation, through which Caelestius professed both that he wished to be instructed and that he agreed with Innocent’s decrees. Indeed, the holy Doctor clearly indicates this in several places (below, *On Original Sin*, nos. 9, 24; *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, no. 5; *Against Julian*, book 6, no. 38).

### XVI. The African council of 214 bishops held at Carthage replies to Zosimus. It defends the judgment pronounced by Innocent against Pelagius and Caelestius and advises Zosimus to conduct a new examination of Caelestius.

After the African bishops received the letter that Pope Zosimus had sent in Caelestius’s favor, they urgently appealed to him in their own letter to leave matters in the state in which they then stood until he had been more fully informed about Caelestius’s case, since Caelestius had first been accused before them. The letter was issued by bishops either summoned to Carthage for this purpose or fortuitously present in that city. That a genuine council nevertheless took place is shown by the fact that, in replying to their letter, Zosimus addressed his own letter to Aurelius and the others who had been present at the Council of Carthage (below, Appendix, part 2).

It is highly probable that as soon as Zosimus’s first letter in support of Caelestius arrived, Bishop Aurelius notified the bishops of the less distant regions—such as Proconsular Africa, Numidia, and Byzacena—so that they might assemble with him for deliberation on so important a matter. When the nearer bishops arrived, he immediately wrote to Zosimus, asking that their letter reach Rome, if possible, before the two months granted by Zosimus had elapsed.

The remaining bishops subsequently joined them, and from them the council of 214 bishops was finally formed. Prosper states that it was held before Caelestius was condemned by Zosimus (ibid.). Augustine calls it an African council in more than one place (below, *On Original Sin*, nos. 8, 9, 24; and volume 2, *Letter* 215, no. 2), perhaps because it consisted of bishops from several provinces, though not from all of them; in this way he distinguishes it from the plenary and general council of the following year.

It appears that the council should be assigned to the beginning of November, since the subdeacon Marcellinus, who carried its decisions to the pontiff, was preparing to depart on the sixth day before the Ides of that month (below, Appendix, part 2). It is nevertheless possible that, because of the importance of the matter under discussion and the preparation of the records to be sent to Rome, the council lasted somewhat longer.

At this synod decrees and constitutions were issued, which afterward were embraced by the whole world, by Rome, and by the emperors Honorius and Arcadius (ibid.). These decrees supplied the material for the eight or nine African canons against the Pelagians, which had previously been wrongly attributed to the Council of Milevis but are now recognized as having been enacted by the general Council of Carthage held on the Kalends of May in 418.

The synod prefixed to its decrees a letter to Zosimus, in which the Fathers addressed him as follows:

“We have determined that the judgment pronounced against Pelagius and Caelestius through the venerable bishop Innocent, from the See of the blessed Apostle Peter, should remain in force until they openly confess that by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord we are assisted not only in knowing justice but also in doing it, in such a way that without that grace we are able neither to possess, think, say, nor do anything belonging to true and holy piety” (ibid.).

They added that it was not enough for less perceptive people that Caelestius had said in general terms that he agreed with Innocent’s letters. He had to anathematize openly the errors he had set down in his statement, lest, if he failed to do so, many of the less discerning should believe that those poisons of faith had been approved by the Apostolic See—because that See had declared his statement Catholic—rather than corrected, because he had answered that he agreed with Pope Innocent’s letters (below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, no. 5).

The African bishops also recalled to Zosimus Innocent’s judgment concerning the Synod of Diospolis (below, *On Original Sin*, no. 9). They took care to expose to him the deceptions and tricks in the profession of faith that Pelagius had sent to Rome (ibid., no. 24), and at the same time to refute all the sophistries of the heretics, so that they might overcome them by reasoning no less than by the authority of their sacred office (below, Appendix, part 2).

When Zosimus reproached them as though they had rashly believed Caelestius’s accusers, they in turn showed him that he had placed confidence in Caelestius’s words somewhat too quickly (ibid.). Finally, they explained to the pontiff everything that had previously been done among them concerning Caelestius’s case, and sent him the records then compiled on the matter, whether in Caelestius’s presence or in his absence. Zosimus does not conceal that the volume of their letter seemed unusually long to him (ibid.).

Those bishops also appear to have excused before the pontiff the deacon Paulinus, who had been ordered to come to Rome to give an account of the accusation he himself had brought against Caelestius six years earlier. They perhaps prevented him from going there because Caelestius’s case no longer concerned Paulinus but the whole Church, as Paulinus himself indicates in the statement he sent to Zosimus on the seventh day before the Ides of November (ibid.).

There is likewise no doubt that a decree was made for a more general and plenary synod to be held in the following year, after the Paschal celebrations, from all the provinces of Africa. This was carried out in May.

These are the facts that it has been possible to discover concerning that celebrated African council and the subsequent letter sent by it through the subdeacon Marcellinus (ibid.). Although very many writings on this affair passed between Rome and Africa and between Africa and Rome under Pope Zosimus (below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, no. 5), nothing remains of all that was sent to Zosimus by the African bishops.

We rightly lament the loss of those distinguished records, which would have preserved the Africans’ courage in defending the grace of Christ and supporting Innocent’s decree. It is certain that a substantial portion of the credit for this belongs to Augustine’s intelligence and diligence.

### XVII. In 418 Zosimus replies to the Fathers of the African council. A plenary council of all Africa is again held at Carthage and issues nine canons against the Pelagians.

Zosimus appears not to have given a separate reply to the first letter of the African council, perhaps because winter prevented him from doing so. Nor does he seem to have written to the Fathers until the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, after receiving their second, later letter—and then to have sent one letter in response to both, a rather brief one.

In it he extols his own dignity in magnificent terms. He asks that the fact that he had chosen to communicate with the Africans by letter concerning Caelestius’s case be credited to him as an act of grace. “Although,” he says, “we possessed such authority that no one could call our judgment into question, we did nothing that we did not voluntarily report to your knowledge in our letters, granting this to brotherly affection,” and so forth.

He nevertheless assures them that he had left everything in precisely the state in which they had asked him to leave it. He appears to imply that he intended to deliberate again about what should be done in the matter (below, Appendix, part 2).

This letter reached Africa on the third day before the Kalends of May, at the time when the bishops were assembling at Carthage to celebrate a new council against the Pelagians. This council was held in the Basilica of Faustus on the first day of May in 418. Ancient copies note that it was assembled from the provinces of Byzacena, Mauretania Sitifensis, Tripolitana, Numidia, Mauretania Caesariensis, and Spain. They record that Aurelius sat in it, together with Donatianus of Telepte, primate of Byzacena, and 203 other bishops. Photius counts 224 besides Aurelius and Donatianus (ibid.).

There is no room for doubt that this was the plenary council of all Africa at which Augustine testifies that he and the other bishops briefly enacted something against the Pelagian heresy (*Letter* 215, no. 2). Certainly at this council they composed the eight or nine canons that were read as belonging to the Council of Milevis, and which Baronius also thought had been enacted by the synod assembled in that city in 416.

The African collection, the ancient Gandavense manuscript, the code of the Canons of the Roman Church, and Photius himself, who read its acts, all assign these canons to this council (below, Appendix, part 2). The third, fourth, and fifth of these canons are also cited by Pope Celestine under the name of the Council of Carthage (ibid.).

Furthermore, the letter of the Council of Milevis to Innocent makes no mention whatsoever of these canons, although it should have sent them to him for confirmation by his authority. Indeed, that synod asked nothing else of the pontiff except that he condemn the two errors of the Pelagians: their attack on original sin and on the necessity of grace. Yet the final three of those canons also strike with anathema those who twisted the words of John, James, and the Lord’s Prayer away from their true meaning, so that we would not recognize from them that no just person in this life is without sin.

Moreover, the five bishops who wrote to Innocent after the Council of Milevis by no means absolutely forbade anyone to say that a person could, with the help of grace, be without sin in this life, provided that no one arrogated such perfection of righteousness to himself. They considered that question still to be submitted to examination (*Letter* 177, nos. 16, 18). Again, in his book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, written somewhat later, Augustine numbers this same question among those that ought not to be debated against heretics but examined peacefully among Catholics (below, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 55).

As for the number of these canons, it is agreed that the Pelagian heresy was struck down by the Council of Carthage. The African collection previously contained only eight: the first two concerned original sin, the middle three the assistance of grace, and the final three the possibility of sinlessness. The oldest manuscripts display a ninth, inserted in third place, condemning those who assigned to infants who died without Baptism some intermediate place of happiness outside both the kingdom of heaven and the company of demons.

Photius recognizes this canon and assigns it the same position. Augustine’s testimony is also not lacking: he says that the recent Pelagian heretics were most justly condemned by the authority of Catholic councils and the Apostolic See because they dared to give unbaptized infants a place of salvation and rest even outside the kingdom of heaven (below, *On the Soul and Its Origin*, no. 17).

The holy Doctor spoke in this way toward the end of 419. It is therefore plausible that the African council of the preceding year informed Zosimus about this Pelagian evasion, and that it was condemned by the Africans in this plenary council of 418 and by that pontiff in his *Tractoria* letter.

Concerning both councils of Africa, Prosper writes in his poem *Against the Ungrateful*:

> You, Africa, pursue the cause of our faith  
> With still more ardor; and, joining your strength  
> With that of the apostolic throne,  
> You crush the savage entrails of war  
> And lay the defeated low over a broad expanse.  
>   
> Your nourishing bishops gathered from every city,  
> And in a famous twofold assembly of elders  
> You decreed what Rome approves,  
> What kingdoms follow.

A little later, overflowing with praise of Augustine, he continues:

> Could a holy council proceed toward any other end,  
> When Aurelius was its leader  
> And Augustine its intelligence?  
> Christ’s grace, watering him with a richer horn,  
> Gave our age a light kindled from the true Light.  
> For God is his food, his life, and his rest;  
> and he is every delight, and so forth (below, Appendix, part 2).

### XVIII. The emperor Honorius penalizes the Pelagians by law. Zosimus finally condemns them by a definitive judgment, which the universal Church accepts.

After the council had ended, Augustine was selected, together with several bishops, to settle the remaining cases and stayed behind at Carthage (below, before the books *On the Grace of Christ*, see the note attached to chapter 50 of book 2 of the *Retractations*). In that city, until he departed for Mauretania Caesariensis [Col. 0069] (*Letter* 193, no. 1), where he was staying on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, various and by no means minor urgent affairs detained him and kept him extremely busy.

Two very welcome reports then greatly refreshed him: one concerned the law that Honorius had issued against the Pelagians, the other the condemnation of those same heretics by Pope Zosimus (below, *On Original Sin*, no. 18).

That law of Honorius still exists. It was issued at Ravenna on 30 April 418. By it the emperor decreed that Caelestius and Pelagius should first be expelled from Rome—if they were then living there, since Pelagius was at that time in Palestine—and that afterward anyone who discovered adherents of their heresy should report them to the magistrates, with the accused ultimately being subjected to the punishment of exile (below, Appendix, part 2).

The praetorian prefects carried out the imperial edict by their own orders: Junius Quartus Palladius in Italy, Monaxius in the East, and Agricola in Gaul. They ordered Pelagius and Caelestius to be expelled from the City according to the emperor’s decree, and all who were convicted of their error to be stripped of their property and punished with perpetual exile (ibid.).

The Pelagians, who interpreted divine law according to their own will, also twisted the imperial law to suit their own meaning. Although the law was perfectly clear, Julian did not blush to claim that the emperor had issued it rather for his side. Augustine wittily replied that Julian ought therefore to cite it before the public authorities (below, *Against Julian*, book 3, no. 3).

The law had indeed been requested, since it is called not merely a constitution but a rescript and a response. Augustine says of it: “If the emperor’s response was rather in your favor…” (ibid.). An ancient code of the Roman Church appears to declare that it was granted in response to the Africans’ petitions by giving it this heading: “The sacred rescript, after the records of the synod written above had been received.”

The Council of Carthage of 418 precedes it there. Since that council was held on the first day of May, it is one day later than the rescript. Yet the Council of 418 could easily have been confused with the council held in 417.

Those who think that Honorius’s law, enacted on 30 April, preceded Zosimus’s judgment believe that it had considerable influence in eliciting that judgment from the pontiff. From another direction Zosimus saw the faithful Romans fighting with one voice and one zeal for Catholic truth against Pelagius’s errors (below, *On Original Sin*, no. 9). His doctrines could certainly not have remained hidden from them, since he had lived among them for a long time; and they knew that Caelestius was his disciple well enough to give the most faithful and firm testimony concerning the matter.

Moreover, after the African council’s replies, some Catholics of the City took care to bring to the pontiff’s attention certain statements and writings of Pelagius, including his commentaries on Paul. Mercator attributes Caelestius’s condemnation to the errors in those commentaries (below, Appendix, part 2).

Since, on the other side, there were also people there who defended the heresy, Rome was torn apart by a most grievous division; in Honorius’s words, “with zeal divided into factions for the assertion of opposing positions, the material for an unpacified dissension had been introduced” (ibid.). Among others, Constantius, formerly a deputy of the prefects but then a servant of Christ living in Rome, distinguished his zeal for God’s grace by blunting the efforts of the Pelagians. After suffering much through their faction, he deserved to be enrolled in the list of holy confessors (ibid.).

This period may perhaps also be the time to which the substance of Julian’s accusation refers, when he charged the Catholics with stirring up seditions in Rome (below, *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book 3, chapter 35).

Since matters in the City stood thus, Zosimus resolved, in accordance with the warnings of the African council, to examine Caelestius again and finally to draw clear and explicit answers from him, so that thereafter no doubt would remain either that he had renounced his errors or that he must be regarded as a treacherous impostor (below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, no. 5).

Caelestius, however, did not dare submit to this examination. He not only abandoned his appointed appearance but also fled from the City (below, Appendix, part 2). Since he did not appear, nothing could any longer restrain Zosimus from pronouncing the judgment that both the obstinacy of the heretics and the welfare of the Church required of him (below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, no. 5).

Accordingly, he brought forth once more the discipline of just severity, which he had interrupted only briefly (ibid.). He approved and confirmed the decrees of the African council (below, Appendix, part 2); and, following the judgment of his predecessor (below, *Against Julian*, book 1, no. 13; book 6, no. 37), he condemned Pelagius and Caelestius with renewed authority (below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 2, no. 5).

He assigned them to the order of penitents if they detested their errors; but if they refused this, he struck them with full anathema (below, *On Original Sin*, no. 25; and volume 2, *Letter* 190, no. 22).

On this matter he wrote both specifically to the Africans and generally to all the bishops of the entire Christian world, sending letters of extraordinary length. Augustine, Prosper, and Pope Celestine cite several fragments of them (below, Appendix, part 2). In them he set out the errors of which Caelestius had been accused by Paulinus, and omitted nothing that pertained either to Caelestius’s case as Pelagius’s disciple or to Pelagius’s case as his teacher.

According to a learned authority, he also inserted in these letters a catalogue of Pelagian errors excerpted from Augustine’s letter to Paulinus. In the same place he made honorable mention of John Chrysostom (ibid.). He asserted the doctrine of original sin with great force (*Letter* 190, no. 23). Nor should we hesitate to identify as Zosimus’s writing the passage in which the authority of the Apostolic See condemned the recent heretics because they granted unbaptized infants a place of rest and happiness outside the kingdom of heaven (below, *On the Soul and Its Origin*, [Col. 0071] no. 17).

There he also taught that no period passes in which we do not need divine assistance, and that in all our actions, cases, thoughts, and movements we ought to expect everything from God’s protection, not from the powers of nature (below, Appendix, part 2).

Among the other condemnable statements in his letters, he included several passages taken from Pelagius’s commentary on Paul. Mercator transcribes these passages and testifies that they were fully inserted into Zosimus’s letter, which he calls the *Tractoria* (ibid.).

The same letter was sent to the Eastern Churches—to Egypt, Constantinople, Thessalonica, and Jerusalem, indeed throughout the whole world—and was subscribed by all the Catholic prelates (ibid.). Hence it was rightly reported in writing that the decree issued in the African council of 214 bishops against the enemies of God’s grace had been embraced by the whole world, and that the Pelagian heresy had been condemned throughout the entire world (ibid.). Honorius likewise indicates this in a sanction addressed to Aurelius in June of the year 419, affirming that the Pelagians had been condemned by all after examination of the judgment.

It is certainly established that Zosimus ordered the same letter to be subscribed by the bishops of Italy; for Bishop Julian was condemned and deprived of his dignity by him because he had refused to subscribe it (ibid.).

At that time, when the Roman clerics—whom the Pelagians subsequently accused of collusion just as they accused Zosimus—were readily assenting to the judgment of their president, the presbyter Sixtus, the very man whom the enemies of grace boasted was the principal defender of their cause (Epistle 191, §1), was the first of all to pronounce an anathema against them before a very large gathering (Epistle 194, §1). He also wrote diligently on this matter to those among whom the Pelagians were accustomed to boast of his friendship: not merely declaring in his own letters that his mind was entirely alien to the heresy, but also beginning to drive its adherents, through fear of the imperial laws, to renounce it (Epistle 191, §1).

Although in his letter dated 21 March Zosimus displays a relaxed attitude and still appears insufficiently inclined to condemn the Pelagians, Augustine nevertheless places his decisive letter against them between the African council of 417 and the plenary council of 418, in such a way as to indicate that it preceded the latter council, or at least followed it so quickly that it cannot be said to have been issued under its influence. “What was written to Pope Zosimus from the African council,” he says, “and his rescript sent to all the bishops of the entire world, and what at the subsequent plenary council we briefly decreed against that very error throughout Africa . . . we have sent to you” (Epistle 215, §2).

The African bishops congratulated Zosimus, as was fitting, on the condemnation of the Pelagians. From their letter written on this subject, Prosper excerpted the following passage, which Celestine also cites:

“But that which you placed in your letter, which you arranged to have sent to all the provinces, saying, ‘Nevertheless, by the prompting of God’—for all good things must be referred to their author, from whom they arise—‘we referred everything to the conscience of our brothers and fellow bishops’: we understood this statement as meaning that you cut down, with the unsheathed sword of truth, as though passing swiftly by, those who exalt human freedom against God’s help. For what did you do more freely than to refer everything to the conscience of our humility? And yet you rightly and wisely saw that this was done by the prompting of God, and you spoke truly and confidently.

“This is so because the will is prepared by the Lord, and he himself touches the hearts of his children with paternal inspirations so that they may do something good. For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the children of God. Thus we may feel that our freedom is not lacking, yet we may not doubt that in every individual movement of the human will toward good his help is more powerful” (below, Appendix, part 2).

### XIX. All the bishops subscribe to the condemnation of the Pelagians, except eighteen, who withdraw after being deposed and demand a general council.

In his decisive letter against the Pelagians, Zosimus asked all the bishops not only to reject them as heretics, but also to confirm their proscription by their own signatures. Mercator in fact reports that this letter was sent throughout the whole world and strengthened by the subscriptions of the holy fathers (below, Appendix, part 2). Prosper is also thought to indicate this when he says that the right hands of all the bishops were armed with Peter’s sword for the beheading of the impious; and then, for their destruction, that the sentence of all the priests was written with one hand (ibid., part 3). Finally, he says that their doctrines were condemned by the councils and by the hand of the world (Prosper, *On the Ungrateful*, chapter 9).

Certainly the Pelagians themselves complained of precisely this in the following words: “A subscription was extorted from simple bishops, seated in their own places, without a synodal assembly” (below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, §34).

On that occasion, says Mercator, Julian and his remaining accomplices refused to subscribe and were unwilling to make themselves of one mind with those same fathers who had subscribed. They were therefore deposed and deprived of office, not only by imperial laws but also by ecclesiastical decrees, and were driven out of all Italy. Many of them, coming to their senses and being corrected of the error mentioned above, returned as suppliants to the Apostolic See and, having been received, recovered their churches (below, Appendix, part 2).

Julian and his accomplices were undoubtedly those eighteen bishops of the Pelagian faction who shortly afterward sent a letter to Rufus of Thessalonica (below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, §3). Nestorius, writing to Pope Celestine on behalf of the Pelagians, names the bishops Julian, Florus, Orontius, and Fabius; the Council of Ephesus adds Persidius and Marcellinus (below, Appendix, part 2).

They were therefore summoned to condemn Pelagius and Coelestius together with the universal Church, and also to subscribe Zosimus’s letter. They, however, declared that they would not do so, alleging that it was unlawful to condemn in an infamous sentence men who were absent and unheard, and who had proscribed in their own writings the errors falsely attributed to them (below, Appendix, part 2).

On this matter Julian wrote two letters to Zosimus (below, *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book 1, chapter 17). One of these, which appears to have preceded his deposition, may perhaps be that very confession of faith which in our own time began to emerge from a Veronese manuscript, written in the name of many bishops—namely, those eighteen who had joined Julian (below, Appendix, part 2).

The first three parts contain a confession of faith that does not differ greatly from the Pelagian and Coelestian statements mentioned above. They nevertheless admit that all die through Adam; but they most explicitly reject original sin, which they call “natural.” They believe that Pelagius and Coelestius sufficiently proved their faith by rejecting the errors falsely imposed upon them.

In the final sections, where they explain why they refuse to condemn those heresiarchs—namely, because they themselves had not been heard—they abuse, for this purpose, the same passages by which Zosimus had earlier attacked the Africans, as though reproaching him for having changed his judgment in this way. They say that although it belongs both to their office and to Christian charity to wish to defend those whom they did not see to be guilty, they nevertheless intend to remain impartial, as they had promised, so as neither to condemn those men unheard nor defend them while absent.

They say that if the Pontiff disapproves of anything in what they have written to him concerning their doctrine and faith, he can indicate this to them. But if they are unjustly attacked, they have resolved not to yield to any harassment, however violent. Moreover, they declare to the Pontiff that they appeal to the judgment of a plenary synod (ibid.).

Zosimus could not possibly have been satisfied with a confession of faith that was wholly Pelagian. Accordingly, it is established that Julian and his associates were deposed by an ecclesiastical judgment pronounced by that same pontiff—a fact that led Augustine to call him Julian’s condemner (below, *Against Julian*, book 1, §13). This judgment was entered into the records, since at the Council of Ephesus the acts of the deposition of Pelagius, Coelestius, Julian, Persidius, Florus, Marcellinus, Orontius, and their associates were read and confirmed (below, Appendix, part 2).

After this condemnation also, as it seems to us, Julian wrote another letter to Zosimus, excerpts of which may be read in Mercator (ibid.). In it he outwardly rejects certain of the errors condemned in Coelestius, although he later did not hesitate openly to teach them. Before this letter reached the Pontiff, it had already been circulated through nearly all Italy by the efforts of certain people deceived by Julian, and had been distributed to many as some remarkable work.

Julian also sent another letter to Rome toward the end of the year 419, to encourage those who followed the Pelagian party. In it he professed that he was not in communion with the Manichaeans—that is, with the Catholics of that time (below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, §4). Augustine in fact testifies that a rupture had occurred between them and the Church (Sermon 181, §3).

For a time they had their own presbyters and bishops. But since that faction had always been very small and weak, they lacked sacred buildings in which to assemble. Consequently, most of them did not hesitate to come into Catholic churches and receive communion together with the Catholics (below, Appendix, part 2). Nevertheless, they were objects of horror to the other members of their faction, and whenever they were discovered by Catholics, they were punished with the greatest severity.

Although the faction loudly claimed that it did not wish to communicate with the Catholics, whom it unjustly called Manichaeans (below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, §42), it nevertheless left nothing undone to remove from itself the penalty of excommunication. These men approached the emperor Honorius and asked him to appoint ecclesiastical judges who would reopen the matter for examination, alleging that they had been condemned through deceit and fraud.

But Count Valerius broke their efforts by his authority and prevented the Emperor from assigning a time and place for their case to be examined again (below, *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book 1, chapter 10). And rightly so: since Honorius did not wish the ancient Catholic faith to be called into question, he judged that no new disputes concerning the faith should be granted to its enemies, but that they should instead be restrained by the severity of the laws and of ecclesiastical discipline. Thus he joined his authority to that of the Church and arranged for Julian and the others from whom Zosimus had taken the episcopate to be expelled from Italy (below, Appendix, part 2).

It is not yet clear when this occurred. Nor perhaps did it happen before the year 419, when the Emperor, by a new sanction establishing penalties of deposition and exile, bound all the bishops to confirm by their subscriptions the condemnation of the heresiarchs. He said that he had established this in order to correct the obstinacy of certain bishops who either supported their perverse arguments by tacit consent or failed to destroy them by public opposition (Epistle 201, among the Augustinian letters).

The Pelagians complained bitterly that they had been denied an opportunity to plead their case, and they wished to turn that denial into an argument for their victory (below, *Against Julian*, book 3, §5). Julian, in a manner bordering on insult, certainly reproached the Catholics for their distrust, because a hearing had been refused to him and his associates (below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, §42).

Augustine replied that their case had been fully examined by the bishops in a competent judgment and did not require another inquiry (ibid., §34; and *Against Julian*, book 3, §5). He further replied that the destructive character of the Pelagian heresy was all too clear, and that most heresies had been condemned without the convocation of general synods. The Pelagians, he said, were at least attempting to disturb the Catholic world, which they could not corrupt; and, with that pride by which they wished to glory not in God but in themselves, they were also seeking the glory of having a synod of East and West assembled on their account (below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, §34).

In this respect they were like the Maximianists, who sought to be admitted to plead their case at the Carthaginian conference, desiring nothing more than to console their insignificance by at least the name of a contest, and thereby to appear to be something in the eyes of those by whom they were despised, since they were being allowed to undertake an examination together with the Catholics (below, *Against Julian*, book 3, §5).

### XX. Augustine exposes Pelagius’s deceptions in the books *On the Grace of Christ* and *On Original Sin*. He also writes to Optatus, to Mercator, and to Sixtus.

After the Pelagian heresy and its authors had already been condemned by Zosimus, while Augustine was still at Carthage after the plenary council of 418, he composed two books against the authors of that heresy. In them, we believe, one may find whatever the African bishops had brought forward in their letter to Zosimus—which we regret has been lost—in order to expose the frauds of Coelestius and Pelagius.

The occasion for these books was perhaps a conversation between Pinianus, his mother-in-law Albina, and his wife Melania with Pelagius, held somewhere in Palestine. Pelagius was indeed there in 415, and in 417 Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem, sent a letter to Rome together with Pelagius and on his behalf. Albina, Pinianus, and Melania, for their part, sent greetings to Augustine from there through Jerome’s letter in 419.

In that conversation they had asked Pelagius to reject in writing all the errors of which he was accused. Pelagius had first replied that he anathematized anyone who either thought or said that the grace of God, through which Christ came into this world to save sinners, was not necessary—not only at every hour or every moment, but also in each of our actions (below, *On the Grace of Christ*, §2).

He then said that he held one Baptism, which he declared was celebrated in infants with the same words of the sacrament as in adults. When he was questioned further, he confessed in his own words that infants receive Baptism for the remission of sins (ibid., §35).

He also read to them the little book which he had sent to Rome to Innocent (below, *On Original Sin*, §1). Before them he complained that he himself had been included in the condemnation of Coelestius—not indeed by Zosimus, for we should not believe that it had yet reached his ears, but by Innocent and the African bishops. Conversely, he boasted that his innocence had been declared by the synod of Diospolis (ibid., §9).

Neither Pinianus nor the matrons present were able to see through the deceit and ambiguities of this schemer. They were therefore delighted to have heard him speak in the manner they desired, but, not daring to trust their own judgment in so important a matter, preferred to consult Augustine, whose insight was exceptionally clear, about his words.

Accordingly, writing under their common name, they informed him of the conversation they had held with Pelagius and asked what he thought about it. The bearer of their letter found the holy bishop, as has already been said, at Carthage. Although he was occupied there with business much heavier than elsewhere, he did not delay his reply, nor did he make it shorter than two volumes: one *On the Grace of Christ*, the other *On Original Sin*.

In these works he shows what Pelagius’s true mind was concerning both subjects, drawing upon the very works which that heresiarch had cited in his letter to Innocent for the purpose of clearing himself, and especially upon his books *On Free Choice*. Since Pelagius made a highly honorific mention of Ambrose in those books and praised his faith with exceptional commendation, Augustine sets against him, at the end of both of his volumes, various testimonies of that same bishop.

In the first volume Augustine shows that Pelagius locates grace either in nature and free choice or in the law and teaching. He further shows that Pelagius wishes grace to assist only what he called the possibility of willing and acting, not willing and acting themselves; and that this assisting grace is given according to merits and helps human beings only so that they may fulfill the commandments more easily.

Thus Augustine demonstrates that all the passages in Pelagius’s shorter works in which he repeatedly boasts that grace is explicitly commended by him can be interpreted as referring to the law and teaching—that is, to divine revelation and to Christ’s example, which likewise belong to teaching—or to the remission of sins. It is not at all apparent, he says, that Pelagius truly recognizes Christian grace: that is, the assistance in doing good which, through the inspiration of the most ardent and luminous charity, is added to nature and teaching (below, *On the Grace of Christ*, §38).

In the second volume Augustine also shows that, in the question of original sin and the Baptism of infants, Pelagius in reality differs in nothing from his disciple Coelestius. In the middle of that volume he refutes the new argument against original sin, perhaps devised by Theodore of Mopsuestia:

“Then,” objected the opponents, “marriage is evil, and the human being whom marriage produces is not the work of God” (above, chapter 11).

In this volume he again demonstrates that the question of original fault is not one of those in which error may occur without danger to the faith, as the Pelagians wished in order not to be called heretics, but that it belongs to a fundamental article of faith.

There too he relates what had taken place at Rome concerning Pelagius and Coelestius under the pontificate of Zosimus, and by what final procedure each had been marked with a sentence of condemnation (below, *On Original Sin*, §7 ff.).

Moreover, in these two volumes he appended the little book presented by Coelestius to the Pontiff (below, *On the Grace of Christ*, §32), together with everything that concerned the same matter. We do not know whether he also arranged to attach Zosimus’s decisive letter, to which he refers Albina, Pinianus, and Melania (below, *On Original Sin*, §24).

Meanwhile, another opportunity was offered to the holy bishop to make his love for the Church still more evident through new labors. Pope Zosimus sent letters compelling both him and several other bishops to travel to Caesarea in Mauretania for some ecclesiastical necessity (Epistle 190, §1; Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 14).

When he therefore departed from Carthage, he proceeded from there to Caesarea in Mauretania (Epistle 193, §1). In the principal city of that province, namely Caesarea—which also gave its name to the region—he was staying on 20 September of that same year, 418.

Although occupied with other matters there, he was compelled to give Bishop Optatus a letter concerning the origin of the soul, at the urging of Bishop Muresse and the vehement insistence of the monk Renatus. He nevertheless indicates that he wrote it after leaving the city of Caesarea, in the words: “While we were staying in the aforesaid town” (Epistle 190, §1).

In this letter he carefully warns that the difficult question must be treated in such a way that the faith remains intact above all: the faith by which we believe that no one is born from Adam except under the bond of condemnation, and that no one is freed from it except by being reborn through Christ. He also warns that the new Pelagian heresy must be avoided, already condemned throughout the Christian world, because by arguing against the grace of God it seeks to tear down the foundations of the most ancient faith.

He also sends Optatus a copy of the recent letters—whether those addressed specifically to the Africans or those sent universally to all the bishops for the condemnation of that heresy—issued by Pope Zosimus. In those letters Pelagius’s own argument against original sin was included among the other statements condemned in him.

Finally, the holy Doctor inserted into this letter of his a fragment from those same letters of Zosimus, which have so far been missing.

After returning to Hippo, Augustine found there letters sent to him by Mercator, together with a book composed through Mercator’s efforts against the Pelagians, which he was sending to the holy Doctor for examination and approval.

Other letters from Mercator had already reached Augustine while he was at Carthage, before he went to Caesarea. In them Mercator complained, somewhat sharply and with a certain indignation, that no reply had been sent to him. Augustine, however, received this most gratefully, because the indignation seemed to him not the beginning of hostility but an indication of affection.

An opportunity then arose to send a reply through Albinus, an acolyte of the Roman Church. Augustine gave him a reply to deliver to Mercator.

The Pelagians had by then been driven to confess that infants believe through those by whom they are brought for Baptism. But they added—as Mercator had reported—that they did not believe in the remission of sins in such a way that sins were remitted to the infants themselves; rather, they believed that this remission took place in others and not in them.

Augustine argues, however, that by this very admission—that infants believe in Baptism in some sense—the opponents cannot avoid admitting original sin in them.

He then shows that they argue in vain from the translation of Enoch and Elijah before death, or from the taking up of living believers at Christ’s coming, in an attempt to persuade people that death is not the punishment of sin.

As for the question of the resurrection—whether some people will truly pass from this mortality to immortality without an intervening death—he wishes to be instructed about it by others, because he loves learning more than teaching. “For,” he says, “the sweetness of truth ought to invite us to learn; but necessity born of charity ought to compel us to teach” (Epistle 193).

That same Albinus, the bearer of the preceding letter, also delivered the shorter of the two letters to Sixtus. In it Augustine congratulates Sixtus, then a Roman presbyter and later pontiff, because he had undertaken the defense of God’s grace against the Pelagians, concerning whom a rumor had circulated that he favored them. Augustine urges him to continue exercising care, not only so that those who still persist in speaking more freely or whispering more secretly may be restrained, but also so that those who, although silent through fear, perhaps do not cease to foster the error in their hearts may be taught and healed (Epistle 191).

Not long after Albinus’s departure, Augustine gave a longer letter to the same Sixtus to be carried to Rome by the presbyter Firmus, who was returning to Rome from Africa. Several years later Augustine said that he had written it at the time when the struggle against the Pelagians was being waged with the greatest intensity (below, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, §55).

There he dissolves their evasions and all their subtler arguments against the grace of God. Among these were the following:

First, that free choice is taken away if we do not possess even a good will without God’s help.

Second, that it is unjust, in one and the same evil situation, for one person to be freed and another punished; and consequently that the grace which Pelagius confessed at the Palestinian synod to be given without any preceding merits is itself the human nature in which we were created.

Furthermore, that people who do not wish to live rightly and faithfully would excuse themselves by saying: “What have we done, since we have lived badly, when we did not receive the grace by which we might live well?”

They also argued that God would be a respecter of persons if, in one and the same situation, his mercy came upon some while his wrath remained upon others.

Thus, they said, he hated one of the unborn—Esau, for example—and loved another, namely Jacob, because he foresaw their future works. “For,” they said, “God foresees, in those whom he takes from this life, how each person would have lived if he had lived; and therefore he causes one whom he knows would have lived wickedly to die without Baptism, punishing in him the evil works not which he committed but which he would have committed.”

Augustine also refutes the same heretics when they argued against original sin as follows: “How,” they said, “does sin pass into the children of faithful parents when we do not doubt that it was remitted in the parents through Baptism?”

Here again he rejects the evasion which Mercator had reported them to have devised: namely, that infants truly respond through the mouths of those carrying them that they believe in the remission of sins, but not because sins are remitted to the infants, but because they are remitted in those in whom the sins are found.

After completely overturning these arguments, Augustine asks Sixtus not to fail to inform him both of whatever else the Pelagians might devise against the Catholic faith and of anything that he himself might argue in defense of the Catholic faith against them (Epistle 194).

In a letter to Asellicus, perhaps sent toward the end of the year 418, Augustine observes that the Pelagian heresy in a certain way falls into Judaism. He further observes that its most vehement advocates, Pelagius and Coelestius, recently deprived even of Catholic communion by judicial sentence, still persist in their condemnation because of their impenitent hearts (Epistle 196, §7).

### XXI. Augustine first sends Valerius the book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. In 419 the bishops, at the command of Honorius, subscribe to the condemnation of the Pelagians. Jerome congratulates Augustine on the destruction of the Pelagian heresy. Certain Pelagian doctrines of Vincentius Victor, and others worse than these, are refuted.

While Augustine was refuting the profane innovations of the Pelagians in his writings, Count Valerius was suppressing their efforts by his authority and influence with the Emperor. In this way he effectively prevented the council which they had requested after their own condemnation from being granted. The holy bishop counts the Count’s service to the Church among his praises (below, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, §2; *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book 1, chapter 10).

The heretics, however, in order to deprive the Church of the patronage of this powerful man and turn him away from Catholic teaching, wrote him a letter in which they implied that Augustine condemned marriage by asserting original sin ( *Retractations*, book 2, chapter 53; Epistle 200; below, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, §2).

Valerius, endowed with a very firm faith, rejected and ridiculed that slander. Augustine nevertheless thought that the Church’s doctrine had to be defended against such an accusation. For this reason he first composed the two books entitled *On Marriage and Concupiscence*.

In the first he demonstrates what the goods of marriage are, distinguishing them from concupiscence. He asserts that concupiscence is altogether an evil—not arising from the nature of marriage, but brought into marriage from the ancient sin—and nevertheless maintains that conjugal chastity makes good use of this evil for the procreation of children.

Because of this concupiscence, he explains, children of the age are born even from legitimate marriages of the children of God. They are bound by the chain of sin, although their parents have been freed from it, and are held captive under the power of the devil unless they too are freed by the same grace of Christ.

He explains how concupiscence remains in the baptized in its activity but not in its guilt. He also teaches that through the holiness of Baptism not only this original guilt but also all other sins and every evil of human beings are to be removed.

He wrote this first book after the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius (below, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 1, §9), at the beginning of 419 or at the end of 418. In that year, 418, he had received three letters from Valerius, one through Bishop Vindemialis and two through the presbyter Firmus, who also brought Sixtus’s letters (Epistle 200, §1).

In his reply, which he sent with the book to Valerius, Augustine testifies that he learned many things about him from Firmus’s report. Among these was perhaps the information he later recalled having learned by hearsay from the same Firmus: namely, that the Pelagians had written to Valerius saying that Augustine condemned marriage by asserting original sin ( *Retractations*, book 2, chapter 53).

That new argument against original guilt he had already begun to refute elsewhere in that year, 418 (below, *On Original Sin*, §38).

Many considerations moved him to dedicate this book chiefly to Count Valerius, although, as he says, it had been composed amid his ecclesiastical cares and not without difficulty because of its length and the complexity of the question (below, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, §40).

Julian nevertheless seized this opportunity to boast that Augustine had written it to a military man for no other reason than to beg his aid against his opponents’ power. Augustine replied:

“We do not ask for the aid of coercive power against you; rather, we praise the service of Christian power for your benefit, that you may be restrained from sacrilegious presumption” (below, *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book 2, chapter 14).

Catholics received the same book with open arms. This provoked complaints from the Pelagians, and, with Julian’s anger inflamed by this public approval, gave rise to numerous writings on both sides.

We do not know whether another constitution of Honorius against the Pelagians, issued at about this time, should be attributed to the prompting of Count Valerius, or rather to the efforts and prayers of Boniface, by then bishop of Rome.

When Zosimus died toward the end of 418, Boniface was appointed in his place, not without some disagreement among the Roman people concerning the appointment of a bishop. Julian shamelessly attributed that disagreement to divine vengeance for the Pelagians condemned by the Roman Church (below, *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book 6, chapter 38).

With the greatest zeal, Boniface fought the enemies of Christ’s grace both by his apostolic authority and through the edicts of the emperors (below, Appendix, part 3). This diligence may therefore perhaps be credited with the letter of Honorius to Bishop Aurelius, written on 9 June of the year 419 (Epistle 201, among the Augustinian letters).

There Honorius indicates that the constitution which he had issued the previous year against Pelagius and Coelestius had most recently been renewed. He also decreed that anyone who knowingly failed to denounce or expel them, wherever in the world they might be, should himself be driven into exile.

He adds that there were bishops who did not openly strive to oppose and overthrow the perverse doctrines of those same heretics, and who even seemed tacitly to approve them in some fashion.

Accordingly, Aurelius was to admonish all of them concerning their duty, and all the bishops were to be compelled to subscribe to the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius, under penalties by which those who refused would be stripped of their dignity, expelled from their cities, and permanently cut off from communion.

Photius mentions this letter against the Pelagians sent by Honorius to Aurelius (below, Appendix, part 2).

This letter, however, appears to be distinct from the constitution which Honorius sent to Aurelius at the same time and by which he more explicitly prescribed the manner of subscribing. This can be understood from Aurelius’s letter to the bishops of the provinces of Byzacena and Arzugitana, issued on the Kalends of August on this matter (ibid.).

In that letter he clearly distinguishes the imperial constitution from the letter addressed to him, and he arranges for the letter itself to be delivered to them.
