He urges all of them to subscribe—both those who had already subscribed to that condemnation at the plenary council of all Africa in the preceding year and those who had been unable to attend it—so that no suspicion of negligence, dissimulation, or some hidden inclination toward the heresy might remain in any of them.

The same letter from the Emperor was likewise addressed to Augustine, whose personal virtue had earned him honors not owed to his see of Hippo. Indeed, more properly than anyone else, this statement in Honorius’s letter applied to him:

“In this matter”—that is, in condemning Pelagius and Coelestius—“our clemency followed the judgment of Your Holiness, by which it is established that they were condemned by all after a just examination of the judgment” (below, Appendix, part 2).

For although the zeal of the African bishops contributed greatly to the victory won by the Church over the Pelagians, its principal praise belongs to Augustine’s diligence and learning. Of him Prosper writes:

> Therefore his industry among all those  
> Who drove the mad beasts from the holy flock  
> Was greater; a greater work, more excellent,  
> Filled the whole world.

(Ibid.)

This was that bishop who, rightly and deservedly called the chief portion of the Lord’s priests, under whose leadership the Catholic army conquered the enemies of God’s grace, and who wrote, with the hand of all the priests, one sentence for their destruction (ibid.).

In this sense Julian reproached Augustine with that glorious “crime,” calling him the head of all the proceedings against the Pelagians about which he complained, and the cause of their misfortunes (below, *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book 2, chapter 104).

Because of Augustine’s outstanding service to the Church, Jerome wrote to him after those same heretics had been defeated, perhaps around the year 418. He testified that his veneration and affection for Augustine—which had already seemed completely full—had nevertheless increased to such an extent that he could not endure even a single hour without mentioning him.

Alluding, no doubt, to the difficulties he had suffered at Rome on account of the faith, Jerome added that Augustine had persevered against the opposing winds through the ardor of faith.

Finally, he appended that exceptional praise of the holy man:

> Well done for your courage: you are celebrated throughout the world. Catholics venerate and honor you as the restorer of the ancient faith; and—what is a sign of even greater glory—all the heretics detest you.

(Epistle 195, among the Augustinian letters.)

In this matter Alypius also shared in Augustine’s glory, having been unjustly called by Julian “the little slave of his sins” (below, *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book 1, chapter 7). Hence, in a letter addressed to both of them in the year 419, Jerome wrote: “I call God as my witness that, if it could be done, taking the wings of a dove I would entwine myself in your embraces—always, indeed, because of the merit of your virtues, but now especially because, with you cooperating and taking the lead, the Coelestian heresy has been slaughtered.” At the end he sends greetings in the name of Albina, Pinianus, Melania, and the younger Paula (Letter 202 among the Augustinian letters). This letter of Jerome, who departed to heaven in the following year, is thought by some to be the last of his letters still extant (Baronius, under the year 412).

During this period, Vincentius Victor, a young man from Caesarea in Mauretania, inexperienced and untrained in Catholic doctrine, rashly undertook to deal with the perplexing question of the origin of souls, which Augustine had asked Jerome to explain; and he fell into certain Pelagian errors, and into others worse than those. For among other things he said: “That the soul deserved to be sinful before every sin.” He maintained that infants overtaken by death before they were baptized could attain forgiveness of original sins. Moreover, he asserted that those whom the Lord had predestined for Baptism could be snatched away from that predestination and die before what the Almighty had predestined for them had been fulfilled. He also held that some of those who had departed this life without the Baptism of Christ meanwhile did not enter the kingdom but went to paradise; afterward, at the resurrection of the dead, they would even attain the blessedness of the kingdom of heaven (*On the Soul and Its Origin*, book 4, no. 22).

At the end of this same year, 419, Augustine refuted Victor in four books. Although the young man was mistaken and held views worse than Pelagius’s (*ibid.*, book 3, no. 19), Augustine saw that he could be defended by the fact that, at the beginning of his work, he modestly and humbly professed that, in judging his own work, he did not trust himself or defend his own opinion if it should be found implausible, but that he desired, once his own judgment had been condemned, to follow what was better and truer (*ibid.*, book 2, no. 22). This modesty, which the outcome proved to be sincere, indicated a good disposition in him; and at the same time it meant that, although he held opinions contrary to the faith, he nevertheless did not depart from the Catholic faith. “For this disposition,” Augustine says, “even in statements that are non-Catholic through ignorance, is itself Catholic through the very forethought and preparation for correction” (*ibid.*, book 3, no. 23).

Accordingly, the holy Doctor restrained the young man’s arrogance with whatever severity was required for the defense of the faith; yet meanwhile he took care to exercise as much leniency as possible. He evidently thought that the young man should not be rashly detested but still instructed, and desired that he be corrected rather than condemned. Nor was his hope disappointed, for he received a reply from Victor in which Victor testified that he had finally abandoned his errors (*Retractions*, book 2, chapter 56).

Toward the end of the same year, 419, two letters of the Pelagians appeared—one sent to Rome, the other to Thessalonica—together with Julian’s four books against the first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. Augustine refuted these volumes in a twofold work, one addressed to Valerius and the other to Claudius; he refuted the letters in books written to Boniface, as we are now about to relate.

## XXII. In the year 420 Augustine composed the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, as well as four books to Boniface against the two letters of the Pelagians.

### [Column 0083]

The first book addressed to the comes Valerius, written around the beginning of the year 419, had scarcely appeared when Julian, a Pelagian bishop who understood that its reading was stirring the minds of Christians to hatred of the heresy, published four large books against it (below, *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 1, no. 9; book 4, no. 20). In these, as he complacently imagined, he completely defeated Augustine’s book, although he did not even reach a quarter of it, contenting himself with attacking what seemed weaker (below, *Against Julian*, book 1, no. 2). He nevertheless thought that he had adequately forestalled any future complaint by his preface, in which he declared that he had passed over in silence whatever contributed nothing to proving the case (below, *Unfinished Work against the Same Julian*, book 1, chapter 12).

Deprived of the protection of truth, he took refuge in insults, with which he repeatedly drenched his four books. He designated Augustine and all Catholics by the name of Manichaeans (below, *Against Julian*, book 1, no. 3). He also disparaged certain people who had returned from the Pelagian sect to the Church, but treated the comes Valerius more respectfully (below, *Unfinished Work against the Same Julian*, book 1, chapter 10). He dedicated these books to Turbantius, a bishop of the same sect (below, *Against Julian*, book 3; *Unfinished Work against the Same Julian*, book 1, chapter 1).

At the same time a letter was sent to Rome, reportedly at Julian’s instigation, through which he sought, as Augustine puts it, either to find or to make as many of his own adherents as he could (below, *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 1, no. 3). He was evidently striving to seduce as many people as possible in that great city, by means of fear and horror of the errors that he attributed to Catholics while slandering them under the name of Manichaeans. In the same letter he recalls the hearing—that is, the synod—which the Pelagian faction was demanding (*ibid.*, no. 42). Julian appears to have wished to deny the letter for some frivolous reason. Augustine, however, caring little whether such a denial was sincere or feigned, allows Julian to deny that this letter was his (below, *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book 1, chapter 18).

What was written in that same letter—that things Augustine, their adversary, had spread had been accepted by their own enemies out of hatred for the truth (below, *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 1, no. 9; book 4, no. 20)—was likewise found in the Pelagian letter of eighteen bishops addressed to the bishop of Thessalonica. Hence it may be conjectured that this letter too was written at about the same time. In it they attempted to draw Rufus, then bishop of Thessalonica, over to their side, requesting his fellowship and that of the other Eastern bishops against the impious Manichaean heresy, which had been embraced throughout the West. For all their efforts were directed toward this: by fastening upon Catholics the charge of the horrible heresy which they themselves equally abhorred, they might conceal their own errors and condemn grace while commending nature, the law, and free will. Julian himself cites this letter (below, *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book 2, chapter 178).

The vigilance and diligence of the Roman Catholics caused both letters to come into the hands of Pope Boniface (below, *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 1, no. 3). He arranged for them to be carried to Augustine by Alypius. From this it is inferred that Alypius had gone to Italy at that time, although we do not know the reason for his journey. It is certain, however, that he went both to Rome and to Ravenna (below, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 1).

At Ravenna he visited the comes Valerius, from whom he received a letter thanking Augustine for the book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* that had been sent to him. Valerius also warned him that the book contained certain passages which the heretics were attacking, and asked him to hear Alypius concerning those passages. After Alypius subsequently went from Ravenna to Rome, Valerius sent him some sheets. These sheets contained excerpts from the first of Julian’s four books, which someone had collected at will, with several passages also altered. Valerius requested that Augustine refute these excerpts as quickly as possible (below, Preface to the *Unfinished Work against Julian*).

At Rome Alypius stayed only a very short time and lived in Boniface’s household. Boniface received him with the greatest friendliness and honored him with exceptional intimacy. Thus Alypius—and, on the same occasion, Augustine—bound himself to this pontiff by the closest bond of friendship (below, *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 1, no. 1). Boniface gave Alypius the two letters mentioned above because he had found Augustine’s name maliciously inserted in them (*ibid.*, no. 3). Alypius therefore returned to Africa carrying these two letters and the aforementioned excerpts.

Augustine immediately recognized that the excerpts had been collected from Julian’s work. He himself would have preferred not to answer them until he had seen the complete work from which they had been taken. Nevertheless, he judged that he should meanwhile hasten his response to them in order to satisfy the comes Valerius (below, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 2, no. 2; *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book 1, chapters 16 ff.). Accordingly, he quickly published a second book addressed to Valerius under the same title, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. In it he so defended the Catholic doctrine of original evil against the adversary’s slanders that he demonstrated its complete remoteness from the Manichaean error. We therefore place it immediately after the first book, with only a short interval between them, because Augustine composed it immediately after receiving Valerius’s thanks for the earlier book; nor does it seem plausible that Valerius waited two full years before thanking him.

He also worked out four books against the two letters of the Pelagians that had been brought to him by Alypius from Boniface. In the first book he refuted the letter said to have been sent by Julian to Rome; in the three following books, the other letter, which had been addressed to Thessalonica in the name of eighteen bishops.

In the first book he exposes the heretical meaning concealed in the Pelagian confession of faith set against the Catholics. In the second he removes from the Roman clergy the charge of having acted treacherously in the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius; and he demonstrates that Catholics neither assert fate under the name of grace nor attribute partiality to God. In the third he explains what Catholics truly say concerning the usefulness of the law; the effect and power of Baptism; the difference between the two Testaments; the justice and perfection of the Prophets and Apostles; the application of the word “sin” to Christ; and, finally, what they teach about the fulfillment of the commandments in the future life. In the fourth book he reveals the Pelagians’ hidden snares in five points of their doctrine: the praise of creation, the praise of marriage, the praise of the law, the praise of free will, and the praise of the saints.

He dedicated this work to Boniface, moved by the honorable account Alypius had given him of that pontiff, and asked him to read it not so much for the purpose of learning as for examination and correction. At the beginning of the work, recalling the Pelagians’ insulting conduct toward him, he says: “I hope in the Lord our God that they who tear me with a slanderous tooth, because I oppose them on behalf of the little ones . . . will not do so without the reward that is in heaven” (below, *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 1, no. 3).

## XXIII. Alypius brings these books to Italy around the beginning of the year 421. Constantius issues an edict against the Pelagians. Augustine composes six other books against Julian.

Alypius carried the four books to Boniface (below, *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book 1, chapter 75), and likewise brought the second book *On Marriage and Concupiscence* to Valerius (*ibid.*, chapters 7, 52). It is therefore clear that, either at the end of the year 420 or at the beginning of 421, he crossed over to Italy again. Augustine himself, in replying to the excerpts from Julian that had been sent to him, responded immediately, with such diligence and speed that it is impossible to suppose that Alypius could have caused that response to be sent late to Valerius. The Pelagians, moreover, attempted to defame this overseas journey of Alypius in such a way that we may easily infer that it had been undertaken against them. And certainly we shall see that these heretics attacked the emperor Constantius at about the same time.

Julian therefore reproaches Augustine for shouting “with women, and with all the camp-followers and tribunes, to whom your colleague Alypius, as you say, recently brought eighty or more horses fattened throughout Africa” (*ibid.*, chapter 42). Further on he boasts in these terms: “The greatness of our cause is most evident, as is shown both by consideration and weighing of the facts which we defend, and by your fear—your fear which, fighting against our blood by the outpouring of money, the lavish distribution of inheritances, the sending of horses, the sedition of peoples, and the corruption of authorities, makes you ashamed to profess your faith, which is attacked by us,” etc. (*ibid.*, chapter 74). Elsewhere again: “Why have you stirred up all Italy with such great factions? Why have you raised seditions at Rome by hiring crowds? Why have you fattened, throughout almost the whole of Africa, herds of horses from the resources of the poor, horses which, with Alypius escorting them, you sent to tribunes and centurions? Why have you corrupted the powers of this world by the inheritances offered by matrons, so that the straw of public fury might burn against us? Why have you disturbed the peace of the Churches? Why have you stained the reign of a religious Prince with the impiety of persecutions?” (*ibid.*, book 3, chapter 35).

Augustine rebukes Julian’s extraordinary vehemence and shamelessness in accusation with these most prudent words: “Either you are slandering, or you do not know what you are saying; and therefore you speak these things either as a liar or as a rash man. What is worse than you if you invented these things yourself? What is more foolish if you believed those who invented them? And as for what you even dared to write, without fearing that your books might reach those places where my colleague Alypius was received while crossing or coming by land and sea—when I read your most blatant falsehoods there, they cannot be read without your being mocked, or rather detested—which impudence, I do not say, but madness, does this resemble?” (*ibid.*, book 1, chapter 42).

The edict issued by Constantius against the Pelagians at precisely this time had plainly given Julian a new cause for anger, perhaps because Alypius’s embassy and request had moved the emperor to issue it. The chronographers agree that this emperor died in the year 421, after reigning for only six months, with the seventh having begun according to Olympiodorus. Prosper and Idacius place his accession in the year 420; Theophanes places it in the year 421, on the sixth day before the Ides of February. The *Theodosian Code* agrees with Theophanes: in its laws issued from 10 March 421 to 28 July, the name of Constantius is recorded.

The first of these laws was written to Volusianus, from which we learn that Coelestius was then active in the City. Constantius states there that he had already issued an edict against certain ancient and recent heresies, yet was informed daily that they were spreading more widely. Therefore, so that the disturbances which these dissensions might produce could be avoided, he renewed the same orders and wished that, after a careful investigation of the enemies of the true faith, they should immediately be expelled from Rome and sent far away, Coelestius above all. By his own subscription he added that it was Volusianus’s responsibility to ensure that this edict was observed (below, Appendix, part 2).

Accordingly, to obey Constantius, Volusianus himself promulgated a decree expelling Coelestius from Rome and the entire neighboring region as a disturber of the divine faith and public peace, threatening the penalty of proscription against those by whom he might be concealed. Photius mentions the edict of Constantius to Volusianus concerning the expulsion of Coelestius (*ibid.*).

Nevertheless, Coelestius’s courage did not fail on that account. Several years later, under Pope Coelestine, he came to the City in the year 424 or somewhat later, seeking a hearing as though his case had not yet been discussed (below, Appendix, part 3).

Since the enemies of grace did not cease to rage around the enclosures of the Lord’s flock and to search everywhere for entrances through which they might plunder Christ’s sheep, Augustine did whatever lay within his office to cure their madness altogether or at least prevent them from harming others (below, *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 1, no. 2). It was therefore not at all enough for him to have answered, in the later book addressed to Valerius, the excerpts from Julian’s work that had been sent to him. Afterward, having obtained Julian’s complete work through the favor of Bishop Claudius, he resolved to publish a new and fuller response to it.

This additional labor necessarily had to be undertaken for another reason: after examining Julian’s work more carefully, Augustine had discovered that the excerpts Valerius sent him differed in certain respects from the original. He therefore had good reason to fear that Julian himself, or someone else comparing the response with the work itself, might accuse him of fraud—a charge which the adversary in fact did not fail to level against the holy Doctor with the greatest insolence.

Since Augustine places this second refutation of Julian immediately after his four books to Boniface, it may be affirmed that it was published in the year 421 or shortly afterward. In it he mentions Jerome as already dead. Thus, while we see no reason to place it much later within the present year, it is also clear that it cannot be assigned any earlier date, since Jerome died only on 30 September 420. Augustine himself indicates the amount of study, diligence, and labor he devoted to it by calling it a work of such magnitude and elaboration (*Retractions*, book 2, chapter 62). On this occasion, someone not without justification declares that the holy Doctor, who is remarkable in all the other books he published against the Pelagians, appears in this work almost divine (Henricus Noris, *Pelagian History*, book 1, chapter 21).

At the beginning he declares that he does not disregard the insults and reproaches Julian heaped upon him as though they had nothing to do with him. They provided him with abundant material both for joy and for sorrow: joy, because of the rich reward he hoped for in heaven; sorrow, because of Julian himself, whom he could not help loving, whatever Julian might say against him (below, *Against Julian*, book 1, no. 35).

Since Julian called those who affirmed original sin “Manichaeans,” Augustine shows that this accusation falls upon the most distinguished of the Fathers, both Greek and Latin; this is the subject of the first part of the first book. The second part is devoted to demonstrating that the Manichaeans are greatly aided by several rash statements made by Julian himself.

In the second book he overturns five Pelagian arguments against original sin by the authority of earlier Doctors of the Church—namely, ten illustrious bishops: Irenaeus, Cyprian, Reticius, Olympius, Hilary, Gregory of Nazianzus, Ambrose, Basil, John of Constantinople, and Innocent; the testimony of the priest Jerome, a holy and exceptionally learned man, is added as well.

Since he knew perfectly well that the adversary would have no sense of shame and would undoubtedly not blush to say that all these celebrated men had likewise been caught in the same error, Augustine accordingly sets one of his own books against each of Julian’s four books in succession, examining everything Julian had said except those passages that had no bearing on the central question.

In the third book he proves especially that concupiscence is evil, although marriage is good and instituted by God. Chaste married people make good use of this evil; continent believers make better use of it by not using it. This evil is entirely different from what the Manichaean, in his delirium, claimed had been mixed into us from some other substance coeternal with God.

In the fourth book he teaches that the virtues of unbelievers are not true virtues. Among other matters, he incidentally shows how grace is given not according to merits and yet is not to be attributed to fate.

In the fifth he observes that the Christian multitude knows that, by the merit of sin, the image of God suffers here in infants such great torments, and that if they die without Baptism they are excluded from the kingdom of God. He then proves that the first parents assumed coverings because of the shame arising from sin; that sin can be the punishment of a preceding sin; that from the same condemned mass some are freely chosen while others are made vessels of wrath; that concupiscence is always evil, even in those who do not consent to it; that marriage can exist without intercourse; and that Christ’s flesh differs from the flesh of other human beings, which is flesh of sin, etc.

In the sixth book he demonstrates original sin from the Baptism of infants, from the words of the Apostle, and from the exorcism and exsufflation of those being baptized. By the example of the cultivated olive and the wild olive he suitably explains how sinful children who must be regenerated can be born from parents who have been regenerated and made righteous. Original sin was voluntary in the first parents; in us it is foreign in respect of the individuality of the act, yet it is ours through the contagion of propagation, etc.

Immediately after this work he places the *Enchiridion* addressed to Laurentius, which Augustine composed after Jerome’s death and in which he honors Jerome with the praise “of blessed memory.” Although he wished the book to bear the more general title *On Faith, Hope, and Charity*, he devoted most of it to setting forth the doctrine of Christian grace.

## XXIV. The Pelagians make a futile attempt to win over the Eastern Churches. Pelagius is condemned in Syria and Julian in Cilicia. Where the faction, still obstinate in heresy, eventually withdrew.

The Pelagians often attempted to throw the East into turmoil no less than the West, especially after Zosimus’s judgment, from which they never ceased appealing to a general synod until the year 431. Accordingly, from among their bishops who had been driven from their sees, they sent some to Constantinople. There, concealing the impiety of their error, they disguised themselves and their cause under a false appearance.

By that time Atticus had succeeded blessed John Chrysostom in that city. He was a worthy rival of Chrysostom’s faith and, in this case, applying both his knowledge and his episcopal authority, rejected their embassy, setting against them the Church’s ancient faith. He pursued them so vigorously that he would not even grant them permission to remain in the city (below, Appendix, part 2). He also sent to Rome the proceedings he had drawn up against them. Coelestius is counted among these envoys by those who think that this is the event meant by Augustine when he says that Coelestius was defeated at Constantinople by the army of Christ (below, *Against Julian*, book 3, no. 4). Others nevertheless believe that it refers to Coelestius’s expulsion from the Constantinopolitan Church, which preceded Zosimus’s judgment (above, chapter 14).

Moreover, as we have already observed, Julian and seventeen other Pelagians who assumed the episcopal title wrote to Rufus, bishop of Thessalonica, in order, if they could somehow manage it, to draw him over to their side (below, *Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 1, no. 3). We do not know how he received their letter, but we know for certain that Rufus never withdrew from the unity of the Church. If the Pelagians had obtained anything from him that served their error, Julian would certainly not have refrained from proclaiming it publicly. In any event, the bishop of Thessalonica was especially bound to the Apostolic See and was obliged to subscribe to the judgment of the Roman pontiffs, since other metropolitans in Illyricum were subject to him by authority of that same See.

There is no doubt that these heretics also attempted to win over the Ephesian Church, where Coelestius, because of his prolonged residence there, may have enjoyed various connections. Indeed, this appeared to be the very Church which, through imprudence, had admitted that arch-heretic into the company of the presbyters and therefore seemed more obligated than all the others to undertake his defense.

Nevertheless, you could not adapt Prosper’s following verses to any occasion more suitably than to this one:

“I pass over how greatly famed Ephesus  
was stirred by a well-aroused tumult,  
not allowing vessels of wrath, blasts of disease,  
and seeds of death to remain within its walls.”  
(Below, Appendix, part 2.)

It is entirely unclear in what year all these Churches professed their hatred of the Pelagians. It may nevertheless be thought that this did not happen before the end of the year 421, since Augustine, in his work against Julian, written, as we believe, in that same year 421 or shortly afterward, makes no mention of it, although the occasion would have invited such a reference. He recalls only that Coelestius had been defeated at Constantinople, an event which had occurred before the year 418.

Neither this holy bishop nor Prosper knew of any other synodical declaration by an Eastern Church in defense of the faith against Pelagius himself. For when Pelagius, who had apparently been acquitted at the synod of Diospolis after deceiving the bishops, was pursued by his accusers before another synod presided over by Theodotus, bishop of Antioch, that slippery man could not hide before this assembly. Convicted of heresy, he was expelled from the holy places of Jerusalem.

Mercator, the sole surviving witness of this notable event, cites the letters of Theodotus and Praylius, bishop of Jerusalem, written on this matter to the bishop of the city of Rome (*ibid.*). Pelagius’s accusers at that time were certainly those same celebrated men, Heros and Lazarus, who alone had been willing to undertake that office against him, and whom Mercator had shortly before indicated without naming them. It therefore appears that, as soon as they were able, they ought to have pursued Pelagius before Theodotus.

For this reason Joannes Garnerius thinks that Theodotus and Praylius wrote the aforementioned letters against that arch-heretic as early as the year 417, before they had learned of Innocent’s death (Garnerius on Mercator, pp. 25 and 209). Yet although it may have happened that Theodotus was already occupying the episcopal see in the year 417 itself, nothing compels us to believe that Praylius wrote about Pelagius at approximately the same time in both directions. For we saw that, in that very year, after he had been raised to episcopal dignity, he sent letters to the Roman pontiff on that account, and that they reached Rome only in September (above, chapter 15).

The council of Theodotus may therefore be placed somewhat later, either after Zosimus’s condemnation of Pelagius had been promulgated in the year 418, or even after Jerome’s death, which occurred on 30 September 420. For Jerome certainly would not have failed, had he still been alive, to inform Augustine of news so eagerly desired.

Since Cilicia belonged to the patriarchate of Antioch, the Pelagians were also condemned there in a provincial synod. Moreover, that famous Theodore of Mopsuestia, who was called the parent of this heresy, who had defended it in a work published against Jerome and Augustine, and who shortly before had provided refuge to Julian and other leading patrons of the same cause, himself pronounced an anathema against Julian in that very council.

Mercator reports that this happened after Julian’s departure from Cilicia. Julian had evidently left the West around the year 421 and, having crossed the sea and traversed, as Mercator says, the East—that is, Asia Minor—had withdrawn with his companions in error and exile (below, Appendix, part 2). Some even think that Julian’s stay with Theodore, and the evils that spread from there throughout the surrounding region, gave the Cilician synod cause to be held (Garnerius on Mercator, p. 219).

According to Mercator, Julian had approached Theodore so that he might receive new strength from him for defending the Pelagian heresy and, as though better instructed by Theodore’s teaching, might undertake another work against Augustine. There is no doubt that Julian himself had also been Theodore’s instigator and encourager in publishing books against those who affirmed original sin, if indeed Theodore had not already published such works several years earlier, as we have observed (above, chapter 10).

Where Pelagius fled after being expelled from Jerusalem is unknown; nor is any further mention of him found in the records of history. In any case, he was already of sufficiently advanced age that he could not have long survived the sorrow which, given his pride of spirit, he must have drawn from the offense and hatred of everyone against him.

As for the followers of his heresy, when they realized that they had been condemned by the West and rejected by the East, most of them returned to sounder counsels. They abjured their errors, abandoned Julian, to whom they had clung, condemned Pelagius, and implored the mercy of the Apostolic See. The Church judged that pardon should be extended to them, received those who returned, and even restored them to their sees (below, Appendix, part 2).

Writing around the year 420, Julian accused certain deserters from the Pelagian doctrine who had returned to the Catholic faith, though he concealed their names. Possidius too, who committed the acts of Augustine’s life to writing around the year 432, testified that very many had returned from the Pelagians and that, as the truth of the right faith increasingly overcame the darkness of the detestable error, others were still returning (Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 18).

Among those whom the devout mother Church embraced on their return, we know one: Turbantius, to whom Julian had dedicated his first work against Augustine, and whom he called holy and conspicuous for the great splendor of his virtues (below, *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book 1, chapter 1). In the second refutation of Julian, Augustine calls him “brother” (*ibid.*, book 2, chapter 11), because, like the others, he had evidently had his episcopal dignity restored.

Julian, however, and those who hardened their minds with him in heresy, when, as Augustine puts it, the army of Christ, “spread everywhere,” defeated them wherever they appeared (*ibid.*, book 3, no. 4), each withdrew wherever he could. It is not unlikely that some of them stayed in Gaul, where at this time various bishops gave grounds for suspicion that they were attached to Pelagian errors. For on the seventh day before the Ides of July in the year 425, Valentinian III ordered that the same bishops be summoned by Patroclus of Arles to renounce these errors within twenty days; if they did not do so, others would be appointed in their place and they themselves would be forced to leave the soil of the country (below, Appendix, part 2).

Some also carried their heresy into Britain. There, during the time of Pope Coelestine, a certain Pelagian named Agricola, son of Severianus, a Pelagian bishop, was corrupting the Churches of Ireland by persuading them to accept his doctrine. Coelestine therefore sent Bishop Germanus of Auxerre, so that, after expelling the heretics, he might direct the Britons toward the Catholic faith (*ibid.*).

Some people wrongly confused this Severianus with Sulpicius Severus. Concerning the latter, Gennadius left a written account that he was deceived by Pelagius in his old age (so the old Corbie manuscript). He immediately adds, however, that, recognizing the fault of his loquacity, Severus maintained silence until death, so that the sin he had contracted by speaking might be completely corrected by silence.

During the reigns of Honorius and Theodosius, Bishop Fastidius also transmitted Pelagius’s doctrines to the Britons. His book addressed to the widow Fatalis survives among Augustine’s spurious works, disfigured by the opinions and words of that arch-heretic (Appendix, volume 6, *Book on the Christian Life*).

After an embassy had been sent from Britain, the Gallic bishops learned that the Pelagian plague was spreading more widely there. They held a large synod, at which Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, was chosen together with Lupus of Troyes. To suppress the heresy there, Germanus crossed over once and again: first with Bishop Lupus in the year 429, and afterward with Severus of Trier, a disciple of that same Lupus, in the year 447 (below, Appendix, part 2).

Where Julian ended up, and how futilely he and his associates made new attempts and schemes in the East during the time of Nestorius before the fathers of the Ephesian synod, we shall relate elsewhere (below, *On Julian and His Writings*, notice to the *Unfinished Work against Julian’s Second Reply*).

As for Coelestius, who, after returning to Rome around the year 424, as we related above, was expelled from Italy at the order of Pope Coelestine, he met Nestorius in Constantinople, together with Julian and other bishops of the same faction. There they petitioned the emperor Theodosius II for permission to hold a council; Nestorius, in their favor, wrote to Coelestine. But when Mercator presented Theodosius with a petition against them in the year 429, they were ordered to leave the city (below, Appendix, part 2). What happened to Coelestius thereafter we nowhere find recorded.

## XXV. Around the year 426 the monks of Adrumetum disagree among themselves over the question of grace and free will. Augustine brings them to agreement in a book composed on the same subject.

Some time after Pope Zosimus had condemned the Pelagians and they had been expelled from the West, a disagreement arose among the monks of Adrumetum concerning a lengthy letter to Sixtus. It was a happy and fortunate disagreement, since it produced two books of such great importance to the Church: one, *On Grace and Free Will*, and the other, *On Rebuke and Grace*—probably around the year 426. There is no reason to date these books later than that, since they are listed in the *Retractions*, composed around 427; nor should they be placed earlier, because there they occupy the final position.

At that time Adrumetum was a celebrated city in Byzacena, a province of Africa. There was a monastery there inhabited by monks, among whom was a certain Florus, a native of Uzalis (Letter 216, §2 ff.). Once, prompted by charity, he had undertaken a journey to his homeland with a companion, Felix, likewise a monk of Adrumetum. While staying there, he discovered some short works of Augustine, namely the letter to Sixtus (Letter 214), which he copied—with Felix dictating it and with the consent of the monks of Uzalis. Later Florus went from Uzalis to Carthage, while Felix returned to his own monastery, carrying the holy Doctor’s book with him.

When he began reading that work to the brethren, without the knowledge of the abbot Valentinus, five of them, or scarcely more, failed to grasp the author’s meaning and turned the medicine into an illness. They stirred up great disturbances in the monastery, asserting that grace was defended by others who understood this teaching more correctly in such a way as to abolish free will, and that we were not to be judged at the last judgment according to each person’s works. Some also seem to have doubted whether the writing was Augustine’s. When Florus returned from Carthage, the tumult broke out again. They rose up against him as though he were the author of the wounds they had suffered from the book, attributing to him all the monastery’s disorders and disagreements because they could not grasp his words as he attempted to resolve questions of such difficulty. He himself, however, followed the genuine and catholic faith.

Throughout that period this disagreement remained confined within the monastery, while Valentinus knew nothing of it. Florus nevertheless thought it his duty to inform him. The abbot did not doubt that the work was a genuine production of Augustine or that it presented orthodox teaching. He knew the holy Doctor’s style well, as well as that angelic wisdom which shone forth in his writings. He saw that Christian grace was commended in this very book with such a bright and powerful eloquence that he could not permit himself to doubt its author. He therefore read it through with delight and received, with profound reverence, the light and consolation that the holy man’s most gracious admonitions pour into humble souls.

At the same time, he worked to suppress those impious questions, which had arisen from the ignorance of some of his brethren. He resolved to send certain men to Evodius, the bishop of Uzalis, so that they might bring back from him the instruction necessary for properly understanding Augustine’s book. When that holy bishop learned of the disputes by which they were contending among themselves over free will and divine justice, he wrote back to Abbot Valentinus and his monks in these words:

> “Honourable brothers have reported to us that I know not what questions have arisen among you concerning free will and the justice of God. We commend your zeal, but we do not wish it to be contentious. For contention creates disturbance, whereas zeal requires piety. The man first created possessed the fullest exercise of free will. I mean Adam. But when free will itself was wounded, it was weakened. Thus free will still exists in man, but it is wounded. Hence it is said: ‘My strength is weakened through poverty’ (Psalm 30:11); and: ‘The light of my eyes is not with me’ (Psalm 37:11). To restore this, the physician Christ the Saviour was sent, so that he might save what had perished and heal what had been corrupted.”

And after other remarks:

> “Let them therefore read,” he said, “the sayings of the holy men of God from former times, as I have already said—men who possess a pious affection for the divine gift. When they do not understand them, let them not be quick to criticize, but let them pray that they may understand.”

We possess this fragment of Evodius’s letter through James Sirmond, who merely indicated that the same letter was found in a manuscript of the Abbey of St Maximin at Trier. He omitted the rest, which, as he says, is all worthy of being brought to light, except that it is somewhat poorly corrected (Sirmond, *History of the Predestinarians*, chapter 1).

Those for whom Augustine’s book had not sufficed did not declare themselves satisfied by Evodius’s response either. They therefore decided to visit Augustine himself, although their own abbot opposed the plan. He also tried, but in vain, to cure them through the assistance of a certain holy priest named Sabinus, who explained the book to them in a polished interpretation. Since he now knew of no other remedy, he reluctantly consented to their departure, lest their wounds be increased by a rebuff, and even supplied them with the money necessary for the journey. He gave them no letter for Augustine, however, lest he himself should appear, like them, to be wavering in uncertainty concerning the truth of Augustine’s teaching.

Thus the defenders of liberty against grace, setting out freely and in disorderly fashion (Letter 216, §1)—that is, contrary to the order of monastic discipline—undertook their journey, carrying with them the writing that had been disputed. No more than two of them are named: Cresconius and Felix (Letter 214, §1). This Felix may have been different from the man who had brought the aforementioned writing to the monastery at Adrumetum; yet he too seems to have travelled with them, since they are called his companions (Letter 216).

After they had departed, the other brethren in the monastery enjoyed quiet and peace. Although these men had no letter of introduction to Augustine, they nevertheless presented themselves as monks from the congregation at Adrumetum. The holy Bishop received them, perceiving in them a simplicity too great to make him suspect deceit or fraud (Letter 214, §5).

They therefore told him that some of their brethren preached grace in such a way as to deny free will and assert that we are not to be judged according to our works. Others, however, acknowledged together with grace both human free will and the justice of God, by which he will repay each person according to his works. They also accused Florus of being the author of the disagreement by which their congregation was being torn apart (ibid., §1).

Augustine instructed the monks and explained his letter to Sixtus to them. Through them he also wrote to Valentinus and to the brethren in the community at Adrumetum who had accused him, discussing that extremely difficult question concerning the will and grace (Letter 215, §2). He asked Valentinus to send Florus to him, conjecturing what was in fact the case: that some were rioting against Florus because they did not understand what he was saying (Letter 214, §6).

Augustine had wished to send, through Cresconius and Felix, various documents relating to the history of the Pelagian heresy [Col. 0095]. But they would not allow time for these to be copied, since they were hastening back to the monastery so that they might celebrate Easter there with their brethren—Easter, which in the year 427 fell on 3 April—after the cause of their disagreements had been removed and with complete agreement among their minds (Letter 214, §5).

This plan of theirs moved the holy Bishop to give them the aforementioned letter to Valentinus before Easter. Nevertheless, he kept them with him beyond that feast, in order to strengthen them further against the Pelagian danger (Letter 215, §§1–2). They suppose that the reason for this delay was provided by another Felix, who arrived to see Augustine somewhat later, only after his companions; and it is plausible that the holy Doctor learned from him the true state of the dispute.

During their longer stay, therefore, Augustine not only read his letter to Sixtus to these monks, but also read to them the letters of the Councils of Carthage and Milevis, as well as the letter of the five bishops to Innocent together with the Pope’s individual replies to them; the letter of the African council to Zosimus and Zosimus’s rescript sent to all the bishops throughout the world; and finally the canons established by the plenary council of all Africa against the Pelagian heresy. To all this he added a reading of Cyprian’s book *On the Lord’s Prayer*, in which that blessed martyr magnificently commends the grace of God. He omitted nothing that might make them sound and steadfast in the faith, without denying either free will or the necessity of grace.

Moreover, impelled by the charity with which the holy man burned toward his brethren (see below, *On Grace and Free Will*, §1), he composed a book on this very subject, giving it the title *On Grace and Free Will, to Valentinus and the Monks with Him*. First, he demonstrates from Scripture both that man is truly endowed with free will and that, nevertheless, he can do nothing good without the assistance of grace. He then proves that grace is not given according to merits and explains in what sense eternal life, which is repaid for good works, is truly grace.

Next, he shows that neither knowledge of the law, nor nature, nor the mere remission of sins is that grace which is given through Christ. Rather, through Christ’s grace the law is fulfilled, nature is set free, and sin is prevented from ruling. He refutes the Pelagian refuge by which they objected that, although grace is not given according to the merits of good works, it is nevertheless given according to the merits of a good will preceding faith and prayer (ibid., §27).

He takes up the question why God commands what he himself is going to give, and whether he commands certain things that we are unable to do. He proves that charity, without which the commandments are not fulfilled, exists in us only from God. He teaches that God works in human hearts to incline their wills wherever he wishes—toward good, according to his mercy, or toward evil, according to their merits—by a judgment sometimes hidden, but always just (ibid., §§34, 43).

Finally, he gives a clear example of freely bestowed grace, not repaid for merits, in those infants who are saved while others, whose case is the same as theirs, perish.

He urges the people of Adrumetum to reread this book frequently. If they understand its teaching, they are to give thanks to God; but if they encounter anything obscure in it, they are to strive to obtain understanding through pious prayers. Above all, they must reject from themselves that contentious knowledge and bitter zeal which the Apostle James so strongly condemns (ibid., §46).

He further commends the reading of the same book to them at great length in another work which he later addressed to these same monks (see below, *On Rebuke and Grace*, §1), trusting that, with the assistance of divine grace, once they had read it more carefully and understood it more deeply, all the disagreements that had arisen among them on this subject would be quieted (Letter 215, §8).

He also read this work to Cresconius and his companions and gave it to them to carry back to their monastery, together with the other documents relating to the condemnation of the Pelagians that he thought should be sent there. At the same time he entrusted them with a second letter to Valentinus and his brethren, in which he addressed them concerning the sending of Florus to him in these words:

> “If I have any claim upon you, let brother Florus come to me.” (ibid.)

### XXVI. Another book, entitled *On Rebuke and Grace*, is sent to the same people of Adrumetum.

Valentinus received Augustine’s book and letters with the greatest reverence (Letter 216, §§1–2). Although the ignorance of some of his brethren had caused it to appear that he and others who were innocent of blame had been rebuked along with them, he nevertheless rejoiced greatly that their curiosity had produced such happy fruits and had brought him an acquaintance with teaching so useful and so delightful.

Valentinus certainly did not fail to order Florus to go to Augustine. He also gave him a letter explaining to the holy Bishop everything that had taken place in his monastery, together with a profession of his own faith, which he affirmed was also Florus’s faith. In the same letter he asked Augustine to pray to God for peace in his monastery and tranquillity amid such storms of contention. Finally, he added that whatever Florus might request from Augustine for establishing the rule and discipline of his monastery, Augustine should not hesitate to prescribe.

Florus gladly undertook the journey and went with several others to the holy Bishop. When Augustine discovered in him the catholic faith concerning free will and grace, and learned from Valentinus’s letter that peace among the brethren had nearly been restored, that they were united in the truth, and that they were ardent in charity, he was filled with no ordinary joy.

The holy man rejoiced exceedingly that divine mercy had, through its marvellous goodness, turned the devil’s wickedness to the advancement of God’s servants. Thus the very devices by which the enemy of the human race had attempted to overthrow some of them harmed no one and contributed to the instruction of many (see below, *On Rebuke and Grace*, §1)—namely, those who had opposed Florus because they failed to grasp the meaning of his words. For afterward they seem to have corrected their error.

This explains why Augustine, who in his first letter to Valentinus had stated as a fact that there were some in the monastery who truly denied free will (Letter 214), and who later, perhaps instructed by the report of the other Felix, had spoken about the matter with a certain hesitation—saying that there were some who defended grace in such a way as to deny free will, or who thought that free will was denied when grace was defended (see below, *On Grace and Free Will*, §1)—later said in the *Retractions*, after receiving Valentinus’s response and hearing Florus, that he had composed the book for the sake of those who, thinking that free will was denied when God’s grace was defended, defended free will in such a way as to deny God’s grace, asserting that grace was given according to our merits (*Retractions* II.66).

Augustine also learned, perhaps from Florus himself, that there was someone in the monastery at Adrumetum who objected:

> “Why are we preached to and commanded to turn away from evil and do good, if we do not do this ourselves, but God works in us both the willing and the doing? Let those who rule over us merely command us what we ought to do, and pray for us that we may do it; but let them not rebuke and accuse us if we fail to do it. How can it not be counted as my fault that I did not receive from him something which, unless it is given, can be obtained from no other source?” (see below, *On Rebuke and Grace*, §§4–6).

This false inference, by which that monk attempted to bring the doctrine of grace into disrepute, moved Augustine to defend the same doctrine in a new work against those who defended free will not according to grace but against grace (ibid., §17).

This is the book which he entitled *On Rebuke and Grace* and addressed to the same Valentinus and the monks with him. Yet he was not attacking them in it, since their hearts were rightly disposed toward God; indeed, the very man who had raised the objection may have abandoned that opinion. The holy Doctor expressly states that he was acting not against the people of Adrumetum, but against those who, being concerned with nothing but earthly things, did not wish to be rebuked by preachers of grace for the evils they committed—or, at least, against the human thoughts themselves that might enter the minds of some (ibid., §6). Indeed, in the course of the discussion he attacks those who had not yet been regenerated through Baptism.

In this book above all, Augustine began to explain more clearly the foundations of predestination, which he had previously set forth less plainly and distinctly (see below, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, §55). Consequently, those who opposed this mystery at Massilia were extremely hostile to the work. Conversely, it brought great consolation and light to Prosper and the other defenders of grace.

At the beginning of the book he sets forth the catholic faith concerning the law, free will, and grace. He teaches that the grace of Christ is that by which alone human beings are liberated from evil and without which they can do no good; grace not only shows them what they should do, but also enables them to do it with love.

He teaches that the rebuke of evil people who have not received this grace is neither unjust, since they are evil by their own will, nor useless—although it must be acknowledged that it is only through God that rebuke becomes beneficial. Perseverance in the good is truly a great gift of God. Yet the person who, without receiving this gift, falls back into sin by his own will is worthy not only of rebuke but also, if he remains in evil until death, of eternal condemnation.

Why one person receives this gift and another does not is inscrutable. None of the predestined can perish. Therefore the perseverance that is not received by all who are called here “sons of God” is given to all who truly are sons by God’s foreknowledge and predestination.

He addresses the question of Adam: how could Adam have sinned by failing to persevere if he had not received perseverance? Augustine shows that Adam was initially given an assistance by which he could persevere, and without which he could not persevere if he wished, but not an assistance by which he would be made to wish. Through Christ, however, an assistance is now given not only without which we cannot persevere, even if we wish to do so, but also an assistance so great and so constituted that it causes us to wish to persevere.

He proves that the number of the predestined, to whom this kind of gift belongs, is certain and can neither be increased nor diminished. Since it is unknown who belongs to that number and who does not, medicinal rebuke must be applied to all who sin, lest they themselves perish or cause others to perish.

Finally, he concludes that grace does not prevent rebuke, nor does rebuke deny grace.

### XXVII. The monk Leporius, expelled from Gaul because of doctrines opposed to the faith of the Incarnation and divine grace, is brought to correction in Africa through Augustine.

In the foregoing book Augustine asserts that, up to that time, no one had been found so blind and so ignorant in the faith as to dare say that Christ, born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary as a son of man, had nevertheless merited by living well through free will and performing good works without sin to be the Son of God (see below, *On Rebuke and Grace*, §30).

Cassian, however, attributes this very teaching to certain persons, among whom Leporius was one of the chief (see below, Appendix, part 2). Leporius himself openly confesses the matter in his book of correction. This recantation, therefore, which must chiefly be attributed to Augustine’s labour and diligence, seems certainly later than the book just mentioned, but earlier than the final work against Julian. For in that work, because of certain words of Julian’s which seemed in some way relevant to the matter, the holy Doctor so plainly charges the Pelagians with this error that, having learned elsewhere that they had added this impiety, he may reasonably be thought to have learned elsewhere of the fact that they had added this impiety (see below, *The Unfinished Work against Julian* IV.84).

Leporius, a monk professed in Gaul, stood out among the others for the purity of his life. Yet he attributed his virtue not to divine assistance but solely to free will and his own powers, following Pelagian teaching. That he had been imbued with this teaching by Pelagius himself seems to be indicated by Cassian’s words: “Proceeding from the instruction, or rather the depravity, of Pelagius.”

Moreover, he then plunged into a much more dangerous abyss. For he was counted among the principal leaders [Col. 0099] of those who at that time revived, from the principles of the Pelagian heresy, the ancient impiety of the Ebionites and laid the foundations of the Nestorian position.

Among other things, these men said that the solitary man Jesus Christ had lived without any contamination of sin. They had advanced so far as to assert that human beings, if they wished, could be without sin without God’s assistance. Then, breaking out into still greater madness, they said that Jesus Christ had come into this world not to provide redemption for the human race but to offer examples of good actions.

Cassian writes that this plague had arisen in his own time, especially in the city of Beligara—or, as another reading has it, “from the great city of Veligara.” Whether he intended to designate Belica, or whether the text should be read “from the great city of the Belgae,” a description that would fit Augusta Treverorum, may be left to the judgment of others.

Nevertheless, Cassian’s own statement makes clear that Leporius was either the first, or among the first, to defend this same heresy in Gaul (see below, Appendix, part 2). Facundus also recorded that Leporius taught in Gaul the same doctrine which Nestorius later disseminated in the East (Facundus, I.4).

Leporius published his errors in a written letter, which gravely offended the orthodox and produced enormous scandals. Cassian, who may already have been in Provence from the year 415 onward, states that he admonished Leporius to come to his senses. Other learned men from Gaul did the same, but in vain (see below, Appendix, part 2).

Accordingly, the Gallic bishops Proculus and Cylinnius rebuked the erring monk as his arrogance deserved and condemned his impious doctrines. Expelled from Gaul, he crossed over to Africa with several companions in error. There, through the work of certain African bishops, but especially through Augustine, and with divine light shining upon him, he was freed from his blindness. He acknowledged his error and renounced its deadly character with the utmost detestation.

For he not only confessed it in Africa with profound sorrow and a kind of devout boldness; since his error had also been made public in Gaul, he wished his correction to become public there as well. He therefore sent a book there, filled with the groans of his repentance, in which he condemned his former ravings—if we may use Cassian’s words—in so magnificent a manner that his correction is scarcely less admirable than the unshaken faith of many others (ibid.).

On this occasion Augustine, together with Aurelius, Florentius, and Secundinus, wrote a joint letter to the bishops Proculus and Cylinnius, reporting that those who had crossed over with Leporius had also been corrected and healed with him (Letter 219).

### XXVIII. Twelve statements concerning grace, belonging to the catholic faith, are brought forward against certain remnants of Pelagian error detected in Vitalis.

Another offshoot of the Pelagian heresy produced far greater harm to the Church, especially in Gaul. It spread more widely and struck deeper roots because at first sight it appeared less injurious to the grace of Christ the Saviour, which it even seemed to magnify to no small degree.

Certain beginnings of this movement appeared with a new doctrine taught by Vitalis, a man otherwise catholic. Since he had been educated in the Church of Carthage, he owed a particular reverence to the teaching of Cyprian, the bishop of that city. Augustine nevertheless complained that Vitalis was rashly departing from it.

The holy Doctor did not believe Vitalis to be a Pelagian heretic. But he had heard that Vitalis was not so orthodox that none of that error had reached him or remained in him. The Pelagians, Augustine writes to him, attribute everything that pertains to the faithful and pious life of human beings to the free choice of the will, so that they think these things should be sought from ourselves rather than requested from the Lord.

“But you,” he continues, “if what I hear about you is true, do not wish the beginning of faith—which is also the beginning of a good, that is, a pious, will—to be God’s gift. Rather, you maintain that we possess this beginning from ourselves, so that we begin to believe. As for the other goods of the religious life, you agree that God gives them by his grace to those who already ask, seek, and knock in faith.”

Vitalis then responded to the Apostle Paul’s statement that God works in us both to will and to accomplish, as follows:

> “God works through his law and through his Scriptures so that we may will, whether we read them or hear them. But whether we consent or do not consent to them is so much our own affair that, if we wish, it comes to pass, whereas, if we do not wish, we render God’s working ineffectual in us.”

He interpreted the Psalmist in much the same way. He thought that the statement that the steps of a man are directed by the Lord was made because a person wills to follow the path when he follows God’s teaching, preceded by persuasion and followed by consent. He does this by natural freedom if he wishes, and does not do it if he does not wish; and he receives reward or punishment according to what he has done.

Augustine refuted this error of Vitalis—the same error later embraced by those called Semipelagians—chiefly in a letter written to Vitalis (Letter 217). The Church, he argued, offers prayers to God for unbelievers, so that they may be converted, and gives thanks for those same people once they have been converted to the faith. It also prays for the faithful, so that they may persevere, by God’s gift, in what they have begun to be.

Augustine did not think Vitalis’s mind so corrupt as to reject these practices. He also made use of Cyprian’s book on the Lord’s Prayer and another entitled *On Mortality*.

He proposed to Vitalis twelve statements concerning grace that settled the whole question, since each of them made clear that God’s grace precedes human wills and prepares them through grace, rather than being given because of their merits. The statements are these:

1. The unborn have done nothing good or evil in their own life; nor do they enter the miseries of this life according to the merits of some previous life. Rather, those born carnally according to Adam contract the contagion of ancient death through their first birth, and they are not freed from the punishment of eternal death—which, proceeding from one person, passes to all in a just condemnation—unless they are reborn through grace in Christ.

2. God’s grace is given neither to infants nor to adults according to merits.

3. To adults it is given for each individual act.

4. It is not given to all human beings; and to those to whom it is given, it is given not only without regard to the merits of their works, but also without regard to the merits of their will. This is especially evident in infants.

5. To those to whom it is given, it is given as God’s gratuitous mercy.

6. To those to whom it is not given, it is not given by the just judgment of God [Col. 0101].

7. We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each person may receive according to what he has done through the body, not according to what he would have done if he had lived longer, whether good or evil.

8. Infants too will receive good or evil according to what they have done through the body—that is, during the time they were in the body, when they believed or did not believe through the hearts and mouths of those carrying them, when they were baptized or not baptized, and so forth.

9. Blessed are the dead who die in the Lord; whatever they would have done had they lived longer does not concern them.

10. Those who believe in the Lord with their own heart do so by their own will and free choice.

11. On behalf of those who do not wish to believe, we who already believe act rightly when we pray to God that they may wish to believe.

12. On behalf of those among them who have believed, we ought rightly and truly to give thanks to God, and we are accustomed to do so, as for benefits received.

He says that he reduced these teachings to the number twelve so that they might more easily be committed to memory and held more distinctly. For catholic Christians, he says, it is absolutely certain that all these teachings belong to the true and catholic faith.

Finally, at the end of the letter he adds that, if Vitalis persists in his error, he must be dealt with differently, lest he lead others into error: that is, the obstinate man must be cut off from the body of the Church.

This letter to Vitalis appears to have been written after the disagreement among the people of Adrumetum and after the books composed to settle it. Vitalis, struggling with the same question as they, thought that human free will and God’s justice could not otherwise be preserved unless it were said that both faith and consent to divine persuasion come from us—that is, from our own will—so that each person would receive reward or punishment for what he had done through natural freedom.

But in the book *On Grace and Free Will*, Augustine had asserted the opposite: that faith itself and a good will come from God’s gift (see below, *On Grace and Free Will*, §16 ff.). Perhaps moved by this, Vitalis began to contradict him more openly and to respond to the testimonies of Paul and the Psalmist cited in that book (ibid., §32).

Augustine therefore presses and explains against Vitalis the verse from Psalm 36, which he had merely mentioned in the earlier book. He also refutes more fully, on the basis of the Church’s prayers for unbelievers, the argument that he had touched upon only briefly in that book.

### XXIX. Toward the end of Augustine’s life, the Semipelagians of Massilia rise up against the doctrine of predestination. Augustine defends it in his books to Prosper and Hilary, *On the Predestination of the Saints* and *On the Gift of Perseverance*.

During this final period of his life Augustine undertook another work against Julian’s second response. He continued it until the end of his life but left it unfinished. We shall discuss that unfinished work below, in a special introduction to it.

We shall now explain on what occasion God led the blessed Bishop, whom he had chosen as a defender of his grace, to affirm the doctrine of predestination before departing from this life. This doctrine necessarily followed from what Pelagius, even against his will, had conceded at the synod in Palestine: that grace is not given according to merits (see below, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, §41).

There were therefore many people at Massilia and elsewhere in Gaul who, through ignorance, persuaded themselves that everything Augustine had written in his books against the Pelagians concerning the calling of the elect according to God’s good pleasure was wholly contrary to the opinion of the Fathers and the judgment of the Church (Letter 225, §2).

They also thought that this doctrine produced negligence and lukewarmness in both saints and sinners, since, however they behaved, nothing other than what God had determined could happen to them. Consequently, even if the doctrine were entirely true, they thought it ought not to be made public, since, although it was not at all necessary, it would produce extremely dangerous effects and render the exhortations of those who encouraged others vain and ineffectual.

Their alienation from that catholic doctrine, from which they drew such offensive consequences, drove them into the well-known errors of the Semipelagians—a name they rightly acquired. Earlier they had held better and more orthodox views; but, lacking definite rules and foundations, they shifted their minds and opinions now in one direction, now in another (ibid., §6).

They thought that the beginning of faith and perseverance to the end were so much within our power that they were not gifts of God (see below, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, §42), or that God gave only such perseverance as a person could abandon by his own will (Letter 226, §4).

There were even some who departed so little from the paths of the Pelagians that they seemed to acknowledge no grace other than reason and free will, given by the Creator to a human being who had previously merited nothing (Letter 225, §4).

Nevertheless, those who embraced these errors were distinguished men, who had acquired great authority among the more simple through their devotion to every virtue and through the reputation for integrity that they enjoyed.

No one, however, is more exposed to accepting the impious opinions of the Pelagians—unless they guard themselves against themselves—than such men. Nor are people generally found more ready to misuse God’s benefits by becoming proud of them and attributing them to themselves than those who have been enriched by him with the greatest number of gifts.

This plague had seized a large part of the servants of Christ at Massilia—that is, the monks. No one is unaware that John Cassian, who had established the monastery there, propagated this same error in his writings, especially in his thirteenth *Conference*, which he published around the year 426, one year after Valentinian had ordered the Gallic bishops who followed Pelagius’s doctrines to be deposed and expelled.

The same error also gained considerable authority from the fact that some of those who defended it held the highest priestly rank, namely the episcopate, which they had recently attained (ibid., §7).

Hilary himself, the bishop of Arles who had succeeded Honoratus toward the end of 428, followed and admired Augustine in other matters of doctrine. Yet he was troubled by Augustine’s teaching concerning predestination and expressed some complaint about it. He wished to discuss his thoughts on this subject with the holy Doctor.

[Col. 0103] The authority of men so illustrious and so outstanding in the Church both for piety and for rank made their error more dangerous both to themselves and to others. The respect owed to them drew the inexperienced into imitation and at the same time restrained the tongues of the more knowledgeable through an unprofitable silence, so that scarcely anyone could be found who either admonished them or opposed the error they were teaching, except for a few fearless lovers of perfect grace (Letter 225, no. 7). Among these were Prosper and a certain Hilary, different from the bishop of Arles, since he belonged to the lay order (Letter 226, no. 9). This Hilary had once enjoyed the delights of Augustine’s companionship and had been nourished by the wholesome milk of his teaching. Therefore, although at that time, as is believable, he was enjoying the sight of his homeland and relatives, he nevertheless regarded himself as an exile. He seems to have left Augustine’s company with the intention of securing the salvation of his brother, who was bound by the marriage tie. The outcome proved that this had happened by divine providence. For, in addition to the defense of grace that he undertook in Gaul, his brother, with his wife’s consent, embraced continence, and both of them vowed to God that they would preserve it perfectly to the end of their lives (ibid., no. 2). In our opinion, nothing prevents us from thinking that this Hilary was the same man who, around the year 414, wrote to Augustine from Sicily about the errors of the Pelagians. Besides being tormented in spirit by the loss of the holy Teacher’s presence, he was also deeply distressed that doctrines so clear, taught by that holy man, were not only rejected but even criticized by those who understood them least. Accordingly, although, as a layman, he reverently displayed the respect that ecclesiastical custom requires toward men of such superior rank, he nevertheless did not remain silent when an opportunity arose; rather, according to the strength God had given him, he defended Catholic doctrine.

Prosper, who succeeded Augustine in the task and labor of defending grace, was an Aquitanian and, in Gennadius’s words, *sermone scholasticus*, that is, highly learned; altogether, he was a man distinguished both in character and in eloquence and zeal (Letter 226, no. 10), and not unworthy of the holy Bishop’s acquaintance. Although he indicates in some way that he himself belonged only to the lay order, when he declares that he was by no means the equal of the authority of the aforementioned Semi-Pelagians, who surpassed him greatly both in the merits of their lives and in the highest priestly dignity. He had never seen Augustine, but had merely sent him respectful greetings in letters conveyed through the deacon Leontius, through whom he also received the holy Bishop’s reply. Nevertheless, instructed both by reading Augustine and by God’s revelation, he recognized how utterly perverse it was to say that, once predestination and prevenient grace had been denied, the beginning of salvation depended on the one who is saved rather than on the one who saves, and that the human will supplied help to divine grace rather than grace subjecting the human will to itself (ibid., 225, nos. 6, 7). Disregarding the hostile efforts of others, he not only remained steadfast in this faith but also defended it against its attackers, using both the works of the holy Teacher and the testimonies of Scripture cited there, and arguments which he himself drew from the foundations Augustine had laid—fighting, that is, with powerful reasoning and those vigorous assertions in which, according to Gennadius’s testimony as well, he was strong.

At the first beginnings of this dispute, the people of Massilia preferred for a while to attribute the fault to their own slowness rather than condemn a doctrine they did not understand. Indeed, some among them wished to consult Augustine and asked him to publish a clearer and more explicit explanation of the matter. But, by the providential will of the merciful God, it happened that the book *On Rebuke and Grace* was brought to Massilia at that time. In that book the monks of Hadrumetum received such a full and decisive answer to the very issues that troubled the Massilians that the book seemed to have been written to settle the disturbances of controversy that had arisen in Gaul. When they saw the book, those who followed Augustine’s apostolic doctrine drew from it new light and greater support for defending it. Others, however, whose minds had already been occupied by error and were obstructed by their own darkness, found there nothing but further grounds for offense and more fervent hatred of the truth (ibid., no. 2).

Defending their own view in the name of antiquity, they branded the doctrine of predestination with the mark of novelty. In Augustine’s writings composed against the Pelagians, they asserted that whatever the holy Teacher had discussed there concerning the calling of the elect according to God’s purpose was contrary to the opinion of the Fathers and to the Church’s understanding. They said that no one had ever understood the relevant passages of Paul in that way. When asked how they themselves wished those passages to be explained, they admitted that no interpretation they found satisfactory occurred to them; instead, they ordered that one remain silent about matters whose profundity no one had reached. They produced statements from Augustine’s works written before the Pelagian heresy, as though these fully agreed with their own opinion. Moreover, whatever Augustine had opposed to himself from the other side in the book *On Rebuke and Grace*, they insistently repeated as supporting their position. What displeased them most, however, was the distinction made there between the grace given to Adam and that now given to us. Finally, they did not want the example of predestination to be taken from infants, since, they claimed, Augustine himself had previously held a different view of them in his books *On Free Will* (ibid., no. 3).

When the defenders of truth were oppressed by the authority of those whom the spirit of Pelagian impiety so mocked, they were compelled to ask the holy Bishop to oppose his own authority to theirs. Hilary wrote two letters to him on this subject. The first, which has been lost, may have dealt with that offensive formula concerning the proclamation of predestination which Augustine said his opponents had thrown in his face (below, *On the Gift of Perseverance*, no. 58). In the second, after Hilary had discussed the complaints of the opponents, he says: “Whatever you may wish or be able to do on behalf of that grace which, in you, we little ones admire together with the great, we shall receive with the greatest gratitude, as though it had been decreed for us by an authority most dear and most revered.” He also indicates that he had urged Prosper to write letters on the same matter, which he sends to Augustine together with his own (Letter 226, no. 10).

These letters of Prosper still exist. At their beginning he declares that he is writing to the holy Teacher not merely from the desire to greet him, as he had done in an earlier letter, but also out of devotion to the faith by which the Church lives. “Since your most vigilant diligence,” he says, “keeps watch for all the members of Christ’s body, and since you fight with the power of truth against the snares of heretical doctrines, I did not think that I needed to fear in any way being burdensome or troublesome to you in a matter that concerns the salvation of many and therefore your own piety. Rather, I believed that I would be guilty if I did not refer to the faith’s special champion matters which I understand to be extremely dangerous” (Letter 225, no. 1).
