After explaining the considerable venom contained in those remnants of Pelagian depravity, he adds: “We hope that not only our weakness will be strengthened by the support of your discussions, but that those whom the darkness of this opinion obscures, though distinguished by merits and honors, will also receive the most purified light of grace” (ibid., nos. 6, 9).

Although Augustine was troubled that anyone still dared to oppose Catholic doctrine, confirmed by so many and such manifest divine testimonies, he was nevertheless moved by Prosper and Hilary—men who, as we have said, belonged to the lay order, but whom he himself calls his dearest sons (below, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, no. 1)—and by their zeal and pious concern for those in error. He therefore wrote two books in their name, that is, to Prosper and Hilary. Both are found in the old Noaillian, Pratellian, and Metensian codices, and in Prosper himself: in *On Predestination*, part 3; at the beginning of *Prosper’s Responses to the Excerpts of the Genoese*; and in volume 1, in the variant reading at the end of the *Retractations*. The second book, however, has long been called *On the Gift of Perseverance*, perhaps because its title was altered by copyists.

In the first book he shows that the gift of God consists not only in the increase of faith but also in its beginning. He does not deny that he once thought otherwise about this matter and erred in works written before he was a bishop. But he indicates that he was later convinced chiefly by this testimony: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7). He proves that this testimony must also be understood of faith itself. He teaches that faith is among those things which must be counted as works, by which the Apostle denies that God’s grace is preceded. Grace removes hardness of heart; and all who come to Christ come because they are taught by the Father. Those whom he teaches, he teaches through mercy; those whom he does not teach, he does not teach through judgment. The passage from his own 102nd letter that had been brought against him can be correctly explained without compromising the doctrine of grace and predestination. He notes the difference between grace and predestination. By predestination, God foreknew those things which he himself was going to do. He wonders that the opponents of predestination, who are said not to want to be led into uncertainty about God’s will, prefer to entrust themselves to their own weakness rather than to the firmness of God’s promise. He shows that they misuse the text, “If you believe, you will be saved” (Rom. 10:9). The truth of grace and predestination shines forth in infants who are saved, distinguished by none of their own merits from the others who perish; for they are not distinguished by a foreknowledge of merits which they would have possessed had they lived longer. The most splendid example of predestination and grace, however, is the Savior himself, who acquired the status of Savior and only-begotten Son of God without any preceding merits of works or faith. The predestined are called by a particular calling proper to the elect. They were chosen before the foundation of the world, not because it was foreknown that they would believe and become holy, but so that they might become such through that very election of grace.

In the first part of the second book he proves that the perseverance by which one perseveres in Christ to the end is a gift of God. It would be ridiculous to ask this from God if one does not believe that it is given by God. Yet, according to Cyprian’s exposition, almost nothing else is requested in the Lord’s Prayer than perseverance. By that exposition the enemies of grace themselves were defeated before they were born. He teaches that the grace of perseverance is given not according to the merits of those who receive it, but to some through mercy and withheld from others by God’s just judgment. Why one adult rather than another is called, and likewise why one of two infants is taken up while the other is left, is inscrutable. More inscrutable still is why, among two godly persons, perseverance is given to one and not to the other. Yet this is absolutely certain: the former is among the predestined, while the latter is not. He observes that the mystery of predestination is shown by the Lord’s words concerning the people of Tyre and Sidon, who would have repented if the signs performed among them had been performed among Chorazin. He demonstrates that the example of infants is useful for confirming the truth of predestination and grace in adults, and he answers an objection by the opponents who had wrongly applied to this matter a passage from the third book of his work *On Free Will*. In the later part of the book he refutes their claim that the doctrine of predestination is harmful to the usefulness of exhortation and correction. On the contrary, he asserts that predestination is beneficially preached so that a person may glory not in himself but in God. The objections raised by these people against predestination can likewise be turned, in no dissimilar way, against God’s foreknowledge or against that grace which they agree is necessary for all other good things, except the beginning of faith and the perfection of perseverance. For the predestination of the saints is nothing other than the foreknowledge and preparation of God’s benefits, by which all who are delivered are most certainly delivered. Nevertheless, he orders that predestination be preached in a suitable manner, and not in such a way that, among the uneducated multitude, it seems to be refuted by the very fact of its proclamation. Finally, he commends to us the Lord Jesus, the most illustrious example of predestination set before our eyes.

Here they observe that Augustine treated the matter in those two books against his opponents with such light and force that he seems not so much to have exerted the powers of his own intellect as to have spoken under the inspiration of the divine Spirit (Rivius, book 4, chapter 10, no. 3).

The holy man adorned this excellent work—perhaps the last of those he was permitted to complete perfectly after the *Retractations*—with an outstanding conclusion, leaving there a record of the great modesty of his spirit in these final words:

“Those who read these things, if they understand them, should give thanks to God. But those who do not understand them should pray that he may be their inner teacher, from whose presence come knowledge and understanding. Those who think that I am in error should consider carefully, again and again, what has been said, lest perhaps they themselves be in error. But since, through those who read my labors, I become not only more learned but also more corrected, I acknowledge God as gracious to me. And this above all I expect from the teachers of the Church, if what I write comes into their hands and they deign to know what I write.”

[Note: [Col. 0107] More notable records of events occurring after Augustine’s death and near to his time concerning the remnants of the Pelagians—namely, under the Roman pontiffs Celestine, Sixtus, Leo, Gelasius, Hormisdas, Felix IV, and Boniface II—are presented below in the Appendix, together with Prosper’s *Apologies* against those same heretics, written in defense of the blessed defender of grace.]

[Col. 0107]

## FROM AUGUSTINE’S BOOK *ON HERESIES*, TO QUODVULTDEUS, HERESY 88

The heresy of the Pelagians is the most recent of all at the present time, having arisen from the monk Pelagius. Coelestius followed him as teacher so closely that their followers are still called Coelestians. They are so hostile to the grace of God—through which we have been predestined for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ and in him (Eph. 1:5), through which we are rescued from the power of darkness so that we may believe in him and be transferred into his kingdom (Col. 1:13), because of which he says, “No one comes to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6:66), and through which charity is poured into our hearts (Rom. 5:5), so that faith works through love (Gal. 5:6)—that they believe a human being can fulfill all the divine commandments without this grace. If that were true, the Lord would seem to have said in vain, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Finally, when Pelagius was rebuked by the brethren because he attributed nothing to the help of God’s grace in carrying out his commandments, he yielded to their correction only to the extent that he did not place grace before free will but, with faithless cunning, placed it beneath free will. He said that grace is given to human beings so that what they are commanded to do through free will they may fulfill more easily through grace. By saying “more easily,” he plainly wished it to be believed that, although with greater difficulty, human beings could nevertheless fulfill the divine commands without divine grace.

They say that the grace of God, without which we can do no good, exists only in free will, which our nature received from him without any preceding merits of its own. God assists it through his law and teaching only so that we may learn what we ought to do and what we ought to hope for, not so that, through the gift of his Spirit, we may do what we have learned must be done. Thus they acknowledge that knowledge is given to us by God, by which ignorance is driven away, but deny that charity is given, by which one lives piously. Their position is therefore that, although knowledge—which without charity puffs up—is God’s gift, charity itself—which builds up so that knowledge does not puff up—is not God’s gift (1 Cor. 8:1).

They also destroy the prayers offered by the Church, whether for unbelievers and those who resist the teaching of God, that they may be converted to God, or for the faithful, that their faith may increase and that they may persevere in it. They insist that human beings do not receive these things from God but possess them from themselves, saying that God’s grace, by which we are delivered from impiety, is given according to our merits. Pelagius, fearing that this position would be condemned at the episcopal judgment in Palestine, was indeed compelled to condemn it; but in his later writings he is found teaching it.

They go so far as to say that the lives of the righteous in this world contain absolutely no sin, and that the Church of Christ is perfected in this mortal life so that it is entirely “without spot or wrinkle” (Eph. 5:27), as though it were not Christ’s Church that cries out to God throughout the whole world, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12).

They also deny that infants, born carnally according to Adam, contract the contagion of the ancient death at their first birth. They assert that they are born entirely without any bond of original sin, so that there is absolutely nothing that must be forgiven them at a second birth. They say that they are baptized for this reason: that, adopted through regeneration, they may be admitted to the kingdom of God and transferred from good to better, rather than released by this renewal from some evil inherited obligation. For even if they are not baptized, they promise them—outside the kingdom of God, certainly, but nevertheless—a certain eternal and blessed life of their own.

They also say that Adam, even if he had not sinned, would have died bodily, and that he died not as the result of the guilt’s merit but by the condition of nature. Other objections are made against them as well, but these are the principal ones, from which it can be understood that all, or almost all, the others depend.

[Col. 0109]

[Note: [Col. 0107] On the books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, see book 2, chapter 33, of the *Retractations*, volume 1, column 643, from the words “Necessity also came” through the words “with great waves of anxiety.” M.]

## SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, *ON THE MERITS AND FORGIVENESS OF SINS AND ON THE BAPTISM OF INFANTS*, THREE BOOKS TO MARCELLINUS

[Note: [Col. 0109] Written in the year of Christ 412.]

[Note: [Col. 0109] The three books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins* have been revised in this new edition against three old Roman codices of the Vatican Library and ten Gallican manuscripts: one from the library of the most illustrious de Saint-Georges, royal-designated archbishop of Tours; one of the Church of Laon; one belonging to the Dominicans of the major convent in Paris on the Rue Saint-Jacques; one of the Sorbonne College; and codices from the abbeys of Corbie, Saint-Remi, Pratelles, Bec, Casal, and Cygirannus. They were also compared with variant readings collected through the care of the Louvain scholars from four Belgian manuscripts, as well as with the principal editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain—that is, those of Johann Amerbach, Desiderius Erasmus, and the Louvain theologians.]

[Note: [Col. 0109] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C)

## BOOK ONE

[Col. 0109]

He refutes those who say that Adam, even if he had not sinned, would have died, and that nothing from his sin was transmitted by generation to his descendants. He proves that human death followed not from the necessity of nature but from the merit of sin. He also teaches that Adam’s entire offspring was bound by Adam’s sin, showing that infants are baptized in order to receive the remission of original sin.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1. Preface

Although we are amid the great and pressing anxieties and vexations caused by those who abandon the law of God [Note: [Col. 0109] Perhaps by the Donatists, who at that time were attacking the Catholics. See Augustine’s letters 133 and 131.], even if we also attribute these very circumstances to the merits of our own sins, I did not wish to remain in your debt any longer, dearest Marcellinus, because of your zeal, by which you are dearer and more pleasing to me; indeed, to speak truthfully, I could not do so. Either the very charity by which, in the One who is unchangeable, we are one and are changed for the better, or the fear that I might offend God in you—God who gave you such a desire, and whom I serve by serving the one to whom he gave it—compelled me; yes, it compelled me, led me, and drew me to the best of my ability to resolve the questions that you had assigned to me in writing. Thus this matter prevailed for a little while in my mind over other concerns, until I had accomplished something by which it would be clear that I had served, though not adequately, yet obediently, your good will and that of those who care about these matters.

## CHAPTER TWO

### 2. Adam would not have died if he had not sinned

Those who say that Adam was created in such a way that he would have died even without the merit of sin—not as the punishment of guilt but by the necessity of nature—plainly try to refer the statement made in the Law, “On the day when you eat, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2:17), not to the death of the body but to the death of the soul, which occurs in sin [Note: [Col. 0109] The editions of Amerbach and Erasmus read, “which is in sin.” The Casal manuscript reads, “which sin produces,” omitting the preposition *in*.]. By this death, the Lord indicated that unbelievers were dead, when he said, “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. 8:22).

What, then, will they answer when we read that God, rebuking and condemning the first man even after his sin, said to him: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19)? For Adam was earth not according to the soul but, as is obvious, according to the body, and he was going to return to earth through the death of that same body. Although according to the body he was earth and bore an animal body in which he had been created, nevertheless, if he had not sinned, he would have been changed into a spiritual body and would have passed into that incorruption which is promised to the faithful and the saints without the danger of death [Note: [Col. 0110] Two Belgian manuscripts and one Vatican manuscript read, “without the punishment of death.”].

We ourselves not only feel within us a desire for this, but also recognize it through the Apostle’s reminder, where he says: “For in this we groan, desiring to be clothed over with our dwelling that is from heaven, if indeed, once clothed, we shall not be found naked. For we who are in this dwelling groan, being burdened, because we do not wish to be unclothed but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Cor. 5:2–4). Therefore, if Adam had not sinned, he would not have been unclothed of the body but clothed over with immortality and incorruption, so that what was mortal might be swallowed up by life—that is, so that he might pass from the animal state into the spiritual.

## CHAPTER THREE

### 3. To be mortal is different from being subject to death

There was no reason to fear that, if he lived here longer in an animal body [Note: [Col. 0110] Louvain, from three Belgian manuscripts: “if, by living here longer…”], he might be weighed down by old age and gradually grow old until he reached death. For if God granted to the garments and footwear of the Israelites that they were not worn out over so many years (Deut. 29:5), why should it be surprising if his power granted the obedient man, who possessed an animal and mortal body [Note: [Col. 0111] Four Gallican manuscripts of excellent quality and two Belgian manuscripts read, “who possessed this animal mortal body.” Some others read, “this animal, that is, mortal body,” and so forth.], a certain condition in that body by which he could remain for many years without deterioration [Note: [Col. 0111] Earlier editions read, “old.” Almost all the manuscripts, however, read, “of years.” Three others read, “aged”], for as long as God wished, passing from mortality to immortality without an intervening death?

For just as this flesh which we now have is not invulnerable simply because it need not necessarily be wounded, so that body was not therefore immortal simply because it need not necessarily die. I think that such a condition was granted even in an animal and mortal body to those who were transferred from here without death. For Enoch and Elijah did not wither with old age over so long a span of life. Yet I do not believe that they have already been changed into that spiritual quality of body which is promised in the resurrection, the first instance of which preceded in the Lord. Perhaps, however, they do not need even these foods, which restore those who consume them; rather, since they were transferred, they live in such a way that they possess a satiety like that of Elijah during the forty days when he lived without food on a cup of water and a cake of bread (4 Kings 2:11) [Note: [Col. 0111] The manuscripts read *collyrida*—“a cake”—rather than *collyride*.]. Or, if they do need such supports, perhaps they are fed in paradise in the way Adam was fed before he deserved to leave it because of sin. For, as I suppose, he obtained from the fruits of the trees refreshment against exhaustion and from the tree of life stability against aging.

## CHAPTER FOUR

### 4. The death of the body also resulted from sin

Besides the fact that, in punishing him, God said, “You are earth, and into earth you shall go”—a statement which, unless it refers to the death of the body, I do not know how to understand—there are also other testimonies which make it completely evident that the human race deserved the death not only of the spirit but also of the body because of sin.

The Apostle says to the Romans: “If Christ is in you, the body is indeed dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. And if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:10–11). I think that so clear and open a statement needs not an interpreter but merely a reader [Note: [Col. 0111] The Casal manuscript reads, “a reporter.”]. “The body,” he says, “is dead,” not because of its earthly fragility, because it was made from the dust of the earth, but because of sin. What more do we seek? And he most carefully did not say “mortal,” but “dead.”

## CHAPTER FIVE

### 5. Mortal, dead, and destined to die

Before it was changed into that incorruption which is promised in the resurrection of the saints, it could be mortal although it was not destined to die, just as our present body can, so to speak, be capable of illness although it is not destined to become ill. What flesh is there that cannot become ill, even if it should die for some reason before becoming ill? In the same way, that body was already mortal; a change into eternal incorruption would have consumed that mortality if righteousness—that is, obedience—had remained in the human being. But the mortal body itself did not become dead except because of sin. Since the future change in the resurrection will possess not only no death—the death that came about because of sin—but also no mortality, which the animal body possessed before sin, he did not say, “He who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will give life to your dead bodies,” although he had previously said, “the body is dead.” Rather, he says, “he will give life to your mortal bodies,” so that they may then be not only no longer dead but not even mortal, when the animal body rises as spiritual, this mortal body puts on immortality, and what is mortal is swallowed up by life (1 Cor. 15:44, 53–54).

## CHAPTER SIX

### 6. How the body is dead because of sin

It would be remarkable if anything clearer than this exposition were sought. Unless perhaps we must listen to the objection made against this clarity, namely, that we should understand the dead body here in the sense in which it is said, “Put to death your members which are upon the earth” (Col. 3:5). But in that sense the body is put to death because of righteousness, not because of sin; for in order to do righteousness we put to death our members which are upon the earth.

Or, if they think that “because of sin” was added so that we should not understand that sin has been committed but that sin should not be committed—as though he were saying, “The body is dead because of sin not being committed”—what then does it mean that, after adding “but the spirit is life,” he added “because of righteousness”? It would have been enough if he had added, “the life of the spirit” [Note: [Col. 0112] Amerbach and Erasmus: “It would be enough if he added.” Louvain: “if he were to add in this way.”], so that here too one might understand “because of sin not being committed.” In that case we would understand both statements as referring to one thing: that the body is dead and the spirit is life because of sin not being committed.

Indeed, even if he had intended to say only “because of righteousness”—that is, “because of righteousness being done”—both statements could be referred to this: that the body is dead and the spirit is life because of righteousness being done [Note: [Col. 0112] Amerbach and Erasmus: “both could be referred to this.”]. But now he said both that the body is dead because of sin and that the spirit is life because of righteousness, assigning different merits to different things: to the death of the body, the merit of sin; to the life of the spirit, the merit of righteousness. Therefore, if, as cannot be doubted, the spirit is life because of righteousness—that is, through the merit of righteousness—then what else can or ought we understand by “the body is dead because of sin” than “through the merit of sin,” if we do not arbitrarily distort and twist the Scripture’s most explicit meaning?

The light of the words that follow also contributes to this. When he was defining the grace of the present time, he said that the body is dead because of sin, because, in the body not yet renewed through the resurrection, the merit of sin remains—that is, the necessity of death. He said that the spirit is life because of righteousness, because, although we are still burdened with this body of death, we already breathe toward the righteousness of faith through the renewal begun according to the inner person [Col. 0113] [Note: [Col. 0113] Perhaps, “righteousness.”]. Yet, so that human ignorance might not hope for nothing concerning the resurrection of the body, he also said that the very thing which, because of the merit of sin, he had called dead in the present age would be given life in the future because of the merit of righteousness—not in such a way that it would merely become living from dead, but also immortal from mortal.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

### 7. The life of the body is to be hoped for, since the life of the spirit has already preceded it

Although I fear that a manifest matter may be made obscure by explaining it, nevertheless attend to the light of the apostolic statement. “If Christ,” he says, “is in you, the body is indeed dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness.”

This was said so that people would not think that they had received no benefit, or only a small benefit, from the grace of Christ because they must necessarily die bodily. They ought to understand that the body still bears the merit of sin and is bound to the condition of death, but that the spirit has already begun to live because of the righteousness of faith—the spirit which itself had been extinguished in the human being by a certain death of unbelief.

“Therefore,” he says, “do not think that little has been bestowed upon you through the fact that Christ is in you: although the body is dead because of sin, your spirit now lives because of righteousness. Nor should you therefore despair of the life of the body itself. For if the Spirit of him who raised Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you.”

Why is the smoke of controversy still cast over so great a light? The Apostle cries out: “The body is indeed dead in you because of sin, but your mortal bodies also will be given life because of righteousness, because of which your spirit is already life—something that will be wholly completed through the grace of Christ, that is, through his Spirit dwelling in you.” And still there is objection!

He also explains how life turns death within itself into life by putting death to death [Note: [Col. 0113] The editions read, “so that life may turn death within itself into life by putting it to death.” The Vatican manuscripts more suitably read, “so that life, that is, the spirit, by putting the body to death, may make it spiritual and alive.” The Cygirannus codex reads, “so that life may turn death within itself into life by giving life to it and putting it to death.”]. “Therefore, brothers,” he says, “we are debtors not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live” (Rom. 8:10–13). What else does this mean than: If you live according to death, everything will die; but if, by living according to life, you put death to death, everything will live? [Note: [Col. 0113] Four Gallican manuscripts and some Belgian manuscripts read, “if you give life to death.”]

## CHAPTER EIGHT

### 8. In what sense Paul’s words are to be understood

Likewise, when he says, “Through a human being came death, and through a human being the resurrection of the dead,” what else can this mean than the death of the body? For when he said this, he was speaking about the resurrection of the body and urging it with the most intense and ardent insistence.

What, then, does he say here to the Corinthians: “Through a human being came death, and through a human being the resurrection of the dead. For just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be given life” (1 Cor. 15:21–22), unless it is the same as what he also says to the Romans: “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin, death” (Rom. 5:12)?

They want this death to be understood as the death not of the body but of the soul, as though something different had been said to the Corinthians—“Through a human being came death”—where they are not permitted at all to understand the death of the soul, because the subject was the resurrection of the body, which is contrary to the death of the body. For this reason, only death is mentioned there as having come through a human being, and not sin as well, because the subject was not righteousness, which is contrary to sin, but the resurrection of the body, which is contrary to the death of the body.

## CHAPTER NINE
### 9. Sin passed to all by propagation, not merely by imitation

You indicated in your letter that they are trying to twist this apostolic testimony—“Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death”—into some other novel opinion; but you did not say what exactly they think these words mean. From what I have learned elsewhere, however, they hold that the death mentioned there is not bodily death—which they do not want Adam to have deserved by sinning—but the death of the soul, which occurs in sin itself [Note: The printed editions have *sit* (“is”); the manuscripts have *fit* (“becomes”). One manuscript, the Cygirannian, reads *quo ipso peccato fit* (“which becomes [death] through that very sin”). See above, §2.]. They also hold that sin itself passed from the first man into other human beings not by propagation but by imitation. For this reason they refuse to believe that original sin is remitted in infants through Baptism, since they insist that no such sin exists at all in those being born.

But if the Apostle had wished to mention the sin that entered this world not by propagation but by imitation [Note: Several manuscripts have *intravit* (“entered”).], he would have called its author not Adam but the devil, of whom it is written: “From the beginning the devil sins” (1 John 3:8). Of him we also read in the Book of Wisdom: “But through the devil’s envy death entered the world.” Since this death came from the devil to human beings not because they were propagated from him, but because they imitated him, the text immediately adds: “But those who belong to his side imitate him” (Wisdom 2:24–25). Accordingly, when the Apostle mentioned the sin and death that passed from one person to all by propagation, he made that one the author from whom the propagation of the human race took its beginning.

### 10.

They certainly imitate Adam—those who transgress God’s command through disobedience. But one thing is an example for those who sin by their will; another is an origin for those born with sin. The saints of Christ also imitate him in pursuing righteousness. Hence the same Apostle says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). Yet beyond this imitation, his grace also works inwardly in our illumination and justification, by that work of which the same preacher says: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7).

[Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read *Haec enim gratia* (“For this grace”); less correctly.] By this grace he also incorporates baptized infants into his body, although they are certainly not yet able to imitate anyone. Therefore, just as the one in whom all are made alive [Note: This is the manuscript reading. The editions have: “in whom all will be made alive, besides that.”], in addition to offering himself as an example to those who imitate him for righteousness, also gives the faithful the utterly hidden grace of his Spirit, which he secretly infuses even into infants, so also the one in whom all die, besides being an example of imitation to those who willingly transgress the Lord’s commandment, has also corrupted in himself, through the hidden decay of his carnal concupiscence, all who come from his stock [Note: Most manuscripts have *venturos* (“those who will come”), rather than *venientes* (“those who come”).].

For this reason, and for no other, the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.” If I were to say this, these people would resist me and loudly proclaim that I was speaking and thinking incorrectly. For in these words they would understand no statement concerning any human being [Note: Several manuscripts add *haec dicere* (“to say this”); the printed editions have *qui diceret haec* (“who would say this”). It is a gloss absent from some manuscripts.] except the very one they refuse to understand in the Apostle. But because these are the words of someone whose authority and teaching they cannot withstand, they reproach us for slowness of understanding while trying to twist words spoken with such clarity into something else.

“Through one man,” he says, “sin entered into the world, and through sin death.” This concerns propagation, not imitation. For if it concerned imitation, he would have said, “Through the devil” [Note: The editions of Amerbach and Erasmus read *nam per diabolum diceret* (“for he would have said, ‘through the devil’”), omitting *si imitationis* (“if it concerned imitation”), which Lovanius and several manuscripts add, although it is not necessary.]. Everyone agrees that this first man is the one called Adam. “And so,” he says, “it passed into all human beings.”

### Chapter X

#### 11. The distinction between actual and original sin

Next consider the statement that follows: “In whom all sinned.” How carefully, precisely, and unambiguously it is expressed! If you understand the sin that entered the world through one man as the sin “in whom all sinned” [Note: The Greek reads *eph’ hō*, which does not agree in gender with *hamartia* (“sin”), the noun used there to signify sin. Compare *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 4, §7.], then it is certainly clear that there are individual sins proper to each person, in which only those whose sins they are sin, and that there is another, single sin in which all sinned, because all were that one man.

But if it is not sin that is understood, but that one man in whom all sinned, what could be clearer than this? We read that those who believe in Christ are justified in him through the hidden sharing and inspiration of spiritual grace, by which whoever clings to the Lord becomes one spirit with him, although Christ’s saints also imitate him. Let someone show me any comparable statement about those who imitated his saints: has anyone ever been said to be justified in Paul, or in Peter, or in any of those whose authority is so eminent among God’s people? We are said to be blessed in Abraham, certainly, as it was said to him: “In you all nations will be blessed” (Genesis 12:3; Galatians 3:8), because of Christ, who according to the flesh is his offspring. This is stated even more clearly when the same thing is expressed as follows: “In your offspring all nations will be blessed” (Genesis 22:18).

I do not know whether anyone can find in the divine Scriptures that anyone is said to have sinned or to sin in the devil, although all the wicked and ungodly imitate him. Yet when the Apostle says of the first man, “In whom all sinned,” the dispute about the propagation of sin still continues, and some sort of cloud of imitation is set against it [Note: Good manuscripts read: “while the dispute about the propagation of sin still continues, some sort of cloud of imitation is set against it.”].

#### 12.

Consider also what follows. After saying, “In whom all sinned,” he adds: “For until the law sin was in the world.” That is, the law could not remove sin, although it entered in so that sin might abound—whether this means the natural law, under which each person, once he begins to use reason, adds his own sins to original sin, or the law given to the people in written form through Moses. For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness would have come entirely through the law. But Scripture confined everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ (Galatians 3:21–22).

“Sin was not counted,” however, when there was no law. What does “was not counted” mean except “was not known, and was not thought to be sin”? Yet God the Lord did not regard it as though it did not exist, since it is written: “All who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law” (Romans 2:12).

### Chapter XI

#### 13. What the Apostle means by the reign of death

“But death reigned,” he says, “from Adam to Moses”—that is, from the first man even to the law itself, which was promulgated by divine authority, because the law itself could not remove the reign of death. He means by the reign of death the condition in which the guilt of sin so dominates human beings that it does not permit them to come to eternal life, which is true life, but draws them even toward the second death, which is eternal in punishment.

Only the grace of the Savior destroys this reign of death in any person. This grace was also at work in the ancient saints, all those who, before Christ came in the flesh, nevertheless belonged to his assisting grace and not to the letter of the law, which could command but could not help. This was hidden in the Old Testament according to the most just dispensation of the times; now it is revealed in the New.

Therefore death reigned in all from Adam to Moses who were not helped by Christ’s grace, so that the reign of death might be destroyed in them—even in those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression [Note: Some manuscripts read *in similitudine* (“in the likeness”) rather than *in similitudinem* (“into the likeness”). This is how the Cygirannian manuscript reads. Other manuscripts have *ergo in eis* (“therefore in them”); the editions have *ergo et in eis* (“therefore also in them”).]—that is, those who had not yet sinned by their own individual will as he did, but had drawn original sin from him. He is “the form of the one to come,” because in him the pattern of condemnation was established for future descendants who would be created from his stock, so that all might be born from one person into condemnation, from which only the Savior’s grace delivers them.

I know that most Latin manuscripts read as follows [Note: Compare Letter 157, §19.]: “Death reigned from Adam to Moses over those who sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression.” Those who read it this way also refer it to the same meaning: they understand those to have sinned “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” who sinned in him, so that they were created like him—just as human beings come from a human being, sinners from a sinner, the dying from one who is dying, and the condemned from one who is condemned [Note: The Remigian manuscript and several Belgian manuscripts read *damnandi* (“who are to be condemned”).]. But the Greek manuscripts from which the Latin translation was made, either all or nearly all of them, have the wording that I first gave.

#### 14.

“But,” he says, “the gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through the trespass of one, much more did the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abound for many.” He does not mean “more many,” that is, many more human beings—for more are not justified than are condemned—but “abounded much more.”

Adam, through his one trespass, generated the guilty. Christ, however, by his grace both releases and forgives the trespasses that human beings have added by their own will to the original sin in which they were born. He states this more clearly in what follows.

### Chapter XII

#### 15. One sin common to all

Consider more carefully what he says: “Because of the trespass of one, many died.” Why because of that one person’s trespass, and not rather because of their own individual trespasses, if imitation rather than propagation is to be understood here?

But consider what follows: “And the gift is not like what came through one who sinned. For judgment from one trespass led to condemnation, but grace from many trespasses led to justification.” Let them now say where that imitation has a place in these words. “From one,” he says, “to condemnation.” From one what, if not from one trespass? He explains this when he adds: “But grace from many trespasses to justification.”

Why, then, does judgment from one trespass lead to condemnation, while grace from many trespasses leads to justification? If there is no original trespass, does not judgment, just as grace leads to justification, also lead human beings to condemnation because of many trespasses? For grace does not forgive many trespasses without judgment also condemning many trespasses.

Or if they are led from one trespass to condemnation because all the trespasses that are condemned were committed in imitation of that one trespass, then for the same reason they should be understood to be led from one trespass to justification, because all the trespasses forgiven in those who are justified were committed in imitation of that one trespass.

But surely the Apostle did not understand this when he said: “Judgment from one trespass led to condemnation, but grace from many trespasses led to justification”? On the contrary, let us understand the Apostle and see that judgment is said to proceed from one trespass to condemnation because it would be sufficient for condemnation even if human beings had no sin except original sin.

Although the condemnation of those who have joined their own sins to original sin is more severe—and is more severe for each person in proportion to the gravity of the sin committed [Note: The editions have *quanto gravius quisque peccavit* (“the more gravely each person sinned”); the manuscripts have *quanto gravius quis peccavit* (“the more gravely a person sinned”).]—nevertheless, even original sin alone not only separates a person from the kingdom of God, into which even they themselves confess that infants who die without receiving Christ’s grace cannot enter; it also makes them strangers to salvation and eternal life, since there can be no other salvation and eternal life than the kingdom of God, into which only fellowship with Christ brings us.

### Chapter XIII

[Col. 0118]

#### 16. How death came through one and life through one

Accordingly, from Adam, in whom all sinned, we derived not all our sins, but only original sin [Note: One Belgian manuscript has *traximus* (“we drew”) instead of *traduximus* (“we transmitted” or “derived”).]. From Christ, however, in whom all are justified [Note: Six manuscripts have *justificantur* (“are justified”).], we obtain forgiveness not only of that original sin but also of the other sins that we ourselves have added.

Therefore the gift is not like what came through one who sinned. For judgment from one trespass—if it is not forgiven, that is, original sin—can already lead to condemnation; but grace from many forgiven trespasses, that is, not only from original sin but also from all the others, leads to justification.

#### 17.

“For if, because of one trespass, death reigned through one, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ.”

Why did death reign through one because of one trespass, unless it is because they were held by the bond of death in that one in whom all sinned, even if they added no personal sins? Otherwise [Note: Amerbach and Erasmus read *non solum* (“not only”).] death did not reign through one because of one trespass, but because of the many trespasses of many people, through each person who sinned.

For if the others died because of another man’s trespass because they followed him, who sinned before them, by imitating him, then he too—and all the more so—died because of another’s trespass: the devil had preceded him in sinning and had himself persuaded him to sin. But Adam did not persuade his imitators; and many who are said to be his imitators either have never heard that he existed and committed such an act, or do not believe it at all.

How much more reasonably, then, as I have already said, would the Apostle have made the devil the author, saying that sin and death passed from that one through all, if he had wished to speak here not of propagation but of imitation? Adam is much more reasonably called an imitator of the devil, since he had the devil as the persuader of his sin, than anyone could be called an imitator of one who persuaded no one to do such a thing, or whom he does not know.

What does “those who receive the abundance of grace and righteousness” [Note: The editions read *quod* (“what”) rather than *qui* (“those who”).] mean except that the grace of forgiveness is given not only for the sin in which all sinned, but also for the sins they added? Such righteousness is bestowed on these people that, although Adam consented to the one who persuaded him to sin, they do not yield even to one who compels them.

And what does “they will reign much more in life” mean, when the reign of death draws many more into eternal punishment, except that we understand the same people to be spoken of in both cases—those who pass from Adam to Christ, that is, from death to life—because they will reign without end in eternal life, for longer than death reigned in them temporarily and with an end?

#### 18.

“Therefore, just as through one trespass condemnation came to all human beings, so also through one justification justification of life came to all human beings.”

If we attend to imitation, this “one trespass” can only be the devil’s. But since it is clear that Adam, not the devil, is meant, it remains that we must understand not imitation but the propagation of sin.

### Chapter XIV

#### No one justifies except Christ

The statement about Christ, “through one justification,” expresses the matter more precisely than if he had said, “through the righteousness of one.” For he is speaking of the justification by which Christ justifies the ungodly; he did not offer this as an example to be imitated, but he alone can accomplish it.

The Apostle could rightly say: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11:1). But he would never say: “Be justified by me, as I also have been justified by Christ.” There can be, and are, and have been many righteous human beings who are worthy of imitation; but no one is both righteous and justifying except Christ.

Hence it is said: “To the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness” (Romans 4:5). Therefore, whoever dares to say, “I justify you,” must also say, “Believe in me.” No saint could rightly say this, except the Holy One of holies: “Believe in God, and believe in me” (John 14:1) [Note: The editions have *creditis* (“you believe”); the manuscripts have *credite* (“believe”), as Augustine commonly follows the Greek *pisteuete*.]. Thus, because he himself justifies the ungodly, faith is counted as righteousness for the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly.

### Chapter XV

#### 19. He confirms that sin comes through propagation, just as righteousness comes through regeneration. How all are sinners through Adam and all are righteous through Christ

If imitation alone makes people sinners through Adam, why does imitation alone not also make people righteous through Christ? For he says: “Just as through one trespass condemnation came to all human beings, so also through one justification justification of life came to all human beings.”

Accordingly, these “one and one” should have been not Adam and Christ, but Adam and Abel. For although many sinners preceded us during the course of this life, and those who sinned later imitated them, these people nevertheless insist that only Adam is meant as the one in whom all sinned by imitation, because he was the first of human beings to sin.

Accordingly, Abel should have been named as the one in whom all human beings are similarly justified by imitation, since he was the first human being to live righteously. Or, if Christ was established as the head of the righteous for the sake of a particular period belonging to the beginning of the New Testament, then Judas, his betrayer, should have been established as the head of sinners.

But if Christ is the one in whom all are justified because his imitation alone does not make people righteous, but grace regenerates them through the Spirit, then Adam is likewise the one in whom all sinned because his imitation alone does not make people sinners, but punishment generates them through the flesh.

For this reason also the text says “all” and “all.” Those who are generated through Adam are not all the same people who are regenerated through Christ; nevertheless, the statement is rightly made because, just as no one’s bodily generation occurs except through Adam, so no one’s spiritual generation occurs except through Christ.

For if some could be generated in the flesh without Adam [Note: The editions read *regenerari* (“be regenerated”); the manuscripts read *generari* (“be generated”).], and some could be generated in the spirit without Christ, they would not properly be called “all” in either case. Yet he later calls these same “all” “many.” For a group can be “all” in some respect even when it is small. Bodily generation has many, and spiritual generation also has many, although the latter does not have as many as the former.

Nevertheless, just as bodily generation includes all human beings, so spiritual generation includes all righteous human beings. For just as no one is a human being apart from the former, so no one is a righteous human being apart from the latter; and there are many in both. For just as through the disobedience of one man the many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one man the many will be made righteous.

#### 20.

“The law entered in so that trespass might abound.” Human beings added this to original sin by their own will, not through Adam. But this too is released and healed through Christ, because “where sin abounded, grace abounded exceedingly” [Note: The editions have *superabundavit et gratia* (“grace also abounded exceedingly”). The conjunction *et* (“also”) is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek of the Apostle.].

Thus, just as sin reigned in death—including the sin that human beings did not draw from Adam but added by their own will—so grace might also reign through righteousness unto eternal life. Yet there is no righteousness apart from Christ, as there are sins apart from Adam.

Therefore, when he said, “just as sin reigned in death,” he did not add “through one” or “through Adam,” because above he had also spoken of that sin which abounded when the law entered, and this is certainly not original but already belongs to the will of the individual.

But when he said, “so also grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life,” he added, “through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 5:12–21), because through the flesh’s generation only that which is original sin is drawn [Note: In the *Enchiridion*, written many years later, Augustine stated (§13) that it could not implausibly be said that infants are bound not only by the sins of their first parents but also by the sins of their own parents from whom they were born, and that before regeneration they are held under the divine sentence: “I will repay the sins of the fathers upon the children.” The Master of the Sentences, book 2, chapter 33, shows that Augustine said this not as an assertion of his own position, but while reporting various opinions. He did, however, state it with the rule and moderation that he required in *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 6, §14—namely, “that in the depths of Scripture’s meaning it is better to devote oneself to careful inquiry than to rash affirmation.”]; but through the Spirit’s regeneration forgiveness is effected not only of original sins but also of voluntary sins.

### Chapter XVI

#### 21. Unbaptized infants are condemned with the mildest condemnation, though they are nevertheless condemned. The grace of the body was lost as punishment for Adam’s sin

Accordingly, it can rightly be said that infants who leave the body without Baptism will be in the mildest possible condemnation. But the person who proclaims that they will not be in condemnation is greatly deceived and greatly deceives others, since the Apostle says: “Judgment from one trespass led to condemnation,” and shortly afterward: “Through one trespass condemnation came to all human beings.”

When Adam sinned by disobeying God, his body—although it was animal and mortal—then lost the grace by which it had obeyed his soul in every respect. Then there arose in him that shameful bestial movement at which he blushed in his nakedness. Then also, through a disease arising from sudden and deadly corruption, it came about that, having lost the stability of the age in which they had been created, they proceeded through successive ages toward death.

Although they lived many years afterward, they began to die on the day when they received the law of death, by which they would grow old. For whatever moves gradually toward an end through continual change does not remain still even for a moment of time, but slips onward without interruption—not toward completion, but toward decay.

Thus what God had said was fulfilled: “On the day when you eat from it, you will die by death” (Genesis 2:17). Therefore, because of this disobedience of the flesh, because of this law of sin and death, everyone who is generated carnally needs to be regenerated spiritually, so that he may not only be brought to the kingdom of God but also be freed from the condemnation of sin.

They are therefore born in the flesh simultaneously subject to the sin and death of the first man, and in Baptism they are reborn simultaneously joined to the righteousness and eternal life of the second man. As it is also written in Ecclesiasticus: “From a woman sin had its beginning, and through her we all die” (Ecclesiasticus 25:33). Whether it is said to be from the woman or from Adam, both refer to the first man, since, as we know, the woman is from the man, and the flesh of both is one. Hence also the statement that is written: “And the two will be one flesh. Therefore,” says the Lord, “they are no longer two but one flesh” (Matthew 19:5–6).

### Chapter XVII

#### 22. Personal sin must not be attributed to infants

For this reason those who say that infants are baptized so that what they contracted as their own in this life may be forgiven them, and not what they derived from Adam, are not difficult to refute. When they themselves reflect for a little while, without any desire to quarrel, on how absurd and unworthy of discussion their claim is, they will immediately change their position.

If they refuse to do so, we should not despair so greatly of human understanding that we fear they may persuade anyone of this. They themselves, unless I am mistaken, were driven to say this by the prejudice of some other opinion. Since they necessarily admitted that sins are remitted in the baptized, but did not want to admit that the sin they confessed to be remitted in infants was derived from Adam, they were forced to accuse infancy itself—as though an accuser of infancy would be safer the less able the accused was to answer him.

But let us leave these people aside, as I have said. No speech or proof is needed to establish the innocence of infants as far as concerns the life they lead in themselves from the time of their recent birth, if human understanding, unsupported by any aid from argument, does not recognize it.

### Chapter XVIII

#### 23. He refutes those who say that infants are baptized not for the remission of sin but to obtain the kingdom of heaven

But those who say that infants newly brought forth from their mothers’ wombs receive Baptism not for the remission of sin, but so that, not possessing spiritual generation [Note: The Corbie manuscript and two others read *procreationem habentes* (“possessing spiritual generation”), omitting the negative.], they may be created in Christ and become participants in the kingdom of heaven—sons and heirs of God, and co-heirs of Christ—appear to offer something worthy of consideration and examination.

Yet when they are asked whether the unbaptized, who have not been made co-heirs of Christ and participants in the kingdom of heaven, at least possess the benefit of eternal salvation in the resurrection of the dead, they struggle intensely and find no way out.

For what Christian could endure the claim that someone can attain eternal salvation without being reborn in Christ, when Christ willed this rebirth to take place through Baptism, at the very time when this Sacrament was to be instituted for those being regenerated in the hope of eternal salvation?

Hence the Apostle says: “He saved us, not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy, through the washing of regeneration” (Titus 3:5). Yet he says that this salvation is held in hope while we live here, when he says: “For in hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8:24–25).

Who would dare to affirm, then, that infants can be saved eternally without this regeneration, as though Christ had not died for them? For “Christ died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6). These infants, as is clear, have committed nothing ungodly in their own lives. If they are also held by no bond of ungodliness originally, how did the one who died for the ungodly die for them?

If they are wounded by no sickness of original sin, why are they carried with devout fear to Christ the physician—that is, to receive the Sacrament of eternal salvation? Why is it not said to them in the Church: “Take these innocent ones away; the healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are sick; Christ did not come to call the righteous, but sinners”? Such an invention has never been said, is never said [Note: The manuscripts have *nunquam dicatur* (“let it never be said”).], and will never be said at all in the Church of Christ.

### Chapter XIX

#### 24. Infants are called believers and likewise penitents. Only sins separate human beings from God

And lest anyone think that infants ought to be brought to Baptism because, just as they are not sinners, so they are not righteous, how do some recall that the merit of this age was praised by the Lord, when he said: “Let the little children come to me; for of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19:14)?

If this was said not because of a likeness to humility—which makes people little—but because of the praiseworthy life of children, then they are certainly righteous. For it could not rightly have been said otherwise: “Of such is the kingdom of heaven,” since it can belong only to the righteous.

Perhaps, however, it is not fitting to say that the Lord praised the life of infants when he said, “Of such is the kingdom of heaven,” since the true interpretation is that he placed a likeness to humility in their early age.

Nevertheless, perhaps we should hold to what I said: infants ought to be baptized because, just as they are not sinners, so they are not righteous. But when it had been said, “I have not come to call the righteous,” as though someone had replied, “Whom, then, have you come to call?”, he immediately added: “But sinners to repentance” (Luke 5:32).

Accordingly, just as he does not come to call them if they are righteous, so also, if they are not sinners, he does not come to call them—he who said, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.” And so they seem to rush into the Baptism of the one who does not call them not merely uselessly but even irreverently—God forbid that we should think this.

The physician therefore calls them—not those who are healthy, but those who are sick—and he has not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance. And because they are not yet held liable for any sins of their own lives, the original sickness in them is healed by the grace of the one who saves through the washing of regeneration.

#### 25.

Someone may say: “How, then, are they also called to repentance? Can such tiny children repent of anything?” [Note: This is how the Vatican manuscript reads. Other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, have *tantillus* (“so tiny”).]

The answer is: If they should not be called penitents because they do not possess the faculty of repentance [Note: The editions have *nondum habent* (“do not yet possess”); the manuscripts have *non habent* (“do not possess”).], neither should they be called believers, because likewise they do not yet possess the faculty of believing.

But if they are rightly called believers because, through the words of those who carry them, they in some manner profess faith, why are they not also first regarded as penitents, since through the same words of those who carry them they are shown to renounce the devil and this world?

All this occurs in hope, through the power of the Sacrament and of the divine grace that the Lord has given to the Church. Otherwise, who does not know that if a baptized infant reaches the age of reason, does not believe, and does not abstain from unlawful desires, what he received as an infant will profit him nothing?

Nevertheless, if after receiving Baptism he departs from this life, once the guilt to which he was originally subject has been released, he will be perfected in that light of truth which, remaining unchangeably forever, illumines the justified by the presence of the Creator.

For only sins separate human beings from God. They are released by Christ’s grace, through whom, as mediator, we are reconciled when he justifies the ungodly.

### Chapter XX

#### 26. No one rightly approaches the Lord’s table unless baptized

These people are terrified by the Lord’s statement: “Unless someone has been born again, he will not see the kingdom of God.” When explaining this, he said: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (John 3:3, 5).

For this reason they try to grant unbaptized infants salvation and eternal life on the basis of their innocence, but, because they have not been baptized, to exclude them from the kingdom of heaven—a novel and astonishing presumption, as though salvation and eternal life could exist outside Christ’s inheritance, outside the kingdom of heaven.

They apparently have somewhere to flee and hide, because the Lord did not say, “If someone is not born again of water and the Spirit, he will not have life,” but said, “He will not enter the kingdom of God” [Note: Lovanius has “into the kingdom of heaven.” Amerbach, Erasmus, and our manuscripts at this place have “into the kingdom of God.”].

For if he had said the former, no doubt could arise from this passage. Let doubt, then, be removed. Let us now hear the Lord, not the suspicions and conjectures of mortals. Let us hear the Lord, I say—not, indeed, speaking here about the Sacrament of the washing [Note: Lovanius has “the washing of the holy [sacrament],” adding *sancti* (“holy”) from only one manuscript.], but about the Sacrament of his holy table [Note: The Cygirannian manuscript omits *sanctae* (“holy”).], to which no one rightly approaches unless baptized:

“Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves.”

What more are we seeking? What can be answered to this, unless obstinate contention strains its sinews against the steadfastness of manifest truth?

[Col. 0124] **27.** Or will anyone dare to say even this: that this statement does not apply to infants, and that they can have life in themselves without sharing in this body and blood [Note: [Col. 0124] Augustine writes that this statement was used by the Apostolic See against the Pelagians when this very matter was under discussion, *Letter* 186 to Paulinus, §§28–29. Pope Innocent evidently used it in his letter to the Fathers of the Council of Milevis, which is numbered 182 among Augustine’s letters. Augustine transferred Innocent’s relevant words into *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 2, §7. Moreover, after Augustine’s death, Pope Gelasius, writing to the bishops throughout Picenum, likewise refuted the Pelagians on the basis of this statement and taught that no one was excepted. Fulgentius, when asked by the deacon Ferrandus what should be thought concerning the salvation of an Ethiopian youth who was baptized while dying but died before receiving the Eucharist, showed, both from many passages of Scripture and from Augustine’s sermon to the Infants, “that each of the faithful becomes a participant in the Lord’s body and blood when, in Baptism, he is made a member of Christ’s body; nor is he alienated from participation in the bread and cup, even if, before eating that bread and drinking the cup, he departs from this world established in the unity of Christ’s body.” Compare *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 3, §§7–9, and *Tractate* 26 on John.] For he does not say, “Whoever has not eaten,” as he says concerning Baptism, “Whoever has not been reborn”; rather, he says, “Unless you eat,” as though addressing those who were able to hear and understand—something infants plainly cannot do? But whoever says this does not consider that, unless this statement applies to everyone, so that they cannot have life without the body and blood of the Son of Man, the older age also concerns itself with this in vain. If you attend not to the speaker’s intention but to his words, it can seem to have been said only to those to whom the Lord was then speaking, since he does not say, “Whoever has not eaten,” but, “Unless you eat.” And what of what he says in the same passage about this very matter: “The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6:54, 52)? Accordingly, we understand that sacrament also to apply to us, who did not yet exist when he said these things, because [Note: [Col. 0124] All the manuscripts have, “who.”] we cannot say that we do not belong to the world for whose life Christ gave his flesh. Who, moreover, doubts that by “the world” human beings are meant—those who, by being born, come into this world? For, as he says elsewhere, “The children of this world marry and are given in marriage” (Luke 20:34). Therefore flesh was also given for the life of infants, since it was given for the life of the world; and if they do not eat the flesh of the Son of Man, neither will they have life.

**28.** This is also the meaning of the following: “The Father loves the Son, and has given everything into his hand” [Note: [Col. 0124] Printed editions have *into his hands*. The manuscripts, in accordance with the Vulgate, have *into his hand*.]. “Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; but whoever is unbelieving toward the Son will not have life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3:35–36). In which of these two classes, then, shall we place infants: among those who believe in the Son, or among those who are unbelieving toward the Son? “Among neither,” someone says, “because, since they cannot yet believe, they should not be counted unbelievers.” The ecclesiastical rule does not indicate this [Note: [Col. 0124] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read, “The ecclesiastical rule does not judge this.”], for it adds baptized infants to the number of the faithful. Furthermore, if those who are baptized are counted among believers because of the power and celebration of so great a sacrament, although they themselves neither perform with their heart and mouth what pertains to believing and confessing: surely those who lack the sacrament must be counted among those who do not believe in the Son. And therefore, if they depart from the body empty of this grace, what was said will follow them: “They will not have life” [Note: [Col. 0125] The manuscripts have, “They will not see life.”], “but the wrath of God remains upon them.” Why is this [Note: [Col. 0125] Printed editions have, “And why is this?” The word “and” is absent from the manuscripts.], when it is clear that they have no sins of their own, if they are not also held liable for original sin?

**CHAPTER XXI**

**29. Why some infants depart deprived of Baptism and others do not is inscrutable.** It is well that he does not say, “The wrath of God will come upon him,” but, “remains upon him.” For nothing frees anyone from that wrath under which all are subject to sin, and of which the Apostle says, “For we too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians 2:3), except the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. The reason why this grace comes to one person and not to another may be hidden, but it cannot be unjust. “Is there injustice with God? Certainly not” (Romans 9:14). But first our necks must be submitted to the authority of the holy Scriptures, so that each person may arrive at understanding through faith. For it was not said without reason: “Your judgments are like a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7). As though terrified by the depth of this abyss, the Apostle cries out: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” He had prefaced this with a statement of wondrous profundity: “For God has shut up all in unbelief, so that he might have mercy upon all.” Struck, as it were, by the horror of this profundity, he says: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who first gave to him, that he should be repaid?” [Note: [Col. 0125] Most manuscripts have, “so that he might be repaid.”] “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory forever and ever. Amen” (Romans 11:32–36). We therefore have far too little understanding to examine the justice of God’s judgments—to examine gratuitous grace, which, with no preceding merits, is not unjust. This grace is less disturbing when it is bestowed on the unworthy than when it is denied to other equally unworthy people.

**30.** For those who think it unjust that infants departing from the body without Christ’s grace should be deprived not only of the kingdom of God—which they themselves admit they cannot enter unless reborn through Baptism—but also of eternal life and salvation, ask how it is just that one person is released from original ungodliness and another is not, when the condition of both is the same. Let them answer, according to their own view, how it is likewise just that Baptism is granted to one, so that he may enter the kingdom of God, but not granted to another, when the cause of both is equal. If it troubles them that, of two people who are equally sinners by origin, one is released from this bond because Baptism is granted to him, while the other is not released because such grace is not granted to him, why does it not trouble them equally that, of two people innocent by origin, one receives Baptism, by which he can enter the kingdom of God, while the other does not receive it and therefore cannot approach the kingdom of God? In both cases we are brought back to that exclamation: “O the depth of the riches!” Then, among the baptized infants themselves, let someone tell me why one is snatched away “lest wickedness change his understanding” (Wisdom 4:11), while another lives on, destined to become impious. If both were snatched away, would both not enter the kingdom of heaven? Yet there is no injustice with God.

What of this: who would not be moved, who would not be compelled to cry out in the presence of such a great depth, when some infants are tormented by an unclean spirit, others suffer nothing of the kind, and still others are sanctified even in their mothers’ wombs, like Jeremiah (Jeremiah 1:5)—although, if original sin exists, all are equally guilty, and, if it does not exist, all are equally innocent? Whence comes such great diversity, unless his judgments are inscrutable and his ways unsearchable?

**CHAPTER XXII**

**31. He refutes those who think that souls are thrust into bodies corresponding to their merits because of sins committed elsewhere, and that they are afflicted in those bodies to a greater or lesser degree.** Or should we now regard as exploded and rejected the idea that souls, having first sinned in their heavenly dwelling, gradually and little by little come into bodies corresponding to their merits and, in proportion to their former life, are afflicted by bodily evils to a greater or lesser degree? Although Holy Scripture most clearly contradicts this opinion—for, when commending grace, it says, “Before they were born, and before they had done anything good or evil” [Note: [Col. 0126] The Louvain edition has, “and before they had done anything.” Corrected according to the manuscripts. Some manuscripts have, “before they had done anything good or evil,” omitting “and.” The Vatican manuscripts have, “and before they had done anything.”], “so that God’s purpose according to election might remain, not from works but from him who calls,” it was said, “The elder shall serve the younger”—even those who hold this view do not escape the difficulties of this question. Confined and entangled in them, they too are forced to cry out, “O the depth!”

For how does it happen that a person who from early childhood is more modest, more intelligent, more temperate, victorious to a great extent over lusts, who hates greed, detests luxury, and rises more advanced and better suited to the other virtues, nevertheless finds himself in a place where Christian grace cannot be preached to him? “How then shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how shall they believe in him whom they have not heard? And how shall they hear without a preacher?” (Romans 10:14). Yet another person, slow-witted, devoted to lusts, covered with crimes and wicked deeds, is so directed that he hears, believes, is baptized, and is snatched away—or, if he is kept here, lives here commendably.

Where did these two acquire such different merits? I do not mean so that one should believe and the other not believe, which belongs to the will itself, but so that one should hear what he is to believe and the other should not hear—for this is not in human power. Where, I ask, did they acquire such different merits? If they lived some life in heaven, so that because of their deeds they were driven or slipped down to earth [Note: [Col. 0126] The phrase “or slipped down” is absent from some manuscripts.] and were confined in bodily receptacles corresponding to their former life, then surely the one who was not burdened greatly in this mortal body, so that he had a good intelligence and was troubled by milder desires which he could easily overcome, must be thought to have lived better before entering this body. Yet he did not merit having that grace preached to him by which alone he could be freed from the danger of the second death.

The other, according to their belief, entangled in a heavier body because of worse merits and therefore dull of heart, overcome by ardent desire for the enticements of the flesh, and by a most wicked life adding worse earthly sins to the former sins for which he had supposedly merited coming into this condition—either heard on the cross, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), or attached himself to some apostle, by whose preaching he was changed and made safe through the washing of regeneration, “so that where sin abounded, grace might abound still more.” I entirely fail to see what answer they can give to this—those who, wishing to defend God’s justice by human conjectures and ignorant of the depth of grace, have woven implausible fables [Note: [Col. 0127] Ambrosiaster has, “what they should answer this.” Louvain has, “what they should answer here.” The manuscripts more correctly have, “what they should answer from this,” a phrase familiar to Augustine.].

**32.** Much could be said about the marvelous callings of human beings, whether those we have read about or those we have experienced, by which the opinion of those who believe that human souls lived certain individual lives before these bodies, and came into them to experience here different good or evil things in accordance with the diversity of their merits, could be overturned [Note: [Col. 0127] Most manuscripts have *diverse* (“in different ways”).]. But the need to bring this work to an end does not allow us to linger over these matters. Nevertheless, I shall not keep silent about one thing that I discovered among many marvels.

According to those who suppose that, because of the merits of an earlier life lived in the heavenly realms before this body, souls are burdened to a greater or lesser degree by earthly bodies, who would not affirm that those sinned more wickedly and savagely before this life who deserved to lose the light of their minds so completely that they were born almost like animals in their understanding? I do not mean merely the very slow-witted—for this is commonly said of others—but so senseless that, even with their hair curled [Note: [Col. 0127] Am., Erasmus, and five manuscripts have *curati* (“tonsured” or “cared-for”). Other manuscripts, along with the Louvain edition, have *cirrati* (“with curled hair”). In the margin of the Cygirannensis manuscript an old hand has written: “Or *cerriti*, that is, madmen.” The word is derived from Ceres, in whose rites people seized by frenzy were not fully in possession of their minds.], they provide sensible people with the delightful spectacle of foolishness, provoking laughter—people whom the common crowd calls *moriones*, a name derived from Greek.

Yet one such person was so Christian that, although in his marvelous foolishness he was exceedingly patient under every insult directed against him, he could not endure an insult against the name of Christ or against the religion with which he had been imbued. Thus he did not cease attacking with stones the sensible people who blasphemed and whom he heard saying such things in order to provoke him; nor did he spare even his masters in that cause [Note: [Col. 0127] Am., Erasmus, and the manuscripts add after “or against the religion in himself,” “reverence.”].

I therefore think that such people are predestined and created so that those who are able may understand that God’s grace, and the Spirit who blows where he wills (John 3:8), does not pass over any kind of intelligence among the children of mercy; and likewise does not pass over any kind of intelligence among the children of Gehenna, so that “whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31).
