But those who assert that souls receive different earthly bodies according to the merits of their former life, that some are burdened more and others less by these bodies [Note: [Col. 0127] Am. and all our manuscripts have, “receive whatever souls”; several of them also have, “different bodies on earth.”], and that human abilities vary according to the same merits, so that some are sharper and others duller, and that, according to the merits of that former life, divine grace too is distributed for the liberation of human beings—what will they be able to answer concerning this man? How will they attribute to him both a most depraved former life, so that he was born foolish because of it, and a life so meritorious that, because of it, he was preferred in Christ’s grace to many of the sharpest minds?

**33.** Let us therefore yield and submit to the authority of Holy Scripture, which neither knows how to be deceived nor deceives. Just as we do not believe that those not yet born had done anything good or evil by which their merits could be distinguished, so let us have no doubt that all are under sin, which entered the world through one man and spread through all human beings, and from which no one is freed except by the grace of God through our Lord Jesus Christ.

**CHAPTER XXIII**

**Christ is also the Savior and Redeemer of infants.** His healing coming is not needed by the healthy but by the sick, because he came not to call the righteous but sinners. No one will enter his kingdom unless he has been reborn of water and the Spirit, nor will anyone possess salvation and eternal life apart from his kingdom. For whoever has not eaten his flesh, and whoever is unbelieving toward the Son, will not have life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.

From this sin, this sickness, and this wrath of God—of which they are naturally children, and from which, even though they do not have personal sin because of their age, they nevertheless derive original sin—none frees them except the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world [Note: [Col. 0128] The old manuscript of Saint-Amand has, “the sin of the world.”] (John 1:29); none except the Physician who came not for the healthy but for the sick; none except the Savior, of whom it was said to the human race, “Today a Savior has been born for you” (Luke 2:11); none except the Redeemer, by whose blood our debt is erased.

For who would dare say that Christ is not the Savior and Redeemer of infants? From what, then, does he save them, if there is no original sickness of sin in them? From what does he redeem them, if through the origin of the first man they were not sold under sin? Therefore let no one promise infants eternal salvation on the basis of our own opinion, apart from Christ’s Baptism—a salvation that divine Scripture does not promise and that must be preferred to every human judgment.

**CHAPTER XXIV**

**34. Punic Christians call Baptism “salvation” and the Eucharist “life.”** The Punic Christians very appropriately call Baptism itself nothing other than “salvation,” and the sacrament of Christ’s body nothing other than “life.” From where does this come, unless from an ancient and, as I believe, apostolic tradition, through which they hold implanted in the churches of Christ the conviction that, apart from Baptism and participation in the Lord’s table, no human being can attain not only the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 0128] The printed editions have, “can attain not only not the kingdom of God,” repeating the negative particle; the latter occurrence is absent from the manuscripts.], but also salvation and eternal life?

Scripture itself testifies to this, in accordance with what we have said above. For what else do those who call Baptism by the name “salvation” hold than what was said: “He saved us through the washing of regeneration” (Titus 3:5), and what Peter says: “In a corresponding form Baptism now saves you” (1 Peter 3:21)? And what else do those who call the sacrament of the Lord’s table “life” hold than what was said: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven”; and, “The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world”; and, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:51, 52, 54)?

If, then, as so many and such great divine testimonies harmoniously declare, no one may hope for salvation or eternal life without Baptism and the Lord’s body and blood, salvation and eternal life are promised to infants without these things in vain. Furthermore, if nothing separates a person from salvation and eternal life except sins, then through these sacraments nothing but the guilt of sin is removed in infants. Concerning this guilt it is written that no one is clean, “even if his life should be but one day” (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint). Hence there is also the statement in the Psalms: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb” (Psalm 50:7). Either this is said in the general person of humanity itself, or, if David is speaking specifically about himself, he was certainly born not from fornication but from a lawful marriage.

Let us therefore not doubt that blood was shed also for the Baptism of infants. Before it was shed, it was given and commended in the sacrament in such a way that he said: “This is my blood, which will be poured out for many for the remission of sins” (Matthew 26:28). Those who refuse to admit that infants are under sin deny that they are freed. For from what are they freed, if they are held bound by no servitude of sin?

**35.** “I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness” (John 12:46). What does he show by saying this except that everyone who does not believe in him is in darkness, and that by believing he ensures that he does not remain in darkness? What else do we understand these darknesses to be but sins? But whatever else these darknesses may be understood to mean, surely whoever does not believe in Christ will remain in them. And they are certainly punitive, not like the nocturnal darknesses necessary for living creatures’ rest.

**CHAPTER XXV**

**Some wrongly inferred from the Gospel that infants are immediately illumined after birth.** Therefore, if infants do not pass into the number of believers through the sacrament divinely instituted for this purpose, they will certainly remain in these darknesses.

**36.** Nevertheless, some believe that infants are illumined immediately after birth, understanding in this way what is written: “This was the true light which illumines every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9). If this is so, it is very surprising how those illumined by the only Son, who in the beginning was the Word, God with God, are not admitted to the kingdom of God and are not heirs of God, nor co-heirs with Christ. Even those who hold this view admit that this is not granted to them except through Baptism.

Moreover, if they are already illumined but are not yet fit to attain the kingdom of God, at least they ought gladly to receive Baptism itself, by which they become fit for this. Yet we see them resist it with great weeping. We disregard that ignorance in this age to such a degree that we complete in them, even while they resist, the sacraments which we know benefit them. For why does the Apostle also say, “Do not be children in your minds” (1 Corinthians 14:20), if their minds have already been illumined by that true light which is the Word of God?

[Col. 0130] **37.** Therefore, what is stated in the Gospel—“This was the true light which illumines every human being coming into this world”—was said for this reason: no human being is illumined except by that light of truth which is God: lest anyone should think that he is illumined by the one from whom he hears in order to learn [Note: [Col. 0130] Printed editions have, “from whom he hears something.” The word “something” is absent from the manuscripts.]—not, I say, even if he should have some great human being as teacher, but not even if he should happen to have an angel as teacher [Note: [Col. 0130] The particle “but,” before “not even if he should have an angel,” may be omitted; and in fact it is omitted in the manuscripts.].

The word of truth is supplied externally through the ministry of bodily speech. Yet “neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:7). A person hears either a human being or an angel speaking; but, so that he may perceive and recognize that what is said is true, his mind is sprinkled inwardly by that light which remains eternal [Note: [Col. 0130] Louvain has, “which remains forever.” The word “in” is absent from the other printed editions and from the manuscripts.], and which also shines in the darkness. But just as this sun is not comprehended by the blind, although in some way it clothes them with its rays, so the light is not comprehended by those in the darkness of foolishness.

**38.** But why, after saying “which illumines every human being,” did he add “coming into this world”? From this arose the opinion that, at bodily birth, immediately after emerging from the mother’s womb, he illumines the minds of newborn infants. Although in Greek it is written [Note: [Col. 0130] *Erchomenē*], in such a way that “the light itself coming into this world” can also be understood, nevertheless, if “a human being coming into this world” must be accepted, I think it was either simply said in this way, as many statements are found in Scripture from which nothing is lost if the words are removed; or, if it must be believed that it was added for some distinction, perhaps it was said to distinguish spiritual illumination from bodily illumination, which illumines the eyes of the flesh either through the heavenly luminaries or through various fires [Note: [Col. 0130] The Louvain edition has *quibuscumque* (“any whatsoever”). But Augustine commonly uses *quibusque* for *quibuscumque*.].

Thus he may have said “the inner human being coming into this world,” because the outer human being is corporeal, like this world—as though he were saying, “He illumines every human being coming into the body,” in accordance with what is written: “I received a good soul, and I came into an undefiled body” (Wisdom 8:19–20).

Or, if it was said for the sake of some distinction, it may have been said in this way: “He illumines every human being coming into this world,” as though it said, “He illumines every inner human being,” because when the inner human being truly becomes wise, he is illumined by none other than the one who [Note: [Col. 0130] All manuscripts, along with Ambrose, have “who.”] is the true light.

Or, if he wished to call the very faculty by which the human soul is called rational—still quiet, as it were, and almost asleep, yet implanted and in some manner sown in infants—the illumination, as the creation of the inner eye, then we must not resist the view that this faculty is made when the soul is created; and it is not absurd to understand this as occurring when a human being comes into the world.

Nevertheless, even that eye, although already created, must remain in darkness if it does not believe in the one who said, “I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness.” That this occurs in infants through the sacrament of Baptism [Note: [Col. 0131] The word “Baptism” is absent from some manuscripts.] is not doubted by Mother Church, who lends them a mother’s heart and mouth [Note: [Col. 0131] The printed editions omit “and mouth.” It is found in the better manuscripts. In the others the text is corruptly read either as “corrected,” or “with a right heart the mother provides for them”; in some manuscripts “affection” or “bosom” is added.], so that they may be imbued with the sacred mysteries, because they are not yet able to believe with their own heart for righteousness or confess with their own mouth for salvation (Romans 10:10). Yet no believer hesitates to call them believers, since their name derives from believing, although during the sacraments it is not they themselves but others who have answered on their behalf.

**CHAPTER XXVI**

**39. He concludes that all are subject to original sin.** It would take too long if we discussed each testimony in the same way. I therefore think it more useful to gather together in a mass those passages that may occur to us or that may seem sufficient, by which it may become clear that the Lord Jesus Christ came in the flesh for no other reason, and, taking the form of a servant, became obedient even to death on a cross (Philippians 2:7–8), except that, through this dispensation of most merciful grace, he might give life, save, free, redeem, and illumine all those for whom, constituted as members in his body, he is the head for the purpose of attaining the kingdom of heaven—those who had previously been placed in the death of sins, in sickness, slavery, captivity, and darkness, under the power of the devil, the ruler of sinners.

Thus he became the mediator between God and human beings, through whom, after the hostilities of our ungodliness had been ended by the peace of his grace, we might be reconciled to God for eternal life, rescued from the eternal death that threatened those in such a condition. For once this has been shown more abundantly, it will follow that those who do not need life, salvation, liberation, redemption, or illumination cannot belong to this dispensation of Christ, which was accomplished through his humility.

And since Baptism belongs to this dispensation—through Baptism they are buried with Christ so that they may be incorporated as his members, that is, as his faithful—Baptism is plainly not necessary for those who have no need of that benefit of remission and reconciliation which takes place through the mediator.

Furthermore, since those who concede that infants ought to be baptized cannot oppose the authority of the whole Church, which was doubtless handed down through the Lord and the Apostles, they must concede that infants need those benefits of the mediator, so that, washed [Note: [Col. 0131] The editions of Ambrose, Erasmus, and Louvain have, “so that, offered.” The older editions and most manuscripts have, “so that, washed.”] through the sacrament and the charity of the faithful, and thus incorporated into Christ’s body, which is the Church, they may be reconciled to God, so that in him they may become alive, saved, freed, redeemed, and illumined. From what, if not from the death, vices, guilt, subjection, and darkness of sins? Since they have committed none of these things at that age through their own life, original sin remains.

**CHAPTER XXVII**

**40. He gathers testimonies from Scripture.** This reasoning will be stronger once I have gathered together the many testimonies I promised. We have already cited: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Luke 5:32). Likewise, when he had entered Zacchaeus’s house, he said: “Today salvation has come to this house, because he too is a son of Abraham. For the Son of Man came to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:9–10). The same is shown by the lost sheep, for whose sake the ninety-nine were left and which was sought and found; and by the drachma that was lost from the ten (Luke 15:3–10).

Therefore, as he says, “repentance and remission of sins had to be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:46–47). Mark also testifies at the end of his Gospel that the Lord said: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:15–16). Who does not know that for infants to believe means to be baptized, while not to believe means not to be baptized?

From the Gospel of John, although we have already cited several passages, consider these also. John the Baptist said concerning him: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). And he himself said of himself: “Those who are of my sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they will never perish” (John 10:27–28). Since infants do not begin to belong to his sheep except through Baptism, plainly, if they do not receive it, they will perish; for they will not have the eternal life that he will give to his sheep. Again, in another place: “I am the way, the truth, and the life. No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14:6).

**41.** Accepting this teaching, observe with how many attestations the Apostles declare it. Peter says in his First Letter: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who, according to the abundance of his mercy, regenerated us [Note: [Col. 0132] The Cygirannensis manuscript has, “who, according to the abundance of his mercy, regenerated us.”] unto the hope of eternal life through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, into an immortal and undefiled inheritance [Note: [Col. 0132] The manuscripts have “uncontaminated.”], flourishing, kept in heaven for you, who are preserved by the power [Note: [Col. 0132] Most manuscripts have “in truth.”] of God through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.”

And a little later: “You may be found,” he says, “unto the praise and honor of Jesus Christ, whom you did not know; in whom, although now you do not see him, you believe, and when you see him you will rejoice with unspeakable joy and honored rejoicing [Note: [Col. 0132] Some manuscripts omit “joy” here.], receiving the testament of faith, the salvation of your souls” (1 Peter 1:3–9).

Again, in another place: “But you,” he says, “are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for adoption, so that you may proclaim the virtues of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Peter 2:9). And again: “Christ,” he says, “suffered for our sins, the just for the unjust, so that he might bring us to God.” Likewise, when he had recalled that eight people were saved in Noah’s ark: “In a corresponding form,” he says, “Baptism now saves you” (1 Peter 3:18–21).

Therefore infants are alien from this salvation and light and will remain in perdition and darkness unless they are joined through adoption to God’s people, holding fast to Christ, the just one who suffered for the unjust, so that he might bring them to God.

**42.** The following passages from John’s Letter also occurred to me as necessary for this question. “But if we walk in the light,” he says, “as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ his Son will cleanse us from every sin” (1 John 1:7).

Again, in another place: “If we receive,” he says, “the testimony of human beings, the testimony of God is greater, because this is the testimony of God, which is greater [Note: [Col. 0133] “Which is greater” is absent here from the Gallican manuscripts. It does occur in the Latin text of the Vulgate edition, but is absent from the Greek. Several of those manuscripts also omit “because he has testified concerning his Son.”], because he has testified concerning his Son. Whoever believes in the Son of God has the testimony [Note: [Col. 0133] Louvain has, “the testimony of God.” The word “of God” is absent here from our manuscripts and from the editions of Ambrose and Erasmus, nor does it occur in the Greek text of John.] in himself. Whoever does not believe God makes him a liar, because he has not believed [Note: [Col. 0133] Only the Louvain edition has, “does not believe.” The Greek has *ou pepisteuken*, “has not believed.”] the testimony that he has given concerning his Son. And this is the testimony: God has given us eternal life, and this life is in his Son. Whoever has the Son has life; whoever does not have the Son does not have life” (1 John 5:9–12).

Therefore infants will have not only not the kingdom of heaven, but not even life, if they do not have the Son, whom they cannot have except through his Baptism. Again, in another place: “For this purpose,” he says, “the Son of God was manifested, that he might destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8). Therefore infants will not belong to the grace of the manifestation of the Son of God if he does not destroy the works of the devil in them [Note: [Col. 0133] According to Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain, “if he does not destroy.”].

### 43.

Now attend to the testimonies of the apostle Paul concerning this matter—naturally all the more numerous because he wrote more Epistles, and because he took greater care to commend the grace of God against those who gloried in [Note: [Col. 0133] Here the printed editions have unnecessarily added “concerning” (*de*).] works and, being ignorant of the righteousness of God and seeking to establish their own, were not subject to the righteousness of God (Rom. 10:3).

In the Epistle to the Romans: “The righteousness of God,” he says, “is upon all who believe; for there is no distinction. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus, whom God set forth as a mercy seat [Note: [Col. 0133] Lov. has “propitiator.” The other printed editions and the manuscripts have “mercy seat,” as do all the books again, together with Lov., in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, no. 21. The Greek is *hilastērion*.] through faith in his blood, to demonstrate his righteousness because of the purpose [Note: [Col. 0133] The printed editions have “because of the remission.” But the manuscripts consistently read “because of the purpose”; and the editions themselves have the same reading in the place of *On the Spirit and the Letter* just cited. Ambrosiaster follows this reading.] of the preceding sins, in the forbearance of God [Note: [Col. 0133] The manuscripts have “forbearance.”], to demonstrate his righteousness at the present time, so that he may be just and justify the one who is of faith in Jesus” (Rom. 3:22–26).

Likewise, in another place: “To the one who works,” he says, “the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt. But to the one who does not work yet believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness. Thus David also speaks of the blessedness of the person to whom God credits righteousness without works: Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven, and whose sins have been covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin.”

A little later: “Now it was not written,” he says, “for his sake alone, that it was reckoned to him [Note: [Col. 0134] The printed editions add “as righteousness.” It is absent from the manuscripts and also from the Greek text of the Apostle.], but also for our sake, to whom it will be reckoned, if we believe in him who raised Jesus Christ our Lord from the dead, who was delivered up because of our offenses and raised for our justification” (Rom. 4:4–8, 23–25).

And a little later: “For while we were still weak, at the proper time Christ died for the ungodly” (Rom. 5:6).

And elsewhere: “We know,” he says, “that the law is spiritual; but I am carnal, sold under sin. For I do not understand what I do: for I do not do what I wish, but I do what I hate. But if I do what I do not wish, I agree with the law, that it is good [Note: [Col. 0134] Here too the word “is” has been added; it is omitted in the manuscripts and in the Greek.]. Now, however, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me. For I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh—for willing is present with me, but I do not find the means of accomplishing good. For I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish, that I do. But if I do what I do not wish, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me. I find, therefore, this law for me who wish to do good: evil is present with me. For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person; but I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:14–25).

Let those who can say that human beings are born not in this body of death say also that they do not need the grace of God through Jesus Christ, by which they may be delivered from this body of death.

A little later: “For what was impossible for the law [Note: [Col. 0134] The printed editions have *legi*, “for the law,” in the dative. But the manuscripts have *legis*, “of the law,” in agreement with the Greek *tou nomou*. Augustine likewise has this reading in Sermon 152], because it was weakened through the flesh, God did, sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh; and, on account of sin, he condemned sin in the flesh” (Rom. 8:3).

Let those who dare say that Christ ought to have been born in the likeness of sinful flesh, unless we had been born in sinful flesh.

### 44.

Likewise, to the Corinthians: “For I delivered to you first of all,” he says, “what I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures” (1 Cor. 15:3).

Likewise, to the same Corinthians in the second Epistle: “For the love of Christ constrains us, judging this: that if one died for all, then all died. And he died for all, so that those who live may no longer live for themselves but for him who died and rose for them. Therefore from now on we know no one according to the flesh; and even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him no longer. Therefore, if anyone is a new creation in Christ, the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new [Note: [Col. 0134] At this point the manuscripts do not have “all things”; nor does it occur in the Greek Bibles or in the Latin Corbeiensis manuscripts]. But all things are from God, who reconciled us to himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation. How so? Because God [Col. 0135] was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself, not reckoning their offenses against them, and placing in us the word of reconciliation. Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us; we entreat you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God. He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God. And as fellow workers we also plead that you not receive the grace of God in vain. For he says: In an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you. Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 5:14–6:2).

If infants do not belong to this reconciliation and salvation, who seeks them for the Baptism of Christ? [Note: [Col. 0135] Two manuscripts read, “what seeks them?”] But if they do belong to it, they are among the dead [Note: [Col. 0135] Am., Er., and the manuscripts have “they are dead.”], for whom he died; nor can they be reconciled and saved by him unless he forgives their offenses and does not reckon them against them.

### 45.

Likewise, to the Galatians: “Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, who gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from the present evil age” (Gal. 1:3–4).

And elsewhere: “The law was appointed because of transgressions [Note: [Col. 0135] Thus the manuscripts read. The printed editions, however, have “was set in place.” And below, “ordained through angels.” See the *Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians*], until the seed should come to whom the promise was made, ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not mediator of one party; but God is one. Is the law therefore against the promises of God? Certainly not. For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would indeed be from the law. But Scripture confined all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through the faith of Jesus Christ” (Gal. 3:19–22).

### 46.

To the Ephesians also: “And you, when you were dead in your offenses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience, among whom we all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of our impulses, and we were by nature children of wrath, even as the others. But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, and when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ—by whose grace we have been saved.”

And a little later: “By grace you have been saved through faith; and this is not from yourselves, but is the gift of God; not from works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them.”

And a little later: “You were at that time without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants and the promise, having no hope and without God in this world. But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far away have been brought near in the blood of Christ [Note: [Col. 0135] The printed editions have “but now.” “But” is absent from the manuscripts]. For he is our peace, who made both one and broke down the middle wall of the barrier, the hostility, in his flesh, abolishing the law of commandments expressed in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself into one new person, making peace, and transform both in one body for God through the cross, putting the hostility to death in himself. And when he came, he preached peace [Col. 0136] to you who were far away and peace to those who were near, because through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Eph. 2:1–18).

Likewise, elsewhere: “As the truth is in Jesus, put off, according to your former way of life, the old person, who is corrupted according to deceitful desires. Be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new person, who was created according to God in righteousness and the holiness of truth.”

And elsewhere: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption” (Eph. 4:21–24, 30).

### 47.

To the Colossians also he speaks in this way: “Giving thanks to the Father, who has made us fit to share in the lot of the saints in light, who delivered us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins” (Col. 1:12–14).

And elsewhere: “You are filled in him, who is the head of every principality and power; in whom also you were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping away of the body of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ, buried with him in Baptism, in which you also rose through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead. And you, when you were dead in offenses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made alive together with him [Note: [Col. 0136] The manuscripts read, “he made alive with him”], forgiving us all offenses, wiping out the bond written against us in decrees, which was hostile to us; he removed it from our midst and fastened it to the cross. Stripping off the flesh, he exposed the principalities and powers, triumphing over them confidently in himself” (Col. 2:10–15).

### 48.

And to Timothy: “This saying is trustworthy and worthy of all acceptance: that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the first. But for this reason I received mercy, so that Christ Jesus might first display in me all patience, as an example for those who would believe in him for eternal life” (1 Tim. 1:15–16).

He also says: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a redemption for all” (1 Tim. 2:5–6).

In the second Epistle to the same man: “Therefore do not be ashamed of the testimony of our Lord, nor of me, his prisoner; but labor together with the Gospel according to the power of God, who saves us and calls us with his holy calling, not according to our works but according to his purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal ages, but has now been manifested through the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has indeed abolished death but has brought life and incorruption to light through the Gospel” (2 Tim. 1:8–10).

### 49.

To Titus also: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the manifestation of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ, who gave himself for us, so that he might redeem us from all iniquity and cleanse for himself a people abundant, zealous for good works” (Titus 2:13–14).

And elsewhere: “When the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared, he saved us, not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy, through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us most abundantly [Col. 0137] through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life” (Titus 3:4).

### 50.

The Epistle to the Hebrews, although its authorship is uncertain to some [Note: [Col. 0137] Jerome often testifies to its uncertainty among the Latins of his time in his *Commentaries on Isaiah*, chapters 6 and 8; on Zechariah, chapter 8; on Matthew, chapter 26; and in the *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 16, concerning Paul, and chapter 70, concerning Gaius, and elsewhere. But concerning its acceptance among the Greeks as Paul’s, he writes in Epistle 129, to Dardanus: “This,” he says, “must be said to our people: that the Epistle written to the Hebrews is accepted not only by the churches of the East, but by all the writers of the Greek-speaking Church from ancient times as belonging to the apostle Paul.” Here, on the authority of the old Corbeiensis manuscript, we correct the editions, which until now generally read, “but by all the churches and writers of the Greek-speaking Church,” or “by the churches and writers of the Greek language.” See Augustine, *City of God*, book 16, chapter 22, and *On Christian Doctrine*, book 2, no. 13.], nevertheless, since I have read that some who hold opinions contrary to our position concerning the Baptism of infants have wished to enlist it as a witness for certain of their views, and since the authority of the Eastern Churches—where this Epistle is also counted among the canonical books—moves me more, we must observe what testimonies it contains in our favor.

At its very beginning we read: “In many portions and in many ways God formerly spoke to the fathers through the Prophets; but in these last days he has spoken to us in his Son, whom he appointed heir of all things, through whom he also made the ages. Since he is the radiance of his glory and the expression of his substance, and since he also upholds all things by the word of his power, having made purification of sins through himself, he sat at the right hand of the majesty on high” (Heb. 1:1–3).

And shortly afterward: “For if the word spoken through angels was made firm, and every transgression and disobedience received a just recompense of reward, how shall we escape if we neglect so great a salvation?”

And elsewhere: “Therefore, since the children shared in blood and flesh, he himself likewise partook of the same, so that through death he might abolish the one who held the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who through fear of death were subject to slavery throughout their whole life. For this reason he had to be made like his brothers in every respect, so that he might become a merciful and faithful high priest before God, to make atonement for the sins of the people” (Heb. 2:2–3, 14–17).

And elsewhere: “Let us hold fast our confession. For we do not have a priest [Note: [Col. 0137] The Lov. edition has “high priest.” The other editions, together with our manuscripts, have “priest.” In the Greek the same word, *archiereus*, occurs here as in the passages cited shortly before from Hebrews 2 and 7, where we read “high priest”]. who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but one who has been tested in every respect according to our likeness, without sin” (Heb. 4:15).

And elsewhere: “He has an untransgressible priesthood; therefore he is also able to save completely those who approach God through him, since he always lives to intercede for them. For such a high priest was fitting for us: righteous, without malice [Note: [Col. 0137] In the manuscripts “without malice” is consistently read as “without blemish,” not only here but also below, book 2, no. 19. The Greek is *akakos*.], undefiled, separated from sinners, made higher than the heavens, having no daily necessity, as the high priests do, first to offer sacrifice for their own sins and then for those of the people; for this he did once, offering himself” (Heb. 7:[Col. 0138] 24–27).

And elsewhere: “For Christ did not enter a sanctuary made by hand, which is a likeness of the true one, but into heaven itself, to appear before the face of God for us—not so that he should offer himself repeatedly, as the high priest enters the holy places once a year with another’s blood. Otherwise he would have had to suffer repeatedly from the foundation of the world. But now, once at the consummation of the ages, he has appeared for the abolition of sin through his sacrifice. And just as it is appointed for human beings to die only once, and after this comes judgment, so Christ also was offered once, to bear the sins of many; he will appear a second time, without sins, to those who await him for salvation” (Heb. 9:24–28).

### 51.

The Apocalypse of John also testifies that these praises are offered to Christ in a new song: “You are worthy to receive the book and to open its seals, because you were slain and redeemed us for God by your blood, from every tribe, language, people, and nation” (Rev. 5:9).

### 52.

Likewise, in the Acts of the Apostles, the apostle Peter declared the Lord Jesus to be the author of life, rebuking the Jews because they had killed him, speaking as follows: “But you dishonored and denied the Holy and Righteous One, and asked for a murderous man to be granted to you; but you killed the author of life” (Acts 3:14–15).

And elsewhere: “This is the stone rejected by you builders, which has become the cornerstone. For there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:11–12).

And elsewhere: “The God of our fathers raised Jesus, whom you killed by hanging him on a tree. God exalted him by his glory as Prince and Savior, to grant repentance to Israel and forgiveness of sins in him” (Acts 5:30–31).

Likewise, in another place: “To him all the Prophets bear witness, that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through him” (Acts 10:43).

Likewise, in the same book the apostle Paul says: “Therefore let it be known to you, brothers, that through him forgiveness of sins is proclaimed to you; and from all the things from which you could not be justified in the law of Moses, in him everyone who believes is justified” (Acts 13:38–39).

### 53.

Before such a great mass of testimonies, whose pride against the truth of God would not be crushed? Many other testimonies can indeed be found, but care must also be taken not to neglect bringing this work to an end.

As for the books of the Old Testament, I thought it unnecessary to add many testimonies of the divine utterances in support of this position, since in those books what is concealed beneath the veil, as it were, of earthly promises is revealed in the preaching of the New Testament.

The Lord himself briefly demonstrated and defined the usefulness of the ancient books when he said that what had been written about him in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms had to be fulfilled—and that these things were precisely that Christ had to suffer, rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins had to be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:44–47).

And Peter says what I mentioned shortly before: that all the Prophets bear witness to him, that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of sins through him.

### 54.

[Col. 0139] Nevertheless, it is more useful to draw a few testimonies also from the Old Testament itself, which may serve either as a supplement, or rather as an accumulation of evidence.

The Lord himself, speaking through the prophet in the Psalm, says: “To the saints who are in his land, he has made all my desires wonderful in them.” Not their merits, but my desires. For what is theirs except what follows? “Their infirmities have been multiplied; above what they were weak [Note: [Col. 0139] The printed editions have “above that in which they were weak.” The manuscripts do not have “that”].”

For this reason the law also entered, so that the offense might abound. But what does he add? “Afterward they hastened”: when their infirmities had multiplied—that is, when sin had abounded—they sought the physician more eagerly, so that where sin had abounded, grace might abound even more (Rom. 5:20).

Finally, he says: “I will not gather their assemblies from blood,” because through the many sacrificial blood offerings, when they first gathered in the tabernacle or temple, sinners were convicted rather than cleansed. “Therefore,” he says, “I will no longer gather their assemblies from blood.” For one blood was given for many, by which they might truly be cleansed.

Finally, what follows is: “Nor will I remember their names through my lips” (Ps. 15:3–4), as though they had been renewed [Note: [Col. 0139] Two manuscripts, one Belgic and one Vatican, read “as though they had been cleansed”; another reads “as though they had been renewed.”]. For previously their names were: children of the flesh, children of the age, children of wrath, children of the devil, unclean, sinners, ungodly. But afterward: children of God; for the new person, a new name; a new song, newly sung through the New Testament [Note: [Col. 0139] Most manuscripts lack the words “singing a new song.” Perhaps, with “new” deleted there, the better reading would be: “a new song sung through the New Testament.”].

Let human beings not be ungrateful for the grace of God, the small together with the great, from the lesser to the greater.

The voice of the whole Church is: “I have gone astray like a sheep that is lost” (Ps. 118:176). The voice of all the members of Christ is: “All we like sheep have gone astray, and he was delivered up for our sins.” This entire passage of prophecy occurs in Isaiah; when the eunuch of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, had it explained to him by Philip, he believed in him (Acts 8:27–39).

See how often he commends this very point and repeatedly impresses it upon certain proud or contentious people—I do not know whom: “A man,” he says, “in affliction and one who knows how to bear infirmities; therefore his face also turned away; he was dishonored and not esteemed. He bears our infirmities and is in pains for us; and we considered him to be in pain, in affliction, and under punishment. But he was wounded because of our sins and weakened because of our iniquities. The discipline of our peace was upon him; by his bruising we were healed. All we like sheep have gone astray, and the Lord delivered him up for our sins. And because he was ill-treated, he did not open his mouth; like a sheep he was led to slaughter, and like a lamb before the one who shears it he was without a voice; so he did not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away. Who will recount his generation? For his life will be taken from the earth; because of the iniquities of my people he was led to death. Therefore I will give the wicked for his burial, and the rich for his death, because he committed no iniquity [Col. 0140], nor was deceit found in his mouth. The Lord wills to cleanse him from affliction. If you give your soul for your offenses, you will see offspring of long life [Note: [Col. 0140] All our manuscripts have “of very long life.”]. And the Lord wills to take his soul away from pains, to show him light, and to form him through understanding, to justify the righteous one who serves many well; and he himself will bear their sins. Therefore he himself will inherit many and will divide the spoils of the strong, because his soul was delivered to death, he was reckoned among the transgressors, and he himself bore the sins of many and was delivered because of their iniquities” (Isa. 53:3–12).

Consider also that passage of the same prophet which, declaring it fulfilled in himself and acting also as a reader, he himself recited in the synagogue: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he sent me to preach good news to the poor, to refresh those who are in anguish of heart [Note: [Col. 0140] Am., Er., and the Gallican manuscripts have “he sent me to preach to the humble, to refresh those who are.” One Vatican manuscript has “to refresh those who.” Another has “to be refreshed, those who.”], to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind” (Isa. 61:1; Luke 4:16–21).

Let us all therefore acknowledge him, and let none of us who wish to cling to his body, enter his fold through him, and attain the perpetual life and salvation that he promised to his own be excepted [Note: [Col. 0140] In all our manuscripts, “to belong.”]. Let us all, I say, acknowledge him who committed no sin and bore our sins in his body upon the tree, so that, separated from sins, we might live for righteousness; by whose scars we were healed, when we were weak [Note: [Col. 0140] Something appears to be omitted here.], like wandering sheep (1 Pet. 2:22, 24–25).

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### 55. He gathers that all need Christ’s death in order to be saved. Unbaptized infants will be in condemnation with the devil. How all are brought to condemnation through Adam and all to justification through Christ. No one is reconciled to God except through Christ.

Since these things are so, sound faith and sound doctrine have never considered anyone who has approached Christ through Baptism excluded from the grace of the forgiveness of sins, nor have they thought that anyone could have eternal salvation apart from his kingdom.

For this salvation is prepared to be revealed at the last time (1 Pet. 1:5), that is, at the resurrection of the dead—those belonging not to eternal death, which is called the second death, but to eternal life, which the God who does not lie promises to his saints and faithful people. All who share in this life will be made alive only in Christ, just as all die in Adam (1 Cor. 15:22).

For just as absolutely all who belong to generation according to the will of the flesh die only in Adam, in whom all sinned, so absolutely all among them who belong to regeneration according to the will of the Spirit are made alive only in Christ, in whom all are justified. For just as through one person all are brought to condemnation, so through one person all are brought to justification (Rom. 5:18).

There is no middle place available to anyone: whoever is not with Christ can only be with the devil.

Therefore the Lord himself, wishing to remove from the hearts of those who believe wrongly this supposed middle state which some attempt [Col. 0141] to assign to unbaptized infants—so that, as though on account of the merit of their innocence, they might be in eternal life, but because they are not baptized they might not be with Christ in his kingdom—issued a definitive sentence to close their mouths when he said: “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Matt. 12:30).

Set before yourself, then, any infant. If the child is already with Christ, why is he baptized? But if the truth is what it declares—that he is baptized in order to be with Christ—then certainly the unbaptized child is not with Christ; and because he is not with Christ, he is against Christ. For we neither ought nor can weaken or alter his so explicit a sentence.

How, then, is he against Christ, if not because of sin [Note: [Col. 0141] The printed editions have “unless because of sin.” The manuscripts have “if not.”]? Certainly not because of body and soul, both of which are God’s creation.

But if because of sin, what sin could there be at that age except original and ancient sin? There is one flesh of sin, in which all are born for condemnation; and there is one flesh in the likeness of sinful flesh, through which all are freed from condemnation.

Nor was it said “all” in such a way that all who are born in sinful flesh are understood to be cleansed by that flesh which is like sinful flesh; for faith does not belong to all (2 Thess. 3:2). Rather, all who belong to generation through carnal marriage are born only in sinful flesh, and all who belong to generation through spiritual marriage are cleansed only through flesh like sinful flesh. That is: the former through Adam to condemnation, the latter through Christ to justification.

It is as if, for example, we were to say: “There is one midwife in this city who receives everyone, and there is one teacher of letters here who teaches everyone.” In the first statement “everyone” can mean only those who are born; in the second, “everyone” can mean only those who learn. Yet not everyone who is born learns letters.

Still, it is clear to anyone that it was rightly said there, “She receives everyone,” since no one is born except through her hands; and that it was rightly said here, “He teaches everyone,” since no one learns except through his instruction.

### 56.

When all the divine testimonies that I have mentioned are considered—whether I discussed each individually, or heaped many together, or omitted whatever similar testimonies I did not mention—nothing is found except what the universal Church holds: that it must remain vigilant against all profane novelties; that every human being is separated from God unless reconciled to God through the mediator Christ; and that no one can be separated from God except through sins that stand in the way.

Therefore reconciliation occurs only through the forgiveness of sins, through the one grace of the most merciful Savior and through the one sacrifice of the truest Priest. Thus all the children of the woman who believed the serpent, so that she might be corrupted by desire (Gen. 3:1–6), are not delivered from this body of death except through the Son of the Virgin, who believed the angel, so that she might conceive without desire (Luke 1:26–38).

## CHAPTER XXIX

### 57. What the good of marriage is. Four distinctions between good and evil uses.

The good of marriage, therefore, is not the heat of desire, but a certain lawful and honorable manner of using that heat, directed toward producing offspring, not toward satisfying lust. [“This will, [Col. 0142] not that pleasure, is nuptial” [Note: [Col. 0142] This sentence, enclosed in brackets, is absent from all the manuscripts].]

Whatever, then, moves disobediently in the members of this body of death and strives to drag down the whole mind after it, neither rising when the mind wishes nor becoming quiet when the mind wishes—this is the evil of sin, in which every human being is born.

But when it is restrained from illicit corruptions and permitted to propagate the human race in an orderly way for the sole purpose of replenishing it, this is the good of marriage, through which a human being is born within an ordered society.

Yet no one is reborn in the body of Christ unless he is first born in the body of sin.

Now, just as it is evil to use a good thing badly, so it is good to use an evil thing well. These two things, good and evil, together with the other two, good use and evil use, joined to one another, make four distinctions:

- One uses a good thing well when one devotes continence to God.
- One uses a good thing badly when one devotes continence to an idol.
- One uses an evil thing badly when one releases desire into adultery.
- One uses an evil thing well when one restrains desire through marriage.

Therefore, just as it is better to use a good thing well than to use an evil thing well, although both uses are good, so the one who gives his virgin daughter in marriage does well, while the one who does not give her in marriage does better.

I discussed this question at much greater length and more adequately, insofar as the Lord granted it, in two books: one *On the Good of Marriage*, the other *On Holy Virginity*, according to the small measure of my abilities.

Let those who exalt the flesh and blood of the transgressor against the flesh and blood of the Redeemer not defend the evil of desire by means of the good of marriage. Let them not be lifted up in the pride of another’s error [Note: [Col. 0142] All the manuscripts have “in the pride”]—from whose infancy the Lord has given us an example of humility.

He alone was born without sin: a virgin conceived him without a human embrace, not through the desire of the flesh but through the obedience of the mind.

Only she could give birth to medicine for our wound, who, not from the wound of sin, brought forth the shoot of a devout offspring.

## CHAPTER XXX

### 58. For what purpose the Pelagians wished Baptism to be necessary for infants.

Let us now examine more carefully, insofar as the Lord assists us, the very passage of the Gospel in which he says: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not enter the kingdom of God.”

If they were not moved by this sentence, these people would judge that infants should not be baptized at all. But because he did not say, they argue, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not have salvation or eternal life,” but only said, “He will not enter the kingdom of God,” infants are to be baptized for this purpose: that they may also be with Christ in the kingdom of God, where they will not be if they have not been baptized. Nevertheless, if infants die without Baptism, they will possess salvation and eternal life, since they are bound by no bond of sin.

In saying these things, first they never explain by what justice an image of God possessing no sin would be separated from the kingdom of God.

Next, let us see whether the Lord Jesus—the one and only good teacher—did not in this very Gospel reading signify and demonstrate that it is only through the forgiveness of sins that the baptized come to the kingdom of God. [Col. 0143] Indeed, for those who understand correctly, it ought to have been sufficient that he said: “Unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God”; and, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.”

For why should one be born again unless one is to be renewed? And from what is one to be renewed unless from oldness? And what oldness except that in which our old person was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be abolished (Rom. 6:6)?

Or from what cause does the image of God fail to enter the kingdom of God except because an obstacle of sin prevents it?

Nevertheless, as we proposed, let us examine the whole context of the Gospel reading that pertains to the matter under discussion, as attentively and carefully as we can.

59. “There was,” he says, “a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. He came to Jesus by night and said to him: Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher; for no one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him. Jesus answered and said to him: Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God. Nicodemus says to him: How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time and be born? Jesus answered: Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0143] In Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts, *holy* is added here.], he cannot enter the kingdom of God. What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit. Do not marvel that I said to you, ‘You must be born again.’ The Spirit blows where it wills, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit. Nicodemus answered and said to him: How can these things happen? Jesus answered and said to him: You are a teacher in Israel, and you do not know these things? Amen, amen, I say to you, we speak of what we know and testify to what we have seen, and you do not accept our testimony. If I told you earthly things and you did not believe [Note: [Col. 0143] All the manuscripts read, “and you do not believe.” The Louvain editors conclude that Augustine nevertheless read *you did not believe*, as in the printed editions, from the immediately following chapter, no. 60, where he says: “he added that he had told them earthly things and they had not believed.”], how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things? And no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven. And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life. For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life. For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him. Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he does not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God. This is the judgment: that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than the light, for their works were evil. For everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, so that his works may not be exposed. But whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed, because they have been done in God.”

Up to this point the whole connected discourse pertains to the matter about which we are inquiring; from here onward the narrator turns aside to another subject (John 3:1–21).

## CHAPTER XXXI

[Col. 0144]

### 60. Christ the head and the body. Because of the unity of his person, Christ both remained in heaven and walked on earth. How one Christ ascends into heaven. The head and the body are one Christ.

Since Nicodemus did not understand what was being said, he asked the Lord how these things could happen. Let us see what the Lord answers him. Certainly, if he deigns to answer the question, “How can these things happen?”, he will say how the spiritual regeneration of a man coming from carnal generation can take place.

Having therefore briefly noted the ignorance of the man who preferred himself to the others in the matter of teaching, and having reproved the unbelief of all such people because they did not accept the testimony of the truth, he added that he had told them earthly things and they had not believed, asking—or expressing his astonishment at—how they would believe heavenly things. Yet he continues and answers that others will believe [Note: [Col. 0144] The manuscripts read, *may believe*.] if those people do not believe, in answer to the question how these things can happen:

“No one,” he says, “has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.”

Thus, he says, spiritual generation will take place, so that heavenly people may come from earthly ones. They will not be able to attain this unless they become my members, so that the one who descended may himself ascend; for no one ascends except the one who descended.

Unless, therefore, all are changed and lifted up [Note: [Col. 0144] Amerbach and Erasmus read *washed*, wrongly, for *lifted up*.] into the unity of Christ, so that Christ himself, who descended, may ascend, recognizing no other body as his own—that is, his Church—than himself, since the words, “The two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24), are more truly understood of Christ and the Church; and concerning this he himself said, “Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh” (Mark 10:8)—they will not be able to ascend at all, because no one ascends into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven.

Although he became the Son of Man on earth, he did not consider the divinity by which, remaining in heaven, he descended to earth unworthy of the name “Son of Man,” just as he graciously allowed his flesh to be called the Son of God, so that these might not be understood as though there were two Christs [Note: [Col. 0144] Amerbach and the Louvain edition understand, “so that they might not be understood as though there were two Christs,” omitting *these*, which all our manuscripts contain.]—one God and another man [Note: [Col. 0144] This was the error later condemned in Nestorius.]—but one and the same God and man: God, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”; man, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14).

Accordingly, by the distinction between divinity and weakness, the Son of God remained in heaven and the Son of Man walked on earth; but by the unity of person, through which the two substances are one Christ, the Son of God also walked on earth, and that same Son of Man remained in heaven.

Thus faith in more credible things [Note: [Col. 0144] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read, *more credible faith*.] arises from things believed that are more incredible. For if the divine substance, vastly more distant and exalted by incomparable difference, was able, for our sake, to assume human substance in such a way that one person came to be—and thus the Son of Man, who was on earth through the weakness of the flesh, was himself also in heaven through the divinity joined to the flesh—how much more credible is it that other [Col. 0145] holy and faithful human beings become one Christ with the man Christ, so that, when all who ascend through this grace and fellowship of his ascend, the one Christ himself may ascend into heaven, the one who descended from heaven?

Thus the Apostle also says: “Just as in one body we have many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ” (1 Cor. 12:12). He did not say, “So also are Christ’s,” that is, Christ’s body or Christ’s members; but “so also is Christ,” calling the head and the body one Christ.

## CHAPTER XXXII

### 61. The serpent lifted up in the wilderness prefigured Christ hanging on the cross. Infants too are poisoned by the serpent’s bite.

This is a great and wondrous condescension. Since it cannot take place except through the remission of sins, he continues and says:

“And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so the Son of Man must be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

We know what happened then in the wilderness: many were dying from the bites of serpents. Then the people, confessing their sins, entreated the Lord through Moses to remove this poison from them. Thus, at the Lord’s command, Moses lifted up a bronze serpent in the wilderness and instructed the people that whoever was bitten by a serpent should look upon the lifted serpent; those who did this were immediately healed (Num. 21:6–9).

What is the lifted-up serpent except the death of Christ, according to that mode of signification by which the effect is signified through the agent producing it? For death came from the serpent, which persuaded man to commit the sin by which he deserved to die. But the Lord did not transfer sin into his flesh, as though it were the serpent’s poison; nevertheless, he transferred death, so that there might be, in the likeness of sinful flesh, punishment without guilt, and so that in sinful flesh both guilt and punishment might be removed.

Therefore, just as then the person who looked upon the lifted serpent was healed from the poison and freed from death, so now the person who is conformed to the likeness of Christ’s death through faith and his baptism is freed from sin through justification and from death through resurrection.

For this is what he said: “so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.” Why, then, is it necessary that an infant be conformed to Christ’s death through Baptism, if the infant has not been poisoned at all by the serpent’s bite?

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### 62. No one can be reconciled to God except through Christ.

Then he says, in orderly succession:

“God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

The infant, therefore, was destined to perish and would not have eternal life if, through the sacrament of Baptism, he did not believe in [Note: [Col. 0145] The printed editions read, “did not believe in the only-begotten,” omitting the preposition *in*, which is present here in the manuscripts.] the only-begotten Son of God, since he came not to judge the world but so that the world might be saved through him.

This is especially clear because he continues and says:

“Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe has already been judged, because he has not believed in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.”

Where, then, do we place baptized infants except among the faithful, as the authority of the universal Church proclaims everywhere? Therefore they are among those who have believed; this is acquired for them through the power of the sacrament and the response of those who present [Col. 0146] them. Consequently, those who have not been baptized are among those who have not believed.

Moreover, if those who have been baptized are not judged, then these others, because they lack Baptism, are judged.

But when he adds, “This is the judgment: that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than the light,” from whom does he say that the light came into the world except with reference to his own coming? Without the sacrament of his coming, how can infants be said to be in the light? Or how do those who, just as they themselves do not believe, likewise do not think that their infants ought to be baptized—not even when they fear bodily death for them—not also have this as part of their love of darkness?

He says that the works of the person who comes to the light have been done in God, because he understands that his justification belongs not to his own merits but to God’s grace. “For it is God,” says the Apostle, “who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13).

In this way, then, the spiritual regeneration of all who come to Christ from carnal generation takes place. He himself disclosed it; he himself showed it, when he was asked how these things could happen. He did not leave human reasoning free in this matter. Infants must not be alienated [Note: [Col. 0146] The printed editions read, “so that infants may not be alienated.” The particle *so that* is absent from the manuscripts.] from the grace of the remission of sins. There is no other passage to Christ; no one can otherwise be reconciled to God or come to God except through Christ.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### 63. The form, or rite, of Baptism. Exorcism. Two errors concerning infants.

What shall I say about the actual form of the sacrament? I wish that one of those who hold contrary opinions would bring me an infant to be baptized. What is my exorcism doing to that child, if the child is not held in the devil’s household? Surely the person carrying the child would have to answer for that child, since the child could not answer for himself.

How, then, would he say that the child renounced the devil, if the child had nothing belonging to the devil? How would he say that the child turned to God, from whom the child had not turned away? How would he say, among other things, that the child believed the remission of sins [Note: [Col. 0146] Several manuscripts read, “believed, moreover.” Shortly afterward the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus read, “in the remission of sins,” adding the preposition *in*, which is absent from the manuscripts and was rightly removed by the Louvain editors.] when no remission of sins was being granted to the child?

If I thought that he held this view contrary to these facts, I would not permit him even to enter the sacraments with the child. But with what face he would present himself to men in this matter, or with what mind to God, I do not know; nor do I wish to say anything more severe.

Some of them have therefore seen that nothing more detestable or abhorrent could be said or believed than that a false or deceptive form of Baptism was being handed down to infants, in which the words sounded and the rite appeared to be performed [Note: [Col. 0146] So the manuscripts. The editions read, “in which the words sounded, though certainly the rite appeared to be performed.”], while nevertheless no remission of sins took place.

Accordingly, with regard to the Baptism of infants, they concede that it is necessary for them and that they too require redemption, as is contained in the very brief book of one of them; yet he did not wish there to express openly that any sin was forgiven.

But, as you yourself informed me in your letter, they now admit, you say, that in infants too the remission of sins takes place through Baptism. This is not surprising, for redemption could not otherwise be understood. Nevertheless, they say, the sin is not original [Col. 0147]; rather, after they were born, they began to possess sin in their own lives.

### 64.

You therefore see how great the difference now is between them and those against whom I have argued at length and for a long time in this work, and one of whose books, containing such doctrines, I read and refuted as best I could.

Between these people, then, as I had begun to say—those who insist that infants are entirely pure and free from every sin, both original and personal—and those who think that infants, once born, contracted personal sins, from which they believe they ought to be cleansed through Baptism, you see how great the difference is.

The latter, by considering the Scriptures, the authority of the whole Church, and the form of the sacrament itself, have correctly seen that through Baptism the remission of sins takes place in infants. But they either do not wish to say, or cannot say, that whatever it is in them is original [Note: [Col. 0147] So the Vatican and Cygirannian codices. Most other manuscripts read, “but that it is original.” The editions read, “but that it was original.” Shortly afterward those same editions read, “or they cannot see.” But *see* is absent from the manuscripts.].

The former, however, by considering human nature itself—which is readily available for everyone to examine—correctly saw what was easy to see: that at that age infants could not have contracted any sin in their own lives. But, in order not to acknowledge original sin, they say that there is no sin at all in infants.

Let them therefore first agree among themselves in those propositions in which each group speaks truly [Note: [Col. 0147] The Cygirannian codex alone reads, “in those propositions in which each individual speaks truly.”], and then it will follow that they disagree with us in no respect.

For if the first group concedes to the second that the remission of sins takes place in baptized infants, and the second concedes to the first—as the very nature of silent infants proclaims—that infants have not yet contracted any sin belonging to their own lives [Note: [Col. 0147] Most manuscripts read, “any sin of their own.”], then both groups will concede to us [Note: [Col. 0147] The Louvain edition and several manuscripts read, “let the latter concede to the former; let both groups concede to us.”] that nothing remains except original sin, which is forgiven in infants through Baptism.

## CHAPTER XXXV

### 65. There is no sin belonging to the infants’ own lives.

Or is this also in question? [Note: [Col. 0147] So all the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “Is this also to be questioned?”] Shall we debate this and spend time proving and teaching how infants, through their own will—without which there can be no sin belonging to one’s own life—have committed no evil, and therefore are called innocent by everyone?

Does not such great weakness of mind and body, such complete ignorance of things, such total incapacity for any commandment, the absence of any perception or impulse concerning either natural or written law, and the absence of any exercise of reason in either direction proclaim and indicate this far more eloquently in its silent testimony than our speech can?

Let the evidence itself carry some force in persuading us of itself. For nowhere do I find so little to say as where the matter under discussion is clearer than anything that can be said.

Nevertheless, I wish that anyone who thinks otherwise would say what sin he has seen or imagined in a newborn infant, immediately from the womb, whom he already admits requires Baptism for redemption. What evil has that infant committed through his own mind or body in his own life?

If perhaps the infant’s crying is regarded as a weariness and nuisance to adults, it is astonishing if this is attributed to wickedness rather than to misery [Col. 0148]. Or is it because the crying cannot be restrained by any reasoning of his own or by anyone’s prohibition? But this is due to ignorance, in which he lies sunk most deeply. In that same ignorance, once he has grown stronger after a short time, he angrily strikes his mother, and often even her very breasts, which he sucks when hungry [Note: [Col. 0148] Most manuscripts have *demands* instead of *sucks*.]

These things are not merely tolerated in infants; they are even loved in them—and with what feeling except a carnal one, by which even laughter and joking are pleasing, and by which the wit of clever people is seasoned with a kind of absurdity? If such behavior were perceived in the way it is described, would people laugh at them as amusing, rather than as foolish?

We see even fools [Note: [Col. 0148] Three Gallican manuscripts read *long-haired fools* in place of *fools*. See above, no. 32, col. 127.] whom the common people call jesters, brought in for the entertainment of sensible people, and valued more highly among slaves than sensible persons are. So powerful is the carnal affection even of those who are not fools in taking pleasure in another’s misfortune.

For although a man may find another’s foolishness amusing, he would nevertheless not wish to be such himself. And if he knew that his own little son—the child whose babbling the father happily awaits and provokes—would grow up to be such, he would have no doubt that the child should be mourned more pitifully than if he were dead.

But while there is hope of growth, and it is believed that the light of intelligence will come with advancing age, even the insults of infants directed at their parents are not merely harmless but actually pleasing and delightful.

No prudent person, however, would approve of this: that children should not merely be prevented from such words or actions when they can already be prevented, but should even be incited to them by the adults’ eagerness to laugh and their vanity [Note: [Col. 0148] The manuscripts omit *not merely* before *prevented*.]

For generally, at that age, children already recognize their father and mother, and dare not curse either of them unless one parent or both have permitted or commanded it.

But these are the actions of infants who have already broken into speech and can express the movements of their minds through whatever signs of the tongue they are able to produce [Note: [Col. 0148] The editions and some manuscripts add *signs*. Some other manuscripts read *indications*. The older codices have neither, since *through movements* is elegantly understood. From those same manuscripts we restore the verb *produce* in place of *attempt repeatedly to produce*, which appeared in the earlier printed editions. The Paris manuscript of the Augustinians reads *bring forth*.]

Let us rather consider the profound ignorance of newborn infants, from which they have advanced toward this later, temporary babbling foolishness as though progressing toward knowledge and speech.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

### 67. The ignorance of infants, and its origin.

Let us, I say, consider those darknesses of the rational mind in which infants are entirely ignorant even of God, whose sacraments they resist even when they are baptized. I ask when and from where they were plunged into these darknesses.

Did they acquire them here, in this life, and through excessive negligence forget God in their own lives, while they lived wisely and religiously in their mothers’ wombs?

Let those who dare say such things state them; let those who wish listen; let those who can believe. I, however, think that all whose minds are not clouded by obstinate determination to defend their own position cannot possibly hold this view.

Or is ignorance not an evil, and therefore not something to be cleansed? And what does that voice [Note: [Col. 0149] The Louvain edition, from some manuscripts, reads *says*.] mean: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance” (Ps. 24:7)?

Although the sins committed knowingly are more deserving of condemnation, nevertheless, if sins of ignorance did not exist, we would not read the words I have cited: “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance.”

Into those thickest darknesses of ignorance, then, where the soul of a newborn infant—certainly the soul of a human being, certainly a rational soul—lies not merely uneducated but incapable of being taught, why, when, or from where was it thrust?

If it is the nature of man [Note: [Col. 0149] The Louvain edition reads, “if it belongs to human nature.”] to begin in this way, and this nature is not already defective, why was Adam not created in such a condition? Why was he capable of receiving a commandment and able to give names to his wife and to all the animals?

For he said of her, “She shall be called woman”; and, “Whatever Adam called the living creature, that was its name” (Gen. 2:23, 19).

But this infant does not know where he is, what he is, by whom he was created, or from whom he was born. Already guilty of sin, yet not capable of receiving a commandment, he is wrapped and pressed down by such profound darkness of ignorance that he cannot even be awakened as from sleep so as to recognize these things once they are pointed out to him. Instead, we must wait for the time when he will gradually digest this mysterious drunkenness—not over one night, as even the most severe drunkenness usually lasts, but over several months and years.

Until this happens, we tolerate in infants so many things that we punish in adults that they cannot possibly be counted.
