If infants contracted this great evil of ignorance and weakness after they were born in this life [Note: [Col. 0149] The better manuscripts—the Corbeiensis, Remigianus, Cygirannianus, and several others—read, “if infants not born in this life contracted it.”], where, when, and how, through some great act of impiety, were they suddenly enveloped in such darkness?

## CHAPTER XXXVII

### 68. If Adam was not created as we are born, why was Christ, free from sin, born an infant and weak?

Someone may say: If this nature is not pure but the beginning of a defective nature, since Adam was not created in this condition, why did Christ, far more excellent and certainly born from a virgin without any sin, nevertheless appear in this weakness and at this age?

We answer this proposition as follows: Adam was not created in this condition because, since no preceding sin of a parent existed, he was not created in sinful flesh [Note: [Col. 0149] Erasmus’s edition reads, “because, with no preceding sin of a parent, he was created in sinful flesh,” omitting *not*.]. We are in this condition because, since his sin preceded us, we were born in sinful flesh. Christ was in this condition because, in order to condemn sin in sin, he was born in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8:3).

For the issue here is not Adam’s bodily size, since he was not made as an infant but with a fully developed bodily stature. It could be said that animals too were created in this way, and yet their sin did not cause their offspring to be born as small young; what the case is with this we are not now asking.

Rather, the issue is a certain strength of mind and use of reason by which Adam, teachable as he was, could grasp God’s commandment and the law of the command, and could easily [Col. 0150] keep them if he wished.

But now man is born in such a way that, because of dreadful ignorance and weakness—not of the flesh but of the mind—he is entirely unable to do so, although we all acknowledge that in the infant there dwells not another substance but the same substance that existed in the first man, namely, a rational soul.

Indeed, even this great weakness of the flesh seems to indicate something penal, though I do not know exactly what. For it raises the question whether, if those first human beings had not sinned, they would have had such children, unable to use either tongue, hands, or feet.

Perhaps it would have been necessary for infants to be born because of the capacity of the womb. Yet although a rib is only a small part of the body, God did not for that reason make a small wife for the man when he built it into a woman. Thus the omnipotence of the Creator could also have made their children large immediately upon birth.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

### 69. The ignorance and weakness of the infant.

But, to set this aside, God certainly could have granted infants what he has granted even to many animals. Although their young are small, and although they do not advance in mind as their bodies grow, since they do not possess rational souls, even the tiniest of them run, recognize their mothers, and do not need another’s care and assistance to be brought to the breast for suckling. Rather, they themselves know where the breasts are, hidden in their mothers’ bodies, with astonishing ease.

By contrast, a human being is born with feet unfit even for walking and hands not even capable of scratching. Unless, with the assistance of the person feeding him, his lips are applied to the nipple of the breast [Note: [Col. 0150] The better manuscripts read, “with unmoved lips.”], he does not even perceive where it is. Though the breasts lie beside him, when hungry he is more capable of crying than of sucking.

This bodily weakness therefore corresponds entirely to the weakness of the mind. The flesh of Christ would not have been in the likeness of sinful flesh unless this were sinful flesh, whose weight so burdens the rational soul—whether the soul itself has been derived from parents, or created there, or breathed in from above, a question I postpone for now.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

### 70. To what extent sin is annulled through Baptism in infants, likewise in adults, and what benefit follows from this.

In infants, certainly, the grace of God, through the Baptism of the one who came in the likeness of sinful flesh, brings this about: that sinful flesh may be annulled.

It is annulled not in the sense that concupiscence, scattered through and innate in the living flesh, is suddenly consumed and ceases to exist, but so that, when the person who was born dies, it may not harm him, although it was present in him at birth.

For if he lives after Baptism and is able to reach the age capable of receiving a commandment, then he has something with which to struggle and something which, with God’s help, he may overcome—if he has not received God’s grace in vain and does not wish to be rejected.

This is not granted even to adults in Baptism, except perhaps by an ineffable miracle of the almighty Creator: that the law of sin, which is present in the members and fights against the law of the mind, should be utterly [Note: [Col. 0150] From the manuscripts we have added *utterly*.] extinguished and cease to exist. Rather, Baptism brings it about that whatever evil has been done, said, or thought by a person while his mind was subject to that concupiscence is entirely erased and regarded as though it had not been done.

Concupiscence itself, once the bond of guilt by which the devil held the soul through it has been loosed [Note: [Col. 0150] Amerbach and Erasmus read, “by which he held it,” omitting *through*. Shortly afterward in [incomplete in source].], and once the barrier by which the devil separated man from his Creator has been destroyed [Col. 0151], remains in the contest in which “we discipline our body and bring it into subjection” (1 Cor. 9:27). It is to be released for lawful and necessary uses or restrained by continence.

But because the human life known beforehand and foretold by the divine Spirit—who knows far better than we do all things concerning the human race, whether past, present, or future—has been such that “no living person is justified in your sight” [Col. 0152] (Ps. 142:2), it follows that through ignorance or weakness, because our will does not exert all its strength against concupiscence, we yield to it in some unlawful matters.

We yield to it more and more frequently the worse we are, and less and less frequently the better we are.

But since the question whether a human being can be, is, has been, or will be without sin in this life—apart from the one who said, “The ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John 14:30)—must be discussed somewhat more carefully, let this be the end of the present volume, so that we may seek the matter from another beginning.

# BOOK TWO

Augustine argues against those who say that in this life there are, have been, and will be human beings who have absolutely no sin. Having proposed four questions concerning this matter, he teaches first that, through God’s grace and the human being’s own free will, it is possible for a person in this life to be without sin. He then proves that nevertheless no one living in this life is entirely without sin. Third, he shows that this is so because no one wills as much as the situation requires, whether because what is just remains hidden or because doing it does not give pleasure. Fourth, he establishes that no human being, except Christ the one Mediator, either is, has been, or will be free from every sin.

## CHAPTER I

### 1. What has been accomplished so far, and what is to be treated in this book.

Concerning the Baptism of infants, Marcellinus, my dearest son, we have argued sufficiently in the preceding book, as I think, that it is given to them not only for attaining the kingdom of God but also for attaining salvation and eternal life—which no one can possess without the kingdom of God and without fellowship with Christ the Savior, into which he redeemed us by his blood.

In this book, however, I have undertaken to discuss and explain, with whatever diligence and ability he grants, whether anyone in this world lives, has lived, or will live without any sin at all, except the one Mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, “who gave himself as a ransom for all” (1 Tim. 2:5–6).

If, in the course of this discussion, the question of the Baptism or sin of infants should repeatedly be introduced by some necessity or opportunity, this should neither surprise us nor be avoided. Rather, in those places, let us answer as best we can everything that demands our response.

## CHAPTER II

### 2. Some attribute too much to free will. Ignorance and weakness.

The solution to this question concerning a human life without any stealthy intrusion or prior seizure by sin is especially necessary because of our daily prayers.

For some people presume so greatly upon the free choice of the human will that they think we require no divine assistance in order not to sin, once the freedom of the will has been granted to our nature.

It follows that we ought not even to pray that we may not enter into temptation—that is, that we may not be overcome by temptation—whether temptation deceives and overtakes us unawares, or presses and forces us when we are weak.

How harmful and destructive this is to our salvation, which is in Christ; how contrary it is to the religion with which we have been imbued and to the piety by which we worship God; and how fiercely opposed it is to our faith that we should not ask the Lord for such a benefit, or think that the petition in the Lord’s Prayer, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6:13), has been placed there in vain—this cannot be expressed adequately in words.

## CHAPTER III

### 3. How God commands nothing impossible. Works of mercy are remedies for abolishing sins.

They think they speak cleverly, as though none of us knew this, when they say: “If we do not wish to sin, we do not sin; and God would not command a human being to do what was impossible for human will.”

But they do not see that overcoming certain things—whether things wrongly desired or things wrongly feared—sometimes requires great and complete strength of will. The one who willed that it be truthfully said through the prophet, “No living person shall be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142:2), foresaw that we would not apply this strength perfectly in every matter.

Since the Lord foresaw that we would be such people, he graciously gave and made effective certain salutary remedies against the guilt and bonds of sins even after Baptism—namely, works of mercy—when he said: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:37–38).

For who would depart from this life with any hope of attaining eternal salvation if the sentence remained that “whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all of it,” unless there followed shortly afterward: “So speak and so act as those who are to be judged by the law of freedom. For judgment is without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy; mercy, however, triumphs over judgment” (James 2:10, 12–13)?

## CHAPTER IV
### 4. To what extent concupiscence exists in us

[Col. 0153]

In the baptized, it is not concupiscence itself but consent to it alone that causes harm. Concupiscence, therefore, remaining like the law of sin in the members of this body of death, is born with infants; in baptized infants it is released from guilt, but is left for the contest. If they die before the contest, it pursues them with no condemnation. In unbaptized infants it binds them as guilty and, as children of wrath, draws them to condemnation, even if they die in infancy.

But in baptized adults, who already use reason, whatever the mind consents to in that concupiscence for the purpose of sin belongs to their own will. Once all sins have been blotted out, and the guilt by which it originally held them bound has also been removed, concupiscence remains for the contest for the time being. If they do not consent to unlawful things, it will do them no harm at all, until “death is swallowed up in victory” (1 Cor. 15:54), and in perfect peace there is nothing left to conquer.

But it holds guilty those who consent to unlawful things; and unless they are healed by the medicine of repentance and works of mercy, through the heavenly Priest who intercedes for us, it leads them to the second death and condemnation.
[Note: Several manuscripts omit “and condemnation.”] For this reason, when the Lord taught us to pray, among other things he instructed us to say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors; and do not bring us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:12–13).

For evil remains in our flesh—not the nature in which the human being was divinely created, but the defect into which he fell by his will. Having lost his strength there, he is not healed with the ease of will by which he was wounded. Concerning this evil the Apostle says: “I know that good does not dwell in my flesh” (Rom. 7:18). He commands us not to obey this evil when he says: “Therefore, let sin not reign in your mortal body so as to obey its desires” (Rom. 6:12).
[Note: Ambrosius Erasmus and several manuscripts read: “He commands us not to obey this evil.”]

If, then, by an unlawful inclination of the will we have consented to these desires of the flesh’s concupiscence, we say for the healing of this: “Forgive us our debts,” applying the remedy of a work of mercy in what we add: “as we also forgive our debtors.” But so that we may not consent to it, we beg for help, saying: “And do not bring us into temptation”—or, as some manuscripts have it, “do not lead us into temptation.”  
[Note: The words placed in brackets are omitted by almost all manuscripts.]

This does not mean that God himself tempts anyone with such a temptation; for “God is not a tempter of evils, and he himself tempts no one” (James 1:13). Rather, it means that if we should begin to be tempted by our own concupiscence, we may not be abandoned by his help, so that we may be able to conquer in him and not be dragged away after being enticed.

Then we add what will be fulfilled at the end, when “what is mortal will be swallowed up by life” (2 Cor. 5:4): “But deliver us from evil.” For then there will be no such concupiscence with which we must contend and to which we are commanded not to consent.

Thus the whole matter can briefly be requested in three benefits: Forgive us the things in which we have been dragged away by concupiscence; help us not to be dragged away by concupiscence; take concupiscence away from us.

### CHAPTER V

[Col. 0154]

#### 5. The human will needs God’s help

For we are not helped by God to sin; but we cannot do what is just, or fulfill the commandment of justice in every respect, unless we are helped by God. Just as the eye of the body is not helped by the light so that it may depart from that same light, whether closed or turned away; but it is helped by it in order to see, and cannot see at all unless the light helps it—so God, who is the light of the inner human being, helps the sight of our mind so that we may do something good not according to our own justice but according to his.

If we turn away from him, that is our doing; and then we think according to the flesh, then we consent to the unlawful desires of the flesh. God therefore helps those who turn toward him and abandons those who turn away. Yet he also helps us so that we may turn toward him—something this bodily light certainly does not provide.

When, therefore, he commands us, saying, “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zech. 1:3), and we say to him, “Turn us, O God of our salvation” (Ps. 84:5), and, “O God of hosts, turn us” (Ps. 80:8), what else are we saying but, “Give what you command”?

When he commands by saying, “Understand, you foolish among the people” (Ps. 94:8), and we say to him, “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” (Ps. 119:73), what else are we saying but, “Give what you command”?

When he commands by saying, “Do not go after your desires” (Ecclus. 18:30), and we say, “We know that no one can be self-controlled unless God grants it” (Wis. 8:21), what else are we saying but, “Give what you command”?

When he commands, saying, “Do justice” (Isa. 56:1), and we say, “Teach me your ordinances” (Ps. 119:12), what else are we saying but, “Give what you command”?
[Note: In the manuscripts, “Likewise, when he says, ‘Blessed are those who hunger’” follows directly after “Do justice,” and the intervening words are omitted.]

Likewise, when he says, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice, for they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:6), from whom ought we to ask for the food and drink of justice, if not from the one who promises its fullness to those who hunger and thirst for it?

#### 6. Let us therefore drive from our ears and minds those who say that, once we have received freedom of will, we ought not to pray that God help us not to sin.

For even that Pharisee was not blinded by such darkness. Although he was mistaken in thinking that nothing needed to be added to his justice and that he was filled with its fullness, he nevertheless gave thanks to God that he was not like other people—unjust, robbers, adulterers—or like that tax collector; that he fasted twice a week; and that he gave tithes of everything he possessed.

He was no longer asking that anything be added to his justice. Yet, by giving thanks to God for what he had, he confessed that he had received everything from him. Nevertheless, he was rejected, both because, as though already filled, he asked for none of the nourishment of justice, and because he eagerly sought to exalt himself over the tax collector who was hungry and thirsty for it, as though insulting him (Luke 18:10–14).

What, then, will happen to those who, even if they admit that they do not possess justice, or do not possess it fully, nevertheless presume that it must be obtained from themselves, not begged from their Creator, with whom are its granary and its fountain?

Yet this does not mean that we should act in this matter only through prayers, without the efficacy of our own will being added through striving.
[Note: The Lovanienses think this passage was emended thus by Martinus Lipsius. Instead of “through striving” (*adnitendo*), the first editions read “for living well” (*ad bene vivendum*), a reading supported by only two manuscripts, one Belgian and one Vatican. Two other Vatican manuscripts read “for acting and living”; two Belgian manuscripts, “for living”; likewise the Gallican manuscripts, except the Beccensis and one Paris manuscript of the Augustinians’ Greater Convent, which read “through striving.”] For God is called “our helper” (Ps. 62:9), and no one can be helped unless he also makes some voluntary effort. God does not work our salvation in us as he does in senseless stones, or in those beings whose nature he created without reason and will.

Why he helps one person and does not help another; why he helps one only, but another not so much; why he does so for this person in one way and for that person in another—it belongs to him to determine, along with the reason for such hidden equity and the excellence of his power.
[Note: All the manuscripts read “but another only,” omitting “not.”]

### CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0155]

#### 7. Four questions concerning the perfection of justice

The first question is whether a human being can be without sin in this life. For when some say that a person can be without sin in this life, we must not immediately oppose them with heedless rashness.
[Note: All our manuscripts again omit “can.”] If we deny that this is possible, we shall detract both from the free will of the human being who desires this by willing it, and from the power or mercy of God, who brings it about by helping.

But one question is whether it can be; another, whether it is; another, if it is not although it can be, why it is not; and another, whether anyone who has never had any sin at all has existed, or could at some time have existed, or can exist.

If, within this fourfold formulation of the questions, I am asked whether a human being can be without sin in this life, I shall confess that this is possible through God’s grace and his free will. I do not doubt that free will itself belongs to God’s grace—that is, to God’s gifts—not merely so that it may exist, but also so that it may be good, namely, that it may be turned toward carrying out the Lord’s commandments. Thus God’s grace not only shows what must be done, but also helps so that what it has shown may be done. For “what do we have that we have not received?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

Hence Jeremiah also says: “I know, Lord, that a person’s way does not belong to him, nor is it in a man to walk and direct his steps” (Jer. 10:23).

For this reason, in the Psalms, when someone had said to God, “You have commanded that your commandments be kept exceedingly,” he immediately did not presume upon himself but desired that he might do so: “Would that my ways,” he says, “might be directed toward keeping your ordinances; then I shall not be put to shame when I look upon all your commandments.” Who desires what he has so completely in his own power that he needs no help at all to do it?

And from whom he desired this—since it was not from fortune, fate, or anyone other than God—he sufficiently shows in what follows: “Direct my paths according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me” (Ps. 119:4–6, 133). Those are freed from slavery to this accursed domination to whom the Lord Jesus, “when they receive him,” gave the power to become children of God (John 1:12).  
[Note: The words “when they receive him” are absent from the manuscripts. See below, no. 37.]

Those who are told, “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36), were to be freed from this dreadful domination.

On the basis of these and innumerably many other testimonies of the same kind, I cannot doubt either that God has commanded human beings nothing impossible, or that anything is impossible for God when it comes to aiding and helping so that what he commands may be done. Accordingly, a person can, if he wishes, be without sin, helped by God.

### CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0156]

#### 8. The second question: whether any human being is without sin in this life

But if the second point I had set down is asked—whether such a person exists—I do not believe that he does. Rather, I believe the Scripture that says, “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 143:2).

Therefore God’s mercy is necessary, for it “exalts itself over judgment,” and it will not be granted to the one who does not show mercy (James 2:13).

When the prophet said, “I said, I will declare my transgression to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my heart,” he immediately added, “For this every holy person shall pray to you at an appropriate time” (Ps. 32:5–6). He therefore says not “every sinner,” but “every holy person.” For this is the voice of the holy: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

Accordingly, in the Apocalypse of that same Apostle, those 144,000 holy persons who did not defile themselves with women, for they remained virgins, and “no deceit was found in their mouths, for they are blameless” (Rev. 14:4–5)—in Greek, *amômoi gar eisi*, “for they are blameless”—are certainly blameless because they truthfully accused themselves. And no deceit was found in their mouths because, if they had said that they had no sin, they would have deceived themselves, and the truth would not have been in them. In any case, there would have been deceit where the truth was not. For “the just person is an accuser of himself at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18:17), and therefore does not lie.

#### 9. Accordingly, those who understand the Scriptures insufficiently are greatly mistaken concerning what is written: “Whoever is born of God does not sin, and cannot sin, because his seed remains in him” (1 John 3:9), and anything else said in the same manner.

They do not notice that people become children of God insofar as they begin to exist in the newness of the spirit and are renewed in the inner person according to the image of him who created them (Col. 3:10).
[Note: Lovaniensis and several manuscripts read “to renew the inner person.”]

A person’s entire old infirmity is not removed from the hour at which he is baptized. Renewal begins with the forgiveness of all sins, and each person is renewed to the extent that he has spiritual understanding—whoever has such understanding.  
[Note: In the printed editions, “to the extent that he has such understanding” was followed by “to that extent he is renewed.” This does not occur in the manuscripts.]

The rest has been accomplished in hope, until it is also accomplished in reality: even to the renewal of the body itself into a better condition of immortality and incorruption, with which we shall be clothed in the resurrection of the dead.

The Lord himself also calls this regeneration—not, of course, the kind that occurs through Baptism, but that in which what is now begun in the spirit will also be completed in the body. “In the regeneration,” he says, “when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

For although in Baptism the forgiveness of sins is complete and entire, if immediately the human being’s transformation into eternal newness were also complete and entire—not to mention the body, which plainly still tends toward its former corruption and toward death, to be renewed at the end, when there will truly be complete newness—but, leaving the body aside, if complete newness were produced in the mind itself, which is the inner person, the Apostle would not say:
[Note: Two manuscripts read “not less.”] “Although our outer person is being corrupted, the inner person is being renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16).

Certainly, whoever is still being renewed day by day has not yet been wholly renewed; and to the extent that he has not yet been renewed, to that extent he is still in the old condition.  
[Note: In almost all manuscripts the words “and to the extent that he has not yet been renewed” are absent.]

Therefore, insofar as they are still in the old condition, although already baptized, they are still children of this age. But insofar as they are in newness—that is, through the complete and perfect forgiveness of sins, and to whatever extent they have spiritual understanding and conduct lives corresponding to it—they are children of God.  
[Note: Some manuscripts read “insofar as they have been renewed” instead of “insofar as they are in newness.”]

For inwardly we have put off the old person and put on the new, since there we lay aside falsehood and speak the truth, along with the other things by which the Apostle explains what it means to put off the old person and put on the new, who has been created according to God in justice and the holiness of truth (Eph. 4:22–24).

He urges the baptized faithful to do this. They would not still need to be admonished if it had already been perfectly accomplished in Baptism. And yet it has been accomplished, just as we have also been saved. “He saved us through the washing of regeneration” (Titus 3:5).

But elsewhere he explains how this has been accomplished: “Not only this,” he says, “but we ourselves, who have the first fruits of the spirit, groan within ourselves as we await adoption, the redemption of our body. For in hope we have been saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:23–25).

### CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0157]

#### 10. When perfection will come

Full adoption as sons will therefore occur also in the redemption of our body. We now have the first fruits of the spirit, by which we have already become children of God in reality. In other respects, in hope, we are saved, renewed, and children of God; but in reality, because we are not yet saved, we are not yet fully renewed and therefore are not yet children of God, but children of this age.

We therefore advance toward renewal and a just life through that by which we are children of God; and through this we cannot sin at all, until everything has been transformed into this condition—even that by which we are still children of this age.
[Note: The printed editions read “that through which”; “through” is absent from the manuscripts.] For through this latter condition we can still sin. Thus it comes about both that the one who has been born of God does not sin, and that, if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us.

What we are as children of the flesh and of this age will therefore be brought to an end, and what we are as children of God and renewed in spirit will be perfected.

Hence the same John says: “Beloved,”—“Beloved,” all the manuscripts read, “we are children of God,” omitting “now”—“we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be.” What is the meaning of “we are” and “we shall be,” unless it is that we are so in hope but shall be so in reality?

For he continues and says: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

We have therefore already begun to be like him, possessing the first fruits of the spirit; and yet we are still unlike him because of the remnants of the old condition. Accordingly, insofar as we are like him, we are children of God through the spirit’s regeneration; but insofar as we are unlike him, we are children of the flesh and of this age.

From the former source we cannot sin; from the latter, if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves—until everything passes into adoption, “and the sinner is no more; you will seek his place, and you will not find it” (Ps. 37:10).

### CHAPTER IX

[Col. 0158]

#### 11. The Pelagian objection: why a just person does not beget a just person

It is therefore pointless that some also argue as follows: “If a sinner begets a sinner, so that the guilt of original sin may be removed from his infant when he receives Baptism, then a just person ought also to beget a just person.”  
[Note: Some manuscripts read, “they seize upon that argument in order to say.”]

It is as though each person begot children carnally because he is just, rather than because that which moves concupisciently in his members is converted to the use of propagation by the law of sin against the law of the mind. He therefore begets from that by which he still drags along the old condition among the children of this age, not from that by which he has advanced into newness among the children of God.

“For the children of this age beget and are begotten” (Luke 20:34). Hence what is born is such, because “what is born of the flesh is flesh” (John 3:6).

The just, however, are children only of God. Insofar as they are children of God, they do not beget through the flesh, because they themselves were born through the spirit, not through the flesh. But those of them who beget children do so through the flesh insofar as they have not yet transformed all the remnants of the old condition into perfect newness.

Therefore, whoever is born as a son from this old and infirm aspect must himself also be old and infirm. For this reason he too must be renewed in the spirit into another generation through the forgiveness of sin.

If this does not happen in him, a just father will profit him nothing, for he is just in the spirit, through which he did not beget him. If it does happen, even an unjust father will harm him nothing, for the former—the child—has passed through spiritual grace into the hope of eternal newness, while the latter—the father—has remained wholly in the old condition through a carnal mind.

### CHAPTER X

#### 12. Reconciling the Scriptures

The testimony “Whoever is born of God does not sin” is therefore not contrary to the testimony addressed to those already born of God: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

For as long as a human being, although already wholly so in hope and already renewed in reality by a partial spiritual regeneration, nevertheless still carries a body that is subject to corruption and weighs down the soul, it is necessary to distinguish, even in one person, what belongs to each aspect and from which aspect each statement is made.  
[Note: Lovaniensis reads “in hope.” “In” is absent from the other printed editions and from the manuscripts.]

For, as I think, Scripture does not easily give so great a testimony to anyone’s justice as it does to three of God’s servants—Noah, Daniel, and Job—whom the prophet Ezekiel says alone could be delivered from a certain impending anger of God (Ezek. 14:14). In these three men he was evidently prefiguring three classes of human beings who were to be delivered: in Noah, as I think, the just rulers of peoples, because of the governance of the ark, as of the Church;  
[Note: Several manuscripts read, “because of the governance of the waters and of the ark.” Compare the exposition on Psalm 132, no. 5.]

[Col. 0159]

in Daniel, the just who practice continence; in Job, the just who are married.  
[Note: The manuscripts read “the married just.”]

There may perhaps be another interpretation, but it is not necessary to investigate it now.

Nevertheless, how greatly these men excelled in justice is sufficiently clear both from this prophetic testimony and from other divine testimonies. Yet no sober person would therefore say that drunkenness is not a sin, although it overtook so great a man. For, as we read, Noah was drunk at one time (Gen. 9:21), though God forbid that he was habitually drunk.

#### 13. Daniel, after the prayer he poured out to God, says of himself: “While I was praying and confessing my sins and the sins of my people to the Lord my God” (Dan. 9:20).

For this reason, unless I am mistaken, the prophet Ezekiel’s previously mentioned words are addressed to an exceedingly proud person: “Are you wiser than Daniel?” (Ezek. 28:3).

Nor can one here make the argument that some offer against the Lord’s Prayer: “Even if the holy and already perfect Apostles prayed it,” they say, “having no sin at all, they nevertheless said it not for themselves but for the imperfect and still sinful. ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors’ (Matt. 6:12). By saying ‘our,’ they thereby demonstrated, they say, that they belonged to one body, including both those who still had sins and themselves, who were already entirely free from sin.”

This certainly cannot be said of Daniel. I believe that, like a prophet foreseeing that this presumption would one day arise, he had often said in his prayer, “We have sinned.” Yet he did not explain to us why he said this in such a way that we would hear from him, “While I was praying and confessing the sins of my people to the Lord my God.”  
[Note: In Ambrosius Erasmus and Lovaniensis, “my sins and” was incorrectly added here; it was rightly absent from the manuscripts.]

Nor did he leave the distinction confused, as though it were uncertain whether, by saying “when I confessed our sins to the Lord my God,” he meant this because of membership in one body. Rather, with complete clarity, as though he were carefully making the distinction and commending it with the greatest force, he says: “My sins and the sins of the people.”

Who would contradict such obvious evidence except one who prefers to defend what he thinks rather than discover what ought to be thought?

#### 14. Let us now see what Job himself says after God’s great testimony to his justice.

“In truth,” he says, “I know that it is so. For how will a human being be just before the Lord? If he should wish to contend with him, he will not be able to answer him.” And shortly afterward: “Who will oppose his judgment?” Again, a little later: “I know,” he says, “that he will not leave me unpunished. Since I am wicked, why have I not died? Even if I were purified like snow and cleansed with clean hands, you have sufficiently stained me with filth” (Job 9:2–3, 19–20, 28–31).

Likewise, in another of his speeches: “For you have written bitter things against me,” he says, “and made me inherit the sins of my youth;” you have set my foot in confinement, guarded all my works, and examined the soles of my feet, which grow old like a wineskin or like a garment eaten by moths.

“For a human being, born of woman, is of short duration and full of anger; like a flower, when it has blossomed and withered, he departs like a shadow and does not remain. Do you not also bring the care of this one into your judgment? For who will be clean from filth? No one—not even if his life should last a single day.”

And shortly afterward: “You have counted all my necessities,” he says, “and nothing concerning my sins has escaped you; you have sealed my sins in a pouch and marked down whatever I committed unwillingly” (Job 13:26–14:1–5, 16–17).

Behold, Job also confesses his sins and says that he knows in truth that no one is just before the Lord. He therefore knows this in truth because, if we say that we have no sin, the truth itself is not in us.

Accordingly, according to the standard of human conduct, God gives him so great a testimony of justice; but Job himself, measuring himself by that rule of justice which he perceives as far as he can in God, knows in truth that this is the case. He adds: “For how will a human being be just before the Lord? If he should wish to contend with him, he will not be able to answer him.” That is, if, when he is to be judged, he wishes to show that nothing condemnable can be found in him, he will not be able to answer him.  
[Note: Most manuscripts omit the words “that is, if, when he is to be judged, he wishes to show that nothing condemnable can be found in him, he will not be able to answer him.” Perhaps this resulted from the carelessness of copyists, for whom the repeated phrase “he will not be able to answer him” provided an opportunity for error.]

For he would even lose that obedience by which he could obey the one commanding him to confess his sins.

Hence he rebukes certain people, saying, “Why do you wish to contend with me in judgment?” (Jer. 2:29). To forestall this, the other says: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person will be justified in your sight.”

For this reason Job also says, “Who will oppose his judgment? But if I should be just, my mouth will speak wickedly.” That is: If I call myself just against his judgment, where that perfect rule of justice proves me unjust, my mouth will certainly speak wickedly, because it will speak against God’s truth.

#### 15. Showing also the fragility—or rather, the condemnation—of carnal generation resulting from the original transgression of sin, when he was speaking of his sins, as though giving the reasons for them, Job said that a human being born of woman is of short duration and full of anger.

What anger could this be except that by which all are, as the Apostle says, “by nature”—that is, originally—“children of wrath” (Eph. 2:3)? For they are children of the concupiscence of the flesh and of this age.

He subsequently shows that the death of the human being also belongs to this anger. For after saying, “He is of short duration and full of anger,” he added, “And like a flower, when it has blossomed and withered, he departs like a shadow; he does not remain.”

When he adds, “Do you not also bring the care of this one into your judgment? For who will be clean from filth? No one, not even if his life should last a single day,” he clearly means: “You have brought the care of a human being of brief life into your judgment.” However short his life may have been—even if it were only one day—he could not be clean from filth, and therefore he will most justly come into your judgment.

But when he says, “You have counted all my necessities, and nothing concerning my sins has escaped you; you have sealed my sins in a pouch and marked down whatever I committed unwillingly,” is it not sufficiently clear that even those sins are justly charged which are not committed through the enticement of pleasure, but to avoid some trouble, pain, or death?

These too are said to be committed under a kind of necessity, although everything must be overcome through love and delight in justice. What he says, “and you marked down whatever I committed unwillingly,” can also be understood as referring to the statement: “For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I hate—that I do” (Rom. 7:15).

[Col. 0161]

#### 16. What of the Lord himself?

He had borne witness to Job, and Scripture—that is, the Spirit of God—had said that in all that happened to him he did not sin with his lips before the Lord (Job 1:22). Yet afterward, when the Lord spoke to him, he spoke reproachfully, as Job himself bears witness, saying: “Why am I still being judged, while I hear the Lord’s rebukes?” (Job 39:33, according to the Septuagint).

No one is justly rebuked unless there is something in him deserving rebuke.

### CHAPTER XI

#### Job foresaw Christ coming to suffer. The reason for humility in the perfect

And what sort of rebuke is that which is understood from the person of the Lord Christ? He lists before Job the divine works of his power, rebuking him in such a way that Job appears to be told: “Can you do these great things that I can do?”

What purpose could this serve except that Job should understand—this too having been divinely inspired in him, so that he might foresee that Christ would come to suffer—how calmly he ought to endure what he suffered, if Christ, in whom there was absolutely no sin when he became human for our sake, and who possesses such great power as God, nevertheless did not refuse obedience in suffering?
[Note: Perhaps the reading is “for.”]

Understanding this with a purer intention of heart, Job added to his answer: “Before, I heard you by the hearing of the ear; but now, behold, my eye sees you. Therefore I reproached myself, and I wasted away, and I regarded myself as earth and ashes” (Job 42:5–6).  
[Note: All manuscripts read “I understood you before.”]

Why was he displeased with himself in this great understanding? The work of God by which he was human could not rightly have displeased him, since it is said even to God: “Do not despise the works of your hands” (Ps. 138:8).

But certainly, according to that justice by which he knew himself to be just, he reproached himself and wasted away, and regarded himself as earth and ashes. He perceived in his mind the justice of Christ, in whose divinity—and not even in whose soul or flesh—could there be any sin.

According to this justice, which is from God, the Apostle Paul not only condemned but also regarded as refuse that which, according to the justice arising from the law, had been blameless in him (Phil. 3:6–8).

### CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0162]

#### 17. No one is just in every respect

The magnificent testimony of God by which Job was praised is therefore not contrary to the testimony that says, “No living person will be justified in your sight.” It does not establish that there was absolutely nothing in him that could truthfully be reproved either by Job himself or rightly by the Lord God.

Thus, although he was already just, a truthful worshiper of God, and abstained from every evil work, he could truthfully be so called. These are God’s words concerning him: “Have you considered my servant Job? For there is no one like him on the earth, blameless, just, a true worshiper of God, abstaining from every evil work” (Job 1:8).

In the first words he is praised by comparison with the human beings who were on earth. Therefore he excelled all who at that time could be just on earth. It does not follow that he had absolutely no sin merely because he surpassed the others in progress toward justice.

Then comes “blameless,” meaning that no one could justly complain about his life; “just,” because he had advanced in such integrity of conduct that no one could be compared with him; “a true worshiper of God,” since he was also a truthful and humble confessor of his own sins; and “abstaining from every evil work”—though it would be remarkable if this meant abstaining from every evil word and thought as well.

We do not know how great Job was. But we know that he was just, and we also know that he was great in enduring the terrifying trials of tribulations. We know that he suffered all those things not because of his sins, but to demonstrate his justice.

Nevertheless, these words with which he is praised by the Lord could also be said of one who delights in the law of God according to the inner person, but sees another law in his members resisting the law of his mind—especially since he says: “I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I hate—that I do. But if I do what I hate, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.”

Behold, this person too, according to the inner person, is separate from every evil work, because he himself does not do it, but the evil dwelling in his flesh does. Yet, since even that delight in the law of God comes to him only through God’s grace, he still needs liberation and cries out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:15–25).

### CHAPTER XIII

#### 18. Perfect human justice is imperfect

There are therefore just people on earth—great, strong, prudent, continent, patient, pious, merciful, enduring with equanimity all temporal evils for the sake of justice.

But if it is true—indeed, because it is true—“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (1 John 1:8), and “No living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 143:2), they are not without sin. Nor does any one of them go mad with such arrogance as to think that he has no need, for whatever his sins may be, of the Lord’s Prayer.

19. Now what are we to say about Zechariah and Elizabeth, who are so often brought forward against us in the discussions of this question, except that Scripture plainly testifies that Zechariah possessed distinguished righteousness among the chief priests responsible for offering the sacrifices of the Old Testament? We read in the Epistle written to the Hebrews [Note: [Col. 0162] Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read “which is entitled.”], a testimony that I already cited in the preceding book (above, Book 1, no. 50), that Christ alone is the high priest who had no need, as did those called chief priests, first to offer sacrifice daily for his own sins and then for those of the people. “For such a high priest was fitting for us,” he says, “righteous, without malice, undefiled, separated from sinners, made higher than the heavens, having no daily need, as the chief priests do, first to offer sacrifice for their own sins” (Heb. 7:26–27). Zechariah belonged to this number of priests; so did Phinehas; so did Aaron himself, from whom this order began; and so did all the others who lived honorably and righteously in that priesthood. Yet they had need first to offer sacrifice for their own sins, whereas Christ alone, whose future coming they prefigured, was an undefiled priest who had no such need.

20. But what commendation was made concerning Zechariah and Elizabeth that is not included in what the Apostle professed about himself when he had not yet believed in Christ? For he said that, according to the righteousness that is in the Law, he had been blameless. The same is read of them: “Now they were both righteous before God, walking blamelessly in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord” (Luke 1:6). Since, therefore, whatever righteousness they possessed was not pretended before human beings, it is said that they were righteous “before God.” What is written about Zechariah and his wife, “in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord,” he expressed briefly by saying, “in the Law.” For before the Gospel there was not one Law for him and another for them, but one and the same Law, which we read was given through Moses to their ancestors; according to it Zechariah was also a priest and offered sacrifice in his appointed turn.

Yet the Apostle, who at that time possessed a similar righteousness, goes on to say: “Whatever gains I had, these I have counted as loss because of Christ. Indeed, I count everything as loss because of the surpassing knowledge of the Lord Jesus Christ, for whose sake I have considered all things not merely disadvantages but even refuse, that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the Law, but that which is through faith in Christ, the righteousness that is from God, founded on faith; that I may know him and the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings, being conformed to his death, if somehow I may attain to the resurrection of the dead.”

So far is it from being the case that, on account of those words, we should believe Zechariah and Elizabeth to have possessed perfect righteousness without any sin, that we should not even think the Apostle himself to have been perfect according to the highest standard of the same rule—not only in that righteousness of the Law, which he possessed like them and counted as loss and refuse in comparison with the surpassing righteousness that is in faith in Christ, but even in the Gospel itself, where he attained the primacy of so great an apostleship. I would not dare to say this if I did not consider it impious to disbelieve him.

There he continues and adds: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect; but I pursue it, if I may apprehend that for which I have also been apprehended in Christ Jesus. Brothers, I do not consider myself to have apprehended it. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the goal, the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus.” [Note: [Col. 0163] The printed editions read, “if somehow I may apprehend.” “If somehow” is absent from the manuscripts, nor is it repeated in the Latin Bibles of the Corbie manuscript of the Vulgate, or in the Greek manuscripts.]

He himself confesses that he had not yet received, and was not yet perfect in, that fullness of righteousness which he desired to attain in Christ; but that he was still pursuing it with determination, forgetting the past and stretching forward to what lay ahead. Thus we understand that the following statement also applies to him: “Though our outward person is being destroyed, yet our inward person is being renewed day by day” (2 Cor. 4:16). He was already a perfect traveler, so to speak, although he had not yet reached perfection at the end of the journey itself.

Finally, he wishes to take with him as companions in this course those whom he immediately addresses, saying: “Therefore, as many as are perfect, let us think in this way; and if you think differently about anything, God will reveal that also to you” [Note: [Col. 0164] The manuscripts read, “God has revealed it.”]; “nevertheless, let us walk according to what we have attained” (Phil. 3:3–16). This walking is carried out not by the feet of the body, but by the dispositions of the mind and the conduct of life. Thus those who progress day by day in their renewal along the straight path of faith [Note: [Col. 0164] The word “of faith” is absent from all the Gallican manuscripts.] can be perfect possessors of righteousness, having already become travelers who are perfect in that same righteousness.

## CHAPTER XIV

21. Thus, all those who in this life have been commended by the testimonies of the divine Scriptures for their good will and deeds of righteousness, and all who were like them afterward—whether or not they were commended and praised by the same testimonies—as well as those who exist even now or will exist later: all are great, all are righteous, all are truly praiseworthy, but none are without some sin. For from the testimonies of Scripture by which we believe in their praises, we also believe this: that no living person is justified in the sight of God; that we are to pray that he not enter into judgment with his servants; and that the Lord’s Prayer, which he handed down to his disciples, is necessary not only for all the faithful universally but also for each individual.

## CHAPTER XV

22. Objection of the Pelagians. Perfection in one respect. One who has made great progress in righteousness is rightly called perfect.—But the Lord says, “Be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5:48). “He would not command this,” they say, “if he knew that what he commands could not be done.”

The question now is not whether it can be done, if they understand this perfection to mean that a person may live this life without any sin—for we have already answered above that this is possible—but whether anyone actually does so. It has already been established that no one desires as much as the matter requires, as the many testimonies of the Scriptures that I cited above clearly show.

Yet when someone’s perfection is mentioned, we must consider in what respect he is said to be perfect. Shortly before, I cited the Apostle’s testimony, in which he confesses that he is not yet perfect in attaining the righteousness he desires; nevertheless, he immediately says, “Therefore, as many as are perfect, let us think in this way.” He would not say both things unless he were perfect in one respect and not perfect in another.

For example, someone might already be a perfect hearer of wisdom, although those to whom the Apostle said, “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food; for you were not yet able—and indeed you are still not able” (1 Cor. 3:2), were not yet such hearers. Yet he also says to them, “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (ibid. 2:6), clearly intending “perfect hearers” to be understood [Note: [Col. 0165] Ambrosius and Erasmus read, “more perfect.”]. Thus, as I said, it can happen that someone is already a perfect hearer of wisdom, although he is not yet a perfect teacher; he may be a perfect knower of righteousness, although not yet a perfect doer of it; he may be perfect in loving his enemies, although not yet perfect in enduring suffering.

Someone may be perfect in loving all human beings, since he has even advanced to the love of enemies. Yet the question remains whether he is already perfect in this love—that is, whether he loves those whom he loves as much as that unchangeable rule of truth prescribes that they should be loved.

Therefore, when the perfection of any person is read of in Scripture, we must carefully observe in what respect it is stated. For no one is thereby understood to be wholly without sin merely because he is said to be perfect in some respect. Nevertheless, even in this matter one may be called perfect, not because there is no further progress possible for him, but because he has progressed to a very great extent. Thus someone may be called perfect in knowledge of the Law even though something still remains hidden from him; just as the Apostle called certain people perfect while nevertheless saying to them, “If you think differently about anything, God will reveal that also to you; nevertheless, let us walk according to what we have attained.”

## CHAPTER XVI

23. Why God commands what he knows will not be observed.—Nor should we deny that God commands us to be so perfect in the practice of righteousness that we have absolutely no sin. For if something is to exist, it will not be sin if God does not command that it not exist.

“Why, then,” they ask, “does he command what he knows no human being will do?” By the same reasoning one might ask why he commanded those first human beings—who were then only two—to do what he knew they would not do. For we must not say that he commanded it so that one of us might do it if they failed to do so. God commanded only those two not to eat from that tree; and just as he knew what act of righteousness they would not perform, so he also knew what act of righteousness he himself would carry out with regard to them.

In the same way, then, he commands all human beings not to commit any sin, although he foreknows that no one will fulfill this command, so that, for all who impiously and damnably despise his commandments, he himself may do what is just in their condemnation. But for those who obediently and devoutly make progress in his commandments, yet do not fulfill everything he has commanded, and who forgive the sins of others as they wish their own sins to be forgiven, he himself may do what is good in their cleansing.

For how could the one who forgives be forgiven by God’s mercy if sin did not exist? Or how could sin not be forbidden by God’s justice if it did exist?

24. “But look,” they say, “the Apostle says, ‘I have fought the good fight, I have kept the faith, I have finished the course; there remains for me the crown of righteousness’ (2 Tim. 4:7–8). He would not have said this if he had any sin.”

On the contrary, let them explain how he could say these things when there still remained for him so great a struggle in the very passion which he had already said was impending, such a difficult and great contest. Was little still lacking for the completion of his course, when what remained was precisely the point at which he would face a fiercer and more cruel enemy?

If he rejoiced with confidence and security in such words because the certainty of the future contest’s victory [Note: [Col. 0166] The printed editions read, “of the future great contest.” “Great” is absent from the manuscripts.—Since the Benedictines had not yet devoted special attention to editing these books, when they cited the present passage in volume 5, Sermon 299, note (a), they used the reading of the printed editions, “of the future great contest”; and we followed their reading there as well. M.] had already made him certain and secure—he who had already revealed to him that the same passion was imminent—then he spoke these words not on the basis of a fully accomplished reality, but from the firmest hope; and he presented as accomplished what he confidently expected would take place.

Therefore, if he had added to these words, “I now have no sin,” we would likewise understand him to have spoken not of a completed reality but of a future perfection. For the completion of his course included having no sin, which they think had already been accomplished in him when he said these things; just as the completion of his course also included overcoming his adversary in the struggle of his passion, which they themselves must admit still had to be accomplished in him when he said these things.

Thus we say that all of this still had to be perfected at the time when, trusting in God’s promise, he spoke of everything as though it had already been accomplished. For the completion of his course also included his forgiving the sins of his debtors and praying that his own sins might likewise be forgiven [Note: [Col. 0166] The printed editions read, “so that they might be forgiven.” The manuscripts read, “so that it might be forgiven.”]. Through the Lord’s promise he was completely certain that, at that end which was still future but which, because of his confidence, he already described as fulfilled, he would have no sin.

To omit other considerations, I wonder whether, when he spoke those words by which he seemed to these people to have had no sin, the “thorn of the flesh” had already been taken away from him—the very thorn concerning whose removal he had three times pleaded with the Lord and had received the answer, “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:7–9). For the perfection of so great a man it was necessary that the angel of Satan not be taken away from him, since he was buffeted by it lest he be exalted by the greatness of his revelations. And yet does anyone dare either to think or to say that a person living under the burden of this life is entirely free from every sin?

25. Even if there are human beings so outstanding in righteousness that God speaks to us from the pillar concerning them—such as Moses and Aaron among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name—whose great praises for devotion and innocence are proclaimed in truthful Scripture from his earliest childhood, from the time when his mother, fulfilling her vow, placed him in God’s temple and dedicated him as the Lord’s servant—even of such people it is written, “You were gracious to them, and took vengeance upon all their affections” (Ps. 98:6–8).

He takes vengeance in anger upon the children of condemnation; but upon the children of grace he takes vengeance in graciousness, when he disciplines the one he loves and scourges every son whom he receives (Prov. 3:12; Heb. 12:6). No vengeance, discipline, or scourging from God is owed except on account of sin—apart from the one who was prepared for scourging so that he might experience all things according to likeness, without sin, and might be the Holy of holies, the priest who intercedes even for the saints. Even they truthfully say of themselves, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12).

Accordingly, even those who argue against these points, although they live chaste lives and are praiseworthy in conduct, and although they do not hesitate to do what the Lord commanded the rich man who sought his advice about attaining eternal life—when the man replied that he had already fulfilled all the commandments of the Law, the Lord told him that, if he wished to be perfect, he should sell everything he had and give it to the poor, and transfer his treasure to heaven (Matt. 19:20–21)—nevertheless none of them dares to say that he is without sin.

As we believe, they do not say this with a deceitful mind. But if they are lying, by that very fact they begin either to increase or to possess sin.

## CHAPTER XVII

26. The third question: why no one is without sin in this life.—Let us now examine what I placed third. Since, with divine grace assisting the human will, a person can be without sin in this life, why is no one so? I could answer very easily and truthfully: because human beings do not will it. But if I am asked why they do not wish to be, we enter upon a lengthy discussion.

Nevertheless, without prejudicing a more careful inquiry, I will say briefly even this much. People do not wish to do what is righteous, either because they do not know whether it is righteous or because it does not please them. For the more certainly we know that something is good, the more vehemently we desire it, and the more ardently we delight in it.

Ignorance and weakness, therefore, are vices that hinder the will from being moved to perform a good work or to abstain from an evil one. But for what was hidden to become known, and for what did not please to become pleasing, this is the work of God’s grace, which assists human wills. The reason they are not assisted is likewise found in them, not in God—whether those predestined to condemnation are so predestined on account of the iniquity of pride, or whether they are to be judged and instructed against that very pride, if they are children of mercy [Note: [Col. 0167] Three Vatican manuscripts and all our Gallican manuscripts read, “to be judged, so that they may be instructed as children of mercy.” Nevertheless, Fulgentius supports the other reading, which is found in all the earlier editions, in Book 1 to Monimus, chapter 28. We carefully examined this passage of Fulgentius not only in printed copies but also in the very ancient Corbie manuscript.].

Thus, when Jeremiah had said, “I know, O Lord, that a person’s way is not his own, nor does it belong to a man to walk and direct his steps,” he immediately added, “Correct me, O Lord; but with judgment, and not in your anger” (Jer. 10:23–24). It is as though he said: “I know that it belongs to my correction that I am less assisted by you, so that my steps may be perfectly directed. Nevertheless, do not deal with me in this matter as in the anger with which you have determined to condemn the wicked, but as in the judgment by which you teach your own people not to be proud.” Hence it is said elsewhere, “Your judgments will help me” (Ps. 118:175).

[Col. 0168] 27. Therefore, do not attribute the cause of any human fault to God. For pride is the cause of all human vices. To convict and remove it, such a remedy came from heaven: to the human being made proud through pride, God descended in humility through mercy, displaying and commending clear and manifest grace in the very human being whom, with such great love beyond his fellows, he took to himself.

For even he did not become so united to the Word of God that, through this union, he became one Son of God and that same one Son of Man because of preceding merits of his own will. There had to be only one such person. If this could happen not through God’s own gift but through the free choice of a human being, there would be two, three, or more such persons.

This, therefore, is especially commended; this, as far as I dare to judge, is especially taught and learned in the treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in Christ. Therefore each of us sometimes knows how to undertake, perform, and complete a good work, and sometimes does not; sometimes delights in it, and sometimes does not delight in it, so that we may know that both what we know and what pleases us are not within our own power but are divine gifts.

Thus we are healed of the vanity of self-exaltation and learn how truly the following words are spoken—not of this earthly land but spiritually: “The Lord will give sweetness, and our land will give its fruit” (Ps. 84:13). A good work pleases us all the more as God, the supreme and unchangeable good and the author of every kind of good, is loved more.

Now, so that God may be loved, “his love has been poured into our hearts,” not through us, “but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

## CHAPTER XVIII

28. The good will is from God.—People labor to discover what good in our will is truly ours and is not from God; how this could be discovered, I do not know. Apart from what the Apostle said when speaking about human goods—“What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7)—even reason itself, which people such as we are can bring to bear on these matters, greatly troubles anyone who searches earnestly. We must not defend grace in such a way that we seem to take away free choice; yet again, we must not assert free choice in such a way that, through proud impiety, we are judged ungrateful toward God’s grace.

29. For some have wished to defend the Apostle’s statement I cited by saying that whatever good will a person possesses must be attributed to God, because it could not exist in that person if the person himself did not exist. Since a person has nothing except from God, both in being something and in being human, why should whatever good will exists in that person not also be attributed to God the author, since it would not exist unless there were someone in whom it could exist?

But by this reasoning one could also say that an evil will must be attributed to God its author, because it too could not exist in a human being unless there were a human being in whom it existed; and God is the author of the human being’s existence. Thus even that person’s evil will—which could not exist at all unless it had a human being in whom it could exist—could not exist [Note: [Col. 0168] Lovaniensis reads: “Thus his evil will too, which could not exist at all unless it had a human being in whom it existed, must be referred to God the author” [Col. 0169] . We have removed the final words, “must be referred to God the author,” restoring the reading found here, “thus his evil will also”; the implied completion is, “God the author would be responsible.” We found this reading in the printed editions of Ambrosius and Erasmus and in all the manuscript codices, although some of them incorrectly add “beginning” after “evil will.” Below, too, along with Ambrosius and Erasmus, they read, “must be referred to God the author.” In one Paris edition of 1644 the passage reads: “Thus whatever is of an evil will, which could not exist at all unless it had a human being in whom it existed.”]. It is wicked to say this.

[Col. 0169] 30. Therefore, unless we establish that not only the freedom of the will—which can turn freely this way and that, and which belongs among those natural goods that even an evil person can misuse—but also the good will, which already belongs among those goods that an evil person cannot use, can exist in us only from God, I do not know how we can defend the statement, “What do you have that you did not receive?”

For if a certain free will is from God and can still be either good or evil, while the good will is from us, then what comes from us is better than what comes from him. But since this is absurd beyond measure, they must admit that we also obtain the good will from God.

Indeed, it would be astonishing if the will could stand in some middle state so that it was neither good nor evil. Either we love righteousness, and the will is good; if we love it more, it is better; if less, less good. Or, if we do not love it at all, the will is not good. Who would hesitate to say that a will that in no way loves righteousness is not merely evil but the worst kind of will?

Therefore, if the will is either good or evil, and if we certainly do not have the evil will from God, it remains that we have the good will from God. Otherwise I do not know what other gift of his we should enjoy when we are justified by him.

For this reason, I think it is written, “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 8:35); and in the Psalms, “The steps of a person are directed by the Lord, and he will delight in his way” (Ps. 36:23); and in the Apostle’s words, “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13).

31. Therefore, since our turning away from God is ours—and this is the evil will—but our turning toward God is something we cannot do unless he himself arouses and assists us—and this is the good will—what do we have that we did not receive? And if we received it, why do we boast as though we had not received it?

Accordingly, “whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31). To those to whom God has wished to grant this, it is a matter of his mercy, not of their merit; but to those to whom he has not wished to grant it, it is a matter of truth. For a just punishment is owed to sinners, since “the Lord God loves mercy and truth” (Ps. 84:12); “mercy and truth have met one another” (Ps. 84:11); and “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10).

Who could explain how frequently divine Scripture mentions these two things together? Sometimes even their names are changed, so that “grace” is used for “mercy.” Hence we read, “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14). Sometimes “judgment” is used for “truth,” as in, “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Ps. 100:1).

[Col. 0170] 32. But why he wishes to convert some and punish others for turning away—although no one can justly criticize him for being merciful in granting a benefit, or for being truthful in exercising vengeance, just as no one could justly criticize him in the case of the Gospel laborers, to some of whom he paid the agreed wage and to others granted even a wage not agreed upon (Matt. 20:9–10)—that belongs to his own counsel of hidden justice.

## CHAPTER XIX

Through grace come both knowledge of the good and delight in it.—Let us understand as much as has been granted to us, and, if we can, let us recognize that the Lord God, who is good, sometimes withholds from even his saints, in relation to some righteous work, either certain knowledge or victorious delight, so that they may learn that the light by which their darkness is illuminated is from him, not from themselves, and that the sweetness by which their land produces its fruit is from him.

33. When we pray to him for his assistance in doing and completing righteousness, what else do we ask except that he reveal what was hidden and make pleasing what did not please us? We learned from his grace that this too must be asked of him: by his grace we came to know what had previously been hidden; by his grace we loved what had previously not pleased us, so that whoever boasts might boast not in himself but in the Lord.

For human beings’ being lifted up in pride proceeds from their own will, not from God’s work; God neither compels nor assists them toward this. A certain desire for self-rule therefore comes first in the human will, so that through pride it becomes disobedient. Even if this desire had not existed, nothing would have been troublesome; and when a person had willed this, he would have been able to will otherwise without difficulty.

But as a just punishment that was owed, such a vice followed, so that obedience to righteousness became troublesome. Unless this vice is overcome with the assistance of grace, no one turns to righteousness; unless it is healed through the operation of grace, no one enjoys the peace of righteousness.

Whose grace conquers and heals it, except that of the one to whom it is said, “Restore us, God of our salvation, and turn away your anger from us” (Ps. 84:5)? And if he does this, he does it in mercy, so that it may be said, “He has not dealt with us according to our sins, nor repaid us according to our iniquities” (Ps. 103:10). And for those for whom he does not do this, it is by judgment that he does not do it.

Who will say to him, “What have you done?”—to him whose mercy and judgment are sung with devout hearts by the saints?

For this reason he also heals his saints and faithful ones more slowly from certain vices, so that the good may please them less than is sufficient for the fulfillment of righteousness in every respect, whether while it remains hidden or even when it has become manifest. Thus, insofar as the most complete rule of his truth is concerned, no living person is justified in his sight.

Yet he does not wish us to be condemnable in this matter, but humble, commending this same grace to us, lest, having attained ease in everything, we think that what belongs to him belongs to us. Such an error is strongly opposed to religion and devotion.

Nevertheless, we must not conclude that we should remain in these same vices. Rather, we must strive vigilantly and pray to him fervently against pride itself, on account of which we are humbled in them, understanding at the same time that both our striving and our praying in this way are gifts from him. Thus, in everything, looking not to ourselves but having our hearts raised upward, let us give thanks to the Lord our God; and when we boast, let us boast in him.

## CHAPTER XX

34. He answers the fourth question: apart from Christ, no one has been or can be without sin.—The fourth matter now remains. Once it has been explained, may this lengthy discourse finally come to an end, insofar as the Lord assists us. The question is whether anyone born of human beings not only has been or will be entirely without any sin, but whether anyone could ever have been or could be so.

It is utterly certain that no one except the one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, either is, was, or will be without sin.

We have already said much about the Baptism of infants. If they have no sin, then not only are there countless human beings without sin; there have also been, and will be, such people. But if what we discussed in the second place is truly established—namely, that no one is without sin (above, nos. 8–9)—then infants too are certainly not without sin.

From this it follows that, even if someone could have existed in this life who was so perfected by virtue as to reach such fullness of righteousness that he had absolutely no sin, it would nevertheless be unquestionable that he had previously been a sinner and had been converted from that condition into this newness of life [Note: [Col. 0171] The word “life” is absent from all the Gallican manuscripts.].

For in the second question a different matter was being sought, while in this fourth one another matter is proposed. In the second, the question was whether someone might, by God’s grace and through the zeal of his will, reach in this life the perfect life that is entirely without sin. In this fourth question, however, we ask whether there was, or could have been, among human beings someone who did not reach perfect righteousness from a condition of sin, but who had never been bound by any sin whatsoever [Note: [Col. 0171] Lovaniensis reads, “through the zeal of the will, it was asked”; “this” is omitted, although it appears in the other books. The manuscripts omit “or could be.”].

Therefore, if all the many things we have said about infants are true, there is no one among human beings, nor has there been, nor will there be, except the one Mediator in whom our reconciliation and justification are established, through which, once the enmity of sins has been ended, we are reconciled to God.

It is therefore not irrelevant, insofar as seems sufficient for the present subject, to recall a few things from the very beginning of the human race, so that the mind of the reader may be instructed against certain matters that could cause difficulty.

## CHAPTER XXI

35. Adam and Eve: God strongly commended obedience to human beings.—After those first human beings, the one man Adam and Eve his wife, refused to preserve obedience after receiving God’s command, a just and deserved punishment followed them. For the Lord had threatened that on the day they ate the forbidden food, they would surely die.

[Col. 0172] Since they had received permission to eat from every tree that was in paradise—and God had also planted the tree of life there—but he had forbidden them to eat from that one tree which he called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil (Gen. 2:9, 16–17), a name signifying the consequences of experience, namely, what good they would feel from preserving the command and what evil they would experience from transgressing it, they are rightly understood to have abstained from the forbidden food before the devil’s wicked persuasion and to have eaten what had been permitted, including the other trees and especially the tree of life.

For what could be more absurd than to believe that they obtained nourishment from the other trees but not also from the one that was likewise permitted and that, by its special benefit, did not allow animal bodies to be changed through the decay of age [Note: [Col. 0172] Only the Lovaniensis edition reads, “to be changed through the lapse of ages.”] and grow old toward death?
