It granted this benefit to the human body from its own substance and, through a mystical sign, showed what would be bestowed through wisdom—which it prefigured—upon the rational soul, so that, vivified by its nourishment, the soul would not be turned toward the decay and death of wickedness.

For it is rightly said of wisdom, “She is a tree of life to those who embrace her” (Prov. 3:18). As that tree was so in the bodily paradise, so wisdom is in the spiritual paradise: the former supplying vigor to the senses of the outward person, the latter to those of the inward person, each providing life without any change over time for the worse.

They therefore served God with the devotion of obedience, which had been strongly commended to them and by which alone God is worshiped. How great this obedience is in itself, and how sufficient it alone is to preserve a rational creature under the Creator, could not have been made clearer than by their being forbidden a tree that was not evil.

Far be it from us to suppose that the Creator of all good things, who made everything and, behold, it was very good (Gen. 1:31), would have planted anything evil in the abundance even of that bodily paradise. Rather, they were forbidden that tree so that human beings, for whom service under such a Lord was supremely beneficial, might be shown how great the good of obedience alone is—obedience that he had required solely from his servant, whom it was advantageous to obey not for the sake of the master’s dominion but rather for the servant’s benefit [Note: [Col. 0172] The manuscripts read either “of the client” or “of the one who must make amends.”].

They were forbidden that tree although, if they had eaten from it without the prohibition, they would have suffered no evil at all. Thus it might be clearly understood that what they suffered after using it against the prohibition was not inflicted by the tree as harmful and destructive food, but solely by the violation of obedience.

## CHAPTER XXII
#### 36. The human condition before sin

Before they transgressed it, they were pleasing to God, and God was pleasing to them; and although they bore an animal body, they felt nothing disobedient within it stirring against them. For the order of justice brought this about: since their soul had received its servant-body from the Lord, just as the soul itself obeyed its own Lord, so its body obeyed the soul and rendered it a service suited to life, without any resistance. Hence they were naked and were not ashamed.

For natural modesty now causes the rational soul to be ashamed that, in the flesh over which it received the right of authority, it cannot, because of some weakness, bring it about that the limbs do not move when it does not wish them to **[Col. 0173]**, and move when it wishes them to. For this reason, in every chaste person they are rightly called the shameful members (*pudenda*): they are aroused against the ruling mind, as though they themselves possessed authority, whenever they please. The only control that virtue exercises over them is to prevent them from reaching impure and unlawful corruptions.

This disobedience of the flesh, which exists in the very movement itself—even when it is not permitted to achieve its effect—was not present in those first human beings when they were naked and were not ashamed. For the rational soul, mistress of the flesh, had not yet become disobedient to its Lord, so as to experience in reciprocal punishment its servant-flesh disobeying it, together with a certain sense of shame and distress. Certainly, the soul itself did not inflict this experience upon God through its disobedience. For God has no reason to be ashamed or distressed if we do not obey him, since we cannot in any way diminish his supreme power over us; but we have reason to be ashamed that the flesh does not serve our command. This happens through the weakness that we deserved by sinning, and it is called “sin dwelling in our members” (Rom. 7:17, 23).

This sin, then, is also a punishment for sin. Accordingly, after that transgression had occurred, and the disobedient soul had turned away from the law of its Lord, its servant—namely, its body—began to have against it a law of disobedience. The human beings were ashamed of their nakedness when they noticed in themselves a movement that they had not previously perceived. This perception is called the opening of the eyes (Gen. 3:7); for they were not wandering among those trees with their eyes closed. Thus it is also written concerning Hagar: “Her eyes were opened, and she saw a well” (ibid. 21:19).

Then those human beings covered their shameful members: God had made those members for them, but they themselves made them shameful.

### CHAPTER XXIII

#### 37. The corruption of nature through sin, and its renewal through Christ

From this law of sin is born the flesh of sin, to be cleansed through the sacrament of him who came “in the likeness of sinful flesh, so that the body of sin might be destroyed” (Rom. 8:3). This body is also called “the body of this death,” from which wretched humanity is delivered only by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord (ibid. 7:24–25).

For this law, the beginning of death, passed from them into their descendants just as the labor with which all human beings labor upon the earth passed into them, and just as childbirth with its pains passed into women. These were judgments which they deserved from God when they were convicted of sin; and we see them fulfilled not only in them but also in their descendants—in some more, in others less, yet in all.

Since, therefore, the first justice of those first human beings consisted in obeying God and in not having in their members a law of desire opposed to the law of their mind, now, after their sin, our sinful flesh has been born from them. Among those who obey God, it is regarded as a great achievement not to obey the desires of that same desire, and to crucify the flesh within themselves with its passions and desires, so that they may belong to Jesus Christ, who represented this in his own cross **[Note: All Gallican manuscripts read, “represented this in his own flesh.”]**. By his grace he gave them power to become children of God **[Col. 0174]**.

For he did not give this to all human beings, but to as many as received him, so that they might be born anew to God by the Spirit—those who had been born into the world through the flesh. For this is what was said concerning them: “But to as many as received him, he gave power to become children of God, who were born not of flesh, nor of blood, nor of the will of man, nor of the will of the flesh, but of God.”

### CHAPTER XXIV

#### 38. What benefit has been bestowed upon us through the incarnation of the Word. In what respect Christ’s birth from the flesh is like and unlike ours. The children even of believers must be baptized

After this he added: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:12–14), as though he were saying:

It is indeed a great thing that this has happened to these people: that those who had previously been born from the flesh into the world, although created by God himself, should be born from God. But something far more marvelous has happened: whereas for them it was natural to be born from the flesh, and it was a gift to be born from God, he who was naturally born from God, in order to bestow this gift, graciously deigned also to be born from the flesh. This is what is meant by: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

Through this, he says, it came about that we, who were born flesh from flesh, should afterward become spirit from being born of the Spirit, and should dwell in God; for God, who was born God from God, afterward became flesh by being born from the flesh, and dwelt among us.

For the Word that became flesh was “in the beginning,” and was God with God. Yet his participation in our lower things, so that ours might be in his higher things, maintained a certain middle position even in the birth from the flesh. Thus we were born in sinful flesh, while he was born in the likeness of sinful flesh; we were born not only from flesh and blood but also from the will of man and from the will of the flesh **[Note: Most manuscripts read, “and from the pleasure of the flesh”; likewise shortly afterward, “nor from the pleasure of the flesh.”]**; but he was born only from flesh and blood, not from the will of man, nor from the will of the flesh, but from God.

Therefore we are subject to death because of sin, while he, for our sake, was subject to death without sin. And just as his lower things, through which he descended to us, were not altogether made equal to our lower things, in which he found us here, so our higher things, through which we ascend to him, will not be made equal to his higher things, in which we shall find him there.

We shall become children of God by his grace; he was always the Son of God by nature. We shall at some time, after being converted, cling to God while remaining unequal to him; he, never having turned away, remains equal to God. We shall be participants in eternal life; he is eternal life.

Therefore he alone, even after becoming human while remaining God, never had any sin, nor did he assume sinful flesh **[Note: In place of “nor did he assume sinful flesh,” most manuscripts read, “nor did he assume flesh with sin.” Perhaps the intended wording is “nor did he assume sinful flesh,” with “he had” understood.]**, although he took his flesh from the sinful flesh of his mother **[Note: The printed editions read, “from the nature of sinful flesh.” Two Sorbonne manuscripts and one manuscript of Casalès Abbey read, “from the material of sinful flesh.” The oldest Corbie manuscript and the other Gallican manuscripts, as well as three Vatican manuscripts and the four Belgian manuscripts seen by the Louvain editors, read, “from the sinful flesh of his mother.” Compare Book 5 against Julian, chapter 9, and Book 10 of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, sections 18 and 20.]**.

Whatever he assumed from it, he certainly either cleansed **[Col. 0175]** before assuming it or cleansed it by assuming it. Therefore he created the Virgin mother whom he would choose, who conceived not according to the law of sinful flesh—that is, not through the movement of carnal desire—but by devout faith **[Note: The manuscripts read, “but by faith itself.”]**, deserving that the holy offspring should be formed within her; and he chose her from whom he would be created **[Note: The manuscripts of Ambrose and Erasmus read, “whom he had chosen he created.”]**.

How much more, then, must sinful flesh be baptized in order to escape judgment, if flesh without sin was baptized as an example for imitation?

### CHAPTER XXV

#### 39. The Pelagian objection

What we answered above against those who say, “If a sinner fathered a sinner, then a righteous person ought also to have fathered a righteous person” (above, section 11), we also answer to those who say that someone born from a baptized person ought already to have been regarded as baptized.

“Why,” they ask, “could he not have been baptized in his father’s loins, if, according to the Epistle written to the Hebrews, Levi could be tithed in Abraham’s loins?” (Heb. 7:9–10).

Those who say this should observe that Levi was not subsequently tithed because he had already been tithed in Abraham’s loins, but because he was appointed to the honor of the priesthood in such a way that he was to receive tithes, not provide them. Otherwise his other brothers, who provided tithes to him, would not have been tithed either, since they too had already been tithed in Abraham’s loins by Melchizedek.

But lest anyone say that Abraham’s sons could rightly have been tithed for this reason—that although they had already been tithed in their father’s loins, tithing was something that had to be performed repeatedly for each person **[Note: Several manuscripts read, “something that had to be performed every year,” omitting “repeatedly,” which the other manuscripts also omit; and below, instead of “from fruits,” they all read “from crops.”]**, just as the Israelites customarily give frequent tithes to the Levites throughout their lives, every year—indeed, from all their crops, whereas Baptism is a sacrament given only once, so that if someone had already received it while he was in his father, he ought to be regarded as baptized when he was born from one who had been baptized—let anyone who says this consider circumcision. Circumcision was performed once, yet it was performed separately upon each individual.

Therefore, just as at the time of that sacrament one who was born from a circumcised person had to be circumcised, so now one who is born from a baptized person must be baptized.

But the Apostle says: “Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy” (1 Cor. 7:14). “Therefore,” they say, “the children of believers ought not to have been baptized.”

I am astonished that this is said by people who deny that sin is transmitted originally from Adam. If they understand the Apostle’s statement in such a way that they believe children are born sanctified from believers, why do they themselves not hesitate to say that those children must also be baptized? Why, finally, do they refuse to admit that some original sin is transmitted from a sinful parent, if some holiness is transmitted from a holy parent?

Even if holy children are propagated from believers, this does not contradict our assertion when we say that, if they are not baptized, they proceed to condemnation—those to whom they themselves also close the kingdom of heaven, although they say that such children have neither any personal sin nor original sin.

Or, if they consider it unworthy **[Col. 0176]** that holy people should be condemned, how is it worthy that holy people should be excluded from the kingdom of God? They should rather consider how no sin can be transmitted from sinful parents if some holiness is transmitted from holy parents, and uncleanness from unclean parents. For the one who said, “Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy,” said both.

Let them also explain how it is just that children born holy from believers and unclean from unbelievers are nevertheless equally forbidden to enter the kingdom of God if they have not been baptized. What benefit, then, does that holiness provide them?

For if they admitted that those unclean children born from unbelievers are condemned, while distinguishing them from the holy children of believers by saying that the latter cannot enter the kingdom of God unless they have been baptized, but nevertheless are not condemned because they are holy, there would at least be some distinction. But as things stand, they say equally that those born holy from holy parents are holy, and those born unclean from unclean parents are unclean; that they are not condemned because they have no sin, yet that they are excluded from the kingdom of God because they do not have Baptism. Who could believe that minds of such a kind do not see this absurdity?

But attend for a little while to our judgment—or rather, to that of the Apostle himself, who said, “From one came condemnation upon all,” and “From one came justification unto life” (Rom. 5:16, 18)—and observe how what he said in dealing with another matter, “Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy,” is not contrary to it.

### CHAPTER XXVI

#### The manifold forms of sanctification. The sacrament of catechumens

Sanctification is not of one kind. I think that catechumens too are sanctified in a certain manner proper to them through the sign of Christ and the prayer of the laying on of hands **[Note: A Remigian manuscript reads, “through the prayer and the laying on of hands.”]**. And what they receive, although it is not the body of Christ, is nevertheless holy, and holier than the foods by which we are nourished, because it is a sacrament **[Note: Catechumens received the sacrament of salt; concerning this there survives canon 5 of the Third Council of Carthage. Augustine again calls it a sacrament in Book 1 of *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*, section 50, and a form sanctified by blessing. In Book 1 of the *Confessions*, chapter 11, speaking of his own catechumenate, he says: “I was already being marked with the sign of his cross and seasoned with his salt.”]**.

Yet the same Apostle said that the foods by which we are nourished for the support of this present life are sanctified through the word of God and prayer (1 Tim. 4:5)—the prayer by which, naturally, we ask to refresh our little bodies.

Therefore, just as this sanctification of foods does not cause what enters the mouth not to pass into the stomach and be expelled into the latrine through the process of decay by which all earthly things dissolve—hence the Lord also exhorts us toward another food that does not perish (John 6:27)—so the sanctification of a catechumen, if he has not been baptized, does not avail him for entering the kingdom of heaven or for the remission of sins.

Consequently, that sanctification also, whatever kind it may be, which the Apostle said exists in the children of believers, has absolutely no bearing on this question concerning Baptism and the origin or remission of sin.

For in the same passage he also says that unbelieving spouses are sanctified in believing spouses, speaking as follows **[Col. 0177]**: “For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the brother. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy” (1 Cor. 7:14).

I do not think anyone can understand these words so unbelievingly—whatever else he may understand in them—as to suppose that, merely because a man’s wife is a Christian, the non-Christian husband need no longer be baptized, has already attained the remission of sins, and will enter the kingdom of heaven because he is said to have been sanctified in his wife.

### CHAPTER XXVII

#### 43. Why those born from baptized persons are baptized

Whoever is still troubled by the question of why those born from baptized persons are baptized should accept this brief answer.

**[Col. 0177]**

Just as the generation of sinful flesh through one Adam brings condemnation upon all who are generated in that manner, so the generation of the Spirit of grace through one Jesus Christ leads to the justification of eternal life all those who are predestined and regenerated in that manner **[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read, “who are predestined in that manner.”]**.

The sacrament of Baptism is certainly the sacrament of regeneration. Therefore, just as one who has not lived cannot die, and one who has not died cannot rise again, so one who has not been born cannot be born again. From this it follows that no one could have been born anew in his parent without having been born.

But if he has been born, he must be born again, because “unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3:3). Therefore even an infant must be imbued with the sacrament of regeneration, lest he depart from this life badly without it; and this occurs only for the remission of sins.

Christ also demonstrated this in that very passage when, asked how these things could happen, he recalled what Moses had done in the raising up of the serpent. Since, therefore, through the sacrament of Baptism infants are conformed to the death of Christ, we must confess that they are freed from the serpent’s bite if we do not wish to depart from the rule of Christian faith. Yet they received that bite not in their own personal life, but in the one upon whom it was first inflicted.

#### 44. Pelagian objection

Nor should we be deceived by the argument that personal sins do not harm even the parent after conversion **[Note: The printed editions read, “that if even the parent’s sins do not harm him after conversion.” “If” is absent from the manuscripts, but in the following clause they add *enim*, a particle absent from the printed editions.]** **[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “confession” instead of “conversion.”]**. “How much less,” they say, “can they harm his son?”

But those who think this do not observe that, just as the parent’s personal sins do not harm him because he has been reborn in spirit, so the sins transmitted from the parent will harm the one born from him unless he is reborn in the same manner.

For parents who have been renewed beget children carnally not from the first fruits of their newness, but from the remnants of their old condition. Their children, wholly old from the remnants of their parents’ old condition and propagated in sinful flesh **[Note: Ambrose, Erasmus, and all the manuscripts read, “wholly old, propagated in sinful flesh,” omitting the conjunction “and.”]**, escape through the sacrament of spiritual regeneration and renewal the condemnation owed to the old person **[Note: Most manuscripts read, “through spiritual regeneration.”]**.

We must especially observe and remember this, because of the questions that have arisen or may still arise concerning this matter: **[Col. 0178]** Baptism alone brings about the full and perfect remission of all sins; but the condition of the human being himself is not immediately changed in its entirety. Rather, the spiritual first fruits, as they make good progress and increase in newness day by day, transform within themselves what is old according to the flesh, until everything is renewed in such a way that even the body’s animal weakness reaches spiritual strength and incorruption.

### CHAPTER XXVIII

#### 45. The law of sin called “sin.” How desire remains in the baptized after its guilt has been destroyed

This law of sin—which the Apostle also calls “sin” when he says, “Therefore let not sin reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires” (Rom. 6:12)—does not remain in the members of those who have been born again from water and the Spirit as though its remission had not occurred. In Baptism the remission of sins is wholly full and perfect, with all the enmities by which we were separated from God destroyed.

Rather, it remains in the oldness of the flesh as something conquered and destroyed, unless it revives in some way through unlawful consent and is recalled to its own kingdom and dominion.

The life of the Spirit, in whose newness the baptized are reborn by God’s grace, is so distinct from this oldness of the flesh, in which this law of sin—or sin already remitted—exists, that it was not enough for the Apostle to say that such people are not in sin. He also said that they are not in the flesh itself before they depart from this mortal life.

“For those who are in the flesh,” he says, “cannot please God. But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit—if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (Rom. 8:8–9).

Yet just as those who turn its members toward good works make good use of the flesh itself, although it is corruptible—and are not in the flesh because they neither think nor live according to it—so, finally, those who courageously and patiently expend their lives for their brothers, for the faith, or for any true and holy justice make good use even of death, which is the punishment of the first sin.

In the same way faithful married people make good use of that law of sin which, already remitted, remains in the oldness of the flesh. Because they belong to the newness of Christ, they do not allow desire to dominate them; but because they still bear the oldness of Adam, they beget immortal children for regeneration through mortal generation, together with that propagation of sin to which those who have been reborn are not held liable, and through which those who are born are released by being reborn.

As long, therefore, as the law of desire remains in the members, its guilt is remitted while the reality itself remains. But it is remitted to the one who has received the sacrament of regeneration and has already begun to be renewed.

From the oldness of desire that remains, the one who is born needs to be born again in order to be healed. For faithful parents, born carnally and reborn spiritually, have begotten children carnally; but before the children were born, how could they have been born again?

Nor should you be surprised that I said that, while the law of sin remains in the form of desire, its guilt is remitted through the grace of the sacrament **[Col. 0179]**. For just as wicked deeds, words, and thoughts have already passed away and no longer exist with respect to the movements themselves of mind and body, yet their guilt remains after they have passed and no longer exist, unless it is remitted through the forgiveness of sins, so, conversely, in this case the law of desire has not passed away but still remains; nevertheless its guilt is remitted, and it will not exist when the full remission of sins takes place in Baptism.

Indeed, if departure from this life immediately follows, there will be nothing at all to hold the person liable, since everything that held him has been released.

Therefore, just as it is not surprising that the guilt of past words, deeds, and thoughts remains before the remission of sins, so conversely it should not be surprising that the guilt of remaining desire passes away after the remission of sins.

### CHAPTER XXIX

#### 47. All the predestined are saved through the one Mediator Christ and through one and the same faith. Christ is also the Savior of infants. Christ as an infant was free from ignorance and mental weakness

Since these things are so, from the time when sin entered this world through one human being, and death through sin, and so death passed into all human beings (Rom. 5:12), throughout the entire course of this carnal generation and corruptible age—whose children beget and are begotten—there has been no human being living in this life of whom it could truthfully be said that he is wholly without sin, except the one Mediator who reconciles us to our Creator through the remission of sins.

Our same Lord has never denied this remedy of his, at any time of the human race before the final judgment still to come, to those whom, through his most certain foreknowledge and future beneficence **[Note: The printed editions read, “and most righteous beneficence.” All our Gallican, Vatican, and Belgian manuscripts instead read, “and future beneficence,” or simply “beneficence.”]**, he predestined to reign with him in eternal life.

Before the birth of his flesh, the weakness of his passion, and the power of his resurrection, he instructed those who lived at that time, through faith in those future events, for the inheritance of eternal salvation. Those who were present when these things were happening he instructed through faith in events then present, and they saw the things foretold being fulfilled. Those who came afterward, and ourselves, and those who will come later, he continues to instruct through faith in things already past **[Note: The printed editions read, “through faith in things already past.” “Things” is absent from the manuscripts.]**.

There is therefore one faith that saves all who are spiritually reborn from carnal generation **[Note: This is how it appears in all the manuscripts. The printed editions instead read, “who are saved by being reborn from carnal generation into spiritual generation.”]**—a faith completed in the one who came to be judged and to die for us, the judge of the living and the dead. Yet, for the sake of appropriate signs, the sacraments of this one faith have varied through different periods.

#### 48. Christ is the Savior of infants

The same Savior, therefore, is the Savior of infants and adults. Of him the angels said, “Today a Savior has been born for you” (Luke 2:11); and of him it was said to the Virgin Mary, “You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21).

This plainly demonstrates that he is called by the name Jesus **[Col. 0180]** for the salvation that he grants us; for *Jesus* means “Savior” in Latin.

Who, then, would dare to say that the Lord Christ is Jesus only for adults and not also for infants? He came in the likeness of sinful flesh in order to destroy the body of sin. In this most weak body, whose infant limbs are suited or adequate to no useful purpose, the rational soul is weighed down by pitiable ignorance.

I certainly could not believe that this ignorance existed in that infant in whom the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. Nor could I suspect in Christ as an infant that weakness of mind which we see in infants.

Through this weakness, even when infants are disturbed by irrational impulses, they are restrained by no reason or command, but sometimes by pain or fear of pain. Thus one sees in them altogether the children of that disobedience which moves in the members against the law of the mind and does not become quiet when reason wishes it to. Indeed, it too is often restrained either by bodily pain, as though by a beating, or by fear, or by some similar movement of the mind—not, however, by an act of commanding will.

But because there was in Christ a likeness of sinful flesh, he willingly underwent the changes of the various ages, beginning from infancy, so that this flesh might appear capable of reaching death even through growing old—unless he had been killed while still young.

Yet death, which is owed to disobedience in sinful flesh **[Note: Several manuscripts read, “now owed to disobedience.”]**, was undertaken in the likeness of sinful flesh by an act of obedience.

For as he was going to that death and about to suffer it, he said: “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me; but so that all may know that I do the will of my Father, rise, let us go from here” (John 14:30–31).

After saying this, he went to the death he did not owe, becoming obedient even unto death.

### CHAPTER XXX

#### 49. Response to the Pelagian objection

Therefore, those who say, “If the sin of the first human being caused us to die, then the coming of Christ should cause believers in him not to die,” and who add as though it were a reason, “For the transgression of the transgressor did not harm us more than the incarnation or redemption of the Savior benefited us,” should rather attend to this, hear this, and believe without hesitation what the Apostle stated without ambiguity:

“Through a human being came death, and through a human being came the resurrection of the dead. For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:21–22).

He was speaking of nothing other than the resurrection of the body. Therefore he said that the death of all bodies came through one human being, and promised that the resurrection of all bodies unto eternal life would come through one Christ.

How, then, did that one harm us more by sinning than this one benefited us by redeeming us, when through the sin of the former we die temporarily, but through the redemption of the latter we rise not to temporal life but to everlasting life?

Our body, therefore, is dead because of sin; but Christ’s body alone died without sin, so that, when his blood was poured out without guilt, the written obligations of all sins might be erased—obligations by which those who believe in him had previously been held as debtors by the devil **[Col. 0181]**.

Therefore he says: “This is my blood, which will be poured out for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. 26:28).

### CHAPTER XXXI

#### 50. Why death itself is not abolished together with sins through Baptism

He could also have granted believers that they would not experience the death of this body. But if he had done this, a certain felicity would have been added to the flesh, while the strength of faith would have been diminished.

For people fear this death so much that they would say Christians were happy for no other reason than that they could not die at all. Consequently, no one would hasten to the grace of Christ for the sake of that blessed life which is to follow this death, through the virtue of despising death itself. Instead, people would believe in Christ more indulgently in order to remove the distress of death.

He therefore bestowed more grace; without doubt, he gave more to his faithful. For what great thing would it be, seeing that those who believed did not die, to believe that one would not die? How much greater, how much stronger, how much more praiseworthy it is to believe in such a way that one hopes, though destined to die, to live without end!

Finally, at the end he will grant this to some: they will not experience this death through a sudden transformation **[Note: See Book 2 of the *Retractations*, chapter 33, and Letter 193 to Mercator.]**, but will be caught up together with those who rise in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so will always live with the Lord (1 Thess. 4:16).

And rightly so, since there will no longer be descendants who believe for this reason—not hoping for what they do not see, but loving what they see. Such faith is weak and feeble, and should not be called faith at all, since faith has been defined in this way: “Faith is the substance of those who hope, the conviction of things that are not seen” **[Note: Louvain reads, “the substance of things hoped for.” Ambrose, Erasmus, and our manuscripts consistently read, “the substance of those who hope.” The Greek is *elpizomenōn*, which, being a middle-voice verb, was understood actively by some and passively by others.]**.

Accordingly, in the same Epistle to the Hebrews, where this too is written, after listing certain people who pleased God through faith, he says:

“According to faith, all these died without receiving the promises, but seeing them from afar, greeting them, and confessing that they were strangers and pilgrims upon the earth.”

A little later he concluded the same praise of faith in this way:

“And all these, having received testimony through faith, did not obtain the promises; for they provided better things for us, so that they might not be made perfect without us” (Heb. 11:1, 13, 39–40).

This praise of faith would not exist—and, as I have already said, there would not be faith at all—if people, in believing, pursued visible rewards; that is, if the reward of immortality were granted to believers in this present age.

For this reason the Lord himself also wished to die, so that, as it is written of him, through death he might destroy the one who held the power of death, that is, the devil, and free those who through fear of death were subject to slavery throughout their entire lives (ibid. 2:14–15).

This testimony also sufficiently demonstrates that the death of the body occurred through the devil as its prince and author—that is, through the sin which he persuaded us to commit. For otherwise he could not most truly be said to possess the power of death.

**[Col. 0182]** Thus he who was dying without any sin, whether original or personal, said what I recalled shortly before: “Behold, the prince of this world will come”—that is, the devil, who held the power of death—“and he will find nothing in me”—that is, no sin on account of which he caused human beings to die.

And as though someone had said to him, “Why, then, are you dying?” he replied: “But so that all may know that I do the will of my Father, rise, let us go from here.” That is: “I am dying without having the cause of death in sin under the author of sin; rather, through obedience and justice I have become obedient even unto death.”

That testimony, therefore, also demonstrates that the faithful’s overcoming of the fear of death belongs to the struggle of faith. This would certainly have been absent if believers had immediately obtained immortality.

### CHAPTER XXXII

#### 52. Why Christ withdrew his presence from the world after the resurrection

Although the Lord performed many visible miracles, from which faith might germinate as though from certain tender beginnings and grow from that infancy into its full strength—for faith is stronger insofar as it no longer seeks such things—he nevertheless wished what we hope has been promised to be awaited invisibly, so that “the righteous might live by faith.”

Thus even he who rose on the third day did not wish to remain among human beings. After showing those whom he deigned to have as witnesses an example of the resurrection in his own flesh, he ascended into heaven, also removing himself from their eyes and granting no one’s flesh anything like what he had demonstrated in his own flesh.

He did this so that they too might live by faith and, through patience, await invisibly for the time being the reward of that righteousness in which one lives by faith—a reward that will afterward be visible.

I believe that what he said concerning the Holy Spirit should also be referred to this meaning: “He cannot come unless I depart.” This means: “You will not be able to live justly by faith—which you will possess as my gift, that is, from the Holy Spirit—unless I remove from your eyes what you are looking at, so that your heart may advance spiritually by believing in invisible things.”

Speaking again of the Holy Spirit, he commends this righteousness of faith in the following way: “He will convict the world concerning sin, concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment: concerning sin, because they did not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me” (John 16:7–10).

What is this righteousness by which they would not see him **[Note: The Corbie manuscript reads, “they saw.”]**, except that the righteous should live by faith, and that, not looking at the things that are seen but at the things that are unseen, we should await in the spirit, through faith, the hope of righteousness?

### CHAPTER XXXIII
53. He answers the objection of the Pelagians. But those who say, “If this death of the body had occurred because of sin, surely we would not die after the remission of sins which the Redeemer has granted us,” do not understand how God releases us from the liability of sins so that they may not harm us after this life, yet allows them to remain for the contest of faith, so that those who are making progress may be instructed and exercised through them in the struggle for righteousness. For someone else, not understanding this, might say: “If God said to man on account of sin, ‘In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread,’ and, ‘The earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you’ [Col. 0183; Gen. III, 19], why does this labor remain even after remission, and why does the earth of the faithful also produce these hard and harsh things?” Likewise, if it was said to the woman on account of sin, “In groaning you shall give birth” (Gen. III, 16), why do faithful women also suffer the same pains in childbirth after the remission of sins? Yet it is certain that, on account of the sin they had committed, the first human beings heard and merited these things from God. The words of the divine book that I have cited concerning man’s labor and the woman’s childbirth are resisted only by someone who, wholly alien to the Catholic faith, opposes those same Scriptures.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

54. Why punishment is still exacted after sin has been forgiven. Since such people are not lacking, just as we answer them when this question is put forward—saying that before remission there are punishments for sins, but after remission there are contests and exercises for the righteous—so we must also answer those who are similarly troubled by the death of the body. We should acknowledge that it too came about because of sin, yet not disdain to confess that, after the remission of sins, it was left to us as a contest, so that by overcoming its great terror those who are making progress might be trained.

For if it were a small virtue of faith, which works through love, to overcome the fear of death, the glory of the martyrs would not be so great, nor would the Lord say, “Greater love has no one than this, that he lay down his life for his friends” (John XV, 13). John says the same in his Epistle: “As he laid down his life for us, so we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers” (I John III, 16). Therefore, supreme patience would by no means be praised in undergoing or despising death for righteousness if death were not a great and exceedingly grievous affliction. Whoever conquers its fear through faith obtains for that very faith great glory and a just reward. Hence it is not surprising both that death of the body would not have come upon man unless sin had preceded it, so that such a punishment would follow, and that after the remission of sins it comes upon the faithful, so that the strength of righteousness may be exercised in conquering its fear.

55. For the flesh that was first made was not sinful flesh; in it man refused to preserve righteousness amid the delights of paradise. Therefore God decreed that, after his sin, sinful flesh propagated through descent should strive through labors and hardships to recover righteousness. For this reason Adam, after being dismissed from paradise [Note: [Col. 0183] The printed editions read, “Adam, expelled from paradise.” But the manuscripts read, “dismissed.”], dwelt opposite Eden—that is, opposite the seat of delights—in order to signify that sinful flesh, which had not preserved obedience amid delights before it became sinful flesh, was to be instructed through labors, which are contrary to delights.

Therefore, just as those first human beings, although afterward living righteously—and thus rightly believed to have been freed through the Lord’s blood from ultimate punishment—did not, in that life, merit being restored to paradise, so sinful flesh, even if a person lives righteously in it after his sins have been forgiven, does not immediately merit escaping that death which it drew from the descent of sin.

56. Something similar is intimated to us concerning the patriarch [Col. 0184] David in the Book of Kings. When the prophet had been sent to him and, because of the sin he had committed, threatened him with evils that would come upon him through God’s anger, he obtained pardon by confessing his sin, the prophet replying that his offense and crime had been forgiven (II Sam. XII, 13). Yet the things God had threatened followed, so that he might be humbled by his son.

Why, then, is it not said here also: “If God had threatened that because of that sin, why did he fulfill what he had threatened after the sin had been forgiven?” The reason is that, if the question is put in this way, the most correct answer will be that the sin was forgiven so that the man would not be prevented from attaining eternal life, whereas the consequence of that threat followed so that the man’s piety might be exercised and tested in that humility. Thus God both inflicted death of the body upon man because of sin and, after the remission of sins, did not remove it, so that righteousness might be exercised.

## CHAPTER XXXV

57. We must not turn aside to the right or to the left. Let us therefore hold fast an unchanging confession of faith. There is only one who was born without sin, in the likeness of sinful flesh; who lived without sin amid the sins of others; and who died without sin because of our sins.

Let us not turn aside to the right or to the left. To turn aside to the right is to deceive oneself by saying that one is without sin; to turn aside to the left is, through some unknown perverse and depraved security, to surrender oneself to sins as though they would go unpunished. For the Lord knows the ways that are on the right—the one who alone is without sin and can erase our sins—and the ways that are on the left are perverse: friendships with sins (Prov. IV, 27).

Those young men who were twenty years old also prefigured the new people. They entered the promised land and are said to have turned neither to the right nor to the left [Note: [Col. 0184] He appears to be referring to Num. XIV. After condemning to death in the wilderness all those who had been counted from twenty years old and upward, God decreed that the others, younger in age, should be brought into the promised land. They are praised in Josh. XXIII, 6, 8 as not having turned aside from the law, neither to the right nor to the left.].

An age of twenty years is not, of course, to be compared with the innocence of little children. Rather, unless I am mistaken, this number sketches and echoes something mystical. For the Old Testament excels in the five books of Moses, while the New Testament is preeminent in the authority of the four Gospels. These numbers, multiplied by one another, arrive at twenty: four times five, or five times four, is twenty.

Such a people, as I have said, instructed in the kingdom of heaven through the two Testaments, Old and New, will enter the promised land, turning neither to the right through proud presumption of righteousness nor to the left through complacent enjoyment of sin [Note: [Col. 0184] Four Gallican manuscripts and three Vatican manuscripts read “love of sin.”]. There we shall hope that sins will no longer need to be forgiven us, nor fear that they will be punished in us, having been freed by that Redeemer who, although not sold under sin, redeemed Israel from all its iniquities—whether committed in anyone’s own life [Note: [Col. 0184] Thus all the Gallican manuscripts. The printed editions read “of anyone.” Augustine perhaps avoided this expression because of the error of those who attributed the sins of their own lives to every human being, even to infants. See above, Book I, nos. 22, 31, 63, 64.] or inherited originally.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

58. Whether the soul is derived through descent. In obscure matters, where the Scriptures do not assist us, rashness in judging must be avoided. The Scriptures are clear in matters necessary for salvation. For not a few have yielded to the authority and truth of the divine writings. Although they did not wish openly to state in their writings that remission of sins is necessary for little children, they nevertheless confessed that redemption is necessary for them; using another expression, likewise drawn from Christian instruction, they said absolutely nothing else.

Nor should those who faithfully read, faithfully hear, and faithfully retain the divine writings doubt [Note: [Col. 0185] Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read “that it is so.”] that from that flesh which was first made sinful flesh through the will of sin, sinful flesh was afterward propagated through succession into all, carrying with it the condemnation of iniquity and death—except for the one likeness of sinful flesh, which nevertheless would not exist unless sinful flesh also existed.

59. But concerning the soul—whether it too was propagated in the same way and bound by a liability from which it must be released (for we cannot say that only the flesh of an infant, and not also its soul, needs the help of the Savior and Redeemer, or that it is alien to the thanksgiving expressed in the Psalms, where we read and say, “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his rewards: he who is gracious to all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from corruption” [Col. 0186; Ps. CII, 2–4]); or whether, although not propagated, it nevertheless needs remission of that very sin and its own redemption because it is joined to sinful flesh, which weighs it down—while God, through his supreme foreknowledge [Note: [Col. 0186] The Belgian manuscripts and two Gallican manuscripts read “through his own foreknowledge.”], judges that little children [Note: [Col. 0186] The printed editions read “that the little children.” The manuscripts read “that little children.”] do not deserve to be absolved from this liability, even though, before they are born, they have done nothing anywhere in their own life, whether good or evil; and how God, even if he does not create souls through descent, is nevertheless not the author of that same liability, on account of which the redemption of the sacrament is necessary also for the soul of an infant [Note: [Col. 0186] Most manuscripts read, “redemption is necessary, and [he is the author] of the infant’s misery”; supply “he is the author.” The printed editions read, “redemption is necessary for the soul of the infant.”]—this is a great question and requires another discussion. Yet it must be treated, in my judgment, with this moderation: cautious inquiry should be praised rather than rash assertion condemned.

When a very obscure matter is debated without the support of certain and clear testimonies from the divine Scriptures, human presumption ought to restrain itself and do nothing by inclining toward either side. Even if I do not know how any of these positions can be demonstrated and explained, I nevertheless believe that the authority of the divine utterances would be perfectly clear on this matter too, if a person could not remain ignorant of it without forfeiting the salvation that has been promised.

You have here a work undertaken with effort—may it be as useful as it is lengthy—according to my abilities. Perhaps I would defend its length if I did not fear that, in defending it, I would make it still longer.

# BOOK THREE, OR THE LETTER TO THE SAME MARCELLINUS

[Col. 0185]

In it Augustine refutes the errors of Pelagius concerning the question of the merits of sins and the Baptism of infants, as well as certain arguments against original sin that Pelagius had inserted into his expositions of Paul.

To his most beloved son Marcellinus, Augustine, bishop, servant of Christ and of Christ’s servants, sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0185]

1. Pelagius regarded as a holy man. His expositions of Paul. Concerning the questions that you had proposed to me, asking me to write something to you against those who say that Adam would have died even if he had not sinned, and that nothing from his sin was transmitted by propagation to his descendants—especially on account of the Baptism of infants, which the whole Church practices with profoundly pious and maternal devotion—and concerning the claim that in this life there are, have been, and will be human children who have absolutely no sin, I had already completed two lengthy books.

In them I seemed to myself not indeed to have met every movement of every mind in this matter—for I do not know whether that could be done by me or by anyone, and indeed I do not doubt that it cannot be done—but nevertheless to have done something by which defenders of the faith handed down by our ancestors against the innovations of those who think otherwise would not be entirely without weapons.

But a few days later I read some writings of Pelagius, a man said, I hear, to be holy and considerably advanced as a Christian. They contained very brief expositions of the letters of the apostle Paul [Col. 0186] [Note: [Col. 0186] Mercator cites Pelagius’s Commentaries on Paul in his *Commonitorium*, chapter 2, and quotes many of his statements there; nearly all of them are read in virtually the same words in the Commentaries falsely published under Jerome’s name.].

There I discovered that, when he reached the passage where the Apostle says that through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so passed into all human beings (Rom. V, 12), he presented an argument of certain people who deny that infants bear original sin. I confess that I did not refute it in those lengthy volumes of mine, because it had not entered my mind at all that anyone could think or say such things.

Therefore, since I did not wish to add anything to that work, which I had already brought to a definite conclusion, I thought that I should insert in this letter both the argument itself, in the very words in which I read it, and what I think against it.

## CHAPTER II

2. Pelagius’s objection. Infants counted among believers and the faithful. The argument is stated as follows:

“But those who oppose the transmission of sin,” he says, “try to attack it in this way: ‘If Adam’s sin harmed even those who do not sin [Col. 0187], then Christ’s righteousness also benefits even those who do not believe, because he says that, just as through one person people are saved, indeed even more so than through one person they previously perished.’”

As I said, I answered nothing to this argument in the two books that I wrote to you, nor did I at all propose to refute it. Now, then, first observe how, when they say, “If Adam’s sin harms even those who do not sin, Christ’s righteousness also benefits even those who do not believe,” they judge it utterly absurd and utterly false that Christ’s righteousness should benefit those who do not believe. From this they think it follows that the sin of the first man could not harm infants who do not sin, just as Christ’s righteousness cannot benefit any who do not believe.

Let them therefore say what Christ’s righteousness benefits baptized infants. Let them say absolutely whatever they wish. Certainly, if they remember that they are Christians, they do not doubt that it benefits them in some way. Whatever benefit it provides, however, it cannot, as they themselves also assert, benefit those who do not believe. Thus they are compelled to count baptized infants among believers and to agree with the authority of the holy Church everywhere [Note: [Col. 0187] In most manuscripts either “authority” or “holy” is absent.], which does not regard them as unworthy of being called faithful, since, even according to these people, Christ’s righteousness could benefit them only if they believed.

Therefore, just as the spirit of those through whom they are reborn conveys faith to them by its response, a faith that they could not yet possess by their own will, so the sinful flesh of those through whom they are born conveys to them a guilt that they have not yet contracted through their own life. And just as the spirit of life regenerates them as faithful people in Christ, so the body of death had generated them as sinners in Adam. For the former generation is carnal, the latter spiritual; the former makes children of the flesh, the latter children of the spirit; the former children of death, the latter children of resurrection; the former children of the world, the latter children of God; the former children of wrath, the latter children of mercy. Consequently, the former binds them by original sin, while the latter frees them from the bond of every sin.

3. Finally, with regard to what we cannot attain by the sharpest understanding, we must be compelled to agree with the authority of God. It is good that they themselves remind us that Christ’s righteousness cannot benefit anyone except believers, while they confess that it benefits infants in some way. Hence, as we have said, they must necessarily place baptized infants among believers without any evasion.

Consequently, if they are not baptized, they will be among those who do not believe. Therefore they will not have life, but the wrath of God remains upon them, since “whoever does not believe the Son shall not have life, but the wrath of God remains upon him”; and they have been judged, since “whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John III, 36, 18); and they will be condemned, since “whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark XVI, 16).

Let these people now see by what righteousness they attempt or endeavor to assert that human beings who are without sin belong not to eternal life but to the wrath of God, and are judged and condemned by divine judgment—if, just as they have no personal sin, they also have no original sin.

[Col. 0188]

4. As for the other things that Pelagius suggests are said by those who dispute against original sin, I have answered them sufficiently, as far as I think, clearly and fully in those two lengthy books of mine. If this seems to some people insufficient or obscure, let them pardon me and reconcile themselves with those who perhaps criticize it not because it is too little, but because it is too much. And those who still do not understand what I believe I have stated clearly in proportion to the nature of the questions should not slander me on the grounds of negligence or lack of ability; rather, let them pray to God to grant them understanding.

## CHAPTER III

5. Pelagius praised by some. Arguments against original sin that Pelagius presents in his Commentary. Nevertheless, we must carefully observe that this man, whom those who knew him describe as a good and praiseworthy man [Note: [Col. 0188] All the Gallican manuscripts omit “good,” while retaining in most cases the preposition *ac*, or altering it so that some read “a man fit to be praised.”], did not introduce this argument against the transmission of sin in his own person, but reported what those who do not approve it say. He did not merely report the point that I have just stated and answered; he also reported the other points to which I recall having already responded in those books. For, after he had said, “If Adam’s sin harmed even those who do not sin, then Christ’s righteousness also benefits even those who do not believe”—a point which, in what I have answered, you see does not merely fail to overthrow what we say, but even reminds us what we ought to say [Note: [Col. 0188] Most manuscripts read, “which do not refute what we say, but also remind us what to say”; shortly afterward they read “They add this also,” rather than “There is also this.”]—he continued:

For after saying, “They say, ‘If Adam’s sin harmed even those who do not sin, then Christ’s righteousness also benefits even those who do not believe,’” he continued:

“Next they say, ‘If Baptism cleanses that ancient offense, those who are born from two baptized parents ought to be free from this sin, since they could not transmit to their descendants what they themselves did not have.’” [Note: [Col. 0188] Most manuscripts read “They add this also,” rather than “There is also this.”]

He adds:

“There is also this: if the soul is not derived through descent, but only the flesh is, then the flesh alone possesses the transmission of sin, and the flesh alone deserves punishment. For they say that it is unjust that a soul born today, not formed from Adam’s mass, should bear an ancient sin belonging to another.

“They also say that there is no reason to allow God, who forgives personal sins, to impute the sins of others.”

6. Do you see, I ask, how Pelagius has introduced all of this into his writings not in his own person but in the person of others? He knew so well that this was some sort of novelty, now beginning to sound against the ancient opinion implanted in the Church, that he was either ashamed or afraid to confess that he himself held it.

Perhaps he himself does not realize that he is saying that a human being is born without sin, while admitting that Baptism is necessary for that person, in which the remission of sins takes place; and [Note: [Col. 0188] The particle “and” is absent from the manuscripts. The printed editions, two of whose oldest editions, Amerbach and Erasmus, read “and that a human being is condemned without Baptism,” are mistaken, against the manuscripts, which consistently read “without sin” in both places.] that a human being who is without sin is condemned without Baptism and must be counted among those who do not believe—for certainly the evangelical Scripture cannot deceive, and it most clearly says, “Whoever does not believe will be condemned”; and finally, that the image of God, though without sin, is not admitted into the kingdom of God, since “unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III, 5).

Thus such a person would either be plunged without sin into eternal death or, even more absurdly, possess eternal life outside the kingdom of God. Yet when the Lord foretold what he would say to his own at the end, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,” he also made clear what the kingdom itself was of which he spoke, concluding: “Thus they will go into eternal burning, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. XXV, 34, 46).

I therefore believe that this exceptionally Christian man does not at all hold these and other consequences that follow from this error, since they are so perverse and opposed to Christian truth. But it may be that he is still moved by the arguments of those who hold this position against the transmission of sin, and is waiting to hear or learn what is said against them. For that reason he did not wish to conceal what those who hold this position say, so that the question might be brought forward for discussion; yet he removed it from his own person, lest he himself also be judged to hold it.

## CHAPTER IV

7. Jesus is also the Jesus of infants. He shows that the ancients had no doubt about the original sin of infants. Even if I am unable to refute the arguments of these people, I nevertheless see that we must adhere to what is most clearly stated in the Scriptures, so that obscure matters may be revealed from them. Or, if the mind is not yet capable of seeing what has been demonstrated or investigating what is hidden, these things must be believed without any hesitation.

What could be clearer than the many and great testimonies of the divine utterances, by which it is most plainly evident both that no human being can attain life and eternal salvation apart from fellowship with Christ, and that no one can be unjustly condemned by divine judgment—that is, separated from that life and salvation?

It follows that, since nothing else is done when infants are baptized except that they are incorporated into the Church—that is, joined to Christ’s body and members—it is clear [Col. 0189] that they belong to condemnation unless this is granted to them [Note: [Col. 0189] Many manuscripts read “unless provision has been made for them.”]. They could not, however, be condemned if they had no sin at all. Since that age could contract no sin in its own life [Note: [Col. 0189] The printed editions read “no sin in its own life.” Six Gallican manuscripts, however, read “no sin in its own life.” The point is apparently to exclude a double error: one that attributes to infants the sin of a life lived either before the body or within the body. Hence, in Letter 217 to Vitalis, no. 16, he says: “Nor according to the merits of some earlier life, which no individual could have as his own.” See above, Book I, no. 31.], it remains either to understand—or, if we cannot yet do so, at least to believe—that infants draw original sin with them.

8. Therefore, if the Apostle’s words—“Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and so passed into all human beings” (Rom. V, 12)—contain something ambiguous and can be led or transferred to another meaning, is this also ambiguous: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John III, 5)? Is this also ambiguous: “You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (Matt. I, 21)? Is this also ambiguous: “It is not the healthy who need a physician, but the sick”—that is, Jesus [Col. 0190] is not necessary for those who have no sin, but for those who are to be saved from sin (ibid. IX, 12)? Is this also ambiguous: “Unless people eat his flesh”—that is, unless they become participants in his body—“they will not have life” (John VI, 54)?

In these and many other testimonies, which I now pass over—clear as daylight through divine illumination and certain through divine authority—does not truth proclaim without any ambiguity not only that unbaptized infants cannot enter the kingdom of God, but also that they cannot have eternal life apart from Christ’s body, into which they are incorporated through the sacrament of Baptism?

Does not truth testify without any doubt that they are carried to Jesus—that is, to Christ the Savior and Physician—in the pious arms of those who carry them for no other reason than that through the medicine of his sacraments they may be healed from the plague of sin? [Note: [Col. 0190] Chapter 5 begins here in the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus.]

Why, then, do we hesitate to understand the Apostle’s words, about which we may have had some doubt, in a way that makes them agree with these testimonies about which we cannot doubt?

9. Nevertheless, throughout the entire passage in which the Apostle speaks of the condemnation of many through the sin of one and the justification of many through the righteousness of one, nothing seems ambiguous to me except what he says: “Adam was a type of the one who was to come” (Rom. V, 14). This statement truly agrees not only with the interpretation by which it is understood that his future descendants were to be generated with sin according to the same pattern [Note: [Col. 0190] Amerbach and Erasmus read “and according to the same pattern.”], but these words can also be directed toward various other interpretations.

For at one time we too have said something else about them, and perhaps we shall say something else, though it will not be contrary to this interpretation (Letter 157, no. 20; above, Book I, no. 13; below, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book II, no. 46, and *Against Julian*, Book VI, no. 9). Pelagius himself also explained the passage in more than one way.

But the other things said there, if they are carefully observed and examined, as I attempted to do, however inadequately, in the first of those two books, although the language may be somewhat obscure because of the nature of the matters themselves, cannot have any other meaning than the one by which the universal Church has from ancient times maintained that faithful infants obtain remission of original sin through Christ’s Baptism.

## CHAPTER V

10. Cyprian’s testimony. Hence blessed Cyprian showed with good reason what the Church has preserved as believed and understood from the beginning. When he asserted that infants newly born from the mother’s womb were already suitable for receiving Christ’s Baptism—having been consulted as to whether this should be done before the eighth day—he tried as far as he could to demonstrate that they were complete, so that no one might think that, because infants had previously been circumcised on the eighth day, they still needed to be made complete because of the number of days [Note: [Col. 0190] Some manuscripts read, “so that no one, because of the number itself.”] (Cyprian, Letter 64, to Fidus).

Although he had thus provided them with a great defense and protection [Note: [Col. 0190] The Lovaniensian edition alone reads “And.”], he nevertheless confessed that they were not free from original sin. For if he denied this, he would remove the reason for the very Baptism on account of which he defended their being received.

If you wish, you can read the letter of that celebrated martyr concerning the Baptism of infants; it cannot be unavailable at Carthage. But I have thought that a few passages should be transferred from it into this work, insofar as seemed sufficient for the present question. Pay careful attention to them.

“As far as concerns the case of infants,” he says, “whom you stated were within the second or third day from their birth and ought not to be baptized, and whom you thought should be considered in light of the law of the ancient circumcision, so that you did not think that one who had been born should be baptized and sanctified before the eighth day: our council took a very different view.

“For in this matter, which you thought ought to be done, no one agreed with you. Rather, we all judged that God’s mercy and grace should be denied to no human being who is born. For since the Lord says in his Gospel, ‘The Son of Man did not come to destroy human souls but to save them’ (Luke IX, 56), as far as lies within us, no soul is to be destroyed, if this can be done.”

Do you notice what he says and how he understands it? Without that saving sacrament, it is destructive and deadly not only for the flesh but also for an infant’s soul to depart from this life [Note: [Col. 0191] Several manuscripts read “without any sacrament.”]. Even if he had said nothing else, it would have been for us to understand that a soul cannot perish without sin.

But shortly afterward, while defending the innocence of infants, see what he nevertheless most explicitly confesses concerning them:

“Moreover, if anything could prevent people in any way from attaining grace, then more serious sins would be able to prevent adults, those advanced in age, and the elderly. But if, when they afterward believe, no one is prevented from receiving remission of sins, Baptism [Col. 0191], and grace—even those guilty of the gravest offenses and who had sinned greatly against God long before—how much more should no one prevent an infant, who, being newly born, has committed no sin, except that, having been born carnally according to Adam, he has contracted the contagion of ancient death through his first birth?

“He approaches more easily to receive the remission of sins for this very reason: that those sins being remitted are not his own, but those of another” [Note: [Col. 0191] Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read “to receive the remission, for this very reason.”].

11. Do you see with what confidence this great man speaks from the ancient and indisputable rule of faith? He brought forward these most certain proofs so that what was uncertain—the matter about which the person to whom he was replying had consulted him, and concerning which he mentions that a decree of the council had been established [Note: [Col. 0191] The old Corbeiensis codex reads “that the decree had been agreed upon.” Most other manuscripts read “that the decree had agreed.”—might be confirmed by them: namely, that no one would hesitate to baptize an infant before the eighth day after his birth if the infant were brought forward.

For the council was not then establishing or confirming as something new, or as something challenged by anyone’s opposition, the proposition that infants were held bound by original sin. Rather, since another question was being considered and debated there—because of the law of bodily circumcision, whether they ought to be baptized before the eighth day—no one agreed with the person who denied this [Col. 0192]. The matter was no longer something to be consulted about or debated, but was regarded as firm and certain: the soul would perish with regard to eternal salvation if it ended this life without receiving that sacrament, even though infants newly born from the womb were bound only by the liability of original sin. Thus, although the remission of sins was much easier for them because the sins were another’s, it was nevertheless necessary.

The uncertain question concerning the eighth day was resolved by these certainties, and the council judged that every day assistance ought to be given to a human being who has been born, lest he perish eternally [Note: [Col. 0192] The printed editions read “that it is permitted to give assistance.” All the Gallican, Belgian, and Vatican manuscripts read “that assistance ought to be given,” although some of them have “to give assistance.”].

An explanation was also given concerning bodily circumcision itself: it was a shadow of what was to come. This does not mean that we should understand Baptism as needing to be administered on the eighth day after a person’s birth, but that we are spiritually circumcised in Christ’s resurrection. He rose from the dead on the third day after the day of his passion, yet, in the sequence of the days of the week by which time moves forward, on the eighth day—that is, on the first day after the Sabbath [Note: [Col. 0192] The printed editions read “not because.” The Cygirannensis codex more aptly reads “not so that.”].

## CHAPTER VI

12. Universal agreement concerning original sin. And now certain people are attempting, with the audacity of some new dispute [Note: [Col. 0192] Five Gallican manuscripts read “a new dispute.”], to make uncertain for us what our ancestors presented as utterly certain when resolving matters that seemed uncertain to some.

I do not know when this first began to be debated. But I do know that even Saint Jerome—who to this day is occupied in ecclesiastical literature with a reputation for and labor of such outstanding learning—uses this as a most certain proof, without any debate, in resolving certain questions in his books.

For in what he wrote on the prophet Jonah, when he came to the passage where even little children are mentioned as punished by fasting, he says:

“The older age begins and reaches down to the youngest. For no one is without sin, not even if his life has lasted a single day, and the years of his life are numbered [Note: [Col. 0192] Amerbach, Erasmus, and many manuscripts read “and the years of his life are innumerable,” corruptly, for “and the years of his life are counted.”] (Job XIV, 5). For if the stars are not pure in God’s sight, how much more are the worm and corruption” (ibid. XXV, 5–6), “and those who are held liable through the sin of Adam who offended” (Jerome, on chapter 3 of Jonah)?

If we could easily question this most learned man, how many interpreters of the divine Scriptures in both languages and writers of Christian discussions would he mention who, from the time Christ’s Church was established, held no other view, received no other view from their ancestors, and handed down no other view to posterity?

Although I have read far fewer works, I do not remember ever hearing anything else from Christians who accept both Testaments—not only those established in the Catholic Church, but also those belonging to any heresy or schism. Nor do I remember reading anything else among those whose writings on these matters I have been able to read [Col. 0193], who followed, or believed that they followed, or wished to be believed to follow, the canonical Scriptures.

I do not know where this issue has suddenly emerged for us. For a short time ago [Note: [Col. 0193] We believe this was in the year 411, when the conference with the Donatists was held at Carthage. At that time Augustine records below, in *The Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 46, that he saw Pelagius.] I happened to hear, in passing, the words of some people who were speaking casually among themselves while we were at Carthage: infants are not baptized in order to receive remission of sins, they said, but in order to be sanctified in Christ.

Disturbed by this novelty—and since it was not an appropriate occasion for me to say anything in response, and since these were not people whose authority concerned me—I easily regarded it as something already past and extinguished. But now, behold, it is being defended with zeal against the Church [Note: [Col. 0193] The words “against the Church” are absent from almost all the manuscripts.]; behold, it is also being committed to memory through writing; behold, the matter is being brought to such a crisis that our brothers are consulting us about it; behold, we are compelled to dispute and write against it.

## CHAPTER VII
[Col. 0193]

### 13. Jovinian’s Error. The Opinions of Any Debaters Are Not to Be Regarded as Canonical Authority. How Original Sin Is Alien. We Were All One Man in Adam

A few years ago there arose at Rome a certain Jovinian, who is said to have persuaded even consecrated virgins of more advanced age to marry—not by enticing them because he wished to take any of them as a wife, but by arguing that virgins dedicated to religious devotion had no greater merit before God than married believers. Yet it never occurred to him to attempt to assert that human children are born without original sin. Indeed, if he had maintained this, women would have been much more inclined to marry, since they would expect to bear children entirely pure.

When the brethren sent Jovinian’s writings to Jerome for refutation—for he had even dared to write—Jerome found in them not only nothing of this kind, but, in refuting certain of his foolish arguments, brought this forward among many other proofs as something entirely certain concerning humanity’s original sin, a matter about which he evidently believed even Jovinian himself had no doubt (Jerome, *Against Jovinian*, book 2, shortly after the beginning). His words in that discussion are these:

> “He who says that he remains in Christ,” he says, “ought himself to walk as he walked” (1 John 2:6). Let the opponent choose whichever of the two he wishes; we grant him the choice. Does he remain in Christ, or does he not remain? If he remains, then let him walk as Christ walked. But if it is presumptuous to promise a likeness to the Lord’s virtues, then he does not remain in Christ, because he does not walk as Christ did. He committed no sin, and deceit was not found in his mouth; when he was reviled, he did not revile in return, and like a lamb before its shearer, so he did not open his mouth (Isaiah 53:9; 1 Peter 2:22–23). The ruler of this world came to him and found nothing in him (John 14:30). Although he had committed no sin, God made him sin for us (2 Corinthians 5:21).
>
> But we, according to the Epistle of James, “all offend in many things” (James 3:2), and no one is free from sins, even if his life should last only a single day (Job 14:5). “For who can boast that he has a clean heart, or who can confidently say that he is pure from sins?” (Proverbs 20:9). And we are held liable in a likeness of Adam’s transgression. Hence David also says, “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Psalm 50:7 [51:5]).

### 14. These Statements Are Not Cited as Though We Rely on the Opinions of Any Debaters as Canonical Authority

I have recalled these things not because we rely on the opinions of just any debaters as though they possessed canonical authority, but so that it may be evident that, from the beginning up to the present time, when this novelty arose, this doctrine concerning original sin was guarded with such steadfastness in the faith of the Church that those who expounded the Lord’s utterances more readily brought it forward as something entirely certain in order to refute other falsehoods than anyone attempted to refute it as false.

Moreover, in the holy canonical Books the clearest and fullest authority for this doctrine is in force. The Apostle cries out: “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so death passed into all men, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12). Therefore it cannot plainly be said that Adam’s sin harmed even those who did not sin, since Scripture says, “in whom all sinned.” Nor are these sins called alien as though they had no relation at all to infants. For all sinned in Adam at the time when, by that implanted power in his nature by which he was able to beget them, they were still all that one man.

[Note: Printed editions read *insita in qua* (“implanted in which”). The manuscripts correct this, though they differ among themselves: some read *insita vis est in qua* (“the implanted power is that in which”); others, *insita vi in qua* (“by the implanted power in which”); and still others, *insita vi qua* (“by the implanted power through which”).]
