They are called alien, however, because they were not yet living their own individual lives; rather, whatever existed in the future stock of descendants was contained in the life of one man.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 15. The Origins of the Errors. The Comparisons Drawn from the Foreskin of the Circumcised and from the Chaff of Wheat

“They allow no reason,” they say, “for God, who forgives personal sins, to impute another’s sins.”

He does forgive them—but to those regenerated by the Spirit, not to those generated by the flesh. And he imputes not sins that are now alien, but their own. For they were alien when those who would carry them through propagation did not yet exist; but now, through carnal generation, they belong to those in whom they have not yet been forgiven through spiritual regeneration.

### 16. The Objection from the Baptized Parents of Baptized Children

“But if Baptism,” they say, “cleanses that ancient offense, those who are born from two baptized parents ought to be free from this sin. For they could not transmit to their descendants what they themselves never possessed.”

This is where the error commonly gains strength: people are capable of asking questions about matters they are not capable of understanding. To what listener, or in what words, can I explain how mortal and corrupted beginnings do not harm those who have been initiated through other, immortal beginnings, and yet do harm those whom the very persons whom they no longer harm have begotten from those same corrupted beginnings? How can this be understood by someone whose rather slow mind is obstructed both by prejudice in favor of his own opinion and by the most burdensome bond of obstinacy?

Nevertheless, if this case had been undertaken against those who altogether forbid infants to be baptized, or contend that they are baptized unnecessarily, saying that children born of believers necessarily inherit their parents’ merit, then I ought perhaps to rouse myself more laboriously and energetically to convict that opinion.

If, among dull and contentious people, the obscurity of nature’s processes made it difficult for me to refute falsehood and persuade them of the truth, I might perhaps resort to examples that were familiar and readily available. I would in turn ask them this: Since they are troubled by how sin that is cleansed through Baptism remains in those whom baptized people beget, let them explain how the foreskin that is removed through circumcision remains in those whom the circumcised beget; and how the chaff that human labor separates with such care remains in the grain that grows from purified wheat.

## CHAPTER IX

### 17. Christians Do Not Always Beget Christians, nor the Cleansed the Cleansed

By examples such as these I might perhaps in some measure attempt to persuade people who thought that the sacraments of cleansing were needlessly administered to the children of the cleansed—namely, to show by what sound reasoning the children of baptized people are baptized, and how it can happen that, when a person possesses both kinds of seed, that of death in the flesh and that of immortality in the spirit, what harms his son generated through the flesh does not harm him regenerated through the Spirit, and that what is cleansed in one by forgiveness must likewise be cleansed in the other by a similar forgiveness—like circumcision, or like threshing and winnowing.

But since we are now dealing with people who admit that the children of baptized people ought to be baptized, how much better is it to proceed in this way:

You who assert that children ought to have been born without sin from people cleansed of the stain of sin—why do you not observe that it could likewise be said to you that Christian children ought to have been born from Christian parents? Why, then, do you think they must become Christians? Was there not a Christian body in their parents, to whom it was said, “Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ?” (1 Corinthians 6:15).

Or perhaps a Christian body was indeed born from Christian parents, but it did not receive a Christian soul? This is much more astonishing. For whichever view you hold concerning the soul—and surely, with the Apostle, you do not believe that before it was born it had done anything good or evil—it was either drawn from the stock of its parents and ought likewise to have been Christian, just as a Christian body is generated from Christians; or, having been created by Christ, whether in a Christian body or for the sake of a Christian body, it ought to have been created or sent as a Christian soul.

Unless perhaps you will say that Christian human beings could beget a Christian body, but Christ himself could not produce a Christian soul.

Yield, then, to the truth, and observe that, just as it could happen—as you yourselves admit—that from Christians there might be born someone who is not a Christian, and from members of Christ someone who is not a member of Christ, and—so that we may address also all those who, although falsely, are nevertheless held under some name of religion—that from the consecrated there might be born someone not consecrated, so also it can happen that from the cleansed there is born someone not cleansed.

What answer will you give as to why someone who is not a Christian is born from Christians, unless it is because generation does not make Christians, but regeneration does? Give yourselves, therefore, this explanation as well: no one is cleansed from sins by being born, but all are cleansed by being reborn.

And so, because people are cleansed through being reborn, the person who is born from people cleansed in this way must be reborn, so that he too may be cleansed.

[Note: Both the Ambrosian edition and the manuscripts read *renascatur* (“may be reborn”). Louvain reads *renascitur* (“is reborn”).]

For parents were able to transmit to their descendants what they themselves did not possess—not only in the way wheat transmits chaff, and a circumcised man transmits the foreskin, but also in the way that you yourselves acknowledge: believers transmit unbelief to their descendants. This unbelief is no longer theirs through the Spirit, by which they have been regenerated, but is the defect of mortal seed through which they were generated in the flesh.

For surely, although you judge that infants are to be made believers through the sacrament of the faithful, you do not deny that they are born unbelievers from believing parents.

## CHAPTER X

### 18. Whether the Soul Is Derived from the Parents

“But if the soul is not derived from the parents, but only the flesh,” they say, “then only the flesh possesses transmitted sin, and only the flesh deserves punishment.” For this is what they think when they say, “It is unjust that a soul born today, not from Adam’s mass, should bear so ancient a sin belonging to another.”

Consider, I beg you, how carefully Pelagius—who was a discerning man—recognized the difficulty of the question concerning the soul. For I have transcribed these words just quoted from his book. He did not say, “Since the soul is not derived from the parents,” but, “If the soul is not derived from the parents.” He was acting most appropriately concerning so obscure a matter, about which we can find no certain and clear testimonies in the holy Scriptures, or can find them only with the greatest difficulty: he spoke hesitantly rather than confidently.

Therefore I too respond to this proposition without rash assertion:

If the soul is not derived from the parents, what justice is there in compelling a soul newly created, entirely free from every fault, and wholly untouched by every contagion of sin, to endure in infants the sufferings of the flesh, its various torments, and—what is more terrible—the attacks of demons?

For the flesh does not suffer any of these things in such a way that the soul, which lives and feels there, does not rather undergo the punishments.

If this can be shown to be just, then it can likewise be shown by what justice the flesh also incurs original sin in the flesh of sin, to be cleansed through the sacrament of Baptism and the mercy of grace.

But if that cannot be shown, I do not think that this can be shown either.

Let us therefore either endure both matters as hidden and remember that we are human beings, or, if necessity should require it, let us undertake a separate discussion concerning the soul with sober caution.

## CHAPTER XI

### 19. What the Sting of Death Is

For the present, however, let us understand the Apostle’s statement—“Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so death passed into all men, in whom all sinned”—in such a way that we are not judged to resist, with excessive folly and misery, so many and such clear testimonies of the divine Scriptures. Through these we are taught that no one can obtain life and eternal salvation apart from fellowship with Christ—fellowship that takes place in him and with him when we are imbued with his sacraments and incorporated into his members.

The statement made to the Romans, “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all men,” was made in the same sense as the statement made to the Corinthians: “By a man came death, and by a man came also the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.”

No one doubts that the passage in Corinthians concerns the death of the body, since the Apostle was dealing at length and with great emphasis with the resurrection of the body. For this reason he appears there to have said nothing about sin, because the question was not about righteousness.

Here, however, in the Epistle to the Romans, he set forth both matters and commended both at great length: sin in Adam, righteousness in Christ; death in Adam, and life in Christ. I examined and explained all these words of the Apostle’s discourse in the first of those two books, as I have already said, as far as I was able and thought sufficient.

### 20. The Sting of Death Is Sin

Nevertheless, in the passage to the Corinthians, where he had long treated the subject of the resurrection, he also brought the discussion to a conclusion in such a way that he left us no reason to doubt that the death of the body likewise occurred because of sin.

For after he had said, “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. And when this corruptible has put on incorruption, and this mortal has put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written: Death is swallowed up in victory. Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” he added: “The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law” (1 Corinthians 15:21–22, 53–56).

[Note: At this point, and again below, the manuscripts read, “Where is your contention, O death?” Nevertheless, in the second occurrence they agree with the printed editions: “Where is your victory, O death?”]

Since, therefore, as the Apostle’s clearest words show, death will be swallowed up in victory when this corruptible puts on incorruption and this mortal puts on immortality—that is, when God gives life to our mortal bodies because of his Spirit dwelling in us—it is clear that the sting of this bodily death, which is opposed to the resurrection of the body, was sin.

It was the sting by which death was made, not a sting made by death. For we die because of sin; we do not sin because of death.

Thus “the sting of death” is spoken of in the same way as “the tree of life”: not because human life made it, but because human life was made through it. Likewise, “the tree of knowledge” means the tree through which human knowledge was made, not something that human beings made through their own knowledge.

So too the sting of death is that by which death was made, not something made by death. In the same way we speak of a deadly cup—the cup by which someone has died or may die—not something prepared by the person who is dying or has died.

The sting of death, therefore, is sin. By the puncture of sin the human race was mortified.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “the puncture was made by sin,” rather than “by the puncture of sin.”]

Why do we continue asking whose death this is—whether the death of the soul or of the body; whether the first death, by which we are all now dying, or the second, by which the wicked will then die? There is no reason to agitate the question, and no room for evasion. The Apostle’s words themselves, which address the matter, provide the answer:

“When this mortal,” he says, “has put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written: Death is swallowed up in victory. Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death? The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.”

He was speaking about the resurrection of the body, by which death will be swallowed up in victory when this mortal puts on immortality. Then death itself will be mocked, for it will be swallowed up in victory through the resurrection of the body.

Then it will be said to it: “Where is your victory, O death? Where is your sting, O death?” This, therefore, will be said to bodily death. For victorious immortality will swallow it up when this mortal puts on immortality.

To bodily death, I say, it will be said:

“Where is your victory, by which you had overcome everyone so completely that even the Son of God had to engage you and overcome you—not by avoiding you, but by accepting you?”

You conquered in those who were dying; you were conquered in those who were rising. Your victory, by which you had swallowed the bodies of the dying, was temporary; our victory, by which you have been swallowed up in the bodies of those rising, will endure forever.

“Where is your sting?” That is, sin, by which we were pierced and poisoned, so that you might also fix yourself in our bodies and possess them for so long a time?

[Note: The printed editions read, “so that you might also become in our bodies.” The manuscripts support the reading translated above.]

“The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.”

We all sinned in one, so that we might all die in one. We received the law not so that we might end sin through correction, but so that we might increase it through transgression. For “the law entered in so that sin might abound,” and Scripture confined all things under sin.

But thanks be to God, who gave us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 15:57), so that “where sin abounded, grace abounded even more” (Romans 5:20), and so that “the promise through faith in Jesus Christ might be given to those who believe” (Galatians 3:22). Thus we conquer death through immortal resurrection, and its sting, sin, through gratuitous justification.

## CHAPTER XII

### 21. The Commandment Concerning a Menstruating Woman Is Not to Be Understood Figuratively. The Necessity of the Sacraments

Let no one, then, deceive himself or deceive others concerning this matter. This clear meaning of Holy Scripture removes every ambiguity.

Just as death is drawn from our origin into this body of death, so sin has been drawn from our origin into this flesh of sin. For the healing of this condition—and because he came to heal what had been drawn in through propagation and increased through the will, and also to raise up this very flesh—the physician came in the likeness of sinful flesh. He is not needed by the healthy but by the sick, and he did not come to call the righteous but sinners (Mark 2:17).

Accordingly, when the Apostle urged believers not to separate themselves from unbelieving spouses, he said:

“For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified in the brother; otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy” (1 Corinthians 7:14).

This must either be understood as we have explained elsewhere (*On the Sermon on the Mount*, book 1, section 45), and as Pelagius explained when treating the same Epistle to the Corinthians:

Examples had already preceded—of men whom their wives had won for Christ, of women whom their husbands had won, and of children whom the Christian will of even one parent had prevailed upon to make Christians;

or, if the Apostle’s words seem more naturally and almost necessarily to require it, some kind of sanctification must be understood there by which the unbelieving husband and wife were sanctified in the believing spouse, and by which the children of believers were born holy.

This may be because any man or woman who had learned it from the law abstained from intercourse during the woman’s menstrual blood—for Ezekiel places this among the commandments that are not to be understood figuratively (Ezekiel 18:6)—or because of some other sprinkling of holiness arising from the very relationship of marriage and children, which is not explicitly stated there.

Nevertheless, this must be held without hesitation: whatever that sanctification may be, it is not effective for making people Christians or for remitting sins unless, through Christian and ecclesiastical instruction, they are made believers through the sacraments.

For unbelieving spouses are not cleansed from iniquity—which compels those separated from the kingdom of God to go into condemnation—even if they cling to holy and righteous spouses. Nor are infants born of any holy and righteous parents absolved from the guilt of original sin unless they have been baptized in Christ. We ought to speak on behalf of such children all the more earnestly because they themselves are less able to speak on their own behalf.

## CHAPTER XIII

### 22. Conclusion. We Must Be Concerned That Infants Be Baptized

The purpose of that disputation, whose novelty must be opposed by the ancient truth, is to make it appear that infants are baptized altogether unnecessarily. But this is not stated openly, lest the Church’s salutary custom, so firmly established, be unable to tolerate those who violate it.

[Note: The manuscripts read, “so firm,” rather than “so firmly established.”]

But if we are commanded to help orphans, how much more ought we to labor on behalf of these children, who, if Christ’s grace is denied them, will remain even more abandoned and wretched than orphans, although they are still under the care of their parents—children who cannot themselves demand that grace?

### 23. On the Claim That Some People Have Lived or Live Without Any Sin

As for what they say—that some people who already possess the use of reason have lived or are living in this world without any sin—it is something to be desired, something to be attempted, and something to be sought through prayer. Yet it must not be confidently assumed as accomplished.

[Note: Louvain reads “confessed” rather than “confidently assumed.”]

For whatever sins remain in those who desire and strive for this and ask for it through worthy supplication are daily forgiven through what we truthfully say in prayer:

“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

Whoever says that this prayer was unnecessary in this life for any holy person who knows and does the will of God—apart from the one Holy of holies—is greatly mistaken, and cannot possibly please the very one whom he praises.

But if he thinks himself to be such a person, he deceives himself, and the truth is not in him (1 John 1:8), for no other reason than that he thinks what is false.

That physician, therefore, who is needed not by the healthy but by the sick, knows how to heal us and bring us to perfection for eternal salvation. Although death has been inflicted because of sin’s desert, he does not remove it in this world from those whose sins he forgives. He does this so that, even while overcoming the fear of death, they may undertake the struggle on behalf of the sincerity of their faith.

And in the case of some of his righteous people as well, since they can still become exalted, he does not help them toward perfect righteousness, so that, while “no living person is justified in his sight” (Psalm 142:2), we may always owe thanksgiving to his forgiveness, and thus be healed through holy humility from that first cause of all vices—namely, the swelling of pride.

[Note: After the word *sanemur* (“we may be healed”), older codices insert “thanks be to God” and continue, “This epistle …”]

While my plan was giving birth to a short epistle, a lengthy book has been born. Would that it were as perfect as it has finally become complete.

[Additional textual notes: At §13, Erasmus and Louvain read *sanctimoniae* (“religious devotion”) corruptly; see the *Expositions on Psalm 99*, §13. At §15, Erasmus and Louvain read *quanquam* (“although”); the manuscripts correct this to *quamque* (“and how”). At §17, the printed editions read *sic anima etiam* (“thus the soul also”); *sic* is superfluous and absent from the manuscripts. The manuscripts read *Credite* (“Believe”), rather than *Cedite* (“Yield”). At §19, some manuscripts add, “and explained both.” At §20, some manuscripts read *faceret* (“made”) rather than *fecerit* (“has made”); the manuscripts read *resurrectione* (“by the resurrection”), whereas the printed editions have *resurrectionis* (“of the resurrection”); and the printed editions read: “To bodily death, I say, it will then be said: ‘Where is your victory, O death, by which you had here overcome everyone so completely?’” At §21, see the *Commentaries on Paul* among Jerome’s works, volume 8, which belong either to Pelagius or to one of his disciples. The printed editions read “and through the sacraments”; the conjunction is absent from the manuscripts. Some manuscripts read *pro se* (“for themselves”) rather than *per se* (“of themselves”). At §23, the printed editions add *propriae voluntatis* (“of their own will”), but this is absent from the manuscripts; they also read “in that prayer,” and “for any even holy person,” while *that* and *even* are absent from the manuscripts. Some manuscripts punctuate, “so that, also overcoming its fear”; although the Louvain editors prefer the other reading, see above, book 2, §54. The printed editions read *disputatio magna* (“a great disputation”), and all the Gallican manuscripts *disputatio mea* (“my disputation”); the Vatican manuscripts agree, except one, which reads *dispositio mea* (“my plan”), a reading that appears more fitting.]

[Col. 0199]

[Note: For the book *On the Spirit and the Letter*, see book 2, chapter 37 of the *Retractions*, volume 1, column 645, from the words “To whom I had written to the tribune Marcellinus” through column 646, ending with the words “Dearest son Marcellinus.” It explains that Marcellinus the tribune—to whom so many other works of Augustine must be credited as occasioned by his requests—also gave occasion for the following work by raising a question from the books *On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, which, as we said above, were published in A.D. 412. In the *Retractions*, *On the Spirit and the Letter* follows these books not immediately but fourth in order, and was undoubtedly written near the end of that same year, 412, or somewhat before the killing of Marcellinus, which occurred in September 413. This same work is cited in *On Faith and Works*, §21, and in book 3 of *On Christian Doctrine*, §46. M.]

Saint Aurelius Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, One Book

[Note: Written toward the end of the year 412.]

[Note: Five Vatican manuscript codices and eleven Gallican manuscripts were used to correct *On the Spirit and the Letter*: the codex of the most illustrious lord of Saint-Georges, archbishop-designate of Tours; the Sorbonne codex; the codex of the Augustinians of the larger convent in Paris; the codex of the Dominicans, likewise in Paris, on the Rue Saint-Jacques; the codex of the Church of Laon; the codex of the Abbey of Saint-Remigius at Reims; and those of the abbeys of Saint-Cyprian, Corbie, Saint Michael of the Mount in Periculo Maris, Bec, and Pratelles. Also used were the variant readings of the Louvain editors, extracted from three Belgian copies, and the older editions of this work: the Ambrosian, Erasmus’s, and Louvain editions.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and the *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C)

Marcellinus wrote that he had been deeply moved because, in the preceding work, he had read that it was possible for a person to be without sin in this life if he wished, with God’s help, although no example of such perfect righteousness existed anywhere among human beings.

Augustine takes this as an occasion to argue against the Pelagians concerning the assistance of God’s grace. He shows that God does not help us divinely to perform righteousness merely by giving a law full of good and holy commandments, but by assisting and strengthening our own will, without which we cannot do good, through the Spirit of grace bestowed upon us. Without this assistance, the teaching of the law is a letter that kills, because it holds the ungodly guilty of transgression rather than justifying them.

Returning to the question proposed—which he begins to resolve at the start of the book and returns to again at its conclusion—he demonstrates that many things are possible with God’s help, as no one denies, although no example of any of them exists anywhere. Thus he concludes that perfect righteousness among human beings exists without an example, yet is not impossible.

## CHAPTER I

### 1. The Occasion for Writing This Book. Something May Be Possible Even Though It Has Never Happened

After reading the little works that I recently composed for you, my dearest son Marcellinus, concerning the baptism of infants and the perfection of human righteousness—concerning which no one in this life appears either to have attained or to be going to attain it, except the one Mediator, who endured human experiences in the likeness of sinful flesh while entirely free from sin—you wrote back that you had been troubled because, in the later of the two books, I said that it was possible for a person to be without sin if his will did not fail him, with divine assistance supporting it, and yet that, apart from the one in whom all will be made alive (1 Corinthians 15:22), no one had been or would be found in whom this perfection existed while he lived in this world.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the two books” rather than “the later of the two books.”]

It seems absurd to you to say that something can happen for which there is no example, since, as I believe, you do not doubt that a camel has never passed through the eye of a needle, and yet Christ said that even this was possible for God (Matthew 19:24, 26).

You may also read that twelve thousand legions of angels could have fought for Christ so that he would not suffer (Matthew 26:53), and yet this did not happen; that it could have happened that the nations were exterminated at one time from the land given to the children of Israel (Deuteronomy 31:3), yet God willed that this take place gradually (Judges 2:3); and six hundred other examples may occur to us of things that we admit either did happen, could have happened, or can happen, although we cannot produce examples showing that they did happen.

[Note: The Georgian manuscript omits “twelve thousand”; it is not found in the Gospel, although Augustine cites it again below, section 62. Nor do Hilary of Poitiers and Pope Leo read this passage differently in the places cited. The words enclosed in brackets occur only in edition GG.]

Therefore we must not deny that it is possible for a human being to be without sin merely because there is no human being—apart from him who is not only human but also God by nature—in whom we can demonstrate that this perfection exists.

## CHAPTER II

### 2. The Error of Those Who Say That a Person Lives Without Sin in This World Is Less Harmful. The Error of Those Who Deny the Necessity of Grace Is More Serious and Must Be Refuted with the Greatest Zeal

Perhaps you will reply that the things I mentioned as having been possible, although they did not happen, are divine works; whereas for a human being to be without sin belongs to the human person’s own work. It is the highest work, by which full, perfect, and entirely complete righteousness is achieved. Therefore, you may say, we should not believe that no one either has been, is, or will be in this life who has completed this work, if it can be completed by a human being.

But you must consider that, although carrying this out belongs to the human person, this too is a divine gift, and therefore you must not doubt that it is a divine work. “For it is God,” says the Apostle, “who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

### 3. Those Who Say That a Person Lives or Has Lived Without Any Sin

Accordingly, those who say that a person lives—or has lived—in this world without any sin at all are not especially troublesome, and we must press them to demonstrate, if they can, that this is so.

For if someone could teach that the testimonies of Scripture—which I believe establish that no human being living here, even while exercising free choice, is found without sin—are to be understood differently from how they sound, and could demonstrate that one person or several had lived here without any sin, then anyone who did not oppose him, but instead congratulated him greatly, would be driven by no small impulses of envy.

Indeed, if no one is, was, or will be perfect in such purity—which I more strongly believe—yet someone defends or supposes that such a person exists, existed, or will exist, then, as far as I can judge, the error is not great or dangerous, provided that the person is deceived with a certain benevolence, and provided that whoever holds this view does not think himself to be such a person unless he has truly and clearly recognized that he is.

### 4. Those Who Think That Human Will Can Perfect or Advance in Righteousness Without God’s Help Must Be Opposed Most Fiercely

But we must resist with the greatest force and intensity those who think that, without God’s assistance, the power of the human will by itself can either perfect righteousness or make progress toward it by persevering in it.

When they begin to be pressed on how they presume to assert that this can happen without divine help, they restrain themselves and do not dare to utter this claim, because they see how impious and intolerable it is.

But they say that these things do not happen without divine help because God created human beings with free choice of the will, and, by giving commandments, himself teaches how a person ought to live. In this respect, they say, he certainly helps by removing ignorance through instruction, so that a person may know what he ought to avoid and what he ought to seek in his actions. By following the way that has been shown, through free choice naturally implanted in him, and by living temperately, justly, and piously, he may merit to attain the blessed and eternal life.

## CHAPTER III

### 5. True Grace Is the Gift of the Holy Spirit, Through Which Delight in and Love of the Good Arise in the Soul

We, however, say that the human will is divinely assisted in doing righteousness in such a way that, besides being created with free choice of the will, and besides receiving instruction that commands how it ought to live, a person receives the Holy Spirit. Through the Spirit, delight in and love of that supreme and unchangeable good which God is come to exist in the soul, even now while we still walk by faith and not yet by sight (2 Corinthians 5:7).

Thus, with this pledge of a free gift bestowed upon it, the soul grows ardent to cling to its Creator and is inflamed to approach participation in that true light, so that it may be well with it because of him from whom it has its being.

For free choice is capable of nothing except sinning if the way of truth is hidden from it. And once what ought to be done and toward what one ought to strive begins to be known, it is not done, undertaken, or lived well unless it also gives delight and is loved.

But “the love of God is poured out into our hearts,” not through free choice arising from ourselves, “but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

## CHAPTER IV
### [Chapter IV—inherited heading; supplied text begins at §6]

#### 6. The teaching of the law without the life-giving Spirit is a letter that kills

That teaching by which we receive the command to live continually and rightly is a letter that kills unless the life-giving Spirit is present. For what we read—“The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6)—must not be understood only in this way: that when something is written figuratively and its literal meaning is absurd, we should not accept it as the words sound, but, looking to what it signifies, nourish the inner person with spiritual understanding—for “to set the mind on the flesh is death, but to set the mind on the Spirit is life and peace” (Rom. 8:6). This would be the case, for example, if someone were to understand much of what is written in the Song of Songs carnally, directing it not toward the fruit of radiant love but toward the feeling of lustful desire.

The Apostle’s statement, “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life,” must therefore not be understood only in that way, but also—and most especially—in the sense in which he says elsewhere most plainly:

[Col. 0203. The printed editions read “that”; the manuscripts more correctly read “in which.”]

“I would not have known desire unless the law had said, ‘You shall not desire.’” And shortly afterward he says: “Taking occasion through the commandment, sin deceived me, and through it killed me” (Rom. 7:7, 11). Behold what “the letter kills” means.

[The Gallican manuscripts all omit “something is said.”]

Certainly, when it says, “You shall not desire,” it is not speaking figuratively of something that should not be understood according to the sound of the words; rather, it is a perfectly clear and salutary command, and whoever fulfills it will have no sin at all. For this reason the Apostle chose a general statement by which he embraced everything, as though this were the voice of the law prohibiting every sin: [Col. 0204] “You shall not desire.” No sin, after all, is committed except through desire; therefore the law that gives this command is good and worthy of praise.

But when the Holy Spirit does not help by inspiring a good desire in place of evil desire—that is, by pouring love into our hearts—that law, although good, increases the evil desire by prohibiting it. It is like the force of water: if it continues to flow in one direction, it becomes more violent because of an obstacle placed against it; and once it has overcome the obstacle’s mass, it rushes down with a greater accumulation and rolls more violently along the downward slopes. Somehow, the very thing that is desired becomes more pleasurable when it is forbidden. This is what it means that sin deceives through the commandment and through it kills, when transgression is added as well—for transgression does not exist where there is no law (Rom. 4:15).

### Chapter V

#### 7. What is to be discussed here

Let us, if you please, consider the whole passage of the apostolic letter and examine it as the Lord may assist us. For I wish, if I can, to demonstrate that the Apostle’s statement, “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life,” was not spoken about figurative expressions, although it can appropriately be understood in that way as well.

[The printed editions read “and there”; the Cygirannensis manuscript reads “and thus”; four other manuscripts read “and that.”]

Rather, it was spoken chiefly about the law plainly prohibiting what is evil.

When I have shown this, it will certainly become clearer that living well is a divine gift—not only because God gave human beings free will, without which one can live neither badly nor well; and not only because he gave a command by which he teaches how one ought to live; but because through the Holy Spirit he pours love into the hearts of those whom he foreknew in order to predestine, predestined in order to call, called in order to justify, and justified in order to glorify (Rom. 8:29–30).

When this has become clear, you will see, I think, that it is said in vain that only those things which are works of God are possible without an example—as we mentioned the passage of a camel through the eye of a needle, and whatever other things are impossible for us but easy for God—and that, for this reason, human righteousness should not be counted among them, since it ought to belong not to God’s work but to human work. If its perfection is possible in this life, there is no reason why it should be believed to be without an example.

The futility of this claim will become sufficiently evident when it has also become clear that human righteousness itself must be attributed to God’s work, although it does not occur without the human will. Therefore we cannot deny that its perfection is possible even in this life, because all things are possible for God (Mark 10:27)—both those he accomplishes by his own will alone and those which he has determined can be accomplished by him with the wills of his creatures cooperating.

Accordingly, whatever of these things he does not accomplish is indeed without an example among completed works; but in God and in his power it has a cause by which it could be accomplished, and in his wisdom a reason why it was not accomplished. Even if this reason is hidden from human beings, let them not forget that they are human, nor for that reason attribute folly to God because they do not fully grasp his wisdom.

#### 8. The Apostle’s explanation to the Romans

Consider, then, the Apostle explaining this in his letter to the Romans and sufficiently demonstrating that what he wrote to the Corinthians—[Col. 0205] “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life”—must be understood more in the manner we have stated above. For the letter of the law, which teaches that one must not sin, kills if the life-giving Spirit is absent: it makes sin known rather than avoided, and thus causes it to increase rather than diminish, because transgression of the law is added to evil desire.

### Chapter VI

#### 9. The abundance of sin through the law

The Apostle therefore wished to commend the grace that came through Jesus Christ to all the nations, so that the Jews would not exalt themselves over the other nations on account of having received the law. After saying that sin and death had entered the human race through one man, and righteousness and eternal life through one man—clearly indicating that the former was Adam and the latter Christ—he says:

“But the law entered in so that sin might abound; but where sin abounded, grace abounded even more, so that just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

[The Gallican manuscripts all omit “unto death.”]

Then, raising an objection against himself, he says: “What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound? By no means.” For he saw that what he had said—“The law entered in so that sin might abound; but where sin abounded, grace abounded even more”—could be perversely understood by perverse people, as though he had said that sin was beneficial because of the abundance of grace.

[The Louvain edition reads, “grace might abound even more.”]

He dispelled this notion by answering, “By no means,” and added: “We who have died to sin, how shall we live in it?” That is: since grace has brought about our death to sin, what else shall we do if we live in it except show ourselves ungrateful to grace?

Someone who praises the benefit of medicine does not say that diseases and wounds—the things from which medicine heals a person—are beneficial. Rather, the more medicine is praised, the more the wounds and diseases from which it delivers us are condemned and abhorred. In the same way, praise and proclamation of grace constitute the condemnation and denunciation of sins.

The ugliness of the human illness had to be demonstrated, since no holy and good commandment profited a person against his iniquity; indeed, his iniquity was increased rather than diminished by it, since “the law entered in so that sin might abound.” Thus, convicted and confounded, a person might see that he needs not merely a teacher but also God as a helper, by whom his ways may be directed so that no iniquity may rule over him (Ps. 118:133), and that, by fleeing to the aid of divine mercy, he may be healed. Thus, where sin abounded, grace might abound even more—not through the merit of the sinner, but through the help of the one who comes to his aid.

#### 10. The same healing mystically shown in Christ’s passion and resurrection

The Apostle next shows that this same healing was mystically demonstrated in Christ’s passion and resurrection, saying:

“Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death? We were therefore buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. [Col. 0206] For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be so in the likeness of his resurrection—knowing this, that our old man was crucified together with him so that the body of sin may be abolished, so that henceforth we might not serve sin. For whoever has died has been justified from sin. But if we have died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him, knowing that Christ, having risen from the dead, dies no more, and death shall no longer rule over him. For in that he died, he died to sin once for all; but in that he lives, he lives to God. So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 5:20–6:11).

[The manuscripts read, “so that the body of sin might be abolished.”]

[The printed editions read, “and also.” The manuscripts read, “but also,” in accordance with the Greek: ἀλλὰ καί.]

[Most manuscripts read, “death shall no longer rule over him.”]

It is certainly quite clear that, through the mystery of the Lord’s death and resurrection, the ending of our former life and the beginning of the new have been symbolized, and the abolition of iniquity and renewal of righteousness have been demonstrated. From where, then, does such a great benefit come to a person through the letter of the law—

[The Belgian manuscript of Saint-Amand omits “through the letter of the law.”]

—unless through faith in Jesus Christ?

### Chapter VII

#### 11. From what source good works proceed

This holy thought preserves the children of human beings who hope in the protection of God’s wings, so that they may be intoxicated by the abundance of his house and drink from the torrent of his delight—

[The Gallican and Vatican manuscripts read, “and drink from the torrent of delight.”]

—for with him is the fountain of life, and in his light we shall see light. He extends his mercy to those who know him and his righteousness to those who are upright in heart. He extends his mercy not merely because they know him, but also so that they may know him; nor does he extend his righteousness merely because they are upright in heart, but also so that they may become upright in heart—the righteousness by which he justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5).

This thought does not lift a person into pride—

[Thus most manuscripts. Three other manuscripts read, “does not remove him into pride.” The printed editions read, “does not bring pride.”]

—for this vice arises when each person places excessive confidence in himself and makes himself his own head for living. Through this disposition one departs from that fountain of life, from which alone righteousness—namely, the good life—is drunk, and from that unchangeable light, through participation in which the rational soul is, in a certain way, kindled so that it too becomes a made and created light.

Thus John was “a burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35); yet, acknowledging from where he shone, he said: “We have received from his fullness”—from whose fullness, unless from that one in comparison with whom John was not the light? For “that was the true light which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:16, 9).

Accordingly, after he had said in the same psalm, “Extend your mercy to those who know you, and your righteousness to those who are upright in heart,” he continues: “Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of sinners move me: there all those who work iniquity have fallen; they have been driven out and were unable to stand” (Ps. 35:8–13).

[The printed editions read, “let not the hands of sinners move me.” The manuscripts read, “let not the hand of sinners move me”; several of them have “of the sinner” instead of “of sinners.”]

By this impiety, through which each person attributes to himself what belongs to God, he is driven into his own darkness, which consists of works of iniquity. He himself plainly performs these works and is capable [Col. 0207] of accomplishing them.

[The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions read, “he himself performs them, who is capable of accomplishing these things.”]

But he does not perform works of righteousness except insofar as he receives from that fountain and from that light in which life is in need of nothing, and in which there is neither change nor the shadow of alteration (James 1:17).

#### 12. Paul’s humility and his defense of grace

For this reason the Apostle Paul, who had formerly been called Saul (Acts 13:9), chose this name, as I see it, for no other reason than to show himself to be small, as though the least of the Apostles—

[Most manuscripts read, “as though the least.”]

—while fighting powerfully and vigorously against the proud and arrogant, and against those who presume upon their own works, in defense of this grace of God.

For grace truly appeared more evident and brilliant in him: while he had been violently persecuting the Church of God and performing deeds for which he deserved the severest punishment, he received mercy instead of condemnation and obtained grace instead of punishment. Rightly, therefore, he cries out and contends in its defense, and, in a profound and exceedingly hidden matter, he does not care about the resentment

[Here the printed editions add “especially.”]

of those who do not understand and twist his sound words into a perverse meaning—provided only that he proclaims without hesitation the gift of God, by which alone the children of promise are saved: the children of divine beneficence, the children of grace and mercy, the children of the New Covenant.

First, all his salutations have this form: “Grace to you and peace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (at the beginning of the Epistles). Moreover, in the letter to the Romans almost the entire discussion concerns this very question, and does so with such force and in so many ways that it certainly tires the reader’s attention, but with a useful and salutary fatigue, exercising the limbs of the inner person more than breaking them.

### Chapter VIII

#### 13. Observance of the law; the character of Jewish boasting; fear of punishment; circumcision of the heart; the point at which the Pelagians acknowledge God as the author of our justification

These are the matters I mentioned above. This is why he rebukes the Jew and says that he is called a Jew but by no means fulfills what he professes:

“But if you are called a Jew, and rest in the law, and boast in God, and know the will, and approve what is excellent—

[The printed editions read, “his will.” The word “his” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle.]

[Greek: *tà diaphéronta* (τὰ διαφέροντα).]

—instructed by the law, and are confident that you yourself are a guide of the blind, a light of those who are in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of infants, having the form of knowledge and truth in the law: you, then, who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who preach that one must not steal, do you steal? You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege? You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God through transgression of the law? For ‘the name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you,’ as it is written.

“Circumcision indeed profits, if you keep the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision. Therefore, if uncircumcision keeps the requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision? And will not uncircumcision by nature, fulfilling the law, judge you who, with the letter and circumcision, are a transgressor of the law?

[All manuscripts read, “fulfilling the law.” The printed editions read, “bringing the law to completion.”]

“For it is not the one who is a Jew outwardly, nor is circumcision outwardly in the flesh; but the one who is a Jew inwardly, [Col. 0208] and circumcision is of the heart, in the Spirit—

[The printed editions, together with some manuscripts, read, “and circumcision of the heart by the Spirit.”]

—not in the letter, whose praise is not from human beings but from God” (Rom. 2:17–29).

Here he made clear how he had said, “You boast in God.” For certainly, if such a Jew truly boasted in God in the manner demanded by grace—which is given not on the merits of works but freely—his praise would be from God, not from human beings.

But they boasted in God as though they alone had deserved to receive his law, in accordance with the words of the Psalm: “He has not dealt so with any nation, nor made his judgments known to them” (Ps. 147:20). Yet they supposed that they fulfilled this law of God by their own righteousness, when in fact they were rather its transgressors. Thus it produced wrath for them (Rom. 4:15), as sin abounded, being committed by those who knew.

For even those who did what the law commanded, when the Spirit of grace did not help them, did so out of fear of punishment, not out of love of righteousness. Consequently, before God there was not the will that appeared in the deed before human beings; rather, they were held guilty because God knew that, if they could do so with impunity, they would prefer to commit those very acts.

He calls circumcision of the heart a will that is pure from every unlawful desire. This is not brought about by the letter teaching and threatening, but by the Spirit helping and healing. Therefore the praise of such people is not from human beings but from God, who by his grace supplies the grounds for their praise. Of him it is said, “In the Lord my soul shall be praised” (Ps. 33:3), and to him it is said, “With you is my praise” (Ps. 21:26)—not like those who want God to be praised because they are human beings, but themselves because they are just.

#### 14. The Pelagian claim concerning God as the author of our justification

“But we praise,” they say, “God as the author of our justification, in that he gave the law, by observing which we might know how we ought to live.”

They do not hear what they read: “No flesh shall be justified from the law before God.” Something may indeed be accomplished before human beings, but not before the one who examines the heart and the innermost will, where he sees—although the one who fears the law may do something else—what that person would nevertheless prefer to do if it were permitted.

And lest anyone think that the Apostle here said that no one is justified by that law which contains many figurative commandments in the old sacraments—including circumcision of the flesh, which infants were commanded to receive on the eighth day (Lev. 12:3)—he immediately added which law he meant, saying: “For through the law comes knowledge of sin.”

That, then, is the law about which he later says: “I would not have known sin except through the law. For I would not have known desire unless the law had said, ‘You shall not desire’” (Rom. 7:7). For what else does “through the law comes knowledge of sin” mean?

### Chapter IX

#### 15. The righteousness of God manifested through the Law and the Prophets

At this point perhaps human presumption, ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish its own, might say that the Apostle rightly said, “No one will be justified from the law.” For the law merely shows what must be done and what must be avoided, so that the will may fulfill what the law has shown, and thus a person may be justified—not through the command of the law but through free will.

[Most manuscripts lack the words “not through the command of the law but through free will.”]

But, human being, pay attention to what follows. He says: “But now, apart from the law, the righteousness of God has been manifested, witnessed by the Law and the Prophets.”

Does this not sound loudly enough even to deaf ears? “The righteousness of God,” he says, “has been manifested.” Those who wish to establish their own righteousness are ignorant of this righteousness and unwilling to submit to it (Rom. 10:3).

[Only the printed editions add, “and to this.”]

He says, “The righteousness of God has been manifested.” He did not say, “the righteousness of a human being,” or “the righteousness of one’s own will,” but “the righteousness of God”—not the righteousness by which God is just, but the righteousness with which he clothes a person when he justifies the ungodly.

The Law and the Prophets bear witness to this righteousness. The Law does so by commanding, threatening, and justifying no one, thereby sufficiently indicating that a person is justified by the gift of God through the help of the Spirit. The Prophets do so because Christ’s coming fulfilled what they foretold.

For he goes on to add: “But the righteousness of God is through faith in Jesus Christ”—that is, through the faith by which one believes in Christ. Just as this is called the faith of Christ, not the faith by which Christ believes, so that is called the righteousness of God, not the righteousness by which God is just. Both are ours; but they are called God’s and Christ’s because they are given to us by his generosity.

Therefore the righteousness of God [Col. 0209] is without the law—not manifested without the law.

[The manuscripts omit “of God” here.]

For how could it be witnessed through the law if it were manifested without the law? Rather, the righteousness of God is without the law in this sense: God bestows it through the Spirit of grace upon the believer without the help of the law—that is, without being helped by the law.

[Am. Er. and most manuscripts read, “without being helped by the law.”]

For through the law he shows a person his weakness, so that, fleeing through faith to God’s mercy, he may be healed.

[The Louvain edition reads, “so that he may be healed.”]

For it is said of God’s wisdom that it carries law and mercy on its tongue (Prov. 3:16, according to the Septuagint): law, by which it makes the proud guilty; and mercy, by which it justifies the humbled.

Therefore, “the righteousness of God is through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe; for there is no distinction. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God”—not their own glory. For “what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

They therefore lack the glory of God. And see what follows: “Having been justified freely by his grace” (Rom. 3:20–24). They were not justified by the law, nor justified by their own will, but justified freely by his grace. This does not mean that it occurs without our will; rather, the law reveals our will to be weak, so that grace may heal the will, and the healed will may fulfill the law—not placed under the law and not in need of the law.

### Chapter X

#### 16. How the law is not imposed on the just

“For the law is not imposed on the just”—although it is good if someone uses it lawfully. By connecting these two statements as though they were contrary to one another, the Apostle admonishes and moves the reader to investigate and resolve the question.

How is the law good if someone uses it lawfully (1 Tim. 1:9, 8), if what follows is also true: “Knowing this, that the law is not imposed on the just”? For who uses the law lawfully except the just person? Yet the law is not imposed on him, but on the unjust.

Or must the unjust person use the law lawfully in order to be justified—that is, in order to become just—so that, like a pedagogue, it may lead him to grace (Gal. 3:24), through which alone he can fulfill what the law commands?

For through grace he is justified freely, that is, without any preceding merits of his works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace (Rom. 11:6). It is given, after all, not because we have done good works, but so that we may be able to do them; that is, not because we have fulfilled the law, but so that we may be able to fulfill the law.

For he said, “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17). Of him it was said: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-Begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:14).

This is the glory of which it was said: “For all have sinned and lack the glory of God.” And this is the grace of which he immediately says: “Having been justified freely by his grace.”

The unjust person therefore uses the law lawfully in order to become just. Once he has become just, he no longer uses it as a vehicle after reaching his destination—or rather, to use the Apostle’s comparison mentioned above, as a pedagogue after he has been instructed.

For how is the law not imposed on the just if it is also necessary for the just—not so that the unjust may be led by it to justifying grace, but so that the just person may use it lawfully?

Perhaps—indeed, not perhaps, but certainly—the just person uses the law lawfully

[The earlier printed editions read, “uses.”]

when he imposes it upon the unjust to frighten them, so that, when the disease of their ingrained desire begins to be increased in them by the stimulus of prohibition and the accumulation of transgression, they may flee through faith to justifying grace and, delighted by the sweetness of righteousness through the gift of the Spirit, escape the punishment threatened by the letter.

Thus the two statements will not be contrary, nor will they conflict with each other: the just person may use the good law lawfully, and yet the law is not imposed on the just. For he was not justified by that law, but by the law of faith, through which he believed that divine grace could in no way come to the aid of his weakness in fulfilling what the law of works commanded.

[Two Belgian manuscripts omit “of works.”]

#### 17. The exclusion of boasting

For this reason he says: “Where, then, is your boasting? It has been excluded. Through what law? The law of works? No, but through the law of faith” (Rom. 3:27).

Perhaps by “boasting” he meant the praiseworthy boasting that is in the Lord, and said that it had been excluded—not so that it might be driven away, but so that it might stand forth prominently. Hence certain silversmith craftsmen are called *exclusores*, “finishers” or “polishers.”

This is also the meaning of the Psalm: “That those who have been tested as silver may stand forth” (Ps. 67:31)—that is, that those who have been tested by the word of the Lord may stand forth. For elsewhere it is said: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire” (Ps. 11:7).

Or perhaps he wished to refer to the defective boasting that arises from pride—namely, the boasting of those who think they live justly and boast as though they had not received anything. He says that this boasting has been excluded not through the law of works—

[The printed editions read, “as though they had not received it; which he says has been excluded not through the law of works.” The manuscripts correct this reading.]

—but through the law of faith: that is, it has been expelled and cast away, because through the law of faith each person recognizes that, if he lives well in any respect, [Col. 0211] he has this from God’s grace, and that he will obtain the perfection of his love of righteousness from no other source.

### Chapter XI

#### 18. Piety is wisdom; the righteousness of God is called that which God effects

This thought makes a person pious, because piety is true wisdom. I call “piety” what the Greeks call *theosebeia* (θεοσέβεια). It is this that is commended when it is said to a human being, as we read in the book of Job: “Behold, piety is wisdom” (Job 28:28).

If *theosebeia* were rendered into Latin according to the origin of the word, it could be called the worship of God. This worship consists chiefly in the soul’s not being ungrateful to him. Hence, in the true and unique sacrifice itself,

[The printed editions read, “and in the unique sacrifice”; the word “in” is absent from the manuscripts.]

we are admonished to give thanks to the Lord our God.

The soul will be ungrateful if it attributes to itself what comes from God, especially righteousness. It becomes inflated by righteousness as though by its own works and as though obtained by itself from itself—not in the ordinary manner in which people boast of riches, bodily form, eloquence, and other external or internal, bodily or spiritual goods, which even criminals commonly possess, but as though it were boasting wisely of things that are properly the goods of the good.

[Two Belgian manuscripts omit “wisely.”]

Driven away by this vice from the stability of the divine substance, certain great men have even fallen into the disgrace of idolatry.

Thus the same Apostle, in the same Epistle in which he is a vigorous defender of grace, after saying that he was a debtor to Greeks and barbarians, to the wise and the foolish, and that, so far as it depended on him, he was ready to evangelize those who were in Rome, says:

“For I am not ashamed of the Gospel; for it is the power of God unto salvation for everyone who believes, for the Jew first and for the Greek. For the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as it is written: ‘The just shall live by faith.’”

This is the righteousness of God that was veiled in the Old Testament and revealed in the New. It is called the righteousness of God because, by imparting it, he makes people just, just as salvation is called the Lord’s (Ps. 3:9) because he makes people safe.

This is the faith from which and unto which it is revealed—

[The printed editions read, “and in which.” The manuscripts are corrected to read, “and unto which.”]

—from the faith of those who proclaim, that is, into the faith of those who obey. Through this faith of Jesus Christ—that is, the faith Christ has bestowed upon us—we believe that what enables us to live justly comes from God and that it will become more complete. Therefore, with that piety by which God alone is to be worshiped, we give him thanks.

### Chapter XII

#### 19. Knowledge of God through created things; the law without grace

With good reason, then, the Apostle turns from this point to mention with abhorrence those who, inflated and made light by the vice I recalled above, lifted themselves up by themselves as though through empty space, only to find no place of rest and to be shattered by their fall, descending into the images (*figmenta*) of idols as though into stones.

[The Cambronensis manuscript reads “fragments” (*fragmenta*).]

Because he had commended the piety of faith, through which, having been justified by God, we ought to be grateful to him, he introduces what we should detest as its opposite:

“For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all impiety and injustice of human beings who suppress the truth in injustice, because what can be known of God is manifest among them; for God has manifested it to them. For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly perceived through the things that have been made—both his eternal power and divinity—[Col. 0212] that they may be without excuse; because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools, and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible human beings, birds, four-footed animals, and serpents” (Rom. 1:14–23).

[The printed editions read “so that”; the manuscripts and the Greek omit “so.”]

Observe how he did not say that they were ignorant of the truth, but that they suppressed the truth in wickedness. But since it occurred to him that someone might ask where those people could have obtained knowledge of the truth, given that God had not given them the law, he did not leave this unexplained.

[The printed editions read “since it occurred,” omitting “but.”]

He said that they had arrived at an understanding of the invisible things of the Creator through the visible things of creation.

[The Louvain edition reads, “of the invisible Creator.”]

For in truth, just as great minds persisted in seeking, so they were able to find.

[The manuscripts read, “thus great minds.”]

Where, then, was their impiety? Clearly, in this: although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their thoughts. Their particular vice is vanity: they deceive themselves while seeming to themselves to be something, although they are nothing (Gal. 6:3).

Finally, by covering themselves with this swelling of pride—the foot of which that holy singer prays may not come against him—

[All manuscripts read *cantator* (“singer”).]

—he who said, “In your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:12, 10), they turned away from the light of unchanging truth, and their foolish heart was darkened.

It was not a wise heart, although they had known God, but rather a foolish one, because they did not glorify God as God or give thanks. For he said to the human being, “Behold, piety is wisdom.” Thus, when they claimed to be wise, what this must mean is that, by attributing this very thing to themselves, they became fools.

#### 20. The knowledge of the Creator through creation does not justify

What need is there to discuss what follows? Through this impiety, into what did those people—those people, I say, who were able to know the Creator through creation—fall, and where were they submerged? The continuation of the Epistle itself teaches this better than we recount it here, since God resists the proud (James 4:6).

For we have not undertaken in this work to expound the Epistle, but chiefly strive, by its testimony, to demonstrate as far as we can that we are divinely helped in carrying out righteousness not because God gave the law filled with good and holy commandments, but because our will itself—without which we cannot perform what is good—is helped and raised up by the imparted Spirit of grace. Without this help, that teaching is a letter that kills, because it holds the ungodly guilty of transgression rather than justifying them.

For just as the knowledge itself of the Creator profited nothing for salvation those who knew the Creator through creation,

[All our manuscripts omit “of the Creator.”]

[Col. 0213]

because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, claiming to be wise, so the knowledge itself does not justify those who learn through the law how a human being ought to live, because, wishing to establish their own righteousness, they are not subject to the righteousness of God (Rom. 10:3).

[The printed editions add here, “of God.”]

### Chapter XIII
### CHAPTER XIII

#### 21. The law of works and the law of faith

It is worthwhile to consider how the law of deeds—that is, of works—by which boasting is not excluded, and the law of faith, by which it is excluded, differ from one another, provided that we are able to attend and discern. [Note: Col. 0213. The Louvain edition, with some manuscripts, reads: “For rightly, indeed.”]

For someone will quickly say that the law of works belongs to Judaism, but the law of faith to Christianity, because circumcision and the other such works belong to the law, whereas Christian practice no longer observes them. But we have been working for a long time to show how greatly this distinction is mistaken, and perhaps we have already demonstrated it to you and to others of similar discernment. Nevertheless, since the matter is important, it is not inappropriate to linger over its clarification with still more testimonies.

He himself speaks of the law by which no one is justified, which, he says, entered in so that transgression might abound (Rom. 5:20). Yet, lest anyone inexperienced in the matter should on this account condemn it and sacrilegiously accuse it, he defends it, saying:

> “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not! But I did not know sin except through the law. For I would not have known covetousness unless the law said, ‘You shall not covet.’ Thus, taking occasion through the commandment, sin produced in me every kind of covetousness.” 

He also says:

> “The law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good. But sin, so that it might appear to be sin, through what is good worked death in me” (Rom. 7:7–13).

It is therefore the letter that kills, which says, “You shall not covet.” Of this same letter he also says what I mentioned shortly before:

> “Through the law comes knowledge of sin. But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, attested by the Law and the Prophets; the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ upon all who believe, for there is no distinction. For all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. God set him forth as a propitiatory offering [Note: Col. 0213. Three Vatican manuscripts read *propitiatorem*, “propitiator,” instead of *propitiatorium*, “propitiatory offering.”] through faith in his blood, to demonstrate his righteousness on account of the purpose of the preceding sins in God’s forbearance [reading uncertain], to demonstrate his righteousness at the present time, so that he might be just and the one who justifies him who is of the faith of Jesus.”

Then he adds the passage that concerns our present discussion:

> “Where, then, is your boasting? It has been excluded. Through what law? Of works? No, but through the law of faith” (Rom. 3:20, 27).

The law of works, therefore, is itself the law that says, “You shall not covet,” because through it comes knowledge of sin.

I therefore want to know whether anyone would dare say to me that the law of faith does not say, “You shall not covet.” For if it does not say this, why should we, secure and unpunished because we stand within it, sin with impunity? This is what those people thought the Apostle meant, of whom he says:

> “And, as some allege that we say, ‘Let us do evil so that good may come,’ whose judgment is just” [Note: Col. 0214. Most manuscripts read: “whose condemnation is just”] (Rom. 3:8).

But if the law of faith itself also says, “You shall not covet”—as so many [Note: Col. 0214. The manuscripts omit “so many,” and likewise omit “and apostolic” below.] Gospel and apostolic commandments do not cease to testify and proclaim—why is it not itself called the law of works? For the fact that it does not contain the works of the ancient sacraments, namely circumcision and the others, does not mean that the works it contains in its sacraments, appropriate to the present age, are not works. [Note: The printed editions read “appropriate now to this age”; the manuscripts omit “now.”]

Nor, when the law was mentioned because through it comes knowledge of sin and therefore no one is justified by it, was the question really about the works of the sacraments. Thus boasting was not excluded through that law, but through the law of faith, by which the righteous person lives. But does knowledge of sin not also arise through this law, since it too says, “You shall not covet”?

#### 22. What, then, is the difference?

I shall state it briefly. What the law of works commands by threatening, the law of faith obtains by believing. The former says, “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17); the latter says:

> “Since I knew that no one could be continent unless God granted it—and that it was itself a matter of wisdom to know whose gift this was—I went to the Lord and entreated him” (Wis. 8:21).

This is that wisdom called piety, by which the Father of lights is worshiped, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift (James 1:17). He is worshiped through the sacrifice of praise and thanksgiving [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read “through acts of praise and thanksgiving”], so that his worshiper may boast not in himself but in him (2 Cor. 10:17).

Accordingly, through the law of works God says, “Do what I command”; through the law of faith one says to God, “Give what you command.” The law commands for this reason: that it may admonish faith concerning what it should do. That is, if the one commanded cannot yet do it, he may know what to ask; but if he can immediately do it and does so obediently, he must also know by whose gift he is able.

“For we have not received,” says that same most steadfast preacher of grace, “the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Cor. 2:12).

What, however, is the spirit of this world except the spirit of pride? It is through this spirit that the foolish heart of those people was darkened who, although they knew God, did not glorify him as God by giving thanks. It is by no other spirit that those are deceived who, ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own righteousness, are not subject to God’s righteousness.

Hence, in my view, the more truly a child of faith is the person who knows from whom to hope for what he does not yet possess, rather than the one who attributes to himself what he does possess. Yet preferable to both is the person who both possesses something and knows from whom he possesses it—provided that he does not believe himself to be what he is not yet [Note: Col. 0214. Some printed editions add “already”: “provided that he does not believe himself already to be …”], lest he fall into the fault of that Pharisee who, although he gave thanks to God for what he possessed, nevertheless asked for nothing to be given him, as though he needed nothing for the increase or perfection of his righteousness (Luke 18:11–12).

Having considered and examined these matters according to the abilities the Lord graciously grants, we conclude that a person is not justified by the commandments of a good life except through faith in Jesus Christ—that is, not by the law of works but by the law of faith; not by the letter but by the Spirit; not by the merits of works but by gratuitous grace.

### CHAPTER XIV

#### 23. The Decalogue also kills unless grace is present

Although the Apostle appears to rebuke and correct those to whom circumcision was being commended in such a way that he calls circumcision itself, and the other observances of that kind, by the name of “the law”—observances that Christians now reject as shadows of what was to come, holding fast to what was figuratively promised through those shadows—nevertheless, when he says that no one is justified by the law, he intends this to be understood not only of those sacraments that contained figures promising future realities, but also of those works by which anyone who performs them lives justly. Among these is the commandment, “You shall not covet.”

To make what we are saying clearer, let us examine the Decalogue itself. Moses certainly received on the mountain the law to be administered to the people, written on tablets of stone by the finger of God; it is comprised of ten commandments (Exod. 31:18; Deut. 9:10; Exod. 20). Nothing there was commanded concerning circumcision, nothing concerning animal sacrifices, which Christians no longer offer.

Of those ten commandments, excepting the observance of the Sabbath, let someone tell me what a Christian is not required to observe: whether the prohibition against making or worshiping idols and any gods besides the one true God; the prohibition against taking God’s name in vain; the command to honor parents; or the commands to avoid fornication, murder, theft, false testimony, adultery, and coveting another’s property. [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read “not coveting another’s property.”] Who could say that a Christian ought not to keep any of these?

Or perhaps the Apostle does not call the law written on those two tablets the letter that kills, but rather the law of circumcision and the other ancient sacraments that have now been abolished? But how could we think this, since the commandment “You shall not covet” is contained in it—through which commandment, although it is holy and just and good, sin, he says, deceived him and through it killed him? For what else does “the letter kills” mean?

#### 24. The letter and the Spirit

The passage addressed to the Corinthians makes this even clearer, where he says, “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.” He wishes no other letter to be understood there than the Decalogue itself, written on those two tablets. For he says:

> “You are Christ’s letter, administered through us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God; not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts. Such confidence we have through Christ toward God—not that we are competent to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves, but our competence is from God, who made us competent ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit. [Note: The manuscripts have the genitive construction “not of the letter but of the Spirit,” following the Greek. The printed editions here read “not the letter but the Spirit”; elsewhere, in sections 30 and 35, they agree with the ancient codices and the Greek.] For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.

> “Now if the ministry of death, engraved in letters on stones, came with glory, so that the children of Israel could not gaze steadily at Moses’ face because of the glory of his countenance, which is passing away, why will the ministry of the Spirit not be even more glorious? For if the ministry of condemnation has glory [Note: The Louvain edition reads “if the ministry of condemnation is in glory”], much more will the ministry of righteousness abound in glory” (2 Cor. 3:2–9).

Much can be said about these words [Note: The printed editions read, “Much can be said about these words,” whereas the manuscripts more suitably read, “Much can be said about these expressions”], but perhaps at another time it will be more appropriate. For now, observe which letter he calls deadly, to which he introduces the life-giving Spirit as its opposite.

It is certainly the ministry of death engraved in letters on stone, and the ministry of condemnation, because “the law entered so that transgression might abound.” Yet the commandments themselves are so useful and salutary to the person who performs them that, unless someone performs them, he cannot possess life.
