Or was the Decalogue called the letter that kills because of the one commandment concerning the Sabbath, since whoever observes that day even now as the letter sounds is carnally minded—and to be carnally minded is death (Rom. 8:6)—while the other nine commandments, when rightly observed exactly as they are written, are to be considered as belonging not to the law of works by which no one is justified, but to the law of faith by which the righteous person lives?

Who could think so absurdly as to say that the ministry of death engraved in letters on stone is derived not from all ten commandments but from the one alone concerning the Sabbath?

Where, then, do we place the statements, “The law produces wrath, for where there is no law there is no transgression” (Rom. 4:15); “Until the law, sin was in the world, but sin is not counted where there is no law” (Rom. 5:13); and the statement we have already mentioned so many times, “Through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Rom. 3:20)? Above all, where do we place the statement in which he expressed most clearly the matter under discussion: “I would not have known covetousness unless the law said, ‘You shall not covet’”?

#### 25. The law exposes sin but does not give life

Consider the whole passage and see whether he says anything there on account of circumcision or the Sabbath or any other shadowy sacrament, rather than saying it entirely because the letter that prohibits sin does not give life to a person [Note: The manuscripts read “does not give life”; the printed editions read “does not justify”], but instead kills him by increasing covetousness and piling up iniquity through transgression—unless grace, through the law of faith that is in Christ Jesus, sets him free, when love is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5).

For after saying, “So that we may serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter,” he continues:

> “What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not! But I did not know sin except through the law. For I would not have known covetousness unless the law said, ‘You shall not covet.’ But sin, taking occasion through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetousness. For apart from the law sin was dead. I was once alive apart from the law, but when the commandment came, sin revived. I died, and the commandment that was intended for life was found to be death for me. For sin, taking occasion through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.

> “Therefore the law indeed is holy, and the commandment holy and just and good. So what is good became death for me [Note: The printed editions read, “So what is good—for good it is—became death for me.” The manuscripts lack the words “for good it is,” which are enclosed in parentheses in the editions]. Certainly not! Rather, so that sin might appear to be sin, through what is good it worked death in me, so that through the commandment sin might become exceedingly sinful.

> “For we know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin. For I do not understand what I do: I do not do what I wish, but what I hate, that I do. If I do what I do not wish, I agree with the law that it is good. But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.

> “For I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh. For willing is present with me, but carrying out the good is not. For I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish, that I do. If I do what I do not wish, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.

> “I find, then, the law for me who wish to do good: evil is present with me. [Note: The printed editions read, “the willing of evil is present with me.” The word “willing” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Apostle’s text.] For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person, but I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read “taking me captive in the law of sin.” The printed editions read “leading me captive into the law of sin, which is…”], which is in my members.

> “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. Therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7:6–25).

#### 26. The letter of the law makes guilty unless the newness of the Spirit is present

The oldness of the letter therefore makes people guilty through knowledge of sin, rather than freeing them from sin, unless the newness of the Spirit is present. Hence it is also written elsewhere, “Whoever increases knowledge increases sorrow” (Eccl. 1:18)—not because the law itself is evil, but because the good commandment is contained in the letter that displays it, not in the Spirit who gives assistance.

If the commandment is carried out through fear of punishment rather than love of righteousness, it is carried out slavishly rather than freely, and therefore it is not truly carried out. For the fruit is not good if it does not arise from the root of love.

But when there is faith working through love (Gal. 5:6), a person begins to delight in the law of God according to the inner person. This delight is a gift not of the letter but of the Spirit, even though another law in the members still wars against the law of the mind, until the whole oldness has passed away, transformed into the newness that increases day by day in the inner person. The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord frees us from this body of death.

### CHAPTER XV

#### 27. Grace hidden in the Old Testament is revealed in the New

This grace lay concealed under a veil in the Old Testament, and was revealed in the Gospel of Christ through the most orderly arrangement of the ages, as God knows how to order all things.

Perhaps its very concealment is signified by the fact that in the Decalogue given on Mount Sinai, the only commandment presented in a figurative form and thereby concealed is the one concerning the Sabbath. [Note: Col. 0217. The Louvain edition and fewer manuscripts read: “the commandment [was] figuratively [presented].”] The Sabbath is the day of sanctification. [Note: Col. 0217. The word “day” is absent here from the manuscripts.] Nor is it without significance that, among all the works God made, sanctification first resounded there, where he rested from all his works (Gen. 2:3). But this is not the place to discuss that matter.

Nevertheless, what I think is sufficient for the matter at hand is this: it was not without reason that the people were commanded to abstain from every servile work on that day. This signifies that not to sin is sanctification—that is, the gift of God through the Holy Spirit. In the law written on the two tablets of stone, this alone among the other commandments was placed in the shadow of a figure, in which the Jews observe the Sabbath. By this very fact it was signified that the time had then come for grace to be concealed—a grace that was to be revealed in the New Testament through Christ’s passion, as through the tearing of the veil [Note: Col. 0218. The printed editions read “by the tearing”] (Matt. 27:51).

“For when one passes over to Christ,” he says, “the veil will be taken away.” [Note: Col. 0218. Four manuscripts read “when you pass over.”]

### CHAPTER XVI

#### 28. Why the Holy Spirit is called the finger of God

“Now the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:16–17).

This is the Spirit of God, by whose gift we are justified, through whom it comes about that we delight in not sinning. Where this Spirit is, there is freedom; apart from this Spirit, there is delight in sinning, and there is slavery. We must abstain from the works of that slavery. [Note: The printed editions add “that is, keeping a spiritual Sabbath”; this is absent from the manuscripts.]

This Holy Spirit, through whom love is poured into our hearts—the fullness of the law—is also called the finger of God in the Gospel (Luke 11:20). Since those tablets too were written by the finger of God, and since the finger of God is the Spirit of God through whom we are sanctified, so that, living by faith, we may work good through love, who would not be moved by this correspondence and, at the same time, this difference? [Note: Col. 0218. The manuscripts read “this correspondence and, at the same time, this difference”; the printed editions read “this correspondence and the same subsistence.”]

Fifty days are counted from the celebration of Passover, which was commanded through Moses to be carried out by the slaughter of the figurative lamb (Exod. 12), clearly signifying the future passion of the Lord, up to the day on which Moses received the law written on tablets by the finger of God. Similarly, after fifty days had been completed from the slaughter and resurrection of him who was led like a sheep to be sacrificed (Isa. 53:7), the finger of God—that is, the Holy Spirit—filled the believers who had gathered together in one place (Acts 2:2–4).

### CHAPTER XVII

#### 29. Comparison of the Mosaic law and the new law

In this marvelous correspondence there is certainly a great difference between the two events. There, the people were prevented by terrifying fear from approaching the place where the law was given (Exod. 19); here, the Holy Spirit came upon those who had gathered together in one place while awaiting him who had been promised.

There, the finger of God worked on tablets of stone; here, in human hearts. There, therefore, the law was placed externally, so that the unrighteous might be terrified; here, it was given internally, so that they might be justified.

“For ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ ‘You shall not murder,’ ‘You shall not covet,’ and whatever other commandment there is”—which is certainly written on those tablets—“is summed up in this saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’” Love does no harm to one’s neighbor. Therefore love is the fullness of the law (Rom. 13:9–10).

This love has not been written on tablets of stone, but has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5). The law of God, therefore, is love. The wisdom of the flesh is not subject to it, nor indeed can it be (Rom. 8:7). But when the works of love are written on tablets in order to terrify the wisdom of the flesh, the law is the law of works, and the letter kills the transgressor. When love itself is poured into the hearts of believers, the law is the law of faith, and the Spirit gives life to the one who loves.

#### 30. The distinction between the letter and the Spirit agrees with the Apostle’s words

Now observe how this distinction agrees with the apostolic words that I mentioned earlier for another purpose and postponed discussing more carefully. He says:

> “It has been manifested that you are Christ’s letter, administered through us, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God; not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts.”

See how he shows that the former is written outside the human person, to terrify him externally, while the latter is written within the person, to justify him internally.

He called the tablets of the heart “fleshly,” not in the sense of belonging to carnal wisdom, but as though they were living and endowed with perception, in comparison with stone, which is without sensation.

When shortly afterward he says that the children of Israel could not gaze steadily to the end at Moses’ face, and that for this reason he spoke to them through a veil, this signifies that the letter of the law justifies no one. Rather, a veil has been placed over the reading of the Old Testament until one passes over to Christ and the veil is removed—that is, until one passes over to grace and understands that justification comes to us from him, by which we do what he commands.

He commands for this reason: so that, when we fail in ourselves, we may flee to him. Therefore, after saying most carefully, “Such confidence we have through Christ toward God,” lest this be attributed to our own strength, he immediately commended the source of the matter under discussion, saying:

> “Not that we are competent to think anything from ourselves, as though from ourselves, but our competence is from God, who also made us competent ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life.”

### CHAPTER XVIII

#### 31. The old law ministers death; the new law ministers righteousness

Since the law, as he says elsewhere, was established because of transgression (Gal. 3:19)—that is, this letter written outside the human person—he therefore calls it both the ministry of death and the ministry of condemnation.

But this ministry, namely that of the New Testament [Note: The Louvain edition reads “the New Testament”], he calls the ministry of the Spirit and the ministry of righteousness, because through the gift of the Spirit we work righteousness and are freed from the condemnation of transgression.

Therefore the former is brought to an end, while the latter remains, because the terrifying tutor will be removed when love succeeds fear. “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom.”

He says that this ministry comes not from our merits but from mercy:

> “Therefore, since we have this ministry, just as we have received mercy, we do not lose heart; rather, we reject the hidden things of shame, not walking in cunning nor adulterating the word of God through deceit.”

By this cunning and deceit he wants hypocrisy to be understood, through which [Note: Col. 0219. Some printed editions and manuscripts read “because”] the proud wish to appear righteous. Hence, in that psalm which the Apostle himself recalls as testimony to this very grace, he says:

> “Blessed is the one whose sin the Lord has not counted, and in whose mouth there is no deceit” (Rom. 4:8; Ps. 32:2).

This is the confession of humble saints, not the boast of those claiming to be what they are not.

A little later he says:

> “For we do not preach ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord [Note: The printed editions add “our Lord.” This is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek], and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake. For God, who said, ‘Let light shine out of darkness,’ has shone in our hearts to illuminate the knowledge of his glory in the face of Christ Jesus.”

This is the knowledge of his glory: that we know him to be the light by which our darkness is illuminated.

Observe how he emphasizes the same point:

> “But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, so that the surpassing power may be of God and not from us.”

A little later, commending this same grace more abundantly in the Lord Jesus Christ, he reaches the garment of the righteousness of faith. Clothed in it, we shall not be found naked; and for this reason, weighed down by mortality [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read “weighed down mortally”], we groan, desiring to be clothed over with our heavenly dwelling, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life.

See what he adds:

> “He who has prepared us for this very thing is God, who has given us the pledge of the Spirit.”

And shortly afterward he says:

> “So that we might become the righteousness of God in him” (2 Cor. 3–5).

This is that righteousness of God—not the righteousness by which God himself is righteous, but that by which we are made by him. [Note: Col. 0220. Some more recent editions add *justi facti*, “made righteous.”]

### CHAPTER XIX

#### 32. Christian faith concerning the assistance of grace. Prophecy of Jeremiah concerning the New Testament. Law. Grace.

Let no Christian stray from this faith, which alone is Christian. Nor should anyone, when ashamed to say that we are made righteous by ourselves, without God’s grace working this in us—because he sees that the faithful and devout cannot bear this assertion when it is made [Note: Col. 0220. The manuscripts read “cannot be borne”; the printed editions read “cannot be believed”]—turn instead to say that we cannot be righteous without the working of God’s grace because he gave the law, established teaching, and commanded good precepts.

Without the Spirit’s assistance, that law is unquestionably the letter that kills. But when the life-giving Spirit is present, he causes the very thing to be loved inwardly that the law, written outwardly, caused to be feared.

#### 33. Jeremiah’s prophecy concerning the New Testament

Consider this briefly in the testimony that was most splendidly proclaimed through the prophet concerning this matter [Note: The Louvain edition reads “was proclaimed most splendidly”]:

> “Behold, the days are coming [Note: The printed editions read “will come,” but the manuscripts read “are coming”], says the Lord, and I will complete a New Testament over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah—not according to the testament that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out [Note: The Ambrosian edition and only two of the Vatican manuscripts read “to cast them out.” But whenever this testimony is repeated below, the other Vatican and Gallican manuscripts consistently agree with the reading “to lead them out.”] from the land of Egypt. For they did not remain in my testament, and I disregarded them, says the Lord.

> “For this is the testament that I will establish with the house of Israel: After those days, says the Lord, I will give my laws into their hearts, and I will write them on their minds; and I will be their God, and they will be my people. And no one will teach his fellow citizen and no one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord,’ because all will know me, from the least to the greatest of them, because I will be merciful toward their iniquity, and I will remember their sins no more” (Jer. 31:31–34).

What shall we say to this? In the ancient books, apart from this prophetic passage, the New Testament is either nowhere or only rarely mentioned in such a way that it is expressly called by that name. For in many places it is signified and foretold as something future, but not in such a way that the name itself is also written.

Consider carefully, therefore, what distinction God testified that there is between the two testaments, namely the Old and the New.

#### 34. The law is not at fault; grace fulfills it

After saying, “Not according to the testament that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out from the land of Egypt,” observe what he adds:

> “For they did not remain in my testament.”

He attributes to their fault the fact that they did not remain in God’s testament, lest the law they then received appear to be at fault. For this is the law that Christ did not come to abolish but to fulfill (Matt. 5:17).

Nevertheless, the impious are not justified by that same law, but by grace. This is what the life-giving Spirit accomplishes, without whom the letter kills.

“For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly have come from the law. But Scripture confined everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ.”

Through this promise—that is, through God’s gift—the law itself is fulfilled. Without this promise, it makes people transgressors: either up to the point of an evil deed, if the flame of covetousness breaks through even the barriers of fear, or at least in the will alone, if fear of punishment overcomes the pleasure of lust.

When he says, “Scripture confined everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ,” he is stating the benefit of this confinement. For to what purpose did it confine them, except as he says elsewhere:

> “Before faith came, we were kept under the law, confined for the faith that was later to be revealed” (Gal. 3:21–23)?

The law, therefore, was given so that grace might be sought; grace was given so that the law might be fulfilled.

The law was not left unfulfilled through any fault of its own, but through the fault of the wisdom of the flesh. This fault had to be exposed through the law and healed through grace.

“For what was impossible for the law [Note: The Louvain edition reads “for the law”; other printed editions and the manuscripts read “of the law,” in agreement with the Greek], in that it was weakened through the flesh, God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and, because of sin, condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteousness of the law might be fulfilled in us who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit” (Rom. 8:3–4).

Hence, in this prophetic testimony also, when he says, “I will complete a New Testament over the house of Israel and over the house of Judah,” what does “I will complete” mean except “I will fulfill”? It means: not according to the testament that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out from the land of Egypt.

### CHAPTER XX

#### 35. The old law and the new law

That testament was old, therefore, because this one is new. Why, then, is the former old and the latter new, when the same law is fulfilled through the New Testament that said in the Old, “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17)?

“Because they did not remain in my testament, and I disregarded them, says the Lord.”

Thus, because of the guilt of the old person—which was not healed by the letter that commanded and threatened—that testament is called old. This one, however, is called new because of the newness of the Spirit, which heals the human being from the fault of oldness.

Finally, consider what follows and see how clearly it reveals what people who trust in themselves refuse to look upon:

> “For this is the testament that I will establish with the house of Israel: After those days, says the Lord, I will give my laws into their hearts, and I will write them on their minds.”

Here is the source of the Apostle’s statement that we mentioned above:

> “Not on tablets of stone but on tablets of the heart, because not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God.”

I believe that the Apostle mentioned the New Testament in that passage for no other reason—there he says, “who made us competent ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit” (2 Cor. 3:3, 6)—than that he was contemplating this prophecy when he said, “not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshly hearts.” For here it says, “I will write them on their hearts,” where the New Testament is expressly promised.

### CHAPTER XXI

#### 36. The law written on hearts

What, then, are the laws of God written by God himself on hearts, except the very presence of the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God? When he is present, love is poured into our hearts; love is the fullness of the law and the goal of the commandment.

For although the promises of the Old Testament are earthly, it nevertheless contains—apart from the sacraments that were shadows of things to come, such as circumcision, the Sabbath, other observances of days, ceremonies concerning certain foods [Note: Col. 0222. See *Retractions* 2.37], and the manifold rite of sacrifices and sacred observances, which suited the oldness of the carnal law [Note: Col. 0222. The Ambrosian and Louvain editions and most manuscripts read “which suited the carnal law”] and the servile yoke—such commandments of righteousness as we are also now commanded to observe. They are especially expressed on those two tablets without the shadow of figurative signification: “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not murder,” “You shall not covet,” and whatever other commandment there is, which is summed up in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Exod. 20:14–17).

Yet because, as I have said, earthly and temporal promises are recounted in that testament—good things of this corruptible flesh, although eternal and heavenly things belonging to the New Testament are figured by them [Note: Col. 0222. The printed editions read “were figured”]—the good of the heart itself, the good of the mind, the good of the spirit—that is, intelligible good—is now promised when it says:

> “I will give my laws into their minds, and I will write them on their hearts.”

Thus he signified that they would not fear the law that terrifies externally, but would love the very righteousness of the law dwelling within them.

### CHAPTER XXII
### 37. The eternal reward

Then he added the reward as well: “And I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” This is what that man says to God: “But for me, it is good to cling to God” (Ps. 72:28). “I will be their God,” he says, “and they shall be my people.” What good is better than this, what happiness more blessed than this: to live for God, to live from God, with whom is the fountain of life, and in whose light we shall see light (Ps. 35:10)?[^c0022-18]

Of this life the Lord himself says: “And this is eternal life, that they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3)—that is, that they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you sent as the one true God.[^c0022-1] For he himself also promises this to those who love him, saying: “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments; and whoever loves me will be loved by my Father; and I will love him, and I will show myself to him” (ibid. 14:21)—namely, in the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father, not in the form of a servant, in which he will show himself even to the ungodly.[^c0022-2]

Then what is written will come to pass: “Let the ungodly be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of the Lord” (Isa. 26:10), when the wicked will go into eternal fire, but the righteous into eternal life (Matt. 25:46). This eternal life, as I have mentioned, has been defined as consisting in knowing the one true God.

John says the same thing: “Beloved, we are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). This likeness is now beginning to be restored, as long as the human being is renewed inwardly from day to day (2 Cor. 4:16), according to the image of him who created him (Col. 3:10).

### CHAPTER XXIII

### 38. The present restoration compared with the perfection of the life to come

But in comparison with the perfection of that eminence which will then exist, what—and how great—is this present state? The Apostle, applying some sort of example drawn from familiar things to those ineffable realities, compared the smallness of childhood with mature adulthood. “When I was a child,” he says, “I spoke as a child, I understood as a child, I thought as a child; but when I became a man, I put away the things that belonged to a child.”

Then, showing in sequence why he said this, he continues: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face. Now I know in part; but then I shall know even as I have been known” (1 Cor. 13:11–12).

### CHAPTER XXIV

### 39. The eternal reward proper to the New Testament, foretold through the prophet. How that reward will belong to all. The Apostle, a forceful defender of grace. The law written in hearts and the reward of eternal contemplation belong to the New Testament. Who are the lesser and greater among the blessed?

Accordingly, through this prophet also, whose testimony we are examining, the following is added, so that in this reward, in this end, in this perfection, the consummation of blessedness and eternal life may consist. For after he had said, “I will be their God, and they shall be my people,” he immediately added: “And they shall no longer teach each one his fellow citizen and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all [Col. 0224] shall know me, from the least to the greatest of them.”

Certainly now is already the time of the New Testament, whose promise was made through the Prophet in these words that we have recalled from that prophecy. Why, then, does he still say that each one teaches his fellow citizen and his brother, “Know the Lord”? Or is this perhaps not said when the Gospel is preached, since its very proclamation consists in saying this everywhere? For why does the Apostle call himself a teacher of the Gentiles (1 Tim. 2:7), unless what he himself says is being fulfilled: “How will they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how will they believe him whom they have not heard? And how will they hear without a preacher?” (Rom. 10:14).

Since this preaching is now spreading everywhere, how is this the time of the New Testament concerning which the Prophet said, “And they shall no longer teach each one his fellow citizen and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all shall know me, from the least to the greatest of them,” unless he joined to that same New Testament the eternal reward—namely, the most blessed contemplation of God himself—by promising it?

### 40.

What, then, is meant by “all, from the least to the greatest of them,” except all who belong spiritually to the house of Israel and to the house of Judah—that is, to the children of Isaac, to the seed of Abraham? For this is the promise that was made to him: “In Isaac shall your seed be called.” “For not all who are descended from the flesh are children of God; rather, the children of the promise are counted as seed.”[^c0022-3]

The word of the promise is this: “At this time I will come, and Sarah shall have a son.” And not only this, but Rebecca also, having conceived from one union with Isaac our father. For before the children had been born, or had done anything good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works but from him who calls—it was said to her, “The elder shall serve the younger” (Rom. 9:7–13).

This is the house of Israel, or the house of Judah, because of Christ, who came from the tribe of Judah. This is the house of the children of the promise, not of their own works,[^c0022-4] but of God’s gift. For God promises what he himself brings about. He does not promise something while another accomplishes it; that would no longer be promising, but foretelling.

Therefore it is “not from works, but from him who calls,” lest it be theirs and not God’s; lest the reward be reckoned not according to grace but according to debt (Rom. 4:4), and thus grace no longer be grace. The Apostle, the least of the apostles, is an energetic defender and champion of this grace—he who labored more than all of them, “yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:9–10).

“For all,” he says, “shall know me”: all of the house of Israel and the house of Judah. For “not all who are from Israel are Israel.” Rather, they are all to whom it is said in the Psalm, concerning the morning reception—that is, concerning the new light, namely, the New Testament: “All the seed of Jacob, magnify him; let all the seed of Israel fear him” (Ps. 21:1, 24).

Entirely all the seed—absolutely all the seed of those who were promised and called, but of those who were called according to the purpose. “For those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, [Col. 0225] he also glorified” (Rom. 8:28, 30).

Therefore it is “from faith, so that the promise may be firm according to grace for all the seed”—not only for the seed that is from the law, that is, which comes from the Old Testament into the New, but also for the seed that is from faith, without a law previously set before it.[^c0022-5]

Now Abraham is from faith—that is, those who imitate Abraham’s faith. He is “the father of us all,” as it is written: “I have appointed you the father of many nations” (Rom. 4:16–17). All these, therefore—predestined, called, justified, and glorified—shall know God by the grace of the New Testament, from the least to the greatest of them.

### 41.

Just as the law of works written on tablets of stone, and its reward—the promised land, which the carnal house of Israel received after it had been delivered from Egypt—belong to the Old Testament, so the law of faith written in hearts, and its reward—the vision of contemplation, which the spiritual house of Israel will receive after being delivered from this world—belong to the New Testament.

Then what the Apostle says will come to pass: “Whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease, or knowledge will be abolished”—namely, that childish knowledge in which one lives here, which is partial, through a mirror and in an enigma. For because of this, prophecy is necessary, while future things continue to succeed past things. Because of this, tongues are necessary—that is, a multiplicity of significations—when one thing and then another is brought to the attention of one who does not yet contemplate the eternal light of manifest truth with a wholly purified mind.

But when the perfect has come, and all that is partial has been abolished (1 Cor. 13:8–9), then he who, having assumed flesh, appeared to flesh will show himself to those who love him. Then there will be eternal life, “that we may know the one true God” (John 17:3). Then “we shall be like him” (1 John 3:2), because then “we shall know even as we have been known” (1 Cor. 13:12).

Then no one will teach his fellow citizen or his brother, saying, “Know the Lord”; for all shall know him, from the least to the greatest of them.

This may be understood in several ways. It may mean that there too each of the saints differs from another in glory as one star differs from another (ibid. 15:41). Nor does it matter at all whether the phrase is “from the least to the greatest,” as it is stated, or whether it were said “from the greatest to the least.” The sense would likewise be unaffected if by the lesser we understood those who are able only to believe, and by the greater those who, insofar as this life permits, were also able to understand the incorporeal and immutable light.[^c0022-6]

Or the lesser may be understood as those later in time, and the greater as those earlier in time. For all will receive together the contemplation of God that was promised, because “they provided something better for us, so that they might not be perfected without us” (Heb. 11:40). And for this reason the earlier are found as lesser,[^c0022-7] because they were delayed [Col. 0226] less—just as, in the Gospel parable, those who came later to the vineyard are said to receive the denarius first (Matt. 20:8–12).

Or, in whatever other way—which perhaps presently escapes me—the lesser and greater are to be understood.

### CHAPTER XXV

### 42. The distinction between the Old and New Testaments

Nevertheless, attend as carefully as you can to what I am striving with such effort to demonstrate. When the Prophet promised the New Testament, saying that it would not be according to the covenant previously made with the people of Israel after their deliverance from Egypt, he said nothing about a change of sacrifices or of any sacraments, although these too were undoubtedly to follow, as we see that they did, and as the same prophetic Scripture testifies in many other places. He commended only this distinction: that God would give his laws in the minds of those who belonged to this covenant, and would write them in their hearts.[^c0022-19] From this the Apostle took his language: “not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God; not on tablets of stone, but on tablets of human hearts” (2 Cor. 3:3).

The eternal reward of this justification would not be a land from which the Amorites, Hittites, and the other nations mentioned there were expelled (Josh. 12), but God himself, to whom it is good to cling (Ps. 72:28), so that the good of God which they love may be God himself whom they love. Nothing separates him from human beings except sins, and these are forgiven only through that same grace.

Thus, after he had said, “For all shall know me, from the least to the greatest of them,” he immediately added: “For I will be merciful toward their iniquity, and I will remember their sins no more.”

Through the law of works the Lord says, “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17). Through the law of faith the Lord says, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). He was speaking about good works—that is, about the fruits of the branches.[^c0022-8]

Since this distinction between the Old and New Testaments is evident—that in the former the law is written on tablets, while in the latter it is written in hearts, so that what terrifies outwardly in the former delights inwardly in the latter, and so that there one becomes a transgressor through the letter that kills, while here one becomes a lover through the Spirit that gives life—it must not therefore be said that God helps us to perform righteousness and works in us both willing and doing according to his good pleasure (Phil. 2:13) merely because the commands of righteousness resound outwardly in our senses. Rather, he does so because he gives increase inwardly (1 Cor. 3:7), pouring out love in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5).

### CHAPTER XXVI

### 43. A question concerning the Apostle’s statement about the Gentiles who are said naturally to do the things of the law and to have the law written in their hearts

We must examine how the Apostle can say: “For when Gentiles, who do not have the law, naturally do the things of the law, these, although they do not have the law, are a law for themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts” (Rom. 2:14–15). Otherwise it might seem that there is no certain distinction belonging to the New Testament, since the Lord promised that he would write his laws in the hearts of his people, [Col. 0227] while the Gentiles possess this naturally.

This question, which has arisen as no small difficulty, must therefore be investigated. Someone might say: If God distinguishes the New Testament from the Old by this—that in the Old he wrote his law on tablets, whereas in the New he wrote it in hearts—then how are the believers of the New Testament distinguished from the Gentiles who have the work of the law written in their hearts and naturally do the things of the law? Would they not already be superior to that old people, which received the law on tablets, and prior to the new people, to whom through the New Testament what nature has already provided for these is granted?

### 44.

Or perhaps the Apostle was speaking of those Gentiles who have the law written in their hearts and who belong to the New Testament? To determine this, we must consider the context from which his statement arose.

First, commending the Gospel, he says: “For it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and to the Greek. For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as it is written: ‘But the righteous shall live by faith.’”

Then he speaks about those ungodly people for whom, because of their pride, even knowledge of God was of no benefit, since they did not glorify him as God or give thanks. From there he turns to those who judge and do such things as they condemn—clearly with reference to the Jews, who gloried in God’s law, although he does not yet name them explicitly. Therefore he says:[^c0022-9]

“Wrath and indignation, tribulation and anguish upon every soul of a human being who works evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek; but glory and honor and peace to everyone who works good, to the Jew first and also to the Greek. For there is no partiality with God. For whoever sinned without the law will also perish without the law; and whoever sinned under the law will be judged by the law. For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified.”

He then adds the passage under discussion and says: “When Gentiles who do not have the law naturally do the things of the law,” and the rest that I have already quoted above.

Accordingly, he does not seem here to signify by the name “Gentiles” any others than those whom he had signified above by the name “Greek,” when he said, “to the Jew first and also to the Greek.”

Moreover, if the Gospel is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, “to the Jew first and also to the Greek”; and if wrath, indignation, tribulation, and anguish fall upon every human soul that works evil, “upon the Jew first and also upon the Greek,” while glory, honor, and peace belong to everyone who works good, “to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Rom. 1:16; 2:14)—and if this Greek is signified by the name “Gentiles” as those who naturally do the things of the law and have the work of the law written in their hearts—then surely those Gentiles whose law is written in their hearts belong to the Gospel, since for those who believe, it is the power of God for salvation.

But to what Gentiles who do good would he promise glory, honor, and peace if they were outside the grace of the Gospel? Since there is no partiality with God, and it is not the hearers of the law but the doers who are justified, whether a Jew or a Greek—that is, anyone from the Gentiles—believes, he will equally have salvation in the Gospel.

“For there is no distinction,” as he says later: “For all have sinned [Col. 0228] and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace” (Rom. 3:23–24). How, then, could he say that a Greek who does the law is justified without the grace of the Savior?

### 45.

For he would not contradict himself when he says, “The doers of the law will be justified,” as though they were justified by works and not by grace, since he says that a person is “justified freely by faith without works of the law” (ibid. 3:28). By saying “freely,” he means nothing other than that works do not precede justification. For elsewhere he plainly says: “If it is by grace, then it is not from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (ibid. 11:6).

But “the doers of the law will be justified” must be understood in such a way that we know they are not doers of the law in any other manner than by being justified. Justification does not come afterward to those who are already doers; rather, justification precedes their becoming doers.

For what else does “justified” mean than “made righteous”—by him, of course, who justifies the ungodly (ibid. 4:5), so that an ungodly person becomes righteous?

If we were to speak in such a way as to say, “Human beings will be liberated,” this would certainly be understood as liberation being added to those who were already human beings. But if we said, “Human beings will be created,” it would not be understood that those who already existed as human beings were being created; rather, that through the very act of creation they would become human beings.

Thus, if it had been said, “The doers of the law will be honored,” we would not correctly understand it except as honor being added to those who were already doers of the law. But since it is said, “The doers of the law will be justified,” what else has been said than “the righteous will be justified”? For the doers of the law are certainly righteous.

Accordingly, this is equivalent to saying, “The doers of the law will be created”—not those who already were, but so that they may become doers. In this way even the Jews who heard the law would understand that they needed the grace of the one who justifies them in order to be able to become doers.[^c0022-10]

Or certainly “they will be justified” is said as though it meant “they will be regarded as righteous” or “they will be counted as righteous,” just as it was said of a certain man, “But wishing to justify himself” (Luke 10:29)—that is, wishing to be regarded and counted as righteous.

This is why we say one thing when we say, “God sanctifies his saints,” and another when we say, “Hallowed be your name” (Matt. 6:9). The former is said because he himself makes holy those who were not holy; the latter because what is always holy in him should also be regarded as holy by human beings—that is, reverently feared.[^c0022-11]

### 46.

If, therefore, in mentioning Gentiles who naturally do the things of the law and have the work of the law written in their hearts, he intended those who believe in Christ—because they do not come to faith as the Jews do, with the law previously set before them—there is no reason for us to try to distinguish them from those to whom the Lord, promising the New Testament through the Prophet, said that he would write his laws in their hearts.

For they too, through the grafting which he says was performed from a wild olive into the cultivated olive, belong to that same olive—that is, to that same people of God (Rom. 11:24). Rather, this apostolic testimony agrees with the prophetic one: belonging to the New Testament means having the law [Col. 0229] of God written not on tablets but in hearts. That is, it means embracing the righteousness of the law in the innermost affection, where faith works through love (Gal. 5:6).

For God justifies the Gentiles by faith. Scripture, foreseeing this, announced it beforehand to Abraham, saying: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gal. 3:8). Through this grace of the promise, the wild olive was grafted into the olive, and the believing Gentiles became children of Abraham in the seed of Abraham, which is Christ (ibid. 3:8, 16), following the faith of Abraham, who, without having received the law on tablets and before possessing circumcision itself, “believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness” (Gen. 15:6; Rom. 4:3).

Thus, what the Apostle said about such Gentiles—that they have the work of the law written in their hearts (Rom. 2:15)—is like what he says to the Corinthians: “not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts” (2 Cor. 3:3).

In this way they become members of the house of Israel, when their uncircumcision is counted as circumcision, because they demonstrate the righteousness of the law not by cutting the flesh but by guarding it through the love of the heart. For “if the uncircumcision keeps the righteous requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision?” he says (Rom. 2:26).

And therefore, in the house of the true Israel, in which there is no deceit (John 1:47), they are participants in the New Testament, because God gives his laws in their minds and writes them in their hearts with his finger, the Holy Spirit, by whom love is poured out there (Rom. 5:5), and love is the fullness of the law (ibid. 13:10).

### CHAPTER XXVII

### 47. To fulfill the law naturally means the same as to fulfill it according to nature restored by grace

Nor should it trouble us that he said they naturally do the things of the law, and did not say “by the Spirit of God,” “by faith,” or “by grace.” For this is what the Spirit of grace accomplishes: he restores in us the image of God, in which we were naturally made.

The defect is contrary to nature, and grace certainly heals it. For this reason it is said to God: “Have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40:5).

Accordingly, human beings naturally do the things of the law; those who do not do them fail to do so because of their own defect.[^c0022-12] Through this defect the law of God was erased from their hearts. Consequently, when the defect has been healed and the law is written there, they naturally do the things of the law—not because grace has been denied through nature, but rather because nature has been restored through grace.

For through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and thus death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned (Rom. 5:12). And therefore, because there is no distinction, all lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace.

Through this grace righteousness is written in the inner person, having been erased by sin. And this mercy is extended over the human race through Christ Jesus our Lord. “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5).

### 48.

But if those who naturally do the things of the law are not yet to be counted among those whom the grace of Christ justifies, but rather among those of whom we read, know, or hear that even though they are ungodly and do not truly and righteously worship the true God, they nevertheless perform certain deeds in their ungodly lives which, [Col. 0230] according to the rule of righteousness, we cannot merely criticize, but which we rightly and deservedly praise—although, if the end for which they are done is examined,[^c0022-13] scarcely any are found that deserve the praise or defense due to righteousness—

### CHAPTER XXVIII

### The image of God not entirely erased in unbelievers. Venial sins

Nevertheless, since the image of God in the human soul has not been so thoroughly worn away by the stain of earthly affections that no final traces, as it were, of its features remain—traces from which it may rightly be said that even in the impiety of their lives people do or understand some things belonging to the law—if this is what is meant by the statement that Gentiles who do not have the law, that is, the law of God, naturally do the things of the law, and that such people are a law for themselves and have the work of the law written in their hearts—that is, what was impressed there through the image of God when they were created has not been entirely erased—even so, the distinction by which the New Testament differs from the Old will not be obscured. Through the New Testament the law of God is written in the hearts of the faithful, whereas through the Old it was written on tablets.

For what is written there through renewal is what was not entirely erased through age. Just as the image of God itself is renewed in the mind of believers through the New Testament, although impiety had not completely destroyed it—for what remained was precisely what prevents the human soul from being anything other than rational—so too the law of God, which injustice had not entirely erased, is certainly written anew there through grace.

Nor could the law written on tablets produce this writing—which is justification—in the Jews; it could produce only transgression. They too were human beings, and they possessed that power of nature by which the rational soul both perceives and does something lawful.[^c0022-14] But piety, which transfers a person into another life, blessed and eternal, possesses the immaculate law that converts souls (Ps. 19:8), so that they may be renewed from that light and so that these words may be fulfilled in them: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Ps. 4:7).

Having turned away from it, they deserved to grow old and decay.[^c0022-15] But they cannot be renewed except by Christian grace, that is, except through the intercession of the Mediator. “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all.”

If those about whom we are speaking are estranged from his grace—those who, in the manner sufficiently discussed above, naturally do the things of the law—what benefit will their excusing thoughts provide them on the day when God judges the hidden things of human beings (Rom. 2:14–16), except perhaps that they may be punished less severely?

For just as certain venial sins, without which this life is not lived, do not prevent the righteous from attaining eternal life, so some good works, without which the life of even the worst person is scarcely found, provide no benefit toward eternal salvation to the ungodly.

Nevertheless, just as the saints differ in glory in the kingdom of God as one star differs from another (1 Cor. 15:41), so in the condemnation of eternal punishment it will be more tolerable for Sodom than for another city (Luke 10:12), and some will be “sons of Gehenna” twice as much as others (Matt. 23:15). Thus it will not be irrelevant to God’s judgment [Col. 0231] that, within damnable impiety itself, one person has sinned more or less than another.

### 49.

What, then, did the Apostle intend to establish by this? Having restrained the Jews’ boasting, he said, “It is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified.” He immediately added his statement concerning those who do not have the law but naturally do the things of the law.

If by these he did not mean those who belong to the grace of the Mediator, but rather those who, although they do not worship the true God with genuine piety, nevertheless possess certain good works in an ungodly life, then perhaps he believed that this very point should establish what he had said above: that there is no partiality with God, and what he said afterward, that God is not the God of the Jews only but also of the Gentiles (Rom. 3:29).

For however small the works of the law naturally implanted in them may be, they would not be found in those who had not received the law except from the remnants of the image of God. God does not despise this image when they believe in him with whom there is no partiality.

But whichever of these interpretations is accepted, it remains certain that God’s grace was promised to the New Testament also through the Prophet, and that this same grace was defined in it as the writing of God’s laws in human hearts, so that they might reach that knowledge of God where no one teaches his fellow citizen or brother, saying, “Know God,” because all shall know him, from the least to the greatest of them.

This is the gift of the Holy Spirit, through whom love is poured out in our hearts—a love not of just any kind, but the love of God proceeding from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith (1 Tim. 1:5). By this love the righteous person, living in this pilgrimage, is brought after the mirror and the enigma to the vision itself, and whatever was partial is brought to completion, so that he may know face to face, even as he has been known (1 Cor. 13:12).[^c0022-16]

“For he asked one thing of the Lord,” and this he seeks: “that he may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of his life,” in order “to contemplate the delight of the Lord” (Ps. 27:4).

### CHAPTER XXIX

### 50. Righteousness is a gift from God

Therefore, let no one boast of what he seems to possess, as though he had not received it (1 Cor. 4:7), or think that he received it because the letter appeared outwardly, either to be read or to sound in the ears.

“For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Gal. 2:21). But if he did not die for nothing, “he ascended on high, led captivity captive, and gave gifts to human beings” (Ps. 68:19; Eph. 4:8). Whoever possesses anything possesses it from him.

But whoever denies that he possesses it from him either does not possess it, or what he possesses will be taken away from him (Luke 8:18; 19:26).

For there is one God who justifies circumcision from faith and uncircumcision through faith (Rom. 3:30). This was not said to indicate some difference, as though “from faith” meant one thing and “through faith” another, but to vary the expression.

Elsewhere, speaking about the Gentiles—that is, about the uncircumcision—he says: “Foreseeing,” says Scripture, “that God justifies the Gentiles from faith” (Gal. 3:8). Likewise, when he was speaking about circumcision, to which he himself belonged, he says: “We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from the Gentiles; yet knowing that a human being is not justified [Col. 0232] from works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we too have believed in Christ Jesus” (Gal. 2:15–16).

Here he says that the uncircumcision is justified from faith and circumcision through faith, provided that circumcision holds the righteousness of faith.[^c0022-17]

Thus the Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, attained righteousness—the righteousness that is from faith—by obtaining it from God, not by presuming upon themselves. But Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness. Why? “Because it was not from faith, but as though from works” (Rom. 9:30–31)—that is, as though they themselves were producing it, rather than believing that God was producing it in them.

“For it is God who works in us both willing and doing according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13). And so they “stumbled over the stone of stumbling” (Rom. 9:32).

For what he meant by “not from faith, but as though from works,” he explained most openly when he said: “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they were not subject to the righteousness of God. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (ibid. 10:3–4).

Do we still doubt what the works of the law are, by which a person is not justified if he believes them to be his own, without the help and gift of God that comes through faith in Jesus Christ? Do we suspect that they are circumcision and similar practices, because certain things of this kind are also read elsewhere concerning these sacraments?

But here they certainly did not wish to establish circumcision as their own righteousness, since God himself established it by commanding it. Nor can this be understood of those works concerning which the Lord says to them: “You reject the commandment of God in order to establish your traditions” (Matt. 15:3; Mark 7:9). For he says, “Israel, pursuing the law of righteousness, did not attain the law of righteousness”; he did not say, “pursuing their traditions,” that is, following after them.

The only distinction, then, is this: they attributed to themselves the commandment “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17), and his other holy and good commandments. Yet, in order that a human being may do them, God works in the human being through faith in Jesus Christ, who is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes.

That is, once a person has been incorporated into him through the Spirit and has become his member, he can work righteousness, because Christ gives inward increase. Of his works he himself also said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

### 51.

For this reason, then, the righteousness of the law is set forth: “Whoever does it shall live by it” (Lev. 18:5). Thus, when each person has recognized his own weakness, he may attain justification, do what is required, and live by it—not through his own powers, nor through the letter of the law itself, which cannot accomplish this, but by obtaining the Justifier through faith. For the work by which the one who does it will live is accomplished only by one who has been justified.

Justification, moreover, is obtained through faith. Concerning this it is written: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will ascend into heaven?’”—that is, to bring Christ down—“or, ‘Who will descend into the abyss?’”—that is, to bring Christ back from the dead. But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart”—that is, it says, “the word of faith which we preach: for if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Rom. 10:5–9). One is righteous to the extent that one is saved.

Through this faith we believe that God will also raise us from the dead: for the present, in spirit, so that “in the newness of his grace we may live temperately, righteously, and devoutly in this age” (Tit. 2:12); afterward, also in our flesh, which will rise to immortality. This is the achievement of the spirit, which precedes the flesh in its resurrection appropriate to it—that is, in justification. [Note: [Col. 0233] Five manuscripts read: “which obtains for it the achievement of the spirit.”]

“For we were buried with Christ through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life” (Rom. 6:4). Therefore, by the faith of Jesus Christ we obtain salvation, both insofar as it is begun for us in reality and insofar as its completion is awaited in hope. “For everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord will be saved” (Joel 2:32; Rom. 10:13).

“How great is the abundance of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you, but perfected for those who hope in you!” says the Psalmist (Ps. 30:20). Through the law we fear God; through faith we hope in God. But grace is hidden from those who fear punishment. When the soul struggles under this fear, whenever it has not conquered evil desire and that fear has not withdrawn like a strict guardian, let it flee through faith to the mercy of God, so that he may give what he commands and, through the sweetness of grace inspired by the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0233] Nearly all manuscripts read, “of inspired grace.”], make what he commands more delightful than what hinders it.

Thus the great abundance of his sweetness—that is, the law of faith, his love written and poured out in hearts—is perfected in those who hope in him [Note: [Col. 0233] Several manuscripts read, “in her.”], so that the healed soul may do good not from fear of punishment but from love of righteousness.

## CHAPTER XXX

### 52. Whether free will is nullified by grace

Do we then nullify free will through grace? Certainly not; rather, we establish free will. For just as the law is not nullified but established through faith (Rom. 3:31), so free will is not nullified but established through grace.

The law is not fulfilled except through free will [Note: [Col. 0233] Several manuscripts read, “without free will.”]. Through the law comes knowledge of sin; through faith, the obtaining of grace against sin; through grace, the healing of the soul from the defect of sin [Note: [Col. 0233] Thus the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus and most manuscripts. Lovaniensis reads, “the healing of the soul through the abolition of sin.”]; through the soul’s healing, freedom of will; through free will, love of righteousness; and through love of righteousness, the performance of the law.

Accordingly, just as the law is not nullified but established through faith, because faith obtains the grace by which the law may be fulfilled, so free will is not nullified through grace but established, because grace heals the will by which righteousness may freely be loved.

All these things, which I have linked together as though in a chain, have their own expressions in the holy Scriptures. The law says: “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17). Faith says: “Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Ps. 41:5). Grace says: “Behold, you have been made well; now do not sin anymore, lest something worse happen to you” (John 5:14). Healing says: “Lord my God, I cried out to you, and you healed me” (Ps. 30:3). Free will says: “I will sacrifice to you freely” (Ps. 54:8). Love of righteousness says: “The wicked have told me of their delights [Note: [Col. 0234] The Lovaniensis edition adds here, “their own.”], but not as does your law, Lord” (Ps. 119:85).

Why, then, do wretched human beings dare to boast of free will before they have been freed, or of their own powers if they have already been freed? They do not attend to the fact that the very expression “free will” plainly signifies freedom. “Where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17).

If they are slaves of sin, why do they boast of free will? “For by whatever anyone is overcome, by this he is enslaved” (2 Pet. 2:19). But if they have been freed, why do they boast as though it were their own work, and glory as though they had not received it? Are they free in such a way that they do not wish to have as Lord even the one who says to them, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), and, “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36)?

## CHAPTER XXXI

### 53. Whether faith is in our power

Someone will ask whether faith itself—in which the beginning of the connection I have mentioned concerning salvation, or toward salvation, seems to lie—is established within our power. We shall see this more easily if we first examine somewhat more carefully what power is.

There are two things, namely, willing and being able. Hence neither does the one who wills immediately have the ability, nor does the one who is able immediately will; for just as we sometimes will what we cannot do, so we sometimes can do what we do not will. If the words themselves are carefully examined, it becomes sufficiently clear that the word “will” has given rise to “will” or “volition,” while “ability” has given rise to “power” [Note: [Col. 0234] The manuscripts read, “it is sufficiently clear from the words themselves”; some of them, “it is sufficiently clear, and from the words themselves,” etc.]. Therefore, just as the one who wills has volition, so the one who can has power.

But for something to be done by power, the will must be present. No one is ordinarily said to have done something by his power if he did it unwillingly [Note: [Col. 0234] Two Vatican and three Gallican manuscripts read, “to have done it by his will.” The editors of a later Lovaniensis edition of 1647 preferred this reading.]. Yet, if we consider the matter more subtly, even what someone is compelled to do unwillingly, if he does it, he does it willingly. But because he would prefer something else, he is said to do it unwillingly—that is, not wanting to do it. He is compelled by some evil to do what he would willingly avoid or remove from himself.

For if his will were so strong that he preferred not to do this rather than suffer that, he would certainly resist the one compelling him and would not do it. Accordingly, if he does it, then, although not with a full and free will, nevertheless he does it only by will. Since the result follows that will, we cannot say that the one acting lacked the power. If, yielding to the one compelling him, he wanted to do it but could not, we would say that he possessed a will, albeit an extorted one, but lacked the power. When, however, he did not do it because he did not want to, power was present, but the will was lacking so long as, by resisting the one compelling him, he did not act.

This is why even those who compel or persuade commonly say: “What you have the power to do, why do you not do, so that you may be free of this evil?” And those who altogether cannot do what they are compelled to do because they are believed able commonly reply in excuse: “I would do it if it were in my power.”

What more, then, are we seeking, since we call that “in one’s power” where the capacity to act accompanies the will [Note: [Col. 0235] Two Vatican manuscripts omit “to act.”]? Thus each person is said to have something in his power if, when he wills, he does it, and, when he does not will, he does not do it.

### 54. Whether faith is in our power

Now attend to the matter we have proposed for examination: whether faith is in our power. We are speaking here of the faith we exercise when we believe something, not of the faithfulness we give when we make a promise; for that too is called faith.

But we use the expressions differently. We say, “He did not have faith in me,” and differently, “He did not keep faith with me.” The first means, “He did not believe what I said”; the second, “He did not do what he said.”

According to the faith by which we believe, we are faithful to God; according to the faithfulness by which what is promised is done [Note: [Col. 0235] Lovaniensis reads, “by which he promises.”], God himself is also faithful to us. For the Apostle says: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able” (1 Cor. 10:13).

It is therefore the faith by which we believe God, or believe in God, that we are asking about: whether it is in our power. For concerning this it is written: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness”; and, “To the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness” (Gen. 15:6; Rom. 4:3, 5).

Consider now whether someone believes if he does not wish to, or does not believe if he does wish to. If this is absurd—for what is believing except consenting that what is said is true? And consent is certainly an act of one who wills—then faith is in our power.

But, as the Apostle says, “There is no power except from God” (Rom. 13:1). What reason, then, is there why we should not also be told concerning this: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7). For God also gave us the capacity to believe [Note: [Col. 0235] Lovaniensis reads, “For God also gave us this, that we should believe.” “This” is absent from the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, as well as from five Vatican manuscripts, two Belgian manuscripts, and nearly all the Gallican manuscripts.].

Nowhere, however, do we read in the holy Scriptures, “There is no will except from God.” And rightly is this not written, because it is not true. Otherwise God would also be the author—God forbid—of sins, if there were no will except from him; for an evil will is already sin by itself, even if the deed is absent, that is, even if it does not have the power to carry itself out.

Furthermore, when an evil will receives the power to fulfill what it intends [Note: [Col. 0235] Thus many manuscripts. The printed editions read, “what is intended.”], this proceeds from God’s judgment, with whom there is no injustice (Rom. 9:14). He punishes in this way as well, and not unjustly because he does so secretly. The unjust person does not know that he is being punished until he has felt an evident punishment [Note: [Col. 0235] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “judgment”], unwillingly experiencing how great is the evil he willingly committed.

This is what the Apostle says concerning certain people: “God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to do what is improper” (Rom. 1:24). The Lord also said to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19:11).

But when power is given, necessity is not thereby imposed. Thus, when David received the power to kill Saul, he preferred to spare him rather than strike him (1 Sam. 24 and 26). From this we understand that the wicked receive power for the condemnation of their evil will, while the good receive it for the testing of their good will.

## CHAPTER XXXII

### 55. What faith is to be praised

Since faith is in our power, because each person believes when he wills, and when he believes, he believes willingly, we must next ask—or rather recall—which faith the Apostle commends with such intense struggle.

For it is not good to believe just anything. What, then, is the meaning of: “Brothers, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4:1) [Note: [Col. 0236] Three Vatican manuscripts read, “whether it is from God.”]?

Nor should the statement in the praises of love, “It believes all things” (1 Cor. 13:7), be understood in such a way that we detract from anyone’s love if he does not immediately believe whatever he has heard. Indeed, does not that same love advise us not readily to believe anything evil about a brother, and, when something of that sort is said, judge that it concerns itself above all with not believing it [Note: [Col. 0236] The printed editions read, “indicate that it concerns itself.”]?

Finally, love itself, which believes all things, does not believe every spirit. Accordingly, it believes all things—but in God; for it is not said, “It believes everyone.” No one, therefore, doubts that the Apostle commends the faith by which God is believed.

### 56. Further distinctions concerning faith

But another distinction must still be made [Note: [Col. 0236] The printed editions read, “but there is still something to be distinguished.” The manuscripts omit “to be.”]. Those who are under the law attempt to accomplish their righteousness through fear of punishment. They therefore do not accomplish the righteousness of God, because love accomplishes it. Love takes pleasure only in what is permitted; fear does not. Fear is compelled to have in action what is permitted, while in the will it has something else, and, if it could, would prefer that what is not permitted were permitted.

They too, therefore, believe God; for if they did not believe at all, they would certainly not fear the punishment of the law. But this is not the faith commended by the Apostle, who says: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again into fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:15).

That fear, then, is servile. Consequently, although the Lord is believed in it, righteousness is not loved; condemnation is feared. But the children cry, “Abba, Father.” One of these two words comes from circumcision and the other from the foreskin—from the Jews first and from the Greeks [that is, Gentiles], because there is one God “who justifies circumcision by faith and the foreskin through faith” (Rom. 3:30).

When they cry out, they are asking for something. And what do they ask for except what they hunger and thirst for? And what is this except what was said concerning them: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6)?

Let those who are under the law therefore pass over to this, so that from slaves they may become sons. Yet not in such a way that they cease to be servants, but so that, as sons, they may serve their Lord and Father freely, because they have received this as well. For the Only-Begotten gave power to those who believe in his name to become children of God (John 1:12). He also urged them to ask, seek, and knock, so that they might receive, find, and have the door opened to them. He added a rebuke, saying: “If you, though evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?” (Matt. 7:7–11).

When, therefore, the law inflamed sin, the sting of death (1 Cor. 15:56), so that, taking occasion, sin through the commandment might produce every form of covetous desire [Col. 0237] (Rom. 7:8), from whom is self-control to be requested except from the one who knows how to give good gifts to his children? Or does the foolish person not know that no one can be continent unless God grants it (Wis. 8:21)? To know this, he himself needs wisdom.

Why, then, does he not hear the Spirit of his Father speaking through the apostle of Christ—or Christ himself, speaking in his Gospel—when he says, “Ask, and you will receive” (Matt. 7:7)? He also speaks in his apostle, saying: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach, and it will be given to him; but let him ask in faith, without doubting” (Jas. 1:5–6).

This is the faith by which “the righteous lives” (Rom. 1:17). This is the faith by which one believes in him who justifies the ungodly (Rom. 4:5). This is the faith through which boasting is excluded (Rom. 3:27)—whether so that the boasting by which we inflate ourselves may depart, or so that the boasting by which we glory in the Lord may prevail.

This is the faith by which the abundance of the Spirit is obtained, concerning which it is said: “For through the Spirit, by faith, we await the hope of righteousness” (Gal. 5:5). Here one may still ask whether he meant “the hope of righteousness” by which righteousness hopes [Note: [Col. 0237] The manuscripts read, “which righteousness hopes for.”], or the hope by which righteousness itself is hoped for.

For the righteous person, living by faith, certainly hopes for eternal life. Likewise, faith that hungers and thirsts for righteousness advances in it through the renewal of the inner person from day to day (2 Cor. 4:16), and hopes to be satisfied in it in eternal life, where what is said of God in the Psalm will take place: “He satisfies your desire with good things” (Ps. 103:5).

This is the faith by which those to whom it is said are saved: “You have been saved by grace through faith; and this is not from yourselves, but is the gift of God; not from works, lest anyone should boast. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared so that we might walk in them” (Eph. 2:8–10).

Finally, this is the faith that works through love (Gal. 5:6), not through fear—not by fearing punishment, but by loving righteousness. From where, then, does this love—that is, charity, through which faith works—come, except from where faith itself obtained it? For it would not be in us, however great it may be in us, unless it were poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5).

It is called the love of God poured into our hearts not because it is the love with which he himself loves us, but because it makes us lovers of him; just as the righteousness of God is that by which we are made righteous through his gift (Rom. 3:24), and the salvation of the Lord is that by which he makes us safe (Ps. 3:9), and the faith of Jesus Christ is that by which he makes us faithful (Gal. 2:16).

This is the righteousness of God, which he not only teaches through the commandment of the law but also gives through the gift of the Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### 57. Whence comes the will to believe

It follows that we should inquire briefly whether that will by which we believe is itself also a gift of God, or whether it is employed from the free will naturally implanted in us.

If we say that it is not a gift of God, we must fear that we may think we have found something to answer the Apostle when he rebukes us and says: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7). We could then reply: “Behold, we have the will to believe, which we did not receive; behold, here is what we boast of having not received.”

But if we say that a will of this kind is itself nothing other than a gift of God, we must again fear that unbelievers and ungodly people may seem, not without reason, to excuse themselves as though justly, saying that they did not believe because God did not wish to give them this will.

The statement, “For it is God who works in us both to will and to work, for good will” (Phil. 2:13), already concerns grace [Note: [Col. 0238] Lovaniensis reads, “it is grace.” Other printed editions read, “it concerns grace.” The manuscripts likewise have “it concerns grace”; but in them, consistently, “by which faith” is read as “which faith.”]. Faith obtains this grace so that the good works of human beings may be possible—works that faith performs through love, which is poured into the heart through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

If we believe in order to obtain this grace, and certainly believe willingly, the question is where this will comes from. If it comes from nature, why does it not belong to everyone, since the same God is the Creator of all? If it is a gift of God, why is this gift not given to everyone, since he wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4)?

### 58. Free will as an intermediate power

Let us first say the following and see whether it adequately answers this question: free will, naturally granted by the Creator to the rational soul, is an intermediate power, which can either be directed toward faith or inclined toward unbelief.
