Therefore, a person cannot be said to possess this will by which he believes God without having received it [Note: [Col. 0238] Nearly the Lovaniensis edition alone reads, “and therefore not”;], since, when called by God, it rises from free will, which he received naturally when he was created.

God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth; yet not in such a way that he takes away from them free will, by using which either well or badly they are most justly judged.

When this happens, unbelievers act against the will of God when they do not believe his Gospel. Yet they do not thereby overcome that will; rather, they defraud themselves of a great and supreme good and entangle themselves in punitive evils. They will experience in punishments the power of the one whose mercy in gifts they despised.

Thus the will of God is always unconquered. It would be conquered if it did not find something to do with those who despise it, or if they could in any way escape what he has decreed concerning such people.

For example, suppose he says: “I want all these people, my servants, to work in the vineyard and, after their labor, to rest and feast, while whoever among them does not wish this shall always grind in the mill.” Anyone who despises this would seem to act against the will of his Lord. But he would overcome it only if, while also despising the mill, he escaped it—and under God’s power this is impossible.

Hence it is written: “God spoke once,” that is, immutably—although the statement may also be understood of the one Word. Then, adding what he spoke immutably, he says: “These two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and to you, Lord, mercy, for you will repay each person according to his works” (Ps. 62:12–13).

That person, therefore, who has despised God’s mercy by refusing to believe will be guilty for condemnation under his power [Col. 0239]. But whoever believes and entrusts himself to God to be absolved from all sins, healed from all vices, and kindled and enlightened by his warmth and light [Note: [Col. 0239] We have restored this passage from two Vatican manuscripts, the Sorbonicus, and several other Gallican manuscripts. In earlier editions it was corruptly read: “Whoever will have believed in him who did not despise being absolved from all sins, healed from all vices, and kindled and enlightened by his warmth and light.”], will have good works from his grace. Through these he will also be redeemed in the body from the corruption of death, crowned, and satisfied with good things—not temporal but eternal—beyond what we ask or understand (Eph. 3:20).

### 59. The order set forth in the Psalm

The Psalm maintained this order where it says: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his rewards: he who is gracious to all your iniquities, who heals all your diseases, who redeems your life from corruption [Note: [Col. 0239] Most manuscripts read, “who will redeem.”], who crowns you with compassion and mercy, who satisfies your desire with good things” (Ps. 103:2–5).

And lest the deformity of this old condition—that is, of mortality—despair of such great blessings, it says: “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s.” It is as though he were saying: “What you have heard belongs to the new person and to the New Testament.”

Recall these same things with me for a little while, I ask you, and contemplate with delight the praise of mercy—that is, the praise of God’s grace. “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and do not forget all his rewards.” It does not say, “tributions,” but “his recompenses,” because he repays good for evil [Note: [Col. 0239] The manuscripts read, “not attributions.” From these the printed editions are corrected in the next phrase, where they had read “who recompenses” instead of “because he recompenses.”].

“He who is gracious to all your iniquities”: this takes place in the sacrament of baptism.

“He who heals all your diseases”: this takes place in the present life of the faithful person, while the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, so that we do not do what we want (Gal. 5:17); while another law in the members fights against the law of the mind; while willing is present but accomplishing the good is not [Note: [Col. 0239] The printed editions read, “but we do not find the accomplishment of the good.” “We find” is absent from the manuscripts.] (Rom. 7:23, 18).

These are the diseases of the old condition. If we advance with persevering purpose, they are healed from day to day as the new condition grows, through faith that works through love.

“He who redeems your life from corruption”: this takes place in the final resurrection of the dead.

“He who crowns you with compassion and mercy” (Ps. 103:2–4): this takes place in the judgment, where, when the righteous King has sat upon his throne to repay each person according to his works, who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will boast that he is clean from sin? (Prov. 20:8–9; Matt. 16:27).

For this reason it was necessary there to mention the compassion and mercy of the Lord, where debts could already seem to be demanded and merits repaid in such a way that there would be no place for mercy. He therefore crowns with compassion and mercy, but even so according to works.

For the one to whom it is said, “I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25:35), will be separated to the right: “For judgment is without mercy for the one who has not shown mercy” (Jas. 2:13); but “blessed are the merciful, for God will show mercy to them” (Matt. 5:7).

And when those on the left have gone into eternal fire, while the righteous have gone into eternal life (Matt. 25:46), this is because, as he says, “this is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). Through that knowledge, vision, and contemplation, the soul’s desire will be satisfied with good things (Ps. 103:5).

This alone is sufficient for it; beyond this it has nothing to desire, long for, or seek. For one who burned with desire for this satisfaction said to the Lord Christ: “Show us the Father, and it is enough for us.” He was answered: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” [Note: [Col. 0240] The printed editions read, “Whoever sees me sees the Father.” The manuscripts consistently read “has seen,” in accordance with the Greek.] (John 14:8–9).

For this is eternal life: “that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” But if the one who has seen the Son has also seen the Father, then certainly the one who sees the Father and the Son also sees the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son. Thus we neither take away free will, nor does our soul fail to bless the Lord, forgetting none of his rewards. Nor does it ignore the righteousness of God and wish to establish its own (Rom. 10:3); rather, it believes in him who justifies the ungodly and lives by faith until it is brought to vision—by faith, namely, which works through love.

This love is poured into our hearts not through the sufficiency of our own will, nor through the letter of the law, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### 60. The will to believe comes from God

If this discussion is sufficient to resolve that question, let it be sufficient. But if the answer is that care must be taken lest anyone think God should be blamed for the sin committed through free will, since, in the statement “What do you have that you did not receive?”, even the will by which we believe is attributed to God’s gift because it arises from free will, which we received when we were created, then let him attend and see that this will is to be attributed to the divine gift not only because it comes from free will, which was naturally created with us, but also because God acts through the persuasive force of things perceived, so that we may will and believe.

He does this either externally, through evangelical exhortations—where even the commandments of the law accomplish something if they remind a person of his weakness so that by believing he may flee to justifying grace—or internally, where no one has power over what enters his mind, but consenting or dissenting belongs to his own will.

When God acts with the rational soul in these ways so that it believes him—for no one can believe just anything by free will [Note: [Col. 0240] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “by any free will.” Amerbach and most manuscripts read, “just anything by free will.” One Vatican manuscript reads, “just any free will.”] if there is no persuasion or calling for it to believe—then God certainly works in the human being even the will to believe, and his mercy always precedes us.

To consent to God’s calling or dissent from it, as I have said, belongs to one’s own will. This fact not only does not weaken the statement, “What do you have that you did not receive?”, but also confirms it. For the soul cannot receive and possess the gifts about which it hears this unless it consents. Accordingly, what it possesses and what it receives belong to God; but receiving and possessing belong, in turn, to the one who receives and possesses.

Now, if someone presses us to investigate that profound question—why one person is persuaded in such a way that he is convinced [Note: [Col. 0241] Several manuscripts read, “why he persuades one in this way,” omitting “that he is convinced.” Others read, “why he persuades one in this way so that he persuades.”] and another is not—two answers alone occur to me for the present, and I am pleased to give them: “O the depth of riches!” (Rom. 11:33); and, “Is there injustice with God?” (Rom. 9:14).

If this answer displeases anyone, let him seek out people more learned—but let him beware lest he find people more presumptuous [Note: [Col. 0241] Two manuscripts read, “more presumptuous still.”].

## CHAPTER XXXV

### 61. Conclusion of the work

Let us therefore finally conclude this book, whose great length I do not know whether it has accomplished anything—not with you, whose faith I know, but with the minds of those for whose sake you wished me to write. They prefer to defend their own opinion against not merely one statement of ours but—speaking more mildly, and not saying “against the one who spoke in his apostles”—certainly against the vehement, intense, vigilant struggle of so great an apostle Paul [Note: [Col. 0241] Several manuscripts read, “against the apostle Paul,” omitting “so great.”], rather than hear him beseeching them by the mercy of God and saying, through the grace of God given to him, not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sobriety, each according to the measure of faith that God has apportioned (Rom. 12:1, 3).

### 62. What you proposed and what this work has accomplished

But attend to what you proposed to me and to what we have accomplished through this lengthy work of discussion.

You were certainly moved by the statement that it could be possible for a human being to be without sin if his will were not lacking, with divine assistance, although no one has been, is, or will be in this life of such perfect righteousness.

For this is how I put the matter to you in the books I had previously written on the subject:

> “If I am asked,” I said, “whether a human being can be without sin in this life, I shall confess that this is possible through the grace of God and a human being’s free will. I do not doubt that free will itself belongs to the grace of God—that is, to the gifts of God—not merely so that it exists, but also so that it may be good, that is, so that it may be turned toward carrying out the Lord’s commandments. In this way the grace of God not only shows what must be done, but also helps make it possible to do what it has shown” (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 2, §7).

But it seemed absurd to you that something which can happen should have no example. From this arose the question of this book. Accordingly, it was our task to show that something can be possible even though there is no example of it.

At the beginning of this discussion we therefore set forth certain examples from the Gospel and the Law: the passage of a camel through the eye of a needle (Matt. 19:24); the twelve thousand legions of angels who could have fought for Christ if he had wished (Matt. 26:53); and the nations whom God says he could have exterminated at one stroke from before his people (Deut. 31:3; Judg. 2:3). None of these things happened [Col. 0242].

To these may also be added what is read in the Book of Wisdom: how many new punishments God could inflict upon the ungodly at will, with creation serving him (Wis. 16:24)—yet he did not inflict them [Note: [Col. 0242] The manuscripts read “bring forth”; and below, “he brought forth,” instead of “he inflicted.”].

One may also mention the mountain which faith could transfer into the sea (Mark 11:23), although we have neither read nor heard that this was ever done [Note: [Col. 0242] Eusebius’s account, translated by Rufinus, had not yet come into his hands. In book 7, chapter 24 of his *Ecclesiastical History*, Eusebius reports that Gregory, bishop of Neocaesarea in Pontus, performed such a miracle, moving a mountain or rock from its place. Bede also mentions this event in book 3 of his *Commentary on Mark*, chapter 11.].

For whoever says that any of these things is impossible for God—you see how foolish he is and how he speaks against the faith of God’s Scripture. Many other examples of this kind may occur to someone reading or reflecting, whose possibility for God we cannot deny, even though there is no example of them.

### 63. Righteous living is also a work of God

But because it can be said that those are divine works, whereas living righteously belongs to our works, I undertook to show that this too is a divine work. I have perhaps done so at greater length in this book than is sufficient; yet, against the enemies of God’s grace, I seem to have said too little.

Nothing pleases me so much as saying a great deal where his Scripture gives me the strongest support: namely, that “the one who boasts should boast in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17), and that in everything we should give thanks to the Lord our God, having our hearts lifted upward, from whom comes every good gift and every perfect gift (Jas. 1:17).

For if something is not God’s work because it is done through us, or because we act while he gives us the ability, then neither is it God’s work for a mountain to be transferred into the sea, since the Lord said that this could happen through human faith and attributed it to their work, saying: “If you have faith in you like a grain of mustard seed, you will say to this mountain, ‘Be lifted up and cast into the sea,’ and it will happen, and nothing will be impossible for you” (Mark 11:23–24; Luke 17:6).

Certainly he said, “for you,” not “for me” or “for the Father.” Yet a human being does this in no way except through God’s giving and working.

Behold, then, how perfect righteousness is without an example among human beings, and yet is not impossible. It would occur if a will as great as the matter requires were applied. It would be that great if nothing pertaining to righteousness escaped our knowledge, and if these things delighted the soul in such a way that this delight overcame whatever other pleasure or pain interferes with them [Note: [Col. 0242] The printed editions read, “pleasure or pain.” The manuscripts read, “of pleasure or of pain.”].

That this is not so belongs not to impossibility but to the judgment of God. For who does not know that it is not in a human being’s power what he knows, and that it does not follow that what has been recognized as desirable will be desired, unless it delights him as much as it ought to be loved [Note: [Col. 0242] Two Belgian manuscripts read, “as much as it ought to be found delightful.”]? This, however, is the soul’s state of health.

## CHAPTER XXXVI
### 64. When the Commandment of Love Will Be Perfectly Fulfilled. Sins of Ignorance. What Kind of Sinless Righteousness Can Be Posited in This Life. Perfect Righteousness, Although Not Found Here, Is Not Impossible

But perhaps someone may think that nothing is lacking in our knowledge of righteousness, since the Lord, “bringing the word to completion and cutting it short upon the earth” (Isaiah X, 23; Romans IX, 28), said that the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon two commandments. Nor did he leave them unmentioned [Note: [Col. 0243] Several manuscripts read, “nor did he leave it unmentioned.”], but expressed them in the clearest words: “You shall love,” he says, “the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind; and you shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew XXII, 37–40). What could be truer than that, when these commandments are fulfilled, righteousness is altogether fulfilled?

Yet whoever considers this should also consider how often “we all offend” (James III, 2), when we suppose that what we do pleases—or does not displease—God, whom we love; and afterward, having been admonished through his Scripture or by a sure and evident reasoning, when we have learned what does not please him, we ask in repentance that he forgive us. Human life is full of such lessons. But why do we know less of what pleases him, unless because he is also less known to us? “For now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face.” Who, however, would dare to suppose that, when we have arrived at what he says—“that I may know even as I am known” (1 Corinthians XIII, 12)—the love of God among those who contemplate him will be as great as it now is among the faithful, or that this present love is in any way to be compared with that love as though it were close at hand? [Note: [Col. 0243] The printed editions read, “or in that way”; the manuscript reading is better.]

Moreover, if greater knowledge brings greater love, then certainly, to the extent that love is lacking now, to that extent we must believe that righteousness is lacking in its perfection [Note: [Col. 0243] The printed editions read, “so much then will be lacking for its perfection.” The word “then” is absent from the manuscripts.]. For something can be known or believed and yet not loved; but what is neither known nor believed cannot be loved. Now, if by believing the saints were able to attain such great love that the Lord himself testified that there could be no greater in this life—so that they would lay down their lives for the faith or for their brothers (John XV, 13)—then, when we have passed from this pilgrimage, in which we now walk by faith (2 Corinthians V, 7), to the sight that we hope for though we have not yet seen it, and await through patience (Romans VIII, 25), then without doubt love itself will be not merely greater than what we have here, but far greater than what we ask or understand (Ephesians III, 20). Yet even then it cannot be more than love “with all the heart, with all the soul, and with all the mind.” For nothing remains in us that can be added to the whole; if something remains, it is not the whole.

Accordingly, we shall fulfill in that life, when we see face to face, this first commandment of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0243] The printed editions here added “will be”; and below, after “consequent,” they read, “which we shall fulfill in that life.”], by which we are ordered to love God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind, and to which the second commandment concerning the love of our neighbor is consequent. But this commandment is given to us even now so that we may be admonished what we ought to seek by faith, toward which we ought to send our hope in advance, and toward which we ought to stretch ourselves, “forgetting the things that are behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead” (Philippians III). Accordingly, so far as I see it, a person has made great progress in the righteousness that is to be perfected if, while progressing, he has come to know how far he is from the perfection of righteousness.

### 65.

But if one may speak of a certain lesser righteousness suited to this life, in which “the righteous lives by faith” (Romans I, 17), although he is a pilgrim away from the Lord and therefore walks by faith, not yet by sight, it is not unreasonable to say that even to this righteousness belongs the injunction not to sin. For the fact that our love of God cannot yet be as great as the love owed to full and perfect knowledge of him must not already be counted as guilt. It is one thing not yet to attain the whole of charity [Note: [Col. 0244] Several manuscripts read “to carry out” (*exsequi*).]; it is another to follow no desire at all.

Therefore, although a human being loves God far less than he can love him when he beholds him, he ought nevertheless to desire nothing unlawful. Thus, even among things accessible to the bodily senses, the eye can take pleasure in no darkness, although it cannot fix its gaze upon the most brilliant light.

But behold, let us now posit a human soul in this corruptible body which, although it has not yet absorbed and consumed every movement of earthly desire through that surpassingly eminent perfection of love for God, nevertheless, within this lesser righteousness, gives no consent whatever to that desire in performing anything unlawful. For the immortal life the command is: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy VI, 5); for this life: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires” (Romans VI, 12). For that life: “You shall not covet” (Exodus XX, 17); for this: “Do not follow your desires” (Ecclesiasticus XVIII, 30). For that life: to seek nothing more than to remain in that perfection; for this: to possess in one’s conduct what one is doing and to hope for that perfection as one’s reward [Note: [Col. 0244] Five manuscripts read, “what he says.” Perhaps the phrase should be understood as “toward which he strives” or “toward which he progresses.” See below, *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*, no. 31.]. Through that righteousness the righteous person will live without end in the sight that he desired in this life [Note: [Col. 0244] One of the Vatican manuscripts reads, “without faith.”]; through this, the righteous person lives by faith, in which he desires that other life with assured fulfillment.

(Once these points have been established, the sin of a person living by faith will consist in consenting at some time to some unlawful pleasure—not only in committing those dreadful crimes and disgraces, but also in lesser matters: for example, lending an ear to a voice that ought not to be heard, or a tongue to something that ought not to be said; or thinking something in the heart in such a way that one would prefer what unlawfully pleases to be lawful, although one knows by the commandment that it is unlawful. This too is consent to sin, and it would certainly occur unless punishment caused fear [Note: [Col. 0244] We suspect that something is disordered here. For the material enclosed in parentheses does not fit sufficiently with the words that follow; perhaps it should be placed somewhat earlier, namely before “But behold, let us now posit.”].)

Do such righteous people living by faith not need to say [Note: [Col. 0244] The Cygirannus manuscript alone omits “not”; and below, in place of “and prove false,” it reads, “or prove false.” In a smaller Paris polemical edition of 1644, the negative particle was likewise omitted, and “lest they prove false” was afterward substituted. We have changed nothing here except the punctuation.], “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew VI, 12)? Do they thereby prove false what is written, “In your sight no living person shall be justified” (Psalm CXLII, 2)? Or this: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I, 8)? Or this: “There is no one who will not sin” (3 Kings VIII, 46)? Or this: “There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Ecclesiasticus VII, 21)? (Neither of these two testimonies speaks of the past—that is, “he has sinned”—but of the future: “he will sin.”) And what of the other passages that Holy Scripture recalls in the same sense?

But since these statements cannot be false, I see that the consequence must be that, however great or of whatever kind the righteousness we can define in this life may be, no human being exists in it who has absolutely no sin. Every person must give in order to receive, forgive in order to be forgiven (Luke VI, 38, 37); and, if he possesses any righteousness, he must not presume that it comes from himself, but from the grace of God who justifies. Yet he must still hunger and thirst for righteousness from him (Matthew V, 6), who is the living bread (John VI, 51) and with whom is the fountain of life (Psalm XXXV, 10). He works justification in his saints as they labor amid the trials of this life, while nevertheless there remains something that he may generously add to those who ask and mercifully forgive those who confess.

### 66.

But let these people, if they can, find someone living under the burden of this corruption to whom God has nothing left to forgive—unless, that is, they admit that such a person was assisted not only by the instruction of the law that was given [Note: [Col. 0245] Some manuscripts read, “given” in the masculine or neuter form. Most others read the feminine form, agreeing with “law.”], but also by the Spirit of grace infused into him, in which case they will incur not the charge of some particular sin, but that of impiety itself.

Certainly, if they properly understand those divine testimonies, they cannot find such a person at all. Nevertheless, it must in no way be said that God lacks the power by which the human will might be so assisted that not only this righteousness which comes from faith (Romans X, 6) might be perfected in every respect in a human being now, but also that righteousness according to which one will afterward live eternally in the very contemplation of God. For suppose that God should now wish to clothe someone in this corruptible body with incorruption (1 Corinthians XV, 53), and command him to live here among human beings destined to die, yet himself not to die at all; suppose that, with all oldness utterly consumed, no law in his members should resist the law of his mind (Romans VII, 23), and that he should know God, present everywhere, as the saints will afterward know him. What madman would dare to affirm that God could not do this?

But people ask why he does not do it; and those who ask do not consider that they themselves are human beings. I know that, just as impossibility is not found in God, neither is iniquity (Romans IX, 14). I know that “he resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James IV, 6). I know that the one to whom, lest he be exalted, there was given a thorn in the flesh—an angel of Satan to buffet him—was told, when he had entreated once, twice, and a third time: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians XII, 7–9).

There is therefore something hidden and profound in the judgments of God, so that even the whole mouth of the righteous may be closed in praise of themselves and opened only in praise of God. But who can search out this something, who investigate it, who know it? “How unsearchable are his judgments, and how inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, that he should be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things; to him be glory forever and ever. Amen” (Romans XI, 33–36).

## [ON NATURE AND GRACE]

[Col. 0245]

### NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING WORK

Augustine assigned the book *On Nature and Grace* the final place among several writings of the year 415 in Letter 169 to Evodius, sent during that same year, 415: “I have also written,” he says, “a fairly large book against the heresy of Pelagius, at the urging of certain brothers to whom he had persuaded a most pernicious opinion against the grace of Christ.”

This same book had already been begun, but was not yet finished, when Orosius sailed from Africa to Palestine, in the spring of that very year, 415. For shortly after arriving there, at the assembly in Jerusalem, at which Pelagius himself was present, Orosius expressly affirmed that he was responding fully to Pelagius’s book, at the disclosure and request of Pelagius’s own disciples.

At this same time Jerome was speaking of a certain work by Augustine that he had not yet seen, in which Augustine was said to be attacking Pelagius by name: “He is also said,” Jerome writes in the third dialogue against the Pelagian heresy, “to be forging other books specifically against your name.” Although Augustine did not insert into this work of his the name of Pelagius, whose book he was refuting, he did so lest the offended adversary become still more incorrigible. For Augustine thought that he would benefit Pelagius if, while preserving their friendship, he continued to spare his modesty, although he ought no longer to spare his writings. He expresses this intention in the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 47. In that later passage he immediately adds a letter written back to him by Timasius and Jacobus as an expression of gratitude for having received the volume *On Nature and Grace*. They declared that they were astonished that responses had been given to the Pelagian disputation point by point.

In the following year Augustine sent this work, together with Pelagius’s own book, to John, bishop of Jerusalem, in a letter written for this purpose, Letter 179, so that John might at last understand the mind of the new heresiarch. He also gave the same books—Pelagius’s and his own—to be carried to Pope Innocent in the year 416, together with Letter 177, addressed to him in the name of five bishops; Innocent replied in Letter 183.

This concerns the passage in Letter 183, no. 5; and in Letter 177, no. 6, where Timasius and Jacobus are praised as religious and honorable young men, servants of God, who had abandoned the hope they had placed in the world and served God in continence. In Letter 179, no. 2, they are described as young men of very honorable birth and educated in the liberal disciplines; in *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 17, they are called servants of God, good and honorable men. Julian, in his work addressed to Florus—namely, book 4 of the *Imperfect Work*—cites the book addressed to Timasius and maliciously declares it to be against free will.

[Col. 0247]

[Note: [Col. 0247] Concerning the book *On Nature and Grace*, see book 2, chapter 42, of the *Retractations*, col. 647, from the words “There also came” through the words “The book which you sent,” together with note (c). M.]

### SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO: ONE BOOK ON NATURE AND GRACE, ADDRESSED TO TIMASIUS AND JACOBUS, AGAINST PELAGIUS

[Note: [Col. 0247] Written in the year of Christ 415.]

[Note: [Col. 0247] We collated the book *On Nature and Grace* against sixteen Gallican manuscript copies from various libraries: namely, the Sorbonne; the Colbert Library; the library of the Paris abbey of Saint Genevieve; the library of the Church of Reims; the abbey of Saint Arnulf at Metz; the abbey of Saint Albinius at Angers; the abbey of Saint Cygirannus; the abbey of Saint Peter at Chartres; the abbey of Casale Benedicti; the abbey of Saint Michael in Periculo Maris; the abbey of Saint Audoenus at Rouen; and also the abbeys of Pratel, Bec, and Jumièges; finally, two copies from the Cistercian abbey. We also consulted five copies from the Roman Vatican Library, as well as the variant readings of two Belgian manuscripts excerpted by the Louvain theologians, and finally the ancient and principal editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 0247] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C)

At the beginning it is established what is known concerning nature and grace: namely, that nature, propagated from the flesh of Adam the transgressor, now needs the assistance of grace, since it is no longer as God originally created it—blameless and sound. Through grace it is both redeemed from the wrath of God and directed toward the perfection of righteousness.

The punitive defect of nature belongs to a most just punishment. Grace itself, however, is not given in return for merits but bestowed freely; and those who are not liberated through it are justly condemned.

Next, Pelagius’s book, which supports this same nature against grace, is refuted by answering each point in turn. Among other things, the principal issue is that, wishing to persuade people that a human being can be without sin, Pelagius maintains that nature has not been weakened or changed by sin; otherwise, he thinks absurdly, the material of sin would become a punishment, if a sinner had been weakened for the purpose of committing more sins.

Furthermore, when he recalls righteous people from both the Old and the New Testament whom he believes to have been without sin, he says that the possibility of not sinning is inherent in human nature. He attributes this possibility to the grace of God because God is the author of that nature, in which the possibility of not sinning has been inseparably implanted. Finally, the opinions of the ancients whom Pelagius cites in his support—especially Hilary, Ambrose, and Augustine himself—are examined.

## CHAPTER I

### 1. The Occasion for Publishing This Short Work. What the Righteousness of God Is

Dearest sons, Timasius and Jacobus, I set aside for a little while the matters that were in hand and read through, quickly but with no ordinary attention, the book you sent. I saw in it a man inflamed with the most ardent zeal against those who, although they ought to accuse the human will for their sins, instead accuse human nature and attempt to excuse themselves through it.

He has burned fiercely against this pestilence, which even authors of secular literature have sternly condemned, exclaiming: “The human race falsely complains about its nature” (Sallust, *Prologue to the Jugurthine War*). This author has likewise reinforced that very opinion with all the powers of intellect at his command.

Nevertheless, I fear that he may rather lend support to those who have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge: for, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, they are not subject to the righteousness of God.

What this righteousness of God is of which he speaks, he subsequently makes clear by adding: “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans X, 2–4). Whoever understands that this righteousness of God is established not in the commandment of the law, by which fear is instilled, but in the help of Christ’s grace—to which alone the fear of the law, like a pedagogue, profitably leads (Galatians III, 24)—understands why he is a Christian.

For if righteousness comes through the law, then “Christ died for nothing” (Galatians II, 21). But if he did not die for nothing, then the ungodly person is justified in him alone: for faith is counted as righteousness for the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly (Romans IV, 5). “All have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely through his blood” (Romans III, 23–24).

But whoever is not thought to belong among all those who have sinned and lack the glory of God clearly has no need to become a Christian, because “it is not the healthy who need a physician, but the sick.” Therefore he came not to call the righteous, but sinners (Matthew IX, 12–13).

## CHAPTER II

### 2. Faith in Christ Is Not Necessary for Salvation If a Human Being Can Live Righteously Without It

Accordingly, if the nature of the human race, produced from the flesh of that one transgressor, can suffice by itself to fulfill the law and perfect righteousness, it ought to be secure of its reward—that is, of eternal life—even if, among some people or in an earlier age, faith in the blood of Christ remained unknown to it.

For God is not unjust, so as to deprive righteous people of the reward of righteousness if the sacrament of Christ’s divinity and humanity, which was manifested in the flesh (1 Timothy III, 16), was not announced to them. For “how could they believe in what they had not heard? Or how could they hear without someone preaching?” “Faith comes from hearing,” as it is written; “and hearing through the word of Christ” (Romans X, 14, 17).

But, he says, “I ask: Have they not heard?” “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Psalm XVIII, 5).

But before this began to happen, and before that preaching had finally reached the ends of the whole earth—for even now there remain remote peoples, although, as is reported, very few, to whom it has not yet been preached—what will human nature do, or what has it done, if it either did not previously hear that this would happen or has not yet learned that it has happened? What will it do except believe in God, who made heaven and earth, by whom it naturally understands that it too was made, and by living rightly fulfill his will, without having been instructed by any faith in Christ’s passion and resurrection?

If this could happen or can happen, then I too say what the Apostle said concerning the law: “Then Christ died for nothing.” For if this were possible, they could all do it even if Christ had not died; and if they were unjust, they would be unjust because they wished to be so, not because they could not be righteous.

But if no one could be justified without the grace of Christ, then let him absolve this person also, if he dares, according to his own words: for if that person was such because he could not possibly be otherwise, he was without guilt.

## CHAPTER III

### 3. Nature Was Created Sound but Later Corrupted by Sin

Human nature was originally created blameless and without any defect. But this human nature in which each person is born from Adam already needs a physician, because it is not sound.

All the good that it possesses in its formation, life, senses, and mind comes from God most high, its creator and craftsman. But the defect that darkens and weakens these natural goods, so that illumination and healing are necessary, was not contracted from a blameless craftsman; rather, it comes from original sin, which was committed through free choice.

Accordingly, punitive nature belongs to a most just punishment. For although [Note: [Col. 0249] Perhaps, “although” (*etsi*).] “we are now a new creation in Christ” (2 Corinthians V, 17), nevertheless “we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest”; but God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, “even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ,” by whose grace we have been saved (Ephesians II, 3–5).

## CHAPTER IV

### 4. Grace Is Freely Given

This grace of Christ [Note: [Col. 0249] Erasmus, the Gallican manuscripts, and the Vatican manuscripts read, “therefore this grace.”], without which neither infants nor adults can be saved, is not given in return for merits but bestowed freely; and for this reason it is called grace.

“Being justified,” he says, “freely through his blood.” Therefore those who are not liberated through it—whether because they have not yet been able to hear, because they have refused to obey, or because, when they were unable by reason of age to hear, they did not receive the bath of regeneration, which they could have received and through which they would have been saved—are justly condemned.

For they are not without sin, whether the sin they inherited originally or the sin they added through evil conduct. “All have sinned,” whether in Adam or in themselves, “and lack the glory of God.”

## CHAPTER V

### 5. It Was Just for All to Be Condemned

The entire mass therefore owes punishment; and if the punishment of condemnation owed by all were rendered to all, it would unquestionably be rendered justly.

Those who are liberated from that mass through grace are therefore called not vessels of their merits but “vessels of mercy” (Romans IX, 23). Whose mercy, if not that of the one who sent Christ Jesus into this world to save sinners (1 Timothy I, 15)—those whom he foreknew, predestined, called, justified, and glorified (Romans VIII, 29–30)?

Who, then, could be so utterly and insanely mad as not to give unspeakable thanks for the mercy that liberates those whom God willed to liberate, while he could in no way rightly accuse the justice that condemns all without exception?

## CHAPTER VI

### 6. The Pelagians’ Exceptionally Strong and Swift Intellects

If we understand this according to the Scriptures, we are not compelled to argue against Christian grace or to say things by which we might attempt to show that human nature does not need a physician in infants because it is sound, and that in adults it can suffice by itself for righteousness if it wishes.

These statements appear to be cleverly made, but they belong to “the wisdom of speech by which the cross of Christ is emptied of its power” (1 Corinthians I, 17). This is not “the wisdom that comes down from above” (James III, 15).

I do not want to say what follows, lest we seem to be doing an injury to our friends, whose exceptionally strong and swift intellects we wish to run not in a perverse direction but in a straight one.

## CHAPTER VII

### 7. He Undertakes the Refutation of Pelagius’s Book. Pelagius’s Distinction Between “Being” and “Being Able”

Therefore, just as the author of this book you sent was inflamed with zeal against those who seek a defense for their sins from the weakness of human nature, so we ought to be inflamed with an even greater and much more ardent zeal, lest the cross of Christ be emptied of its power.

It is emptied if it is said that, apart from Christ’s sacrament, one can in some way attain righteousness and eternal life. I do not want to say that this is done knowingly—for then I should judge the one who wrote it not even to be considered a Christian—but rather, as I am more inclined to believe, unknowingly: with great force indeed, but I want that force to be sound, not like the force madmen are accustomed to possess.

### 8.

First he distinguishes between asking whether something can be—that is, a question concerning possibility alone—and asking whether it exists. No one doubts that this distinction is true. For it follows that what exists could have existed; but it does not follow that what can exist also exists.

Since the Lord raised Lazarus (John XI, 43–44), he unquestionably could do so. But since he did not raise Judas [Note: [Col. 0250–0251] Peter Lombard, in *Sentences* 1, distinction 43, final chapter, to show that God can do many things that he does not will to do, after citing the statement concerning the Tyrians and Sidonians in the *Enchiridion*, no. 24—“Nor indeed did God unjustly will that they should not be saved, although they could have been saved if he had willed it”—immediately appended this very passage from the present book, interpreting it of Judas’s resurrection in mind: “The same author says in the book *On Nature and Grace*: ‘The Lord raised Lazarus in body; must it be said that he could not raise Judas in mind? He certainly could, but did not will to do so.’”], should one say, “He could not”? He could, therefore, but he did not wish to. For if he had wished to, he would have done this also by the same power, because “the Son gives life to whom he wishes” (John V, 21).

But observe where this true and evident distinction tends and what it attempts to accomplish. “We,” he says, “are dealing only with possibility; and unless something certain has been established concerning it, we consider it extremely serious and out of order to pass on to another matter.”

He turns this over in many ways and at length, lest anyone suppose that he is asking anything other than whether it is possible not to sin. Among the many things by which he pursues this point, he also says:

“Again I repeat: I say that a human being can be without sin. What do you say? That a human being cannot be without sin?”

“Nor do I,” he says, “say that a human being is without sin, nor do you say that a human being is not without sin. We are arguing about can and cannot, not about is and is not.”

Then, concerning certain passages from Scripture that are customarily brought against them, he says that they do not belong to this question, in which one asks whether a human being can or cannot be without sin:

“For example, ‘No one is clean from defilement’ (Job XIV, 4, according to the Septuagint); ‘There is no person who does not sin’ (3 Kings VIII, 46); ‘There is no righteous person on earth’ (Ecclesiastes VII, 21); ‘There is no one who does good’ (Psalm XIII, 1); and other similar passages,” he says, “refer to non-being, not to non-possibility.”

For examples of this kind show what certain people were like at some particular time, not that they could not have been otherwise. Hence they are rightly found to be guilty. For if they were such because they could not have been otherwise, they would be without guilt.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 9. Those Who Could Not Be Justified Are Also Condemned

Observe what he has said. “I say that an infant born in a place where he could not be helped through Christ’s baptism, and overtaken by death, was such—that is, departed without the bath of regeneration—because he could not have been otherwise.”

Let him therefore absolve that child and open to him the kingdom of heaven, contrary to the Lord’s sentence (John III, 5). But the Apostle does not absolve him, for he says: “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans V, 12).

Therefore, by the condemnation that runs through the entire mass, he is rightly excluded from the kingdom of heaven, although he was not only not a Christian but could not have been one.

## CHAPTER IX

### 10. One Who Had Not Heard the Name of Christ Could Not Be Justified. The Emptying of Christ’s Cross

“But he is not condemned,” they say, “because when it is said that all sinned in Adam, this was said not because sin was drawn in through birth, but because of imitation.”

If Adam is therefore called the author of the sins of all who followed him because he was the first sinner among human beings, why is Abel not rather than Christ set forth as the head of all the righteous, because he was the first righteous person among human beings?

But I am not speaking of an infant. A young man or an old man died in a region where he could not hear the name of Christ. Could he become righteous through nature and free choice, or could he not?

If they say that he could, there is what it means to empty the cross of Christ: to maintain that anyone can be justified without it through natural law and the choice of his will.

Let us say here also: “Then Christ died for nothing.” For all could have done this even if he had not died; and if they were unjust, they would be unjust because they wished to be so, not because they could not be righteous.

But if he could not be justified at all without the grace of Christ, then let him absolve this person also, if he dares, according to his own words: for if that person was such because he could not possibly be otherwise, he was without guilt.

## CHAPTER X

### 11. Pelagius Subtly Confesses Grace

But he presents an objection to himself as though it had been made by someone else and says: “He can indeed be so, but through the grace of God, you will say.”

Then, as though replying, he adds:

“I thank your Humanity for not merely declining to attack or being content simply to acknowledge my assertion [Note: [Col. 0252] Amerbach, Erasmus, and some manuscripts read, “or you are not content merely to acknowledge.”], which you were previously attacking, but also for not refusing to approve it. For to say, ‘He can indeed, but through this or that’—what else is it than not only to agree that the thing can exist, but also to show how or in what manner it can exist? No one proves the possibility of anything more effectively than one who also acknowledges its quality, since a quality cannot exist without the thing itself.”

After saying this, he again raises an objection against himself:

“But you,” he says, “will say that in this passage you seem to reject the grace of God, since you do not mention it.”

Then he replies:

“Do I reject it, when by confessing the thing I must also confess that by which the thing can be accomplished? Or do you reject it, when by denying the thing you undoubtedly also deny whatever it is by which the thing is accomplished?”

He has forgotten that he is now answering someone who does not deny the thing, whose objection he had proposed shortly before: “He can indeed, but through the grace of God.”

How, then, can the person who says to him, “It can be, but through the grace of God,” deny the possibility for which Pelagius is laboring so strenuously?

Nevertheless, setting aside the person who now confesses the thing, since Pelagius is still arguing against those who deny that it is possible for a human being to be without sin, what does this have to do with us? Let him argue against whomever he wishes, provided that he confesses what is denied with the most criminal impiety: that without the grace of God a human being cannot be without sin.

He therefore says:

“Whether through grace, through assistance, through mercy, or through whatever it is by which a human being can be without sin, whoever acknowledges the thing itself acknowledges it.”

## CHAPTER XI

### 12. When We Discuss Grace, We Mean Not the Grace Belonging to the Institution of Nature but to Its Restoration

I confess to your Charity that, while reading these words, I was suddenly filled with joy because he did not deny the grace of God, through which alone a human being can be justified. This is what I especially detest and dread in the disputations of such people.

But as I continued reading the rest, I began to suspect his meaning from the examples he gave. He says:

“For [Note: [Col. 0252] Amerbach, Erasmus, and some manuscripts read “now”; others read “whether.” And below: “whether, then, of functions,” etc.] if I say, ‘A human being can discuss, a bird can fly, a hare can run,’ and do not also mention through what means these things can be accomplished—that is, the tongue, wings, and feet—have I denied the qualities of these functions, when I have confessed the functions themselves?”

It certainly appears that he has mentioned things that operate by nature. For these members—the tongue, wings, and feet—were created for natures of this kind. He did not posit anything like what we wish to be understood by grace, without which a human being is not justified, since in that case we are dealing with natures being healed, not instituted.

From this point I began to read the rest with concern and discovered that my suspicion had not been unfounded.

## CHAPTER XII

### 13. The Purpose of the Threats of the Law. Perfect Travelers

Before I come to that, observe what he said. When treating the question of the difference among sins, he raised the objection that some people say “certain slight sins, because they occur so frequently, cannot all be avoided.” He denied that such sins “ought to be reproved even with a mild correction if they cannot be avoided at all.”

He was evidently not paying attention to the Scriptures of the New Testament, where we learn [Note: [Col. 0253] Perhaps, “we learn” (*discimus*).] that this is the purpose of the law when it reproves: that, because of the wrongs committed, people may flee to the grace of the merciful Lord. The law is like a pedagogue who confines them within the same faith [Note: [Col. 0253] The Cygirannus manuscript reads, “into that faith.”], which was afterward revealed; and in that faith the wrongs committed are forgiven, and, with the same grace assisting, they are not committed.

This is the way of those who are making progress, although those who make good progress are called perfect travelers. The highest perfection, however, is that to which nothing can be added, when what one is journeying toward has begun to be possessed.

## CHAPTER XIII

### 14. The Refutation of Pelagius Continues

As for the objection put to him, “Are you yourself without sin?” [Note: [Col. 0253] Erasmus and most manuscripts here and somewhat below, no. 14, read, “which is said to them.” The same is true in no. 30.], it truly does not pertain to the matter under dispute.

But when he says that “the fact that he is not without sin ought rather to be attributed to his negligence,” he speaks well. Yet let him also deign to pray to God that this wicked negligence may not dominate him. A certain person prayed for this when he said: “Direct my paths according to your word, and let no iniquity dominate me” (Psalm CXVIII, 133).

Otherwise, while he trusts in his own diligence as though it were his own strength, he may attain neither true righteousness here nor that righteousness there which must undoubtedly be desired and hoped for in its perfection.

## CHAPTER XIV
15. Not Everything Has Been Written Down. And what some say to him—“Nowhere is it written in these exact words that a human being can be without sin”—he easily refutes: “For the question is not in what words any proposition is expressed.” Nevertheless, perhaps not without reason: although Scripture several times speaks of human beings as “blameless,” it never speaks of anyone as “without sin,” except the one alone of whom it is plainly said, “Him who knew no sin” (II Cor. 5:21). And in the passage where the priests were under discussion [Note: Nearly all manuscripts: “where the holy priests were under discussion”], “For he experienced all things according to likeness, without sin” (Heb. 4:15)—that is, in the flesh which had the likeness of sinful flesh, although it was not sinful flesh; yet it would not have had that likeness unless all the rest were sinful flesh.

Now how are we to understand this: “Everyone who is born of God does not sin, and he cannot sin, because his seed remains in him” (I John 3:9), when the apostle John himself, as though he were not born of God, or were speaking to those not yet born of God, plainly stated, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (ibid. 1:8)? In the books which I wrote on this subject to Marcellinus, I tried, as best I could, to explain this (On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, Book 2, §§8–10). And I do not find it objectionable to say that the statement “he cannot sin” means the same as if it were said, “He ought not to sin.” For what madman would say that one ought to sin, when sin is called sin precisely because it ought not to be done?

CHAPTER XV

16. Pelagius Corrupts a Passage of the Apostle James by Adding an Interrogation Mark. Certainly, when the apostle James says, “But no human being can tame the tongue,” I do not think it should be understood in the way he wished to explain it: “as though it were said by way of reproach, as if one were saying, ‘What then? No human being can tame the tongue?’—rebuking and saying, ‘You can tame wild beasts, but you cannot tame the tongue?’—as though it were easier to tame the tongue than wild beasts.”

I do not think that this is the meaning here. If he wished to imply that the tongue was easy to tame, the remaining statements would have followed by way of comparison with wild beasts. But instead there follows: “An unquiet evil, full of deadly poison” (James 3:8)—certainly more harmful than wild beasts and serpents. For the one kills the flesh, but the other kills the soul: “The mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wisdom 1:11).

Therefore Saint James did not pronounce that statement, nor intend it to be pronounced, as though taming the tongue were easier than taming wild beasts. Rather, he was showing how great the evil of the tongue is, since no human being can tame it, although human beings tame beasts. Nor did he say this so that we should negligently allow this evil to retain dominion over us, but so that we should seek the help of divine grace in taming the tongue. For he did not say, “No one can tame the tongue,” but “No human being”; so that, when it is tamed, we may acknowledge that this happens through God’s mercy, God’s help, and God’s grace.

Let the soul therefore strive to tame the tongue, and while striving let it ask for help. Let the tongue pray that the tongue may be tamed by him [Note: Several manuscripts: “by him giving [it]”] who said to his disciples, “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20). Thus we are admonished to do this by commandment, while, in our striving and inability through our own strength, we pray for divine assistance.

CHAPTER XVI

17. The Same Passage from James Explained Further. Accordingly, after he had emphasized the evil of the tongue, saying among other things, “This ought not to be so, my brothers,” he immediately indicated, once he had completed what he was saying about these matters, by what help the things he said ought not to happen would not happen.

“Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show by his good conduct his works in the meekness of wisdom. But if you have bitter jealousy and contention in your hearts, do not boast and be liars against the truth. This is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but earthly, unspiritual, demonic. For where jealousy and contention exist, there is instability and every evil work. But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to persuasion, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial, without hypocrisy” (James 3:10, 13–17).

This is the wisdom that tames the tongue: it comes down from above; it does not spring forth from the human heart. Does anyone dare to deprive even this wisdom of the grace of God and, in the most arrogant vanity, place it within human power? Why then is it prayed for, if it comes from human beings that it may be possessed? Or is this prayer also opposed, lest an injustice be done to free will, which is sufficient for itself, by the power of nature, to fulfill all the commandments of righteousness?

Let the same apostle James, then, be contradicted when he admonishes and says, “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him. But let him ask in faith, without doubting” (ibid. 1:5). This is the faith to which the commandments compel us: the law commands, and faith obtains.

For by means of the tongue, which no human being can tame but which the wisdom descending from above tames, we all stumble in many things (ibid. 3:2). For this apostle did not pronounce this in some different way from what he said when he declared, “No human being can tame the tongue.”

CHAPTER XVII

18. Who Are Said to Be in the Flesh. Sins of Ignorance. To Whom the Wisdom of God Is Given When They Ask for It. Nor should anyone similarly object, as though it proved the impossibility of not sinning, what has been said: “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God—indeed, it cannot be. Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom. 8:7–8).

For he said “the wisdom of the flesh,” not the wisdom that comes down from above. And it is clear that by being “in the flesh” he meant not those who have not yet departed from the body, but those who live according to the flesh. The question at issue is not found there.

What I would like to hear from him, if I could, is whether those who live according to the Spirit—and who, for this reason, although still living here, are already in some sense not in the flesh—live according to the Spirit by the grace of God, or whether they are sufficient unto themselves through their own will and through the power of nature given to them when they were created. For “the fullness of the law is love” (ibid. 13:10), and “God’s love has been poured into our hearts,” not through ourselves, “but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (ibid. 5:5).

19. This man also discusses sins of ignorance and says that “a person ought to be vigilant beforehand lest he be ignorant; and therefore ignorance is blameworthy, because through his own negligence a person does not know what he ought to have known had he applied diligence.” Yet he argues about everything rather than praying and saying, “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” (Ps. 118:73).

It is one thing not to have taken care to know what one ought to know—sins of negligence that even seemed to be expiated through certain sacrifices of the law. It is another thing to desire to understand but be unable, and to act against the law because one does not understand what it wishes to be done.

Therefore we are admonished to ask wisdom from God, who gives generously to all—certainly to all who ask in the manner and to the extent in which so great a thing ought to be sought.

CHAPTER XVIII

20. What Prayer Pelagius Acknowledged to Be Necessary. He admits that “sins committed must nevertheless be expiated by divine means and that the Lord must be entreated on their behalf,” namely, in order to obtain forgiveness. For “what has been done cannot be made undone” by that “power” of nature and human will so highly praised by him—indeed, as he himself admits, it cannot. Therefore, because of this necessity, it remains that one must pray for forgiveness.

But as to being helped so that one may not sin, he has nowhere said anything—I have not found it in this book. His silence on this matter is altogether astonishing, since the Lord’s Prayer teaches us to ask for both: that our debts be forgiven us, and that we not be led into temptation. The former concerns the expiation of past sins; the latter, the avoidance of future sins.

Although this does not happen unless the will is present, the will alone is not sufficient for it to happen. Therefore prayer is offered to the Lord for this purpose, neither superfluously nor shamelessly. For what could be more foolish than to pray to do what lies within one’s own power?

CHAPTER XIX

21. Pelagius Denies That Human Nature Has Been Depraved or Corrupted by Sin. Now observe, on the point most relevant to the matter, how he attempts to show human nature as though it were entirely without any defect, and how, by the wisdom of the word by which “the cross of Christ” is emptied of its force (I Cor. 1:17)—he struggles against the clearest passages of Scripture. But the cross will certainly not be emptied of its force; rather, this cleverness will be overthrown. For when we have demonstrated this, perhaps the mercy of God will be present so that he himself may repent of having said these things.

“First,” he says, “we must discuss the claim that nature is said to have been weakened and changed through sin. Therefore, above all, I think we must ask what sin is,” he says, “whether it is some substance, or a name entirely lacking substance [Note: Most manuscripts: “a name lacking all substance”], by which not a thing, not an existent entity, not some body, but an act improperly performed is expressed.”

Then he adds: “I believe that this is so. And if this is so,” he says, “how could something lacking substance have weakened or changed human nature?”

Observe, I beg you, how, without understanding what he is doing, he endeavors to overturn the most salutary words of the healing Scriptures. “I said, ‘Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you’” (Ps. 40:5).

What is healed if nothing has been wounded, injured, weakened, or corrupted? Moreover, if there is something to be healed, from what has it been corrupted? You hear a person confessing; what need have you of an argument? “Heal my soul,” he says. Ask him from what that which he begs to be healed has been corrupted, and hear what follows: “For I have sinned against you.”

Let him question this man; let him ask him what he thinks ought to be asked, and let him say: “You who cry out, ‘Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you,’ what is sin? Is it some substance, or a name entirely lacking substance, by which not a thing, not an existent entity, not some body, but merely an act improperly performed is expressed?”

The man replies: “It is as you say: sin is not some substance, but this name merely expresses an act improperly performed.”

And the other replies: “Why then do you cry out, ‘Heal my soul, for I have sinned against you’? How could something lacking substance corrupt your soul?”

Would he not, overcome by sorrow over his wound and unwilling to be diverted from prayer by an argument, answer briefly and say: “Please leave me. If you can, argue instead with him who said, ‘Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners’ (Matt. 9:12–13)—where he plainly called the righteous ‘the healthy’ and sinners ‘the sick’”?

CHAPTER XX

22. Even If Sin Is Not a Substance, How Could It Corrupt Nature? Do you see where this argument is heading and toward what it reaches out its hands? It is intended to make us think that the statement “You shall call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins” (ibid. 1:21) was altogether made in vain.

For how will he save them where there is no illness? The sins from which the Gospel says Christ’s people are to be saved are not substances, and, according to this man, they cannot corrupt anything.

Brother, it is good that you remember you are a Christian. Perhaps it would be enough simply to believe these things. Yet because you wish to argue—and this is not harmful, but even beneficial, if the firmest faith precedes it—let us not suppose that human nature cannot be corrupted by sin. Rather, believing the divine Scriptures that it has been corrupted by sin, let us inquire how this could have happened.

Since we have learned that sin is not a substance, is it not clear—even leaving other things aside—that not eating is also not a substance? For one departs from substance, since food is a substance. But abstaining from food is not a substance, and yet the substance of the body, if it entirely abstains from food, grows so weak, is so disordered by failing health, is so drained of strength, and is so weakened and broken by exhaustion that, if it somehow continues to live, it can scarcely be restored to the food from which it was corrupted by abstinence.

So sin is not a substance. But God is a substance, indeed the highest substance, and the one true food of rational creation. By departing from him through disobedience, and through weakness becoming unable to receive and rejoice in what it ought, you hear the soul say: “My heart is struck down like grass and has withered, for I have forgotten to eat my bread” (Ps. 101:5). [Note: The printed editions read, “I have been struck down.” But many manuscripts read, “It has been struck down.” Augustine likewise uses the latter reading in his exposition of the same psalm, Sermon 1.]

CHAPTER XXI

23. Adam Freed by Christ’s Mercy. Observe how he continues to press arguments that seem plausible against the truth of Holy Scripture. The Lord Jesus says—and he is called Jesus because he saves his people from their sins—“Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. 9:12–13).

Hence the Apostle also says, “The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance: Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (I Tim. 1:15).

Against this trustworthy saying, deserving of full acceptance, he says that “this sickness ought not to have been contracted through sins, lest the punishment of sin should consist in their committing further sins.”

So great a helper and physician is sought also for little children. [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “Therefore.”] Yet this man says: “What are you looking for? Those for whom you seek a physician are healthy. Nor was the first human being condemned to death for this reason, since afterward he did not sin.”

As though he had learned anything afterward about Adam’s perfection in righteousness, except what the Church proclaims: that he too was freed by the mercy of the Lord Christ.

“This man’s descendants,” he also says, “were not only no weaker than he, but fulfilled even more commandments, since he neglected to fulfill one.”

He sees these descendants being born in a condition in which, certainly, Adam was not made: not only incapable of understanding a commandment, which they do not perceive at all, but scarcely capable even of the breast when they are hungry. Yet when the one who saves his people from their sins wishes to save them by his grace in the bosom of Mother Church, human beings contradict him and, as though they knew better than he how to regard the creature established by him, pronounce in an unsound voice that these children are healthy.

CHAPTER XXII

24. Sin Itself and the Punishment of Sin. He says that “punishment is the material of sin, if the sinner has been weakened for the purpose of committing further sins.”

He does not consider how deservedly the light of truth abandons the transgressor of the law. Once abandoned by that light, he necessarily becomes blind, stumbles more often, is tormented by falling, and, once tormented, does not rise—so that he hears the voice of the law only for the purpose of being admonished to implore the grace of the Savior.

Is there no punishment for those of whom the Apostle says, “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their reasoning, and their foolish heart was darkened”? This darkening was already punishment and retribution. Yet through this punishment—that is, through the blindness of the heart produced by the withdrawal of the light of wisdom—they fell into more numerous and more serious sins.

“For claiming to be wise, they became fools.” This is a grave punishment, if anyone understands it. And from this punishment, observe where they went: “They exchanged the glory of the immortal God for the likeness of an image of mortal human beings and of birds and four-footed animals and reptiles.” They did these things because of the punishment of sin, by which their foolish heart was darkened.

Yet because these acts, although punitive, are themselves also sins, he adds and says: “Therefore God gave them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity.”

Observe how God condemned them more gravely by giving them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity. Observe also what they do as a result of this punishment [Note: The printed editions read, “what”; the manuscripts, “which”]: “They dishonor their bodies among themselves.”

And because this punishment is itself also iniquity, he makes the point more clearly by saying: “They exchanged the truth of God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.”

“For this reason,” he says, “God gave them over to dishonorable passions.”

Observe how many times God exacts punishment, and how from the same punishment more numerous and more serious sins arise. “Their women exchanged natural use for that which is contrary to nature; and likewise the men, abandoning the natural use of women, burned with desire for one another, men committing disgraceful acts with men.”

And to show that these acts are sins in such a way that they are also punishments for sins, he added: “Receiving in themselves the due recompense for their error.”

Observe how many times he punishes, and how the same punishment produces and multiplies sins.

Again, observe: “Since they did not approve of having God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a debased mind, to do what ought not to be done, filled with all iniquity, deceit, malice, greed, full of envy, murder, strife, fraud, ill will; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insolent, arrogant, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents, foolish, faithless, heartless, ruthless” (Rom. 1:21–31).

Let this man now say: “Sin ought not to have been punished in such a way that the sinner would commit more sins through the punishment.”

CHAPTER XXIII

25. God Abandons Only Those Worthy of Abandonment. We Are Sufficient for Sinning, but Not Likewise for Returning to Righteousness. Death Is a Punishment, Not the Cause of Sin. Perhaps he will reply that God does not compel people to do these things, but merely abandons those who deserve to be abandoned.

If he says this, he speaks most truly. For once abandoned, as I have said, by the light of righteousness and thereby plunged into darkness, what else can they produce than all the works of darkness I have mentioned, until it is said to them—if they obey the command—“Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead, and Christ will shine on you” (Eph. 5:14)?

Truth calls them dead, and so does the statement, “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matt. 8:22). Truth therefore calls dead those whom this man says could not have been harmed or corrupted by sin, because, evidently, he has learned that sin is not a substance.

No one says to him that human beings were made in such a way that they could indeed pass from righteousness into sin, but could not return from sin to righteousness. Rather, in order to enter sin, free will was sufficient, by which the person corrupted himself. But in order to return to righteousness, he needs a physician, because he is not healthy; he needs one who gives life, because he is dead.

Regarding this grace, he says absolutely nothing, as though a person could heal himself by his own will alone because he was able to corrupt himself by his own will alone.

We are not saying that bodily death contributes to sin, since there it is only punishment: no one sins by dying bodily. But the death of the soul contributes to sin; its life—that is, its God—has abandoned it, and it necessarily performs dead works until it comes back to life through Christ’s grace.

As for hunger, thirst, and the other bodily afflictions, far be it from us to say that they create a necessity of sinning. Through these afflictions the life of the righteous has been exercised, shining more brilliantly and gaining greater glory by overcoming them through patience—but with the help of God’s grace, the help of God’s Spirit, and the help of God’s mercy; not exalting itself through proud will, but obtaining strength through humble confession.

For he knew to say to God, “For you are my patience” (Ps. 70:5).

Regarding this grace, help, and mercy, without which we cannot live well, I do not know why he says absolutely nothing. Indeed, by defending nature as sufficient for righteousness if only the will is present [Note: Lov. reads, “if his will is present.” Other printed editions and the manuscripts read, “if only the will is present”], he most plainly contradicts the grace of Christ by which we are justified.

But why bodily death remains, for the exercise of faith, after the guilt of sin has been released through grace, although death came from sin—this too I discussed, as best I could, in the books addressed to Marcellinus, of holy memory [Note: Marcellinus the tribune died in September 413, “under the odium of the Heraclean tyranny,” as Jerome writes in Book 3 Against the Pelagians, “an innocent man slain by heretics.” Honorius calls him “a man of distinguished memory” in a law issued on 30 August 414, in Book 16 of the Theodosian Code, On Heretics, law 55.] (On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, Book 2, §§49–56).

CHAPTER XXIV

26. Christ Died by Power. Even Evils Are Beneficial through God’s Mercy. As for his statement that the Lord could have died without sin, even his birth was an act of the power of mercy, not a condition imposed by nature. Thus he also died by power; and this is our price, by which he redeemed us from death.

Their argument attempts to empty this of its force, since they defend human nature in such a way that free will could have no need of this price in order to be transferred from the power of darkness and from the ruler of death into the kingdom of Christ the Lord.

Yet when the Lord went forth to his passion, he said: “Behold, the ruler of this world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” [Note: The Reims manuscript reads: “Behold, the ruler of this world is coming, and he finds nothing in me.”]—certainly no sin on account of which the ruler of death could justly put him to death.

“But,” he said, “so that all may know that I do the will of my Father, rise; let us go from here” (John 14:30–31). That is: I do not die from the necessity of sin, but by the will of obedience.

27. He Says That No Evil Is the Cause of Any Good. [Note: In many manuscripts, “to no one” instead of “no evil.”] As though punishment were good, although many have been corrected by it. There are therefore evils that, through the wondrous mercy of God, are beneficial.

Did the man who said, “You hid your face from me, and I was troubled,” suffer anything good? Certainly not. Yet this very trouble was, in a certain way, medicinal for him against pride.

For he had said in his prosperity, “I shall never be moved,” and attributed to himself what he had from the Lord. “What do you have that you did not receive?” (I Cor. 4:7).

Therefore it was necessary to show him from where he had received it, so that in humility he might recover what he had lost through pride.

“Lord,” he says, “in your favor you gave strength to my beauty. In my prosperity I said, ‘I shall never be moved,’ although this came from you, not from me. Then you hid your face from me, and I was troubled” (Ps. 29:7–8).

CHAPTER XXV

28. The Disposition of Those Who Err. With Certain Heretics We Must Deal Not So Much by Arguments as by Prayers. A proud mind has no understanding of this at all [Note: Three Gallican manuscripts and the Belgian manuscripts read: “A proud friend has no understanding of this.”] But the Lord is great, and he persuades it in the manner he knows.

We are more inclined to seek what we can say in response to objections raised against our error than to consider how health-giving those objections are, so that we may be free from error. Therefore, with these people we must deal not so much by arguments as by prayers on their behalf, just as we pray for ourselves.

For we do not say to them what this man has set against himself: that sin was necessary in order to provide a reason for God’s mercy. Would that there had been no misery, so that this mercy would not have been necessary.

But because the iniquity of sin was all the more serious inasmuch as the human being could more easily have avoided sin—no weakness yet holding him—there followed a most just punishment: that he should receive in himself the due recompense of his sin, losing, in a certain sense, the obedience of his body placed beneath him, which he himself had contemptuously refused to render above all to his Lord.
