And because we are now born under that same law of sin which wars in our members against the law of the mind (Rom. 7:23), we ought neither to murmur against God nor argue against what is perfectly clear, but, because of our punishment, seek and pray for his mercy.

CHAPTER XXVI

29. An Illustration Showing That God’s Grace Is Necessary for Every Good Work. Observe carefully how he said: “God also applies his mercy to this part, whenever it is necessary, because after sin human beings must be helped in this way—not because God desired the cause of this necessity.”

Do you see how he does not say that God’s mercy is necessary so that we may not sin, but because we have sinned?

Then he adds: “But a physician must also be ready to treat someone who has already been wounded; he ought not, however, to desire that a healthy person be wounded.”

If this comparison corresponds to the matters under discussion, human nature certainly cannot be wounded by sin, since sin is no substance.

But just as, for example, someone who is lame because of a wound is healed so that, once the past injury has been cured, his future walking may be directed aright, so the heavenly physician heals our evils not merely so that they may no longer exist, but so that thereafter we may walk correctly. Yet even when healthy, we will be able to do this only with his help.

When a human physician has healed someone, he leaves the person thereafter to God, so that the restored health may be strengthened and preserved by suitable support from bodily elements and nourishment. God provides these things for those living in the flesh, and they were also among the resources the physician employed while treating the sick.

For no physician heals anyone from things he himself has created, but from the resources of the one who created everything necessary for the healthy and the diseased [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read this way. The printed editions read, “from his works.” See below, §70.]

But God himself, through the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (I Tim. 2:5), spiritually heals the sick or gives life to the dead—that is, justifies the ungodly. And when he has brought a person to perfect health, that is, to perfect life and righteousness, he does not abandon him if he is not abandoned, so that he may always live piously and righteously.

For just as the bodily eye, even when completely healthy, cannot see unless it is aided by the brightness of light, so a human being, even when perfectly justified, cannot live rightly unless divinely aided by the eternal light of righteousness [Note: The Cistercian manuscript reads, “of eternal light.”].

God therefore heals not only to erase what we have sinned, but also to grant that we may not sin.

CHAPTER XXVII

30. Sin Is Removed by Sin. The Heavenly Physician Does Not Receive the Order of Healing from the Sick, but from Himself. What the Righteous Have to Fear. He handles and develops with considerable cleverness—and, as far as he thinks, refutes and disproves—the statement made to him that sin was necessary for a human being, so that the occasion for pride or glory might be removed and he could not be without sin [Note: The Cygirannensis manuscript reads, “the statement made to him.”]

For he considers it utterly absurd and foolish that sin should have existed so that there would be no sin, since pride itself is certainly also sin. As though an ulcer were not painful, and an incision did not cause pain, so that pain might be removed by pain.

If we had not experienced this, and if, in some lands where such things had never occurred, we heard of it, we would certainly laugh at it, perhaps even using this man’s words and saying: “It is utterly absurd that pain should have been necessary so that there would be no pain from an ulcer.”

31. “But,” they say, “God can heal everything.” Indeed, this is what he does: he heals everything. But he does so according to his own judgment, and he does not receive the order of healing from the sick.

Without doubt he wished to make the Apostle exceedingly strong, yet he said to him, “Power is made perfect in weakness.” And when the Apostle prayed repeatedly, he did not remove from him some “thorn in the flesh,” which he says was given to him so that he would not be exalted by the greatness of his revelations (II Cor. 12:7–9).

For other vices have force only in evil deeds, whereas pride must be guarded against even in good deeds. Therefore they are admonished not to perish more grievously by attributing God’s gifts to their own power and exalting themselves than they would if they did no good at all. They are told: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling, for God is the one who works in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:12–13).

Why, then, “with fear and trembling,” and not rather with confidence, if God is at work? Because, on account of our will, without which we cannot work well, it can quickly creep into the human mind that whatever good it does it considers to be its own alone, and says in its prosperity, “I shall never be moved.”

Therefore he who had given strength to its beauty in his favor briefly hid his face, so that the one who had said this might become troubled; for that swelling had to be healed by these very pains.

CHAPTER XXVIII

32. God Withdraws Slightly, Lest We Become Proud. It is not therefore said to a human being, “You must sin so that you may not sin.” Rather, it is said to a human being: “God withdraws somewhat from that in which you take pride, so that you may know that it is not yours but his, and learn not to be proud.”

And what of the Apostle’s statement? Is it not so astonishing that, unless it came from him—whom it would be impious to contradict when he speaks the truth—it would be unbelievable?

Who among the faithful does not know that the first persuasion to sin came from Satan (Gen. 3:1–6), and that he is the original author of all sins? Yet some are handed over to Satan so that they may learn not to blaspheme (I Tim. 1:20).

How, then, is Satan’s work excluded by Satan’s work? Let him consider these and similar matters, lest what sounds clever to him prove, when examined, to be dull.

Moreover, he also introduces comparisons by which he more strongly indicates what ought to be answered. “What more can I say,” he asks, “except that it may be believed that fires are extinguished by fires, if it may be believed that sins are cured by sins?” [Note: The printed editions read, “if this may be believed.” The manuscripts correct the reading.]

What if someone cannot extinguish fires with fires, but pains can nevertheless, as I have shown, be healed by pains? Poisons can also be driven out by poisons, if one seeks and learns this. For if he notices that fevers are sometimes broken by certain medicinal heats, he may perhaps also concede that fires are extinguished by fires.

CHAPTER XXIX

33. Not Every Sin Is Pride. How Pride Is the Beginning of Every Sin. “How,” he asks, “shall we separate pride itself from sin? Why press this point, when it is clear that pride itself is also sin?”

“To sin,” he says, “is as much to be proud as to be proud is to sin. For inquire what any sin may be, and see whether you can find any sin without calling it pride.”

He develops and attempts to prove this proposition as follows: “Every sin,” he says, “unless I am mistaken, is contempt of God; and every contempt of God is pride. For what is as proud as to despise God? Therefore every sin is also pride, as Scripture says, ‘The beginning of every sin is pride.’”

Let him inquire carefully, and he will find that in the law the sin of pride is clearly distinguished from other sins. Many sins are committed through pride, but not everything done wrongly is done proudly—certainly not by the ignorant, certainly not by the weak, and certainly often not by those who weep and groan.

Indeed, although pride itself is a great sin, it exists by itself without other sins; and, as I have said, it often arrives and steals in with a swift step not into sins but into good deeds themselves.

Yet the statement “The beginning of every sin is pride,” which this man understood differently, was made with complete truth. Pride cast down the devil, from whom sin’s origin arose, and then, with envy following, it overthrew the human being who was standing, in the very place from which the devil had fallen.

For that serpent sought the door of boasting through which he might enter when he said, “You will be like gods” (Gen. 3:5). Therefore it is said, “The beginning of every sin is pride,” and, “The beginning of human pride is apostasy from God” (Ecclus. 10:15, 14).

CHAPTER XXX

34. How Human Sin Is His Own, Although Grace Is Needed to Heal His Weakness. What does he mean when he says: “Then how will he be subject to God for the guilt of that sin which he has recognized as not his own? For it is not his own,” he says, “if it is necessary. Or, if it is his own, it is voluntary; and if it is voluntary, it can be avoided”?

We reply: It is entirely his own; but the vice by which it is committed has not yet been completely healed. It grew from a soundness that was not rightly used. From this vice, now sick either through weakness or through blindness, he commits further sins.

For this he must pray to be healed, so that thereafter he may live in perpetual health. He must not become proud, as though a human being were healed by the same power by which he was corrupted.

CHAPTER XXXI
## CHAPTER XXXI

### 35. Why God does not immediately heal pride itself. How secretly pride lies in wait.

I have said this in such a way as to confess that I do not understand the deeper counsel of God [Note: [Col. 0263] Some Belgian manuscripts read “judgment” (*judicium*)], namely, why God does not immediately heal pride itself, which lies in wait for the human mind even in right actions. For its healing, devout souls implore him with tears and great groans to extend his right hand to those striving to overcome it and, in a certain sense, trample and crush it.

For whenever a person rejoices that, in some good work, he has also overcome pride, pride raises its head out of that very joy and says: “Look at me! I am alive. Why are you celebrating your triumph? I am alive precisely because you are celebrating your triumph.” Perhaps it is pleasant to celebrate a triumph over it as though it had already been conquered, before the proper time—although at noon, as I suppose, its final shadow will be swallowed up. Scripture promises that noon in these words: “He will bring forth your righteousness like the light, and your judgment like the noonday,” if what is written above is fulfilled: “Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him; and he himself will act” (Ps. XXXVI, 6, 5)—not, as some think, that they themselves act. [Note: [Col. 0264] Here chapter 32 begins in Am. and Er.]

For he seems to have had no others in mind when he said, “And he himself will act,” except those who say, “We act”—that is, “We ourselves justify ourselves.” We too certainly work, but we cooperate with him as he works, because his mercy goes before us. It goes before us so that we may be healed, and follows after us so that, once healed, we may be strengthened [Note: [Col. 0264] The Cygirannensis codex and several Vatican manuscripts read “follows” (*subsequitur*)]; it goes before us so that we may be called, and follows after us so that we may be glorified; it goes before us so that we may live devoutly, and follows after us so that we may live with him forever—for “without me you can do nothing” (John XV, 5).

Both statements have been written: “My God, his mercy will go before me” (Ps. LVIII, 11), and “Your mercy will follow me all the days of my life” (Ps. XXII, 6). Let us therefore reveal our way to him by confession, and praise it not by self-defence. For if it is not his way but ours, it is certainly not right. Let us reveal it by confessing, since it is not hidden from him even if we try to conceal it. “It is good to confess to the Lord” (Ps. XCI, 2).

## CHAPTER XXXII [Note: [Col. 0264] In Am. and Er., chapter 33.]

### 36. Pride must also be guarded against in right actions. Free will is not removed when grace is preached.

He will give us what pleases him if what displeases him in us also displeases us. As it is written, he will turn our paths away from his way (Ps. XLIII, 19), and he will make ours the way that is his, because he provides it to those who believe and hope in him, so that he himself may act.

For this is the just way. Those who have zeal for God but not according to knowledge, and who wish to establish their own righteousness, are not subject to the righteousness of God. “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 2–4)—he who said, “I am the way” (John XIV, 6).

Yet while they were already walking on this way, a divine voice frightened them lest they become elated as though they possessed their own strength for walking on it. For those to whom the Apostle says, “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling; for it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Phil. II, 12–13), the Psalm also says for this very reason: “Serve the Lord in fear, and rejoice in him with trembling; embrace discipline, lest the Lord become angry, and you perish from the right way when his anger is kindled briefly against you.”

It does not say, “Lest the Lord become angry and fail to show you the right way,” or “fail to bring you into the right way.” Rather, it could frighten those already walking there by saying, “Lest you perish from the right way.” Why is this, except because pride—which, as I have said so many times and must often say again, must also be guarded against in right actions—is to be guarded against even on the right way? Otherwise, while a person attributes what belongs to God to himself, he loses what belongs to God and returns to what is his own.

Therefore let us do what this psalm concludes: “Blessed are all who trust in him” (Ps. II, 11–13)—that is, so that he himself may act and himself show his way. To him it is said, “Show us, Lord, your mercy,” and let him himself give salvation, so that we may be able to walk, to whom it is said, “And give us your salvation” (Ps. LXXXIV, 8). Let him himself lead us on that same way, to whom it is said, “Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth” (Ps. LXXXV, 11). Let him himself bring us to those promised things to which the way leads, to whom it is said, “Indeed, your hand will lead me there, and your right hand will bring me through” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 10). Let him himself feed us there as we recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, of whom it is said, “He will make them recline, and will pass by and serve them” (Luke XII, 37).

When we recall these things, we do not abolish the freedom of the will; we preach the grace of God. For whom do these things benefit except one who wills—but one who wills humbly, not exalting himself on the strength of his will as though that strength alone were sufficient for the perfection of righteousness?

## CHAPTER XXXIII [Note: [Col. 0265] In Am. and Er., chapter 34.]

### 37. Even being entirely without sin does not make a human being equal to God.

Far be it from us to say to him what, as he reports, certain people say against him: “A human being is compared with God if it is asserted that he can be without sin” [Note: [Col. 0265] He does not prove that this was objected to Pelagius; Jerome, however, uses this argument against him in his letter to Ctesiphon: “Did God,” he says, “command me to be what God is, so that there would be nothing between me and the Lord Creator, so that I would be higher than the rank of angels, so that I would possess what angels do not possess? Of him it is written as something proper to him, ‘He committed no sin.’”].

As though an angel, because he is without sin, were thereby compared with God! I certainly hold this view: even when there is in us such great righteousness that nothing at all could be added to it, the creature will not be equal to the Creator. If, however, some think that our progress will one day be so great that we shall be changed into God’s substance and become altogether what he is, let them see how they can establish their position. I confess that I am not persuaded of this.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### 38. We most truly say that we are not without sin. One must not lie even for the sake of modesty. The praise of humility must not be placed on the side of falsehood.

I readily give the author of this book considerable credit for the following: against those who say, “What you assert does indeed seem reasonable, but it is arrogant to say that a human being can be without sin,” he responds in such a way that, if the assertion is true, it must in no way be called arrogant.

He says with great acuteness and truth: “On which side should humility rather be placed? Without doubt, on the side of falsehood, if pride is proved to lie on the side of truth.” Accordingly, he is right to approve the placing of humility more on the side of truth than on the side of falsehood.

It follows that the one who said, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I, 8), must unquestionably have spoken truly, lest [Note: [Col. 0266] Am., Er., and five manuscripts read “nor” (*nec*)] it appear that he said something false for the sake of humility. For this reason he added, “And the truth is not in us.” It might perhaps have been enough to say, “We deceive ourselves,” unless he had considered that some might think the statement “we deceive ourselves” was made because even someone who praises himself for a genuine good becomes elated. By adding, “And the truth is not in us,” he clearly showed—as this author also rightly approves—that it is altogether untrue if we say that we have no sin, lest humility established on the side of falsehood lose the reward of truth.

### 39.

Moreover, when he appears to plead God’s cause by defending nature, he does not realize that, by calling that same nature sound, he rejects the mercy of the physician. The one who created it is also its savior. We must not praise the Creator in such a way that we are compelled—or rather, truly convicted—to say that the Savior is superfluous.

Let us therefore honor human nature with praises appropriate to it, and refer those praises to the glory of its Creator. But because he created us, let us be grateful in such a way that, because he heals us, we are not ungrateful. Let us indeed attribute the defects he heals not to God’s work but to human will and to his just retribution. Yet just as we confess that it was in our power to prevent them from occurring, so let us acknowledge that their healing belongs more to his mercy than to our power.

This author places the mercy and medicinal assistance of the Savior only in the forgiveness of past sins, not in assistance for avoiding future sins. Here he is most perniciously mistaken. Here, even though unknowingly, he prevents us from watching and praying lest we enter into temptation, since he insists that avoiding this lies entirely within our own power.

## CHAPTER XXXV

### 40. Why the sins of certain people were written down. Despair thinks it will destroy itself in sins if it does not do what lust urges. Whether the saints died without sin.

A person of sound judgment does not say that the “examples of certain people whom we read to have sinned” were “written down” for the purpose of making us despair of not sinning or somehow providing us with security in sinning. Rather, they were written so that we might learn either the humility of repentance or that salvation should not be despaired of even in such falls.

Some people, having fallen into sins, perish even more through despair. They not only neglect the medicine of repentance but become slaves of lust and criminal desires, in order to fulfil dishonorable and wicked longings—as though they would perish if they did not do what lust urges, when certain condemnation already awaits them. Against this exceedingly dangerous and destructive disease, it is useful to recall even the sins into which righteous and holy people have fallen.

### 41.

He appears, however, to ask an acute question: “How are we to believe that these saints departed from this life—with sin or without sin?” If the answer is “With sin,” it might be thought that condemnation followed them, which it would be impious to believe [Note: [Col. 0266] Most manuscripts read “to say” (*dicere*)]. If, on the other hand, it is said that they departed this life without sin, this would prove that at least as death approached a human being had been without sin in this life.

Yet, though he is very acute, he pays too little attention to the fact that even the righteous say in prayer, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” and that the Lord Christ, after explaining this same prayer while teaching it, most truthfully added: “For if you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you your sins.”

Through this daily spiritual incense, in a certain sense, which is brought before God upon the altar of the heart—of which we are admonished to keep the heart above—even if one does not live without sin in this life, one may die without sin, provided that what is repeatedly committed through ignorance or weakness is repeatedly erased by forgiveness.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

### 42. The holy Virgin Mary lived entirely without sin. No other saint was without sin.

He then recalls those “who are reported not merely to have refrained from sinning but also to have lived righteously: Abel, Enoch, Melchizedek, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joshua son of Nun, Phinehas, Samuel, Nathan, Elijah, Joseph, Elisha, Micah, Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, Mishael, Ezekiel, Mordecai, Simeon, Joseph to whom the Virgin Mary was betrothed, and John.”

He also adds women: “Deborah, Hannah the mother of Samuel, Judith, Esther, the other Hannah, daughter of Phanuel, Elizabeth, and the very Mother of our Lord and Savior,” whom he says “piety requires us to confess to have been without sin.”

With the exception, therefore, of the holy Virgin Mary—concerning whom, out of honor to the Lord, I wish no question whatsoever to be raised [Note: [Col. 0267] The printed editions read “to raise” (*habere*); the manuscripts read “to be raised” (*haberi*)] when sins are under discussion—for how do we know what greater measure of grace was given her for overcoming sin in every respect, since she merited to conceive and bear the one whom it is established had no sin? [Note: [Col. 0267] Two of five Vatican manuscripts read: “For how do we know that a greater measure of grace was given her for overcoming sin in every respect, since she conceived …” Saint Thomas also read this way in *Summa theologiae* III, q. 27, a. 4.]

With this Virgin excepted, if we could gather all those holy men and women while they were living here and ask whether they were without sin, what should we think they would have answered? Would it have been what this author says, or what the apostle John says?

I ask you: however outstanding their holiness may have been in this body, if they could have been asked this question, would they not [Note: [Col. 0267] The word “not” (*nonne*) was added in Lov. from one Belgian manuscript; it is absent from the other editions and manuscripts] all have cried out with one voice, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us”? Or would they perhaps have answered more humbly than truthfully?

Yet this author now approves—and rightly approves—the principle “not to place the praise of humility on the side of falsehood.” Therefore, if they said this truthfully, they would have had sin; but because they confessed it humbly, the truth would have been in them [Note: [Col. 0267] In Er. and Lov. the word order is changed: “which they would confess humbly, because the truth would be in them.”]. If, on the other hand, they lied, they would nevertheless have had sin, because the truth would not have been in them.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

### 43. Why Scripture did not mention the sins of everyone.

“Perhaps they will say,” he says, “Could Scripture mention the sins of everyone?” Whoever says this will be telling him the truth; and I do not see that he has offered any effective response to it, although I see that he did not wish to leave it unanswered.

Please consider what he says: “This can rightly be said of those whose good or evil deeds Scripture does not mention. But concerning those whose righteousness it records, it would certainly also have remembered their sins if it had perceived that they had committed any.”

Let him then say that the faith of those people was not sufficiently relevant to their righteousness—those who, going before and following after in a great multitude, accompanied the Lord’s ass with praises and, even amid the shouting of hostile opponents who asked why they were doing this, cried out, saying, “Hosanna to the Son of David; blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matt. XXI, 9) [Note: [Col. 0268] The manuscripts of Lov. likewise read this, in agreement with the Vulgate; the printed editions have “Son of David” in the vocative.].

Let him dare to say, if he can, that no one in that great multitude had any sin whatsoever. If it is absurd to say this, why did Scripture, which took care to record the great good of their faith, record none of their sins?

### 44.

But perhaps he himself saw this, and therefore added the following: “Suppose that at other times, because of the size of the crowds, it concealed and passed over the sins of everyone. In the very beginning of the world, however, when there were only four human beings, what,” he asks, “are we to say? Why did it not wish to mention the offenses of everyone? Was it because of the size of a great multitude, which did not yet exist? Or because it remembered only the one who had committed sins, while it could not remember the one who had committed none?”

He adds further words to establish this view more fully and clearly [Note: [Col. 0268] The manuscripts read “to these things” (*adhuc*); Lov. reads “to these” (*ad haec*), and below “more clearly” (*planius*) for “more fully” (*plenius*)]: “Certainly,” he says, “at the first period Adam and Eve, from whom Cain and Abel were born, are reported to have been only four human beings. Eve sinned, and Scripture disclosed this; Adam also transgressed, and the same Scripture did not keep silent about it (Gen. III). Scripture likewise testified that Cain sinned (ibid. IV), indicating not only their sins but also the character of their sins. If Abel too had sinned, Scripture would certainly have said so; but it did not. Therefore neither did he sin; indeed, it showed him to be righteous. Let us therefore believe what we read, and let us consider it impious to assert what we do not read.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

### 45. Why some thought that Cain had begotten children by his mother Eve. The sins of the righteous; and how someone can be righteous without being sinless. Whatever is lacking in love arises from a defect.

In saying this, he pays too little attention to what he himself had said shortly before: that once the human race had multiplied, the size of the crowd might have enabled Scripture to conceal and pass over the sins of everyone.

If he had considered this carefully enough, he would have seen that even in one person there may be a crowd and multitude of minor sins, which either could not have been written down or, even if they could, ought not to have been. For what was written had to be limited in scope, and the reader had to be instructed by a few examples concerning many necessary matters.

Scripture did not wish to record how many human beings there then were, or who they were—that is, how many sons and daughters Adam and Eve produced and what names they gave them. Hence some people, insufficiently considering how much Scripture silently passes over, thought that Cain had intercourse with his mother and begot the offspring that is mentioned, supposing that Adam’s sons had no sisters because Scripture was silent about them at that point. Later, by recapitulating, Scripture supplied what it had omitted, saying that Adam begot sons and daughters (Gen. V, 4), without indicating the time of their birth, their number, or their names.

In the same way, it was not necessary to mention if Abel, although rightly called righteous, at some time laughed a little too freely, or joked in relaxation of spirit, or saw something that aroused desire, or plucked fruit somewhat too immoderately, or was made somewhat more crude by an excess of food, or, while praying, thought of something that diverted his attention elsewhere—or how often such things and many similar things might have crept upon him.

Or are these not sins concerning which we are generally warned to be on guard and to restrain them by the apostolic command: “Therefore, let not sin reign in your mortal body so as to obey its desires” (Rom. VI, 12)?

We must struggle against these desires in a daily and perpetual conflict, so that we do not obey them in doing what is forbidden or less fitting. For it is certainly from this defect that the eye is directed or allowed to rest where it ought not. If this defect grows strong and prevails, adultery is also committed in the body; in the heart it occurs all the more quickly, because thought is swifter and encounters no delay or physical impediment.

Those who have to a great extent restrained this sin—that is, this desire arising from a defective affection—so that they did not obey its desires or present their members to it as weapons of unrighteousness, have deserved to be called righteous; and this also through the help of God’s grace. Yet because sin often creeps in through the lightest matters and sometimes through carelessness, they were righteous, but they were not without sin.

Finally, if in the righteous Abel the love of God—which alone truly makes anyone righteous—still had room to be increased and ought to have been increased [Note: [Col. 0269] Understand: “which could and ought to have been increased in this life.” He says in *On the Spirit and the Letter*, §65: “For if such love of God as is owed to full and perfect knowledge cannot yet exist, this should not already be counted as guilt.” See below, *On the Perfection of Righteousness*, §15], whatever was lacking arose from a defect. And who does not have something lacking until the strength is reached at which all human weakness is swallowed up?

## CHAPTER XXXIX

### 46. The same argument is discussed.

He concluded this section with a grand statement when he said: “Let us therefore believe what we read, and let us consider it impious to assert what we do not read”—a statement that would be sufficient even if he had said it about everyone.

I, however, reply that we are not bound to believe everything we read, on account of the Apostle’s statement, “Examine everything; hold fast to what is good” (1 Thess. V, 21). Nor is it impious to assert something that we do not read. We may in good faith assert something of which we have personal experience, even if we have perhaps not read it.

Perhaps he will respond here: “When I said this, I was speaking about the holy Scriptures.” Would that he wished to assert—not merely nothing other than what he reads in those writings, but nothing contrary to what he reads! Let him faithfully and obediently hear what is written: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. V, 12). Let him not weaken the grace of so great a physician by refusing to admit that human nature has been corrupted.

Would that, as a Christian, he would read that, apart from Jesus Christ, “there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which we must be saved” (Acts IV, 12), and would not defend the possibility of human nature in such a way that it is believed that a human being can be saved by free will even without this name!

## CHAPTER XL

### 47. For what purpose Pelagius thought Christ was necessary for us.

Perhaps he thinks that Christ’s name is necessary so that, through his Gospel, we may learn how we ought to live, but not so that we may be aided by his grace in living well.

At the very least, let him acknowledge from this that there are pitiable shadows in the human mind: a person may know how to tame a lion and yet not know how to live. Or is free will and the natural law sufficient even for him to know this?

This is the “wisdom of speech” by which the cross of Christ is emptied of its power. But the one who said, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise”—because this cross cannot be emptied—overturns that wisdom by the foolishness of preaching, through which believers are healed (1 Cor. I, 17, 19, 21).

For if natural possibility, through free will, is sufficient both to understand how one ought to live and to live well, then Christ died for nothing (Gal. II, 21); then the offense of the cross has been abolished.

Why should I not cry out here as well? Indeed, I will cry out, and with Christian grief rebuke these people: “You have been severed from Christ, you who are justified in nature; you have fallen away from grace” (ibid. V, 11, 4). For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish your own, you are not subject to God’s righteousness.

For just as Christ is the end of the law, so too Christ is the Savior of defective human nature, “for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 3–4).

## CHAPTER XLI

### 48. How “all” is to be understood in the Apostle’s words, which occasion the dispute.

As for the statement he brought against those whom he is addressing—“For all have sinned” (ibid. III, 23)—it is clear that the Apostle was speaking of those who existed at that time, namely Jews and Gentiles.

But the statement I mentioned—“Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned”—embraces both ancient and recent generations, ourselves and our descendants.

He also cites a testimony by which he attempts to prove that when “all” is said, it does not always have to be understood as absolutely everyone, with no one omitted. “Just as,” he says, “through one man’s offense there was condemnation for all, so also through one man’s righteousness there is justification of life for all.”

It is beyond doubt, he says, that through Christ’s righteousness not everyone has been sanctified, but only those who wished to obey him and were cleansed by the washing of his Baptism.

This testimony does not prove what he wants. For just as it says, “Through one man’s offense there was condemnation for all,” so that no one would be omitted, likewise in the statement that “through one man’s righteousness there is justification of life for all” (ibid. V, 18), no one is omitted—not because everyone believes in him and is washed in his Baptism, but because no one is justified except one who believes in him and is washed in his Baptism.

Thus “all” is said so that no one may in any way be believed capable of being saved by some means other than him. For just as, when one teacher of letters has been appointed in a city, we quite correctly say, “This man teaches everyone here to read and write”—not because all the citizens learn their letters, but because no one learns unless he teaches that person—so no one is justified except one whom Christ has justified.

## CHAPTER XLII

### 49. A human being can be without sin, but only with the assistance of grace. In the saints, possibility comes together with its realization.

“But suppose,” he says, “I agree that he testifies that everyone has been a sinner. He says what they were, not that they could not have been something else. Therefore, even if all human beings could be proved to have been sinners, this would in no way harm our definition, since we defend not so much what human beings are as what they could be.”

Here he does well to agree, at least sometimes, that “no living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. CXLII, 2) [Note: [Col. 0271] Two Vatican manuscripts read, “Here he does well” (*hoc recte facit*)].

Yet he insists that this is not the issue; rather, the issue is the very possibility of not sinning, and there is no need for us to contend with him about that. For I am not greatly concerned whether there have been, are, or could be here some people who have had, now have, or will have the perfect love of God, to which nothing could be added. For this love is the truest, fullest, and most perfect righteousness [Note: [Col. 0271] Most manuscripts read, “it is the truest,” omitting *enim*].

I confess and maintain that this can occur through the human will assisted by God’s grace [Note: [Col. 0271] Two Gallican manuscripts read “since in the human will,” omitting “that”]; I need not contend too fiercely about when, where, or in whom it occurs. Nor do I dispute the possibility itself, since, when the human will has been healed and aided, possibility itself comes to the saints together with its realization. This occurs when the love of God is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. V, 5), to the fullest extent that our sound and purified nature can receive it.

God’s cause is therefore better defended—for this is what he says he is doing when he claims to defend nature—when both the Creator and the Savior are acknowledged than when, by defending the creature as though it were sound and possessed unimpaired powers, the Savior’s help is rendered empty.

## CHAPTER XLIII

### 50. God does not command the impossible.

It is true that he says: “God, being as good as he is just, made such a human being [Note: [Col. 0271] Am. and Er. read “to whom” (*cui*)] that he was capable of being free from the evil of sin, if he had wished.”

For who does not know that the human being was made sound and blameless, established with free will and the unrestricted power to live justly?

But the discussion now concerns the man whom robbers left half-dead on the road. Struck and pierced by severe wounds, he cannot rise to the summit of righteousness in the way he was able to descend from it. Even if he is already in the inn, he is still being treated (Luke X, 30, 34).

God therefore does not command the impossible. Rather, by commanding, he admonishes us both to do what we can and to ask for what we cannot. Let us now see what he can do and what he cannot.

This author says: “What nature can do is not a matter of the will.” I reply: a human being is indeed not righteous by the will if nature can accomplish it; but medicine will be able to accomplish what the defect cannot.

## CHAPTER XLIV

[Col. 0272]

### 51. The state of the question between the Pelagians and Catholics. The ancient righteous were saved by the same faith in Christ as we are.

What need is there now to linger over many other matters? Let us come more deeply to the issue on which alone, or almost alone, we disagree with these people.

As he himself says, “It does not belong to the present discussion to ask whether there have been or are any people in this life without sin, but whether they could have been or can be without sin,” so I, even if I concede that there have been or are such people, nevertheless in no way affirm that they could have been or can be so except as justified by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, and him crucified.

The faith that saved the righteous of ancient times is the same faith that saves us: faith in the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus; faith in his blood, faith in his cross, faith in his death and resurrection. Since we have the same spirit of faith, we too believe, and therefore we speak (2 Cor. IV, 13).

### 52.

Let us now consider what answer he gives to the objection raised against him—a question that truly appears intolerable to Christian hearts.

He says: “But this is what troubles many, you will say: that you defend the possibility of a human being’s being without sin without the grace of God.”

Precisely this is what troubles us; precisely this is what we object to. He states the matter itself: this is exactly what we find most difficult to endure. We cannot, in the love that we have for others and for them, tolerate Christians discussing such things in this way.

Let us therefore hear how he escapes from the objection posed by this question. “O blindness of ignorance,” he says, “O sluggishness of an uneducated mind, which thinks that a thing is being defended without God’s grace when it hears that the thing is to be attributed to God alone!”

If we did not know what follows, merely hearing these words would lead us to think that we had believed false reports about them, spread by rumor and asserted by certain suitable brothers as reliable witnesses [Note: [Col. 0272] The Belgian manuscript of Saint-Amand reads, “and by certain suitable witnesses,” omitting “brothers”].

For what could have been said more briefly and more truly than that the possibility of not sinning, however great it is or will be in a human being, must be attributed to God alone? This is what we too say. Let us join right hands.

## CHAPTER XLV

### 53. Pelagius’s other analogies and arguments are examined. Should the remaining points be heard?

They certainly should be heard—and corrected or avoided.

“For when it is said,” he says, “that the power itself does not belong at all to human free choice but to the author of nature, namely God, how can it be understood apart from God’s grace when it is judged to belong properly to God?”

It is beginning to become clear what he means. But lest we be mistaken, he explains it more fully and clearly:

“But to make this more evident,” he says, “we must discuss it at somewhat greater length. For we say that the possibility of anything lies not so much in the power of human choice as in the necessity of nature.”

He illustrates what he means with examples or analogies:

“For example,” he says, “I can speak. The fact that I can speak is not mine; the fact that I speak is mine—that is, it belongs to my own will. And because the fact that I speak is mine, I can do either: speak or not speak. But because the fact that I can speak is not mine—that is, it does not belong to my choice and will—I must always be able to speak. And if I should wish not to be able to speak, I nevertheless cannot be unable to speak, unless perhaps I remove that member by which the function of speaking can be performed.”

Many things could indeed be said by which a person might deprive himself of the possibility of speaking without removing the member with which we speak. For example, something might happen that took away the voice itself, so that no one could speak while the members remained. The human voice is not a bodily member. Yet this could occur through some internal member being impaired, without that member being removed [Note: [Col. 0273] In the Paris edition of the *Polemicorum* of 1644: “No one could speak while the members remained—for the human voice is not a bodily member”—followed by “yet this can occur through some internal member being impaired,” and so forth].

But lest I seem to press the point verbally, and someone contentiously reply, “To impair something is also to remove it,” we can certainly bring this about by closing and fastening the mouth with bonds so firmly that we are entirely unable to open it. Nor would opening it then lie within our power, although closing it was within our power while the integrity and health of the members remained.

## CHAPTER XLVI

### 54. Necessity does not conflict with the choice of the will.

But what does this have to do with us? Let us see what he puts together next:

“For whatever is constrained by natural necessity,” he says, “is deprived of the choice and deliberation of the will.”

There is some difficulty here as well. It would be utterly absurd for us to say that our desire to be blessed does not belong to our will because we cannot altogether will not to be blessed, through some good constraint of nature. Nor do we dare say that God possesses not a will but a necessity for righteousness because he cannot will to sin.

## CHAPTER XLVII

### 55. The same argument is discussed.

Consider also what follows:

“This,” he says, “can likewise be understood of hearing, smell, and sight: hearing, smelling, and seeing are within our power, but the ability to hear, smell, or see is not within our power; rather, it consists in a natural necessity.”

Either I do not understand what he is saying, or he does not. For how is the possibility of seeing not within our power if the inability to see is within our power, since blindness is within our power and, if we wish, can deprive us of the ability to see?

On the other hand, how is seeing within our power if we wish, when, even with the integrity of the nature of our bodies and eyes preserved, we cannot see even when we wish—for example, at night, when the lights supplied from outside have been removed, or when someone shuts us up in a dark place?

Likewise, if whether we can hear or cannot hear is not within our power but is determined by the constraint of nature, while what we hear or do not hear belongs to our own will, why does he not consider how much we hear unwillingly—sounds that penetrate our senses even when our ears are blocked, such as the nearby screech of a saw or the grunting of a pig?

Indeed, blocking the ears shows that it is not within our power not to hear when our ears are open. Such blocking may perhaps even remove the sense itself, so that it is also within our power to be unable to hear.

As for smell, does he not pay too little attention [Note: [Col. 0274] Most manuscripts read: “what he says, unless he pays too little attention to what he says”] when he says that “the ability or inability to smell is not within our power, but that smelling or not smelling is within our power”—that is, within free will? Suppose we are placed amid strong and unpleasant odors, and someone leaves us there with our hands bound, while the integrity and health of our members remain entirely intact. We may wish not to smell, but we cannot do so, because when we are compelled to draw breath, we simultaneously inhale the odor we do not want.

## CHAPTER XLVIII
### 56. The assistance of grace in an unimpaired nature

As, then, these analogies are false, so also is the point for which he wished to employ them. For he goes on to say: “In the same way, therefore, what is meant by the possibility of not sinning must be understood as follows: that not sinning is ours, but being able not to sin is not ours.”

If he were speaking of the unimpaired and healthy nature of humanity—which we do not now possess (“For in hope we were saved; but hope which is seen is not hope; and if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” [Rom. 8:24–25])—even then he would not rightly say that merely not sinning is ours, although sinning would be ours. For even then there would be God’s assistance, and it would present itself to those willing, like light to healthy eyes, so that, assisted by it, they might see.

[Note: At Col. 0274 the printed books read “and there too there would be.”]

[Note: The reading was “to present itself.” On the authority of two Vatican manuscripts, “it would present itself” has been restored.]

But since he is discussing this present life, in which “the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” (Wis. 9:15), I wonder with what state of mind he supposes that, even without the assistance of the medicine of our Savior, not sinning is ours, while he maintains that the ability not to sin belongs to nature—a nature so plainly corrupted that it is itself a greater corruption not to see this.

## CHAPTER XLIX

### 57. Nothing is taken away from God’s omnipotence by the fact that He can neither sin, nor die, nor kill Himself

“Because not sinning,” he says, “is ours, we can sin and not sin.”

What if someone else were to say: “Because not wishing for unhappiness is ours, we can both not wish it and wish it”? [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “something” for “something else.”] Yet we absolutely cannot desire it. For who could in any way wish to be unhappy, even if he desires something else through which unhappiness overtakes him against his will?

Furthermore, since not sinning belongs much more properly to God, shall we dare to say of Him that He can both sin and not sin? Far be it from us to say that God can sin. For, as fools suppose, He will not therefore cease to be omnipotent because He can neither die nor deny Himself (2 Tim. 2:13).

What, then, is he saying, and by what rules of expression is he trying to persuade us of what he does not wish to consider? He adds further:

“Because, however, being able not to sin is not ours, if we wish not to be unable not to sin, we cannot be unable not to sin.”

He has expressed this awkwardly, and therefore rather obscurely. It could be stated more plainly in this way: “Because being able not to sin is not ours, whether we wish it or not, we are able not to sin.”

For he does not say: “Whether we wish it or not, we do not sin”; for without doubt we sin if we wish to. But nevertheless, whether we wish it or not, he asserts that we possess the possibility of not sinning, which he says has been implanted in nature.

It can tolerably be said of a man with sound feet that, whether he wishes it or not, he possesses the ability to walk; but if his feet are broken, he does not possess it even if he wishes to. The nature of which he speaks has been corrupted. “Why does earth and ashes boast?” (Sir. 10:9). It has been corrupted and implores a physician: “Save me, Lord,” it cries (Ps. 12:1); “Heal my soul,” it cries (Ps. 41:4).

Why does he obstruct these cries, so that, by defending a possibility as though it were present, he prevents future healing?

## CHAPTER L

### 58. Grace is attacked even by those who are pious and fear God

And observe what he adds, by which he thinks that claim is confirmed:

“No will can take away what is proved to be inseparably implanted in nature.”

Whence, then, comes the statement: “So that you may not do the things you wish” (Gal. 5:17)? Whence also this: “For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I hate, this I do”? Where is the possibility that is proved to be inseparably implanted in nature?

Behold, people do not do what they wish. And he was certainly speaking about not sinning, not about flying, since they were human beings, not birds. Behold, a person does not do the good he wishes, but does the evil he does not wish; willing is present to him, but accomplishing the good is not present (Rom. 7:15, 18). Where is the possibility that is proved to be inseparably implanted in nature?

Let him transform anyone he wishes into himself, if the Apostle is not saying these things about himself; certainly he is transforming a human being into himself. Yet this man maintains that human nature itself possesses an inseparable possibility of not sinning.

But by these words—although the speaker does not know it, while the one who suggests that such things be said to the unwary, including those who fear God, does know it—the result is that the grace of Christ is emptied, while human nature is made to appear sufficient for its own righteousness.

[Note: A number of Gallican manuscripts read “so that the cross of Christ may be emptied.”]

## CHAPTER LI

### 59. In what sense Pelagius attributed the possibility of not sinning to God’s grace

To avoid the hostility aroused by Christians who cry out for their salvation and say, “Why do you say that a person can refrain from sinning without the assistance of God’s grace?” he says:

[Note: Here the printed editions add “also.”]

“The very possibility of not sinning lies not so much in the power of free choice as in the necessity of nature.”

Whatever is placed in the necessity of nature is undoubtedly regarded as belonging to the author of nature, namely, God. How, then, he asks, can something be thought to be asserted without God’s grace when it is shown to belong properly to God?

The hidden meaning has been made explicit; it can no longer be concealed. He attributes the possibility of not sinning to God’s grace because God is the author of the nature into which he says the possibility of not sinning has been inseparably implanted.

“When he wills, therefore, he does it; because when he does not will, he does not do it.”

[Note: This is the reading of the old Cygirannensis codex. The Amiens, Erasmus, and Louvain editions read “may do it”; other manuscripts agree, three Vatican manuscripts continuing: “because when he does not will, he does not do it.”]

For where there is an inseparable possibility, weakness of will—or rather, the will’s dependence and need of perfection—cannot befall it.

If this is so, whence comes the statement: “Willing is present, but accomplishing the good is not present”? For if the author of this book were speaking of that human nature which was originally created unimpaired and healthy, this statement might in some measure be accepted. Yet that nature ought not to be said to possess an inseparable possibility—that is, so to speak, an unlosable possibility—if it could be corrupted and require a physician to heal the eyes of the blind and restore the possibility of seeing that had been lost through blindness.

For I suppose that a blind person wishes to see, but cannot. If he wishes and cannot, the will is present, but the possibility has been lost.

[Note: The Louvain edition adds here *potuit* (“was able”).]

## CHAPTER LII

### 60. The same argument considered

Observe further what great masses he attempts to break through, in order to advance his position, if only he could do so. For he raises an objection against himself, saying:

“But the flesh is opposed to us, according to the Apostle” (Gal. 5:17), you will say.

Then he replies:

“How can it happen that the flesh is opposed to any baptized person, when according to the same Apostle he is understood not to be in the flesh? For he says: ‘But you are not in the flesh’” (Rom. 8:9).

It is good that he says that the flesh cannot be opposed to the baptized; whether this is true we shall see later (in the following chapter). But for the moment, because he could not entirely forget that he was a Christian, though he remembered it only faintly, he withdrew from his defense of nature.

Where, then, is the inseparability of the possibility? Perhaps those who have not yet been baptized are not included in human nature? Here—precisely here—he could awaken, if he paid attention, and he can do so.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “awaken”; the printed editions read “keep watch.”]

“How can it happen,” he says, “that the flesh is opposed to any baptized person?”

Therefore the flesh can be opposed to those who are not baptized. Let him explain how, since they too possess that nature which he has defended so vigorously. Certainly he either admits that nature to be corrupted in them, if the wounded man has already left the inn healed in the case of the baptized, or if he is healthy in the inn to which the merciful Samaritan brought him for healing (Luke 10:30–35).

Moreover, if he grants even to these people that the flesh is opposed to them, let him say what has happened, since both—the flesh and the spirit—are creatures of one and the same Creator, and are without doubt good because He is good. Unless the explanation is that this is the fault inflicted by the will’s own choice; and that, in order for it to be healed in nature, there is need of the very Savior by whom nature was established as Creator.

If we acknowledge that this Savior, and that medicine of his by which “the Word became flesh so that he might dwell among us” (John 1:14), is necessary for the little and the great—that is, from infants’ cries to the gray hairs of old age—then the whole controversy in this question is dissolved.

## CHAPTER LIII

### 61. What grace of God is being discussed here; the ungodly person is not freed from desire even at death

Now let us see whether the flesh is also said to be opposed to the baptized. I ask to whom the Apostle was speaking when he said:

“The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another, so that you may not do the things you wish” (Gal. 5:17).

He wrote this, I believe, to the Galatians, to whom he says:

“Therefore, does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works miracles among you do so from works of the law, or from hearing with faith?” (Gal. 3:5).

Thus it is evident that he is speaking to Christians, and to those to whom God had given the Spirit; therefore, also to the baptized.

Behold, the flesh is found to be opposed even to the baptized, and that possibility which he says has been inseparably implanted in nature is absent. [Note: Four Vatican manuscripts read “this” for “that.”] Where is his statement: “How can it happen that the flesh is opposed to any baptized person”?

However he understands “flesh”—for in truth it is not the good substance of nature that is called flesh here, but the carnal vices—nevertheless, even the baptized have the flesh opposed to them. And how is it opposed? So that they do not do what they wish.

Behold, the will is present in a person. Where is that possibility belonging to nature? Let us acknowledge that grace is necessary and cry out: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?” And let the answer be given to us: “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24–25).

### 62. The grace by which humanity is created is not the issue, but the grace by which it is saved

When it is rightly said to such people, “Why do you say that a person can be without sin without the assistance of God’s grace?” the question is not about that grace by which humanity was created, but about this grace by which it is saved through Jesus Christ our Lord.

For the faithful pray: “Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13). If the possibility is present, why do they pray? Or from what evil do they pray to be delivered, if not especially from “this body of death”? From this, only the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord delivers.

It is not from the substance of the body, which is good, but from carnal vices; and a person is not delivered from these without the grace of the Savior—not even when, through bodily death, he departs from the body.

And to make this point, what had the Apostle said above?

“I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. 7:23).

Behold the defect of human nature inflicted by the disobedience of the will. Let him be permitted to pray, so that he may be healed. Why is so much presumed about nature’s possibility? It has been wounded, injured, afflicted, and lost; it requires true confession, not false defense.

Let the grace of God be sought—not the grace by which nature is established, but that by which it is restored. He alone declares this grace unnecessary, though he does so by remaining silent. [Note: The printed editions read “answers”; the manuscripts more correctly read “answered.”] If he had said absolutely nothing about God’s grace, nor proposed that question for himself to resolve in order to remove from himself the hostility regarding it, he might have been thought to hold what the truth requires, but not to have said it, since not everything must be said everywhere.

But he proposed the question of grace and answered it according to what he held in his heart. The question has been settled—not as we wished, but in a way that shows what he thought when we were uncertain.

## CHAPTER LIV

### 63. A hypothetical dialogue

Then, with many words from the Apostle, he attempts to show—on a point about which there is no controversy—that “the flesh is so often named by him that he wishes it to be understood not as substance, but as the works of the flesh.”

What has this to do with the matter? The vices of the flesh are opposed to the human will; nature is not accused, but a physician is sought for the vices.

What is the point of his asking, “Who made the human spirit?” and answering himself, “Without doubt, God”? He likewise asks, “Who created the flesh?” and answers again, “The same, I believe, God.” A third time he asks, “Is the God who created both good?” and replies, “No one doubts it.” He asks further, “And is each thing that a good author created good?” and answers this as well: “It must be confessed.”

Then he concludes:

“If, therefore, both the spirit is good and the flesh is good, as having been created by a good author, how can two good things be opposed to one another?”

I omit saying that his entire argument would be thrown into confusion if someone asked him, “Who made heat and cold?” He would answer, “Without doubt, God.” I do not ask many questions. Let him himself conclude whether these things can either be called not good or fail to appear opposed to one another.

Perhaps here he will say: “These are qualities of substances, not substances.” That is true. But they are natural qualities and undoubtedly belong to God’s creation. Substances are said to be opposed to one another—not in themselves, but through their qualities—as water and fire are said to be opposed.

What if flesh and spirit are like this? We do not affirm that they are; but we have said it to show that his argument does not reach its conclusion by a necessary inference.

For opposites can also fail to oppose one another and instead be tempered by one another and produce good health, as dryness and moisture, cold and heat, through the proper balance of all of which bodily health consists.

But that the flesh is opposed to the spirit, so that we do not do what we wish, is a defect, not nature. Let medicinal grace be sought, and let the controversy end.

### 64. The contradiction in applying this argument to the unbaptized

How, then, can these two good things, created by the good God, be opposed to one another in unbaptized people, contrary to his argument? Or will he regret having said this as well, speaking under some impulse of Christian faith?

When he said, “How can it happen that the flesh is opposed to any person already baptized?” he indicated that the flesh can be opposed to the unbaptized. For why did he add “already baptized,” when he could have said without that addition, “How can it happen that the flesh is opposed to anyone,” and then supplied his argument to prove it—that both are good, created by the good God, and therefore cannot be opposed to one another?

If, then, the unbaptized, to whom he certainly admits that the flesh is opposed, press him with his own questions and say:

“Who made the human spirit?”

He will answer: “God.”

They will likewise ask him:

“Who created the flesh?”

He will answer: “The same, I believe, God.”

They will ask him a third time:

“Is the God who created both good?”

And he will reply: “No one doubts it.”

Then let them ask the one remaining question:

“Is each thing that the good author created good?”

He will confess that it is.

Then they will cut his throat with his own sword, bringing forward his conclusion and saying:

“If, therefore, the spirit is good and the flesh is good, as having been created by the good author, how can two good things be opposed to one another?”

Perhaps then he will answer:

“Forgive me, for I ought not to have said that the flesh cannot be opposed to any baptized person, thereby admitting that it is opposed to you unbaptized people. I ought instead to have said without exception that the flesh is opposed to no one.”

Behold the predicament into which he brings himself. Behold what the man says who does not wish to cry out with the Apostle:

“Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

“But why,” he says, “should I cry out, since I am already baptized in Christ? Let those cry out who have not yet received such a benefit, if indeed they say even this.”

But this defense of nature does not permit even them to cry out in these words. For nature is not present in the baptized while absent from the unbaptized.

Or, if he grants that it is corrupted even in them, so that they rightly cry out, “Wretched man, who will deliver me from this body of death?” and are helped by what follows, “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord,” then at last let him concede that human nature requires Christ the physician.

## CHAPTER LV

### 65. “The body of death” is said of a defect, not of substance

I ask, then, where nature lost that freedom which it longs to have given back to it when it says, “Who will deliver me?” [Note: Several manuscripts read “this” for “that.”] For the one who says that he desires to be delivered from “this body of death” is not accusing the substance of the flesh; the nature of the body, like that of the soul, must also be attributed to God as the good author. Rather, he is speaking of the body’s vices.

Death separates the body from the body; but the vices contracted from it remain attached, and to them a just punishment is due—a punishment which the rich man also encountered in hell (Luke 16:22–26).

The one who says, “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” could certainly not deliver himself from this. Wherever nature lost that freedom, the possibility belonging to nature is certainly inseparable. It possesses the ability through natural support; it possesses the will through free choice. Why, then, does it seek the sacrament of Baptism?

Is it because of past offenses, so that only those things may be forgiven which cannot be made not to have happened? Leave the man alone; let him cry out what he was crying out. For he desires not merely to be rendered immune from punishment for past sins through pardon, but also to be strong and capable thereafter of not sinning.

“For I delight in the law of God according to the inner person, but I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind.” He sees that it exists; he does not remember that it once existed. He is pressed by present things, not recalling past ones.

Nor does he merely see it warring against him; he also sees it taking him captive under the law of sin which is in his members—not which was in them. This is why he cries out:

“Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?”

Let him be permitted to pray; let him be permitted to implore the help of the most powerful physician. What is being opposed? What is being shouted down? Why is the wretched man forbidden to seek Christ’s mercy—and forbidden by Christians at that?

Those who were walking with Christ also tried to prevent the blind man from seeking light by crying out. Yet amid the tumult of those who opposed him, he heard the one crying out (Mark 10:46–52). To this man, therefore, the answer was given:

“The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

[Note: The printed editions read “the blind men.” The manuscripts, which read “the blind man,” should be followed, in accordance with Mark 10; or else the text should subsequently read “he hears them crying out,” not, as in the printed editions, the singular “he hears him crying out.”]

### 66. The unbaptized should also implore the Savior’s grace

Moreover, if we obtain even this from them—that the unbaptized should implore the help of the Savior’s grace—that is certainly not a small victory against that false defense of nature and of free choice as self-sufficient. For a person who says, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me?” is not self-sufficient; nor can someone be said to possess complete freedom who still asks to be delivered.

## CHAPTER LVI

### The same argument considered

Nevertheless, let us also examine whether those who have been baptized do the good things they wish, with no desire of the flesh opposing them.

But he himself recalls what we should say about this when, concluding this passage, he says:

“As we have said, the passage containing the words ‘the flesh desires against the spirit’ must necessarily be understood not of the substance of the flesh, but of the works of the flesh.”

We say the same: it is spoken not of the substance of the flesh, but of the works that proceed from carnal desire—that is, from sin—concerning which he commanded that it should not reign in our mortal body, so as to obey its desires (Rom. 6:12).

## CHAPTER LVII

### 67. Who is said to be under the law

But let him also observe that it was said to the baptized:

“The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you may not do the things you wish.”

And lest he make them sluggish by this struggle itself, or appear by this statement to have given them license to sin, he adds:

“But if you are led by the Spirit, you are no longer under the law” (Gal. 5:17–18).

A person is under the law when, through fear of the punishment threatened by the law, rather than through love of righteousness, he feels himself abstaining from the act of sin, still not free and not detached from the will to sin. For he is guilty in that very will, by which he would prefer, if it were possible, that there were nothing to fear, so that he might freely do what he secretly desires.

“Therefore, if you are led by the Spirit,” he says, “you are no longer under the law”—certainly the law that instills fear but does not bestow love, “the love of God poured out in our hearts,” not through the letter of the law but “through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

This is the law of freedom, not of slavery, since it is the law of love, not of fear. Concerning it the Apostle James also says: “But whoever looks intently into the perfect law of freedom” (James 1:25).

Thus that man was no longer terrified by God’s law as a slave, but delighted in it according to the inner person; nevertheless, he still saw another law in his members warring against the law of his mind.

So here also: “If you are led by the Spirit,” he says, “you are no longer under the law.” To the extent that a person is led by the Spirit, he is not under the law; to the extent that he delights in God’s law, he is not under the law’s fear. For “fear has torment” (1 John 4:18), not delight.

## CHAPTER LVIII

### 68. The same argument considered

Accordingly, if we think correctly, just as we ought to give thanks for healed members, so we ought to pray for those that are to be healed, so that we may enjoy the most complete health, to which nothing can be added, the perfect sweetness of God, and full freedom.

We do not deny that human nature can be without sin; nor should we deny in any way that it can be perfected. We do not deny its ability to make progress, but we attribute its perfection to the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. We say that, with his help, it becomes righteous and blessed—by him who created it so that it might exist.

Thus the objection that some people say is brought against him is easily refuted: “The devil opposes us.”

To this objection we answer with precisely the words he himself answered:

“Let us resist him, and he will flee. ‘Resist the devil,’ says the blessed Apostle, ‘and he will flee from you’” (James 4:7). “From this it must be understood what power can harm those from whom he flees, or what virtue he must be understood to possess, since he can prevail only over those who do not resist.”

These are also my words, for nothing could be said more truly. But the difference between us and these people is that when we resist the devil, we not only do not deny that God’s help must be sought; we also proclaim it. They, however, attribute such power to the will that they take prayer away from piety.

For it is precisely so that we may resist the devil and he may flee from us that we pray:

“Lead us not into temptation” (Matt. 6:13).

For this reason also we have been admonished, as though by a commander exhorting his soldiers:

“Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Mark 14:38).

## CHAPTER LIX

### 69. The same argument considered

As for his argument against those who say, “Who would not wish to be without sin, if this lay within human power?”—he argues correctly that by this very statement they confess that it is not impossible, since either many or all wish it.

But let him confess from what source this is possible, and there will be peace. For this is the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, by which he nowhere wished to say that we are helped when we pray not to sin.

If perhaps he secretly believes this, let him forgive those who suspect otherwise. He himself causes this suspicion: though he suffers so much hostility on this matter, he wishes to be understood as holding this view, but does not wish to confess or openly declare it.

What great difficulty would it have been for him to say this, especially since he had undertaken to discuss and explain the matter as though it were an objection raised by his opponents?

Why did he wish to defend nature alone there, and assert that because humanity was created in such a way that it could refrain from sinning if it did not wish to sin, the possibility belonging to that creation should therefore be attributed to God’s grace? Why did he refuse to say anything about the fact that human nature itself, through the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, is either healed because it has been corrupted or assisted because it is not sufficient for itself?

## CHAPTER LX

### 70. Whether anyone can live without sin in this life

Whether there has been, is, or can be anyone in this world who lives so righteously as to possess absolutely no sin may be a question among true and devout Christians. But whoever doubts that this can be the case after this life is foolish.

Yet I do not wish to dispute even about this present life. Although it does not seem to me that the statement “No living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 143:2), or similar passages, can be understood otherwise, nevertheless, would that it could be shown [Note: The printed editions read “yet”; this is corrected from the manuscripts.] either that these testimonies can be better understood in another way, or that perfect and complete righteousness, to which nothing at all remains to be added, has existed in someone yesterday while he was living in this body, exists today, and will exist tomorrow.

This could be granted provided that far more people remain those who, while not doubting that they need to say truthfully until the last day of this life, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12), nevertheless trust that their hope in Christ and in his promises is true, certain, and firm.

Yet those who deny that, only with the help of the grace of Christ the Savior crucified and by the gift of his Spirit, anyone can reach either the fullest perfection or any degree whatsoever of genuine and godly righteousness—I do not know whether they can rightly be counted among any kind of Christians.

## CHAPTER LXI

### 71. He answers the testimonies of Catholic writers that Pelagius had produced on his own behalf: Lactantius, Hilary, Ambrose, and Jerome

[Note: Lactantius is the author from whom Pelagius drew his first testimonies.]

Accordingly, the testimonies that he quoted—not from the canonical Scriptures, but from certain short works of Catholic interpreters—intending to answer those who would say that he alone defended these positions, are so inconclusive that they are neither against our position nor against his own.

Among them he also wished to insert something from my books, counting me as someone who seemed worthy of being mentioned with those writers. I should therefore not be ungrateful; and, with the greater affection of a friend, I would not wish him to be mistaken, since he has conferred this honor upon me.

As for the first passages he quoted, since I did not find the name of the person who said them there—either because that person did not write them, or because the copy you sent did not contain the name owing perhaps to some scribal error—what need is there to discuss them?

Especially since, being free regarding the writings of any such persons—for I owe unreserved assent only to the canonical Scriptures—I am not troubled [Note: A Sorbonne manuscript reads “I am troubled”; the Amiens, Erasmus, and Louvain editions read “I am not troubled.”] by what he quoted from the writings of one whose name I did not find there:

“It was necessary that the teacher and instructor of virtue should become like a human being, so that by conquering sin he might teach humanity that it could conquer sin” [Note: The printed editions read “virtues”; the manuscripts read “virtue.”] (Lactantius, *Institutes*, book 4, chapters 24–25).

How this was said, let the author of the statement see how it can be explained. We, meanwhile, have no doubt that Christ did not have sin in himself for him to conquer, since he was born in the likeness of sinful flesh, not in sinful flesh.

He quoted another statement by the same writer as follows:

“And again, by subduing the desires of the flesh, he was to teach that sinning is not a matter of necessity but of intention and will.”

I understand “the desires of the flesh”—if unlawful desires are not meant there—to refer to things such as hunger, thirst, relief from weariness, and anything of that kind. Through these things some people fall into sins, although the things themselves are blameless. This was absent from the Savior, even though, as the Gospel testifies, we see that such things existed in him because of the likeness of sinful flesh.

[Note: Erasmus, the Amiens edition, and several manuscripts read “but of one’s own will.”]

## CHAPTER LXII

### 72. Doing and perfecting righteousness

The blessed Hilary, whose words he quoted, says:

“For only when we have been perfected by the Spirit and transformed into immortality—a state ordained for those who are pure in heart—shall we behold that which is immortal in God” (Hilary, on Matthew 5: “Blessed are the pure in heart”).

I do not know what he said here against our position, or how it assists this man, except that he testified that a person can be pure in heart. Who denies that? But this occurs through the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, not through free choice alone.

Likewise, in recalling that Hilary said:

“What writings of Job had he read, so that he might abstain from every evil thing? Because he worshiped God with his mind alone, free from vices; but to worship God is the proper duty of righteousness”—

Hilary said what Job did, not what he perfected in this world, nor what he either did or perfected without the grace of the Savior, whom he also prophesied.

Even someone who has sin can abstain from every evil thing if he does not permit sin to reign in him, though a reprehensible thought may steal upon him and he does not permit it to reach the completion of an act.

But it is one thing not to have sin and another not to obey its desires. It is one thing to fulfill the commandment “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17), and another, through a certain effort of abstinence, at least to do what is likewise written: “Do not follow your desires” (Sir. 18:30).
