Yet he knows that he can rightly do none of this without the grace of the Savior.

To do righteousness, therefore, is to struggle in the true worship of God in an inner conflict against the inner evil of desire. To perfect it is to have no adversary at all.

The one who fights is still in danger and is sometimes struck, even if he is not knocked down. But the one who has no adversary rejoices in complete peace.

And the one in whom no sin dwells is most truly said to be without sin—not the one who says, through abstaining from an evil act, “It is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me” (Rom. 7:20).

### 73. Job’s confession and Hilary’s testimony

Job himself does not remain silent about his sins. It is rightly pleasing to this friend of yours that humility should in no way be placed on the side of falsehood. [Note: Four Vatican and the Gallican manuscripts read “our friend.” The reading “your friend” is preferable: Augustine refers to Timasius and James.] Therefore, because Job is a truthful worshiper of God, he certainly makes a truthful confession of what he confesses.

When Hilary himself was explaining the passage of the Psalm where it is written, “You have rejected all who depart from your ordinances,” he said:

“For if God rejected sinners, he would reject everyone, since no one is without sin. But he rejects those who depart from him, whom they call apostates” (Hilary, on Psalm 118 [119]).

You see how he did not say, “because no one was without sin,” as though speaking of the past, but “because no one is without sin.” As I said, I do not dispute this.

For whoever refuses to yield to the Apostle John—who himself does not say, “If we say that we have not had sin,” but “if we say that we do not have sin” (1 John 1:8)—how will he yield to Bishop Hilary?

I cry out for the grace of Christ, without which no one is justified, against the claim that nature’s free choice is sufficient by itself. Indeed, Hilary himself cries out for that grace. Let him be obeyed when he says:

“Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

[Note: Some printed editions read “let him be believed.”]

## CHAPTER LXIII

### 74. He brings forward other testimonies of Ambrose

Saint Ambrose, in the passage that this man cites, truly resists those who say that a person cannot be without sin in this life.

In order to say these things, Ambrose took his occasion from Zechariah and Elizabeth, who are mentioned in the Gospel as having walked in all the ordinances of the law blamelessly. Yet does he deny that this is accomplished through the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord?

There is no doubt that the righteous lived by this faith even before Christ’s Passion. He grants the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, through whom love is poured into our hearts; and all who are righteous are righteous through this love alone.

The bishop mentioned above also admonishes us to obtain this Spirit through prayers—so that the will, when it is not divinely assisted, is plainly insufficient—when he says in his hymn:

> And by diligent vows he grants  
>  
> that we may be worthy of the Holy Spirit.

[Note: The Louvain edition alone among nearly all the editions reads “he persists.”]

[Note: This Ambrosian hymn is sung by the Cistercian monks at Terce on Palm Sunday and on the days immediately following.]

75. I too shall mention something from this very work of Saint Ambrose, from which he has cited what he thought worth mentioning. “It seemed,” he says, “to me.” It may not have seemed so to him alone, since he declares that it seemed so to him. For it seemed so not merely by human will, but as it pleased him who, he says, speaks in me—Christ [Note: [Col. 0284] Four Vatican manuscripts read, “the Spirit”—who works so that what is good may also seem good to us. For he has mercy on whom he wills, and calls him. And therefore whoever follows Christ, when asked why he wished to become a Christian, can answer, ‘It seemed so to me.’ When he says this, he does not deny that it seemed so to God; for the will of human beings is prepared by God. Thus, for God to be honored by a holy person is the grace of God.”

Behold what he understands, if he takes pleasure in Ambrose’s words: that the will of human beings is prepared by God, and that it is no great question who is perfected, or when, provided that it is in no way doubted that this cannot occur without the grace of Christ. Moreover, how much would it have mattered if he had paid attention to a single sentence of the words of Ambrose that he quoted. For after Ambrose had said:

“For since the Church has been gathered from the Gentiles, that is, from sinners, how can she be immaculate if she is made from the defiled, unless first, through the grace of Christ, she is washed from sin, and then, through the quality of not sinning, she abstains from sins?”

he added what it is apparent that this man did not wish to add. For Ambrose said:

“Nor is she immaculate from the beginning; for this is impossible for human nature. But through the grace of God and through her own quality, since she now does not sin, she comes to appear immaculate” (Ambrose, on chapter 1 of Luke).

Who does not understand why he did not add these words? What is being accomplished now in this [Col. 0285] age is precisely that the holy Church may reach that most immaculate purity which all the saints desire. In the age to come, she will lead the purest life in divine eternity, neither having any evil persons mingled with her nor having any law of sin within her resisting the law of the mind.

Yet let him attend to what Bishop Ambrose said according to the Scriptures: “Nor is she immaculate from the beginning; for this is impossible for human nature.” For by “from the beginning” he certainly means the state in which we are born from Adam. Adam himself, without doubt, was made immaculate; but among those who are by nature children of wrath, deriving from him what was corrupted in him, he defined it as impossible for human nature to be immaculate from the beginning.

## CHAPTER LXIV

### 76. The same argument discussed

Likewise John, Bishop of Constantinople, whose statement he quoted, says that sin is not a substance but a malicious act. Who denies this? And because it is not natural, he therefore says that a law was given against it, and that it descends from freedom of choice. Who denies this either? But the matter now concerns human nature, which has been corrupted; it also concerns the grace of God [Note: [Col. 0285] The printed editions read: “But the matter does not concern human nature, which exists in this life; rather, it concerns the grace of God.” The manuscripts correct this reading.] by which it is healed through Christ the physician. It would not need him if it were healthy; yet this man defends it as able not to sin, as though it were healthy, or as though the freedom of its will were sufficient for itself.

77. What Christian, likewise, is unaware of what he reports that the most blessed Sixtus, bishop of the Roman Church and martyr of the Lord, said [Note: [Col. 0285] The words which Pelagius himself presented as belonging to Sixtus, bishop and martyr of Rome, Augustine later learned, from his reading—perhaps Jerome’s letter to Ctesiphon—that they belonged to the philosopher Sextus, a Pythagorean. Jerome, exposing this error, attributes its source to Rufinus.]:

“Because God allowed human beings the freedom of their choice, so that by living purely and without sin they might become like God”?

But it belongs to that very choice to hear and believe the one who calls, and to ask from the one in whom one believes for help not to sin. For he certainly says that they will become like God. They will become like God through the love of God, which has been poured into our hearts—not through the possibility of nature, nor through the free choice that is in us, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

And when the same martyr says, “A pure mind is a holy temple for God, and a clean and sinless heart is the best altar for him,” who does not know that a clean heart is to be brought to this perfection while the inner person is renewed day by day—not, however, without the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord? Likewise, when he himself says, “A chaste and sinless person has received from God the power to be a child of God,” he certainly gave this warning: when someone has become so chaste and sinless—for the question of where and when this is accomplished is open to some discussion, though among devout people it is properly investigated, and among them it is nevertheless agreed both that it can occur and that it cannot occur without the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus—then, as I had begun to say, Sixtus wisely warned that when someone has become such a person, and is thereby rightly counted among the children of God, he must not think that the power was his own, although he received it by the grace of God. For he did not possess it in his nature, which had already been corrupted and depraved, just as we read in the Gospel: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12). They were certainly not children of God by nature, nor would they be so at all unless, by receiving him, they had received through his grace this kind of power. This is the power which the strength of love claims for itself—a power that is not in us except through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.

## CHAPTER LXV

### 78. The same argument discussed

But when the venerable presbyter Jerome said, in the passages which he is reported to have spoken while expounding what is written, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God”: “Those whom no consciousness of sin accuses”; and added: “The pure in heart sees the Pure; the temple of God cannot be polluted” (Jerome, on chapter 5 of Matthew)—this is certainly what is being pursued among us by striving, laboring, praying, and obtaining, so that through the grace of God we may be brought through Jesus Christ our Lord to that perfection in which we can behold God with a pure heart.

Likewise, when he reports that the aforementioned presbyter said, “God created us with free choice, and we are dragged by necessity neither toward virtue nor toward vice; otherwise, where there is necessity, there is no crown” (Jerome, Against Jovinianus, book 2), who does not recognize this? Who does not embrace it with his whole heart? Who would deny that human nature was created otherwise? But in doing what is right there is no bond of necessity precisely because there is freedom of love [Note: [Col. 0286] The editions of Amerbach and Erasmus read, “because love exists.”].

## CHAPTER LXVI

### 79. A certain necessity of sinning

Return, then, to the apostolic statement: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5). By whom, unless by the one who ascended on high, led captivity captive, and gave gifts to human beings (Ephesians 4:8)?

But since a certain necessity of sinning arises from the vices of nature, not from the condition in which nature was created, let a person listen and learn to say to God, so that this same necessity may not exist: “Bring me out of my necessities” (Psalm 24:17). For in such prayer also there is a struggle against the tempter, who fights against us by means of that very necessity. Therefore, with grace assisting us through Jesus Christ our Lord, both the evil necessity will be removed and full freedom will be granted.

## CHAPTER LXVII

### 80. Just as diseases, so sins, are avoided in two ways

Let us come to our own writings. “Again,” he says, “Bishop Augustine says in his books On Free Choice: Whatever this cause of the will may be, if it cannot be resisted, one yields to it without sin; but if it can be resisted, one must not yield to it, and one will not sin. Or does it deceive the unwary? Then let him beware lest he be deceived. Or is it such a great deception that it cannot be avoided at all? If that is so, then there are no sins. For who sins in something that cannot possibly be avoided? Yet people do sin; therefore it can be avoided.”

I recognize these words: they are mine. But let him also deign to recognize everything that was said above. For the subject is the grace of God, which assists us as medicine through the Mediator, not the impossibility of righteousness. Therefore resistance can be made to that cause, whatever it may be—certainly it can. For in [the text is corrupt: “Possidius”] we ask for this assistance when we say, “Do not bring us into temptation.” We would not ask for this assistance if we believed that resistance were altogether impossible.

Sin can be avoided, with the help of him who cannot be deceived. Indeed, this too belongs to avoiding sin: if we truthfully say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12–13). For bodily disease is also avoided in two ways: so that it does not occur, and so that, if it occurs, it may quickly be healed. To prevent it, let us take care by saying, “Do not bring us into temptation”; so that it may quickly be healed, let us take care by saying, “Forgive us our debts.” Whether, therefore, it threatens or is already present, it can be avoided [Note: [Col. 0287] See Retractations, book 1, chapter 9, sections 5–6.].

81. But so that my view on this matter may be sufficiently clear not only to him but also to those who have not read my books On Free Choice, which he has read, and who perhaps read this work without having read those books, I ought to quote from those very books what he would have included in his own writings if he held the same view. No controversy between us on this matter would then remain.

Immediately after the words of mine that he quoted, I added what might have occurred to him, and treated the matter as fully as I could, saying:

“And yet certain acts committed through ignorance are also disapproved and judged to require correction, as we read in the divine authorities.”

Then, introducing examples, I also spoke about weakness, saying:

“There are also acts done under necessity which are to be disapproved, when a person wishes to do what is right and cannot. For where do those words come from: ‘For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I hate, that I do’?”

And, after citing other testimonies of the divine writings to the same effect:

“But all these,” I said, “are the voices of human beings coming from that condemnation of death. For if this is not the punishment of humanity but its nature, then none of these things are sins.”

Then, a little later:

“It remains, therefore,” I said, “that this just punishment comes from the condemnation of humanity. Nor is it surprising that, either through ignorance, a person does not have freedom of will to choose what he should rightly do, or that, when a carnal habit resists him—a habit which, through the violence of mortal succession, has in a certain way naturally grown strong—he sees what ought rightly to be done and wishes to do it, yet cannot accomplish it. For this is the most just punishment of sin: that each person lose what he refused to use well, although he could have used it without any difficulty if he had wished. That is, the person who knowingly does not do what is right loses the knowledge of what is right; and the person who, although able to do what is right, refused to do so, loses the ability to do it when he wishes.

“For there are truly two punitive conditions in every sinful soul: ignorance and difficulty. From ignorance comes the disgrace of error; from difficulty comes the affliction of torment. But to approve falsehoods as truths, so that one errs unwillingly, and to be unable to refrain from lustful acts because of the carnal bond that resists and torments one with pain, is not the nature in which humanity was created, but the punishment of one condemned. When we speak of free will for doing what is right, we are speaking of that condition in which the human being was created.”

From this point, then, the following answer was given to human beings who, because the vices of ignorance and difficulty had been transmitted and infused into their offspring from the first human being, were presenting what seemed a just complaint:

“To them,” I said, “a brief answer is given, so that they may be silent and cease murmuring against God. They might perhaps rightly complain if no human being ever emerged victorious over error and lust. But since the one who calls back the person who has turned away, teaches the believer, comforts the one who hopes, exhorts the one who loves, helps the one who strives, and hears the one who prays, is everywhere present in many ways through creation serving its Lord, it is not counted against you as guilt that you are ignorant unwillingly, but that you neglect to seek what you do not know. Nor is it counted against you that you do not bind up wounded limbs, but that you disdain the one who wishes to heal you.”

Thus I exhorted people, as far as I could, to live rightly, and I did not nullify the grace of God, without which human nature, already darkened and corrupted, cannot be enlightened and healed. The whole controversy with these people concerns this matter: that we not frustrate the grace of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord, by a perverse defense of nature.

Concerning this nature I also said a little later (On Free Choice, book 3, sections 50–54):

“We use the word ‘nature’ in two different ways when speaking precisely. In one sense we mean human nature as it was when the first human being was created blameless in his kind; in another sense we mean the condition in which we are born, ignorant and subject to the flesh, as the punishment of that condemned person. In this sense the Apostle says, ‘For we too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest’” (Ephesians 2:3).

## CHAPTER LXVIII

### 82. How people are to be exhorted to faith, repentance, and progress

If, then, we wish to rouse and kindle minds that are cold and sluggish toward right living through Christian exhortations, let us first exhort them to the faith by which they become Christians and submit to his name, without which they cannot be saved.

But if they are already Christians and neglect to live rightly, let them be chastened by fear and lifted up by praise of rewards. Let us take care, however, to remember to exhort them not only to good works but also to devout prayers, and to instruct them in this sound doctrine: once they have begun to live well, they should give thanks to God for having done something without difficulty; and whenever they experience some difficulty, they should persist in obtaining from the Lord, through the most faithful and persevering prayers and ready works of mercy, the ability to act with ease.

As for those who make progress in this way, I am not greatly concerned about where or when they are perfected in the fullest righteousness. Wherever and whenever they are perfected, I affirm that they can be perfected only by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

Certainly, when they clearly discover that they have no sin, they must not say that they have no sin [Note: [Col. 0288] Amerbach, Erasmus, and some more recent editions of the Polemical Works read, “that they do not have sin,” an obvious error.], lest the truth not be in them. The truth is not in those who, although they have sin, say that they do not.

## CHAPTER LXIX

### 83. God commands nothing impossible, because everything is made easy by love

The commandments are very good, if we use them lawfully (1 Timothy 1:8). Precisely because it is firmly believed that the just and good God could not have commanded what is impossible, we are thereby instructed both what to do in easy matters and what to ask for in difficult ones. For all things are made easy by love. To love alone Christ’s burden is light (Matthew 11:30), or rather, love itself is that one burden which is light.

Accordingly it is said, “His commandments are not burdensome” (1 John 5:3). Therefore, whoever finds them burdensome should consider that it could not have been said divinely, “They are not burdensome,” unless there could be an affection of the heart for which they are not burdensome. Let that person ask for what he lacks, so that he may fulfill what is commanded.

The statement addressed to Israel in Deuteronomy, if understood devoutly, holily, and spiritually, means the same thing. For when the Apostle recalled this testimony, “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (here the text has, “in your hands” [Note: [Col. 0289] This may indicate either the book of Deuteronomy used by Pelagius, whom Augustine is refuting, or at least the Deuteronomy according to the Septuagint, which adds “and in your hands.” Compare Questions on Deuteronomy, book 5, question 54]; for spiritual hands are in the heart), he says, “This is the word of faith that we preach” (Deuteronomy 30:14; Romans 10:8).

When, therefore, each person turns to the Lord his God, as commanded there, with all his heart and with all his soul, God’s commandment will not be burdensome to him. For how can it be burdensome when it is a commandment of love? Either a person does not love, and therefore it is burdensome, or he loves, and it cannot be burdensome. He loves if he turns to the Lord his God, as Israel is admonished there, with all his heart and with all his soul.

“I give you a new commandment,” he says, “that you love one another” (John 13:34); and, “The one who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law”; and, “Love is the fullness of the law” (Romans 13:8, 10).

In this sense also it was said, “If they walked along good paths, you would find the paths of righteousness easy” (Proverbs 2:20, according to the Septuagint). How, then, is it said, “Because of the words of your lips I have guarded against difficult paths” (Psalm 16:4), unless both statements are true? The paths are difficult for fear, but easy for love.

## CHAPTER LXX

### 84. The degrees of love produce degrees of righteousness

Thus, beginning love is beginning righteousness; advanced love is advanced righteousness; great love is great righteousness; perfect love is perfect righteousness. But it is love arising from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith. It is greatest in this life when life itself is despised for its sake; yet I wonder whether it does not have room to grow when it has passed beyond mortal life.

Wherever and whenever it is so full [Note: [Col. 0290] The Louvain edition reads, “becomes full,”], that nothing can be added to it, it is nevertheless not poured into our hearts by the resources of nature or of the will [Note: [Col. 0290] Amerbach, Erasmus, and five manuscripts read, “works.” See above, section 29.] that are in us, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us. He both assists our weakness and cooperates with our health.

This is the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, belong eternity and goodness, for ever and ever. Amen.

# [ON THE PERFECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTEOUSNESS]

[Col. 0289]

## INTRODUCTORY NOTE TO THE FOLLOWING BOOK

Augustine passed over this little work in silence in his Retractions, evidently because he considered it part of the series of letters which he was planning to revise separately. For in all the manuscripts its beginning is marked by the following epistolary greeting: “To the holy brothers and fellow bishops Eutropius and Paul, Augustine.” Nevertheless, this letter has always held such a place among all readers that it is called a book, not only in those volumes that contain its exemplar but also in the writings of the ancients who cite it.

Among the more distinguished scholars, and those more deeply engaged in reading Augustine, Possidius, in his Catalogue, chapter 4, and Fulgentius, in book 1 of his work To Monimus, chapter 3, call this work the Book on the Perfection of Human Righteousness. Nearly all handwritten copies agree. But the Audoen manuscript, the Pratell manuscript, and certain others add to the same title these words: “Against those who assert that a human being can become righteous by his own powers alone.”

In the manuscript of the Church of Reims this title is found: “Book on the Definitions Said to Be Those of Coelestius.” Prosper, in his book Against the Collator, chapter 43, urges the reading, among other books of Augustine, of the work which he says was written to the priests Paul and Eutropius against the questions of Pelagius and Coelestius.

From this passage of Prosper, in which he listed certain of Augustine’s works against the Pelagians without much regard for their order, no one can properly prove, because they are named there first, that the Book on the Perfection of Human Righteousness is later in time than either the books On Marriage and Concupiscence or the first six books Against Julian.

Indeed, at the end of this book Augustine does not yet dare to criticize those who affirm that righteous people either exist or have existed in this life entirely without any sin. As in the book On the Spirit and the Letter, section 3, and in the book On Nature and Grace, sections 49 and 70, Augustine still thinks here that one should not resist that opinion too strongly.

Nothing, therefore, had yet been definitively settled on this matter, nor had the three famous canons of the Council of Carthage held in the year 418—canons six, seven, and eight—yet been formulated against that opinion. By their authority Augustine thereafter commands that it be avoided as a destructive error, as can be seen throughout the books Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, especially book 4, section 27, where he says:

“Let us now consider that third point, which no less causes every member of Christ and his whole body to recoil in horror: they contend that in this life there are, or have been, righteous people who have no sin at all.”

Certainly, in the year of Christ 414, when he wrote Letter 157 in response to Hilary concerning questions being raised in Sicily, he speaks of sinlessness—ἀναμαρτησία (anamartēsia)—in exactly the same manner and almost the same words as in the conclusion of this book.

“But these people,” he says in that letter, section 4, “are to some extent tolerable when they say that there is or has been here someone, apart from the one Holy of holies, who had no sin at all. But what they say—that free choice is sufficient for a human being to fulfill the Lord’s commandments even without being assisted toward good works by the grace of God and the gift of the Holy Spirit—is wholly to be anathematized and detested with every possible execration.”

When these words are compared with the closing words of the following book, nothing seems more probable than that the book itself, in which the definitions of Coelestius brought from Sicily are likewise refuted, was written not long after that letter.

Possidius places it immediately after the book On Nature and Grace in his Catalogue, and places the book On the Proceedings of Pelagius after it. Augustine, however, in Letter 169, sent to Evodius toward the end of the year 415, does not mention this work. He does indicate there that he had replied to Orosius’s Memorandum, in which Orosius said that the bishops Eutropius and Paul had already given Augustine a certain memorandum concerning several heresies.

Some understand this to mean nothing other than the letter which they sent him together with the definitions of Coelestius. In any event, it is not rash to believe that, not long after Orosius’s arrival in Africa—namely, before the middle of the year 415—they gave him those same definitions, and that Augustine first sent a reply to Orosius against them and shortly afterward wrote back to Eutropius and Paul.

Coelestius, whose name those definitions bore, had written to his parents from the monastery before he fell into the Pelagian doctrine, as Gennadius testifies in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers: three letters in the form of little books, necessary for all who desire God.

After Coelestius later professed the Pelagian heresy, he himself published a little book in which, among other things, he confessed that through the baptism of Christ even infants are redeemed. This was done in the Church of Carthage, in an episcopal judgment held there at the beginning of the year 412, as we learn from the letter to Pope Innocent, numbered 175 among Augustine’s letters, sections 1 and 6; from the aforementioned Letter 157, section 22; from book 1 On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, section 62, and book 2, section 58; from the book On Original Sin, section 21; and from book 3 Against Julian, section 8.

Another book, lacking its author’s name but said to have been Coelestius’s, divided into chapters, is mentioned in the immediately following book On the Proceedings of Pelagius, sections 29, 30, and 63. Finally, in the year 417 there existed several works or little books of Coelestius, which he is said to have cited at Rome in ecclesiastical proceedings before Zosimus, in the book On the Grace of Christ, sections 31 and 36.

The work of Coelestius which Augustine here, at the beginning of the Book on the Perfection of Human Righteousness, testifies that he had seen with certainty—and from which he understood that these definitions or arguments were not foreign to Coelestius’s ingenuity—may perhaps have been the same work that Jerome cites in his letter to Ctesiphon, written in the year 413 or 414, in these words:

“One of his disciples”—that is, of Pelagius—“indeed, by now his teacher and leader of the entire army, and a vessel of perdition against the Apostle, running through thickets of solecisms, not, as his followers boast, of syllogisms, thus philosophizes and argues:

‘If I can do nothing without God’s help, and if everything I accomplish in each action is his, then it is not I who labor but God’s assistance in me that will be crowned; and he gave me free choice in vain, since I cannot fulfill it unless he is always helping me. For the will that needs another’s aid is destroyed. But God gave free choice, and it will not otherwise be free unless I do what I wish. Thus either I use once for all the power that has been given to me, so that free choice may remain free; or, if I need another’s aid, freedom of choice is destroyed in me.’”

[Col. 0291]

# S. AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO

## LETTER, OR BOOK, TO THE BISHOPS EUTROPIUS AND PAUL [Note: [Col. 0291] Written around the end of the year 415]

# ON THE PERFECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTEOUSNESS

[Note: [Col. 0291] In correcting this book we used four manuscript codices from the Vatican library and thirteen from Gaul: the Colbertine, Sorbonne, Reims Major Church, Chartres Abbey of Saint Peter, Angers Saint-Albin, Rouen Saint-Ouen, Jumièges, Pratell, Bec, Mont-Michel, two from the Cistercian abbey, and Corbie. We also compared the variant readings of four Belgian manuscripts and three early editions, those of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain.] [Note: [Col. 0293] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the Retractions, volume 1. M.] (C)

Having received a sheet containing definitions said to be those of Coelestius, Augustine first dismantles, one by one, the arguments by which he—or some other associate in error—wrongly defined that a human being can be without sin in this life. He teaches that the perfection and fullness of righteousness by which a human being is entirely without sin is neither possible through the powers of nature, especially corrupted nature, without grace, nor ever present in this current life.

He then proceeds to the authorities which the same sheet had gathered from the Scriptures: some commanding a human being to be immaculate and perfect, some stating that God’s commandments are not burdensome, and finally some apparently opposed to those authorities which Catholics commonly bring forward against the Pelagians.

[Col. 0291]

To the holy brothers and fellow bishops EUTROPIUS and PAUL, AUGUSTINE.

## CHAPTER I

Your Charity, which is so great and so holy in you [Col. 0292] that it takes pleasure even in serving one who commands, asked me to respond to the definitions said to be those of Coelestius.

For the sheet which you gave me is headed as follows: “Definitions, as they are said to be, of Coelestius.” I believe that this heading belongs not to him but to those who brought the sheet from Sicily, where Coelestius is said not to be present, but where many [Note: [Col. 0293] The Louvain edition reads, “For there are many,” erroneously and against the earlier editions and all the manuscripts. In Letter 157 to Hilary, written shortly before this work, section 22, when Augustine recalls Coelestius and the condemnation of his errors by the Council of Carthage, he feared that Coelestius himself might be in Sicily, attempting to disturb the faith of Catholics: “But whether it is he himself,” he says, “or others who share his error—for there are more of them than we can hope, and where they are not refuted they also seduce others to their sect, and thus multiply, so that I do not know where they will burst forth,” and so on.] chatter such things, and, as the Apostle says, are themselves in error and lead others into error (2 Timothy 3:13).

Nevertheless, we too may suppose that this doctrine belongs to him, or at least to some of his associates [Note: [Col. 0293] So all the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “his followers.” This is not unreasonable, since Coelestius had become “by now a teacher and leader of the entire army,” as Jerome says in his letter to Ctesiphon, written in 413 or 414.]. For these brief definitions—or rather, arguments—are not unlike his ingenuity, which I observed in another work whose authorship is known to be his. Nor do I think that the brothers who brought these things from Sicily heard without reason that he had taught or written them.

I would like, if I could, to comply with your fraternal kindness by responding just as briefly. But unless I also recall the points to which I am replying, who could judge how I have replied? Nevertheless, with the help of your prayers before the mercy of the Lord, I shall try, as far as I can, to keep my speech from extending beyond what is necessary.

## CHAPTER II

### First argument

“Above all,” he says, “the person who denies that a human being can be without sin must be asked what kind of sin it is: something that can be avoided, or something that cannot be avoided. If it cannot be avoided, it is not sin; if it can be avoided, a human being can be without the sin that can be avoided. For neither reason nor justice permits even the calling of something sin which cannot be avoided in any way.”

We reply that sin can be avoided if corrupted nature is healed by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord. For nature is not healthy to the extent that it either does not see through blindness what ought to be done or does not accomplish it through weakness, while the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, so that a person does not do the things he wishes (Galatians 5:17).

### Second argument

“Again,” he says, “it must be asked whether sin is of the will or of necessity. If it is of necessity, it is not sin; if it is of the will, it can be avoided.”

We reply as above. And in order to be healed, we call upon the one to whom it is said in the Psalm, “Bring me out of my necessities” (Psalm 24:17).

### Third argument

“Again,” he says, “it must be asked what sin is: natural or accidental. If it is natural, it is not sin; but if it is accidental, it can depart. What can depart can be avoided; and what can be avoided is something from which a human being can be free.”

The answer is that sin is not natural, but that for nature—especially corrupted nature, from which we have become by nature children of wrath (Ephesians 2:3)—the freedom of the will is insufficient for not sinning unless it is healed by the assisting grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord [Col. 0294] [Note: [Col. 0294] Later editions added “accidental” here, thereby reinforcing another error of the earlier editions. They read afterward, “nature, children of wrath,” and “it is insufficient for not sinning.” The manuscripts provide the corrected text.].

### Fourth argument

“Again,” he says, “it must be asked what sin is: an act or a thing. If it is a thing, it must have an author; and if it is said to have an author, someone other than God will seem to be introduced as the author of something. But if it is impious to say this, it must be confessed that every sin is an act, not a thing. Therefore, if it is an act—or rather, because it truly is an act—it can be avoided.”

We reply that sin is indeed called and is an act, not a thing. But limping in the body is also, by the same reasoning, an act and not a thing. For the thing is the foot itself, or the body, or the person who limps with a defective foot. Yet a person cannot avoid limping unless he has a healed foot.

The same thing can happen in the inner person, but through the grace of God by Jesus Christ our Lord. The very defect by which a person limps is neither the foot, nor the body, nor the person, nor the limping itself—for limping is not present when he is not walking, although the defect by which he limps when he walks remains within him.

Let him therefore consider what name he wishes to give to that defect: does he want to call it a thing, an act, or rather an evil quality of a thing by which the act becomes deformed?

Likewise, in the inner person, the mind is a thing, robbery is an act, and avarice is a defect—that is, a quality according to which the mind is evil even when it does nothing by which it serves its avarice, even when it hears, “You shall not covet” (Exodus 20:17), condemns itself, and nevertheless remains avaricious. But through faith it is renewed—that is, healed—day by day (2 Corinthians 4:16), though this too occurs only through the grace of God by Jesus Christ our Lord.

## CHAPTER III

### Fifth argument

“Again,” he says, “it must be asked whether a human being ought to be without sin. Certainly he ought. If he ought, he can; if he cannot, then he ought not. And if a human being ought not to be without sin, then he ought to be with sin; and sin will no longer be sin if it is established that one ought to have it” [Note: [Col. 0294] The Louvain edition reads, “if it is established that it ought to be possessed.” But Amerbach, Erasmus, and the Colbert manuscript have “that it ought to be,” omitting “possessed.”].

“Or if even this is absurd to say, it must be confessed that a human being ought to be without sin, and it is established that he is bound to nothing other than what he can do.”

We reply with the same comparison by which we already replied above. When we see a lame person who can be healed, we rightly say, “This person ought to be without lameness”; and if he ought, he can. Yet when he wishes to do so, he cannot immediately. He can only do so once treatment has been applied, he has been healed, and medicine has assisted his will.

This takes place in the inner person with respect to sin, as though it were his lameness [Col. 0295] [Note: [Col. 0295] The printed editions read, “as though with respect to his lameness.” The manuscripts do not have “with respect to.”], through the grace of the one who came not to call the righteous but sinners, because the healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are ill do (Matthew 9:12–13).

### Sixth argument

“Again,” he says, “it must be asked whether a human being has been commanded to be without sin. Either he cannot, and it is not commanded; or, since it is commanded, he can. For why would something be commanded which could not possibly be done?”

We reply that a person is wisely commanded to walk with upright steps, so that when he recognizes that he cannot do so, he may seek the medicine which, for healing the inner person’s lameness of sin, is the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

### Reasoning 7

Again, he says, it must be asked whether God wishes man to be without sin. Without doubt he does wish it, and without doubt it is possible. For who is so foolish as either to doubt that something can happen which he does not doubt God wishes to happen?

The answer is: If God did not wish man to be without sin, he would not have sent his sinless Son to heal human beings from their sins. This is accomplished in believers who are making progress through the renewal of the inner person from day to day, until perfect righteousness comes about, like complete health.

### Reasoning 8

Again, he says, it must be asked how God wishes man to exist: with sin or without sin. Without doubt, he does not wish him to exist with sin. One must consider how great the impiety and blasphemy would be to say that man can exist with sin, which God does not wish, while denying that he can exist without sin, which God does wish—as though God had created someone so that he could be what God did not want, but could not be what God did want, and so that he might exist contrary to God’s will rather than according to it.

The answer has already been given above. But I see that I must add that we have been saved in hope. Now hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience (Rom. 8:24–25). Full righteousness, then, will exist when there is complete health; complete health will exist when there is complete love—for love is the fullness of the law (Rom. 13:10); and complete love will exist when we see him as he is (1 John 3:2). [Col. 0295] For nothing will be added to love when faith has arrived at vision.

[Note: Am. Er. and the Vatican and Gallican manuscripts read, “For it will not be that nothing will be added” (*neque enim non erit*).]

## CHAPTER IV

### Reasoning 9

Again, he says, it must be asked through what man comes to be with sin: through the necessity of nature, or through freedom of choice. If through the necessity of nature, he is free from guilt; but if through freedom of choice, it must be asked from whom he received that freedom of choice—without doubt, from God. Now what God gave is certainly good; this cannot be denied. In what sense, then, is it proved to be good if it is more inclined toward evil than toward good? For it is more inclined toward evil than toward good if, through it, man can be with sin but cannot be without sin.

The answer is that it was through freedom of choice that man came to be with sin; but then a punitive corruption followed, and from freedom produced necessity. Hence faith cries out to God, “Deliver me from my necessities” (Ps. 24:17). When placed under these necessities, we are either unable to understand what we wish, [Col. 0296] or, having understood it, we wish it but are unable to accomplish it. Indeed, freedom itself is promised to believers by the Liberator. “If the Son sets you free,” he says, “then you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

For nature, having been conquered by the vice into which the will fell, lost its freedom. Hence another Scripture says, “For by whatever anyone is overcome, to that he is enslaved” (2 Pet. 2:19). Therefore, just as “a physician is not needed by the healthy but by those who are ill” (Matt. 9:12), so a liberator is not needed by the free but by slaves, so that they may express their gratitude for freedom by saying, “You have saved my soul from necessities” (Ps. 30:8).

For health itself is true freedom, which would not have been lost if the will had remained good. But because the will sinned, the harsh necessity of possessing sin followed the sinning will, until the whole sickness is healed and such freedom is received that, just as the will to live happily necessarily remains, so there may also be a willing and happy necessity to live well and never sin.

[Note: One Vatican manuscript reads *tota* (“whole”) instead of *tanta* (“so great”).]

### Reasoning 10

“Therefore,” he says, “God made man good, and besides making him good, he further commanded him to do good. How impious it would be to confess that man is evil, although he was neither made evil nor commanded to be evil, and to deny that he can be good, although he was made good and was commanded to do good!”

We answer: Since man did not make himself good, but God made him good, God—not man himself—restores him so that he may be good, while freeing the willing, believing, and invoking man from the evil that he himself brought upon himself. This takes place as the inner person is renewed day by day by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, so that the outward person may rise on the last day to eternal life, not to punishment.

[Note: The printed editions read *praeterquam quod* (“and besides the fact that”). Am. Er. and the manuscripts omit *quod*.]

[Note: The manuscripts read *homo exterior novissimo die* (“the outward person on the last day”), omitting *in*.]

## CHAPTER V

### Reasoning 11

“Again,” he says, “it must be asked in how many ways all sin consists: in two, unless I am mistaken—either in doing what is forbidden or in failing to do what is commanded. Certainly everything that is forbidden can be avoided just as everything that is commanded can be performed. For something would not be forbidden or commanded if it could neither be avoided nor fulfilled. And how will we deny that man can be without sin when we must confess that he can both avoid everything that is forbidden and do everything that is commanded?”

We answer that there are many divine commandments in the Holy Scriptures, and it would be excessively laborious to mention them all. But the Lord, who “completed and shortened his word upon the earth” (Rom. 9:28), said that the Law and the Prophets depend upon two commandments, so that we might understand that whatever else has been divinely commanded finds its end in these two and must be referred to them: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind”; and, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” “On these two commandments,” he says, “the whole Law and the Prophets depend” (Matt. 22:40, 37).

Whatever, therefore, we are forbidden by God’s law, and whatever we are commanded to do, is forbidden and commanded [Col. 0297] so that we may fulfill these two commandments. Perhaps the general prohibition is, “You shall not covet” (Exod. 20:17), and the general commandment is, “You shall love” (Deut. 6:5).

Accordingly, the Apostle Paul briefly embraced both in one passage. The prohibition is, “Do not be conformed to this age”; the command is, “But be transformed in the renewal of your mind” (Rom. 12:2). The former pertains to not coveting; the latter to loving. The former pertains to self-restraint; the latter to righteousness. The former to turning away from evil; the latter to doing good. By not coveting, we are stripped of the old self; by loving, we are clothed with the new.

Yet no one can be self-restrained unless God grants it (Wis. 8:21), and the love of God is poured into our hearts not through ourselves but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5). This occurs day by day in those who make progress by willing, believing, and invoking, and who, “forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead” (Phil. 3:13), advance toward it.

For this reason the law commands these things: so that when man fails in fulfilling them, he may not, swollen with pride, exalt himself, but, wearied, may flee to grace; and thus, by terrifying him, the law may lead him to love Christ in the manner of a pedagogue.

## CHAPTER VI

### Reasoning 12

“Again, it must be asked,” he says, “how man cannot be without sin: by will or by nature. If by nature, it is not sin; if by will, the will can very easily be changed by the will.”

We answer by urging consideration of the magnitude of this presumption: it is said not merely that the will can be changed—which, with the help of God’s grace, must not be denied—but that it can be changed very easily, by the will. Yet the Apostle says, “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to each other, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Gal. 5:17).

He does not say, “These are opposed to each other so that you do not wish to do what you can do,” but, “so that you do not do the things you wish.” Why, then, has the desire of the flesh—which is certainly culpable and corrupt, and is nothing other than the desire for sin, which the same Apostle commands not to reign in our mortal body (Rom. 6:12)—not been changed by that will which the Apostle clearly expressed by saying, “so that you do not do the things you wish,” if the will can easily be changed by the will?

We certainly do not thereby accuse nature, whether of the soul or of the body, which God created and which is wholly good. Rather, we say that, having been corrupted by its own will, it cannot be healed without God’s grace.

### Reasoning 13

“Again,” he says, “it must be asked: if man cannot be without sin, whose fault is it—his own or someone else’s? If it is man’s own, how is it man’s fault if this is something that cannot be otherwise?”

We answer that it is man’s fault that he is not without sin because it happened through man’s will alone that he came into this necessity, [Col. 0298] although man’s will alone cannot overcome it.

## Reasoning 14

“Again,” he says, “if human nature is good—as no one except Marcion or Manichaeus will dare deny—how, then, is it good if it is impossible for it to be free from evil? For who would doubt that every sin is evil?”

We answer that human nature is good and that it can be free from evil. For this is why we cry out, “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13): a deliverance that is not completed so long as “the body that is subject to corruption weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15).

But grace works this through faith, so that one day it may be said, “Where, O death, is your contention? Where, O death, is your sting? The sting of death is sin, and the strength of sin is the law” (1 Cor. 15:55–56). For by forbidding, the law increases the desire for sin unless the Spirit pours out love—the love that will then be full and perfect, when we see face to face.

### Reasoning 15

“And this,” he says, “must also be said: God is certainly just; this cannot be denied. Yet God imputes every sin to man. This too, I think, must be confessed, because whatever is not imputed as sin is not sin. And if there is some sin that cannot be avoided, how is God called just if he is believed to impute to anyone what cannot be avoided?”

We answer that long ago the cry was raised against the proud: “Blessed is the one whose sin the Lord has not imputed” (Ps. 32:2).

[Note: The manuscripts read *imputabit* (“will not impute”). The Greek is *logisētai*.]

For he does not impute sin to those who faithfully say to him, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). And he does not impute it justly, because what he says is just: “In the measure with which you measure, it will be measured back to you” (Matt. 7:2).

Sin exists whenever love is absent where it ought to be, or is less than it ought to be, whether this can be avoided by the will or cannot be avoided. For if it can be avoided, the present will causes it; but if it cannot, the past will caused it. Yet it can be avoided—not when the proud will is praised, but when the humble will is assisted.

## CHAPTER VII

### Reasoning 16

After this, the man who wrote these things introduces his own person as though disputing with another. He has himself questioned, and has the questioner say to him, “Give me a man without sin.”

He replies, “I give you one who can be without sin.”

Again the questioner says to him, “Who is he?”

He replies, “You yourself.”

“If you say,” he continues, “‘I cannot be that man,’ the answer must be, ‘Whose fault is that?’ If you say, ‘Mine,’ it must be said, ‘How is it yours if you cannot be that man?’”

Again he has himself questioned and addressed in this way: “Are you yourself without sin, you who say that man can be without sin?”

He replies, “If I am not without sin, whose fault is that?”

“If he says,” he continues, “‘Yours,’ the answer must be, ‘How is it mine if I cannot be without sin?’”

We answer that there need be no dispute with them over these words, because he did not dare to say that any man—or himself—was without [Col. 0299] sin; he merely replied that man can be without sin, which we too do not deny. What is being asked is when, and through whom, he can be without sin.

For if he is already without sin, there would be no need for every faithful soul placed in this body of death to pray and say, “Forgive us our debts,” since all past sins were already forgiven in holy Baptism. Whoever tries to persuade Christ’s faithful members that this prayer should not be made is declaring nothing other than that he himself is not a Christian.

Moreover, if man can be without sin by himself, then Christ died for nothing (Gal. 2:21). But Christ did not die for nothing. Therefore man cannot be without sin, even if he wishes to be, unless he is helped by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

This is being brought to completion now in those who are making progress, and it will be fulfilled in every respect when the struggle with death has been brought to an end and the love nourished by believing and hoping has been perfected through seeing and possessing.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 17

Next he undertakes to establish his argument by divine testimonies. Let us examine carefully what kind of argument it is.

“Testimonies,” he says, “by which it is proved that man has been commanded to be without sin.”

We answer: The question is not whether this is commanded, for that is perfectly clear; the question is whether what is plainly commanded can be fulfilled in this body of death, where the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, so that we do not do what we wish.

Not everyone who ends this life is freed from this body of death; only the one who receives grace in this life and does not receive it in vain, but acts through good works, is freed from it. It is one thing to leave this body, which the last day of every human life compels all people to do; it is another thing to be freed from this body of death, which God’s grace alone, through Jesus Christ our Lord, grants to his holy and faithful people (Rom. 7:24–25).

After this life, the reward is given in its completed form, but only to those who in this life acquire the merit of that same reward. No one will attain the fullness of righteousness after departing from here unless, while here, he has pursued it by hungering and thirsting for it. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:9).

### 18

As long, therefore, as we are pilgrims away from the Lord and walk by faith, not by sight (2 Cor. 5:6–7)—whence it is said, “The righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4)—this is our righteousness during our pilgrimage: that we now strive toward that perfection and fullness of righteousness in which love will already be full and perfect in the sight of its beauty.

We do this by disciplining our body and bringing it into subjection; by cheerfully and wholeheartedly giving alms through acts of kindness, and forgiving the sins committed against us; and by persevering without ceasing in prayer. We do these things within sound doctrine, by which right faith, firm hope, and pure love are built up.

[Col. 0300] This is our righteousness now: by it we run, hungering and thirsting, toward the perfection and fullness of righteousness, so that afterward we may be satisfied by it.

Therefore, when the Lord had said in the Gospel, “Do not perform your righteousness before men in order to be seen by them” (Matt. 6:1), so that we would not measure this race of ours by the end of human glory, he did not continue his exposition of righteousness beyond these three: fasting, almsgiving, and prayer.

By fasting he signified every form of bodily discipline; by almsgiving, every form of kindness and benevolence, whether giving or forgiving; and by prayer he indicated all the principles of holy desire.

For in bodily discipline concupiscence is restrained—a concupiscence that ought not merely to be restrained but not to exist at all, and that will not exist in that perfection of righteousness where there will be absolutely no sin. Yet even in the use of things permitted and lawful, it often displays its immoderation.

In genuine benevolence, by which the righteous person cares for his neighbor, things are sometimes done that cause harm although they were thought to be beneficial. At times, through weakness, or because what is expended in kindness and labor is insufficient for the needs of others, or because it accomplishes little in them, weariness creeps in and darkens the cheerfulness in which God takes delight in the giver (2 Cor. 9:7). It creeps in all the more as a person has made less progress, and all the less as he has made greater progress.

When these and similar matters are considered, we rightly say in prayer, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” This is so provided that we do what we say: that we love even our enemies. But if someone who is still a little child in Christ does not yet do this, he must nevertheless forgive from the depths of his heart the person who has sinned against him, when that person repents of what he has done and asks forgiveness, if he wishes the heavenly Father to hear his prayer.

[Note: The printed editions read *indesinenter insistendo et hoc faciendo* (“persevering without ceasing and doing this”). The manuscripts read *indesinenter instando, et haec faciendo* (“persevering without ceasing in prayer, and doing these things”).]

### 19

In this prayer, if we do not wish to be contentious, we have a sufficient mirror in which to inspect the life of the righteous—those who live by faith and run perfectly, although they are not without sin. Hence they say, “Forgive us,” because they have not yet reached the destination toward which they are running.

The Apostle says:

“Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect. Brothers, I do not consider myself to have grasped it; but forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the goal toward the prize of God’s heavenly calling in Christ Jesus. Therefore, as many as are perfect, let us think this way” (Phil. 3:12–15).

That is, as many as run perfectly, let us think this way: that we are not yet perfect, so that we may be perfected there, although we now run perfectly. When perfection comes, what is partial will be abolished; that is, it will no longer be partial but complete. For the reality itself will succeed faith and hope—not something to be believed and hoped for, but something to be seen and possessed. Love, however, which is greater than these three, will not be taken away (1 Cor. 13:10, 13), but will be increased and brought to completion when it beholds what it believed and obtains what it hoped for.

[Note: Am. Er. and several manuscripts read: “It will not be taken away, but will be increased and brought to completion.”]

In that fullness [Col. 0301] of love the commandment will be fulfilled: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Deut. 6:5). For as long as there is any carnal concupiscence that must be restrained by self-control, God is not loved with the whole soul in every respect. The flesh does not desire apart from the soul, although the desire is attributed to the flesh, because the soul desires carnally.

The righteous person will be without any sin whatsoever when there is no law in his members resisting the law of his mind (Rom. 7:23), but he loves God with his whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind. This is the first and greatest commandment (Matt. 22:37–38).

Why, then, should this perfection not be commanded to man, even though no one possesses it in this life? For one does not run correctly if one does not know toward what one must run. How could it be known if it were not shown by commandments?

Let us therefore run so that we may attain. All who run correctly will attain—not as in the theatrical race, where all run but only one receives the prize (1 Cor. 9:24). Let us run by believing, hoping, and desiring. Let us run by disciplining the body and cheerfully and wholeheartedly giving alms through doing good and forgiving evil. Let us pray so that the strength of those who run may be helped. And thus let us hear the commandments of perfection, so that we may not neglect to run toward the fullness of love.

## CHAPTER IX

### 20

With these points established, let us carefully hear the testimonies cited by the man to whom we are replying, as though we ourselves had produced them.

“In Deuteronomy: ‘You shall be perfect before the Lord your God’ (Deut. 18:13). Again there: ‘And there shall be no one uncompleted among the children of Israel.’

[Note: In Deuteronomy 23:18, according to the Septuagint, the term is *teliskomenos*, “initiated.” Nevertheless, this testimony does not seem to have been taken from another passage in Deuteronomy.]

Again, the Savior in the Gospel: ‘Be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect’ (Matt. 5:48).

Again, the Apostle in the Second Letter to the Corinthians: ‘Finally, brothers, rejoice; be perfect’ (2 Cor. 13:11).

Again, in the Letter to the Colossians: ‘Admonishing every person and teaching every person in all wisdom, so that we may present every person perfect in Christ’ (Col. 1:28).

Again, in the Letter to the Philippians: ‘Do everything without grumbling and hesitation, so that you may be blameless and sincere, as spotless children of God’ (Phil. 2:14–15).

Again, in the Letter to the Ephesians: ‘Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and spotless in his sight’ (Eph. 1:3–4).

Again, in the Letter to the Colossians: ‘Although you were once alienated and enemies in your understanding through evil works, now he has reconciled you in the body of his flesh through his death; present yourselves holy, spotless, and blameless’ (Col. 1:21).

[Note: All the manuscripts read *inimicis sensus ejus in operibus malis* (“enemies of his understanding in evil works”).]

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read *ut exhiberet vos* (“so that he might present you”).]

Again, in the Letter to the Ephesians: ‘So that he might present to himself a glorious Church, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, but holy and spotless’ (Eph. 5:27).

Again, in the First Letter to the Corinthians [Col. 0302]: ‘Be sober and righteous, and do not sin’ (1 Cor. 15:34).

Again, in the Letter of the holy Peter: ‘Therefore, girding the loins of your mind, being sober, hope perfectly in the grace that is being offered to you, as obedient children, not being conformed to the former desires of your ignorance; but, according to the one who called you, the Holy One, be holy yourselves in all your conduct, because it is written, “You shall be holy, because I am holy”’ (1 Pet. 1:13–16).

Hence blessed David also says: ‘Lord, who will dwell in your tabernacle, or who will rest upon your holy mountain? The one who walks without spot and practices righteousness’ (Ps. 15:1–2).

And elsewhere: ‘I shall be spotless with him’ (Ps. 18:24).

And elsewhere: ‘Blessed are the spotless in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord’ (Ps. 119:1).

Likewise in Solomon: ‘The Lord loves holy hearts, but all the spotless are acceptable to him’” (Prov. 11:20, according to the Septuagint).

Some of these testimonies encourage those who are running to run perfectly; others mention the very end toward which they are to strive by running.

A person who enters without spot may reasonably be understood not as one who is already perfect, but as one who runs blamelessly toward perfection itself, free from sins that merit condemnation and not neglecting to cleanse even venial sins through almsgiving.

For a pure prayer cleanses our entrance—that is, the journey by which we strive toward perfection. Prayer is pure when one says truthfully, “Forgive us, as we also forgive” (Matt. 6:12). Thus, since what is not imputed is not held against us, our journey toward perfection is considered blameless—that is, without spot. When we reach that perfection, there will no longer be anything to be cleansed through forgiveness.

[Note: Am. Er. read *dum reprehenditur* (“while it is reproved”), omitting the negative particle. The negative particle is restored here from the manuscripts.]

[Note: The printed books read *pervenerimus* (“when we have reached it”); the manuscripts read *venerimus* (“when we have come to it”).]

## CHAPTER X

### 21

Next he introduces testimonies to show that the divine commandments are not burdensome. Who, however, does not know that, since the general commandment is love—for “the end of the commandment is love” (1 Tim. 1:5), and “the fullness of the law is love” (Rom. 13:10)—what is done through love rather than fear is not burdensome?

Those who try to fulfill God’s commandments through fear struggle under them. But perfect love casts out fear (1 John 4:18) and makes the burden of the commandment not merely fail to press down with the weight of a load, but actually lift us like wings.

Nevertheless, in order to possess this love, even as much as can be possessed in this body of death, the freedom of our will is insufficient unless it is helped by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom. 7:24–25). For, as must often be said, love is poured into our hearts not through ourselves but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5).

Scripture mentions that God’s commandments are [Col. 0303] not burdensome for no other reason than this: the soul that finds them burdensome should understand that it has not yet received the strength by which the Lord’s commandments become what they are declared to be—easy and pleasant. It should pray with the groaning of its will to obtain the gift of ease.

For the one who says, “Let my heart be made spotless”; and, “Direct my paths according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me” (Ps. 119:80, 133); and, “Your will be done, as in heaven so also on earth”; and, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6:10, 13); and other prayers of this kind, which it would take too long to enumerate, is certainly praying that he may do God’s commandments.

The commandments would not be given if our will did nothing in the matter; nor would they be prayed for if the will alone were sufficient. They are therefore declared not to be burdensome so that the person for whom they are burdensome may understand that he has not yet received the gift by which they cease to be burdensome, and may not suppose that he fulfills them when he performs them in such a way that they remain burdensome.

For God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7). Yet when a person finds the commandments burdensome, he must not be broken by despair; rather, he should be compelled to seek, ask, and knock.

[Note: Am. Er., together with the Gallican and Vatican manuscripts, adds *levem* (“light”) here.]

[Note: Lov. reads *facultatis* (“of ability”); the reading here is *facilitatis* (“of ease”).]

### 22

Let us therefore hear also, in the testimonies he next introduced, God declaring that his commandments are not burdensome.

“That God’s commandments,” he says, “are not only not impossible but not even burdensome.”

“In Deuteronomy: ‘The Lord your God will turn and rejoice over you for good, just as he rejoiced over your fathers, if you listen to the voice of the Lord your God, to keep and do all his commandments, statutes, and judgments that are written in the book of this law; if you turn to the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul.

“For this commandment that I command you today is not burdensome, nor is it far from you. It is not in heaven, so that you may say, “Who will ascend into heaven and take it for us, so that we may hear it and do it?” It is not beyond the sea, so that you may say, “Who will cross the sea and take it for us, so that we may hear it and do it?” For the word is very near you, in your mouth, in your heart, and in your hands, so that you may do it’” (Deut. 30:9–14).

“Again, the Lord in the Gospel: ‘Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is pleasant and my burden is light’” (Matt. 11:28–30).

“Again, in the Letter of the holy John: ‘This is the love of God, that we keep his commandments; and his commandments are not burdensome’” (1 John 5:3).

Having heard these legal, evangelical, and apostolic testimonies, let us be built up into the grace that those who do not understand it fail to recognize. In ignorance of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, they are not subject to God’s righteousness.

For if they do not understand from Deuteronomy how the Apostle Paul recalled that one believes with the heart unto righteousness, while confession is made with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10:3, 10)—because “a physician is not needed by the healthy but by those who are ill” (Matt. 9:12)—then at least, through this testimony of the Apostle John, which he placed last in support of this position, they ought to be admonished.

He says, “This is the love of God, that we keep his commandments; and his commandments are not burdensome.” They ought to be admonished [Col. 0304] that God’s commandment is not burdensome to the love of God, which is poured into our hearts only through the Holy Spirit, not through the freedom of the human will. By giving the human will more than is proper, they fail to understand God’s righteousness.

Yet this love will be perfect when all punitive fear has departed.

## CHAPTER XI

### 23

After this he presented testimonies that are customarily cited against them. He did not resolve them; rather, by recalling what seemed to be contrary testimonies, he bound the questions even more tightly.

For he says:

“Testimonies from Scripture that must be set forth in opposition to those who incompetently suppose that they can destroy, by the authority of Scripture, either freedom of choice or the possibility of not sinning.

“They are accustomed to object,” he says, “that the holy Job said, ‘Who is clean from sin? Not even an infant whose life upon the earth is a single day’” (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint).

Then, as though answering this testimony with other testimonies, he adduces what Job himself said: “For I am a righteous and blameless man, made a laughingstock” (Job 12:4, according to the Septuagint).

He does not understand that a person can be called righteous when he has come very close to the perfection of righteousness, so that he has become near to it. We do not deny that many have been able to reach this state even in this life, in which one lives by faith.

### 24

This is also confirmed by the testimony that he next added, spoken by the same Job: “Behold, I am near my judgment, and I know that I shall be found righteous” (Job 13:18).

This is the judgment of which it is said elsewhere, “He will bring forth your righteousness like the light, and your judgment like midday” (Ps. 37:6). In the end, he did not say, “I am there,” but, “I am near.”

If he wished this to be understood as his judgment—not the judgment by which he himself will judge, but the judgment by which he will be judged at the end—then all the righteous will be found in that judgment who do not deceitfully say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

For through this forgiveness the righteous will be found righteous, because they have wiped away by almsgiving the sins they had in this life.

[Note: Most manuscripts read, “and because they washed away through almsgiving the sins they had in this life.”]

Hence the Lord says, “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11:41). Finally, this will be said to the righteous as they enter the promised kingdom: “For I was hungry, and you gave me food” (Matt. 25:35), and other words of this kind.

But it is one thing to be without sin, which in this life was said of the Only-Begotten alone; it is another to be without blame, which could be said of many righteous people even in this life. For there is a certain manner of good living about which no just complaint can be made even in this human society.

Who could justly complain about a person who wishes evil to no one, faithfully cares for those whom he can help, and does not hold on to the desire for revenge against anyone’s injuries, so that he can truthfully say, “As we also forgive our debtors”? And yet, precisely by saying truthfully, “Forgive us, as we also forgive,” he declares that he is not without sin.

### 25

This is why he says, “There was no injustice in my hands, but my prayer was pure” (Job 16:18). His prayer was pure because he was not unjustly asking forgiveness: he was genuinely granting it.

[Col. 0305] ### 26

And when he says of the Lord, “For he has inflicted many afflictions upon me without cause” (Job 9:17), he does not say, “He inflicted none with cause,” but “many without cause.” His many afflictions were not inflicted on account of his many sins, but for the testing of his patience. On account of the sins without which, as he confesses elsewhere, he was not, he judges that he ought to have suffered fewer afflictions (Job 6:2–3).

### 37

Likewise, when he says, “For I have kept his ways and have not turned aside from his commandments, nor shall I depart from them” (Job 23:11), he kept God’s ways because he did not deviate so far as to abandon them, but made progress in them by running—even if at times, as a weak person, he stumbled or faltered. He made progress by diminishing his sins until he reached the place where he would be without sin.

For he cannot make progress in this way except by keeping God’s ways. But the apostate turns aside from the Lord’s commandments and departs from them—not the person who, even if he has sin, does not abandon perseverance in struggling against it until he reaches the place where no struggle with death remains.

In this struggle, therefore, we put on the righteousness by which one lives here through faith, and in a certain sense we put on this righteousness as armor. We also take up judgment—the judgment that we make against ourselves and for ourselves when, by accusing our sins, we condemn them. Hence it is written, “The righteous person is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18:17).

For this reason he also says, “I was clothed with righteousness, and I surrounded myself with judgment as with a cloak” (Job 29:14). Such clothing is generally more suited to war than to peace: it belongs where concupiscence is still being conquered, not where righteousness will be complete, with no enemy whatsoever, after the last enemy, death, has been destroyed.

[Note: The manuscripts read *judicabit* (“will judge”); the printed editions read *judicavit* (“judged”).]

[Col. 0305] 28. But when that same holy Job again says, “For my heart shall not reproach me throughout all my life” (Job 27:6), then, in this life in which we live by faith, our heart does not reproach us if that same faith by which one believes with the heart unto righteousness [Note: The Amerbach and Erasmus editions and the manuscripts read “in which”; the Louvain editors deleted “in.”] does not neglect to reproach our sin. Hence the Apostle says, “For I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I hate, that I do” (Rom. 7:15). It is good not to desire wrongly, and this is the good that the righteous person who lives by faith desires (Hab. 2:4); yet he does what he hates, because he desires wrongly, although he does not follow his desires (Ecclus. 18:30). If he does follow them, then he truly acts so as to yield, consent, and obey the desire of sin. Then his heart reproaches him, because it is he himself whom it reproaches—not that sin of his which dwells in his members. [Note: One of the Vatican manuscripts omits “because it is he himself whom it reproaches.”]

[Col. 0306] When, however, he does not allow sin to reign in his mortal body so as to obey its desires, and does not present his members as weapons of wickedness to sin (Rom. 6:12–13), sin is indeed present in his members, but it does not reign, because its desires are not obeyed. And therefore, while he does what he does not wish—that is, he does not wish to desire wrongly, yet he does desire wrongly—he consents to the law, because it is good. For he himself desires what the law also desires: he desires not to desire wrongly, and the law says, “You shall not desire wrongly” (Exod. 20:17). Since he desires what the law also desires, he undoubtedly consents to the law; yet he desires wrongly, because he is not without sin. But now it is no longer he himself who does this; rather, it is the sin dwelling in him.

Therefore his heart does not reproach him throughout his entire life—that is, in his faith, because the righteous person lives by faith, and thus his faith is his life. For he knows that what is good does not dwell in his flesh, where sin dwells. Yet he lives without consenting to it, by the faith [Note: The Amerbach and Erasmus editions and most manuscripts read “because.”] through which he calls upon God to help him as he fights against sin. That sin should not be present there at all is something he desires, but accomplishing the good is not yet within his power (Rom. 7:15–21). It is not that doing good is beyond him, but accomplishing it perfectly is. For by not consenting, he does good; by hating his wrongful desire, he does good; by not ceasing to give alms, he does good; by forgiving the one who sins against him, he does good; by asking that his debts be forgiven and truthfully saying that he too forgives his debtors, and by praying not to be led into temptation but to be delivered from evil, he does good. Yet accomplishing the good perfectly is beyond him; that will occur when the wrongful desire dwelling in his members no longer exists.

Therefore his heart does not reproach him when it reproaches the sin dwelling in his members, and finds no unbelief in him to reproach. [Note: Several manuscripts read, “which finds no unbelief in him to reproach.”] Thus he is neither reproached by his heart in his life—that is, in his faith—nor proved not to be without sin. Job himself also confesses this about himself when he says, “Nothing concerning my sins was hidden from you. You sealed up my iniquities in a bag and marked whether I had transgressed anything unwillingly” (Job 14:16–17).

We have therefore shown, as best we could, how the testimonies that he cited from the words of holy Job should be understood. Yet he has not thereby resolved what he proposed that Job likewise said: “For who is pure from sin? Not even an infant whose life upon earth is but a single day.”

## CHAPTER XII

29. “Again,” he says, “they commonly propose, ‘Every human being is a liar’” (Ps. 115:2).
