He does not resolve this proposition, which he has himself brought forward against himself [Note: Most manuscripts read “against themselves.”]; rather, by recalling other testimonies as though they were contradictory, he leaves the divine utterances in dispute before those who do not understand Holy Scripture. For he says:

“To these one should reply that it is written in the Book of Numbers, ‘A truthful man’” (Num. 24, according to the Septuagint). And concerning holy Job it is read as follows: “There was a man living in the region of Ausitis, named Job, truthful, blameless, righteous, a worshiper of God, abstaining from every evil thing” (Job 1:1).

I am astonished that he dared to cite this testimony, in which it is said, “abstaining from every evil thing,” since he wanted this to be understood as abstaining from every sin, although earlier he had said that sin is an evil act, not a thing [Note: The Amerbach and Erasmus editions and all but one manuscript read “that sin is an evil act.”] (ch. 2, §4). Let him therefore remember that even if it is an act, it can still be called a thing. A person abstains from every evil thing if, regarding the sin without which he is not, he either never consents to it at all or, if at some time he is pressed by it, is not crushed by it—like a stronger wrestler who, even if he is sometimes held, does not thereby lose the superiority in which he is found.

Certainly a person is read of as blameless and without complaint; [Col. 0307] but no one is read of as without sin except the Son of Man, who is also the one and only Son of God.

30. “Likewise,” he says, “in Job himself: ‘And a marvel held the truthful man.’ Again, in Solomon concerning Wisdom: ‘Lying men will not remember her, but truthful men will be found in her’” (Ecclus. 15:8). “Again, in the Apocalypse: ‘And no lie was found in their mouth; they are without blemish’” (Rev. 14:5).

To these we too reply, explaining how a human being is to be called truthful by the grace and truth of God, although by himself he is undoubtedly a liar. Hence it was said, “Every human being is a liar.” [Note: The printed editions read, “This testimony,” omitting “also,” which the manuscripts retain.] This is also the force of the testimony from Wisdom that he himself cited: “But truthful men will be found in her.” For those who will undoubtedly be found to be liars in themselves will be found truthful in her—not in themselves. Thus it is written, “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8). When he said “darkness,” he did not add “in the Lord”; but when he said “light,” he added “in the Lord,” because they could not be light in themselves, so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31).

Those men in the Apocalypse are called such because no lie was found in their mouth. They did not say that they had no sin; for if they did, they would deceive themselves, and the truth would not be in them (1 John 1:8). Furthermore, if the truth were not in them, a lie would be found in their mouth. But if, because of envy, they were without sin and nevertheless said that they were not without sin, that very statement would be a lie, and the saying “No lie was found in their mouth” would be false. Therefore they are without blemish because, just as they themselves forgave their debtors, so they were cleansed when God forgave them.

Behold, we have explained, as far as we were able, how the testimonies he cited for his own case should be understood. But he has not explained at all how the statement “Every human being is a liar” should be understood; nor will he be able to explain it until he corrects the error by which he believes that a human being can be truthful without the help of God’s grace, through his own will alone.

## CHAPTER XIII

31. He next proposed another question and did not resolve it; rather, he enlarged it and made it more difficult by bringing forward against himself the testimony [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “prophetic”; several manuscripts, together with the Amerbach and Erasmus editions, read “proved”], “There is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13:1, 3), and by citing apparently contrary testimonies through which he might show that there are people who do good. He did indeed show this; but it is one thing not to do good, and another thing not to be without sin, even though a person does many good things.

Therefore the testimonies he cited are not contrary to the statement that in this life there is no human being without sin. He himself, however, did not show how the words “There is none who does good, not even one” should be understood. For, he says, holy David stated, “Hope in the Lord and do goodness” (Ps. 36:3). This is a commandment, not a completed deed; and those of whom it was said, “There is none who does good, not even [Col. 0308] one,” were certainly not carrying out this commandment.

He also says that holy Tobias stated, “Do not be afraid, my son; we lead a poor life, but we shall have many good things if we fear God, withdraw from every sin, and do good things” (Tob. 4:23). Truly, a person will have many good things when he has withdrawn from every sin. For then he will have no evils, so that he will not need to say, “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13).

Nevertheless, even now everyone who is making progress, progressing with right intention, withdraws from every sin; and he becomes more distant from it the nearer he comes to the fullness and perfection of righteousness. For even wrongful desire—which is sin dwelling in our flesh—although it still remains in mortal members, does not cease to diminish in those who are making progress.

It is one thing to withdraw from every sin that is now present in action, and another thing to have withdrawn from every sin, which will occur in that perfection. Yet neither the one who has already withdrawn nor the one who is still withdrawing should be denied the performance of good.

How, then, was it said, “There is none who does good, not even one”—the statement he proposed and left unresolved? It can only be because that psalm censures a certain people among whom there was not even one who did good, since they wished to remain human beings’ children and not God’s children, by whose grace a person becomes good so as to do good.

For here we should understand the good of which it says there: “God looked down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there was anyone who understood or sought God” (Ps. 13:1–3). This good, namely, seeking God, was not done by anyone, not even by one—but this was among that class of human beings which is predestined to destruction. [Note: On this passage Fulgentius says in *To Monimus*, book 1, chapter 5: “I think that nothing else should be understood in that statement of Saint Augustine by which he affirms that some are predestined to destruction except destruction of punishment, not of sin; not to the evil which they unjustly commit, but to the torment which they will most justly suffer; not to the sin by which they either do not receive or lose the benefit of the first resurrection, but to the punishment which their own wickedness wrongly produces for them and divine justice rightly repays.”]

Upon these, divine foreknowledge looked down and pronounced sentence.

## CHAPTER XIV

32. “Again,” he says, “they cite what the Savior said: ‘Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone’” (Luke 18:19; Mark 10:18). He does not resolve this proposition at all; instead, he set against it, as though in opposition, other testimonies by which he might prove that a human being can also be good.

For he said that one should reply that the same Lord says elsewhere, “A good person brings good things out of the good treasure of his heart” (Matt. 12:35), and again, “Who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil” (Matt. 5:45). “And elsewhere,” he says, “it is written, ‘Good things were created for the good from the beginning’” (Ecclus. 39:30); and again, “Those who are good will inhabit the earth” (Prov. 2:21).

The reply should be framed so that the statement “No one is good except God alone” may also be understood. This may be because all created things, although God made them very good, are not good when compared with the Creator—or, compared with him, they are not. For in the highest [Note: The Louvain edition reads “most high.”] and most proper sense he said of himself, “I am who I am” (Exod. 3:14).

Thus [Note: The printed editions read “just as,” less correctly.] it was said, “No one is good except God alone,” just as it was said of John, “He was not the light” (John 1:8), although the Lord calls him a lamp (John 5:35), as he calls the disciples, to whom he said, “You are the light of the world; no one lights a lamp and puts it under a bushel” (Matt. 5:14–15). Yet in comparison with that light which is the true light, enlightening every human being who comes into this world (John 1:9), John was not the light.

Or it may be because even the children of God, compared with themselves as they will be in that eternal perfection, are so good that they are still also evil. I would not dare to say this of them—for who would dare to call evil those whose Father is God?—unless the Lord himself had said, “If you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?” (Matt. 7:11). By saying “your Father,” he showed that those whom he nevertheless did not fail to call evil were already God’s children.

He did not, however, explain how these people can be good while no one is good except God alone. For this reason the man who had asked what good he should do was admonished to seek the one whose grace made him good, to whom being good is identical with being—for he is immutably good and cannot possibly be evil. [Note: The Louvain edition reads, “because he is immutably good, he cannot”; the conjunction “and,” found in the other printed editions and the manuscripts, is omitted.]

## CHAPTER XV

33. “Again,” he says, “they cite: ‘Who can boast that he has a pure heart?’” To this also he replied with many testimonies, wishing to show that a human being can have a pure heart. Yet he does not say how the statement he proposed as being spoken against him—“Who can boast that he has a pure heart?”—should be understood, lest divine Scripture appear in this testimony and in those by which he replied to contradict itself.

We, however, reply to him that the question “Who can boast that he has a pure heart?” follows because the preceding statement is, “When the righteous king has sat upon the throne.” However great the righteousness with which a person is endowed, he must consider that, when the righteous King [Note: The Amerbach and Erasmus editions and the manuscripts read “Judge.”] has sat upon the throne, something in him that he himself does not see may be found worthy of condemnation. The transgressions of the one whose knowledge they cannot escape cannot escape him—not even those of which it was said, “Who understands his transgressions?” (Ps. 19:12).

When, therefore, the righteous King has sat upon the throne, “who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will boast that he is clean from sin?” (Prov. 20:8–9)—unless perhaps those who wish to boast in their own righteousness and not in the mercy of that Judge.

34. Nevertheless, the things he added in reply are also true: “The Savior says in the Gospel, ‘Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God’” (Matt. 5:8). And David says, “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? The innocent in hands and pure in heart” (Ps. 24:3–4). And elsewhere, “Do good, O Lord, to the good and upright in heart” (Ps. 125:4). Likewise, in Solomon: “Good is the substance of the one whose conscience has no sin” (Ecclus. 13:30). And there also: “Turn away from sin, direct your hands, and cleanse your heart from every sin” (Ecclus. 38:10). Likewise, in the Epistle of John: “If our heart does not reproach us, we have confidence toward God, and whatever we ask, we shall receive from him” (1 John 3:21–22).

This is accomplished by the will: by believing, hoping, loving, disciplining the body, giving alms, forgiving injuries, praying persistently, praying for strength to make progress, and truthfully saying, “Forgive us, as we also forgive,” and, “Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:12–13). The purpose of all this is that the heart may be cleansed and every sin removed; and that whatever the righteous Judge finds hidden and insufficiently cleansed when he has sat upon the throne may be forgiven by his mercy, so that it may be made entirely sound and pure for the sight of God.

“For judgment is without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy. But mercy triumphs over judgment” (Jas. 2:13). If this were not so, what hope would there be? For when the righteous King has sat upon the throne, “who will boast that he has a pure heart? Or who will boast that he is clean from sin?” Then, through his mercy, those who are righteous, fully and perfectly cleansed, “will shine in the kingdom of their Father like the sun” (Matt. 13:43).

35. Then [Note: The manuscripts read “fully and perfectly”; the printed editions read “full and perfect.”] the Church will be fully and perfectly “without spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind,” because then it will also truly be glorious. For when he says not merely that he might present the Church to himself without spot or wrinkle, but adds “glorious” (Eph. 5:27), he sufficiently indicates when it will be without spot, wrinkle, or anything of that kind [Note: The printed editions read “or anything of that kind”; three Vatican manuscripts read “or any such thing.”]: namely, when it is glorious.

It should not now be said to be glorious amid such great evils, such great scandals, such a great mixture of very wicked people, and such great insults from the ungodly, because kings serve it—a circumstance in which there is a more dangerous and greater temptation. Rather, it will then be glorious, when what the same Apostle says comes to pass: “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:4).

Since the Lord himself, according to the form of a servant by which the Mediator united himself to the Church, was not glorified except by the glory of the resurrection—hence it was said, “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39)—how can his Church be said to be glorious before its resurrection?

He therefore now cleanses it “by the washing of water with the word” (Eph. 5:26), washing away past sins and driving from it the dominion of the evil angels. Then, perfecting its healings, he causes it to arrive at that glorious state, without spot or wrinkle. “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8:30).

I think that this mystery is signified by the words, “Behold, I cast out demons and perform healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected” (Luke 13:32)—that is, “I am brought to completion.” For he said this in the person of his body, which is the Church, assigning “days” to distinct and ordered periods. He also signified this in his own resurrection by the three-day period. [Note: The printed editions read, “the Church of God: assigning.” This is corrected from a Vatican manuscript.]

[Col. 0311] 36. I think there is a difference between being upright in heart and being pure in heart. The upright in heart presses forward toward what lies ahead, forgetting what is behind, so that by a straight course—that is, by right faith and intention—he may arrive where the pure in heart dwells (Phil. 3:13–14).

Thus the individual clauses should each be applied to their proper subjects in the passage: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place? The innocent in hands and pure in heart.” The innocent in hands will ascend, and the pure in heart will stand: the former concerns conduct, the latter the end. [Note: The printed editions read, “the former concerns faith,” but this is incorrect and conflicts with the manuscripts.]

The statement “Good is the substance of the one whose conscience has no sin” should likewise be understood more deeply. Then there will truly be good substance—that is, true riches—when all poverty has passed away, that is, when all weakness has been brought to an end. [Note: The printed editions and the manuscripts, except one Vatican manuscript, read “when all weakness has been completed.”]

For now, a person should turn away from sin as he withdraws from it by making progress and is renewed day by day [Note: Most manuscripts read “withdraws and is renewed”; the Amerbach edition reads “withdraw,” and the Louvain edition, “withdraws and be renewed.”]; he should direct his hands toward works [Note: Most manuscripts read “work”; one manuscript reads “a work.”] of mercy and cleanse his heart from every sin, showing mercy so that what remains may be forgiven. [Note: One of the Vatican manuscripts reads, “cleanse his heart while, through works of mercy, he earns that what remains,” and so forth.]

This is rightly understood, for our salvation and without empty or vain boasting, in what holy John said: “If our heart does not reproach us, we have confidence toward God, and whatever we ask, we shall receive from him.” He seems here to have warned us that our heart should not reproach us in the very act of praying and asking; that is, when we begin to say, “Forgive us, as we also forgive,” we should not be pierced by the realization that we do not do what we say, nor even dare to say what we do not do, and thereby lose confidence in asking.

## CHAPTER XVI

37. He also set against himself the testimony of Scripture that is usually cited to them: “There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin” (Eccles. 7:20). And he apparently replied with other testimonies, because “the Lord says concerning holy Job: ‘Have you considered my servant Job? For there is no one like him on earth, a blameless man, a true worshiper of God, abstaining from every evil’” (Job 1:8).

We have already discussed this above. Yet he has not shown us how Job, if these words are to be understood in this way, could have been without any sin on earth, while the statement he says is written—“There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin”—remains true.

## CHAPTER XVII

38. “Again,” he says, “they cite: ‘No living person shall be justified in your sight’” (Ps. 143:2). He replied to this testimony as though for no other purpose than to make the Scriptures appear to quarrel among themselves, whereas we ought to demonstrate their harmony.

For he says: “To this one should reply that the Evangelist testifies concerning holy Zechariah and Elizabeth, saying, ‘They were both righteous before God, walking in all the commandments and ordinances of the Lord without blame’” (Luke 1:6).

Those two righteous people had certainly read, among the commandments themselves, how they should cleanse their sins. For Zechariah, as is said in the Epistle to the Hebrews concerning every priest taken from among human beings, undoubtedly offered sacrifices even for his own sins (Heb. 5:3). How the phrase “without blame” should be understood, we have already shown sufficiently, as I believe (ch. 11, §§23–28).

“And the blessed Apostle,” he says, “says, ‘That we should be holy and without blemish in his sight’” (Eph. 1:4). This is what is being accomplished, so that we may be such—if “without blemish” is understood to mean those who are altogether without sin. But if those are without blemish who are without crime, we cannot deny that there have been and are such people even in this life. For no one is without any sin merely because he has no criminal stain.

Thus, when the Apostle was choosing ministers to be ordained, he did not say, “If anyone is without sin,” which could not be found; but he said, “If anyone is without crime” (Titus 1:6), which could indeed be found. [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads “be found.”] Yet he has not shown how, according to his own case, we ought to understand what is written: “No living person shall be justified in your sight.”

The meaning is clear and is made more evident by the preceding verse: “Do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person shall be justified in your sight.” He fears judgment because he desires mercy, and mercy triumphs over judgment. This is the meaning of “Do not enter into judgment with your servant”: do not judge me according to your own standard, since you are without sin, “for no living person shall be justified in your sight.” That this is spoken of the present life is understood without difficulty; and the statement “shall not be justified” refers to that perfection of righteousness which does not exist in this life.

## CHAPTER XVIII

39. “Again,” he says, “they cite: ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us’” (1 John 1:8). He attempted to reply to this most evident testimony with supposedly contrary testimonies, since “the same holy John says in the same Epistle, ‘But I say this, brothers, so that you may not sin. Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him, and he cannot sin’” (1 John 3:9).

“Again, there: ‘The one who is born of God does not sin, because God’s generation preserves him, and the evil one does not touch him’” (1 John 5:18). “Again,” he says, “there, where he speaks of the Savior: ‘He appeared in order to take away sins. Everyone who remains in him does not sin. Everyone who sins has not seen him or known him. Again, there: Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is; and everyone who has this hope in him sanctifies himself, just as he is holy’” (1 John 3:5–6, 2–3).

Yet although all these testimonies are true, the statement he proposed and did not resolve is also true: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

Accordingly, insofar as we have been born of God, we remain in the one who appeared to take away sins—that is, in Christ—and we do not sin. This means that “the inner person is renewed day by day” [Note: The Amerbach and Erasmus editions and the manuscripts read “that the inner person is renewed,” omitting “human being.”] (2 Cor. 4:16). But insofar as we have been born from that human being through whom sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings (Rom. 5:12), we are not without sin. For we are not yet without that person’s weakness, until the entire weakness in which we were born from the first human being—and in which we are not without sin—is healed by that renewal which takes place day by day, since through that renewal we have been born of God.

As long as the remnants of this weakness remain in the inner person, although they diminish day by day in those who are making progress, if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.

How is it true, then, that “everyone who sins has not seen him or known him,” since, according to the vision and knowledge that will exist in direct sight, no one sees or knows him in this life, while according to the vision and knowledge that exists in faith, there are many who sin—certainly the apostates themselves, who nevertheless once believed in him—so that it cannot be said of any of them, according to the vision and knowledge that still exists in faith, that he has not seen or known him?

I think the meaning must be that the renewal which is to be perfected sees and knows him, whereas the weakness that is to be removed neither sees nor knows him. As long as any remnants of it remain within, if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.

Therefore, although through the grace of renewal we are children of God, because of the remnants of weakness it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. Then there will be no sin, because no weakness, whether within or without, will remain.

And everyone who has this hope in him sanctifies himself, just as he is holy. He sanctifies himself not by himself, but by believing in and calling upon the one who sanctifies his saints. The perfection of this sanctification—which now progresses and grows day by day—will remove all remnants of weakness.

## CHAPTER XIX

40. “Again,” he says, “they cite: ‘It depends not on the one who wills or runs, but on God who shows mercy’” (Rom. 9:16). To this, he says, “one should reply that the same Apostle says elsewhere concerning a certain man, ‘Let him do what he wishes’” (1 Cor. 7:36).

“Again,” he says, “to Philemon concerning Onesimus: ‘I wanted to keep him with me, so that he might minister to me on your behalf; but I wished to do nothing without your counsel, so that your good deed might not be as though compelled, but voluntary’” (Philem. 13–14).

“Again, in Deuteronomy: ‘He set life and death before you, good and evil; choose life, so that you may live’” (Deut. 30:15, 19). “Again, in Solomon: ‘God established human beings from the beginning and left them in the hand of their own counsel. He added commandments and precepts; if you wish the commandments, they will preserve you, and afterward you will render a faithfulness pleasing to God. He placed water and fire before you; stretch out your hand toward whichever you wish. Before human beings are good and evil, life and death; and poverty and honor come from the Lord God’” (Ecclus. 15:14–18).

“Again, in Isaiah: ‘If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and do not obey me, the sword shall devour you. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things’” (Isa. 1:19–20).

Here, however much they may conceal themselves, they reveal themselves. For they show that they are arguing against the grace or mercy of God, which we wish to obtain when we say, “Your will be done, as in heaven so on earth,” or, “Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:10, 13).

Why do we ask for these things in prayer with such deep groaning if it depends on the one who wills and runs, and not on God who shows mercy? This does not mean that it takes place without our will, but that the will does not accomplish what it undertakes unless it is divinely helped. This is the soundness of faith, which makes us seek so that we may find, ask so that we may receive, and knock so that it may be opened to us (Luke 11:9). Whoever argues against this closes the door of God’s mercy against himself. I do not wish to say more about so great a matter, because I entrust it more suitably to the groans of the faithful than to my own words.

41. Nevertheless, observe, I beg you, what sort of argument it is to say that God’s mercy is not necessary for the one who wills and runs—although that mercy even precedes him so that he may run—because the Apostle says of a certain man, “Let him do what he wishes.” This occurs, I think, where he goes on to say, “He does not sin if he marries.” As though wishing to marry were something great, when the question under discussion concerns the aid of divine mercy.

Or does willing even there accomplish anything unless God, by the providence through which he governs all things, joins male and female? Or because the Apostle wrote to Philemon, “So that his good deed might not be as though compelled, but voluntary,” is good voluntary in any other way than when God works in us both willing and working according to his good will (Phil. 2:13)?

Or because it is written in Deuteronomy, “I have set life and death, good and evil, before human beings,” and he admonished them to choose life—is the admonition itself not also from mercy? Or would choosing life accomplish anything unless God inspired the love by which life is chosen and granted that it be possessed after being chosen? Concerning this it is said, “For his anger is in his indignation, and life is in his will” (Ps. 30:6).

Or because it was said, “If you wish the commandments, they will preserve you,” should one not give thanks to God for having wished the commandments, when a person abandoned to every light of truth could not have wished them?

With fire and water placed before a person, he does indeed stretch out his hand toward whichever he wishes; but the one who calls is higher [Note: An old Corbie manuscript reads “more deeply” here and in the following occurrence; four other manuscripts consistently read “higher” in both places.], calling more deeply than every human thought. For the beginning of correction is faith, as it is written, “You will come and pass through from the beginning of faith” (Song 4, according to the Septuagint). Each person chooses the good according to the measure of faith that God has allotted to him (Rom. 12:3).

And “No one can come to me,” says the Prince of faith, “unless the Father who sent me draws him.” That he is speaking of faith, by which one believes in him, he explains clearly afterward, when he says: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life; but there are some among you who do not believe.” For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who believed and who would betray him. And he said, “Therefore I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been granted to him by my Father” (John 6:44, 64–66).

42. He thought he had found something important for his case in the prophet Isaiah, because God said, “If you are willing and listen to me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and do not listen to me, the sword shall devour you. For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things.”

As though the entire law were not filled with conditions of this kind; or as though these commandments had been given to the proud for any other reason than that the law was established because of transgression, until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made (Gal. 3:19).

Therefore “the law came in so that the trespass might increase; but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5:20). That is, human beings were to receive commandments while proudly trusting in their own powers; then, failing in those powers and becoming transgressors as well, they would seek a liberator and savior. In this way the fear of the law, having made them humble, would lead them, like a tutor, to faith and grace.

Thus, after weaknesses had multiplied, “they hastened afterward” (Ps. 16:4), and Christ came at the fitting time to heal them. The righteous of ancient times also believed in his grace, aided by that same grace, so that they joyfully recognized him beforehand, and some even foretold that he would come: among the people of Israel, Moses, Joshua the son of Nun, Samuel, David, and others like them; outside that people, Job; before that people, Abraham, Noah, and whatever others divine Scripture either mentions or leaves unmentioned.

For there is one God and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5), without whose grace no one is freed from condemnation—whether from the condemnation inherited from the one in whom all sinned, or from that which each person afterward added through his own iniquities.

## CHAPTER XX
43. What, then, is the meaning of what he placed at the end: “If someone says, ‘Can it happen that a person does not sin even in word?’ the answer is,” he says, “If God wills it, he can; for God wills it, therefore he can.” Likewise he says: “If someone says, ‘Can it happen that a person does not transgress even in thought?’ the answer is, ‘If God wills it, he can; for God wills it, therefore he can.’” See how he did not wish to say, “If God helps him, he can,” to whom it is said, “Be my helper; do not forsake me” (Ps. 26:9)—not, certainly, for acquiring bodily goods and avoiding bodily evils, but for practicing and fulfilling righteousness. For this reason we say, “Do not bring us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13).

And no one is helped unless he himself also does something; he is helped, however, if he calls upon God, if he believes, if he has been called according to the purpose: “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. 8:29–30).

We therefore run when we make progress, while our health runs forward in those who are making progress (just as a scar is also said to “run” when a wound is being treated well and carefully), so that, perfected in every respect, we may be entirely without any infirmity of sin. God not only wills this; he also brings it about and helps us to accomplish it. [Col. 0316] And the grace of God accomplishes this with us through Jesus Christ our Lord—not only through commands, sacraments, and examples, but also through the Holy Spirit, by whom charity is secretly poured into our hearts (Rom. 5:5), and this charity “intercedes with inexpressible groanings” (ibid. 8:26), until health is perfected in us and God is revealed to us to be seen as he is in eternal truth.

## CHAPTER XXI

44. Whoever, therefore, thinks that in this life there has been or is any human being, or any human beings, except for the one Mediator between God and human beings, for whom the forgiveness of sins was not necessary, contradicts divine Scripture, where the Apostle says: “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (ibid. 5:12).

Such a person must, with impious obstinacy, assert that there can be human beings who, without Christ the Mediator liberating and saving them, are free and safe from sin, although Christ said: “It is not the healthy who need a physician, but those who are ill. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. 9:12–13).

Whoever, however, says that after receiving forgiveness of sins someone has lived, or lives, so righteously in this flesh that he has absolutely no sin, contradicts the apostle John, who says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8). He did not say, “We have had no sin,” but, “We have no sin.”

If someone asserts that this refers to the sin that dwells in our mortal flesh, according to the vice contracted through the will of the first human being who sinned—a sin whose desires the Apostle Paul commands us not to obey (Rom. 6:12)—but that the person who has consented to that same sin in no evil deed, word, or thought at all, although it dwells in the flesh, does not sin, even though concupiscence itself is stirred (and has received the name “sin” in another sense, because to consent to it is sin, while it is stirred in us against our will), he distinguishes these matters subtly. But let him consider what happens with regard to the Lord’s Prayer, in which we say, “Forgive us our debts.” Unless I am mistaken, there would be no need to say this if we never consented, even slightly, to the desires of that same sin—whether through a slip of the tongue or by indulging a thought—but only needed to say, “Do not bring us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:12–13).

Nor would the apostle James say, “We all offend in many things” (Jas. 3:2). For no one offends unless an evil desire, contrary to the rule of righteousness, persuades him—whether by deceiving or overpowering him—to do, say, or think something that he ought not, by desiring or avoiding it.

Finally, if, except for our Head, the Savior of his body, some human beings are asserted either to have been or to be in this life righteous without any sin—whether because they never consent to its desires, or because what is involved is not to be counted as sin, since God does not charge it against their piety [Note: [Col. 0316] The Corbie manuscript and one of the Belgian manuscripts read, “so that he does not charge this against their piety.”] [Col. 0317]—although one person is blessed without sin in one way, and another is blessed because the Lord does not charge sin against him (Ps. 26:9), I do not think we should resist too strongly.

For I know that this has seemed so to certain people, whose opinion on the matter I do not dare to criticize, although I cannot defend it either [Note: [Col. 0317] Three French manuscripts and two Vatican manuscripts read, “I do not dare.”]. But plainly, whoever denies that we ought to pray that we not enter into temptation [Col. 0318]—and he denies this who maintains that God’s help is not necessary for human beings in order not to sin, but that the human will, once it has received the law, is sufficient by itself—I do not doubt that such a person must be removed from the ears of everyone and anathematized by the mouth of everyone.

## [ON THE PROCEEDINGS OF PELAGIUS]

[Col. 0317]

### INTRODUCTION TO THE BOOK ON THE PROCEEDINGS OF PELAGIUS

In the year of Christ 415, Pelagius, accused of heresy in Palestine, was brought to trial once and again. Concerning the first trial, which John, bishop of Jerusalem, held in an assembly of presbyters around the thirtieth of July, Augustine writes in the following book, sections 39 and 55, that no official proceedings were drawn up. The time and day of this assembly could be learned from Orosius, a Spanish presbyter who attended it and recorded in his *Apology* some matters worthy of remembrance from its proceedings [Note: [Col. 0317] See below, Appendix, part 2.]. There he says that, after many arguments had been advanced by both sides, Bishop John finally pronounced the decision that brothers and letters should be sent to the blessed Innocent, pope of Rome, and that everyone should follow whatever he decided.

A second trial, with a written record of the proceedings, was subsequently held at Diospolis, a city of Palestine, by fourteen bishops. Augustine names each of the bishops in his first book against Julian, sections 19 and 32, in the following order: Eulogius, John, Ammonianus, Porphyry, Eutonius, another Porphyry, Fidus, Zoninus, Zoboennus, Nymphidius, Chromatius, Jovinus, Eleutherius, and Clematius. Moreover, no one doubts that Eulogius himself was bishop of Caesarea and primate of the province of Palestine, since Augustine consistently places him before the other thirteen bishops, including John of Jerusalem himself.

We understand that the synod was held as the Nativity of the Lord was approaching from Lucian’s letter concerning the revelation of the body of the martyr Stephen [Note: [Col. 0317] It appears in the Appendix to volume 7.]. After relating that three visions had been divinely shown to him in the year 415—the first on December 3, the second on the tenth, and the third on the seventeenth—and that he had reported the matter to John at Jerusalem, while John had ordered him to search for the tomb by digging up the ground, he then testifies that, after finding the tomb, he immediately went back to John, who, he says, was at Lydda, that is, Diospolis, holding a synod.

This evidently fell around December 21. For Lucian continues by saying that John came with two other bishops, Eutonius of Sebaste and Eleutherius of Jericho, and that, in their presence, the relics of the martyr were transferred on the twenty-sixth of that same month.

A certain Annianus, a deacon of Celeda, is thought to have defended Pelagius’s case at the synod. Some learned men more readily interpret Jerome’s words about this deacon than about Pelagius, in his letter to Alypius and Augustine, number 202 among Augustine’s letters, section 2, where he writes: “Whatever he denies having said at that wretched synod of Diospolis, he professes in this work.” When Jerome called the synod of Diospolis “wretched,” we think he did so for no other reason than that he knew from the proceedings that Pelagius had deceived it.

Having seen those same proceedings, Pope Innocent declared that he could neither condemn nor approve the judgment of those bishops (letter 183 among Augustine’s letters, section 4). Augustine, for his part, calls them “pious judges” in the following book, section 4, and “Catholic judges” in the first book against Julian, section 19. They had absolved Pelagius because, after he had abjured the errors charged against him, they judged him Catholic. Yet Augustine often cites those same fourteen bishops against Julian as witnesses to Catholic truth.

In letters 175, section 4, and 177, section 2, written to Innocent in the year 416, Augustine indicated that he possessed nothing concerning the proceedings of the synod except hearsay. In letter 179, section 4, he earnestly asked John of Jerusalem to send them to him. But he had them in his possession when he wrote letter 186 to Paulinus around the middle of the year 417. This book, therefore, having been published immediately after he received the proceedings, is assigned to the beginning of that same year, 417.

Although this work is called *On the Proceedings in Palestine* in the book *On Original Sin*, section 15—a title by which Prosper likewise designates it in his book against the *Collator*, chapter 43—the title *On the Proceedings of Pelagius* must be retained. This title appears both in ancient copies and at the head of Augustine’s own *Retractations* of the work (*Retractations* 2.47).

He evidently gave the work this title either because it had already become customary for the proceedings of Pelagius and his acquittal to be so called [Note: [Col. 0317] *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, section 53], by which Pelagius boasted that he had been cleared; or because this work was to deal with the very proceedings that Pelagius himself had previously published in abbreviated and corrupted form. Hence Possidius, in his *Index*, chapter 4, titled it the book *Against the Proceedings of Pelagius*.

From this book Photius gained a very accurate knowledge of the synod of Diospolis and recorded it in manuscript 54 of his library [Col. 0319] [Note: [Col. 0319] See below, Appendix, part 2, M.]. From this one may understand that Augustine’s book was among those which Possidius says, in his *Life of Augustine*, chapter 11 or 21, section 59, were translated into Greek. Photius there called Aurelius himself—the bishop of Carthage for whom the book was written—by that title; before him, Prosper did so in his book against the *Collator*, chapter 43. Even if the title did not formerly make this clear, both men could easily discover it from reading the book, section 23.

[Col. 0319]

[Note: [Col. 0319] Concerning the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, see book 2, chapter 47, of the *Retractations*, vol. 1, col. 649, from the words “About the same time” up to “After they had come into our hands.” M.]

### SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON THE PROCEEDINGS OF PELAGIUS

To Aurelius, bishop. One book. [Note: [Col. 0319] In the editions the title was: “The book of the divine Aurelius Augustine, bishop of Hippo, to the holy bishop Aurelius, concerning the proceedings of Pelagius, against the adversaries of the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.”] [Note: [Col. 0319] Written at the beginning of the year 417.] [Note: [Col. 0319] The book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius* has been purged of countless errors with the help of ancient copies: one French manuscript from the Colbert Library, and four Italian manuscripts—namely, the Roman manuscript, whose variant readings Velser wrote in the margin of his book, and three others preserved in the libraries of the Grand Duke of Florence. We also compared four editions of this same short work: Vels., that is, the edition prepared under the direction of Marcus Velser and Antonius Velser and produced at Augsburg in the year of Christ 1611; Suar., the edition prepared by Francisco Suárez from a copy supplied to him by a learned man whom he considered entirely trustworthy, and published after Suárez’s death in the sixth prolegomenon to the books *On Grace*, chapter 7; the edition Mas., which came from the workshop of Bernard Masius at Louvain in 1647; and finally Vign., that is, the edition which Jerome Vignier caused to be published in the Augustinian Supplement.] [Note: [Col. 0319] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.] (C)

The individual charges of error brought against Pelagius before the Palestinian Synod, together with his responses to them, are examined in detail. Although Pelagius obtained an acquittal from the Synod, Augustine shows that suspicion of heresy nevertheless still remained in him. Finally, he shows that the man was acquitted by the judgment of the Synod in such a way that the heresy itself, on account of which he had been brought to trial, was unequivocally condemned.

[Col. 0319] 1. After the ecclesiastical proceedings came into our hands [Note: [Col. 0319] Velser’s edition and the Colbert manuscript read, “into your hands.” The other editions, however, correctly emend this to “into our hands,” with the support of the second book of the *Retractations*, chapter 47.], holy Pope Aurelius, in which Pelagius was pronounced Catholic by fourteen bishops of the province of Palestine, my hesitation came to an end—the hesitation that had made me doubt whether to discuss his defense itself more fully and confidently.

I had already read this defense in a certain little document that he himself had sent me [Note: [Col. 0319] See below, section 57.]. But because I had not received with it any letter from him addressed to me [Note: [Col. 0319] Perhaps, “addressed to me.”], I feared that something might be found in my words different from what was read in the episcopal proceedings. Thus, if Pelagius denied that he himself had sent me that little document—for he could not easily be convicted on the testimony of only one witness—I might instead be accused by those who favored his denial either of having introduced a forgery or, to put it more mildly, of having believed recklessly.

Now, therefore, as I examine what the proceedings attest [Note: [Col. 0319] So the ancient manuscripts, the Vatican and Colbert manuscripts. The editions, however, read: “Now therefore I examine what the proceedings attest.”], it seems to me that, with the doubt removed as to whether he acted in his own defense in this way [Note: [Col. 0319] Velser’s first edition and the manuscripts read, “as it seemed to me.”], Your Holiness, and everyone who reads this, will judge more easily and more certainly both his defense and this work of ours. [Col. 0320]

## CHAPTER I

2. First, therefore, I give ineffable thanks to the Lord God, my ruler and guardian [Note: [Col. 0320] The Colbert manuscript reads, “our ruler and guardian.”], because my opinion concerning the holy brothers and our fellow bishops who sat as judges in that case did not deceive me.

They rightly approved his answers, caring not how he had stated the matters being objected to in his writings, but what answer he gave concerning them in the present examination. For unsound faith is one thing, and careless expression another.

Finally, among the matters read out as objections from the little book given by our holy brothers and fellow bishops, the Gauls Heros and Lazarus, to Bishop Eulogius [Note: [Col. 0320] To Bishop Eulogius: see below, section 9]—who, because of the serious illness of one of them, as we later learned more reliably, were quite unable to be present—the first objection was this: in one of his books he wrote, “No one can be without sin unless he has knowledge of the law.”

After this was read, the Synod said: “Did you publish this, Pelagius?” He replied: “I did say it, but not in the way they understand it. I did not say that someone who has knowledge of the law cannot sin; rather, that knowledge of the law helps one not to sin, as it is written, ‘He gave them the law for assistance’” (Isa. 8:20, according to the Septuagint).

When they heard this, the Synod said: “What Pelagius has said is not alien to the Church.” Certainly, what he answered is not alien to the Church; but what was brought forward from his book has a different meaning. The bishops, however, being Greek speakers and hearing those words through an interpreter, did not take the trouble to investigate this. They considered only what the man being questioned said he had meant, not the words in which the same opinion had been written in his book.

3. It is one thing for a person to be helped by knowledge of the law not to sin, and another thing for no one to be without sin unless he has knowledge of the law.

For when, for example, we see that threshing floors can be threshed without threshing sledges, although sledges are useful if they are present; that boys can proceed to school without tutors, although the assistance of tutors is not useless for this purpose; that many recover from illness without physicians, although the assistance of physicians is plainly beneficial; and that people can live on other foods without bread, although the great value of bread’s assistance is not denied—and many other examples that readily occur to anyone who reflects while we remain silent—we are plainly reminded that there are two kinds of assistance.

Some kinds are such that, without them, the thing they assist cannot be accomplished: no one sails without a ship, no one speaks without a voice, no one walks without feet, no one sees without light, and many things of this sort. Among these is also the fact that no one lives rightly without the grace of God.

Other kinds of assistance, however, help us in such a way that, even if they are absent, the thing for which we require them can be accomplished in another way. Such are the examples I mentioned: a threshing sledge for threshing grain, a tutor for leading a boy, a medicine compounded by human skill [Note: [Col. 0321] The manuscripts read, “compounded by human kindness.”] for restoring health, and other things of this sort.

We must therefore ask which of these two kinds knowledge of the law belongs to—that is, how it helps one not to sin. If it belongs to the first kind, so that this cannot be accomplished without it, then Pelagius not only answered correctly at the trial but also wrote correctly in his book. But if it belongs to the second kind, so that it helps when present, while the thing it helps can nevertheless be accomplished in another way even when it is absent, then he answered correctly at the trial—something the bishops rightly approved—when he said that “a person is helped by knowledge of the law not to sin.” But he did not write correctly in his book, “No one is without sin unless he has knowledge of the law.” The judges left this unexplored because they were ignorant of the Latin language and contented themselves with the confession of the man pleading his case. In particular, no opponent was present who could have forced the interpreter, by explaining the words of the book, to reveal their meaning and show why the brothers had not been moved without reason.

Very few people are learned in the law. But the multitude of Christ’s members, spread everywhere and unskilled in a law so deep and manifold, is commended by the piety of simple faith, the firmest hope in God, and sincere charity. Endowed with these gifts, it trusts that by the grace of God it can be cleansed from sins through Jesus Christ our Lord.

## CHAPTER II

4. If Pelagius were to answer that he had called “knowledge of the law” that knowledge without which a person cannot be free from sins—the knowledge conveyed through the teaching of faith to novices and little ones in Christ, by which those who are to be baptized are also catechized so that they may know the Creed—then this is not ordinarily what is meant when someone is said to possess knowledge of the law; rather, it refers to the knowledge by which people are called learned in the law.

Nevertheless, if he were to call these words—which are few in number but great in weight, and which, according to the custom of all the Churches, are faithfully imparted to those about to be baptized—“knowledge of the law,” asserting that he had spoken of this knowledge when he said, “No one is without sin unless he has knowledge of the law,” which must be handed on to believers before they come to the forgiveness of sins, even then he would be surrounded not by disputants but by an innumerable multitude of baptized infants crying out.

They would not cry out in words, but by the very truth of their innocence: “What is this, what is this that you have written—‘No one can be without sin unless he has knowledge of the law’? Look at us: we are a great flock of sinless lambs, yet we do not possess knowledge of the law.”

These children would at least, though their tongues were silent, compel him to be silent, or perhaps even to confess either that he had now been corrected from that perversity [Note: [Col. 0322] Perhaps, “corrected” in the sense of “amended.”], or certainly that he had always understood what he now said in the ecclesiastical examination, but had not expressed that opinion in his book with sufficiently careful wording. Therefore, his faith should be approved and his book amended.

For, as it is written, “There is one who slips in speech but not in his heart” (Ecclus. 19:16).

If he were to say this—or if he should say it now—who would not readily forgive him for having written those same words too carelessly and negligently, provided that he did not defend the opinion contained in them, but said that his opinion was the one approved by the truth?

We should believe that the pious judges also considered this—if, that is, they were able to understand sufficiently what was carefully interpreted from his Latin book, just as they judged that his response, delivered in Greek and therefore easily understood, was not alien to the Church.

But now let us examine the rest.

## CHAPTER III

5. The episcopal Synod added and said: “Let another chapter be read.” It was read that Pelagius had written in the same book, “Everyone is governed by his own will.”

After this was read, Pelagius replied: “I said this also on account of free choice, to one choosing the good God is a helper; but when a person sins, he himself is at fault, as possessing free choice.”

When they heard this, the bishops said: “Nor is this alien to ecclesiastical teaching.” For who would condemn free choice, or deny it, when God’s help is preached together with it? Therefore the respondent’s statement rightly pleased the bishops. Nevertheless, the brothers who knew what such people usually argue against God’s grace ought certainly to have been disturbed by what was written in his book: “Everyone is governed by his own will.”

For this was said as though God governs no one, and as though it had been written in vain: “Save your people, and bless your inheritance; shepherd them and lift them up forever” (Ps. 28:9). Otherwise, if they are governed by their own will without God, they would remain like sheep without a shepherd (Mark 6:34)—which God forbid.

For, without doubt, to be directed is more than to be governed. Whoever is governed does something, and is governed by God so that he may act rightly. But whoever is directed is scarcely understood to do anything himself. Nevertheless, the grace of the Savior does so much for our wills that the Apostle does not hesitate to say: “As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God” (Rom. 8:14).

Nor can free will do anything better in us than to commend itself to him to be directed by him who cannot act wrongly. And when it has done this, it should not doubt that it was helped by him to do so—to whom it is said in the Psalm, “My God, his mercy will precede me” (Ps. 59:11).

6. Indeed, in the book in which Pelagius wrote those chapters, he placed something after the proposition in which he said, “Everyone is governed by his own will, and each person is left to his own desire” [Note: [Col. 0323] The Colbert manuscript reads, “proposition.”], drawing upon the testimony of Scripture. This makes it sufficiently clear that a person ought not entrust himself to be governed by himself.

For, concerning this very matter, Solomon’s Wisdom says: “I too am a mortal human being, like everyone else, descended from the earthly one who was formed first” [Note: [Col. 0323] Suárez: “who was made”; Masius: “who was fashioned”; the first editions and the manuscripts: “who was formed.”], and so on up to the end of the chapter, where we read: “One is the entrance into life for all, and alike the exit. Therefore I desired, and understanding was given to me; I called upon God, and the spirit of wisdom came to me” (Wis. 7:1–7).

Is it not clearer than daylight how this man, considering the misery of human frailty, did not dare entrust himself to be governed by himself? Rather, he desired, and understanding was given to him—understanding of which the Apostle says, “But we have the mind of the Lord” (1 Cor. 2:16); and he called upon God, and the spirit of wisdom came to him.

It is by this spirit, not by the strength of their own will, that those who are sons of God are governed and led.

7. Likewise, in the same book of chapters, he included a passage from the Psalm as though to prove that “everyone is governed by his own will”: “He loved cursing, and it shall come upon him; he did not desire blessing, and it shall be far from him” (Ps. 109:18).

Who does not know that this is a vice not of nature, as God created it, but of the human will, which withdrew from God?

Nevertheless, if he had not loved cursing, had desired blessing, and in this very matter had denied that his will was helped by divine grace, he would have been abandoned to govern himself—ungrateful and impious—so that, rushing headlong without God as his governor, he might learn through punishments that he could not govern himself by himself.

The same applies to the testimony that he placed under the same heading in that book: “He has set before you water and fire; stretch out your hand toward whichever you wish. Before human beings are good and evil, life and death; whichever pleases them shall be given to them” (Ecclus. 15:17–18).

It is clear that if a person stretches out his hand toward fire, and evil and death please him, the human will brings this about. But if he loves good and life, the will does not merely accomplish this; it is also divinely helped.

The eye is sufficient for itself not to see—that is, for darkness. But it is not sufficient for itself to see by its own light unless the assistance of a bright light is supplied to it from outside.

But far be it that those who are called according to the purpose—those whom God foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. 8:29)—should be abandoned to their own desire so that they perish [Note: [Col. 0324] Suárez reads, “should be permitted.”].

This is what the vessels of wrath suffer, vessels perfected for destruction. In their very destruction God makes known the riches of his glory in the vessels of his mercy (ibid. 9:22–23).

For this reason, after saying, “My God, his mercy will precede me,” the Psalm immediately adds, “My God has shown me among my enemies” (Ps. 59:11–12).

Thus what is written happens to them: “God gave them over to the desires of their heart” (Rom. 1:24). But this does not happen to those who are predestined and governed by the Spirit of God, for their voice is not empty: “Do not hand me over, Lord, to my sinful desire” (Ps. 140:9).

Indeed, even against those desires prayer was offered in these words: “Take away from me the desires of the belly, and do not let the desire for intercourse seize me” (Ecclus. 23:6).

God grants this to those whom he governs in submission to himself, but not to those who think themselves capable of governing themselves and, with the proud neck of their own will, disdain to have him as their governor.

8. Since these things are so, how could the children of God who know this—who rejoice that they are governed and led by the Spirit of God—have failed to be disturbed when they heard or read that Pelagius had written, “Everyone is governed by his own will, and each person is left to his own desire”?

And yet, when questioned by the bishops, he perceived what evil those words conveyed and replied that “he had said this on account of free choice,” immediately adding, “to one choosing the good God is a helper; but when a person sins, he himself is at fault, as possessing free choice.”

The pious judges approved this statement as well, but they did not wish to consider or investigate either how carelessly those words had been placed in his book or in what sense they had been written. They considered it sufficient that he had confessed free choice in such a way that God was the helper of the person choosing good, while the sinner was at fault, his own will being sufficient for this purpose.

Accordingly, God governs those for whom he is the helper when they choose good. And they govern whatever they govern well because they themselves are governed by the Good.

9. It was next read that Pelagius had written in his book [Col. 0325]: “On the day of judgment, the wicked and sinners are not to be spared, but are to be burned in eternal fires.”

This had disturbed the brothers, so that they thought it ought to be brought forward as an objection, because it was stated as though all sinners were to be punished by eternal torment, with no exception for those who have Christ as their foundation, even though they build upon it wood, hay, and straw. Concerning these the Apostle says: “If anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire” (1 Cor. 3:15).

But when Pelagius replied, “I said this according to the Gospel, where it is said concerning sinners, ‘They will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life’” (Matt. 25:46), Christian judges could in no way find the evangelical and dominical sentence displeasing. They did not know what had disturbed the brothers in the words taken from Pelagius’s book, since they were accustomed to hearing the arguments of Pelagius and his disciples.

In the absence of those who had given the holy Bishop Eulogius the book against Pelagius, no one pressed him to distinguish by some exception between sinners who would be saved through fire and sinners who would be punished by eternal torment. Had the judges understood why the objection had been raised, Pelagius would rightly have been condemned if he refused to make the distinction.

10. But when Pelagius added, “And if anyone believes otherwise, he is an Origenist,” the judges understood this to refer to what the Church rightly detests in Origen: namely, the belief that even those whom the Lord says will be punished by eternal torment, and the devil himself and his angels, will, after a very long period of purification, be released from their punishments and join the saints who reign with God in the fellowship of blessedness.

Thus the Synod said that the statement was “not alien to the Church,” not according to Pelagius, but rather according to the Gospel: wicked people and sinners of the kind whom the Gospel judges worthy of such punishment will be burned in eternal fires. And whoever agrees with Origen in the detestable claim that the punishment of such people can at some point end—although the Lord called it eternal—holds a position that must be condemned.

As for those sinners of whom the Apostle says that, after their work has been burned up, they will be saved as through fire, nothing was clearly brought forward against Pelagius concerning them, and therefore the judges made no ruling about them.

Accordingly, Pelagius does not inappropriately call someone an Origenist who says that the wicked and sinners whom the truth condemns to eternal punishment can at some point be released from it. But, in turn, whoever considers no sinner worthy of mercy at God’s judgment may give him whatever name he wishes, provided that he understands that this error too is not accepted by ecclesiastical truth.

“For judgment will be without mercy for the one who has shown no mercy” (Jas. 2:13).

11. But how this judgment will take place is difficult to grasp from the Holy Scriptures, for what will occur in one way is signified in many ways. Thus at one time the Lord says that, against those whom he does not admit into his kingdom, he will shut the door [Note: [Col. 0325] Only the later editions read *clausurum* (“that he will shut”).], while they cry out and say, “Open to us! We ate and drank in your name,” and the other things which they are written as saying; he will answer them, “I do not know you, you who work iniquity” (Luke 13:26–27). At another time he recalls that he will order those who did not wish him to reign over them to be brought before him and slain in his presence (ibid. 19:27). At another time he says that he will come with his angels in his majesty, so that all nations will be gathered before him; he will divide them and place some at his right hand. Recalling their good works, he will carry them [Note: [Col. 0326] Vignerius reads *reponat* (“place back”). Perhaps one should read *eos portet* (“carry them”).] into eternal life; others he will place at his left, and, charging them with the barrenness of their good works, condemn them to eternal fire (Matthew 25:31–46). At another time he orders the wicked and lazy servant who neglected to invest his money (Luke 19:22–24), or the man found at the banquet without a wedding garment, to be cast, with hands and feet bound, into the outer darkness. At another time, after receiving the five wise virgins, he shuts the door against the other five, the foolish ones (Matthew 25:10–12).

These and whatever else does not presently occur to me are spoken concerning the future judgment, which will certainly be carried out not upon one or five people but upon many. For if there were only one who was ordered to be cast from the banquet into the darkness because he did not have a wedding garment, it would not immediately follow that the statement “For many are called, but few are chosen” was made (ibid. 22:11–14), since, with one person cast out and condemned, many would rather appear to have remained in the house. But to discuss all these matters now at sufficient length would take too long.

This much, however, I can say briefly—without prejudging what is commonly said in financial accounts, “the better reckoning”—that one particular mode of judgment, inscrutable to us, is signified throughout the Holy Scriptures in many ways, while the diversity of merits in rewards and punishments is preserved. As far as the matter now under discussion is concerned, this is sufficient: if Pelagius had said that all sinners without exception were to be punished with eternal fire and eternal punishment, anyone who approved that judgment would first have pronounced sentence upon himself. For who will boast that he is clean from sins? (Proverbs 20:9, according to the Septuagint.)

But because he said neither “all” nor “some,” but used an indefinite expression [Note: [Col. 0326] In the manuscripts, and in the editions of Velsius and Suarius, the reading was *sed nec indefinite posuit* (“but he did not even use an indefinite expression”).], and replied that he had said this according to the Gospel, the statement was indeed confirmed by episcopal judgment. Yet it is still unclear what Pelagius thinks, and after this episcopal judgment it is not impertinent to inquire further [Note: [Col. 0326] The same manuscripts, Velsius, and Suarius read *sed adhucne aliquid sentiat* (“but whether he still thinks anything at all”). Perhaps for *sed aliudne aliquid sentiat* (“but whether he thinks something else”).].

## CHAPTER IV

12. Pelagius was also charged with having written in his book, “Evil does not even enter into thought.” He replied, “We did not state it in that way; rather, we said that a Christian ought to strive not to think evil”—which the bishops approved, as was proper. For who doubts that evil ought not to be thought? And indeed, if what he says in his book, “evil is not even thought,” is read as “evil is not even to be thought” [Col. 0327], this is ordinarily understood [Note: [Col. 0327] This passage was horribly corrupted through the scribes’ fault in the manuscripts, which read: *Et revera in libro suo ad malum cujus ita legitur, nec cogitandum, quod in hac intelligi solet.* Nothing was changed in Velsius’s edition, except that, in place of *ad malum cujus*, a conjecture—“*ad Melaniam*”—was written in the margin of the book. Without the support of any old manuscript, certain later editors rashly introduced this conjecture into the text.], namely, that evil ought not even to be thought. But whoever denies this says what else except that evil ought to be thought? If that were true, it would not be said in praise of charity, “It does not think evil” (1 Corinthians 13:5).

Nevertheless, the statement that evil does not “enter into the thought” of the righteous and holy is not asserted with sufficient precision, because *thought* is also commonly used when something comes into the mind, even if consent does not follow. The thought that incurs guilt and is rightly forbidden, however, is not without consent. It could therefore have happened that those who thought this should be charged against Pelagius had read a faulty manuscript, as though Pelagius had said, “Evil does not even enter into thought”—that is, that what is evil does not enter the minds of the righteous and holy.

This opinion is certainly most absurd. For when we condemn evils, we cannot express them in words unless they have been thought. But, as we have said, the thought of evil is called culpable when it draws consent along with it.

## CHAPTER V

13. When the judges had approved this response of Pelagius as well, another statement was read from his little book: “The kingdom of heaven was also promised in the Old Testament.” Pelagius replied:

“This too can be proved from the Scriptures. Heretics, however, deny it in order to insult the Old Testament. Following the authority of the Scriptures, I said this because it is written in the prophet Daniel, ‘And the saints shall receive the kingdom of the Most High’” (Daniel 7:18).

When his response had been accepted, the Synod said, “Neither is this contrary to ecclesiastical faith.”

14. Did our brothers, then, have no reason for bringing these words forward among the other charges? Certainly not. The name “Old Testament” is ordinarily used in two ways: first, according to the authority of the divine Scriptures; and second, according to the most common usage of speech.

For the Apostle Paul says to the Galatians:

“Tell me, you who desire to be under the law, have you not heard the law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and the other by a free woman; but these things are an allegory [Note: [Col. 0327] Velsius and Suarius read *quae sunt allegoria*, omitting *in*. Perhaps the reading should be *allegorica* (“allegorical”).]. For these are the two Testaments: one indeed generating slavery, which is Hagar. For Mount Sinai is in Arabia, which is joined to the Jerusalem that now exists; and it is in slavery with its children. But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.”

Since the Old Testament pertains to slavery—for it was also said, “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Galatians 4:21–30)—while the kingdom of heaven pertains to freedom, how can the kingdom of heaven also belong to the Old Testament?

But since, as I said, we also commonly speak in such a way that we call all the Scriptures of the Law and the Prophets, contained under canonical authority and given before the Lord’s incarnation [Col. 0328], by the name “Old Testament,” who is even moderately learned in ecclesiastical literature and does not know that the kingdom of heaven could have been promised in those Scriptures, just as it also belongs to the New Testament, to which the kingdom of heaven pertains?

For it is certainly written there most explicitly:

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a New Testament with the house of Israel and with the house of Jacob, not according to the Testament which I established with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt” (Jeremiah 31:31–32).

This was done on Mount Sinai. But at that time the prophet Daniel, who had said [Note: [Col. 0328] Perhaps *diceret* (“would say”) should be read instead of *dixisset* (“had said”).], “The saints shall receive the kingdom of the Most High,” did not yet exist. In these words he was prophesying a reward belonging not to the Old but to the New Testament, just as those same Prophets foretold Christ himself as destined to come, by whose blood the New Testament was consecrated. The Apostles became ministers of this Testament, as the blessed Paul says: “He also made us competent ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit. For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6).

In that Testament which is properly called “old” and was given on Mount Sinai, nothing is found to be promised explicitly except earthly happiness. Hence the land into which the people were led after being conducted through the wilderness is called “the land of promise.” Peace and a kingdom, victories over enemies, abundance of children and earthly produce, and whatever else is of this kind—these are the promises of the Old Testament. Although spiritual realities belonging to the New Testament are represented by them, the person who receives the law of God for the sake of those earthly things is himself an heir of the Old Testament.

For the things that are promised and bestowed according to the Old Testament are those desired according to the old human being. But the things represented there that pertain to the New Testament seek new human beings. Nor did that great Apostle fail to know what he was saying when he declared that the two Testaments were distinguished allegorically by the slave woman and the free woman, assigning sons of the flesh to the old covenant and sons of promise to the new:

“Not those who are children of the flesh are children of God,” he says, “but the children of promise are counted as offspring” (Romans 9:8).

The children of the flesh therefore belong to the earthly Jerusalem, which is in slavery with her children; but the children of promise belong to the Jerusalem above, our free mother in the eternal heavens. From this it becomes clear who belong to the earthly kingdom and who belong to the kingdom of heaven.

Those who, even at that time, understood this distinction by the grace of God and became children of promise were, in the hidden counsel of God, reckoned heirs of the New Testament, even though they appropriately administered the Old Testament, divinely given to the old people according to the distribution of the ages [Col. 0328] [Note: [Col. 0328] Suarius’s edition reads *pro temporum distributione* (“according to the distribution of the ages”).].

15. How, then, could the children of promise—the children of the free Jerusalem, eternal in the heavens—not rightly be disturbed when this apostolic and catholic distinction seemed to be removed by Pelagius’s words, and Hagar, in a certain sense, seemed to be regarded as equal to Sarah [Col. 0329]?

He therefore insults the Old Testament with heretical impiety who, with the boldness of sacrilegious impiety, denies that it comes from the good, supreme, and true God—like Marcion, like Manichaeus, and whatever other plague holds this opinion.

Therefore, to express as briefly as I can what I think about this matter: just as the Old Testament is insulted if it is denied to be from the good and supreme God, so the New Testament is insulted if it is made equal to the Old.

But when Pelagius, in answer to the question why he had also said that the kingdom of heaven was promised in the Old Testament, cited the testimony of the prophet Daniel, who most explicitly prophesied that the saints would receive the kingdom of the Most High, it was rightly judged that this was not contrary to catholic faith—not according to the distinction by which the earthly promises made on Mount Sinai are shown to belong properly to the Old Testament, but also not improperly according to the common usage by which all the canonical Scriptures given before the Lord’s incarnation are classified under the name “Old Testament.”

For the kingdom of the Most High is nothing other than the kingdom of God. Nor will anyone dare to contend that the kingdom of God is one thing and the kingdom of heaven another.

## CHAPTER VI

16. After this, Pelagius was charged with having written in the same book, “A person can be without sin if he wishes,” and with having said flatteringly in a letter to a widow:

“May piety find a place with you where it has found one nowhere else; may justice, an exile everywhere, find a home in you; may truth, which now no one knows, become familiar and friendly to you; and may the law of God, which is almost universally despised, be honored by you alone.”

And again to the same woman:

“O happy and blessed are you, if justice—which is believed to exist only in heaven—is found on earth in you alone!”

And in another book addressed to her, after the prayer of our Lord and Savior, while teaching how the saints ought to pray, he says:

“That person raises his hands worthily to God; that person pours out prayer with a good conscience, who can say: ‘You know, Lord, how holy, innocent, and clean from every annoyance [Note: [Col. 0329] The later editions, following what we think was a conjecture by Antonius Velsius, read *ab omni malitia* (“from all malice”).] and iniquity and robbery are the hands that I extend to you; how just and clean, and free from every lie, are the lips with which I offer supplication to you, asking you to have mercy on me.’”

In response to this Pelagius said:

“We did indeed say that a person can be without sin and keep God’s commandments if he wishes, for God gave him this possibility. But we did not say that anyone is found who has never sinned from infancy to old age. Rather, having turned away from sins, a person can, through his own labor and the grace of God, be without sin; yet by this he is not thereby incapable of turning back in the future. The remaining statements that they have attributed to us are found neither in our books, nor have we ever said anything of the kind.”

When they heard this, the Synod said:

“Since you deny having written such things, do you anathematize those who hold them?”

Pelagius replied:

“I anathematize them as fools, not as heretics, since this is not a dogma.”

Then the bishops gave judgment, saying:

“Now, since Pelagius has anathematized in his own voice this uncertain foolish talk [Col. 0330], rightly replying that a person can be without sin with God’s help and grace, let him also respond to the other chapters.”

17.
