Could or should the judges have condemned matters unknown and uncertain when no one was present to prove that Pelagius had written the statements said to have been reprehensibly addressed to the widow? It would plainly have been insufficient merely to produce a book and read these passages from his writings, unless witnesses were also brought forward, if he denied, even while they were being read, that those writings were his.

Nevertheless, in this matter too the judges did what they could do: they asked Pelagius whether he anathematized those who held opinions such as he denied having written or expressed. When he replied that he anathematized them as fools [Note: [Col. 0330] The printed editions read *quos ibi* or *quos ille*. The Colbertine manuscript reads *quos ubi*.], what more ought the judges to have sought concerning this matter in the absence of his opponents?

18. Is it perhaps also necessary to examine whether it was rightly said that those who held such an opinion should be anathematized “not as heretics but as fools, since it was not a dogma”? But from this serious question—how far someone should be defined as a heretic—the judges rightly abstained for the present [Note: [Col. 0330] The manuscripts and the first edition of Velsius and Suarius read *abstulerunt* (“removed themselves”).].

For if someone should say, for example, that eaglets, suspended from the father’s talon and exposed to the rays of the sun, are released to the ground as illegitimate if they blink their eyes—light in some way providing the proof—then, if this happens to be false, he is not for that reason to be judged a heretic.

This statement is found in the writings of learned men and has become widely known by reputation. It should not be thought foolish even if it is untrue; nor does it harm the faith for which we are called faithful, or aid what is believed. But if someone should argue from this opinion that rational souls are present in birds because human souls are transformed into them, then this must be driven from the ears and mind as a heretical plague. It must be demonstrated that, even if this claim about eagles is true—as many remarkable things about bees are true before our eyes—reason nevertheless differs greatly from the nature of irrational animals, however remarkable their instinct may be. Reason is shared not by human beings and beasts but by human beings and angels.

Many foolish things are also said by the ignorant and vain, without their being heretics. Such are the statements of those who rashly judge arts belonging to others, which they have not learned, or who, through excessive and blind affection, either praise those whom they love or blame those whom they hate. The same applies to whatever else in ordinary human speech is uttered or committed to writing and letters, not as an established dogma but casually, as it happens to occur at the moment, through the frivolity of foolishness.

Finally, many people, after being briefly admonished about such matters, soon regret having said them. They had not retained them as fixed opinions adopted by deliberate judgment, but had poured them out as though snatched from anywhere and not considered. It is scarcely possible to be free from these faults; and who is there who does not stumble in speech and offend in a word? (Sirach 19:16; James 3:2.)

The difference lies in how serious the matter is; it matters where it comes from; and, finally, it matters whether the person corrects himself when admonished or, by stubbornly defending it, turns into a dogma what he had said through frivolity rather than conviction.

Since every heretic is consequently also a fool, but not every fool must immediately be called a heretic, the judges rightly said that Pelagius had anathematized the uncertain foolish talk in his own voice. For even if it were heresy, it would undoubtedly be foolish talk. Accordingly, whatever its precise character, they called it by the general name of a fault.

Whether these statements had been spoken from some dogma, or whether they were not fixed and settled opinions but errors easily corrected, the judges did not think it necessary to investigate at that time, since the man being heard had denied that the statements were his, whatever their form.

19. When we were reading this defense of Pelagius [Note: [Col. 0331] Suarius reads *definitionem* (“definition”) instead of *defensionem* (“defense”).] in the document we had previously received [Note: [Col. 0331] See below, no. 57.], certain holy brothers were present. They said that they possessed books of Pelagius written as exhortations or consolations to a certain widow whose name was not stated [Note: [Col. 0331] Mercator calls her Livania in the *Commonitorium* concerning Caelestius.]. They urged that it be investigated whether these statements, which Pelagius denied were his, might have been written there, since they themselves also claimed not to know this.

When those books were then read from the beginning, the passages in question were sought and found. Those who produced the codex affirmed that for nearly four years they had possessed these books as Pelagius’s books, and that they had never heard anyone express doubt as to whether they were his.

Considering, therefore, that the well-known fidelity of these servants of God could not lie about this matter, it seemed that we were left to believe that Pelagius had lied in the episcopal judgment—unless we thought it possible that, even so many years earlier, something had been circulated under his name without having been written by him. For these men did not say that they had received the same books from him, or that they had heard from him that they were his.

Some of our brothers also told me that certain little works had arrived in Spain under my name which those who had read other works of ours did not recognize, although others believed them to be ours.

20. The statement that Pelagius acknowledged as his own still remains obscure, but I think that it will become clear in the later parts of these proceedings. He says:

“We did indeed say that a person can be without sin and keep God’s commandments if he wishes, for God gave him this possibility. But we did not say that anyone is found who has never sinned from infancy to old age. Rather, having turned away from sins, a person can, through his own labor and the grace of God, be without sin; yet by this he is not thereby incapable of turning back in the future.”

In these words it is entirely unclear what he calls the grace of God. The catholic judges could understand no other grace than the one that apostolic teaching strongly commends to us. For this is the grace by which we hope to be delivered from “the body of this death” through Jesus Christ our Lord:

## CHAPTER VII

And for the obtaining of this grace we pray that we may not enter into temptation (Matthew 6:13).

This grace is not nature, but that by which our frail and corrupted nature is helped. This grace is not knowledge of the law, but the grace of which the Apostle says: “I do not nullify the grace of God; for if justification comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21). Therefore it is not the killing letter but the life-giving Spirit.

For knowledge of the law without the grace of the Spirit produces every kind of desire in a person. “I would not have known sin,” he says, “except through the law; for I would not have known desire unless the law said, ‘You shall not desire.’ But, taking occasion through the commandment, sin produced in me every kind of desire.”

In saying this he does not blame the law; indeed, he praises it when he says: “The law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good. Did then what is good become death to me? Certainly not! Rather, sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good.”

Again he praises the law when he says: “We know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, sold under sin. For I do not understand what I do. For I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate. But if I do what I do not want, I agree with the law that it is good.”

He already knows the law, praises it, and agrees with it—that is, he agrees that it is good—for what the law commands, he also wills, and what it forbids and condemns, he also hates. Yet what he hates, he does.

Thus knowledge of the holy law is present, and yet the corrupt desire is not healed; a good will is present, and yet an evil action prevails. Hence, while two laws struggle against each other, the law of the mind being opposed by the law in the members and taking the person captive under the law of sin, the one who confesses cries out:

“Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?”

“The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

## CHAPTER VIII

21. It is therefore not nature—which has been sold under sin and wounded by corruption and therefore desires a redeemer and savior—nor knowledge of the law, through which the recognition but not the defeat of desire is produced [Note: [Col. 0332] Mas., Vignerius, and the Roman manuscript read *e vitio* (“from corruption”).], that delivers from the body of this death, but the grace of the Lord through Jesus Christ our Lord.

## CHAPTER IX

This is not dying nature, nor the killing letter, but the life-giving Spirit.

The man already possessed nature together with freedom of will, for he said, “To will is present with me.” But he did not possess nature together with health, free from corruption, for he said, “I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh.”

He already possessed knowledge of the holy law, for he said, “I did not know sin except through the law.” But he did not possess the strength to do and complete righteousness, for he said, “I do not do what I want, but I do what I hate,” and, “I do not find how to accomplish the good” (Romans 7:7–25).

Therefore neither freedom of will nor the commandment of the law could deliver him from the body of this death, because he already possessed both: one in nature [Col. 0333], the other in instruction. He was instead asking for the help of God’s grace through Jesus Christ our Lord.

## CHAPTER X

22. The bishops believed that Pelagius was confessing this grace, which they knew to be thoroughly familiar in the catholic Church, when they heard him say that “a person who has turned away from sins can, through his own labor and the grace of God, be without sin.”

But because of the book which the servants of God gave me to refute [Note: [Col. 0333] Timasius and Jacobus.], who had been his disciples and, because they greatly loved Pelagius, said that it was his, in which, when he had raised this question for himself, he most explicitly stated this—since many had already been offended by the way he spoke against God’s grace—that he called “the grace of God” the fact that our nature received, at its creation, the possibility of not sinning, because it was created with free will; because of this book, then, I, and many brothers because of his discussions, which they say are very familiar to them, still remain concerned about the ambiguity of these words of his. We fear that something may lie hidden in them, and that he may later explain to his disciples that he said this without prejudice to his own doctrine, arguing as follows:

“I did indeed say that a person can be without sin through his own labor and God’s grace; but you know perfectly well what grace I mean, and you can recall by reading that it is the grace in which we were created by God with free will.”

Thus, while the bishops believed that he had spoken of the grace by which we have been adopted into a new creation—not the grace by which we were created as human beings—for divine Scripture most explicitly commends this grace, they acquitted him as a catholic, unknowingly acquitting a heretic.

What also makes me suspicious is that, although in the same book to which I replied he had most explicitly said, “Abel the righteous never sinned at all,” he now says, “We did not say that anyone is found who has never sinned from infancy to old age; rather, having turned away from sins, a person can, through his own labor and the grace of God, be without sin.”

For he did not say that the righteous Abel, having turned away from sins, became without sin during the rest of his life, but that “he had never committed any sin at all.” Therefore, if that book is his, it must certainly be corrected in light of this very response.

I do not wish him now to say that he was lying, lest he perhaps claim that he had forgotten what he wrote in that book [Note: [Col. 0333] The Colbertine manuscript reads *quid* (“something”) instead of *quod* (“what”).]. Let us therefore examine what follows. For the later portions of the ecclesiastical proceedings contain material by which, with the Lord’s help, we can show that, even though Pelagius appears to some to have been cleared in that examination—and was certainly acquitted at least by the human judges—this heresy, which we do not wish to see advance further and progress toward worse things, was unquestionably condemned.

## CHAPTER XI

23. The following charges were brought against Pelagius; they were reported as having been found in the teaching of his disciple Caelestius:

“Adam was created mortal, and whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died. Adam’s sin injured himself alone and not the human race. The Law leads to the kingdom in the same way as the Gospel. Before Christ’s coming there were human beings without sin. Infants newly born are in the same condition in which Adam was before the transgression. Neither through Adam’s death or transgression does the whole human race die, nor through Christ’s resurrection does the whole human race rise again.”

These charges were presented in such a way that it was also said that Your Holiness and the other bishops with you had heard and condemned them at Carthage. As you recall, I myself was not there; but afterward, when I had come to Carthage, I reviewed the proceedings and remember some things from them. I do not know, however, whether all these statements are contained in those records [Note: [Col. 0334] The printed editions read *ejus* (“his”). The Colbertine manuscript reads *eis*, with *gestis* (“proceedings”) understood.].

But what difference does it make if some of them perhaps were not mentioned there and therefore were not condemned, since it is certain that they deserve condemnation?

Then some other chapters were brought forward, with a mention of my name inserted. These had been sent to me from Sicily when the catholic brothers there were disturbed by such questions. I answered them sufficiently, as it seems to me, in a book written to Hilary, who had consulted me about them in his letter (Letter 157, written to Hilary).

These statements were:

“A person can be without sin if he wishes. Infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life. If baptized rich people do not renounce everything, then, even if they appear to do something good, it is not credited to them, and they cannot possess the kingdom of God.”

24. Concerning these charges, as the proceedings testify, Pelagius replied:

“Regarding the possibility of a person’s being without sin, it was said above,” he said. “But concerning the claim that there were people without sin before the Lord’s coming, we too say that before Christ’s coming certain people lived holy and righteous lives, according to the tradition of the Holy Scriptures. The remaining statements were not made by me, even according to the testimony of those who brought the charges; I am therefore not required to answer for them. Nevertheless, to satisfy the holy Synod, I anathematize those who hold or have ever held such opinions.”

After this response of his, the Synod said:

“Pelagius, who is present, has sufficiently and rightly answered these aforementioned chapters by anathematizing the statements that were not his.”

We therefore see and hold that not only Pelagius but also the holy bishops who presided over that judgment condemned such pernicious errors of this heresy:

“Adam was created mortal”—to which, so that the meaning of the statement might be explained more fully, was added, “whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.”

“Adam’s sin injured himself alone and not the human race.”

“The Law leads to the kingdom in the same way as the Gospel.”

“Infants newly born are in the same condition in which Adam was before the transgression.”

“Neither through Adam’s death or transgression does the whole human race die, nor through Christ’s resurrection does the whole human race rise again.”

“Infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life.”

“Baptized rich people, unless they renounce everything, even if they appear to do something good, are not credited with it, and cannot possess the kingdom of God.”

It is certain that all these statements were condemned in that ecclesiastical judgment, with Pelagius anathematizing them and the bishops pronouncing their decisions [Col. 0335].

25. Since these questions and the most contentious assertions of these opinions were already raging everywhere, the weakness of many brothers was being disturbed. Therefore, compelled by the loving concern which, through the grace of Christ, we ought to have for the Church of Christ, we also wrote to Marcellinus, of blessed memory, who endured those most troublesome disputants every day and consulted me by letter, concerning some of these questions, especially concerning the baptism of infants.

Later, at your command, I also labored as much as I could in the Basilica of Majorum [Note: [Col. 0335] The later editions read *Majorini*. The first edition of Velsius and Suarius, together with the manuscripts, reads *Majorum*. The title of the cited sermon 294 agrees with this reading.], holding in my hands the letter of the glorious martyr Cyprian, reciting and discussing his words on this matter, so that this wicked error might be removed from the hearts of certain people who had been persuaded of the things we see condemned in these proceedings. I was assisted by your prayers.

These were the matters which certain people holding such opinions tried to persuade some of the brothers to accept, even threatening them with the Eastern Churches: unless the brothers held these views, they could be condemned by the judgment of those churches.

Behold, fourteen bishops of the Eastern Church [Note: [Col. 0335] Augustine lists their names in Book 1, no. 19, of *Against Julian*], in that land to which the Lord displayed the presence of his flesh [Note: [Col. 0335] The Roman and Colbertine manuscripts read *incarnationis* (“of his incarnation”).], would not have acquitted Pelagius unless he condemned these statements as opposed to the catholic faith.

Therefore, if he was acquitted because he anathematized such opinions, then without doubt those opinions were condemned. This will appear much more fully and clearly in what follows.

26. Let us now examine those two statements which Pelagius did not wish to anathematize, because he acknowledged that they were his, but explained how he understood them in order to remove whatever was objectionable in them.

“Regarding the possibility,” he said, “of a person’s being without sin, it was said above.”

It was indeed said, and we remember it. But the statement was softened and approved by the judges because the grace of God, which had been omitted in those chapters, was added.

The other statement requires closer examination as to how he answered it:

“But concerning the claim,” he said, “that there were people without sin before the Lord’s coming, we too say that before Christ’s coming certain people lived holy and righteous lives, according to the tradition of the Holy Scriptures.”

He did not dare to say, “We too say that before Christ’s coming there were people without sin,” although this was the statement charged against him from Caelestius’s teaching. He understood how dangerous and troublesome it would be. Instead he said, “We too say that before Christ’s coming certain people lived holy and righteous lives.”

Who could deny this? But this is one thing, and being without sin is another. For even those who were living holy and righteously truly said, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

Even today many live righteously and holily [Col. 0336], yet they do not lie in prayer when they say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

This, then, pleased the judges: the way Pelagius asserted that he understood the matter, not the way Caelestius was charged with having stated it. Let us now discuss the remaining matters as best we can.

## CHAPTER XII
27. It was alleged against Pelagius that he said, “The Church here is without spot or wrinkle.” This was also the basis of the Donatists’ long conflict with us in our Conference. We pressed them chiefly on the mixture of wicked men with the good, like chaff with wheat, because of the likeness to the threshing floor; and by the same comparison we can answer these men as well—unless perhaps they wish the Church to be understood as consisting only of the good, whom they assert to have absolutely no sin, so that the Church here may be without spot or wrinkle. But if that is so, I repeat what I mentioned shortly before: How are those people members of the Church of whom humble truth cries out, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8)? Or how will the Church pray for what the Lord taught it to pray: “Forgive us our debts,” if in this world the Church is without spot or wrinkle? Finally, they themselves must be asked whether or not they admit that they have any sins. If they deny it, they must be told that they deceive themselves and that the truth is not in them. But if they admit that they have sin, what else will they be admitting than their wrinkle or spot? These people, therefore, are not members of the Church, because the Church is without spot or wrinkle, whereas they have spot and wrinkle.

28. But to this charge he replied with vigilant caution, which the Catholic judges undoubtedly approved. “It was said by us,” he said, “but in this sense: that through the washing the Church is cleansed from every spot and wrinkle, and the Lord wills it to remain so.” To this the Synod said: “This also pleases us.”

For who among us denies that all sins are forgiven in Baptism and that all the faithful rise from the washing of regeneration without spot or wrinkle? Or what Catholic Christian does not approve what also pleases the Lord—namely, that the Church will remain without spot or wrinkle? For by God’s mercy and truth the present work is directed toward bringing the holy Church to that perfection in which it will remain forever without spot or wrinkle.

But between the washing, where all former spots and wrinkles are removed, and the kingdom, where the Church will remain perpetually without spot or wrinkle, there is this intervening time of prayer, in which it must say, “Forgive us our debts.” For this reason it was alleged that they said, “The Church is here without spot or wrinkle,” to see whether [Note: [Col. 0336] Perhaps, “so that they might not.”] by this statement they might dare to forbid the prayer by which the baptized Church asks day and night for the forgiveness of sins.

Regarding this intervening period between the forgiveness of sins that takes place in the washing and the future permanence without sins in the kingdom, nothing was accomplished with Pelagius, and nothing was pronounced by the bishops. Only this was indicated briefly: that he had not said it in the manner in which the charge seemed to represent him as having said it. For when he said, “It was said by us, but in this sense,” what did he wish to convey except that he had not said it in the way those who brought the charge believed he had? What the judges nevertheless had in mind when they said that this pleased them—that is, Baptism, by which the holy Church that is now being cleansed is washed from sins, and the kingdom, where it will remain without sins—is sufficiently clear, so far as I judge.

**CHAPTER XIII**

29. Next, charges were brought from the book of Coelestius, stating what each chapter contained, more according to its meaning than its exact wording. Those who had submitted the document against Pelagius said that Coelestius developed these points at greater length, but that they had been unable at that time to include everything.

Thus, they stated that the first chapter of Coelestius’s book contained this: “Because we do more than is commanded in the Law and the Gospel.” Pelagius replied: “They attributed this to us; but we said it, in accordance with the Apostle, of virginity, concerning which Paul says, ‘I have no command of the Lord.’” The Synod said: “This also the Church accepts.”

I have read the sense in which Coelestius placed this statement in his book—if, indeed, he does not deny that the book is his. He said it in order to persuade people that, by the nature of free choice, we possess such a great possibility of not sinning that we even do more than is commanded, since many preserve perpetual virginity, which is not commanded, whereas fulfilling the commandments is sufficient for not sinning.

But the response given by Pelagius, which the judges approved, was not understood in this way: that those who additionally preserve virginity, which is not commanded, observe all the commandments of the Law and the Gospel. Rather, it was understood only in this sense: virginity, which is not commanded, is something greater than conjugal chastity, which is commanded, and to preserve the former is certainly to do more than to preserve the latter. Yet neither of these is possessed without the grace of God, since the Apostle, speaking of this matter, says: “Now I wish all people to be as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that” (1 Corinthians 7:7).

And when the disciples said to the Lord, “If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is not advantageous to marry”—or, as the Latin more accurately says, “it is not advantageous to take a wife”—he replied: “Not all receive this saying, but those to whom it has been given” (Matthew 19:10–11).

The bishops therefore declared that the Church accepts this: that persevering virginity, which is not commanded, is greater than the chastity of marriage, which is commanded. But in what sense Pelagius—or Coelestius—had said the statement, the judges did not know.

**CHAPTER XIV**

30. At this point other capital charges were brought against Pelagius from Coelestius’s chapters—charges that unquestionably deserved condemnation, and without whose anathematization he would certainly have been condemned along with them.

It was alleged that in the third chapter Coelestius had written that the grace and help of God are not given for individual acts, but exist in free choice or in the Law and teaching. And again, that God’s grace is given according to our merits, because if he gives it to sinners, he appears unjust; and that he added these words: “Therefore grace itself has also been placed in my will, whether I have been worthy or unworthy. For if we do everything through grace, when we are overcome by sin, it is not we who are overcome, but God’s grace, which wished to help us in every way but was unable.”

And again he said: “If it is God’s grace when we conquer sins, then he himself is at fault when we are overcome by sin, because he either could not or did not wish to preserve us altogether.”

Pelagius replied to these statements: “Let those who say that they belong to Coelestius see whether they are his. I myself have never held them in this way, but I anathematize anyone who holds them in this way.”

The Synod said: “The holy Synod receives you, since you condemn the objectionable statements in this manner.”

With respect to all these points, Pelagius’s explicit anathematization of them and the bishops’ complete judgment condemning them are certainly clear. Whether Pelagius, Coelestius, both, neither, or others—either with them or under their names—held or still hold these views may be uncertain or hidden. Nevertheless, this judgment has made it sufficiently clear that they have been condemned, and that Pelagius himself would likewise have been condemned unless he too had condemned them. Now, after this judgment, whenever we argue against opinions of this kind, we are arguing against a condemned heresy.

31. I shall also say something more reassuring [Note: [Col. 0338] The printed editions read latius, “more extensively.” The Roman copy has laetius, “more reassuringly,” that is, in such a way that my fear and anxiety may be removed.]. Earlier I was afraid (above, §20), when Pelagius said that, with the help of God’s grace, a person could be without sin, lest perhaps he should say that this same grace was the possibility belonging to the nature created by God with free choice, as it is stated in that book which I accepted as his [Note: [Col. 0338] The book of Pelagius received by James and Timasius, to which Augustine replied in *On Nature and Grace*.], and to which I replied, and thus deceive the judges, who did not know the matter, in that way.

Now, however, since he anathematizes those who say that God’s grace and help are not given for individual acts, but exist in free choice or in the Law and teaching, it is sufficiently evident that he means by grace the grace preached in Christ’s Church, which is given through the ministration of the Holy Spirit, so that we may be helped in each of our individual acts. Hence we always pray for timely help, lest we be led into temptation.

Nor am I now afraid that, when he said, “No one can be without sin unless he has knowledge of the Law,” and explained this as placing the help for not sinning in knowledge of the Law (above, §2), he might intend that same knowledge of the Law to be understood as God’s grace. Behold, he anathematizes those who hold this view. Behold, he does not wish either the nature of free choice or the Law and teaching to be understood as the grace by which we are helped in our individual acts.

What remains, then, except that he understands it as the grace which the Apostle says is given through the ministration of the Holy Spirit (Philippians 1:19)? Of this the Lord says: “Do not consider how or what you should speak; for it will be given to you in that hour what you should speak. For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matthew 10:19–20).

Nor need we fear that, when he says, “All are governed by their own will,” and explained that he said this because of free choice, with God as the helper of the one choosing what is good (above, §5), he may here too have called the nature of free choice and the teaching of the Law a helper [Note: [Col. 0338] Some printed editions read adjutorium, “help.”].

For since he rightly anathematized those who say that God’s grace and help are not given for individual acts, but exist in free choice or in the Law and teaching, God’s grace or help is certainly given for individual acts, apart from free choice or the Law and teaching. Consequently, we are governed by God in each individual act when we act rightly; and it is not in vain that we pray, “Direct my paths according to your word, and let no iniquity rule over me” (Psalm 118:133).

32. But what follows this once again troubles me. When the fifth chapter of Coelestius’s book was brought against Pelagius, it was alleged that they “affirm that each person can possess all virtues and graces, and remove the diversity of graces that the Apostle teaches.”

Pelagius replied: “It was said by us, but they criticized it maliciously and incompetently. For we do not remove the diversity of graces; rather, we say that God gives to the one who is worthy to receive all graces, just as he gave them to the Apostle Paul.”

To this the Synod said: “Accordingly, you too have understood, in an ecclesiastical sense, the gift of graces contained in the holy Apostle.”

Here someone may ask: What, then, troubles you? Will you deny that all virtues and graces were present in the Apostle? For my part, if all those graces are meant which the Apostle himself mentioned together in one passage—and I think that the bishops understood them in this way when they approved the statement and declared it to have been made “in the ecclesiastical sense”—I do not doubt that the Apostle Paul possessed them.

For he says: “And some indeed God has appointed in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers, then powers, then gifts of healings, helps, administrations, kinds of tongues” (1 Corinthians 12:28).

What, then? Shall we say that the Apostle Paul did not possess all these? Who would dare say so? For by the very fact that he was an apostle, he certainly possessed apostleship.

But he also possessed prophecy. Was his not prophecy? For the Spirit expressly says: “In the last times some will depart from the faith, giving heed to deceitful spirits and doctrines of demons” (1 Timothy 4:1).

He was also a teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth (1 Timothy 2:7); and he performed powers and healings. For he shook off a viper that had bitten him without harm (Acts 28:5), and a paralytic rose immediately at his word, his health restored (Acts 14:9).

What he means by “helps” is unclear, since the force of this word extends widely. Yet who would say that he lacked this grace, through whose labor the salvation of human beings was evidently so greatly assisted?

And what was more illustrious than his administration, since through him the Lord then governed so many Churches and now governs them through his letters?

As for kinds of tongues, how could these have been lacking in him when he himself says, “I thank God that I speak in the tongues of you all” (1 Corinthians 14:18)?

Since, therefore, we must believe that none of these things was lacking in the Apostle Paul, the judges approved Pelagius’s response that “all graces had been given to him.”

But there are also other graces that are not mentioned here. For although the Apostle Paul was a very eminent member of Christ’s body, he did not receive more numerous and greater graces than the very head of the whole body, whether in the flesh or in the soul of a human being—that is, the Word of God, who assumed his creature into the unity of his person so that he might be our head and we might be his body.

Indeed, if all things could exist in each individual member, the likeness drawn from the members of our body for this purpose would appear pointless. Some things are common to all members, such as health and life; but other things belong specifically to individual members. Thus the ear does not perceive colors, nor the eye sounds. Hence it is said: “If the whole body were an eye, where would hearing be? If the whole were hearing, where would smelling be?” (1 Corinthians 12:17).

This is not said as though it were impossible for God to grant the ears the power of sight and the eyes the power of hearing. Nevertheless, what the Apostle signified by the body of Christ, which is the Church, and by the diversity of Churches [Note: [Col. 0340] Perhaps, “of graces.”] as by different members, so that there might also be gifts proper to individuals, is certain [Note: [Col. 0340] Suarius has “is uncertain.”].

Therefore it is now clear both why those who brought the charge did not want the distinction of graces removed, and why, on account of the Apostle Paul, in whom we recognize all the gifts mentioned in that one passage, the bishops were able to approve Pelagius’s response.

33. What, then, is the reason I said that this chapter had made me anxious? It is this statement of Pelagius: “God gives all graces to the one who is worthy to receive them, just as he gave them to the Apostle Paul.”

I would not be at all anxious about this response of his, except insofar as it bears on this case, in which our chief concern must be to prevent the grace of God from being attacked while we remain silent and conceal so great an evil.

Since he did not say, “God gives them to whomever he wishes,” but said, “God gives all graces to the one who is worthy to receive them,” I could not read it without becoming suspicious [Note: [Col. 0340] The printed editions read suspectus, “suspicious” or “suspected.” This would be correct if the preceding text read non potuit, “he could not”; otherwise one should read sollicitus, “anxious,” or, according to the Colbertine manuscript, suspiciosus, “suspicious.”].

For the very name of grace, and the meaning of that name, is removed if it is not given freely but is received by one who is worthy. Or perhaps someone will say that I am doing the Apostle an injustice because I do not say that he was worthy of grace? On the contrary, I do him an injustice and bring punishment upon myself if I do not believe what he himself says.

Did he not define grace in such a way as to show that it was called grace because it was given freely? Indeed, he himself says: “But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Romans 11:6). Again he says: “To the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt” (Romans 4:4).

Therefore, whoever is worthy has a debt owed to him. But if it is owed, it is not grace; for grace is given, whereas a debt is repaid. Grace, therefore, is given to the unworthy, so that the debt may be repaid to the worthy. Yet the one who makes them possess whatever he will repay to the worthy is the one who gave to the unworthy what they did not possess.

34. Perhaps he will say: “I did not say that the Apostle was worthy because of works, but because of faith; for I did not mean that his works, which he had not previously possessed as good works, merited this, but that his faith merited it.”

What then? Do we suppose that faith does not act? On the contrary, it truly acts—the faith that works through love (Galatians 5:6).

However much the works of unbelievers may be praised, we know that the same Apostle’s statement is true and unconquerable: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Romans 14:23).

He therefore often says that righteousness is reckoned to us not from works but from faith, although faith works through love, so that no one may think that one reaches faith by the merits of works. Faith itself is the beginning from which good works begin, since, as has been said, whatever is not from it is sin.

For this reason it is also said to the Church in the Song of Songs: “You shall come, and you shall pass over from the beginning of faith” (Song of Songs 4:8, according to the Septuagint).

Therefore, although faith obtains the grace of doing good, we certainly did not merit faith itself by any faith of our own. Rather, in the giving of faith by which we would follow the Lord, his mercy went before us (Psalm 58:11).

Did we give faith to ourselves and make ourselves believers? Here too I shall cry out with complete conviction: “He made us, and not we ourselves” (Psalm 99:3).

The apostolic teaching commends nothing else when it says: “For I say, through the grace of God that has been given to me, to everyone who is among you, not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think soberly, according as God has allotted to each a measure of faith” (Romans 12:3).

This is also the meaning of the statement: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7). For we received even that from which whatever good we have in our actions begins.

35. What, then, does the same Apostle mean when he says, “I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith; henceforth there remains for me the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the just judge, will repay me on that day” (2 Timothy 4:7–8), if these things are not repaid to the worthy but given to the unworthy?

Whoever says this pays too little attention to the fact that the crown could not have been repaid to one who was worthy unless grace had first been given to one who was unworthy.

He says, “I have fought the good fight”; but the same man says, “Thanks be to God, who gave us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57).

He says, “I have finished the course”; but the same man says, “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Romans 9:16).

He says, “I have kept the faith”; but the same man says, “For I know whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to preserve my deposit until that day” (2 Timothy 1:12)—that is, what I have entrusted to him. Some manuscripts do not have “deposit,” but the clearer reading, “what I have entrusted.”

And what do we entrust to God except what we pray that he may preserve, among which is our faith itself? For what else did the Lord commend to God concerning the Apostle Peter when he prayed and said to him, “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32), except that God should preserve his faith, lest it fail by yielding to temptation?

Therefore, blessed Paul [Note: [Col. 0341] Two manuscripts read, “O blessed Paul.”], great preacher of grace, I shall say—and I shall not fear, for who will be less angry with me for saying this than you, who said what had to be said and taught what had to be taught?—I shall say, then, and shall not fear: the crown is indeed repaid to your merits, but your merits are gifts of God.

36. The worthy Apostle therefore receives his due reward; but grace freely gave him the apostleship, which was not his due, when he was unworthy [Note: [Col. 0341] Most printed editions read gratiae, “of grace.” The Colbertine manuscript and Suarius have gratia, “grace.”].

Will I regret having said this? Far from it. I shall defend myself from this charge by his own testimony, and no one will call me presumptuous unless he dares to call him a liar.

He himself cries out and bears witness; and in order to commend God’s gifts in himself, and to glory not in himself but in the Lord (1 Corinthians 1:31), he says not only that he possessed no good merits by which he might become an apostle, but even declares that his merits were evil, in order to manifest and proclaim God’s grace.

“I am not worthy,” he says, “to be called an apostle.” What else does this mean than “I am not deserving”? For many Latin manuscripts have precisely that reading.

This is exactly what we are investigating: all those graces are contained in the office of apostleship. It was neither fitting nor necessary for an apostle to lack prophecy, or to fail to be a teacher, or not to shine through powers and gifts of healings, or not to provide helps, or not to govern Churches, or not to excel in kinds of tongues. The single name “apostleship” embraces all these things.

Let us therefore consult him; rather, let us listen to him. Let us say to him: “Holy Apostle Paul, the monk Pelagius says that you were worthy to receive all the graces of your apostleship. What do you yourself say?”

“‘I am not worthy,’ he says, ‘to be called an apostle.’”

What? In order to honor Paul, shall I dare to believe Pelagius about Paul more than I believe Paul? I shall not do so. If I did, I would burden myself rather than honor him.

Let us also hear why he was not worthy to be called an apostle: “Because I persecuted the Church of God,” he says.

If we followed human judgment, who would not think that such a person ought rather to be condemned by Christ than called by him? Who could love the preacher without detesting the persecutor?

Therefore he speaks most rightly and truly: “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God.”

Having done such great evil, then, from where did you merit such great good?

Let all nations hear his reply: “But by the grace of God I am what I am.”

Is grace commended in any other way than by being given to one who is unworthy? “And his grace,” he says, “toward me was not empty.”

He also enjoins this upon others, thereby showing the exercise of the will, when he says: “We also exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain” (2 Corinthians 6:1).

And how does he prove that God’s grace toward him was not empty except by what follows: “But I labored more abundantly than all of them”?

Therefore he did not labor in order to receive grace; he received grace in order to labor. Thus, through grace, he who was unworthy freely received what made him worthy to receive the rewards due to him.

Nor did he dare to claim even that labor for himself. For after saying, “I labored more abundantly than all of them,” he immediately added: “Not I, but the grace of God that is with me” (1 Corinthians 15:9–10).

O great teacher, confessor, and preacher of grace! What is this: “I labored more,” yet “not I”? When the will raised itself somewhat, piety immediately kept watch, and humility trembled, because weakness recognized itself.

37. As the proceedings indicate, the holy John, bishop of the Church of Jerusalem, also rightly used this testimony. When asked what had taken place before the trial in his presence [Note: [Col. 0343] Namely, the gathering held at Jerusalem at the end of July 415, described by Orosius in his *Apology*. It is included below in the second part of the Appendix.], he himself recounted it to our co-bishops, who had presided together at that trial.

For he says that, when some people were whispering and saying that Pelagius taught that “a person can be perfected without the grace of God”—that is, that a person can be without sin, as he had said above—he replied:

“Blaming him” [Note: [Col. 0343] The printed editions consistently read culpam, “the fault.” It should be corrected from the words below, §55: “John said that he had blamed this.”], “on this point as well, I brought forward the fact that the Apostle Paul, laboring greatly but not according to his own power, rather according to the grace of God, said: ‘I labored more abundantly than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God that is with me’; and again: ‘It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy’ (Romans 9:16); and also: ‘Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain’ (Psalm 126:1). We mentioned many other similar passages from the holy Scriptures.”

“But when they did not accept what we were saying from the holy Scriptures, and continued whispering, Pelagius said: ‘I too believe this. Let him be anathema who says that a person can advance toward every virtue without God’s help.’”

**CHAPTER XV**

38. Bishop John related this in the presence of Pelagius. Pelagius could certainly have said respectfully: “Your Holiness is mistaken; you do not remember correctly. In response to those testimonies that you cited from the Scriptures, I did not say, ‘I too believe this.’ For I do not understand them in such a way that God’s grace labors with a person so that the fact that he does not sin is ‘not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy.’”

**CHAPTER XVI**

39. There are indeed certain commentaries on Paul’s Letter to the Romans said to be by Pelagius, in which he asserts that the statement, “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy,” was “not spoken in the person of Paul,” but that Paul used the voice of someone asking and rebuking when he said this, as though such a statement ought not to be made at all.

When Bishop John plainly recognized this statement as belonging to the Apostle and cited it for the purpose of preventing Pelagius from thinking that anyone could avoid sin without God’s grace, and when he said that Pelagius had replied, “I too believe this,” Pelagius did not answer, while hearing this in person, “I do not believe this.” He ought therefore either to deny that commentary as his own, or not hesitate to correct and amend it, where he intended the Apostle to be understood as not having held this meaning but rather as having issued a rebuke.

Whatever Bishop John said about our absent brothers—whether our co-bishops Heros and Lazarus, or the presbyter Orosius, or others whose names are not expressly recorded there [Note: [Col. 0343] Perhaps Avitus, Passerius, and Domno, formerly a military commander. Their names, which were not expressed in the proceedings of Diospolis, are found below, in part 2 of the Appendix, in Orosius’s *Apology*, chapter 3.]—I believe he understands that it cannot prejudice them. If they had been present, they might perhaps have been able—far be it from me to say “to convict him of falsehood”—to recall something he had forgotten, or to point out where a Latin interpreter had misled him, even without any intention to lie, through some difficulty in understanding another language.

This is especially so because the matter was not being conducted in formal proceedings [Note: [Col. 0344] Most editions read, “the matter is not being conducted in formal proceedings.” Suarius and the Colbertine manuscript more accurately have “was being conducted.” Perhaps the reading should be “it was not conducted by proceedings,” with the preposition in deleted, as below, §55. Augustine is speaking of what took place before Bishop John at the Jerusalem gathering before the trial at Diospolis, as is clear from §37.], which were established usefully so that wicked people might not lie and good people might not forget something.

But if anyone brings some charge from this against our brothers just mentioned and summons them before an episcopal judgment [Note: [Col. 0344] Suarius reads “recalls them.”], they will attend as they are able. Why should we labor over the matter here, when even the judges themselves, after the account of our co-bishop, did not wish to pronounce anything on it?

**CHAPTER XVII**

40. Since Pelagius, being present, silently acknowledged that he had said that he believed those testimonies of Scripture, how did he fail to see, when shortly before recalling the Apostle’s testimony and finding him to have said, “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God; but by the grace of God I am what I am,” that he ought not to have said, when the abundance of the graces received by that same Apostle was under discussion, that he was “worthy to receive them”? He himself not only said that he was unworthy, but also proved it by giving another reason, and by that very fact truly commended grace as grace.

But if perhaps he was unable to think of or remember what had been related earlier by Saint John, he should have considered his most recent response and noticed what he had anathematized shortly before when the statements of Coelestius were brought against him.

Among those statements was the allegation that Coelestius had said, “God’s grace is given according to our merits.” If Pelagius truly anathematized this, what does it mean that he says all graces were given to the Apostle according to his merit? Is being worthy to receive something different from receiving it according to merit? Can he demonstrate by some subtle argument that someone is worthy but does not merit it?

Yet Coelestius—or whoever else was responsible for all the preceding statements that he anathematized—does not allow him to obscure or hide behind this word. For he presses the point and says: “Grace itself has also been placed in my will, whether I have been worthy or unworthy.”

If Pelagius rightly and truthfully condemned the statement that “God’s grace is given according to merits, and to the worthy,” with what intention did he think or with what mouth did he say: “We say that God gives all graces to the one who is worthy to receive them”? Who would not become anxious about this response or defense of his if he carefully considered it?

41. Why, then, someone may ask, did the judges approve it? I admit that I myself am now uncertain for that very reason. But perhaps either their brief statement easily escaped the judges’ attention and consideration, or, thinking that it could somehow be correctly understood, and believing that they had clear confessions from him on this matter, they judged that no controversy should be raised against him over a single word.

The same thing might perhaps have happened to us if we had sat with them at that trial. If, instead of “worthy,” the text had said “predestined,” or something similar, it would certainly have caused no scruple or heightened concern. Yet if one says that the person who is justified by the election of grace is called worthy—not because of any preceding good merits, but by designation, just as he is called elect—it is difficult to judge whether this can be said with certainty, or even without the slightest offense to understanding.

As far as I am concerned, I would easily pass over this word if the book to which I replied had not made me anxious about Pelagius’s meaning by saying that there is no grace of God at all except our nature with free choice, a created grace [Note: [Col. 0345] Perhaps, “created freely.”]. I feared that he had inserted this word not through careless speech but through deliberate concern for his doctrine.

The remaining and final charges moved the judges so strongly that they considered them deserving of condemnation even before Pelagius’s response.

**CHAPTER XVIII**

42. For in the sixth chapter of Coelestius’s book it was alleged that the following statement occurred: “The children of God cannot be called such unless they have been made entirely without sin.” Consequently, according to this statement, the Apostle Paul would not be a son of God, since he said, “Not that I have already received it, or have already been perfected” (Philippians 3:12).

In the seventh chapter: “Forgetfulness and ignorance are not subject to sin, because they do not occur according to the will but according to necessity.” Yet David says, “Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorance” (Psalm 24:7), and sacrifices are offered under the Law for ignorance just as for sin (Leviticus 4).

In the tenth chapter: “There is no free choice if it needs God’s help, since each person has it in his own will either to do something or not to do it.”

In the twelfth chapter: “Our victory does not come from God’s help but from free choice.” He is said to have supported this with the words: “The victory is ours, because by our own will we took up arms; likewise, when we are overcome, that is ours, because by our own will we refused to arm ourselves.”

He also cited the testimony of the Apostle Peter, that “we are partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4). And he is said to have constructed this syllogism: “If the soul cannot be without sin, then God too is subject to sin, since a part of him—that is, the soul—is liable to sin.”

In the thirteenth chapter he says: “Forgiveness is not granted to penitents according to the grace and mercy of God, but according to the merits and labor of those who have become worthy of mercy through repentance.”

**CHAPTER XIX**

43. After these statements had been read, the Synod said: “What does the present Pelagius the monk say regarding these chapters that have been read? For the holy Synod and the holy Catholic Church of God reject them.”

Pelagius replied: “I say again that, according even to their own testimony, these statements are not mine, and therefore, as I said, I owe no defense concerning them. But those that I have confessed to be mine, I affirm to be correct. Those that I said were not mine, I reject according to the judgment of the holy Church, pronouncing anathema upon everyone who opposes or contradicts the teachings of the holy Catholic Church.

“For I believe in the Trinity of one substance, and I believe all things according to the teaching of the holy Catholic Church. But if anyone holds a view foreign to this, let him be anathema.”

**CHAPTER XX**

44. The Synod said: “Now, since satisfaction has been made to us by the statements of the present Pelagius the monk, who agrees with the pious doctrines but rejects and anathematizes what is contrary to the faith of the Church [Note: [Col. 0346] The Colbertine manuscript reads, “the ecclesiastical faith.”], we declare that he belongs to ecclesiastical communion and is Catholic.”

**CHAPTER XXI**
45. If these are the proceedings [Note: [Col. 0346] The same manuscript reads: “but if these are the proceedings.”] by which Pelagius’s friends rejoice that he has been cleared, then we, since he took sufficient care to demonstrate his friendship toward us as well by producing and having read in this trial our personal letters—which are included in the proceedings—do indeed desire and wish for his salvation in Christ; but as for this acquittal of his, which is believed more than it is clearly demonstrated, we ought not rashly to rejoice. In saying this I do not accuse the judges either of negligence, collusion, or—something certainly far from them—consciousness of impious doctrines. Yet although their judgment has been rightly approved and praised according to its merit, Pelagius does not seem to me to have been cleared in the eyes of those who know him more fully and certainly [Note: [Col. 0346] Two manuscripts read *arctiusque*: “more closely.”]. For, judging as they did about a man they did not know, especially in the absence of those who had submitted a written accusation against him, they were quite unable to examine the man himself with sufficient care; nevertheless, they utterly destroyed the heresy itself, if they follow the judgment of those who were contending on behalf of his perversity. But those who know well what Pelagius has been accustomed to teach—whether those who resisted his arguments or those who rejoice that they have been freed from his error—how can they not regard him with suspicion, when they read not a simple confession of his past errors and their condemnation, but a confession of such a kind [Note: [Col. 0346] Suar. and the Colbertinus manuscript read “defense.”] as though he had never thought otherwise than the view approved in this trial in his responses?

CHAPTER XXII.

46. For, to speak especially of myself, I first learned of Pelagius, while he was absent and living in Rome, by hearing his name spoken with great praise. Later, reports began to reach us that he was arguing against the grace of God. Although I was grieved by this, and was told it by people whom I believed, I nevertheless wanted to know from him himself, or from some book of his, whether he held anything of the kind, so that, if I began to refute him, he could not deny it. After he came to Africa, he was received, in my absence, on our shore—that is, at Hippo—where, as I learned from our people [Note: [Col. 0346] So Suar. and the Colbertinus manuscript. In Velser’s first edition, the words “I learned from our people” were omitted, and it read “as you know from our people.” In later editions this became “as you know.”], nothing of this sort was heard from him at all; for he departed from there sooner than had been expected. Later, as I recall, I saw him once or twice in Carthage, when I was fully occupied with the business of the Conference [Note: [Col. 0347] Suar. reads “when I was occupied with the business concerning the Conference.”] that we were to hold with the Donatist heretics; but he also hastened overseas. Meanwhile, these doctrines were being vigorously spread by those who were regarded as his disciples, until a certain Coelestius came before an ecclesiastical tribunal and received a sentence worthy of his perversity. We thought it would be more beneficial to proceed against them if, without naming the men, their errors themselves were refuted and exposed, and if the men were corrected more by fear of ecclesiastical judgment than punished by the judgment itself. Accordingly, we did not cease either to argue against those evils in books or to address them in public sermons.

CHAPTER XXIII.

47. But when that book was also given to me by God’s servants, the good and honorable men Timasius and James, in which Pelagius most openly attempted to resolve for himself the question of God’s grace that had been raised against him by himself as an opponent—a question from which he was already suffering great unpopularity—by declaring that God’s grace was human nature created with free choice, occasionally and only faintly [Note: [Col. 0347] The printed editions read “which he held.”] joining to it either the assistance of the law or even the forgiveness of sins, then it became entirely clear to me how poisonous his perversity was and how hostile to Christian salvation.

Yet even then, in the work by which I refuted that same book, I did not insert Pelagius’s name. I thought I would accomplish more if, while preserving our friendship, I continued to spare his modesty, although I could no longer spare his writings. Hence I now regret that in this trial he said at one point: “I anathematize those who hold or have ever held this view.” It would have been enough for him to say, “those who hold this view,” so that we might believe that he had been corrected. But when he added, “or have ever held it,” first, how unjustly did he dare to condemn those who were undeserving—those who had been free from the error which they had learned either from others or from him himself? Further, who among those who know that he not only once held these views but also taught them would not rightly suspect that he had pretended to anathematize those who hold them, since he did not hesitate in the same way to anathematize those who had once held them—among whom they will remember that he himself was a teacher?

Behold, to say nothing of others, with what eyes and with what face will he look upon Timasius and James, his own friends and beloved former disciples, to whom I wrote the book in which I responded to his book [Note: [Col. 0347] The book *On Nature and Grace*.]? Certainly I did not think that the manner in which they wrote back to me should be concealed and passed over; rather, I appended below a copy of their letter.

CHAPTER XXIV.

48. “To the truly most blessed Lord and deservedly venerable father, Bishop Augustine, Timasius and James send greetings in the Lord.

“God’s grace, administered through your word, has so restored and refreshed us that we may quite genuinely say, ‘He sent his word and healed them’ (Ps. 106:20), most blessed Lord and deservedly venerable father. Indeed, we have found that Your Holiness examined the text of that book with such care that we are astonished to find responses given to every point, both to those things which a Christian ought to refute, detest, and flee, and to those in which he does not seem to have erred sufficiently; although, by some cunning of which I know not the nature, he believed that even in those matters God’s grace ought to be suppressed.

“But there is one thing that affects us amid so great a benefit: that this splendid gift of God’s grace has shone forth so late. For it happened [Note: [Col. 0348] Suar. reads “happens.”] that certain people were absent, to whose blindness this illumination of such clear truth was owed. Nevertheless, even if more slowly, we do not despair that the same grace will reach them, with God’s favor—he who wishes all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4).

“As for us, although long ago, through the spirit of charity [Note: [Col. 0348] Other printed editions read “of clarity.”] that is in you, we learned to reject the subjection [Note: [Col. 0348] The Florentinus manuscript reads “subsection.”] of that error, we now give thanks also for this: that we have learned to disclose to others what we formerly believed, while Your Holiness’s more abundant discourse opens a way of ease [Note: [Col. 0348] Suar. reads “of felicity.”].

“And in another hand: ‘May the mercy of our God glorify Your Blessedness, keep you safe, and mindful of us, forever.’” (*Letter* 168, among Augustine’s letters.)

CHAPTER XXV.

49. If, then, he too had confessed that he had once been so involved in this error as a man taken by it, but now anathematized those who hold it, whoever failed to congratulate him—now that he had taken the path of truth—would himself be abandoning the entrails of charity. But now it is not enough that he has failed to confess that he was freed from that plague; he has also anathematized those who have been freed from it, although they love him so much that they desire his own liberation as well. Among these are the men who expressed their goodwill toward him in the letter they sent to me. Indeed, they were thinking especially of him when they said that they were distressed that I had written that book so late:

“‘For it happened,’ they say, ‘that certain people were absent, to whose blindness this illumination of such clear truth was owed. Nevertheless, even if more slowly,’ they say, ‘we do not despair that, with God’s favor, the same grace will reach them.’”

They too thought that the name, or names, should still be kept silent, so that, while friendship remained alive, the error rather than the friends might die.

50. But now, if Pelagius thinks of God and is not ungrateful for his mercy—for God brought him before the judgment of bishops precisely so that he would not afterward dare to defend these anathemas and might recognize them as detestable and to be rejected—he will receive our letter with greater gratitude, since by expressly naming him we are opening the sore in order to heal it, rather than sending the earlier letter [Note: [Col. 0348] Understand: “he received it.”], in which, because we feared causing pain, we increased the swelling, something we regret.

But if he becomes angry with me, let him consider how unjustly he is angry, and, in order to overcome his anger, let him at last seek from God the grace which he confessed in this trial to be necessary for each of our actions, so that, with God’s help, he may obtain a true victory. For what benefit are all the great praises of him in the bishops’ letters, which he thought ought to be recalled, or even read and cited, on his behalf—as though all who heard his forceful and, in a certain sense, ardent exhortations to the good life could easily have known that he held these perverse opinions?

CHAPTER XXVI.

51. In my own letter, which he produced, I not only refrained from praising him; I also urged, as far as I could, and without provoking him, to think rightly about the grace of God [Note: [Col. 0349] The Roman manuscript reads “without provoking anyone”; the Colbertinus reads “without mentioning him.”]. I called him “Lord” in the greeting, as we are accustomed, in the manner of letters, to write even to certain non-Christians; nor was this a lie, since in some sense we owe all people a willing servitude, so that they may attain the salvation that is in Christ.

I called him “most beloved,” which I say even now, and, although he may be angry, will continue to say; for unless I retain love toward him, while he is angry, I shall do myself greater harm.

I called him “most desired,” because I greatly wished to converse with him in person. For I had already heard that, whenever any mention was made of this matter, he openly and contentiously attempted to argue against the grace by which we are justified.

Finally, the brief text of the letter itself indicates this. After I had given thanks that he had gladdened me by his writings, assuring me of the welfare of himself and his people—for if we want them to be corrected, we must also want them to be saved in bodily health—I immediately wished that the Lord would repay him with good things, not those pertaining to bodily health, but rather those which he thought, or perhaps still thinks, are placed solely in the freedom and power of the will; and at the same time I wished him eternal life on account of this.

Then, because in his letter, to which I was replying, he had praised certain good qualities in me very generously and kindly, I also asked him to pray for me, so that I might become by the Lord’s action such as he already believed me to be. In this way, while admonishing him, I indicated against his view that even the righteousness which he thought ought to be praised in me is “not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:16).

This is everything contained in that brief letter of mine, and it was dictated with this intention. It reads as follows:

CHAPTERS XXVII AND XXVIII.

52. “To the most beloved and most desired brother Pelagius, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

“I give very great thanks that you have deigned to gladden me by your letter and to assure me of your welfare. May the Lord repay you with good things, so that you may always be good and live with him forever, most beloved and most desired brother.

“As for me, although I do not recognize in myself the praises of me contained in your letter of kindness, I cannot nevertheless be ungrateful for your goodwill toward my lowliness. At the same time I urge you rather to pray for me, so that I may become by the Lord’s action such as you now believe me to be.

“And in another hand: ‘Being mindful of us, may you remain safe and please the Lord, most beloved and most desired brother.’” (*Letter* 146.)

CHAPTER XXIX.

53. Even in the subscription, where I wrote “may he please the Lord,” I signified that this depends more upon the Lord’s grace than upon human will alone, since I neither urged, commanded, nor taught this, but merely wished it. Yet just as, if I had urged, commanded, or taught it, I would have shown that it also pertained to free choice without thereby detracting from God’s grace, so, because I wished it, I commended God’s grace but did not extinguish the choice of the will.

Why, then, did he produce this letter in the trial? If he had held this view from the beginning, perhaps he would in no way have been summoned to an episcopal trial, even by good brothers who had nevertheless been offended by the perversity of his arguments. Moreover, just as I gave an account of this letter of mine, so, if necessary, those whose letters he cited could give an account of theirs, stating what they had thought, what they had not known, or for what reason they had written.

Therefore, no matter whose friendship with saints Pelagius boasts of, no matter whose letters praising him he reads, and no matter what proceedings of his acquittal he produces, unless, having confessed that he set down in his books those things which are proved by the testimony of competent witnesses against the grace of God by which we are called and justified, he anathematizes them, and thereafter writes and argues against those very things, he will by no means appear corrected to those who know him more fully.

CHAPTER XXX.

54. I shall not keep silent about what followed this trial and has increased this suspicion. A certain letter came into our hands said to be Pelagius’s, written to a certain presbyter who was his friend and who, as the same letter relates, had kindly admonished him not to become the occasion by which anyone would separate himself from the body of the Church.

Among other matters, whose insertion would be lengthy and unnecessary, Pelagius is said to have written:

“By the judgment of fourteen bishops our definition was approved, in which we said that a person can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments if he wishes. This judgment,” he says, “overwhelmed the mouth of contradiction with confusion [Note: [Col. 0350] The Colbertinus manuscript has an illegible or missing reading here.] and divided from one another the whole association conspiring for evil.”

Whether Pelagius truly wrote this letter, or whether it was fabricated by someone under his name, who does not see how this error boasts as though it were victorious because of the judgment in which it was convicted and condemned?

For he set down these words as they are read in his book called the *Book of Chapters*, not as they were brought forward in the trial, nor as they were repeated in his own response. Even those who brought the charge, through I know not what carelessness, omitted a word over which there is considerable controversy. For they wrote that he had said: “A person can, if he wishes, be without sin and keep God’s commandments if he wishes.” Nothing was said there about ease.

Then, in his own response, he said: “We did say that a person can be without sin and keep God’s commandments if he wishes.” He too did not say “keep them easily,” but only “keep them.”

Again, in another place, among the matters on which Hilary consulted me and to which I replied, the charge was presented in this form: “A person can be without sin if he wishes.” To this he responded: “It was stated above that a person can be without sin.” Here too, therefore, neither those who brought the charge nor he who responded added the word “easily.”

Earlier, in the account of the holy bishop John, it is likewise recalled:

“While they were insisting and saying, ‘He is a heretic, for he says that a person can, if he wishes, be without sin,’ and when we questioned him about this, he replied: ‘I did not say that human nature has received the capacity to be impeccable; I said that whoever wishes to labor and strive for his own salvation, so as not to sin and to walk in God’s commandments, possesses this possibility from God.’

“Then, when some whispered and said that Pelagius was saying that a person could be perfected without God’s grace, he said, ‘Blaming this, I also added that the Apostle Paul, laboring greatly—not according to his own virtue but according to God’s grace—said, “I labored more abundantly than all of them, yet not I, but the grace of God with me”’ (1 Cor. 15:10),” together with the rest that I have already quoted above (no. 37).

55. What, then, does it mean that in this letter they dared to boast so greatly that they claimed to have persuaded the fourteen bishops not only of the possibility of not sinning but also of the ease of not sinning, as it is set down in Pelagius’s *Book of Chapters*, even though, although the same charges were brought and repeated so many times in the proceedings, this is nowhere found?

For how is this word not contrary even to Pelagius’s own defense and response, when Bishop John said that he had answered before him in such a way as to make it understood that “the person who wishes to labor and strive for his salvation can avoid sin,” and when he himself, in conducting his defense before the proceedings [Note: [Col. 0351] That is, before the bishops of the Synod of Diospolis, who had earlier responded to the charges before John, before the proceedings had been drawn up.], said that “by his own labor and by God’s grace a person can be without sin”?

How, then, does it happen easily, if labor is required for it? I think that all human understanding will acknowledge with us that where there is labor, there is no ease.

And yet the letter, full of fleshly boasting and arrogance, flies forth, overtaking the delayed proceedings and outstripping them in speed, rushing into people’s hands, so that it may be said that the fourteen eastern bishops approved not only that “a person can be without sin and keep God’s commandments,” but also that he can “keep them easily”—without mentioning God as the helper, but only saying “if he wishes.” Thus, with divine grace—on behalf of which the struggle was waged so fiercely—silently suppressed, only unhappy human pride remains to be read in the letter, deceiving itself as though victorious.

Was this not precisely what Bishop John said he condemned, and what he cast down, as though he had hurled three thunderbolts, the three divine testimonies, against the giant mountains built up against the supremacy of heavenly grace? Or would the other bishops who sat with him as judges have endured Pelagius saying, “We did say that a person can be without sin and keep God’s commandments if he wishes,” whether in their minds or with their own ears, unless he had immediately added, “For God gave him this possibility”—something they did not know he meant of nature, not of that grace which they knew from apostolic preaching?

He then added: “But we did not say that there is anyone who, from infancy to old age, has never sinned, but that a person who has turned away from sins can, by his own labor and God’s grace, be without sin.”

They also declared this in their own judgment, saying that he had answered correctly that a person, with God’s help and grace, can be without sin [Note: [Col. 0352] The Roman manuscript reads “who also.”]. What else were they afraid of except that, by denying this, they might appear to do injury not to human possibility but to God’s grace itself?

Yet it was not defined when a person becomes without sin, although it was judged that this can happen with the assistance of God’s grace. It was not, I say, defined whether, in this flesh that lusts against the spirit, there has been, is, or will be someone who, now using reason and the choice of the will, whether amid this multitude of human beings or in the solitude of monks, has no longer needed to say in prayer—not only for the sake of others but also for himself—“Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12); or whether this gift is perfected only when we become like him and see him as he is (1 John 3:2), when the words will be spoken not by those who are still fighting, “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind” (Rom. 7:23), but by those who are triumphant, “O death, where is your victory? O death, where is your sting?” (1 Cor. 15:55).

This question ought perhaps to be examined peacefully, not between Catholics and heretics, but among Catholics themselves [Note: [Col. 0352] “Perhaps” has been added here from the Colbertinus manuscript.] [Note: [Col. 0352] The matter was settled one or two years later by the Council of Carthage, canons 6–8. See the Admonition to the book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness* above.].

CHAPTER XXXI.

56. How, then, can it be believed that Pelagius—if this letter is indeed his—truly confessed God’s grace, which is neither nature created with free choice, nor knowledge of the law, nor merely the forgiveness of sins, but that grace which is necessary in each of our actions; and truly anathematized anyone who thought otherwise, when in his letter he added the ease of not sinning, about which no question was raised in this trial, as though the judges had also approved this word, while he did not mention God’s grace, by confessing which and adding it he escaped ecclesiastical condemnation?

CHAPTER XXXII.

57. There is another matter about which I must not remain silent. In the written statement of his defense, which he sent to me through our fellow citizen Charus of Hippo, a deacon from the East [Note: [Col. 0352] The Roman manuscript reads “your fellow citizen.”], he did something that differs from what is contained in the episcopal proceedings.

What the proceedings contain is much better and firmer, and altogether clearer in defense of Catholic truth against the plague of that heresy. For when I read that written statement before the proceedings came to us, I did not know that he had used the very words he used when he was present at the trial. There are only a few differences, and not very substantial ones, which do not greatly concern me.

CHAPTER XXXIII.
