But I was troubled that he could appear to have retained a defense of certain propositions of Coelestius which he plainly anathematized in the proceedings. For he denied that some of them were his own, saying only that “he was not required to give satisfaction for them”; yet in the same written statement he did not wish to anathematize them. They are these:

“Adam was created mortal, and whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.

“Adam’s sin harmed only Adam himself and not the human race.

“The law leads to the kingdom of heaven in the same way as the Gospel.

“Newborn infants are in the same condition in which Adam was before his transgression.

“Neither through Adam’s death or transgression does the whole human race die, nor through Christ’s resurrection does the whole human race rise again.

“Infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life.

“Baptized rich people, unless they have renounced everything, are not credited with whatever good they seem to do, nor will they possess the kingdom of heaven.” [Note: [Col. 0353] Augustine repeats below, at no. 65, the principal doctrines of the Pelagian heresy.]

To these statements he replied in that written statement as follows:

“All these things, according to their testimony, were not said by me, nor am I required to give satisfaction for them.”

But in the proceedings he spoke about these very matters as follows:

“According to their testimony, these things were not said by me, for which I ought not to give satisfaction; nevertheless, in order to satisfy the holy Synod, I anathematize those who hold or have ever held them.”

Why, then, was this not written in the written statement as well? Surely not much ink, writing, time, or space on the written statement would have been required if it had been done so. But who would not believe that this was arranged so that this document might circulate everywhere as though it were an abridgment of those proceedings [Note: [Col. 0353] The Colbertinus manuscript reads “might run.”]? In it, people might suppose that the license to defend any of those propositions had not been taken away, since they had merely been charged against him and had not been proven against him, but had not been anathematized and condemned either.

58. Later, in the same written statement, he collected many chapters from the book of Coelestius that had been brought against him. He did not include the two responses which the proceedings contain, by which he anathematized those same chapters, but appended a single response to all of them together. I would have thought that this had been done out of a desire for brevity, unless I saw that it mattered greatly to the issue troubling us.

For he concluded as follows:

“Again I say that these things also, according to their testimony, are not mine, for which, as I have said, I am not required to give satisfaction. But those things which I have confessed to be mine, I affirm that I rightly teach; those things which I said were not mine, I reject according to the judgment of the holy Church, anathematizing everyone who opposes the teachings of the holy and Catholic Church, and likewise those who, fabricating falsehoods, have brought accusations against us.”

The proceedings do not contain this final sentence, but it has no bearing on the matter about which we must be concerned. Let those who fabricate falsehoods and bring accusations against them indeed be anathema.

But when I first read, “Those things which I said were not mine, I reject according to the judgment of the holy Church,” not knowing that the judgment of the Church had already been made—for this is left unstated here—and not having read the proceedings, I supposed nothing other than that he had promised to hold this view of those chapters which the Church had not yet judged but would judge at some time, and that he would reject what the Church had not yet rejected but would reject at some time. This, I thought, was also the meaning of what he added: “anathematizing everyone who opposes or contradicts the teachings of the holy Catholic Church.”

But in fact, as the proceedings testify, an ecclesiastical judgment had already been made about these matters by fourteen bishops. According to that judgment, he said that he rejected all these things and pronounced anathema upon those who, by holding such views, opposed a judgment that the proceedings show had already been made.

For the judges had already said:

“What does the present monk Pelagius say about these chapters that have been read? For the holy Synod and the holy Catholic Church of God reject them.”

But those who do not know this and read the written statement suppose that some of those positions may legitimately be defended, as though it had not been judged that they were contrary to Catholic doctrine, and as though Pelagius had declared himself ready to hold about these matters what the Church had not judged but would judge.

He therefore did not write in the written statement now under discussion in such a way that the truth contained in the proceedings could be recognized: namely, that all those doctrines by which the same heresy was spreading and growing strong through contentious audacity had been condemned by ecclesiastical judgment, with fourteen bishops presiding.

If he feared that this matter would become known as it truly stands, let him correct himself rather than grow angry at our vigilance, however late and imperfect. But if it is false that he feared this, and if—as human beings we suspect—things are otherwise, let him forgive us, provided that henceforth he oppose those things which were anathematized and rejected in the proceedings at which he was heard, lest, by sparing them, he appear not merely to have believed them before but to believe them still.

CHAPTER XXXIV.

59. For this reason I wished to write this book to Your Reverence, perhaps not without cause so lengthy in a matter so grave and weighty: so that, if it does not displease your judgment, it may, through your authority—which is far greater than the efforts of our insignificance—be made known to those whom you consider necessary, in order to suppress the vanities and contentious arguments of those who think that, once Pelagius had been acquitted, those doctrines pleased the eastern bishops who judged him—doctrines that most perniciously flourish against the Christian faith and against the grace of God by which we are called and justified, and which Christian truth has always condemned and has also condemned by the authority of these fourteen bishops, who would likewise have condemned Pelagius himself if those doctrines had not been anathematized by him.

Now, since we have discharged toward this man the obligation of fraternal charity and faithfully expressed our concern for and on behalf of him, let us see how it can be briefly understood that, although he has been clearly acquitted in the eyes of human beings, the heresy itself—always condemnable by divine judgment—was nevertheless condemned also by the judgment of the fourteen eastern bishops.

CHAPTER XXXV.

60. This is the final sentence of that judgment. The Synod said:

“Now, since we have received satisfaction from the statements of the present monk Pelagius, who indeed agrees with pious doctrines but rejects and anathematizes what is contrary to the faith of the Church, we acknowledge him to belong to ecclesiastical and Catholic communion.”

In the brevity of their sentence, the holy bishops who judged him included two matters sufficiently clear concerning the monk Pelagius: first, that “he agrees with pious doctrines”; second, that “he rejects and anathematizes what is contrary to the faith of the Church.” On account of these two things Pelagius was declared to belong to “ecclesiastical and Catholic communion.”

Let us therefore see, by briefly recapitulating everything, in which of his statements both points became clear—so far as human beings could judge in the present circumstances—from the matters brought against him. In those accusations which he answered were not his own, he was said to reject and anathematize what was contrary to them. Let us therefore gather the whole case together briefly, if we can.

61. Since it was necessary that what the Apostle Paul foretold should be fulfilled—“There must also be heresies among you, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (1 Cor. 11:19)—after the ancient heresies another heresy has now been introduced, not by bishops, presbyters, or any other clerics, but by certain people who were, as it were, monks. It argued against the grace of God that is ours through Jesus Christ our Lord, under the pretext of defending free choice, and attempted to overthrow the support (*firmamentum*) of the Christian faith [Note: [Col. 0355] Suar. reads *fundamentum evertere*, “to overthrow the foundation.”], concerning which it is written: “Through one man, death, and through one man, the resurrection of the dead; for as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ” (1 Cor. 15:21–22).

It also denied God’s assistance in our actions, saying that, in order not to sin and to fulfill righteousness, human nature—which was created with free choice—could be sufficient, and that this itself was God’s grace, because we were created in such a way that we could do this by our will; and that God had given the assistance of the law and his commandments, and forgave past sins to those who turned to him. God’s grace, it said, was to be reckoned as present only in these things, not in the assistance given for each of our individual actions.

“For a person can be without sin and can easily keep God’s commandments, if he wishes.”

62. When this heresy had deceived many and troubled the brothers whom it had not deceived, a certain Coelestius, who held such views, was brought before the judgment of the Church of Carthage and condemned by the sentence of the bishops [Note: [Col. 0355] This judgment was held before Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, at the beginning of the year 412, as is understood from the *Letter to Innocent*, which is Augustine’s Letter 175, §§1 and 6.].

Then, several years later, when this heresy was brought against Pelagius, who was said to be its teacher, he too came before an episcopal tribunal [Note: [Col. 0355] In the year 415, Pelagius, accused of heresy, came to trial, which was held at Diospolis in December.]. After everything that the Gallic bishops Heros and Lazarus had set down in the written accusation submitted against him had been read—for they were absent and had excused themselves because one of them was ill—fourteen bishops of the province of Palestine, after Pelagius had responded to everything, declared him free from the perversity of this heresy according to his responses; nevertheless, they condemned the heresy itself without any hesitation.

For, in accordance with his answer to the charges brought against him, they approved the statement that “a person is assisted by knowledge of the law so as not to sin, as it is written, ‘He gave them the law as an assistance’” (Isa. 8:20, according to the Septuagint). Yet they did not thereby approve that this knowledge of the law was that grace of God concerning which it is written: “Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24–25) [Note: [Col. 0356] Suar. and the Colbertinus manuscript read “they judged.”].

Nor did they therefore approve the statement attributed to Pelagius, “All are governed by their own will,” as though God did not govern them. For he responded that he had said this on account of free choice, for which God is an assistant when it chooses the good, whereas the person who sins is himself at fault, as belonging to free choice.

They also approved the statement that the wicked and sinners are not to be spared on the day of judgment but are to be punished with eternal fires. Since he replied that he had said this “according to the Gospel,” they approved it because it is written: “These will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46).

He had not said that all sinners belong to eternal punishment, so that he might rightly appear to have spoken against the Apostle, who says that some will be saved, yet as through fire (1 Cor. 3:15).

For this reason they approved that “the kingdom of heaven was also promised in the Old Testament,” since he cited the testimony of the prophet Daniel, where it is said: “And the saints will receive the kingdom of the Most High” (Dan. 7:18). Here, by “Old Testament,” they understood him to mean not only that which was given on Mount Sinai, but all the canonical Scriptures provided before the Lord’s coming [Note: [Col. 0356] The printed editions read “administered”; the Colbertinus manuscript reads “provided.”].

But the statement that “a person can be without sin, if he wishes” was not approved in the sense in which it appeared to have been set down by him in his book—as though this lay solely within human power through free choice. For this was judged to be what he meant by saying “if he wishes.” Rather, it was approved in the sense of his present response—or rather, in the sense in which the bishops, in their brief judicial intervention, stated it more concisely and clearly: that a person, with God’s assistance and grace, can be without sin.

Yet it was not defined when the saints will attain this perfection: whether in this body of death or when death will be swallowed up in victory.

### 63

Among the things that had also been brought against Pelagius as doctrines of his disciple Coelestius, he acknowledged some as his own, but replied that he had understood them differently from the way in which they were being brought against him. Thus there was the statement: “Some people lived holily and justly before Christ’s coming.” Coelestius, however, was reported to have said that “they were without sin.”

Likewise, Coelestius was accused of having said, “The Church is without spot or wrinkle.” Pelagius replied: “I did say this, but in the sense that the Church is cleansed from every spot and wrinkle by the washing, and that the Lord wills it to remain in that condition.”

There was also the statement attributed to Coelestius: “For we do more than is commanded in the Law and the Gospel.” Pelagius replied that he had spoken of virginity, about which Paul says, “I have no commandment of the Lord” (1 Cor. 7:25).

Again, Coelestius was accused of affirming that “each person can possess all virtues and graces,” thereby removing the diversity of graces taught by the Apostle. Pelagius replied: “I do not remove the diversity of graces; rather, I say that God gives to the person who is worthy to receive them all the graces, just as he gave them to the Apostle Paul.”

### 64

The bishops who judged the case did not approve these four statements when understood as Coelestius was said to have understood them, but according to the way Pelagius answered them. [Note: The Colbertine manuscript reads *viderunt* (“they saw”); the printed editions have *videtur* (“it is seen”).]

For they saw that being without sin is one thing, while living holily and justly is another—as Scripture also testifies that certain people lived before Christ’s coming. And although the Church is not now without spot or wrinkle, nevertheless it is cleansed from every spot and wrinkle by the washing of regeneration, and the Lord wills that it remain so. Indeed, it will remain so, because it will certainly reign in eternal blessedness without spot or wrinkle.

They also saw that perpetual virginity, which has not been commanded, is unquestionably something greater than conjugal chastity, which has been commanded—although many who persevere in virginity are nevertheless not without sin.

They saw, moreover, that the Apostle Paul possessed all the graces that he lists together in one passage. They could understand, however, either that he was worthy to receive them—not according to his merits, but rather in some way according to predestination—for he himself says, “I am not worthy,” or “I am not fit to be called an apostle” (1 Cor. 15:9); or else the wording eluded their intention, and Pelagius himself must determine how he intended it. These are the points on which the bishops declared that Pelagius agreed with pious doctrines.

### 65

Let us now, by recapitulating, examine somewhat more carefully those matters which they said he rejected and anathematized as contrary to the faith. For it is chiefly in this that the whole of this heresy consists.

Apart, therefore, from the statements he was said to have inserted in his books while flattering some widow—I do not know whom—which he replied were “neither in his books nor ever spoken by him,” and he anathematized those who held such views “not as heretics, but as fools”—these are the matters whose thickets of heresy we grieved to see sprouting daily, indeed already becoming a forest:

“Adam was made mortal, and whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.

“Adam’s sin injured Adam alone and not the human race.

“The Law leads to the kingdom in the same way as the Gospel.

“Newly born infants are in the same condition in which Adam was before his transgression.

“Neither through Adam’s death or transgression does the whole human race die, nor through Christ’s resurrection does the whole human race rise again.

“Infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life.

“If baptized rich people do not renounce everything, then whatever good they may appear to do is not counted to them, and they cannot possess the kingdom of God.

“God’s grace and assistance are not given for individual acts, but reside in free choice and in the Law and teaching.

“God’s grace is given according to our merits; and therefore grace itself is placed in the human will, whether the person becomes worthy [Note: Perhaps *fuerit*, “whether he has become,” rather than *fiat*, “whether he becomes.”] or unworthy.

“The children of God cannot be called such unless they have been made entirely without sin.

“Forgetfulness and ignorance are not subject to sin, because they do not occur according to the will but according to necessity.

“There is no free choice if it needs God’s assistance, since each person has his own will either to do something or not to do it.

“Our victory does not come from God’s assistance but from free choice.

“From Peter’s statement that we are ‘partakers of the divine nature,’ it follows that the soul can be without sin in the same way as God.”

I myself read this last statement in the eleventh chapter of a book which does not bear its author’s name but is said to be by Coelestius. It is expressed in these words:

“How,” he says, “has anyone become a participant in that of which he is declared to be a stranger in condition and power?”

For this reason the brothers who brought these charges understood him as having said that the soul was of the same nature as God and was a part of God; for they took his words to mean that he considered the soul to be of the same condition and power as God.

At the end of the charges was placed the following:

“Forgiveness is not granted to penitents according to the grace and mercy of God, but according to the merit and labor of those who, through repentance, have become worthy of mercy.”

The judges approved Pelagius, who denied that all these statements—and any arguments inserted to support them—were his, and who anathematized them. Therefore they declared that, by rejecting and anathematizing doctrines contrary to the Church’s faith, he had condemned them.

Accordingly, however Coelestius may or may not have stated these things, and however Pelagius may or may not have held them, let us rejoice that such great evils of this new heresy were condemned by that ecclesiastical judgment, and let us give thanks and praise to God.

### 66

As for the deeds said to have been perpetrated after this judgment, with incredible boldness, by some band of criminals—I do not know whom—who are reported to have strongly supported Pelagius in his perversity: that the servants and maidservants of God belonging to the care of the holy presbyter Jerome were subjected to a most wicked massacre; that a deacon was killed; that the monastery buildings were burned; and that, by God’s mercy, Jerome himself was scarcely protected from this assault and attack of the impious by a more strongly fortified tower [Note: This is relevant to Pope Innocent’s Letter 32 to John of Jerusalem, beginning: “The most noble and holy virgins Eustochium and Paula lamented that the devil had perpetrated in the places of your Church plunderings, murders, fires, every crime of extreme madness, etc.” Also relevant is his Letter 33 to Jerome, which begins: “The Apostle testifies that contention has never accomplished anything good in the Church.” These letters are reproduced below in the second part of the Appendix.]—I think that we should rather remain silent and await what our fellow bishops there judge ought to be done about such great evils. Who could believe that they can overlook them?

For the impious doctrines of such people must be refuted by Catholics everywhere, even by those who live far from those regions, so that they may not be able to do harm wherever they can reach. But impious deeds, the restraint of which belongs to episcopal discipline, must be punished where they are committed, especially by those who are present or nearby, with pastoral diligence and godly severity. [Note: The first editions have *coertio* (“restraint”); the manuscripts agree on *coercitio*, except for one, which has *cohibitio*.]

We, therefore, situated so far away, ought to wish that these matters may there receive such an ending that it will no longer be necessary for anyone anywhere to judge them, but that we may instead have something suitable to preach: namely, that the minds of all who have been grievously wounded by the report of those crimes, which has flown everywhere, may be healed through the mercy of God.

[Col. 0360]

Let this, then, be the end of this book. If, as I hope, it has deserved to please your judgment, then, with the Lord’s assistance, it will be useful to its readers—commended more by your name than by mine, and made known to many more widely through your diligence. [Note: At the end of the book, the editions add: “Here ends the book of Saint Augustine to the holy bishop Aurelius, concerning the proceedings against Pelagius the heretic, against the adversaries of the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ.”]

[Col. 0359]

[Note: Concerning the books *On the Grace of Christ* and *On Original Sin*, see Book 2, chapter 50, of the *Retractions*, vol. 1, col. 650, from the words “After the Pelagian heresy” through the words “Let us rejoice in salvation.” M.]

## SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO  
## TWO BOOKS ON THE GRACE OF CHRIST AND ON ORIGINAL SIN, AGAINST PELAGIUS AND COELESTIUS

[Note: Written in the year of Christ 418. For in that year the Pelagian heresy was condemned by Zosimus, as Augustine himself states in Book 2, chapter 50, of the *Retractions*. This was at the same time that a universal council against that heresy was held at Carthage by the African bishops, recorded on the Kalends of May in the same year, 418. After that council Augustine remained at Carthage, and his stay in that city lasted for a considerable period, as is understood from canon 94 of the African Council, or canon 127 of the Code of Canons of the African Church, as well as from Letter 93 to Mercator, section 1. During this interval, before he departed from there for Caesarea in Mauretania, he composed these books for Albina, Pinianus, and Melania. For this reason, in the *Retractions*, he places them immediately before the proceedings against Emeritus, which were completed at Caesarea on September 20 of that same year, 418. Julian, in his work addressed to Turbantius, maliciously attacked a passage from the book *On the Grace of Christ*. Augustine defended it in Book 4 against Julian, section 47, where he says that the title of this first book of his, as he calls it, “to the holy Pinianus,” is *On Grace against Pelagius*.]

[Note: The book *On the Grace of Christ* and the book *On Original Sin* have been newly corrected on the authority of the Vatican manuscript and four Gallican manuscripts belonging to the Colbert Library, the Abbey of Saint Victor in Paris, the Abbey of Casalis Benedicti, and the Abbey of Saint-Cyran; variant readings from the Belgian manuscript of the Abbey of Saint-Amand were also helpful. We also examined the earlier editions, those of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.]

(C)

# BOOK ONE  
## ON THE GRACE OF CHRIST

Augustine shows that Pelagius disguises his opposition to grace by professing it. For Pelagius either places grace in nature and free choice, or in the Law and teaching. Moreover, he says that divine grace assists only the possibility of willing and acting, as he calls it, and not willing and acting themselves; and he further holds that this assisting grace is given by God according to human merits, and that it helps people only so that they may more easily fulfill the commandments.

Augustine examines passages in Pelagius’s own short works in which Pelagius loudly claimed that he had commended God’s grace. He demonstrates that these passages can be interpreted as referring to the Law and teaching—that is, to divine revelation and Christ’s example, which likewise belong to teaching—or to the remission of sins. He further shows that it is not at all apparent whether Pelagius truly acknowledges Christian grace: that is, assistance in doing good, added to nature and teaching through the inspiration of a most ardent and radiant love. Finally, Pelagius is made to listen to Ambrose, whom he had praised so highly, speaking certain noble words in commendation of divine grace.

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0359]

### 1

How greatly we rejoice in your bodily and especially your spiritual salvation, most sincere brothers, beloved by God—Albina [Note: The editions have *Albine*. The Vatican codex and all our Gallican manuscripts have *Albina*. The title of the work agrees with this in the manuscripts of *Retractions*, Book 2, chapter 50, and in Possidius, *Index*, chapter 4: “To Albina,” etc. She was the mother-in-law of Pinianus and the mother of Melania. Compare Letter 124, written by Augustine to them while they were in Africa in 411, and Letter 126, written to Albina herself.], Pinianus, and Melania—we cannot express. We leave it to you to reflect upon and believe this; let us now rather speak about the matters concerning which you consulted us.

Since the messenger was in haste, and since our occupations here at Carthage are much more pressing than anywhere else, we dictated these things as best we could, insofar as God deigned to grant us the ability.

## CHAPTER TWO

### 2

You wrote to me that you had dealt with Pelagius so that he would condemn in writing whatever was said against him; and that, in your hearing, he had said:

“I anathematize anyone who thinks or says that the grace of God by which Christ came into this world to save sinners (1 Tim. 1:15) is not necessary—not only at every hour or every moment, but also in each of our individual acts; and those who try to take this grace away will suffer eternal punishments.” [Note: The majority of the manuscripts read *sortiantur* (“may suffer”); the editions have *soriuntur*.]

Anyone who hears these words and does not know his position—as he expressed it clearly enough in his books, not in those which he says were stolen from him uncorrected or which he altogether denies as his own, but in those which he mentions in his writings sent to Rome—will think that he holds precisely what the truth teaches.

But anyone who notices what he says more openly in those works ought also to regard these words with suspicion. For even if he places the grace of God by which Christ came into the world to save sinners solely in the remission of sins, he can adapt these words to that interpretation. He may say that grace is necessary at every hour, every moment, and in each individual act for this reason: that, by constantly retaining and remembering that our sins have been forgiven, we may not sin thereafter, aided not by any provision of strength but by the powers of its own will, as it recalls in each individual act what the remission of sins has bestowed upon it. [Note: The editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain have *recordantes* (“as we recall”); the manuscripts more suitably have *recordantis* (“of the one recalling”), namely, of the will. The phrase “what the remission of sins has accomplished for us” cannot be referred elsewhere.]

Likewise, since they are accustomed to say that Christ gave us assistance in not sinning because, by living justly and teaching justly, he left us an example, they can adapt these words in this way also: that this kind of grace is necessary to us at every moment and in each individual act, namely, so that in all our conduct we may contemplate the example of the Lord’s conduct. [Note: Amerbach and Erasmus have *justoque dicendo* (“and by teaching justly”); perhaps *justaque docendo* should be read.]

But your faith clearly perceives how sharply this confession must be distinguished from the confession of grace that is at issue. Nevertheless, it can be concealed beneath the ambiguity of such words.

## CHAPTER THREE

### 3

But why should this surprise us? Pelagius himself condemned, without any hesitation, in the episcopal proceedings those who say that God’s grace and assistance are not given for individual acts but reside in free choice or in the Law and teaching. We thought that all his evasions concerning this matter had been exhausted. He also condemned those who teach that God’s grace is given according to our merits. Yet in the books he published in defense of free choice, which he mentions in the letter he sent to Rome, he is shown to hold nothing other than what he appeared to have condemned.

For he places the grace and assistance of God by which we are helped not to sin either in nature and free choice, or in the Law and teaching. Thus, when God helps a person to turn away from evil and do good by revealing and showing what ought to be done, he is understood to provide assistance—not also by cooperating and inspiring love, so that the person may do what he has learned ought to be done.

### 4

For when he establishes and distinguishes three things by which he says that the divine commandments are fulfilled—possibility, will, and action—he means by possibility that by which a person can be just; by will, that by which he wishes to be just; and by action, that by which he is just.

Of these three, he confesses that the first—that is, the possibility—was given by the Creator of nature. It is not in our power, he says, but we possess it even if we do not wish to possess it. The other two—that is, will and action—he asserts to be ours, and attributes them to us in such a way that he insists they come from us alone.

Finally, he says that God’s grace does not assist those two which he wants to belong entirely to us, namely, will and action, but assists that which is not in our power and which comes to us from God, namely, possibility. It is as though what belongs to us—that is, will and action—were so effective for turning away from evil and doing good that they did not need divine assistance, while what comes to us from God—that is, possibility—were so weak that it always needed the help of grace. [Note: The Louvain edition alone reads: “that is, possibility, so weak that it always needs assistance from grace.”]

## CHAPTER FOUR

### 5

But lest anyone perhaps say that we do not understand correctly what he says, or that with malicious intent we twist into another meaning words that were not spoken in that sense, hear his own words:

“We distinguish these three things in this way and divide them, as it were, into a fixed order. In the first place we set ability, in the second willing, and in the third being. We place ability in nature, willing in choice, and being in the result.

“The first of these, namely ability, properly belongs to God, who conferred it upon his creature. The other two, however, namely willing and being, must be referred to the human being, because they descend from the source of free choice.

“Therefore praise for the good will and the good work belongs to the human being—indeed, to both the human being and God, who gave the possibility of that will and work and who always assists that possibility itself with the help of his grace.

“But the fact that a person can will and accomplish good belongs to God alone. Thus that one thing can exist even if the other two do not; but the other two cannot exist without it.

“Therefore I am free to have neither a good will nor a good action. But I can in no way fail to possess the possibility of good. It is present in me even if I do not wish it to be, and nature never finds rest from its activity in this respect.

“Some examples will make this meaning clearer to us. The fact that we can see with our eyes does not belong to us; but whether we see well or badly does belong to us.” [Note: Another example, omitted here, is discussed in the book *On Nature and Grace*, section 55.]

“And to embrace everything generally: the fact that we can do, say, or think every good thing belongs to the one who gave us this ability and assists this ability. But whether we do, speak, or think well belongs to us, because we can also turn all these things toward evil.

“Therefore—since this must often be repeated because of your slander—when we say that a person can be without sin, and by confessing the possibility we have received praise God, who has granted us this ability, there is no opportunity there for praising the human being, since only God’s role is being discussed. For the subject is not willing or being, but only that by which a person can be.”

## CHAPTER FIVE

### 6

Here, expressed with complete care and in these very words, is the whole doctrine of Pelagius in the third book of his work *In Defense of Free Choice*. He takes such pains to distinguish these three things—one, ability; another, willing; and the third, being—that is, possibility, will, and action, that whenever we read or hear him confess the assistance of divine grace by which we turn away from evil and do good, whether he places it in the Law and teaching or elsewhere, we know what he is saying and do not err by understanding him otherwise than he intends.

We must understand that he does not believe either our will or our action to be assisted by divine help, but only the possibility of willing and acting. Of these three, he affirms that we possess only this possibility from God, as though what God himself placed in nature were weak, while the other two, which he wanted to belong to us, were so firm, strong, and self-sufficient that they needed none of God’s assistance. Accordingly, God does not help us to will or to act, but only helps us to be able to will and act.

The Apostle, however, says: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.” And so that they might know that they were divinely assisted not only in their ability to act—for they had already received this in nature and teaching—but also in the action itself, he did not say, “For God is the one who works in you the ability,” as though they already possessed willing and acting by themselves and did not need his assistance in these two things. Rather, he said: “For God is the one who works in you both willing and accomplishing” (Phil. 2:12–13); or, as it is read in other manuscripts, especially the Greek ones, “both willing and acting.” [Note: Greek: *to energein* (τὸ ἐνεργεῖν), “to act” or “to work.”]

See whether the Apostle did not foresee, by the Holy Spirit, long beforehand those who would become adversaries of God’s grace. These two things—willing and acting—which Pelagius wanted to belong to us in such a way that they were not assisted by divine grace, the Apostle says that God works in us.

## CHAPTER SIX

### 7

Nor should Pelagius deceive the unwary and simple—or even himself—by saying, “Therefore praise for the good will and the good work belongs to the human being,” and then appearing to correct himself by adding, “Indeed, to both the human being and God.”

He did not say this because, according to sound teaching, he intended it to mean that God works in us both willing and acting. He shows quite clearly why he said it by immediately adding: “who gave the possibility of that will and work.”

It is clear from his earlier words that he places this possibility in nature. But lest he appear to have said nothing about grace, he added: “and who always assists that possibility itself with the help of his grace.” He did not say, “the will itself,” or “the action itself.” If he had said that, he would not appear to have departed from apostolic teaching. Instead he said, “that possibility itself,” namely, the one among the three which he placed in nature, “he always assists with the help of his grace.”

Thus, according to him, praise belongs to both God and the human being in willing and acting—not because the human being wills in such a way that God nevertheless inspires the will with the ardor of love, nor because the human being acts in such a way that God nevertheless cooperates, without whose assistance what is a human being? Rather, he adds God to this praise because, unless there were the nature in which God created us, by which we could will and act, we would neither will nor act.

### 8

Although he confesses that this natural possibility is assisted by God’s grace, it is not clear here either what grace he means or to what extent he considers nature to be assisted by it. But, as can be understood from other passages where he speaks more explicitly, he does not want it to be understood as anything other than the Law and teaching, by which natural possibility is assisted.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

For in one place he says:

“Here the most ignorant of people think that we do injury to divine grace because we say that it cannot perfect holiness in us without our will—as though God had issued a command and did not also supply the assistance of his grace to those whom he commanded, so that what human beings are commanded to do through free choice they might more easily fulfill through grace.”

And as though he were about to explain what grace he means, he continued:

“We confess that this grace exists not, as you think, only in the Law, but also in God’s assistance.”

Who would not wish him here to show what grace he wants us to understand? For this is precisely why we should especially expect him to say that what he calls grace is not something he confesses only in the Law.

But while he leaves us suspended in this expectation, observe what he added:

“For God helps us through his teaching and revelation, while he opens the eyes of our heart; while he shows us the future, so that we may not be occupied with present things; while he lays bare the snares of the devil; while he illuminates us with the manifold and ineffable gift of heavenly grace.” [Note: Amerbach and Erasmus have “with the manifold and ineffable gift of heavenly grace.”]

Then, concluding his argument as though with a kind of final vindication, he says:

“Does the person who says these things appear to you to deny grace? Or does he not confess both human free choice and God’s grace?”

In all this he has not departed from commending the Law and teaching. He carefully insists that this is the assisting grace, and he develops precisely what he had proposed when he said, “but also in God’s assistance.”

Finally, he thought that God’s assistance should be indicated in many ways by mentioning teaching and revelation, the opening of the eyes of the heart, the showing of future things, the uncovering of the devil’s snares, and illumination by the manifold and ineffable gift of heavenly grace—all, of course, so that we may learn the divine commandments and promises.

Thus to place God’s grace in the Law and teaching means this.

## CHAPTER EIGHT

### 9

From this, therefore, it is apparent that Pelagius confesses the grace by which God demonstrates and reveals what we ought to do, not the grace by which he gives and assists us to do it. For the knowledge of the Law is useful, if assistance is lacking, chiefly in this respect: it makes transgression of the commandment occur.

“For where there is no law,” says the Apostle, “neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15). And again: “I would not have known covetousness unless the Law had said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Rom. 7:7).

Thus Law and grace are so different that the Law not only accomplishes nothing but is also greatly harmful unless grace assists. Yet this is shown to be the usefulness of the Law: that it makes those whom it renders guilty of transgression flee to grace in order to be freed and to be assisted in overcoming evil desires.

For the Law commands rather than assists; it teaches that there is a disease but does not heal it. Indeed, insofar as the disease is not healed by it, it is increased, so that the medicine of grace may be sought more attentively and earnestly.

“For the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). “For if a law had been given that could give life” [Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and the Cygirannus manuscript read “could justify”], “then righteousness would truly have come from the Law.”

Yet, in showing how the Law also assists, he adds:

“But Scripture confined all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ. Therefore,” he says, “the Law was our pedagogue to Christ Jesus” (Gal. 3:21–22, 24).

It is useful, therefore, for the proud to be confined more tightly and clearly under sin, so that they may not presume to establish righteousness by free choice, as though relying on their own powers. Rather, “every mouth may be stopped, and the whole world may become accountable to God, because no flesh will be justified by the Law in his sight.”

“For through the Law comes knowledge of sin. But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the Law, testified to by the Law and the Prophets” (Rom. 3:19–21).

How, then, has it been manifested apart from the Law, if it is testified to by the Law? It has not been manifested without the Law, but the righteousness is apart from the Law, because it is God’s righteousness—that is, a righteousness which comes to us not from the Law but from God. It is not a righteousness feared because it is known at his command, but one held through love because it is given by him, so that “whoever boasts may boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:31). [Note: The manuscripts read this way. The editions have “It is not so manifested apart from the Law.”]

## CHAPTER NINE

### 10

What, then, does Pelagius mean by assigning to the Law and teaching the grace by which we are helped to perform righteousness—a grace which, however much it assists, assists us chiefly so that grace may be sought?

No one can fulfill the Law through the Law. “For the fullness of the Law is love” (Rom. 13:10). But “the love of God has not been poured into our hearts through the Law, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

Accordingly, grace is demonstrated through the Law, so that the Law may be fulfilled through grace.

What advantage does Pelagius gain by saying the same thing in different words, so that it is not understood that he places grace in the Law and teaching, by which he asserts that nature’s possibility is assisted? As far as I understand, he is afraid that this will be recognized because he condemned those who say that God’s grace and assistance are not given for individual acts but reside in free choice or in the Law and teaching. Yet he thinks he can remain concealed while expressing the meaning of the Law and teaching in one formulation after another.

## CHAPTER TEN

### 11

In another passage, after asserting for a long time that the good will is produced in us not by God’s assistance but by ourselves, he raised against himself a question from the Apostle’s Letter and said:

“And how,” he asks, “will that statement of the Apostle stand: ‘For God is the one who works in you both willing and accomplishing’?”

Then, as though resolving this objection—which he saw to be strongly opposed to his doctrine—he continued:

“He works in us the will that is good and the will that is holy, while he sets us, who are devoted to earthly desires and love only present things like dumb animals, on fire with the greatness of future glory and the promise of rewards; while, through the revelation of wisdom, he arouses our stunned will into desire for God; while he persuades us of everything that is good.” [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “which elsewhere you do not fear to deny”; the printed text has “which elsewhere he does not fear to deny.”]

What could be clearer? He says that the grace by which God works in us the will that is good is nothing other than the Law and teaching.

For in the Law and teaching of the holy Scriptures the greatness of future glory and rewards is promised. The revelation of wisdom also belongs to teaching; the persuasion of everything good also belongs to teaching. And although there may seem to be some difference between teaching and persuading—or rather exhorting—even this is encompassed by the general character of teaching, which is contained in various speeches and writings. For the holy Scriptures both teach and exhort, and human activity can also be involved in teaching and exhorting.

But let Pelagius at some point acknowledge that grace by which the greatness of future glory is not only promised but also believed and hoped for; by which wisdom is not only revealed but also loved; by which what is good is not only recommended but also made persuasive. [Note: The edition of Amerbach and the Victorinus manuscript read: “But we do not want him to confess this grace. Let these people confess it at some point.” Erasmus has: “But we do not want this grace. Let him confess this grace at some point.”]

For “faith does not belong to everyone” (2 Thess. 3:2) who hears through the Scriptures the Lord promising the kingdom of heaven. Nor is everyone persuaded to come to him who says, “Come to me, all you who labor” (Matt. 11:28), even though many are urged to come.

But whose faith it is, and who are persuaded to come to him, he himself clearly demonstrated when he said: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.” And shortly afterward, speaking of those who did not believe, he said: “I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6:44, 66).

Pelagius ought to confess this grace if he wishes not merely to be called a Christian but also to be one.

## CHAPTER ELEVEN

### 12

What, then, shall I say about the revelation of wisdom? No one could easily hope to attain in this life the greatness of the revelations granted to the Apostle Paul. And surely, in those revelations, what else should we believe was customarily revealed to him except what pertained to wisdom?

Yet he says:

“So that I might not be exalted because of the greatness of my revelations, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan to buffet me. Concerning this I pleaded with the Lord three times that he might remove it from me. And he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness’” (2 Cor. 12:7–9).

Without doubt, if the Apostle had already possessed the highest love, to which nothing could be added, and which could not at all be puffed up, would the angel of Satan have been necessary, by whose buffeting the exaltation that could arise from the greatness of his revelations might be restrained?

What else is exaltation than inflation? And surely it is most truly said of love: “Love does not envy; love is not puffed up” (1 Cor. 13:4).

This love, therefore, was still increasing day by day even in so great an Apostle, as long as his inner person was being renewed day by day (2 Cor. 4:16). It was doubtless to be perfected when it could no longer be puffed up.

At that time his mind was still in a condition in which it could be inflated by the greatness of revelation, until it was filled with the solid structure of love. For he had not yet reached, by attaining it, that toward which he was running by advancing.

## CHAPTER TWELVE

### 13

Therefore, when he was unwilling to endure the distress by which his exaltation was restrained before the ultimate and highest perfection of love existed in him, he was rightly told: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.”

This weakness was not, as Pelagius thinks, weakness “of the flesh alone,” but of both flesh and spirit. For, in comparison with that highest perfection, the spirit too was weak; and therefore, so that it might not be exalted, the thorn in the flesh—the angel of Satan—was understood to have been given to him. [Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain read “when he was exalted”; the manuscripts have *quin extolleretur*, “so that he might not be exalted,” in the construction “to whom, so that he might not be exalted.”]

Nevertheless, in comparison with carnal or merely natural people, who do not yet perceive what belongs to the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:14), he was exceedingly strong.

Therefore, if power is perfected in weakness, whoever does not acknowledge that he is weak is not perfected.

This grace, by which power is perfected in weakness, brings those who are predestined and called according to God’s purpose (Rom. 8:28) to the highest perfection and glorification. Through this grace we are enabled not only to know what ought to be done, but also to do what we have learned; and not only to believe what ought to be loved, but also to love what we have believed.

## CHAPTER THIRTEEN
14. If this grace is to be called teaching, let it certainly be described in such a way that God is believed to pour it, with ineffable sweetness, more deeply and inwardly—not only through those who plant and water externally, but also through himself, who secretly supplies the growth [Note: [Col. 0367] Morel considers *qui incrementum subministrat* (“who supplies the growth”) to be the reading required. See *Elementa Critica*, p. 148.] (I Cor. 3:7)—so that he not only displays the truth but also imparts love. For God teaches those who are called according to his purpose in this manner, granting them simultaneously to know what they should do and to do what they know. Hence the Apostle says to the Thessalonians: “Concerning brotherly love, you have no need for anyone to write to you; for you yourselves have been taught by God to love one another.” And to prove that they had been taught by God, he added: “For indeed you do this toward all the brothers throughout all Macedonia” (I Thess. 4:9–10). It is as though this were the surest indication that you have been taught by God: that you do what you have been taught.

Thus all who are called according to his purpose are, as it is written in the Prophets, “taught by God” (Isa. 54:13; John 6:45). But whoever knows what ought to be done and does not do it has not yet been taught by God according to grace, but according to the law; not according to the spirit, but according to the letter. Although many appear to do what the law commands out of fear of punishment, not out of love of righteousness—the righteousness which the Apostle calls “their own, which is from the law,” as though it were commanded rather than given. But if it has been given, it is not called our righteousness, but God’s, because it becomes ours in such a way that it comes to us from God. For he says: “That I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Jesus, righteousness from God” (Phil. 3:9).

So great is the distinction between law and grace that, although there can be no doubt that the law is from God, the righteousness which is from the law is nevertheless not from God; whereas the righteousness perfected through grace is from God. For “righteousness from the law” is so called when it is performed because of the law’s curse [Note: [Col. 0368] The printed editions read “the law’s command.” The manuscripts, Cygerannensis and Casalinus, have “the law’s curse,” which is more suitable to the antithesis: by it evil is announced to the transgressor, so that the command is made terrifying.]; “righteousness from God” is so called when it is given through the gift of grace. Thus the command is not terrifying but pleasant, as it is prayed in the Psalm: “You are sweet, Lord, and in your sweetness teach me your righteousness” (Ps. 118:68)—that is, so that I may not be slavishly compelled to be under the law through fear of punishment, but may delight in being with the law through free love. For a free person fulfills a command when he fulfills it willingly. And in this way whoever learns does altogether whatever he has learned ought to be done.

CHAPTER XIV

15. Concerning this manner of teaching, the Lord also says: “Everyone who has heard from my Father and learned comes to me” (John 6:45). Therefore, of one who has not come, it is not rightly said: “He has indeed heard and learned that he ought to come, but he does not wish to do what he has learned.” This is altogether not rightly said of that manner of teaching by which God teaches through grace. For if, as the Truth says, “everyone who has learned comes,” then whoever does not come has plainly not learned.

Who does not see that someone may come or not come by the choice of his will? But this choice can exist by itself if he does not come; if he comes, however, it cannot exist without being assisted—and assisted in such a way that he not only knows what ought to be done but also does what he has learned. Accordingly, when God teaches—not through the letter of the law, but through the grace of the Spirit—he teaches in such a way that whatever each person has learned, he not only sees by knowing it, but also desires by willing it and accomplishes by doing it. In this divine manner of teaching, the will itself and the action itself are assisted, not merely the natural possibility of willing and acting.

For if this grace assisted only our ability, the Lord would have said: “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned is able to come to me.” But he did not say that. Rather, he said: “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me.” Pelagius places the ability to come in nature—or, as he has recently begun to say, in grace, however he understands that grace, “by which,” as he says, “the possibility itself is assisted.” But coming is already a matter of will and action. It does not follow that whoever is able to come also comes, unless he wills and does so. But everyone who has learned from the Father not only is able to come, but comes. Here there is already the advance of ability, the affection of will, and the effect of action.

CHAPTER XV

16. What, then, is the purpose of these examples, unless they have truly made his meaning clearer to us, as he promised—not so that we ought to accept their meaning, but so that we may understand more plainly and openly what he himself meant? “What we are able to see,” he says, “with our eyes is not ours; but whether we see well or badly, that is ours.”

Let the Psalm answer him, where it says to God: “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity” (Ps. 118:37). Even if this is said of the eyes of the mind, it is certainly from them that there proceeds into these bodily eyes the seeing either well or badly—not in the sense in which people are said to see well when they look with healthy eyes and badly when they are bleary-eyed, but seeing well so as to come to someone’s aid, and seeing badly so as to desire. For although by these outward eyes one sees both the poor person to whom help is given and the woman who is desired, mercy or lust proceeds from the inner eyes toward seeing well or badly.

Why, then, is it said to God, “Turn my eyes away, lest they see vanity”? Why is something belonging to our power requested, if God does not assist the will?

CHAPTER XVI

17. “What we are able to say,” he says, “is God’s; but whether we speak well or badly is ours.” The one who speaks well does not teach this. “For,” he says, “it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20). “And, to embrace everything generally,” he says, “our ability to do, say, and think every good thing belongs to him who gave us this ability, who assists this ability.”

Here again he repeats the meaning stated above: of those three things—possibility, will, and action—only possibility is assisted. Finally, adding what completes his intention, he says: “But whether we act, speak, or think well is ours.” He has forgotten what he had previously seemed to correct, when, after saying, “Therefore human praise consists in good will and good action,” he added: “Rather, it belongs both to man and to God, who gave the possibility of that very will and action.”

Why, even in these examples, did he not remember this, so that at least at their conclusion he might say: “Our ability to do, say, and think every good thing belongs to him who gave us this ability, who assists this ability; but whether we act, speak, or think well belongs both to us and to him”? He did not say this. But, unless I am mistaken, I seem to see what he feared.

CHAPTER XVII

18. For when he wanted to show why the matter is ours, he said: “Because we are able to turn all these things toward evil as well.” This, then, is what he feared: he did not say, “It belongs both to us and to God,” lest someone answer him:

“If what we do, say, and think well belongs both to us and to God because he gave us the ability to do so, then what we do, say, and think badly also belongs both to us and to God, because he gave us the ability to do either. Thus—God forbid—as we are praised with God in good works, so we would be blamed with him in evil works.”

For that possibility which he gave us makes us as able to do good as to do evil.

CHAPTER XVIII

19. Concerning this possibility Pelagius speaks in the first book of his work *On Free Choice* as follows:

“We have,” he says, “the possibility of either side implanted by God, like a certain—as I may put it—fruit-bearing and fertile root, which produces and brings forth different things according to the will of man, and which, at the discretion of its own cultivator, can either shine with the flower of virtues or bristle with the thorns of vices.”

Here he establishes one and the same root of good and evil, without observing what he is saying, contrary to evangelical truth and apostolic teaching. For the Lord says that neither a good tree can produce evil fruits nor an evil tree good fruits (Matt. 7:18). And when the Apostle Paul says that greed is the root of all evils (I Tim. 6:10), he certainly urges us to understand that love is the root of all good things.

Therefore, if the two trees—the good and the evil—are two people, the good and the evil, what is a good person except one of good will, that is, a tree with a good root? And what is an evil person except one of evil will, that is, a tree with an evil root? The fruits of these roots and trees are deeds, words, and thoughts: good ones proceed from good will, and evil ones from evil will.

CHAPTER XIX

20. A person makes a good tree when he receives God’s grace. For he does not make himself good from being evil by himself; rather, he becomes good from him, through him, and in him who is always good. And not only is the same grace necessary for him to be a good tree, but also for him to produce good fruits, since without it he cannot do anything good.

For it is he himself who cooperates in producing fruit in good trees: externally he waters and cultivates through whatever minister he chooses, while inwardly he himself gives the growth (I Cor. 3:7). A person makes an evil tree when he makes himself evil, when he falls away from the unchangeable good. For from that falling away arises the origin of evil will. This falling away does not initiate [Note: [Col. 0370] The Vatican Manuscript reads *nuntiat* (“announces”).] another evil nature, but corrupts the nature that was created good. When the corruption has been healed, no evil remains, because corruption was present in the nature, but corruption was not the nature.

CHAPTER XX

21. That possibility, therefore, is not—as he supposes—one and the same root of good and evil. Love, the root of good, is one thing; greed, the root of evil, is another. They differ from each other as much as virtue and vice do.

But that possibility is capable of either root, because a person can not only possess love, by which he becomes a good tree, but can also possess greed, by which he becomes an evil tree. Yet the greed of man, which is a vice, has man as its author—or the deceiver of man—not the creator of man. For it is “the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the ambition of the world,” which is “not from the Father but from the world” (I John 2:16).

Who does not know that Scripture commonly uses the name “world” for those by whom this world is inhabited?

CHAPTER XXI

22. But love, which is a virtue, comes to us from God, not from ourselves, as Scripture testifies when it says: “Love is from God, and everyone who loves has been born from God and knows God, because God is love” (I John 4:7–8).

In accordance with this love, the statement is better understood: “Whoever has been born from God does not sin,” and, “He cannot sin” (I John 3:9). For love, according to which he has been born from God, does not act wrongly and does not think evil (I Cor. 13:4–5).

Therefore, when a person sins, he sins not according to love but according to greed, according to which he has not been born from God, since, as has been said, that possibility is capable of either root.

When Scripture says, “Love is from God,” or, what is more, “God is love”; when the Apostle John cries out most plainly, “See what kind of love the Father has given us, that we should be called and should be children of God” (I John 3:1)—when this man hears, “God is love,” why does he still insist that, of those three things, we have from God only possibility, while we have good will and good action from ourselves? It is as though good will were something other than love, which Scripture cries out is from God and given by the Father so that we might be his children.

CHAPTER XXII

23. But perhaps our preceding merits caused love to be given to us. This is how he understands God’s grace in the book he wrote to the sacred virgin [Note: [Col. 0371] This is the letter to Demetrias, which appears in volume 2 of the Appendix.], which he also mentioned in the letter he sent to Rome.

For there, after inserting the testimony of the Apostle James, who says, “Submit yourselves to God; resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7), he adds:

“He shows how we ought to resist the devil: namely, if we are submissive to God and, by doing his will, merit divine grace, and more easily resist the evil spirit with the help of the Holy Spirit” (chapter 25).

See with what truthful heart he condemned in the ecclesiastical judgment at Palestine those who say that God’s grace is given according to our merits! Or do we still doubt that he holds and most openly preaches this view? How, then, was that confession truthful in the episcopal examination? Or perhaps he had already written this book, in which he openly says that grace is given according to our merits—a view which he condemned without any objection in the Eastern synod? He should therefore have confessed that he had once held this view but no longer held it, so that we might rejoice openly in his correction.

But now, when this among other charges had been brought against him, he replied:

“Whether these are Coelestius’s opinions, let those who say that they are Coelestius’s see to it; but I have never held them in this way. I anathematize those who hold them” [Note: [Col. 0371] *Book on the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 30.].

How has he never held this view, if he had previously composed this book? Or how does he anathematize those who hold it, if he composed this book afterward?

24. But lest he perhaps reply that by saying, “By doing God’s will, we may merit divine grace,” he meant only that grace is added to the faithful and those who live piously so that they may resist the tempter courageously, although they had already first received grace in order to do God’s will, listen to other words of his concerning this matter.

“He who runs to the Lord,” he says, “and desires to be ruled by him—that is, suspends his own will upon God’s will—who by continually cleaving to him becomes, according to the Apostle, one spirit with him (I Cor. 6:17), accomplishes this only through the freedom of choice.”

See what a great matter he says is accomplished only through freedom of choice. Accordingly, he thinks that without God’s assistance we cleave to God. For this is what “only through the freedom of choice” means: that once we have cleaved to him without his assistance, then, because we have cleaved to him, we merit being assisted.

CHAPTER XXIII

He continues and says:

“He who uses it well”—that is, he who uses freedom of choice well—“surrenders himself wholly to God and puts his entire will to death, so that he can say with the Apostle, ‘It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me’ (Gal. 2:20); and he places his heart in the hand of God, so that he himself may incline it wherever he wills” (Prov. 21:1) [Note: [Col. 0372] In Lovaniensis, “God” is added here.].

This is certainly a great assistance of divine grace: that God himself should incline our heart wherever he wills. But, according to this man’s folly, we merit this great assistance only when, without any assistance, we run to the Lord solely through freedom of choice; desire to be ruled by him; suspend our will upon his will; and, by continually cleaving to him, become one spirit with him.

According to him, we accomplish these exceedingly great goods only through freedom of choice, so that, with these preceding merits, we may consequently obtain his grace in such a way that he himself inclines our heart wherever he wills.

How, then, is it grace if it is not given freely? How is it grace if it is repaid as a debt? How does the Apostle speak truly when he says, “It is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God—not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. 2:8–9)? And again: “But if it is by grace,” he says, “it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Rom. 11:6).

How, I ask, is this true if such great works precede, making for us a merit by which we obtain grace, so that it is not given to us freely but repaid as a debt? Is it therefore the case that, in order to reach God’s assistance, we run to God without God’s assistance? And in order that, cleaving to God, we may be assisted by God, do we cleave to God without being assisted by God?

What greater or comparable thing could grace itself provide to man, if he could already become one spirit with the Lord without grace, solely through freedom of choice?

CHAPTER XXIV

25. But I should like this man to say whether that Assyrian king [Note: [Col. 0372] The Colbertine Manuscript reads “Ahasuerus.”]—whose bed the holy woman Esther abhorred—when he sat upon the throne of his kingdom, clothed entirely in the robe of his splendor, covered with gold and precious stones, exceedingly terrifying, and, lifting his face inflamed with majesty, looked at her like a bull in the violence of his anger [Note: [Col. 0372] Here the particle *in* has been restored from the manuscripts]; and the queen was afraid, her color changed in a faint, and she leaned upon the head of her delicate attendant who went before her—whether, I say, that king had already run to the Lord, desired to be ruled by him, suspended his will upon God’s will, and, by continually cleaving to him, become one spirit with him solely through freedom of choice; whether he had surrendered himself wholly to God, put his entire will to death, and placed his heart in God’s hand [Col. 0373].

I think that anyone who forms such an opinion of that king as he was at that time is not foolish but insane. And yet God “turned and transferred his anger into gentleness” (Esther 5, according to the Septuagint).

Who does not see that it is much greater to turn and transfer anger into its opposite, gentleness, than to incline a heart that has been seized by neither affection, but stands midway between the two, toward one of them?

Let them read, then, and understand; let them observe and confess that God works in human hearts—not merely through the law and teaching sounding externally, but by an internal and hidden, wondrous and ineffable power—not only true revelations but also good wills.

CHAPTER XXV

26. Let Pelagius, then, cease to deceive both himself and others by arguing against God’s grace. God’s grace must be proclaimed not merely on account of one of those three things—namely, the possibility of good will and action—but also on account of good will and good action.

For he defines that possibility as effective for either side. Yet he does not therefore want our sins also attributed to God, just as, because of that same possibility, he wants our good works attributed to God. Divine grace should not be commended merely because it assists natural possibility.

Let him cease saying: “Our ability to do, say, and think every good thing belongs to him who gave us this ability, who assists this ability; but whether we act, speak, or think well is ours.” Let him cease, I say, saying this.

For God has not only given and assists our ability; he also works in us to will and to act (Phil. 2:13). This is not because we do not will or do not act, but because without his assistance we neither will nor do anything good.

For how can it be said, “The ability to act well is God’s, but the action is ours,” when the Apostle says that he prays to God on behalf of those to whom he is writing, both that they do no evil and that they do what is good? He does not say, “We pray that you may be able to do no evil,” but “that you may do no evil”; nor, “that you may be able to do good,” but “that you may do good” (II Cor. 13:7).

For those of whom it is written, “As many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God” (Rom. 8:14), are plainly led to do what is good by him who is good.

How does Pelagius say, “Our ability to speak well is God’s, but speaking well is ours,” when the Lord says, “It is the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you”? He does not say, “It is not you who gave yourselves the ability to speak well”; rather, he says, “It is not you who speak” (Matt. 10:20).

Nor does he say, “It is the Spirit of your Father who gives or gave you the ability to speak well,” but, “who speaks in you”—not indicating an advance in possibility [Note: [Col. 0373] The manuscripts read *provectum* (“advance”) rather than *profectum* (“progress”).], but expressing the effect of cooperation.

How does this exalted advocate of free choice say, “Our ability to think well is God’s, but thinking well is ours” [Col. 0374], when the humble preacher of grace answers him: “Not that we are competent of ourselves to think anything as from ourselves, but our competence is from God” (II Cor. 3:5)? He does not say, “the ability to think,” but “to think.”

CHAPTER XXVI

27. Let Pelagius also openly acknowledge this grace of God, which is manifest in the divine utterances, and let him not conceal that he has thought otherwise for so long through a most shameless shame; rather, let him reveal it through salutary sorrow, so that the holy Church may not be disturbed by his obstinate persistence but may rejoice in his truthful correction.

Let him distinguish knowledge and love as they must be distinguished [Note: [Col. 0374] The printed editions read “thought and choice.” The reading has been corrected on the authority of the manuscripts.], because “knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (I Cor. 8:1). Knowledge does not puff up when love builds up.

Although both are gifts of God, one lesser and the other greater, let him not so exalt our righteousness over the praise of our Justifier that he attributes the lesser of these two to divine assistance but arrogates the greater to human choice [Note: [Col. 0374] The printed editions read “here.” The Vatican Manuscript’s “thus” is preferable.].

And if he agrees that we receive love from God’s grace, let him not suppose that any good merits of ours preceded it. For what good merits could we have had when we did not love God? In order that we might receive the love by which we would love, we were loved when we did not yet possess it.

The Apostle John says this most plainly: “Not that we loved God, but that he loved us” [Note: [Col. 0374] The printed editions add “first,” but it is absent from the manuscripts and from the corresponding passage in John.]. And elsewhere: “Let us love,” he says, “because he first loved us” (I John 4:10, 19).

This is altogether most excellent and entirely true. For we would have no basis from which to love him unless we received it from him when he first loved us.

What good would we do if we did not love? Or how could we fail to do good if we loved? For although God’s command sometimes appears to be fulfilled not by those who love but by those who fear, nevertheless, where there is no love, no good work is credited, nor is it rightly called a good work, because “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23), and “faith works through love” (Gal. 5:6).

Accordingly, whoever wishes to confess God’s grace truthfully should confess the grace by which God’s love is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5) in such a way that he does not doubt at all that, without it, nothing belonging to true devotion and true righteousness can be done.

Not like this man, who, when he says that grace is given “so that what God commands may be fulfilled more easily,” sufficiently shows what he thinks about it: namely, that even without grace, although less easily, what God commands can nevertheless be done.

CHAPTER XXVII

28. In the book to the sacred virgin, which I also mentioned above, when he says, “May we merit divine grace, and more easily resist the evil spirit with the help of the Holy Spirit,” he plainly indicates his meaning.

Why did he insert the word “more easily”? Or was the meaning not complete in the form, “so that we may resist the evil spirit with the help of the Holy Spirit”? Who does not understand how much harm this addition has caused?

He evidently wants it to be believed that the powers of nature are so great—powers which he exalts only to bring them down—that even without the assistance of the Holy Spirit one can nevertheless resist the evil spirit somehow, although less easily.

CHAPTER XXVIII

29. Likewise, in the first book *On Free Choice*, he says:

“Although we possess within us a freedom of choice so strong and so firm for not sinning, which the Creator of human nature implanted generally in nature, nevertheless, because of his immeasurable kindness, we are fortified by his daily assistance.”

What need is there of this assistance if freedom of choice is so strong and so firm for not sinning? But here too he wants it understood that assistance exists so that grace may make easier what, although less easily, he thinks can nevertheless be done without grace.

CHAPTER XXIX

30. Elsewhere in the same book he says:

“So that what human beings are commanded to do through free choice, they may more easily fulfill through grace.”

Remove the word “more easily,” and the meaning is not only complete but sound if it is stated thus: “So that what human beings are commanded to do through free choice, they may fulfill through grace.”

But when “more easily” is added, it is tacitly suggested that the fulfillment of a good work can also take place without God’s grace. This meaning is refuted by the one who says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

CHAPTER XXX

31. Let him correct all these matters, lest, if human weakness has erred in the depth of great questions, diabolical deceit or obstinacy should also be added to that error—whether by denying what he has thought or by defending what he has thought wrongly, after he has recognized from the clear truth quoted above that he ought not to have thought it.

For in all the writings of Pelagius and Coelestius that I have been able to read, I have nowhere found them confessing this grace by which we are justified—that is, by which God’s love is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us—in the manner in which it ought to be confessed.

I have nowhere found them recognizing, as they ought to be recognized, the children of promise, of whom the Apostle says: “It is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of promise are counted as offspring” (Rom. 9:8).

For what God promises is not accomplished by us through choice or nature; he himself accomplishes it through grace.

32. To say nothing for the moment of Coelestius’s writings, or of the pamphlets of his which he cited in ecclesiastical judgments [Note: [Col. 0375] He refers again below, no. 36, to the pamphlet cited by Coelestius in the ecclesiastical proceedings at Rome, and in *On Original Sin*, nos. 2, 5, and elsewhere. Those proceedings were conducted in the presence of Coelestius, who gave his responses, under Zosimus in the year of Christ 417, as he testifies in book 2 of *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, no. 5. See Zosimus’s letters below, Appendix, part 2.], all of which, along with other letters that we considered necessary, we have taken care to send to you, so that, after carefully examining them all, you may observe that he does not place the grace of God by which we are assisted—whether in turning away from evil or in doing good—outside the natural choice of the will, except in the law and teaching.

Thus he asserts that even prayers are necessary for this purpose: to show a person what he should desire and love.

But to set all this aside for the moment, Pelagius himself recently sent both a letter and a pamphlet concerning his faith to Rome, writing to Pope Innocent of blessed memory, whose death he did not know about. In this letter he says that there are certain charges by which people try to defame him: one, that he denies the sacrament of Baptism to infants and promises the kingdom of heaven to some without Christ’s redemption; the other, that he says a person can avoid sin in such a way as to exclude God’s help, and trusts so much in free choice that he rejects the assistance of grace.

Although, concerning the Baptism of infants, he concedes that it ought to be given to them, this is not the place for us to discuss more carefully how perversely he understands the truth against the Christian and Catholic faith. For now, we must complete the discussion of the assistance of grace which we have undertaken.
