Let us therefore see what answer he gives also to the matter he has raised. Omitting his spiteful complaints about his enemies, when he came to the point itself he spoke as follows.

CHAPTER XXXI

33. “Behold,” he says, “let this letter clear me before Your Beatitude, in which we state plainly and simply that we possess an unimpaired freedom of choice for sinning and not sinning, and that in all good works it is always assisted by divine aid.”

You therefore see, in accordance with the understanding the Lord has given you, that these words of his are insufficient to resolve the question. For we are still asking by what assistance he says free choice is helped, lest, as he commonly does, he wishes the law and teaching to be understood.

For if you ask why he said “always,” he may answer: “Because it is written, ‘He will meditate on his law day and night’” (Ps. 1:2).

Then, after inserting certain remarks concerning the condition of man and his natural possibility of sinning and not sinning, he added:

“We say that this power of free choice exists generally in all—in Christians, Jews, and Gentiles. Free choice exists equally in all by nature, but in Christians alone it is assisted by grace.”

Again we ask: by what grace? And again he may answer: by Christian law and teaching.

34. Moreover, whatever he understands by grace, he says that it is given to Christians themselves according to their merits, although, as I mentioned above (chapter 22, no. 23), he condemned in Palestine, in that celebrated defense of his, those who say this.

For these are his words:

“In them”—that is, in those who are not Christians—“the good of their condition is naked and unarmed.” Then, continuing:

“But in those who belong to Christ, it is fortified by Christ’s assistance.”

You see that, in light of what we said above, it remains uncertain what assistance he means.

But he continues concerning those who are not Christians and says:

“They are to be judged and condemned because, although they possess free choice, through which they could come to faith and merit God’s grace, they misuse the freedom granted to them. But those are to be rewarded [Note: [Col. 0377] Perhaps “he believes” (*credat*).] who, using free choice well, merit the Lord’s grace and keep his commandments.”

It is therefore manifest that he says grace is given according to merits, whatever grace he may mean, or however he may mean it—although he does not state it openly. For when he says that those who use free choice well are to be rewarded, and therefore merit the Lord’s grace, he admits that a debt is repaid to them.

Where, then, is the Apostle’s statement: “Being justified freely by his grace” (Rom. 3:24)? Where is also the statement: “You have been saved by grace”? And lest they should think this was through works, he added, “through faith.” Again, lest they should think that even faith itself should be attributed to them without God’s grace, he says: “And this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God” (Eph. 2:8).

Therefore, that from which everything begins which we are said to receive deservedly, we receive without merit—that is, faith itself.

Or if it is denied that faith is given, what is meant by the statement: “As God has allotted to each a measure of faith” (Rom. 12:3)? But if it is said to be given in such a way that it is repaid according to merits and not given as a gift, what is meant by the further statement: “To you it has been granted for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1:29) [Note: [Col. 0377] The manuscripts read “but also to suffer for him,” omitting *ut* (“that”), a wording not repeated in the Greek. ]?

He testified that both were granted as gifts: believing in Christ and suffering for Christ.

But these people attach faith to free choice in such a way that grace appears to be repaid to faith—not freely given, but owed. And consequently it is no longer grace, because unless it is freely given, it is not grace.

CHAPTER XXXII

35. But from this letter Pelagius wishes the reader to pass to his book on the faith [Note: [Col. 0377] We present it below, Appendix, part 2.], which he mentioned to you [Note: [Col. 0377] Am. Er. and the manuscripts read “to us.”]. In it he discussed many matters about which he had not been questioned.

But let us examine the matters concerning which we are dealing with them. After bringing to an end, at whatever length he wished, a discussion extending from the unity of the Trinity to the resurrection of the flesh—subjects about which no one had asked him—he says:

“And we hold one Baptism, which we say is to be celebrated with the same words of the sacrament for infants as for adults.”

You certainly said that you had also heard this from him in person. But what benefit is there in his saying that the sacrament of Baptism is celebrated for infants with the same words as for adults, when what we ask about is the reality, not words alone?

More significant is what he answered when you yourselves questioned him orally, as you write: “Infants receive Baptism for the remission of sins.” For here too he did not say “in the words of the remission of sins,” but confessed that they are baptized into the remission itself. Yet if you asked him what sin he believed was remitted to them, he would deny that they possessed any.

CHAPTER XXXIII

36. Who would believe that, beneath this seemingly clear confession, a contrary meaning lay hidden, unless Coelestius had revealed it? In his pamphlet, which he cited in the ecclesiastical proceedings at Rome, he both confessed that “infants are baptized for the remission of sins” and denied that they “have any original sin.”

But let us now attend not to the Baptism of infants, but rather to what Pelagius thought concerning the assistance of grace, even in the pamphlet on his faith which he sent to Rome.

“We confess,” he says, “free choice in such a way that we say we always need God’s help.”

Here again we ask what assistance he admits that we need. Again we find the statement ambiguous, since he can answer that by it he means the law or Christian teaching, by which that natural possibility is assisted.

But we seek in their confession that grace of which the Apostle says: “God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power and love and self-control” (II Tim. 1:7).

It does not follow that whoever possesses the gift of knowledge, by which he knows what he ought to do, also possesses love, so that he does it.

CHAPTER XXXIV
37. I also read those works which he mentions in the same letter that he sent to Pope Innocent of blessed memory, except for one letter, which he says he sent to the holy bishop Constantius as a brief communication. Nowhere, however, could I find him confessing that grace by which not only the natural capacity of the will and action—which he says we possess even if we neither will nor perform the good—is assisted, but the will itself and the action are assisted by the supply of the Holy Spirit.

## CHAPTER XXXV

38. “Let them read,” he says, “the letter which we wrote nearly twelve years ago to the holy bishop Paulinus. In perhaps three hundred verses it confesses nothing other than the grace and assistance of God, and that we can do absolutely no good without God.”

I therefore read this letter and found that throughout almost the whole of it he dwells only on the faculty and possibility of nature, and establishes God’s grace almost exclusively there. Christian grace, however, he touches upon so briefly, merely mentioning the name, that he seems to have feared nothing so much as appearing to be silent about it. Whether, nevertheless, he wishes it to be understood as the remission of sins, or also as the teaching of Christ—which includes the example of his conduct, as he does in places in some of his shorter works—or whether he believes that some assistance toward doing good is added to nature and teaching through the inspiration of the most ardent and luminous charity, is entirely unclear.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

39. “Let them also read,” he says, “the letter to the holy bishop Constantius, where, although briefly, I plainly joined God’s grace and assistance to the free will of man.”

As I said above (ch. 34, §37), I did not read this letter. But if it is not unlike the others that he mentions, and of which I have knowledge, it too contains nothing of what we are seeking.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

39. “Let them also read,” he says, “what we composed in the East for the sacred virgin of Christ, Demetrias [Note: Col. 0378. See this letter in the Appendix to volume 2.], and they will find that we praise human nature in such a way that we always add the assistance of God’s grace.”

I certainly read this work, and it had almost persuaded me that he was confessing the grace at issue, although in many passages of the work he seemed to contradict himself. But when other writings came into my hands, which he had composed later and at greater length, I saw how he could mention grace even there while concealing what he meant beneath an ambiguous generality, using the word “grace” to blunt resentment and avoid offense.

For at the beginning of the work, where he says, “Let us devote ourselves zealously to the task, and let us not distrust the moderate capacity [Note: [Col. 0379] Amerbach and the manuscripts read *mediocritate* (ablative, “moderate capacity”) for *mediocritati* (dative, “moderate capacity”). In the letter to Demetrias, Appendix to volume 2, the reading is *de mediocritate* (“concerning moderate capacity”).] of our talent, which we believe is assisted by the faith of the mother and the merit of the virgin,” he seemed to me to confess the grace by which we are assisted in doing something. I had not considered that he might place this assistance solely in the revelation of teaching.

41. Again, elsewhere in the same work:

“But if even without God,” he says, “human beings show what sort of beings they were made by God, see what Christians can do, whose nature has been restored for the better through Christ and who are also assisted by the help of divine grace.”

By nature restored for the better he wishes the remission of sins to be understood. He demonstrated this sufficiently elsewhere in the same book, where he says, “Even those who through long practice of sin have become hardened in a certain way can be restored through repentance.” Here too, however, he can place the assistance of divine grace in the revelation of teaching.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

42. Again, elsewhere in the same letter:

“For if even before the Law,” he says, “and long before the coming of our Lord and Savior, certain people are reported to have lived justly and holily, how much more, after the illumination of his coming, should we believe that we can do so—being restored through the grace of Christ and reborn as better human beings, cleansed and purified by his blood, and urged toward the perfection of righteousness by his example? We ought to be better than those who lived before the Law.”

Observe how here too, although in different words, he places the assistance of grace in the remission of sins and in Christ’s example. Then he adds:

“Better even than those who lived under the Law, since the Apostle says, ‘Sin shall not rule over you; for you are not under the Law but under grace’ (Rom. 6:14). And since,” he says, “we have now spoken sufficiently, as I think, let us form the perfect virgin, who, kindled by both, may always bear witness through the holiness of her conduct to the goodness both of nature and of grace.”

In these words you should notice that he wished to conclude what he was saying in such a way that we should understand the goodness of nature as what we received when we were created, and the goodness of grace as what we receive when we contemplate Christ’s example [Note: Amerbach reads *imitemur* (“imitate”); the source also lists Erasmus, but supplies no reading after that siglum.]—as though sin had not been pardoned to those who were or are under the Law because they either did not have Christ’s example or did not believe in it.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

43. Other words of his show that this is what he thinks—not in this book, but in the third book *On Free Will*. There, addressing the person against whom he is arguing, because that person had cited the Apostle’s words, “I do not do the good that I want,” and, “I see another law in my members warring against the law of my mind,” together with the other words found there, he replied:

“For what you wish to understand from the Apostle, all ecclesiastical men assert that he said in the person of a sinner and of one still under the Law, who was held, as it were, by a necessity of sinning because of excessive habit of vice; although he desired the good by his will, he was nevertheless driven headlong into evil by habit. In the person,” he says, “of one man, he depicts the people still sinning under the old Law; and he says that they are to be freed from this evil of habit through Christ, who first forgives all sins through Baptism to those who believe in him, and then urges them through imitation of himself toward perfect holiness, conquering the habit of vice by the example of virtue.”

See how he wishes those who sin under the Law to be understood as being assisted, so that, justified by the grace of Christ, they may be freed—as though the Law alone were insufficient for them because of their excessive habit of sinning, unless Christ’s example of virtue, presented in evangelical teaching for contemplation and imitation, should be added. Certainly, here there was the greatest reason to explain what grace he meant, since the Apostle concluded the very passage to which he is responding by saying: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:15, 23–25).

Since he places this grace not in Christ’s assistance in virtue but in the example of imitation, what more ought we to expect from him wherever he mentions the name of grace beneath an ambiguous generality?

## CHAPTER XL

44. Again, in the same book addressed to the sacred virgin, where we have already discussed the matter above, he says:

“Let us be subject to God, and by doing his will let us merit divine grace, and let us resist the evil spirit more easily with the assistance of the Holy Spirit.”

In these words it is certainly clear that he wishes us to be assisted by the grace of the Holy Spirit not because, without that Spirit, we cannot resist the tempter even through the mere possibility of nature, but so that we may resist more easily. Yet it is credible that he establishes this assistance, whatever its quality and however slight its extent, in the fact that knowledge is added to us through the Spirit’s revelation in teaching—knowledge which by nature we either cannot possess or can possess only with difficulty.

These are the points I was able to observe in the book he wrote to the virgin of Christ, where he appears to confess grace. You can plainly see what sort of grace this is.

## CHAPTER XLI

45. “Let them also read,” he says, “my recent short work, which we were recently compelled to publish *On Free Will*. They will recognize how unjustly those who desire to defame us by denying grace have acted, since throughout almost the entire text of the work we confess both free will and grace perfectly and fully.”

This work consists of four books. I read them, and from them I took the material that I proposed to examine and discuss, and I treated it as well as I could before we came to this letter of his that was sent to Rome.

But in these four books, whatever he seems to say about grace by which we are assisted to turn away from evil and do good, he says in such a way that he never departs from the ambiguity of his words. Thus he can explain them to his disciples in such a way that they believe there is no assistance of grace by which the possibility of nature is helped, except in the Law and in teaching. He even thinks that prayers themselves, as he most plainly affirms in his writings, are to be employed for no other purpose than that teaching may be opened to us through divine revelation—not that the human mind may be assisted so that what it has learned ought to be done may also be accomplished through love and action.

For he does not depart at all from his most evident doctrine, in which he establishes those three things: possibility, will, and action. He says that only possibility is always assisted by divine help; but he thinks that the will and the action need no assistance from God.

The assistance itself by which he says natural possibility is helped he places in the Law and in teaching, which he admits are also revealed to us by the Holy Spirit, and for this reason he allows that we ought to pray. Yet he thinks that this assistance of the Law and teaching existed also in prophetic times, while the assistance of grace—which is properly called grace—consists, in his view, in Christ’s example. You see that this too belongs to the teaching preached to us in the Gospel: as though, once the road had been pointed out on which we ought to walk, we were sufficient for ourselves through the powers of free will, needing no assistance from anyone else in order not to fail on the way.

Although he also maintains that this road can be discovered by nature alone, he says that it is easier to find if grace assists.

## CHAPTER XLII

46. This, then, is what I was able to understand, according to my capacity, from Pelagius’s writings when he mentions grace.

You see, however, that those who think in this way, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness, desire to establish their own” (Rom. 10:3), and are far from that righteousness which is from God and not from ourselves (Phil. 3:9). They ought to have noticed and acknowledged this especially in the sacred canonical Scriptures. But because they read them according to their own understanding, they evidently do not even see the evident things in those Scriptures [Note: The manuscripts read, “especially in the sacred canonical Scriptures.” The editions reverse the order: “in the sacred Scriptures, especially the canonical ones.” The printed editions read *aperte*, “plainly”; the manuscripts read *aperta*, “the evident things.”].

Would that at least in the writings of Catholic men—whose correct understanding of the Scriptures they do not doubt—they would carefully attend to what should be thought about the assistance of divine grace, and would not pass it over because of their excessive attachment to their own opinion.

For this same Pelagius, in that very recent short work by which he defends himself—that is, in the third book *On Free Will*—praises Saint Ambrose. Listen to how he praises him.

## CHAPTER XLIII

47. “Blessed,” he says, “is Ambrose the bishop, in whose books above all the Roman faith shines forth; a certain beautiful flower among Latin writers, whose faith and utterly pure understanding of the Scriptures not even an enemy has dared to criticize.”

See with what and how great praises he extols this holy and learned man, though he certainly cannot be compared with the authority of canonical Scripture. Pelagius commends him in this way because he thinks that in one passage of Ambrose’s books he can use Ambrose as a witness to prove that a human being can be without sin.

That is not the issue now. The issue is the assistance of grace by which we are helped not to sin and to live justly.

## CHAPTER XLIV

48. Let him therefore hear that venerable bishop speaking and teaching, in the second book of his *Exposition of the Gospel according to Luke* (Book 2, §84, on Luke 3:22), that the Lord also cooperates with our wills:

“You see, therefore,” he says, “that everywhere the Lord’s power cooperates with human efforts, so that no one can build without the Lord, no one can guard without the Lord, and no one can begin anything without the Lord. And therefore, according to the Apostle, ‘Whether you eat or drink, do everything for the glory of God’” (1 Cor. 10:31).

You see how Saint Ambrose, in these words, removed even what people commonly say—“We begin, and God brings to completion”—by saying, “No one can even begin anything without God.”

Again, in the sixth book of the same work, when he was discussing the two debtors of a single moneylender:

“According to human judgment,” he says, “the one who owed more perhaps offended more. But through the mercy of the Lord the matter is changed, so that the one who owed more loves more, provided that he receives grace” (Book 6, §25, on Luke 7:41).

Here the Catholic teacher most plainly proclaims that even the love by which one person loves more belongs to the gift of grace.

## CHAPTER XLV

49. Finally, blessed Ambrose says in the ninth book of the same work [Note: Here the printed editions, following the customary division of this work of Ambrose into ten books, read “in the tenth.” All the manuscripts read “in the ninth.”] that repentance itself—which is unquestionably brought about by the will—is nevertheless brought about through the mercy and assistance of the Lord. He speaks as follows:

“Good are the tears that wash away guilt. In the end, those whom Jesus looks upon weep [Note: The printed editions add *plorant delictum*, “weep over their offense.” Neither the manuscripts nor Ambrose include the word *delictum*.]. Peter denied him the first time and did not weep, because the Lord had not looked upon him; he denied him the second time and did not weep, because the Lord had not yet looked upon him; he denied him the third time, Jesus looked upon him, and he wept most bitterly” (Book 10, §89, on Luke 22:61).

Let these men read the Gospel and see that the Lord Jesus was then inside, when he was being questioned by the chief priests, while the apostle Peter was outside and below in the courtyard with the servants, sometimes sitting and sometimes standing by the fire, as the most truthful and harmonious narrative of the Evangelists demonstrates.

Therefore it cannot be said that the Lord looked upon him visibly with bodily eyes, admonishing him. And so what is written there—“The Lord looked upon him” (Luke 22:61)—was accomplished inwardly; it was accomplished in the mind, it was accomplished in the will [Note: Two manuscripts, one from Casale and the other from Victorinus, read: “It was accomplished inwardly, in the mind, in the will.”].

The Lord secretly came to his aid through mercy; he touched his heart, reminded him, visited Peter by his inward grace, and moved and brought forth the emotion of the inner person into outward tears.

See how God, by assisting, is present to our wills and actions; see how he works in us both willing and acting.

50. Again, in the same book the same Saint Ambrose says:

“For if Peter,” he says, “fell, though he had said, ‘Even if all are scandalized, I will not be scandalized’ (Matt. 26:33), who else can rightly presume concerning himself? Finally, David, because he had said, ‘In my prosperity I said, I shall never be moved,’ confesses that his own boasting harmed him, saying, ‘You turned your face away, and I was troubled’” (Ps. 29:7–8).

Let Pelagius hear this great man teaching and imitate him in faith, since he praised his teaching and faith. Let him hear humbly and imitate faithfully; let him not stubbornly presume upon himself, lest he perish.

Into what sea does Pelagius wish to plunge, from which Peter was rescued by the Rock?

## CHAPTER XLVI

51. Let him hear the same bishop of God saying in the sixth book of the same work:

“Why they did not receive him, the Evangelist himself has recorded, saying: ‘Because his face was set toward Jerusalem.’ But the disciples were eager for him to be received into Samaria. Yet God calls those whom he deigns to call, and makes religious whom he wills” (Book 7, §27, on Luke 9:53).

O the understanding of this man of God, drawn from the very fountain of God’s grace! “God,” he says, “calls those whom he deigns to call, and makes religious whom he wills.”

See whether this is not the prophetic statement, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion,” and the apostolic statement, “So then it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” [Note: Erasmus’s edition reads, “but it is God who shows mercy.”] (Exod. 33:19; Rom. 9:15–16).

As a man of our own time who belongs to him says, “He calls whom he deigns to call, and makes religious whom he wills” [Note: The Casale manuscript reads, “a man of God.”].

Will anyone dare to say that the person who “runs to the Lord, desires to be governed by him, suspends his will upon God’s will, and by continually clinging to him becomes one spirit with him, according to the Apostle” (Pelagius’s words above, §24), is not yet religious?

Yet Pelagius says that this entire great work of the religious person is accomplished “only by freedom of the will.”

By contrast, blessed Ambrose, whom Pelagius himself praises so extravagantly, says: “The Lord God calls whom he deigns to call, and makes religious whom he wills.”

Therefore, in order that a person may run to the Lord, desire to be governed by him, suspend his will upon God’s will, and by continually clinging to him become one spirit with him, according to the Apostle (1 Cor. 6:17), God makes religious whom he wills. And a person does all this only if he is religious.

Therefore, unless God makes it happen that he does this, who does it?

## CHAPTER XLVII

52. But because this question—where the free choice of the will and God’s grace are discussed—is so difficult to distinguish that when free will is defended, God’s grace seems to be denied, while when God’s grace is asserted, free will seems to be taken away, Pelagius can wrap himself in the shadows of this obscurity. He can say that he agrees even with the passages we have cited from Saint Ambrose, and proclaim that he thinks and has always thought the same things, then attempt to explain each passage in such a way that it may be believed to agree with his own opinion.

Therefore, as far as this question of divine grace and assistance is concerned, attend to the three things that he distinguished most plainly: being able, willing, and being [Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “acting.”]; that is, possibility, will, and action.

If, then, he agrees with us that not only possibility exists in a human being—even when he neither wills nor does what is good—but that the will and action themselves also exist, that is, that we may will well and act well, which are not in a person except when he wills well and acts well; if, as I said, he agrees that the will and action themselves are divinely assisted, and assisted in such a way that without that assistance we can neither will nor do anything good; and if he agrees that this is the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, in which he makes us righteous by his righteousness, not ours, so that our true righteousness is the righteousness that comes from him—then, as far as I understand, no controversy about the assistance of God’s grace will remain between us.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

53. As for the reason why Pelagius praised Saint Ambrose in this way—namely, because he found in Ambrose’s writings, in his praise of Zechariah and Elizabeth, that a human being can be without sin in this life—although it must not be denied that all things are possible for God, if this is what God wills, let Pelagius nevertheless consider more carefully how the statement was made.

It was made, as I see it, according to a kind of conduct among human beings that is commendable and praiseworthy, and that no one could justly bring forward as a charge or accusation. Zechariah and his wife are therefore reported to have had this standing before God (Luke 1:6), because they deceived no one through dissimulation, but were known to God’s eyes just as they appeared to human beings.

The statement was not made according to that perfection of righteousness in which we shall live truly and altogether [Note: Several manuscripts read “entirely.” The same variant occurs shortly below, in ch. 49, §54, where the phrase is “entirely perfect righteousness.”] immaculate and perfect. The Apostle Paul too said that, according to the righteousness that comes from the Law, he had been blameless—a Law according to which Zechariah also lived blamelessly.

But the Apostle counted this righteousness as refuse and loss in comparison with the righteousness that we hope for (Phil. 3:6, 8), and which we ought now to hunger and thirst for (Matt. 5:6), so that one day we may be filled with it in its visible reality, whereas now it exists in faith, so long as “the righteous live by faith” (Rom. 1:17).

## CHAPTER XLIX

54. Finally, let Pelagius hear that venerable bishop himself, when he was expounding the prophet Isaiah [Note: This work of Ambrose is not extant. Augustine cites it again in *On Original Sin* 47; *On Marriage and Concupiscence* 1.40; *Against Julian* 1.11 and 2.24; and *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians* 4.30. Ambrose himself mentions the same work in *Exposition of Luke* 2.56, on Luke 11:19.], saying that no one in this world can be without sin.

No one can say that by “in this world” he meant “in the love of this world.” For he was speaking about the Apostle, who said, “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20).

The bishop mentioned above, explaining this meaning, says:

“The Apostle says that he and many others are perfect while still situated in this world; yet, if you look to true perfection, they could not be perfect. For he himself said, ‘Now we see through a mirror in an obscure form, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know just as I am known’ (1 Cor. 13:12).

“Thus they are immaculate in this world, and they will be immaculate in the kingdom of God. Yet if you examine the matter minutely, no one can be immaculate, because no one is without sin.”

Therefore that testimony of Saint Ambrose, which Pelagius uses on behalf of his own opinion, was either spoken according to a certain manner of understanding—one that is indeed plausible but has not been examined minutely—or, if that holy and humble man truly thought Zechariah and Elizabeth possessed the highest and entirely perfect righteousness, to which nothing could be added, then he certainly corrected his statement by examining his opinion more closely.

## CHAPTER L

55. Let Pelagius also attend to the fact that in the very passage from which he took the testimony of Ambrose that pleased him, Ambrose said this as well: “That a person should be immaculate from the beginning is impossible for human nature” [Note: Perhaps the reading should be “that human nature should be immaculate from the beginning.”].

Here the venerable Ambrose plainly testifies that natural possibility—which Pelagius refuses faithfully to regard as corrupted by sin and therefore boastfully exalts—is powerless and weak. He does so certainly against Pelagius’s will, but not against apostolic truth, where we read: “We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3).

This is the nature that was corrupted and condemned through the sin of the first human being, a sin that arose from his free will. Divine grace alone, through the Mediator between God and human beings and through the almighty physician, comes to its aid.

We have already been discussing for a long time the assistance in our justification by which God works all things together for good for those who love him (Rom. 8:28), whom he loved first (1 John 4:19), granting them that he might be loved by them.

From this point onward, therefore, with the Lord’s help, let us begin to set forth also what seems sufficient concerning the sin that entered the world through one human being together with death, and thus passed into all human beings (Rom. 5:12), against those who have more openly broken out into an error opposed to this truth.

# BOOK TWO: ON ORIGINAL SIN

[Col. 0385]

Augustine shows that, in the question of original sin and the Baptism of infants, Pelagius in reality disagrees in no respect with his disciple Coelestius. Coelestius, unwilling to confess original sin and even daring openly to deny it, was condemned first at Carthage and afterward at Rome by episcopal judgments. For they held that this question was not, as the heretics wished, one of those matters in which it is possible to err without endangering the faith; rather, their error attacks the very foundations of the Christian faith.

Augustine then refutes those who argued that the doctrine of original corruption detracted from the goodness of marriage and inflicted an injury upon God himself, the creator of the human being generated through marriage.

## CHAPTER I

1. Now pay careful attention to how cautiously you ought to listen concerning the Baptism of infants to people of this sort. They do not dare openly to deny to that age the washing of regeneration and the remission of sins, lest Christian ears be unable to tolerate it. Yet they persist in defending and maintaining their opinion that bodily generation is not held under the obligation of the sin of the first human being, even though they seem to grant that infants are baptized for the remission of sins.

You yourselves wrote that, with Pelagius present, you had heard him say—he recited to you from the booklet which he also claimed to have sent to Rome—that infants “ought to be baptized with the same words of the Sacrament” as adults.

After those words, who would have thought that any question on this matter needed to be raised against them? Or, when someone did raise one, who would not have seemed utterly slanderous if their explicit words had not been read—words in which they deny that infants bear original sin and insist that all are born without any defect?

## CHAPTER II

2. Coelestius, however, was more uninhibited in this error, to such an extent that, in the episcopal judgment at Carthage, he refused to condemn those who say:

“That Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race; and that infants who are born are in the same state in which Adam was before his transgression.”

And in the city of Rome, in the booklet that he gave to the most blessed Pope Zosimus, he asserted the matter even more explicitly: “No infant is bound by original sin.”

We have transcribed these words from the ecclesiastical acts of Carthage.

## CHAPTER III

3. “Bishop Aurelius said: ‘Let the following items be read.’

“And it was read:

‘That Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race.’

“When this had been read, Coelestius said:

‘I have said that I am uncertain about the transmission of sin, yet in such a way that I agree with anyone to whom God has granted the grace of knowledge, since I have heard different views from men who are certainly presbyters established in the Catholic Church.’

“Deacon Paulinus said:

‘Tell us their names.’

“Coelestius said:

‘The holy presbyter Rufinus [Note: In his *Commonitorium regarding the name of Coelestius*, Mercator writes that a certain Rufinus, a Syrian by nationality, first introduced the question of the transmission of sin to Rome under Pope Anastasius. Some identify him with Rufinus of Aquileia, who is noted by Jerome in his letter to Ctesiphon as having preceded Pelagius in the error concerning *anamartēsia*—sinlessness. Others identify him with another Rufinus, known from Jerome’s sixty-sixth letter, perhaps the same person who rejects the transmission of sin in the book *On the Faith*, which Jacobus Sirmond published under the name of Rufinus, a presbyter of the province of Palestine. Certainly it is scarcely, or not at all, credible that Rufinus of Aquileia went to Rome under Pope Anastasius or stayed there with Pammachius.] of Rome, who stayed with the holy Pammachius. I heard him say that there is no transmission of sin.’

“Deacon Paulinus [Note: This Paulinus, Mercator testifies in his *Commonitorium regarding the name of Coelestius*, was deacon to Ambrose, bishop of Milan, and, at Augustine’s urging, author of his Life. He testifies that he lived in Africa and wrote the Life when John was praetorian prefect—that is, in 412, 413, or 422. The judgment in question was held at Carthage at the beginning of 412, as Augustine’s Letter 173 to Innocent, §§1 and 6, shows. Compare above, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, §23.] said:

‘Is there anyone else?’

“Coelestius said:

‘I have heard many others say it.’

“Deacon Paulinus said:

‘Tell us their names.’

“Coelestius said:

‘Is one priest not enough for you?’”

And after some intervening material, elsewhere:

“Bishop Aurelius said:

‘Let the rest of the booklet be read.’

“And it was read:

‘That infants who are born are in the same state in which Adam was before the transgression,’ up to the end of the shorter booklet inserted above.”

## CHAPTER IV

“Bishop Aurelius said:

‘Have you at some time taught, Coelestius, as the deacon Paulinus said, that infants who are born are in the same state in which Adam was before the transgression?’

“Coelestius said:

‘Let him explain what he meant by “before the transgression.”’

“Deacon Paulinus said:

‘Deny that you taught this. There are only two possibilities: either deny that you taught it, or now condemn it.’

“Coelestius said:

‘I have already said: let him explain how he used the phrase “before the transgression.”’

“Deacon Paulinus said:

‘Deny that you taught those things.’

“Bishop Aurelius said:

‘I ask what I have gathered from this objection [Note: The manuscripts read *hujus* (“of this person”); the printed editions read *hujusmodi* (“of this sort”).]. I say that Adam, established in paradise, was first made, as it is said, incapable of destruction, and afterward, through transgressing the commandment, was made corruptible. Is this what you are saying, brother Paulinus?’

“Deacon Paulinus said:

‘That is so, lord.’

“Bishop Aurelius said:

‘The question the deacon Paulinus wishes to hear answered is certainly whether the state of infants being baptized today is such as Adam’s was before the transgression, or whether they derive from the same origin of sin from which they are born and therefore bear the guilt of transgression.’

“Deacon Paulinus said:

‘Did he teach this, or does he deny it?’

“Coelestius said:

‘I have already spoken about the transmission of sin: I have heard many people established within the Catholic Church destroy the doctrine, and I have also heard others affirm it. Although this is a matter for discussion, it is not heresy. I have always said that infants need Baptism and ought to be baptized. What more does he seek?’”

4. You can see that Coelestius granted Baptism to infants in such a way that he refused to confess that the sin of the first human being—which is washed away by the washing of regeneration—passes into them, although he did not dare to deny it either. Because of this uncertainty, he did not condemn those who say:

“That Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race; and that infants who are born are in the same state in which Adam was before the transgression.”

## CHAPTER V

5. In the booklet that he published at Rome, which was presented there to the ecclesiastical proceedings, he speaks about this matter in such a way that he shows himself to believe what he had said here that he doubted. For these are his words:

“We confess,” he says, “that infants ought to be baptized for the remission of sins, according to the rule of the universal Church and according to the teaching of the Gospel, because the Lord established that the kingdom of heaven can be granted only to the baptized (John 3:5). Since they do not possess this by the powers of nature, it is necessary that it be granted through the freedom of grace [Note: Perhaps “the generosity” or “liberality” of grace.].”

If he had said nothing more on this subject, who would not have believed that he confessed that original sins are also remitted to infants in Baptism, since he said that they ought to be baptized for the remission of sins?

This, then, also explains what you wrote: that Pelagius answered you “that infants are baptized with the same sacramental words as adults.” You were delighted to hear what you desired to hear, yet you preferred to consult us further about his words.

## CHAPTER VI

6. Pay attention, then, to what Coelestius said most openly, and there you will see what Pelagius concealed from you.

Coelestius adds:

“We did not say that infants are to be baptized for the remission of sins in order to appear to affirm sin through transmission. That is far removed from Catholic understanding. Sin is not born with a human being; it is subsequently committed by the human being. It is shown to belong not to nature but to the will.

“It is therefore fitting to confess the matter in this way, lest we appear to create different kinds of Baptism; and it is necessary to guard against this, lest, under cover of the mystery, it be said—against the injury of the Creator—that evil is transmitted to a human being through nature before the human being has committed it.”

Pelagius either feared or was ashamed to disclose this opinion of his to you. His disciple, however, openly professed it before the Apostolic See, without any winding paths of obscurity. He neither feared nor was ashamed to do so.

7. But the bishop of that See, whose mercy was exceedingly great, saw that Coelestius was being driven headlong by such presumption, like a madman. He preferred to restrain him gradually through his own questions and Coelestius’s answers, until he might perhaps recover his senses, rather than strike him with a stern sentence and drive him into the precipice toward which he already seemed to be leaning.

That is why I did not say, “He had openly fallen,” but rather, “He seemed to be leaning”—because earlier in the same booklet, before speaking about such questions, he had said:

“If perhaps some error of ignorance has slipped into anyone, let it be corrected by your judgment.”

## CHAPTER VII

8. Holding to this preliminary statement of his, the venerable Pope Zosimus dealt with the man whom the wind of false doctrine had inflated [Col. 0389], urging him to condemn the matters that had been brought against him by the deacon Paulinus and to assent to the letters of the Apostolic See that had come from his predecessor of blessed memory.

He refused to condemn the charges brought by the deacon. But he did not dare to resist the letters of blessed Pope Innocent. Rather, “he promised that he would condemn everything condemned by that See.” And so, like a madman, he was treated gently so that he might come to rest; yet he was not thought to have been released from the bonds of excommunication.

Nevertheless, a period of two months was allowed to pass while a reply was being sent from Africa, and during that time he was given an opportunity to recover his senses through a certain medicinal leniency in the sentence. For if, laying aside the vanity of his obstinacy, he had wished to attend to what he had promised, and had carefully read the same letters to which he had answered that he would consent, he would have been healed.

But after the reply had been sent from the African council of bishops, read everything that followed and led with complete justice to the sentence pronounced against him, since we have transmitted everything.

## CHAPTER VIII
9. Hence Pelagius too, if he considers himself and his writings without deceit, does not rightly say that he ought not to have been held by the same judgment. For he deceived the Palestinian judgment; therefore he seems to have been acquitted there. But he could not deceive the Roman Church—where you know he was very well known—completely, although he did make some attempt to do so [Note: [Col. 0389] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read *utrumque* (“both”).]. But, as I have said, he achieved nothing whatever. For the most blessed Pope Zosimus recalled what his predecessor, worthy of imitation, had thought about those proceedings. He also considered what the faith of the Romans, celebrated in the Lord (Rom. I, 8), thought of him—those Romans whose united zeal he saw burning harmoniously in defense of Catholic truth against his error. He had lived among them for a long time, and his doctrines could not remain hidden from them; they knew him to be a disciple of Coelestius and could therefore give the most faithful and decisive testimony about this matter.

What, then, the holy Pope Innocent judged concerning the proceedings of the Palestinian synod, by which Pelagius boasts that he was acquitted—you may read it in the letter he wrote back to us, and it was also recalled when [Note: [Col. 0389] Am. and Er. read *eum* (“him”). Lov. and the manuscripts better read *cum* (“when”), so that Innocent’s own judgment on the Palestinian proceedings is understood to be recalled in the African synod’s letter to Zosimus. These letters have hitherto been sought in vain.] the African synod replied to the venerable Pope Zosimus. We sent this reply to Your Charity together with the other instructions; nevertheless, it seems that it should not be passed over in this work either.

CHAPTER IX

10. When we five bishops wrote him a letter [Note: [Col. 0389] Letter 177 among Augustine’s letters, no. 2.], we had mentioned those Palestinian proceedings, whose reputation had already reached us. We said that ecclesiastical proceedings had taken place in the East, where he lived, by which he was thought to have been acquitted. Among other things he replied:

“Since,” he said, “there are in those proceedings certain matters which, when brought against him, he partly suppressed by avoiding them and partly confused in complete obscurity by turning many words back upon himself; and since he cleared himself of some charges by a method that, for the moment, could appear more false than true, denying some and twisting others through a false interpretation—would that, as is more greatly to be desired, he might now turn from that error of his to the true way of the Catholic faith, and desire and wish to be cleared, considering the daily grace and recognizing the help of God, so that he might truly appear, and be approved by all, to have been corrected by manifest reason—not by the judgment of the proceedings, but by his heart’s conversion to the Catholic faith. Hence we can neither approve nor condemn their judgment, since we do not know whether the proceedings are true; or, if they are true, it is clear that he evaded rather than cleared himself in the fullness of truth” [Note: [Col. 0390] Letter of Innocent among Augustine’s letters, 183, §§3–4.].

You plainly see in these words how the most blessed Pope Innocent does not seem to speak as though of an unknown person. You see what judgment he pronounced concerning Pelagius’s acquittal. You see what his successor, the holy Pope Zosimus, ought to have recalled—and did recall—in order to confirm without hesitation the judgment of his predecessor concerning him.

CHAPTER X

11. Now pay close attention to how it can be shown that Pelagius deceived the Palestinian judges, to say nothing of other matters, in this very question of the baptism of infants. Otherwise someone might accuse us—or merely suspect—that, in what we have said, we concealed from you the position in which Coelestius was more outspoken, even though Pelagius himself holds the same view, rather than that we have grasped anything certain.

It has already become sufficiently clear above why Coelestius refused to condemn the statement that “Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone, and not the human race; and that infants who are born are in the condition in which Adam was before the transgression.” He saw that, if he condemned these propositions, he would affirm that sin passed from Adam into infants.

When these propositions were brought against Pelagius, on the ground that he too held them together with Coelestius, he condemned them without any qualification. Although I know that you have read this, since this is not written for you alone, let the reader not be reluctant to return to the proceedings themselves—or, if he does not possess them, to seek them out even with some effort. We transcribe the actual words below.

CHAPTER XI

12. “The synod said: Since Pelagius has now anathematized [Note: [Col. 0390] In *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 16, *anathematizavit* (“has anathematized”). Perhaps one should read *cum anathematizaverit* (“since he has anathematized”).] the foolish and uncertain statement, rightly responding that a human being can, with God’s help and grace, be ἀναμάρτητον—that is, without sin—let him also respond to the other chapters.

“Another chapter in the teaching of Coelestius, a disciple of Pelagius, drawn from matters heard and reported at Carthage by the holy Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, together with the other bishops:

“Adam was created mortal, and whether he sinned or did not sin, he would have died.

“Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone, and not the human race.

“The law leads to the kingdom in the same way as the Gospel.

“Before Christ’s coming there were human beings without sin.

“Newborn infants are in the condition in which Adam was before the transgression.

“Neither through Adam’s death or transgression does the entire human race die, nor through Christ’s resurrection does the entire human race rise again.

“The holy bishop Augustine, responding in Sicily to his disciples through Hilary concerning the following chapters, wrote a book [Note: [Col. 0391] Letter 157, to Hilary.] containing these statements:

“‘A human being can be without sin, if he wishes.’

“‘Infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life.’

“‘Baptized rich people, unless they renounce everything, are not credited with whatever good they may appear to do, nor can they possess the kingdom of God.’

“Pelagius said: ‘Concerning the possibility of a human being’s being without sin, this has already been stated above. But concerning the claim that there were human beings without sin before the Lord’s coming, we too say that, before Christ’s coming, certain people lived holily and justly, according to the tradition of the holy Scriptures. As for the rest, and in accordance with their own testimony, these are not propositions for which I ought to give satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0391] In the same book, no. 24: “But the rest, according to their own testimony, were not stated by me, and I ought not to give satisfaction for them.” The same words are repeated there, no. 57.]. Nevertheless, in order to satisfy the holy synod, I anathematize those who hold or have ever held these views.’”

CHAPTER XII

13. Behold: to omit other matters, you see that Pelagius anathematized those who hold “that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone, and not the human race, and that infants who are born are in the condition in which Adam was before the transgression.” What else, then, could the judging bishops understand him to be confessing here except that sin passes from Adam into infants?

Coelestius refused to confess this; therefore he refused to condemn these propositions, whereas Pelagius condemned them. Accordingly, if I show that Pelagius himself thinks nothing else about infants than that they are born without the contagion of any fault whatsoever, what difference will there be between him and Coelestius in this question, except that one was more outspoken and the other more concealed; one more stubborn and the other more deceitful—or, certainly, one more forthright and the other more crafty?

Coelestius was unwilling to condemn in the Church of Carthage what he later confessed that he held in Rome, and he declared himself ready to be corrected if error had crept into him as into a human being. Pelagius, however, condemned that doctrine as contrary to the truth lest he himself be condemned by the Catholic judges, and afterward reserved it for his own defense—either condemning it deceitfully or interpreting it craftily.

CHAPTER XIII

14. But I see that I am now most justly required not to delay demonstrating whether Pelagius himself holds the same view as Coelestius. In the first book of his more recent work, which he wrote in defense of free will and which he mentioned in the letter he sent to Rome, he says:

“Every good and evil by which we are either praiseworthy or blameworthy does not arise with us but is performed by us. For we are born capable of either, not full of either; and just as we are begotten without virtue, so we are begotten without vice. Before the action of one’s own will, the only thing in a human being is what God created.”

You surely see what doctrine is contained in these words of Pelagius: the doctrine held by both men, that infants are born without any contagion of fault from Adam.

It is therefore not surprising that Coelestius refused to condemn those who say “that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone, and not the human race, and that infants who are born are in the condition in which Adam was before the transgression.” But it is greatly surprising with what boldness Pelagius condemned these propositions.

For if, as he says, “evil does not arise with us, we are begotten without vice, and before the action of one’s own will the only thing in a human being is what God created,” then Adam’s sin certainly harmed Adam alone, because it made no passage into his offspring. For sin is not something other than evil; nor is sin something other than vice; nor did God create sin.

Yet Pelagius says: “Evil does not arise with us; we are begotten without vice; and the only thing in those being born is what God created.” Accordingly, since he considers it entirely true, according to his own view, that “Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone, and not the human race,” why did Pelagius condemn this except in order to deceive the Catholic judges?

The same may also be said of the other proposition: “If evil does not arise with us, and we are begotten without vice, and the only thing in the human being at birth is what God created,” then undoubtedly “infants who are born are in the condition in which Adam was before the transgression”—a condition in which there was no evil or vice, and in which there was only what God had created.

And yet Pelagius anathematized those “who hold or have ever held that infants newly born are in the condition in which Adam was before the transgression”—that is, without any evil, without any vice, possessing only what God created. Why, then, did Pelagius condemn this too, except in order that the Catholic synod might be deceived and the new heretic not be condemned?

CHAPTER XIV

15. You know what follows, and I [Note: [Col. 0392] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions read *ergo* (“therefore”).] also included it in the book that I wrote to our venerable elder Aurelius concerning the proceedings of the Palestinian synod. I rejoiced that the whole question had been settled by that response of Pelagius, and he seemed to me to have confessed most openly that there is original sin in infants by anathematizing those who believed that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race, and who thought that infants were in the condition in which that first man was before the transgression.

But afterward, when I had read his four books, from the first of which I transcribed the words quoted above, and had found that he still held an opinion about infants contrary to the Catholic faith, I began to wonder even more [Note: [Col. 0392] Am., Er., and the manuscripts read *prius* (“earlier”).] at so shameless a falsehood in an ecclesiastical judgment concerning so great a question.

For if he had already written those same books, how could he say that he anathematized those who had ever held such views? But if he composed that work afterward [Note: [Col. 0392] Perhaps, “undertook” or “labored over.”], how could he have anathematized those who hold such views?

Unless, perhaps, he should absurdly say that he condemned those who had once held and who now hold such views, but that, concerning the future—that is, concerning those who were going to continue holding them—he could prejudice neither himself nor others; and that therefore he had not lied, because he was afterward discovered to hold those views.

But he does not say this—not only because it is absurd, but because it cannot be true. For in those same books he speaks against the passage of sin from Adam into infants, while boasting of the proceedings of the Palestinian synod, where he was thought to have truly condemned those who hold such views and to have secured his acquittal by deception.

CHAPTER XV

16. What relevance does it have to the matter now before us that he replies to his disciples, “He condemned those propositions because he too says that the first sin harmed not only the first man but also the human race—not by propagation, but by example”? That is, not because those who were propagated from Adam drew some fault from him, but because all who sinned afterward imitated him as the first sinner.

Or what relevance does it have that he says, “Infants are not in the condition in which Adam was before the transgression because they are not yet able to receive a command, whereas Adam could; nor do they yet use the freedom of rational will, whereas, if he had not used it, no command would have been given to him”?

What relevance does this have, when by interpreting the words brought against him in this way he thinks he has rightly condemned the proposition that “Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone, and not the human race, and that infants who are born are in the condition in which Adam was before the sin,” while, after condemning these propositions, he nevertheless does not deceitfully hold what is found in the little works he later wrote: “that infants are born without any evil or any vice, and that the only thing in them is what God created”—not the wound inflicted by the enemy?

CHAPTER XVI

17. By saying these things and interpreting in another way the words brought against him for another purpose, does he thereby demonstrate that he did not deceive the judges? He certainly does not accomplish this. The more craftily he explains these matters, the more covertly he deceived them.

For when the Catholic bishops heard a man anathematizing those who say, “Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone, and not the human race,” they thought that he held nothing other than what the Catholic Church is accustomed to proclaim. Hence the Church truly baptizes infants for the remission of sins—not sins they committed by imitation, because of the example of the first sinner, but sins they drew from him by being born, because of the fault of origin.

And when they heard him anathematizing those who say that infants who are born are in the condition in which Adam was before the transgression, they thought that he meant nothing other than those who believe that infants have drawn no sin from Adam and, accordingly, are in the condition in which Adam was before the sin.

For this was what was brought against him [Note: [Col. 0393] The Vatican manuscript reads: “This was what was brought against him there.”], not something else that was at issue. Therefore, when Pelagius explains it in such a way as to say that infants are not in the condition in which Adam was before the sin because they are not yet equal to him in firmness of mind or body—not because any guilt of propagation has passed into them—let this be said in reply:

“When those propositions were brought against you for condemnation [Note: [Col. 0393] Two manuscripts read *damnata* (“condemned”); likewise a little later, “you who held condemned propositions.”], the Catholic bishops did not understand them in this way. Therefore, when you condemned them, they believed you to be Catholic. What they thought you held had to be acquitted; what you actually held had to be condemned.

“You, therefore, were not acquitted, since you held propositions that had to be condemned. Rather, that which you ought to have held was acquitted. In order that you might be thought acquitted, you were believed to hold praiseworthy doctrines, while the judges did not understand that you were concealing those that had to be condemned.

“You were rightly judged a companion of Coelestius, whose manifest partner you show yourself to be. And although you concealed your books during the judgment, you published them after the judgment.”

CHAPTER XVII

18. Since these things are so, you surely perceive that the episcopal councils, the Apostolic See, the whole Roman Church, and the Roman Empire—which by God’s favor is Christian—were most rightly moved against the authors of so wicked an error [Note: [Col. 0394] Possidius, *Life of Augustine*, chapter 18: “When the most pious emperor Honorius heard and followed this judgment, which had been pronounced by the Catholic Church of God against them, he also decreed by his laws that they should be condemned and counted among the heretics.” The laws of Honorius are given below, in the second part of the Appendix.], until they should recover from the snares of the devil.

For who knows whether God might perhaps grant them repentance for recognizing, confessing, and even proclaiming the truth, and for truly condemning condemnable falsehood? However these men may wish to regard themselves, we cannot doubt that the Lord’s mercy has provided for many who followed them because they saw them associated with Catholic communion.

19. Now pay careful attention to how Pelagius attempted to creep in and deceive even the episcopal judgment of the Apostolic See in this very question of the baptism of infants.

In the letter he sent to Rome to Pope Innocent of blessed memory—whom they did not find alive, and which was therefore delivered to the holy Pope Zosimus and sent from there to us—Pelagius says that “people defame him by saying that he denies the sacrament of Baptism to infants and promises the kingdom of heaven to some without Christ’s redemption.”

But these charges are not brought against them in the way he presented them. For they do not deny the sacrament of Baptism to infants, nor do they promise the kingdom of heaven to anyone without Christ’s redemption. Thus, in explaining the grounds on which he complained of being defamed, he framed the issue in such a way that he could easily answer the charge brought against him while preserving his own doctrine.

CHAPTER XVIII

The charge brought against them is that they refuse to confess that unbaptized infants are subject to the condemnation of the first man and that original sin has passed into them, to be cleansed through regeneration. They insist that infants should be baptized solely in order to receive the kingdom of heaven—as though, apart from the kingdom of heaven, those who cannot possess eternal life without participation in the body and blood of the Lord could have anything other than eternal death.

This is what is charged against them concerning the baptism of infants—not what he presented, in such a way that he could answer the charge as though it were an objection to his own formulation, in accordance with his doctrines.

20. Finally, observe how he answers, and see how he prepares hiding places for falsehood through ambiguity, casting darkness over the truth. Thus, when we first read these words, we almost rejoiced that they were sound or had been corrected.

His fuller discussions in his books, however, where he is compelled to reveal himself no matter how much he conceals himself, made us suspicious of these statements as well. When we examined them more attentively, we found their ambiguity.

After saying that he had “never heard even an impious heretic say this” concerning infants, he added:

“For who is so ignorant of evangelical teaching that he would not only attempt to affirm this, but could even lightly say or think it? And who is so impious as to wish infants to be excluded from the kingdom of heaven, while he forbids them to be baptized and reborn in Christ?” [Note: [Col. 0395] The printed editions read *putat* (“thinks”). The manuscripts have *vetat* (“forbids”), which is adopted here.]

CHAPTER XIX

21. He says these things in vain; they do not clear him. They themselves have never denied that infants cannot enter the kingdom of heaven without Baptism. That is not the issue. The issue concerns the cleansing of original sin in infants. Let him clear himself on that point—he who does not wish to admit that the laver of regeneration in infants contains something that it cleanses.

Let us therefore attend to the rest of what he is going to say. After introducing the Gospel testimony that no one can enter the kingdom of heaven unless he is born again of water and the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0395] The printed editions read “water and the Holy Spirit”; *Holy* is absent from the manuscripts.] (John III, 5)—a matter about which, as we said, no question is raised among them—he continued:

“Who is so impious as to forbid a child of whatever age the common redemption of the human race?”

This too is ambiguous: what kind of redemption does he mean? Is it redemption from evil to good, or from good to something better? For Coelestius too, in his booklet at Carthage, confessed the redemption of infants, and yet refused to confess that sin had passed from Adam into them.

CHAPTER XX

22. But observe what Pelagius adds next:

“And forbid him who was born for an uncertain life to be reborn for perpetual and certain life?”

That is: Who is so impious as to forbid someone born for an uncertain life to be reborn for perpetual and certain life?

When we first read these words, we believed that by “uncertain life” he meant this temporal life, although it seemed to us that he ought rather to have called it mortal than uncertain, since it ends in certain death. Nevertheless, as long as it is lived, since it is undoubtedly uncertain at every moment, we thought that he meant nothing other than this mortal life, which he preferred to call uncertain.

Accordingly, although he plainly refused to confess that infants who depart from this life without the sacrament of Baptism suffer eternal death, our concern about him was for a time comforted by what seemed a sound line of reasoning. We said:

“If perpetual life, as he seems to confess, can belong only to those who have been baptized, then those who die unbaptized will certainly be overtaken by perpetual death. This could not justly happen to those who committed no sins in this life, unless there were original sin.”

CHAPTER XXI

23. But afterward some brothers reminded us that Pelagius might have been able to say this because, concerning this question, he was reportedly accustomed to answer those who asked him in the following way:

“I know where infants who die without Baptism do not go; where they go, I do not know” [Col. 0396]—that is, he said that he knew they did not go to the kingdom of heaven, but that he did not know where they went. He either said or says this [Note: [Col. 0396] This addition, “or says,” is not superfluous, as the scholars of Louvain thought, and should not be deleted. It indicates that Pelagius may perhaps not yet have departed from his error.], because he did not dare to say that they go to eternal death—those whom he believed to have committed no evil here and whom he refused to admit had drawn original sin.

Thus these words of his, sent to Rome as a major proof of his acquittal, are so ambiguous that they can provide hiding places for his doctrine, from which heretical meaning may spring out to lie in wait—when no one is present who can answer, as though a vulnerable person were found in solitude.

24. But in the book of his Faith [Note: [Col. 0396] It is presented below, in the second part of the Appendix.], which he sent to the same Pope Innocent together with the letter he had written to him, he exposed himself while attempting to conceal himself much more clearly. He said:

“We hold one Baptism, which we say is celebrated in infants with the same words of the sacrament as in adults.”

He did not at least say, “with the same sacrament.” If he had said that, the statement would still have been ambiguous. But he said, “with the same words of the sacrament,” as though the remission of sins were pronounced to infants by the sound of words and not effected in them by the reality itself.

For a time he seemed to be saying something compatible with the Catholic faith. But he was unable to deceive that See to the end.

After the replies of the African council—into whose province that deadly doctrine had indeed crept, although it had not occupied or penetrated it so broadly and deeply—other statements of his also came to light in the city of Rome, where he had lived for a very long time and had previously engaged in these discussions and disputes. Through the care of faithful brothers, these statements were brought forward, and Pope Zosimus appended them to his letter, which he composed for circulation throughout the Catholic world, as matters deserving execration, as you may read.

There Pelagius, as though expounding the Apostle Paul’s Letter to the Romans, argues and says:

“If Adam’s sin harmed even those who do not sin, then Christ’s righteousness also benefits even those who do not believe.”

And other statements of this kind, all of which, with the Lord’s help, have been refuted and dismantled in the books we wrote concerning the baptism of infants (Book 3, §§5–6).

In those purported expositions he did not dare to raise these objections in his own person. But he said such things where he was widely known and could not conceal what he thought and said. In the books of which I mentioned something above from the first [above, §14], he argues openly and without disguise, with all the force of disputation he can muster, that human nature in infants is in no way corrupted through propagation. By arrogating salvation to that nature, he begrudges it a Savior [Note: [Col. 0396] Erasmus reads *salvatori* (“the Savior”), which is less correct.].

CHAPTER XXII

25. Since these things are so, and since it is now established that there arose a deadly and heretical error—a doctrine which, with the Lord’s help, the Church is now avoiding more openly—what remains but that these two men, Pelagius and Coelestius, should either be brought to repentance or, if they refuse, be altogether condemned?

They are reported or shown to be the authors of this perversity; or, if they are not its authors but learned it from others, they are nevertheless celebrated as its advocates and teachers, through whom it would creep and grow more widely—by their words, their writings, the appropriate evidence, and the reputation arising and spreading from all these things.

What remains, then, except that every Catholic, according to the strength he receives from the Lord, should rebuke this pestilence and vigilantly resist it? Thus, when the truth is defended under the necessity of answering, without a spirit of contentiousness, the unlearned may be instructed, and what the enemy contrived for destruction may be turned to the Church’s benefit, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “There must also be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest among you” (I Cor. XI, 19).

CHAPTER XXIII

26. Therefore, after the many things we have been able to discuss in writing against this error, which is hostile to the grace of God that He bestows through Jesus Christ our Lord upon the small and the great, we must now examine what they assert in their effort to evade cleverly the disrepute of heresy:

“That this is a question outside the danger of faith.”

They say this so that, if they are convicted of having deviated in this matter, they may appear to have erred not criminally but, as it were, civilly.

Thus Coelestius spoke at Carthage in the ecclesiastical proceedings:

“I have already spoken,” he said, “about the transmission of sin, because I have heard many people within the Catholic Church destroy it, and others affirm it, although this is a matter of inquiry, not of heresy. I have always said that infants need Baptism and ought to be baptized. What else does he seek?”

He said this as though he wished to indicate that the matter should then be judged heresy if he denied that infants ought to be baptized. But now, since he admits that they should be baptized—even if he does not give as the reason for their Baptism the reason that the truth supplies, but one that has nothing to do with the faith—he does not think that he is in error [Note: [Col. 0397] Perhaps, “that he is not erring criminally”; *arbitratur* (“he thinks”) would then be deleted.], and therefore does not think that he should be judged a heretic. [Note: [Col. 0397] Here begins chapter 33 in Erasmus and the Erfurt edition.]

Likewise, in the booklet he presented at Rome, after explaining his faith—from the Trinity of one divinity to the future resurrection of the dead, about which no one had questioned him and concerning which no issue had been raised, to the extent that he wished to speak—when his discourse reached the matter at hand, he said:

“But if questions have arisen outside the faith, concerning which there is disagreement among many, I have not established them by a definitive authority as the author of any doctrine. Rather, I offer for examination by your Apostolate those things which I have received from the fountain of the Prophets and Apostles, so that, if perhaps some error of ignorance has crept into a human being [Note: [Col. 0397] The printed editions read *obrepserit* (“has crept in”). The manuscripts have *obrepsit*, adopted here.], it may be corrected by your judgment” [Note: [Col. 0397] Erasmus and the Erfurt edition read, “corrected by our knowledge.” This is erroneous, as is clear from §7 below, where those same editions, together with others, read “corrected by your judgment.”].

Clearly, by prefacing his statement in this way, he intended that, if any error appeared in him, he would seem to have erred not in matters of faith but in questions outside the faith. In such a case, although the error ought to be corrected, it would not be corrected as heresy; and once corrected, he would be said to have erred in such a way that he would nevertheless not be judged a heretic [Note: [Col. 0397] The Casalensis and Cygirannensis manuscripts read, “and whoever has not been corrected.”].

27. But this opinion deceives him greatly. These questions, which he thinks are outside the faith, are very different from those in which, while preserving the faith by which we are Christians, either what is true is unknown and a definitive judgment is suspended, or something is conjectured through human and weak suspicion otherwise than it actually is.

For example, one may ask what or where the paradise was in which God placed the human being whom He formed from dust, while Christian faith does not doubt that paradise existed. Or one may ask where Elijah or Enoch now is—whether there or somewhere else—although we do not doubt that they live in the bodies in which they were born.

One may ask whether the Apostle was taken up into the third heaven in the body or outside the body, although it is an impudent inquiry on the part of those who wish to know what the one to whom this was granted testifies that he himself did not know, while certainly preserving the faith (II Cor. XII, 2).

One may ask how many heavens there are, into the third of which he recalls having been taken. Or one may ask whether the elements of this visible world are four or more; what causes the sun or moon to be eclipsed in those eclipses whose times astrologers are accustomed to predict by a definite reckoning of periods; why the people of ancient times lived so long, as Holy Scripture testifies; and whether, in proportion to their longer lifespan, they began to beget children at a later puberty.

One may ask where Methuselah could have lived, since he was not in the ark and, according to the reckoning of years found in many Greek and Latin manuscripts, appears to have survived the Flood; or whether we should instead believe the fewer manuscripts—very rare ones—in which the number of his years is recorded in such a way that it is shown that he died before the Flood.

Who does not perceive that, in these and countless similar questions—whether they concern the most obscure works of God or the hidden recesses of Scripture, which are difficult to encompass and define within any single category—many things may be unknown while the Christian faith remains intact, and that one may err in some matters without the crime of holding a heretical doctrine?

CHAPTER XXIV

28. But in the case of the two human beings through one of whom we were sold under sin and through the other redeemed from sins; through one of whom we were cast down into death and through the other freed for life; [Note: [Col. 0398] Am., Er., and the manuscripts read *quoniam ille* (“because that one”).] one of whom destroyed us in himself by doing his own will rather than the will of Him by whom he was made, while the other saved us in himself by doing not his own will but the will of Him by whom he was sent (John IV, 34; V, 30)—in the case, then, of these two human beings, the Christian faith is properly established.

“For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (I Tim. II, 5). “For there is no other name under heaven given among human beings by which it is necessary for us to be saved” (Acts IV, 12). And God “has established faith for all” [Note: [Col. 0398] The printed editions read *hominibus* (“human beings”); corrected from the manuscripts.] in him, raising him from the dead (Acts XVII, 31).

Therefore, without this faith—that is, without faith in the one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus; without faith, I say, in his resurrection, which God established for all, and which certainly cannot truly be believed without his incarnation and death—without faith, then, in Christ’s incarnation, death, and resurrection, Christian truth does not doubt that even the righteous of ancient times could not be cleansed from sins and justified by God’s grace in order to be righteous.

This applies both to those righteous people whom Holy Scripture mentions and to those whom it does not mention but who nevertheless must be believed to have existed: whether before the Flood, or from that time until the giving of the law, or during the time of the law—not only among the children of Israel, as were the Prophets, but also outside that people, as was Job.

Their hearts too were cleansed by faith in the same mediator, and love was poured into them through the Holy Spirit (Rom. V, 5), who “breathes where he wills” (John III, 8), not following merits but also creating the merits themselves. For God’s grace would in no way be grace unless it were wholly gratuitous.

29. Although death reigned from Adam to Moses (Rom. V, 14), because even the law given through Moses could not conquer it—for the law was not given in such a way that it could give life (Gal. III, 21)—it was nevertheless given to reveal those who were dead and needed grace in order to be made alive: those cast down not only by the propagation and domination of sin, but also convicted by the transgression added through the law itself.
