This was not so that anyone who understood this even then in God’s mercy would perish, but so that, destined through the reign of death for punishment and exposed even to himself through transgression of the law [Note: [Col. 0399] The Vatican manuscript reads: “destined for eternal punishment, he himself also exposed to himself.”], he might seek God’s help, so that where sin abounded, grace might abound even more (Rom. V, 20)—the grace that alone frees us from this body of death (Rom. VII, 24–25).

CHAPTER XXV
Although, then, even the law given through Moses could not take away from any human being the reign of death, there were nevertheless men of God in the time of the law—not under the law, which terrifies, convicts, and punishes, but under grace, which delights, heals, and liberates. There were those who said, “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb”; and, “There is no peace in my bones because of my sins” (Ps. 37:4); and, “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within my inward parts”; and, “Strengthen me with your principal Spirit”; and, “Do not take your Holy Spirit from me” (Ps. 50:7, 12, 14, 13). There were those who said, “I believed, and therefore I spoke” (Ps. 115:1). For they too were cleansed by the same faith by which we are cleansed. Hence the Apostle also says, “But having the same spirit of faith, according to what is written, ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke,’ we too believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Cor. 4:13).

From that same faith it was said, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and bear a son; and they shall call his name Emmanuel,” which is interpreted, “God with us” (Isa. 7:14; Matt. 1:23). From that same faith it was said of him, “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, rejoiced like a giant to run his course; his going forth is from the summit of heaven [Col. 0399], and his circuit reaches even to the summit of heaven; and there is no one who can hide from his heat” (Ps. 18:6–7). **[Note: The printed editions read “heaven” (coelo); the manuscripts, “of heaven” (coeli).]** By that same faith it was said to him, “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the scepter of righteousness is the scepter of your kingdom. You have loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 45:7–8). By the same spirit of faith they saw these things as future, by which they are believed by us as having already occurred. [Col. 0400] For those who were able to prophesy these things to us in faithful love were surely themselves not excluded from sharing in them.

And what else is the meaning of the Apostle Peter’s words, “Why do you test God by placing upon the neck of the disciples a yoke which neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we shall be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they too were” (Acts 15:10–11), unless it is that they too were saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, not through the law of Moses, through which there was made not healing but knowledge of sin? “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, attested by the Law and the Prophets” (Rom. 3:20–21). If, then, it has now been manifested, it existed even then, but was hidden. Its concealment was signified by the veil of the temple, which was torn at the death of Christ in order to signify its revelation (Matt. 27:51).

Therefore, even then this grace of the one Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, existed among the people of God. But it was present hidden, like rain in a fleece, which God separates for his inheritance—not as something owed, but as something freely bestowed (Ps. 68:9). Now, however, as though that fleece had been dried out—that is, with the Jewish people rejected—it is seen openly among all the nations, like rain spread across the threshing floor (Judg. 6:36–40).

## CHAPTER XXVI

**30.** Let us not, then, as Pelagius and his disciples do, divide the ages by saying: first, righteous people lived according to nature; next, under the law; and third, under grace. “According to nature,” they say, means from Adam onward through that very long period during which the law had not yet been given. At that time, they claim, the Creator was known under the guidance of reason, and the manner in which one ought to live was inscribed in their hearts—not by the law of the letter, but by nature.

But when morals had become corrupted, they say, and nature, already disfigured, began to be insufficient, the law was added to it so that, like the moon, it might have its former brightness restored after being worn down by rust. But when, as they argue, an excessive habit of sinning prevailed—one that the law was too weak to heal—Christ came **[Note: The printed editions read “is too weak” (valet); the manuscripts, “was too weak” (valeret).]** and, as a physician, himself came to the aid of this almost hopeless disease, not through disciples but personally.

**31.** By arguing in this way, they attempt to exclude the ancient righteous from the grace of the Mediator, as though the human being Christ Jesus had not been Mediator between God and those people, because he was not yet human when those righteous people lived, not yet having taken flesh from the Virgin’s womb.

If this were so, the Apostle would certainly not say: “By a human being came death, and by a human being the resurrection of the dead; for as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:21–22). According to their empty talk, those ancient righteous people, with nature sufficient for themselves, needed neither the human Mediator Christ, through whom they might be reconciled to God, nor will they be made alive in him, since they are shown not to belong to his body and members according to that by which he became human for the sake of human beings.

But if, as Truth speaks through his Apostles, “as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive,” because “by that human being came death, and by this human being the resurrection of the dead”—what Christian would dare to doubt that even those righteous people who pleased God in more recent periods of the human race **[Note: Perhaps “more remote” (remotioribus).]** [Col. 0401] will come to the resurrection of eternal life and not to eternal death, because they will be made alive in Christ; that they will be made alive in Christ because they belong to Christ’s body; that they belong to Christ’s body because Christ is also their head (1 Cor. 11:3); and that Christ is also their head because there is one Mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus?

This would not have been true of them unless they had believed, through his grace, in his resurrection. And how could this have happened if they had not known that he would come in the flesh, and had not lived justly and devoutly according to this faith? For if Christ’s incarnation did not benefit them because it had not yet happened, neither does Christ’s judgment of the living and the dead benefit us, because it has not yet happened. But if by faith in this judgment, which has not yet happened but is still future, we shall stand at Christ’s right hand, then surely they are members of Christ through faith in his incarnation, which at that time had not yet happened but was still future.

## CHAPTER XXVII

**32.** Nor should it be thought that the ancient righteous benefited only from Christ’s divinity, which always existed, and not also from knowledge of his humanity, which did not yet exist. For when the Lord Jesus said, “Abraham desired to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced,” if he wished his “day” to be understood as his time, he certainly bore witness that Abraham had been imbued with faith in his incarnation.

According to this incarnation, he has a temporal existence; but his divinity transcends all time, because through it all times were made. Even if someone should think that “day” ought to be understood as the eternal day, which no tomorrow ends and no yesterday precedes—that is, as eternity, in which he is coeternal with the Father—how could Abraham truly have desired it unless he knew the future mortality of the one whose eternity he sought?

Or if someone restricts the meaning of these words so as to say that nothing should be understood in the Lord’s statement, “He sought my day,” except, “He sought me, who am the enduring day, the unfailing light”—as when we speak of the Son’s life, of which the Gospel says, “So he gave the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26), not understanding the Son as one thing and his life as another, but understanding the Son himself to be life, since he said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6), and since it is said of him, “He is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20)—so that Abraham desired to see his divinity, equal to the Father, without having foreknown his incarnation, just as certain philosophers also sought him without having learned anything about his flesh: would anyone also rightly understand Abraham’s command that his servant place his hand under Abraham’s thigh and swear by the God of heaven (Gen. 24:2–3) in any other way than that Abraham knew from which thigh the God of heaven would come, taking flesh?

## CHAPTER XXVIII

**33.** When Melchizedek blessed Abraham, he also offered a testimony concerning this flesh and blood, well known to Christian believers (Gen. 14:18–20). Thus, long afterward, the Psalms would say of Christ what had not yet happened but was still future, while the one faith of the fathers—which is also ours—[Col. 0402] sang the same words: “You are a priest for ever, according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 110:4).

To those who find death in Adam, Christ is beneficial because he is the Mediator to life. He is not Mediator because he is equal to the Father. For by that equality he is as far from us as the Father is; and how can there be mediation where the very same distance exists? Therefore the Apostle does not say, “One Mediator of God and human beings, Christ Jesus,” but “the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5).

He is Mediator, then, insofar as he is human: lower than the Father insofar as he is nearer to us; higher than us insofar as he is nearer to the Father. This is expressed more clearly as follows: lower than the Father because he was in the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7); higher than us because he was without the stain of sin.

## CHAPTER XXIX

**34.** Therefore, whoever maintains that human nature, at any stage, does not need the second Adam as physician because it was not corrupted in the first Adam is shown to be an enemy of God’s grace—not in some question in which one may doubt or err without endangering the faith, but in the very rule of faith by which we are Christians.

What, then, is the meaning of their praising human nature as though it had once been corrupted by lesser moral evils, while they do not consider that people were then submerged under sins so great and intolerable that, except for one man of God and his wife, their three sons and the same number of daughters-in-law, the whole world was destroyed by the flood through God’s just judgment, just as the small territory of Sodom was later destroyed by fire (Gen. 7 and 19)?

From the time, then, when through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned (Rom. 5:12), the whole mass became the possession of the one who destroys it. Therefore no one—absolutely no one—has been, is, or will be freed from it except by the grace of the Redeemer.

## CHAPTER XXX

**35.** Scripture does not state whether, before Abraham, righteous people or their children were marked by some bodily and visible sacrament. Abraham himself, however, received the sign of circumcision, the seal of the righteousness of faith (Rom. 4:11). He received it in such a way that afterward he was commanded to circumcise all the male children of his household, those only recently born from their mothers’ wombs, on the eighth day of their birth, so that even those who could not yet believe with the heart unto righteousness might nevertheless receive the seal of the righteousness of faith.

This was commanded with such great severity that God said that the person whose foreskin had not been circumcised on the eighth day would perish from his people (Gen. 17). If the justice of so terrible a punishment is sought, will not all their argumentation about free choice and the praiseworthy health and purity of nature, however clever it may be, recoil shattered and broken?

For what evil, I ask, did an infant commit by his own will, so that, if another neglected him and did not circumcise him, he himself should be condemned—with a condemnation so severe that that person would perish from his people? The threat was not one of temporal death, since of the righteous, when they died, it was said instead, “And he was gathered to his people” (Gen. 25:17), or, “He was gathered to his ancestors” (1 Macc. 2:69). For afterward no temptation is feared by a human being [Col. 0403] that could separate him from his people, if his people are themselves the people of God. **[Note: The Am. edition and the manuscripts read “since” (quoniam).]**

## CHAPTER XXXI

**36.** What, then, is the meaning of so great a condemnation for an act involving no personal will? It is not, as some Platonists suppose, that each infant’s soul is being repaid for what it committed by its own will before this life, when it possessed free choice to live either well or badly before inhabiting this body. For the Apostle Paul says most explicitly that, before they were born, they had done nothing either good or evil (Rom. 9:11).

How, then, is an infant rightly punished with that destruction unless because he belongs to the mass of destruction, and is rightly understood to have been born from Adam, condemned by the obligation of an ancient debt, unless he is freed from it—not according to the debt, but according to grace? What grace, except the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord?

This grace was prophesied, among the other ancient sacraments, even by circumcision of the foreskin itself. For the eighth day, in the recurring sequence of weeks, is the Lord’s day, on which the Lord rose. And “the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4); hence the circumcision knife was made of stone, and the flesh of the foreskin was the body of sin.

## CHAPTER XXXII

**37.** Therefore, after the sacraments were changed, when the one whom they signified as destined to come had come, the help of the Mediator was not changed. Even before he came in the flesh, he was freeing his ancient members through faith in his incarnation.

And when we were dead in sins and in the foreskin of our flesh, we were made alive together with Christ, in whom we were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand (Col. 2:13, 11), which was prefigured by circumcision made by hand, so that the body of sin might be abolished (Rom. 6:6), the body with which we were born from Adam.

The propagation of a condemned origin condemns us unless we are cleansed by the likeness of sinful flesh, in which he was sent without sin, yet condemned sin from sin (Rom. 8:3), having been made sin for us. **[Note: One Cygirannensis manuscript reads, “for he was made sin for us.”]**

Hence the Apostle says: “We beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God. **[Note: The same manuscript reads “to be reconciled to God.”]** He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him” (2 Cor. 5:20–21). God, then, to whom we are reconciled, made him sin for us—that is, a sacrifice by which our sins would be forgiven—for sacrifices offered for sins are called “sins.” And certainly he himself was sacrificed for our sins, possessing no defect, alone among human beings having what was required even then among animals: the absence of defect, signifying that one without defect would come to heal defects.

Therefore, on whatever day after birth an infant is baptized in Christ, he is circumcised as though on the eighth day, because in him he is circumcised who rose on the third day after he was crucified, but on the eighth day in the sequence of weeks. He is circumcised for the stripping away of the body of the flesh (Col. 2:11)—that is, so that the debt contracted through the contagion of carnal generation may be discharged by the grace of spiritual regeneration.

For no one is clean from defilement—what defilement, I ask, except that of sin?—not even an infant [Col. 0404] whose life upon the earth is but one day (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint).

## CHAPTER XXXIII

**38.** They argue as follows: “Then marriage is an evil, and the human being whom marriage produces is not God’s work?” As though the good of marriage were the disease of concupiscence, in which those who do not know God love their wives, something the Apostle forbids (1 Thess. 4:5); rather than conjugal chastity, by which carnal desire is directed toward the proper use of producing children.

Or could a human being be anything other than God’s work, whether he is born from marriage, fornication, or adultery? But in this question—where what is being asked is not for what the Creator is necessary, but for what the Savior is necessary—we must not consider what good there is in the procreation of nature, but what evil there is in sin, by which it is certain that nature has been corrupted.

Both are propagated together: nature and nature’s defect, one of which is good and the other evil. The former is received from the Creator’s generosity; the latter is drawn from the condemnation of origin. **[Note: All manuscripts read, “from the origin of condemnation.”]** The cause of the former is the good will of the supreme God; the cause of the latter is the evil will of the first human being. The former indicates God as the creator of the creature; the latter indicates God as the punisher of disobedience. Finally, the same Christ, because of the former, is the maker of the human being; because of the latter, he became human in order to heal it.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

**39.** Marriage, then, is good in all that properly belongs to marriage. These are three things: the ordered purpose of begetting children, fidelity in chastity, and the sacrament of the marital union.

With regard to the ordered purpose of begetting children, it is written: “I want younger women to marry, bear children, and manage households” (1 Tim. 5:14). With regard to fidelity in chastity: “The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband does; likewise, the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does” (1 Cor. 7:4). With regard to the sacrament of marriage: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:6).

We remember that in other works of ours, which are not unknown to you, we have discussed these matters sufficiently, insofar as the Lord enabled us (On the Good of Marriage, no. 3 ff.). Because of all these things, “marriage is honorable in all, and the marriage bed is undefiled” (Heb. 13:4).

For to the extent that marriage is good, it makes much good even from the evil of lust, since lust itself does not use lust well, but reason does. Lust is that which the Apostle identifies as resisting the law of the mind, in the disobedient law of the members (Rom. 7:23). **[Note: Thus the Gallican manuscripts. The Louvain edition omits “in”; the Am. and Er. editions subsequently read: “which the Apostle calls the law of the members, resisting the law of the mind, of the disobedient.” This is acceptable if “law of the members” is corrected.]** Reason, however, using lust well, is itself within the law of marriage.

For if no good could be made from evil, God would not have created a human being even from adulterous intercourse. Therefore, just as the damnable evil of adultery is not attributed to God when a human being is born from it—since God himself makes a good work from the evil work of human beings—so whatever is shameful in that disobedience of the members, because of which those who sinned were ashamed and covered the same members with fig leaves (Gen. 3:7), is not attributed to marriage, on account of which conjugal intercourse is not only lawful but also useful and honorable [Col. 0405]. Rather, it is attributed to the sin of disobedience, whose consequence was that the human being, disobedient to God, also experienced his own members as disobedient to him.

Ashamed of them because they moved, not at the command of his will, but as though by their own will at the stimulus of lust, he judged them shameful and arranged that they be covered. For a human being ought not to have been ashamed of God’s work, nor should he in any way have been ashamed of what appeared good to the Creator to establish. Thus neither God nor human beings were displeased by that simple nakedness when nothing was shameful, because nothing had yet occurred that deserved punishment.

## CHAPTER XXXV

**40.** Marriage would certainly have existed even without the prior occurrence of sin, since there was no other reason why a helper should be made for the man—not another man, but a woman. And the words of God, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. 1:28), are not a prediction of sins destined to be condemned, but a blessing upon marriages destined to be fruitful.

By these ineffable words of his—that is, by the divine principles living in the truth of his wisdom, through which all things were made—God implanted the power of seed in the first human beings.

But if nature had not been dishonored by sin, let us not suppose that marriage in paradise would have been such that, for sowing offspring, the genital members would be moved by the heat of lust rather than by the command of the will **[Note: The printed editions and manuscripts read “not by the nature of the will”; this is corrected from Book 1 of *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, no. 7.]**, as the foot is moved for walking, the hand for working, and the tongue for speaking. Nor would the integrity of virginity have been violated by the violence of turbulent heat in order to conceive offspring, as now occurs. **[Note: The Victor manuscript and the Vatican manuscript read “would have been stirred” (incitaretur).]** Instead, it would have obeyed the command of the most tranquil love; and in that way there would have been neither the pain and blood of a virgin having intercourse nor the groaning of a mother giving birth.

These things are not believed because they are unknown in our present condition of mortality. For nature, changed for the worse by corruption, does not find an example of that original purity. But we are speaking to believers who know how to believe the divine utterances even without examples drawn from experience.

For how can I now demonstrate, without any parents, a human being made from dust, and a wife made for him from his side (Gen. 2:7, 22)? And yet faith believes what the eye no longer finds.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

**41.** Thus the tranquility of the first marriage without the passion of lust, and the movement of the genital members like that of the other members—not for the stimulation of unrestrained heat, but according to the command of the will—such as marriage would have remained if the shame of sin had not intervened, cannot now be demonstrated. But it can rightly be believed on the basis of what has been written by divine authority.

For just as I cannot now find anyone engaging in intercourse without the itching of lust, I cannot find anyone giving birth without pain and groaning, or anyone being born without future death. Yet according to the truth of the holy Scriptures, the groaning of a woman giving birth and the death of a human being would not have existed if sin had not preceded them.

The same is true of that from which those who covered their members [Col. 0406] were ashamed, because this too is written in the same holy Scriptures as having followed the prior sin. Unless an indecent movement had announced those members to their eyes—not eyes that were closed, but eyes not open to this matter, that is, not attentive—they would not have perceived anything in their bodies, which God had made wholly worthy of praise, as shameful or requiring concealment. For unless the deed that disobedience dared to commit had come first, the disgrace that modesty wished to hide would not have followed.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

**42.** It is therefore clear that this is not to be attributed to marriage, since marriage would exist even if it did not exist. Its goodness is not removed by this evil; rather, marriage turns even this evil to good use.

But because, under the present condition of mortals, intercourse and lust now occur together, those who do not wish or do not know how to distinguish them suppose that when lust is reproved, lawful and honorable marital intercourse is also being reproved.

They do not consider that the good of marriage, from which marriage takes its glory, is offspring, chastity, and the sacrament; whereas the other thing is not marriage’s good but the evil of carnal concupiscence, of which marriage too is ashamed.

But because the good of marriage—namely, the propagation of children—cannot be achieved without that evil, when one comes to this act, privacy is sought, witnesses are removed, and even the presence of the children themselves, if any have already been born and have begun, with advancing age, to perceive such things, is avoided. Thus marriage is permitted to perform what is lawful, while taking care to conceal what is shameful.

This is why even infants, who cannot sin, are nevertheless born not without the contagion of sin—not because of what is lawful, but because of what is shameful. From what is lawful, nature is born; from what is shameful, defect. God is the author of the nature that is born, he who created the human being and joined male and female by the law of marriage. The author of the defect, however, is the cunning of the devil who deceives and the will of the human being who consents.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

**43.** God did nothing here except condemn, by a just judgment, the human being who sinned by his will together with his descendants. Therefore whatever had not yet been born was deservedly condemned in that transgressing root. In that condemned lineage, carnal generation holds the human being; only spiritual regeneration frees him.

Therefore, regenerated parents, if they persevere in the same grace, will doubtless not be harmed by this on account of the remission of sins wrought in them, unless they make bad use of it—not only in every unlawful corruption, but even with their spouses, when they devote themselves to the begetting of children not with the purpose of propagation but in the service of satisfying lustful pleasure.

To avoid fornication, the Apostle grants husbands and wives that they should not defraud one another except by mutual consent for a time, so that they may devote themselves to prayer; he grants this as a concession, not as a command (1 Cor. 7:5–6). For by explicitly granting permission, he clearly indicates the fault.

Marital intercourse, which the marriage documents also declare to be for the purpose of begetting children, is in itself wholly good—not merely good in comparison with fornication [Col. 0407]. Although, because of the body of death, which has not yet been renewed by resurrection, it cannot occur without a certain animal-like movement of which human nature is ashamed, intercourse itself is not a sin when reason uses lust for good rather than being overcome by it for evil.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

**44.** This concupiscence of the flesh would be harmful even merely because it existed, unless the remission of sins were beneficial in such a way that what is in them **[Note: Possibly, “what is present in them”]** could be present in one who is born and also harm him, while in one who has been reborn it could be present without harming him.

For it harms those who are born to such an extent that, unless they are reborn, it is of no benefit that they were born from parents who have been reborn. The defect of origin remains in the offspring, so that it makes him guilty **[Note: The Cygirannensis and Casalensis manuscripts read “so that it makes him guilty”; other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read “so that it produces guilt”]**, even if the parent’s guilt has been washed away by the remission of the same defect **[Note: Two manuscripts read “has been absolved”]**—until every defect by which one sins through consenting to it is consumed by the final regeneration.

This means the renewal even of the flesh itself, which is promised to occur in the resurrection, when we shall not only commit no sins but also possess no vicious desires to which we might consent and thereby sin. It is toward this blessed perfection that the grace of the holy washing now given brings us.

For just as the regeneration of the spirit now causes all past sins to be forgiven, so through its merit the regeneration of the flesh will also occur unto eternal life, when, as the flesh itself rises incorruptibly, all the incentives to sin will be healed. But that salvation has been accomplished in hope, not yet possessed in reality; it is not held in the present, but awaited through endurance.

## CHAPTER XL

And therefore not only all sins—which are now forgiven in Baptism and make people guilty when they consent to vicious desires and sin—but also the vicious desires themselves, to which, if no consent is given, no guilt of sin is contracted, and which will have no existence in that other life, are all cleansed by the same washing of Baptism.

**45.** The guilt of the defect of which we are speaking will therefore remain in the carnal offspring of those who have been regenerated until it is washed away there also by the washing of regeneration.

One who has been regenerated does not regenerate children of the flesh, but begets them; and therefore he transmits to them not what he has been regenerated into, but what he has been begotten as. Thus, whether a guilty unbeliever or an absolved believer, neither begets absolved children; both beget guilty children. **[Note: The printed editions read “regenerates”; the manuscripts read more aptly here, “begets” (generat).]** In the same way, not only the seeds of the wild olive but also the seeds of the olive tree do not produce olive trees but wild olive trees.

Thus the first birth holds the human being under condemnation, from which only a second birth can free him. The devil holds him; Christ frees him. The deceiver of Eve holds him; the Son of Mary frees him. He who came to the man through the woman holds him; he who was born from a woman who did not experience a man frees him. He who introduced the cause of lust to the woman holds him; he who was conceived in a woman without lust frees him.

That one was able to hold them all through one person, and only one person frees them from his dominion [Col. 0408]—one whom he was unable to hold.

Finally, the very sacraments of the Church, which the Church celebrates with the authority of so ancient a tradition **[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “celebrate,” which is not bad if it is referred to the Pelagians.]**—so that these people, although they think the sacraments are performed in infants more as a pretense than in truth, nevertheless do not dare reject them by open repudiation—these very sacraments, I say, of the holy Church sufficiently indicate that infants, even those newly born from the womb, are freed from the devil’s service through the grace of Christ.

For apart from the fact that they are baptized for the remission of sins in a faithful rather than deceptive mystery, the opposing power is first exorcised and expelled from them; and they respond, through the words of those who carry them, that they renounce it. Through all these consecrated and evident signs of hidden realities, they are shown to pass from the worst captor to the best Redeemer, who, having taken upon himself weakness for our sake, bound the strong man in order to plunder his goods (Matt. 12:29). For what is weak in God is stronger not only than human beings but also than angels (1 Cor. 1:25).

Thus God, freeing the little ones together with the great, demonstrates in both what Truth spoke through the Apostle. He does not rescue only those advanced in age, but also the little ones, from the power of darkness, so that he may transfer them into the kingdom of the Son of his love (Col. 1:13).

**46.** Nor should anyone be surprised and say, “Why does the goodness of God create what the malignity of the devil possesses?” For he grants this to the seeds of his creation from that goodness by which he also makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45).

By this goodness he also blessed the seeds themselves, or established them by blessing them. Sin, which deserves condemnation, did not remove that blessing of nature, which is worthy of praise. Although sin had power, through the justice of God who punishes, to cause human beings to be born with the defect of original sin, it did not have power to prevent human beings from being born.

In the same way, among those advanced in age, whatever defects of sin may exist do not remove the human being from humanity; God’s good work remains amid however many evil works of the impious.

For even if a human being placed in honor, without understanding, is compared with animals and becomes like them (Ps. 49:13), he does not become so like them that he is an animal. He is compared with them through defect, not through nature; not through a defect of the beast, but through its nature. For the human being is of such great excellence in comparison with a beast that the defect of a human being is the nature of a beast; yet human nature is not thereby changed into the nature of a beast.

Thus God condemns the human being because of the defect by which nature is dishonored, not because of nature, which is not removed by the defect. But let us not suppose that beasts are liable to the punishment of condemnation. It is right that they be free from misery, since they cannot share in blessedness.

What, then, is surprising or unjust about a human being being subjected to an unclean spirit—not because of his nature but because of his uncleanness, which he contracted in the stain of origin, coming not from God’s work but from human will—when the unclean spirit itself is good insofar as it is a spirit and evil insofar as it is unclean? The former comes from God’s work; the latter from its own will.

[Col. 0409] Nature, then, which is stronger—that is, angelic nature—holds the lower nature, human nature, subjected through association with defect. Therefore the Mediator, stronger than the angels, became weak for the sake of human beings. Thus the pride of the captor is destroyed by the humility of the Redeemer: the one who boasts of angelic strength over the sons of man is conquered by the human weakness assumed by the Son of God. **[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads “sons of human beings.”]**

## CHAPTER XLI

**47.** [Col. 0410] As we are now bringing this book to a conclusion, we think it appropriate to have Ambrose, the bishop of God, respond to the slanderous verbosity of these people concerning original sin, just as we did concerning grace. Pelagius especially praises Ambrose among ecclesiastical writers of the Latin language for his completely sound faith. In the destruction of original sin, the grace of God is commended even more clearly. **[Note: See the book On the Grace of Christ, nos. 47–55.]**

In the work he wrote On the Resurrection, Saint Ambrose says:

“I fell in Adam; in Adam I was expelled from paradise; in Adam I died. He does not restore me unless he finds me in Adam, so that, just as in Adam I am liable to guilt and subject to death, so in Christ I may be justified” (Book *On Faith in the Resurrection*). **[Note: The manuscripts read “does not restore”; the printed editions, less well, “would restore.” Ambrose reads, “how he restores.”]**

Again, writing against the Novatians, he says:

“All human beings are born under sin; their very birth is in defect, as you have read when David says: ‘Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in offenses my mother gave birth to me’ (Ps. 51:5). Therefore Paul’s flesh was the body of death, as he himself says: ‘Who will free me from this body of death?’ (Rom. 7:24). But Christ’s flesh condemned sin, which it did not experience in being born and which it crucified in dying, so that in our flesh there might be justification through grace, where previously there had been a flood of sin through guilt” (Book 1 of On Penance, chapter 2 or 3).

Again, when the same Ambrose was explaining the prophet Isaiah and speaking of Christ, he says:

“Therefore he was also tempted in every respect as a human being and endured all things in the likeness of human beings; but, as one born from the Spirit, he abstained from sin” (Heb. 4:15). “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. 116:11), and no one is without sin except the one God. It was therefore preserved that, from man and woman—that is, through the commingling of bodies—no one should appear free from sin. But whoever is free from sin is also free from this kind of conception.” **[Note: Ambrose’s work on Isaiah does not survive.]**

Again, when he was explaining the Gospel according to Luke, he says:

“For it was not intercourse with a man that opened the secret places of the virgin womb, but the Holy Spirit poured immaculate seed into an inviolate womb. For the Lord Jesus alone, among all those born from woman, was holy in every respect; he did not experience the contagions of earthly corruption because of the newness of his immaculate birth, and he drove them away by his heavenly majesty” (Book 2, no. 56, on chapter 2).

48. Yet Pelagius contradicts these words of the man of God, Ambrose, whom he himself praised with such high commendation, when he says, “Just as we are begotten without virtue, so we are begotten without vice.” What remains, then, except either that Pelagius condemn this error of his, or that he regret having praised Ambrose in such a manner? But since blessed Ambrose spoke these things according to the Catholic faith, as a Catholic bishop, it follows that Pelagius, who deviated from this path of faith, was rightly condemned by the authority of the Catholic Church together with his disciple Coelestius—unless he should regret not having praised Ambrose, but having held opinions contrary to Ambrose. I know that you read insatiably whatever is written for the building up or strengthening of the faith; nevertheless, this book, however useful it may be for that purpose, must at last be brought to an end.

# [ON MARRIAGE AND CONCUPISCENCE]

[Col. 0409]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING BOOKS, ON MARRIAGE AND CONCUPISCENCE

When Augustine reviewed the two books addressed to the count Valerius, he appended them immediately to his response to the speech of the Arians, which was placed after the proceedings with Emeritus. These proceedings, moreover, are recorded under the year of Christ 418, on 20 September. Therefore, we have no doubt that at least the first of the following books was written either toward the end of that same year 418 or at the beginning of 419. For Augustine himself says of this first book in Book One Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, no. 9:

> “My book, against which he recalls having replied in four little books, I wrote after the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius. I thought this should be said,” he continues, “because he says that my words were taken up by his enemies in hatred of the truth, lest anyone should therefore suppose that the new heretics, enemies of Christ’s grace, were condemned on account of this book of mine.”

From these words you can easily understand that this first book, after the Pelagians had been condemned in 418, appeared approximately at that same time.

As soon as the book appeared, the Pelagians began publicly to criticize it, for they understood that its reading was stirring the minds of Catholics to hatred of their heresy. Among them was Julian, inflamed with zeal to support the Pelagian heresy, who immediately attacked that single book of Augustine in four books. Someone extracted a number of passages from Julian’s books and sent the excerpts to Count Valerius. Valerius arranged for them to be carried from Ravenna to Rome to Alypius, so that Alypius, when he himself had returned to Africa, might hand those excerpts over to Augustine for a speedy refutation, in addition to the letters in which Valerius thanked him for the earlier book dedicated to himself.

Augustine immediately recognized that these materials had been collected from Julian’s work. Although he would have preferred not to reply to them before receiving the complete work from which they had been taken, he nevertheless thought that he must hasten in order to satisfy Count Valerius. Accordingly, without any delay, he replied to these excerpts and composed a second book under the same title, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. We judge that it should be assigned to the year of Christ 420, since the holy Doctor wrote it immediately after receiving Valerius’s thanks for the earlier book; nor does it seem likely that Valerius waited two years or more to testify to this expression of gratitude.

That Valerius, whom Augustine honors with the titles “Illustrious” and “Count,” was occupied with public affairs—not, indeed, with forensic affairs, but with military ones. We therefore are not easily persuaded to believe, with the learned scholar, that he was the same man who was *comes rei privatae* in 425, consul in 432, and finally *magister officiorum* under the younger Theodosius in 435. For neither did those offices belong to military service, nor did the prefects under Theodosius have anything in common with those under Honorius.

[Note: [Col. 0411] See also Book 2, chapter 53, of the *Retractions*, vol. 1, col. 651, from the words “I wrote two books” through the words “Amid the duties of your military service.” M.]

[Col. 0411]

## LETTER TO COUNT VALERIUS

[Note: [Col. 0411] This is number 200 among the Augustinian letters, vol. 2.]

In this letter Augustine sends him the first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, dedicated to him. (C)

To the illustrious lord, most worthy of distinction, and most beloved son in the love of Christ, VALERIUS, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1. Why he has written this letter.

For a long time I was troubled that, although I had written several times, I had earned no reply from Your Sublimity. Suddenly, however, I received three letters from Your Kindness: one addressed not to me alone, sent through my fellow bishop Vindemialis, and, not long afterward, two through my fellow presbyter Firmus. This holy man, united to us by a most familiar affection—as you were able to learn from him—spoke much with us about your excellence and truthfully conveyed what sort of person he knew you to be in the depths of Christ. He overcame not only the letters which the aforementioned bishop had brought, or which he himself had carried, but also those letters which we complained that we had not received. And therefore his account of you was more pleasing to us, because he said what you could not write back even if I asked you, lest you become, contrary to what Holy Scripture forbids (Prov. 27:2), the herald of your own praises. Although I too fear writing these things to you, lest I incur the suspicion of flattery, illustrious lord, most worthy of distinction, and most beloved son in the love of Christ.

### 2. Valerius’s virtues.

Your praises in Christ—or rather, the praises of Christ in you—consider what delight and joy it was for me to hear them from one who could not deceive me because of his faithfulness, and could not fail to know them because of his friendship with you. Yet we have also heard other things from other persons, though not so many or so certain: how sound and Catholic your faith is; how devout your expectation of things to come; what love you have for God and for the brethren; how, amid the highest honors, you do not hold proud opinions; how you do not place your hope in uncertain riches, but in the living God, and are rich in good works (1 Tim. 6:17–18); how your house is a place of rest and consolation for the saints, and a terror to the ungodly; how great your concern is that no one should lie in wait for the members of Christ while covered by the name of Christ, whether among His former enemies or among His more recent ones; and how watchful you are for the salvation of these same enemies, while hostile to their error. These and similar things, as I said, we usually hear from others; but now, through the brother mentioned above, we have learned them more fully and with stronger testimony.

### 3. Valerius’s conjugal chastity.

But as for conjugal chastity, so that we too might praise and love it in you, would we have heard of it except from one of your more intimate associates, who knew your life not superficially but thoroughly? Therefore, concerning this good of yours, a gift of God, I am also pleased to speak with you more familiarly and at somewhat greater length. I know that I am not a burden to you if I send something rather long, so that by reading it you may remain with us for a longer time. For I have also learned that, amid your many and great cares, you readily and willingly read our works, and take great pleasure even in those which we have written for others, whenever they have been able to come into your hands. How much more, then, in what is written to you, where I shall speak as though you were present, and where you will deign to attend more closely and receive it more graciously? From this letter, therefore, proceed to the book which I have sent along with it. Its opening will more suitably explain both why it was written and why it was sent especially to you.

[Col. 0413]

## TWO BOOKS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON MARRIAGE AND CONCUPISCENCE, ADDRESSED TO COUNT VALERIUS

[Note: [Col. 0413] We have collated the two books *On Marriage and Concupiscence* with four ancient Vatican manuscripts and eleven Gallican manuscripts: one belonging to the Church of Reims, one to the Sorbonne College, one to the abbey of Casal Benedicti, two to Saint Michael’s, and others from the abbeys of Cygirannus, Corbie, Pratelles, Saint Benignus of Dijon, Cîteaux, and Saint Victor of Paris; in addition, with the variant readings of the Louvain edition from five Belgian manuscripts, and with the three most distinguished editions. Am., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: [Col. 0413] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and the *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.] (C)

## BOOK ONE

[Note: [Col. 0414] Written approximately at the beginning of the year 419.]

He explains the proper and natural goods of marriage. He proves that carnal concupiscence is not to be counted among those goods: for it is altogether an evil, which does not arise from the nature of marriage but has come upon marriage from the ancient sin. Nevertheless, marriage makes good use of this evil for the procreation of children. Because of this concupiscence, even from legitimate marriages children of God are born who are not children of God but children of the world; they are bound by the chain of sin, although their parents have been freed from it by grace, and are captives under the power of the devil unless they likewise are freed by the same grace of Christ. He explains how concupiscence remains in the baptized in its activity but not in its guilt. He teaches that, through the holiness of baptism, not only this original guilt but also all other sins and absolutely every evil of human beings are to be removed. Finally, he confirms by the authority of Ambrose that the evil of concupiscence must be distinguished from the goodness of marriage.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1. The subject of this work.

The new heretics, my dearest son Valerius, who contend that the medicine of Christ, by which sins are healed, is not necessary for infants born through the flesh, most maliciously cry out that we are condemners of marriage and of the divine work by which God creates human beings from males and females. They say this because we maintain that those born from such intercourse contract original sin, concerning which the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). We do not deny that they remain under the devil, regardless of the sort of parents from whom they are born, unless they are reborn in Christ and, through His grace, rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of Him who did not wish to be born from the intercourse of the two sexes (Col. 1:13).

Because we say this—which is contained in the most ancient and most firmly established rule of the Catholic faith—these recent and perverse advocates of a doctrine who say that there is no sin in infants to be washed away by the bath of regeneration slander us, faithlessly or ignorantly, as though we condemned marriage and as though we were saying that the work of God—that is, the human being born from marriage—was the work of the devil. They do not notice that the goodness of marriage cannot be accused because of the original evil drawn from it, any more than the evil of adultery and fornication can be excused because of the natural good born from them.

For just as sin, whether drawn from one source or the other by infants, is the work of the devil, so the human being, whether born from one source or the other, is the work of God. The purpose of this book, therefore, is that, insofar as the Lord deigns to help us, we may distinguish the evil of carnal concupiscence—on account of which the human being born through it contracts original sin—from the goodness of marriage. For this concupiscence, which shameless people shamelessly praise, would not exist as a thing of shame unless the human being had sinned beforehand. Marriage, however, would exist even if no one had sinned; for the sowing of children in the body of that life would then take place without this disease, without which it cannot now take place in the body of this death [Col. 0414] (Rom. 7:24).

[Note: [Col. 0413] At the end of this chapter, after “in the body of this death,” two polemical editions, the Paris and Louvain editions, add four or five lines, namely: “For the body of this death was not such in paradise before sin,” etc. These words belong to Book Two, no. 6.]

## CHAPTER TWO

### 2. Why he wrote the work to Valerius.

There are three principal reasons why I wished to write to you especially about this matter, which I shall briefly explain. The first is that, by Christ’s gift, you have great regard for conjugal chastity. The second is that you have effectively resisted, by your authority, by corrective action, and by persistence, those profane novelties against which we are contending here in argument. The third is that I learned that something written by them had come into your hands. Although you have mocked it with the strongest faith, it is nevertheless good that we should also know how to help defend what we believe. For the Apostle Peter commands us to be ready to give an answer [Note: [Col. 0413] Six manuscripts read “for confession.” Four, followed by the edition of Am., read “for an answer and confession.” The Greek is *pros apologian*, “for defense” or “for an explanation.”] to everyone who asks us for a reason concerning our faith [Note: [Col. 0414] The word “faith” was also present here in several manuscript Bibles. It is absent from the current printed Latin editions, as well as from the Greek.] and hope (1 Pet. 3:15). And the Apostle Paul says: “Let your speech always be gracious, seasoned with salt, so that you may know how you ought to answer each person” (Col. 4:6).

These are the matters that chiefly compelled me to provide you in this volume with whatever kind of discourse the Lord might deign to grant. I have never approved of thrusting any of my little works upon an illustrious man of such great rank as yourself—especially one already enjoying an office that allows no leisure, but still occupied with public affairs, and those military ones—when he had not asked me to read them, doing so not merely without due care but shamelessly. If, therefore, I have now done anything of this kind for the reasons I have mentioned, graciously forgive me and turn your kindly attention to what follows.

## CHAPTER THREE

### 3. Conjugal chastity is a gift of God. The difficulty concerning the chastity of unbelievers. No one is truly chaste except the faithful.

That conjugal chastity also is a gift of God is shown by the most blessed Paul, where, speaking about this matter, he says: “Now I wish all people to be as I myself am; but each has his own gift from God, one in this way [Note: [Col. 0415] In all the manuscripts: “one in this way, another indeed in this way.”], another in that way” (1 Cor. 7:7). See: he said that this too is a gift from God. It is inferior to that continence in which he wished all to be as he himself was, yet it is still a gift from God.

From this we understand that, when these things are commanded so that they may be done, nothing else is being shown except that we ought to have within us a particular will to receive and possess them. But when they are shown to be gifts of God, we learn from whom they must be requested if they are not possessed, and to whom thanks must be given if they are possessed. We also learn that our wills have little power to seek, receive, and retain these things unless they are divinely assisted.

### 4. What, then, are we to say when conjugal chastity is found even among certain ungodly people? Is it to be said that they sin because they misuse a gift of God, not referring it to the worship of Him from whom they received it? Or perhaps these things should not be regarded as gifts of God [Note: [Col. 0415] Several manuscripts read, “these things should not be called gifts.”] when unbelievers perform them, according to the Apostle’s statement: “Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23).

But who would dare to say that a gift of God is sin? The soul and body, and whatever good things are naturally implanted in soul and body, are gifts of God even in sinners, because God, not they themselves, made them. But concerning the things they do, it has been said: “Everything that is not from faith is sin.”

When, therefore, people without faith do these things which appear to belong to conjugal chastity—whether they are seeking to please human beings, themselves or others; whether they are avoiding human annoyances in matters which they desire viciously; or whether they are serving demons—it is not that sins are restrained, but that some sins are overcome by other sins. Therefore, let no one who does not preserve the fidelity of marriage to his wife for the sake of the true God be called truly chaste.

## CHAPTER FOUR

### 5. The natural good of marriage. Every association naturally rejects a dishonest associate. What true conjugal chastity is. Virginity and chastity are not true unless devoted to the true faith.

The union of male and female for the purpose of begetting is a natural good of marriage. But the person who uses this good bestially uses it badly, so that his intention is directed toward the pleasure of lust and not toward the will to procreate.

Although among certain animals lacking reason, such as most birds, a kind of quasi-alliance between mates is maintained, along with the communal skill of nest-building, the division of periods for incubating the eggs, and the alternating care of feeding the young, so that when they mate they seem rather to be conducting the business of perpetuating their kind than of satisfying lust, of these two things the former is like a human activity in animals, while the latter is animal-like in human beings.

But what I said belongs to the nature of marriage—that male and female are joined in a partnership for begetting and thus do not defraud one another, just as every association naturally refuses a dishonest associate [Note: [Col. 0416] Am. and Er. read, “the dishonesty of associates.”]—this evident good, when unbelievers possess it, they turn into evil and sin because they use it unbelievingly.

In the same way, faithful marriages turn that concupiscence of the flesh by which the flesh desires against the spirit (Gal. 5:17) into the service of righteousness. Their intention is to beget those who are to be regenerated, so that those who are born from them as children of the world may be reborn as children of God.

Therefore, those who beget children without this intention, this will, and this purpose—namely, to transfer them from the members of the first human being into the members of Christ—but instead, as unbelieving parents, glory in unbelieving offspring, do not possess true conjugal chastity, even if their observance is so great [Note: [Col. 0416] Some Vatican manuscripts read, “even if they are so observant.”] that, according to the marriage contract, they have intercourse solely for the procreation of children.

For since chastity is a virtue, whose opposite is unchastity, and since all virtues, including those that operate through the body, dwell in the mind, how can a body reasonably be declared chaste when the mind itself fornicates against the true God? That fornication is condemned by the holy psalm where it says: “For behold, those who distance themselves from you will perish; you have destroyed everyone who commits fornication away from you” (Ps. 72:27).

Therefore, neither conjugal, nor widowed, nor virginal chastity should be called true unless it is devoted to the true faith. Since consecrated virginity is rightly preferred to marriage, what Christian of sound mind would not place even Christian Catholic married women who have had more than one husband [Note: [Col. 0416] Three Vatican manuscripts read, “even Christian women who have had one husband,” omitting “non-.”] above not only Vestal virgins but also heretical virgins? Such is the power of faith, concerning which the Apostle says, “Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23), and concerning which it is likewise written to the Hebrews: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11:6).

## CHAPTER FIVE

### 6. Condemnation of lust is not condemnation of marriage. The origin of shame in the human body. Adam and Eve were not created blind. What the opening of the eyes meant in the first parents.

Since these things are so, those who suppose that marriage is condemned whenever carnal lust is criticized are plainly mistaken, as though this disease arose from marriage and not from sin.

Were not those first married couple, whose marriage God blessed by saying, “Be fruitful and multiply” (Gen. 1:28), naked and unashamed? Why, then, did shame arise from those members after sin, unless an indecent movement arose there—a movement that, if human beings had not sinned, marriage certainly would not have had?

Or perhaps, as some think because they pay too little attention to what they read, human beings were created blind at first, like dogs; and, even more absurdly, did not gain sight by growing as dogs do, but by sinning? Far be it from us to believe this.

But the reason those who think this are troubled is what is read: “She took from its fruit, ate, and gave it to her husband with her, and they ate; and the eyes of both were opened, and they recognized that they were naked” (Gen. 3:6–7). Because they understand this too little, they suppose that their eyes had previously been closed, since divine Scripture testifies that they were then opened.

But did Hagar, Sarah’s maidservant, when she opened her eyes while her son was thirsting and crying and saw a well (Gen. 21:19), previously have her eyes closed? Or were those two disciples walking along the road with the Lord after His resurrection walking with closed eyes, of whom the Gospel says that their eyes were opened in the breaking of bread and they recognized Him (Luke 24:31, 35)?

What is written of the first human beings—“The eyes of both were opened”—we should understand as meaning that they became attentive to perceiving and recognizing what had newly occurred in their bodies. That body, in any case, lay naked before their open eyes every day and was known [Note: [Col. 0417] Several manuscripts read, “lay before their eyes at will.”].

Otherwise, how could Adam, when all the land animals and flying creatures had been brought to him, assign them names with his eyes closed? He could not do so without distinguishing them, and he could not distinguish them without seeing. Finally, how was the woman herself shown to him, when he said, “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2:23)?

At last, if anyone should be so contentious as to say that Adam could have recognized these things not by seeing but by touching [Note: [Col. 0417] The printed editions add “and knowing,” which is absent from the manuscripts.], what will he say about the statement that the woman saw the tree from which she had been forbidden to eat, and saw that it was beautiful for the eyes to look upon (Gen. 3:6)?

They were therefore naked and were not ashamed (Gen. 2:25), not because they did not see, but because they had felt nothing shameful in the members they saw. For it is not said, “They were both naked, and they did not know,” but, “They were not ashamed.” Since nothing impermissible had preceded, nothing shameful had followed.

## CHAPTER SIX

### 7. The disobedience of the flesh justly repaid to the human being. Shame because of disobedient members.

At that point, when the human being had first transgressed God’s law, he began to have in his members another law opposing his mind, and he felt the evil of his disobedience when he found the disobedience of his flesh most deservedly repaid to him.

For the serpent had promised him this very opening of the eyes through deception, so that he might know something which it would have been better not to know. Then the human being perceived in himself what he had done; then he distinguished evil from good—not by being free from evil, but by suffering it.

For it was unjust that his servant—that is, his body—should obey him who had not obeyed his own Lord. Why is it that the eyes, lips, tongue, hands, feet, and the movements of the back, neck, and sides are placed under our control, so that they may move toward the activities appropriate to them, when we possess a healthy body free from impediment; but when the time comes for children to be begotten, the members created for this work do not serve the will’s command? Instead, lust, as though it possessed an authority of its own, is awaited to move them—and sometimes it does not move when the mind wishes, while at other times it moves when the mind does not wish it.

Would human freedom of choice not blush at this—that, by scorning God who commanded it, it had lost its own authority even over its own members? Where could it be shown more fittingly that human nature was corrupted as a just consequence of disobedience than in those disobedient places through which nature itself is perpetuated by succession? For this is why these bodily parts are specifically called by the name “nature.”

When those first human beings felt this movement in their flesh, indecent because it was disobedient, and were ashamed of their nakedness, they covered those same members with fig leaves (Gen. 3:7), so that what was not moved by the will of those who desired it might at least be covered by the choice of those who felt shame. And because they were ashamed of what they indecently desired, what was fitting was achieved by covering it.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

### 8. The evil of lust does not remove the good of marriage.

Since, therefore, the good of marriage could not perish even with this evil added to it, the imprudent think that this is not an evil but belongs to that good. Yet it is distinguished not only by subtle reasoning but also by the most common natural judgment, which was displayed in those first human beings and is still maintained by married people today.

What they afterward did by procreation is the good of marriage; what they earlier covered in shame is the evil of concupiscence, which everywhere avoids being seen and seeks secrecy through shame. Accordingly, marriage boasts because it makes some good even from that evil; it is ashamed because it cannot be carried out without it.

It is as if someone with an injured foot reached some good destination even by limping: the arrival is not bad because of the evil of limping, nor is the limp good because of the goodness of reaching the destination. So neither should we condemn marriage because of the evil of lust, nor praise lust because of the good of marriage.

## CHAPTER EIGHT

### 9. The disease of concupiscence in marriage is a matter not of the will but of necessity. What the will of the faithful should be in the use of marriage. Who is to be considered to use concupiscence without being conquered by it. How the holy Fathers formerly used marriage.

This, then, is the disease concerning which the Apostle, speaking even to married believers, says: “For this is the will of God, your sanctification: that you abstain from fornication, that each of you know how to possess his own vessel in sanctification and honor, not in the disease of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God” (1 Thess. 4:3–5).

Therefore, the faithful married person must not only refrain from using another’s vessel—as those do who desire other men’s wives—but must also know that even his own vessel is not to be possessed in the disease of carnal concupiscence.

This should not be understood as though the Apostle had forbidden conjugal intercourse, that is, lawful and honorable intercourse. Rather, this intercourse [Note: [Col. 0418] Some later editions read, “but that this intercourse should be.” Shortly afterward, where the text now has “which is now joined to it,” the later editions read “so that it may not be a matter of the will”; this reading is incorrect and contrary to the manuscripts.]—which would have had no diseased lust attached to it if the freedom of choice had not been lost through the preceding sin—now has this attached to it and is not a matter of the will but of necessity, without which, nevertheless, the will itself cannot attain its purpose in begetting children.

In the marriages of the faithful, this will is not directed toward the purpose that children destined to pass away should be born into this world, but that children destined to remain should be reborn in Christ [Note: [Col. 0419] Manuscripts read, “transient children.”]. If this occurs, it will be the reward of a marriage blessed with complete happiness; if it does not occur, there will still be peace for spouses of good will.

The person who, with this intention of heart, possesses his own vessel—that is, his wife—certainly does not possess her in the disease of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God, but in sanctification and honor, like the faithful who hope in God.

A person uses that evil of concupiscence rather than being conquered by it when he restrains and checks it as it surges in disordered and indecent movements; and he relaxes and employs it only with concern for procreation, so that he may beget carnally those who are to be regenerated spiritually, not so that he may subject the spirit to the flesh in sordid servitude.

No Christian should doubt that the holy fathers from Abraham and before Abraham used marriage in this way—those of whom God testifies that they pleased Him—since even some of them were permitted to have several wives, where the purpose was the multiplication of offspring, not the desire for varied pleasure.

## CHAPTER NINE

### 10. Why a man was sometimes permitted to have several wives, but a woman was never permitted to have several husbands. Nature favors singularity in those who rule.

For if the multiplicity of wives had not displeased the God of our fathers, who is also our God, because it allowed lust to display itself more abundantly, holy women too would each have served several men. If any woman did this, what except the shamefulness of concupiscence would compel her to have several husbands, when this license would not produce more children?

Nevertheless, the fact that it belongs more properly to the good of marriage that there should be not one man and many women but one man and one woman is sufficiently indicated by the first union of husband and wife, divinely established, from which marriages were to take their beginning and in which the more honorable example was to be observed.

As the human race advanced, certain good women were joined to certain good men, several to one. From this it appears that the former arrangement sought dignity and modesty more earnestly, while the latter was permitted by nature for the sake of fertility. For dominion too is more naturally exercised by one over many than by many over one.

Nor can there be doubt that, according to the natural order, men are more suited to rule women than women are to rule men. In preserving this order, the Apostle says, “The head of the woman is the man” (1 Cor. 11:3), and, “Women, be subject to your husbands” (Col. 3:18). The Apostle Peter likewise says: “Thus Sarah obeyed Abraham, calling him lord” (1 Pet. 3:6).

Although this is so—that nature favors singularity among those who rule, while we more readily observe plurality among those who are subordinate—several women would never lawfully be joined to one man unless several children were born from that arrangement. Therefore, if one woman has intercourse with several men, since this brings her not a multiplication of offspring but a repetition of lust, she cannot be a wife but is a prostitute.

## CHAPTER TEN

### 11. The sacrament of marriage. Marriage is indissoluble. The law of the world concerning divorce differs from the law of the Gospel.

Since not only fertility, whose fruit is offspring, and not only chastity, whose bond is fidelity, but also a certain sacrament of marriage is commended to married believers, the Apostle says: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church” (Eph. 5:25).

The reality of this sacrament, without doubt, is that male and female joined in marriage should remain inseparably united for as long as they live, and that it is not lawful, except on account of fornication, for one spouse to be separated from the other (Matt. 5:32).

For this is preserved in Christ and in the Church: that the living should remain with the living forever, separated by no divorce. Such observance of this sacrament exists in the city of our God, on His holy mountain (Ps. 47:2)—that is, in the Church of Christ—among all married believers, who are without doubt members of Christ, that even when women marry or men take wives for the purpose of begetting children, it is not lawful to abandon a barren wife in order to take a fertile one.

If someone does this, he is not guilty according to the law of this world, where, once a divorce has intervened, it is permitted without crime for one person to contract another marriage with another. The Lord Himself testifies that holy Moses also permitted this to the Israelites because of the hardness of their hearts. But according to the law of the Gospel, he is guilty of adultery, as is the woman too if she marries another (Matt. 19:8–9).

So enduring are the rights of marriage once entered into between the living that spouses who have been separated from one another remain spouses more truly than they are spouses with those to whom they have subsequently attached themselves. For they would not be adulterers with the others unless they remained spouses to one another.

Finally, when the husband with whom a true marriage existed has died, a true marriage can be formed with the person with whom there had previously been adultery. Thus something marital remains among the living [Note: [Col. 0420] The manuscripts read this way; the printed editions read, “Thus a certain marital bond remains.”] which neither separation nor union with another can remove.

It remains, however, for the burden of the crime, not as the bond of the covenant. In the same way, the soul of an apostate [Note: [Col. 0420] Several manuscripts read, “the apostate soul.”], as though withdrawing from the marriage-bond with Christ, does not lose, even after faith has been abandoned, the sacrament of faith which it received in the bath of regeneration. For if it had lost it when it departed, it would undoubtedly be restored to it when it returned. But whoever has departed possesses it for the accumulation of punishment, not for the earning of reward.

## CHAPTER ELEVEN
## 12. A Mutual Vow of Continence Does Not Dissolve Marriage. The True Marriage of Mary and Joseph. How Joseph Was Christ’s Father. All the Goods of Marriage Were Present in the Marriage of Mary and Joseph

When, by mutual consent, people resolve to abstain permanently from the use of carnal desire, far be it from us to say that the marital bond between them is broken. Rather, it will be firmer, insofar as they have entered into agreements with one another that ought to be observed with greater affection and concord—not through bodily bonds of pleasure, but through the voluntary affections of their souls.

For the angel did not falsely say to Joseph, “Do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife” (Matt. 1:20). She is called his wife on account of the original pledge of betrothal, which he had neither known through intercourse nor was going to know through intercourse. [Col. 0421] The title “wife” had neither perished nor remained false where there had been no bodily union and none was to be.

For she was a virgin, and therefore was both holier and more wonderfully pleasing to her husband: fruitful without a husband, unlike him in offspring, but equal in faith. For this reason both deserved to be called, by virtue of their faithful marriage, the parents of Christ—not only she as his mother, but also he as her husband and therefore his father: both in mind, not in flesh. Yet whether he was a father only in mind, or she a mother in both mind and flesh, both were parents of his humility, not of his sublimity; of his weakness, not of his divinity.

For the Gospel does not lie where we read: “And his father and mother were amazed at what was said about him.” And elsewhere: “And his parents went every year to Jerusalem.” A little later: “And his mother said to him, ‘Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been seeking you sorrowfully.’” But he, to show that he had another father besides them, who had begotten him without a mother, answered them: “Why were you seeking me? Did you not know that I must be in the things that belong to my Father?” And again, lest it be thought that by this statement he had denied those persons as his parents, the Evangelist immediately added: “And they did not understand the word that he spoke to them. And he went down with them and came to Nazareth, and he was subject to them” (Luke 2:33, 41, 48–51). Subject to whom, except his parents? And who was subject except Jesus Christ, who, “though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized”? Why, then, was he subject to those who were far beneath the form of God, except because “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6–7), of whose form they were parents?

But since she had given birth without his sowing, clearly both would not have been parents even of that servant’s form unless they had also been husband and wife to one another without bodily union. Hence, when the sequence of generations recalls Christ’s parents through the connection of succession, it ought rather to have been brought down to Joseph, as it was done (Matt. 1:16; Luke 3:23), lest injury be done in that marriage to the male sex, which is naturally the more prominent, since nothing would be lost to the truth: Joseph as well as Mary was from the seed of David, from whom Christ was foretold to come.

## 13. The Whole Good of Marriage Was Fulfilled in Them

Thus every good of marriage was fulfilled in those parents of Christ: offspring, fidelity, and sacrament. We recognize the offspring as the Lord Jesus himself; fidelity, because there was no adultery; sacrament, because there was no divorce.

## Chapter XII

All Flesh That Is Born from Intercourse Is Sinful Flesh

Only in this case was there no marital intercourse, because it could not take place in sinful flesh without that shameful desire of the flesh which arises from sin. He who was to be without sin chose to be conceived without it—not in sinful flesh, but “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. 8:3). In this way he also taught that all flesh born from intercourse is sinful flesh, since the only flesh that was not born from it was not sinful flesh.

Although marital intercourse undertaken with the intention of procreation is not itself sin—for the good will of the soul leads the bodily pleasure that follows, rather than following where bodily pleasure leads; nor is human choice dragged beneath sin’s domination when the wound of sin is rightly reduced to the use of procreation. A certain itching of this wound reigns in the foulness of adultery, fornication, every kind of sexual violation, and impurity; but in the obligations of marriage it is subject to service.

[Note: [Col. 0422] Some manuscripts: “necessities.”] There, such shamefulness is condemned as a master; here, honesty is ashamed of such a servant. Therefore, why should those who cease intercourse by mutual consent not remain married, if Joseph and Mary remained married, although they never began to have intercourse?

## Chapter XIII

### 14. Before Christ Was the Time for Marrying; After Christ Is the Time for Continence

This propagation of children, which among the holy fathers was supremely dutiful for generating and preserving the people of God, among whom Christ’s prophecy had to precede, no longer has that necessity. The abundance of children to be spiritually begotten from all nations, regardless of where they were born carnally, is now evident.

And what is written—“A time for embracing, and a time for refraining from embracing” (Eccles. 3:5)—is understood to have been divided between that former time and this present one.

[Note: [Col. 0422] Some Vatican manuscripts: “through both this time.”] The former was the time for embracing; the latter is the time for refraining from embracing.

### 15.

Accordingly, when the Apostle was speaking about this, he said: “But this I say, brothers: the time is short. It remains that those who have wives should be as though they had none; and those who weep as though they did not weep; and those who rejoice as though they did not rejoice; and those who buy as though they did not possess; and those who use this world as though they did not use it. For the form of this world is passing away. I want you to be without anxiety” (1 Cor. 7:29–32).
