[Note: [Col. 0422] All manuscripts: “as though they did not buy.”]

To explain this briefly, I understand all these statements as follows. “This I say,” he says, “brothers: the time is short.” The people of God are no longer to be propagated carnally through generation, but gathered spiritually through regeneration.

It remains, therefore, that those who have wives should not be enslaved to carnal desire; that those who weep because of present evil should rejoice in hope of future good; that those who rejoice because of some temporal advantage should fear eternal judgment; that those who buy should possess in such a way that they do not cling through love; and that those who use this world should consider themselves passing through it, not remaining in it. “For the form of this world is passing away.” “I want you,” he says, “to be without anxiety”—that is, I want you to have your heart above, in the things that do not pass away.

Then he adds: “The unmarried man is concerned with the things of the Lord, how he may please the Lord; but the married man is concerned with the things of the world, how he may please his wife” (1 Cor. 7:32–33). In this way he explains, in a certain sense, what he had said above: “Those who have wives should be as though they had none.” For those who have wives in such a way that they are concerned with the things of the Lord, how they may please the Lord, and are not concerned with pleasing their wives in the things of the world, are as though they had none.

This happens more easily when the wives too are such that their husbands please them not because they are rich, eminent, noble in birth, or physically attractive, but because they are faithful, devout, chaste, and good men.

[Note: Am. Er. and six manuscripts: “because it happens with that happiness.” Two manuscripts: “because it happens with that ease.” One Vatican manuscript, in a second hand: “because it happens easily.”]

## Chapter XIV

### 16. A Certain Intemperance Is to Be Tolerated in Married People. Marital Intercourse for the Sake of Pleasure Alone Is Not Without Fault, but Receives Pardon Because of Marriage

Among married people, just as these things are to be desired and praised, so other things must be tolerated, lest one fall into damnable crimes, that is, fornication or adultery.

To avoid this evil, even the intercourse of spouses that does not take place for the sake of procreation but serves victorious desire—intercourse concerning which they are commanded not to defraud one another, lest Satan tempt them because of their lack of self-control—is not commanded according to precept, but is permitted according to pardon.

For it is written: “Let the husband render the debt to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband; likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife. Do not defraud one another, except by mutual consent for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer; and return again to the same, lest Satan tempt you because of your lack of self-control. But I say this according to pardon, not according to command” (1 Cor. 7:3–6).

Where pardon must be given, it cannot reasonably be denied that there is some fault. Since intercourse undertaken with the intention of procreation is not blameworthy, and properly belongs to marriage, what does the Apostle permit according to pardon except that spouses, when they do not exercise continence, demand from one another the bodily debt—not from the will to propagate, but from the pleasure of desire?

Yet this pleasure falls into fault not because of marriage, but receives pardon because of marriage. Therefore marriage is praiseworthy even for this reason: it causes what does not belong to marriage itself to be forgiven on account of marriage. For even this intercourse, by which desire is served, is not conducted in such a way as to prevent the offspring that marriage seeks.

## Chapter XV

### 17. In the Use of a Spouse: What Is Without Fault, What Has Venial Fault, and What Has Mortal Fault

Yet it is one thing not to have intercourse except from the will to procreate, which has no fault; another thing to seek bodily pleasure through intercourse, but not with anyone other than one’s spouse, which has venial fault. For although intercourse does not take place for the purpose of propagating offspring, nevertheless the propagation of offspring is not obstructed on account of this desire, whether by an evil vow or by an evil act.

Those who do this, although they are called married, are not so. They retain none of the reality of marriage, but use its honorable name as a covering for their shame.

[Note: Most manuscripts with Am.: “as a covering for their shame.”]

They are exposed, however, when they go so far as to abandon the children who are born against their will.

[Note: Three Vatican manuscripts: “in the streets.”]

For they hate to nourish or possess those whom they feared to beget. Thus, when dark iniquity rages against its own offspring, whom it begot unwillingly, it is brought into the light by manifest iniquity, and hidden shamefulness is convicted by open cruelty.

Sometimes this lustful cruelty—or cruel lust—goes so far that it even procures poisons of sterility. And if these have accomplished nothing, it destroys and expels the conceived fetus by some means from within the womb, wishing its offspring to perish before it could live; or, if it was already living in the womb, to be killed before it was born.

In short, if both spouses are such, they are not married; and if they were such from the beginning, they came together not through marriage but rather through sexual violation. If only one of them is such, I dare say that either she is, in a certain sense, her husband’s prostitute, or he is his wife’s adulterer.

## Chapter XVI

### 18. The Weakness of Incontinence Is to Be Received into the Honor of Marriage, Lest It Fall into the Ruin of Sexual Crimes

Since marriage cannot now be what it could have been among the first human beings, if sin had not preceded it, let it be what it was among the holy fathers. The shameful desire of the flesh, which was neither in paradise before sin nor permitted to be there after sin, necessarily exists in this body of death; but it must not be served. Rather, it must itself be compelled to serve only the propagation of offspring.

Or, since the present time—the time of refraining from embracing, as we have already said—has no necessity for this duty, because there is everywhere among all nations such abundance of children to be spiritually begotten, let whoever can accept that higher good of continence accept it.

But whoever cannot accept it, if he takes a wife, does not sin; and if a woman does not exercise continence, let her marry. “It is good for a man not to touch a woman.” But since not all accept this saying, only those to whom it has been given (Matt. 19:12, 11), it remains that “because of fornications each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband” (1 Cor. 7:28, 1–2).

[Note: [Col. 0424] Printed editions read “because of fornication”; the manuscripts read “because of fornications,” in accordance with the Greek.] Thus the weakness of incontinence, lest it fall into the ruin of sexual crimes, is received into the honor of marriage.

What the Apostle says concerning women—“Therefore I want younger women to marry”—can also be said concerning men: “I want younger men to take wives.” Thus it applies to both sexes: to bear children, to be fathers and mothers of households, and to give the adversary no occasion for slander (1 Tim. 5:14).

## Chapter XVII

### 19. The Goods of Marriage

In marriage, however, the goods proper to marriage should be loved: offspring, fidelity, and sacrament. Offspring, not merely so that it may be born, but also so that it may be reborn—for it is born for punishment unless it is reborn for life.

Fidelity, however, is not merely the fidelity that even unbelievers possess when they jealously guard the flesh. What husband, however impious, wants an adulterous wife? Or what woman, however impious, wants an adulterous husband? This is indeed a natural good in marriage, but it is nevertheless carnal.

A spouse who is a member of Christ ought to fear adultery for the sake of the spouse, not for his or her own sake, and ought to hope from Christ for the reward of the fidelity shown to the spouse.

[Note: [Col. 0424] One Vatican manuscript: “but the mind of the Christian spouse.”]

But the sacrament—which neither separated nor adulterous spouses lose—should be guarded by married people in concord and chastity.

[Note: Lov.: “which does not permit spouses to be separated or adulterated, when they guard it in concord and chastity.” Other printed editions, Am. and Er.: “which separated or adulterated spouses do not lose, when they guard it in concord and chastity.” The reading is corrected with the help of the older books, especially the Gallican manuscripts of Rheims, Cygirannus, and Michaelinus, and three Vatican manuscripts.]

For this alone is what even a childless marriage retains by the law of piety, after the hope of fertility for which it had been joined has been lost.

Let whoever wishes to praise marriage praise these marital goods within marriage. But the desire of the flesh is not to be counted as a good of marriage; it is to be tolerated.

[Note: Three manuscripts: “the shameful desire.”]

For it is not a good arising from natural marriage, but an evil arising from ancient sin.

## Chapter XVIII

### 20. Why Children of Wrath Are Born from a Holy Marriage

Because of this, even from the just and legitimate marriages of the children of God are born not children of God but children of the world. For those who beget, if they have already been regenerated, do not beget from what makes them children of God, but from what still makes them children of the world.

The Lord’s saying is: “The children of this world beget and are begotten” (Luke 20:34). Since we are still children of this world, our outward person is being corrupted; from this, too, children of this world are begotten, and they do not become children of God unless they are reborn. But insofar as we are children of God, our inner person is renewed day by day (2 Cor. 4:16).

Although the outward person itself has been sanctified through the washing of regeneration and has received the hope of future incorruption, for which reason it is rightly called the temple of God: “Your bodies,” the Apostle says, “are the temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God; and you are not your own, for you were bought with a great price. Therefore glorify and carry [Note: “And carry” is absent from many manuscripts. It is also absent from the Greek witnesses.] God in your body” (1 Cor. 6:19–20).

All this was said not only on account of present sanctification, but especially on account of that hope of which he says elsewhere: “But we ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body.”

If, then, according to the Apostle, the redemption of our body is awaited, surely what is awaited is still hoped for and is not yet possessed. Hence he adds: “For in hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:23–25).

Therefore it is not through what we await, but through what we endure, that carnal children are propagated.

Far be it, then, from a faithful man, when he hears the Apostle say, “Love your wives” (Col. 3:19), to love the desire of the flesh in his wife—a desire he ought not to love even in himself—when he hears another Apostle say: “Do not love the world or the things in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him, because everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age, which is not from the Father but from the world. And the world will pass away” [Note: Some manuscripts: “passes away.”] “and its desire; but whoever does the will of God remains forever, just as God remains forever” (1 John 2:15–17).

## Chapter XIX

### 21. Thus Sinners Are Born from the Just, as Wild Olives from Olive Trees

Whatever is born from this desire of the flesh is born for the world, not for God. But it is born for God when it is reborn from water and the Spirit.

[Note: The printed editions add “holy.”]

Regeneration alone remits the guilt of this desire; and therefore generation transmits it.

[Note: The printed editions read: “which generation transmits.” Six manuscripts read: “and therefore generation transmits it.” The printed editions likewise have this reading when the passage is repeated in Book 6 Against Julian, chapter 1 or 3.]

Therefore what has been generated must be regenerated, so that, since it cannot happen otherwise, what has been transmitted may likewise be remitted.

[Note: Five manuscripts have this reading, with which the other codices agree in Book 6 Against Julian, chapter 1 or 3. More manuscripts here omit “likewise” and read: “must be regenerated (since it cannot happen otherwise), so that what has been transmitted may be remitted.” The printed editions read: “must be regenerated, since it cannot otherwise be effected, so that what has been transmitted may be remitted.”]

For that what has been remitted in the parent should be transmitted to the offspring [Note: The printed editions here read “into the offspring”; but in Book 6 Against Julian, chapter 2 or 5, they agree with the manuscripts in reading “in the offspring.”] happens in marvelous ways, but it nevertheless happens.

Divine providence arranged this in certain trees, so that these invisible and unbelievable things might have some visible example for unbelievers, though they are nevertheless true. Why should we not believe that the reason the wild olive grows from the olive was established for this purpose? Or should we not believe that, in something created for human use, the Creator provided and instituted what could serve as an example for the human race?

It is therefore marvelous how those who have been freed by grace from the bond of sin nevertheless beget children bound by that same bond, whom it is likewise necessary to free. We confess that this is marvelous.

But that the offspring of wild olives was hidden even in the seeds of olives—when would this also be believed unless experience proved it? Accordingly, just as a wild olive is produced from the seed of a wild olive, and from the seed of an olive nothing but a wild olive is produced, although there is a great difference between a wild olive and an olive, so from the flesh of a sinner and from the flesh of a just person the same sinner is produced in both cases, although there is a great difference between a sinner and a just person.

The person born is not yet a sinner by action; he is new by birth but old by guilt: a human being from the Creator, a captive from the deceiver, one in need of a redeemer.

But it is asked how captivity can be transmitted to offspring even from parents who have already been redeemed. Since this cannot readily be investigated or explained in speech, it is not believed by unbelievers—as though the example we have given of the wild olive and the olive, that a dissimilar kind should produce similar offspring, could easily be discovered by reason or explained by speech.

[Note: The printed editions read: “could easily be discovered by reason or explained by speech.” The manuscripts read “discovers” and “explains.”]

Yet this can be observed by anyone who wishes to investigate it by experience. Let it therefore stand as an example, through which what cannot be observed may also be believed.

## Chapter XX

### 22. Even Unbaptized Infants Are in the Power of the Devil. Exorcism and Renunciation of the Devil in Infants

Christian faith does not doubt—and the new heretics have begun to attack this—that those who are washed in the washing of regeneration are redeemed from the power of the devil, and that those who have not yet been redeemed through such regeneration, including the infant children of the redeemed, remain captives under the power of that same devil unless they too are redeemed by the same grace of Christ.

For we do not doubt that the benefit of God spoken of by the Apostle applies to people of every age: “He rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 1:13).

Whoever denies that infants are rescued when they are baptized from this power of darkness—of which the devil is prince, that is, from the power of the devil and his angels—is convicted by the truth of the Church’s own sacraments. No heretical novelty is permitted to remove or change these within Christ’s Church, whose head governs and assists the whole body, the small together with the great.

Accordingly, in truth and not in falsehood, the devil’s power is exorcized in infants. They renounce him—not by their own action, but through the hearts and mouths of those who carry them—so that, rescued from the power of darkness, they may be transferred into the kingdom of their Lord.

What, then, is in them by which they remain under the devil’s power until they are rescued from it through the sacrament of Christ’s Baptism? What is it except sin? For the devil found no other means by which he could enslave human nature to his own right, although a good Creator had established it as good.

Infants have committed no personal sin in their own lives. Original sin therefore remains, by which they are held captive under the devil’s power unless they are redeemed from it by the washing of regeneration and the blood of Christ, and pass into the kingdom of their Redeemer, the power of their captor being frustrated, and power being given them to become children of God from children of this world (John 1:12).

## Chapter XXI

### 23. Sin Did Not Arise from the Goods of Marriage. The Sacrament of Marriage Is Great in Christ and the Church, but Small in Husband and Wife

Now, if we were in some way to question those marital goods and ask how sin could have been transmitted from them to infants, the act of propagating offspring would answer us:

“I would have been happier in paradise if sin had not been committed. For that blessing of God belongs to me: ‘Be fruitful and multiply’” (Gen. 1:28). For this good work, the distinct limbs of the two sexes were created—limbs that already existed before sin, although they were not shameful.

The fidelity of chastity would answer: “If sin had not existed, what could have made me more secure in paradise, where neither my desire would have goaded me nor another’s desire tempted me?”

The sacrament of marriage would also answer: “Before sin, this was said of me in paradise: ‘A man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’” (Gen. 2:24). The Apostle calls this a great sacrament in Christ and the Church (Eph. 5:32). What is great in Christ and the Church is therefore small in each individual husband and wife, but it is nevertheless an inseparable [Note: Er. and six manuscripts: “inseparable.”] sacrament of union.

Which of these things in marriage is the source from which the bond of sin could pass to posterity? Surely none. And yet the goodness of marriage would be complete in these three goods, by which good marriages are still good today.

## Chapter XXII

### 24. Desire and Shame Arise from Sin. The Law of Sin. The Shamelessness of the Cynics

But if that desire of the flesh were questioned—the desire by which the parts of the body became shameful, although they had not previously been shameful—would it not answer that it began to exist in the human limbs after sin?

For this reason the Apostle calls it, in his own words, the law of sin (Rom. 7:23): it made the human being subject to itself because he did not wish to be subject to his God. It is also the desire from which the first married couple were ashamed when they covered their shameful parts (Gen. 3:7), and from which everyone is now ashamed when they seek private places for intercourse and do not dare to have as witnesses even their children, whom they have begotten from it.

The error of the Cynic philosophers resisted this natural modesty with marvelous shamelessness, since they believed that, because it was lawful and honorable, intercourse should be performed openly with one’s spouse. Hence the impurity of this shamelessness rightly received the name “canine”: for this reason they were called Cynics.

## Chapter XXIII

### 25. In the Regenerated, Desire Without Consent Is Not Sin. In What Sense Desire Is Called Sin. Whatever Is Born through Desire Is Rightly Subjected to the Devil Because of Sin. The Devil Is to Be Punished More Severely Than Human Beings

This desire, then, this law of sin dwelling in the limbs, to which the law of righteousness forbids obedience—the Apostle saying, “Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires; and do not present your members to sin as weapons of iniquity” (Rom. 6:12–13)—this desire, I say, which is cleansed only by the sacrament of regeneration, certainly transmits the bond of sin through generation to posterity, unless they too are released from it through regeneration.

Desire itself, however, is no longer sin in those who have been regenerated, when they do not consent to it for unlawful acts and the members are not given over by the ruling mind so that they may carry out those acts.

[Note: [Col. 0428] The manuscripts read “do not present”; the printed editions read “do not present [them].”]

[Note: [Col. 0428] Some manuscripts: “that he may carry it out.”]

Thus, if what is written—“You shall not desire” (Exod. 20:17)—is not fulfilled, at least what is read elsewhere should be fulfilled: “Do not go after your desires” (Sir. 18:30).

But because, in a certain manner of speaking, it is called sin both because it was made through sin and because it makes sin if it prevails, its guilt is effective in the one begotten; but Christ’s grace, through the forgiveness of all sins, does not allow that guilt to be effective in the regenerated person if he does not obey it, as it were commanding evil works.

[Note: [Col. 0428] The Louvain editors omitted “because,” although it occurs in Am., Er., and all the manuscript codices. Perhaps the reading should be: “but [that which] is called sin in a certain manner of speaking …”]

[Note: The Benignian manuscript reads “but its true guilt.” “True” was substituted by a later hand for another word. Some books read “it makes him guilty; its guilt is of value,” which is less satisfactory. Morel, *Elem. crit.*, pp. 329–330, reads the passage as follows: “But because, in a certain manner of speaking, it is called sin both because it was made through sin and because, if it prevails, it truly makes sin; its guilt is effective in the one who has been begotten.”]

It is therefore called sin because it was made through sin, although in the regenerated it is no longer itself sin, just as a speech is called “tongue” because the tongue produces it, and writing is called “hand” because the hand produces it.

Likewise, it is called sin because it makes sin if it prevails, just as cold is called “lazy” not because it is made by lazy people, but because it makes people lazy.

### 26.

This wound inflicted on the human race by the devil compels everything born through it to be under the devil, as though he were rightly plucking fruit from his own tree—not because human nature is from him, for it is from God alone, but because the defect is not from God.

Human nature is not condemned on account of itself, since it is praiseworthy as God’s work, but on account of the damnable defect by which it has been corrupted. And on account of what condemns it, it is also subjected to the damnable devil: for the devil himself is an unclean spirit. What belongs to him as spirit is good; what belongs to him as unclean is evil. He is spirit by nature and unclean by defect. Of these two, the former is from God, the latter from the devil himself.

Thus he does not hold human beings—whether adults or infants—because they are human, but because they are unclean. Whoever, therefore, is surprised that God’s creature is subjected to the devil should not be surprised: God’s creature is subjected to God’s creature, the lesser to the greater, because the human being is subjected to the angel. Yet this is not on account of nature, but on account of defect, because the unclean is subjected to the unclean.

This is the fruit produced by him from the ancient stock of uncleanness that he planted in the human being. At the final judgment he himself will suffer the greater punishments insofar as he is more unclean. Nevertheless, even those for whom that condemnation will be more tolerable are subject to him as their prince and author of sin, because there will be no cause of condemnation except sin.

## Chapter XXIV

### 27. Original Sin Is Transmitted through Lust. Venial Sins in Married People. The Desire of the Flesh Is Both Daughter and Mother of Sin

Therefore, because children are born not from the good by which marriage is good, but from the evil of desire, which marriage uses well, yet for which marriage itself is ashamed, the devil holds infants as guilty.

For although marriages are themselves honorable in all the goods that properly belong to them, even when they have an undefiled marriage bed (Heb. 13:4), not only as regards fornications and adulteries, which are damnable crimes, but also as regards those excesses of intercourse that do not occur for the sake of offspring with the will ruling, but for the sake of pleasure with desire prevailing—excesses that are venial sins in married people.

Nevertheless, when the act of procreation is undertaken, that lawful and honorable intercourse cannot take place without the heat of desire, so that what belongs to reason, not to desire, may be carried out.

Certainly, whether this heat follows or precedes the will, it is nevertheless the heat itself that, as though by its own command, moves the limbs—limbs that cannot be moved by the will. Thus it reveals itself not as a servant of one who commands, but as the punishment of a will that disobeys; it is moved not by free choice but by some enticing stimulus, and for this reason it is shameful.

From this desire of the flesh—which, although it is no longer counted as sin in those who have been regenerated, nevertheless enters nature only from sin—from this desire of the flesh, I say, as sin’s daughter and, when consent is given to shameful acts, also the mother of many sins, whatever offspring is born is bound by original sin unless it is reborn in him whom the Virgin conceived without this desire. Therefore, when he deigned to be born in the flesh, he alone was born without sin.

## Chapter XXV

### 28. Desire Remains after Baptism Like Weakness after an Illness Has Been Healed. Desire Decreases in Those Who Make Progress and Increases in Those Who Lack Continence

If it is asked how this desire of the flesh remains in the regenerated person, in whom the forgiveness of all sins has been effected—since through it offspring is conceived, and the child of even a baptized parent is born carnally—or, more precisely, if sin can exist in a baptized parent without being sin, why that same thing should be sin in the offspring, the answer is that the desire of the flesh is forgiven in Baptism not so that it ceases to exist, but so that it is not counted as sin.

Although its guilt has already been removed, it nevertheless remains until all our weakness is healed through the progressive renewal of the inner person day by day, when the outer person has put on incorruption.

It does not remain substantially, like some body or spirit, but is an affection of a certain evil quality, like weakness. Therefore something does not remain that has not been forgiven, since it happens as it is written: “The Lord is gracious toward all our iniquities.” But until what follows also happens—“who heals all your weaknesses, who redeems your life from corruption” (Ps. 102:3–4)—the desire of the flesh remains in this body of death.

We are commanded not to obey its vicious desires in order to commit unlawful acts, lest sin reign in our mortal body. Yet this desire decreases daily in those who make progress and exercise continence, especially as old age approaches.

Those who wickedly serve it, however, acquire such great strength from it that often, even when their limbs are failing with age and the bodily parts are less able to move for that act, it does not cease to rage with greater shamefulness and insolence.

## Chapter XXVI

### 29. How Desire Remains in the Baptized in Act but Passes Away in Guilt

In those, then, who are regenerated in Christ and receive forgiveness of absolutely all sins, it is necessary that the guilt of this desire—which nevertheless still remains—also be forgiven, so that, as I have said, it is not counted as sin.

For just as, in the case of sins that cannot remain because they pass away when they are committed, their guilt nevertheless remains, and unless it is forgiven will remain forever, so, when the guilt of that desire is forgiven, it is removed.

[Note: “That is, of desire.”]

For not to have sin is not to be guilty of sin. If, for example, someone commits adultery and never commits it thereafter, he is nevertheless guilty of adultery until the guilt itself is forgiven through indulgence.

He therefore has sin, although what he committed no longer exists, because it passed away with the time in which it was done. For if ceasing to sin meant not having sins, it would be enough for Scripture to admonish us in this way: “My son, have you sinned? Do not do it again.” But this is not enough; it adds: “And pray for forgiveness of your former sins, so that they may be forgiven you” (Sir. 21:1).

They therefore remain unless they are forgiven. But how do they remain if they are past, except because they have passed away in act but remain in guilt? In the opposite way, then, it can happen that something remains in act but passes away in guilt.

## Chapter XXVII
### 30. The Desires of Concupiscence Are Evil; We Ought to Will That They Not Exist

For concupiscence of the flesh does something, even when there is not offered to it either [Col. 0431] the consent of the heart, in which it might reign, or the members as weapons by which what it commands may be carried out. But what does it do except produce those very evil and shameful desires? For if they were good and lawful, the Apostle would not forbid us to obey them, saying: “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, so as to obey its desires.” For he does not say, “so as to have its desires,” but “so as to obey its desires.” Since these desires are greater in some and lesser in others, according as each person has progressed in the renewal of the inner human being, let us maintain in this the struggle of righteousness and chastity, so that we do not obey them.

Nevertheless, we ought to will that the desires themselves should not exist, even if we cannot attain this in the body of this death. For this reason, in another passage the same Apostle, speaking as though introducing his own person, instructs us, saying: “For I do not do what I will, but I do what I hate”—that is, I have concupiscence—because he would not wish even to have concupiscence, so that he might be perfect in every respect. “But if,” he says, “I do what I do not will, I agree with the law that it is good,” because the law also does not will what I do not will. For it does not will me to desire, when it says, “You shall not desire”; and I do not will to desire. Thus the will of the law and my own will agree in this.

But because he did not wish to desire, and yet did desire, although he did not in any way serve that same concupiscence by consenting to it, he added and said: “Now, however, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.”

### CHAPTER XXVIII

#### 31. Who Could Say, “It Is No Longer I Who Do It”?

A person is greatly mistaken if, while consenting to the concupiscence of his flesh, deciding and resolving to do what it desires, he thinks that he may still say, “It is not I who do it,” even if he hates it because he consents to it. Both things are present together: he himself hates it, because he knows that it is evil; and he himself does it, because he has resolved to do it.

But if he also adds what Scripture forbids, saying, “Do not offer your members to sin as weapons of iniquity” (Rom. 6:12–13), so that he completes bodily what he has resolved in his heart to do, and therefore says, “It is not I who do it, but sin dwelling in me,” because, while deciding and carrying it out, he displeases himself—then he is so greatly mistaken that he does not even recognize himself. For he is wholly the one who decides in his heart and carries out the act in his body, yet still does not think that he himself is the one who does it.

### CHAPTER XXIX

#### When the Good Is Brought to Perfection

Therefore, when someone says, “It is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me,” he speaks truly if he merely desires; not if he decides with the consent of his heart, or even completes the act through the service of his body.

#### 32. The Apostle then adds:

“For I know that good does not dwell in me—that is, in my flesh. For to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find.”

This is said because the good is brought to perfection when there are no evil desires, just as evil is brought to perfection when one obeys evil desires. When such desires exist but are not obeyed, evil is not brought to perfection, because they are not obeyed; nor is good brought to perfection, because they exist. Yet good is accomplished in part, because the evil concupiscence is not consented to; and evil remains in part, because there is concupiscence at all.

[Col. 0432] Therefore the Apostle does not say that doing good is not present with him, but that accomplishing it is not. For he does much good [Note: [Col. 0432] Several manuscripts read: “For he does much good.”] who does what is written: “Do not go after your desires” (Ecclus. 18:30). But he does not bring it to perfection, because he does not fulfill what is written: “You shall not desire” (Exod. 20:17).

The law therefore said, “You shall not desire,” so that, finding ourselves lying in this sickness, we might seek the medicine of grace; and so that, in this commandment, we might know both the goal toward which we ought to strive as we make progress in this mortal life and the goal that can be reached by us in that most blessed immortality. For unless it were someday to be brought to perfection, it would never have been commanded.

### CHAPTER XXX

#### 33. How Concupiscence Held the Apostle Captive; What the Law of Sin Was for the Apostle

Then, repeating his earlier statement in order to commend it more fully, the Apostle says: “For I do not do the good that I will, but I do the evil that I do not will. But if I do what I do not will, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.”

And he continues: “I find therefore a law for me who desire to do good, that evil is present with me.” This means: I find that a law is present for me who desire to do what the law wills, because it is not the law itself—which says, “You shall not desire”—but the evil that I do not will that is present with me, because, though I do not will it, I nevertheless have concupiscence [Note: [Col. 0432] Several manuscripts read: “because both I do not will it and I have concupiscence.”].

“For I delight,” he says, “in the law of God according to the inner human being; but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members.”

This delight in the law of God according to the inner human being comes to us from the great grace of God. In it our inner human being is renewed from day to day as it makes continual progress in it. For this is not fear that tortures [Note: [Col. 0432] Two Belgian manuscripts read: “that lies dormant.”], but willing love. We are truly free where we do not take delight against our will.

#### 34. But when he says:

“I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind,” this is the very concupiscence of which we are speaking, the law of sin in the flesh of sin.

When he says, “and taking me captive under the law of sin,” this means: under itself, which is in my members. Or by “taking me captive” he means “trying to take me captive,” that is, compelling me to consent and to carry out the desire. Or rather—and this is beyond dispute—he means “taking me captive according to the flesh.” Unless carnal concupiscence held the flesh captive—the concupiscence that he calls the law of sin—it would certainly not stir up in it any illicit desire that the mind ought not to obey.

But since he did not say, “taking my flesh captive,” but “taking me captive,” this led people to seek another interpretation, and we accepted “taking captive” as though he had said “trying to take captive.”

Yet why would he not say “taking me captive” if he wished his flesh to be understood? Was it not said of Jesus, when his flesh was not found in the tomb, “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him” (John 20:2)? Is this therefore not correctly said because it does not say, “the flesh” or “the body of my Lord,” but “my Lord”?

### CHAPTER XXXI

#### 35. The Flesh and the Affect of the Flesh

Although [Col. 0433], a little earlier, the Apostle himself clearly showed how he could rightly say of his flesh, “taking me captive.” For when he had said, “I know that good does not dwell in me,” explaining this very statement he added, “that is, in my flesh.”

This flesh, therefore, is held captive under the law of sin, in which good does not dwell—that is, the flesh. But here he called “flesh” that diseased affect of the flesh, not the bodily structure itself, whose members must not be offered as weapons to sin—that is, to the very concupiscence that holds this carnal part of us captive.

As far as the bodily substance and nature itself are concerned, in faithful men—whether married or continent—it is already the temple of God. Nevertheless, if no part whatever of our flesh were held captive—not, indeed, under the devil, since there too remission of sin has taken place, so that sin is not imputed, which is properly called the law of sin, but under that very law of sin, that is, under its own concupiscence—how could what the same Apostle says be true: “awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body” (Rom. 8:23)?

The redemption of our body is therefore still awaited to the extent that it is still captive in some part under the law of sin. Hence, crying out here also, he says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

What are we to understand here except that “the body, which is corrupted, weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15)? When, therefore, this same body receives incorruptibility, there will be complete liberation from this body of death—a liberation not experienced by those who will rise for punishment.

The body of this death is therefore understood to include the fact that another law in our members indeed wars against the law of the mind, while the flesh desires against the spirit—even though it does not subjugate the mind, because the spirit also desires against the flesh (Gal. 5:17). Thus, although the law of sin itself holds some part of the flesh captive, from which it resists the law of the mind, it nevertheless does not reign in our mortal body, provided that its desires are not obeyed.

For even enemies against whom war is waged can both be inferior in the struggle and hold something captive after being defeated. Although that which is held in our flesh under the law of sin is still held there, it nevertheless exists in the hope of redemption. For that vicious concupiscence will not remain at all, while our flesh, healed of that plague and sickness and clothed wholly in immortality, will remain in eternal blessedness.

#### 36. The Apostle adds and says:

“Therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin.”

This is to be understood as follows: with my mind I serve the law of God by not consenting to the law of sin; but with my flesh I serve the law of sin by having sinful desires, from which, although I do not consent to them, I am not yet entirely free.

Finally, let us observe what he introduces after this: “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”

Even now, he says—even when the law in the members wars against the law of the mind and holds some part captive in this body of death—there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.

Hear why: “For the law of the Spirit of life,” he says, “[Col. 0434] in Christ Jesus has freed me from the law of sin and death” (Rom. 7:15–8:2).

How has it freed me except by dissolving its guilt through the remission of all sins, so that, although it still remains and is diminished more and more from day to day, it is nevertheless not imputed as sin?

### CHAPTER XXXII

#### 37. The Law of Sin with Guilt in Unbaptized Infants; Through Adam the Human Race Became a Wild Olive

[Col. 0434] This remission of sins, so long as it does not take place in the offspring, means that the law of sin is present there in such a way that it is also imputed as sin—that is, its guilt is present with it and holds it liable to eternal punishment [Note: [Col. 0434] The printed editions read: “which holds him liable.” The word “him” is absent from the manuscripts; several of them read “which” rather than “who.”].

For the parent transmits to carnal offspring what he himself is carnally born as, not what he has been spiritually reborn as. The very thing that he is carnally born as, although, once its guilt has been removed, it does not prevent its fruit, nevertheless lies hidden as though in the seed of an olive. Even if, because of the remission of sins, it harms no oil [Note: [Col. 0434] Several manuscripts read: “it harms no olive tree.”]—that is, the life according to Christ, who was named from oil, that is, from chrism, and “the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17)—nevertheless it is concealed there.

What is covered in a regenerated parent, as in the seed of an olive, without any guilt because it has been remitted, is plainly possessed in an offspring not yet regenerated, as in a wild olive, together with guilt, until the same grace remits it there also.

From the time when Adam, by sinning, was changed from such an olive—one in which there was not even seed of the kind from which the bitterness of a wild olive could arise—into a wild olive, because it was so great a sin, involving so great a change of nature for the worse, he made the whole human race a wild olive. Thus, just as we now see in trees themselves, if divine grace converts anything from it into an olive, then the defect of the first birth—original sin, transmitted and drawn from carnal concupiscence—is remitted, covered, and not imputed. Nevertheless, it remains within, from which a wild olive may grow [Note: [Col. 0434] Thus the old Benignian manuscript. The printed editions instead read “from which nevertheless,” omitting “it remains within.”], unless it too is reborn into an olive by the same grace.

### CHAPTER XXXIII

#### 38. Through Baptism There Is Remission of All Sins, and Complete Healing in the Resurrection; What Is Received Must Be Ascribed [to God]; Daily Cleansing

Blessed, therefore, is the olive whose iniquities have been remitted and whose sins have been covered; blessed is the one to whom the Lord has not imputed sin (Ps. 32:1–2).

But that which has been remitted and covered and is not imputed, until the complete transformation into eternal immortality takes place, still possesses a hidden force from which the bitter wild olive may be propagated, unless there too the same cultivation by God remits it, covers it, and does not impute it.

There will, however, be nothing at all defective even in carnal seed when the same regeneration—which now takes place through the sacred washing, cleansing and healing every evil of the human being until the end—makes that same flesh through which the carnal soul was produced itself spiritual also. It will then possess no concupiscence of the flesh resisting the law of the mind and will produce no carnal seed.

This is how we should understand what the same Apostle says: “Christ loved the Church [Col. 0435] and gave himself for her, to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word, so that he might present the Church to himself glorious, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind” (Eph. 5:25–27).

This, I say, must be understood so that, through the same washing of regeneration and the word of sanctification, every evil of regenerated human beings is wholly cleansed and healed—not only the sins that are all remitted now in Baptism, but also those contracted afterward through human ignorance or weakness. This does not mean that Baptism is repeated as often as one sins; rather, because Baptism is given once, it brings about the obtaining of forgiveness for the faithful not only for sins committed previously but also for those committed afterward.

For what benefit would repentance before Baptism have if Baptism did not follow, or repentance afterward if Baptism did not precede it? Even in the Lord’s Prayer, which is our daily cleansing, with what benefit or effect would it be said, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12), unless it were said by those who have been baptized?

Likewise, no matter how great one’s generosity in almsgiving and beneficence, for whose sins would it be useful if he had not been baptized?

Finally, the blessedness of the kingdom of heaven itself—where the Church will have no spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind, where there will be nothing blameworthy and nothing hypocritical, where there will be not only no guilt but also no concupiscence of sin at all—whose will it be except that of the baptized?

### CHAPTER XXXIV

#### 39. Through the Holiness of Baptism Not Only Sins but Every Evil Must Be Removed; The Church Is Not Yet Free from Every Spot

Accordingly, not only all sins but absolutely every evil of human beings is removed through the holiness of the Christian washing. By this washing Christ cleanses his Church so that he may present it to himself—not in this age but in the future—without spot or wrinkle or anything of that kind.

For those who now say that the Church is already such, and yet are themselves within it—since they also confess that they have sins, if they speak the truth—clearly, because they are not cleansed from sins, the Church has a spot in them. But if they speak falsely, because they speak with a divided heart, the Church has a wrinkle in them.

If they say that they possess these things but that the Church herself does not, then let them confess that they are not members of her and do not belong to her body, so that even by their own confession they may be condemned.

### CHAPTER XXXV

#### 40. The Pelagians, Who Praise the Concupiscence of the Flesh as a Natural Good, Are Refuted by the Authority of Blessed Ambrose [Col. 0436]

We have taken care, in a lengthy discussion, to distinguish this concupiscence of the flesh from the goods of marriage because of the new heretics who, whenever it is criticized, bring an accusation as though marriage itself were being criticized. By praising it as a natural good, they seek to strengthen their deadly doctrine, according to which offspring born through it do not inherit any original sin.

Concerning this concupiscence of the flesh, therefore, blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan, through whose priestly ministry I received the washing of regeneration, spoke briefly when, in explaining the prophet Isaiah, he was indicating the carnal birth of Christ:

> “Therefore,” he says, “he was also tempted in every respect as a human being and endured all things in the likeness of human beings; but, as one born from the Spirit, he abstained from sin” (Heb. 4:15). “For every human being is a liar” (Ps. 116:2), “and no one is without sin except the one God. It was therefore preserved that, from man and woman—that is, through that commingling of bodies—no one should appear free from transgression. But whoever is free from transgression is also free from conception of this kind.”

Did not holy Ambrose, by the truth of this statement, condemn not the goodness of marriage but rather the vanity of these heretics, although they had not yet appeared?

I thought this worth recalling because Pelagius praises Ambrose in the following manner:

> “Blessed Ambrose the bishop, in whose books above all the Roman faith shines forth; he was distinguished among Latin writers as a kind of beautiful flower, and not even an enemy dared to criticize his faith and his most pure understanding of the Scriptures” (*On Free Will*, book 3).

Let him therefore repent of what he thought against Ambrose, lest he have to repent of having praised Ambrose in this way.

You have here a book burdensome because of its length and difficult because of the question involved—a book whose dictation was as laborious for me as its reading must be for you. At what small intervals of time it has found, or may find, you at leisure. I would not, in the midst of my ecclesiastical duties, have imposed upon you, amid your public responsibilities, a work which I have labored over as far as the Lord has deigned to help me, unless I had heard from a man of God who knows you more intimately that you read with such pleasure that you even devote some nighttime hours vigilantly to reading.

## Into the Following Book

### Augustine in the Preface to the *Unfinished Work against Julian*

I wrote a book to Count Valerius, entitled *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, because I had learned that the Pelagians were saying to him that we condemn marriage. Finally, in that work I distinguished, with such discussion as I could, the good of marriage from the evil of carnal concupiscence, which conjugal chastity uses well.

After receiving this book, the aforementioned distinguished man sent me on a small sheet some statements excerpted from a work by Julian, the Pelagian heretic. In that work Julian thought that he had answered, in four books, the one book of mine that I have mentioned writing on *Marriage and Concupiscence*. The statements had been sent to him by someone unknown to me, who had arranged for them to be excerpted from Julian’s first book in whatever manner he wished. Valerius asked me to answer them as quickly as possible.

Thus it happened that, under the same title, I also wrote a second book, against which Julian composed eight other books with excessive verbosity.

### The Same, in Letter 207, to Claudius

Whoever, therefore, reads that second book of mine to Count Valerius, likewise written to him, just as he reads the first, should know that in certain matters I did not answer Julian, but rather the person who selected those passages from his books and did not set them down as he found them, but thought that they should be altered somewhat—perhaps so that, in that form, he might make his own what was plainly another’s.

# BOOK TWO [Note: [Col. 0437] Written in the year of Christ 420.]

[Col. 0437]

In this second book Augustine refutes statements of Julian, excerpted by an unknown hand from the first of the four books that Julian had published against the earlier book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, and brought to Augustine at the initiative of Count Valerius. He vindicates the Catholic doctrine concerning original evil from the adversary’s accusations and sophistries, and above all demonstrates that it is far removed from the wicked heresy of the Manichaeans.

### CHAPTER I

#### 1.

Amid the cares of your military service, the distinguished rank that you bear in accordance with your merits, and the necessary business of the state, my most beloved and honored son Valerius, it cannot be adequately expressed with what joy of mind I am delighted to see you burning with such zeal for the divine Scriptures against heretics.

Accordingly, after I read the letter of Your Excellency in which you thank me for the book that I wrote to you, and also urge me to learn through my brother and fellow bishop Alypius what arguments they draw from certain passages of that same heretical book, I was moved to write this response.

I learned this not only from the report of my aforementioned brother, but also by reading the sheets that he produced and that, after his departure from Ravenna, you yourself arranged to send to Rome. In them I was able to find the adversaries’ empty talk, and I proposed, with the Lord’s help, to answer it with as much truth and authority from the divine Scriptures as I could.

### CHAPTER II

#### 2.

The sheet to which I am now replying bears this title at the beginning:

> “Chapters from Augustine’s book, against which I have excerpted a few passages from the books.”

Here I see that the person who sent these writings to Your Excellency wished to excerpt them from some books—so I suppose—for the sake of a quicker response, lest he delay answering your request.

When I considered what books these might be, I thought they were those mentioned by Julian in the letter that he sent to Rome [Note: [Col. 0437] See book 1 of the *Unfinished Work against Julian*, chapter 18], a copy of which also reached me [Note: [Col. 0437] The elegant Cygirannian manuscript and certain others read: “a copy of which reached me,” omitting “also.” The word is likewise absent from the manuscript copies of the *Unfinished Work against Julian*, book 1, chapter 17.].

There he says:

> “They also say that the marriages now being contracted were not instituted by God, as is read in Augustine’s book, against which I have now answered in four little books.”

I believe these passages were excerpted from those books. It might therefore have been better for our purpose to labor at criticizing and refuting his entire work, which he set forth in four volumes, unless I had also been unwilling to postpone my reply, just as you did not postpone sending the writings to which an answer was required [Note: [Col. 0437] He later did this in six books published against Julian, after he had obtained Julian’s complete work. In book 1 of the *Unfinished Work against Julian*, chapter 19, he states that Julian’s work, which he sought in order to refute it, reached him only after a delay.].

#### 3.

From the book that I sent to you, and that is very well known to you, he set down the following words of mine, which he attempted to refute:

> “They most maliciously proclaim that we are condemners of marriage and of the divine work by which God creates human beings from males and females, because we say that those born from such a commingling inherit original sin; and, whatever kind of parents they are born from, we do not deny that they still remain under the devil unless they are reborn in Christ” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, §1).

In these words he omitted the testimony of the Apostle that I inserted, by which he felt himself hard pressed [Note: [Col. 0438] The printed editions read “oppressed.”].

For after I had said that human beings born into the world inherit original sin, I immediately added [Note: [Col. 0438] This is the proper reading, “I immediately added, ‘Concerning this the Apostle says,’” supported by several manuscripts and by book 1, chapter 17, of the *Unfinished Work against Julian*. The printed text reads: “I immediately introduced what the Apostle says.”]:

> “Concerning this the Apostle says: ‘Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned’” (Rom. 5:12).

After omitting this testimony, as I have said, he joined together the other statements quoted above.

For he knows how the faithful hearts of Catholics are accustomed to understand these apostolic words that he omitted—words so straightforward and shining with such great light, which the new heretics strive to obscure and distort through dark and tortuous interpretations.

#### 4.

Then he added other words of mine, where I said:

> “They do not observe that the good of marriage cannot be accused because of the evil of original sin that is drawn from it, just as the evil of adultery and fornication cannot be excused because of the natural good that is born from them. For just as sin, whether it is transmitted from one source or the other, is the work of the devil, so a human being, whether born from one source or the other, is the work of God” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, §1).

Here too he omitted the passages in which he feared the Catholic ears.

For before we came to these words, we had said:

> “Therefore, because we say this—which is contained in the ancient and most firmly established rule of the Catholic faith—these recent advocates of a perverse doctrine, who say that there is no sin in infants to be washed away by the washing of regeneration, slander us either faithlessly or ignorantly, as though we condemned marriage and as though we said that the work of God, that is, the human being born from marriage, is the work of the devil.”

After omitting these words of ours, he follows with those of ours that he set down, as quoted above.

In what he omitted, he feared this: it agrees with the whole heart of the Catholic Church and addresses the faith handed down and founded from ancient times in a kind of clear voice; it also moves that faith most vigorously against them by what we said, namely, “because they say that there is no sin in infants to be washed away by the washing of regeneration.”

For everyone brings infants to the Church for no other reason than that the original sin drawn in the first birth may be expiated through the regeneration of the second birth.

#### 5.

Then he returns to our earlier words, which I do not know why he repeats:

> “We say that those who are born from such a commingling inherit original sin, and, whatever kind of parents they are born from, we do not deny that they still remain under the devil unless they are reborn in Christ.”

He had already stated these words of ours shortly before.

Then he adds what we said about Christ:

> “Who did not wish to be born from the same commingling of the two sexes.”

But here too he omitted what I added:

> “So that through his grace they might be rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of the one who did not wish to be born from the same commingling of the two sexes.”

Observe, I beg you, which words of ours he avoided, as though he were altogether an enemy of the grace of God that comes through Jesus Christ our Lord.

For he knows that, according to the Apostle’s statement concerning God the Father, “who rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 1:13), it is utterly wrong and impious to separate infants from that kingdom. For this reason, no doubt, he preferred to omit these words rather than include them.

#### 6.

After this he set down that passage of ours in which we said:

> “For this shameful concupiscence, which shameless people shamelessly praise, would not exist at all unless the human being had sinned previously. Marriage, however, would exist even if no one had sinned; the generation of children would take place without this sickness.”

This is as far as he set down my words. For he feared what I added:

> “In the body of that life, without which it cannot now take place in the body of this death.”

Here too, so as not to allow my statement to reach its conclusion, but rather to mutilate it in a certain way, he feared the Apostle’s testimony in which he says:

> “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

For the body of this death did not exist in paradise before sin. This is why we said that, “in the body of that life,” which existed there, the generation of children could have taken place without this sickness, whereas now it cannot take place without it “in the body of this death.”

But before the Apostle came to this recollection of human misery and divine grace, he had said:

> “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members.”

After these words he cried out:

> “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:23–25).

Therefore, in the body of this death, such as it was in paradise before sin, there certainly was not another law in our members warring against the law of our mind [Note: [Col. 0439] Two manuscripts and two editions of the polemical works—the Paris edition of 1644 and the Leuven edition of 1647—read: “before sin it did not exist; certainly there was not,” and so forth. Two Vatican manuscripts read: “before sin certainly there was no other law in our members resisting the law,” and so forth. This same reading was found in book 1 of the *Unfinished Work against Julian*, chapter 71.].

For even when we do not wish it, and when we do not consent, and do not offer our members to it so that it may fulfill what it desires, it nevertheless dwells in them and troubles the mind that resists and opposes it. Thus the struggle itself, even if it is not condemnable because it does not complete iniquity, is nevertheless wretched because it does not possess peace.

I have therefore sufficiently shown that he wished to present my words as though they needed refutation in such a way that in some places, after removing the middle portions, he interrupted the statements, and in others, by not adding the endings, he shortened them. I have also adequately shown why he did this.

### CHAPTER III

#### 7.

Now let us examine what he set forth from our writings in the manner he chose, and what he opposed from his own writings. His words now follow, and, as the person who sent you the sheet indicated, he first wrote something from the preface, plainly from those books from which he excerpted a few passages.

It reads as follows:

> “The teachers of our time,” he says, “and the authors of the wicked sedition that still burns, have resolved to reach the insults and destruction of those human beings whose holy endeavors consume them by means of the ruin of the whole Church. They do not understand how much honor they have conferred upon those whose glory they have shown could not be overthrown except together with the Catholic religion.
>
> “For if anyone says either that human beings possess free choice or that God is the creator of those who are born, he is called a Coelestian and a Pelagian. Therefore, lest they be called heretics, they become Manichaeans; and while fearing a false disgrace, they incur a true crime—like wild beasts surrounded by wings so that they may be driven into nets, and, because they lack reason, thrust into genuine destruction by an empty fear” [Note: [Col. 0440] See below, *Unfinished Work*, book 1, chapter 3.].

#### 8.

It is not as you say, whoever you are who said these things; it is not so. You are greatly mistaken, or are attempting to deceive. We do not deny free choice. But “if the Son sets you free,” says the Truth, “then you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

You begrudge this liberator, you who grant a vain freedom to those who are captives. For “by whatever a person is overcome,” as Scripture says, “to that he is enslaved” (2 Pet. 2:19). No one is released from this bond of servitude except through the grace of the liberator, from which no human being is exempt.

For “through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12).

God is therefore the creator of those who are born in such a way that all proceed from one into condemnation unless they have a liberator in rebirth. For he himself is called the potter, making from the same mass one vessel for honor according to mercy and another for dishonor according to judgment (Rom. 9:21). To him the Church sings: “Mercy and judgment” (Ps. 101:1).

Therefore, it is not as you say, deceiving both yourself and others, when you say:

> “If anyone says either that human beings possess free choice or that God is the creator of those who are born, he is called a Coelestian and a Pelagian.”

The Catholic faith says these things.

But if someone says that human beings possess free choice for rightly worshiping God without God’s help, and if anyone says that God is the creator of those who are born in such a way as to deny that infants are redeemed from the power of the devil, that person is called a Pelagian and a Coelestian.

We both say that human beings possess free choice and that God is the creator of those who are born. On this account you are not Coelestians and Pelagians.

But you say that anyone can be free to do good without God’s help, and that infants are not rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of God (Col. 1:13). On this account you are Coelestians and Pelagians.

Why do you hold out the covering of a common doctrine to deceive, so that you may conceal your own crime, from which your name has been given to you? And, in order to frighten the unlearned with a wicked designation, why do you say, “Therefore, lest they be called heretics, they become Manichaeans”?

9. Hear briefly, then, what is at issue in this question. Catholics say that human nature, created good by the good Creator God, has been corrupted by sin and needs Christ the physician. The Manichaeans say that human nature was not created good by God and corrupted by sin, but that man was created by the prince of eternal darkness from the mingling of two natures, which have always existed, one good and one evil. The Pelagians and Coelestians say that human nature was created good by the good God, but that in infants at birth it is so sound that they do not need Christ’s medicine at that age. Recognize, then, your own name in your doctrine, and stop charging the Catholics who refute you with a doctrine and name that belong to someone else. For Truth refutes both parties: both the Manichaeans and you.

To the Manichaeans it says: “Have you not read that he who made them from the beginning made them male and female? And he said, ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.’ Therefore they are no longer two but one flesh. What God has joined, let no man separate” (Matt. 19:4–6). In this way it demonstrates both that God is the creator of human beings and that God is the one who joins husband and wife, against the Manichaeans, who deny both these things.

To you, however, it says: “The Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost” (Luke 19:10). But you, excellent Christians, answer Christ: “If you came to seek and save what was lost, you did not come for infants; they were not lost, and they were born saved. Go to adults. From your own words we bring a charge against you: ‘Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick’” (Matt. 9:12).

Thus it comes about that the Manichaean, who says that an evil nature is mingled with human nature, at least wishes the good soul to be saved from it by Christ; whereas you contend that, since infants are sound in body [Note: [Col. 0441] “In body” is absent from nearly all manuscripts. But it occurs in Book III of the Unfinished Work against Julian, chapter 137.], there is nothing in them for Christ to save. Accordingly, the Manichaean indeed reprehensibly denounces human nature, but you praise it cruelly. For those who believe you as its praiser would not bring their infants to the Savior.

What does it profit you, holding so wicked an opinion [Note: [Col. 0441] The Benignianus manuscript reads “wickedly.”], not to fear what happens to you in order that you may fear salutarily and be made human [Note: [Col. 0441] Erasmus and Lovaniensis, together with later editions, read “not to fear.” But Cygirannensis has “so that it happens to you that you may fear salutarily and you make yourself human.” The Cygirannensis reading is better: nearly all the other manuscripts agree with it in reading “not to fear what happens to you,” namely, the punishments or laws already established by Emperor Honorius against the Pelagian heretics. Julianus accused the Roman clergy, terrified by these measures, of having had no shame in committing the crime of betrayal by declaring that human nature was evil, as we shall see below, in Book II against the Two Letters of the Pelagians, no. 5.], rather than an animal [Col. 0442] surrounded by wings so that it may be driven into nets? You ought to have held to the truth and, for love of it, not feared. But now you do not fear in such a way that, if you feared, you would escape the nets of the wicked one [Note: [Col. 0442] Amianus, Erasmus, and all the manuscripts read “wicked” (maligna).] rather than fall into them. Mother Catholic terrifies you because she fears for you and for others through you; and if, through her sons placed in positions of authority, she acts so that you will fear, she does not act from cruelty but from charity.

But you, a very brave man, consider it cowardly to fear human beings. Fear God, then, and do not attempt with such obstinacy to overthrow the ancient foundations of the Catholic faith. Indeed, would that your bold spirit at least feared human beings in this matter! Would that, I say, it at least feared cowardice [Note: [Col. 0442] Erasmus and later editions add “rather.” It was not found in the manuscripts, nor is it elegantly omitted.], lest audacity destroy it.

## CHAPTER IV

10. Let us examine the other points that he connects with this. But what shall I do? Shall I set out each individual statement of his and answer it? Or, passing over what the Catholic faith contains, shall I deal only with and refute the points in which he departs from the path of truth and attempts to graft the Pelagian heresy, like poisonous shoots, onto Catholic branches?

The latter is certainly shorter. But I think I must take care lest someone, after reading my book but not reading everything he has said, suppose that I was unwilling to set out the points on which these statements of his depend, and from which they are presented as though they consequently proved true what I refute as false. Therefore, let the reader not begrudge giving careful attention and consideration to both things inserted in this little work of ours: what he said and what I answer.

11. The writer who sent the document to Your Dilection prefaced the following points in this way: “Against those,” he says, “who condemn marriage and assign its offspring to the devil.”

Not, then, against us, who neither condemn marriage—which we also praise in its proper order with the appropriate proclamation—nor assign its offspring to the devil. The offspring of marriage are human beings, properly generated from it, not the sins with which they are born. Nor are human beings under the devil because they are human beings, which is where the offspring of marriage is concerned, but because they are sinners, which is where the propagation of vices is concerned. For the devil is the author of guilt, not of nature.

12. Consider also the points by which he thinks he agrees with us under this prefixed title [Note: [Col. 0442] Printed editions read “this”; most manuscripts read “this one.”]. “God,” he says, “who had fashioned Adam from clay, constructed Eve from a rib (Gen. 2:22), and said, ‘She shall be called Life, because she is the mother of all living things.’”

That is not, in fact, how it is written. But what does that have to do with us? It often happens that memory fails concerning the wording while the meaning is nevertheless retained [Note: [Col. 0442] Lovaniensis and later editions read “is retained in the books.” This addition was absent from the older books. See Book IV of the Unfinished Work, chapter 4.]. Nor did God give Eve the name “Life”; her husband did. For it is written: “And Adam called the name of his wife Life, because she herself is the mother [Col. 0443] of all the living” (Gen. 3:20).

Perhaps, however, he understood this as meaning that God gave Eve that name through Adam, as through a prophet [Note: [Col. 0443] Erasmus and most manuscripts read “prophecy.”]. For in the fact that she was called Life and mother of the living there is a great mystery of the Church, about which it would take too long to speak now and which is unnecessary for the work undertaken.

For when the Apostle says, “This is a great mystery, but I speak of Christ and the Church,” Adam himself said, “For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.” Yet the Lord Jesus recalls in the Gospel that God said this (Eph. 5:31–32; Gen. 2:24; Matt. 19:4–5), because God certainly spoke through a human being what the human being had foretold prophetically.

Consider, then, what follows: “At her first naming,” he says, “he showed for what work she had been prepared and said, ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth’” (Gen. 1:28). For which of us denies that woman was prepared for the work of bearing children by the Lord God, the good Creator of all good things?

See what he adds: “Therefore,” he says, “God, the creator of male and female, formed members appropriate for generation and ordained that bodies should be begotten from bodies; yet the power of operation intervenes in their effectiveness [Note: [Col. 0443] Printed editions read “the power of God’s operation intervenes.” “Of God” is absent from the manuscripts and also from Book IV of the Unfinished Work, chapter 5. The entire sentence depends on the words “Therefore God.”], administering everything that exists by the power by which he created it.”

We confess that this too is Catholic teaching. And what he adds next is also true: “If, then,” he says, “a fetus comes only through sex, sex only through the body, and the body only through God, who would doubt that fertility must rightly be attributed to God?”

13. After these statements—which were truly and Catholicly spoken, indeed truly written in the divine books, though not spoken by him in a Catholic manner, because they were not spoken with the intention of a Catholic heart—the reason for which he said them now begins to introduce the Pelagian and Coelestian heresy [Note: [Col. 0443] Some manuscripts read “he begins to introduce the Pelagian and Coelestian heresy.”].

For consider what follows: “But you,” he says, “who say, ‘Whatever sort of parents they may be born from, we do not deny that they are still under the devil unless they are reborn in Christ,’ show us, then, what the devil recognizes as his in the sexes, by which he may rightly possess their offspring, as you say. Is it the diversity of the sexes? But that is in the bodies God made. Is it intercourse? But this is claimed no less by the privilege of blessing than by that of institution. For it is God’s voice: ‘A man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.’ It is God’s voice: ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth.’ Or perhaps it is fertility itself? But fertility is the very purpose for which marriage was instituted.”

## CHAPTER V

14. You see, then, how he asks us what the devil recognizes as his in the sexes, by which those born from whatever kind of parents are under him unless they are reborn in Christ: whether we say that the diversity of the sexes belongs to the devil, or intercourse, or fertility itself.

We answer, then, that none of these does. The diversity of the sexes belongs to the instruments of generation; the intercourse of the two belongs to the sowing of children; and fertility itself belongs to the blessing of marriage. All these things, however, are from God. But in all these matters he did not wish to mention the concupiscence of the flesh, which is not from the Father but from the world (1 John 2:16), whose prince is called the devil.

The devil did not find this concupiscence in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0444] The most ancient Benignianus manuscript reads “God.”], because the Lord did not come to human beings through it. Hence the Lord himself says, “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he finds nothing in me” (John 14:30) [Note: [Col. 0444] Almost all the printed editions read “he will find nothing.”]—nothing, certainly, of sin, neither what is drawn from one at birth nor what is added by one who lives.

This man did not wish to mention concupiscence among all the natural goods he recalled, although it is precisely because of it that even marriages, which glory in all those goods, are subject to shame. For why is the act of married couples withdrawn and hidden even from the eyes of their children, unless it is because they cannot engage in the intercourse that is praised without the lust that causes shame?

Even those who first covered their shameful parts were ashamed of this (Gen. 3:7). Those parts had previously not been shameful, but were like works of God to be proclaimed and gloried in [Note: [Col. 0444] Several, but more recent, manuscripts read “to be praised and proclaimed,” omitting “and gloried in.”]. They covered them, then, when they became ashamed; and they became ashamed when, after their disobedience, they felt their disobedient members.

This praiser of it was also ashamed of it. He mentioned the diversity of the sexes, he mentioned intercourse, he mentioned fertility; but he was ashamed to mention that. It is not surprising that those who praise what we see those who generate being ashamed of are themselves ashamed.

15. But he adds and says: “By what means, then, are those whom God made under the devil?” And, as though answering in our voice, he says: “By sin, not by nature.”

Then, referring his own answer to our response, he says: “But just as a fetus cannot exist without the sexes, so sin cannot exist without the will.”

Yes—precisely so. “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). Through the evil will of that one man, all sinned in him, when all were that one man; and for this reason each individual drew original sin from him.

“For you say,” he continues, “that they are under the devil because they are born from the intercourse of both sexes.”

I plainly say that they are under the devil because of sin. They are not free from sin because they were born from that intercourse, which cannot perform even what is honorable without the lust that causes shame.

The most blessed Ambrose, bishop of the Church of Milan, also said this when he declared that Christ’s bodily birth was free from sin because his conception was free from the intercourse of the two sexes, and that no human being conceived through that intercourse is without sin. For these are his words:
