“Therefore,” he says, “he was tempted in every respect as a human being and endured all things in the likeness of human beings; yet, as one born of the Spirit, he abstained from sin (Heb. 4:15). For ‘every human being is a liar’ (Ps. 115:2), and no one is without sin except God alone. Therefore,” he says, “it was preserved as a fact that, when born from a man and a woman—that is, through that intercourse of bodies—no one appears to be free from sin. But whoever is free from sin is also free from conception of this kind [Note: [Col. 0445] Ambrose, On Isaiah.].”

Will you also dare to call this man a Manichaean, O Pelagians and Coelestians? The heretic Jovinianus called him that, against whose impiety that holy man also defended the perpetual virginity of holy Mary after childbirth.

If, then, you do not dare to call him a Manichaean, why do you call us Manichaeans when we defend the Catholic faith in the same matter and with the same judgment? Or, if you boast that even that most faithful man understood this according to the Manichaeans, boast away—boast away—so that you may more perfectly fill up Jovinianus’s measure [Note: [Col. 0445] Several manuscripts omit “more perfectly”; the Benignianus manuscript has “defect” in its place.]. Together with that man of God, we patiently endure your curses and insults.

And yet your heresiarch Pelagius praises Ambrose’s faith and utterly pure understanding of Scripture so highly that he says not even an enemy dared to criticize him. Consider, then, how far you have advanced, and at last restrain yourselves from Jovinianus’s presumption.

Although Jovinianus, by praising marriage excessively, made it equal to holy virginity, he nevertheless did not deny that Christ the Savior and Redeemer was necessary for the offspring of marriage, even from the womb, and that they needed to be saved from the power of the devil. You deny this. And because we resist you for the salvation of those who cannot yet speak on their own behalf and for the foundations of the Catholic faith, you boast that we are Manichaeans.

But let us now examine what follows.

## CHAPTER VI

16. Again, asking a question, he says: “Whom, then, do you confess to be the author of infants? The true God?”

I answer: “The true God” [Note: [Col. 0445] Lovaniensis reads “He answers.”].

Then he adds: “But he did not make evil.”

And again he asks whether we confess the devil to be the author of infants. Again he answers: “But he himself did not create human nature.”

Then, as though drawing a conclusion, he says: “If intercourse is evil, the formation of bodies is deformed, and therefore you also assign the bodies to an evil author.”

I answer him: I do not assign bodies to an evil author, but sins, on account of which it happened that, although everything in bodies—that is, in God’s works—was pleasing, there nevertheless occurred to male and female something of which they would be ashamed; so that the intercourse was not of the kind that could have existed in the body of that life, but of the kind we see in the body of this death, in which they blush.

“But God,” he says, “divided in sex what he joined in operation. Therefore the intercourse of bodies comes from the one from whom the origin of bodies comes.”

We have already answered above that these things are from God, but not sin—not the disobedience of the members through the concupiscence of the flesh, which is not from the Father.

Then he says: “Therefore, so many good things—namely, bodies, sexes, and unions—cannot have evil offspring; nor are human beings made by God for this purpose, that they should be held by the devil, as you say, by legitimate right” [Col. 0446].

It has already been said that they are not held for the reason that they are human beings, which is the name of nature, whose author the devil is not, but because they are sinners, which is the name of guilt, whose author the devil is.

## CHAPTER VII

17. Yet among all the names of good things—bodies, sexes, and unions—he does not name lust or the concupiscence of the flesh. He is silent because he is ashamed; and it is remarkable—if one may put it so—that he is shameless in his shame: he is ashamed to name what he is not ashamed to praise.

Finally, observe how he preferred to signify it by circumlocution rather than name it. “After the man,” he says, “knew his wife through natural appetite.”

Here again he did not wish to say, “He knew his wife through the concupiscence of the flesh,” but “through natural appetite.” By this we can still understand the righteous and honorable will by which he wished to beget children, not that lust of which he is so ashamed that he prefers to speak ambiguously to us [Note: [Col. 0446] The manuscripts read “ambiguously” in the masculine or neuter form rather than the adverbial form “ambiguously.”], rather than clearly express what he means.

What is “natural appetite”? Is it not also a natural appetite to wish to be saved, and to wish to receive, nourish, and educate children—an appetite belonging to reason, not lust?

But because we know his intention, we think that by these words he wished to signify nothing other than the lust of the genital members. Do these words not seem to you to be fig leaves [Note: [Col. 0446] Erasmus and several manuscripts read “fig-tree leaves.”], under which something else is hidden—namely, the very thing that causes shame? Thus he has woven for himself the barriers of this circumlocution, just as those first people sewed themselves coverings.

Let him weave and say [Note: [Col. 0446] Lovaniensis reads “he wove and said.”]: “After the man knew his wife through natural appetite, divine Scripture says: ‘Eve conceived and bore a son, and called his name Cain.’ But let us hear,” he says, “what Adam says: ‘I have acquired a man through God’ (Gen. 4:1). From this it is clear that he whom Scripture testifies was acquired through God is God’s work.”

Who could doubt this? Who, especially a Catholic Christian, could deny it? Man is God’s work. But the concupiscence of the flesh, without which, if sin had not preceded it, man would have been sown in obedience to a peaceful will, with the genital members obeying as the other members do, is not from the Father but from the world (1 John 2:16).

18. But now, I beg you, look somewhat more attentively at what name he has found by which once again to conceal what he is ashamed to reveal. “For Adam had begotten him,” he says, “by the power of his members, not by a diversity of merits.”

What he means by “a diversity of merits,” I confess I do not understand. But by “the power of his members,” I believe he meant what he is plainly ashamed to say. For he preferred to say “the power of the members” rather than “the concupiscence of the flesh.”

Certainly, even if he did not think of it, he has signified something that appears relevant to the matter. For what is more powerful than human members when they do not serve the human will? Although their use may be restrained by temperance or continence, their movement is nevertheless not under human control.

Adam therefore begot children by this “power,” as he calls it, “of his members,” of which he was ashamed after sin and before he begot them. If he had not sinned, however, he would not have begotten them by the power of his members but by the obedience of his members. He himself would have been powerful enough to command them by his will, with them subject to him, if he too had served, by that same will, one more powerful than himself.

## CHAPTER VIII

19. “After some time,” he says, “divine Scripture again says: ‘Adam knew Eve his wife, and she conceived and bore a son, and called his name Seth, saying, “The Lord has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel, whom Cain killed”’ (Gen. 4:25).”

Then he adds: “As evidence of the institution of intercourse, divinity is said to have raised up the seed itself.”

This man did not understand what is written. He thought that the words “The Lord has raised up for me another seed in place of Abel” were said so that it would be believed that God had aroused in him the desire for intercourse, by whose movement the seed would be aroused so that it could be poured into the woman’s womb.

He does not know [Note: [Col. 0447] Printed editions here add “for another reason.”] that the statement was not “He aroused seed for me” but “He gave me a son.” Adam did not say this after his intercourse, in which he emitted seed, but after his wife’s childbirth, in which, by God’s gift, he received a son.

For what kind of rejoicing is there—unless perhaps among lustful people who possess their own vessel in the disease of desire, contrary to the Apostle’s command (1 Thess. 4:5)—if seed is poured out in the final pleasure of intercourse [Note: [Col. 0447] Amianus reads “if seed is poured out apart from the pleasure of intercourse.” Erasmus reads “if seed is poured out apart from the will involved in intercourse.”], without conception or childbirth following, when the true offspring of marriage is found?

20. I do not say this because anyone other than the supreme and true God should be thought to be the creator either of human seed or of the human being formed from seed [Note: [Col. 0447] Amianus, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read “to exist as the creator of the human being.”]. Rather, if sin had not preceded, human beings would have emerged from the peaceful obedience of the members at the command of the will.

Nor is the issue now the nature of seed [Note: [Col. 0447] Lovaniensis reads “the nature of human seed.” Amianus, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read “the nature of man.”], but its defect. That nature has God as its author; from this defect, however, original sin is drawn.

For if seed itself has no defect, what is meant by what is written in the Book of Wisdom: “Not unaware that their generation was wicked, and their natural malice, and that their thinking could not be changed forever; for their seed was accursed from the beginning” (Wis. 12:10–11) [Note: [Col. 0447] The printed editions read “for their seed was accursed”; “their” is absent from the manuscripts and from the sacred Bibles.]?

Whoever these words concern, they concern human beings. How, then, is the wickedness of every human being natural and the seed accursed from the beginning, unless reference is made to the fact that “through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12)?

And whose evil thought cannot be changed forever except because it cannot change itself, unless divine grace comes to its aid? When that aid does not come, what are human beings except what the Apostle Peter says: “Like irrational animals, creatures born naturally for captivity and destruction” (2 Pet. 2:12) [Note: [Col. 0448] Here and shortly below, Lovaniensis and some manuscripts read “in captivity and in destruction.”]?

Accordingly, in one passage the Apostle Paul recalls both things: the wrath of God with which we are born and the grace by which we are freed: “We all,” he says, “once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of our inclinations; and we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest. But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ, by whose grace we have been saved” (Eph. 2:3–5).

What, then, is the natural wickedness of man, the seed accursed from the beginning, those naturally born for captivity and destruction, and nature’s children of wrath? Was this nature so created in Adam? Far from it. But because in him it was corrupted, it has now flowed and continues to flow naturally through all human beings, so that no one frees them from this destruction except the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

## CHAPTER IX

21. What, then, is the point of what he adds concerning Noah and his sons, namely, that they “were blessed in the same way as Adam and Eve, God saying, ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth, and rule over it’” (Gen. 9:1–2)?

To these words of God he adds his own, saying: “Therefore this pleasure, which you wish to appear diabolical, already existed in the aforementioned married couples; and just as it remained through a good institution, so also it remained through a blessing. For there is no doubt that the words ‘Increase and multiply, and fill the earth’ were spoken to Noah and his sons concerning this intercourse of bodies, the use of which had by then become established.”

There is no need to repeat the same things at length. The issue here is the defect by which good nature has been corrupted, whose author is the devil—not the goodness of nature itself, whose author is God. Yet God did not withhold his goodness even from nature after it had been corrupted and depraved. He did not take away from man [Note: [Col. 0448] Printed editions and most manuscripts read “human beings”; the Benignianus manuscript reads “man.”] fertility, vitality, health, or the very substance of soul and body, sensation and reason, food, nourishment, and growth. He also makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and rains upon the just and the unjust (Matt. 5:45), and every good thing belonging to human nature comes from the good God, even in those human beings [Note: [Col. 0448] The printed editions add “is” after “human beings.”] who will not be freed from evil.

22. Yet here too he spoke of pleasure, because pleasure can also be honorable. He did not speak of the concupiscence of the flesh or of lust, which causes shame. But in what follows he disclosed his embarrassment and could not conceal what nature itself forcefully prescribed.

“And that saying,” he continues, “‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’ (Gen. 2:24).” Then, adding his own words to these words of God, he says: “To express the truth of the works, the prophet approached near the danger of shame.”

O completely open confession, wrenched forth by the force of truth [Col. 0449]!

The prophet, then, in order to express the truth of the works, approached near the danger of shame because he said, “The two shall be one flesh,” where he wished the intercourse of male and female to be understood.

Let the reason be stated why, in expressing God’s works, the prophet approached near the danger of shame. Is it really the case that human works ought not to be shameful but plainly ought to be gloried in, while divine works are shameful? Is it really the case that, in proclaiming and expressing God’s works, the prophet’s love or labor is not honored but his modesty is endangered?

For what could God have done that would make his herald ashamed to speak of it? And, what is more serious, why should a man be ashamed of some work that not man but God performed in man, when all craftsmen work with as much labor and skill as they can [Note: [Col. 0449] The better manuscripts read “as much as possible” rather than “as much labor.”] so that they will not be ashamed of their works?

But certainly it is that of which those first human beings were ashamed that now causes us shame [Note: [Col. 0449] Some manuscripts read “now” rather than “certainly”], when they covered their shameful parts. That is the punishment of sin; that is the wound and trace of sin; that is the enticement and fuel of sin; that is the law in the members resisting the law of the mind; that is the disobedience arising from ourselves against ourselves, repaid to the disobedient by a most just reciprocity.

We are ashamed of this, and rightly ashamed. For if this were not so, what would be more ungrateful or irreligious than for us to be ashamed in our members not of our defect or punishment but of the works of God?

## CHAPTER X

23. This man also says many useless things about Abraham and Sarah, explaining how they received a son by promise. At last he names concupiscence, but he does not add “of the flesh,” because that itself causes shame.

Yet sometimes there is reason to glory in the name “concupiscence,” since there is also “the concupiscence of the Spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17), and there is also a concupiscence for wisdom (Wis. 6:21).

He says, then: “Surely you have defined this concupiscence, without which there is no fertility, as naturally evil [Note: [Col. 0449] Lovaniensis reads “evil.”]. How, then, is it aroused in the aged through a heavenly gift? Now prove, if you can, that this belongs to the work of the devil, which you see God bestowing as a gift.”

He speaks as though the concupiscence of the flesh had previously been absent from them and God had given it to them. It was undoubtedly present in the body of this death; what was lacking was fertility, whose author is God, and that was granted when God willed it.

But far be it from us to say what he thought we would say: that Isaac was begotten without the heat of intercourse.

## CHAPTER XI

24. But let him now say why the soul of the child would perish from his people if he were not circumcised on the eighth day; what sin he himself had committed, what offense he had given God, that he should be punished by so severe a sentence for another person’s negligence, if there were no original sin.

For concerning the circumcision of infants God commanded as follows: “The male who is not circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin [Note: [Col. 0449] Erasmus, Lugdunensis, Venetiensis, and Lovaniensis read “in his flesh”; M. reads “flesh.”] on the eighth day—his soul shall perish from his people, because he has broken my covenant” (Gen. 17:14).

Let him say, if he can, how that eight-day-old child, so far as he himself was concerned an innocent infant, broke God’s covenant. Yet God or Holy Scripture would in no way say this falsely.

He therefore broke God’s covenant—not the covenant concerning the commanded circumcision, but the one concerning the prohibition of the tree—when through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.

This was signified as being cleansed by circumcision on the eighth day, that is, by the sacrament of the Mediator who was to come in the flesh. For by the same faith in Christ who was to come in the flesh, die for us, and rise again on the third day—which, after the seventh day of the week, would be the eighth—also the righteous of ancient times were saved.

“He was handed over because of our sins and rose again because of our justification.” From the time circumcision was instituted among the people of God, which was then the sign of the righteousness of faith (Rom. 4:25, 11), it was effective as a sign of the cleansing of original and ancient sin even in infants [Note: [Col. 0450] From the Benignianus manuscript we add “thus,” and also “in” before “infants.”], just as Baptism, from the time it was instituted, began to be effective for the renewal of man [Note: [Col. 0450] In Amianus and Erasmus, chapter 12 begins here.].

This is not to say that before circumcision there was no righteousness of faith. For while he was still uncircumcised, Abraham himself was justified by faith, the father of the nations that would follow his faith. But in earlier times the sacrament of justification by faith was entirely hidden.

Nevertheless, the same faith in the Mediator saved the righteous of ancient times, the little with the great—not the Old Testament, which generates for slavery (Gal. 4:24), nor the law, which was not given in such a way that it could give life (Gal. 3:21), but the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom. 7:25).

For as we believe that Christ came in the flesh, so they believed that he would come; as we believe that he died, so they believed that he would die; as we believe that he rose again, so they believed that he would rise again; and both we and they believed that he would come for the judgment of the living and the dead.

Therefore, by defending human nature wrongly, let him not hinder it from salvation, since we are all born under sin and are freed by the one who alone was born without sin.

## CHAPTER XII

25. “This intercourse of bodies,” he says, “with heat, pleasure, and seed, was made by God and is approved as praiseworthy in its own measure; sometimes it even becomes a great gift of the godly.”

He said “with heat”; he said “with pleasure”; he said “with seed.” Yet he did not dare to say “with lust.” Why, unless because he is ashamed to name what he is not ashamed to praise [Note: [Col. 0450] Amianus, Erasmus, and all the manuscripts read “he is ashamed to name it, he is not ashamed to praise it,” omitting “what”?]

The gift of the godly is the fruitful propagation of children, not the shameful agitation of the members. Nature in health would not have had this agitation in generating children; now, however, corrupted nature has it.

Accordingly, the one who is born from it needs to be reborn in order to be a member of Christ; and the one from whom he is born, if he has already been reborn, needs to be freed from that law of sin which exists in the body of this death.

Since this is so, how does he add and say, “You must therefore confess that the original sin which you had invented has perished”?

I did not invent original sin, which the Catholic faith believes from ancient times [Col. 0451] [Note: [Col. 0451] The manuscripts read “believes.” The printed editions read “believed.”]. But you, who deny it, are undoubtedly a new heretic.

By God’s judgment, all who are generated with sin are under the devil unless they are regenerated in Christ.

## CHAPTER XIII

26. But because he had been speaking about Abraham and Sarah, he added and said: “If you say, ‘The use existed in them, but there was no offspring,’ I shall reply: ‘The one whom the Creator promised, the Creator gave. What is born is not the work of intercourse but the work of God, who is born. For he who first made man from dust (Gen. 2:7) fashions everyone from seed. Therefore, just as the clay that was taken as material was not the author of man, so now that force of pleasure, which produces and mingles seeds, does not fulfill the place of the operation; rather, it offers to God from the treasuries of nature the material from which he deigns to make man.’”

Everything he has said here, except his statement that seeds are produced and mingled by pleasure, he would correctly say if he were trying to defend a Catholic understanding in these matters. But because we know what he is striving to accomplish through them, he clearly speaks perversely even when he says things that are correct.

That one point, then—apart from which I do not deny that the rest is true—is not true for this reason: that pleasure, namely the concupiscence of the flesh, does not produce the seeds. Rather, the seeds already created in bodies by the true God, by whom the bodies themselves are also created, are not made by pleasure [Note: [Col. 0451] Amianus, Erasmus, and all the manuscripts read “are not made pleasure,” omitting the preposition “by.”], but are aroused and emitted with pleasure.

Whether the seeds of both sexes are mingled with pleasure in the woman’s womb, let women determine from what they feel in their hidden organs. It is not fitting for us to be pointlessly curious about such matters.

That lust, however, which ought to cause shame and from which the very members are called “shameful,” did not exist in the body of that life which was in paradise before sin. It began in the body of this death as a retributive disobedience after sin.

Without that lust, the act of married couples in generating children could have been performed, just as many acts are performed through the obedience of the other members without any such burning of the limbs [Note: [Col. 0451] Lovaniensis reads “any.”]: they are moved by the command of the will, not aroused by the heat of lust.

### 27

“Consider the rest,” he says. “The authority of the Apostle also confirms this. For when blessed Paul was speaking about the resurrection of the dead, he said: ‘Fool, what you sow is not made alive.’ And below: ‘But God gives it a body as he wills, and to each of the seeds its own body’ (1 Cor. 15:36–38). ‘If, then,’ he says, ‘God assigns to human seed—which no prudent or pious person denies—a body of its own, just as he does to all things, how will you prove anyone to have been born guilty?’

“Finally, I ask you to consider what snares suffocate the assertion of natural sin. But come,” he says, “I beg you, deal more gently with yourself. Believe me, God made you too; but, as must be admitted, a grave error has infected you. For what could be said more profanely than that God either did not make man, or—as you say—made him for the devil, or certainly that the devil is God’s image, that is, that he fashioned man? The latter is recognized as no less foolish than impious.

“Is God, then,” he says, “so destitute and shameless that he had nothing to give holy men as their reward except what the devil infused into those who had been deceived, in vice [Note: [Col. 0452] Lovaniensis reads *in initio*, ‘in the beginning.’ But Am. Er. and most manuscripts read *in vitio*, ‘in vice.’ Perhaps *in vitium*, ‘into vice,’ should be read, since *in praemium*, ‘as a reward,’ precedes.]?

“Do you wish to know that God is also proved to have bestowed this generative power upon those who are not holy? At the time, then, when Abraham, terrified by fear of a barbarian nation, called Sarah, who was his wife, his sister, it is reported that Abimelech, king of that region, took her away for the use of the night. But God, who was concerned for the honor of the holy woman, came to Abimelech in a dream and restrained the king’s boldness, threatening him with death if he continued to violate the marriage.

“Then Abimelech said: ‘Will you destroy an ignorant and righteous nation, Lord? Did they not themselves say that they were related? Abimelech therefore rose in the morning, took a thousand didrachmas [Note: [Col. 0452] The manuscripts have *didragma*, in accordance with the Greek.] of silver, sheep, calves, male and female servants, and gave them to Abraham; and he sent the woman away from him untouched. Abraham, however, prayed to God for Abimelech; and God healed Abimelech, his wife, and his female servants.’”

But why he related all this at such length, understand briefly from what he immediately added: “‘God,’ he says, ‘when Abraham prayed, healed by the hidden power of his dispensation [Note: [Col. 0452] Most manuscripts read *curavit potentia dispensationis secretae*, ‘he healed by the hidden power of his dispensation.’ Some then have *quae mota est*, ‘which was moved’; others *quae nota est*, ‘which is known’; but most, omitting *quae*, have *ammota* or *admota*, ‘removed’ or ‘applied.’ All the manuscripts have *verecundis*, ‘the genitals.’ Perhaps the reading should be *curavit potentiam dispensationis secretae*, ‘he restored the power of his hidden dispensation.’ For Julianus shortly before calls this the ‘power of generation,’ and above, in section 18, the ‘power of the members’; likewise below, in book 5 of *Against Him*, chapter 5, he speaks of a ‘hidden dispensation.’], which had been removed from the genitals of base women, because God had closed from without every womb in the house of Abimelech’” (Gen. 20).

“See, therefore,” he says, “whether that should be called naturally evil which an angered God sometimes takes away and, when appeased, restores. He himself,” he says, “makes the children of both the pious and the impious, since the fact that they become parents belongs to nature, which rejoices in God as its author; but the fact that they are impious belongs to the perversity of their pursuits, which comes to each person from free choice.”

### CAPUT XIV

#### 28

To all these many things that he has said we respond that none of the divine testimonies he inserted was spoken about the shameful lust which, as we say, was not in the bodies of the blessed when they were naked and were not ashamed (ibid. 2:25).

For, first, that statement of the Apostle about seeds was spoken about grains of wheat, which first die so that they may be made alive. This apostolic sentence, for reasons I do not know, he did not wish to complete; for he quoted it only this far: “Fool, what you sow is not made alive.” But the Apostle adds: “unless it dies.”

In my judgment, however, he wanted those who read these things—people who either do not know or do not remember the holy Scriptures—to understand what was said about grains as referring to human seed. Thus he not only abbreviated the sentence by failing to add “unless it dies,” but also omitted what follows, where the Apostle made clear what seeds he was speaking about. For the Apostle says: “And what you sow, you do not sow the body that is to be, but a bare grain, perhaps of wheat or of some other kind.”

After omitting these words, he joined together what the Apostle says next: “But God gives it a body as he wills, and to each of the seeds its own body” (1 Cor. 15:36–38), as though the Apostle had been speaking of a man engaging in intercourse when he said: “Fool, what you sow is not made alive”—so that we might understand that human seed is made alive not by the man who sows children through intercourse, but by God.

For he had previously said that “that pleasure does not perform the function of the operation, but offers God from the treasures of nature the material from which he may deign to fashion man.” He then added the testimony, as though the Apostle had said: “Fool, what you sow is not made alive”—that is, “it is not made alive by you, but God fashions a man from your seed.” It is as though the intervening words, which he omitted, had not been spoken by the Apostle, and his sentence stood as though he were speaking about human seed: “Fool, what you sow is not made alive; but God gives it a body as he wills, and to each of the seeds its own body.”

Finally, after these words of the Apostle, he introduces his own argument in this way: “If, then,” he says, “God assigns to human seed—which no prudent or pious person denies—a body of its own, just as he does to all things,” as though the Apostle had spoken about human seed in that passage.

#### 29

When I considered more carefully what advantage this fraud could bring to his purpose, I could discover nothing except that he wanted to enlist the Apostle as a witness in order to prove that God fashions man from human seed—which is also what we say. Since no testimony occurred to him, he fraudulently abused this one, fearing, of course, that if it became clear that the Apostle had spoken not about human seed but about grains, we would be reminded of the point from which his argument could be refuted: he is a bashful namer but a shameless advocate of lustful pleasure, not of religious intention.

For he can himself be refuted by the very seeds that farmers sow in the fields. Why should we not believe that God could have granted the blessed man in paradise, from his own seed, what we see granted to farmers from the seed of wheat—so that seed might be sown in that way without any shameful lust, with the genital members obedient to the command of the will, just as wheat is sown without any shameful lust, with the farmers’ hands obedient to the command of their will?

In the case of parents, the desire to beget children would have been more honorable than the desire of plowmen to fill their granaries. Then the omnipotent Creator, everywhere present with his undefiled [Note: [Col. 0453] Am. Er. and many manuscripts read *incommutabili*, “unchangeable,” instead of *incontaminabili*, “undefiled.”] presence and creative power, would have fashioned from human seed in the woman whatever he willed—as he still does—just as from grains of wheat he fashions in the earth whatever he wills. Blessed mothers would have conceived without lustful pleasure and given birth without painful groaning, since in that happiness, and in a body not yet subject to this death but belonging to that life, women would have had nothing shameful in receiving seed, just as they would have had nothing painful in giving birth to their offspring.

Whoever does not believe [Note: [Col. 0453] The printed editions read *Quisquis autem non credit*, “Whoever, however, does not believe.” *Autem* is absent from the manuscripts.]—or does not wish to believe—that God could have granted this by his will and kindness to human beings living in that paradisal happiness before every sin is not a praiser of desirable fertility but a lover of shameful pleasure.

### CAPUT XV

#### 30

Likewise, what relevance does the other testimony from the divine book have—the one he cited concerning Abimelech, when, by God’s will, every womb in his household was closed so that his women could not give birth, and was opened again so that they could? What does this have to do with the matter? What does it have to do with that shameful lust which is now under discussion?

Did God take lust itself away from those women and restore it when he wished? Rather, the inability to give birth was a punishment, whereas the ability to give birth was a benefit, in the manner of this corruptible flesh [Note: [Col. 0454] Most manuscripts read *corporis*, “body,” instead of *carnis*, “flesh.”].

For God would not have bestowed upon this body of death such a benefit as would belong only to that body of life which existed in paradise before sin: namely, that conception should occur without itching lust and birth without torturing pain.

Why should we not understand—since Scripture says that every womb was closed from without—that the women were prevented by some pain from enduring intercourse, a pain inflicted when God was angry [Note: [Col. 0454] The Vatican manuscripts read *irascente*, “when he was angry.” Several others read *suscitante*, “when he stirred up.”], and removed when he showed mercy?

For if lust had to be removed in order to prevent the sowing of offspring, it would have had to be removed from the men, not the women. A woman could have intercourse by her will even if the lust that stimulated her had ceased, provided that the lust by which the man was aroused had not failed him.

Unless perhaps, because it is written that Abimelech himself was healed, he will say that masculine lust was restored to him. Yet if he had lost it, why was he divinely warned not to have intercourse with Abraham’s wife? He says that Abimelech was healed because his household was healed from that affliction.

### CAPUT XVI

#### 31

Let us now examine those three possibilities, any one of which, he says, would be the most profane thing imaginable: either that God did not make man, or that God made man for the devil, or that the devil is God’s image—that is, that the devil fashioned man.

He himself confesses that the first and the last of these are not said by us, provided that he is not senseless or excessively obstinate. The question concerns the middle alternative, which he placed second, where he is so mistaken that he supposes us to say that God made man for the devil—as though, in the case of human beings whom God creates from human parents, God intended, cared about, and arranged by the plan of his work that the devil should have servants whom he himself is unable to make.

Far be it from any kind of piety, even childish piety, to suspect this. In his goodness God makes human beings: the first without sin, and the rest under sin, for the purposes of his profound designs.

For just as, concerning the malice of the devil himself, God knows what he is doing, and what he does is just and good, although the one about whom he acts is unjust and evil—and God did not therefore refuse to create him because he foresaw that he would become evil—so, concerning the entire human race, although no human being is born without the stain of sin, the supremely good God accomplishes a good work: making some as vessels of mercy, whom grace distinguishes from those who are vessels of wrath; and others as vessels of wrath, in order to make known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy.

Let him now go and argue against the Apostle, whose sentence this is—or rather, against the potter himself, to whom the Apostle forbids us to reply, saying: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Will the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” (Rom. 9:20–23).

Does he therefore deny that the vessels of wrath are under the devil? Or, because they are under the devil, does someone other than the one who makes the vessels of mercy make them? Or does he make them from some other material and not from the same lump?

Let him say here: “Then God makes vessels for the devil,” as though God did not know how to use them for his just and good works, just as he makes use of the devil himself.

### CAPUT XVII

#### 32

Or does he feed and nourish the children of destruction, the goats on the left hand (Matt. 25:33), for the devil, because he makes his sun rise over the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust (ibid. 5:45)?

Thus he creates the evil in the same way that he feeds and nourishes the evil: what he grants them in creating belongs to the goodness of nature; and the increase he gives them by feeding and nourishing them is not an aid to their evil, but a good aid to that same good nature which the good God created.

Insofar as they are human beings, it is good, belonging to the nature whose author is God. But insofar as they are born with sin and will perish if they are not reborn [Note: [Col. 0455] Am. Er. and many manuscripts read *perituri qui non renascuntur*, “those who will perish if they are not reborn.” The same reading occurs below, in *Unfinished Work*, book 3, chapter 142, and book 5, chapter 64.], they belong to the seed cursed from the beginning (Wis. 12:11), through the fault of that ancient disobedience.

Yet the maker makes good use even of the vessels of wrath, in order to make known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy, so that no one may attribute it to his own merits if, belonging to the same lump, he is freed by grace; rather, “whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord” (2 Cor. 10:17).

### CAPUT XVIII

#### 33

Departing from this most truthful and firmly established apostolic and catholic faith, and joining the Pelagians, he does not want those who are born to be under the devil, lest infants be carried to Christ so that they may be rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into his kingdom (Col. 1:13).

And so he accuses the Church spread throughout the whole world, in which everywhere all infants who are to be baptized are exsufflated for no other reason than that the prince of this world may be driven out from them (John 12:31). For it is necessary that the vessels of wrath be possessed by him when they are born from Adam, unless they are reborn in Christ and, having been made vessels of mercy by grace, are transferred into his kingdom.

When he comes against this most firmly established truth, he does not wish to appear to attack the whole Church of Christ. Instead, as though addressing and correcting me alone, and as though admonishing me, he says: “God made you too; but, as must be admitted, a grave error has infected you.”

I readily acknowledge and give thanks that God made me. Yet I would have perished with the vessels of wrath if he had made me only from Adam and had not remade me in Christ. Since he does not believe this, being possessed by Pelagian impiety, if he persists in so great an evil to the end, let the Catholics judge what kind and how great an error has infected him—or rather, has plainly destroyed him.

### CAPUT XIX

#### 34

Consider what follows: “But let us learn from the Apostle that children conceived in marriage are naturally good. Speaking of the wicked, he says: ‘Abandoning the natural use of the female, they burned in their desires for one another, males committing shameful acts with males’ (Rom. 1:27).

“He therefore shows,” he says, “that the use of the female is both natural and, in its proper measure, praiseworthy; but that the disgrace arises from one’s own will, exercised against the modesty of the institution.

“Accordingly,” he says, “in those who use it properly, both the kind and the measure of desire are rightly praised; but in the shameful, its excess is punished. Finally, at the same time God invigorated the bodies of Abraham and Sarah, withered by age” (Gen. 21:1), “when in Sodom he punished the same thing with a fiery rain” (ibid. 19:24–25).

“If, then,” he says, “you think the vigor of the members should be condemned because through it the Sodomites forgot their crimes [Note: [Col. 0456] Am. Er. and some manuscripts read *obligati*, “bound,” instead of *obliti*, “forgetful.” The Cygirannensis manuscript has *obvoluti*, “wrapped up”; the Casalensis has *obruti*, “overwhelmed.” Other manuscripts and Lovaniensis read *obliti*. This is a manner of expression familiar to Julianus; thus, in book 5 against him, chapter 7: “Let him be stained with the filth of crimes.”], you will also condemn the creation of bread and wine, since divine Scripture has indicated that they too sinned through these things.

“For the Lord says through the prophet Ezekiel: ‘Nevertheless, these were the iniquities of your sister Sodom: pride; she and her daughters overflowed in fullness of bread and abundance of wine, and they did not assist the poor and needy’ (Ezek. 16:49).

“Choose now,” he says, “which you prefer: either regard the union of bodies as a divine work, or declare the creation of bread and wine to be likewise evil. If you do this, you will plainly be convicted of being a Manichaean.

“Whoever keeps the proper measure of natural desire uses a good thing well; whoever does not keep the proper measure uses a good thing badly.

“What do you say, then?” he asks. “Thus the good of marriage cannot be accused because of the original evil drawn from it, just as the evil of adultery cannot be excused because of the natural good born from it” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, section 1).

“By these arguments,” he says, “you have conceded what you had denied and taken away what you had conceded; and you labor at nothing more than making yourself poorly understood. Show bodily marriages without intercourse, or give this act some single name and call the marriage either good or evil.

“You certainly promised to define marriages as good. If marriage is good, if the human being who is the fruit of marriage is good, and if this fruit cannot be an evil work of God, since it is born through what is good and from what is good, where, then, is the original evil, which has been destroyed by so many precedents?”

### CAPUT XX

#### 35

To this I reply that not only children born from marriage, but also those born from adultery, are in some respect good, according to the work of God by which they were created. But according to original sin, they are born under condemnation from the first Adam—not only if they are generated from adultery, but also if they are generated from marriage—unless they are regenerated in the second Adam, who is Christ.

When the Apostle says of the wicked, “Abandoning the natural use of the female, they burned in their desires for one another, males committing shameful acts with males,” he did not say “the conjugal use,” but “the natural use,” intending us to understand the use made of those members created for the purpose that the two sexes might unite through them for generation.

Consequently, when someone uses those same members with a prostitute, the use is natural, but it is not praiseworthy; it is culpable. If someone uses a part of the body that was not instituted for generation even with his wife, the act is contrary to nature and shameful.

Indeed, the same Apostle first says concerning the women: “For their females exchanged the natural use for that which is against nature” (Rom. 1:26); then, concerning males committing shameful acts with males, he speaks of “abandoning the natural use of the female.”

Therefore, by this term—that is, “natural use”—conjugal intercourse is not praised; rather, filthier and more criminal acts are condemned than those committed illicitly with women while nevertheless using the natural organs.

### CAPUT XXI

#### 36

We do not blame bread and wine because of the luxurious and the drunkards, any more than we blame gold because of the covetous and greedy. Accordingly, we do not blame the honorable intercourse of married couples because of the shameful lust of the body.

That intercourse could have existed without any preceding commission of sin, and married people would not have been ashamed of it. But lust arose after sin, and they were compelled to cover it because they were ashamed (Gen. 3:7).

Thus, although later married people use it well and lawfully, they have retained the practice of avoiding human eyes in such an act, and thereby confessing that what is shameful is shameful, even though no one ought to be ashamed of what is good.

In this way two things are indicated: the good of the union that deserves praise, from which children are generated, and the evil of shameful lust, from which those who are generated must be regenerated lest they be condemned.

Therefore, whoever lawfully has intercourse while shameful lust is present uses an evil thing well; whoever does so unlawfully uses an evil thing badly. For it more properly receives the name of evil than of good—that thing of which both the evil and the good are ashamed.

We more readily believe the one who says, “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Rom. 7:18), than this man who calls that good which, if he is ashamed of it, he confesses to be evil, and if he is not ashamed of it, adds shamelessness to it, an even worse evil.

We were therefore right to say: “Thus the good of marriage cannot be accused because of the original evil drawn from it, just as the evil of adultery cannot be excused because of the natural good born from it.” For human nature, whether born from marriage or from adultery, is the work of God.

If it were evil, it ought not to be generated; if it did not contain evil, it would not need to be regenerated. To bring both points together in one statement: if human nature were evil, it ought not to be saved; if it contained no evil, it would not need to be saved.

Whoever says that it is not good denies the Creator of what was created as good. Whoever denies that evil is present in it begrudges the merciful Savior of what has been corrupted.

Therefore, in human beings who are born, adulteries are neither to be excused because of the good created from them by the good Creator, nor marriages to be accused because of the evil that must be healed there by the merciful Savior.

### CAPUT XXII

#### 37

“Show,” he says, “bodily marriages without intercourse.”

I do not show marriages without bodily intercourse; but neither does he show that the same intercourse can exist without shame. In paradise, however, if sin had not preceded it, generation would indeed not have occurred without the union of the two sexes, but the union would have occurred without shame.

There would have been a tranquil obedience of the members in intercourse, not the shameful lust of the flesh.

Accordingly, marriage is good, from which a human being is generated in an orderly manner; and the fruit of marriage is good, namely, the human being who is thus born. But sin is evil, and every human being is born with it.

For God made and makes man; but through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned (Rom. 5:12).

### CAPUT XXIII

#### 38

“With a novel kind of argument,” he says, “you both profess to be Catholic [Note: [Col. 0458] The printed editions add *te*, “yourself.” *Te* is absent from the manuscripts.] and give support to Manichaeus by saying that marriage is both a great good and a great evil.”

He plainly does not understand what he is saying, or pretends not to understand. Either he does not understand, or he does not want to be understood [Note: [Col. 0458] Lovaniensis reads *non vult intelligere*, “he does not want to understand.” The same applies below, “what we mean to understand.”] concerning what we say.

If he does not understand, he is hindered by the preoccupation of error. If he does not want what we say to be understood, it is the fault of obstinacy by which he defends his error.

Jovinianus, too, who attempted a few years ago to establish a novel heresy, said that Catholics were supporting the Manichaeans because they preferred holy virginity to marriage in opposition to him.

But this man will reply that he does not share Jovinianus’s opinion concerning the indifference of marriage and virginity. Nor do I say that they hold this opinion. Nevertheless, by recognizing that Jovinianus accused Catholics of Manichaeism, let these new heretics acknowledge that this is not a new charge.

We therefore say that marriage is good, not evil. But just as the Arians accuse us of being Sabellians, although we do not say that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one and the same person, as the Sabellians say, but that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one and the same nature, as Catholics say, so the Pelagians accuse us of being Manichaeans, although we do not say that marriage is evil, as the Manichaeans say, but that evil befell the first human beings—that is, the first married couple—and passed from them into all human beings, as the Catholics say.

But just as the Arians, while fleeing the Sabellians, fell into something worse because they dared to distinguish, not the persons of the Trinity, but the natures, so the Pelagians, while perversely attempting to avoid the plague of the Manichaeans, are convicted of holding a more pernicious view than the Manichaeans themselves concerning the fruit of marriage, because they believe that infants have no need of Christ the physician.

### CAPUT XXIV

#### 39

“You define,” he says, “that a man born from fornication is not guilty, but that one born from marriage is not innocent. For this is where what you said leads: that natural good can subsist even from adulteries, while original evil is also drawn from marriage.”

He is utterly unsuccessful in trying to distort what is right before an intelligent reader. Far be it from us to say that a man born from fornication is not guilty.

Rather, we say that a man, whether born from marriage or from fornication, is something good because God is the author of nature, and that he draws something evil because of original sin.

Therefore, when we say that “natural good can subsist even from adulteries, while original evil is also drawn from marriage,” this does not lead to the conclusion to which he tries to force it: that one born from adultery is not guilty, or one born from marriage is not innocent.

Instead, a person born from either is made guilty through generation because of original sin, and both must be absolved through regeneration because of the good of nature.

### CAPUT XXV

#### 40

“One of these two things,” he says, “is true, the other false.”

I answer him with equal brevity: rather, both are true; neither is false.

“It is true,” he says, “that the man born from adultery cannot excuse the guilt of the adulterers, because what the adulterers did belongs to the fault of the will, while what they generated pertains to the praise of fertility. For if someone sows stolen wheat, the crop that is born is not liable to accusation.

“Thus I blame the thief, but praise the crop. I declare innocent the one who is born from the nobility of the seeds, since the Apostle says: ‘God gives it a body as he wills, and to each of the seeds its own body’” (1 Cor. 15:38). “But I condemn the criminal who sinned through the perversity of his intention.”

### CAPUT XXVI

#### 41

To this he adds and says: “But plainly, if evil is drawn from marriage, marriages can be accused but cannot be excused; and you place their work and fruit under the devil’s jurisdiction, because every cause of evil is devoid of good.

“But the man,” he says, “who is born from marriage is attributed not to crimes but to seeds. The cause of the seeds lies in the constitution of the bodies; whoever uses those bodies badly wounds the merit of the good, not the kind of thing itself.

“Clearly, then,” he says, “it is evident that good is not the cause of evil [Note: [Col. 0459] Most manuscripts read *bonam non esse causam mali*, “that a good thing is not the cause of evil,” instead of *bonum non esse causam mali*, “that good is not the cause of evil.”].

“If, then,” he says, “original evil is also drawn from marriage, the union of marriage is the cause of evil. It must therefore be evil, since it is through it and from it that an evil fruit has appeared, as the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘A tree is known by its fruits’” (Matt. 7:16).

“How,” he says, “do you expect to be heard when you say that marriage is good, although you define that nothing but evil proceeds from it? It is therefore established that marriages are guilty [Note: [Col. 0459] Thus the manuscripts read here and in book 5 of *Unfinished Work*, chapter 23. The printed editions instead have *mala*, “evil.”] if original sin is derived from them, and that they cannot be defended unless their fruit is approved as innocent. But they are defended and pronounced good; therefore their fruit is approved as harmless.”

#### 42

In replying to this, I first want the attentive reader to understand that these people are doing nothing except trying to establish that a savior is not necessary for infants, whom they deny to have any sins from which they need to be saved.

This great perversity, so hostile to the grace of God that has been given through Jesus Christ our Lord, who came to seek and save what was lost (Luke 19:10), attempts to insinuate itself into the hearts of those who understand poorly by praising the works of God—that is, by praising human nature, praising seed, praising marriage, praising the union of the two sexes, and praising fertility.

All these things are good. I do not wish to say “by praising lust,” because he himself is ashamed even to name it, so that he may appear to praise something other than lust itself.

Accordingly, by failing to distinguish the evils that have befallen nature from the goodness of nature itself, he does not show nature to be healthy—for that is false—but prevents it, though sick, from being healed.

And so he grants that what we said—that “the man born from adultery cannot excuse the guilt of adultery because of the good born from it”—is true. He establishes and confirms this point as best he can even by the comparison of a thief sowing stolen wheat, from which a good crop is certainly born.

But he does not wish to agree that the other statement we made is true: “The good of marriage cannot be accused because of the original evil drawn from it.” For if he agreed, he would be not a Pelagian heretic but a Catholic Christian.

“Plainly,” he says, “if evil is drawn from marriage, marriages can be accused but cannot be excused; and you place their work and fruit under the devil’s jurisdiction, because every cause of evil is devoid of good.”

He attaches the rest of his argument to this in order to prove that a good thing cannot be the cause of evil [Note: [Col. 0460] Am. Er. and many manuscripts read *causam mali bonam esse non posse*, “that the good cause of evil cannot exist,” rather than *causam mali bonum esse non posse*, “that a good thing cannot be the cause of evil.”]. For this reason, since marriage is good, he argues that it cannot be the cause of evil; and consequently that a sinner who needs a savior cannot possibly be born from it.

This is as though we were saying that marriage is the cause of sin, although a person born from marriage is not born without sin.

Marriage was instituted for the sake of generating, not for the sake of sinning. For this reason the Lord’s blessing upon marriage is: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28).

The sin that is drawn from birth does not belong to marriage, but to the evil that befell the human beings whose union constitutes marriage. For the evil of shameful lust can exist without marriage, and marriage could exist without it. But it belongs to the condition of the body—not of that life, but of this death—that now marriage cannot exist without it, although it can itself exist without marriage.

For shameful lust of the flesh certainly exists without marriage when it commits adultery, fornication, and every kind of obscenity, which are utterly contrary to the chastity of marriage. Or it exists when none of these acts is committed, because a person allows them by no consent, yet the organ rises and moves and causes movement, and often in sleep reaches the completion of its motion in a semblance of the act itself.

This evil, therefore, is not even within marriage itself the evil of marriage. Rather, they have it prepared in this body of death, whether they wish it or not, and without it they cannot fulfill what they wish.

It did not come to marriage from its institution, which is blessed, but from the fact that through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.

#### 43

What, then, does he mean when he says, “A tree is known by its fruits,” since we read that the Lord said this in the Gospel?

Was the Lord speaking there about this matter, and not rather about the two wills of human beings—namely, calling the good will a good tree and the evil will an evil tree, because good works arise from a good will and evil works from an evil one, and good cannot come from evil or evil from good?

If we place marriage as a good tree, according to the evangelical comparison he recalled, then by contrast we will certainly have to place fornication as an evil tree.

Therefore, if man is called the fruit of marriage as though something good comes from a good tree, then plainly man ought not to be born from fornication. “A bad tree cannot produce good fruits” (Matt. 7:18).

But if he says that adultery should not be placed in the position of the tree, but rather human nature, from which man is born, then here too the tree will not be marriage but human nature, from which man is born.

Thus that evangelical comparison contributes nothing to this question, because marriage is not the cause of the sin drawn from the one who is born and cleansed in the one who is reborn; rather, the voluntary sin of the first man is the cause of original sin.

“You say again,” he says, “that just as sin, whether it is drawn from this source or that, is the work of the devil, so man, whether born from this source or that, is the work of God.”

I did say this, and I said it most truthfully. If he were not a Pelagian but a Catholic, he too would say nothing else within the Catholic faith [Note: [Col. 0461] One Vatican manuscript reads *et ipse catholicus diceret*, “he too would say as a Catholic.” The Cygirannensis manuscript reads *et ipse catholice diceret*, “he too would speak in a Catholic manner.”].

### CAPUT XXVII

#### 44

What, then, is the question he puts to us: “By what means is sin found in an infant? Through the will, or through marriage, or through the parents?”

For he speaks in this way, as though he were responding to all these alternatives and, by purging each of them of sin, wished nothing to remain through which sin could be found in the infant.

Now listen to his very words: “By what means, then,” he says, “is sin found in an infant? Through the will? There was none in him. Through marriage? But marriage belongs to the work of the parents, whom you had previously stated did not sin in this act; but, as appears from what follows, you had not truly granted this.

“Marriage itself, therefore, must be accursed, since it caused the evil. But only marriage indicates the work of persons [Note: [Col. 0461] The manuscripts read *O sed illae*, “Oh, but those alone.”].

“Therefore the parents who by their union caused the sin are rightly liable to condemnation. If we follow your opinion, there can now be no doubt that married couples must be handed over to eternal punishment, since through their labor it was brought about that the devil attained dominion over human beings.

“And where is what you said shortly before, that man is the work of God? For if, through origin, there is evil in human beings, and through evil the devil’s right over human beings, you are saying that the devil is the author of human beings, since the origin of those who are born comes from him.

“But if you believe that man is made by God and that married couples are innocent, see how it cannot stand that original sin is drawn from them.”

45. To all these points the Apostle replies: he neither blames the will of the infant, which is not yet personally present in him for sinning, nor marriage insofar as it is marriage, since it has from God not only its institution but also its blessing, nor the parents insofar as they are parents, married to one another lawfully and legitimately for the procreation of children [Note: [Col. 0462] In the Louvain editions, *conjugatos* (“married”) is printed.]: “Through one man,” he says, “sin entered into this world, and through sin, death; and so it passed through to all human beings, in whom all sinned.” If these people would receive this with Catholic ears and minds, they would not harbor rebellious dispositions against the faith and grace of Christ, nor would they vainly attempt to twist these apostolic words, so clear and manifest, toward their own peculiar heretical interpretation, asserting that this was said because Adam sinned first, and that thereafter whoever wished to sin found in him an example of sinning; so that sin, they claim, passed to all human beings not by generation from that one man, but by imitation of him.

Yet surely, if the Apostle had wished imitation to be understood here, he would have said that sin entered this world through the devil rather than through one man, and that it passed through all human beings. For it is written concerning the devil: “Those who belong to his party imitate him” (Wis. 2:25). But he said “through one man,” from whom the generation of human beings certainly began, in order to teach that original sin had passed through generation to all.

46. What else do the Apostle’s subsequent words indicate? After saying this, he added: “For until the law sin was in the world”—that is, because even the law could not remove sin. “But sin,” he says, “was not reckoned when there was no law.” It was therefore present, but it was not reckoned, because what was to be reckoned was not exposed. For, as he says elsewhere, “Through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Rom. 3:20).

“But death reigned,” he says, “from Adam to Moses”—that is, what he had said above, “until the law”; not that thereafter, from Moses onward, sin no longer existed, but because the law given through Moses could not remove the reign of death, which certainly reigns only through sin. Its reign, moreover, consists in plunging mortal human beings into a second death as well, one that is everlasting.

But over whom did it reign? “Even over those,” he says, “who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one to come.” Of whom to come, if not of Christ? And what sort of type, if not one by contrast? Elsewhere also he says briefly: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:22). As that occurred in the one, so this occurs in the other: that is the type.

But this type is not similar in every respect. Therefore the Apostle immediately continued: “But the gift is not like the trespass. For if many died through the trespass of one, much more have the grace of God and the gift by the grace of the one man Jesus Christ abounded to many.” What does “much more … abounded” mean, except that all who are freed through Christ die temporally on account of Adam, but on account of Christ himself will live without end?

“And the gift,” he says, “is not like what came through the one who sinned. For the judgment from one trespass resulted in condemnation, but the grace from many trespasses resulted in justification.” From one—what, except a trespass? For he continues: “But the grace from many trespasses.” Let them say how the result could be condemnation from one trespass, unless even one original sin, which passed through to all human beings, is sufficient for condemnation. Grace, however, results in justification from many trespasses because it not only cancels that one sin which is inherited by origin, but also the other sins added in each person by the movement of his own will.

“For if death reigned through the one man because of one trespass, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ. Therefore, just as through one trespass the result for all human beings was condemnation, so through one act of righteousness the result for all human beings is justification of life.”

Let them persist in the vanity of their minds and say that one man did not transmit a hereditary stock but merely offered an example of sin. How, then, is the result of one trespass condemnation for all human beings, and not rather the result of the many trespasses of each individual? It is because, even if that one trespass alone existed, it is sufficient to bring about condemnation without the addition of the others—just as it brings condemnation upon infants who die, born from Adam, if they are not reborn in Christ.

What, then, does this man ask of us, which he does not wish to hear from the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0463] The printed editions read *qui* (“who”); the manuscripts, *quod* (“which”).]: “By what is sin found in the infant—through the will, or through marriage, or through the parents?” Let him hear, then, by what sin is found in the infant, and let him be silent: “Through the trespass of one,” says the Apostle, “the result for all human beings was condemnation.”

He said “all” for condemnation through Adam, and “all” for justification through Christ. Yet Christ certainly does not transfer all those who die in Adam to life. He said “all” and “all” because, just as no one comes to death except through Adam, so no one comes to life except through Christ. It is like what we say of a teacher of letters, if he is the only one in the city: “This man teaches everyone here to read”—not because everyone learns, but because no one learns except from him.

Finally, those whom he had first called “all,” he later called “many,” signifying by both expressions the same people. “For just as through the disobedience of one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of one the many will be made righteous” (Rom. 5:12–19).

47. Let him ask again: “By what is sin found in the infant?” Let the sacred pages answer him:

“Through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin, death; and so it passed through to all human beings, in whom all sinned.”

“Because of one trespass many died.”

“The judgment from one trespass resulted in condemnation.”

“Because of one trespass death reigned through one.”

“Through one trespass the result for all human beings was condemnation.”

“Through the disobedience of one man the many were made sinners.”

There: this is how trespass is found in the infant. Let him now believe in original sin; let him allow infants to come to Christ so that they may be saved.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

[Col. 0464]

“What is this that he says: ‘This man who is born does not sin; that man who begot him does not sin; this one who created him does not sin? Through what cracks, amid so many safeguards of innocence, do you imagine that sin entered?’”

Why does he seek a hidden crack when he has a completely open door? “Through one man,” says the Apostle; “through the trespass of one,” says the Apostle; “through the disobedience of one man,” says the Apostle. What more does he seek? What could be clearer? What could be stated more insistently?

48. “If sin,” he says, “comes from the will, then it is an evil will that makes sin; if from nature, then nature is evil.”

I answer quickly: sin comes from the will. Perhaps he asks whether this is also true of original sin. I answer: certainly, original sin also; for this too was sown through the will of the first man, so that it might be in him and pass to all.

But concerning what he then added—“If it comes from nature, then nature is evil”—I ask him, if he can answer: Just as it is clear that all evil works arise from an evil will as from an evil tree, so from where does he say that the evil will itself—that is, the evil tree of evil fruits [Note: [Col. 0464] The printed editions read “that is, of fruits,” omitting “itself”; we have supplied it from the manuscripts.]—arose? If from an angel, what was that angel himself except a good work of God? If from a human being, what was that human being himself except a good work of God? Indeed, since an evil will arose in the angel from the angel [Note: [Col. 0464] The printed editions read “of the angel from the angel”; the manuscripts, “in the angel from the angel.”], and in the human being from the human being, what were these two before these evils arose in them except a good work of God and a good and praiseworthy nature?

There, then: evil arises from good, and there was absolutely nowhere from which it could arise except from good. I mean the evil will itself, which no evil preceded—not the evil works, which arise only from an evil will as from an evil tree.

Yet the evil will could not arise from good merely because it was made by the good God, but because it was made from nothing, not from God.

What, then, is the meaning of his saying: “If nature is the work of God, how is the work of the devil allowed to pass through the work of God?” Did not the work of the devil, when it first arose in the angel who became the devil, arise within the work of God? Therefore, if evil, which previously existed nowhere at all, could arise within God’s work, why could evil which already existed somewhere not pass through the work of God—especially since the Apostle uses this very expression, saying, “And so it passed through to all human beings”? Are human beings not the work of God? Sin therefore passed through human beings—that is, the work of the devil passed through the work of God.

Or, to say the same thing another way: the work of the work of God passed through the work of God [Note: [Col. 0464] Earlier printed editions add the following gloss: “and, to say the same thing another way (because the work of the devil, that is, sin, which arose through the devil himself, who is God’s creature or work, passed through another work of God, that is, the human being), the work of the work of God passed through the work of God.” We have removed the gloss on the authority of four manuscripts, supported by copies of the *Opus imperfectum*, book 5, chapters 26 and 63.].

And therefore God alone is immutable and of the most powerful goodness: he who, even before there was any evil, made all things good, and who works good in every way through the evils that arose in the good things made by him.

## CHAPTER XXIX

49. “In one human being,” he says, “the intention is rightly blamed and the origin praised, because there are two things that are assigned to opposite sources. But in the infant there is only one thing, nature alone, because there is no will. That one thing, therefore,” he says, “must be attributed either to God or to the devil. If nature is from God,” he says, “there cannot be original evil in it [Note: [Col. 0465] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read *adscribitur* (“is attributed”) above, rather than *adscribetur* (“will be attributed”).]. If it is from the devil, there will be nothing by which the human being can be claimed for the divine work. He who defends original evil is therefore perfectly a Manichaean.”

Let him rather hear what is true against these claims. In one human being the intention is rightly blamed and nature praised, because there are two things that are assigned to opposite sources. But in the infant also there are not merely one thing—that is, nature, in which the human being was created by the good God. The infant also has a defect, which passed through one man to all human beings, as the Apostle understands, not as Pelagius, Coelestius, or any disciple of theirs misunderstands.

Of these two things, then, which we have said are present in the infant, one is attributed to God and the other to the devil. And the fact that both, on account of one of them—that is, the defect—are subjected to the power of the devil is not incongruous, because this does not occur by the devil’s power, but by God’s. The defect is subjected to defect, and nature to nature, because both are present in the devil as well. Thus, when the beloved and chosen are rescued from the power of darkness, to which they are rightly subjected, it becomes evident what is bestowed upon the justified good by the good God, who works well even through evils [Note: [Col. 0465] The manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions read: “what is bestowed upon the justified good by God, who works good things well through evils.”].

50. As for what this man thought he was saying religiously: “If nature is from God, there cannot be original evil in it,” does not another person seem [Note: [Col. 0465] The Louvain editions read “would seem.”] to speak more religiously by saying: “If nature is from God, no evil at all can arise in it”? And yet this is false. The Manichaeans wished to assert precisely this, and they attempted to fill not God’s creature, made from nothing, but God’s own nature with every evil.

Evil arose only in what is good—not, however, in the highest and immutable good, which is God’s nature, but in what was made from nothing through God’s wisdom.

There is therefore something by which the human being may be claimed for the divine work, because he would not be human unless he were created by the divine work. But evil would not be in infants unless the first human being had sinned by his will and original sin had been inherited through an impaired origin [Note: [Col. 0465] The printed editions read “and inherited from an origin.” The word “from” is absent from the manuscripts.].

It is not therefore, as this man says, that “he who defends original evil is perfectly a Manichaean”; rather, he who does not believe in original evil is perfectly a Pelagian.

For it was not from the time when the pestilential teaching of Manichaeus began that infants began to be baptized, exorcized, and exsufflated in the Church of God, so that through these very rites it might be shown that they cannot be transferred into the kingdom of Christ unless rescued from the power of darkness (Col. 1:13). Nor is it in the books of Manichaeus that we read [Note: [Col. 0465] The printed editions read “or when we read”; “when” is absent from the manuscripts.] that “the Son of Man came to seek and save what was lost” (Luke 19:10); or that “through one man sin entered into this world” (Rom. 5:12), together with the other passages bearing on the same judgment that we mentioned above; or that God “visits the sins of the fathers upon the children” (Exod. 20:5); or what is written in the Psalm: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb” (Ps. 50:7); or: “Humanity was made like vanity; its days pass like a shadow” (Ps. 143:4); or: “Behold, you have made my days old, and my substance is as nothing before you; surely every living human being is altogether vanity” (Ps. 38:6); or what the Apostle says: “Every creature has been subjected to vanity” (Rom. 8:20); or in the book of Ecclesiastes: “Vanity of vanities” [Note: [Col. 0466] Several manuscripts read “vanity of those who make vanity.”], “and all is vanity: what abundance is there for a human being in all his labor at which he labors under the sun?” (Eccl. 1:2–3); or in the book of Ecclesiasticus: “A grievous yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40:1); or what the Apostle says: “In Adam all die” (1 Cor. 15:22); or what holy Job says when speaking of his sins:

“For a human being, born of woman, is short-lived and full of anger; like a flower of grass he withers, and he flees like a shadow and does not remain. And have you not also taken account of him, and caused him to enter into judgment before you? For who will be pure from defilement? No one—not even if his life upon the earth should be but one day” (Job 14:1–5, according to the Septuagint).

What defilements he meant, since he wished them to be understood as sins, the passage itself indicates, where it plainly becomes clear what he is discussing. There is also the passage in the prophet Zechariah, where the filthy garment is removed from the priest and it is said to him: “Behold, I have taken away your sins” (Zech. 3:4).

I think that all these passages, and others of the same kind, which indicate that every human being is born under sin and under a curse, are not read in the darkness of the Manichaeans, but in the light of Catholics.

51. What should I say about the interpreters of the divine Scriptures themselves, who flourished in the Catholic Church, and about how they did not attempt to twist these matters into other meanings, because they were steadfast in the most ancient and strongest faith and were not shaken by a novel error?

If I wished to gather them and make use of their testimonies, the task would be excessively long. Moreover, with respect to the canonical authorities, from which we must not turn away, I might perhaps appear to have presumed less than I ought.

Nevertheless, to pass over the most blessed Ambrose, to whom Pelagius, as I have already mentioned, bore such great testimony concerning integrity in the faith (above, book 1, no. 40)—although that same Ambrose defended nothing else in infants as making Christ the necessary physician except original sin (Ambrose, *On Isaiah*, cited above, book 1, no. 40)—surely no one will say, nor even be able to say, that Cyprian of the most glorious crown was a Manichaean, since he suffered martyrdom before that plague appeared in the Roman world.

Yet in his book *On the Baptism of Infants* he defended original sin so firmly that he said for this reason that an infant ought to be baptized even before the eighth day, if necessary, lest its soul perish. He wished it to be understood that the infant comes more easily to the pardon of baptism the more it is forgiven—not its own sins, but others’ sins (Cyprian, letter formerly 59, now 64, to Fidus).

Let this man dare to call such men Manichaeans, and let him smear with this unspeakable crime the most ancient tradition of the Church, by which, as I have said, infants are exorcized and exsufflated so that they may be rescued from the power of darkness—that is, from the devil and his angels—and transferred into the kingdom of Christ.
