For our part, we are more prepared to endure every curse and insult with these men and with the Church of Christ, established in the antiquity of this faith, than to be praised with the preaching of Pelagians of whatever eloquence [Note: [Col. 0467] The Ambrosian and Erasmian editions read “than to be praised by Pelagians of whatever eloquence.”].

## CHAPTER XXX

52. “Again,” he says, “you assert and say: ‘There would be no concupiscence if the human being had not sinned before; but marriage would exist even if no one had sinned.’”

I did not say, “There would be no concupiscence,” because there is also a concupiscence that is worthy of glory, by which wisdom is desired (Wis. 6:21). Rather, I said, “There would be no shameful concupiscence” (above, book 1, no. 1). Let my words be reread—the very words he himself included—so that it may become clear how fraudulently he cites them.

But let him call it by whatever name he wishes. I said that the thing of which I was speaking would not exist unless the human being had sinned before: it is the thing of which those in paradise were ashamed, who covered their shameful parts. No one denies that it followed because the sin of disobedience had preceded it.

Anyone who wishes to understand what they felt ought to consider what they covered. They made themselves loin-coverings from fig leaves, not garments (Gen. 3:7). In Greek these loin-coverings are called *perizōmata* (περιζώματα). What the *perizōmata* cover is known to everyone; some Latins have translated them as *campestria*. Who, then, is unaware of which parts of the body are covered by those who wear the *campestre*? Roman youths covered these parts when they exercised naked in the field; hence this type of covering received that name [Note: [Col. 0467] See *The City of God*, book 11, chapter 17.].

## CHAPTER XXXI

53. “Those marriages,” he says, “which, as you say, could have existed without concupiscence, without bodily movement, without the necessity of the sexes, you pronounce praiseworthy. But these marriages that now take place you define as invented by the devil. Thus,” he says, “those marriages which you dream could have been instituted you judge good, whereas these of which divine Scripture says, ‘A man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh’ (Gen. 2:24), you declare to be evil and demonic, and finally claim that they ought to be called a disease, not a marriage.”

It is not surprising that the Pelagians attempt to twist our words into whatever meanings they wish, since they are accustomed to do the same even with the sacred Scriptures—not merely where something is obscurely said, but where the testimonies are clear and open, as is also the custom of other heretics.

Who could say that marriages could exist “without bodily movement, without the necessity of the sexes”? For God made the sexes, since “he made them male and female” (Gen. 1:27), as it is written. How could those who were to be joined, and who through that very union were to generate, fail to move their bodies, when no bodily approach of one human being to another occurs if bodily movement is absent?

The question here, then, is not about bodily movement, without which they could not unite at all, but about the shameful movement of the genitals. That movement would certainly not exist, and yet the generative union would not be absent, if the genitals served not lust but the will, as the other members do.

Even now, in this body of death, do we not command the foot, the arm, the finger, the lip, and the tongue, and are they not immediately extended at our bidding? Indeed, what is more remarkable, when we wish, and when we are not compelled by an urgent abundance, we command the fluid contained internally in the bladder to flow, and it obeys. Rather, we command even the hidden viscera and nerves in which that fluid is contained to propel it, press it out, and expel it; and, when health is present, they serve the will without difficulty [Note: [Col. 0468] The printed editions read “the fluid placed within, which and when.” Either “which” should be deleted—it is absent from three Vatican manuscripts—or “when we wish” should be supplied in its place, as it was corrected by an ancient hand in the Benignian manuscript.].

How much more easily and peacefully, if the genital members of the body obeyed, would the member itself be extended and the human being be generated, unless the disobedience of these members had been repaid to those human beings as a just punishment for their disobedience?

The chaste feel this punishment; without doubt, if they could, they would prefer to generate children at the command of the will rather than through the stimulation of pleasure. But the unclean, who on account of this disease love not only prostitutes but even wives, exult in this punishment of the flesh with a still heavier punishment of the mind.

## CHAPTER XXXII

54. Far be it from us, then, to say what this man falsely attributes to us: “These marriages that now take place were invented by the devil.” They are precisely the marriages that God instituted from the beginning.

He did not remove this good of his, instituted for the generation of human beings, even from condemned human beings; nor did he remove from them the senses of the flesh and the bodily members—clearly his own gifts—even though they were already destined to die under the deserved sentence of condemnation.

These, I say, are the marriages of which it was said—apart from the fact that here it was represented figuratively in that great sacrament of Christ and the Church—“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.” This was said before sin; and if no one had sinned, it could have been fulfilled without shameful lust [Note: [Col. 0468] Here, after “fulfilled,” two manuscripts and several editions add “in the body of that life.”].

Even now, although it does not occur without that lust in this body of death, the same thing nevertheless continues to occur: a man clings to his wife, and the two are one flesh.

Therefore, although it is said that marriages now are one thing, while they could have been another if no one had sinned, this is said not according to their nature but according to a certain quality changed for the worse. Thus one person is said to be different although he is the same human being, if he has changed his life either for the better or for the worse. For one thing is a righteous person, another a sinner, although the human being himself remains the same.

So there are marriages without shameful lust, and marriages with shameful lust; yet according to the institution by which a woman is lawfully joined to a man, conjugal fidelity concerning the marital debt is preserved free from the sin of adultery, and children are generated according to legitimate custom: they are the very same marriages that God instituted.

The devil has not injured the marriages themselves, but the human beings from whom marriages arise, wounding them through the ancient persuasion of sin—persuading them to disobedience, for which, by divine judgment, the reciprocal disobedience of the members was imposed as its repayment. In that disobedience, although the married pair were ashamed of their nakedness, they nevertheless could not wholly lose the goodness of marriage instituted by God.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

55. From this point he proceeds from those who are joined in marriage to those who are born from them, on whose account we labor in this controversy with such extensive arguments against the new heretics. Compelled by a hidden prompting of God, he says something in which, by his own confession, he dissolves this entire knot.

For he wishes to arouse greater hatred against us because we say that infants are born under sin even from legitimate marriages:

“Those, then,” he says, “who were never born you say could have been good; but these who have filled the world, for whom Christ died, you define as the work of the devil, born from disease, and guilty from their beginning. I have therefore proved,” he says, “that you are doing nothing other than denying that God is the creator of these human beings who exist.”

I certainly say that the creator of all human beings, although all are born under sin and perish unless they are reborn, is none other than God. The defect was sown through the devil’s persuasion, by which they were born under sin; it was not the created nature by which they are human beings.

If shameful lust did not move the members except when we wished, it would not be a disease. If even lawful and honorable intercourse between married people did not blush at it, avoiding public view and seeking privacy, it would not be a disease. If the Apostle did not forbid people to possess their wives in this disease, it would not be a disease.

For what the Greek has, ἐν πάθει ἐπιθυμίας (“in the passion of desire”), some have translated into Latin as *in morbo desiderii* (“in the disease of desire”) or *of concupiscence*; others as *in passione concupiscentiae* (“in the passion of concupiscence”) (1 Thess. 4:5), or in some other way, as it is found in different manuscripts. But in the Latin language, especially according to ecclesiastical usage, *passio* (“passion”) is ordinarily understood only in a pejorative sense [Note: [Col. 0469] Ambrose and all the manuscripts read “not for reproach,” omitting “only”; the Louvain editors think that Erasmus added “only.”].

56. Whatever this man may think about shameful carnal concupiscence, consider what he has said about the infants on whose behalf we labor, so that they may be believed to need a Savior and not die without salvation. I repeat his words:

“Those, then,” he says, “who were never born you say could have been good; but these who have filled the world, for whom Christ died, you define as the work of the devil, born from disease, and guilty from their beginning.”

If only he would dissolve the knot of the controversy as he has dissolved the knot of this question! Will he now claim that he was speaking about adults? The discussion concerns infants; it concerns those who are being born. He stirs up hostility against us because we define as guilty those for whom Christ died.

Why, then, did Christ die for them if they are not guilty? Precisely from this point—from the point where he thought indignation should be aroused—we shall establish our case.

He says: “How are infants guilty, for whom Christ died?”

We reply: Rather, how are infants not guilty, for whom Christ died?

This controversy seeks a judge [Note: [Col. 0470] All the manuscripts read *quaerat* (“should seek”).]. Let Christ judge, then, and let him himself say for whose sake his death was beneficial.

“This is my blood,” he says, “which will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matt. 26:28).

Let the Apostle judge together with him, since Christ himself speaks in the Apostle. He also cries out and says concerning God the Father: “He did not spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8:32).

I think that Christ was delivered up for all of us in such a way that in this matter infants are not separated from us.

But why should we labor over this point, when even this man no longer argues against it? For he not only confesses that Christ died even for infants, but also attacks us on the ground that we call those same infants guilty for whom Christ died.

Let the Apostle, then, who said that Christ was delivered up for us all, also say why Christ was delivered up for us. “He was delivered up,” he says, “for our trespasses, and he was raised for our justification” (Rom. 4:25).

If, therefore, as this man both confesses, declares, says, and charges, infants too are among those for whom Christ was delivered up, and Christ was delivered up for our trespasses, then infants certainly have original trespasses for which Christ was delivered up.

He has something in them to heal who, as he himself says, declared that “the physician is not needed by the healthy but by the sick” (Matt. 9:12). He has a reason to save them, who came into the world, as the Apostle Paul says, “to save sinners” (1 Tim. 1:15). He has something in them to forgive, who testifies that he shed his blood for the forgiveness of sins. He has a reason to seek them, who came, as he says, “to seek and save what was lost” (Luke 19:10). The Son of God has something in them to release, since he came for this purpose, as the Apostle John says, “to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8).

The enemy, then, of the salvation of infants is the person who asserts their innocence in such a way as to deny that medicine is necessary for the wounded and injured.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

57. Now attend to what follows and what he adds. “If,” he says, “before sin, that from which human beings would be born was created by God, but that by which the parents would be moved was created by the devil, then holiness will doubtless be attributed to those being born, and guilt to those begetting.”

Since this very plainly condemns marriage, remove this interpretation, I beg you, from the midst of the Churches, and truly believe that “all things were made through Jesus Christ, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

He speaks as though we were saying that some substance in human beings was created by the devil. The devil persuaded human beings to evil as sin; he did not create it as nature. But he certainly persuaded nature, because the human being is nature, and by persuading it he corrupted it.

For the one who wounds does not create the limbs but afflicts them [Note: [Col. 0470] One manuscript reads “but corrupts them.”]. Yet wounds inflicted upon bodies make the limbs limp or difficult to move, but not the power by which a human being is righteous [Note: [Col. 0471] One of the Vatican manuscripts reads “upright.”].

But the wound called sin wounds the very life by which one lived rightly. This wound the devil then inflicted, very much greater and deeper than the sins known to human beings [Note: [Col. 0471] Here the manuscripts add “very great.” In its place Ambrose and Erasmus read “the wound.” See book 6 of the *Opus imperfectum*.].

Thus, through the great sin of the first human being, our nature, having been changed for the worse, was not only made sinful but also generates sinners [Note: [Col. 0471] The printed editions read “generated sinners.”]. Yet that sickness through which the power of living well perished is certainly not nature but a defect.

In the same way, bodily ill health is not some substance or nature but a defect. And although not always, nevertheless in most cases the ill health of parents is somehow transmitted and appears in the bodies of their children.

58. This sin, which changed the human being himself for the worse in paradise, because it is much greater than we can judge, is inherited by everyone who is born and is forgiven only in one who is reborn. Thus, even from parents who have already been reborn, in whom it has been forgiven and covered, it is inherited as guilt by their children at birth, unless the second, spiritual birth liberates those whom the first, carnal birth bound.

The wondrous Creator has produced a wondrous example of this in the olive and the wild olive: not only from the seed of the wild olive, but even from the seed of the cultivated olive, a wild olive alone arises.

Therefore, although in human beings generated by nature and regenerated by grace there is this carnal concupiscence resisting the law of the mind, because it has been forgiven in the forgiveness of sins it is no longer reckoned to them as sin, nor does it cause harm unless consent is given to something unlawful through its movements.

Their offspring, however, because it is sown not through spiritual but through carnal concupiscence, is like a wild olive of our stock arising from that cultivated olive. Thus it inherits guilt by being born from it, and unless it is liberated from that plague by being reborn, it cannot be freed.

How, then, does this man assert that we attribute holiness to those being born and guilt to those begetting, when truth rather shows that, even if there was holiness in those begetting, original guilt is present in those being born, and is abolished only in those being reborn?

## CHAPTER XXXV
59. Since this is so, let him think what he pleases about this carnal concupiscence and this lust—imperious to the shameless, to be subdued by the chaste, yet shameful both to the chaste and to the shameless—for, as I see, he is greatly pleased with it. Let him not hesitate to praise what he is ashamed to name; let him call it, as he has called it, “the vigor of the members,” and let him not fear the horror of chaste ears; let him call it “the power of the members,” and let him not shrink from immodesty. Let him say, if he is not ashamed, that if no one had sinned in paradise, this vigor might there have flourished like a flower [Note: [Col. 0471] More manuscripts read *vigere*, “to thrive.” Some read *vivere*, “to live.”]; nor would there have been any need to cover what would move in such a way that no one would be put to shame by it; rather, with the wife ready, it would always have been exercised and never restrained, lest such great pleasure ever be denied to such great happiness. For far be it from us to suppose that that blessedness could either lack in that place what it wanted or feel in its body or mind what it did not want. Accordingly, if the movement of lust anticipated the will of the human beings, the will would immediately follow it; the wife, who for this reason ought never to be absent, whether she was about to conceive or already pregnant, would at once be brought near [Note: [Col. 0472] The printed editions read: “and the wife, who for this reason ought never to be absent, but whether she was about to conceive …” The text has been corrected according to the manuscripts.]; and either offspring would be generated or natural and praiseworthy pleasure fulfilled; and the man’s seed would perish, lest the appetite for so good a concupiscence be defrauded. The spouses would only not turn to that use which is against nature, but whenever pleasure prompted them, they would use the members created for this purpose, the genital members.

Yet what if that use contrary to nature should perhaps also give pleasure? What if that praiseworthy lust should neigh after this pleasure as well? Would they follow it because it was pleasant, or resist it because it was shameful? If they followed it, where would any consideration of honor be? If they resisted it, where would be the peace of such great happiness?

If at this point he should perhaps blush and say that such great peace and such perfect order could have existed in those matters that carnal concupiscence would never anticipate the will of those human beings, but would arise when they themselves wished it; and that they would wish it when it was necessary for begetting children, so that no emission of seed would be fruitless, no intercourse would occur without conception and birth, with the flesh obeying their command and lust obeying their command—if he says this, let him at least consider that what he describes does not now exist in human beings. And if he does not wish to admit that lust is a defect, let him at least say that, through the disobedience of those human beings, carnal concupiscence itself was also corrupted, so that what would then have moved obediently and orderly now moves disobediently and disorderly. Thus, even for chaste married people, it does not obey their command, but moves when it is not necessary and, when it is necessary, sometimes sooner and sometimes later; it does not [Note: [Col. 0472] Nearly all manuscripts omit *non*, “not.”] follow their nod, but displays movements of its own.

Those disobedient human beings therefore received this disobedience of its own, and transmitted it by propagation into us. For it was certainly not moving at their command, but in a disorderly fashion, when they covered the members that had previously been a source of glory and had now become a source of shame.

60. But, as I said, let this man think what he pleases about this lust, proclaim it as he pleases, praise it as much as he pleases—as he indicates in many passages, he takes great pleasure in it—so that the Pelagians, whoever among them do not enjoy carnal marriage on account of their professed continence, may be delighted, if not by its uses, at least by its praises [Note: [Col. 0472] The manuscripts read, “do not enjoy the flesh of spouses.”]. Let him at least spare infants, so that he does not praise them uselessly and defend them cruelly; let him not say that they are saved; let him allow them to come not to Pelagius their praiser, but to Christ their Savior.

For, to bring this book to a close, since his discourse—the one written in the little document you sent—ended in this way, let him grant that Jesus is also Jesus for infants. And just as he confesses that all things were made through him insofar as he is the Word, God, so let him also confess that infants are saved by him insofar as he is Jesus, if he wishes to be a catholic Christian. For it is written in the Gospel: “And they shall call his name Jesus; for he shall save his people from their sins” (Matt. 1:21). He is therefore called Jesus because *Jesus* means “Savior” in Latin. “He shall save his people,” and infants certainly belong to that people. But he shall save them from their sins; therefore infants too have original sins, on account of which Jesus—that is, the Savior—can also be their Savior.

# [On the Soul and Its Origin]

[Col. 0473]

## Prefatory Notice to the Following Books on the Soul and Its Origin

Vincentius Victor, a young man born in Caesarea of Mauritania and converted from the faction of the Rogatists—which was a schism of the Donatists occupying a portion of Mauritania around the city of Cartenna—provided the material for these four books. It was said that Victor still held in high esteem the reputation of that Vincentius who had presided over the same faction after Rogatus, so much so that for this reason he wished that man’s name to be his own surname [Note: [Col. 0473] See below, Book 3, no. 2.].

Now when this Victor happened upon one of Augustine’s writings in which Augustine admitted that he did not know whether all souls were propagated from Adam’s one soul, or whether each individual human being received from God an individual soul, as Adam himself had received one, without propagation, he nevertheless said that he did know that the soul was by nature spirit, not body. Victor was equally displeased with both points: first, that so great a man as Augustine should teach with hesitation what ought to be held concerning the origin of the soul, especially since he considered the propagation of souls plausible; and second, that Augustine should emphatically declare the nature of the soul to be incorporeal. Accordingly, he dedicated to the presbyter Peter the two books he wrote against Augustine on this subject. They contain several opinions of the Pelagian heretics, as well as others still worse.

Renatus, a monk who was then at Caesarea—the same man, apparently, who, when Augustine was present in that city in the autumn of 418, had delivered to him the letter of Bishop Optatus asking about the origin of the soul [Note: [Col. 0473] See Augustine’s Letter 190, no. 1]—was a layman by social standing but thoroughly orthodox in faith. He carefully copied these same books of Victor and sent them from Caesarea to Hippo during the summer. Augustine, however, received them only toward the end of autumn, in the year commonly thought to be 419. As soon as the holy Doctor had read them, he immediately composed the first of the four following books for the monk Renatus; he then wrote the second in the form of a letter to the presbyter Peter; and the final two to Victor himself, though somewhat later, as is shown by the words of Book 2, no. 7: “But if the Lord wills that I write to that young man himself, as I desire.”

In the *Retractations*, this labor of Augustine’s is listed immediately after the works of the year 419, namely, in fifth place after the *Proceedings with Emeritus*, which were completed at Caesarea in September of 418. It therefore belongs to the end of 419 or the beginning of 420. It was written after the Pelagians had already been condemned by the authority of the Catholic councils and the Apostolic See, though very recently [Note: [Col. 0473] See below, Book 2, no. 17, and Book 1, no. 34]—an event that had happily occurred in the year of Christ 418.

In the first book, written to Renatus, Augustine demonstrates that Victor had unjustly criticized his view of the nature of the soul and his hesitation concerning its origin. He restrains the young man’s arrogance and shows that, by daring to undertake a question beyond his powers to solve, he had fallen into serious and unheard-of errors. He also demonstrates that the testimonies of Scripture which Victor thought proved that souls are made by God rather than propagated, and are newly breathed into each individual at birth, are ambiguous and wholly inadequate to confirm Victor’s opinion.

In the second book, he warns Peter not to allow it to be thought that, by praising Victor’s books written to him about the origin of the soul, he had approved them, or that he regarded the rash statements of that young man which were contrary to Christian faith as Catholic doctrines. He points out Victor’s various and extremely serious errors and refutes them briefly. Finally, he urges Peter himself to lead Victor toward correcting them.

In the third book, written to Victor himself, he shows what Victor ought to correct in his books if he wishes to be regarded as a Catholic. He briefly touches upon Victor’s opinions and paradoxes, which had already been refuted in the preceding books to Renatus and Peter, and reduces them to eleven heads of error.

In the fourth book to the same Victor, Augustine first demonstrates that he is unjustly blamed for his hesitation concerning the origin of souls and that Victor wrongfully compared him to cattle because he had not dared to define anything on this matter. He then shows that Victor also rashly rejected Augustine’s unhesitating assertion that the soul is spirit, not body, in a futile attempt to defend the claim that the soul is corporeal by nature and that the spirit is distinct from the soul in a human being.

[Col. 0475]

[Note: [Col. 0473] On the four books *On the Soul and Its Origin*, see Book 2, chapter 56, of the *Retractations*, vol. 1, col. 653, from the words “At the same time” to the words “I thought it should be written.” M.]

## The Four Books of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, on the Soul and Its Origin

[Note: [Col. 0475] Written toward the end of the year of Christ 419.]

[Note: [Col. 0475] For correcting the four books *On the Soul and Its Origin*, besides one Vatican manuscript, we used eleven Gallican manuscripts supplied to us by various abbeys: two from Saint Remigius of Reims; one from Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris; another from the abbey of Couture at Le Mans; another from Saint-Martin of Séez; and the remaining ones from Prémontré, Saint-Michel, Casal, Corbie, Cygirannus, and Cîteaux. We also consulted the variant readings of five Belgian manuscripts held at Louvain, and compared the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 0475] We further compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.]

(C)

# BOOK ONE: TO THE MONK RENATUS

After receiving two books by Vincentius Victor, who rejected Augustine’s view of the nature of the soul and his hesitation concerning its origin, Augustine shows that the young man, thinking arrogantly of himself, had fallen into intolerable errors by deciding a matter so obscure. He then demonstrates that the testimonies of Scripture by which Victor thought he could prove that souls are made by God rather than propagated, and are newly breathed into each individual at birth, are ambiguous and wholly inadequate for this opinion.

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0475]

1. We had already regarded your sincerity toward us, dearest brother Renatus, your brotherly goodwill, and the affection of our mutual love as established. But now you have shown them to us as even more firmly established by your friendly diligence, because last summer you sent me two books by a man whom I utterly did not know, though for that reason not to be despised, Vincentius Victor—for that is how I found his name written at the beginning of the books. Since I had been absent, they were delivered to me only at the end of autumn.

How could you, my dearest friend, either have been able or have thought you ought not to bring to my attention the writings of any person whatsoever, when such writings had come into your hands—even if they were addressed to someone else—if my name was nevertheless mentioned and read in them, and if they contradicted statements of mine that I had published in certain little works? You have done what my most sincere and beloved friend ought to have done.

## CHAPTER TWO

2. Yet I am somewhat distressed by the fact that I am still less well known to Your Holiness than I would wish. For you thought that I would receive this as though you had injured me by making known what another man had done. But see how far this is from my mind: I do not even complain that I have been injured by that man.

When he held opinions different from mine on certain matters, ought he to have kept silent? I should therefore be grateful to him that he did not remain silent, so that we too may read what he wrote. He ought indeed to have written only to me rather than about me to another [Note: [Col. 0475] Most manuscripts read, “you ought indeed.”]; but because I was unknown to him, he did not dare to intrude upon me by refuting my statements. Nor did he think he should consult me about matters on which he seemed to himself to have no doubt at all, but to possess a clear and certain opinion.

He obeyed a friend of his who, he says, compelled him to write. And if, in the course of argument, he expressed anything that reflected insult upon me [Col. 0476], I would not believe that he did so with the intention of abusing me, but rather from the necessity of one who held a different opinion. For when a man’s disposition toward me is unknown and uncertain, I think it better to suppose that he has better intentions than to condemn what has not been investigated.

Perhaps he acted out of love for me, knowing that what he wrote might reach me, since he did not want me to err in matters in which he himself did not think that he was in error. Therefore I ought also to be grateful for the goodwill of one whose opinion I must reject. Accordingly, in those matters on which he does not think rightly, he still seems to me to require gentle correction, not harsh hatred—especially because, as I hear, he has recently become a Catholic, for which we ought to congratulate him.

He has been freed from the division and error of the Donatists, or rather of the Rogatists, by which he was formerly held—provided that he understands Catholic truth as he ought, so that we may truly rejoice in his conversion.

## CHAPTER THREE

3. He possesses eloquence with which he can explain what he thinks. We must therefore deal with him and wish that he may think rightly, lest he make useless things pleasing and cause what he has expressed eloquently to appear true. Even in his eloquence, however, he has much to correct and much that must be restrained from excessive exuberance. This also displeased you in him, as a serious man, as your writings show.

But this defect is either easily corrected or, without harm to the faith, loved by superficial minds and tolerated by serious ones. We already have some people who are frothy in speech but sound in faith. There is therefore no reason to despair that this feature too—although tolerable if it persists—may nevertheless be cleansed and moderated, and either brought or restored to a complete and solid standard. This is especially so because he is said to be young, so that what he lacks in experience he may make up by diligence, and what the immaturity of loquacity belches forth may be refined by the maturity of age.

What is troubling and dangerous [Col. 0477], or destructive, is that when eloquence is praised, folly should be persuaded, and a pestilential drink should be swallowed from a precious cup.

## CHAPTER FOUR

4. To begin now to demonstrate what must especially be avoided in his argument: he says that the soul was indeed made by God and is not a part or nature of God—which is entirely true. But when he refuses to admit that it was made from nothing, and mentions no other creature from which it was made, he gives it God as its author in such a way that it is believed to have been made neither from no existing thing, that is, from nothing, nor from some thing that is not what God is, but from God himself.

He does not realize that he is thereby driven back to the position from which he thinks he has withdrawn: namely, that the soul is nothing other than God’s nature. Consequently, something would also be made from God’s nature by that same God, so that the material from which he makes would himself be the maker. Thus God’s nature would be changeable, and that nature of God, changed for the worse, would be condemned by that same God.

With your faithful understanding, you see how impossible this opinion is, how it must be excluded from a Catholic heart, and how far it must be avoided. The soul was made either from breath, or it itself was made the breath of God, in such a way that it is not from God’s own substance but was created by him from nothing.

For when a human being breathes, he cannot make breath from nothing; he draws it from the surrounding air and gives it back. We must not therefore suppose that some airs already surrounded God, of which he drew a small portion by breathing and exhaled it when he breathed into the face of the human being, thereby making the soul in that manner. Even if this were so, what he breathed could still be from some underlying, breath-bearing thing rather than from God himself.

But far be it from us to deny that the Almighty could make from nothing the breath of life by which the human being would become a living soul. We must not be forced into the alternatives of supposing either that something already existed which God was not, from which he made the breath, or that he made from himself what we see to be changeable. For what is from him must necessarily be of the same nature as he is; and consequently it must also be unchangeable.

But the soul, as everyone admits, is changeable. It is therefore not from him, because it is not unchangeable as he is. If, however, it was made from no other thing, then it was unquestionably made from nothing—but by him.

## CHAPTER FIVE

5. But when he argues that the soul is not spirit but body, what else does he intend to accomplish than to make us consist not of soul and body but of two, or even three, bodies? For when he says that we consist of spirit, soul, and body, and asserts that all three are bodies, he clearly thinks that we are composed of three bodies.

How much absurdity follows him in this opinion I think should be demonstrated to him rather than to you. Yet this is a tolerable error in a man who has not yet learned that there is something which, although it is not body, can nevertheless bear a certain resemblance to body.

## CHAPTER SIX

6. But who could tolerate this? In the second book, when he was attempting to solve the extremely difficult question of original sin, insofar as it concerns body and soul, if the soul is not drawn from the parents but is newly breathed in by God, he strives to unravel this troublesome and profound problem and says:

“Rightly, through the flesh, it restores its former condition, which it seemed for a little while to have lost through the flesh, so that through that by which it had deserved to be defiled it might begin to be reborn.”

You see, surely, that a man who dared to undertake what exceeded his powers has fallen into such an immense precipice that he said the soul deserved to be defiled through the flesh, although he cannot possibly say where it derived this merit before the flesh.

For if it begins to acquire the merit of sin from the flesh, let him say, if he can, how it deserved, through the flesh, to be defiled before its own sin. For this merit by which it was sent into sinful flesh so that it might be defiled by it was surely derived either from itself or—from what is much more abhorrent—from God.

It could not have derived from the flesh, before the flesh, the merit by which it was sent into the flesh to be defiled. If, then, it derived this merit from itself, how did it derive it, when before the flesh it had done nothing evil? But if it is said to have derived this merit from God, who could hear it? Who could endure it? Who could permit such a thing to be said with impunity?

For the question here is not what it deserved so that it might be judged worthy of condemnation after the flesh, but what it deserved before the flesh so as to be condemned in such a way that it would be sent into the flesh to be defiled. Let him explain this, if he can—the man who dared to say that the soul deserved to be defiled through the flesh.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

7. Likewise, in another passage, when he presented for solution the same question in which he had entangled himself, he spoke as though in the person of his opponents:

“Why,” they say, “did God punish the soul with so unjust a penalty that he wished to banish it into a body, when it begins to be sinful through association with the flesh, although it could not have been sinful?”

In the whirlpool of this question, full of reefs, he ought certainly to have avoided shipwreck and not ventured into a place from which he could not rescue himself by passing through it, but perhaps only by turning back—that is, by repenting.

He attempts to free himself from the foreknowledge of God, but in vain. God’s foreknowledge foreknows as sinners those whom he will heal; it does not make them sinners. For if he frees from sin those souls whom he himself entangled in sin while they were innocent and pure, he heals a wound that he inflicted upon us, not one that he found in us.

But may God avert it, and may it be wholly absent from us, that we should say that when God cleanses the souls of infants in the bath of regeneration, he is then correcting evils of his own which he himself caused in them, when he joined souls possessing no sin to sinful flesh, by whose original sin they would be defiled. Yet this man, accusing them, says that they deserved to be defiled through the flesh, and he cannot say where they deserved so great an evil before the flesh.

## CHAPTER EIGHT

8. Thinking, therefore, that he could dissolve this question by appealing to God’s foreknowledge, he only entangles himself further and says:

“If the soul deserved to be sinful, although it could not have been sinful, nevertheless it did not remain in sin, because, having been prefigured in Christ, it ought not to be in sin, just as it could not have been.”

What does he mean by saying that it “could not have been sinful” or “could not have been in sin,” unless, I suppose, he means that it could not have been so if it had not come into the flesh? For if it is not drawn from a parent, it could not have been sinful through original sin, or in any way been in original sin, except through the flesh.

We therefore see it freed from sin by grace, but we do not see where it deserved to be bound to sin. What, then, does he mean when he says, “If it deserved to be sinful, nevertheless it did not remain in sin”? If I ask him why it did not remain in sin, he will answer most correctly that the grace of Christ freed it. Therefore, just as he says from what the soul of an infant was freed as sinful, so let him also say from what it deserved to become sinful.

9. But what does he say, when this very thing that he had stated beforehand has happened to him? For, in proposing this question to himself, he said:

“Other reproaches are heaped up, presented by the querulous murmurs of those who bark at us; and, shaken as though by some whirlwind, we are repeatedly dashed against immense rocks.”

If I said this about him, he might perhaps be angry. These are his own words. After prefacing them, he proposed the question in which he displayed the very rocks against which he had been dashed and suffered shipwreck.

For he has been driven to this point, carried against, struck upon, and fixed in such dreadful cliffs that he cannot extricate himself at all except by correcting what he said. He is unable to show by what merit the soul was made sinful, although he did not fear to say that, before any sin of its own, it deserved to become sinful.

Who deserves so immense a punishment without sin that, being conceived in another’s iniquity, before leaving its mother’s womb it is already not without sin? By free grace, without any preceding merits of their own, Christ frees from this punishment the souls of infants who are regenerated in him; otherwise grace would no longer be grace (Rom. 11:6).

Therefore let this very intelligent man, who dislikes our cautious hesitation in so profound a matter, though it may not be learned, say, if he can, by what merit the soul reached this punishment—a punishment from which grace frees it without merit. Let him say this, so that, if he can, he may defend what he said by some argument.

I would not demand this of him unless he himself had said that the soul deserved to be sinful. Let him state whether its merit was good or evil. If it was good, by what good merit did it come into evil? If it was evil, where did it obtain an evil merit before any sin?

I ask again: if it was good, then grace does not free it gratuitously but according to a debt, since a good merit preceded it; and thus grace will no longer be grace. But if it was evil, I ask what that evil was. Was it the fact that it came into the flesh—something it would not have done unless the One in whom there is no iniquity had himself sent it?

Thus he will never attempt to establish this opinion of his except by plunging himself into worse difficulties: the opinion in which he said that the soul deserved to be sinful.

As for those infants whose original sin is washed away in Baptism, he has found, in some fashion, something to say: since God’s foreknowledge could not have harmed those predestined to eternal life by allowing them for a short time to be involved in another’s sin. This could be said tolerably enough if the man did not entangle himself in his own words by saying that the soul deserved to be sinful. He cannot free himself from this unless he regrets having said it.

## CHAPTER NINE

[Col. 0480]

10. But when he wished to answer concerning those infants who are overtaken by death before they are baptized in Christ, he dared to promise them not only paradise but also the kingdom of heaven. He found no way out, lest he be forced to say that God condemns innocent souls to eternal death—souls whom he inserts into sinful flesh without any preceding merit of sin.

Yet, sensing in some way what evil he had said [Note: [Col. 0480] More manuscripts read, “what he had said wrongly.”], namely, that the souls of infants are redeemed into eternal life and the kingdom of heaven without any grace of Christ, and that original sin can be removed in them without Christ’s Baptism, in which the remission of sins takes place, he saw into what depth of a shipwreck-filled whirlpool he had thrown himself and said:

“Certainly, I judge that continual offerings should be made for them, and that the sacrifices of the priests should be offered continually on their behalf.”

Here is another position from which he will never escape unless he regrets having said it. For who offers the body of Christ except for those who are members of Christ?

Since Christ said, “Unless one is born of water and the Spirit [Note: [Col. 0480] The printed editions read, “of water and the Holy Spirit.” The word “holy” is absent from the manuscripts.], he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5), and elsewhere, “Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it” (Matt. 10:39), no one becomes a member of Christ except either by Baptism in Christ or by death for Christ.

11. For this reason that thief—the one who was not a follower before the Lord’s cross, but became a confessor on the cross—about whom a precedent is sometimes seized upon or attempted against the sacrament of Baptism, is counted by Saint Cyprian among the martyrs who are baptized in their own blood. This occurs to many unbaptized people during a raging persecution [Note: [Col. 0480] See Book 4, *On Baptism against the Donatists*, no. 29, and *Questions on Leviticus*, question 84; Book 2 of the *Retractations*, chapters 18 and 55.].

For so great was the weight assigned to it, and so much did it count before him who knew how to weigh such things, that the thief confessed the crucified Lord as much as if he had been crucified for the Lord. His faith then blossomed from the wood when that of the disciples withered—unless it revived through the resurrection of the One whose death had caused it to wither through fear.

They despaired of the One who was dying; he hoped in the One who was dying beside him. They fled from the Author of life; he entreated the companion in punishment. They mourned the death as though he were merely human; he believed that he would reign after death. They abandoned the guarantor of salvation; he honored his companion on the cross.

In him was found the measure of a martyr: he believed in Christ at the very moment when those who were destined to become martyrs had failed. This was clear to the Lord’s eyes, who immediately granted such blessedness to one who had not been baptized, as though he had been cleansed by the blood of martyrdom (Luke 23:43).

But who among us would not also consider with what faith, hope, and love a person could accept death for the living Christ, when he sought life in the dying Christ?

Moreover, it is not implausibly said that the thief who then believed, crucified beside the Lord, was bathed in the water that flowed from the wound in his side, as though in a most sacred baptism. I will say nothing of the fact that no one knows or can prove that he had not been baptized before he was condemned.

Let each person accept these matters as he wishes, provided that no one uses the example of this thief to set aside the Savior’s command concerning Baptism. Let no one promise unbaptized infants some intermediate place—whether of rest or happiness, wherever it may be—between condemnation and the kingdom of heaven.

The Pelagian heresy also promised this to them: it neither feared condemnation for infants, since it thinks that they have no original sin, nor hoped that they would attain the kingdom of heaven if they did not reach the sacrament of Baptism. But this man, while confessing that infants are bound by original sin, dared to promise them the kingdom of heaven even without Baptism—something not even those dared to promise who assert that infants are entirely without any sin.

See in what snares of presumption he entangles himself, unless he regrets having written such things.

## CHAPTER TEN

12. As for Dinocrates, the brother of the holy Perpetua, the account itself is not canonical Scripture, nor did she—or whoever wrote it—write in such a way as to say that the boy, who had died at the age of seven, had died without Baptism. It is believed that she was heard on his behalf when martyrdom was imminent, so that he might be transferred from punishments to rest.

For children of that age can already lie and speak the truth, confess and deny. Therefore, when they are baptized, they also recite the creed and answer for themselves when questioned.

Who, then, knows whether, after Baptism, during the time of persecution, that boy was alienated from Christ by his impious father through idolatry, and therefore went into condemnation, from which he emerged only through the prayers of his sister, who was destined to die for Christ?

## CHAPTER ELEVEN

13. But even if this were granted to him—though it cannot in any way be granted without violating the Catholic faith and ecclesiastical rule—that a sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood should be offered for unbaptized people of any age, as though they might be helped to reach the kingdom of heaven through such piety on the part of their own people, what will he answer concerning the many thousands of infants who are born to the impious, never come into the hands of the devout through any divine or human compassion, and depart from this life at that tender age without the bath of regeneration?

Let him say, if he can, by what means these souls deserved to become sinful in such a way that they would not afterward be freed from sin at all. If I ask why they deserve condemnation if they are not baptized, the proper answer is: on account of original sin. If I then ask where they derived original sin, he will answer: certainly from sinful flesh.

If, therefore, I ask where they deserved to be condemned into sinful flesh, although they had done nothing evil before the flesh, let him find what answer he can give [Note: [Col. 0481] In some manuscripts the words “let him find what answer he can give” are transposed to below, after “may cleanse the defiled.”]. Thus they are condemned to undergo the contagion of others’ sins, so that neither Baptism regenerates those badly generated nor sacrifices cleanse the defiled.

For these infants were born, or are still being born, among such people and from such people, so that no such assistance can be offered to them. Here, certainly, every argument fails.

For we are not asking where souls deserved to be condemned after association with sinful flesh. We are asking where souls deserved to be condemned to undergo association with sinful flesh when they had no sin before that association with sinful flesh.

One cannot say: “The contagion of another’s sin, shared for a short time, did them no harm, since redemption had been prepared for them in God’s foreknowledge.” For we are now speaking of those who depart from the body before Baptism, and for whom no redemption comes to their aid.

One cannot say: “Those whom Baptism does not cleanse will be cleansed by frequent sacrifices offered for them. God, foreseeing this, wished them to cling for a short time to the sins of others without any danger of eternal condemnation and with the hope of eternal happiness.” For we are now speaking of those whose birth among the impious and from the impious could find no such means of assistance.

Indeed, if such aid could be provided, it would undoubtedly be unable to benefit the unbaptized—just as the sacrifices for dead sinners mentioned from the Book of Maccabees (2 Macc. 12:43) would have been of no benefit to them if they had not been circumcised.

14. Let him therefore find, if he can, what to say when he is asked what the soul, without any sin—whether original or personal—deserved, so as to be condemned to undergo another’s original sin in such a way that it could not be freed from it.

And let him see which of two alternatives he should choose: whether to say that even the souls of infants who die and depart from this life without the bath of regeneration, for whom no sacrifice of the Lord’s body is offered, are released from the bond of original sin, even though the Apostle teaches that all go into condemnation through one (Rom. 5:16), and that grace does not come to their aid so that they may be rescued through one into redemption; or whether to say that souls possessing neither personal nor original sin, and innocent, simple, and pure in every respect, are punished by the just God with eternal condemnation when he himself inserts them into sinful flesh without intending to free them.

## CHAPTER TWELVE
15. I affirm that neither of these two alternatives should be stated—and not the third either, namely, that souls sinned elsewhere before entering the flesh, so that they deserved to be condemned in the flesh. For the Apostle has most explicitly determined that those not yet born in the flesh had done nothing either good or evil (Rom. 9:11). Hence it is clear that infants, since they need remission of sins, have contracted no sin except original sin.

Nor should we assert the fourth alternative: that the souls of infants who will die without Baptism are banished and condemned by the just God into sinful flesh because he foresaw that, had they reached an age at which they could exercise free choice, they would have lived wickedly. Indeed, this man himself, placed in such great difficulty, did not dare to say this. Rather, he has already spoken sufficiently clearly and briefly against this absurdity where he says: “God would have been unjust if he wished to judge a human being who had not been born, without the completed works of his own will.”

He said this in response to the question raised against those who say: Why did God make a human being whom, as one who foreknew the future, he knew would not be good? He would have judged someone not yet born if he had refused to create him for the reason that he foresaw that he would not be good. And surely, as this man himself saw, God ought to have judged a human being on the basis of his completed deeds [Col. 0483], not on the basis of things foreknown and never permitted to occur.

For if sins that a person would have committed had he lived are condemned even though they were not committed in one who has died, then no benefit was conferred on the one who was snatched away lest wickedness change his understanding (Wis. 4:11). He would be judged according to the wickedness that would have been in him, not according to the innocence that was found in him. Nor could there be security concerning any baptized person who has died, since after Baptism people can not only sin in some manner but can also become apostates.

What, then, if the baptized person who was snatched away was destined to become an apostate, had he lived? Shall we think that no benefit was conferred on him by being snatched away lest wickedness change his understanding, and shall we decide that, because of God’s foreknowledge, he must be judged not as a faithful member of Christ but as an apostate? How much better would it be, if sins not yet committed or even conceived, but foreknown and future, are punished, for those two to have been cast out of paradise before sinning, lest sin be committed in so holy and blessed a place?

Moreover, foreknowledge itself is utterly emptied of meaning if what is foreknown will not occur. For how can something be rightly said to be foreknown as future if it will not be future? How, then, are sins punished that do not exist—that is, sins committed neither before the flesh, when this life had not yet begun, nor after the flesh, when death has intervened?

**CHAPTER XIII**

16. This intervening period, from the time when the soul was sent into the flesh until it is released from the flesh, since it is the period of an infant’s soul, which has not yet exercised the age of free choice, provides no basis on which the soul could be condemned for not having received Baptism except original sin. We do not deny that the soul is justly condemned for this sin, since a just law has established punishment for sin. But we ask why it was condemned to undergo this sin, if it is not drawn from that one sin committed by the first father of the human race.

Therefore, if God does not condemn the innocent, nor make guilty those whom he sees to be innocent; if souls are not freed either from original sins or from their own sins except by Christ’s Baptism in Christ’s Church; if souls had absolutely no sin before entering the flesh; and if sins cannot be condemned by a just law before they are committed—and still less sins that are never committed—let this man state none of these four alternatives. Instead, if he can, let him explain for what merit the souls of infants who depart without Baptism are sent into sinful flesh, though they have committed no sin, so that there they may find sin on account of which they could justly be condemned.

But if, avoiding these four positions condemned by sound doctrine—that is, if he does not dare to say that God makes souls sinful when they exist without any sin; or that original sin is released in them without Christ’s sacrament; or that they sinned somewhere before being sent into the flesh; or that sins they never possessed are condemned in them—if, not daring to say these things to us because they ought not to be said, he should assert that infants do not contract original sin and have no ground for condemnation if they depart this life without receiving the sacrament of regeneration [Col. 0484], he will unquestionably fall under condemnation into the Pelagian heresy, which is itself deserving of condemnation.

To prevent this from happening to him, how much better it is for him to retain my hesitation concerning the origin of the soul, rather than dare to affirm what he neither comprehends by human reason nor defends by divine authority—lest, while fearing to confess ignorance, he be compelled to profess folly.

**CHAPTER XIV**

17. At this point he may perhaps say that his opinion is defended by divine authority, since he believes that he can prove from testimonies of the holy Scriptures that souls are made by God, not through propagation, but are newly breathed into each individual. Let him prove it, if he can, and I shall acknowledge that I have learned from him what I have sought with great earnestness. But let him look elsewhere, lest perhaps he find something; for he has not proved this by the testimonies he has already brought forward.

Everything he has adduced here is certain with respect to some matter; but with respect to the question being asked about the origin of the soul, these passages are shown to be ambiguous. It is certain that God gave human beings breath and spirit, as the prophet says: “Thus says the Lord, who made heaven and founded the earth and all that is in it, who gives breath to the people upon it and spirit to those who tread upon it” (Isa. 42:5).

This man wants this testimony to be understood in support of the opinion he defends, so that when it says, “he gives breath to the people,” it may be believed that God does not make souls for the people through propagation, but breathes new souls into them. Let him therefore dare to say that God himself did not give us flesh, because the origin of flesh has been drawn from parents. And when the Apostle says of the grain of wheat, “God gives it a body as he wills” (1 Cor. 15:38), let him deny, if he dares, that wheat comes from wheat and its stalk from seed according to its kind.

If he does not dare to deny this, how does he know, then, how the words “he gives breath to the people” are to be understood—whether God draws that breath from parents or breathes it in as something new?

18. How does he also know whether this is a repetition of the same statement: “who gives breath to the people upon it, and spirit to those who tread upon it,” so that both expressions are understood to refer to one matter, and whether the prophet intended to signify not the soul or spirit by which human nature lives, but the Holy Spirit?

For if the Holy Spirit could not be signified by breath, the Lord would not have breathed upon the disciples after his resurrection and said, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). Nor would it have been written in the Acts of the Apostles: “Suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a violent breath being carried along, and divided tongues appeared to them as if of fire, which also rested upon each one of them, and they were all filled with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:2–4).

What if the prophet foretold this when he said, “who gives breath to the people upon it”? And, as though explaining what he had called breath, repeated himself and said, “and spirit to those who tread upon it”? For this was most clearly accomplished when they were all filled with the Holy Spirit.

Or, if the one hundred and twenty people who were then present in one place should not yet be called a people, certainly when four or five thousand believed together, were baptized, and received the Holy Spirit (Acts 4:31), who could doubt that the people received the Holy Spirit together, and that the multitude walking upon the earth—that is, human beings treading upon the earth—received him?

The breath given in relation to human nature, whether it is given through propagation or newly breathed in—neither of which, I say, should be affirmed until one or the other becomes clear beyond doubt—is not given to those treading upon the earth, but to those still enclosed in the mother’s womb.

Therefore he gave breath to the people upon the earth and spirit to those treading upon it when many believed together and were filled together with the Holy Spirit. He gives this to his people, even if not to all at once but to each at his own time, until, as some depart this life and others enter it, the full number of that same people is completed. [Note: The manuscripts read, “even if not to all at once, at each one’s own time,” omitting “but.”]

Thus in this passage of holy Scripture “breath” is not one thing and “spirit” another, but the same statement is repeated. Just as “the one who dwells in the heavens” is not one person and “the Lord” another, nor “laugh” one thing and “mock” another, but the same statement is repeated where we read, “He who dwells in the heavens will laugh at them, and the Lord will mock them.”

Likewise, when it says, “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:4, 8), it certainly does not mean one thing by “inheritance” and another by “possession,” or one thing by “nations” and another by “the ends of the earth”; it is a repetition of the same statement. If he pays attention to what he reads, he will find innumerable expressions of this kind in the divine utterances.

19. The word that the Greek has as πνοήν (*pnoēn*) the Latins have translated variously: sometimes as *flatus* (“breath”), sometimes as *spiritus* (“spirit”), and sometimes as *inspiratio* (“inspiration”). For the Greek manuscripts have this word in the prophetic testimony we are now discussing, where it says, “who gives breath to the people upon it”: that is, πνοήν (*pnoēn*).

It is the same word where the human being was animated: “And God breathed into his face the breath of life” (Gen. 2:7). It is also the same word in the Psalm where it is sung: “Let every spirit praise the Lord” (Ps. 150:6). It is also the same in the book of Job, where it is written: “But the inspiration of the Almighty is what gives understanding.”

He did not wish to say “breath” but “inspiration,” although the Greek has πνοή (*pnoē*), the same word found in the prophet’s words we are now discussing. And certainly in this passage, I do not know whether it ought to be doubted that the Holy Spirit is signified. The subject was wisdom and its source in human beings: “For it is not the number of years,” he says, “but it is the spirit in human beings; and the inspiration of the Almighty is what gives understanding” (Job 32:7–8, according to the Septuagint). By this repetition, it may be understood that when he said, “the spirit is in human beings,” he was not speaking of the human spirit.

For he wished to show where they obtain wisdom: not from themselves. He explained this by repeating himself and saying, “The inspiration of the Almighty is what gives understanding.”

Likewise, elsewhere in the same book he says: “The understanding of my lips shall understand what is pure; the divine Spirit who made me, and the inspiration of the Almighty, teaches me” (Job 33:3–4, according to the Septuagint). Here too, what he calls “inspiration,” or “breathing in,” is πνοήν (*pnoēn*) in Greek, the word translated as “breath” in the prophet’s words.

Therefore, when it is rashly denied that the words “who gives breath to the people upon it, and spirit to those who tread upon it” refer to the human soul or spirit—although the Holy Spirit can much more plausibly be understood there—how could anyone dare to define that the prophet intended in that passage to signify the soul or spirit by which our nature lives [Col. 0486]?

Certainly, even if he had said most explicitly, “who gives a soul to the people upon the earth,” it would still have to be asked whether God gives it from the origin of the preceding generation, just as from the origin of the preceding generation he nevertheless gives the body [Note: The manuscripts omit “he himself” (ipse).]—not only to a human being or an animal, but also to a grain of wheat or to any other thing—as he wills; or whether he breathes in a new soul, as the first human being received one.

**Note:** The passage may perhaps be read as follows: “How could anyone dare to define that the prophet intended in that passage to signify the soul or spirit by which our nature lives as given by God not through propagation?”

20. There are also those who understand these prophetic words in such a way that when he says, “He gave breath to the people upon it,” that is, upon the earth, they want “breath” to be understood only as the soul; but when he adds, “and spirit to those who tread upon it,” they believe that the Holy Spirit is signified. They take this to follow the order in which the Apostle also says: “Not first the spiritual, but the animal; afterward, the spiritual” (1 Cor. 15:46).

From this prophetic statement an elegant meaning can also be drawn: that he said “those who tread upon it” in order to indicate “those who despise it.” For those who receive the Holy Spirit despise earthly things out of love for heavenly things.

All these interpretations are not contrary to the faith—whether someone understands both expressions, “breath” and “spirit,” as referring to what belongs to human nature; or understands both as spoken of the Holy Spirit; or refers “breath” to the soul and “spirit” to the Holy Spirit.

But if the human soul and spirit are also to be understood here, then, just as there should be no doubt that God gives them, it must still be asked from where he gives them: whether through propagation, just as he himself gives—but nevertheless gives through propagation—the members of the body; or whether he gives them as something new, distributing them to individuals by breathing them in. We want this to be defended by the authority of the divine utterances through some entirely certain testimony, not through ambiguous passages, as this man does.

21. By the same reasoning, the words of God, “For the spirit shall go forth from me, and I have made every breath” (Isa. 57:16), must be understood as referring to the Holy Spirit where he says, “The spirit shall go forth from me”; concerning this the Savior also says, “He proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26). But the words “I have made every breath” cannot be denied to refer to every soul.

Yet God himself also makes every body. And no one doubts that he makes the human body through propagation. Accordingly, although it is established that he makes the soul, it must still be asked from where he makes it: whether through propagation, as with the body, or by breathing it in, as he made the first soul.

22. He also added a third testimony, since it is written: “He who forms the spirit of a human being within him” (Zech. 12:1). As though this were denied! The question is from where he forms it. For who but God forms the bodily eye of a human being? And I think that he forms it not outside but within him [Col. 0486; note: understand, “forms”]. Yet it is nevertheless certain that it comes through propagation. Since, then, he also forms the human spirit within him, it must be asked whether he does so by a new breathing-in or by drawing it from propagation.

**[Col. 0487] 23.** We also know how the mother of the Maccabean youths, more fruitful in virtue when her sons suffered than in offspring when they were born, encouraged them, saying:

“My children, I do not know how you appeared in my womb” [Note: Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice here and shortly afterward read, “I do not know how you appeared in my womb”; the Vulgate supports this reading, saying, “I do not know how you appeared in my womb.” Lovaniensis, however, has, “I do not know how you came into my womb,” with this note: “The manuscripts consistently read this, not only in this passage but also in two others below. I believe Augustine used this version because it closely expresses the Septuagint, where the accusative is likewise found.” The Greek reads: Οὐκ οἶδα ὅπως εἰς τὴν ἐμὴν ἐφάνητε κοιλίαν (*ouk oida hopōs eis tēn emēn ephēnate koilian*). M.]

“For I did not give you spirit and soul, nor did I form the appearance and limbs of each of you; but God, who made the world and all that is in it, and who made the human race and investigates the deeds of all, will himself restore spirit and soul to you in great mercy” (2 Macc. 7:22–23). [Note: The text probably ought to read “origin” (*ortum*); the Greek has γένεσιν (*genesin*).]

We know these words, certainly; but we do not see how they support what he asserts. For what Christian would deny that God gives human beings soul and spirit? Yet I think this man likewise cannot deny that God gives human beings a tongue, an ear, a hand, a foot, all the bodily senses, and the form and nature of all their limbs. How could he deny that these are gifts of God unless he forgot that he was a Christian?

But just as it is established that these things are made and given by him through propagation, so it must also be asked from where the human spirit and soul are produced by him, by whom they are produced and given: whether from the parents, or from nothing, or—as this man asserts, though it must be avoided at all costs—from some existing nature of his breath, not created from nothing but from God himself.

**CHAPTER XV**

24. Since, then, the testimonies of Scripture that he cites by no means teach what he tries to persuade us of—for with respect to this question they do not express it at all—what does he mean when he constantly asserts, “We say that the soul comes from the breath of God, not through transmission, because it is given by God”?

As though the body were given from anyone other than the one by whom it is created, from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things (Rom. 11:36)—although it is not from his nature but from his workmanship.

“Nor is it from nothing,” he says, “because it proceeds from God.” We are not yet merely advising that it must be asked whether this is so; rather, we firmly affirm without hesitation that what he says is absolutely not true—namely, that the soul is neither through transmission nor from nothing.

It must be one of two alternatives: if it is not through transmission, it is from nothing. Otherwise it would be from God in such a way as to belong to God’s nature, which it is wholly sacrilegious to believe. But we still demand or seek certain testimonies that it is not through transmission—not testimonies such as those he has offered, by which what we are asking is not demonstrated.

25. If only, in the midst of so deep a question, while he does not know what to say, he would imitate the mother of the Maccabeans! She knew that she had conceived sons from a man and that they had been created for her by the Creator of all things, whether according to body or according to soul and spirit. Nevertheless she said, “I do not know how you came into my womb.”

I wish he would say what it was that she did not know. She certainly knew what I have just mentioned: how they had come into her womb according to the body, since she could not doubt that she had conceived them from a man. She also confessed—and she certainly knew this—that God had given them soul and spirit, and that he himself had formed their appearance and limbs.

What, then, did she not know? Perhaps what we too do not know: whether the soul and spirit that God undoubtedly gave them had been drawn from their parents, or whether he had breathed them in as something new, as he had done for the first human being?

But whether she was ignorant of this or of some other matter concerning the formation of human nature, she said that she did not know it; she did not rashly defend what she did not know.

Yet he would not say to her what he was not ashamed to say to us [Note: Four manuscripts read “what he was not ashamed to say about us” (*quod de nobis dicere*)]: “A human being, when placed in honor, did not understand; he was compared with senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. 48:13). Behold, this woman said of her sons, “I do not know how you came into my womb,” and yet she is not compared with senseless beasts.

She said, “I do not know”; and as though they were asking her why she did not know, she added: “For I did not give you spirit and soul.” Therefore the one who gave them knows from where he made what he gave—whether he drew it from propagation or breathed it in as something new. “I did not form the appearance and limbs of each of you”; the one who formed them knows whether he formed them together with the soul or whether he gave them a soul after they had already been formed.

How, then, did she not know by which of these means her sons had entered her womb, while she nevertheless knew that the one who gave everything would restore everything? Let this man choose what this woman did not know amid the profound and hidden secret of human nature. Only let him not judge her to be a liar, nor compare the woman who was ignorant with senseless beasts.

Whatever it was that she did not know certainly belonged to human nature; yet a human being could be ignorant of it without fault.

Therefore I too say of my soul: “I do not know how it came into my body; for I did not give it to myself.” The one who gave it knows whether he drew it from my father, or created it new, as he did for the first human being. I too shall know if he himself teaches me, whenever he wishes. But for now I do not know, and I am not ashamed, as this man is, to confess that I do not know what I do not know [Note: Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice read: “Nor am I ashamed to confess that I do not know what I do not know.” M.]

**CHAPTER XVI**

26. “Learn,” he says; “behold, the Apostle teaches.” I shall certainly learn if the Apostle teaches, for it is God who teaches through the Apostle. But what, finally, does the Apostle teach?

“Behold,” he says, “when he was speaking to the Athenians, he explained this consistently, saying: ‘Since he himself gives life and spirit to all.’”

Who denies this? “But understand,” he says, “what the Apostle says: ‘he gives,’” he says, “not ‘he gave,’ referring it to an unlimited and continuous time, not declaring it concerning the past and completed action. And what he gives without cessation, he always gives, just as he himself is always the one who gives.”

I have set down his words just as I found them in the second book of his writings that you sent.

First observe how far he has proceeded while attempting to affirm what he does not know. For he has dared to say that God gives souls not only now and in this present age, but throughout infinite time without cessation, indeed always, to those who are being born.

“He always gives,” he says, “just as he himself is always the one who gives” [Col. 0489].

It is clear enough what the Apostle said [Note: Two manuscripts read *quod* (“that”) for *quid* (“what”).], and far be it from me to deny that I understand it. But what this man says, he too ought to understand is contrary to the Christian faith, and he should take care not to say it any further.

For when the dead have risen, no one will then be born. Therefore at that time he will not give souls to those being born, but will judge with their bodies the souls he gives in this present age. He does not, then, always give, although he himself is always the one who now gives.

Nor, because the blessed Apostle did not say “he gave” but “he gives,” does it follow that what this man wants to establish is established—namely, that God does not give souls through propagation. He himself gives them even if he gives them through propagation.

For he gives human beings the members of the body, the bodily senses, the bodily form, and the entire substance of the body, although he gives these through propagation.

When the Lord says, “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven” (Matt. 6:30), he does not say “he clothed it,” as when he first established it, but says “he clothes it,” referring to what he does now. Yet for this reason we will not deny that lilies are produced from the origin of their own kind.

What, then, if the soul and spirit of a human being are likewise given by God as long as they are being given, and yet are given through the propagation of their own kind? I neither defend nor refute this. But if it is to be defended or refuted, I insist that this must be done by clear, not ambiguous, testimonies.

Nor should I therefore be compared with senseless beasts because I declare that I do not yet know this. Rather, I should be compared with cautious people, because I do not dare to teach what I do not know.

As for him, I do not in return compare him with beasts, as though repaying an insult with an insult. I admonish him as a son to confess that he does not know what he does not know, and not attempt to teach what he has not yet learned—lest he be compared not with beasts but with those people of whom the Apostle says that they desire to be teachers of the law, understanding neither what they say nor the matters about which they make assertions (1 Tim. 1:7).

**CHAPTER XVII**

27. For why is it that he fails to pay attention to the Scriptures of which he speaks, so that when he reads that human beings are from God, he insists that they are from God not also according to the body but only according to soul and spirit?

When the Apostle says, “We are from him” (Acts 17:28), this man does not want the words referred to the body but only to the soul and spirit.

If bodies are not from God, then what is written is false: “From him and through him and in him are all things” (Rom. 11:36).

Moreover, when the same Apostle says, “For just as the woman is from the man, so also the man is through the woman,” let this man explain what kind of propagation he intended to signify: of the soul, of the body, or of both.

But he does not want souls to be from propagation. It remains, then, that according to him and all who destroy the propagation of souls, the Apostle signified only the male and female body [Note: The manuscripts read *significaret* (“would signify”).] when he said, “Just as the woman is from the man, so also the man is through the woman,” because woman was made from man so that afterward man might be born through woman.
