If, then, in saying this the Apostle did not want souls and spirits also to be understood, but only the bodies of both sexes, why did he immediately add, “But all things are from God” (1 Cor. 11:12), unless bodies too are from God?

For this is how he speaks: “Just as the woman is from the man, so also the man is through the woman; but all things are from God.”

Let this man choose what the words refer to. If they refer to bodies, then bodies too are from God.

What, then, is the meaning of his wanting “from God” to be understood wherever he reads it in Scripture, when human beings are under discussion, not as including bodies but only souls and spirits?

But if “all things are from God” was spoken both of the body of either sex and of soul and spirit, then the woman is from the man in every respect.

The woman is from the man, the man through the woman, and all things are from God. What “all things” could these be except those of which he was speaking: the man from whom the woman came, the woman who came from the man, and the man who was born afterward through the woman?

For the man from whom the woman came was not through the woman; rather, it was the man who was later born from the man through the woman, as human beings are born even today.

Accordingly, if the Apostle was speaking of bodies when he said these things, then unquestionably the bodies of both sexes are from God.

But if he does not want anything belonging to human beings to be from God except souls and spirits, then the woman is from the man according to soul and spirit as well, and nothing remains for those who argue against the propagation of souls.

If, however, he divides the matter in such a way as to say that the woman is from the man according to the body but from God according to soul and spirit, how will the Apostle’s statement, “But all things are from God,” be true, if the woman’s body is so from the man that it is not from God?

Therefore, in order that the Apostle should speak truth rather than this man be preferred to the Apostle, the woman is from the man, whether according to the body alone or according to the whole reality that constitutes human nature. We affirm none of these alternatives as certain, but are still seeking which is true.

And the man is through the woman, whether the whole of human nature is derived from the father [Note: Printed editions read “from a part”; most manuscripts read “from the father,” preferable here and above in §25.], which is born through the woman, or only the flesh, which remains a question.

Yet all things are from God, about which there is no question: body, soul, and spirit, both of man and of woman. Even if these were not born or drawn from God or flowed from him in such a way as to belong to his nature, they are nevertheless from God. For from the one by whom they were created, founded, and made, they derive their existence.

28. “But,” he says, “when the Apostle says, ‘He himself gives life and spirit to all,’ and then adds, ‘He made every race of human beings from one blood’ (Acts 17:25–26), he referred soul and spirit in their origin to the author, but the body to propagation.”

On the contrary, one who does not wish rashly to deny the propagation of souls before it becomes plainly clear whether this is so or not has something to understand in these words of the Apostle: that when he said “from one blood,” he said “from one human being,” signifying the whole from a part according to a manner of speech.

For if this man is permitted to understand the whole from a part in what is written, “And the human being became a living soul” (Gen. 2:7), so that the spirit, of which Scripture is silent there, may also be understood, why should others not be permitted to understand “from one blood” in such a way that soul and spirit may also be understood there, since the human being signified by the word “blood” consists not only of body but also of soul and spirit?

Just as one who defends the propagation of souls should not be overwhelmed by the fact that it is written of the first human being, “In whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12)—for it does not say, “In whom the flesh of all sinned,” but “all,” meaning all human beings, since a human being is not flesh alone—so this man should not use the words “every race of human beings from one blood” to press the defenders of the propagation of souls, as though only flesh therefore belonged to propagation.

If what these people assert [Note: Perhaps the singular, “this man asserts,” should be read.] is true—that soul does not come from soul, but only flesh from flesh—then “from one blood” was said so that the whole human being would not be signified by a part, but only the flesh of one human being.

But the words, “In whom all sinned,” would then have to be understood as referring only to the flesh of all human beings, which was transmitted from him, with Scripture signifying a part from the whole.

If, however, what is true is that the whole human being is propagated from the whole human being—that is, body, soul, and spirit—then “in whom all human beings sinned” was said literally, whereas “from one blood” is figurative: the whole is signified by a part, namely, the whole human being, who consists of soul and flesh—or rather, as this man likes to put it, of soul, spirit, and flesh.

For the divine utterances customarily signify the whole from a part and a part from the whole. The whole is signified from a part where we read, “All flesh will come to you” (Ps. 64:3), because the whole human being is understood from “flesh.” A part is signified from the whole when Christ is said to have been buried, although only his flesh was buried.

As for the statement included in this testimony of the Apostle—that he himself gives life and spirit to all—I think, according to the preceding discussion, that it troubles no one. He himself gives them; but we are still asking from where he gives them: whether by a new breathing-in or through propagation. For he is quite rightly said to give the substance of the flesh as well, although it is not denied that he gives it through propagation.

**CHAPTER XVIII**

29. Let us now examine the testimony from Genesis where the woman, made from the man’s side, was brought to him, and he said: “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.”

This man thinks that Adam ought to have said, “Soul from my soul” or “Spirit from my spirit,” if the soul or spirit too had been drawn from him.

But those who assert the propagation of souls believe that they can fortify their position more invincibly from this fact: Scripture says that God took a rib from the man’s side and built it into a woman, but it does not add that he breathed into her face the breath of life.

“Therefore,” they say, “this is because she had already been animated from the man. For if she had not been, holy Scripture would certainly not have defrauded us of knowledge of this matter.”

As for Adam’s words, “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,” and the fact that he did not say “spirit” or “soul,” “from my spirit” or “from my soul,” they can respond as was demonstrated above: that the words “my bone and my flesh” are to be understood as the whole from a part, though what was taken away was animated, not dead.

Nor should we deny that the Almighty could have done this merely because no human being can cut something from human flesh together with its soul.

For when Adam continued by adding, “She shall be called Woman, because she was taken from her man” (Gen. 2:23), why did he not instead say what would have confirmed their opinion, “Because her flesh was taken from her man”?

Those who hold the contrary view can therefore say that, since Scripture does not say that the woman’s flesh was taken from her man, but that the woman was taken from her man, she should be understood as a whole, together with soul and spirit.

Although the soul has no sex, nevertheless, when women are called women, they need not be understood with the soul excluded. Otherwise they would not be instructed to adorn themselves in this way: “Not with braided hair, or gold, or pearls, or expensive clothing, but—as is fitting for women who profess piety—through good conduct” (1 Tim. 2:9–10).

Piety is certainly inward, in the soul or spirit, and yet they are called women even when they are instructed to adorn themselves inwardly, where there is no sex.

30. Since these men have contended with one another in alternating argument, I judge between them in this way: I admonish both not to trust what is unknown and rashly affirm what they do not know.

For even if it had been written, “He breathed the breath of life into the woman’s face, and she became a living soul,” it still would not follow that the soul is not propagated from parents unless we also read that the same thing was written of their son.

It could have happened that an inanimate member taken from the body needed to be animated, while the son’s soul was drawn from the father through the mother by the transmission of propagation.

Since Scripture is silent, the matter has been concealed, not denied—but neither has it been affirmed. Accordingly, if somewhere it is not silent, the claim must be established by clearer evidence.

Thus those who defend the propagation of souls gain nothing from the fact that God did not breathe into the woman’s face; nor should those who deny it persuade themselves that they know the truth merely because Adam did not say, “Soul from my soul.”

For just as, while the question remained unresolved, Scripture could have been silent about the woman receiving a soul when God breathed upon her as he had breathed upon her man, so, while the same question remained unresolved, Scripture could have been silent so that Adam did not say, “Soul from my soul.”

Accordingly, if the soul of the first woman came from the man, then the whole was signified by a part where we read, “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh,” since the whole woman was taken from the man, not flesh alone.

But if she did not come from the man and God breathed a soul into her as he had into the man, then a part was signified by the whole where we read, “She was taken from her man,” since not all her flesh was taken.

31. Therefore, since these testimonies, insofar as they pertain to this matter, are plainly ambiguous and do not resolve the question, I nevertheless know this: those who infer from the fact that it was not said, “Soul from my soul,” but “bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh,” that the woman’s soul is not derived from the man’s soul, argue in the same way as the Apollinarists—or whoever else they may be—argue against the Lord’s soul, which they deny for the reason that they read, “The Word [Col. 0493] became flesh” (John 1:14). “For if the soul were there as well,” they say, “it ought to have been said, ‘The Word became man.’”

But they are answered by pointing out that Scripture commonly uses the name “flesh” for the whole human being, as in, “And all flesh shall see the salvation of God” (Isaiah 40:5; Luke 3:6). For flesh without a soul cannot see anything. Moreover, in many other passages of the holy Scriptures it is shown without any ambiguity that Christ the man possesses not only flesh but also a human soul—that is, a rational soul. Therefore those who defend the propagation of souls could also accept that “bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh” was said by synecdoche, from the part signifying the whole, so that the soul too is understood there, just as we understand that the Word became flesh not without a soul—provided that, just as the other testimonies teach that Christ possessed a human soul, they too established the propagation of souls by means of some unambiguous testimonies.

Conversely, therefore, we also admonish those who deny the propagation of souls to assert, on the basis of certain proofs, that new souls are breathed in by God. Then they should defend the claim that “bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh” was not said figuratively, with the part signifying the whole so that the soul is understood together with it, but literally of flesh alone.

## CHAPTER XIX

32. Since this is so, I see that this book must now be brought to a close. For it contains everything that seemed especially necessary to me, so that those who read it may know that they must take care not to agree with this man—whose two books you sent me—in believing that souls are from God’s breath in such a way that they are not from nothing.

Whoever believes this, even if he denies it in words, nevertheless proclaims in reality that souls possess God’s substance and are his offspring, not by gift but by nature. For no sensible person can deny that, from whatever source someone derives the origin of his nature, from that same source he derives the genus of his nature.

Yet this man is so self-contradictory that he says souls are God’s offspring by gift, not by nature, and nevertheless says that they derive their origin from him, not having been made from nothing. Thus he does not hesitate to refer them back to God’s nature, which he had previously denied.

33. We certainly do not forbid the defense of the view that new souls are breathed in without propagation, provided that it is defended by people who are able to find either in the canonical Books something unambiguous with which this exceedingly difficult question may be resolved, or in their own reasoning something that is not contrary to Catholic truth.

It must not be defended by people such as this man has shown himself to be: unable to find anything to say, unwilling to suspend his judgment, and not measuring his powers at all, he nevertheless dared to say that “the soul deserved to be defiled through the flesh, and deserved to become a sinful soul,” although he could find no merit—whether good or evil—that it possessed before the flesh.

He also said that “original sin can be forgiven for infants who leave the body without baptism, and that the sacrifice of Christ’s body should be offered for them,” although they have not been incorporated into Christ through his sacraments in his Church; and that “those who depart this life without the washing of regeneration go not merely to rest but may even reach the kingdom of heaven.”

There are many other absurdities as well. It seemed too long to collect them all and arrange them in this book. Therefore, far be it from us that the propagation of [Col. 0494] souls, if it is false, should be refuted by such people, or that the breathing-in of new souls, if it is true, should be defended by such people.

34. For this reason, whoever wishes to defend the claim that new souls are breathed into those being born rather than drawn from their parents must in every way beware of each of the four things I mentioned above. That is:

- They must not say that God makes souls sinful through another’s original sin.
- They must not say that infants who depart without baptism can reach eternal life and the kingdom of heaven once original sin has been removed by any other means.
- They must not say that souls sinned somewhere before the flesh and that, as a punishment for this, they were thrust into sinful flesh.
- They must not say that sins which were not found in them, but were foreknown, were justly punished, even though they were not permitted to reach the life in which they would commit those sins.

Let them say none of these four things, since each of them is false and impious. Let them also find the most certain testimony of the Scriptures on this matter, and defend their opinion—not only without my opposition, but with my support and gratitude.

But if they do not find the most certain authority for this matter in the divine words, and are driven by their lack of resources to assert one of those four things, let them restrain themselves, lest through that same poverty they be driven to say, in accordance with the Pelagian heresy—condemned long ago and most recently condemned again—that the souls of infants do not have original sin.

For it is better for a person to confess that he does not know what he does not know than, while rashly daring to defend what he does not know, either to fall into a condemned heresy or to create a new one.

There are many other false and absurd statements by this man in which he departs from the path of truth, though not so dangerously. Since there are many of them, and since, if the Lord wills, I also wish to write something about his books for him personally, I shall perhaps demonstrate there all of them—or, if I cannot do so, most of them.

## CHAPTER XX

35. As for this book, which I thought ought to be written for you rather than for anyone else—you who, as a true Catholic and good friend, have faithfully and kindly cared both for our faith and for my reputation—you shall give it to whomever you can for reading or copying, or to whomever you judge it ought to be given.

In it I thought that this young man’s presumption should be restrained and refuted, while nevertheless I love him. I do not wish him to be condemned but corrected, and to make such progress in the great house that is the Catholic Church, to which divine mercy has brought him, that he may be in it a vessel sanctified for honorable use, useful to the Lord and always ready for every good work, both by living well and by teaching sound doctrine.

[Note: In the manuscripts, “speaking.”]

Moreover, if I ought to love him—as I do—how much more ought I to love you, brother, whose goodwill toward me and whose careful and sober Catholic faith I know extremely well. It was therefore in consequence of this that you took care, with genuinely fraternal and wholly sincere affection, to have those books which displeased you, and in which you discovered that my name had been placed otherwise than you wished, copied and sent to me.

So far am I from being angry with your affection because you did this that, if you had not done it, I ought rather to be angry with you with full right as a friend. I therefore give abundant thanks.

How I received your action I have indicated more clearly by the fact that, as soon as I had read those books, I wrote this one to you without any delay.

[Note: The Vatican manuscript reads, “you will judge.”]

# BOOK TWO: TO THE PRESBYTER PETER

Augustine admonishes Peter not to allow it to be thought that, by praising the books on the origin of the soul which Vincentius Victor had written to him, he had approved them, or that he considered as Catholic dogmas the things which Victor had rashly written contrary to the Christian faith. He points out various and extremely serious errors of Victor and refutes them briefly. Finally, he urges Peter himself to lead Victor to correct them.

To his most beloved lord, brother, and fellow presbyter, PETER, Augustine the bishop sends greetings in the Lord.

## CHAPTER I

1. Two books by Vincentius Victor, which he wrote to Your Holiness, have reached me. Our brother Renatus sent them to me—a layman indeed, but prudently and religiously concerned on behalf of his own faith and that of those whom he loves.

After reading them, I saw that the man was fluent in speech—not merely to the point of sufficiency but even to the point of exuberance—yet in the matters about which he wished to speak he was not yet instructed as he ought to be. If the Lord grants him this, he may become useful to many. For he possesses no small ability to explain and adorn what he thinks, provided that he first takes care to think correctly.

Erroneous eloquence is exceedingly harmful, because to less educated people, precisely because it is eloquent, it appears true.

I do not know how you yourself received these books. Nevertheless, if what I heard is true, you are said to have leapt for joy when they were read aloud, so that, an old man, you kissed that young man’s head and, a presbyter, the mouth of a layman, and gave thanks that you had learned what you did not know.

In this I do not censure your humility; indeed, I praise you for honoring your teacher—not the man, but the truth itself, which deigned to speak to you through him—provided that you are able to show what truth you received through him.

I would therefore like you to teach me in your reply what he taught you. Far be it from me to be ashamed to learn from a presbyter, if you were not ashamed to learn from a layman, with a humility worthy of praise and imitation—provided that what you learned was true.

[Note: So Am. and the manuscripts. Er. and Lov. read: “and to have learned with a humility worthy of praise and imitation.”]

## CHAPTER II

2. Therefore, beloved brother, I wish to know what you learned from him, so that, if I already knew it, I may rejoice on your behalf, and, if I did not know it, may learn it through you.

Did you not know that there are two things, soul and spirit, according to what is written, “You have released my soul from the spirit” (Job 7, according to the Septuagint)? And that both belong to human nature, so that the whole human being is spirit, soul, and body?

Yet sometimes the two are together called by the name “soul,” as in, “And man became a living soul” (Genesis 2:7). For the spirit is understood there as well.

At other times both are called by the name “spirit,” as in, “And bowing his head, he gave up his spirit” (John 19:30), where the soul too must necessarily be understood.

And did you know that both are of one substance? I think you already knew these things. But if you did not know them, you should understand that you have not learned something whose ignorance involves great danger.

If there is anything more subtle to be discussed here, it is better to discuss it with the man himself, whose eloquence we now know: whether, when “soul” is said so that the spirit is understood together with it, both are soul and the spirit is something belonging to the soul; or whether, as he thought, this name is applied by synecdoche; or whether both are spirit and the part properly called “soul” is a part of the spirit; or whether this too is called by synecdoche, when “spirit” is said so that the soul is understood together with it. For this is what he prefers.

But these matters, as I said, are discussed subtly, and ignorance of them is harmless—or at any rate involves no great danger.

3. I also wonder whether he taught you that some senses belong to the body and others to the soul. Before hearing him, did you, a man of such age and dignity, think that the faculty by which white and black are distinguished—the faculty that sparrows see along with us—and the faculty by which justice and injustice are judged—the faculty that Tobias possessed even after the loss of his bodily sight—were one and the same?

[Note: Only Lov. reads, “the faculty by which sparrows also see with us.” Below, it reads, “by which Tobias saw.” The reading is not unreasonable, since it refers to the sense.]

[Note: The manuscripts consistently read “Tobis.”]

If this is so, then whenever you heard or read, “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep unto death” (Psalm 12:4), you must have thought only of the eyes of the flesh.

[Note: The printed editions read “in death”; the manuscripts read “unto death,” in accordance with the Greek.] Or, if that passage is obscure, surely when you recalled the Apostle’s words, “The eyes of your heart having been enlightened” (Ephesians 1:18), you must have believed that we have a heart beneath the forehead and above the cheeks.

Far be it from me to think this of you. Therefore this too was not taught to you by that man.

4. But if, before this teaching which you now rejoice that you have discovered, you perhaps thought that the nature of the soul was a portion of God, then you did not know that this was plainly false and involved a dreadful danger.

And if you learned from him that the soul is not a portion of God, give as much thanks to God as you can that you did not depart from the body before learning this. For you would have departed as a great heretic and a dreadful blasphemer.

Nevertheless, I could never think this of you either: that as a Catholic and by no means contemptible presbyter, you believed that the nature of the soul was a portion of God. Therefore I confess to Your Charity that I fear this man may have taught you something that is actually contrary to the faith you held.

## CHAPTER III

5. For just as I do not think that you ever believed, within the Catholic faith, that the soul is a portion of God, or that the soul and God are in any way of the same nature, so I fear that perhaps you agreed with this man that “God did not make the soul from nothing, but that it is from him in such a way that it emanated from him.”

This is one of the expressions he used among the others by which, in this question, he strayed toward an immense precipice.

But if he taught you this, I do not want you to teach it to me. Indeed, I want you yourself to unlearn what you learned.

It is not enough merely not to believe or say that the soul is a part of God. For we do not say that the Son or the Holy Spirit is a part of God either, and yet we say that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are of one and the same nature.

It is therefore not enough for us not to say that the soul is a part of God. We must also say that the soul and God are not of one and the same nature.

Accordingly, he was right to say that souls are God’s offspring “by gift, not by nature,” and therefore not the offspring of all people but of the faithful. Yet he fell back again into the error toward which he had been turning, and said that God and the soul are of the same nature—not in those words, but with an open and unmistakable meaning.

For when he says that the soul is from God in such a way that God created it neither from another nature nor from nothing but from himself, what is he trying to persuade us of except what he denies in other words: namely, that the soul is of the same nature as God?

Every nature is either God, who has no author, or it is from God, because it has him as its author. But what has God as its author and is from him is either made or not made.

Now what is not made and yet is from him was either begotten by him or proceeds from him. What is begotten is the only-begotten Son; what proceeds is the Holy Spirit. This Trinity is of one and the same nature.

For these three are one, each individually is God, and together they are one immutable and eternal God, without any beginning or end in time.

But the nature that has been made is called a creature, while God is the Creator—that is, the Trinity.

A creature is therefore said to be from God in such a way that it was not made from his nature. It is said to be from him because it has him as its author, so that it exists—not because it was born from him or proceeded from him, but because it was created, founded, and made by him.

Some creatures were made from nothing else—that is, entirely from nothing—such as heaven and earth, or rather the whole matter of the entire structure of the world, created together with the world.

Others were made from a nature already created and existing, such as man from dust, woman from man, and human beings from their parents.

Every creature is nevertheless from God, who creates either from nothing or from something; he does not beget or produce creatures from himself.

6. In saying these things to a Catholic, I am reminding you rather than teaching you. I do not think they are new to you, or even that you heard them previously without believing them. Rather, as I suppose, you are reading my letter in such a way that you recognize here the faith that you and I share, by the Lord’s gift, in the Catholic Church.

If, then, as I began to say, I am speaking with a Catholic, from where do you believe the soul comes—not the soul of each one of us, but the first soul given to that first man?

If you believe that it was made from nothing and nevertheless breathed in by God, you believe what I do.

But if you believe that it was made from some other creature which lay before God the Craftsman as matter from which a soul could be made—just as dust was the matter from which Adam was made, or his rib that from which Eve was made, or water that from which fish and birds were made, or earth that from which the various terrestrial animals were made—this is not Catholic and is not true.

But if you suppose—far be it from you—that God made or makes souls neither from nothing nor from any other creature, but from himself, that is, from his own nature, then you learned this from that man. Yet I do not congratulate or flatter you; you have strayed far from the Catholic faith along with him.

[Note: The printed editions read “far indeed”; “indeed” is absent from the manuscripts.]

For it would be more tolerable—although it would still be false, but, as I said, more tolerable—to believe that the soul was created from some other creature already made by God than to believe that it was created from God’s nature. Otherwise what is mutable, what sins, what becomes impious, and what, if it persists in impiety at the end, will be condemned without end, would be referred back to God’s nature with dreadful blasphemy.

Cast away, brother, cast away, I beg you, this—not truly faith, but an error of execrable impiety, lest you, a serious man led astray by a young man, and a presbyter by a layman, be removed from the number of the faithful—something may the Lord avert—while you suppose this to be the Catholic faith.

For one must not deal with you as with him, nor is your dreadful error—although it passed from him to you—worthy of the same pardon as that young man’s.

He recently came to the Catholic fold to be healed; you are counted among the Catholic pastors. We do not want the sheep that has come from error to the Lord’s flock to be cared for in such a way that, before being healed, it destroys the shepherd through its deadly infection.

7. But if you say, “He did not teach me this, nor did I in any way agree with his error, however much I may have been enticed by the sweetness of his eloquent and polished speech,” I give immense thanks to God.

But I ask why, as it is said, you kissed his head and gave thanks for having learned from him what you had been ignorant of until you heard his discussion. Or, if it is false that you did and said this,

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “and learned.” The Vatican manuscript and the very ancient Remigianus read: “Or, if it is false that you did this, I ask that the empty rumor may be refuted by your letter.”]

I ask you to be kind enough to make this known to us, so that the empty rumor may be refuted by your letter.

But if it is true that, with that humility, you gave thanks to the man, I rejoice if he did not teach you what I showed above to be detestable and to be avoided.

## CHAPTER IV

I do not criticize you for having shown such humility and gratitude toward your teacher if, while he was discussing something else, you learned something true and useful. But I ask what that might have been. Was it perhaps that the soul is not spirit but body?

I do not consider it a great loss to Christian doctrine to be ignorant of this. And if the kinds of bodies are discussed subtly, learning this requires more difficulty than it offers benefit.

If the Lord wills me to write to that young man himself, as I desire, Your Charity will perhaps learn there also what else he did not teach you—provided that you rejoice in having learned this from him.

But lest it be something else that is certainly useful and necessary to the faith, I ask that you not hesitate to reply.

8. For he rightly and very beneficially believes that souls are judged after they have left their bodies, before they come to that judgment at which they must be judged after their bodies have been restored, and that in the very flesh in which they lived here they will either be punished or glorified.

Did you yourself really not know this? Who has become deaf to the Gospel with such obstinacy of mind that he does not hear this in the poor man who, after death, was carried into Abraham’s bosom, and in the rich man whose torment in hell is described, or, having heard it, does not believe it?

[Note: The Cygirannensis manuscript and two Belgian manuscripts read “whose torment in hell”; the printed editions read “hell’s torment.”]

But did he teach you how the soul, without a body, could desire a drop of water from the poor man’s finger (Luke 16:22–24), when he himself admitted that the soul seeks bodily nourishment only to repair the ruins of its corruptible body?

These are his words:

“Do we believe,” he says, “that because the soul seeks food or drink, nourishment passes into the soul itself?”

And shortly afterward:

“From this it is understood,” he says, “and proved that the supports provided by food do not belong to the soul but to the body. Clothing is also provided for the body in a similar way in addition to food, so that the provision of nourishment may seem necessary to that for which it is appropriate to have clothing as well.”

After explaining this opinion of his clearly enough, and illuminating it with a certain comparison, he added:

“What, then, do we suppose? Does any tenant fail to care for his dwelling? If he notices that its roof trembles, its wall totters, or its foundation gives way, does he not seek beams, gather materials, and pile them up, so that he may carefully and diligently support the impending collapse, lest the tenant appear to be threatened by the danger of his dwelling?”

[Note: The manuscripts read “to hang over the dwelling.”]

“So,” he says, “recognize that the soul desires food for its flesh, from which it undoubtedly conceives that desire.”

That young man certainly explained his own thoughts in words as clear and adequate as possible, asserting that nourishment is required not for the soul but for the body: the soul cares for the body, indeed, but as one dwelling in a house and supporting through prudent replenishment the impending ruins of the dying flesh.

Let him therefore also explain to you what that soul of the rich man wished to shore up—a soul that no longer had a mortal body, yet thirsted and sought a drop of water from the poor man’s finger.

Here is something for this teacher of old men to exercise himself upon. Let him inquire, and, if he can, discover for what purpose that soul begged for moist nourishment, however small, in the underworld, when it was already without its crumbling dwelling.

## CHAPTER V

9. I congratulate him that he believes God to be incorporeal, since in this at least he has distinguished himself from Tertullian’s ravings. For Tertullian maintained that God, like the soul, is corporeal.

[Note: Tertullian, *On the Soul*. See Augustine, *On Heresies*, chapter 86, and Letter 190.]

But while disagreeing with Tertullian on this point, this man attempts to persuade us of something more astonishing: that God is incorporeal, yet does not make the breath from nothing, but exhales a corporeal breath from himself.

O doctrine worthy of having every generation prick up its ears, worthy in the end of having aged men—and even presbyters—as its pupils! Let him read aloud in an assembly what he has written; let him invite the known and unknown, the educated and uneducated, to hear it recited.

“Elders, gather with the younger; learn what you did not know; hear what you had never heard.”

Behold: according to this teacher, God does not create the breath from something else that exists in some fashion, nor from what does not exist at all. Rather, since he is incorporeal, he breathes a body from what he himself is.

Thus, before his nature is changed into a body of sin, he himself changes his nature into a body.

Or does he say that, when he makes the breath, God does not change anything from his own nature? Then he does not make it from himself, for God himself is not one thing and his nature another. What utterly insane person could think this?

But if he says that God makes the breath from his nature in such a way that he himself remains whole, that is not the issue. The issue is whether what is not from elsewhere or from nothing, but is from him, is not what he is—that is, whether it is not of the same nature and essence.

For even when he begets the Son, he remains whole. But because he begot him from himself, he did not beget something other than what he is.

Apart from the fact that he assumed humanity and the Word became flesh, the Word of God is indeed another person, but he is not another thing. That is, he is another person, but not a different nature.

And how is this so except because he was not created from another or from nothing, but was born from him—not so that he might be better than he was, but so that he might exist at all, and that he might be what the one from whom he was born is: that is, of one and the same nature, equal, coeternal, altogether alike, equally immutable, equally invisible, equally incorporeal, equally God—altogether what the Father is, except that the Son himself is Son, not Father?

But if God himself remains whole, and yet creates from himself—not from nothing or from something else—something different and inferior, and if a body emanates from the incorporeal God, far be it from a Catholic mind to accept this. For this is not an outflow from the divine fountain but a fabrication of the human heart.

## CHAPTER VI

10. As for how ineptly he labors to defend the soul, which he thinks is corporeal, from the body’s passions—when he discusses the soul’s infancy, paralytics, the soul’s oppressed senses, and bodily limbs being amputated without the soul’s being cut apart—I ought to deal not with you but with him.

He must sweat to give an account of his statements, lest we seem to wish to burden the gravity of an old man with the work of a young man.

As for his argument that similarities of character found in children do not come from the seed of the soul, this is indeed the necessary conclusion of all who destroy the propagation of the soul. But those who affirm propagation do not place the weight of their argument there.

For they see that children also differ from their parents in character. They think this happens because one and the same person often has different dispositions at different times, not because he has received another soul, but because his life has changed for the better or the worse.

[Note: Some manuscripts read “the soul from which it was propagated.”]

Thus they say that it is not impossible for a soul not to possess the dispositions of the person from whom it was propagated, since that same soul can have different dispositions at different times.

Therefore, if you think that you learned from this man that the soul is not transmitted by descent—if only you had truly learned it—I would gladly hand myself over to you as a teacher.

But learning something and thinking that one has learned it are different matters.

If, then, you think you have learned what you still do not know, you have not really learned it. You have rashly believed what you willingly heard, and false speech has stolen upon you through pleasing speech.

I do not say this because I am already certain that it is false that souls are breathed in as new rather than drawn from the origin of their parents. On this matter I still think we must inquire of those who can teach it.

I say it because this man discussed the matter in such a way that he not only failed to resolve the question, which still requires examination, but also made statements whose falsity admits of no doubt.

For while he wished to prove doubtful matters, he dared to assert without doubt things that must be rejected.

## CHAPTER VII

11. Will you hesitate to reject what he said when speaking about the soul?

“Do you not wish,” he says, “for the soul to contract a condition from sinful flesh, to which you see sanctification in turn pass through the flesh, so that through that same flesh the soul may restore the condition through which it had lost its merit?”

Or is it that, because the body is cleansed in baptism, what is believed to be conferred through baptism does not pass to the soul or spirit?

Rightly, therefore, through the flesh it recovers its former condition, which it seemed briefly to have lost through the flesh, so that through that by which it deserved to be defiled it might begin to be reborn” (below, book 3, section 9).

Consider in these words how greatly this teacher of yours has gone astray.

He said that “the soul recovers through the flesh the condition through which it had lost its merit.” Therefore the soul had some condition and some good merit before the flesh, which he wants it to recover through the flesh when the flesh is cleansed by the washing of regeneration.

Thus it had lived somewhere before the flesh in a good condition and with good merit. It lost that condition and merit when it came into the flesh.

He said that “through the flesh it recovers its former condition, which it seemed briefly to have lost through the flesh.” Therefore, before the flesh, it had an ancient condition—for that is what “former” means. And what sort of condition could this have been except a blessed and praiseworthy one?

He asserts that this condition is restored through the sacrament of baptism, although he does not want the soul to derive its origin from that propagation which plainly was once happy in paradise.

[Note: Three manuscripts read “through propagation”; the other manuscripts and printed editions read “through origin.”]

How, then, can he say elsewhere that he “consistently maintains that the soul is not from transmission, nor from nothing, nor through itself, nor before the body”?

Here, he wants souls to have lived somewhere before the body, so blessedly that the same blessedness is restored to them through baptism.

And, as though he had again forgotten himself, he adds:

“So that through it”—that is, through the flesh—“it may begin to be reborn, through which it had deserved to be defiled.”

Above, he had indicated that good merit had been lost through the flesh. Now, however, he indicates an evil merit by which it came or was sent into the flesh, saying, “through which it had deserved to be defiled.”

For if it deserves to be defiled, that is plainly not good merit. Let him say what it sinned before being defiled through the flesh, so that through the flesh it might deserve to be defiled.

Let him say, if he can, what he cannot possibly say. For he is wholly unable to find anything true to say here.

## CHAPTER VIII

12. A little later he says:

“Therefore, if the soul deserved to be sinful, although it could not be sinful, nevertheless it did not remain in sin, because, being prefigured in Christ, it ought not to be in sin, just as it could not be” (above, book 1, section 8, and below, book 3, section 11).

I ask you, brother: do you think that you at least read and considered these words afterward, and reflected on what you praised in the man while he was reciting them, or for what you gave thanks after the recitation?

What, I beg you, does “Therefore, if the soul deserved to be sinful, although it could not be sinful” mean?

What do “deserved” and “could not” mean, when it could not have deserved this unless it had been sinful, and it could not have been sinful unless it had been able to be so? Thus, before any evil merit existed, by sinning it would make a merit for itself, from which it could proceed to other sins if the Lord abandoned it.

Did he perhaps say “which could not be sinful” because, unless it came into the flesh, it could not be sinful?

What, then, did it deserve, so that it might be sent to the place where it could be sinful, since, if it had not come there, it could not be sinful elsewhere?

Let him say what it deserved.

For if it deserved to be sinful, it had already sinned in some way, by which it deserved to be sinful again.

But perhaps these matters may seem obscure, or may be claimed to be obscure, although they are perfectly clear. For he ought not to have said that “the soul deserved to be sinful through the flesh,” since he will not be able to find any good or evil merit belonging to it before the flesh.

## CHAPTER IX

13. But let us come to clearer matters.

When he was being pressed by great difficulties concerning how souls could be bound by the chains of original sin if they did not derive their origin from the first soul that sinned, but were breathed by the Creator into sinful flesh pure from every taint and transmission of sin—so that no one might say to God that, by breathing them in, he made them guilty—he first attempted to reinforce this opinion by appealing to God’s foreknowledge.

He said that God “had prepared redemption for them.” In the sacrament of this redemption infants are baptized so that the original sin they drew from the flesh may be washed away—as though God were correcting his own works, because he had made innocent souls subject to defilement.

But after he came to speak about those who do not receive such assistance, and who die before being baptized, he said:

“Here I do not put myself forward as an authority, but I infer something from an example. We say that some account must be given of infants of this kind who, although predestined for baptism, are overtaken by the death of the present life before they are reborn in Christ.

For we read,” he says, “that this was written about such people:

‘He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding or deceit should mislead his soul. For this reason God hastened to bring him out from the midst of iniquity, for his soul was pleasing to God; and, being perfected in a short time, he fulfilled a long period of life’” (Wisdom 4:11, 14, 13).

Who would disdain to have this man as a teacher?

Are infants whom people generally want to have baptized, but who, while preparations are being made, die first, such that, if they were delayed a little in this life so that they might die immediately after baptism, wickedness would change their understanding and deceit would mislead their souls—and, to prevent this from happening to them, were they helped by being snatched away before they were baptized?

Then in baptism itself they would have been changed for the worse and deceived by deceit if they had been snatched away after baptism.

O admirable doctrine, worthy to be followed!

[Note: Some manuscripts add here, “or rather, detestable and accursed.”]

But this is what he presumed upon your prudence—you who were present when he recited these words—and especially upon yours, to whom he wrote and to whom he handed over the books he had recited, trusting that you would believe that the passage about infants who were not baptized had been written about them, when it was written about the premature deaths of all the saints.

Foolish people think that these saints were treated badly if they were snatched quickly from this life and were unable to reach the years that human beings earnestly desire for themselves as a great divine gift.

But what does it mean to say that “infants predestined for baptism are overtaken by the death of the present life before they are reborn in Christ,” as though some force of fortune, fate, or anything else did not permit God to fulfill what he predestined?

And how does he himself snatch them away because they pleased him? Does he both predestine them to be baptized and himself prevent what he predestined from taking place?

## CHAPTER X
14. But consider what he still dares to say, since he is displeased that, in so deep a question, our hesitation is more cautious than learned. “I would venture to say,” he says, “that these children may attain forgiveness of original sins, though not so as to be brought into the heavenly kingdom; just as the Lord granted the confessed but unbaptized thief not the kingdom of heaven but paradise (Luke 23:43), while the statement nevertheless remains: ‘He who has not been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit will not enter the kingdom of heaven’ (John 3:5). Especially since the Lord professes that there are many dwelling places with his Father, in which many and diverse merits of those dwelling there are indicated: so that the unbaptized person may be brought to forgiveness, and the baptized to the palm, which is prepared through grace.”

[Note: [Col. 0503] Lov.: “You see the man [separating] those dwelling places.” Am. and Er.: “You see the man equally [separating] the dwelling places”; they omit the word “paradise,” which, however, most and older manuscripts here retain with the added conjunction “and.”]

You see how this man separates paradise and the dwelling places that are with the Father from the kingdom of heaven, so that places of everlasting happiness may abound even for the unbaptized. Yet, when he says this, he does not see that he is unwilling to separate the dwelling place of any baptized child from the kingdom of heaven in such a way that he is not also afraid to separate from it the very house of God the Father, or certain parts of that house. For the Lord Jesus did not say, “In the whole of creation,” or “in any part of the whole”; he said, “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14:2). How, then, can the unbaptized person be in the house of God the Father, when he cannot have God as Father unless he has been reborn? Let him not be ungrateful to God, who deemed him worthy to free him from the division of the Donatists or Rogatists, by attempting to divide the very house of God the Father and place some part of it outside the kingdom of heaven, where the unbaptized might be able to dwell. And how does he presume that he himself will enter the kingdom of heaven, when he excludes from that kingdom as large a part as he wishes of the house of its own King?

But concerning that thief, who, crucified beside the Lord, placed his hope in the Lord even while he was crucified, and concerning Dinocrates, the brother of Saint Perpetua, he argues that forgiveness of sins and some seat among the blessed may also be granted to the unbaptized [Col. 0504]—as though someone, whom it would be sacrilegious not to believe, had informed him that these men had not been baptized. Concerning them, however, I explained more fully what I thought in the book that I wrote to our brother Renatus (above, Book 1, §§11–12). Your Affection will be able to learn this if you do not disdain to read it; for that book will not be able to refuse one who asks.

## CHAPTER XI

15. Yet this man is seething and is being choked by dreadful difficulties. For perhaps he pays closer attention than you do to the evil of what he says—namely, that original sin is removed from little children apart from Christ’s Baptism. Finally, so that he might, however belatedly, take refuge in the Church’s sacraments in this matter, he says: “For these, certainly, I judge that constant offerings should be made and that the sacrifices of priests should continually be offered.”

If you please, regard him also as a censor, if it was not enough for you to have him as a teacher, so that you may offer the sacrifice of Christ’s body even for those who have not been incorporated into Christ. When he dared to insert so novel a thing, so alien to ecclesiastical discipline and the rule of truth, into his books, he did not say, “I think”; he did not say, “I suppose”; he did not say, “I judge”; he did not even say, “I suggest” or “I say,” but “I judge”—so that, if we were offended by the novelty or perversity of the opinion, we might be terrified by the authority of his decree.

You must see, brother, how you can tolerate this man as a teacher. [Note: [Col. 0504] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions have “these things.”] Catholics, however, who think soundly—among whom you too ought to be numbered—must not agree to listen to one who issues judgments of this sort. Rather, they should wish him to recover his senses and grieve, and to repent with salutary correction for having held, or rather even written, such opinions.

“But this,” he says, “I establish by the example of the Maccabees who fell in battle. When they had secretly taken away things forbidden [Note: [Col. 0504] We print *auferrent* (“had taken away”) from the Erfurt, Lyons, and Venice editions and from the sense of the cited passage, 2 Maccabees 12:40; Morel likewise considers this reading necessary (*Elementa critica*, p. 314). B has *offerrent* (“had offered”).] and had fallen in the very combat, we find,” he says, “that the priests adopted the following decision: that, since the guilt arising from the forbidden things had bound the souls of those men, the offering of sacrifices should restore them” (2 Maccabees 12:39–46).

He says this as though he had read that those sacrifices were offered for the uncircumcised, just as he judged that our sacrifices should be offered for the unbaptized. Circumcision, after all, was the sacrament of that former age, prefiguring the Baptism of our age.

## CHAPTER XII

16. Nevertheless, in comparison with what he later appeared to be, he is still making the more tolerable error. For it is as though he had repented—not of what he ought to have repented, namely, that he had dared to assert that original sin could be remitted to the unbaptized, and that forgiveness of all sins could be granted to them, so that they might be sent to paradise, that is, to a place of such great happiness, and might be deemed worthy to have blessed dwelling places in the Father’s house—but rather of having granted them a dwelling place of lesser blessedness outside the kingdom of heaven. He added and said:

“Or, if perhaps someone should object to the paradise temporarily granted in the meantime to the soul of the thief or to Dinocrates—for a reward in the kingdom of heaven still remains for them at the resurrection; although that principal pronouncement stands in the way: ‘He who has not been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit will not enter the kingdom of heaven’—nevertheless, let him also accept my assent in this matter, since I am not envious, provided that he enlarges both the effect and the intention of divine mercy and foreknowledge.” [Col. 0505]

I have transcribed these words as they are found in his second book. Could anyone possess greater audacity, rashness, or presumption in the error of this matter? He himself recalls the Lord’s sentence; he himself mentions it; he himself inserts it into his writing; he himself says, “Although that principal pronouncement stands in the way: ‘He who has not been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit will not enter the kingdom of heaven’”; and yet he dares to raise his neck in defiance of the principal pronouncement of his own judgment!

“Let him also accept,” he says, “my assent, since I am not envious”—the assent of one who says that the souls of the unbaptized temporarily merit paradise. He mentions the thief and Dinocrates as though by way of prescription, or rather prejudice, on behalf of these souls; and says that at the resurrection they will be transferred to better things and receive the reward of the kingdom of heaven: “although,” he says, “the principal pronouncement stands in the way.”

Now, then, consider for yourself, I ask you, brother: what sentence will the Prince pronounce upon anyone who gives assent against the authority of the principal pronouncement?

17. The authority of the Catholic councils and of the Apostolic See rightly condemned the recent heretics, the Pelagians, because they had dared to grant unbaptized children a place of rest and salvation, even apart from the kingdom of heaven. They would not have dared to do this unless they denied that these children had original sin, which needed to be absolved through the sacrament of Baptism.

This man, however, while speaking as a Catholic, says that children are bound by original sin; yet he absolves them from such a bond without the washing of regeneration and, in his mercy, sends them after death to paradise; then, after the resurrection, in even greater mercy, he introduces them into the kingdom of heaven.

Such a merciful Saul seemed to himself when he spared the king whom God had commanded to be killed. But that mercy, rightly condemned as disobedient—or that disobedience, merciful in appearance—was rejected and condemned (1 Samuel 15). Let a man beware lest he deserve mercy from that One against whose sentence the man acts who was made by him.

Truth thunders through the mouth of its own body: “If anyone has not been reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5). And, in order to exempt from this sentence the martyrs who happened to be killed for Christ’s name before they could be washed in Christ’s Baptism, he says elsewhere: “Whoever loses his life for my sake will find it” (Matthew 10:39).

And lest anyone who has not been reborn through the washing of the Christian faith be promised the abolition of original sin, the Apostle cries out: “Through one offense condemnation came upon all human beings” (Romans 5:18). Against this condemnation, the Lord, showing that there is one means of salvation, says: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16). The mystery of this faith is fulfilled in little children through the response of those by whom they are carried, lest, if it were not done, all should go from the one source into condemnation.

And yet, against such manifest voices, which Truth sings out, a vanity more foolish than merciful comes forward and says: “Children do not merely avoid condemnation, even though no washing of the Christian faith absolves them from the bond of original sin; they also enjoy the happiness of paradise temporarily after death, and after the resurrection they will possess the happiness of the kingdom of heaven.”

Would this man dare to assert such things against the most firmly grounded Catholic faith, if he had not dared to undertake a question concerning the origin of the soul that exceeded his powers?

## CHAPTER XIII

18. He is indeed constricted by dreadful difficulties on the part of those who say: “Why did God punish the soul with such unjust severity, wishing to confine it in a body of sin, when it begins to be sinful through association with flesh, although it could not have been sinful?” For they certainly say: “The soul could not have been sinful unless God had mixed it with sinful flesh.”

Since this man could not discover by what justice God did this—especially in view of the eternal damnation of little children who die without Baptism, for whom original sin has not been expiated—why, then, did the just and good God, by sending into a body drawn from Adam the souls of little children whom he foreknew would receive no assistance from the sacrament of Christian grace, bind them with the bond of original sin, though they were free from every guilt of inherited origin, and in this way make them liable to eternal damnation? Since he could not find an answer, and did not wish to say that these souls themselves also derive their origin from that one sinful source, he preferred to escape by a pitiable shipwreck rather than, with the sails lowered and the oars of his argument restrained, check his rash course through prudent deliberation.

For youthful disdain made light of our old-age caution, as though this most troublesome and dangerous question required the force of eloquence more than the counsel of prudence. He himself foresaw this too, but in vain. For, as though he were about to set before himself these objections as coming from his opponents, he says: “From this point other reproaches are heaped up amid the barking of complaining murmurs, and, shaken as though by some whirlwind, we are repeatedly dashed against enormous rocks.”

Having announced these things, he set before himself the aforementioned question, full of reefs, where he was shipwrecked away from the Catholic faith—unless, by repenting, he repairs what he broke. Avoiding that whirlwind and those rocks, I did not wish to entrust the ship to them [Note: [Col. 0506] The printed editions read, “I therefore.”]; and I wrote about this matter in such a way as to display rather the reason for my hesitation than the rashness of presumption (On Free Will, Book 3, §§59–62; On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, Book 2, §59; Letter 166 to Jerome, and Letter 190 to Optatus).

When he found this little work of mine with you, he mocked it and committed himself to those cliffs with a more courageous than prudent charge. But where this overconfidence has brought him, I think you now see; and I give fuller thanks to God if you had already seen it before. For, unwilling to restrain his headlong course because of its dangerous turn, he met with a pitiable collision, asserting that God grants to little children who die without Christian regeneration both paradise now and the kingdom of heaven afterward.

## CHAPTER XIV

19. As for whatever testimonies from Scripture he brought forward, by which he attempted to prove that God draws souls not from the propagation of that first soul but, as with the first soul, breathes them individually into each person, they are, so far as this question is concerned, so uncertain and ambiguous that they can very easily be understood otherwise than he wishes. I have already demonstrated this sufficiently, as far as I believe, in the book that I wrote to our friend whom I mentioned above (above, Book 1, §17 ff.).

The very testimonies he employed, in which God is said either to give, make, or form souls, do not show from where he gives, makes, or forms them—whether from the propagation of that first soul or by breathing, as he did the first soul. Yet this man, simply from the fact that Scripture says that God gives, makes, or forms souls (Isaiah 42:5; 57:16; Zechariah 12:1), already thinks that the propagation of souls has been denied. But, according to the testimony of the same Scripture, God also gives, makes, or forms bodies; nevertheless, no one doubts that they are given, made, or formed by him from the propagation of seed. [Note: [Col. 0507] All manuscripts read, “from the seed of propagation.”]

20. Likewise, because it is written that God made every nation of human beings from one blood (Acts 17:26), or because Adam said, “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh” (Genesis 2:23), he thinks that the souls of children are denied to come from their parents, or that the soul of that woman is denied to come from the man—because it is not said there, “from one soul,” nor here, “soul from my soul.” As though, if it were said not “from one blood” but “from one soul,” something other than the whole human being would be understood, and the propagation of the body would thereby be denied.

Likewise, if it had been said, “Soul from my soul,” the flesh would certainly not have been denied, although it was evident that it had been taken from him. Scripture often signifies the whole by a part, just as it also signifies a part by the whole. For certainly, if that passage had said not “from one blood” but “from one man,” that the human race had been established, the testimony he brought forward would not prejudice those who deny the propagation of souls, although a human being is neither soul alone nor flesh alone, but both together. They would answer that Scripture could signify, from the whole, a part—namely, from the man, only the man’s flesh.

Thus, those who defend the propagation of souls contend that what is said, “from one blood,” signifies through blood the human being—that is, the whole by a part. For just as it seems to help the former that it is said “from one blood,” and not “from one man,” so it seems to help the latter that it is said: “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death, and thus it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12); it is not said, “in whom the flesh of all sinned.”

Likewise, just as it seems to help the former that it is said, “This now is bone from my bones and flesh from my flesh,” because a part is named, not the whole, so again it helps the latter that what follows immediately is said: “She shall be called woman, because she was taken from her man.” [Col. 0508] They say that it ought to have been said, “because her flesh was taken from her man,” if not the whole woman—that is, together with the soul—but only the flesh were taken from the man.

When both sides have been heard, however, anyone who judges without partisan zeal plainly sees that those testimonies in which a part is named should not be brought against those who defend the propagation of souls, because Scripture could there signify the whole by a part, just as, when we read “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), we understand not flesh alone but the whole human being. Nor should those passages in which the whole human being is mentioned be brought against those who destroy the propagation of souls, because Scripture could there signify a part by the whole, just as we confess that Christ was buried, although only his flesh was buried.

Accordingly, we say that the propagation of souls should neither be rashly asserted nor rashly rejected; rather, we point out that other testimonies must be sought—testimonies that are not ambiguous.

## CHAPTER XV

21. Therefore, what this man taught you, and for what you gave thanks, I still do not know. That question remains as it was: concerning the origin of souls, whether God gives, makes, or forms them for human beings from the propagation of that one soul whom he first breathed into man, or from his own breath, as he did for the first man. The Christian faith does not doubt that he gives, makes, and forms them.

When this man tried to solve that question without considering his own powers, he destroyed the propagation of souls and asserted that the Creator breathes souls, pure from every contagion of sin, not from nothing but from himself. In doing so, he branded God’s nature with the reproach of mutability, although this was unnecessary. And, while wishing to provide an explanation so that God would not be thought unjust if he binds with the bond of original sin souls that are pure from every sin—including those whom he does not redeem through Christian regeneration [Note: [Col. 0508] Thus the Germanensis codex and the Victorinus; printed editions read “whom he redeems.”]—he said things that I do not want you to have learned from him.

For he grants unbaptized children so much salvation and happiness that even the Pelagian heresy could not grant as much. And yet, concerning the many thousands of little children who are born among the ungodly and die among the ungodly—not those whom human beings could assist through Baptism whenever they wished, but those concerning whose baptism no one could or can even think, and for whom no one has offered or will offer the sacrifice that he judged should be offered even for us who are baptized [Note: Am. Er. and most manuscripts: “that he judged should be offered even for the unbaptized”]—he could find nothing to say.

If he were asked what these souls had merited, that God should insert them into sinful flesh, neither to be washed in Baptism nor cleansed by the sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood, but to be condemned eternally [Note: [Col. 0508] Two Belgian manuscripts read, “should have inserted them into sinful flesh.” All our manuscripts read *inserit* (“inserts”); corruptly.] , he would either be completely at a loss—and our hesitation would at last please him—or else, on behalf of all the little children who die throughout the world without Christian Baptism, even though their names are not known in the Church of Christ and they have not been incorporated into Christ’s body, he would judge that Christ’s body ought to be offered, without mentioning their names.

## CHAPTER XVI

22. Far be it from you, brother, to approve these things [Col. 0509]; far be it from you either to rejoice that you have learned them or to presume to teach them. Otherwise he himself will be found far better than you. For at the beginning of his first book he spoke modestly and humbly beforehand, saying: “When I desire to obey you, I incur the appearance of presumption” [Note: The printed editions have *incurri*, “I incurred”; two manuscripts have *incurro*, “I incur”].

And shortly afterward he says: “Since I do not even believe myself capable of proving what I shall say, I should always strive not to defend my own opinion if it is shown to be untenable; and I should take it to heart, once my own judgment has been condemned, to pursue what is better and more true. For just as it is characteristic of an excellent purpose and a praiseworthy plan to be easily led toward what is more true, so it is characteristic of a bad and obstinate judgment to be unwilling to bend quickly toward the path of reason.”

If he said these things truthfully, and feels as he spoke, then he certainly bears within him a spirit of great promise. Likewise, at the end of his second book he says:

“Nor should you perhaps think that the following ought to be attributed to your envy: that I place the judgment of my statements in your power. And lest the gaze of some inquisitive reader be troubled and offended by traces remaining among the interwoven fibers of the elements—[Note: In the manuscripts, *illicitas*, “unlawful,” rather than *illitas*, “interwoven”]—tear apart with a severe finger the sequence woven across the page; and punish me, exempt from this judgment, with the inks that have marked unworthy utterances [Note: Am. and Er.: “punish me, exempt from this judgment”; they and Lov. read, “with the ink that has signified unworthy utterances.” We read *atramenta* (“inks”) from most manuscripts and *signaverunt* (“have marked”) from the Germanensis codex. Three manuscripts cited by Lov. read: “Let the inks punish me, exempt from this judgment, which have signified unworthy utterances.”]; lest on this occasion both your judgment of me, in which you are exceedingly indulgent toward me, and my follies, which had remained hidden, be mocked.”

## CHAPTER XVII

23. Since, then, he fortified his books at the beginning and secured them at the end, and placed upon your shoulders the religious duty of correcting and amending him, let him find in you what he requested [Col. 0510]: that you should amend him in mercy and rebuke him; but as for “the oil of the sinner,” which would make his head fat (Psalm 140:5), let it be far from your hands and eyes—that is, the indecent flattery of one who praises and the deceptive softness of one who soothes.

If you neglect to amend him when you see that he needs amendment, you act against charity. But if he does not seem to you to need correction because you think that he has held these opinions rightly, you think against the truth. Thus he is better—the one who is readier to be corrected, provided that a corrector is not lacking—than you, if you either knowingly and mockingly disregard one who is in error, or unknowingly follow the same error.

Therefore, examine soberly and attentively everything in those same books that he wrote to you and delivered to you, and perhaps you will find more things deserving blame than I have found. Whatever in them is to be approved and praised, if there is anything you truly did not know and learned from his exposition, openly declare what it is, so that everyone may know that you gave thanks for this, not for the many things in those books that deserve disapproval—everyone, that is, who either heard them with you while he was reading them aloud or later read the same books.

Otherwise, in his polished eloquence, as in a precious cup with which he invites you, though you do not drink, they may drink poison if they do not know what you have drunk from it and what you have not drunk, and, on account of your praise, suppose that everything in it should be drunk for their health. Yet what is it to hear, to read, and to absorb into memory what has been said, except to drink?

But the Lord foretold concerning his faithful that even if they should drink something deadly, it would not harm them (Mark 16:18). Accordingly, those who read with discernment, approving what ought to be approved according to the rule of faith and rejecting what ought to be rejected—even if they commit to memory things that ought to be rejected—are not harmed by any poisonous perversity of doctrine.

I shall not regret having warned or admonished Your Gravity and Religiousness, whether through mutual affection or through affection that came first, however you receive what I thought should be entrusted to you. I shall give abundant thanks to him whose mercy it is most salutary to trust, if this letter either finds your faith alien from and uncorrupted by the perversities and errors that I have been able to expose from this man’s books, or makes it so.

# BOOK THREE. TO VINCENTIUS VICTOR

[Col. 0509]

Augustine shows Vincentius Victor what he must correct in his books concerning the origin of the soul if he wishes to be a Catholic. The matters already refuted in the preceding books addressed to Renatus and Peter he briefly touches upon in this third work addressed to Victor himself, reducing them to eleven heads of error.

## CHAPTER I

1. I want you, dearest son Victor, first to consider this: if I despised you, I would certainly not have done what I thought ought to be written to you. [Col. 0510] Yet do not abuse our humility in such a way as to suppose that you have been approved merely because you see that you have not been despised.

For I love you not so that you may be followed, but so that you may be corrected. And since I do not despair that you can be corrected, do not be surprised that I cannot despise one whom I love. For if I ought to have loved you before you entered into communion with us, so that you might become a Catholic, how much more ought I now to love you, as one already in communion, so that you may not become a new heretic, and so that you may be the kind of Catholic whom no heretic can resist!

As is apparent from the gifts of intellect that God has already bestowed upon you, you will certainly be wise if you do not believe yourself to be so, and if you piously, humbly, and earnestly ask wisdom from him who makes the wise. You should prefer not to be deceived by error rather than to be honored by the praises of those who err.

## CHAPTER II

2. At first, the title bearing your name in your books made me concerned for you. When I had asked those who knew you, and perhaps were present, who Vincentius Victor was, I heard that you had been a Donatist—or rather a Rogatist—but had recently entered into communion with the Catholic Church. [Col. 0511]

I rejoiced as much as we usually rejoice over those whom we learn have been freed from that error—indeed, much more, because I saw that your intellect, with which I took pleasure in your writings, had not remained among the adversaries of truth. But those who reported this added something that saddened me amid that joy: they said that you had wished to be called Vincentius because you still held in your mind, as though he were a great and holy man, the successor of Rogatus who was called by that name, and for this reason had wished his name to be your surname.

There were also those who said that you had even boasted that he had appeared to you in some vision and had helped you compose these books, about which I have undertaken to deal with you in this work, by dictating to you what you were to write, insofar as the matters and arguments themselves were concerned [Note: The Cistercian manuscript: “so that he dictated to you the books you were to write”].

If this is true, I am no longer surprised that you were able to say the things you said—things of which, if you patiently heed my admonition and consider and examine those books with a Catholic mind, you will undoubtedly repent. For the one who, as the Apostle exposes him, “transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Corinthians 11:14), has transformed himself for you into the one whom you believe to have been or to be an angel of light.

He is less effective at deceiving Catholics when he transforms himself not into angels of light but into heretics; yet I would not want you, now a Catholic, to be deceived by him. Let him, then, be tormented that you have learned what is true, all the more because he had rejoiced that he had persuaded you of what is false.

To keep you from loving a dead man whose love can harm you but cannot benefit him, consider briefly what I now urge upon you. He is certainly not holy and just if you escaped the snares of the heretical Donatists or Rogatists. But if you think him holy and just, then by entering into communion with Catholics you have perished.

You are evidently pretending to be a Catholic if in your mind you follow the character of the man whom you love. And you know how fearfully it is written: “The Holy Spirit will flee what is feigned” (Wisdom 1:5).

But if, by entering into communion truthfully, you are not pretending to be a Catholic, why do you still love a dead heretic so much that you wish to boast of bearing the name of one whose error you no longer hold? We do not want you to have such a surname, as though you were a monument to a dead heretic. We do not want your book to bear such a title, one that we would call false if we read it on his tomb.

For we do not know Vincentius Victor to be the victor, but the vanquished—and would that he had been vanquished profitably, just as we want you to be vanquished by the truth!

You seem to have acted astutely and cleverly when, calling your books those dictated to you by his revelation, you named them “Vincentius Victor,” as though, by revealing to you what you were to write, he had conquered error. Why do you do these things, my son? Be a true, not a feigned, Catholic, lest the Holy Spirit flee from you and Vincentius be of no benefit to you—the Vincentius into whom the most wicked spirit transformed himself in order to deceive you. Those are his teachings, persuaded upon you by whatever fraud.

If, after being admonished, you correct them with pious humility and Catholic peace, they will be judged to have been the errors of an earnest young man who desired correction rather than persistence in error. But if, God forbid, he persuades you to contend stubbornly on their behalf, then they must be condemned as heretical doctrines together with their author—by pastoral and medicinal care, before dreadful contagions spread through the unwary crowd [Note: The Victorinus codex reads *vulnus*, “wound,” less correctly. Augustine is alluding to Virgil, *Georgics* 3.468–469: “Check the fault with iron at once, before the dreadful contagions spread through the unwary crowd”], while salutary discipline is neglected under the name, rather than in the truth, of love [Note: Am., Er., and the Pratellensis manuscript read *medicina*, “medicine,” instead of *disciplina*, “discipline”].

## CHAPTER III

3. If you ask what those errors are, you can certainly read my writings to our brothers Renatus, servant of God, and the presbyter Peter, to whom you thought that the very matters we are now discussing ought to be written, “obeying,” as you claim, “the will of one who asked.” They will undoubtedly give them to you to read if you wish, and will even thrust them upon you without your asking.

Nevertheless, here too I shall not keep silent about the matters that I especially want corrected in those books of yours and in your faith.
