First is this: “You do not wish the soul to have been made by God in such a way that he made it from nothing, but from himself” [Col. 0512] (above, Book 1, §4, and Book 2, §5). You do not think it follows from this that the soul is of God’s nature, because you yourself recognize how impious that would certainly be.

To avoid that impiety, you must speak of God as the soul’s author in such a way that it was made by him, not from him. For what is from him, like the only-begotten Son, is of the same nature as he is. But, so that the soul would not be of the same nature as he is, it was made by him, but not from him. Either, then, say from what it was made, or admit that it was made from nothing.

What do you mean when you say that it is “a certain portion of the breath of God’s nature”? Do you deny that the very breath of God’s nature, of which this is a portion, is of the same nature as God? If you deny this, then God made even that breath from nothing, the portion of which you wish the soul to be. But if he did not make it from nothing, say from what God made it. If he made it from himself, then—God forbid—he is the material of his own work.

But you say, “When he makes a breath or exhalation from himself, he himself remains whole,” as though even the fire of a lamp did not remain whole when another lamp is lit from it, although the new flame is of the same nature, not another nature.

## CHAPTER IV

4. “But,” you say, “when a wineskin is inflated by us, no portion of our nature or quality is infused into it [Col. 0513], since this very spirit, when drawn in, fills and stretches the wineskin and is expelled without any diminution of us.”

You continue to add to and dwell upon these words of yours, and you press the analogy as though it were necessary, by which we are to understand how God, without any loss to his nature, makes a soul from himself, and how something made from him is not himself. For you say:

“Is the inflation of a wineskin a portion of our soul? Or do we fashion human beings when we inflate wineskins? Or do we suffer any loss of ourselves when we divide our breaths in different directions? We suffer no loss when we transmit breath from ourselves into something else; and while the full quality and entire quantity of our own breath remains in us, we remember no loss that we experience from inflating wineskins.”

Observe how greatly this analogy, which seems to you sufficiently elegant and appropriate, deceives you. You say that God, who is incorporeal, breathes forth a corporeal soul—not from nothing, but from himself—while we, although we emit something corporeal, nevertheless emit something more subtle than our bodies; and we exhale it not from our soul but from this air, through the inward parts of the body.

For the lungs draw in and expel this aerial spirit like bellows, moved by the soul, by whose command the other members of the body are also moved. Besides solid and liquid nourishment, from which food and drink come, God has surrounded us with this third nourishment, the air, which we take in so that we can remain for a long time without food and drink; but without this third nourishment, which the air surrounding us on every side supplies as we inhale and exhale, we cannot live even for a short interval of time.

Just as food and drink must not only be taken in but also expelled through passages established for that purpose, lest they harm us either by failing to enter or by failing to leave, so this third, breath-like nourishment, because it is not permitted to remain within us and is not corrupted by lingering there but is expelled as soon as it is taken in, has been given not different passages but the same ones—namely, the mouth, the nostrils, or both—through which it enters and through which it exits.

5. Prove for yourself what I am saying: emit your breath by blowing, and see whether you can endure it if you do not take it back. Take it in again by breathing, and see what distress you suffer if you do not release it again. This, then, is what we do when, as you say, we inflate a wineskin—something we do in order to live—except that then we draw in somewhat more breath so that we may emit somewhat more, constraining the breath—that is, the wind—with which the wineskin is to be filled and stretched, not by calm inhalation and exhalation, but by the force of panting.

How, then, can you say: “We suffer no loss when we transmit breath from ourselves to something else; and, while the full quality and entire quantity of our own breath remains in us, we do not recall experiencing any harm from inflating wineskins”? It is evident, my son, that if you have ever inflated a wineskin, you did not notice what you had done. For what you lose by blowing [Note: [Col. 0513] Am. Er. and most manuscripts read: “by blowing into.”], you do not immediately perceive when you take it back. But you can learn this very easily, if you would rather do so than defend your words—since they have already been spoken—not by inflating a wineskin, but by being yourself inflated, and puffing up your hearers, whom you ought to edify with true matters [Note: [Col. 0513] The Cistercian manuscript has: “whom you ought to edify not with words but with realities.”], with the empty noise of windy speech.

In this matter I send you to no teacher except yourself. Breathe into a wineskin, close your mouth at once, and hold your nostrils shut; then at least perceive that what I say is true. When you begin to suffer intolerable distress, what will you wish to receive through your open mouth and nostrils, if, when you have blown, you think that you have lost nothing? See what a predicament you are in unless, by drawing in, you take back what you had returned by pouring out. See what losses and damage that blowing would have caused, had breathing not restored them. For unless what you expended to fill the wineskin returns to you in the same way, with access opened so that you may be nourished, what will remain for you—not only with which to inflate it, but with which you yourself may live?

6. You ought to have considered these matters when you wrote. You ought not to have introduced God to us by this comparison with inflated or inflating wineskins, as though he blows souls from another nature that already existed, just as we make breath from the surrounding air; or, alternatively—which both conflicts with this comparison and is full of impiety—you ought not to have suggested that God, without suffering any loss in himself, nevertheless brings forth or produces something mutable from his own nature, as though he himself were the material of his own work.

If, then, we are to apply some comparison from our breath to this matter, what ought rather to be believed is this: just as we do not make breath from our own nature, but, because we are not omnipotent, from the surrounding air that we draw in and return when we inhale and exhale; and when we blow, we make breath that is neither living nor sentient, although we ourselves live and perceive—so God, not from his own nature, but because he is so omnipotent that he can create whatever he wills even from what altogether does not exist, that is, from nothing, can make breath that is living and sentient; yet, while he himself is immutable, he makes it mutable [Note: [Col. 0514] Here the printed editions add: “he makes it.”].

## CHAPTER V

7. What, then, did you intend by adding to this comparison, as an example, the blessed Elisha, because he revived a dead man by blowing into his face (2 Kings 4:34–35)? Do you really think that Elisha’s breath became [Note: [Col. 0514] We add “became” from the manuscripts.] the boy’s soul? I cannot believe that you have strayed so far from the truth.

If, therefore, the very soul that had been taken from the living boy so that he might die was returned to him so that he might live again [Note: [Col. 0514] In the manuscripts: “might revive”; and shortly afterward, “of the one reviving.”], what relevance has your statement that “nothing was diminished from Elisha,” as though something had passed from him by which the boy might live? But if this was said because Elisha blew and remained whole, why did you need to say this of Elisha reviving a dead man, when you could equally have said it of anyone blowing without reviving anyone?

You certainly spoke carelessly—for it is far from you to believe that Elisha’s breath became the soul of the boy who revived—when you wished to distinguish the first work of God from the work of this prophet by saying that God blew once, whereas Elisha blew three times. For you said:

“Elisha breathed into the face of the dead son of the Shunammite woman, after the pattern of the first creation. And when,” you say, “divine power, through the prophet’s breath, rekindled the lifeless limbs and restored them to their former vigor, nothing was diminished from Elisha, through whose breath the dead body received again its soul and spirit—except that the Lord breathed once into the face of man, and he lived, while Elisha breathed three times into the face of the dead man, and he revived.”

These words of yours sound as though the only difference were the number of times he blew [Note: [Col. 0515] The Cistercian manuscript has: “as though the number of times he blew were lacking.”], so that the prophet might be thought to have done what God did. This, too, must therefore be corrected. There was a very great difference between that work of God and Elisha’s work: God breathed the breath of life by which man was made a living soul; Elisha, however, breathed a breath that was neither sentient nor living, but signified something symbolically.

In short, in order that this boy might revive, the prophet did not make him alive; rather, by loving him, he obtained that God might do this [Note: [Col. 0515] The old German manuscript and Victorinus have: “but by loving him,” omitting the second “him.”]. As for your claim that he blew three times, you were misled either by your memory, as commonly happens, or by a corrupt manuscript. What more is there to say? You ought not to seek examples and arguments to support this position; rather, you should correct and change your opinion. Therefore, do not believe, do not say, and do not teach “that God made the soul not from nothing but from his own nature,” if you wish to be catholic.

## CHAPTER VI

8. Do not believe, say, or teach “that throughout infinite time, and thus always, God gives souls, just as he himself is always the one who gives” (above, book 1, §26), if you wish to be catholic. For there will be a time when God will not give souls, although he himself will not cease to exist.

What you said—“he always gives”—could indeed have been understood to mean that he gives without interruption so long as human beings generate and are generated, just as it is said of certain people: “always learning and never arriving at a knowledge of the truth” (2 Tim. 3:7). For “always” in that passage is not understood to mean that they never cease learning, since plainly they do not learn when they have ceased living in this body or when they have begun to burn in the punishment of the fire of Gehenna.

But you did not allow your statement to be understood in this way when you said, “he always gives,” since you thought that it should be referred to infinite time. And this was not enough: as though you were being asked to explain more clearly what you meant by “he always gives,” you added and said, “just as he himself is always the one who gives.” Sound and catholic faith altogether condemns this. Far be it from us to believe that God always gives souls, just as he himself is always the one who gives.

For he is always himself in such a way that he never ceases to exist. He will not, however, always give souls; rather, when the age of generation has ended and there are no longer any people being born to whom they may be given, he will unquestionably cease to give them.

## CHAPTER VII

9. Do not believe, say, or teach “that the soul lost some merit through the flesh, as though it had possessed good merit before the flesh” (above, book 2, §11), if you wish to be catholic. For the Apostle says that those not yet born had done nothing either good or evil (Rom. 9:11). How, then, could the soul have possessed good merit before the flesh, when it had done nothing good? Or will you dare to say that it lived well before the flesh, when you cannot show that it even existed?

How, then, can you say: “You do not wish the soul to contract from the flesh of sin a sickness, toward which you see sanctification pass in turn through the flesh, so that through that same flesh it may recover the condition through which it had lost its merit”? These doctrines—that the soul possessed some good condition and good merit before the flesh—have been condemned by the Catholic Church not only among the ancient heretics but, more recently, among the Priscillianists as well, if you are unaware of it.

10. Do not believe, say, or teach “that through the flesh the soul recovers its former condition and is reborn through that by which it had deserved to be defiled” (above, book 1, §6, and book 2, §11), if you wish to be catholic.

To pass over the fact that you said, “Therefore, deservedly, through the flesh it recovers its former condition, which it seemed for a little while to have lost through the flesh, so that through that by which it had deserved to be defiled it may begin to be reborn”—to pass over this, you have very recently proved yourself wholly contradictory to yourself [Note: [Col. 0516] The printed editions read: “you yourself have very recently proved yourself contradictory to yourself.” The manuscripts correct the wording.]. A little earlier you had said that the soul recovers through the flesh the condition through which it had lost its merit; there, “merit” can in no way be understood except as good merit, which you certainly wish to be restored through the flesh in baptism. Then again you said that it had deserved to be defiled through the flesh, where “merit” can no longer be understood as good but only as evil merit.

To leave that aside, it is altogether un-Catholic to believe that the soul possessed either good or evil merit before the flesh.

## CHAPTER VIII

11. Do not believe, say, or teach “that the soul deserved to become sinful before all sin” (above, book 1, §8, and book 2, §12), if you wish to be catholic. For it is a very evil merit to have deserved to become sinful. Such an evil merit could in no way have existed before all sin, especially before the soul came into the flesh, when it could possess neither evil nor good merit.

How, then, can you say: “If, therefore, the soul deserved to be sinful, although it could not be sinful, nevertheless it did not remain in sin, because, prefigured in Christ, it ought not to be in sin, just as it could not be”? Consider what you are saying and stop saying it. How did it deserve, and how could it not be sinful? How, I ask you, did the soul deserve to be sinful when it had not lived wickedly? How did it become sinful when it could not be sinful?

Or if you say “it could not” because it could not be sinful apart from the flesh, how, then, did it deserve to be sinful—and by that merit to be sent into the flesh—when before the flesh it could not be sinful and therefore could not deserve anything evil?

## CHAPTER IX

12. Do not believe, say, or teach “that infants who are overtaken by death before they are baptized can attain the remission of original sins” (above, book 1, §§10–12, and book 2, §§13–14), if you wish to be catholic.

The examples that mislead you—whether the thief who confessed the Lord on the cross (Luke 23:43), or Dinocrates, the brother of the holy Perpetua—give no support to this erroneous opinion.

As for that thief, although he might have been counted by divine judgment among those who are cleansed by confession of martyrdom, you do not even know whether he was not baptized. To pass over the belief that he may have been sprinkled, while hanging beside the Lord, with the water that sprang forth together with blood from the Lord’s side, and cleansed by such a most holy baptism: what if he had been baptized in prison, something which, later, during a time of persecution, some were able secretly to obtain? What if he had been baptized even before he was arrested? The public laws could not therefore spare him from bodily death, since by divine grace he had received remission of sins.

What if, already baptized, he had fallen into the crime and offense of banditry, and, being not without baptism but rather repentant, received forgiveness for the crimes he had committed after baptism? His faithful piety was evident both to the Lord in his heart and to us in his words.

For if we maintain that those of whom it is not written whether they were baptized departed this life without baptism, we slander the Apostles themselves, since, apart from the Apostle Paul (Acts 9:18), we do not know when they were baptized. But if it could be made known to us that they themselves were baptized by what the Lord said to blessed Peter—“The one who has been washed does not need [anything] except to wash his feet” [Note: [Col. 0517] In the manuscripts: “does not need to wash,” omitting “except the feet.”] (John 13:10)—what are we to say about the others, concerning whom we do not even read such a statement: Barnabas, Timothy, Titus, Silas, Philemon, and the evangelists Mark and Luke themselves, not to mention countless others? Far be it from us to doubt that they were baptized merely because we do not read of it.

As for Dinocrates, a seven-year-old boy—at which age boys, when they are baptized, already recite the Creed and answer the questions for themselves—I do not know why it did not seem possible to you that, though baptized, he could have been brought back by his impious father to the sacrileges of the Gentiles, and for this reason have been in the punishments from which he was freed when his sister prayed for him. For did you read that he had either never been a Christian or had died as a catechumen? Moreover, the account itself is not contained in that canon of Scripture from which testimonies ought to be produced in questions of this kind.

## CHAPTER X

13. Do not believe, say, or teach “that those whom the Lord predestined for baptism can be snatched from his predestination and die before what the Omnipotent predestined has been fulfilled in them” (above, book 2, §13), if you wish to be catholic.

For I do not know what power is here granted to chance against the power of God, so that, when such accidents occur, what he predestined is prevented from happening. There is no need to enlarge upon the abyss of impiety into which this error swallows the one who errs; it is enough briefly to admonish a prudent man who is ready to be corrected.

These are your own words: “We say,” you write, “that an account must be given of infants of this kind, who, although predestined for baptism, are overtaken by the death of the present life before they are reborn in Christ.”

Are those who are predestined for baptism overtaken by death before they reach it? And did God predestine what he foresaw would not happen, or did he not know that this would not happen [Note: [Col. 0517] Am. Er. and several manuscripts read: “did not foresee that it would happen,” omitting the negative particle. The Sagiensis manuscript reads: “foresaw that it would happen.”], so that either his predestination would be frustrated or his foreknowledge deceived? You see how much could be said here, except that I should hold to what I said shortly before, in order to admonish you briefly on this point.

14. Do not believe, say, or teach “that it is written concerning infants who are overtaken by death before they are reborn in Christ: ‘He was taken away lest wickedness should change his understanding, or deceit should beguile his soul. Therefore he hastened to remove him from the midst of iniquity; for his soul was pleasing to God; and, being perfected in a short time, he fulfilled a long age’” (Wis. 4:11, 14, 13), if you wish to be catholic.

This does not apply to them at all. It applies rather to those who, having been baptized and living piously, are not permitted to live here for long—not perfected in years, but perfected in wisdom.

This error, by which people suppose that the passage was spoken about little children dying before baptism, inflicts intolerable injury upon the most holy washing, if a child who could have been snatched away after baptism is taken away beforehand lest wickedness change his understanding or deceit beguile his soul—as though that wickedness and deceit were believed to exist in the same baptism, by which he would be changed for the worse and deceived if he were not taken away beforehand.

Furthermore, since his soul was pleasing to God, he hastened to remove him from the midst of iniquity, so that he did not even delay for a little while in order to fulfill what he had predestined in him; rather, he preferred to act against his own predestination [Note: [Col. 0518] The Cygirannensis manuscript reads: “that he might do something else.” The passage is obscure and perhaps corrupt.], as though in haste lest what had pleased him in the unbaptized child be destroyed in baptism—as though the child were destined to perish there, where he must be taken in order that he not perish.

Who, then, would believe, say, write, or recite that these words written in the Book of Wisdom were spoken about little children who died without baptism, if he considered them as he ought?

## CHAPTER XI

15. Do not believe, say, or teach “that there are certain dwelling places outside the kingdom of God, which the Lord said were in his Father’s house” (above, book 2, §14), if you wish to be catholic.

For he did not say, as you yourself cited the passage, “There are many dwelling places with my Father.” If he had said this, they would have to be understood as being nowhere other than in his Father’s house. Rather, he plainly said: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14:2).

Who, then, would dare to separate any parts of God’s house from the kingdom of God, so that earthly kings are found to reign not only in their own house, nor only in their own country, but also far and wide across the sea, while the King who made heaven and earth is said not to reign in his entire house?

16. But perhaps you will say that everything does indeed belong to the kingdom of God, because he reigns in heaven, on earth, in the abysses, in paradise, and in hell—for where does he not reign, whose supreme power is everywhere?—but that the kingdom of heaven is one thing, which no one may enter unless washed in the bath of regeneration, because of the Lord’s true and fixed judgment; while the kingdom of earth, or of other parts of creation, is another, where certain dwelling places of God’s house may exist which, although belonging to the kingdom of God, do not belong to the kingdom of heaven, where God’s kingdom is more exalted and blessed.

Thus, you may argue, no parts or dwelling places of God’s house are impiously separated from the kingdom of God; yet not all dwelling places are prepared in the kingdom of heaven [Note: [Col. 0519] Am. Er. and most manuscripts read: “for the inhabitants,” rather than “dwelling places.”]. Those that are not in the kingdom of heaven may nevertheless be inhabited happily by those to whom God wishes to give them, even though they are unbaptized; thus they may be in the kingdom of God, although, because they are not baptized, they cannot be in the kingdom of heaven.

17. Those who say this seem to themselves to be saying something because they attend negligently to the Scriptures and do not understand how the kingdom of God is spoken of when we pray, saying, “Your kingdom come” (Matt. 6:10) [Note: [Col. 0519] The printed editions and the Cygirannensis manuscript have: “may arrive.” In these same books, however, as in the other manuscripts, we later read that we pray “that it may come.”].

The kingdom of God is called that realm in which his faithful household will reign with him, blessedly and eternally, in its entirety. According to the power that he possesses over all things, he certainly reigns even now. What, then, do we pray to come, unless that we may deserve to reign with him?

Under his power, however, there will also be those who burn in the punishment of eternal fire. Shall we therefore say that they too will be in the kingdom of God? It is one thing to be honored by the gifts of the kingdom of God, and another to be restrained by the laws of the kingdom of God [Note: [Col. 0519] Am. Er. and most manuscripts read: “For the kingdom of God is one thing to be honored by its gifts, and another to be restrained by its laws.”].

To make it most plainly evident to you that the kingdom of heaven is not to be distributed to the baptized while other parts of the kingdom of God are given, as you think, to the unbaptized, listen to the Lord himself. He did not say, “If anyone is not reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven,” but, he said, “he cannot enter the kingdom of God.”

These are his words on this subject to Nicodemus: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone has been born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.” Notice that here he did not say “the kingdom of heaven,” but “the kingdom of God.”

When Nicodemus replied and said, “How can a man be born when he is old? Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time and be born?” [Note: [Col. 0519] Lov. has: “and be reborn.” The other books, following the Greek, have: “and be born.”] the Lord, repeating the same statement more plainly and clearly, said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:3–5).

Notice that here too he did not say “the kingdom of heaven,” but “the kingdom of God.” What he had said, “unless someone has been born again,” he explained by saying, “unless someone has been born again of water and the Spirit.” And what he had said, “he cannot see,” he explained by saying, “he cannot enter.” Yet the phrase “the kingdom of God” that he had used he did not repeat under another name [Note: [Col. 0519] The printed editions read: “but the phrase he had used.”].

There is no need now to seek or discuss whether “the kingdom of God” and “the kingdom of heaven” are to be understood with some distinction, or whether one reality is called by two names. It is enough that the one who has not been washed in the bath of regeneration cannot enter the kingdom of God.

You now, I think, understand how far from the truth it is to separate certain dwelling places established in God’s house from the kingdom of God. Therefore, since you have thought that some people who have not been reborn of water and the Spirit will dwell in certain dwelling places that the Lord said were many in his Father’s house, I admonish you—if you permit it—not to delay correcting this, so that you may hold the catholic faith.

## CHAPTER XII

18. Do not believe, say, or teach “that the sacrifice of Christians should be offered for those who have departed from the body unbaptized” (above, book 1, §13, and book 2, §15), if you wish to be catholic.

For you have not shown that the sacrifice you mentioned from the Books of the Maccabees—the Jewish sacrifice (2 Macc. 12:39–46)—was offered for those who had departed from the body uncircumcised.

In stating this opinion of yours, so novel and contrary to the authority and discipline of the whole Church, you also used an extremely presumptuous expression, saying: “For them, certainly, I judge that frequent offerings and the sacrifices of priests should continually be offered.” Thus, as a layman, you placed yourself above God’s priests, neither submitting to them as a learner nor even joining them as a fellow seeker, but presiding over them as a judge.

Put such things away, my son. One does not walk in this way along the path that Christ taught us to be himself—the humble path. No one enters his narrow gate with such swelling pride.

## CHAPTER XIII

19. Do not believe, say, or teach “that some of those who have departed this life without Christ’s baptism do not meanwhile go into the kingdom of heaven but into paradise, and afterward, at the resurrection of the dead, also attain the blessedness of the kingdom of heaven” (above, book 2, §16), if you wish to be catholic.

Even the Pelagian heresy did not dare to grant this to them, although it holds that little children do not contract original sin. You, although as a Catholic you confess that they are born with sin, nevertheless, through some even more perverse novelty of opinion, assert that without saving baptism they are both absolved from the sin with which they are born and introduced into the kingdom of heaven.

Nor do you consider how much worse you think in this matter than Pelagius. Fearing the Lord’s statement by which the unbaptized are not permitted to enter the kingdom of heaven, he did not dare to send little children there, although he believed them free from every sin. You, however, so disregard the statement, “If anyone has not been reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God,” that—apart from the error by which you dare to separate paradise from the kingdom of God—you do not hesitate to promise both absolution from guilt and the kingdom of heaven to certain little children whom, as a Catholic, you believe are born guilty, even though they died without baptism.

It is as though you could then be a true Catholic in asserting original sin against Pelagius if, against the Lord, you became a new heretic by destroying his teaching concerning baptism. We do not wish you, beloved, to be a victor over heretics in such a way that error conquers error and, what is worse, the greater error conquers the lesser.

For you say: “But if perhaps someone should object that paradise was temporarily granted in the meantime to the soul of the thief or of Dinocrates, since the reward of the kingdom of heaven still remains for them at the resurrection, although that principal judgment stands in the way, ‘For whoever has not been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit will not enter the kingdom of heaven,’ nevertheless let him also hold my ungrudging assent in this matter, provided he magnifies both the effect and the affection of divine mercy and foreknowledge.”

These are your words, in which you confess that you agree with the claim that certain unbaptized people were temporarily granted paradise in such a way that the reward of the kingdom of heaven still remains for them at the resurrection—against the principal judgment by which it has been established that the one who has not been reborn of water and the Holy Spirit will not enter that kingdom.

Fearing to violate this principal judgment, Pelagius did not believe that even those would enter the kingdom of heaven without baptism whom he did not believe to be guilty. You, however, both confess that little children are guilty of original sin and yet absolve them without the bath of regeneration, send them to paradise, and afterward allow them also to enter the kingdom of heaven.

## CHAPTER XIV

20. Correct these and similar matters, and any others that, upon more attentive and unhurried examination, you may perhaps find in your books, without any further delay, if you possess a catholic spirit—that is, if you truly spoke beforehand when you said “that you should not be so trusting toward yourself as to think that what you have said can be proved; and that you should always strive not to defend even your own opinion if it is exposed as untenable; and that you should take to heart, with your own judgment condemned, to pursue what is better and what is truer.”

Now prove, my dearest, that you did not speak these words deceitfully, so that the Catholic Church may rejoice in your character—not only ingenious but also cautious, devout, and modest—and not burn with the madness of contentious heresy.

Now is the time for you to show with what sincerity of heart you spoke these good words of yours that I have recalled. Immediately afterward you added: “For just as it is characteristic of an excellent purpose and praiseworthy counsel to be easily led toward what is truer, so it is characteristic of a wicked and stubborn judgment not to bend quickly toward the path of reason” (above, book 2, §22).

Be, therefore, a person of excellent purpose and praiseworthy counsel, and be easily led toward what is truer. Do not be of a wicked and stubborn judgment, unwilling to bend quickly toward the path of reason.

For if you spoke these words generously—if they did not merely sound upon your lips, but you felt them inwardly and sincerely in your heart—you will hate delay in the great good of your correction. It was not enough for you to say that it is characteristic of a wicked and stubborn judgment not to bend toward the path of reason unless you added “quickly.” By this you showed how detestable is the person who never does this, since one who does it slowly seems to you worthy of such severe blame that he is rightly called wicked in judgment and stubborn.

Listen, then, to yourself, and make use above all and especially of the fruits of your own eloquence [Note: [Col. 0521] The Belgian manuscript of Saint-Amand has: “and make use above all and especially of the fruits of your own spoken words.” The Tournai manuscript has: “and make use above all and especially of the fruits of your greatest eloquence.” Our oldest German manuscript has: “and make use above all and especially of what you have said,” omitting “fruits.” The text is faulty unless one reads: “of what you have said.”], so that with the gravity of your mind you may bend more quickly toward the path of reason than you turned away from it through the slippery inexperience of your age, with insufficient learning and little prudence.

21. It would take too long to examine and discuss everything in your books—or rather, everything in yourself—that I wish to have corrected, and at least to give you a brief account of each point requiring correction.

Nevertheless, do not therefore despise yourself or suppose that your intelligence and eloquence should be valued lightly. Nor have I found your knowledge of the holy Scriptures to be small. But your learning is less than would have been fitting for such talent and effort.

Thus I do not wish you to become vain by attributing more to yourself than is appropriate, nor again to grow cold by casting yourself down and despairing. If only I could read your writings with you and point out by conversation rather than by writing what ought to be corrected. We could complete this task more easily by speaking together than by letters; if it had to be written, it would require many volumes.

Nevertheless, I earnestly admonish you concerning these fundamental matters, which I have wished to set out under a definite number: do not delay correcting them, and make them wholly foreign to your faith and preaching. Thus, whatever capacity for disputation you possess, use it—as God’s gift—profitably for the edification, not the destruction, of sound and salutary doctrine.

## CHAPTER XV

22. These, then, are the matters about which I have already argued as best I could; but I shall briefly repeat and review them.

The first is that you said “God made the soul not from nothing but from himself.”

The second is that “through infinite time, and thus always, God gives souls, just as he himself is always the one who gives.”

The third is that “the soul lost through the flesh some merit that it had possessed before the flesh.”

The fourth is that “through the flesh the soul recovers its former condition and is reborn through that same flesh through which it had deserved to be defiled.”

The fifth is that “the soul deserved to become sinful before all sin.”

The sixth is that “infants overtaken by death before they are baptized can attain the remission of original sins.”

The seventh is that “those whom the Lord predestined for baptism can be snatched from his predestination and die before what the Omnipotent predestined has been fulfilled in them.”

The eighth is that “it is written concerning infants who are overtaken by death before they are reborn in Christ: ‘He was taken away lest wickedness should change his understanding’”—and the other things read in the Book of Wisdom in that connection.

The ninth is that “there are certain dwelling places outside the kingdom of God, among those which the Lord said were in his Father’s house.”

The tenth is that “the sacrifice of Christians should be offered for those who have departed from the body unbaptized.”

The eleventh is that “some of those who have departed this life without Christ’s baptism do not meanwhile go into the kingdom but into paradise, and afterward, at the resurrection of the dead, also attain the blessedness of the kingdom of heaven.”

23. These eleven matters, for the present, are plainly and greatly perverse and opposed to the catholic faith. Now do not hesitate to uproot and cast them from your mind, your speech, and your writing, if you wish us to rejoice that you have not merely crossed over to the Catholic altars but are truly catholic.

For if each of these matters is defended stubbornly, they can produce as many heresies as there are opinions. Consider, therefore, how dreadful it would be if all those things were found in one man which would be condemnable individually in separate persons.

But if you fight for none of them contentiously—indeed, if you defeat them with faithful words and writings—you will be more praiseworthy as a censor of yourself than if you had reproved anyone else with sound reasoning, and a more remarkable corrector of them than if you had never held those opinions.

May the Lord be present to your mind and pour into your spirit, through his own Spirit, such readiness for humility, such light of truth, such sweetness of charity, and such peace of devotion that you would rather be victorious over your own mind in what is true than over anyone who contradicts you in what is false.

But far be it from you to suppose that, by holding these opinions, you have departed from the catholic faith, although they are contrary to the catholic faith, if before God—whose eye is deceived in no one’s heart—you sincerely recall having said [Note: [Col. 0523] Five manuscripts have “if you repent.” The others, with the printed editions, read “if you reconsider.”]:

“that you should not be so trusting toward yourself as to think that what you have said can be proved; and that you should always strive not to defend even your own opinion if it is exposed as untenable, because you take to heart, with your own judgment condemned, to pursue what is better and what is truer.”

For this disposition, even when expressed in statements that are un-Catholic through ignorance, is itself catholic because it has already anticipated and prepared for correction.

But let this be the end of this volume, where the reader may rest for a little while, so that his attention may be renewed by another beginning for what follows.

# BOOK FOUR: TO VINCENTIUS VICTOR

[Col. 0523]

First, he shows Vincentius Victor that he was unjustly criticized for his hesitation concerning the origin of souls, and that Victor unjustly compared him to animals because he had dared to define nothing on this matter. Then, because he unhesitatingly said that the soul is spirit and not body, Victor rashly censured him as well, attempting to establish that the soul is corporeal by nature and that the spirit is distinct from it in human beings. Refuting him, Augustine, after carefully examining the arguments by which Victor tried to prove that the soul is corporeal, shows that this same soul is also called “spirit” in Scripture, although in truth that name properly denotes the soul’s faculty by which we reason and understand.

## CHAPTER ONE
1. Now receive also what I wish to say to you about myself, if I can—that is, if he grants it in whose hand both we and our words are. For you have criticized me twice, explicitly mentioning my name; and although at the beginning of your book you declared yourself extremely conscious of your own inexperience and lacking the support of learning, while, when you mentioned me, you called me highly learned and most experienced, nevertheless, in matters where you thought you knew what I either confess that I do not know or, though I do not know it, presume that I do know, you did not hesitate—with the freedom that was appropriate [Note: [Col. 0523] Several manuscripts: “with the freedom that was not appropriate.”]—to criticize not merely an old man as a young man, and a bishop as a layman, but even a man whom, in your judgment, you had called highly learned and most experienced.

I, however, neither know myself to be highly learned and most experienced, indeed I know with complete certainty that I am not; and I do not doubt that it can happen that some unlearned and ignorant person happens to know something that a learned and experienced person does not know. [Note: [Col. 0523] Am., Er., and several manuscripts: “some learned layman.”] In this I praise you outright: you preferred truth to a human being, even if it was not truth that you had grasped, but certainly truth that you thought you had grasped [Note: [Col. 0523] Printed editions: “never”; corrected from the manuscripts.]; rashly, indeed, because you thought you knew what you do not know, but freely, because you did not respect the person and chose to disclose what you thought.

Hence you ought to understand how much greater concern we should have to recall the Lord’s sheep from errors, if it is shameful even for sheep to conceal from their shepherds whatever faults they have discovered in them. Would that you had criticized in me those things that deserve just criticism! For I ought not to deny that, in my conduct no less than in my many writings, there are many things that can rightly and without rashness be censured. If you had criticized some of these, I might perhaps have shown you what I would wish you to be in matters where you had not criticized wrongly; and [Note: [Col. 0523] Morel considers that *meque* should be read; see *Elementa Critica*, p. 147.], as an older man to a younger, and a superior to a subordinate, I would have offered you an example of correction—one that would have been all the more salutary the more humbly it was offered. But you criticized in me things that humility does not compel me to correct, but truth compels me partly to acknowledge and partly to defend. [Col. 0524]

## CHAPTER II

2. These things are as follows: first, that concerning the origin of souls which were given, or are given, to human beings after the first man, I did not dare to define anything, because I confess that I do not know; second, that I said I knew the soul to be spirit, not body. On this second point you criticized two things: first, that I did not believe it to be a body; second, that I believed it to be spirit. For it seems to you both that the soul is a body and that it is not spirit.

Listen, then, to my defense against your criticism; and, through this occasion on which I defend myself to you, learn in your own case what you should correct. Recall the words of your book where you first mentioned me:

“I know,” you say, “that most men, and easily the most learned of them, as well as men of judgment, have maintained silence, or have spoken nothing more explicit, when, after beginning their exposition, they withheld a definition from their discussions—as I recently read in writing in the work of Augustine, that highly learned and celebrated bishop [Note: [Col. 0524] Printed editions and several manuscripts: “just as I have recently read through ...”]: men who, as I think, explored the secrets of this matter with greater modesty and restraint, swallowed within themselves the judgment of their investigation, and professed that they could determine nothing further from that point onward. But, believe me, it seems to me sufficiently, and more than sufficiently, absurd and contrary to reason that a human being should be ignorant of himself, or that one who is believed to have attained knowledge of all things should be unknown to himself.

“What difference, then, is there between a human being and an animal [Note: [Col. 0524] Manuscripts: “What difference does a human being have from an animal?” and likewise below consistently omit “from.”] if he does not know how to investigate and discuss his own condition and nature—so that what is written may rightly apply to him: ‘Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them’ (Ps. XLVIII, 13)? For since the good God created nothing without reason, and produced the human being himself as a rational animal, capable of understanding, endowed with reason, and alive to sensation, one who should distribute all things devoid of reason by a prudent ordering [Note: [Col. 0524] Am. and Er.: “who should distribute by all experience of reason and prudent ordering”; some manuscripts: “by an ordering of prudence.”], what could be said more incongruously than that he deprived him of knowledge of himself alone? And since the wisdom of the world, which stretches itself even to knowledge of the truth by a superfluous investigation—for it cannot know through whom it is possible to recognize what is true—has nevertheless attempted to discern something near, indeed akin, to the truth concerning the nature of the soul, how unbecoming and shameful it is for any religious person either to know nothing about this very matter or to have completely forbidden himself to know it.”

3. This eloquent and brilliant chastisement of our ignorance compels you to know everything that pertains to human nature, so that, if you are ignorant of any one of these things, you are compared—not by my judgment, but by your own—to animals. Although you seem to touch upon these matters more emphatically [Note: [Col. 0525] Printed editions: “more emphatically”; manuscripts: *insignitius*, “more notably” or “more pointedly.”] because you said, “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand,” since we possess the honor of the Church, which you do not, nevertheless you too possess the honor of nature, by which you are preferred to animals—animals to which, according to your own judgment, you must be compared if you are ignorant of anything that plainly belongs to your nature.

For you did not direct this criticism merely against those who are ignorant of what I am ignorant of—that is, the origin of the human soul. Indeed, I do not wholly fail to know it: I know that God breathed into the face of the first man, and that the man became a living soul (Gen. II, 7); yet, unless I had read this, I could not have known it by myself. Rather, you said: “What difference is there between a human being and an animal if he does not know how to investigate and discuss his own condition and nature?” You seem to have understood this as though a human being ought to investigate and discuss his entire condition and nature in such a way that nothing about himself remains hidden from him.

If that is so, I shall compare you to animals if you do not tell me the number of your hairs. But if you grant that, however much progress we make in this life, there are some things pertaining to our nature that we do not know, I ask how far and to what extent you grant this—lest perhaps this too belong among the things of which we do not know the origin of our souls in every respect. Nevertheless, we know without ambiguity what pertains to the salvation of faith: that the soul is given by God, and that it is not of the same nature as God.

Or do you perhaps think that each person is ignorant of his nature only to the extent that you are ignorant of it, and knows it only to the extent that you are able to know it? Thus, if someone knows a little less than you, you compare him to animals because you were able to know that thing; and, in the same justice, if someone knows a little more than you, he will compare you to animals. Tell us, then, to what extent you permit us not to know our nature, so that our distinction from animals may remain secure. Yet consider whether the person who knows that he is ignorant of some aspect of his nature is farther removed from animals than the person who thinks he knows what he does not know.

The whole nature of a human being certainly consists of spirit, soul, and body. Therefore anyone who wishes to separate the body from human nature is foolish. Yet physicians who are called anatomists have investigated the nature of the body—through limbs, veins, nerves, bones, marrow, and vital inner organs—by dissecting living human beings for as long as they were able to remain alive in the hands of those examining them [Col. 0526; Note: [Col. 0526] Er. and Lov.: “by cutting apart”; erroneously.]. They did this so that they might know the nature of the body; yet they did not compare us to animals because we do not know these things.

Unless perhaps you are going to say that those should be compared to animals who do not know the nature of the soul, rather than those who do not know the nature of the body. You therefore ought not to have made your preliminary statement in that way. For you did not say, “What difference is there between a human being and an animal if he does not know the condition and nature of his soul?” Rather, you said, “if he does not know how to investigate and discuss his own condition and nature.” Our condition and our nature are reckoned together with the body, although each of the things of which we consist may be discussed separately.

For my part, if I wished to explain how much I could discuss with the greatest knowledge concerning human nature, I would fill several volumes. Yet I confess that there are many things I do not know.

## CHAPTER III

4. To what, then, do you wish to relate what we discussed in the preceding book concerning the breath of a human being? Does it pertain to the nature of the soul, because the soul produces it in the human being; or to the body, which is moved by the soul in order to produce it; or to this air, by whose alternation it is shown to be produced; or rather to all three—to the soul, which moves the body; to the body, which receives and returns the breath through movement; and to that surrounding air which, entering, nourishes it, and, leaving, relieves it?

And yet you, a learned and eloquent man, certainly did not know this when you believed, said, wrote, and read before an assembled crowd that “from our nature we inflate a wineskin,” and that “in our nature we have nothing less” [Note: [Col. 0526] Thus the manuscripts. Printed editions read: “and from our nature we inflate a wineskin, and our nature has nothing less in us.”]—although you could very easily have learned where we do this, not by searching through divine and human writings, but by observing yourself whenever you wished.

How, then, can I entrust you with teaching me about the origin of souls, when I confess that I do not know it, if you did not know the source of what you continually do through your own nostrils and mouth? May the Lord grant that, having been admonished by me, you yield rather than resist a truth so obvious and so perfectly clear. Do not question your lungs about inflating a wineskin in such a way that you prefer to have them inflated against me rather than to heed them as they teach you and give you a true answer—not by speaking and arguing, but by breathing in and breathing out.

Accordingly, I would not take it badly if you rebuked and reproached me for my ignorance concerning the origin of souls. Indeed, I would give great thanks if you struck it, not only with harsh insults, but also shook it out with true statements. For if you could teach me what I do not know, I ought to endure you striking me not merely with words but even with blows, with the greatest patience.

## CHAPTER IV

5. For I confess to Your Affection that, as far as this question is concerned, I greatly desire to know one of two things, if I can: either what I do not know concerning the origin of souls, or whether it is necessary for us to know this while we live here. For what if it belongs among those matters about which we are told: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not investigate what is too strong for you; but always think upon what the Lord has commanded you” (Ecclus. I, 22)?

Yet I wish to know this either from God himself, who knows what he creates, or from some learned person who knows what he is saying—not from a person who does not know what he is breathing. No one remembers his infancy, and do you think that a human being can know, except by God’s teaching, from what point he began to live in his mother’s womb? This is especially so if human nature remains so hidden from him that he does not know not only what he has within himself, but even what approaches him from outside.

Will you, dearest son, teach me—or anyone else—from what source human beings receive their souls at birth, when you still did not know from what source living human beings are nourished in such a way that, if that nourishment is withdrawn for a little while, they immediately die? Will you teach me—or anyone else—from what source human beings receive their souls, when you still did not know from what source wineskins are filled when they are inflated?

Would that, just as you do not know the origin of souls, I at least knew whether it were necessary for me to know this in this life. For if it belongs among those higher things which we are forbidden to investigate and scrutinize, we must fear that we sin in this matter not by ignorance but by seeking it. Nor should we think that it does not belong among those higher things merely because it concerns not God’s nature but ours.

## CHAPTER V

6. What of the fact that certain works of God are more difficult to know than God himself, insofar as he can be known? We have learned that God is Trinity; but how many kinds of animals he created—at least of the land animals that could enter Noah’s ark—we still do not know. Unless perhaps you have already learned this.

It is also written in the Book of Wisdom: “For if they were able to know enough to judge the world, how did they not more easily find its Lord?” (Wis. XIII, 9). Or is something not higher for us simply because it is within us? The nature of our soul is more interior than the body. As though the soul could not more easily know the body externally through the eyes of that very body than internally through itself! What is there in the body’s intestines where the soul itself is not present? And yet it investigated even the internal and vital organs through the body’s eyes, and whatever it was able to learn from them, it learned through the body’s eyes. Certainly the soul was there even when it did not know those organs. And although our internal organs cannot live without the soul, the soul was more able to give them life than to know them.

Or perhaps is the body more beyond the soul’s knowledge than the soul herself is? [Note: [Col. 0527] Printed editions and several manuscripts read: “is she herself more beyond knowledge than her body?”] If the soul wishes to investigate and discuss when human seed is changed into blood, when into solid flesh, when the bones harden, and when they begin to develop marrow; how many kinds of veins and nerves there are, by what courses and windings they irrigate and bind the whole body; whether the skin should be counted among the nerves, and the teeth among the bones—for they differ in that they lack marrow; and how fingernails differ from both, since they resemble them in hardness, while being cut and growing, like hair; what is the function of the veins that carry not blood but air, which are called arteries—if the soul desires to know these and similar matters concerning the nature of its body, are we then to say to a human being [Note: [Col. 0527] Am. and Er.: “then certainly it must be said”; Lov.: “then it must be said”; manuscripts: “are we then to say”], “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not investigate what is too strong for you”?

But if it investigates what it does not know concerning its own origin, is that not too high or too strong for it to grasp? You consider it absurd and contrary to reason that the soul should not know whether it was divinely breathed into human beings or derived from parents, although it does not remember this past event and counts it among those things—like infancy and the other early stages after birth—that it has irrevocably forgotten, if indeed it occurred with any awareness on its part when it occurred.

Yet you do not consider it absurd or contrary to reason that the soul should not know the body subject to it, and should be entirely ignorant of something not belonging to its past but wholly to its present: whether it moves the veins so that it may live in the body, and the nerves so that it may operate the body’s limbs; and, if this is so, why it does not move the nerves unless it wishes, while the beating of the veins proceeds without interruption even if it does not wish it; from which part of the body it governs the rest—what they call the ἡγεμονικόν (*hegemonikon*, the governing faculty): whether from the heart, or from the brain, or through movements distributed from the heart and sensations from the brain, or from the brain for sensations and voluntary movements but from the heart for involuntary pulsations of the veins; and, if it performs those two functions from the brain, why it feels even when it does not wish, but does not move the limbs unless it wishes.

Since, then, no one but the soul performs these functions in the body, why does it not know what it does, or from where it does it? It is not shameful for it to be ignorant of these things; yet you consider it shameful if it does not know from where or how it was made, although it did not make itself. No one knows how or from where the soul performs these things in the body. Why, then, do you not think that this belongs among the higher and stronger matters?

## CHAPTER VI

7. But here I raise an even greater question for you: why do very few people know the source from which they do what everyone does? Perhaps you will say: “Because they have learned anatomy or empiricism, branches contained within the medical discipline, which only a few attain; while the others did not wish to learn these things, although they could have if they had wished.”

I pass over the question why many attempt to learn these things but cannot, being hindered—strangely enough—by a sluggish intellect from learning from others what is done by themselves and within themselves. But this itself is the greatest question: why do I need no skill to know that the sun, the moon, and the other stars are in the sky, while I need skill to know, when I move my finger, where I begin—from the heart, or from the brain, or from both, or from neither? Why do I need no teacher to know what is so far above me, while I expect to learn from another human being the source from which what is done in me is done by me?

For although we are said to think in the heart, and know what we think without any other person knowing it, we nevertheless do not know in what part of the body we have the very heart in which we think, unless we learn it from someone else who does not know what we are thinking. I am not unaware that when we hear the command to love God with our whole heart, this is not said of that piece of flesh lying beneath our ribs, but of the power by which thoughts are formed. It is rightly called by this name because, just as movement does not cease in the heart, from which the pulse spreads throughout the veins, so we do not cease to turn something over in thought.

Nevertheless, since every sensation is present to the soul and through the soul to the body, why is it that even in darkness and with our eyes closed, by the bodily sense called touch, we can count our external limbs, while, through the soul’s own inward presence—by which it is present to all the things it vivifies and animates—we know none of our internal organs? I believe that no one knows this: not empirical physicians, not anatomists, not dogmatic physicians, and not methodical physicians; indeed, no human being.

8. Whoever has attempted to learn these things is not told without reason: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not investigate what is too strong for you.” For these things are not higher than our stature can reach, but higher than our conjecture can comprehend; nor are they stronger than human strength, but stronger than the power of human understanding can penetrate.

And yet they are not the heaven of heaven, nor the dimensions of the stars, nor the measure of the sea and lands, nor the lowest underworld. We are the ones who cannot comprehend ourselves; we surpass the measure of our knowledge in height and strength; we cannot contain ourselves, and yet we are certainly not outside ourselves.

Nor should we be compared to animals because we do not completely discover what we are. Yet you think we should be compared to animals if we have forgotten what we were—provided that we ever knew it. For my soul is not now drawn from my parents, nor is it now breathed in by God. Whichever of these he did, he did it when he created me; he does not now do it concerning me or in me. That event was done and completed; it is neither present nor recent for me.

I do not even know whether I once knew this and have forgotten it, or whether, when it happened, I was not then able to perceive and know it.

## CHAPTER VII

9. Look: now, at this very moment [Note: [Col. 0529] Printed editions omit the second *modo* (“now”).], while we exist, while we live, while we know that we live, while we are absolutely certain that we remember, understand, and will [Note: [Col. 0529] Several manuscripts: “we know with absolute certainty.”]—we who boast that we are great investigators of our own nature do not know at all what our memory, understanding, or will is capable of.

A certain friend of mine, named Simplicius, a man of outstanding and astonishing memory from his youth onward, was once asked by us what verses Virgil had placed above the final verses in all his books. He answered immediately, quickly, and from memory. We also asked him to recite the preceding verses, and he did so. We believed that he could recite Virgil backward.

From whatever place we wished, we asked him to begin, and he did so. We also wanted him to do the same with prose, from whatever speech of Cicero he had committed to memory; he followed upward through as much as we wished. While we were marveling, he called God to witness that he had not known before that experiment that he could do this. [Note: [Col. 0529] Some manuscripts omit “God,” reading simply: “he testified that he had not known.”] Thus, as far as memory was concerned, his mind learned its capacity only then; and whenever it learned it, it could do so only by testing and experimenting. [Note: [Col. 0529] The Leuven editors rejected the negative particle, although it is present here in the manuscripts.] Yet before he tested it, he was the same person. Why, then, did he not know himself?

10. Often we presume that we will retain something in memory, and because we think so, we do not write it down. Later, when we wish, it does not come to mind; we regret that we believed it would return, or that we did not bind it with letters so that it would not escape. Then suddenly, when we are not looking for it, it comes back.

Were we not present when we were thinking about it? And yet we are not now what we were when we cannot think about it. What, then, is this by which, in some inexplicable way, we are withdrawn from ourselves and denied to ourselves, and likewise, in some inexplicable way, brought before ourselves and restored to ourselves? [Note: [Col. 0530] Printed editions read: “What then is it that we do not know? How are we withdrawn and denied to ourselves? Thus I do not know ...”; some manuscripts: “What then is it that we are not? ...” The text is corrected from the oldest Germanensis manuscript.] It is as though we were other people and were somewhere else when we search for what we placed in our memory and do not find it; as though we ourselves could not reach ourselves, placed as if elsewhere, and reached ourselves only when we find it.

Where do we search, except within ourselves? And what do we search for, except ourselves? It is as though we were not within ourselves and had withdrawn somewhere from ourselves. Do you not attend to this and shudder at such a great depth? What else is this than our nature—not what it once was, but what it now is? And behold, it is sought more than it is comprehended.

Often I thought that I would understand a question placed before me if I reflected upon it. I reflected, but could not. Often I did not expect to understand, and yet I could. Therefore the powers of my understanding are certainly not known to me—and I believe they are not known to you either.

11. Perhaps you despise me for confessing this, and for this reason as well you will compare me to animals. I, however, do not cease to advise—or, if you do not consider me worthy of advice, at least to remind—you to recognize instead the common weakness in which strength is perfected. Do not presume unknown things to be known, lest you be unable to reach the truth.

For I think there is something that you too seek to understand but cannot; yet you would not seek it unless you hoped that you could. Thus you too do not know the powers of your understanding, although you profess knowledge of your nature and do not confess your ignorance with me.

What shall I say about the will, where our free choice is certainly proclaimed? The blessed apostle Peter wished to lay down his life for the Lord (John XIII, 37). He plainly wished it; for he was not deceiving God when he promised it. Yet his will itself did not know how much strength it possessed. Thus so great a man, who had recognized the Son of God, was hidden from himself.

We know, then, that we wish or do not wish something. But even when our will is good, we do not know—if we are not deceiving ourselves—how much it is worth, how much strength it has, or to which temptations it yields and to which it does not, dear son.

## CHAPTER VIII

12. Consider, then, how many things concerning our nature we do not know—not past things but present ones, and not merely matters pertaining to the body but also matters pertaining to the inner human being—and yet we are not compared to animals.

And because I do not entirely fail to know the past origin of my soul, but do not know it fully—for I know that it was given to me by God, yet that it is not of God—you judged me worthy of such abuse.

When can I list all the things we do not know concerning the nature of our spirit and soul? Rather, we should cry out to God with what he cried out in the Psalm: “Your knowledge has become wonderful beyond me; it has prevailed, and I cannot attain it” (Ps. CXXXVIII, 6). Why did he add “beyond me,” unless he inferred from himself how incomprehensible God’s knowledge was, since he could not comprehend himself?

The Apostle was caught up into the third heaven and heard ineffable words that are not permitted for a human being to speak. He says that he does not know whether this happened to him in the body or outside the body (II Cor. XII, 2–4), and he does not fear being compared by you to animals. He knew that his spirit was in the third heaven and in paradise, but he did not know whether he was in the body.

Now the third heaven and paradise were certainly not the apostle Paul himself; but his body, soul, and spirit were himself. Behold: he knew great, exalted, and divine things that he himself was not; yet he did not know something that pertained to his own nature. Who would not marvel at such great ignorance of oneself amid such great knowledge of hidden things?

Finally, who would believe this unless the one who does not deceive had said it: “We do not know what we ought to pray for” (Rom. VIII, 26)? Our chief concern ought to be to stretch ourselves toward the things that lie ahead. Yet you compare me to animals if I have forgotten something concerning my origin among the things that lie behind, although you hear that the same apostle says: “Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, according to my purpose I pursue the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus” (Phil. III, 13–14).

## CHAPTER IX

13. Or perhaps, because I said, “We do not know what we ought to pray for,” you think I should be mocked and judge me like irrational animals? That would perhaps be more tolerable. For when, with sound and proper judgment, we prefer our future to our past, and prayer is necessary for us not because of what we were but because of what we will be, it is certainly much more troublesome not to know what we should pray for than not to know how we came into existence.

But let it come to your mind where you have read this—or recall it by rereading—and do not throw the stone of this reproach at me, lest it reach the one you do not wish to strike. For that very Apostle, the teacher of the Gentiles, said: “We do not know what we ought to pray for.” He taught this not only by word but also demonstrated it by his own example.

Against his own benefit and the perfection of his salvation, he ignorantly prayed that the thorn of the flesh—which he said had been given to him so that he would not be exalted by the greatness of his revelations—might depart from him. And because the Lord loved him, he did not do what he ignorantly asked (II Cor. XII, 7–9).

Yet when he says, “We do not know what we ought to pray for,” he immediately adds: “But the Spirit himself intercedes for us with ineffable groanings. He who searches hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because he intercedes for the saints according to God” (Rom. VIII, 26–27)—that is, he causes the saints to intercede.

This is the Spirit whom God sent into our hearts, crying, “Abba, Father” (Gal. IV, 6), and in whom we cry, “Abba, Father” (Rom. VIII, 15). Both statements are made: that we have received the Spirit crying, “Abba, Father,” and that we cry, “Abba, Father,” in the Spirit. The second explains how he said “crying”: that is, causing us to cry, so that, because he causes it, we cry.

Let that Spirit, then, teach me this as well when he wishes, if he knows that it is beneficial for me to know from where I derive my origin according to the soul. But let that Spirit teach me who searches the depth of God [Note: [Col. 0532] Several manuscripts: “the depths of God.”]—not a human being who does not know from where a wineskin is inflated. Yet far be it from me to compare you to animals on this account. You were ignorant of this not because you were unable, but because you had not paid attention.

## CHAPTER X

14. But perhaps, although the matters investigated concerning the origin of souls are higher than the source from which we draw and return breath, you nevertheless trust that you have learned these higher matters from the holy Scriptures—from which, through faith, we have learned things that no human intellect could investigate. [Note: [Col. 0532] Manuscripts: “can investigate.”]

For it is far more excellent to know that the flesh will rise again and live without end than to know whatever physicians have been able to discover about it by investigation—things that the soul perceives through no sensation, although by its presence it gives life to everything it does not know. And it is far better to know that the soul which has been reborn and renewed in Christ will be blessed forever than to know whatever we are ignorant of concerning its memory, understanding, and will.

We could in no way know these more excellent and better things unless we believed the divine utterances. Perhaps, then, you think that you can rely on these utterances so as not to hesitate to produce a definite opinion about the origin of souls.

First, if this were so [Note: [Col. 0532] Most manuscripts instead read: “you are the first to hesitate to offer a definite opinion. If this were so ...”], you ought not to have attributed to human nature itself the fact that a human being knows how to investigate and discuss his own condition and nature, but to God’s gift. For you said, “What difference is there between a human being and an animal if he does not know this?”

What need, then, is there to read anything in order to know this, if by the very fact that we differ from animals we ought already to know it? Just as no Scripture is needed for me to know that I live—my nature makes it impossible for me not to know this—so, if knowing that belongs to nature, why do you offer me scriptural testimonies about this matter, so that I may believe them? Are only those who read the Scriptures distinguished from animals? Were we not created in such a way that we differ from animals before we could reach any written texts?

What, I ask, is this that you attribute so greatly to our nature: that, by the very fact that it differs from animals, it should already know how to investigate and discuss the origin of souls; and yet you make it so incapable of this knowledge that it cannot know it by human means unless it believes divine witnesses?

## CHAPTER XI

15. Moreover, you are mistaken in this respect as well. For the divine testimonies that you wished to bring forward to settle this question do not reveal what you claim. They demonstrate something else, without which we truly cannot live piously: namely, that we have God as the giver, creator, and fashioner of our souls.

But how he does this—whether by breathing new souls into them or by drawing them from their parents—they do not express, except in the case of that one soul which he gave to the first man. Read carefully what I wrote to our brother, the servant of God, Renatus (above, Book I, §17 and following). Since I demonstrated this there, it was not necessary to write it here as well.

You wanted me to define what you yourself had defined, so that I would be forced into the same narrow straits into which you yourself were forced, and you spoke so many and such grave things against the catholic faith that, if you faithfully and humbly recall and consider them [Note: [Col. 0532] Printed editions read *eas* (“them”); manuscripts more correctly read *ea* (“these things”).], you will plainly see how much it would have benefited you to have known that you did not know what you do not know—and how much it benefits you if you know it even now. [Col. 0532]

For if understanding pleases you in human nature—since, truly, if we did not possess it, we would differ from animals in nothing as far as souls are concerned—understand what you do not understand, lest you fail to understand anything at all. Do not despise the person who, in order to understand truthfully what he does not understand, understands that he does not understand it.

Read and understand why it was said in the sacred Psalm: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. XLVIII, 13). In this way you will humbly avoid this reproach yourself rather than arrogantly casting it at another.

For it was said of those who regard this life alone as life, living according to the flesh and hoping for nothing after death, like animals—not of those who neither deny that they know what they know nor fail to confess that they do not know what they do not know, and who understand their weakness rather than trusting in their own strength.

16. Therefore, son, let my old-age fear not displease your youthful presumption. [Note: [Col. 0533] The manuscripts consistently read *juvenali* (“youthful” or “of youth”).] For if, concerning what we are investigating about the origin of souls, I cannot learn it from God or from some spiritual person teaching it, I am more ready to defend the proposition that God rightly willed us not to know this, as he has willed us not to know many other things, than rashly to say that it is either so obscure that I cannot bring it to the understanding of others, or even understand it myself; or that it might assist heretics, who try to persuade people that the souls of infants are entirely free from all guilt.

They do this lest that same guilt return and rebound upon God the author, on the ground that, by giving innocent souls—which he foresaw would receive no assistance from the laver of regeneration—to sinful flesh, he compelled them to become sinful, with no grace of Baptism to rescue them from eternal condemnation. Countless souls of infants, after all, depart from their bodies before they are baptized.

Far be it from me, in trying to dissolve this argument, to say what you yourself have said: “That the soul deserved to be defiled through the flesh and to be sinful, although it had no prior sin by which it could rightly be said to have deserved this”; and “that original sins are forgiven even without Baptism”; and “that at the end the kingdom of heaven is also granted to the unbaptized.”

If I were not afraid to utter these and similar poisons against the faith, perhaps I would not be afraid to define something about this matter. How much better, then, not to discuss and affirm separately what I do not know about the soul, but simply to hold what I see the Apostle teaching most openly: that from one human being all who are born from Adam go into condemnation (Rom. V, 18), unless they are reborn in Christ in the manner in which he ordained that they should be reborn before they die bodily—those whom the most merciful giver of grace has predestined to eternal life, while being also the most just retributor of punishment for those whom he has predestined to eternal death.

This is not only because of those things which they add voluntarily, but also, if infants add nothing, because of original sin. This is my definition in that question: that the hidden works of God should retain their secret, while my faith remains secure.

## CHAPTER XII
17. Now, insofar as the Lord deigns to grant it, I must also answer the point where, speaking about the soul, you repeated my name and said: “For we do not allow, as the most learned Bishop Augustine professes, that it is incorporeal and itself a spirit.” Let us first discuss whether the soul is to be considered incorporeal, as I said, or corporeal, as you maintain. Then let us consider whether Scripture also calls it a spirit, although properly speaking spirit is the name not of the whole soul but of a part of it.

First, I should like to know how you define a body. For if nothing is a body except what consists of bodily limbs, then neither earth nor heaven nor a stone nor water nor the stars, nor anything of this kind, will be a body. But if a body is whatever consists of parts, larger and smaller, occupying larger and smaller regions of space, then those things I have mentioned are bodies as well: air is a body, this visible light is a body, and all those things are bodies which the Apostle calls “heavenly bodies” and “earthly bodies” (1 Cor. 15:40).

18. But whether the soul is something of this kind is a question requiring the most scrupulous and subtle investigation.
