Nevertheless, in this respect—something for which I especially congratulate you—you affirm that God is not a body. Yet you again make me uneasy when you say: “If the soul lacks a body, so that it is, as some think, a substance of empty nothingness, airy and insubstantial” [Note: [Col. 0534] Manuscripts: “an airy and insubstantial (or subtle) substance.”]. By these words of yours you seem to believe that everything which lacks a body is a substance of nothingness. If that is so, how dare you say that God lacks a body, and do you not fear that it will follow that He is a substance of nothingness? But if God also lacks a body, as you have already confessed, and if you would not dare to say that He is a substance of nothingness, then whatever lacks a body is not therefore a substance of nothingness.

Accordingly, when someone says that the soul is incorporeal, it does not follow that he wishes it to be regarded as a substance of emptiness and futility, since he also confesses that God, who is not something empty, is incorporeal. Observe, then, how great is the difference between what I say and what you suppose me to say. I do not call the soul an airy substance; otherwise I would confess that it is a body. Air is a body, according to all who know what they are talking about when they speak of bodies. But because I said that the soul is incorporeal, you thought that I had called it not merely a substance of empty nothingness but, for that reason, an airy substance. Yet I have said both that it is not a body—which air is—and that what is filled with air cannot be empty.

Not even your own wineskins could teach you otherwise. For what else is compressed within them when they are inflated except air? They are not so empty that, with the same fullness, they can even bear weights. If perhaps you think that breath is one thing and air another, although breath is simply air in motion—as can also be demonstrated by waving a fan—then take any hollow vessels which you think are empty and, to discover that they are full, push them into water from the side by which they are filled. You will see that no moisture can enter, because the air with which they are full repels it. But when they are placed with their mouths upward [Note: [Col. 0535] Several manuscripts: “with the mouth turned upward.”], or on their side, they receive liquid if any is poured or flows into them, because the air goes out and escapes through the opening.

This could be demonstrated more easily by an actual experiment than in writing. But there is no need to linger over it, since whether or not you understand that air is corporeal in nature, you must not suppose that I called the soul airy, but wholly incorporeal. You yourself confess that God is incorporeal; you do not dare to call Him something empty, yet you cannot deny that He is of an omnipotent and immutable substance [Note: [Col. 0535] Several manuscripts: “but it cannot be denied.”]. Why, then, do we fear that the soul is a substance of empty nothingness if it is incorporeal, when we confess that God is incorporeal and do not call Him a substance of empty nothingness? Thus the incorporeal One could create an incorporeal soul, just as the living One could create a living being, although the immutable created what is mutable and the omnipotent created what is vastly inferior to Himself.

## CHAPTER XIII

19. I do not see why you refuse to let the soul be a spirit, but wish it to be a body. If it is not a spirit because the Apostle distinctly named “spirit,” saying, “May your spirit and soul and body be preserved blameless” (1 Thess. 5:23), then for the same reason it is not a body, because he also distinctly named “body.” But if you maintain that the soul is a body, although he distinctly named the body, allow it also to be a spirit, although he distinctly named the spirit.

Indeed, the soul ought much more to seem to you to be a spirit than a body, because you admit that spirit and soul are of one substance, whereas you do not say that soul and body are of one substance. How, then, is the soul a body, when its nature is different from that of the body, and the soul is not a spirit, when its nature is one and the same as that of the spirit?

Moreover, by this reasoning you are compelled to say that the spirit too is a body. Otherwise, if the spirit is not a body while the soul is a body, spirit and soul are not of one and the same substance. Yet you confess that both, although you regard them as two things, possess one substance. Therefore the spirit too is a body, if the soul is a body; for otherwise they cannot be of one and the same nature.

Accordingly, in your view, when the Apostle says, “Your spirit and soul and body,” these are three bodies. Of these, two—the soul and the spirit—are bodies of one nature, while that body which is also called flesh is of another nature. And from these three bodies, as you suppose, of which one is of a different substance and two are of one and the same substance, the whole human being consists, one thing and one substance.

Yet while asserting these things, you do not want two things of one and the same substance—that is, soul and spirit—to have one name, the name spirit, although two things not of one and the same but of unequal and different substances—that is, soul and body—have one name, as you suppose, the name body.

## CHAPTER XIV

20. But I shall set this aside, lest our controversy be about names rather than things. Let us consider who the inner person is: the soul, or the spirit, or both. From what I see you have written, you call the inner person the soul. For it was of this that you were speaking when you said:

“And when the frozen substance, which could not be grasped, produced another body within the body, compacted by the power and breath of its own nature, then the inner person began to appear; the form of the bodily sheath enclosing him as though in a scabbard, while the structure of the outer person outlined him in its own likeness.”

Then you continue:

“Thus the breath of God made a mind; indeed, breath from God was made a soul, substantially fashioned, corporeal according to its nature, like its own body and conformed to its image.”

After this, beginning to speak of the spirit, you say:

“This soul, which originated from the breath of God, could not exist without its own sensation and inward understanding, which is the spirit.”

As I understand you, then, you want the inner person to be the soul and the innermost person to be the spirit—as though the spirit itself were interior to the soul in the way the soul is interior to the body. It follows that, just as the body receives within its interior hollows another body, which you suppose to be the soul, so the soul must also be believed to have interior empty spaces into which it received a third body, the spirit. Thus the whole human being consists of three: the outer, the inner, and the innermost.

Do you still not see how many utterly absurd consequences follow when you try to assert that the soul is corporeal? Tell me, then: which of these is renewed in the knowledge of God, according to the image of the one who created him (Col. 3:10)—the inner person or the innermost?

I do not see that the Apostle knows of any other inner person besides the inner and outer, that is, another inner person within the inner person, the innermost of the whole human being. But choose whichever you wish to be renewed according to the image of God. How will it receive this image if it has already taken on the image of the outer person?

For if the inner person flowed through the limbs of the outer person and froze—since you also used this word, as though a cast object were formed from a clay shape made out of dust—how can it be reformed according to the image of God while retaining the same form impressed or stamped upon it from the body?

Will it have two images, one from God above and the other from the body below, as it is said of a coin: “head and ship” [Note: [Col. 0536] In Ambrose, “ship,” erroneously “naiva.”] [Note: [Col. 0536] Macrobius helps explain this expression, *Saturnalia* 1.7, where, speaking of Janus, he writes: “When he first struck bronze coinage, he also preserved in this the reverence due to Saturn: since Saturn had been carried here by ship, on one side an image of his head was represented, and on the other a ship, so that the memory of Saturn might also be handed down to posterity. That bronze was so marked is understood even today in the game of chance, when boys toss coins into the air and call out ‘heads’ or ‘ship’ (here, it seems, one should read ‘head’ or ‘ship’), the game bearing witness to antiquity.” In our language, French: “Croix ou Pile” (“heads or tails”).]?

Or perhaps you will say that the soul received the image of the body, while the spirit receives the image of God—as though the soul were contiguous with the body and the spirit with God—and thus it is the innermost person, not the inner person, who is reformed according to the image of God.

But you say this to no purpose. For if that innermost person is spread through all the limbs of the soul in the same way that the soul is spread through the body, then it too has already received the image of the body through the soul, just as the soul’s form fashioned it. Therefore it has no place in which to receive the image of God while this image of the body remains in it—unless, as I said, it is formed like a coin, differently on its lower side and on its upper side.

When you think about the soul, carnal thinking about bodies drives you, whether you wish it or not, toward these absurdities. But God, as you yourself most rightly confess, is not a body. How, then, can a body receive His image?

I beg you, brother, do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewal of your mind (Rom. 12:2), and do not set your mind according to the flesh, for that is death (ibid. 8:6).

## CHAPTER XV

21. But you say: “If the soul lacks a body, what is it that the rich man recognizes in the underworld? Certainly,” you say, “he already knew Lazarus, but he did not know Abraham” [Note: [Col. 0537] The negative particle is absent from some manuscripts.] (Luke 16:19–31). “From where did recognition of Abraham, who had died so long before, come to him?”

In saying this, if you do not think that recognition of a person can arise without the form of a body, then, I suppose, you are constantly looking into a mirror, lest, if you forget your own face, you should be unable to recognize yourself. Tell me: whom does a person know more than himself, and whose face can he see less than his own?

And who can know God, whom you too do not doubt to be incorporeal, if knowledge cannot arise apart from bodily form, as you suppose—that is, if only bodies can be known?

What Christian, discussing matters so great and difficult, would attend so carelessly to the divine words as to say, “If the soul is incorporeal, it must lack form”? Have you forgotten that you have read of “the form of teaching” (Rom. 6:17)? Therefore the form of teaching is corporeal.

Have you forgotten that it is written of Christ Jesus, before He had put on humanity, that He was “in the form of God” (Phil. 2:6)? How, then, do you say, “If the soul is incorporeal, it must lack form,” when you hear of the form of God, whom you confess not to be corporeal, and speak as though form could exist only in bodies?

22. You also say: “Names cease there, where form is not distinguished, and the use of names does nothing there, where there is no designation of persons.” By this you wish to prove that Abraham’s soul was corporeal, because it could be called “Father Abraham.”

We have already said that form exists even where there is no body. But if you think that names do nothing where there are no bodies, then, I ask you, count these names:

“The fruit of the spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control” (Gal. 5:22–23).

Tell me whether you do not recognize the things whose names these are, or whether you recognize them in such a way that you see some outlines of bodies. To say nothing of the others, tell me what shape, what limbs, what color love has. Certainly, if you yourself are not empty, you cannot regard love as something empty.

“The one whose help was invoked,” you say, “was plainly seen and formed as a body.” Let people hear you, then, and let no one invoke God’s help, because no one can see Him as corporeal.

## CHAPTER XVI

23. “Finally,” you say, “the soul’s limbs are described there, so that it truly is a body.” You want “the whole head to be understood by the eye,” because it is said that he lifted up his eyes; “the throat by the tongue, and the hand by the finger,” because it is said: “Send Lazarus, so that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue.”

Yet, lest the names of limbs compel you to conceive God as corporeal, you say that “by these expressions incorporeal powers are to be understood,” because you rightly defend God as not corporeal. What, then, is the reason why these names of limbs do not make God a body for you, but do make the soul a body? Or are they to be understood literally when spoken of a creature, but figuratively and metaphorically when spoken of the Creator?

Then you will give us corporeal wings, since it is not the Creator but a creature, namely a human being, who says, “If I take up my wings like a dove” (Ps. 138:9).

Moreover, if the rich man had a corporeal tongue because he said, “Cool my tongue,” then in us too, while we are still living in the flesh, the tongue itself has corporeal hands, because it is written: “Death and life are in the hands of the tongue” (Prov. 18:21).

I suppose you do not think that sin is either a creature [Note: [Col. 0538] All our manuscripts read “in the Creator.”] or a body. Why, then, does it have a face? Do you not hear in the Psalm: “There is no peace in my bones because of the face of my sins” (Ps. 37:4)?

24. As for your opinion that “that bosom of Abraham” is corporeal, and your assertion that “through it his whole body is recognized,” I fear that in so great a matter you may be thought to be acting playfully and mockingly, not seriously and gravely. You would not be so foolish as to suppose that the corporeal bosom of one man could carry so many souls—or, to speak according to your own language, “carry as many bodies of the righteous as the angels carry there, as they carried Lazarus.”

Unless perhaps you think that only that one soul deserved to reach the same bosom. If you are not joking and do not wish to err in a childish manner, understand “the bosom of Abraham” as a remote and secluded place of rest where Abraham is. It was therefore called Abraham’s—not because it belongs to him alone, but because he was appointed the father of many nations (Gen. 17:4–5), set before them as the chief example of faith [Note: [Col. 0538] Printed editions: “the primacy of faith.” The manuscripts have been followed here.]. In the same way, God wished to be called the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob (Exod. 3:6), although He is the God of innumerable people.

## CHAPTER XVII

25. You should not suppose that I am arguing these points as though I denied that it is possible for the soul of a dead person to experience good or evil in the likeness of its body, just as a sleeping person does. For in dreams, when we undergo hardships and painful experiences, it is truly we who suffer; and unless such things pass away when we awaken, we pay very severe penalties.

But to believe that the things by which we are carried and borne here and there in dreams are bodies belongs to a person who has thought too carelessly about such matters. For it is precisely from these images of visions that the soul is especially shown not to be corporeal—unless you wish to call bodies also all the many things we see in dreams besides ourselves: heaven, earth, sea, sun, moon, stars, rivers, mountains, trees, and animals.

Anyone who believes these to be bodies is extraordinarily foolish. Yet they are entirely similar to bodies. Of this same kind are also those things which are divinely displayed as signifying something else, whether in dreams or in ecstasy. Who can investigate or explain where they come from—that is, what their supposed material may be? Nevertheless, there is no doubt that it is spiritual, not corporeal.

For such appearances, resembling bodies but not being bodies, are formed both by the thought of those who are awake and are held in the depths of memory. From its most hidden recesses they emerge, I do not know by what marvelous and ineffable manner, when we remember them, and they move about as though brought before our eyes.

If the soul were a body, it could not contain in thought or retain in memory so many and such great images of bodies. For according to your definition, “by its corporeal substance this outward body does not exceed its own limits.” By what magnitude, then—since it has no such magnitude—does it contain images of bodies and spaces and regions so vast?

What wonder is it, then, if the soul also appears to itself in the likeness of its body when it appears without the body? For it does not appear to itself with its body in dreams, yet in that very likeness of its body it moves through places both unknown and known, experiencing many things with joy or sorrow.

But I suppose that you would not dare to say that the bodily shape and limbs which the soul appears to have in dreams are a real body. For in that case the mountain which it seems to climb would be a real mountain; the house which it seems to enter would be a corporeal house; the tree and true wood possessing a true body beneath which it seems to lie would be real; the water which it seems to drink would be real; and everything in which it moves as though among bodies would be a body, if the soul itself, which moves amid all these things in a similar image, is also a body.

## CHAPTER XVIII

26. I must say something to you about the written visions of the martyrs, since you also thought that testimony should be drawn from them. Surely the holy Perpetua saw herself in a dream, changed into a man, wrestling with an Egyptian.

Who could doubt that in this likeness of a body it was her soul, not her body, which was present? Her body, remaining in its female sex, lay on a bed with its senses asleep, while her soul wrestled in that likeness of a male body.

What do you say? Was that likeness of a man a real body, or was it not a body, although it possessed the likeness of a body? Choose whichever you wish. If it was a body, why did it not retain the form of its sheath? For the female body of that woman had not acquired male genital organs from which it could be formed by contracting itself and, in your language, “freezing.”

Moreover, I beg you: while the body of the sleeping woman was still alive, when her soul was wrestling, it was in its sheath, enclosed in all the limbs of a living person, and it retained in that body the form from which it had been formed. It had not yet left those limbs, as happens in death; it had not yet drawn members formed from members away from the bodies that formed them by the force of death. From where, then, did the soul’s male body come, in which it seemed to itself to wrestle with its adversary?

But if it was not a body, although it was something similar to a body, in which genuine exertion or genuine joy was experienced, do you now at last see how it can happen that there is in the soul a certain likeness of a body without the soul itself being a body?

27. What if something of this kind occurs in the underworld, and souls recognize themselves there not in bodies but in likenesses of bodies? When we suffer sorrow, even in dreams, although the likeness of limbs is present, the limbs themselves are not corporeal. Yet the likeness is not the punishment—it is the punishment itself. The same is true wherever joyful sensations are experienced.

But since the holy Perpetua was not yet dead, perhaps you do not want this example to be decisive for you. Yet it bears greatly upon the matter what you consider to be the nature of those likenesses of bodies that we have in dreams; and the whole issue is settled if you confess that they are similar to bodies but are not bodies.

Nevertheless, her brother Dinocrates had died. She saw him with the wound that he had borne while alive, the wound by which he had been brought to death. Where is the point for which you labored so strenuously when discussing the severing of limbs, lest the soul also be thought to be cut apart at the same time?

Look: there was a wound in the soul of Dinocrates, and by its force it had expelled her from his body when she was in it. How, then, according to your opinion, when the limbs of the body are cut off, does the soul “withdraw from the blow and gather itself together by condensing into other parts, lest any part of it be amputated by the wound of the body,” even if something is cut from the limbs of a sleeping and unaware person?

You have attributed such vigilance to the soul that, even when occupied with dream-visions, if a blow should suddenly strike an unaware person and the flesh be struck, it promptly and prudently withdraws itself so that it cannot be struck, harmed, or cut apart. Yet, wise man, you do not notice that if the soul withdrew itself from the blow, the blow itself would not be felt.

Find, then, whatever answer you can give: explain how the soul snatches away its parts [Note: [Col. 0540] In Lovaniensis, “grasps” instead of “snatches away.”] and hides them inside, so that when a bodily limb is cut or struck, the soul too is not amputated and injured.

Look at Dinocrates, and explain why his soul did not withdraw from that place of the body which was being devastated by the deadly wound, so that what appeared in his face after the death of his body would not also occur in his soul. Or perhaps you now prefer that we believe these to be likenesses of bodies rather than bodies, so that, just as a wound appears which is not a wound, so what is not a body appears as though it were a body [Note: [Col. 0541] Several manuscripts: “or perhaps you already prefer.”]?

For if the soul can be wounded by those who wound the body, is there nothing to fear lest it can be killed by those who kill the body? The Lord most clearly testifies that this cannot happen (Matt. 10:28). Yet the soul of Dinocrates could not die, although his body died. It appeared as though wounded, just as his body had been wounded, because it was not a body but possessed, in the likeness of a body, also the likeness of a wound.

Moreover, in a body that was not real, there was real misery in the soul, signified by the shadowy wound of the body; from this misery it deserved to be freed through the prayers of his holy sister.

28. What is the point of saying that “the soul receives its form from the body and is extended and grows with the body’s growth,” without noticing how monstrous the soul of a young person or an old person would become if the arm of his infant body had been cut off?

“It contracts itself,” you say, “the hand of the soul, lest it too be amputated with the hand of the body, and it encloses itself by condensing into other parts of the body.” Accordingly, the soul’s arm will remain wherever it is preserved as short as was the bodily arm from which it received its form, because it lost the form by whose growth it could grow along with it.

Thus the soul of a young person or an old person who lost a hand while small emerges with two hands: one was not amputated with the body because it withdrew, but one is youthful or aged, while the other remains infantile, just as it was at first.

Believe me, such souls are not made by the form of the body; they are fabricated by the deformity of error. You will not seem able to escape this error unless, with God’s help, you carefully consider the visions of dreamers and recognize from them that there are things which are not bodies but likenesses of bodies.

For although the things we think about that resemble bodies also belong to this category, when the matter concerns the dead, a more appropriate inference is drawn from the sleeping. Holy Scripture does not call the dead “those who sleep” without reason (1 Thess. 4:12), unless it is because sleep is in some way akin to death’s sleep (Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.279).

## CHAPTER XIX

29. Therefore, if the soul were a body, and if the bodily figure in which it sees itself in dreams had been impressed from its body, no one whose bodily limb had been amputated would see himself in dreams without that limb, just as he lacks it in waking life. Rather, he would always see himself whole, because nothing of his soul had been amputated.

But when people sometimes see themselves whole and at other times see themselves mutilated in whatever part has been cut off, what else does this teach us except that the soul, just as it bears the likeness rather than the reality of other things perceived in dreams, also bears at one time this likeness and at another time that likeness of the body?

Its joy or sadness, pleasure or distress, is real, whether it exists in bodies or in likenesses of bodies.

Did you yourself not say—and say truly—“Food and clothing are not necessary for the soul but for the body”? Why, then, did the rich man in the underworld desire a drop of water? Why did the holy Samuel appear after death, as you yourself also mentioned, clothed in his customary garment (1 Sam. 28:14) [Note: [Col. 0541] Several manuscripts: “solid garment.”]?

Was he seeking to restore the ruins of his soul, as of flesh, by nourishment with moisture? Had Samuel come out of the body clothed? In the rich man there was real distress by which the soul was tormented, but not a real body for which he sought nourishment. Samuel could appear clothed in such a way that he was not a body but that both the soul and the clothing possessed the likeness of a body.

For the soul does not stretch itself out and contract itself into clothing as it does into the limbs of the body, so as to be formed from it.

30. What power of perception souls, even wicked ones, receive after death, when they have been released from corruptible bodies—whether they can behold and recognize, with their inward senses, souls equally wicked or even good, either in the non-bodies that are likenesses of bodies, or in the mind’s good or evil affections, in which there are no apparent outlines of limbs—who can investigate?

This is the source of the fact that, while suffering torment, the rich man recognized the father Abraham, whose bodily appearance was not known to him, although the soul, being incorporeal, could retain a likeness of his body [Note: [Col. 0542] Ambrose, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read “although incorporeal”; Lovaniensis reads “an incorporeal likeness.”].

Who could rightly say that he knew another person unless he knew, insofar as possible, that person’s life and will, which certainly have neither mass nor color? In this way we also know ourselves more certainly than we know others, because our conscience and will are known to us. We plainly see them, yet we do not see in them any likeness of a body.

We do not perceive this in another person, even when he is present, although we know, recall, and contemplate the face of someone absent. But we cannot know, recall, or contemplate our own face in the same way. Nevertheless, we rightly say that we know ourselves more truly than we know that other person. Thus it is clear where the superior and truer knowledge of a person lies.

## CHAPTER XX

31. Since, then, there is one faculty in the soul by which we perceive real bodies through the five bodily senses; another by which, apart from those senses, we see things that are not bodies but resemble bodies, where we also behold ourselves as nothing other than similar to bodies; and another by which we perceive with greater certainty and firmness things that are neither bodies nor likenesses of bodies—such as faith, hope, and love, without any colors, bulges, or likenesses of them—where ought we more properly to exist and, in a certain manner, dwell? Where ought we to be renewed in the knowledge of God according to the image of the one who created us? Is it not in that which I placed third?

There, certainly, we possess neither any sex nor any likeness of sex.

32. For if that form of a male or female soul, distinguished by male or female limbs, is not a likeness of a body but a body, then, whether you wish it or not, whatever appears as male is male, and whatever appears as female is female.

But if, according to your opinion, the soul is both a body and a living body, and it has prominent and hanging breasts, and no beard, and a womb and genital organs such as the limbs of a female body possess, yet is not female, should I not state with greater confidence what is true: “It has an eye, a tongue, a finger, and the other limbs resembling those of a body, and all of this is a likeness of a body, not a body”?

Each person can prove this for himself when imagining the bodies of absent people. He can certainly prove it when recalling both his own shapes and those of others in dreams.

But you cannot produce from the whole order of nature any example of this monstrosity: that there is a real, living, female body, yet no female sex.

For what you say about the phoenix has absolutely no bearing on the matter under discussion. The phoenix signifies the resurrection of bodies; it does not abolish the sex of souls—if, as is believed, it is reborn from its own death.

But I suppose you thought your speech would have little power to win applause if you did not declaim at length about the phoenix in the manner of adolescents. Are there male genital organs in its body while it is not male, or female organs while it is not female?

You, however, should attend to what you are saying, what you are trying to establish and persuade us of. You say that the soul, spread through all the limbs, became rigid by freezing, and that from the crown of the head to the soles of the feet, from the innermost marrow to the surface of the skin, it received the form of the whole body in its entirety.

Accordingly, in a female body it received whatever female organs women possess; this body is real, and these limbs are real, yet it is not female. Why, I ask you, in a real and living body are all the limbs female, yet it is not female? In a real and living body are all the limbs male, yet it is not male? Who would dare to believe, say, or teach such things?

Is it because souls do not beget? Then mules and female mules are neither male nor female. Or is it because souls cannot have intercourse without bodily flesh? But this is also taken away from those who are castrated. Yet when both the act and the movement are removed from them, their sex is not removed, so long as however small a figure of the male limbs remains. No one has ever denied that a eunuch is male.

Moreover, according to your view, the souls of eunuchs still possess their testicles intact. And if someone’s genital organs are completely removed, they will remain wholly and entirely intact in his soul, according to your opinion.

For, as you say, the soul knows how to withdraw when that part of the flesh begins to be cut away, so that the form taken from it, when the thing from which it was taken is amputated, does not perish. Instead, although it had congealed while diffused through the body, it is seized by swift motion and hidden inside, so that it may be preserved intact.

Yet, in the underworld, he is not male, although he carries with him all the male genital organs—he who, when he did not have them in his body, was male solely because of the place where they were located.

These things are false, my son. If you do not want sex to exist in the soul, then neither should the soul be a body.

## CHAPTER XXI

34. Not every likeness of a body is a body. Sleep, and you will see; but when you awaken, distinguish vigilantly what you saw.

In dreams you will appear to yourself as though corporeal. Yet it will not be your body, but your soul; not a real body, but a likeness of a body.

Your body will lie still, while your soul walks. The tongue of your body will be silent, while the soul speaks. Your eyes will be closed, while the soul sees. And certainly the limbs of your body will be alive as they lie there, not dead.

Therefore the form of your soul has not yet been drawn out, as you suppose, frozen as though from its sheath; yet within it the likeness of your flesh is seen whole and intact.

Of this kind are all the likenesses of bodies which, as you read the holy books, you fail to understand in the prophetic visions—likenesses by which events are signified that occur in the present, the past, or the future.

You are deceived in these matters not because the visions themselves are deceptive, but because you do not receive them as they ought to be received. For when the souls of the martyrs were seen (Rev. 6:9), in the same revelation a lamb also was seen “as though slain,” having seven horns (ibid. 5:6). There were horses and other animals, figured as was appropriate. Finally, the stars fell and the heaven was rolled up like a scroll (ibid. 6 and 9), yet the world did not then collapse.

If we understand all these things wisely, we may call the visions truthful, but we do not therefore call the bodies real.

35. A more extended discussion would be required for a very careful treatment of this class of bodily likenesses: whether angels, good or evil, appear in this way when they appear in the form of human beings or of any bodies; or whether they possess some real bodies and are seen in the reality of those bodies; or whether, in dreams or ecstasy, they are seen in these likenesses, not in bodies, while to those who are awake they present real bodies to be seen and, if necessary, touched.

But I do not think that these matters should be sought out and treated in this book.

For now, let what has been said about the soul’s incorporeality suffice. Before you prefer to believe it corporeal, you must first define what a body is, lest, although we agree with one another about the thing itself, we labor in vain over the name.

Nevertheless, I think you can now prudently recognize how many absurdities follow when you conceive of such a body in the soul as is called a body by all educated people: namely, something which, through the intervals of length, breadth, and height, occupies regions of space, smaller regions through its smaller parts and larger regions through its larger parts.

## CHAPTER XXII
36. It remains to show how, although “spirit” is also properly said of not the whole soul but of a part of it, as the Apostle says, “And may your whole spirit and soul and body” (1 Thess. 5:23); or, much more explicitly, in the Book of Job, “You have loosed my soul from my spirit” (Job 7, according to the Septuagint)—nevertheless the whole soul is also called by this name. Yet this question seems much more a matter of names than of realities. For since it is established that there is something in the soul properly called “spirit,” apart from which the soul itself is properly so called, there is no longer any dispute about the realities themselves—especially since I too say that what you say is properly called spirit, namely, that by which we reason and understand, when these terms are distinguished in the manner in which the Apostle says, “And may your whole spirit and soul and body” [Col. 0545]. He also appears to call this spirit “mind” when he says, “With the mind I serve the law of God, but with the flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7:25). For the meaning is, “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17): so that what he calls “mind” there is understood here as “spirit.” It is not as you suppose, that “the whole mind is called [mind], which consists of soul and spirit”—where you have read this, I do not know. For we ordinarily call our mind nothing other than our rational and intellectual faculty. Accordingly, when the same Apostle says, “But be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. 4:23), what else does he say than, “Be renewed in your mind”? For “the spirit of the mind” is nothing other than the mind, just as “the body of the flesh” can be nothing other than flesh. This too is written: “In the stripping off of the body of the flesh” (Col. 2:11), where he calls flesh “the body of the flesh.”

He does, however, also speak in another way of “the spirit of man,” which he entirely distinguishes from the mind: “For if I pray in a tongue,” he says, “my spirit prays, but my mind is unfruitful” (1 Cor. 14:14). But we are not now speaking of this spirit, which is distinct from the mind. It has its own, and likewise difficult, question: for Scripture calls “spirit” by many names and with various meanings. But concerning the spirit with which we reason, understand, and exercise wisdom, we agree that it too is properly called spirit, though it is not the whole soul but something belonging to it.

Yet if you deny that the soul is also spirit because its understanding is distinctly called spirit [Col. 0546], you could equally deny that the whole seed of Jacob is called Israel, since, apart from Judah, the ten tribes that were then in Samaria were also distinctly called Israel (3 Kings 12:28). But why linger over this any longer?

**CHAPTER XXIII**

37. Now attend to how we can more readily show that what is soul is also called spirit, when you hear or read what is written of the Lord at his death: “And, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit” (John 19:30). You want this understood as though the whole were signified by a part, rather than as showing that what is soul can also be called spirit. But, to prove my point more efficiently, I shall call upon you yourself as a witness, and do so promptly and conveniently.

For you defined “spirit” in such a way that animals appear not to possess spirit but soul. They are called irrational because they lack the power of understanding and reason. Thus, when you urged human beings to recognize their own nature, you spoke as follows: “For since the good God created nothing without reason, and brought forth man himself as a rational animal, capable of understanding, endowed with reason, and quick in sensation—one who by prudent ordering distributes all things devoid of reason.”

By these words of yours you sufficiently affirmed what is altogether true: that man possesses reason and is capable of understanding—qualities that animals devoid of reason certainly do not possess. Hence, on divine testimony, you compared those who do not understand to beasts, which plainly do not possess understanding (Ps. 48:13). Elsewhere too it is written: “Do not be like a horse and a mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 32:9).

Since this is so, consider also the words with which you defined and described spirit when you attempted to distinguish it from soul. “This soul,” you say, “which has its origin from the breath of God, could not exist without its own sensation and inward understanding; and this is spirit.” A little later you say: “Although the soul gives life to the body, nevertheless that which senses, understands, and is vigorous must be spirit.” Again, shortly afterward: “The soul will be one thing, and spirit another—wisdom and sensation belonging to the soul.”

By these words you clearly indicate what you take the human spirit to be: namely, our rational faculty, by which the soul senses and understands—not as something is sensed by bodily senses, but as that inward sense from which the term “judgment” (*sententia*) derives. [Note: [Col. 0546] Thus Amerbach and the manuscripts; Erasmus and the Louvain editors read, “senses.”] By this we are unquestionably superior to beasts, since they are devoid of reason. Beasts therefore do not have spirit—that is, understanding and the sense of reason and wisdom—but only soul.

For it was said of them: “Let the waters bring forth moving creatures having living souls”; and, “Let the earth bring forth a living soul” (Gen. 1:20, 24). Thus, to make you know most fully and plainly that what is soul is also called spirit according to the manner of divine utterances, a beast’s spirit is so called. [Note: [Col. 0546] The manuscripts read: “Therefore also [those] in which there is soul.”] Yet beasts certainly do not possess the spirit which your Affection, distinguishing it from soul, defined. It is therefore clear that, as a general term, the soul of a beast could rightly be called spirit, just as we read in Ecclesiastes: “Who knows whether the spirit of the sons of men goes upward, and whether the spirit of the beast goes downward into the earth?” (Eccl. 3:21).

Likewise, in the account of the Flood it is written: “And all flesh that moved upon the earth died—birds, cattle, beasts, and every creeping thing that creeps upon the earth, and every human being, and everything that has the spirit of life” (Gen. 7:21–22). Here, with every ambiguity and evasion removed, we understand “spirit” to be a general name for soul.

The meaning of this name extends so widely that even God is called spirit: “God is spirit” (John 4:24). And this aerial breath, although corporeal, is called in the Psalm “the spirit of the storm” (Ps. 55:9).

Therefore, I think that, having been reminded by these testimonies from the divine Scriptures—which even record that the soul of a beast, which has no understanding, is called spirit—you will no longer deny that what is soul is also called spirit.

Consequently, if you both grasp and understand what has been argued concerning the incorporeal nature of the soul, there is no reason for you to be displeased with my saying that I know it to be not a body but spirit: for it is shown not to be a body, and by a general name it is called spirit.

**CHAPTER XXIV**

38. Therefore, if you receive and read these books [Col. 0547], written for you with devoted affection, with affection in return; if, at the beginning of your first book, you heed both yourself and your own resolve, as you said—“not to defend your opinion if it is shown to be untenable” (above, Book 2, no. 22)—then especially beware of the eleven points about which I warned you in the preceding book (above, Book 3, nos. 22–23).

Beware of saying:

- “that the soul is from God in such a way that he created it neither from nothing nor from another substance, but from his own nature”;
- “that he has given souls throughout infinite time, and therefore always gives them, just as he himself is always the one who gives”;
- “that the soul lost through the flesh some merit which it possessed before the flesh”;
- “that through the flesh the soul recovers its former condition, and through that very flesh is reborn through which it had deserved to be defiled”;
- “that the soul deserved to be sinful before every sin”;
- “that infants who die without the regeneration of Baptism attain forgiveness of original sins” [Note: Several manuscripts read, “who die without the regeneration of Baptism.”];
- “that some whom the Lord predestined to Baptism can be snatched away from his predestination and die before what the Almighty predestined can be fulfilled in them” [Note: The manuscripts omit “can be snatched away from his predestination”; instead they read, “can die beforehand, and that in them what the Almighty …”];
- “that concerning those who expire before being baptized it was said in the passage, ‘He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding’” (Wis. 4:11), together with the other claims pertaining to this interpretation;
- “that some dwelling places are outside the kingdom of God, whereas the Lord said that there are many dwelling places in his Father’s house” (John 14:2);
- “that the sacrifice of Christ’s body and blood should be offered for those who have died unbaptized”;
- “that some of those who die without Christ’s Baptism are meanwhile received into paradise and afterward attain the blessedness of the kingdom of heaven.”

Beware of these things especially, my son; and do not take pleasure in being called Vincentius if you wish to be victorious over error. Nor, when you do not know something, should you suppose that you know it; rather, if you wish to know, learn to acknowledge ignorance. For sin does not lie in being ignorant of the hidden works of God, but in rashly asserting the unknown as known and presenting and defending falsehoods as truths.

As for my own ignorance [Col. 0548]—whether human souls are newly made or come from their parents (although it is not permissible to doubt that, in either case, they are not made from the substance of God the Creator); whether I ought not to be reproved for this ignorance or ought to have it removed by one who can teach me; whether souls possess incorporeal likenesses of bodies, while the souls themselves are not bodies; and whether, while preserving the distinction between soul and spirit, the soul may also universally be called spirit—I think I have persuaded your Affection of these points. But if I have not persuaded you, those who read will judge whether I have nevertheless said what ought to have persuaded you [Note: Thus two manuscripts. The printed editions read, “what I ought to have persuaded.”].

39. If you should perhaps wish to know other matters—of which there are many that seem to me to require correction in your books—do not find it burdensome to come to me, not as a pupil to a teacher, but as a young man to an old man, as a strong man to one who is weak. For although you ought not to have published those books, a person who is corrected and reproved by his own confession possesses a greater and truer glory than one who is praised by the mouth of any person in error.

Yet when your books were read aloud, I do not believe that all your listeners and praisers had previously held, or agreed with you in, everything that sound doctrine rejects. Rather, their minds may have been swept along and struck by the force and rapid flow of your recitation, so that they paid too little attention to these matters; or, at any rate, even those who were able to notice them may have praised in you not the clearest truth of the matters themselves, but the abundance of your words and the power and natural aptitude of your talent. Eloquence is often praised, proclaimed, and loved in a young man who gives promise, even though he does not yet possess the maturity and reliability of a teacher [Note: [Col. 0548] The manuscripts read, “for the most part it is proclaimed,” omitting “praised.”].

Therefore, if you wish both to think rightly yourself and for what you say to be capable not merely of delighting others but also of building them up, you ought to take care with your words, putting aside the applause of others.

# [AGAINST TWO LETTERS OF THE PELAGIANS]

[Col. 0547]

## NOTICE ON THE WORK AGAINST TWO LETTERS OF THE PELAGIANS

While Boniface was governing the Roman Church after Zosimus, two letters of the Pelagians, which were being circulated secretly throughout Italy, were discovered through the vigilance of certain Catholics and brought to Pope Boniface. Julianus was said to have sent one of them to Rome. The other was sent to Thessalonica, under a common name, to Rufus, bishop of that place, by eighteen men who presented themselves as bishops—namely, Julianus himself, and perhaps Florus, Orontius, and the others from among the Pelagians mentioned at the Synod of Ephesus—so as to test the bishop of that place by their cunning and, if possible, bring him over to their party.

Boniface arranged for both letters to be sent to Augustine through Bishop Alypius. Alypius returned from Italy to Africa toward the end of the year 419, bringing back with him not only those letters but also certain excerpts from Julianus’s books, which Count Valerius had sent to him. Against these excerpts Augustine composed a second book, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, probably in the year 420; and, unquestionably around the same time, he produced four books against the two letters of the Pelagians, dedicated to Pope Boniface. He subsequently placed these books in the series of the *Retractions*, immediately after the works composed in the year 420.

When Alypius sailed to Italy again, the same books were carried to Boniface. For Julianus says of them in Book 1, chapter 85, of the *Unfinished Work*: “As in these books which you have now sent through Alypius to Boniface.” In Book 2, chapter 178, he also writes concerning them: “For this is so abominable that, when it had been charged against you by us in the letter which we sent to the East, you attempt in these books, which you recently sent to Boniface, to ward it off from yourself by denying it.”

As for the letter said to have been sent to Rome by Julianus, whose words Augustine quoted in Book 2, no. 2, of *On Marriage and Concupiscence—*“They also say that the marriages now being contracted were not instituted by God, as is read in Augustine’s book, against whom I have now replied in four books”—Julianus denies in Book 1, chapter 18, of the *Unfinished Work* that it was his. “He also mentions,” he says, “a letter which he claims was sent by me to Rome; but from the words he has quoted we have been unable to recognize what writing he is speaking about. For I sent two letters to Zosimus, formerly bishop of that city, concerning these questions, but at a time when I had not yet begun to write books.”

Augustine replies: “This letter is not to Zosimus”—that is, it was not written to him by name—“but to mislead those who in Rome might be misled by such persuasion. But if you do not recognize it, then let it not be yours.” We suspect that Julianus seized upon these words as an opportunity for concealment: “as is read in Augustine’s book, against whom,” and so forth. Perhaps someone later noted these words in the margin, and another person transferred them from there into the text of the letter.

In the first book of the work that follows, Augustine replies to the letter reportedly sent by Julianus to Rome.

In the second book and those that follow, he examines the other letter of the Pelagians to Rufus of Thessalonica. First he shows that Catholics, when they reject the Pelagians, do not thereby fall into Manichaeism. He refutes the charge of prevarication brought against the Roman clergy concerning the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius under Zosimus. He demonstrates that Catholics neither assert fate under the name of grace nor attribute partiality to God.

In the third book he explains, against the Pelagian heresy, what Catholics truly say concerning the usefulness of the Law; what they teach concerning the effect and power of Baptism; what they say about the difference between the two Testaments; what they profess concerning the righteousness and perfection of the Prophets and Apostles; what they say concerning the application of the term “sin” to Christ; and, finally, what they profess concerning the fulfillment of the commandments in the life to come.

In the fourth book, finally, he exposes the snares hidden in the remaining part of the second letter of the Pelagians, in five chapters of their teaching: praise of creation, praise of marriage, praise of the Law, praise of free will, and praise of the saints. Toward the end of the book he produces testimonies from Cyprian and Ambrose in support of the Catholic faith: some concerning original sin, others concerning the assistance of grace, and the final ones concerning the imperfection of present righteousness.

[Col. 0549]

[Note: For the subsequent books, see Book 2, chapter 61, of the *Retractions*, vol. 1, col. 655, from the words “The four books that follow” up to the words “while proclaiming the most celebrated.” M.]

# THE FOUR BOOKS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, AGAINST TWO LETTERS OF THE PELAGIANS, TO BONIFACE, BISHOP OF THE ROMAN CHURCH

[Note: Written in the year 420 or shortly afterward.]

[Note: The four books *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians* were collated with two Vatican manuscript copies and three Gallican ones: one from the abbey of Bec, another from the abbey of Saint Peter at Pratellis, and a third from the abbey of Saint Michael of the Mount in Peril of the Sea; and with the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and the Louvain editors.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions* and *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.]

(C)

## BOOK ONE

Augustine replies to the letter reportedly sent by Julianus to Rome. First he vindicates Catholic doctrine from Julianus’s accusations; then he exposes and refutes the heretical Pelagian meaning concealed in the profession of faith that the author of the letter set against the Catholics.

### CHAPTER I

1. He begins with the preeminence of the Roman episcopate. “I had already known you from the most celebrated report that proclaimed you, and through very frequent and entirely reliable messengers I had learned how full you were of the grace of God, most blessed and venerable Pope Boniface. But after my brother Alypius had also seen you in person, and, received by you with the greatest kindness and sincerity [Col. 0550], had exchanged conversations with you as mutual affection dictated; after living with you, and though for only a short time being joined to you by great affection, he poured both himself and me into your heart, and brought you back to me in his own person—my knowledge of your Holiness became all the greater as our friendship became more certain [Col. 0551].

“For you do not disdain—though you do not set your mind on lofty things, even while presiding from a higher height—to be the friend of the lowly and to return devoted love. For what else is friendship, which derives its name from love and is faithful nowhere except in Christ, in whom alone it can also be eternal and blessed? Therefore, having received you through that brother by whom I came to know you more intimately, I have ventured with greater confidence to write something to Your Beatitude concerning matters which at this time, if there is any episcopal care in us, urge us with a fresh stimulus to vigilance for the Lord’s flock [Note: The Gallican manuscripts read, “if there is any vigilance in us.”].”

2. “For although these new heretics, enemies of the grace of God which is given to the small and the great through Jesus Christ our Lord, are now shown more clearly to be avoided by a more open condemnation [Note: In the same manuscripts, ‘by more evident wickedness.’], they nevertheless do not cease to attack through their writings the hearts of those who are less cautious or less learned. They would have to be answered even if we did not fear that they might deceive some Catholics by plausible speech, so that neither they nor their followers would be confirmed in that wicked error.

“But since they do not cease to rage around the folds of the Lord’s flock and to search everywhere for entrances by which they may plunder sheep purchased at so great a price, and since the watchtower of pastoral responsibility is common to all of us who discharge the office of bishop—although you preside over it at a loftier height—I do what I can in my small share of the office, as much as the Lord deigns to grant me with the help of your prayers: I set before those pestilential and treacherous writings writings that may heal and protect, so that either the fury with which they rage may itself be cured or it may be prevented from harming others [Note: Erasmus and the Louvain editors read, “although you preside over the higher watchtower of pastoral responsibility.” The older edition of Amerbach and the Gallican and Vatican manuscripts more correctly read, “although you preside over it at a loftier height, the watchtower of pastoral responsibility.”].”

3. “These replies of mine to their two letters—one, namely, which Julianus is said to have sent to Rome, I suppose so that through it he might either find or make as many of his followers as he could; and the other, which eighteen men presenting themselves as bishops, participants in his error, ventured to write from Thessalonica, not to just anyone but to the bishop of that place, whom by their cunning they sought to test and, if possible, bring over to their party—I have decided to direct above all to Your Holiness. I offer them not so much for learning as for examination, and, wherever something perhaps displeases you, for correction.

“For my brother informed me that you yourself deigned to give him the letters, which could not have come into your hands except through the most vigilant diligence of our brothers, your sons. I give thanks for your most sincere goodwill toward us, because you did not wish the letters of the enemies of God’s grace to remain hidden from me—letters in which you found my name expressed with malicious and evident misrepresentation.

“But I hope in the Lord our God that, not without the reward which is in heaven, they tear me with a slanderous tooth—those against whom I set myself on behalf of the little ones, so that they may not be left lost to Pelagius, their deceitful praiser, but may be offered for liberation to Christ, the truthful Savior.”

### CHAPTER II

4. He attacks Julianus for asserting that free will perished through Adam’s sin. “Let us now answer Julianus’s letter. ‘Those Manichaeans,’ he says, ‘with whom we now have no fellowship—that is, all those with whom we disagree—say that through the sin of the first man, Adam, free will perished, and that no one now has the power to live well, but that all are compelled to sin by the necessity of their flesh.’”

He calls Catholics Manichaeans, following the example of Jovinianus, who a few years earlier, as a new heretic, destroyed the virginity of holy Mary and equated the sacred virginity with the marriages of the faithful. He made this accusation against Catholics for no other reason than that he wished them to appear to be accusers or condemnators of marriage.

5. Yet, in defending free will, they rush headlong into such a position that people rely on it for doing righteousness rather than on the Lord’s assistance, and so each person glories in himself rather than in the Lord (1 Cor. 1:31).

But who among us says that free will perished from the human race through the sin of the first man? Freedom certainly perished through sin, but it was the freedom that existed in paradise: the possession of complete righteousness together with immortality. For this reason human nature needs divine grace, as the Lord says: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36)—free, of course, to live well and righteously.

So far from free will having perished in the sinner is it that sinners sin through it [Col. 0552]. Indeed, it is especially evident in all who sin with pleasure and love of sin: what pleases them is what they desire [Note: Erasmus and the Louvain editors read, “what pleases them.” Amerbach and the manuscripts read, “what they desire.” Augustine customarily joins this verb with the accusative.].

Hence the Apostle says: “When you were servants of sin, you were free in regard to righteousness.” Thus they are shown to have been able to serve sin only through another kind of freedom. They are therefore free from righteousness only by the choice of their will; but they become free from sin only through the grace of the Savior.

For this reason the admirable Teacher carefully distinguished the very words: “When you were servants of sin,” he says, “you were free in regard to righteousness. What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed? For the end of those things is death. But now, having been freed from sin and made servants of God, you have your fruit in sanctification, and the end is eternal life” (Rom. 6:20–22).

He called them free in regard to righteousness, not freed from righteousness; but he did not call them free from sin, lest they attribute this to themselves. Instead, with the greatest care he preferred to say “freed,” referring this to the Lord’s statement: “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free.”

Since, then, the sons of men do not live well unless they have been made sons of God [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “men” instead of “sons of men.”], what is this man trying to attribute to free will—the power to live well—when this power is given only by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom. 7:25)? The Gospel says: “But to all who received him, he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12).

### CHAPTER III

6. Grace is not given according to merits. But perhaps they will say that people were assisted so that they might have the power to become sons of God, while they first deserved to receive this power by receiving him through free will, without any assistance of grace. This is indeed the intention [Col. 0553] with which they strive to destroy grace: they contend that it is given according to our merits.

Therefore, lest they divide this Gospel statement in such a way as to place merit in the words “All who received him,” and then claim that grace was not given freely but was repaid to this merit in the words that follow—“He gave them power to become children of God”—if they are asked what it means to have received him, will they answer anything other than, “They believed in him”?

To make them understand that this too belongs to grace, let them read what the Apostle says: “In no way be frightened by your adversaries. This is for them a sign of destruction, but for you of salvation—and this is from God; for it has been granted to you for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Phil. 1:28–29). Surely he said that both things had been granted.

Likewise, he says: “Peace to the brethren, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Eph. 6:23). Let them also read what the Lord himself says: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.” And lest anyone suppose that “come to me” means something other than “believe in me,” shortly afterward, when he was speaking about his body and blood, and many were scandalized by his discourse, he said: “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. But there are some among you who do not believe.”

Then the Evangelist added: “For Jesus knew from the beginning who were believers and who would betray him,” and he said, “That is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been granted him by my Father” (John 6:44, 64–66).

He repeated the statement in which he had said, “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.” And he showed that he had said this concerning believers and unbelievers by explaining what he had meant by “unless the Father who sent me draws him”: he repeated the same thing in other words, saying, “unless it has been granted him by my Father.”

That person is drawn to Christ to whom it is granted to believe in Christ. Therefore the power to become children of God is given to those who believe in him, since the very act of believing in him is given. If this power is not given by God, it cannot arise from free will, because that will cannot be free for good which the Liberator has not liberated. But in evil the will has free choice, when either a hidden or manifest deceiver has implanted in it a delight in wickedness, or it has persuaded itself of this.

7. Therefore, contrary to what some say that we claim—and what this man additionally dares to write—not everyone is compelled to sin against his will, as though by the necessity of the flesh. Rather, if they have reached an age at which they use the judgment of their own mind, they remain in sin by their own will and plunge by their own will from sin into sin.

For even the one who persuades and deceives them acts in them only so that they may commit sin willingly—whether through ignorance of the truth, through delight in iniquity, or through both evils, blindness and weakness.

But this will, which is free in evil because it delights in evil, is not free in good because it has not been liberated. Nor can a human being will anything good unless assisted by him who cannot will evil—that is, by the grace of God through Jesus Christ [Col. 0554] our Lord.

“For whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23). Accordingly, the good will that withdraws itself from sin is a believing will, because “the righteous lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4). Believing in Christ belongs to faith. And no one can believe in him—that is [Note: The Vatican manuscripts read, “that is, come.”], come to him—unless it has been granted to him.

No one, therefore, can possess a righteous will unless he has received true grace from above, that is, grace freely given, without preceding merits.

### CHAPTER IV

8. The Pelagians, precipitators of free will. These men do not want this because they are arrogant and proud—not defenders who cleanse free will, but precipitators who, by exalting it, cast it down to destruction. They are indignant at our saying these things for no other reason than that they disdain to glory in the Lord.

Yet Pelagius feared the judgment of the Palestinian bishops. When it was charged against him that he taught that the grace of God is given according to our merits, he denied that he taught this and condemned by an anathema those who did teach it [Note: See above, the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 30.].

Nevertheless, he is found defending nothing else in the books he wrote afterward. He seems to have thought that he had deceived human judges by lying, or somehow concealed his meaning beneath ambiguous words [Note: The Gallican codices read, “that he had done this to human beings,” omitting “judges.”].

### CHAPTER V

9. Julianus’s second accusation: that it is said that marriage was not instituted by God. His third accusation: that sexual intercourse within marriage is condemned. But let us now examine what follows.

“They also say,” he writes, “that the marriages now being contracted were not instituted by God, as is read in Augustine’s book, against whom I have now replied in four little books. Our enemies have adopted Augustine’s statements out of hatred for the truth.”

I see that these most slanderous words of his require a brief answer, because he repeats the same charges later, where he wishes to insinuate as though our opponents say something against us. There, with God’s help, we shall contend with him as the matter appears to require [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “where he wishes to insinuate what they say against our position. There we shall contend with him.”].

For now I answer that marriage was instituted by God, both when it was said, “Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24), and now, because it is written, “A wife is joined to a man by the Lord” (Prov. 19:14).

Even now, nothing else occurs than that a man clings to his wife and the two become one flesh. Indeed, concerning the marriages that are now contracted, the Lord was consulted by the Jews as to whether it was lawful to dismiss one’s wife for any reason. After recalling this testimony of the Law, he added: “Therefore what God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:3–6).

The Apostle Paul also employed this testimony of the Law when he instructed husbands to love their wives (Eph. 5:25, 51). Therefore, far be it from me to have written anything in my book contrary to these divine testimonies. But either through failing to understand, or rather through slander, this man attempts to twist what he read into another meaning [Col. 0555].

The book of mine to which he refers, against which he says he replied in four little books, was written after the condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius. I thought this should be stated because he says that my statements were accepted by his enemies out of hatred for the truth, lest anyone therefore suppose that the enemies of Christ’s grace were condemned as new heretics because of this book of mine.

In that book there is a defense of marriage rather than a condemnation of it.

10. “They also say,” he writes, “that the movement of the genitals and the intercourse of spouses was invented by the devil; and therefore that those who are born innocent [Note: The Gallican manuscripts here and below, in no. 11, read, “those who are born innocently”] are guilty; and that this is done by the devil, not by God, because they are born from this diabolical intercourse. But this is unambiguously Manichaean.”

Rather, just as we say that marriage was instituted by God for the orderly generation of children, so we say that the sowing of offspring could not have occurred, even in paradise, if children were to be begotten there, without the movement of the genitals and without the intercourse of spouses.

But the question is whether their movement and intercourse would have been such as it now is with shameful lust, if no one had sinned. We shall discuss this more carefully later, if God wills.

### CHAPTER VI

11. The Pelagians’ plan in praising the innocence of marital intercourse. What these men want, what they have in mind, and where they are trying to lead the matter are made clear by the words that follow. He says that we claim “therefore that those who are born innocent are guilty, and that this is done by the devil, not by God, because they are born from this diabolical intercourse.”

We do not call the intercourse of spouses diabolical—especially that of the faithful, which occurs for the sake of generating children who are afterward to be regenerated. Nor do we say that any human beings are made by the devil, but by God, insofar as they are human beings.

Yet we do say that even children born from faithful spouses are born guilty, like a wild olive from an olive tree, because of original sin; and that for this reason they are under the devil unless they are reborn in Christ, since the devil is the author of guilt, not of nature.

But when they say that little children do not carry any original sin and therefore are not under the devil, what are they striving to accomplish except to empty out that grace of God in little children by which he has rescued us, as the Apostle says, “from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Col. 1:13)?

For they deny that little children are under the power of darkness even before the assistance of the Lord their Liberator. Thus, while praising the work of the Creator in them, they destroy the mercy of the Redeemer.

Because we confess this mercy both in adults and in little children, he says that this “is unambiguously Manichaean,” although it is the most ancient Catholic teaching by which their new heretical doctrine is overthrown.

### CHAPTER VII
### 12. The fourth calumny: that the saints of the Old Testament are said not to have been free from sins

“He says,” he reports, “that the saints in the Old Testament were not without sins—that is, that they were not freed from crimes through amendment, but were found in guilt, subject to death.”

On the contrary, we say that before the Law, or during the time of the Old Testament, they were freed from sins—not by their own strength, because “cursed is everyone who places his hope in man” (Jeremiah 17:5) [Col. 0556; the printed editions alone read “of the cursed” (*maledicti*), less well]. Without doubt, those whom the divine Psalm also censures are under this curse: “Those who trust in their own strength” (Psalm 48:7). Nor were they freed by the Old Testament, “which generates slavery” (Galatians 4:24), although it was divinely given as part of a definite dispensation; nor by the holy, just, and good Law itself (Romans 7:12), in which it is written, “You shall not covet” (Exodus 20:17), since the Law was not given with power to give life, but was established because of transgression until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made (Galatians 3:21, 19). Rather, they were freed through the blood of that Redeemer who is “the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

But these enemies of God’s grace—which has been given to the small and the great through Jesus Christ our Lord—say that the ancient people of God possessed perfect righteousness, so that they will not be thought to have needed Christ’s incarnation, passion, and resurrection, through faith in which they were saved.

[Textual notes, Col. 0556: Erasmus and Lovanius wrongly insert *in* (“in”) after “nor by”; the manuscripts read as translated. The manuscripts read “he makes this accusation” (*iste … calumniatur*), while the printed editions have the plural, “they make this accusation.” All books then continue, “because they maintain,” which refers to the Pelagians whose cause Julian was advancing by calumny; Augustine quotes Pelagius’s words on this matter in *On the Grace of Christ*, §43. “Thus” may perhaps be read “then” (*inde*). The printed editions add “your” to “Where is boasting?”; it is absent from the Vatican manuscripts and the Greek. The printed editions alone add “was made” after “to his offspring.”]

## CHAPTER VIII

### 13. The fifth calumny: that Paul and the other Apostles are said to have been polluted by lust

“He says,” he reports, “that the Apostle Paul, or all the apostles, were always polluted by immoderate lust.”

Who, even if profane, would dare to say this? But evidently he makes this accusation for the following reason: they maintain that when the Apostle said, “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh; for the willing is present with me, but I do not find the accomplishing of good” (Romans 7:18), and other statements of the same kind, he was not speaking about himself, but was introducing the character of someone else who suffered these things. For this reason that passage in his Epistle must be carefully considered and examined, lest their error lie concealed in some obscurity of it.

Although the Apostle discusses this matter at greater length, defending grace in a great and prolonged conflict against those who gloried in the Law, we shall touch briefly on what is relevant. Thus he says:

“For no flesh will be justified before him by works of the Law. Through the Law comes knowledge of sin. But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the Law, attested by the Law and the Prophets; the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ, for all who believe. For there is no distinction: all have sinned and lack the glory of God, being justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.”

And again:

“Where is boasting? It has been excluded. By what law? By that of works? No, but by the law of faith. For we hold that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the Law” (Romans 3:20–28).

And again:

“For the promise to Abraham or to his offspring that he would be heir of the world was not made through the Law, but through the righteousness of faith. For if those who are of the Law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise has been annulled. For the Law produces wrath; for where there is no Law, there is no transgression” (Romans 4:13–15).

And elsewhere:

“The Law entered so that transgression might increase; but where transgression increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20).

Again, elsewhere:

“Sin will not rule over you, for you are not under the Law but under grace” (Romans 6:14).

And again, elsewhere:

“Or do you not know, brothers—for I am speaking to those who know the Law—that the Law rules over a person as long as he lives? For a woman joined to a husband is bound by law to her husband; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law concerning her husband.”

And shortly afterward:

“Therefore, my brothers, you also have died to the Law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another, to him who was raised from the dead, in order that we may bear fruit for God. For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions that operate through the Law were at work in our members, so that they bore fruit for death. But now we have been released from the Law of death by which we were held, so that we may serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.”

By these and similar declarations that Teacher of the Gentiles clearly shows that the Law could not remove sin, but rather increased it; grace removes it. For the Law knows how to command, and weakness succumbs to the command; grace knows how to help, and through it love is poured in.

But lest anyone, because of these testimonies, disparage the Law and argue that it is evil, the Apostle saw what might occur to those who misunderstood it, and posed the question to himself:

“What then shall we say? Is the Law sin? Certainly not! Yet I did not know sin except through the Law.” He had already said above, “Through the Law comes knowledge of sin.” Therefore it is not removal, but knowledge [Col. 0557; all the manuscripts read *ablatio*, “removal,” while the printed editions read *abolitio*, “abolition”].

### 14. That the Apostle spoke in his own person and in the person of others who are under grace, not under the Law

Here he begins to introduce his own person, as though speaking about himself. The Pelagians do not wish the Apostle himself to be understood here; rather, they say that he transformed himself into someone else—that is, into a person still placed under the Law and not yet freed through grace.

At this point they ought certainly to concede that no one is justified by the Law, as the same Apostle says elsewhere (Galatians 3:11). Yet the Law is useful for the knowledge of sin and for the transgression of the Law itself, so that, once sin has been recognized and increased, grace may be sought through faith.

They are not afraid that the following words should be understood as referring to the Apostle, since he could have spoken of his former life; but they fear the words that follow. For he says here:

“I did not know covetousness except that the Law said, ‘You shall not covet.’ But, taking occasion through the commandment, sin produced in me every kind of covetousness. For apart from the Law sin is dead. I was once alive apart from the Law; but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died. The commandment that was intended for life was found by me to be for death. For sin, taking occasion through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. Therefore the Law is indeed holy, and the commandment is holy, just, and good. Did then what is good become death for me? Certainly not! But, so that sin might appear as sin, through what is good it produced death in me, so that through the commandment either “the sinner” or “sin” might become exceedingly so” (Romans 7:1–13) [Col. 0558; the printed editions read “sinning sin,” while all manuscripts read “sinner or sin”; the Greek is *hamartōlos ē hamartia*].

All this, as I have said, may be understood as the Apostle’s recollection of his former life. By the statement, “I was once alive apart from the Law,” he may have intended the earliest period of his life, from infancy before the years of reason. By what he adds, “When the commandment came, sin revived, and I died,” he shows that he had already become capable of receiving the commandment, but not capable of fulfilling it, and therefore became a transgressor of the Law.

## CHAPTER IX
