### 15. He sins by the will who does not sin only from fear

Nor should it disturb us that he wrote to the Philippians: “According to the righteousness that is in the Law, I was blameless” (Philippians 3:6) [the manuscripts read *qui fuerim*, “that I was”; the printed editions read *quod fuerit*, “that it was”].

For inwardly, in his corrupt affections, he could have been a transgressor of the Law while still fulfilling the Law’s visible works, either from fear of human beings or from fear of God himself—but from dread of punishment, not from love and delight in righteousness [the Vatican manuscripts omit “and delight”].

For it is one thing to do good from the will to do good; it is another to be so inclined by one’s will toward doing evil that one would do it if it could be permitted with impunity. Thus, plainly, the person who does not refrain from sin by the will, but by fear, sins inwardly in the very will.

Knowing that before God’s grace—which is through Jesus Christ our Lord—he had been such in his inner life, the Apostle confesses this most openly elsewhere. Writing to the Ephesians, he says:

“And you, when you were dead in your trespasses and sins, in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the ruler of the power of the air, the spirit that now works in the sons of disobedience, among whom we all once lived in the desires of our flesh, doing the will of the flesh and of our affections; and we were by nature children of wrath, like the rest. But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ—by whose grace we have been saved” (Ephesians 2:1–5).

Again, writing to Titus, he says:

“For we too were once foolish and disobedient, wandering astray, serving various desires and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another.”

Such was Saul when he says that, according to the righteousness that is in the Law, he was blameless. For he had not progressed in the Law and changed his conduct after that abominable life in order to become blameless, as he clearly demonstrates in what follows—since he says that he was changed from these evils only through the grace of the Savior [Col. 0558; the Amsterdam, Erasmus, and manuscript witnesses read “he clearly demonstrates in what follows”; the Lovanius edition reads “he clearly demonstrates these things which follow”].

Adding this very point here also, just as he did to the Ephesians [the printed editions read “just as to Titus”; the manuscripts correct this], he says:

“But when the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared, he saved us—not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy, through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life” (Titus 3:3–7).

[Column 0559] ### 16. On what he says in this passage of the Epistle to the Romans

What he says in this passage of the Epistle to the Romans—“So that sin might appear as sin, through what is good it produced death in me”—agrees with the preceding statements, where he said, “I did not know sin except through the Law,” and, “I did not know covetousness except that the Law said, ‘You shall not covet,’” and earlier, “Through the Law comes knowledge of sin.”

For here too he says “so that sin might appear,” so that by the statement, “Apart from the Law sin is dead,” we should understand not that sin does not exist, but that it is hidden, does not appear, and is entirely unknown, as though it were buried in some darkness of ignorance.

And when he says, “I was once alive apart from the Law,” what does he mean except, “I seemed to myself to be alive”? And when he adds, “When the commandment came, sin revived,” what else does this mean than, “It became prominent and appeared” [the Vatican manuscripts read “flashed forth”]?

Yet he does not say “it lived,” but “it revived.” For it had once lived in paradise, when the transgression against the commandment was sufficiently evident. But when it is drawn from those who are born, it lies hidden as though dead, until its evil, resisting righteousness, is perceived through its prohibition—when one thing is commanded and approved, but another delights and rules. Then sin, in a certain sense, revives in the awareness of the person who has been born: the sin that had once already lived in the awareness of the first human being [Col. 0559; the manuscripts read “first,” while the Amsterdam, Erasmus, and Lovanius editions read “of the first”; Lovanius alone adds “already”].

## CHAPTER X

### 17. The same subject continued

But what follows is not so readily explained as referring to Paul. “We know,” he says, “that the Law is spiritual, but I am fleshly” (Romans 7:14). He does not say, “I was,” but “I am.” Was the Apostle therefore fleshly when he wrote these words? Or is he saying this according to the body?

For he was still in “this body of death” (Romans 7:24), and what is said elsewhere had not yet occurred: “The natural body is sown; a spiritual body will rise” (1 Corinthians 15:44) [Col. 0559; Erasmus and Lovanius add “spiritual” after “had not yet occurred”; the printed editions read “rises,” while the manuscripts read “will rise,” in accordance with the Greek, *egeiretai*].

For then he will be spiritual in his entirety—that is, in both parts of which a human being consists—when the body also will be spiritual. Nor is it absurd that in that life there may also be spiritual flesh, if in this life, among those who still set their minds on carnal things, the spirit itself can also be fleshly.

Thus he said, “I am fleshly,” because the Apostle did not yet possess a spiritual body. In the same way he could say, “I am mortal,” which would certainly be understood as referring to the body, since it had not yet been clothed with immortality.

Likewise, when he added, “Sold under sin,” lest anyone should think that he had not yet been redeemed by Christ’s blood, this too can be understood according to what he says: “We ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait for adoption, the redemption of our body” (Romans 8:23).

For if he says that he was sold under sin in the sense that his body has not yet been redeemed from corruption—or that he was sold at the first transgression of the commandment, so that he possessed a corruptible body “which weighs down the soul” (Wisdom 9:15)—what prevents us from understanding the Apostle as speaking here about himself, saying something that can also be understood as applying to him, even if in his own person he wishes not only himself but all those who know that they struggle in spiritual delight against the inclination of the flesh, without consenting to it, to be included [Col. 0560; the manuscripts read “can,” while the printed editions read “could”; the Gallican manuscripts read “love” (*dilectione*) for “delight” (*delectatione*)]? 

### 18. Whether we perhaps fear what follows

Or do we perhaps fear what follows? For what he says next may lead someone to suspect from these words that the holy Apostle consented to the lust of the flesh in evil actions [Col. 0560; the Vatican manuscripts read *ad opera mala sanctum apostolum suspicetur*, “that one might suspect the holy Apostle concerning evil works”]: 

“What I do, I do not understand; for I do not do what I want, but what I hate, that I do.”

But we must consider what he adds:

“If I do what I do not want, I agree with the Law that it is good.”

For he says that he agrees with the Law rather than with the lust of the flesh. He calls the latter by the name of sin. Therefore he said that he does and performs it, not through the affection of consenting to it and fulfilling it, but through the movement of coveting itself.

“Thus,” he says, “I agree with the Law that it is good”: I agree because I do not want what it does not want.

Then he says:

“But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.”

What does “now” mean except “now, under grace, which has freed the delight of the will from consent to desire”? For “it is not I who do it” is best understood to mean that he does not consent to present his members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin (Romans 6:13).

For if he both covets, consents, and acts, how is he not himself the one who does it, even if he grieves that he does it and groans bitterly at being overcome?

### 19. What follows shows most clearly who is speaking

Does not what follows show most clearly where he is speaking from?

“For I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh.”

If he had not explained this by adding, “that is, in my flesh,” what he said—“in me”—might perhaps have been understood differently.

And so he turns to the same point, repeating and emphasizing it:

“For the willing is present with me, but the accomplishing of good is not.”

To accomplish good is not to covet at all. Good is imperfect, however, when one covets, even if one does not consent to the coveting for evil.

“For I do not do the good that I want,” he says, “but the evil that I do not want, that I do. But if I do what I do not want, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.”

He repeated and emphasized this, as though awakening the very slow from sleep:

“I find therefore a law,” he says, “for me who want to do good: evil is present with me.”

Thus the Law is good for the person who wants to do good, while evil is present through the desire to which the person who says, “It is no longer I who do it,” does not consent.

### 20. Both points are made clearer by what follows

“What follows,” however, makes both points clearer:

“For I delight in the Law of God according to the inner person, but I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members” [the manuscripts read “taking me captive by the law of sin”; below they likewise read “taking me captive—that is, my flesh—by the law of sin,” consistently omitting the preposition *in*, which is also absent from the Greek text of the Apostle].

But the statement “taking me captive” may be troubling if there is no consent. Therefore, on account of these three expressions—the two already discussed, “I am fleshly” and “sold under sin,” and this third one, “taking me captive in the law of sin, which is in my members”—the Apostle may seem to be describing someone who still lives under the Law and not yet under grace.

But just as we explained those two expressions as referring to the flesh, which is still corruptible, so this one too can be understood in the sense that when he said “taking me captive,” he meant “through the flesh,” not through the mind; through movement, not through consent. And he said “taking me captive” because even in the flesh itself the nature is not alien, but ours.

Therefore, just as he himself explained what he meant by “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh,” so from his explanation we ought to understand this passage as though he had said: “taking me captive—that is, my flesh—by the law of sin, which is in my members” [the Gallican manuscripts read “so also”].

### 21. The conclusion of the argument

Then he adds the words on account of which all these things have been said:

“Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

And from there he concludes:

“Therefore I myself with my mind serve the Law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin”—with the flesh, that is, serving the law of sin by coveting; with the mind, serving the Law of God by not consenting to the same coveting.

“Therefore there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has freed you from the law of sin and death” (Romans 7:15–8:2), so that coveting of the flesh may not claim your consent.

The statements that follow demonstrate the same meaning more and more clearly; but a limit must be observed.

### 22. A former interpretation of mine

At one time it had also seemed to me that this speech of the Apostle described a person under the Law [this had seemed so to him in *Exposition of Certain Propositions from the Epistle to the Romans*, propositions 44 and 45; in the *Epistle to the Galatians*, chapter 5, section 47; and *To Simplicianus*, book 1, question 1, sections 7 and 9].

But afterward the following words compelled me to reconsider the matter: “But now it is no longer I who do it.” For the statement that follows also belongs to this:

“Therefore there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.”

And I do not see how a person under the Law could say, “I delight in the Law of God according to the inner person,” since the very delight in good—which does not consent to evil, not from fear of punishment but from love of righteousness, for this is what “delighting together” means—must be attributed only to grace.

## CHAPTER XI

### 23. Again on the same subject

When he says, “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” who could deny that, when the Apostle said this, he was still in this body of death?

The impious are certainly not delivered from it, since their same bodies are restored for eternal punishments. To be delivered from this body of death, therefore, is to have every disease of the lust of the flesh healed—not to receive the body for punishment, but for glory.

This passage also agrees closely with the following:

“We ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait for adoption, the redemption of our body.”

For surely we groan with that groaning in which we say, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death?”

Likewise, when he says, “What I do, I do not understand,” what else does this mean than “I do not want it, I do not approve it, I do not consent to it, I do not do it”?

Otherwise this would contradict what he said above:

“Through the Law comes knowledge of sin”; “I did not know sin except through the Law”; and, “So that sin might appear as sin, through what is good it produced death in me.”

For how could he know through the Law the sin that he does not understand? How could sin appear when it is unknown?

Thus “I do not understand” was said in the sense of “I do not do it,” because I myself do not commit it through any consent. In the same way the Lord will say to the impious, “I never knew you” (Matthew 7:23), although nothing can escape his knowledge; and it is said of Christ, “the one who did not know sin” (2 Corinthians 5:21), meaning “who did not commit it.” For he certainly did not fail to know what he condemned.

### 24. The Apostle includes himself and others under grace

When these and similar matters are carefully considered within the context of this apostolic Scripture, the Apostle is rightly understood to have signified not only himself in his own person, but also others who are established under grace, though not yet with him in that perfect peace in which “death will be swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54).

Afterward he says of this:

“But if Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness. If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Romans 8:10–11).

Once our mortal bodies have been given life, therefore, there will be not only no consent to sin, but not even the lust of the flesh to which one does not consent will remain [Col. 0562; the negative “not” is restored from the manuscripts].

Only that human being could lack in mortal flesh the resistance of the flesh against the spirit who did not come to human beings through the flesh itself. Therefore, since the Apostles were human beings and carried in this mortal life a body that is subject to corruption and weighs down the soul, let us never say, as this accuser does, that they were “always polluted by immoderate lust.”

Rather, we say that they were free from consent to corrupt desires, but that they groaned with such humility and devotion over the lust of the flesh—which they restrained by governing it—that they preferred not to have it rather than to master it.

## CHAPTER XII

### 25. The sixth calumny: that Christ too was not free from sins

Accordingly, when this man added that we say “Christ too was not free from sins, but lied from the necessity of the flesh and was stained by other offenses,” let him determine from whom he heard this or in whose writings he read it. Perhaps he did not understand it and, deceived by malice, twisted it into defamatory interpretations.

## CHAPTER XIII

### 26. The seventh calumny: that not all sins are remitted in Baptism

“He also says,” he reports, “that Baptism does not grant complete forgiveness of sins, nor remove crimes, but merely shaves them, so that the roots of all sins remain in the evil flesh.”

Who but an unbeliever would assert this against the Pelagians? We say, therefore, that Baptism grants forgiveness of all sins and removes crimes; it does not merely shave them, “so that the roots of all sins remain in the evil flesh, like hair on a shaved head, from which sins may grow again and need to be cut off again.” For I have also discovered that they employ this comparison in their calumny, as though we thought and said this.

### 27. On the lust of the flesh after Baptism

But I believe that they are mistaken, or cause others to be mistaken, about this lust of the flesh. With it even a baptized person must struggle in a devout mind, even if he is making the most diligent progress and is led by the Spirit of God (Romans 8:14).

Yet even if this is called sin, it is not called so because it is itself sin, but because it was made through sin—just as a writing is called a hand because a hand made it.

Sins, however, are those things that are illicitly done, said, or thought according to the lust of the flesh or ignorance. Once committed, they continue to hold people guilty unless they are forgiven.

This very lust of the flesh is itself forgiven in Baptism in such a way that, although it has been drawn from those who are born, it harms nothing in those who are reborn. Yet if the reborn beget children carnally, it is drawn forth again and once more becomes harmful to those who are born, unless it is forgiven in those who are reborn in the same manner. It remains present, but will do no harm in the future life, because its guilt, drawn through generation, has been dismissed through regeneration.

Therefore it is no longer sin, but is called this either because it was made through sin, or because it is moved by the delight of sinning, even when it is not consented to because the delight of righteousness prevails over it.

It is not on account of this lust itself, whose guilt has already been removed by the bath of regeneration, that baptized people say in prayer, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” They say this on account of the sins that are committed either through consent to it—when what is pleasing is overcome by what is desired—or when, through ignorance, evil pleases as though it were good.

These sins are committed by action, by speech, or by what is easiest and quickest of all, by thought. Yet who even among the faithful will boast that he has a pure heart, or who will boast that he is clean from sin (Proverbs 20:9)?

The following petition in the prayer, however, is said on account of this lust:

“Do not lead us into temptation, but deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:12–13).

For each person, as it is written, is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire; then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin (James 1:14–15).

## CHAPTER XIV

### 28. Serious offenses and venial sins

All these offspring of desire, together with the ancient guilt of desire itself [the earlier editions needlessly add “which”; it is absent from the manuscripts], have been dismissed through the washing of Baptism.

Whatever this desire now gives birth to—provided that its offspring are not those things that are called not only sins but also crimes—is cleansed by the arrangement of daily prayer, in which we say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive,” and by the sincerity of almsgiving.

No one is so foolish as to say that the Lord’s command does not apply to the baptized:

“Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke 6:37–38).

No one could rightly be ordained as a minister in the Church if the Apostle had said, “If anyone is without sin,” where he says, “If anyone is without crime” (Titus 1:6); or if he had said, “Having no sin,” where he says, “Having no crime” (1 Timothy 3:10).

Many baptized believers are without crime. But I would not say that anyone in this life is without sin, no matter how much the Pelagians may swell with rage and burst in madness against us because we say this—not because any sin remains that is not forgiven in Baptism, but because, while we remain in the weakness of this life, things continue daily to be done by us, and they are daily forgiven to those who pray faithfully and act mercifully [Col. 0564; the printed editions read “because in us,” the Gallican manuscripts “because by us,” and the Vatican manuscripts “because us,” without a preposition].

This is the soundness of the Catholic faith, which the holy Spirit sows everywhere—not the vanity and presumption of heretical perversity.

## CHAPTER XV

### 29. Julian opposes the faith of his associates to Catholic judgments

The first antithesis: concerning free will.  
The second: concerning marriage.  
The third: concerning marital intercourse.

Let us now examine how, after he thought it proper to bring false accusations against us concerning what we believe and to fabricate things that we do not believe, he himself professes the faith either of his own party or of the Pelagians.

“Against these views,” he says, “we argue every day, and for that reason we do not wish to agree with transgressors, because we say that free will exists naturally in all things and could not have perished through Adam’s sin. This is confirmed by the authority of all the Scriptures.”

If you said this as you ought—not against the grace of God—you would not agree with transgressors, but would correct your own understanding. We have discussed this above as much as we could and as much as seemed sufficient.

### 30. Marriage and the transmission of sin

“We say,” he continues, “that the marriages now taking place throughout the world were instituted by God, and that married couples are not guilty, but that fornicators and adulterers must be condemned.”

This is true and Catholic. But what you wish to establish from it—that those born from the intercourse of male and female draw no sin from it, a sin that is expiated by the washing of regeneration—is false and heretical [the printed editions read “what you wish to establish from the intercourse of male and female, namely that no sin…”; the manuscripts correct this].

### 31. The movement of the genitals

“We say,” he continues, “that the movement of the genitals—that is, virility itself, without which intercourse cannot occur—was instituted by God.”

To this we reply that God instituted the movement of the genitals—or, to use his word, virility—without which intercourse cannot occur, in such a way that it possessed nothing shameful. For it was not right that God’s creature should blush at the work of its Creator.

But the disobedience of the members was imposed as a just punishment upon the first human beings for their disobedience. They were ashamed of it when they covered their sexual parts with fig leaves—parts that previously had not been shameful.

## CHAPTER XVI

### 32. The coverings that Adam and Eve sewed for themselves; the opening of Adam’s and Eve’s eyes; shame at nakedness

For after the sin they did not sew tunics to cover their whole bodies, but girdings (*succinctoria*) (Genesis 3:7), which some of our interpreters, less carefully [the manuscripts read “carefully”], translated as “coverings.” This is true, but “covering” is a general term by which every garment and covering may be understood.

The ambiguity should therefore have been avoided: just as the Greek text uses *περιζώματα* (*perizōmata*), which cover only the body’s sexual parts, so the Latin should either have used the Greek term itself—for it has now become customary even in Latin—or should have used *succinctoria*, as some did, or, as others more aptly named them, *campestria*.

This name derives from the fact that, according to ancient Roman custom, young men covered their sexual parts with them when they exercised naked in the field. Hence even today those who cover the same members by girding them are called *campestrati* [the edition of Lovanius reads “today, who,” omitting *-que*, “and”].

Yet if the parts through which the sin was committed had to be covered after the sin, they ought not even to have been clothed in tunics, but should have covered their hand and mouth, because they sinned by taking and eating.

What, then, does it mean that, after the forbidden food had been received and the transgression of the command had occurred, attention was directed toward those members? What new and previously unknown sensation was felt there that compelled them to notice it? This is signified by the opening of their eyes.

Their eyes had not been closed either when he gave names to the cattle and the birds (Genesis 2:20), or when she saw that the tree was beautiful and good (Genesis 3:6–7). Rather, their eyes were opened—that is, made attentive for looking—as it is written of Hagar, Sarah’s servant, that “she opened her eyes and saw a well” (Genesis 21:19), although she certainly did not previously have them closed.

Thus, although they had surely looked upon their nakedness every day without being ashamed, they were suddenly so ashamed of it that they could no longer bear those members to remain naked, but immediately took care to cover them. Did they not therefore—he in open movement and she in concealment—experience those members acting against the determination of their will, although they ought to have ruled them by voluntary command just as they ruled their other members?

They deservedly suffered this, because they themselves had not been obedient to their Lord. They were therefore ashamed that they had not rendered service to their Creator, and in those members from which children were to be procreated they deserved to lose their dominion [Col. 0565; perhaps “over those members”; the printed editions read “receive,” but the manuscripts read “lose”].

## CHAPTER XVII
### 34. Whether sexual desire could have existed in paradise before sin

[Col. 0566]

But, Pelagians, preserving the honor and fruitfulness of marriage, suppose that no one had sinned and choose what sort of life you would wish those human beings to have led in paradise; select one of these four possibilities. For plainly, either they would have had intercourse whenever they wished; or they would have restrained sexual desire whenever intercourse was not necessary; or sexual desire would then have arisen at the command of the will, whenever chaste prudence [Note: [Col. 0566] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “modesty” (*pudentia*).] had foreseen that intercourse was necessary; or, with no sexual desire existing there at all, just as the other members would have served their respective functions at the command of those who willed, so the genital members also would have served their proper function without any difficulty.

Choose whichever of these four you wish. But I think you will reject the first two, in which [Note: [Col. 0566] The printed editions read, “in which” (*quibus*); the manuscripts, “where” (*ubi*).] sexual desire is either obeyed or resisted.

For the first possibility is incompatible with such outstanding chastity; the second, with such great happiness. Heaven forbid that the splendor of so great a blessedness should either have practiced the most shameful slavery by always following sexual desire, or, by resisting it, should have lacked complete peace. Heaven forbid, I say, that the desire of the flesh, arising through disordered agitation not at the appropriate time for procreation, should have had to be satisfied by consenting to please that desire, or restrained by dissenting from it in order to preserve that peace.

### 35. Either remaining view admits the present argument

Whichever of the remaining two possibilities you choose, there is no need to struggle against you in controversy. For even if you do not wish to choose the fourth possibility—that in which there would be complete tranquility among all the obedient members [Note: [Col. 0566] The printed editions alone read, “the obedience of the members.”], without any sexual desire, since the force of your arguments has already made you hostile to it—you will at least approve the third possibility that we proposed: that carnal desire, whose movement reaches the final pleasure [Note: [Col. 0566] The printed editions read, “reaches that final pleasure”; the manuscripts omit “that.”] that greatly delights you, would never have arisen in paradise at the command of the will except when it was necessary for procreation.

If you are willing to place this desire in paradise, and if by such carnal desire—one that neither anticipated, delayed, nor exceeded the command of the will—you think that children could have been generated [Note: [Col. 0566] The printed editions read, “could generate”; the manuscripts, “could have been generated.”] in that happiness, we do not object. For our present argument requires only this: that such desire as you concede could have existed in that happiness is not now found among human beings.

For what it is like now is confessed by the awareness of all mortals, although with shame. It troubles even the chaste, against their will and despite their restraining it through self-control, with restless and disorderly importunity; and very often it withdraws from those who desire it and thrusts itself upon those who do not. Thus, by its disobedience, it testifies that it is nothing other than the punishment for that ancient disobedience.

Therefore, rightly, concerning it both the first human beings then, when they covered their nakedness, and now everyone who considers himself in any sense human—both the modest and the shameless—are confounded. Heaven forbid that this confusion should concern the work of God; it concerns the punishment of the first and ancient sin.

But you, not from religious conviction but from contentious hostility, not for the sake of human modesty but because of your fury, lest this very carnal desire be thought to have been corrupted [Col. 0567] and original sin be derived from it, attempt by argument to restore to paradise [Note: [Col. 0567] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “you will attempt in paradise.”] a desire exactly as it now is. You insist that it could have existed there, either with a shameful consent always following it or with a pitiable dissent sometimes restraining it.

We, however, are not greatly concerned with what you take pleasure in thinking about it. Nevertheless, whatever is born of human beings through it, if it is not reborn, is without doubt condemned; and it must remain under the devil unless it is liberated from him by Christ.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### 36. Julian’s fourth antithesis: that man is God’s work [Col. 0567] and is not compelled by God’s power toward either evil or good

“We defend,” he says, “that human beings are God’s work, and that no one is compelled against his will by his power either toward evil or toward good, but that by his own will he does either good or evil; that in a good work he is always assisted by God’s grace, while toward evil he is incited by the devil’s suggestions.”

To this we reply: human beings are God’s work insofar as they are human beings, but they are under the devil insofar as they are sinners, unless they are rescued from him by the one who became mediator between God and human beings for no other reason than that no sinner could arise from among human beings.

No one is compelled against his will by God’s power either toward evil or toward good; rather, when God abandons him, he goes toward evil in accordance with his merits, and when God assists him, he turns toward good without merits. A person is not good if he does not wish to be; but God’s grace assists him even in this, so that he may wish to be good. For it is not written without reason: “For it is God who works in you [Note: [Col. 0567] The manuscripts read, “in us.”] both to will and to work, according to his good pleasure” (Phil. 2:13); and: “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 8, according to the Septuagint).

## CHAPTER XIX

### 37. The beginning of a good will is a gift of grace. To come to Christ is to believe. The power of grace [Col. 0567]

But you think that in a good work a human being is assisted by God’s grace in such a way that you believe grace does nothing in awakening the will toward that very good work. Your own words make this sufficiently clear.

For why did you not say that a human being is stirred by God’s grace toward a good work, just as you said that he is “incited toward evil by the devil’s suggestions,” but instead said that “in a good work he is always assisted by God’s grace”? It is as though, having begun a good work by his own will and without any grace of God, he were then assisted divinely in the work itself, on account, of course, of the merits of his good will; so that grace is repaid as something owed, rather than bestowed as something unowed. In this way “grace is no longer grace” (Rom. 11:6), but becomes what Pelagius, with feigned sincerity, condemned at the Palestinian hearing: that God’s grace is given according to our merits [Note: [Col. 0567] Above, *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 30.]

Tell me, I beg you, what good did Paul, then still called Saul, desire, and not rather great evils, when, breathing slaughter, he went forth to destroy Christians in the terrifying blindness and fury of his mind? By what merits of good will did God turn him from those evils to good through a marvelous and sudden calling (Acts 9)?

Why should I speak of merits, when he himself cries out: “He saved us, not because of works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy” (Titus 3:5)?

What of the Lord’s statement [Col. 0568] that I have already mentioned: “No one can come to me”—that is understood as, “believe in me”—“unless it has been granted him by my Father” (John 6:66)? Is this given to one who already wishes to believe, on account of the merits of his good will? Or rather, in order that he may believe, is the will itself aroused from above, as in Saul’s case, even if he is so hostile to faith that he persecutes those who believe?

Why, then, did the Lord command us to pray for those who persecute us (Matt. 5:44)? Do we pray that God’s grace may be repaid to them for their good will, or rather that the will itself, which is evil [Note: [Col. 0568] The printed editions read, “their will”; the manuscripts, “the will itself.”], may be changed into good?

As we believe, the saints whom Saul was persecuting did not pray in vain for him (Acts 7:59), that his will might be turned toward the faith which he was destroying. His conversion, moreover, visibly took place from above, accompanied even by an evident miracle.

How many enemies of Christ are daily drawn suddenly to Christ by the hidden grace of God? If I had not taken this expression from the Gospel, how much this man would have said against me because of it—although even now he struggles not against me but against the one who cries out: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44).

For he does not say “leads,” so that we might somehow understand the will to precede. Who is drawn if he already wished to come? And yet no one comes unless he wishes to. Therefore he is drawn in wondrous ways so that he may wish to come, by the one who knows how to work inwardly in the very hearts of human beings—not so that human beings, which cannot happen, should believe while unwilling, but so that from unwilling they may become willing.

## CHAPTER XX

### 38. The power of God’s grace is demonstrated

We do not suspect this to be true through human conjecture; we recognize it through the most evident authority of the divine Scriptures.

It is read in the Books of Chronicles: “And indeed, in Judah the hand of God was present, to give them one heart, so that they might do the command of the king and of the rulers according to the word of the Lord” (2 Chron. 30:12).

Likewise, through the prophet Ezekiel the Lord says: “I will give them another heart, and I will put a new spirit within them; I will remove their heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, so that they may walk in my commandments, observe my ordinances, and perform them” (Ezek. 36:26–27).

What, then, is the meaning of that prayer of Queen Esther, when she says: “Give a well-ordered speech into my mouth, and make my words eloquent in the presence of the lion, and turn his heart toward hatred of the one who attacks us”? Why does she say this to God in prayer if God does not work the will in human hearts?

Perhaps, however, the woman prayed this foolishly. Let us therefore see whether the disposition of the woman praying was put forth in vain and whether the effect of the one hearing her failed to follow.

Behold, she enters before the king. Let us not recount everything at length. Since she was entering contrary to the prescribed order, compelled by great necessity, he looked upon her, as it is written, “like a bull in the rush of his indignation.” The queen was afraid, and her color changed as she fainted; she bent over the head of her maidservant, who was walking before her.

“And God turned [him],” and transferred his indignation into gentleness [Col. 0569]. Why is it necessary to recall what follows, when the divine Scripture testifies that God fulfilled what she had asked (Esth. 14–16), working in the king’s heart what else but the will by which he commanded that what the queen had requested should be done?

God had already heard her so that it might happen: by his most hidden and effective power he turned the king’s heart before he had heard the woman’s petition, transferring it from indignation to gentleness—that is, from a will to harm to a will to favor—according to the Apostle’s statement: “God works [Note: [Col. 0569] The printed editions read, “For God, who works.” The words “for God, who” are absent from the manuscripts.] in you both to will.”

Did the human beings of God who wrote these things—or rather, did the Spirit of God himself, by whose authority these things were written through them—attack human free will? Heaven forbid. Rather, he commended both the most just judgment and the most merciful assistance of the Almighty in all things.

It is enough for a human being to know that there is no injustice with God. But how he arranges these matters, making some vessels of wrath according to merit and others [Note: [Col. 0569] The Vatican and Gallican manuscripts read, “making some vessels of wrath according to merit, and others,” with the corresponding plural forms.] vessels of mercy according to grace (Rom. 9:14, 22–23)—who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor (Rom. 11:34)?

If, then, we belong to the honor of grace, let us not be ungrateful by attributing to ourselves what we have received. For what do we have that we have not received (1 Cor. 4:7)?

## CHAPTER XXI

### 39. Julian’s fifth antithesis: concerning the righteous of the Old Testament [Col. 0569]

“We say,” he declares, “that the saints of the Old Testament passed from this life into eternal life with perfect righteousness—that is, by their devotion to virtue they withdrew from all sins—for although we read that some of them sinned, we nevertheless know that afterward they corrected themselves.”

However great a virtue [Note: [Col. 0569] The Vatican manuscripts read, “however great the virtue.”] you proclaim the ancient righteous to have possessed, it was faith in the Mediator alone that saved them—the one who shed his blood for the remission of sins. For their own voice says: “I believed, therefore I spoke” (Ps. 115:1).

Hence the apostle Paul also says: “But because we have the same spirit of faith, according to what is written, ‘I believed, therefore I spoke,’ we also believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Cor. 4:13).

What does “the same spirit” mean except the spirit possessed also by those righteous people who said these things?

The apostle Peter likewise says: “Why are you putting a yoke on the Gentiles that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear? But we believe that we shall be saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they were” (Acts 15:10–11). [Note: The Louvain edition reads, “that we may be saved”; above, in *On Original Sin*, no. 29, it agrees with the other editions and the manuscripts.]

You do not want this, enemies of this grace [Note: [Col. 0569] The manuscripts have this reading; the printed editions read, “enemies of the grace of Christ,” omitting “this.”]: you do not want the ancients to be believed saved by the same grace of Jesus Christ. Instead, following Pelagius, whose books contain this teaching, you divide the ages and say that before the Law people were saved by nature [Note: The Gallican and Vatican manuscripts read this way; the printed edition reads, “through nature.” See *On Original Sin*, no. 50], then by the Law, and finally through Christ—as though the blood of Christ had not been necessary for human beings in either of the two earlier periods, namely before the Law and under the Law.

Thus you make void what has been said [Col. 0570]: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5).

## CHAPTER XXII

### 40. The sixth antithesis: concerning grace, necessary for all, and the baptism of infants [Col. 0570]

“We confess,” they say, “that the grace of Christ is necessary for everyone, adults and infants alike; and we anathematize those who say that one born of two baptized parents ought not to be baptized.”

We know how you say this—not according to the apostle Paul, but according to the heretic Pelagius: baptism is necessary for infants, you say, not for the remission of sins, but only for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.

For you grant them a place of salvation and eternal life outside the kingdom of God, even if they have not been baptized. And you do not pay attention to what is written: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved; but whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16). [Note: The Vatican manuscripts read, “Whoever has been baptized while believing will be saved.”]

For this reason, in the Church of the Savior infants believe through others, just as through others they acquired the sins that are remitted to them in baptism.

Nor do you consider that those who are without the body and blood of Christ cannot have life, since he himself says: “Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6:54).

Or, if the words of the Gospel compel you to confess that infants leaving the body cannot have life and salvation unless they have been baptized, ask why they are compelled to undergo the punishment of the second death if they were not baptized, when they are judged by the one who condemns no one undeservedly. You will discover what you do not want to discover: original sin.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### 41. The seventh antithesis: concerning the effect of baptism

“We also condemn those,” he says, “who say that baptism does not remove all sins, because we know that complete cleansing is conferred through the mysteries themselves.”

We say this too. But you do not say that infants also are freed through those very mysteries from the bonds of their first birth and their burdened inheritance. Therefore, from the Church of Christ, which has held this from ancient times, you too ought to be separated, just as the other heretics are.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### 42. He refutes the conclusion of Julian’s letter [Col. 0570]

But when he concludes his letter in this way, saying:

“Therefore let no one deceive you, and let the impious not deny that they hold these views. But if they speak the truth, let them be granted a hearing; or certainly let these very bishops who are now at variance condemn what I have said above, namely, that they hold these views with the Manichaeans, just as we condemn what they falsely claim about us; and let complete agreement be established [Note: [Col. 0570] Erasmus and Louvain read, “and let there be”; the Ambrosian edition and the manuscripts read, “and there is.”]. But if they are unwilling, know that they are Manichaeans, and abstain from their associations”—this deserves to be disregarded rather than refuted.

For which of us doubts that anathema must be pronounced against the Manichaeans, who say that neither human beings nor marriage were instituted by the good God, and that the Law given through Moses and administered to the Hebrew people was not given by him?

But we also rightly pronounce anathema against the Pelagians, who are so hostile to the grace of God that comes through Jesus Christ our Lord (Rom. 7:25) that they say it is given not freely but according to our merits, and thus that grace is no longer grace (Rom. 11:6).

They place so much [Col. 0571] in free will, into whose depths the human being has been plunged, that they say a person merits grace by using free will well—although no one can use it well except through grace, which is not paid back as something owed but is freely bestowed by God’s mercy.

They also maintain that infants are already saved [Col. 0572] in such a way that they dare to deny that they must be saved by the Savior [Note: [Col. 0572] The manuscripts read, “by the Savior”; the printed editions read, “to the Savior.”]

While holding and sowing these execrable doctrines, they nevertheless demand a hearing, although, having been condemned, they ought to be doing penance.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0571]

He undertakes to examine a second letter of the Pelagians, filled, like the first, with accusations against the Catholics, which they sent to Thessalonica in the name of eighteen bishops. First, he demonstrates, by comparing the two heresies, that Catholics do not fall into the errors of the Manichaeans when they condemn the doctrines of the Pelagians. He rebuts the accusation of betrayal allegedly committed by the Roman clergy in the later condemnation of Pelagius and Coelestius under Zosimus, showing that the Pelagian doctrines were never approved at Rome, although for a time Zosimus dealt more gently with Coelestius so that he might be brought to correct his errors. In the name of grace, the Catholics neither assert fate nor attribute partiality to God; nevertheless, they truly say that God’s grace is not given according to human merits and that the first desire for the good is inspired by God, so that a human being does not begin at all to be changed from evil to good unless God’s unowed and gratuitous mercy effects this change in him.

## CHAPTER I

### 1. The Pelagians accuse the Catholics under the name of Manichaeans [Col. 0571]

Let us now consider another letter—not Julian’s alone, but one shared [Note: [Col. 0571] The printed editions read, “and”; the manuscripts, “with him” (*ei*).] by him with many Pelagian bishops—which they sent to Thessalonica, and, with the Lord’s help, reply to it as best we can.

Since our work should not become longer than the necessity of the case demands, why should we refute as well those statements that do not contain the treacherous poisons of their doctrine, but seem merely to request, for their own support or in defense of the Catholic faith against what they call the profanation of the Manichaeans, the agreement [Note: The Gallican manuscripts read, “concession.”] of the Eastern bishops?

They strive for nothing else except that, by bringing forward the dreadful heresy whose adversaries they pretend to be, they may conceal their hostility to grace under praise of nature.

For who has ever raised a question against them on this point? Or which Catholic is displeased with them because they condemn those whom the Apostle foretold would depart from the faith, having a seared conscience, forbidding marriage, abstaining from foods that they consider unclean, and not believing that all things were created by God?

Who ever compelled them to deny that every creature of God is good (1 Tim. 4:1–4), or that there is any substance that the supreme God did not make, except God himself, who was made by no one?

These things, which are plainly Catholic, are not criticized or condemned in them. The Catholic faith is not alone in detesting the excessively foolish and harmful [Note: [Col. 0571] The printed editions read, “excessive.” The manuscripts’ reading, “excessively,” is more suitable.] impiety of the Manichaeans; all heretics who are not Manichaeans detest it as well.

Therefore these Pelagians do well in pronouncing anathema against the Manichaeans and contradicting their errors. But they do two evil things for which they themselves must also be anathematized: first, they accuse Catholics under the name of Manichaeans; second, they themselves introduce a heresy of novel error.

For the fact that they do not suffer from the disease of the Manichaeans does not make them sound in faith. Just as in bodies, so also in minds, there is more than one kind of pestilence.

Thus a physician of the body would not immediately declare a person free from danger of death merely because he had denied that the person was dropsical [Note: [Col. 0571] The Gallican manuscripts read, “had declared him free.”], if he had observed that he was ill with another deadly disease. Similarly, truth does not congratulate these people merely because they are not Manichaeans, if they are insane with another kind of perversity. [Col. 0572]

Therefore, what we anathematize together with them is one thing, and what we anathematize in them is another. We detest with them what they themselves rightly reject; yet we detest in them what rightly makes them objectionable.

## CHAPTER II

### 2. The heresies of the Manichaeans and Pelagians are mutually opposed and equally rejected by the Catholic Church

The points on which the Manichaeans and Pelagians are joined in error, and those on which they are separated. The Manichaeans say that the good God is not the creator of all natures; the Pelagians say that God is not the purifier, savior, and liberator of human beings in every age. The Catholic Church refutes both: against the Manichaeans, by defending God’s creation so that no nature may be denied to have been instituted by him; against the Pelagians, by requiring human nature, lost in every age, to be saved.

The Manichaeans condemn the desire of the flesh not as an accidental defect but as a nature evil from eternity; the Pelagians, on the contrary, praise it as though it were no defect at all but an additional natural good.

The Catholic Church refutes both: to the Manichaeans it says, “It is not nature but defect”; to the Pelagians it says, “It is not from the Father but from the world.” Thus it permits both groups to allow this desire to be healed like an illness: the former by ceasing to believe it incurable, the latter by ceasing to proclaim it praiseworthy.

The Manichaeans deny that evil had its beginning for a good human being through free will; the Pelagians say that even an evil human being possesses sufficient free will to perform a good commandment.

The Catholic Church refutes both: to the former it says, “God made the human being upright” (Eccl. 7:30); to the latter it says, “If the Son sets you free, you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

The Manichaeans say that the soul, a fragment of God, possesses sin through mixture with an evil nature; the Pelagians say that the righteous soul, not indeed a fragment but a creature of God, does not possess sin even in this corruptible life.

The Catholic Church refutes both: to the Manichaeans it says, “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matt. 12:33). This would not be said to a human being, who cannot make a nature, unless sin were not nature but defect. To the Pelagians it says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

The Manichaeans and Pelagians contend against one another with these mutually opposed diseases, with different intentions but equal vanity; separated by differing opinions, yet close in their perverse minds.

### 3. Both attack Christ’s grace, nullify his baptism, and dishonor his flesh [Col. 0573]

Now both of them attack Christ’s grace, both nullify his baptism, and both dishonor his flesh—but in different ways and for different reasons.

The Manichaeans say that God’s help is owed on account of the merits of good nature; the Pelagians, on account of the merits of a good will. The former say, “God owes this to the labors of his members”; the latter say, “God owes this to the virtues of his servants.”

For both, therefore, the reward is reckoned not according to grace but according to debt (Rom. 4:4).

The Manichaeans say that the washing of regeneration—that is, the water itself—is superfluous, and insist that it benefits a profane heart nothing. The Pelagians, however, assert that what is said [Note: [Col. 0573] The Vatican manuscripts read, “what is given.”] in holy baptism for the cleansing of sins benefits infants nothing, since they have no sin.

Accordingly, in the baptism of infants, insofar as the remission of sins is concerned, the Manichaeans destroy the visible element, while the Pelagians destroy even the invisible sacrament.

The Manichaeans dishonor Christ’s flesh by blaspheming the Virgin’s birth [Note: [Col. 0573] The Vatican manuscripts read, “by blaspheming the birth,” omitting “of the Virgin.”]; the Pelagians dishonor it by equating the flesh of those who are to be redeemed with the flesh of the Redeemer.

For this reason Christ was born not in sinful flesh but in the likeness of sinful flesh (Rom. 8:3), because the flesh of other human beings is born sinful.

Thus the Manichaeans, detesting all flesh completely, remove from Christ’s flesh its manifest reality; the Pelagians, asserting that no sinful flesh is born, remove from Christ’s flesh its proper dignity.

### 4. The Pelagians should correct their own error

Let the Pelagians therefore stop charging Catholics with what they are not, but let them instead hasten to correct what they themselves are [Note: [Col. 0573] The printed editions omit these words; they are found in the Gallican and Vatican manuscripts.].

Nor should they wish to be considered lovable [Note: [Col. 0573] The Ambrosian edition and the manuscripts omit “to be considered.”] merely because they oppose the hateful error of the Manichaeans; rather, they should recognize that they are rightly hateful because they do not reject their own error.

For two errors can be opposed to one another, yet both must be detested because both are opposed to the truth.

If the Pelagians are to be loved because they hate the Manichaeans, then the Manichaeans must also be loved because they hate the Pelagians. But far be it from the Catholic mother, because of hatred for one group, to choose to love the other, when, with the Lord admonishing and assisting her, she ought to avoid both and desires to heal both.

## CHAPTER III

### 5. The Pelagians’ accusation against the clergy of the Roman Church [Col. 0573]

They also accuse the Roman clergy, writing that “struck by the terror of an order, they were not ashamed to commit the crime of betrayal, so that, contrary to their earlier judgment by which they had supported the Catholic doctrine in official proceedings, they later declared human nature to be evil.”

On the contrary, the Pelagians had falsely hoped that certain Roman Catholic minds could be persuaded of the new and execrable Pelagian or Coelestian doctrine. For those intellects, although perverted by an impious error [Note: [Col. 0574] The Gallican manuscripts read *pervasa* (“pervaded”) for *perversa* (“perverted”).], were nevertheless not contemptible; since they seemed to need careful correction rather than ready condemnation, they were treated somewhat more gently than the stricter discipline of the Church required.

With so many ecclesiastical letters passing back and forth between the Apostolic See and the African bishops, and with official proceedings concerning this matter conducted before that See in the presence of Coelestius and with his answers, what letter of Pope Zosimus, of venerable memory, or what recorded statement can finally be found [Col. 0574] in which he ordered that it ought to be believed that a human being is born without any defect of original sin?

He nowhere said this; he nowhere wrote it at all.

But when Coelestius had included this in his little book, among those matters concerning which he confessed that he still had doubts and wished to be instructed, approval was given—not to the falsity of his doctrine but to the willingness of a man of exceptionally acute intelligence, who, if corrected, would certainly have benefited many, to be corrected.

For this reason his little book was called Catholic: it is characteristic of a Catholic mind that, if it happens to think differently from what truth requires, it does not define that position with certainty but rejects it once it has been exposed and demonstrated.

The Apostle was speaking not to heretics but to Catholics when he said: “Let us therefore, as many as are perfect, think this way; and if you think differently about anything, God will reveal that also to you” (Phil. 3:15).

This was thought to have happened in Coelestius when he replied that he agreed with the letters of Pope Innocent of blessed memory, through which all doubt concerning this matter had been removed.

And in order that this might become more fully and clearly evident in him, letters were awaited from Africa [Col. 0575], where his craftiness had become somewhat more clearly known.

When those letters later arrived, they stated that it was not sufficient for slower and more scrupulous minds that he generally professed agreement with the letters of Bishop Innocent. He had to anathematize openly the errors that he had set down in his little book.

Otherwise, if he did not do this, many people of limited understanding would believe that the poisons of the faith contained in his little book had been approved by the Apostolic See, because that See had declared the book Catholic, rather than believing that they had been corrected, because he himself had replied that he agreed with the letters of Pope Innocent.

Therefore, when his presence was required so that either the man’s cunning or his correction might become clear through definite and lucid answers, and so that nothing ambiguous might remain for anyone, he withdrew and refused to submit to examination.

It was no longer right to postpone what was done for the benefit of others, if it could not benefit the excessive obstinacy and madness of the perverse [Note: [Col. 0574] One Vatican manuscript reads, “if it could not benefit them because of their excessive obstinacy and madness.”].

But if—God forbid—Coelestius or Pelagius had then been judged in the Roman Church in such a way that the doctrines which Pope Innocent had condemned in them and together with them were declared worthy of approval and adherence, then the mark of betrayal would more properly have been branded upon the Roman clergy.

But since, from the beginning, the letters of the most blessed Pope Innocent, replying to the letters of the African bishops, condemned this very error that these men are trying to persuade others to accept; and since his successor, holy Pope Zosimus, never said or wrote that what they think about infants ought to be held; and since, moreover, through repeated formal statements, he compelled Coelestius, who was attempting to clear himself, to agree with the letters of the Apostolic See mentioned above—it is perfectly clear that whatever leniency was shown to Coelestius in the meantime, while the firmness of the most ancient and strongest faith was preserved, was a most merciful exhortation to correction, not the most destructive approval of perversity [Note: [Col. 0575] The Gallican manuscripts read, “it was a most merciful correction of perversity,” omitting the intervening words.].

And the fact that Coelestius and Pelagius were later condemned by the same priest with repeated authority was the expression of a severity temporarily interrupted but now necessarily brought forward, not a betrayal of a truth previously recognized or a new discovery of the truth.

## CHAPTER IV

### 6. The same argument continued

But why should we linger longer in speaking about this matter [Col. 0575], when there exist official proceedings and written documents sent in both directions, in which everything that took place can be learned or reviewed?

From the questions of your holy predecessor and the answers of Coelestius, in which he professed his agreement with the letters of the blessed Pope Innocent, who cannot see how Coelestius was bound and fastened with a salutary bond, so that he would no longer dare to defend the claim that original sin is not remitted in the baptism of infants?

The venerable Bishop Innocent’s words concerning this matter to the Council of Carthage are as follows:

“For he, having once experienced free will, while using his own goods too carelessly, fell and was plunged into the depths of transgression; he found no way by which he could rise from there. Deceived in his freedom forever, he would have lain crushed beneath the oppression of this ruin [Note: [Col. 0575] Amerbach, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read, “he would have remained hidden beneath the oppression of this ruin.” The Louvain edition reads, “he would have lain crushed, overthrown by this ruin.” Compare Innocent’s letter in Augustine, volume 2.] unless Christ’s coming had set him free by his grace. Through the cleansing of a new birth, he purified every past defect by the washing of his baptism” [Note: The Vatican manuscripts read, “every defect of the past.”] (Innocent, Letter 181, no. 7, in Augustine).

What could be clearer or more explicit than this judgment of the Apostolic See?

Coelestius professed his agreement with it when your holy predecessor said to him, “Do you condemn all those things that have been circulated under your name?” He himself replied, “I condemn them according to the judgment of your predecessor, of blessed memory, Innocent.”

Among the other things that had been circulated under his name, the deacon Paulinus had charged Coelestius with saying “that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race, and that infants newly born were in the same state in which Adam was before sin.”

Therefore, if he had condemned Paulinus’s charges with a truthful heart and mouth according to the judgment of the blessed Pope Innocent, what would have remained for him thereafter by which he could contend that there was no defect in infants arising from the transgression of the first human being, a defect that was cleansed in holy baptism through the purification of a new birth?

But his final conduct showed that he had answered deceitfully: he withdrew [Col. 0576] from the examination so that, according to the African letters, he would not be compelled to repeat and anathematize the very words concerning this question that he had set down in his little book.

### 7

What of the fact that the same Pope, in a letter to the bishops of Numidia concerning this very matter—for he had received written reports from both councils, namely the Council of Carthage and that of Milevis—does he not speak most explicitly about infants? For these are his words:

> “But as for what your Fraternity asserts that they preach—that infants can be granted the rewards of eternal life even without the grace of Baptism—this is utterly foolish. For unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, they will not have life in themselves (John 6:54). Those who defend the possibility of their having this without regeneration seem to me to want to invalidate Baptism itself, since they proclaim that these infants possess what we believe is conferred upon them only through Baptism” (Innocent, Letter 182, no. 5, among the Augustinian letters).

What does the ungrateful man say to this, when the Apostolic See had already spared him with the greatest gentleness, as though he had been corrected, on the basis of his own profession? What does he say to this? After the end of this life, will infants—even if, while they live, they are not baptized in Christ—be in eternal life, or will they not?

If he says, “They will,” then how did he reply that he had condemned, according to the judgment of Innocent of blessed memory, the things alleged concerning him? Behold: Pope Innocent of blessed memory says that infants do not have life without the Baptism of Christ and without participation in the body and blood of Christ.

If he says, “They will not,” then how is it that, since they do not receive eternal life, they are consequently condemned to eternal death, if they bear no original sin?

### 8

What do these men say to this—men who dare even to write their slanderous impieties [Note: [Col. 0576] The printed editions omit *audent etiam* (“even dare”). It is restored from the manuscripts.] and dare to send them to Eastern bishops? Coelestius is held to have given his assent in writing to the venerable Innocent: the letters of that renowned bishop are read, in which he writes that unbaptized infants cannot possess life. Who, moreover, will deny that it follows that those who do not have life possess death? Whence, then, does this pitiable punishment in infants arise, if there is no original guilt?

How, then, are the Roman clergy accused by these deserters from the faith and attackers of grace, under Bishop Zosimus, of prevarication—as though they had held a different opinion in the later condemnation of Coelestius and Pelagius from the one they had held under Innocent in the earlier condemnation? For when, through the letters of the venerable Innocent, the ancient faith of the Church had become clear—namely, that infants would remain in eternal death unless they were baptized in Christ—surely anyone who deviated from that judgment would rather be a prevaricator against the Roman Church. [Col. 0577]

But, by God’s favor, this did not happen. Rather, that judgment was preserved by the repeated and steadfast condemnation of Coelestius and Pelagius. Let these men understand that they themselves are guilty of the very thing with which they accuse others, and let them at last be healed of their prevarication against the faith.

For the Catholic faith does not say that human nature is evil insofar as the human being was first established by the Creator; nor is what God now creates when he makes human beings from human beings evil in itself, but rather what it derives from the fault of the first human being.

## CHAPTER V

### 9. He replies to the Pelagians’ accusations: what free will can do without grace; what Catholics think about fate

We must now examine the points which, in their letter, they set before us as accusations, and to which this is our brief reply.

We do not say that, through Adam’s sin, free will perished from human nature; but we do say that, among those subjected to the devil, it is effective for sinning, while it is not effective for living well and piously unless the human will itself has been liberated by God’s grace and aided for every good action, word, and thought.

We say that no one but the Lord God is the creator of those who are born, and that marriage was instituted not by the devil but by God himself. Nevertheless, all are born under sin because of the fault transmitted through descent, and therefore they are under the devil until they are reborn in Christ.

Nor do we assert fate under the name of grace, since we say that God’s grace is preceded by no human merits. If, however, some people prefer to call the will of almighty God by the name “fate,” we avoid profane novelties of language (1 Tim. 6:20), but we do not like to quarrel about words.

### 10

When I considered more carefully why it had seemed to them that they should accuse us of asserting fate under the name of grace, I first examined the words that follow. For this is how they thought they should accuse us:

> “Under the name of grace,” they say, “they assert fate in such a way that they say that unless God inspires an unwilling and resisting person with the desire for the good—and for the good even in its imperfect form—that person can neither turn away from evil nor seize the good.”

Then, somewhat later, when they themselves mention what they defend, I considered what they said on this matter:

> “We confess that Baptism is necessary for every age; and that grace also assists each person’s good purpose, but does not implant a pursuit of virtue in one who resists, because there is no partiality with God” (Col. 3:25).

From these words of theirs I understood that they either think, or want to be thought, to accuse us of asserting fate under the name of grace because we say that God’s grace is given not according to our merits but according to the will of him whose mercy is most compassionate, who said: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.” And it is consequently added: “So then it depends not on the one who wills or runs, but on God who has mercy” (Rom. 9:15–16). [Col. 0578]

From this, some similarly foolish person might even think or say that the Apostle is an advocate of fate. But here these men reveal themselves clearly enough. For when they accuse us of asserting fate under the name of grace because we do not say that God’s grace is given according to our merits, they undoubtedly confess that they themselves say it is given according to our merits.

Thus their blindness could not conceal or disguise the fact that they hold and think what Pelagius, out of deceptive fear, condemned when it was charged against him in the episcopal judgment at Palestine. For it was charged against him—indeed, in the words of his disciple Coelestius—that he too said, “the grace of God is given according to our merits.” Pelagius, detesting this—or at least appearing to detest it—did not delay to anathematize it with his lips alone [Note: [Col. 0578] The Vatican manuscripts read, “which he, as though detesting it,” omitting *detestans vel* (“detesting, or as though detesting”).]

But, as his later books indicate, and as the assertion of these followers of his lays bare [Note: [Col. 0578] The printed editions read *nudata* (“laid bare”). The reading is corrected from the manuscripts.], he preserved it with a deceitful heart, until later the audacity arose to put into writing what at that time his cunning had concealed through fear by denying it.

And still the Pelagian bishops do not shrink back, nor are they even ashamed to send their letters to Catholic Eastern bishops, in which they accuse us of being advocates of fate because we do not say that God’s grace is given according to our merits—something which Pelagius, fearing the Eastern bishops, neither dared to say nor could avoid condemning.

## CHAPTER VI

### 11. The accusation of fate is turned back upon the adversaries

Is it really so, sons of pride, enemies of God’s grace, new Pelagian heretics, that anyone who says that all the good merits of human beings are preceded by God’s grace, and that God’s grace is not given on account of merits—for it would not be grace if it were not given freely but were repaid as something owed to those who deserve it—is, in your view, asserting fate?

Do you yourselves not say, with whatever intention, that Baptism is necessary for everyone at every age? Do you not, in this very letter of yours, place this statement about Baptism alongside your statement about grace? Why has Baptism, which is given to infants, not by its very proximity reminded you what you ought to think about grace?

For these are your words:

> “We confess that Baptism is necessary for every age; and that grace also assists each person’s good purpose, but does not implant a pursuit of virtue in one who resists, because there is no partiality with God.”

For the moment I say nothing about what you have said concerning grace in all these words of yours. Give an account of Baptism: why do you say that it is necessary at every age? Tell us why it is necessary for infants. Surely it is because it confers something good upon them, and that something is neither small nor mediocre but great.

For although [Note: [Col. 0578] The printed editions read *si* (“if”); the manuscripts read *etsi* (“although”).] you deny that they carry the original sin which is remitted in Baptism, you do not deny—indeed, you proclaim—that through the washing of regeneration they are adopted from being sons of human beings as sons of God.

Tell us, then: those infants who were baptized in Christ and departed from the body, by what preceding merits did they receive so sublime a gift?

If you say that they earned it through the piety of their parents, you will be answered: Why is this good sometimes denied to the children of the pious and granted to the children of the impious?

For sometimes offspring born of devout parents are overtaken by death at a tender age, as fresh from the womb as possible [Note: [Col. 0578] The printed editions read *recentissimo* (“most recently”), but the manuscripts have the better reading *recentissima*, referring to *proles* (“offspring”).], before being washed in the bath of regeneration; while an infant born of enemies of Christ is baptized in Christ through the mercy of Christians. A baptized mother mourns her own unbaptized child, while a chaste woman takes up and has baptized the abandoned infant of another woman.

Here certainly the merits of the parents are irrelevant—and, by your admission, so are the merits of the infants themselves. For we know that you do not believe concerning the human soul that it lived somewhere before the earthly body [Note: [Col. 0579] The Vatican manuscripts read, “before the human or earthly body.”] and performed some good or evil deed on account of which it is joined to the flesh, where it would deserve either reward or punishment.

What, then, was the reason that obtained Baptism for this infant and denied it to the other? Do they perhaps have fate because they have no merit? Or is there partiality with the Lord in their case? For you said both things: fate first, and partiality afterward. Since both must be rejected, what remains is the merit which you wish to introduce against grace.

Answer, then, concerning the merits of infants: why do some leave the body baptized and others unbaptized, when neither the merits of their parents make them strong enough to possess, nor deprive them of, so excellent a good—that they should become sons of God from sons of human beings—while neither their parents’ merits nor their own merits are involved?

You are silent, of course [Note: [Col. 0579] The Gallican manuscripts read, “with no merits of their own; and you yourselves,” omitting “You are silent, of course.”]; and you find the charge you bring against us applying more properly to yourselves. For if, where there is no merit, you consequently say that there is fate, and for that reason wish human merit to be understood in God’s grace, lest you be compelled to confess fate, behold, you rather assert fate in the Baptism of infants, whose merit you admit is nonexistent.

But if you grant that in the case of infants who are baptized no merit at all precedes, and yet that there is no fate, why do you accuse us of being advocates of fate when we say that God’s grace is given freely for this reason: so that it may be grace, and not repaid as something owed on account of preceding merits?

You do not understand [Note: [Col. 0579] The printed editions read “not understanding, in justifying,” omitting *in*, which is restored from the manuscripts.] that, in justifying the impious, just as there are no merits precisely because it is God’s grace, so there is no fate precisely because it is God’s grace, and there is no partiality precisely because it is God’s grace.

### 12

Those who affirm fate maintain that acts and events, and even our very wills, depend upon the position of the stars at the time each person is conceived or born—the configurations they call constellations. But God’s grace surpasses not only all the stars and all the heavens, but also all the angels.

Moreover, advocates of fate attribute both human goods and evils to fate. God, however, pursues human beings in their evils by the due retribution of their merits, while he bestows good things through an undeserved grace and merciful will. He does both not through a temporal association with the stars, but through the eternal and deep counsel of his severity and goodness.

We therefore see that neither matter belongs to fate.

If [Note: [Col. 0579] The particle *if* is restored from the manuscripts.] you reply that this very benevolence of God—by which he does not follow merits but bestows undeserved goods through free goodness—ought rather to be called fate, while the Apostle calls it grace, saying, “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God, not from works, so that no one may boast” (Eph. 2:8–9), do you not pay attention? Do you not see that we do not assert fate under the name of divine grace, but that you rather call divine grace by the name of fate?

## CHAPTER VII

### 13. He refutes the accusation concerning partiality

Likewise, partiality [Note: [Col. 0580] The manuscripts read, “Likewise, partiality”; the printed editions read “Likewise, which partiality.”] (*acceptio personarum*) is rightly said to exist where the person who judges, abandoning the merits of the case about which he is judging, supports one party against another because he finds in the person something worthy of honor or pity.

But if someone has two debtors and wishes to forgive one his debt while demanding it from the other, he gives to whomever he wishes but defrauds no one. Nor should this be called partiality when there is no injustice.

Otherwise, to those who understand little, partiality might appear to exist where the master of the vineyard gave the laborers who had worked there for one hour as much as he gave those who had borne the burden and heat of the day, making equal in payment those whose labor had been so unequal.

But what did he reply to those who murmured against the master of the household on account of this supposed partiality?
