> “Friend,” he said, “I am not doing you an injustice. Did you not agree with me for a denarius? Take what is yours and go. I wish to give to this last one as I give to you. Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish? Or is your eye evil because I am good?” (Matt. 20:9–15).

Here, surely, the whole matter is one of justice: “I wish it.” “I repaid you,” he says; “I gave this man a gift. In order to give to him, I took nothing from you; I neither diminished nor denied what I owed you. Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish? Or is your eye evil because I am good?”

Therefore, just as there is no partiality here—for one is honored freely [Note: [Col. 0580] The Gallican manuscripts read “one is honored,” omitting *freely*.] without another being defrauded of what is owed to him—so also, when one person is called according to God’s purpose (Rom. 8:28) and another is not called, the one who is called receives a free gift, of which the calling itself is the beginning; while the one who is not called receives evil, because all are guilty on account of the fact that through one human being sin entered the world (Rom. 5:12).

And in that illustration of the laborers, where one denarius was received both by those who worked for one hour and by those who worked twelve times as long—although, according to human calculations, which are nevertheless vain, the latter ought to have received twelve denarii in proportion to their labor—both groups were made equal in good. They were not divided so that some were liberated and others condemned, because those who labored longer received from the master of the household both the fact that they were called in such a way as to come and the fact that they were nourished in such a way as not to fail.

But where it is said, “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wishes, and he hardens whom he wishes,” and where he makes “one vessel for honor and another for dishonor” (Rom. 9:18, 21), good is given undeservedly and freely, because the one to whom it is not given [Note: [Col. 0580] The negative particle is restored on the authority of the Gallican manuscripts.] is from the same mass; but evil is repaid deservedly and justly, because evil is not unjustly repaid to evil in the mass of perdition.

It is evil for the one to whom it is repaid, because it is his punishment; but for the one by whom it is repaid, it is good, because his action is rightly done.

Nor is there any partiality between two debtors who are equally guilty if one is forgiven and the debt is demanded from the other [Note: [Col. 0580] Lov. reads, “the debt is demanded from one.” The other books read, “the debt is demanded from the other.” The same mode of expression occurs above, no. 13: *alterum exigere*, “to demand it from the other,” rather than *ab altero exigere*.], since what is owed is equally owed by both.

### 14

But so that what we are saying may become clear through the presentation of an example, let us suppose that twins were born to some prostitute and were exposed so that others might take them up. One of them died without Baptism; the other was baptized.

What fate or fortune—which in fact are entirely nonexistent—should we say this was? What partiality could there have been, when there was none with God [Note: [Col. 0581] The printed editions read, “which there is none with God.”], even if there could have been any in these children? They certainly had nothing by which one could be preferred to the other, and they had no personal merits—whether good merits by which one might deserve to be baptized, or evil merits by which the other might deserve to die without Baptism.

Or did they have some merits derived from their parents, where the father was a fornicator and the mother a prostitute? Whatever those merits may have been, they were certainly not different in these children who died under such different conditions; they were common to both.

If, then, neither fate—because no stars decree these things—nor fortune—because chance events do not bring them about—nor any difference of persons or merits caused this, what remains, as far as the baptized child is concerned, except the grace of God, which is freely given to vessels made for honor; and, as far as the unbaptized child is concerned, the anger of God, which is repaid to vessels made for dishonor according to the merits of the mass itself? [Col. 0581]

But in the case of the one who was baptized, we compel you to confess God’s grace and demonstrate that no merit of his preceded it. As for the one who died without Baptism, why the sacrament was lacking to him—although you too admit that it is necessary for every age—and what was punished in him in this way, you must determine, since you do not want there to be original sin.

### 15

In the case of these two twins, who unquestionably had one and the same condition, the Apostle seems to have solved, as though without solving it, the difficulty of the question why one died in one way and the other in another.

For when he himself had proposed something of this kind concerning two twins, on account of which [Note: [Col. 0581] The manuscripts read “on account of which”; the printed editions read “on account of whom.”] it was said—not from works, since they had not yet done anything good or evil, but from him who calls—“The elder shall serve the younger,” and, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated,” and when he had carried the horror of this profound mystery to the point of saying, “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wishes, and he hardens whom he wishes,” he immediately perceived what this would provoke and set against himself the words of one who contradicted him, words which he would restrain by apostolic authority.

For he says:

> “You will say to me then, ‘Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?’”

And to the one who said this he replied:

> “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Will the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me thus?’ Does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?” [Note: [Col. 0581] The manuscripts read, “from the same kneaded mass.”]

Then, following this great and hidden secret as far as he judged it should be disclosed to human beings, he disclosed it, saying:

> “But if God, wishing to show his wrath and make known his power, endured with much patience vessels of wrath made ready for destruction, and in order to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory” (Rom. 9:11–23).

This is [Note: [Col. 0581] The Vatican codices read, “Here is.”] God’s grace—not only assistance but also a demonstration: assistance, certainly, in the vessels of mercy; but in the vessels of wrath, a demonstration. For in them he shows his wrath and makes known his power, because his goodness is so powerful that it makes good use even of evil things. And in them he makes known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy, since what justice in punishment demands from the vessels of wrath, grace in liberation forgives to the vessels of mercy. [Col. 0582]

Nor would the benefit freely bestowed upon some become evident unless God, by condemning others from the same mass, who are equally guilty, to a just punishment, showed what was owed to both groups.

“For who makes you different?” says the same Apostle to a man boasting as though of himself and of his own good [Note: [Col. 0582] The Vatican manuscripts read, “and of his own boasting,” omitting *bono* (“good”).]. “For who makes you different?” Surely it is from the vessels of wrath, from the mass of perdition, which through one man sent all into condemnation.

“Who makes you different?” And as though he had replied, “My faith, my purpose, my merit makes me different,” he says:

> “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7)

That is, as though it were from you that you were made different.

Therefore it is he who makes the distinction, who grants the means by which one is distinguished—removing the deserved punishment and bestowing undeserved grace. It is he who makes the distinction who, when darkness was over the abyss, said, “Let there be light,” and there was light, and he divided—that is, distinguished—between light and darkness (Gen. 1:3–4).

For when there was only darkness, he did not find something that he could distinguish; rather, by making light he created the distinction, so that it might be said to those who have been justified from the ungodly: “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8). Thus, “the one who boasts, let him boast in the Lord,” not in himself (2 Cor. 10:17).

It is he who makes the distinction who, concerning those not yet born and who had done nothing good or evil, so that his purpose according to election might stand—not from works but from him himself, who calls [Note: [Col. 0582] Lov. reads “but from him,” omitting *himself*. The other books have the fuller reading.]—said, “The elder shall serve the younger” (Gen. 25:23). And later, commending the same point through the prophet, he says, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1:2).

He spoke of election [Note: [Col. 0582] All the manuscripts read *electionem* (“election”); the printed editions read *electione* (“by election”).] where God did not find something made by another which he might choose, but himself makes what he finds. Thus it is written concerning the remnant of Israel: “The remnant was made according to the election of grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Rom. 11:5–6).

For this reason you are surely foolish when, while the truth says, “Not from works but from him who calls,” you say that Jacob was loved because of future works which God foresaw he would perform. In this way you contradict the Apostle, who says, “Not from works,” as though he could not have said, “Not from present works, but from future works.”

But he says, “Not from works,” in order to commend grace:

> “But if it is by grace, it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace.”

For grace precedes—not as something owed but as a free gift—so that good works may be done through it [Note: [Col. 0582] The Vatican and Gallican manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions omitted the words “For grace precedes—not as something owed but as a free gift”; they had instead, “grace, certainly, so that through it they may be done.”]. If good works were to precede, grace would be repaid as though on account of works, and thus grace would no longer be grace.

### 16

But so that every hiding place of your darkness might be taken away, I proposed such twins—neither assisted by the merits of their parents—so that, at the beginning of infancy, one would be baptized and the other would die without Baptism. I did this so that you would not say, as you say concerning Jacob and Esau against the Apostle, that God foresaw their future works.

For how could he have foreseen as future works what, because his foreknowledge cannot be deceived, he rather foresaw would not be future for those who would die in infancy?

Or what benefit is there for those who are snatched from this life “lest wickedness change their understanding or deceit deceive their soul” (Wis. 4:11), if even a sin that was neither committed, spoken, nor thought is punished as though it had been committed?

If it is utterly absurd, senseless, and insane to say that any human beings are condemned for sins whose guilt, as you say, they could neither inherit from their parents nor commit—or even think about—then that unbaptized twin brother of the baptized child returns to you [Note: [Col. 0583] The Gallican manuscripts omit “returns to you.”] and silently asks you why he was separated from his brother’s happiness and punished with that misery; why, when the other was adopted as a son of God [Note: [Col. 0583] The Vatican and Gallican manuscripts read, “adopted as sons of God.” The same reading occurs below, book 4, no. 2.], he himself did not receive the sacrament which, as you admit, is necessary for every age.

This is so if, just as there is neither fortune nor fate nor partiality with God, there is likewise no gift of grace without merits and no original sin.

To this infant you submit your tongue and your voice; to this speechless child you have nothing to say.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 17. The desire for even imperfect good is a gift of grace; otherwise grace would be given according to merits

Let us now examine, as far as we can, the very thing which they want to precede in a human being, so that he may be considered worthy of the assistance of grace and so that grace may be repaid to him according to his merit—not given to him as something undeserved but repaid as something owed [Note: [Col. 0583] The printed editions lacked the words “and so that grace may be repaid to him according to his merit—not given to him as something undeserved but repaid as something owed.” They are found in the Vatican manuscripts. In the Gallican manuscripts the reading is: “and so that grace may be repaid to him according to his merit, not as something undeserved; and thus grace,” and so forth.]; and thus grace may no longer be grace.

Let us nevertheless see what this thing is. They say:

> “Under the name of grace they assert fate in such a way that they say that unless God inspires an unwilling and resisting person with the desire for the good, and even with the desire for imperfect good [Note: [Col. 0583] The manuscripts read, “and even with the desire for imperfect good.” The printed editions read, “and with the desire for good in its imperfect form.”], that person can neither turn away from evil nor seize the good.”

We have shown how empty their words are concerning fate and grace. Now we must consider whether God inspires an unwilling and resisting person with the desire for good, so that he is no longer resisting or unwilling but consenting to the good and willing the good.

These men want the desire for good in a human being to begin from the human being himself, so that the merit of this beginning may be followed by the grace of completion—if they even want this much.

For Pelagius more readily says that what is good is fulfilled if grace assists it. By this addition—that is, by adding “more readily”—he plainly indicates that he holds that even if the assistance of grace is lacking, the good can nevertheless be fulfilled, though with greater difficulty, through free will. [Col. 0584]

But with regard to these men, let us not prescribe what they think in this matter on the basis of that author of the heresy. Let us allow them to be free, both with their own free will and from Pelagius himself, and instead attend to the words which they placed in the letter to which we are replying.

### 18

For they thought they should accuse us of saying that God inspires an unwilling and resisting person with the desire not merely for some good but even for imperfect good.

Perhaps, then, they preserve a place for grace in this way at least: they think that without grace a person can have the desire for good, though imperfect good; but that perfect good cannot be achieved more easily through grace, but cannot be achieved at all without grace.

Yet even in this way they say that God’s grace is given according to our merits—something which Pelagius condemned in the East because he feared being condemned by ecclesiastical acts.

For if the desire for good begins from us without God’s grace, that beginning will be the merit to which the assistance of grace comes as something owed. Thus God’s grace will not be given freely but according to our merit.

But the Lord, in replying to the future Pelagius, did not say, “Without me you can do something, though with difficulty”; he said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

And in that same evangelical statement, in replying also to these men of the future, he did not say, “Without me you can complete nothing,” but “do” nothing. For if he had said “complete,” they could say that God’s assistance was necessary not for beginning the good, which comes from us, but for completing it.

Let them hear the Apostle as well. When the Lord says, “Without me you can do nothing,” he comprehends both beginning and completion in this one word. But the Apostle, as an interpreter of the Lord’s saying, distinguishes both more clearly:

> “He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus” (Phil. 1:6).

But in the Holy Scriptures, in that same Apostle, we find still more concerning the matter of which we are speaking.

For we are now speaking about the desire for good. If they want this desire to begin from us and to be perfected by the Lord, let them see what answer they will give to the Apostle when he says:

> “Not that we are competent to think anything as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Cor. 3:5).

The Apostle says “to think something”—obviously something good [Note: [Col. 0584] The Vatican manuscripts add “from us” here.]. But thinking is less than desiring.

For we think everything that we desire, but we do not desire everything that we think, since sometimes we think even what we do not desire. Since thinking is therefore less than desiring—for a person can think of something good which he does not yet desire, and later, by progressing, desire what he previously thought of without desiring it—how are we not competent, as though from ourselves, for what is less, namely, thinking something good, but our sufficiency is from God, while for what is greater, namely, desiring something good, we are competent through free will without divine assistance?

Nor does the Apostle say here, “We are not competent to think what is perfect as though from ourselves”; rather, he says, “to think something,” the opposite of which is “nothing.”

Hence comes the Lord’s saying:

> “Without me you can do nothing.”

## CHAPTER IX

### 19. He interprets the Scriptures which the Pelagians misuse

But surely, when it is written, “It belongs to a human being to prepare the heart, and the answer of the tongue is from the Lord” (Prov. 16:1), they are deceived because they do not understand it correctly and suppose that preparing the heart—that is, beginning the good—belongs to a human being without the assistance of God’s grace.

Far be it from the sons of promise to understand it in this way, as though, when they hear the Lord saying, “Without me you can do nothing,” they should convict him by saying, “Behold, without you we can prepare the heart”; or as though, when they hear the Apostle Paul say, “Not that we are competent to think anything as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God,” they should convict him too by saying, “Behold, from ourselves we are competent to prepare the heart, and therefore also to think something good.”

For who can prepare a good heart without a good thought? [Note: [Col. 0585] In Am., Er., and Lov. *sine* (“without”) was omitted. It was restored in several later editions, supported by the Gallican and Vatican manuscripts.]

Far be it from them to understand the passage in this way, unless they are defenders of their proud free will and deserters of the Catholic faith.

For this reason it is written, “It belongs to a human being to prepare the heart, and the answer of the tongue is from the Lord”: a person prepares the heart, but not without the assistance of God, who touches the heart in such a way that the person prepares the heart [Note: [Col. 0585] Am. reads: “Who touches you? The heart. Let the human being prepare the heart.” Er. and Lov. read: “who touches the heart; the human being prepares the heart.” In several later editions this was corrected conjecturally to: “who, if he touches the heart, the human being prepares the heart.” This is correct, but we have preferred the other reading because it is confirmed by the authority of all our Gallican and Vatican manuscripts.].

But in the answer of the tongue—that is, in the fact that the divine tongue responds to the prepared heart—the human being performs no work; everything comes from the Lord God.

### 20

For just as it is said, “It belongs to a human being to prepare the heart, and the answer of the tongue is from the Lord,” so it is also said, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it” (Ps. 80:11). [Col. 0586]

Although we cannot open our mouth unless he assists us, without whom we can do nothing, we open it through his assistance and through our own action; but the Lord fills it without our action.

For what is preparing the heart and opening the mouth except preparing the will? Yet in the same Scriptures we read, “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 8, according to the Septuagint), and, “You will open my lips, and my mouth will proclaim your praise” (Ps. 50:17).

Behold, God admonishes us to prepare the will in what we read: “It belongs to a human being to prepare the heart.” Yet, for a person to do this, God assists him, because “the will is prepared by the Lord.”

And he says, “Open your mouth,” issuing the command in such a way [Note: [Col. 0585] The printed editions read, “And he will open the mouth, thus commanding,” omitting *dicit* (“he says”). The text is corrected according to the manuscripts.] that no one can do it unless he himself acts by assisting the one to whom it is said, “You will open my lips.”

Are some of these men so foolish [Note: [Col. 0585] The Gallican and Vatican manuscripts read: “Or are these men so utterly foolish?” A possible reading is “Or are they so foolish?”] as to insist that the mouth is one thing and the lips another, and in astonishing folly say that a human being opens the mouth while God opens human lips?

Yet God restrains them even from this absurdity when he says to his servant Moses:

> “I will open your mouth, and I will instruct you what you ought to say” (Exod. 4:12).

Thus, in the statement, “Open your mouth, and I will fill it,” one part appears to belong to the human being and the other to God; but in the statement, “I will open your mouth, and I will instruct you,” both belong to God.

Why is this, except that in the one case he cooperates with the human being who acts, while in the other he alone acts?

21. Therefore God does many good things in a human being that the human being does not do; but the human being does nothing that God does not cause the human being to do. Accordingly, the desire for the good would not come to a human being from the Lord if the good were not good; but if it is good, it comes to us only from him who is supremely and immutably good. For what is the desire for the good except love, about which the Apostle John speaks unambiguously when he says, “Love is from God” (1 John 4:7)? Its beginning does not come from us and its perfection from God; rather, if love is from God, it is wholly from God for us.

May God avert the madness by which we put ourselves first in his gifts and him second, since “his mercy shall go before me” (Ps. 58:11); and he is the one to whom it is faithfully and truly sung, “For you went before him with the blessing of sweetness” (Ps. 20:4). And what is more suitably understood here than the very desire for the good of which we are speaking? For the good begins to be desired when it begins to become sweet. But when good is done out of fear of punishment, not love of righteousness, it is not yet done well; nor is what appears to be done in the deed done in the heart, when a person would prefer not to do it if he could do so with impunity.

Therefore, the “blessing of sweetness” is the grace of God by which it comes about in us that what he commands us pleases us and we desire it—that is, love it. If God does not go before us in this, it is not only not perfected by us; it is not even begun by us. For if without him we can do nothing, surely we can neither begin nor perfect anything without him. To begin, it has been said, “His mercy shall go before me”; to perfect, it has been said, “His mercy shall follow me” (Ps. 22:6).

## CHAPTER X

### 22. According to whose purpose the elect are called

What, then, is the meaning of the statement that follows, where they report what they themselves think and say that they confess that “grace also assists each person’s good purpose, but does not implant a striving for virtue in one who resists”? They speak as though a person possessed by himself, without God’s assistance, a good purpose and a striving for virtue, by the prior merit of which he would deserve to be assisted by the grace that follows.

Perhaps they think that the Apostle said, “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to purpose” [Note: [Col. 0586] The Ambrosian, Erasmian, and some Gallican manuscripts have here and below *cooperantur* (“work together”), rather than *cooperatur* (“works together”).] (Rom. 8:28), in such a way that he intended the human purpose to be understood—the purpose that is followed by the mercy of God who calls, as though by a good merit. They do not understand that the words “who are called according to purpose” were said so that God’s purpose, not a human being’s, might be understood: the purpose by which he chose, before the foundation of the world, those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Rom. 8:28–29; Eph. 1:4).

For not all who are called are called according to purpose, since “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20:16). Those, therefore, who are called according to purpose are the ones chosen before the foundation of the world.

The same purpose of God is meant by what I have already cited concerning the twins Esau and Jacob: “That the purpose of God according to election might remain, not because of works but because of him who calls,” it was said, “The elder shall serve the younger” (Rom. 9:11–13).

This purpose of God is also mentioned in the passage where the Apostle, writing to Timothy, says: “Work together for the Gospel according to the power of God, who saved us and called us with his holy calling, not according to our works but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal ages, but has now been manifested through the appearing of our Savior Jesus Christ” (2 Tim. 1:8–10).

This, then, is the purpose of God of which it is said: “All things work together for good for those who are called according to purpose.”

The good purpose of a human being is indeed assisted by subsequent grace, but it would not itself exist unless grace preceded it. The striving of a human being that is called good, although it is assisted by grace once it has begun to exist, nevertheless does not begin without grace; rather, it is inspired by him of whom the Apostle says, “But thanks be to God, who gave the same earnestness for you in the heart of Titus” (2 Cor. 8:16). If God gives someone the earnestness to act for others, who else will give him the earnestness to act for himself? [Note: [Col. 0587] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have, “to act for himself.”]

[Col. 0588] 23. Since these things are so, I see nothing commanded to a human being in the Holy Scriptures for the purpose of proving free choice that is not found either to be given from God’s goodness or to be demanded in order to demonstrate the assistance of grace. Nor does a human being at all begin to be changed from evil to good through the beginning of faith unless God’s unmerited and gratuitous mercy works this change in him.

Recalling his own thought concerning this mercy, someone says, as we read in the Psalms: “Will God forget to show mercy? Or will he restrain his mercies in his anger? And I said, ‘Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High’” (Ps. 76:10–11). When he said, “Now I have begun,” he did not say, “This is the change of my free choice,” but “of the right hand of the Most High.”

Thus the grace of God should be understood in such a way that from the beginning of his good change to the end of its completion, whoever glories should glory in the Lord (2 Cor. 10:17). For just as no one can perfect the good without the Lord, so no one can begin without the Lord [Note: [Col. 0588] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “For just as no one can begin the good without the Lord, so no one can perfect it without the Lord.”].

But here let this volume end, so that the reader’s attention may be refreshed and restored for what follows.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0587]

He proceeds to refute the remaining accusations that the Pelagians maliciously brought against us in the same letter sent to Thessalonica. Against their heresy, he explains what true Catholics say about the usefulness of the Law; what they teach concerning the effect and power of Baptism; what they say about the difference between the two Testaments, the old and the new; what they say about the righteousness and perfection of the Prophets and Apostles; what they affirm concerning the designation of Christ as “sin,” when he is said to have condemned sin concerning sin in the likeness of sinful flesh, or to have himself been made sin; and finally, what they profess concerning the fulfillment of the commandments in the life to come.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1. Introduction

The accusations they maliciously bring against us continue; they have not yet begun to set out fully what they themselves think. But lest the length of the volumes become wearisome, we divided the accusations they bring into two books. Having completed the former, which is the second book of this entire work, we now begin the other and join it to the first and second as the third.

## CHAPTER II

### 2. The Pelagians’ accusation concerning the use of the Old Law

They say that “we claim that the Law of the Old Testament was not given for the purpose of justifying those who obeyed it, but so that it might become the cause of a more serious sin” [Note: [Col. 0587] The printed editions consistently have *gravior* (“more serious”), but the manuscripts correct this to *gravioris* (“of a more serious [sin]”).].

They utterly fail to understand what we say about the Law, because we say what the Apostle says—an Apostle whom they do not understand. Who could say that those who obey the Law are not justified, when, unless they were justified, they could not obey it? But we say that through the Law it comes about that one hears what God wishes to be done; through grace, however, it comes about that the Law is obeyed.

“For,” says the Apostle, “not the hearers of the Law are righteous before God, but the doers of the Law shall be justified” (Rom. 2:13). Thus the Law makes hearers of righteousness; grace makes doers.

“For what was impossible for the Law,” says the same Apostle, “in that it was weakened through the flesh, God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and concerning sin condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteousness of the Law might be fulfilled in us, who do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit” (Rom. 8:3–4).

This is what we say: let them pray that they may at some time understand, rather than quarrel so that they may never understand. For it is impossible for the Law to be fulfilled through the flesh—that is, through carnal presumption, by which the proud, ignorant of God’s righteousness, meaning the righteousness that comes from God by which a human being becomes righteous, and wishing to establish their own, are not subject to God’s righteousness, as though the Law could be fulfilled by their free choice without divine assistance (Rom. 10:3).

Therefore the righteousness of the Law is fulfilled in those who do not walk according to the flesh—that is, according to the human being who is ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishes to establish his own—but who walk according to the Spirit. And who walks according to the Spirit except whoever is led by the Spirit of God? “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are sons of God” (Rom. 8:14).

Therefore, “the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). Nor is the letter evil because it kills; rather, it convicts the wicked of transgression. For “the Law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.” “Therefore,” he says, “did that which is good become death to me? By no means! But sin, so that it might appear to be sin, worked death in me through that which is good, so that sin might become exceedingly sinful through the commandment [Note: [Col. 0589] The manuscripts consistently read “that sin might become exceedingly sinful.” The printed editions have “that sinning might become exceedingly sinful.”]” (Rom. 7:12–13).

This is what “the letter kills” means. For “the sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the Law” (1 Cor. 15:56). By forbidding, it increases the desires of sin and thereby kills, unless grace gives life by coming to the aid of the sinner.

### 3. The accusation concerning the purpose of the Law

This is what we say; this is why they accuse us of saying that “the Law was given so that it might be the cause of a more serious sin”: they do not listen to the Apostle, who says, “For the Law produces wrath; but where there is no Law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15); and, “The Law was established for the sake of transgression” [Note: [Col. 0589] The Gallican manuscripts have “was proposed.” The Greek is *prosetethē* (“was appointed/established”).], until the offspring should come to whom the promise was made; and, “If a Law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly be from the Law; but Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ” (Gal. 3:19, 21–22).

This is why the Old Testament, from Mount Sinai where the Law was given, “begets into slavery,” and this is Hagar. “But we,” he says, “are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman” (Gal. 4:24, 31).

Therefore those are not children of the free woman who received the letter of the Law, by which they could be shown to be not only sinners but also transgressors; rather, they are the children of the free woman who received the Spirit of grace, by which the holy, righteous, and good Law itself can be fulfilled.

This is what we say: let them attend, and not contend; let them be enlightened, and not bring accusations.

## CHAPTER III

### 4. The accusation concerning the effect of Baptism

They say, “They also assert that Baptism does not truly make people new—that is, that it does not grant full remission of sins—but contend that people become children of God in part, while in part they remain children of the world, that is, children of the devil.”

They lie, they lay traps, they evade the issue. We do not say this. For we say that all human beings who are children of the devil are also children of the world, but we do not say that all children of the world are also children of the devil.

Far be it from us to say that the holy fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and others of this kind, were children of the devil when they begot children through marriage, or that the faithful who continue to beget children even now and hereafter are such. Yet we cannot contradict the Lord when he says, “The children of this world marry and are given in marriage” (Luke 20:34).

Some, therefore, are children of this world and yet are not children of the devil. For although the devil is the author and prince of all sins, not every sin makes people children of the devil. The children of God also sin, since “if they say that they have no sin, they deceive themselves, and the truth is not in them” (1 John 1:8). But they sin in the condition in which they are still children of this world; insofar as they are children of God, they do not sin, because “everyone who has been born of God does not sin” (1 John 3:9).

Unbelief makes people children of the devil. This is properly called “sin,” as though it were the only sin, when no specification is added concerning what kind of sin it is. Thus, when the Apostle is mentioned without saying which apostle, no one understands anyone but Paul, because he is better known through the greater number of his Epistles and worked harder than all the others (1 Cor. 15:10).

Accordingly, when the Lord says of the Holy Spirit, “He will convict the world concerning sin,” he intended unbelief to be understood. For when he explained this, he said, “Concerning sin, because they did not believe in me” (John 16:8–9). And where he says, “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John 15:22), he does not mean that they previously had no sin; rather, he intended that very disbelief to be understood—the disbelief by which they did not believe even the one who was present and speaking to them. They belonged to the one of whom the Apostle says, “According to the ruler of the power of the air, who now works in the sons of disbelief” (Eph. 2:2).

Therefore, in those in whom there is no faith, there are children of the devil, because in the inner person they have no basis on account of which whatever is committed through human weakness, ignorance, or any evil will may be forgiven [Note: [Col. 0590] The Vatican manuscripts have “whatever is committed in the name of weakness or ignorance.” The Gallican manuscripts have “whatever is committed through human weakness,” omitting the first “or.”].

But those who are children of God—even though, if they say that they have no sin, they deceive themselves and the truth is not in them—when they confess their sins, as follows (which the children of the devil do not do, or do not do according to the faith proper to the children of God), find that “he is faithful and righteous to forgive them their sins and cleanse them from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:8–9).

For a fuller understanding of what we are saying, let Jesus himself be heard. He was certainly speaking to the children of God when he said: “If you, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him?” (Matt. 7:11). For if they were not children of God, he would not say to them, “Your Father who is in heaven.” Yet he says that they are evil and know how to give good things to their children.

Are they evil, then, insofar as they are children of God? By no means. They are evil insofar as they are still children of the world, although they have already become children of God through the pledge of the Holy Spirit.

### 5. What Baptism removes and what remains

Baptism therefore washes away all sins—absolutely all sins: sins of deeds, words, and thoughts; whether original or added; whether committed in ignorance or knowingly. But it does not remove the weakness against which the regenerate person struggles when he fights the good fight, and to which he consents when, as a human being, he is overtaken in some offense (Gal. 6:1). Because of the former he rejoices in giving thanks; because of the latter he groans in offering prayers.

For the former he says, “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” (Ps. 115:3); for the latter, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12).

For the former he says, “I will love you, Lord, my strength” (Ps. 17:2); for the latter, “Have mercy on me, Lord, for I am weak” (Ps. 6:3).

For the former he says, “My eyes are always toward the Lord, for he will draw my feet out of the snare” (Ps. 24:15); for the latter, “My eye is troubled because of anger” (Ps. 30:10).

The divine Scriptures are full of countless such passages, spoken by the children of God in faith, in alternating expressions [Note: [Col. 0590] The manuscripts have “in alternating voices.”], sometimes rejoicing in God’s blessings, sometimes grieving over our evils, for as long as they remain, because of the weakness of this life, also children of this world [Note: [Col. 0590] The printed editions have “for as long as they remain children also of the world,” omitting “of this,” which is found in the manuscripts.] (Col. 0591).

Yet God distinguishes them from the children of the devil not only by the washing of regeneration but also by the integrity of the faith that works through love (Gal. 5:6), because “the righteous lives by faith” (Rom. 1:17).

This weakness, with which we struggle until the death of the body through alternating failure and progress, and in which it makes a great difference what prevails in us, will be consumed by another regeneration [Note: [Col. 0591] The printed editions have: “But this is the weakness”; and shortly afterward, “until it is consumed by another regeneration.” On the authority of the manuscripts, we have removed “is” and “until.” In the same sentence the Vatican manuscripts read, “what now prevails in us.”]. Concerning this the Lord says, “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit on twelve thrones” (Matt. 19:28), and so forth.

Here, without any ambiguity, he calls the final resurrection “regeneration.” The Apostle Paul also calls it adoption and redemption, saying: “But we ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body” (Rom. 8:23).

Have we not been regenerated, adopted, and redeemed through the holy washing? And yet there remains a regeneration, adoption, and redemption that will come at the end. We must now patiently await it, so that then we may no longer be children of this world in any respect.

Whoever, therefore, diminishes what we now receive through Baptism corrupts the faith; but whoever attributes to it now what we shall indeed receive through it, but only afterward, cuts off hope.

For if someone asks me whether we have been saved through Baptism, I cannot deny it, since the Apostle says, “He saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit” (Titus 3:5). But if he asks whether through that same washing he has already saved us in every possible respect, I will answer, “That is not so.”

For the same Apostle says again: “For in hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Rom. 8:24–25).

The salvation of the human being has therefore taken place in Baptism, because the sin which he inherited from his parents was forgiven, along with whatever he himself had personally committed before Baptism [Note: [Col. 0591] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “whatever sin he himself committed.”]. But his salvation will afterward be so complete that he will be unable to sin at all [Note: [Col. 0591] The printed editions have “but the salvation of the human being may be so complete.” The Vatican and Gallican manuscripts together provide the corrected reading.].

## CHAPTER IV

### 6. The accusation concerning the Old Testament and the ancient righteous

### The Old Testament as a figure of the New Testament. The saints of the Old Testament belong to the New Testament.

Since these things are so, the other accusations they subsequently bring against us are also refuted. For what Catholic could say what they falsely claim that we say: “The Holy Spirit was not an assistant of virtue in the Old Testament,” unless we understand the Old Testament in the way the Apostle says, “From Mount Sinai, generating into slavery” (Gal. 4:24)?

But because the New Testament was prefigured in it, those men of God who understood this at that time are shown, according to the distribution of the ages, to have been indeed administrators and bearers of the Old Testament, but heirs of the New.

Or shall we deny that the person who says, “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Ps. 50:12), belongs to the New Testament? Or the one who says, “He placed my feet upon a rock, and directed my steps, and put a new song into my mouth, a hymn to our God” (Ps. 39:3–4)?

Or shall we deny that the father of the faithful, who lived before the Old Testament that comes from Mount Sinai, belongs to the New Testament? Concerning him the Apostle says:

“Brothers, I speak according to human judgment: even a human covenant, once confirmed, no one annuls or adds to. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring. He does not say, ‘And to offsprings,’ as though referring to many, but as referring to one: ‘And to your offspring,’ who is Christ. Now this is what I say: the Law, which came four hundred and thirty years later, does not invalidate a covenant previously confirmed by God, so as to cancel the promise. For if the inheritance is from the Law, it is no longer from the promise; but God granted it to Abraham through the promise.”

### 7. The covenant confirmed to Abraham is the New Testament

Here, if we ask whether this covenant, which he says was confirmed by God and cannot be invalidated by the Law that came four hundred and thirty years later, should be understood as new or old, who would hesitate to answer, “New”—but hidden in prophetic mysteries until the time came when it would be revealed in Christ?

For if we say “old,” what will be the covenant that “generates into slavery from Mount Sinai”? The Law was given there four hundred and thirty years later. Paul confirms that this Law cannot invalidate the covenant of promise made to Abraham; and he wants what was done with Abraham to belong rather to us, whom he wishes to be children of the free woman, not of the slave woman; heirs through promise, not through the Law. He says: “For if the inheritance is from the Law, it is no longer from the promise; but God granted it to Abraham through the promise” [Note: [Col. 0592] The Vatican manuscripts consistently read, “God granted it to Abraham through the reaffirmed promise.”].

Thus the Law, which was given four hundred and thirty years later, entered in so that transgression might abound, when the pride of a human being presuming upon his own righteousness is convicted through the transgression; and “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Rom. 5:20), through the faith of the humble person who fails under the Law [Note: [Col. 0592] The Gallican manuscripts have: “through faith; here the humility of the person who fails under the Law is now shown,” and so forth.] and flees to God’s mercy.

Therefore, after saying, “For if the inheritance is from the Law, it is no longer from the promise; but God granted it to Abraham through the promise,” as though someone were asking him, “Why, then, was the Law given afterward?” he added and said, “What, then, is the Law?” To this question he immediately replied, “It was established for the sake of transgression” [Note: [Col. 0592] The Vatican manuscripts here and below have “was established.”], until the offspring should come to whom the promise had been made (Gal. 3:15–19).

He says the same thing again in this way: “For if those who are of the Law are heirs, faith is emptied and the promise is annulled. For the Law produces wrath; but where there is no Law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:14–15).

What he says in the former passage—“For if the inheritance is from the Law, it is no longer from the promise; but God granted it to Abraham through the promise”—he says in the latter as follows: “For if those who are of the Law are heirs, faith is emptied and the promise is annulled.” He sufficiently shows that what God granted to Abraham through the promise belongs to our faith, which certainly belongs to the New Testament.

And what he says in the former passage—“What, then, is the Law?”—and answers, “It was established for the sake of transgression,” he similarly adds in the latter: “For the Law produces wrath; but where there is no Law, neither is there transgression.”

### 8. The righteous before and after Moses are heirs of the promise

Whether Abraham, therefore, or the righteous who lived before him, or those who lived after him up to Moses himself, through whom the covenant was given from Mount Sinai, generating into slavery; whether the other Prophets after Moses and the holy men of God up to John the Baptist—all are children of promise and grace according to Isaac, the son of the free woman. They are heirs of God, not according to the Law but according to the promise, and joint heirs with Christ.

Far be it from us to deny that righteous Noah, the righteous of earlier times, and all who may have been either conspicuously or secretly righteous from Noah up to Abraham belong to the heavenly Jerusalem, which is our mother, although they are found to have existed earlier in time [Note: [Col. 0593] The printed editions have “although she existed earlier in time.” The manuscripts have “although they existed earlier in time.”] than Sarah, who bore the prophecy and figure of that very free mother [Note: [Col. 0593] The Gallican manuscripts have “bears.”].

How much more, then, must all who pleased God after Abraham be regarded as children of promise, since the promise itself was so clearly declared to Abraham that he was called “the father of many nations” (Gen. 17:4–5)? For the generation of the righteous is not found to be more genuine from Abraham onward; rather, the prophecy is found to be clearer.

### 9. Those who belong to the Old Testament

But those who belong to the Old Testament—which is from Mount Sinai, generating into slavery, and which is Hagar—are those who, after receiving the holy, righteous, and good Law, think that the letter alone can suffice for them unto life. Therefore they do not seek divine mercy by which they may become doers of the Law. Instead, ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own righteousness, they are not subject to God’s righteousness (Rom. 10:3).

Of this kind was the multitude that murmured against God in the wilderness and made an idol, and that which, already in the promised land itself, committed fornication after foreign gods. But this multitude too was strongly rejected within the Old Testament itself.

Those also who were there and pursued only the earthly promises that God offers there, ignorant of what those promises signify in relation to the New Testament, kept God’s commandments out of love of obtaining those promises and fear of losing them. Indeed, they did not keep them; they merely seemed to themselves to keep them.

For faith did not work in them through love (Gal. 5:6), but earthly desire and carnal fear. Whoever acts according to the commandments in this way undoubtedly acts unwillingly; and thus he does not act in his heart. For he would much rather not act at all, if he were permitted to do so with impunity according to the things he desires and fears [Note: [Col. 0593] Thus the Vatican manuscripts. The printed editions have “he would rather not act.”].

Accordingly, he is guilty within that very will, where God himself, who commands, looks.

Such were the children of the earthly Jerusalem, concerning whom the Apostle says: “She is in slavery with her children,” belonging to the Old Testament from Mount Sinai, which generates into slavery and is Hagar (Gal. 4:24–25).

Those who crucified the Lord and remained in the same unbelief belonged to this class. Their children too, in the immense multitude of the Jews, still belong to it, although the New Testament has now been disclosed and confirmed through Christ’s blood, as was prophesied, and the Gospel has been proclaimed from the river where he was baptized and began his ministry (Matt. 3:16–17) to the ends of the earth.

These Jews, in accordance with the prophecies that they read, are dispersed throughout all lands, so that Christian truth may not lack testimony even from their own books.

### 10. The Law is good, and its moral precepts remain necessary

God therefore also established the Old Testament, because it pleased him, until the fullness of time, to veil heavenly promises beneath earthly promises set forth as a kind of reward; and to give a people intent upon earthly goods, and therefore possessing a hardened heart, a spiritual law nevertheless written on tablets of stone.

Apart from the sacramental observances of the ancient books, which were commanded solely for the purpose of signifying—although, since they too are to be understood spiritually, the Law is rightly called spiritual in them as well—the remaining precepts that concern piety and good morals, and that cannot by any interpretation be referred to some other signification but must be done exactly as they are stated: no one will doubt that this Law of God was necessary not only for that people then but also for us now, in order to establish a rightly ordered life.

For if Christ has taken away from us the very burdensome yoke of numerous observances—so that we are not circumcised in the flesh, do not sacrifice animal victims, do not rest from even necessary works when the Sabbath returns after the cycle of seven days, and do not observe other things of this kind—but has taught us to hold them spiritually, and, once the shadows that signify have been removed, to keep watch in the light of the realities signified, shall we for that reason say that what is written does not concern us: that whoever finds another person’s lost property must return it to the one who lost it (Lev. 6:3–4), and the many other similar commandments by which one learns to live piously and rightly?

And what of the Decalogue itself, contained on those two tablets of stone, apart from the carnal observance of the Sabbath, which signifies spiritual sanctification and rest? Who could say that Christians ought not to observe that they serve the one God in religious obedience; that they do not worship an idol; that they do not take the name of the Lord in vain; that they honor their parents; that they do not commit adultery, murder, theft, or false testimony; and that they do not covet a wife or any possession belonging to another (Exod. 20)?

Who is so impious as to say that he does not keep these commandments of the Law because he is a Christian and is established not under the Law but under grace?

### 11. The difference between serving under the Law and obeying under grace

But this is the great difference: those who are under the Law do these things because the letter kills, motivated by the desire to obtain earthly happiness or by fear of losing it. Therefore they do not truly do them, because carnal desire, by which sin is exchanged or rather increased [Note: [Col. 0594] Here, on the authority of the manuscripts, we add “by which sin is exchanged or rather increased.”], is not healed by another desire.

These belong to the Old Testament, which generates into slavery, because carnal fear and desire make them slaves, not evangelical faith, hope, and love, which make people free.

But those who are under grace, whom the Spirit gives life, do these things through faith [Note: [Col. 0595] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “through faith and.”], which works through love, in hope of good things—not carnal but spiritual, not earthly but heavenly, not temporal but eternal. Above all, they believe in the Mediator, through whom they do not doubt that the Spirit of grace is supplied to them, so that they may do these things well and may be forgiven when they sin.

These belong to the New Testament: children of promise, regenerated by God the Father and the free woman [Note: [Col. 0595] The printed editions have “and regenerated.” We follow the manuscripts.].

All the righteous of ancient times belonged to this class, including Moses himself, the minister of the Old Testament and heir of the New. For they lived by the one and same faith by which we live: they believed that the incarnation, passion, and resurrection of Christ would take place, whereas we believe that they have taken place.

This continued up to John the Baptist, as though he were a certain boundary of the former dispensation. He did not signify through some shadow of the future, allegorical meaning, or prophetic foretelling that the Mediator himself would come; rather, pointing him out with his finger, he said, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29).

It was as though he were saying: “The one whom many righteous people desired to see, in whose coming they believed from the beginning of the human race, concerning whom the promises were spoken to Abraham, about whom Moses wrote, and to whom the Law and the Prophets bear witness—behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world.”

From John onward, the things that all the righteous of earlier times believed, hoped for, and desired as future began to be spoken of concerning Christ as past or present.

The faith, therefore, is the same both in those who were Christians beforehand in reality though not yet in name, and in those who are not only Christians but are also called by that name. In both groups the grace through the Holy Spirit is the same.

Therefore the Apostle says: “Since we have the same Spirit of faith, according to what is written, ‘I believed, and therefore I spoke’; we also believe, and therefore we speak” (2 Cor. 4:13).

### 12. The apostolic distinction between the Old and New Testaments

The Old Testament is therefore called, according to the usage that has now become established in speech, the Law and all the Prophets who prophesied up to John. It is more distinctly called the Old Instrument than the Old Testament.

But it is called something else when the authority of the Apostles uses the term, whether expressing the name itself or signifying it. The Apostle expresses it when he says: “To this day, whenever Moses is read, the same veil remains over the reading of the Old Testament; it is not revealed, because it is abolished in Christ” (2 Cor. 3:14–15). In this way he clearly refers the Old Testament to the ministry of Moses.

Likewise he says, “So that we may serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter” (Rom. 7:6), signifying the same Testament by the name “letter.”

In another passage he says: “He made us competent ministers of a New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit; for the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” [Note: [Col. 0595] Thus the manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek. The printed editions have “not of the letter but of the Spirit” with the forms altered.]. Here too, by mentioning the New Testament, he intended the Old to be understood [Col. 0596].

Much more clearly, although he does not say either “old” or “new,” he distinguishes the two Testaments by means of Abraham’s two sons, one by the slave woman and the other by the free woman, as we mentioned above.

For what could be clearer than his saying: “Tell me, you who desire to be under the Law, do you not hear the Law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman. But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one by the free woman was born through promise. These things are an allegory. For these are the two Testaments: one indeed from Mount Sinai, generating into slavery, which is Hagar. For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia, joined to the Jerusalem that now exists; for she is in slavery with her children. But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.”

What could be clearer, more certain, or further removed from every obscurity and ambiguity for the children of promise? And shortly afterward: “But we, brothers,” he says, “are children of promise according to Isaac.” Again, shortly afterward: “But we, brothers, are not children of the slave woman but of the free woman; with the freedom with which Christ has set us free” (Gal. 4:21–31).

Let us therefore choose whether we shall call the ancient righteous children of the slave woman or of the free woman. Far be it from us to call them children of the slave woman. Therefore, if they are children of the free woman [Note: [Col. 0596] Thus the Vatican manuscripts. The printed editions have “therefore, children of the free woman,” omitting “if.”], they belong to the New Testament in the Holy Spirit, whom the Apostle sets over against the letter that kills as the Spirit who gives life.

For how could those whose words and books we use to refute and convict these most foolish and ungrateful enemies of the same grace not belong to the grace of the New Testament? [Note: [Col. 0596] The manuscripts have “whom we convict by refuting them.”]

### 13.

But someone will say: How is that called old which was made through Moses four hundred and thirty years later (Gal. 3:17), while that is called new which was made to Abraham so many years earlier? Whoever is moved by this question not contentiously but earnestly should understand first that, when one is called old because it came earlier and the other new because it came later, it is their revelations that are being considered under these names, not their institutions.

For the Old Testament was revealed through Moses, through whom the law was given—holy, just, and good (Rom. 7:12)—through which there would be not the abolition but the recognition of sin; and by it the proud, who wished to establish their own righteousness as though they did not need divine assistance, would be convicted, and, having been made guilty by the letter, would flee to the Spirit of grace—not to be justified by their own righteousness, but by God’s, that is, by the righteousness they would have from God. For, as the same Apostle says, “Through the law comes knowledge of sin; but now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law, testified to by the Law and the Prophets” (Rom. 3:20–21).

The law, precisely because no one is justified by it, bears witness to God’s righteousness. For that no one is justified before God by the law is clear from the statement, “The righteous person lives by faith” (Gal. 3:11). Thus, when the law does not justify the impious person convicted of transgression, it sends him to God, who justifies, and in this way bears witness to God’s righteousness.

The Prophets, moreover, bear witness to God’s righteousness by foretelling Christ, “who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption; so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord’” (1 Cor. 1:30–31).

This law, however, was hidden from the beginning, when nature itself convicted unrighteous people because they did to others what they would not have wished done to themselves. But the revelation of the New Testament took place in Christ, when he was manifested in the flesh; in him appeared the righteousness of God—that is, the righteousness which human beings have from God. For this is why he says, “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law.”

Here, then, is the reason why the one is called the Old Testament: because it was revealed at an earlier time, while this one is called the New Testament because it was revealed later. Further, the Old Testament belongs to the old human being, from whom it is necessary for a person to begin; the New belongs to the new human being, into whom a person ought to pass from oldness.

Therefore, earthly promises are found in the former and heavenly promises in the latter. This too belonged to God’s mercy, lest anyone suppose that even some earthly happiness could be bestowed on anyone except by the Lord, the Creator of the universe. But if God is worshiped on account of that happiness, the worship is servile and belongs to the children of the slave woman. If, however, he is worshiped on account of God himself, so that in eternal life God may be all in all, the service is free and belongs to the children of the free woman, who is our mother, eternal in heaven. She formerly appeared barren, when she did not have conspicuous children; but now we see fulfilled in her what was prophesied:

> “Rejoice, barren woman, who do not bear;  
> break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail;  
> for the children of the deserted woman are more numerous  
> than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1),

that is, more numerous than those of that Jerusalem which was, in a certain sense, married by the bond of the law and serves together with her children.

Therefore, during the time of the Old Testament, we say that the Holy Spirit was in those who even then were, according to Isaac, children of promise—not merely their helper, as these people think sufficient for their doctrine, but also the giver of virtue, which they deny, attributing virtue instead to free choice. They are contradicted by those fathers who knew that they should cry out to God in true devotion:

> “I will love you, Lord, my strength” (Ps. 17:2).

### Chapter V

#### 14. The calumny concerning the righteousness of the Prophets and Apostles

They also say:

> “We do not define all the Apostles or Prophets as fully holy; rather, we say that they were less evil in comparison with worse people, and that this is the righteousness to which God bears witness. Just as the prophet says that Sodom was justified in comparison with the Jews (Ezek. 16:46–57), so we too say, in comparison with criminals, that the saints exercised some virtue.”  
> [Note: [Col. 0597] The manuscripts read *aliquam sanctos*; the printed editions read *aliquos sanctos*.]

Far be it from us to say such things. Either they are unable to understand, or unwilling to pay attention, or, out of a desire to slander, pretend not to know what we say. Let them hear, then—either they themselves, or rather those whom they strive to deceive, the ignorant and uneducated.

Our faith—that is, the Catholic faith—distinguishes the righteous from the unrighteous not by the law of works but by the very law of faith, because “the righteous person lives by faith.” Through this distinction it happens that a person may lead a life without murder, theft, or false testimony; without desiring anyone else’s property; giving parents the honor due to them; chaste even to continence from every kind of sexual intercourse, including marital intercourse; extraordinarily generous in almsgiving; most patient under injuries; not merely taking nothing belonging to another, but not even reclaiming what has been taken from him; or even selling all his possessions and distributing them to the poor, possessing nothing as his own—yet, with all these apparently praiseworthy habits, if he does not hold right and Catholic faith in God, he will depart from this life condemned.

Another person, however, who has good works arising from the right faith that works through love, though not as morally well ordered as the former, supports his lack of continence by the respectability of marriage. He both pays and claims the marital debt of bodily intercourse; he has intercourse not solely for procreation but also for pleasure, although only with his wife, as the Apostle permits to married people by way of concession (1 Cor. 7:6). He does not endure injuries with such patience, but, driven by a desire for revenge, bears them in anger; although, when asked, he forgives, so that he may say, “As we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). He possesses household property and gives alms from it, though not as generously as the former. He takes nothing belonging to another, but, although through ecclesiastical rather than civil judgment, he does reclaim his own.

This person, who appears morally inferior to the other, nevertheless, because of the right faith he has in God—by which he lives, and according to which he accuses himself in all his sins and praises God in all his good works, attributing shame to himself and glory to God, and receiving from him both forgiveness of sins and love for right deeds—will depart from this life set free and will be received into fellowship with those who will reign with Christ.

Why, except because of faith? Although faith without works saves no one—for it is not a rejected faith that works through love—nevertheless sins are forgiven through faith itself, because “the righteous person lives by faith.” Without it, even works that appear good are turned into sins; for “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23).

Because of this great distinction it happens that, although no one doubts that persevering virginal integrity is superior to marital chastity, a woman married twice who professes the Catholic faith is preferred to a heretical virgin. She is not preferred in the sense that the former is better in the kingdom of God, but in the sense that the latter will not be there at all.

Likewise, the person whom we described as morally better, if he possesses right faith, surpasses the other, yet both will be there. If he lacks faith, however, he is so surpassed by the other that he himself will not be there.

#### 15.

Since all the righteous, both those of former times and the Apostles, lived by the right faith that is in Christ Jesus our Lord, and since they possessed such holy conduct together with faith that, although in this life they could not have virtue as perfect as that which will exist after this life, nevertheless whatever sin crept in through human weakness was immediately erased by the devotion of that very faith—how can it be said that they were righteous merely in comparison with the unrighteous whom God will condemn? Through devout faith they were so completely separated from those impious people in the opposite direction that the Apostle cries out:

> “What partnership has the faithful person with the unfaithful?” (2 Cor. 6:15).

But evidently the Pelagians, these new heretics, imagine that they are devout lovers and praisers of the saints if they do not dare to say that the saints possessed imperfect virtue, even though the Chosen Vessel confesses this. Considering where he still stood, and that “the corruptible body weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15), he says:

> “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect. Brothers, I do not consider myself to have apprehended it.”

Yet shortly afterward, although he had denied that he was perfect, he says:

> “Let all of us who are perfect think this way” (Phil. 3:12, 13, 15).

Thus he showed that, according to the condition of this life, there is a certain perfection, and that it also belongs to this perfection for each person to know that he is not yet perfect.

For what was more perfect, or more excellent, among the holy priests of the old people? Yet God commanded them first to offer sacrifice for their own sins (Lev. 9:7; 16:6). And what was holier among the new people than the Apostles? Yet the Lord commanded them to say in prayer, “Forgive us our debts.”

The one hope, therefore, of all the devout who groan under the burden of this corruptible flesh and amid the weakness of this life is that “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the expiation for our sins” (1 John 2:1–2).

### Chapter VI

#### 16. The calumny concerning sin in Christ

Those who are so far removed from the righteous in the opposite direction—even if this were the only difference between them—do not have a righteous advocate.

Far be it from us to say of this righteous advocate, as they slanderously claim, that he “lied because of the necessity of the flesh.” Rather, we say that, “in the likeness of sinful flesh, he condemned sin by means of sin” (Rom. 8:3).

Perhaps because they do not understand this, and, blinded by their desire to slander, do not know the various ways in which the word *sin* is used in the Holy Scriptures, they boast that we affirm sin in Christ.

We therefore say that Christ had no sin, either in his soul or in his flesh; and that, by assuming flesh in the likeness of sinful flesh, he condemned sin by means of sin.

What the Apostle said somewhat obscurely can be explained in two ways: either because likenesses of things are customarily designated by the names of the things to which they are similar, so that the Apostle is understood to have wished to call the very likeness of sinful flesh “sin”; or because sacrifices for sins were called “sins” in the law. All those sacrifices were figures of Christ’s flesh, which is the true and unique sacrifice for sins—not only for those sins that are all washed away in Baptism, but also for those that afterward creep in through the weakness of this life. On account of these sins the whole Church cries out daily to God in prayer, “Forgive us our debts.” They are forgiven through the unique sacrifice for sins, which the Apostle, speaking according to the law, did not hesitate to call “sin.”

Hence there is also that much clearer statement of his, free from any uncertainty at a crossroads of ambiguity:

> “We entreat you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God. He made him who knew no sin to be sin for us, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (2 Cor. 5:20–21).

As for what I mentioned above, “He condemned sin on account of sin”: since it does not say “on account of his sin,” someone might understand it in this way and say that he condemned sin on account of the sin of the Jews, because, on account of the sin of those who crucified him, it came about that he poured out his blood for the remission of sins.

But here, where it says that God made Christ himself, who knew no sin, to be sin, I do not think it can more fittingly be understood in any other way than that Christ was made a sacrifice for sins and for this reason was called “sin.”

### Chapter VII

#### 17. The calumny concerning the fulfillment of the commandments in the future life

Who could tolerate their accusing us of saying “that after the resurrection there will be such progress that people will begin there to fulfill God’s commandments which they were unwilling to fulfill here”?

We say that there will then be absolutely no sin, nor any struggle with sinful desire—as though they themselves dared to deny this. Who will deny that wisdom and knowledge of God will then be perfected in us, and that our rejoicing in the Lord will be so great that it will be complete and true security, unless he is so turned away from the truth that he cannot attain it for this very reason?

But these things will not consist in commandments; they will consist in the reward of the commandments that must be observed here. Contempt for those commandments does not lead to the reward there; rather, here the grace of God grants the desire to keep the commandments. If anything in those commandments is observed imperfectly, grace forgives it, and for this reason we pray both, “Your will be done,” and, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:10, 12).

Here, then, the commandment is that we should not sin; there, the reward is that we cannot sin.

Here, the commandment is that we should not obey the desires of sin; there, the reward is that we do not have sinful desires.

Here, the commandment is:

> “Understand, you foolish among the people; and you senseless, when will you become wise?” (Ps. 94:8).

There, the reward is complete wisdom and perfect knowledge. For the Apostle says:

> “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face. Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, just as I have been fully known” (1 Cor. 13:12).

Here, the commandment is:

> “Rejoice in God our helper” (Ps. 81:2);

and:

> “Rejoice, you righteous, in the Lord” (Ps. 32:1).

There, the reward is to rejoice with perfect and ineffable joy.

Finally, the commandment says:

> “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness”;

but the reward says:

> “For they shall be filled” (Matt. 5:6).

With what, I ask, will they be filled, except with what they hunger and thirst for?

Who, then, is so alien not only from divine judgment but even from human understanding as to say that a person can possess as much righteousness while hungering and thirsting for it as he will possess when he is filled with it?

When we hunger and thirst for righteousness, if the faith of Christ is awake within us, what are we to believe that we hunger and thirst for except Christ? He “became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption; so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord’” (1 Cor. 1:30–31).

And because we now believe in him without seeing him, therefore we thirst and hunger for righteousness. For as long as we are in the body, we are away from the Lord; “for we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:6–7). When we see him, surely arriving at sight itself, we will rejoice with unspeakable joy (1 Pet. 1:8). Then we will be filled with righteousness, because now, in devout desire, we say to him:

> “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 17:15).

#### 18.

How shameless—or rather, how insane—is the pride of those who are not yet equal to the angels of God but think they can already possess righteousness equal to that of the angels of God! They do not consider so great and holy a man who was certainly hungering and thirsting for the perfection of righteousness itself, when he refused to be exalted by the greatness of his revelations. Yet, so that he would not be exalted, he was not left to his own judgment and will; rather, he received “a thorn in the flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet him.” For this reason he pleaded with the Lord three times that it might depart from him, and the Lord said to him:

> “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:7–9).

What power is meant except that which prevents exaltation? And who doubts that this pertains to righteousness?

The angels of God possess the perfection of this righteousness; they always see the face of the Father (Matt. 18:10), and therefore of the entire Trinity, since through the Son they see in the Holy Spirit. Nothing is higher than this revelation. Yet none of the angels who rejoice in that contemplation needs an angel of Satan to buffet him, lest the greatness of the revelation exalt him.

The Apostle Paul did not yet possess this perfection of virtue; he was not yet equal to the angels of God. There remained in him a weakness inclined to exaltation, which had to be restrained even by an angel of Satan, lest he be exalted by the greatness of his revelations.

Although pride was what first cast Satan himself down, the supreme physician, who knows how to make good use even of evil things, employed an angel of Satan against the vice of pride as a salutary though painful remedy—just as an antidote against the venom of serpents is often made even from serpents.

What, then, does “My grace is sufficient for you” mean except: “Do not fail and succumb beneath the buffet of the angel of Satan”?

And what does “Power is perfected in weakness” mean except that, in this place of weakness, the perfection of virtue can exist to the extent that pride is restrained by the very presence of weakness?

That weakness will certainly be healed by the immortality to come. For how can full health be said to exist where medicine against the buffet of an angel of Satan is still necessary?

#### 19.

From this it has come about that the virtue now present in a righteous person is called perfect only in such a way that knowledge of his own imperfection in truth, and confession of it in humility, also belong to his perfection.

This small righteousness is perfect according to the measure of this weakness when a person also understands what he lacks.
