Therefore the Apostle calls himself both imperfect and perfect (Phil. 3:12, 15): imperfect, because he considers how far he is from the righteousness whose fullness he still hungers and thirsts for; but perfect, because he is not ashamed to confess his imperfection and proceeds well in order to arrive.

In this sense we can call a traveler perfect when his progress is advancing well, although his journey is not completed until he has arrived.

Therefore, after saying, “According to the righteousness that is in the law, I was blameless,” he immediately added:

> “Whatever gains I had, these I counted as losses for the sake of Christ. Indeed, I consider everything to be loss because of the surpassing knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord. For his sake I have regarded all things not merely as losses but as refuse, so that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness from God based on faith” (Phil. 3:6–9).

The Apostle clearly says, and certainly not falsely, that according to the righteousness that is from the law he had been blameless. Yet he casts away as refuse the things that had been gains to him, and counts them as losses—not only these things, but all the others he mentioned above—because of the surpassing knowledge, as he himself says, of Christ Jesus our Lord. Without doubt, he still possessed this knowledge by faith, not yet by sight.

For the knowledge of Christ will then be surpassing, when he has been revealed in such a way that what is believed will be seen. Hence elsewhere he says:

> “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:3–4).

The Lord himself says:

> “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21).

The evangelist John says:

> “Beloved, we are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Then the knowledge of Christ will be surpassing. Now it is indeed hidden in faith, but it does not yet appear as surpassing in sight.

#### 20.

The blessed Paul therefore casts away his former righteousness as losses and refuse, so that he may gain Christ and be found in him, not having his own righteousness, which is from the law.

Why does he call it his own if it is from the law? The law is certainly God’s law. Who except Marcion, Manichaeus, and other similar plagues has said otherwise?

Since that law is God’s, he says that the righteousness which is from the law is his own righteousness. He did not wish to possess this righteousness as his own, but cast it away as refuse.

Why, except because this is what we also demonstrated above: those are under the law who, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, have not submitted to the righteousness of God” (Rom. 10:3)?

They think that they can fulfill the law’s commands by the powers of their own free choice; entangled in this pride, they do not turn to grace, which helps them.

Thus the letter kills them: either because they openly make themselves guilty by not doing what it commands, or because they think they are doing what they do not do with the spiritual love that comes from God. They therefore remain either openly unrighteous or deceitfully righteous—plainly crushed in open unrighteousness, and foolishly exalted in deceptive righteousness.

Accordingly, in a remarkable but nevertheless true way, the righteousness of the law is not fulfilled by the righteousness that is in or from the law, but by the righteousness that is in the Spirit of grace.

For the righteousness of the law is fulfilled in those who, as it is written, “do not walk according to the flesh but according to the Spirit” (Rom. 8:4).

The Apostle says that, according to the righteousness that is in the law, he had been blameless in the flesh, not in the Spirit; and he says that the righteousness which is from the law had been his own, not God’s.

We must therefore understand that the righteousness of the law is not fulfilled according to the righteousness that is in or from the law—that is, according to human righteousness—but according to the righteousness that is in the Spirit of grace. Therefore it is fulfilled according to God’s righteousness, that is, the righteousness that a person has from God.

This can be stated more plainly and briefly as follows: the righteousness of the law is not fulfilled when the law commands and a person acts as though by his own powers; it is fulfilled when the Spirit helps and the human will, though free, is liberated by God’s grace and acts.

The righteousness of the law, then, is to command what pleases God and forbid what displeases him. But the righteousness that is in the law is to serve the letter and require no assistance from God outside it for right living.

After saying, “Not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ,” he added, “which is from God.” This, then, is God’s righteousness, which the proud, being ignorant of it, wish to establish as their own.

It is not called God’s righteousness because God is righteous by means of it, but because a human being has it from God.

#### 21.

According to this righteousness of God—that is, the righteousness which is from God for us—faith now works through love (Gal. 5:6). It works so that a person may reach the one in whom he now believes without seeing, and whom, when he sees him, he will find to be what was formerly in faith as through a mirror and in an enigma, but will then be in sight, face to face (1 Cor. 13:12). Then love itself will also be perfected.

For it is exceedingly foolish to say that God is loved as much before he is seen as he will be loved when he is seen. If in this life—no devout person doubting it—the more we love God, the more righteous we are, who could doubt that true and devout righteousness will be perfected when love of God has been perfected?

Then the law will be fulfilled so that absolutely nothing is lacking; according to the Apostle, “the fullness of the law is love” (Rom. 13:10).

Accordingly, after saying, “Not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness from God based on faith,” he added:

> “That I may know him and the power of his resurrection and the fellowship of his sufferings.”

None of these things was yet full and perfect in the Apostle; rather, as one placed on the way, he was running toward their fullness and perfection.

For how had he already perfectly known Christ when elsewhere he says, “Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, just as I have been fully known” (1 Cor. 13:12)?

And how had he already perfectly known the power of Christ’s resurrection, when he still had to know it more fully by experiencing the resurrection of the flesh at the proper time?

And how had he already perfectly known the fellowship of Christ’s sufferings when he had not yet experienced the suffering of death for him?

Finally, he adds:

> “If somehow I may attain the resurrection of the dead.”

Then he says:

> “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect.”

What, then, does he confess that he has not yet received, and in what does he confess that he is not yet perfect, except in that righteousness which is from God—the righteousness he desired and therefore did not wish to possess as his own, as though it were from the law?

For this is what he was speaking about, and this was why he said these things, resisting the enemies of God’s grace, for the granting of which Christ was crucified. These people too belong to their number.

#### 22.

For when he began to say these things, he began as follows:

> “Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers, beware of the mutilation. For we are the circumcision, who serve God in spirit; or, as some manuscripts have it, ‘who serve the Spirit of God’; and who glory in Christ Jesus and put no confidence in the flesh.”

It is clear that he is acting against the Jews, who, observing the law carnally and wishing to establish their own righteousness, were being killed by the letter and not made alive by the Spirit. They gloried in themselves, whereas the Apostles and all the children of promise gloried in Christ.

Then he continued:

> “Although I myself have confidence in the flesh: if anyone else thinks he has reason for confidence in the flesh, I have more.”

After enumerating everything that gives glory according to the flesh, he concluded with the words:

> “According to the righteousness that is in the law, blameless.”

And after saying that these things had been altogether losses, detriments, and refuse to him, so that he might gain Christ, he added the point under discussion:

> “That I may be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, which is from God.”

He confessed that he had not yet received the perfection of this righteousness—which will exist only in that surpassing knowledge of Christ on account of which he said that everything was loss—and therefore that he was not yet perfect.

> “I press on,” he says, “if somehow I may apprehend that for which I was apprehended by Christ Jesus.”

“I may apprehend that for which I was apprehended” has the same meaning as “I shall know fully, just as I have been fully known.”

> “Brothers,” he says, “I do not consider myself to have apprehended it. But one thing: forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the goal, toward the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus.”

The order of the words is: “But I pursue one thing.”

This one thing can rightly be understood as what the Lord also impressed upon Martha when he said:

> “Martha, Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things; but one thing is necessary” (Luke 10:41–42).

Desiring to apprehend this, as one placed on the way, he said that he was pursuing the prize of the heavenly calling of God in Christ Jesus.

Who, then, would hesitate to conclude that, when he has apprehended what he says he is pursuing, he will possess a righteousness equal to the righteousness of the holy angels—none of whom, certainly, is buffeted by an angel of Satan so that he may not be exalted by the greatness of a revelation?

Then, warning those who might already think themselves perfect through the fullness of that righteousness, he says:

> “Let all of us who are perfect think this way.”

It is as though he were saying: If, according to the capacity of a mortal human being and the measure of this life, we are perfect, let us understand that this too belongs to perfection: that we should know ourselves not yet to be perfect with that angelic righteousness which will be ours at Christ’s manifestation.

> “And if you think differently about anything,” he says, “God will reveal this also to you.”

How will he reveal it except to those walking and progressing along the way of right faith, until this pilgrimage is ended and sight is reached?

Consequently he adds:

> “Nevertheless, let us walk in accordance with what we have attained.”

Then he concludes by warning against those with whom this passage of his speech began:

> “Be imitators of me, brothers, and observe those who walk in this way, as you have us for an example. For many walk—of whom I often told you, and now tell you even with tears—as enemies of the cross of Christ. Their end is destruction” (Phil. 3:2–19), and so forth.

These are the very people of whom he had begun by saying, “Beware of the dogs, beware of the evil workers,” and what follows.

All, therefore, are enemies of the cross of Christ who, wishing to establish their own righteousness—the righteousness that is from the law, that is, the letter merely commanding and not the Spirit fulfilling—have not submitted to the righteousness of God.

> “For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith is emptied” (Rom. 4:14).

> “If righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Gal. 2:21).

> “Then the offense of the cross has been removed” (Gal. 5:11).

Accordingly, those are enemies of his cross who say that righteousness comes through the law, whose function is to command, not to help.

But the grace of God, through Jesus Christ the Lord, in the Holy Spirit, helps our weakness.

### 23.

Therefore, whoever lives according to the righteousness that is in the law without faith in the grace of Christ, just as the Apostle recalls that he himself lived blamelessly, must be considered to possess no true righteousness—not because the law is not true and holy, but because wishing to obey the commanding letter without the life-giving Spirit of God, as though by the powers of free choice, is not true righteousness.

The righteousness according to which the righteous person lives by faith is true righteousness, because through the Spirit of grace it comes to a human being from God.

Although it is not without reason called perfect in some righteous people according to the capacity of this life, it is nevertheless small in comparison with that great righteousness which is equal to the angels’ righteousness.

The person who did not yet possess that righteousness called himself perfect because of the righteousness already present in him, and imperfect because of the righteousness still lacking.

This lesser righteousness produces merit; the greater becomes the reward. Therefore whoever does not pursue the lesser does not attain the greater.

Accordingly, after the resurrection of the human being, to deny that the fullness of righteousness will exist, and to think that righteousness will then be as great in the body of that life as it can be in the body of this death, is an extraordinary form of madness.

It is entirely true, however, that people will not then begin to fulfill God’s commandments which they were unwilling to fulfill here. For there will be the most perfect fullness of righteousness, but it will not come about through people then following the commandments and striving by progress toward that fullness; it will come in the twinkling of an eye, just as the resurrection of the dead itself will take place (1 Cor. 15:52).

For that perfect greatness of righteousness will be given as a reward to those who fulfilled the commandments here; it will not itself be commanded to be done.

I speak of their having fulfilled the commandments in such a way that we remember that prayer also belongs to the commandments themselves, in which the holy children of promise truthfully say every day:

> “Your will be done,”

and:

> “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:10, 12).

### Chapter VIII
### 24. The Three Principal Heads of the Pelagian Heresy. The Pelagians’ Mists, and the Five Heads of Their Calumnies

Since, then, the Pelagians are pressed by testimonies and statements of the truth such as these and others of the same kind—so that they may not deny original sin; so that they may not say that the grace of God by which we are justified is given not freely but according to our merits; and so that they may not say that in mortal man, however holy and well-behaved, there is such great righteousness that, even after the laver of regeneration, he has no need of the remission of sins until he ends this life—when, therefore, they are pressed not to make these three assertions, and not by means of them to alienate from the grace of the Savior those who believe them, persuading such people, lifted up in pride, to rush headlong into the condemnation of the devil, they introduce mists of other questions, in which their impiety may remain hidden from simpler people, or from those slower to understand, or from those less instructed in the Holy Scriptures.

These are the mists: praise of creation, praise of marriage, praise of the law, praise of free will, and praise of the saints—as though any one of us disparaged these things, rather than proclaiming them all with the praises due to the honor of the Creator and Savior. Yet creation does not wish to be praised in such a way that it refuses to be healed. And the more marriage is to be praised, the less should the shameful concupiscence of the flesh be attributed to it; this concupiscence is not from the Father but is from the world (I John 2:16). Marriage certainly found it in human beings; it did not make it, since it exists in many even without marriage, and marriage itself could have existed without it if no one had sinned.

The law, too, is holy, just, and good (Romans 7:12); yet it is not itself grace, and nothing is rightly done through it without grace. For it was not given as something able to give life, but was established because of transgression, so that it might confine those convicted under sin, and so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ (Galatians 3:21, 19, 22).

And free will, having been taken captive, is effective only for sin; but for righteousness it is ineffective unless it is liberated and assisted by God. Accordingly, all the saints—whether from that ancient Abel down to John the Baptist, or from the Apostles themselves down to the present time, and thereafter until the end of the age—are to be praised in the Lord, not in themselves. For the voice of the former is: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised” (Psalm 33:3); and the voice of the latter is: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Corinthians 15:10). And this applies to all: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (ibid., 1:31). The common confession of all is: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John 1:8).

## CHAPTER IX

### 25. He Shows That the Catholic Position, Standing Between the Manichaeans and the Pelagians, Refutes Both

But since, in these five matters which I have set forth, in which they seek hiding places and from which they construct their calumnies, they are exposed and convicted by divine testimonies, they have devised the detestable name of the Manichaeans in order to frighten away the uninstructed whom they can, so that they may not lend their ears to the truth against their most perverse doctrines. For the Manichaeans, by blaspheming, condemn the first three of these five matters: they say that neither human creation, nor marriage, nor the law was instituted by the supreme and true God [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “instituted” (*instituta*).].

They do not, however, accept what the truth says: that sin began with free will, and that every evil of angel or human being arose from it. For, straying excessively far from God, they preferred to believe that the nature of evil was always evil and coeternal with God. They also attack the holy Patriarchs and Prophets with every possible curse.

This, then, is how the new heretics think to evade the force of the truth by throwing the name of the Manichaeans against it. But they do not evade it. For the truth pursues them and overthrows both the Manichaeans and the Pelagians together.

When a human being is born, because he is something good insofar as he is human, he refutes the Manichaean and praises the Creator; but insofar as he bears original sin, he refutes Pelagius and has need of a Savior. The assertion that this nature must be healed also strikes at both: it would not need medicine if it were healthy—which is against Pelagius—nor could it be healed at all if it were an eternal and unchangeable evil—which is against the Manichaeans.

Likewise, when we say that concupiscence of the flesh is not to be attributed to marriage, which we praise as established by the Lord, this is against the Pelagians, who place it among marriage’s praises, and against the Manichaeans, who attribute it to an alien evil nature [Note: Here “alien” (*alienae*) is supplied from the manuscripts; it was absent from the Erasmus and Louvain editions. The Amerbach edition read “another” (*aliae*).]; it is an evil accidentally affecting our nature, not something to be separated from it by God’s disjunction [Note: The printed editions read “distinction” (*distinctione*); the manuscripts read “disjunction” (*disjunctione*).], but something to be healed by God’s mercy.

Likewise, when we say that the law is holy, just, and good (Romans 7:12), established not to justify the ungodly but to convict the proud, and established because of transgression, this is against the Manichaeans, since it is praised according to the Apostle; and against the Pelagians, since, according to the Apostle, no one is justified by the law (Galatians 3:19, 11). Therefore the Spirit of grace freely comes to give life to those whom the letter kills—that is, to those whom the good law, by commanding, makes guilty through transgression (II Corinthians 3:6) [Note: The printed editions read “to justify” (*justificandis*); the manuscripts read “to give life” (*vivificandis*), which better corresponds to “kills.”].

Likewise, when we say that free choice in evil must be liberated by the grace of God in order to do good, this is against the Pelagians; but when we say that evil arose from that choice, although previously it did not exist, this is against the Manichaeans.

Likewise, when we honor the holy Patriarchs and Prophets with the praises due to them in God, this is against the Manichaeans; but when we say that even they, although righteous and pleasing to God, needed the Lord’s propitiation, this is against the Pelagians.

Thus the Catholic faith finds both groups, like all other heretics, opposed to it, and by the authority of divine testimonies and the light of truth convicts both.

## CHAPTER X

### 26. The Pelagians Seek Another Hiding Place by Introducing the Unnecessary Question of the Soul’s Origin

The Pelagians also add to the mists of their hiding places an unnecessary question concerning the origin of the soul, in order that, by confusing manifest matters with the obscurity of other matters, they may contrive a place in which to hide.

For they say: “We observe the transmission of souls together with the transmission of sin.” I do not know where or when they have heard this from the speeches or read it in the writings of those who defend the Catholic faith against them. For even if I find something written by Catholics on this subject, the defense of the truth had not yet been undertaken against these men, nor was the purpose to answer them.

But I say this: that original sin is so plainly established according to the Holy Scriptures, and that its forgiveness in little children through the laver of regeneration is so firmly confirmed by the great antiquity and authority of the Catholic faith, and is so widely known through the Church’s clear and universal proclamation, that whatever is argued concerning the investigation or assertion of anyone’s soul-origin, if it conflicts with this, cannot be true.

Therefore, whoever—whether a son or an enemy of the Church—asserts concerning the soul or any obscure matter something by which he destroys what is most true, most firmly established, and most widely known, must either be corrected or avoided.

But let this be the end of this volume, so that what follows may have another beginning.

# BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0609]

After dissolving in the preceding books the accusations directed against Catholics, Augustine now exposes the snares hidden in the remaining portion of the Pelagians’ second Epistle, in the five heads of their doctrine: namely, praise of creation, praise of marriage, praise of the law, praise of free will, and praise of the saints. In these five heads the Pelagians maliciously boast that they oppose the Manichaeans no less than the Catholics, although they are known to refer all five to this purpose: to thrust forward their threefold error—namely, the first two in order to deny original sin; the next two in order to establish that grace is given according to merits; and the fifth in order to say that the saints did not have sin in this life.

Augustine shows that both heresies, that of the Manichaeans and that of the Pelagians, stand opposed to one another and are equally hateful to the Catholic faith. That faith professes, first, that nature is good, created by the good God, but that it nevertheless needs a Savior because of original sin, which passed into all humanity from the transgression of the first man. It then professes that marriage is good and truly instituted by God, but that the concupiscence itself which accompanies marriage is evil, arising from sin. It professes also that God’s law is good, but in such a way that it merely reveals sin and does not remove it. It professes that free will is certainly implanted in human nature, but that it has now been taken captive, so that it cannot perform righteousness unless it has been liberated by grace. Finally, it professes that the saints of both the New and Old Testaments were endowed with true righteousness, though not perfect or so complete that they were without every sin.

At the end he produces testimonies from Cyprian and Ambrose in support of the Catholic faith: some concerning original sin, others concerning the help of grace, and the final ones concerning the imperfection of present righteousness.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0609]

### 1. The Five Hiding Places of the Pelagians

After the matters we have discussed and answered, they repeat the same points for which we convicted their Epistle, but in a different manner. Previously they proposed these matters by objecting to us what they thought we held wrongly; afterward, by explaining what they themselves held, they returned the same points in the opposite form, adding two things they had not said: “They declare baptism necessary for people of every age,” and, “Through Adam death passed to us, not sins.” These matters too must be treated in their proper place.

Accordingly, since in the preceding book, which we have just completed, we said that they held up five matters as obstacles in which their doctrines hostile to the grace of God and the Catholic faith lay hidden—namely, praise of creation, praise of marriage, praise of the law, praise of free will, and praise of the saints—I think it more useful to distinguish by categories everything they defend [Note: Vatican manuscripts read “gradually” (*gradatum*).], the opposites of which they charge us with holding, and to show which of their claims belongs to which of these five matters, so that by this distinction our response may be clearer and more concise [Note: Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “more probable” (*probabilior*).].

## CHAPTER II

### 2. Praise of Creation; Praise of Marriage; Praise of the Law; Praise of Free Will; Praise of the Saints

As regards the human race, which is the subject of the present question, they develop their praise of creation in these statements:

“That God is the creator of those who are born, and that the children of human beings are the work of God; and that every sin descends not from nature but from the will.”

To this praise of creation they attach the claim that “they say baptism is necessary for people of every age,” so that “that creature may be adopted as a child of God,” not because it brings from its parents something that must be cleansed by the laver of regeneration.

To this they add that “they say the Lord Christ was stained by no mark of sin, as far as his infancy is concerned, because they affirm that his flesh was most pure from every contagion of sin, not by any special excellence or singular grace of his own, but by a sharing in the nature that is present in all infants” [Note: Gallican manuscripts omit “of sin.”].

This also pertains to the question they insert “concerning the origin of the soul”: by this they attempt to make all infants’ souls equal to Christ’s soul, since they want all of them likewise to be unstained by any mark of sin.

For this reason they also say: “Nothing evil passed from Adam to the rest, except death.” They say that death “is not always an evil, since for martyrs it is even the cause of rewards; and that what makes it good or evil is not the dissolution of bodies—which will be raised in every class of human beings—but the diversity of merits arising from human freedom.” These are the things they write in this Epistle concerning the praise of creation.

They praise marriage according to the Scriptures, “because the Lord says in the Gospel, ‘He who made them from the beginning made them male and female’ (Matthew 19:4), and said, ‘Increase and multiply and fill the earth’ (Genesis 1:28).” Although this is not written in that passage of the Gospel, it is nevertheless written in the Law. They also add: “Therefore what God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matthew 19:6). We recognize these Gospel words.

In their praise of the law they say: “According to the Apostle, the old law was just, holy, and good (Romans 7:12), and was able to confer everlasting life on those who kept its commandments and lived righteously through faith, such as the Prophets, Patriarchs, and all the saints.”

In their praise of free will they say:

“Free will did not perish, since the Lord speaks through the prophet: ‘If you are willing and heed me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and do not heed me, the sword shall devour you’ (Isaiah 1:19–20). Accordingly, grace also assists the good intention of each person, but does not implant the impulse to resist in the pursuit of virtue, because there is no partiality with God” (Romans 2:11).

They conceal themselves under the praise of the saints, saying:

“Baptism perfectly renews human beings, since the Apostle bears witness that, through the washing of water, the Church from the Gentiles is made holy and immaculate” (Ephesians 5:26). They say also that “the Holy Spirit helped good minds in ancient times,” as the prophet says to God: “Your good Spirit will lead me into the right way” (Psalm 142:10).

They say that all the Prophets and Apostles, and all the saints of both the New and Old Testaments to whom God bears witness, were righteous—not in comparison with criminals, but according to the rule of the virtues—and that in the future there will be a reward both for good works and for evil ones. “Otherwise,” they say, “no one can there fulfill the commandments which he has despised here, because the Apostle said, ‘We must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may receive what belongs to his body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil’” (II Corinthians 5:10).

In all these matters, whatever they say concerning the praise of creation and marriage they attempt to refer to this purpose: that there may be no original sin. Whatever they say concerning the praise of the law and free will they refer to this purpose: that grace may assist nothing except merit, and thus grace may no longer be grace. Whatever they say concerning the praise of the saints they refer to this purpose: that mortal life may appear to contain no sin in the saints, and that they may have no need to pray to God for the forgiveness of their debts.

## CHAPTER III

### Catholics Praise Nature, Marriage, the Law, Free Will, and the Saints in Such a Way as to Condemn the Pelagians and the Manichaeans Together

Whoever, with a Catholic mind, recoils from these wicked and condemnable doctrines in this threefold division should avoid their fivefold hiding places and snares, and should be so cautious between the two that, while turning away from Manichaeism, he does not incline toward Pelagianism; and should likewise separate himself from the Pelagians without joining himself to the Manichaeans. Or, if he is already held by either side, he should not free himself from one group in such a way that he rushes upon the other [Note: The editions read “preserve himself for the other” or “preserve himself for the others”; corrected here according to the manuscripts.].

They appear to be opposed to one another, because the Manichaeans reveal themselves by blaming those five matters, while the Pelagians conceal themselves by praising them.

Therefore whoever, according to the rule of the Catholic faith, glorifies the Creator in human beings who are born, on account of the good creation of flesh and soul—which the Manichaean does not wish to do—yet confesses that, because of the defect which passed into them through the sin of the first man, even infants need a Savior—which Pelagius does not wish to do—condemns and avoids both groups.

He distinguishes the evil of shameful concupiscence from the goodness of marriage in such a way that, unlike the Manichaeans, he does not blame that from which we are born, and, unlike the Pelagians, does not praise that for which we are ashamed.

He maintains that the law given through Moses is holy, just, and good, given by the holy, just, and good God. In this he rejects the Manichaean position, which contradicts the Apostle; yet he says that the law reveals sin without removing it, and commands righteousness without giving it. In this he again rejects the Pelagian position, which contradicts the Apostle.

He asserts free will in such a way that he says the evil of both angel and human being began not from some nature that is always evil—a nature that does not exist—but from free choice itself. This overturns the Manichaean heresy. Yet he does not therefore say that the captive will can recover healthy freedom except by the grace of God. This overturns the Pelagian heresy.

He praises in God the holy people of God, not only those from Christ manifested in the flesh onward, but also those of earlier times, whom the Manichaeans dare to blaspheme. Yet concerning these saints he believes their own confessions rather than the lies of the Pelagians. For the voice of the saints is: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John 1:8).

## CHAPTER IV

### Concerning the Praise of Creation: The Pelagians and the Manichaeans

These matters being so, what advantage is it to the recent heretics, enemies of the cross of Christ and opponents of divine grace, that they appear sound in relation to the error of the Manichaeans while perishing through another plague of their own?

What advantage is it to them that, in their praise of creation, they say that “the good God is the creator of those who are born, through whom all things were made, and that the children of human beings are his work”—whereas the Manichaeans say that they are the work of the prince of darkness—when among both groups, or rather in the hands of both, God’s creature, as it exists in infants, perishes?

For neither group wishes it to be liberated by the flesh and blood of Christ. The Manichaeans do so because they destroy the flesh and blood of Christ, as though he had not assumed such flesh and blood at all in man or from man. The Pelagians do so because they assert that there is no evil in infants from which they need to be liberated through the sacrament of this flesh and blood.

Between them human creation lies in infants: good by its institution, corrupted by its propagation; by its good qualities confessing the best Creator, and by its evils seeking the most merciful Redeemer. It has the Manichaeans as deniers of its good qualities and the Pelagians as deniers of its evils—both as persecutors.

Although infancy cannot speak, by its silent appearance and hidden weakness it nevertheless confronts the impious vanity of both groups. To the Manichaeans it says: “Believe that I was created by the one who creates good things.” To the Pelagians it says: “Allow me to be healed by the one who created me.”

The Manichaean says: “Nothing belongs to this infant except a good soul that must be liberated; everything else, as belonging not to the good God but to the prince of darkness, must be rejected” [Note: The editions read “everything else belongs to the prince of darkness and must be rejected”; the manuscripts have the smoother reading translated here.].

The Pelagian says: “On the contrary, nothing belonging to this infant needs liberation, because we show that the whole of it is already safe.”

Both are lying. Yet the mere accuser of the flesh is already more moderate than the one who is convicted of raging against and condemning everything indiscriminately [Note: The manuscripts read: “the accuser of the flesh, because he is convicted of raging against everything indiscriminately.”].

But neither does the Manichaean help the human soul, since he blasphemes God, the author of the whole human being; nor does the Pelagian allow divine grace to help human infancy, since he denies original sin [Note: The manuscripts read “medicine” rather than “grace.”].

God, therefore, shows mercy through the Catholic faith, which, by refuting both destructive errors, brings help to the infant for salvation. To the Manichaeans it says: “Hear the Apostle crying out: ‘Do you not know that your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit within you?’” (I Corinthians 6:19). Believe that God is the good Creator of bodies, since a temple of the Holy Spirit cannot be the work of the prince of darkness.

To the Pelagians it says: “He was conceived in iniquities, and his mother nourished him in sins in the womb” (Psalm 50:7, according to the Septuagint)—the infant whom you see. Why, by defending him as free from every fault, do you prevent him from being liberated through forgiveness? “No one is clean from uncleanness, not even an infant whose life upon the earth is but one day” (Job 14:5, according to the Septuagint). Allow the unfortunate child to receive remission of sins through him who alone, whether small or great, could have no sin.

### 5.

What advantage, then, is it to them that they say, “Every sin descends not from nature but from the will,” and that by the truth of this statement they resist the Manichaeans, who say that an evil nature is the cause of sin, when, by refusing to admit original sin—which undoubtedly descends from the will of the first man—they make infants emerge from the body guilty?

What advantage is it to them that they “confess baptism necessary for people of every age,” when the Manichaeans say that it is superfluous at every age [Note: Gallican manuscripts read “they say it is superfluous for every age”], if they say that baptism is false in the case of infants, insofar as the remission of sins is concerned?

What advantage is it to them that, against the Manichaeans, who insist that Christ’s flesh was nonexistent or merely simulated, they defend not only the reality of Christ’s flesh but also that “his very soul was unstained by any mark of sin,” when they make all other infants equal to his infancy in an equal purity? Thus Christ’s infancy appears not to preserve its own holiness in comparison with them, while they derive no salvation from it.

### 6.

In the matter of their claim that “through Adam death passed to us, not sins,” they do not have the Manichaeans as opponents. For the Manichaeans too do not assert that original sin passed from the first man—originally pure and upright in body and spirit, but afterward corrupted by free choice—into all humanity, and that it passes into all along with death. Rather, they say that flesh was evil from the beginning, created from an evil body and by an evil spirit, together with that evil spirit [Note: Erasmus and the Louvain edition omit “evil”]. They say that the soul, which is a part of God, comes into a human being according to the merits of its pollution through foods and drink, in which it had previously been confined, and is thus bound through intercourse by the bond of the flesh [Note: The editions add “also” after “through intercourse”; the manuscripts omit it.].

Accordingly, the Manichaeans agree with the Pelagians that the sin of the first man did not pass into the human race: not through the flesh, which they say was never good, nor through the soul, which they claim enters human flesh together with the merits of its impurities, by which it was polluted before the flesh.

But how do the Pelagians say that “only death passed to us through Adam”? If we die because he died, and he died because he sinned, then they say that punishment passes over without guilt and that innocent infants are punished by an unjust penalty, bearing death without any merits deserving death.

Catholic faith knows that this belongs to the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, who for our sake deigned to undergo death—that is, the penalty of sin—without sin. For just as he alone became the Son of man so that through him we might become sons of God, so he alone accepted punishment without evil merits on our behalf, so that through him we might receive grace without good merits [Note: *Consequeremur* (“we might obtain”) was absent from the manuscripts; the reader was to supply *susciperemus* (“we might receive”).]. For just as nothing good was owed to us, so nothing evil was owed to him.

Therefore, commending his love to those to whom he was going to give an unowed life, he willed to suffer for them an unowed death. The Pelagians attempt to abolish this unique prerogative of the Mediator, so that it would no longer be unique in the Lord if Adam suffered death as a deserved penalty because of guilt, while infants, bearing no guilt from him, suffered an undeserved death.

Although much good is conferred upon the good through death, and some have therefore fittingly discussed even the goodness of death, what is to be proclaimed here as well except the mercy of God, by which the punishment of sin is turned to good uses?

### 7.

But they say this because they wish to twist the Apostle’s words into their own meaning. For where the Apostle says, “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings,” they want it to be understood that not sin but death passed over.

What, then, is the meaning of what follows: “in whom all sinned”? Either the Apostle says that all sinned in that one man, of whom he had said, “Through one man sin entered the world,” or in that sin, or certainly in death.

It should not trouble them that he did not say “in which” but “in whom all sinned,” since “death” is masculine in the Greek language [Note: *Ho thanatos*, “death,” with the masculine article and gender]. Let them choose whichever they wish. Either all sinned in that man, and it is therefore said because, when he sinned, all were in him; or all sinned in that sin, because what all would contract by being born was committed in a general way; or it remains for them to say that all sinned in that death.

But I plainly do not see how this can be understood. All die in sin, not in death, for sin precedes and death follows; it is not that death precedes and sin follows. “The sting of death is sin” (I Corinthians 15:56)—that is, the sting by whose piercing death occurs, not the sting with which death pierces.

It is like poison: if it is drunk, it is called “the cup of death,” because death is caused by that cup, not because the cup was made by death or given by death.

If, however, sin cannot be understood in the Apostle’s words—“in whom all sinned”—because in the Greek from which the Epistle was translated, “sin” is feminine in gender [Note: *Hē hamartia*, “sin,” with the feminine article and gender], then it remains that all are understood to have sinned in that first man, because all were in him when he sinned. From him sin is contracted by being born, and it is not removed except by being born again.

Saint Hilary likewise understood the passage “in whom all sinned” in this way. He says: “In whom—that is, in Adam—all sinned.” Then he adds: “It is manifest that all sinned in Adam as in a mass. For he himself, corrupted through sin, begot all those who were born under sin” [Note: The interpretation of Paul cited under Hilary’s name is found in commentaries once attributed to Ambrose; their author is thought to have been Hilary the deacon, a Luciferian by affiliation and a native of Sardinia.].

By writing this, Hilary unambiguously indicated how “in whom all sinned” should be understood.

### 8.

Why, moreover, does the same Apostle say that we are reconciled to God through Christ, except because we had become enemies? And what is this except sin? Hence the prophet also says: “Your sins separate between you and God” (Isaiah 59:2).

Because of this separation, therefore, the Mediator was sent, to remove the sin of the world by which we were separated as enemies, and to make us, once reconciled from being enemies, into sons.

The Apostle was speaking from this basis; from this he went on to say that “through one man sin entered.” These are his preceding words:

“God commends his love toward us, because, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, therefore, having now been justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him. For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved in his life. And not only this, but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.”

Then he adds: “Therefore, just as through one man sin entered this world, and through sin death, and so passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:8–12).

Why do the Pelagians evade the issue? If reconciliation through Christ is necessary for all, then sin passed into all—the sin by which we became enemies and therefore needed reconciliation.

This reconciliation is found in the laver of regeneration and in the flesh and blood of Christ, without which even infants cannot have life in themselves. For just as there was one who brought death because of sin, so there is one who brings life because of righteousness.

“For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (I Corinthians 15:22); and “as through one trespass condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one act of justification justification of life came upon all human beings” (Romans 5:18).

Who, in the face of these apostolic words, has become so hardened by the deafness of wicked impiety that, after hearing them, he insists that death passed into us through Adam without sin—unless he is an opponent of the grace of God and an enemy of the cross of Christ? “Their end is destruction” (Philippians 3:18–19), if they persist in this obstinacy.

But let this suffice concerning their serpentine cunning, by which they wish to corrupt the minds of the simple [Note: Gallican manuscripts read “by which they strive to deceive the simple”] and turn them away from the chastity of the Catholic faith under the pretext of praising creation.

## CHAPTER V

### 9. Concerning the Praise of Marriage

What advantage, moreover, does their praise of marriage bring them? Against the Manichaeans, who attribute marriage not to the true and good God but to the prince of darkness, they oppose them with words of true piety, saying:

“The Lord speaks in the Gospel: ‘He who made them from the beginning made them male and female’ (Matthew 19:4), and says, ‘Increase and multiply and fill the earth’ (Genesis 1:28). ‘Therefore what God has joined, let no human being separate’” (Matthew 19:6).

What advantage is this to them—to lead people from the truth into falsehood? For they say this so that infants may be believed to be born free from every fault [Note: The same manuscripts read, “to seduce through truth into deceptive snares, so that infants may be born free from every fault,” etc.], and thus may not need to be reconciled to God through Christ, since they have no original sin, on account of which reconciliation is necessary for all through the one who came into the world without sin. For just as hostility came upon all through the one through whom sin entered the world [Note: The manuscripts read “just as the hostility of all came through the one through whom sin entered the world”; the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus read “for just as …”].

This is what is believed in the Catholic manner for the salvation of human nature, while preserving the praise of marriage, because the praise of marriage is the just union of the sexes, not the unjust defense of vices.

Accordingly, when they praise marriage and wish to draw people away from the Manichaeans to themselves, they want to change people’s disease, not heal it.

### 10. Concerning the Praise of the Law

Again, what advantage is it to them, in their praise of the law, that they say what is true against the Manichaeans, when from this they want to lead people to what they falsely believe against the Catholics?

For they say:

“We also confess that the old law, according to the Apostle, was just, holy, and good (Romans 7:12), and that it could confer everlasting life upon those who kept its commandments and lived righteously through faith, such as the Prophets, Patriarchs, and all the saints.”

By these words, cunningly framed, they praise the law against grace. For that law, although just, holy, and good, was not able to confer everlasting life upon all those people of God; it was faith in Christ that could do so.

This faith works through love (Galatians 5:6), not according to the letter that kills, but according to the Spirit that gives life (II Corinthians 3:6). To this faith the law leads people as a pedagogue, frightening them on account of transgression (Galatians 3:24), so that what the law itself could not confer might be conferred upon them.

To their words, in which they say that “the law could confer everlasting life upon the Prophets, Patriarchs, and all the saints who kept its commandments,” the Apostle responds:

“If righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21). “If the inheritance is through the law, it is no longer through the promise” (ibid. 3:18). “If those who are of the law are heirs, faith is emptied, and the promise is abolished” (Romans 4:14).

But that no one is justified before God by the law is clear, because “the righteous shall live by faith.” The law, however, is not from faith; rather, “the one who does these things shall live by them” (Galatians 3:11–12).

This testimony from the law, recalled by the Apostle, is understood as referring to temporal life, for fear of losing which people performed the works of the law, not from faith, since transgressors of the law were ordered by that same law to be killed [Note: Gallican manuscripts read “or referring to”; the editions read “which,” and “it ordered them to be killed” has been corrected according to the manuscripts.].

Or, if the words “the one who does these things shall live by them” are to be understood more profoundly as referring to eternal life (Leviticus 18:5), the command of the law was expressed in this way so that human weakness, failing within itself to do what the law commands, might seek help from the grace of God through faith; by his mercy even faith itself is granted.

For faith is possessed according as God has apportioned to each person a measure of faith (Romans 12:3). If people do not possess the spirit of power, love, and self-control from themselves but receive it, as the same teacher of the Gentiles says, “We did not receive a spirit of fear, but of power, love, and self-control” (II Timothy 1:7), then surely the spirit of faith is also received, concerning which he says: “Having the same spirit of faith” (II Corinthians 4:13).

The law therefore speaks truly: “The one who does these things shall live by them.” But in order to do them and live by them, faith is necessary—not the law, which commands this, but faith, which obtains it. Yet this faith itself, in order that it may merit receiving these things, is given freely.

11. Nowhere do these enemies of grace lay more hidden snares to attack that same grace than where they praise the law—a law that certainly deserves praise. For throughout all their arguments, by various turns of phrase and diversity of wording, they want the law itself to be understood as grace: namely, that through it we receive from the Lord God the assistance of knowledge, by which we may know what must be done; but not the inspiration of love, by which, once known, we may do these things with holy love—which is grace in the proper sense. For knowledge of the law without love puffs up rather than builds up, as the same Apostle says most clearly: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1). This statement is similar to the one that says: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6). “Knowledge puffs up” corresponds to “the letter kills”; and “love builds up” corresponds to “the Spirit gives life,” because “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

Knowledge of the law, therefore, makes a proud transgressor; but through the gift of love, it delights him to be a doer of the law. “We do not, then, overthrow the law through faith, but we establish the law” (Rom. 3:31): the law that leads to faith by means of fear. For this reason “the law produces wrath” (Rom. 4:15), so that, once frightened and turned toward fulfilling the righteousness of the law, God’s mercy may bestow grace [Note: [Col. 0617] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “that the grace may grant God’s mercy.”], through Jesus Christ our Lord. He is “the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:30), of whom it is written: “He carries law and mercy upon his tongue” (Prov. 3, according to the Septuagint): law, by which he frightens; mercy, by which he helps—law through the servant, mercy through himself; law as though in the staff which Elisha sent to raise the widow’s son, though the boy did not rise; for “if a law had been given that could make alive, righteousness would indeed be from the law” (Gal. 3:21); but mercy as though in Elisha himself, who, bearing the figure of Christ, was joined to the dead man in order to give him life, as a sign of the great mystery of the New Testament (2 Kings 4:29–35).

## CHAPTER VI

### 12. On the Praise of Free Choice. An Inscrutable Question. Further, That They Praise Free Choice against the Manichaeans

As for the fact that, in opposition to the Manichaeans, they praise free choice by adducing the prophetic testimony, “If you are willing and hear me, you shall eat the good things of the land; but if you are unwilling and do not hear me, the sword shall devour you” (Isa. 1:19–20): what benefit is this to them? For they defend free choice not so much against the Manichaeans as they exalt it against Catholics.

They want the words “If you are willing and hear me” to be understood as though the merit of the grace that follows lay in the preceding will itself, so that grace would no longer be grace, since it would not be free when it is repaid as something owed. But if they understood “If you are willing” in such a way that they would also confess that God prepares that very good will—for it is written, “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 8, according to the Septuagint)—then they would use this testimony as Catholics, and would not merely defeat the old heresy of the Manichaeans but also avoid founding the new heresy of the Pelagians [Note: [Col. 0618] The printed editions omit the negative particle and change *conderent* (“found”) to *contererent* (“crush”).].

### 13.

What benefit is it to them that, in praising free choice itself, they say that “grace assists each person’s good purpose”? This could be accepted without hesitation as a Catholic statement if they did not place merit in the good purpose—a merit to which a reward would then be paid according to what is owed, not according to grace—but instead understood and confessed that the good purpose itself, which grace assists once it has arisen, could not have existed in a human being unless grace had preceded it.

For how can there be a good purpose belonging to a human being without the Lord first showing mercy, when the good will itself is prepared by the Lord? Yet after saying that “grace also assists each person’s good purpose,” they immediately added, “but it does not implant the striving for virtue in one who resists.” This could be understood correctly if it were not said by people whose position is well known. For the hearing of the divine call is first procured by God’s grace itself for the one who resists; then, once he no longer resists, the striving for virtue is kindled in him [Note: [Col. 0618] The printed editions have *aditus* (“access”); the manuscripts have *auditus* (“hearing”). Shortly afterward, where the printed editions read “the striving for virtue,” they have “the spirit of virtue.” Both places are corrected according to the manuscripts.].

Nevertheless, in everything that each person does according to God, his mercy precedes that person (Ps. 58:11). This they do not want, because they want to be not Catholics but Pelagians. For proud impiety takes great pleasure in ensuring that even what a person is compelled to confess as having been given by the Lord does not appear to have been granted to him, but repaid to him—as though the children of destruction, not of promise, had themselves made themselves good, and God had then repaid those whom they had made good by their own efforts with the reward owed for that work.

### 14.

For their very swelling pride has so closed the ears of their hearts that they do not hear: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7); they do not hear: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5); they do not hear: “Love is from God” (1 John 4:7); they do not hear: “God has apportioned the measure of faith” (Rom. 12:3); they do not hear: “The Spirit blows where he wills” (John 3:8), and, “Those who are led by the Spirit of God are the sons of God” (Rom. 8:14); they do not hear: “No one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6:66); they do not hear what Ezra writes: “Blessed is the Lord, the God of our fathers, who put this into the heart of the king, to glorify his house which is in Jerusalem” (3 Esdras 8:28); they do not hear what the Lord says through Jeremiah: “I will put my fear into their heart, so that they will not depart from me, and I will visit them, to make them good” (Jer. 32:40–41).

Most especially, they do not hear what God says through the prophet Ezekiel, where he plainly shows that he is not moved by any good merits of human beings to make them good—that is, obedient to his commands—but rather that he bestows these good things upon them in return for evil, doing this on his own account, not because of them. For he says:

“Thus says the Lord God: I act not for your sake, O house of Israel” [Note: [Col. 0618] The printed editions have: “I shall act, O house of Israel,” omitting “not for your sake” [Col. 0619]. The words are nevertheless found in the manuscripts and in Ezekiel.], “but for the sake of my holy name, which you profaned among the nations to which you entered. And I will sanctify my great name, which has been profaned among the nations and which you profaned in their midst; and the nations shall know that I am the Lord, says Adonai the Lord, when I have been sanctified in you before their eyes. I will take you from among the nations, gather you from all the lands, and bring you into your own land. I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your uncleannesses; I will cleanse you. I will give you a new heart, and I will give a new spirit within you. I will take away the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh. I will put my spirit within you, and I will cause you to walk in my statutes, observe my judgments, and do them.”

And a little later, through the same prophet:

“Not for your sake do I act, says the Lord God; let it be known to you. Be ashamed and confounded because of your ways, O house of Israel. Thus says the Lord God: On the day when I cleanse you from all your iniquities, I will establish the cities, and the desolate places shall be rebuilt, and the devastated land shall be worked [Note: [Col. 0619] The printed editions have “shall be prepared.” The manuscripts have “shall be worked.” The Greek is *ergasthēsetai* (“shall be worked”). Later in this same passage from Ezekiel, Augustine repeats the same word in the passive sense: “they shall be worked and fortified.”], because it had been devastated before the eyes of every passerby. And they shall say: That devastated land has become like a garden of delight; and the cities that were deserted, devastated, and dug up have been settled and fortified. And the nations that remain around you shall know that I, the Lord, have rebuilt the ruins and planted the devastated places. I, the Lord, have spoken, and I have acted.

“Thus says the Lord: I will still be sought by the house of Israel, that I may do this for them. I will multiply them like human sheep, like holy sheep, like the sheep of Jerusalem on its feast days. Thus the deserted cities shall be filled with human sheep, and they shall know that I am the Lord” (Ezek. 36:22–38).

### 15.

What remains for a dead hide by which it can be puffed up, refusing to glory in the Lord when it boasts? What remains for it when, whatever it says it has done—so that, with the merit of a human being preceding, arising from the human being, God might then do what that person deserves—it will be answered, challenged, contradicted: “I act, but for the sake of my holy name; not for your sake do I act, says the Lord God”?

Nothing so overturns the Pelagians, who say that God’s grace is given according to our merits. Pelagius himself condemned this—not by correcting himself, but by fearing the eastern judges [Note: [Col. 0619] The Gallican and Vatican manuscripts have “even if he did not correct himself.” Shortly afterward they also have “Nothing so overturns this,” rather than the reading of the printed editions.].

Nothing so overturns the presumption of those who say, “We act so that we may merit that God act with us.” It is not Pelagius but the Lord himself who answers you: “I act, and not for your sake, but for the sake of my holy name.” For what good can you do with a heart that is not good? But in order that you may have a good heart, he says: “I will give you a new heart, and I will give you a new spirit” [Note: [Col. 0619] The printed editions have “my spirit”; the manuscripts have “a new spirit,” as above.].

Can you perhaps say: “First we walked in his statutes, observed his judgment, and acted so as to become worthy for him to give us his grace” [Note: [Col. 0620] In manuscript B: “so as to become worthy, so that he might…” Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition follow the reading translated here.]? For what good could you do, evil human beings; and how could you do these good things unless you were good? But who makes human beings good except the one who said, “I will visit them, to make them good,” and who said, “I will put my spirit within you, and I will cause you to walk in my statutes, observe my judgments, and do them”?

Are you still not awake? Do you still not hear: “I will cause you to walk; I will cause you to observe; finally, I will cause you to do”? Why do you continue to puff yourselves up? We do walk—it is true; we observe; we do—but he causes us to walk, to observe, and to do. This is the grace of God, which makes us good; this is his mercy, which precedes us.

What merits do the deserted, devastated, and dug-up places possess—places that will nevertheless be rebuilt, worked, and fortified? Is this on account of the merits of their desertion, devastation, and excavation? Far from it. Those are evil merits; these are good gifts. Good things are therefore given to the wicked: they are free gifts, not things owed, and therefore they are grace.

“I,” says the Lord; “I, the Lord.” Does this voice not restrain you, human pride, which says, “I act so that I may merit being rebuilt and planted by the Lord”? Do you not hear: “Not for your sake do I act. I, the Lord, rebuilt the ruins and planted the devastated places. I, the Lord, have spoken, and I have acted”—yet not for your sake, but for the sake of my holy name?

Who multiplies human beings like sheep, like holy sheep, like the sheep of Jerusalem? Who causes those deserted cities to be filled with human sheep except the one who continues by saying, “And they shall know that I am the Lord”?

But with what human sheep does he fill the cities, as he promised? With those he found, or with those he makes? Let us question the Psalm; behold, it answers. Let us listen:

“Come, let us adore and fall down before him, and let us weep before the Lord who made us; for he is our God, and we are the people of his pasture and the sheep of his hand” (Ps. 94:6–7) [Note: [Col. 0620] Lov. has “before.” The other printed editions and the manuscripts have “before the Lord.”].

He therefore makes the sheep with which he fills the deserted cities. And what wonder is this? For to that one sheep—that is, to the Church, whose members are all human sheep—it is said: “For I am the Lord who make you.”

Why do you bring forward free choice to me? It will not be free for doing righteousness unless you are a sheep [Note: [Col. 0620] The Gallican manuscripts have “unless he has become a sheep.” The Vatican manuscripts have “unless it has been set free.”]. He, therefore, who makes human beings into sheep himself frees human wills for obedience to godliness.

### 16.

But why does he make some people into sheep and not others, when “there is no partiality with God” (Rom. 2:11)? This is the question which the blessed Apostle addresses to those who propose it with more curiosity than capacity: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me this way?’” (Rom. 9:20).

This is the question that belongs to that height which the same Apostle, wishing to perceive it, in a certain sense feared, and exclaimed:

“O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, so that he should be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things. To him be glory forever and ever” (Rom. 11:33–36).

Let those who defend merit before grace—and therefore against grace—daring to scrutinize this inscrutable question, cease from wanting to give to God first so that they may be repaid; that is, from wanting to give something first by free choice, so that grace may be repaid to them as a reward. Let them wisely understand, or faithfully believe, that even what they suppose they have given first, they received from him from whom are all things, through whom are all things, and in whom are all things.

But why does one receive and another not receive, when neither deserves to receive, and whoever receives receives without being owed? Let them measure their own strength and not scrutinize matters too difficult for them (Sir. 3:22). Let it suffice for them to know that there is no injustice with God.

For when the Apostle had found no merits by which Jacob had preceded his twin brother with God, he says: “What shall we say, then? Is there injustice with God? Certainly not. For he says to Moses, ‘I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion.’ Therefore it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9:14–16).

Let his free mercy therefore be pleasing to us, even if this deep question remains unsolved. Yet it is solved to the extent that the same Apostle solves it when he says:

“But if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make known his power, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath that had been prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory upon the vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory” (Rom. 9:22–23).

Wrath is not repaid except as something owed, lest there be injustice with God. Mercy, however, even when it is bestowed without being owed, does not constitute injustice with God. From this they understand how freely mercy is bestowed upon the vessels of mercy: the vessels of wrath, with which they share a common mass that is the cause of their destruction, receive the wrath that is owed and justly repaid.

Let this now suffice against those who, through free choice, want to destroy the abundance of grace.

## CHAPTER VII

### 17. On the Praise of the Saints. The Church of the Present Age Is Not Without Spot or Wrinkle. The Snares of the Pelagians

As for their unwillingness that, in praising the saints, we should hunger and thirst for righteousness with the disposition of that tax collector, but instead belch forth as though satiated and full with the vanity of that Pharisee (Luke 18:10–14): what benefit is it to them that, in opposition to the Manichaeans who destroy Baptism, they say, “By Baptism human beings are perfectly renewed,” and bring forward the Apostle’s testimony to this effect, that “through the washing of water he testifies that the Church from the nations is made holy and immaculate” (Eph. 5:26)?

They advance these arguments with a proud and perverse understanding against the prayers of the Church herself. For they say this in order that it may be believed that, after holy Baptism—in which the remission of all sins takes place—the Church no longer has any sin. Yet against them the Church, with all her members, cries out to God from the rising of the sun to its setting: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12).

Moreover, when they themselves are questioned about this matter, what answer they should give they cannot find [Note: [Col. 0622] The Vatican manuscripts have: “she cries out to the Lord, ‘Forgive us our debts.’ Indeed, she also…”]. For if they say that they have no sin, John answers them that they deceive themselves and the truth is not in them (1 John 1:8). But if they confess their sins, since they want to be members of Christ’s body, how can that body—that is, the Church—at this present time be perfectly without spot or wrinkle, as they understand it, when its members do not falsely confess that they have sins [Note: [Col. 0622] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “perfect,” rather than “perfectly.”]?

Therefore, all sins are forgiven in Baptism, and through that washing of water in the word the Church is presented to Christ without spot or wrinkle (Eph. 5:27). For if she had not been baptized, she would say “Forgive us our debts” without effect, until she is brought to glory, where she will have no spot or wrinkle at all in a more perfect sense.

### 18.

It must be confessed that “the Holy Spirit,” even “in ancient times,” not only “assisted good minds”—which they also want to affirm—but also made them good, which they do not want to affirm.

It is also beyond doubt that “all the Prophets and Apostles, or the holy and evangelical and ancient persons to whom God bears witness, were righteous not merely in comparison with criminals but according to the standard of virtue.” This opposes the Manichaeans, who blaspheme the Patriarchs and Prophets. But it also opposes the Pelagians, since all these persons, when questioned about themselves while they lived in this body, would answer with one voice and in complete agreement: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

“It must not be denied,” moreover, “that in the future age there will be a reward both for good works and for evil works, and that no one is commanded there to fulfill commands which he despised here.” But the fullness of perfect righteousness, where sin cannot exist—righteousness for which the saints hunger and thirst here—is to be hoped for here as a command and received there as a reward, while almsgiving and prayers obtain that what has been less perfectly fulfilled here in the commandments may, through the forgiveness of sins, become free from punishment [Note: [Col. 0622] The printed editions have “but plainly this fullness,” omitting “of righteousness.” The passage is restored according to the manuscripts.].

### 19.

Since these things are so, let the Pelagians cease pretending that, through their most treacherous praise of five things—namely, the praise of creation, the praise of marriage, the praise of the law, the praise of free choice, and the praise of the saints—they wish to rescue people from the snares of the Manichaeans, when in fact they wish to entangle them in their own nets [Note: [Col. 0622] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have “most envious praise” rather than “most treacherous praise.”].

That is, they wish to deny original sin and begrudge little children the help of Christ the physician; they wish to say that God’s grace is given according to our merits, so that grace is no longer grace (Rom. 11:6); and they wish to say that the saints did not have sin in this life, so that the prayer taught to the saints by the one who had no sin—and through whom every sin is forgiven to praying saints—would be rendered void [Note: [Col. 0623] The Gallican manuscripts have “and that prayer would not be necessary.”].

Through the deceptive praise of those five goods, they lead incautious and unfeeling people astray into these three evils. I think I have sufficiently answered their most cruel, impious, and arrogant vanity concerning all these matters.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 20. Testimonies of the Ancients Against the Pelagians

But since they say that “their enemies have received our statements out of hatred for the truth,” and complain that “a dogma no less foolish than impious has been accepted throughout the entire West,” and that “simple bishops, sitting in their own places without a synodal assembly, have been forced to subscribe to its confirmation,” whereas it was rather the Church of Christ, both Western and Eastern, that recoiled from their profane novelties of speech (1 Tim. 6:20), I consider it my responsibility not only to bring forward the canonical holy Scriptures as witnesses against them, which we have already done sufficiently, but also to produce certain testimonies from the writings of the saints who before us handled these Scriptures with the greatest renown and glory.

I do not do this as though we equated the authority of any disputant with that of the canonical Books, or as though it were altogether impossible for one Catholic to understand something better or more truly than another Catholic. Rather, I do it so that those who think these people have something to say may be reminded how, before the new empty talk of these men, Catholic bishops followed the divine utterances concerning these matters; and so that they may know that we are defending the right and anciently established Catholic faith against the departing presumption and destructive error of the Pelagian heretics.

### 21.

The most blessed Cyprian, glorious also in the crown of martyrdom, was known not only to the African and Western Churches but also to the Eastern Churches, as his fame and writings were spread far and wide. Even Pelagius himself, the heresiarch of these people, mentions him with the honor certainly due to him. In writing a book of testimonies, Pelagius claims to imitate him, saying that he is doing for Romanus what Cyprian had done for Quirinus.

Let us therefore see what Cyprian thought concerning original sin, which entered the world through one human being (Rom. 5:12). In his letter *On Works and Almsgiving* he speaks as follows:

“When the Lord came and healed those wounds which Adam had carried, and cured the ancient poisons of the serpent [Note: [Col. 0623] So read Ambrose, Erasmus, and the manuscripts, both Gallican and Vatican. Lyons and the new edition of Cyprian have “the ancient serpent.”], he gave the healthy person a law and commanded him not to sin any longer, lest something worse happen to the sinner” (John 5:14).

“We were confined and shut within narrow limits by the prescription of innocence. Human frailty and weakness would have had no means of acting, unless divine mercy had come to our aid once more, displaying works of justice and mercy and opening a certain way of preserving salvation, so that afterward we might wash away whatever stains we contract through almsgiving” (Luke 11:41).

By this testimony, this witness refutes two falsehoods of theirs [Note: [Col. 0624] The Gallican manuscripts have “opposed” rather than “refutes.”]: one, by which they say that the human race derives from Adam no kind of vice that must be cured and healed through Christ; the other, by which they say that the saints have no sin after Baptism.

Again, in the same letter:

“Let each person place before his eyes the devil with his servants—that is, with the people of destruction and death—springing forth into the midst of the people of Christ, with Christ himself present and judging, and challenging them by the very comparison, saying:

‘I have received neither blows on the cheek nor scourging for these whom you see with me; I have endured neither the cross nor shed blood; I have not redeemed my household at the price of suffering and bloodshed. Nor do I promise them the heavenly kingdom, nor restore them to paradise with immortality regained.’”

Let the Pelagians answer: when were we in the immortality of paradise, and how were we expelled from it, so that we might be recalled there by Christ’s grace? And when they cannot find anything here to answer on behalf of their perversion, let them observe how Cyprian understood the Apostle’s statement, “In whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). Let the new Pelagian heretics not dare to level against any Catholic the calumny associated with the old Manichaean heretics, lest they be convicted of committing an equally wicked injury against the ancient martyr Cyprian.

### 22.

For in the letter entitled *On Mortality* he also says:

“The kingdom of God, dearest brothers, has begun to draw near; the reward of life, the joy of eternal salvation, everlasting gladness, and possession of the paradise recently lost are already coming as the world passes away.”

Again, in the same letter:

“Let us embrace the day which assigns each person to his dwelling, which, having snatched us from here and released us from the snares of this age, restores us to paradise and to the kingdom.”

Likewise, in his letter *On Patience*:

“Let the sentence of God be considered, which Adam received at the very beginning of the world and of the human race, when he forgot the commandment and transgressed the law that had been given. Then we shall know how patient we ought to be in this age, since we are born in such a way that here we labor amid pressures and struggles.

“‘Because you listened to the voice of your wife,’ he says, ‘and ate from the tree from which alone I had commanded you not to eat, cursed shall the earth be in all your works. In sorrow and groaning you shall eat from it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you, and you shall eat the food of the field. In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread, until you return to the earth from which you were taken; for you are earth, and to earth you shall go’” (Gen. 3:17–19).

“We are all bound and constrained by the bond of this sentence until, with death erased, we depart from this age.”

And again, in the same letter:
