“For when, in that first transgression of the commandment, the strength of the body departed together with immortality, and weakness came with death, strength cannot be restored unless immortality is restored as well. Therefore, in this frailty and weakness of the body, we must always struggle and contend. This struggle and contention can be sustained only by the strength of patience.”

### 23.

In the letter he wrote to Bishop Fidus [Col. 0625], together with his sixty-six fellow bishops, after Fidus had consulted him about the law of circumcision—whether an infant might be baptized before the eighth day—the matter is handled as though, by divine providence, the Catholic Church were already refuting the future Pelagian heretics from so great a distance.

The one who consulted Cyprian was not in doubt whether those who are born contract original sin, which they wash away by being reborn—for heaven forbid that the Christian faith should ever have doubted this. Rather, he was asking whether the washing of regeneration, by which he did not doubt that original sin was removed, ought to be administered before the eighth day.

In response to this inquiry, the most blessed Cyprian says:

“As far as the case of the infants whom you mentioned is concerned—those who, because they were within the second or third day after their birth, you thought ought not to be baptized, and concerning whom you thought the law of the ancient circumcision should be considered” (Gen. 17:12), “so that you did not think that one who had been born should be baptized and sanctified before the eighth day, the view of everyone in our council was very different [Note: [Col. 0625] The Gallican and Vatican manuscripts have: “the view of everyone in our council was very different.”].

“No one agreed with what you thought should be done. Rather, we all judged that the grace of the merciful God should be denied to no human being who is born. For since the Lord says in his Gospel, ‘The Son of Man did not come to destroy souls but to save them’ (Luke 9:56), as far as lies within us, if it can be done, no soul should be lost.”

And a little later:

“None of us ought to shrink from what the Lord has deigned to do. For even if the infant is newly born from the womb, he is not such that anyone ought to shrink from kissing him when grace is given and peace is bestowed. In the kiss of the infant, each of us, according to his religious devotion, ought to consider the very hands of God, still newly formed, which we in a certain sense kiss in the newly formed and newly born human being, when we embrace what God has made.”

Again, a little later:

“Moreover, if human beings could impede the attainment of grace in any way, more serious sins could impede adults, those advanced in age, and the elderly. But if even the gravest offenders, and those who had long sinned against God, receive the forgiveness of sins when they afterward believe, and no one is barred from Baptism and grace, how much more ought an infant not to be barred—an infant who, being newly born, has committed no sin, except that, having been born carnally according to Adam, he has contracted the contagion of ancient death in his first birth. He approaches all the more easily to receive the forgiveness of sins because the sins forgiven him are not his own but another’s.”

### 24.

What will those who are not merely deserters of God’s grace but also persecutors of it say to these things? What will they say?

How is possession of paradise restored to us? How are we restored to paradise if we were never there? Or how were we there except because we were in Adam? And how do we belong to the sentence pronounced against the transgressor if we do not derive guilt from the transgressor?

Finally, Cyprian judges that infants should be baptized even before the eighth day [Note: [Col. 0625] The printed editions have “Finally, if infants are to be baptized.” The word “if” is absent from the manuscripts.], lest the souls of little children perish through the contagion of ancient death contracted in their first birth. How do they perish if those who are born even of faithful human beings are not held by the devil until they are reborn in Christ and, rescued from the power of darkness, transferred into his kingdom (Col. 1:13)?

And who says that the souls of those who are born will perish unless they are reborn? Surely it is the one who so praises the Creator and creation, the maker and the work, that he restrains and corrects the human horror by which people disdain to kiss infants newly born from the womb, inserting reverence for the Creator himself and saying that, in the kiss of that age, the newly formed hands of God must be considered.

Did he, then, by confessing original sin, condemn nature or marriage? Did he, because he applied the cleansing of regeneration to one born guilty through Adam, thereby deny that God was the creator of those who are born? Did he, because he feared that souls of any age might perish and therefore judged, together with the council of his colleagues, that they should be liberated by the sacrament of Baptism even before the eighth day, thereby accuse marriage—when, in the infant, whether born from marriage or from adultery, simply because he had been born a human being, he showed the newly formed hands of God to be worthy even of the kiss of peace?

If, then, the holy and most glorious bishop and martyr Cyprian could judge original sin in infants to be something that must be healed by Christ’s medicine, while preserving praise of creation and praise of marriage, why does this novel pestilence, which does not dare to call him a Manichaean, think that it should charge Catholics who defend these truths with another person’s crime in order to conceal its own?

Behold, this celebrated interpreter of the divine utterances, before even the faintest scent of the Manichaean pestilence had touched our lands, confesses original sin without any disparagement of God’s work or of marriage. He does not say that Christ was stained by any mark of sin, nor does he compare to him the flesh of sin found in other newborns, for whom he provides the help of cleansing through the likeness of the flesh of sin. Nor is he frightened by the obscure question concerning the origin of souls, so that he refuses to acknowledge that those who are freed by Christ’s grace return to paradise.

Does he say that the condition of death passed from Adam into human beings without the contagion of sin? No. He says that infants, however newly born from the womb, are helped through Baptism not in order to avoid bodily death, but because of the sin that entered the world through one human being.

## CHAPTER IX
## CHAPTER IX

### 25. Cyprian’s testimonies concerning the grace of God

How Cyprian proclaims the grace of God against these men is now clearly evident from his discussion of the Lord’s Prayer. For he says:

> “We say, ‘Hallowed be your name’: not that we wish God to be hallowed by our prayers, but that we ask him for his name to be hallowed in us. For by whom is God hallowed, since he himself hallows? But because he himself said, ‘Be holy, because I too am holy’ (Leviticus 19:2), we ask and entreat that we who have been hallowed in Baptism may persevere in what we have begun to be.”

And elsewhere in the same letter:

> “We add also,” he says, “and say, ‘Your will be done [Column 0627] in heaven [Note: Printed editions have *as in heaven*. The word *as* is absent from the manuscripts.] and on earth’: not that God may do what he wills, but that we may be able to do what God wills. For who resists God, preventing him from doing what he wills? But because the devil resists us, preventing our mind and our conduct from obeying God in every respect, we pray and ask that God’s will be done in us. For this to happen in us, God’s will is necessary—that is, his help and protection—because no one is strong by his own powers, but is kept safe by God’s indulgence and mercy.”

Again, elsewhere:

> “We ask,” he says, “that God’s will be done in heaven and on earth, since both pertain to the completion of our safety and salvation. For since we possess a body from the earth and a spirit from heaven, we ourselves are earth and heaven; and in both—that is, in body and spirit—we pray that God’s will be done. For there is a struggle between flesh and spirit, and a daily conflict between them as they oppose one another, so that we do not do what we ourselves wish: the spirit seeks heavenly and divine things, while the flesh desires earthly and worldly things. Therefore we ask that, between these two, harmony may be brought about by God’s help and assistance, so that while God’s will is carried out both in spirit and in flesh, the soul which has been reborn through him may be preserved [Note: Vatican manuscripts have *may be restored*.]. The apostle Paul plainly and openly declares this in his own words: ‘The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you do not do what you wish’ (Galatians 5:17).”

And a little later:

> “This may also be understood in the following way, dearest brothers: since the Lord commands and teaches us even to love our enemies and to pray also for those who persecute us (Matthew 5:44), let us pray even for those who are still earth and have not yet begun to be heavenly, that God’s will may be done also with regard to them—the will which Christ accomplished by preserving and restoring the human being.”

Likewise, elsewhere:

> “We ask,” he says, “that this bread be given to us daily, so that we who are in Christ and receive the Eucharist daily as food for salvation may not, when some more serious offense intervenes and we are excluded [Note: Printed editions consistently have *absent* here and below. The Gallican and Vatican manuscripts consistently have *excluded*, as does Cyprian.], being forbidden from receiving and communicating in the heavenly bread, be separated from Christ’s body.”

And somewhat later in the same work:

> “When we ask,” he says, “that we may not enter into temptation (Matthew 6:9–13), we are reminded of our weakness and frailty. By praying in this way, no one should presumptuously exalt himself; no one should arrogantly and proudly claim anything for himself; no one should regard the glory of confession or martyrdom as his own. For the Lord himself, teaching humility, said: ‘Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak’ (Matthew 26:41). Thus, while a humble and submissive confession goes before, and everything is given to God, whatever is asked submissively, with fear and reverence toward God, is granted by his own goodness.”

Likewise, in his work addressed to Quirinus—a work in which Pelagius wishes to appear his imitator—he says in the third book:

> “No one should glory in anything, since nothing is ours.”

Adding divine testimonies to this proposition [Column 0628], among other passages he included that apostolic saying by which the mouths of these men above all must be closed:

> “For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

Likewise, in his letter *On Patience*:

> “This virtue,” he says, “is shared by us with God; from him patience begins, from him its glory and dignity take their origin; the source and greatness of patience proceed from God as their author.”

### 26

Does this holy and highly renowned instructor of the Churches in the word of truth deny that free choice exists in human beings because he attributes entirely to God whatever we rightly do? Does he condemn God’s law because he indicates that a human being is not justified by the law itself, when he declares that what the law commands must be obtained from the Lord God by prayers? Does he assert fate under the name of grace, although he says that no one should glory in anything, since nothing is ours? Does he, like these men, believe that the Holy Spirit is the helper of virtue in such a way that the virtue itself which is helped by him arises from us, when, asserting that nothing is ours, he recalls that the Apostle said for this reason, “What do you have that you did not receive?” And does he say that the most excellent virtue—namely, patience—begins not from us and is then aided by the Spirit of God, but that it takes its beginning and origin from him?

Finally, he does not confess that a good intention, the pursuit of virtue, or good minds begin to exist in human beings without the grace of God, since he says that no one should glory in anything, because nothing is ours.

What is so established in free choice as the things which the law says: that an idol must not be worshiped, adultery must not be committed, and murder must not be perpetrated? These and similar crimes are such that, if anyone commits them, he is removed from communion with Christ’s body. Yet if the most blessed Cyprian had thought that our will alone was sufficient for not committing these things, he would not have understood what we say in the Lord’s Prayer—“Give us this day our daily bread”—in such a way as to assert that we ask not to be separated from Christ’s body when, because some more serious offense intervenes, we are excluded and, not communicating, are forbidden the heavenly bread.

Let the new heretics certainly answer: what good merits precede in people who are enemies of the Christian name? For they not only possess no good, but possess even the worst merit. Yet Cyprian understands even in this way what we say in the prayer, “Your will be done in heaven and on earth”: that we should pray also for those who, for this reason, are understood to be earth [Note: The Gallican manuscripts have: *who, because they live carnally, are understood to be earth*.].

Therefore we pray not only for those who are unwilling, but also for those who resist and attack. What, then, do we ask except that the unwilling become willing, the resistant become consenting, and the attackers become loving? From whom, if not from him of whom it is written, “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs 8, according to the Septuagint)?

Let those, then, who resent being told that, if they do no evil and if they do good, they should glory not in themselves but in the Lord, learn to be Catholics.

## CHAPTER X

[Column 0629]

### 27. Cyprian’s testimonies concerning the imperfection of our righteousness

Let us now examine the third point, which no less causes every member of Christ and his entire body to recoil from these men: they contend that there are, or have been, righteous people in this life who possess absolutely no sin [Note: This Pelagian doctrine had already been condemned by the universal African council of 418. See below, in part 2 of the Appendix.]. By this presumption they openly contradict the Lord’s Prayer, in which all the members of Christ cry out with a truthful heart and in daily utterances, “Forgive us our debts.”

Let us see, then, what the most glorious in the Lord, Cyprian, thought about this as well; what he not only said but also committed to writing and memory for the instruction of the Churches—not, of course, of the Manichaeans, but of Catholics.

In his letter *On Works and Almsgiving* he says:

> “Let us therefore acknowledge, dearest brothers, the saving gift of divine indulgence, and let us treat our wounds with spiritual remedies for the cleansing [Note: Printed editions have *for the cleansing*. The manuscripts and Cyprian have *and for the cleansing*.] and purification of our sins, since we cannot exist without some wound to the conscience. Let no one flatter himself so much on the purity and innocence of his heart that, relying on his own innocence, he thinks no medicine should be applied to his wounds, since it is written: ‘Who can boast of having a pure heart? Or who can boast of being clean from sins?’ (Proverbs 20:9). And again, John says in his letter: ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us’ (1 John 1:8) [Note: Cyprian adds here: *But if we confess our sins, the Lord is faithful and righteous to forgive us our sins*.].”

> “But if no one can be without sin, and whoever declares himself blameless is either proud or foolish, how necessary and how kindly disposed is divine clemency! For it knows that certain wounds later arise even in those who have been healed, and it has provided saving remedies for wounds to be treated and healed again [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis have *saved again*. Ambrosius and the manuscripts have *healed again*.].”

Again, in the same work:

> “And since daily sinning in the sight of God cannot be absent, daily sacrifices were not absent [Note: Printed editions have *will not be absent*. Corrected from the manuscripts.], by which sins could be wiped away.”

Likewise, in his letter *On Mortality*:

> “We struggle with greed, with shamelessness, with anger, and with ambition. With carnal vices and worldly enticements there is a constant and troublesome combat. The human mind, besieged and surrounded on every side by the devil’s attacks, scarcely confronts each one and scarcely resists. If greed has been overthrown, lust rises up; if lust has been suppressed, ambition follows; if ambition has been despised, anger exasperates, pride inflates, drunkenness invites, envy breaks harmony, and jealousy cuts friendship apart [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis have *crime*; incorrectly.]. You are compelled to curse, which the divine law forbids; you are forced to swear, which is not permitted. So many persecutions the soul suffers daily [Column 0630], so many dangers press upon the heart [Note: The Gallican manuscripts have: *so many dangers and sins press upon it*], and yet it delights to stand here for a long time among the devil’s swords [Note: Thus in the manuscripts and in Cyprian. Ambrosius, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis have *among the devil’s snares*], when one ought rather to desire and long to hasten more quickly to Christ, with death coming to our aid.”

Likewise, in the same work:

> “The blessed apostle Paul says in his letter: ‘For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain’ (Philippians 1:21), counting it the greatest gain no longer to be held by worldly snares [Note: Cyprian has *by the snares of the world*], and no longer to be subject to any sins and vices of the flesh.”

Again, in his exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, explaining what we ask when we say, “Hallowed be your name,” he says, among other things:

> “We need daily sanctification, so that we who sin daily may cleanse away our offenses through continual sanctification.”

Again, in the same work, when he explained what we say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:9, 12):

> “How necessarily, how wisely, and how beneficially we are reminded that we are sinners, since we are compelled to pray for our sins, so that, while forgiveness is sought from God, the mind may remember its own conscience! To prevent anyone from pleasing himself as though he were innocent and from perishing more through self-exaltation, he is instructed and taught that he sins daily, since he is commanded to pray daily for his sins. Thus John also warns in his letter, saying: ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous [Note: Cyprian has *the Lord is faithful and righteous*, as above, Column 0629, note 3.] to forgive us our sins’” (1 John 1:8–9).

With good reason, in his work addressed to Quirinus, he set forth his most complete judgment on this matter, to which he added divine testimonies: “No one is without defilement and without sin” (Book 3, chapter 54). There he also included those testimonies by which original sin is confirmed—testimonies which these men attempt to twist into I do not know what other perverse new meanings.

These include the statement of holy Job: “No one is without defilement, nor is anyone whose life is even a single day upon the earth” (Job 14:5, according to the Septuagint); and what is read in the Psalm: “I was conceived in iniquity, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb” (Psalm 50:7).

To these testimonies, on account also of those who are already mature in age and are holy—for they too are not without defilement and sin—he added the statement of the blessed John, which he often recalls in many other places:

> “If we say that we have no sin,”

and the rest of the same sentence, which all Catholics do not keep silent about in opposition to these men, who deceive themselves and in whom the truth is not present.

### 28

Let the Pelagians say, if they dare, that this man of God was corrupted by the error of the Manichaeans because he praises the saints while nevertheless confessing that no one in this life reaches such perfection of righteousness that he has absolutely no sin [Note: Lovaniensis has *belongs to such perfection*.]. He confirms his judgment with the manifest truth and divine authority of canonical testimonies.

Does he deny that “all sins are forgiven in Baptism” because he admits that weakness and frailty remain, and therefore says that we sin after Baptism and maintain an unceasing struggle with carnal vices until the end of this life? Or did he for that reason fail to remember what the Apostle said “about the immaculate Church” (Ephesians 5:27), because he commanded that no one should flatter himself so much on the purity and innocence of his heart that, relying on his innocence, he thinks no medicine should be applied to his wounds?

I suppose these new heretics will grant that this Catholic man knew that “the Holy Spirit also helped good minds in ancient times”—indeed, they should grant even what they themselves do not wish to grant: that they could not have good minds except through the Holy Spirit.

I suppose Cyprian knew that “all the Prophets and Apostles, and whatever saints pleased the Lord at any time, were righteous,” not “in comparison with criminals,” as these men falsely accuse us of saying, but “by the rule of virtues,” as they boast of saying. Yet Cyprian also says:

> “No one can be without sin; and whoever declares himself blameless is either proud or foolish.”

For what other reason does he understand it to be written:

> “Who can boast of having a pure heart? Or who can boast of being clean from sins?” (Proverbs 20:9)

I suppose Cyprian did not need to be taught by these men what he knew very well: “that in the future there is a reward for good works and punishment for evil works; but no one can there fulfill the commandments which he has despised here.” Yet he also understands and asserts that the apostle Paul himself—certainly not a despiser of the divine commandments—said, “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21), for no other reason than that he counted it the greatest gain no longer to be held by worldly snares after this life and no longer to be subject to any sins and vices of the flesh.

Thus the most blessed Cyprian understood and discerned in the truth of the divine Scriptures that even the Apostles themselves, although their life was good, holy, and righteous, had endured certain bonds of worldly snares and had been subject to certain sins and vices of the flesh. For this reason they desired death: so that they might be free from these evils and reach that perfect righteousness which would not suffer such things—righteousness that here is to be practiced as a commandment, but there received as a reward [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis have *as a reward*. Ambrosius and the manuscripts have *in the reward*.].

For when what we pray for by saying, “Your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10), has arrived, there will certainly be righteousness in God’s kingdom, since the Apostle says, “For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17).

These three things, among other divine commandments, are indeed commanded. Here righteousness is commanded when it is said, “Practice righteousness” (Isaiah 56:1). Peace is commanded when it is said, “Have peace among yourselves” (Mark 9:50). Joy is commanded when it is said, “Rejoice in the Lord always” (Philippians 4:4).

Let the Pelagians, then, deny that these things will exist in the kingdom of God, where we shall live without end; or, if they wish, let them go so far in their insanity as to contend that righteousness, peace, and joy will be there exactly as they are here among the righteous.

But if they will exist there, and will not be such as they are here, then certainly their practice must be cultivated here as a commandment and their perfection hoped for there as a reward. There, held back by no worldly snares [Note: The printed editions of Ambrosius, Erasmus, and Lovaniensis have *will not be held back*, and end the sentence with the word *said*; from that point they begin a new sentence, *Let us love perfectly*, or, in Lovaniensis, *we shall love*. The Vatican manuscripts do not have *will be* here, but after *subject* add *we shall be*. Neither reading occurs in the Gallican manuscripts.], and subject to no sins or vices of the flesh—for this reason, as Cyprian received this testimony, the Apostle said that death was gain for him—we shall love God perfectly, whose contemplation will be face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12). We shall love our neighbor perfectly as well, when, with the thoughts of the heart revealed, no suspicion of anyone’s evil can trouble anyone concerning anyone else.

## CHAPTER XI

### 29. Testimonies of Ambrose against the Pelagians concerning original sin, the grace of God, and the imperfection of present righteousness

But, in order to refute these men more fully, let us add to the already most glorious martyr Cyprian the blessed Ambrose [Note: The manuscripts have *but now to the most glorious*, without the conjunction *and*.]. For Pelagius praised him so highly that he said not even his enemies could find anything reprehensible in his books.

Since, then, the Pelagians say that there is no original sin with which infants are born, and since they accuse Catholics who resist them on behalf of the ancient faith of the Church of the crime of Manichaeism, let the Catholic man of God Ambrose—praised even by Pelagius for the truth of the faith [Note: Lovaniensis has *of faith*. The other books more correctly have *of the faith*.]—answer them on this matter.

When he was expounding the prophet Isaiah, he said:

> “For this reason Christ is immaculate, because he was not stained even by the ordinary condition of birth.”

And elsewhere in the same work, speaking about the apostle Peter:

> “He himself,” he says, “offered himself, asking that what he had previously thought to be a sin should be washed—not only his feet but also his head (John 13:9). He would have immediately understood that, by the washing of the feet, the filth of the inherited condition of those who fell in the first man is removed.”

Again, in the same work:

> “It was therefore established that, from a man and a woman—that is, through that commingling of bodies—no one appears to be free from sin; but whoever is free from sin is also free from this kind of conception.”

Likewise, writing against the Novatians (Book 1 of *On Repentance*, chapter 3):

> “All human beings are born under sin. Their very birth is in sin, as you have read, when David says: ‘For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother gave birth to me in sins’” (Psalm 50:7).

Again, in his *Apology of the Prophet David*:

> “Before we are born, we are stained by contagion; before we receive the use of light, we receive the injury of our very origin; we are conceived in iniquity.”

Again, speaking of the Lord:

> “For it was fitting that he who was not to have the sin of bodily falling should feel no natural contagion of generation. Therefore David rightly lamented tearfully in himself the very defilements of nature, and that the stain should begin in the human being before life” (chapter 11).

Again, concerning Noah’s Ark:

> “Through one Lord Jesus, therefore, the salvation that would come to the nations is declared—he alone could be righteous while the whole human generation was wandering, for no other reason than that, born of a virgin, he was in no way held by the privilege of the burdened condition of generation [Column 0633] [Note: The printed editions omit *for no other reason than*, and read: *unless he had been born of a virgin, who, by the privilege of the burdened generation, etc.* The passage is restored according to the Gallican manuscripts. The manuscripts again vary: in Book 2 against Julian, section 4, they have *unless he alone were free from bonds, whom the bonds of common nature did not hold?*].”

> “Behold,” he says, “I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother gave birth to me in sins”—says the one who was considered righteous above others. Whom, then, should I call righteous except one who is free from these bonds, whom the bonds of common nature do not hold [Note: The Gallican manuscripts have: *unless he alone is free from bonds, whom the bonds of common nature did not hold?*]?”

Behold this holy man, highly approved in the Catholic faith even by Pelagius’s testimony, refutes the Pelagians who deny original sin with such complete clarity. Yet he neither denies with the Manichaeans that God is the creator of those who are born, nor condemns marriage, which God instituted and blessed.

### 30

The Pelagians say that merit begins with the human being through free choice, and that God subsequently repays it with the assistance of grace. Here too let the venerable Ambrose refute them. In his *Exposition of the Prophet Isaiah* he says:

> “Because human care [Note: Printed editions had *nature* in place of *care*.] is weak for healing without divine help, it requires God as its helper.”

Likewise, in the book entitled *On Flight from the World* (chapter 1):

> “We speak frequently about fleeing this world; and would that our attitude were as cautious and attentive as our speech is easy [Note: The manuscripts have *effect*, rather than *attitude*.]. But what is worse, the enticement of earthly desires frequently creeps in, and a clouding of vanities [Note: The same manuscripts have *outpouring* rather than *clouding*.] occupies the mind, so that what you strive to avoid you think about and turn over in your mind. What is difficult for a human being to guard against is impossible to cast off.

> “Finally, the prophet testifies that this matter is more a matter of prayer than of accomplishment, saying: ‘Incline my heart to your testimonies and not to greed’ (Psalm 118:36). For our heart and our thoughts are not in our power; unexpectedly clouded, they confuse the mind and spirit and draw them elsewhere than you have determined. They recall us to worldly things, implant earthly concerns, introduce pleasures, and weave in enticements. At the very time when we prepare to raise our mind, we are usually cast down to earthly things by empty thoughts inserted into it.

> “Who is so blessed that he always ascends in his heart? But how can this happen without divine help? In no way at all. Indeed, the same Scripture says above: ‘Blessed is the man whose help is from you, O Lord; ascents are in his heart’” (Psalm 83:6).

What could be said more clearly or sufficiently? But perhaps the Pelagians will answer that, precisely because divine help is sought [Note: Printed editions have *may be able*. Corrected from the manuscripts.], a human merit precedes it, and they will call this itself merit, saying that by praying a person becomes worthy of receiving the aid of divine grace.

Let them attend, then, to what this same holy man says in his *Exposition of Isaiah*:

> “To pray to God,” he says, “is itself spiritual grace. For no one says ‘Lord Jesus’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:3).

Hence, also, when expounding the Gospel according to Luke:

> “You see clearly,” he says, “that everywhere the Lord’s power cooperates with human efforts, so that no one can build without the Lord, no one can preserve without the Lord, and no one can begin anything without the Lord” (Book 2 on Luke, chapter 3, section 84, concerning Jesus’ baptism).

Does this great man, Ambrose, destroy free choice because he says these things and commends the grace of God with grateful devotion, as is fitting for the son of promise? Or does he wish that grace to be understood as the kind which the Pelagians, by various expressions, are unwilling to regard as anything other than the law—so that God is thought to help us not in doing what we have learned, but in learning what we should do?

If they think that this man of God held such an opinion, let them hear what he said about the law itself. In *On Flight from the World* he says:

> “The law was able to close the mouth of everyone; it was not able to convert the mind” (chapter 3).

Again, elsewhere in the same book:

> “The law condemns the deed; it does not remove wickedness” (chapter 7).

Let them observe that this faithful and Catholic man agrees with the Apostle, who says:

> “We know that whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are under the law, so that every mouth may be closed and the whole world may become liable to God; because no flesh will be justified before him by the law” (Romans 3:19–20).

For Ambrose took and wrote those words from this apostolic meaning.

### 31

Since the Pelagians now say that there are, or have been, righteous people in this life who have lived without any sin [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions have: *in this life, for this reason, there are or have been those who lived without any sin*.], to such an extent that the future life, which is to be hoped for as a reward, cannot be more advanced or more perfect, let Ambrose answer and refute them here as well.

When he was expounding the prophet Isaiah, on account of what is written, “I have begotten and raised children, but they have rejected me” (Isaiah 1:2), he undertook to discuss the generations which are from God. In that discussion he recalled John’s testimony, where he says, “Whoever is born of God does not sin” (1 John 3:9).

Treating this exceedingly difficult question, he says:

> “Since in this world there is no one who is free from sin, while John himself says, ‘If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar’ (1 John 1:10), but if those born of God do not sin, and we understand this to refer to the innumerable people who are in this world, we must conclude that it concerns those who have obtained the grace of God through the regeneration of the washing.

> “Yet, since the prophet says, ‘All things wait for you, that you may give them food in due season; when you give it to them, they gather it; when you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness; but when you turn your face away, they will be troubled; you will take away their spirit, and they will fail and return to their dust; you will send forth your spirit, and they will be created, and you will renew the face of the earth’ (Psalm 103:27–30), these words may be understood not of some period in particular but of the future, when there will be a new earth and a new heaven.

> “They will therefore be troubled in order to take their beginning; and when you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness [Note: The Gallican manuscripts have: *in order that they may take their beginning, and when you open your hand, all things may be filled with goodness*]. Such goodness does not readily belong to this age. For what does Scripture say about this age? ‘There is no one who does good, not even one’ (Psalm 13:1).

> “If, then, there are different generations, and this entrance into the present life is a receptacle of sins, so much so that even the one who begot is rejected, while another generation does not receive sins, let us see whether there is some regeneration of ours after the course of this life, concerning which it is said, ‘In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his glory’ (Matthew 19:28).

> “For just as the regeneration of the washing is so called because through it we are renewed after the filth of sins has been washed away, so regeneration appears to be the name for that by which, purified from every stain of bodily composition, we are reborn in eternal life with a pure perception of the soul. This is because the quality of that regeneration is purer than that of this washing: in it, not only do no sinful acts occur, but not even any suspicion of sins falls upon our thoughts.”

Again, elsewhere in the same work:

> “We see that it is impossible for anyone who is established in the body to be perfectly immaculate, since even Paul says that he is imperfect. For he says: ‘Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect.’ And yet shortly afterward he says: ‘Therefore, as many as are perfect’ (Philippians 3:12, 15).

> “Unless perhaps there is one kind of perfection in this world and another after that perfection concerning which he says to the Corinthians, ‘When that which is perfect has come’ (1 Corinthians 13:10); and elsewhere, ‘Until we all attain to the unity of faith and the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ’ (Ephesians 4:13).

> “Thus, just as the Apostle calls many who are situated in this world perfect, although, if you consider true perfection, they could not be perfect, because he himself said, ‘Now we see through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known’ (1 Corinthians 13:12), so they are immaculate in this world and will be immaculate in the kingdom of God. Yet if you examine the matter minutely, no one can be immaculate, because no one is without sin.”

Again, in the same work:

> “We see that, while we live this life, we must cleanse ourselves, seek God, and begin with the cleansing of our soul, laying down, as it were, the foundations of virtue, so that after this life we may deserve to attain the perfection of purification [Note: Thus in the manuscripts. The printed editions have *perfection of cleansing*.].”

And again, in the same work:

> “Who would not speak, burdened and groaning, saying, ‘Wretched man that I am, who will free me from this body of death?’ (Romans 7:24). Thus, with the same teacher, we resolve all the varieties of interpretation.

> “For if everyone who recognizes that he is entangled in the troubles of the body is wretched, then every body is wretched. For I would not call happy the person who, confused by certain darknesses of mind, does not know his own condition.

> “This too is not absurd as an interpretation: if the human being who knows himself is wretched, then all are certainly wretched, because each person either recognizes his own weakness through wisdom or fails to know it through foolishness.”

Likewise, in the book *On the Good of Death* (chapters 3 and 11):

> “Let death therefore work in us, so that life may also work—good life after death, good life after victory, good life after the struggle has been brought to an end—so that the law of the flesh may no longer know how to resist the law of the mind (Romans 7:23), and so that we may no longer have any conflict with the body of death.”

Again, in the same work:

> “Therefore,” he says, “since the righteous have this reward, that they see the face of God and that light which enlightens every human being (John 1:9) [Note: The printed editions have *and that they see the light*. The word *that they see* is absent from the manuscripts.], let us henceforth adopt such a devotion that our soul may draw near to God, our prayer may draw near [Note: Here the ancient books restore *our prayer may draw near*], and our desire may cling to him; let us not be separated from him.

> “Even while placed here, let us be joined to God by meditating, reading, and seeking; let us know him as we are able. For here we know in part, because here all things are imperfect, there perfect; here we are children, there mature.

> “He says: ‘Now we see through a mirror in a riddle, but then face to face.’ Then, with face unveiled, we shall be permitted to contemplate the glory of the Lord, which now the souls enclosed in the compacted organs of this body and overshadowed by certain stains and filth of this flesh cannot see sincerely.

> “For who,” he says, “will see my face and live?” (Exodus 33:20). And rightly: for if our eyes cannot endure the rays of the sun, and if someone who gazes at the sun directly for too long is said ordinarily to become blind; if creation cannot look upon creation without injury and harm to itself, how can a person, covered with the outer garments of this body, see without danger to himself the flashing face of the eternal Creator?

> “For who is justified in the sight of God?” (Psalm 142:2). Even an infant of a single day cannot be clean from sin (Job 14:5, according to the Septuagint) [Note: Here too the manuscripts add *from sin*], and no one can glory in the integrity and chastity of his own heart” (Proverbs 20:9).

## CHAPTER XII
### 32. The Pelagian heresy arose long after Ambrose. The Catholic faith is ever vigilant in repelling error. The assembling of a synod is not always necessary for condemning heresies.

It would take too long if I wished to recall everything that Saint Ambrose said and wrote against this heresy of the Pelagians, which arose so much later—not indeed responding to them, but proclaiming the Catholic faith and building people up in it. Nor could or should I recall everything that the most glorious Cyprian placed in his Letters, by which it may be demonstrated that this faith which we hold is truly and genuinely Christian and Catholic [Printed editions read “how”; manuscripts, “that”]:  handed down in ancient times through the sacred Scriptures, then retained and preserved by our fathers up to the present time, when these men attempted to overthrow it, and thereafter to be retained and preserved, by God’s favor.

For the testimonies drawn from his letters show that this and similar teaching was handed down in this way by Cyprian and from Cyprian. What Ambrose wrote about these matters before these men began to boil over demonstrates that it was preserved in this way up to our own times; and the fact that Catholic ears everywhere shuddered at their profane novelties demonstrates that it must thereafter be preserved in the same manner. Moreover, the condemnation of some of them and the correction of others has made it sufficiently clear that this teaching must be preserved in the future.

Whatever they may dare to mutter against the sound faith of Cyprian and Ambrose, I do not think they will burst into such great madness as to dare call those remembered and memorable men of God Manichaeans.

### 33.

What, then, is the meaning of what they now proclaim in the madness of their mind’s blindness—that throughout the entire West a dogma no less foolish than impious has been embraced? For, since the Lord in his mercy and in his merciful governance of his Church watched over it, the Catholic faith remained so vigilant that this dogma, no less foolish than impious, was not embraced by the Church any more than that of the Manichaeans.

Behold Catholic men, holy and learned, as the testimony of the fame of the whole Church confirms, praising both God’s creature, marriage instituted by him, and the law given by him [The printed editions had omitted “by him”; it occurs in the manuscripts.] through holy Moses, as well as free will implanted in human nature and the holy Patriarchs and Prophets, with appropriate and fitting commendations. The Manichaeans condemn all five of these things [Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “unjustly”], partly by denying them and partly even by detesting them. Thus it is evident that these Catholic teachers are far removed from Manichaean opinions.

And yet they affirm original sin; they affirm that God’s grace precedes every merit in relation to free will, so that he may provide truly gratuitous divine assistance; they affirm that the saints lived so justly in this flesh that they needed the aid of prayer for the forgiveness of daily sins, and that perfect righteousness—which cannot possess sin—will be their future reward in the other life, if they have lived justly here.

### 34.

What, then, is the meaning of their claim that “a subscription was extorted from simple bishops [In the printed editions, *De simplicibus episcopis*, ‘Concerning simple bishops.’ The word *de* is absent from the manuscripts.] sitting in their own places, without the assembling of a synod”?

Was a subscription extorted from the most blessed and outstanding men in the Catholic faith, Cyprian and Ambrose, before these men and against these men—men who [The printed editions read “by which”; the manuscripts, “who.”] so plainly overturn their impious doctrines that we can scarcely find anything to say against them that is more obvious [The manuscripts read *manifestatiora*; the printed editions, *manifestiora*]? Or was the assembling of a synod necessary in order to condemn an obvious danger—as though no heresy had ever been condemned except through the assembling of a synod?

On the contrary, very few heresies are found for which such a necessity arose in order to condemn them. There are many more—indeed incomparably more—which, once they arose, deserved to be rejected and condemned there, and from there could become known throughout the other lands as things to be avoided.

But the pride of these men, which raises itself so high against God that it does not wish to glory in him but rather in free will, is understood also to be seeking this glory: that a synod of the East and West should be assembled on their account. Since they cannot corrupt the Catholic world because the Lord resists them, they at least try to disturb it.

Rather, after a suitable and sufficient judgment has been made concerning them through pastoral vigilance and diligence, wherever these wolves appear they must be crushed—either so that they may be healed and changed, or so that they may be avoided for the sake of the salvation and integrity of others. The Shepherd of shepherds assists us: he seeks the lost sheep, even among little ones; he freely makes them holy and just; and, although sanctified and justified, he wisely instructs them to ask for daily forgiveness for their daily sins—for without such sins no one lives here, even when living well—and mercifully hears those who ask.

## [Against Julian]

### Prefatory Notice to the Books Against Julian

In these books the presbyter Jerome is praised as though he were already dead (*Book 1*, no. 34; *Book 2*, no. 36). He departed this life on the day before the Kalends of October in the year of Christ 420. These books therefore cannot be dated earlier than the year 421. Indeed, Augustine himself, in the *Retractations*, reviewed them after the work addressed to Boniface against two letters of the Pelagians, which was published in 420 or not much later.

In the first book, intending to confirm the doctrine of original sin, which he had already explained in the preceding book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, he shows that the accusation of Manichaeism, by which Julian tried to attack Catholics who defended this doctrine, rebounds upon the most distinguished Fathers, both Greek and Latin. In the second part of the book he demonstrates that the Manichaeans receive considerable support from several rash statements made by Julian himself.

In the second book, the author overturns five Pelagian arguments against original sin by the authority of earlier teachers of the Church—namely, ten distinguished bishops: Irenaeus, Cyprian, Reticius, Olympius, Hilary, Gregory of Nazianzus, Ambrose, Basil, John of Constantinople, and Innocent—as well as by the testimony of the presbyter Jerome, a holy and extremely learned man.

Augustine then sets one of his own books against each of Julian’s four books, examining everything Julian said except what had no bearing on the central issue. In his third book, he refutes the adversary’s first book, proving that although God is good and is the creator of human beings, and although marriage is good and was instituted by him, concupiscence is nevertheless evil—the concupiscence by which the flesh lusts against the spirit.

Marriage makes good use of this evil, while continence makes better use of it by abstaining from it. This evil is not, as the mad Manichaean claims, mixed with us from another substance coeternal with God; rather, it arose and was transmitted through Adam’s disobedience and must be expiated and healed through Christ’s obedience. Augustine also shows from Julian’s own statements that lust is evil.

In the fourth book, against Julian’s second book, he teaches chiefly two things: first, that the virtues of unbelievers are not true virtues; second, that concupiscence is evil. Taking the opportunity supplied by Julian’s own statements, he demonstrates this even from the opinions of the Gentiles. Around the middle of the book he briefly shows how grace is given not according to merits and yet is not to be attributed to fate, and how the Apostle’s statement that God wills all people to be saved should be understood.

In the fifth book, refuting the adversary’s third book, he explains why the Christian multitude detests the new heresy that denies original sin: namely, because it knows that the image of God suffers such great torments here in little children and that, if they die without Baptism, they are excluded from the kingdom of God.

He proves that the coverings adopted by the first parents arose from shame resulting from sin. He shows that sin can be the punishment of a preceding sin. He explains that from the same condemned mass some are freely chosen while others are made vessels of wrath. Concupiscence is not therefore worthy of praise because through it human disobedience is punished; rather, it is always evil, even in those who do not consent to it.

He explains how the Apostle’s statement that each person should know how to possess his own vessel is to be understood. He shows that a marriage without intercourse, such as that of Mary with Joseph, is nevertheless a marriage. He demonstrates that Julian vainly argues against original sin from Aristotelian categories. He explains how Christ’s flesh differs from the sinful flesh of other human beings. Catholics do not favor the Manichaeans when they acknowledge the evil of lust and the defect of origin; rather, the Pelagians favor the Manichaeans when they say that “sins are not born from that which is free from sin.”

Finally, in the sixth book, responding to Julian’s fourth book, he confirms that human beings are born with sin from the Baptism of infants, the Apostle’s words, and the rite of exorcism and insufflation performed upon those to be baptized. Through the example of the olive and the wild olive he suitably explains how sinful children in need of regeneration can be born from parents who have been regenerated and justified.

He shows that original sin was voluntary in the first parents and that, although it is alien to us in respect of the action, it is nevertheless ours through the contagion of propagation. By the merit of this sin it comes about that the human race is worn down from infancy by such great miseries, and that infants who die without the grace of regeneration are excluded from the kingdom of God.

He explains how concupiscence remains in act but passes away in guilt. He recalls Paul’s testimonies, perversely interpreted by Julian, to their Catholic meaning. Finally, he interprets the authority of Ezekiel, which Julian abused, according to its legitimate sense.

[On the books *Against Julian*, see *Retractations* 2.62, volume 1, column 655, from the words “Meanwhile, the four books” up to “Your insults and abusive words, Julian.” M.]

## Letter 207 (C) of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo

To the most blessed brother and fellow bishop Claudius, Augustine sends greetings in the Lord.

Since, moved by brotherly affection, you sent me Julian’s four books—which he wrote against one of mine [The first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*]—before I had asked you for them, I thought that nothing would be more appropriate than for you yourself to read what I have written in response and judge whether I have answered correctly and suitably.

For someone—I do not know who—had extracted certain passages from these four books and written them against that same book of mine to the illustrious and religious Count Valerius, knowing that I had written it to him. When these extracts came into my hands through the care of that distinguished man, I did not delay in adding a second volume to the first, in which I refuted all those passages as best I could.

But when I examined the same books more carefully, I discovered that the man who had selected certain passages from them had not set them down exactly as they are found in these books. Thus Julian, or any of his associates, might think that I had been the liar instead, since the extracts taken from these four books and sent to the aforementioned Count could not have become known in precisely the same form as the books themselves.

Whoever, therefore, has read that second book of mine addressed to Count Valerius, as well as the first, should know that in some places I was not responding to Julian, but rather to the man who selected those passages from his books and did not set them down as he found them, but thought that they needed to be altered somewhat—perhaps so that he might make his own, in a certain fashion, what was plainly another’s.

Now, believing the copies sent by Your Holiness to be more accurate, I see that I must answer the author himself, who boasts that he has refuted one of my books in his four books and never ceases to scatter the poisons of his faith everywhere.

I have therefore undertaken this work with the help of the Savior of little ones and great ones. I know that you prayed for me, so that I might complete it, and for those whom we believe and hope will benefit from such labors of ours.

Attend, then, to my response, whose beginning will follow this letter. Farewell in the Lord, remembering us, most blessed brother.

## The Six Books of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, Against Julian, Defender of the Pelagian Heresy

[Written in the year of Christ 421 or shortly thereafter.]

[The six books *Against Julian* were emended with the aid of five Vatican manuscripts and eight Gallican manuscripts: one from the library of the distinguished D. Emeric Bigot; others from the abbeys of Fleury, Casale Benedetto, Pratelles, Saint Michael, Bec, Lyre, and Paris Saint-Victor. Assistance was also provided by variant readings from three Belgian manuscripts, and the old editions were collated. Am. Er. and Lov.]

[Moreover, all the editions mentioned at the beginning of *Retractations* and *Confessions*, volume 1, were compared. M.]

### Book One

Augustine undertakes to defend against Julian the Catholic position on original sin, which he explained in his first book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. Julian dared to attack this position in four larger books and did not hesitate to apply the name of Manichaeans to its defenders.

Augustine shows that this detestable accusation rebounds upon the most distinguished Fathers, both Greek and Latin, adducing their testimonies on the matter and responding specifically to those passages of Basil and John Chrysostom which Julian thinks support him. In the final part of the book he demonstrates that the Manichaean heresy receives considerable support from several rash statements made by Julian himself.

### Chapter One

#### 1.

If I were to say that I despise your insults and abusive words, Julian—words which, in the heat of your anger, you breathed out through four books [An old Fleury codex reads, “which in the heat of your anger you breathed out against me”]—I would be lying. For how can I despise such things when, considering the testimony of my conscience, I see that I ought either to rejoice on my own behalf or to grieve on yours and on behalf of those whom you deceive?

Who could despise either the source of his rejoicing or the source of his grief? For whatever causes us partly to rejoice and partly to grieve, we certainly do not despise.

The cause of my joys is the Lord’s promise, in which he says: “When they say every evil thing against you, lying, on account of me, rejoice and exult, for your reward is abundant [All the manuscripts read, “is abundant.”] in heaven” (Matthew 5:11–12).

Again, the cause of my sorrow is the Apostle’s feeling, where I read: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not on fire?” (2 Corinthians 11:29).

But you too can say these things concerning your doctrine, which you think to be the truth [Am. Er. and several manuscripts read, “concerning your doctrine, which you think to be the truth.”]. Let us therefore, if you please, remove these common matters from consideration—things which can be said by either side, although they cannot truthfully be said by both sides.

#### 2.

First I ask you why you boast that you have responded to my book, at least in appearance, when in your four books you have not even touched, by way of criticism, a fourth part of my one book, and have made such leaps in passing over my arguments as though you entirely despaired [Two manuscripts read, “you despair.”] that anyone could be a reader of both works—of mine and of yours—and detect this.

Finally, even those few portions—scarcely, as I said, a fourth part of my volume—which you judged to be weaker and attempted to overthrow and trample underfoot by the noise of your four larger volumes [All the Vatican manuscripts read “large volumes”], as though by the charge of four-horse chariots, are shown, when the far greater number of other matters you feared to touch are considered, to remain unshaken. It is almost unnecessary to demonstrate this.

Those who wish to know it should rather be advised not to shrink from reading both works: what I wrote and what you wished to answer. The matter itself so declares and indicates this that those who ask us to demonstrate it must be exceedingly slow-witted.

#### 3.

Now, because I see that you have been abandoned by the truth [Erasmus and the Louvain edition read, “abandoned by the truth”; Ambrose and the manuscripts lack the preposition *a*. Thus Tacitus, *Annals* 3.20: “nor did he cease fighting until, abandoned by his men, he fell”—for “by his men”], and have turned to abuse, I shall distribute my argument in such a way that I will first show against how many and what sort of teachers of the Catholic Church you do not hesitate to commit the intolerable insult of calling them Manichaeans, and, when you attack me, against whom you hurl your sacrilegious darts.

Next I shall show that you yourself so assist the condemnable error of the Manichaeans and their unspeakable impiety that they could find no such patron even among those who love them.

Third, as briefly as I can, I shall refute your empty subtleties and elaborated arguments—not with my own opinions, but with the judgments of those who lived before us and defended the Catholic faith against the impious.

Finally, since, if you do not correct yourself, you will necessarily have to attack those teachers of the Catholic Church as well and contend that they too did not maintain the Catholic truth on this question, I shall, with God’s help, defend both their faith and ours against you. There it may also become clear not only how much your words assist the Manichaeans—as I promised to demonstrate in the second place—but also how much the Pelagian doctrine itself, which you all share, assists them.

### Chapter Two

#### 4.

Attend for a little while to how I shall carry out the first part of my division. The issue between us, insofar as it concerns the purpose of my book, which you boast that you have answered in your four books, is this: I say that marriage must be praised in such a way that the fact that all human beings are born subject to the sin of those first human beings in no way belongs to marriage’s fault or condemnation [Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “may be born subject”].

For anyone who denies this attempts to overthrow the very foundations of the Christian faith. This is why I wrote the book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*: to distinguish the good of marriage from the evil from which original sin is drawn.

You, however, say that marriage is without doubt condemned unless what is born from it is free from every bond of sin. For this reason you boast that you have refuted my one book in four books.

In those books, while attempting to turn people away from the deeply grounded Catholic faith and lead them toward the novelty of your error, you often implant in the minds of readers the horror of the Manichaean plague [Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “the error of the Manichaeans”]: as though someone who says that infants born carnally according to Adam contract the contagion of ancient death at their first birth and therefore need a second birth, so that through the washing of regeneration they may first be cleansed from original sin and, adopted as children of God, transferred into the kingdom of the Only-Begotten, were holding with the Manichaeans that evil has a natural origin.

Jovinian also used the name and charge of Manichaeism in this way, denying that the holy virginity of Mary—which had remained while she conceived—remained while she gave birth, as though we would believe with the Manichaeans that Christ was a phantom if we said that he arose from the mother’s uncorrupted virginity.

But with the help of that very Savior, just as Catholics rejected as the sharpest possible argument the argument Jovinian had advanced, and believed neither that holy Mary was corrupted in giving birth nor that the Lord was a phantom, but both that she remained a virgin after childbirth and that Christ’s true body nevertheless arose from her, so they will reject your slanderous empty talk [The Louvain edition reads, “they reject”].

They will neither assert with the Manichaeans that evil has a natural principle, nor hesitate, in accordance with the ancient and true Catholic faith, to believe that Christ is the liberator of infants by cancelling the record of their ancestral debt.

### Chapter Three

#### 5.

But you, who so frequently oppose to us the name of the Manichaeans, look—if you are awake—at what men, what sort of men, and how many defenders of the Catholic faith you dare to attack with so detestable an accusation.

I do not promise to assemble all their opinions on this matter, nor all those whom I shall mention, because that would take too long and I do not think it necessary. I shall set down a few statements from a few men, yet statements by which our opponents must be compelled to blush and yield—if any fear of God or shame before human beings has overcome such great obstinacy in them.

Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, lived not long after the times of the Apostles. He says:

> “People cannot otherwise be saved from the ancient wound of the serpent [Some manuscripts read, “from the wound of the ancient serpent”] unless they believe in him who, in the likeness of sinful flesh, raised up from the earth on the tree of martyrdom, drew all things to himself and gave life to the dead” (*Book 4*, chapter 5).

The same man also says:

> “Just as the human race was bound to death through a virgin, so let it be released through a virgin, with the balance set equally: virgin disobedience through virgin obedience. For while the sin of the first-formed man was receiving correction through the reparation of the Firstborn [Most manuscripts read, “through correction”], the serpent’s cunning was defeated by the simplicity of the dove, and we were released from those bonds by which we had been bound to death” (*Book 5*, chapter 19).

Do you see what this ancient man of God thinks about the ancient wound of the serpent? What he thinks about the likeness of sinful flesh, through which the serpent’s wound is healed in sinful flesh? What he thinks about the sin of the first-formed man, through which we had been bound?

#### 6.

The most blessed martyr and bishop Cyprian speaks much more clearly about the same faith [The manuscripts read, “but in the same faith”]:

> “If anything could hinder people from obtaining grace [The oldest Fleury codex reads, “from the obtaining of grace”], then more serious sins would be able to hinder adults, the mature, and those advanced in age. Yet when the gravest sinners and those who have long sinned greatly against God subsequently believe, forgiveness of sins is granted [Am. Er. and most manuscripts read, “forgiveness”], and no one is prohibited from Baptism and grace. How much less ought an infant to be prohibited—an infant who, having just been born, has committed no sin, except that, born carnally according to Adam, he has contracted the contagion of ancient death at his first birth? He approaches the reception of forgiveness of sins all the more easily because what is forgiven him is not his own but another’s sin” (*Letter 64, to Fidus*).

#### 7.

The ecclesiastical records show that Reticius, bishop of Autun, possessed great authority in the Church during his episcopate. At Rome, under the presidency of Miltiades [The Vatican manuscripts read *Melciade*; others, *Miltiade*], bishop of the Apostolic See, he served as judge with others, condemned Donatus—the original author of the Donatist schism—and acquitted Caecilian, bishop of the Church of Carthage.

When speaking about Baptism, he said:

> “No one is unaware, then, that this is the chief indulgence in the Church: in it we lay down the entire burden of the ancient crime and wipe away the ancient offenses of our ignorance; there we strip off the old human being together with his innate crimes” [This work does not survive].

You hear “the burden of the ancient crime”; you hear “the ancient offenses”; you hear “the old human being together with his innate crimes”—and you dare to construct a ruinous novelty against these things!

#### 8.

Olympius, a Spanish bishop, a man of great glory in the Church and in Christ, said in a certain ecclesiastical sermon:

> “If faith had ever remained incorrupt upon the earth and had held fast the tracks which it abandoned after they had been marked out, it would never have spread the defect of the first-formed man’s deadly transgression [Three Vatican manuscripts read, “the deadly defect of the first-formed man’s deadly transgression”] in his offspring, so that sin would be born together with the human being” [Nothing of this work survives].

Do you have anything which you think you can say against us that you are not also compelled to say against him—or rather, against all of them?

For the Catholic faith of all who believe with one heart and confess with one mouth that through one human being sin entered the world, in which all sinned (Romans 5:12), is one. By its ancient Catholic authority it overthrows your novel presumptions.

#### 9.

Hear still what may move and disturb you further—and, would that it might change you for the better. Who does not know Hilary, the Gallic bishop, a venerable and most vigorous defender of the Catholic Church against heretics?

When he was speaking about Christ’s flesh, observe what he said:

> “Therefore, when he was sent in the likeness of sinful flesh (Romans 8:3), he did not possess sin in the same way that he possessed flesh. But because all flesh is from sin—that is, derived from sin through Adam the ancestor—he was sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, with not sin in him but the likeness of sinful flesh.”

Again, in his *Exposition of Psalm 118*, when he came to the words, “My soul shall live, and it shall praise you” (Psalm 118:175), he said:

> “He does not consider himself to live in this life, since he had said, ‘Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother gave birth to me in sins’ [Am. Er. and the manuscripts read, “conceived me in sins”] (Psalm 50:7). He knows that he was born under the origin of sin and under the law of sin.”

Do you understand what you are hearing? Are you looking for what you should say? If you have any sense of shame, dare to accuse this man—so distinguished among Catholic bishops by such great praise and so conspicuous for his knowledge and reputation—concerning original sin.

#### 10.

But hear still another outstanding steward of God, whom I venerate as a father: “In Christ Jesus, through the Gospel, he himself begot me” (1 Corinthians 4:15), and through this minister of Christ I received the washing of regeneration.

I speak of the blessed Ambrose, whose devotion to the Catholic faith, steadfastness, labors, and dangers, both in his works and in his words, I myself have experienced; and with me the Roman world does not hesitate to proclaim them.

When this man was expounding the Gospel according to Luke, he said:

> “The Jordan was turned back” (Psalm 113:3). “It signified the future mysteries of the saving washing, through which infants who have been baptized are restored to the beginnings of their nature, away from wickedness” (*Book 1 on Luke*, no. 36).

Again, in the same work, he said:

> “For it was not a man’s intercourse that opened the secret places of the virginal womb; rather, the Holy Spirit poured the immaculate seed into an inviolate womb. For the Lord Jesus alone, among those born of woman, is holy in every respect: he did not experience the contagions of earthly corruption because of the novelty of his immaculate birth, and he drove them away by his heavenly majesty” (*Book 2*, no. 56).

Likewise, in the same work:

> “We all die in Adam [Ambrose has *mortui*, ‘we have died’], because through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and thus it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned. Therefore, because of his guilt, death belongs to all” (*Book 4*, no. 67, on Luke 4:38).

Elsewhere in the same Gospel he says:

> “Take care, therefore, lest you be stripped naked beforehand, as Adam was stripped naked when deprived of the keeping of the heavenly commandment and stripped of the garment of faith. Thus he received a mortal wound, in which he would have killed the entire human race unless that Samaritan, descending, had healed his bitter wounds” (*Book 7*, no. 73, on Luke 10:30).

Again, elsewhere in the same work:

> “There was Adam, and in him we were all; Adam perished, and in him we all perished” (*Book 7*, no. 234, on Luke 15:24).

Again, in his *Apology for the Prophet David*:

> “Before we are born, we are stained by contagion; before we enjoy the use of light, we receive the injury of our very origin; we are conceived in iniquity. He did not specify,” he says, “whether it was the parents’ iniquity or ours. ‘And in sins his mother gives birth to each person.’ Here too he did not make clear whether the mother gives birth in her own sins or whether there are already some sins belonging to the one being born. But see whether both should be understood.

“Conception itself is not free from iniquity, since the parents too are not without a fall. If not even an infant of a single day is without sin, how much less are the days of the mother’s conception without sin? We are therefore conceived in the sin of our parents and born in their offenses. But the birth itself too has its contagions, and nature itself has not merely one contagion” (chapter 11).

The same man, in his *Exposition of the Book of Tobit*:

> “Who is this creditor of sin except the devil, from whom Eve borrowed sin [All the manuscripts read, “from whom Eve, stained by sin”; the later printed editions themselves agree with the manuscripts below, no. 32, where they have, with the manuscripts, “from whom Eve was stained”], and at interest on an indebted succession lent it out to the entire human race?” (chapter 9).

Again, in the same work:

> “The devil deceived Eve in order to trip up the man and bind the inheritance” (chapter 23).

The same man, in his *Exposition of Psalm 48*:

> “There is our iniquity, and there is the iniquity of our heel, in which Adam was wounded by the serpent’s tooth. By his wound he left the inheritance of the human succession liable, so that we all limp from that wound” (on verse 6).

### Chapter Four

#### 11.

Go now and accuse me of original sin. Conceal these men; pretend that you do not know what they say; and, as though you did not see all these teachers of the holy Church—so many and so great [Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “so many teachers”]—who, after living excellent lives and conquering the errors of their times, departed most gloriously [Two Vatican manuscripts read, “most glorious”] from this world before you began to boil over, attack me as though they had never existed.

If you had done this unknowingly, I would admit, and would attribute it not to your shamelessness but to your thoughtlessness, that you dare to attack with hostility these lights of the City of God, whom you ought faithfully to have followed.

I would believe, I say, that you had committed this enormous crime without knowing it, if I had not set down in the book to which you either think you responded or wish others to think you responded an utterly clear testimony from the discussion of Saint Ambrose (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 40).

Did you not read there what the aforementioned bishop said when he was explaining Christ’s birth from a virgin’s womb?

> “Therefore he was, as a human being, tempted in every respect, and in the likeness of human beings he endured all things; but, since he was born from the Spirit, he abstained from sin. ‘Every human being is a liar’ (Psalm 115:2), and no one is without sin except the one God. It was therefore established that, from man and woman—that is, through that commingling of bodies—no one appears to be free from sin. But whoever is free from sin is also free from this kind of conception” (*Commentary on Isaiah*).

If you did not read these words of the venerable Ambrose there, how did you undertake to criticize the book in which they were placed? But if you did read them, why do you rage against me and first attack him through me? Why do you try to tear apart my name and make Ambrose a Manichaean by attacking me while silently concealing his name?

12. You see, surely, with whom I endure your curses; you see with whom I share a common cause, which you try to assail and overthrow by calumnies, without any sober consideration. You see how dangerous it is for you to bring so horrible a charge against such men, and how glorious it is for me to hear any charge whatsoever together with such men. If you see this, look—and at last be silent: crush the Pelagian tongue beneath so many Catholic tongues; subject your insolent mouth to so many venerable lips. If you had entered the school of Xenocrates, like Polemo [Note: [Col. 0647] Polemo became a distinguished philosopher after a dissolute youth. See Valerius Maximus, book 6, chapter 9, and Diogenes Laertius, book 4, *Lives of the Philosophers], drunk from a banquet lasting until dawn, you would not have been restrained by shame as great as you ought to feel in this assembly of so many saints. Here, indeed, shame ought to be all the greater, the more genuine the wisdom being learned.

The faces of so many renowned bishops deserve proportionately more reverence than the face of one Xenocrates, as Christ, the teacher of these men, is greater than Plato, Xenocrates’ teacher. I, for my part, mindful of your father Memor, of blessed memory [Note: See Augustine, *Epistle* 101; see also below, Mercator’s *Commonitorium against the Pelagians*, in the second part of the Appendix], who had formed no small friendship with me through correspondence and had made you yourself very dear to me, brought you in—when I saw you in your books not drunk from a banquet until dawn, but disturbed by an insane abuse of language—not into the lecture hall of some philosopher, but into the peaceful and honorable assembly of the holy Fathers, so that you might be calmed and healed.

Please, let it be worth the effort: look at them, as it were, looking at you, and gently and mildly saying to you: “What? Are we, Julian, Manichaeans?” Tell me, what will you answer? With what eyes will you look upon them? What arguments will come to your aid? What categories of Aristotle, with which you seek to leap upon us like a polished disputant, will you produce before their eyes? What edge of your arguments, whether glass-like swords or leaden daggers, will dare to be drawn in their presence? What weapons of yours will not flee from them and leave you unarmed?

[Col. 0648] Or perhaps you will say that you named none of them in this charge? And what will you do when they say to you: “It would have been more tolerable for you to cut down our names with a slanderous tooth than our faith, by whose merit our very names are written in heaven”? Or perhaps you will say to them: “I have not violated your faith by any such charge”? But with what confidence will you dare say this, when you are a man who says that the belief that those born from Adam inherit original sin is Manichaean—a belief which these men confessed and professed, which they learned in the Church of Christ at the time of their early formation, and which they taught in the Church of Christ during the time of their episcopal offices? [Note: The manuscripts read “in the holy Church,” here and below.] Through the Holy Spirit they remitted so many sins—original sins alone—to so many infants whom they were able to baptize.

Again I admonish you, again I entreat you: look upon so many and such great defenders and teachers of the Catholic Church [Note: Thus all manuscripts. Printed editions have *rectores*, “rulers”]. See what grave and unspeakable injury you inflict upon them.

13. Do you therefore think them contemptible because they are all of the Western Church, and because none of the Eastern bishops has been mentioned by us? What then shall we do, since they are Greeks and we are Latins? I think that part of the world ought to suffice for you in which the Lord willed to crown the first of his Apostles with the most glorious martyrdom. If you had been willing to listen to the blessed Innocent, who presided over that Church, you would already then have stripped your dangerous youth of the Pelagian snares.

For what could that holy man have answered the African councils except what the Apostolic and Roman See has held from ancient times, steadfastly together with the rest of the Church? And yet you accuse his successor, Zosimus, of the crime of betrayal because he refused to oppose apostolic teaching and the judgment of his predecessor. But for the moment I say nothing about this, lest I wound your spirit—which I desire to heal rather than provoke—by praising the man who condemned you.

See what you will answer holy Innocent, who knows nothing else about this matter than what those men know, into whose assembly I have introduced you, if that is of any benefit. He too sits among them, later in time but first in rank. He holds with them one true Christian judgment concerning the liberation, through Christ’s grace, of wretched infants from the original evil drawn from Adam.
