He said that Christ cleansed by the washing of his Baptism every past fault—namely, that of the first man, who had been plunged into the depths by free choice [Note: Ambrosiaster, Erasmus, and many manuscripts here and below read “the fault of the past”] (*Epistle* 181, no. 7, among the Augustinian letters). Finally, he defined that infants cannot possibly possess life unless they eat the flesh of the Son of Man (*Epistle* 182, no. 5, among the Augustinian letters; John 6:54).

Answer him—or rather, answer the Lord, whose testimony that bishop used—and say why the image of God should be punished with so capital a penalty that it is deprived of life, if those being born do not inherit original sin. But what can you say, or how can you answer? Even if you dare to call blessed Innocent a Manichaean, you will not dare to call Christ one.

[Col. 0649]

14. There is therefore no reason for you to appeal to the bishops of the East, since they too are Christians, and the faith of both parts of the world is one and the same—because this faith is Christian. The Western land gave you birth, and the Western Church gave you rebirth. Why do you seek to inflict upon it something you did not find in it when you entered its membership? Or rather, why do you seek to take away from it what you too received in it?

For the original sin which you deny, to the ruin of other infants, was either itself remitted to you, whatever your age at baptism, or it too [lacuna; Note: Thus all printed editions. Something nevertheless seems to be missing here. M.]. But if what we have heard is true—that you were baptized as an infant—then although you were innocent of your own sins, because you were born carnally from Adam you nevertheless carried, in your first birth, the contagion of the ancient death; and you were conceived in iniquity. Therefore you were certainly exorcized and breathed upon, so that, having been rescued from the power of darkness, you might be transferred into the kingdom of Christ (Colossians 1:13).

O son badly born from Adam, but well reborn in Christ, you try to take away from your mother the sacraments by which she gave you birth. Was she a Manichaean when she gave you birth in this manner—the manner in which you now no longer wish her to give birth—and when you heap upon her the reproaches of birth [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read “the reproaches of vanity”], so that in her you may close, against others from whom you yourself were born, the entrails of compassion?

You divide from her the name of her husband, so that for the rebirth of infants Christ alone may be Christ, but for adults Christ may be Christ Jesus—because, of course, “Jesus” is interpreted as “Savior.” Yet you do not want him to be Savior for infants, while you proclaim that they have nothing from which he might save them.

## CHAPTER V

15. But you will not lack an illustrious bishop of great name and celebrated reputation, from the regions of the East, whose words, deservedly possessing immense authority, have shone everywhere even after being translated into the Latin language. Let holy Gregory therefore sit with these Fathers also, and with them endure [Note: One manuscript reads “share.”] the empty spite of your accusation—provided that, together with them, he too offers a medicinal judgment against your novel pestilence.

Listen, then, to what he says:

> “Let the image of God cleanse away the stain of bodily inundation [Note: Several manuscripts read, “cleanse away the bodily stain by cleansing”; some, “cleanse away the stain of bodily cleansing”] and raise on wings the flesh of the Word of God joined to itself. And although it would have been better not to have needed such cleansing at all, but to have remained in that original dignity toward which we hasten again after the present correction, and although it would have been better not to have fallen from the tree of life through the most bitter taste of sin, nevertheless, in the second place, after the fall it is better to be amended and corrected than to remain in wickedness.” [Note: Several manuscripts read “after the present cleansing.”]

The same man says again:

> “As in Adam we all died, so also in Christ may we all be made alive. Let us therefore be born with Christ [Note: Some manuscripts read “reborn with Christ”], be crucified with Christ, and be buried with him into death, so that with him we may also rise again to life. For it is necessary for us to undergo this useful and necessary reversal: just as we have fallen from good things into sorrow, so from sorrow we may be restored to better things. For where sin abounded, grace abounded even more, so that those whom the taste of the forbidden tree condemned, [Col. 0650] the cross of Christ might justify with more abundant grace.”

(*Oration on the Nativity of Christ*, shortly after the beginning.)

The same man says elsewhere:

> “Venerate the birth through which you have been freed from the bonds of earthly birth. Honor little and insignificant Bethlehem, through which the way back to paradise has been opened for you.”

(Ibid., near the end.)

Again, speaking elsewhere about Baptism, he says:

> “Let the saying of Christ persuade you of this also: no one can enter the kingdom of heaven unless he has been born again of water and the Spirit” (John 3:5). “Through this, the stains of the first birth are cleansed—the stains by which we are conceived in iniquities and by which our mothers bore us in sins.”

Will you say that this man too thinks or utters the poisons of the Manichaeans? You hear them all saying the same thing with one heart, one mouth, and one faith, and affirming with harmonious testimony that this is the Catholic faith.

16. Does the authority of one Gregory, among the Eastern bishops, seem small to you? He is indeed so eminent a person that he would not say this to everyone unless it came from the Christian faith known to all; nor would they hold him so distinguished and venerable unless they recognized that what he said came from the rule of well-known truth.

But if you wish, let us add holy Basil to him. Indeed, whether you wish it or not, he must be added—especially because, in the fourth volume of this work of yours, you thought you ought to include something from his book written against the Manichaeans, although it has no bearing at all on the cause of original sin entering the world through one man and passing through all human beings.

There he is dealing with the claim that evil should not be believed to be substantial, possessing a certain matter of its own, as the Manichaeans think. Accordingly, he says that evil is “not a substance, but a way of life [*conversatio*; some manuscripts read *conversio*, “conversion”], arising solely from the will”—not in those who have carried the contagion of the ancient death in their first birth, but “in those who have gathered the disease of their way of life from their own will,” that is, in those who are already adults and use reason and freedom of choice.

He says that “this way of life, arising accidentally, can very easily be separated from the will of those who are sick.” He also says:

> “If evil had arisen in such a way that it could no longer be removed from the will—that is, although it had arisen accidentally, if it had arisen in such a way that it could no longer be separated from the will—it could rightly be said that evil was indeed substantial [Note: All manuscripts read “indeed substantial,” omitting “evil”], and that the substance itself, without the evil which had befallen it, could no longer exist. But if it has been added,” he says, “and the beginning of its addition had not substance but will as its source, evil can easily be separated from substance, so that the substance subject to the will may be wholly possessed in purity, with no trace of any evil remaining.”

Holy Basil said these things so rightly that they can also be understood of that very evil which entered the world through Adam and passed through all human beings, because it too was added to human nature. For human nature was not originally created in that condition [Note: The printed editions read “is”; the manuscripts, “was”]; and the beginning of this addition lay not in substance but in will—whether the will of the woman who was deceived by the serpent, or that of her husband, who consented to his deceived wife when she sinned.

But when he says that evil “can easily be separated from the will or from substance,” this is not easy for the human will, but for the mercy of God. This is sufficient against the Manichaeans, who think it impossible for the nature of evil to be changed into good. Therefore holy Basil did not say that the human will itself, or substance or nature, can easily separate evil from itself, but that it can be “easily separated from it.” He weighed his words in such a way that he both refuted the Manichaeans against whom he was arguing and did not exalt human pride against divine grace.

For the Almighty, to whom, according to the Gospel, what is impossible for human beings is easy (Matthew 19:26), will consume the evil that has befallen us—whether from the will of the first man or, in addition, from our own will—by the abundance of his grace, “so that the substance subject to the will,” as you recalled Basil saying, “may be wholly possessed in purity, so that no trace of any evil remains.”

[Col. 0651] This will happen [Note: Some manuscripts read “This happens”], and this is the certain hope of the faithful. But when it will be perfected is clear to the Catholic faith. Then the final enemy, death, will be addressed: “Where is your contest? Where is your sting?” (1 Corinthians 15:55).

17. Likewise, what you recall Basil saying is true:

> “If chastity is a virtue, but the body were substantially evil, it would be impossible to find a chaste body, because a body of shame could not become a body of virtue. But when it is sanctified, it becomes a body of virtue; and thus virtue shares itself with the body, and the body with virtue, through which it also becomes a temple of God. Therefore, if every body were a body of fornication, it would certainly be impossible to find chastity in bodies; and only then could we attribute substantial evil to the nature of bodies. But if the merits of the body have advanced so far, and it has been adorned with such honor and received such a garment of chastity that it deserved to be the house of its Maker and became the bridal chamber of the Son of God, so that the Father and the Son, coming, deigned to choose the bodies as their dwelling—how is the speech of the Manichaeans not proved execrable and ridiculous?”

What could have been said more truly or more consistently with the Catholic rule [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read “more consistently with the Catholic faith.” The other manuscripts read “more consistently with the Catholic rule.” Printed editions change “more consistently” to “more fittingly”]?

This was said against the Manichaeans, who think and affirm [Note: The manuscripts read “maintain”] that bodies originate from the race of darkness—which they call an evil nature coeternal with the good God—and that bodies themselves are unchangeably evil. It was not said against those who hold the true and genuinely Christian faith, confessing that the body is presently corruptible and weighs down the soul (Wisdom 9:15), but that it was not originally created or placed in paradise in this condition, nor will it always remain so; rather, it will be changed through incorruption and immortality.

Nor was it said against those who confess that the body is already beginning to be a temple of God, adorned with conjugal, widowed, or even virginal chastity. For although the flesh desires against the spirit, the spirit nevertheless desires against the flesh (Galatians 5:17), so that the body’s members do not present themselves as weapons of iniquity for sin (Romans 6:13). [Note: An old Floriac manuscript reads “iniquity” rather than “weapons of iniquity.”]

[Col. 0652]

18. But listen to what this holy man Basil says, without any ambiguity, about the sin of the first man, which also concerns us. Although I found it translated, I preferred, for the sake of a more careful fidelity to the truth, to render it word for word from the Greek.

In his sermon *On Fasting* he says:

> “Fasting was ordained by law in paradise. For Adam first received the commandment: ‘You shall not eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil’ (Genesis 2:17). ‘You shall not eat’ [Note: The printed editions read, “and evil you shall not eat. You shall not eat”; the manuscripts, “you shall not eat.”] is fasting, and the beginning of the establishment of the law. If Eve had fasted from the tree, we would not now need this fasting. For it is not the healthy who need a physician, but those who are sick (Matthew 9:12). We became sick through sin; let us be healed through repentance. But repentance without fasting is empty. ‘The earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles’ (Genesis 3:17–18). You have been appointed to grief; are you now to pursue luxury?”

A little later in the same sermon he says:

> “Because we did not fast, we fell from paradise. Let us therefore fast, so that we may return to it.”

(*Sermon* 1.)

If you had read these and similar words of holy Basil, or if you had been willing faithfully to consider what you read, you would certainly never have inserted into these books of yours—where you cast a fog over ignorant people—things that have no bearing on the question disputed between us, and I do not know with what intention.

You hear that we would not need this fasting if the human being had not transgressed the law of fasting in the happiness of paradise; yet you deny that the rest of humanity is born subject to the sin of those people. You hear the statement added, “It is not the healthy who need a physician”; yet you deny that we lost, through the sin of those people, the health in which we were created.

You hear the sentence pronounced against the first sinful man, “The earth shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you,” also applying to us; yet you deny that those are subject to sin whom you see subject to the same sentence. You hear that we must return to paradise from which we fell; yet you deny that the sin of those people—who were then the only human beings in paradise, and in whom we too were present—concerns us.

19. Why say more? See now whether these two men from the East, so distinguished and endowed with such eminent holiness, and, as is reported, even brothers by birth [Note: Gregory of Nyssa was Basil’s brother—not Gregory of Nazianzus, whom Augustine praised above], are sufficient for you. But say that they are not sufficient. We have fourteen other Eastern bishops: Eulogius, John, Ammonianus [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “Ammonius”], Porphyry, Eutonius, Porphyry, Fidus, Zoninus [Note: The printed edition of Louvain reads “Zosimus.” Ambrosius and Erasmus read “Zozinus.” The Vatican manuscripts read “Zonius.” All the Gallican manuscripts read “Zoninus.” See below, no. 32], Zoboennus [Note: Printed editions read “Zoboenus.” The manuscripts read “Zoboennus,” except for three Vatican manuscripts, which have “Zoboemius”], Nymphidius [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “Nymphindius”], Chromatius [Note: Ambrosius and Erasmus read “Ebromatius”], Jovinus, Eleutherius, and Clematius. We can bring them all together, found in one place, into this assembly—the very men who presided as judges over Pelagius and, as human beings, thinking him Catholic when no adversary from the other side was pressing them, pronounced him Catholic.

[Col. 0653]

For unless, in their presence and hearing, he had condemned those who say “that Adam’s sin harmed Adam alone and not the human race; that infants newly born are in the condition in which Adam was before sin; and that infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life,” he could by no means have departed from there except condemned [Note: See *The Proceedings against Pelagius*, nos. 23, 57, 65].

What benefit is it to you that you insert—through some art of tangled reasoning, I do not know whose—various handles and hooks, so that simple things may not become apparent and clear? Who does not see how those judges could have understood these propositions—namely, according to the Catholic faith, which everywhere rescues infants from the power of darkness by exorcizing and breathing upon them—not in the manner in which you explain, or rather construct them?

And yet you were able to say that “Adam’s sin harmed the human race not by propagation but by imitation,” and that “infants newly born are not in the condition in which Adam was before sin, because he was capable of receiving the commandment, whereas they are not yet.” With these fogs Pelagius thinks he deceived that judgment, and you wholeheartedly applaud this wickedness [Note: Most manuscripts read “applauded this wickedness”], laughing that so many bishops were mocked by him.

But could you, by any cleverness, twist into something else or conceal beneath any fig leaves the statement that “infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life”? Pelagius could only condemn those who say this before Catholic judges; and he condemned what he believed, in the presence of human beings, fearing condemnation by human beings. For if you do not believe this, you agree with us. But because you do not agree with us, you undoubtedly believe it. Consequently, the Eastern judges condemn you [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “may condemn you.” A little later: “is anathematized”].

Fearing to be condemned by them, Pelagius condemned those who hold these views, and he must certainly be condemned together with those whom he condemned, because he retained in his heart what he denied with his mouth. For what is anathematized by his words is found in his writings.

But I am not dealing with him now. What do you say, you with whom I now have the issue? Look: so many Eastern judges are present. The ecclesiastical proceedings held among them are read. It is read that Pelagius was accused of saying “that even unbaptized infants possess eternal life.” It is read that Pelagius condemned those who say this; for he could not otherwise have escaped those judges.

What do you yourself now say? Will infants possess eternal life even if they depart this life unbaptized, or will they not possess it? If you say, “They will possess it,” the words of your Pelagius will condemn you, as will all those by whom he himself feared being condemned. But if you say, “They will not possess it,” I ask for what reason the innocent image of God will be punished by deprivation of life [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read “of eternal life,” rather than simply “of life”], if no sin is contracted through human propagation.

If sin is contracted, why are those who hold this view called Manichaeans—those by whom Pelagius would have been condemned, unless he had pretended that he held the same view?

[Col. 0654]

20. For the moment, you have before you bishops not only of the West but also of the East. For those whom we seemed to lack, we have found in greater number among the Easterners. They all believe in one and the same manner that through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and that thus death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned (Romans 5:12). This means that all are believed to be born subject to the sin of that one first man.

If you call anyone who says this a Manichaean [Note: Ambrosius and Erasmus read: “If you call what the Manichaean says this”; this is erroneous], look upon these men; blush before these men; spare these men—or rather, spare yourself, lest the ruler and inhabitant [Note: Some Belgian manuscripts read “judge”] of those men perhaps not spare you. But if you do not call these men Manichaeans, you will not be able to find a reason for calling me one.

For you call me this for no other reason than that, concerning the sin of the first man—which every carnal birth has made all subject to, and from which no one is freed except by spiritual birth—I believe what they believe, hold what they hold, teach what they teach, and preach what they preach.

Yield to these men, and do not strike me [Note: Ambrosius, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read “and you will yield to me.” Some manuscripts read: “Believe these men, and you will believe me”]. Submit to these men, and you will cease from opposing me. Finally, if you do not wish to become my friend through them, at least I ask you not to become their enemy through me.

But how will you avoid becoming their enemy if you persist in this error? How much better, then, to join these men and withdraw from that one [Note: Printed editions read “withdraw.” The manuscripts read “you will withdraw,” or “you withdraw”]. Can Pelagius and Caelestius have so much influence over you that, from the rising of the sun to its setting, you dare not only to abandon so many and such great teachers and defenders of the Catholic faith—ancient men and men near our own age, sleeping and abiding—but even to call them Manichaeans?

I wonder whether this will ever be able to come from your mouth, though the perversity of your error compels you to shout it. But it would be astonishing if, in the face of a human being, there were so great a distance between forehead and tongue that, in this matter, the forehead did not restrain the tongue.

## CHAPTER VI

21. But I know what you are muttering. Say it now, say it; let us hear. At the very end of the work we are now discussing—that is, in the final part of the fourth book—you say:

> “Saint John of Constantinople denies that there is original sin in infants. For in the homily which he delivered concerning the baptized, he says: ‘Blessed is God, who alone works wonders, who made all things and transformed all things. Behold, those who were shortly before captives now enjoy the freedom of serenity; those who were wandering in the error of exile are citizens of the Church; those who were in the confusion of sin now stand among the ranks of righteousness. For they are not merely free, but also holy; not merely holy, but also righteous; not merely righteous, but also sons; not merely sons, but also heirs; not merely heirs, but also brothers of Christ; not merely brothers of Christ, but also coheirs; not merely coheirs, but also members; not merely members, but also a temple; not merely a temple, but also instruments of the Spirit. You see how many are the gifts of Baptism. Yet some think that heavenly grace consists only in the forgiveness of sins [Col. 0655]. We, however, have counted ten honors. For this reason we also baptize infants, although they are not defiled by sin, so that holiness, righteousness, adoption, inheritance, brotherhood with Christ may be added to them, and so that they may be his members.’” [Note: Here the printed editions add “that there be given, or”; this is absent from most manuscripts.]

(*Homily to the Neophytes*.)

22. Do you dare to set these words of holy Bishop John, as though they contradicted the judgments of so many men of such stature, against the concordant fellowship of his colleagues, and to separate him from them and make him their adversary?

Far be it, far be it from us to believe or say such an evil of so great a man. Far be it, I say, that John of Constantinople should resist, concerning the Baptism of infants and their liberation through Christ from their father’s bond [Note: Thus several manuscripts. Printed editions read “from the bond of the father’s handwriting”], so many and such great fellow bishops of his—especially Innocent of Rome, Cyprian of Carthage, Basil of Cappadocia, Gregory of Nazianzus [Note: Some manuscripts omit “Gregory of Nazianzus”], Hilary of Gaul, and Ambrose of Milan.

There are matters on which even the most learned and best defenders of the Catholic rule sometimes differ among themselves without damaging the structure of the faith, and one may say something about a single matter better and more truly than another. But the matter with which we are now concerned belongs to the very foundations of the faith.

Whoever wishes to weaken in the Christian faith what is written—“Through a man came death, and through a man the resurrection of the dead; for as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:21–22)—is attempting to take away everything that we believe concerning Christ.

Christ is altogether the Savior of infants; unless they are redeemed by him, they will perish, because they cannot have life without his flesh and blood. John too thought, believed, learned, and taught this. But you turn his words toward your own doctrine.

He said that infants do not have sins, meaning their own sins. Accordingly, we rightly call them innocent, in keeping with what the Apostle says: that before they were born they had done nothing good or evil (Romans 9:11)—not in keeping with what he says: “By the disobedience of one man the many were made sinners” (Romans 5:19).

Our Cyprian too could have said of infants what John said, since he says “that an infant newly born has committed no sin, and that what is remitted to him is not his own but another’s sin” (*Epistle* 64, to Fidus).

Thus, comparing infants with adults, whose own sins are forgiven in Baptism, John said that they “do not have sins”—not, as you yourself have presented his words, that they are “not defiled by sin,” while intending it to be understood that they are not defiled by the sin of the first man.

But I would not attribute this to you, but to the translator—although in other manuscripts containing the same translation, it reads not “by sin” but “by sins.” Hence I wonder whether someone from your number preferred to write the singular, so that it might be understood as that one sin of which the Apostle says: “Judgment from one offense brought condemnation, but grace from many offenses brought justification” (Romans 5:16).

[Col. 0656] There “one” can mean nothing other than “offense” [Note: Printed editions add “one” here. In the Floriac manuscript, “not unless an offense” is intended]. Since you do not wish infants to be believed defiled, you preferred to say not that they do not have sins—which is what John said, lest they be understood to have their own sins—or “by sins,” as the same translation has in other manuscripts, but “not defiled by sin,” so that the one sin of the first man might come to mind.

But let us not proceed by suspicions. Let this be considered either a scribal error or a variation of the translator. I shall set down the very Greek words spoken by John:

> “Διὰ τοῦτο καὶ τὰ παιδία βαπτίζομεν, καίτοι ἁμαρτήματα οὐκ ἔχοντα.”

That is, in Latin:

> “Ideo et infantes baptizamus, quamvis peccata non habentes.”

“Therefore we also baptize infants, although they do not have sins.”

You clearly see that he did not say that “infants are not defiled by sin,” or “by sins,” but that they “do not have sins.” Understand this as referring to their own sins, and there is no dispute.

But you will say: Why did he not himself add “their own”? Why, we may suppose, except that, speaking within the Catholic Church, he did not think that he would be understood otherwise? Since no one was troubling him with such a question, he spoke more securely, before you began to quarrel.

23. Do you wish to hear what he himself also said most explicitly about this matter? Behold, I add him himself to that number of saints [Note: Two manuscripts read “the holy man”; one reads “the holy men”]. Behold, I establish him among my witnesses—or among our judges—whom you thought to be your patron. Behold, you will now call him a Manichaean too.

Enter, holy John, enter, and sit with your brothers, from whom no reasoning and no temptation has separated you [Note: The Floriac manuscript reads “will separate you”]. Your judgment is needed—your judgment above all—because this young man thinks he has found in your writings something by which he can strike down and nullify the judgments of so many and such great fellow bishops of yours.

If he had truly found such a thing, and if it had become clear that you held what he holds, we could never, with your permission, prefer you alone to so many men of such stature in a matter over which the Christian faith and the Catholic Church have never differed. But far be it from us to suppose that you thought otherwise or that you stood out so prominently in this matter.

Speak, then, and you too say something by which this young man may be confounded and brought to reverence—for he is seeking a stain in me. Forgive me, because when I show him what you think about this matter, he will seek to discover what you think as well.

He says that it is a Manichaean belief to hold that infants need the help of Christ their Liberator in order to be freed from the condemnation to which they have been bound by the sin of the first man. Consequently, when he learns that you hold this too, he will either correct himself from the error of Pelagius or bring against you the charge of Manichaeism.

But let us confer a genuine benefit upon him and pay no attention to his false insult.

24. Listen now, Julian, to what John says together with the other Catholic teachers. In a letter to Olympia he says:

> “When Adam sinned, that great sin, and condemned the whole human race in common, he was paying the penalty in grief.”

[Col. 0657]

Again, concerning the raising of Lazarus:

> “Christ wept,” he says, “because mortality, having been shaken from everlasting things, had fallen so far as to love the underworld. Christ wept because the devil made mortal those who could have been immortal.”

(*Homily on the Raising of Lazarus*.)

What could be expressed more clearly? What answer do you give to this? If Adam, by his great sin, condemned the whole human race in common, is an infant born except under condemnation? And through whom, except Christ, is the infant freed from that condemnation?

If, in the account of Lazarus, mortality is said to have been shaken from everlasting things and to have loved the underworld, who among mortals does not belong to that guilt and fall by which the first man fell from the everlasting life that he would have received had he not sinned? If the devil made mortal all who could have been immortal, why do infants also die if they are not subject to the sin of that first man?

Are infants, then, rescued from the kingdom of death only through him in whom all will be made alive?

### 25

The same John treats in a certain sermon the question of why wild beasts either injure or kill human beings, although the Lord’s decree is clear, by which he subjected them to humanity so that humanity might have power over them (Gen. 1:28). He resolves the question by saying that, before sin, all beasts were subject to human beings; but that their present hostility toward human beings is the punishment for the first sin. His treatment is lengthy, and for that reason I do not insert it all into this work; nevertheless, I ought to include something from it.

“We fear,” he says, “and tremble before wild beasts: I do not deny it. And we have fallen from our dominion: this too I myself affirm. But this does not show that God’s law is false; for at the beginning things were not arranged in this way. Rather, they feared, trembled, and were subject to their lord. And since we have fallen from confidence, plainly we have also fallen from honor. How is this evident? He brought the beasts to Adam to see what he would call them, and Adam did not recoil as though he were afraid.”

A little later he says:

“This one sign alone shows that beasts were not terrifying to human beings from the beginning; but there is another, clearer than this: the conversation that took place between the serpent and the woman. For if beasts had been terrifying to human beings, surely the woman, on seeing the serpent, would not have remained there; she would not have accepted his advice, nor would she have spoken with him so confidently. Rather, at once she would have been frightened by his very appearance and recoiled. But now she both converses and is not afraid. For this fear did not yet exist; but when sin entered, the things that belonged to honor were taken away.”

And shortly afterward:

“As long as he possessed confidence toward God, he was terrifying to the beasts; but because he offended, he now fears even the least of his fellow servants. If this is not so,” he says, “show me that, before sin, beasts were terrifying to human beings. You will not be able to. But if fear entered only afterward, this too is the Lord’s protection [Note: [Col. 0657] So the manuscripts read, in accordance with the Greek. Erasmus and Lovaniensis, however, read *tutela Domini est* as *tulela Donum est*, omitting *et hoc*.]. For if, when the command that had been given was moved and released by the human being, the honor bestowed upon him by God had remained unshaken, he would not easily have risen again” (*Homily 9 on Genesis*).

It is therefore clear that holy John, by this discussion, showed that what entered through one human being [Note: [Col. 0658] The printed editions add *sin*, which is absent from the manuscripts.] became a sin common to all, since the terror of beasts is common to all. Beasts, of course, do not spare infants either; and according to this treatment by John, they would in no way injure or frighten infants unless the latter too were held bound by the guilt of that ancient sin.

### 26

Say it, Julian, say this man too was a Manichaean—for what are you now hesitating to say?—the man who inflicted such injury upon the nature whose innocence you defend, and who asserted the transmission of condemnation. Rather, restrain yourself, if you possess any mind capable of healing, and correct yourself. At last understand how John could say that infants do not have sins: not because they are not held bound by the sin of the first human beings, but because they have committed no sin of their own.

You could have found this in that very homily, if you had read it all. Or, if you did read it, I do not know how it could have escaped you. Or, if it could not have escaped you, I wonder why it did not correct you—provided, that is, that John’s authority has any weight with you. Or, if after reading that sermon and recognizing and examining the passage I am about to cite, you thought you should remain in your opinion, why did you insert any words from it into your work? Perhaps it was so that you might urge us to read the whole thing with you [Note: [Col. 0658] Lovaniensis reads: “that we might read with you.”] and find the place from which we could detect and refute your schemes? For what could be clearer than what he said there:

“Christ came once and found us bound by our father’s bond, which Adam wrote. He introduced the beginning of the debt; our sins increased the interest” (*Homily to the Newly Enlightened*).

Do you hear a man instructed in the Catholic faith and instructing others, distinguishing the debt of the paternal bond—a debt that has adhered to us by inheritance—from those debts whose interest has increased through our own sins? Do you hear what is remitted to infants in Baptism, who have not yet contracted debts of their own, yet could not be free from the paternal bond?

His words, untranslated, are read as follows in Greek:

> «Ἔρχεται ἅπαξ ὁ Χριστὸς, εὗρεν ἡμῶν χειρόγραφον πατρῶον, ὅ τι ἔγραφεν ὁ Ἀδάμ. Ἐκεῖνος τὴν ἀρχὴν εἰσήγαγε τοῦ χρείους, ἡμεῖς τὸν δανεισμὸν ηὐξήσαμεν ταῖς μεταγενεστέραις ἁμαρτίαις.»

Translated literally word for word [Note: [Col. 0658] The printed editions read *Quae verba e verbo* (“These words word for word”). The manuscript reading, *Quae verbum e verbo*, is more harmonious.], they are as follows:

> “Christ came once; he found our paternal bond, which Adam wrote. He introduced the beginning of the debt; we increased the interest by later sins.”

Was he content merely to say “the paternal bond,” unless he added “our”? He wanted us to know that, before we increased the interest through our later sins, the debt of that paternal bond already belonged to us.

### 27

Read also how this same holy man explains that very passage of the Apostle where it is written: “Through one human being sin entered the world.” There he is engaged, more clearly than daylight, with the truth of this Catholic faith. Since it is too long to weave the whole passage into this work, I shall touch upon only a few parts.

“It is evident,” he says, “that it was not the sin itself which arises from transgression of the law, but the sin which arose from Adam’s disobedience, that contaminated everything.”

And shortly afterward:

“Death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who had not sinned. How did it reign? In the likeness of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one who was to come. For this reason Adam is also a type of Christ. In what sense is he a type, they ask? Because just as he became, for those born from him, although they had not eaten from the tree, the cause of death that had been introduced through food, so also Christ became, for those who are from him, although they had done nothing righteous, the provider of the righteousness that he granted to us all through the cross.”

Elsewhere in the same sermon:

“So that when a Jew says to you, ‘How has the world been saved through the power of one Christ?’ you may answer him: ‘Just as the world was condemned through the one disobedient Adam.’ Although grace and sin are not equal, nor are death and life comparable, nor God and the devil equal.”

And a little later:

“But grace was not like the trespass. For if many died through the trespass of one, much more has the grace of God, and the gift in the grace of the one human being Jesus Christ, abounded for many. What he says,” he explains, “is of this kind: If sin prevailed—and the sin of one human being—and grace, the grace of God, not only of the Father but also of the Son, how much more will it prevail? For this is much more reasonable. For one person to be condemned on account of another does not seem very rational; but for one person to be saved on account of another appears both more fitting and more reasonable. If, then, the former occurred, much more will the latter.”

And elsewhere, in what follows:

“Judgment from one trespass led to condemnation, but grace from many trespasses led to justification” (Rom. 5:12–16).

“This,” he says, “is the same as saying that, although sin was able to bring death and condemnation, grace did not kill only that one sin, but also the sins that entered afterward.”

And shortly afterward, on this very point:

“Since [Note: [Col. 0659] The printed editions read “how”; the manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek, read “since.”], then, more good things were introduced, and not only that one sin was destroyed but all the others as well, he demonstrates this by saying: ‘But grace from many trespasses led to justification.’”

And a little later he says:

“For at first he said that, if the sin of one killed all, the grace of one would much more be able to save. After this he shows that not only that one sin was destroyed through grace, but all the others also; and not only were the sins destroyed, but righteousness was also bestowed. Christ did not benefit us merely as much as Adam harmed us, but much more and to a far greater extent [Note: [Col. 0659] Erasmus and all the manuscripts read *majus* (“greater”).].”

After this, while discussing Baptism in the same work, he inserted the words of the Apostle:

“‘Do you not know, brothers,’ he says, ‘that all of us who were baptized in Christ were baptized into his death [Note: [Col. 0660] Most manuscripts read “into his death”; shortly afterward, “through Baptism into death.”]? Therefore we were buried with him through Baptism into death.’ What does ‘we were baptized into his death’ mean? That we too should die as he died. For Baptism is the cross. Therefore, what the cross and the tomb were for Christ, Baptism has become for us—although not in precisely the same things. He died and was buried in the flesh; we, however, in both cases die to sin. For this reason he did not say, ‘We were planted together with death,’ but ‘with the likeness of death’” (Rom. 6:3–5).

“For both this and that are death, but the same thing does not underlie them: the one is the death of Christ’s flesh, ours is the death of sin. Thus, just as that death is real, so is this” (*Homily 10 on the Epistle to the Romans*).

### 28

Can you now doubt that holy John is as far from your position as he is close to the Catholic position? In his discussion, where he explains the Apostle’s passage essential to the question at issue between us—where it is written, “Through one human being sin entered the world,” together with the other statements connected to it—does anything anywhere smell [Note: [Col. 0660] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “smell to anyone.”] of what you say: that this was spoken on account of imitation, not on account of carnal birth?

Does he not say that everything was contaminated by that one sin, and distinguish it from the other sins later committed and introduced—sins which you say belong to imitation, not transmission—so that he says that not only those sins but also this one and those others were destroyed through the grace of Christ [Note: [Col. 0660] In the manuscripts: “and that grace destroyed those sins as well.”]?

Does he not explain the Apostle’s words about Baptism—“All of us who were baptized in Christ were baptized into his death”—by saying that the person baptized in Christ dies to sin just as Christ died in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0660] Two Gallican and two Vatican manuscripts read “in the flesh.”], because to be baptized into Christ’s death means nothing other than to die to sin?

To what sin, then, does an infant die, if he has not contracted original sin? Or are infants perhaps not baptized into Christ’s death? For the Apostle did not say “some,” but “all of us who were baptized in Christ were baptized into his death.”

When infants are baptized with Christian Baptism, will you say that they are not baptized in Christ, lest Bishop John’s definition suffocate you? He says that Baptism is to those baptized in Christ what the cross and tomb were to Christ, so that just as Christ died in the flesh, we should understand these people also to have died to sin.

See what kind of man you wanted to subordinate to your doctrine: a man so great, a defender of the Christian faith and of this Catholic teaching. You acted as though he had said, “Infants are not polluted by the sin of the first human being,” when he actually said that “they do not have sins.” His many and very explicit testimonies make clear that he intended this to be understood only of sins of their own.

## CHAPTER VII

### 29

What help, then, did you gain by producing the testimony of John of Constantinople as though he supported you? Was it so that, with sharp cunning, you might seize upon one word supposedly omitted by him and thereby raise for yourself such a huge mound from the many words with which you were overwhelmed [Col. 0661]? You were so thoughtless and careless that, even in the very homily where you could scarcely find a single testimony by which you might deceive those whom you had misled through a wrong interpretation [Note: [Col. 0661] The printed editions read *potuistis*; the manuscripts read *potuisti*, and some subsequently read *adverteris*.], you did not notice that holy John of Constantinople had stated quite clearly that all human beings, apart from their own debts, are debtors to the paternal bond.

Yet after inserting his words, by which you thought your intention was in some measure assisted, you continue and say:

“Since it is therefore plainly clear that this is the sound and true opinion, fortified first by reason and then by the authority of the Scriptures, and since it has always been celebrated by the learning of holy men—who nevertheless did not bestow authority upon the truth through their own agreement, but received testimony and glory from their association with it—let no agreement of the depraved disturb any prudent person.”

To what do these words of yours tend, except to make it evident either that you neglected to learn the opinions and discussions of Catholic teachers on this matter, or, if you took care to know them, that you are attempting by what fraud to deceive those who do not know them?

For the moment, let me say nothing about reason and the authority of the holy Scriptures. Has the learning of holy men always celebrated this opinion—the opinion by which you deny that infants are born liable to the sin of the first human being? The testimonies of so many great and learned saints whom I have cited do not indicate this. On the contrary, I think you can now see how greatly this opinion has deceived you—unless you are acting deceitfully and already knew this.

But to think better of you: if you are learning this for the first time; if you are only now perceiving that so many saints both learned and taught that infants born through carnal generation are bound by the sin of the first human being and are released from it only through spiritual regeneration—something that we too have learned and teach—then change your mind. Forget this error, indeed this near madness, by which you hurl the reproach of Manichaeism at so many such fathers.

If you did this unknowingly, why do you not reject your wretched ignorance? If knowingly, why do you not lay aside your sacrilegious audacity?

### 30

You are convicted on every side: the testimonies of so many saints are clearer than daylight. Look at the company into which I have brought you.

Here is Ambrose of Milan, whom your teacher Pelagius praised so extravagantly that he said:

“In his books the Roman faith shines forth especially. Among Latin writers he stood out as a certain splendid flower, so that not even an enemy would dare criticize his faith or his most pure understanding of the Scriptures” [Note: [Col. 0661] The manuscripts read *quia* (“because”), rather than *qui* (“who”).].

Here too is John of Constantinople, whom you yourself placed in this very discussion to which I am replying as preeminent among the learned and the saints. Here is Basil, whose words, although they do not pertain to the matter now under discussion, you thought might provide you some assistance. Here also are the others, whose great agreement ought to move you.

This is not, as you write with your slanderous pen, “a conspiracy of the depraved.” In the Catholic Church they became distinguished through their devotion to sound doctrine; armed and girded with spiritual weapons, they waged vigorous wars against heretics; and, having faithfully completed [Note: [Col. 0662] Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read *perfunctis*.] the labors of their stewardship, they fell asleep in the bosom of peace.

“You say,” referring to me, “that one man has come forward who wishes it understood that the whole burden of the battle rests upon him” [Note: [Col. 0662] See below, book 3, section 4.].

Behold: it is not I alone, but so many and such great holy and learned teachers who answer you on my behalf—or together with me—for the salvation of all of us and, if you are wise, for your own salvation as well.

### 31

We do not oppose you, as you falsely accuse us, with “only the murmuring of the people.” Yet the people themselves murmur against you for this reason: this is not the sort of question that can escape even popular understanding [Note: [Col. 0662] The Floriacensis manuscript reads *quaesitio* (“inquiry” or “investigation”) rather than *quaestio* (“question”).].

Rich and poor, exalted and lowly, educated and uneducated, men and women know what is remitted to each age in Baptism. For this reason mothers throughout the world run daily with their infants not merely to Christ—that is, to the Anointed One—but to Christ Jesus—that is, also to the Savior.

But behold the company into which I have brought you. This gathering of saints is not a popular multitude; they are not merely sons but also fathers of the Church. They belong to the number of those concerning whom it was foretold: “In place of your fathers sons have been born to you; you shall appoint them princes over all the earth” (Ps. 44:17). They were begotten as her sons in order to learn these things; they became her fathers in order to teach them [Note: [Col. 0662] All the manuscripts read “begotten”; the printed editions read “reborn.”].

### 32

What is the point of your boast that you rejoice because this truth—which you regard as an error, or wish to have regarded as one—“cannot find an advocate among so great a multitude”? As though its defense were small because the multitude spread throughout the whole world, standing upon this most firm and ancient foundation of the faith, does not differ from itself.

But if you demand advocates whose writings can also be found and whose doctrine is renowned, behold its memorable and venerable assembly and agreement of advocates.

Saint Irenaeus says that the ancient wound inflicted by the serpent is healed by the faith of Christ and by the cross, and that we were bound as though by chains because of the sin of the first-formed human being.

Saint Cyprian says that an infant perishes unless baptized, although what is remitted to him is not his own sin but another’s.

Saint Reticius says that the sin of the old human being, whom we strip off through the washing of regeneration, is not merely old but innate.

Saint Olympius says that a defect was scattered from the first-formed human being into the seed, so that sin might be born together with the human being.

Saint Hilary says that all flesh is from sin, except the flesh of the one who came in the likeness of sinful flesh without sin. He says that the one whose voice is, “I was conceived in iniquities” (Ps. 50:7), was born under the origin of sin and under the law of sin.

Saint Ambrose says that infants who have been baptized are restored from the malice present at the beginning of their nature. He says that, among those born of woman, only the holy Lord Jesus, through the newness of an immaculate birth, experienced none of the contagion of earthly corruption.

He says that we all die in Adam, because through one human being sin entered the world, and the guilt of that one is the death of all.

He says that the whole human race would have perished in Adam’s wound unless that Samaritan, descending, had healed its bitter wounds.

He says that Adam existed, and that all existed in him; Adam perished, and all perished in him.

He says that we are defiled by contagion before we are born, and that human conception is not free from iniquity, because, he says, “we are conceived in the sin of our parents and born in their transgressions.” But birth itself also has its contagions, and nature itself does not possess only one contagion.

He says that the devil is a moneylender, from whom Eve, having been defiled, burdened the whole human race with the interest of a succession held liable.

He says that Eve was deceived by the devil so that she might overthrow her husband and bind the inheritance.

He says that Adam was so corrupted by the serpent’s bite that we all limp from that wound.

He says that, through the mingling of the bodies of man and woman, no one is free from sin; but that the one who is free from sin, namely the Lord Christ, is also free from such a conception.

Saint Innocent says to you that, through the washing of regeneration, every former defect is cleansed—the defect that occurred through the one who, falling by free choice, was plunged into the depths.

He says that infants cannot possess life unless they have eaten the flesh of the Lord and drunk his blood.

Saint Gregory says that it would have been better not to fall away from the tree of life through the exceedingly bitter taste of sin, but that after the fall we ought to be corrected.

He says that we have fallen from good things into sorrow and wishes us to be restored from sorrow to better things, so that those whom the taste of the forbidden tree condemned may be justified by the more abundant grace of Christ.

He says that the birth through which we are freed from the bonds of earthly birth is to be venerated.

He says that, through regeneration by water and the Spirit, the stains of our first birth are cleansed—the stains through which we are conceived in iniquities.

Saint Basil says to you that we contracted the sickness of sin because Eve refused to fast from the forbidden tree.

Finally, he says that we fell from paradise because we did not fast, and that, in order to return there, we must fast.

So many holy bishops say to you with one voice—Eulogius, John, Ammonianus, Porphyrius, Eutonius, another Porphyrius [Note: [Col. 0663] The printed editions lacked *another Porphyrius*. It is restored from the manuscripts. Instead of *Zoninus*, one of the five Vatican manuscripts has *Zorinus*; the other four have *Zozinus*.], Fidus, Zoninus, Zoboennus, Nymphidius, Chromatius, Jovinus, Eleutherius, Clematius:

“We do not absolve Pelagius unless he condemned those who say that infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life.”

Now you answer: can a just God deprive of eternal life an image of his own that is liable to no sin?

### 33

Finally, holy Bishop John—the man whom you honorably mentioned, whom you praised as holy and learned, and whom you said had received testimony and glory through his association with the truth—this same man also says that Adam sinned that great sin in such a way that he condemned the whole human race together.

He says that Christ wept at the death of Lazarus because mortality, having been shaken loose from immortality, loved the realm of the dead; and because the devil made mortal those who could have been immortal.

He says that, before human sin, beasts were subject to human beings in every way; but after that sin entered, we began to fear beasts. He intended that sin of the first human being to be understood as pertaining to all human beings to such an extent that it necessarily follows that no beast would injure infants unless carnal birth also bound them by the chain of that sin.

In the same sermon from which you tried, through your carelessness, to make your way into the hands of the unwary [Note: [Col. 0664] So the Floriacensis manuscript reads. The printed editions have *incautus* (“careless”), rather than *incautis* (“the unwary”).], he says that Christ found us bound both by our paternal bond, which Adam wrote, and by our later personal debts.

He explains the Apostle’s passage on which this entire case rests, where it is written, “Through one human being sin entered the world” (Rom. 5:12), together with the other statements that cohere with this sentence. In his lengthy discussion he does not say what you say: that this sin passed into all human beings not by propagation of the race but by imitation. On the contrary, he demonstrates that the matter is otherwise by not disagreeing with the opinions of his fellow bishops.

For he says that everything was contaminated by the sin of the first human being. And so that no one might think this happened through moral imitation rather than through carnal generation [Note: [Col. 0664] The printed editions read *mortali* (“mortal”), but, unless we are mistaken, the Floriacensis manuscript’s *morali* (“moral”) is more appropriate.], he says that Adam was therefore called a type of the one who was to come because, just as Adam became for those born from him—even though they had not eaten from the tree—the cause of death introduced through food, so Christ became for those who are from him—even though they had done nothing righteous—the provider of the righteousness he granted to all through the cross.

He says that a Jew who denies that the world can be saved through the power of one Christ must be refuted by the sin of the first human being, through whose one disobedience the world was condemned.

He says that it does not seem very reasonable for one person to be condemned on account of another, and yet that this occurred through Adam. From this he more strongly persuades us to believe what appears more fitting and reasonable: that one person is saved on account of another. This is fulfilled in Christ.

But who does not see that, if the sin of the first human being passed into all human beings not by propagation but by imitation, no one would be condemned on account of another? Each person would be condemned by his own sin, which another had not transmitted to him through generation, but which he himself had committed by imitation and through his own will.

He says that through grace not only that one sin of the first human being was destroyed, but also the sins that entered afterward. Here he clearly distinguishes the later sins, which can be said to have been committed through imitation, from that one sin which passed through propagation; and he shows that both were destroyed through grace, so that, in accordance with the Apostle’s intention, regeneration might appear to have accomplished more good than generation had done harm.

For this is how he explains what was said:

“And the gift was not like the trespass. For judgment indeed came from one trespass to condemnation, but grace came from many trespasses to justification” (Rom. 5:16).

By this statement your imitation—the novel contrivance of Pelagian error—is overturned, since it was written by the Apostle Paul and explained by Bishop John.

He also speaks about Baptism itself, explaining the Apostle’s statement, “All of us who were baptized in Christ were baptized into his death” (Rom. 6:3). To be baptized into Christ’s death, he says, means nothing other than to die to sin, just as Christ died in the flesh.

It is therefore necessary either that infants are not [Note: [Col. 0665] We restore the negative particle from the manuscripts.] baptized in Christ, or that, if they are baptized, they are baptized into his death; and thus they too die to sin and, because they do not have sin of their own, are cleansed from the contamination of that other sin—that is, original sin—which has been made common to all.

### 34

Surrounded by so many and such great masses of holy and learned men, will you still think that our cause has been unable to find an advocate among so great a multitude? Or will you call such agreement among Catholic priests a conspiracy of the depraved?

Nor should you despise Saint Jerome because he was a presbyter. Learned in Greek, Latin, and also Hebrew eloquence, he passed from the Western Church to the Eastern Church and lived to an advanced old age amid the holy places and the sacred writings [Note: [Col. 0665] The scholars of Louvain had added here from Belgian manuscripts: “whose eloquence shone for us from East to West like a lamp.” This was followed by: “Here are all, or nearly all, …” But these words are absent not only from the older printed editions but also from the Gallican and Vatican manuscripts.]. He read all, or nearly all, who before him had written anything on ecclesiastical doctrine in either part of the world, and he held and expressed no other opinion on this matter.

When he was explaining the prophet Jonah, he said most explicitly that infants too are held liable by the sin of Adam, who offended (*On the Book of Jonah*, chapter 3).

Will you love your error so much—an error into which, through youthful confidence and human weakness, you fell too incautiously—that, in this great matter on which the substance of the Christian religion rests, you dare not only to disagree with these priests of Catholic unity and truth, who from different regions of the world agree with one another in such great harmony of faith, but even to call them Manichaeans?

If you do not do this, neither do you justly do it to me, whom you see to have followed their footsteps in this same matter through my discussions—those very discussions which make you rage fiercely against me.

But if you sprinkle only me with this reproach, for no other reason than that I feel what they feel concerning the sin of the first human being, hold what they hold, and preach what they preach, who does not see that you openly cast an insult upon me while secretly forming the same judgment about them?

And yet, when you consider—leaving other matters aside—either the words of Bishop John about our paternal bond, which Adam wrote, words that I believe you found in the sermon from which you brought forth what you wished; or the words of Bishop Ambrose, which you read in my book, concerning the fact that no one can be free from sin through the mingling of male and female, but which you feared to touch upon in your own writings—then, although your brow is hard before human beings, your mind blushes before God.

### 35

For my part, because of the affection I have for you—an affection that, with God’s favor, I hope you will not tear from the depths of my heart by any insults—I would rather, my son Julian, that you overcome yourself through a better and stronger youth, and conquer with a more powerful devotion the passion—what else could it be but a human passion?—by which you wish your opinion, whatever its quality, to prevail because it has now become your own.

Just as Polemo gradually removed the crowns of luxury from his head and cast them away, placed his hand beneath his cloak, composed his mouth and countenance into modesty, and finally handed himself over as a disciple to the very man whom he had come to ridicule, so may you cast away, as though they were the crowns of drunkards, the praises of the Pelagians by which you are exalted as their great defender. Let your style—if I may put it mildly—of insult, not be hidden as though beneath a cloak of modesty, but be broken as though by a hand made more capable of correction. Let your breast be filled with truth, and entrust yourself not to Plato’s Xenocrates but to these Christian priests—or rather, through them, to the Lord Christ himself—not as one coming to them for the first time, but as one returning after having departed.

If my advice displeases you, act as you please. If you are corrected—which [Note: [Col. 0666] The printed editions read “in which”; the manuscripts read “which.”] is my greater and more fervent wish—I shall rejoice all the more abundantly and completely. But if, as I abhor, you remain in this perversity, I shall derive from your insults fruitful gain: an increase of heavenly reward for me, and, concerning you, the sharp pain of compassion.

## CHAPTER VIII [Note: [Col. 0666] In the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, “chapter 3.”]

### 36

But since I have now shown how many, what kind, and how great men—defenders and teachers of the Catholic faith—you falsely make into Manichaeans, listen now for a little to how, through your unlearned rashness, you actually assist the true Manichaeans. For I promised that I would demonstrate this as the second part of my discussion.

The Manichaeans, as you have shown that you know well enough, introduce, through the sacrilegious vanity of their wicked error, two natures—one good and the other evil—arising from different principles opposed to one another and coeternal.

Against them the Catholic faith proclaims that only God’s nature is without beginning: namely, the nature of the highest and unchangeable good, that is, of the ineffable Trinity. It says that from this supreme and unchangeable good, as has been stated, the whole created order was established, and that all natures are good, although unequal to the Creator, because they were created from nothing and are therefore mutable.

Thus there is absolutely no nature that is not either God himself or made by him. Consequently, whatever the extent or quality of a nature may be, insofar as it is a nature, it is good.

### 37

They therefore ask us where evil comes from. We answer: from good, but not from the supreme and unchangeable good. Evils, then, arose from lower and mutable goods.

Although we understand that these evils are not natures but defects of natures, we nevertheless understand at the same time that they cannot exist except from and in certain natures; and that nothing is evil except through a falling away from goodness.

But a falling away from what, unless from some nature without doubt? For even an evil will is certainly the will of some nature. Both an angel and a human being are natures. There cannot be the will of no one when there is a will.

And these wills have such power that they make the natures to which they belong possess certain qualities. For if one asks what sort of angel or human being a person of evil will is, the most correct answer is, “Evil”—the designation of quality being derived more from the evil will than from the good nature.

For nature itself is a substance capable both of goodness and of evil. It is capable of goodness through participation in the good by which it was made; but it receives evil not through participation in evil, but through deprivation of good. That is, evil does not arise because nature is mixed with some nature that is evil [Note: [Col. 0667] The printed editions read, “is not mixed with a nature that is something evil,” and shortly afterward, “but because it falls away from nature, etc.” These are corrected from the manuscripts.]—for no nature, insofar as it is nature, is evil—but because it falls away from the nature that is the supreme and unchangeable good, since it was made not from that nature but from nothing.

Otherwise it could not possess an evil will unless it were mutable. A nature, moreover, would not be mutable if it were from God rather than made by him from nothing.

Therefore God is the author of good, since he is the author of natures. The spontaneous falling away of those natures from the good does not indicate from whom they were made, but from what they were made. And this is not something, since it is completely nothing; therefore what is nothing cannot have an author.

38. Therefore, just as Manichaeus opposes the Catholic faith—that is, the faith of truth and true piety [Note: [Col. 0667] Some manuscripts read: “that is, the faith, truth, and true piety.”], who says that good and evil are so opposed to one another that he does not say that a nature becomes evil when it falls away from the good, nor that this falling away itself is its evil [Note: [Col. 0667] Several manuscripts read: “becomes evil.”], but rather says that evil itself is a nature—and, what is more insane, eternal without beginning—and calls it body and spirit: body, namely, from which spirit operates, and spirit, which operates through the body—so it cannot be said how greatly this opponent of the faith assists the one who denies that evils arise from goods and understands in the same sense what the Lord says: “A good tree does not produce evil fruits.” For in that saying the divine Teacher does not designate nature as the tree from which the fruit of which he was speaking comes forth [Note: [Col. 0667] The printed editions read *de qua* (“from which,” feminine); the text has been corrected from the manuscripts.], but the will, whether good or evil, while the fruits are works, which cannot be either good works of an evil will or evil works of a good will. For this is what he says: “An evil tree does not produce good fruits, and a good tree does not produce evil fruits” (Matt. 7:18), as though he were saying: Neither does a good will produce evil works, nor an evil will good works.

For if the origins of those trees—that is, of those wills—are sought, what appears except natures, which God created good? Thus evils have arisen from goods—not evil works from good wills, but evil wills from good natures. What, then, does Manichaeus desire to hear so greatly as that evils cannot be from goods? For since it cannot be denied that evils exist, nothing remains except that they must be from evil, if they cannot be from good natures; and thus an evil nature, without beginning and eternally existing, must have evil as its origin, and there must be two natures, one of good and the other of evil.

For it is necessary that either evils do not exist at all, or that they arise from good natures, or from evil ones. If we say that no evils exist, we say to God in vain, “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13). But if we say that evils arise only from evils, the Manichaean pestilence will triumph, devastate everything, and violate the very nature of God—as though it were mutable—by mingling it with an evil nature. It remains, therefore, that we confess evils to be from goods; for if we deny this, they will be from evils, and we shall certainly lend our support to the Manichaeans.

39. Accordingly, when you say, “Since, according to the judgment of the Gospel, a tree ought to be recognized by its fruits, he who says that marriage is good, although he decisively maintains that nothing but evil proceeds from it, should here be heard,” you evidently want marriage to be regarded as a good tree, from which you do not want a human being bound by the contagion of original sin to be born as though he were an evil fruit. Yet you do not see that, if marriage is a good tree, you must necessarily establish adultery as an evil tree.

Consequently, if the one born from marriage is the fruit of marriage and therefore ought to be without defect, lest an evil fruit be born from a good tree, it follows that the one born from adultery ought not to be born without defect, lest a good fruit be born from an evil tree—for the Lord definitively declares by divine authority that evil fruits do not come from a good tree, nor good fruits from an evil tree.

Therefore, since you escape from this difficulty by saying that a human being cannot be born with a defect from adultery, you will deny that adultery is an evil tree, lest the one who, according to you, is born without defect from adultery appear—contrary to the Lord’s definition—to be a good fruit born from an evil tree. Deny, then, also that marriage is a good tree, and confess that you were mistaken in saying this.

But you will say that the person begotten through adulterous intercourse is not born from adultery. From what, then? “From human nature,” you say, “which even in adulterers is God’s work, not theirs.” Why, then, do you not understand in the same way that the person begotten through marital intercourse is not born from marriage, but likewise from human nature, which even in married couples is God’s work, not theirs? In this way, the evil which those being born contract from a defect of nature is not attributed to the goodness of marriage, just as the good which those being born receive from the institution of nature is not attributed to the wickedness of adultery.

You, however, understand “good tree” not as Christ intended it to be understood—that is, as the good will of a human being—but as God’s work itself, namely, human beings, or marriage, or nature. And because these are good works of God, you say that evil cannot arise from them, since a good tree cannot produce evil fruit.

Thus Manichaeus concludes his reasoning against you in support of his own doctrine; and you assist him by your words in such a way that he desires to hear nothing more than that evils cannot be from goods. Once he has received this, he proceeds to say to you: “If evil cannot be from good, from what will it be except evil? For evils could not suddenly come into existence by themselves, without an author.”

But you say that evil cannot be from good, lest a good tree produce evil fruits contrary to the Gospel’s judgment. “It remains,” he says, “that the nature of evil was eternal and was able to generate evils, since you admit that they cannot exist from goods.”

40. Do you now wish to change the position which you advanced—not by favoring the Manichaeans, but through ignorance of what you were saying—in order to assist the Manichaean pestilence? For how could Christ have said, “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree evil and its fruit evil” (Matt. 12:33), when he was speaking to human beings whom he himself had created, if evil could not arise from his good work, which is the human being, as you think? You make the good work of God—that is, human marriage or nature—a good tree, and therefore say that evil cannot arise from it, because, if we say that evil arises from good, we shall resist the one who said, “A good tree does not produce evil fruits.”

Yet you know that from the good natures of angels and human beings—natures which no evil parents had begotten, but which the supremely good God had made from no parents—there arose not evil fruits, but evil trees themselves, from which evil fruits would arise. The Lord Jesus therefore defeats the Manichaeans, because one human being—that is, one nature—can make both trees; and he defeats you, because an evil tree can arise from a good nature.

From this it is shown to be false that which you say in support of the Manichaeans: “Evils cannot be from goods.” Otherwise, unless they are thought to come from the nature of evil, which their criminal error introduces, evils could not be thought to have existed at all.

41. Nor have you assisted the Manichaeans only in that one passage where you thought a good tree should be mentioned from the Gospel; you have supported them with this perversity in other passages of your discussion as well. Such is the statement where you again said: “Sin cannot be transmitted through nature, because the work of the devil is not permitted to pass through the work of God.”

To this I reply: How is the work of the devil permitted to remain in the work of God if it is not permitted to pass through the work of God? For who would doubt that it is worse for it to remain there than for it to pass from there? [Note: [Col. 0669] The printed editions read: “would think it worse.” Two of the five Vatican manuscripts read: “would think it not worse.” The other three, with several French manuscripts, read: “would doubt it worse.”]

Perhaps you ask how the work of the devil remains in the work of God. Do not look elsewhere; recall the devil himself. He is God’s work, certainly an angelic nature. But envy is the work of the devil himself, and this work both proceeded from him and remains in him.

Your statement, therefore, that “the work of the devil does not pass through the work of God” is empty, since you see that it remains there as well. Do you still not perceive how many thanks Manichaeus gives you? Do you not yet awaken?

For Manichaeus labors to show that evil cannot arise from God’s good work, so that what he himself wants may be believed: that evil cannot be from anything except evil. Here you, his remarkable helper, say, “Through the work of God, evil is not permitted to pass,” so that he can conclude with complete ease that evil cannot arise from it either, since it is not even permitted to pass through it.

## CHAPTER IX

42. Hear another such statement—or rather, a more serious one—in which you repeatedly support the Manichaeans. “Original sin,” you say, “has vanished, because the root of evil cannot be located in that which you call God’s gift” [Col. 0670].

I shall show you with what manifest truth this is refuted. Is not the human mind God’s gift? And yet that enemy-sower placed the root of evil there when, by the serpent’s deceit, he persuaded the human being to sin (Gen. 3:1–6). For unless the human mind had then received the root of evil, it would in no way have given assent to the one who was wickedly persuading it.

What shall I say about avarice, the root of all evils? And where is this found except in the human soul? And what is the human soul except God’s gift? How, then, do you say—unless you do not consider what you are saying—that “the root of evil cannot be located in God’s gift”?

But observe what Manichaeus, whom you greatly assist through these ill-considered statements of yours, says to you. If the existence of a rational creature is God’s gift, and you say that the root of evil cannot be located in God’s gift, how much more plausibly, he says, must one conclude that the root of evil cannot arise from God’s gift?

Thus, with you as his supporter, Manichaeus introduces the root of evil from that nature which he imagines not to have been created by God but to be coeternal with God. For if you say that the root of evil arose from the free will of a good nature created by God—which is what Catholic truth teaches—he easily overcomes you by those words of yours in which you say, “The root of evil cannot be located in God’s gift.” For free will is without doubt God’s gift.

Accordingly, when you said that “the root of evil cannot be located in God’s gift,” you yourself supplied Manichaeus with what he could say against you. For if evil cannot be located in good, as you say to me, much less can evil arise from good, as he says to you. And thus he will conclude that evil exists only from evil. He will seem victorious to himself—and he will indeed be victorious unless resistance is offered both to him and to you.

The truth of the Catholic faith therefore defeats Manichaeus in these statements of yours precisely because it also defeats you. For if it did not defeat you when you say that “the root of evil cannot be located in God’s gift,” it could much less defeat Manichaeus when he says that the root of evil cannot arise from God’s gift.

But in order to defeat both of you, it says that the root of evil can arise from nowhere else and exist in no other place than in a rational nature and in that rational nature itself. Yet for that nature to be rational is nothing other than God’s gift. Since, however, it was made from nothing by the supreme and immutable good, so that it might exist as a good thing, though mutable, it can fall away from the good by which it was made. Thus, from that nature or in that nature there is the root of evil [Note: [Col. 0670] Perhaps: “can fall away.”]—that is, evil is nothing other than the privation of good [Note: [Col. 0670] According to Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venice edition, and the Louvain edition: “this is.” The manuscript reading is retained here.].

43. Furthermore, when you say, “The nature of things does not permit anything evil to be brought forth from good, or anything unjust from the just,” you are speaking in the very words of the Manichaeans. For they assert that evil cannot be brought forth except from evil, and their entire criminal sect rests on this, because they first contend that evil cannot be brought forth from good.

If, with you as its authority, we grant this to them, nothing at all will remain by which we can refute their criminal doctrines. “The unjust from the just” is the same as “evil from good.”

Therefore, in order to resist both you and them, the Catholic faith says that evil has been brought forth only from good, and the unjust only from the just. For the angel and the human being from whom these things were brought forth were previously good and just.

We cannot therefore resist the Manichaeans unless we also obtain from you the admission that evils arose only from goods; and that those evils are not substances, but defects of created substances, through which they fall away from the good because they are mutable, since they were made from nothing.

This is the soundness of Catholic doctrine by which the venom of the Manichaean pestilence is driven out.

44.
