Hence my teacher Ambrose—also praised by the mouth of your evil teacher—says in the book he wrote on Isaac and the Soul: “What, then, is wickedness except the lack of good?” And again he says: “Evils, therefore, arose from goods. For there are no evils except those deprived of goods; yet through evils it came about that goods might stand out. Therefore, the lack of good is the root of wickedness” (ch. 7).

Do you see how blessed Ambrose refutes the Manichaeans by the truly Catholic reasoning? Do you see how, although he did not name them in that same discussion, he nevertheless convicted them by the truth and brevity of these statements?

Behold the man of God against whom, because of original sin—which he asserted in a Catholic manner as a Catholic, you accuse him, at the instigation of the Manichaeans, with the insult of a cursing fury. Yet, contrary to the support you give them, he offers Catholic disputants an unconquerable aid for defeating them.

He cries out against the Manichaeans, “Evils arose from goods.” And on their behalf you cry out against him: “It is necessary that there be some evil from which and through which an evil fruit appeared”; and, “The work of the devil is not permitted to pass through the work of God”; and, “The root of evil cannot be located in God’s gift”; and, “The nature of things does not permit evil to be brought forth from good, or injustice from the just.”

You cry out these things on behalf of the Manichaeans against the voice of Catholic truth uttered through God’s priest. Thus, if you are heard, the Manichaeans will triumph, saying—to pass over the rest—“If the nature of things does not permit evil to be brought forth from good, then evils did not arise from goods, as Ambrose says, but, as we say, from the nature of evil.”

Behold into what an abyss you have fallen by misunderstanding the Lord when he says, “A good tree does not produce evil fruits.” For this was not said of nature, or of marriage, which God instituted, but of the good will of a human being, from which evil works do not arise.

45. But lest you or anyone else perhaps say: “How is it that evil fruits do not arise from the tree which a human being makes—that is, from a good will—while from the nature which God makes there arises an evil tree that produces evil fruits? Is the human being, then, making something better, from which an evil fruit cannot arise, than that which God makes, from which an evil tree can arise?”

Lest anyone fall into this error, let him listen carefully to Ambrose, who says: “What is wickedness except the lack of good? For there are no evils except those deprived of goods, because the lack of good is the root of wickedness.”

From this let him understand why the evil tree is the evil will: because it is a falling away from the supreme good, where created good is deprived of the good that creates it, so that the root of evil in it is nothing other than the lack of good.

The good tree, on the other hand, is the good will because through it the human being is turned toward the supreme and immutable good and is filled with good, so that he may produce good fruit.

Accordingly, God is the author of all goods—that is, of both good nature and good will, which a human being does not produce unless God works in him; for “the will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. 8, according to the Septuagint).

46. But now I see that the order of my plan requires me to do, with God’s help, what I promised to do in the third place: namely, to shatter, by the judgments of the Catholic bishops who lived before us—so far as I am able to find judgments relevant to the matters under discussion—your glassy sophistries and the fragile arguments by which you seem to yourself to be very sharp and polished.

We shall undertake this from another beginning, once the length of this book has been brought to an end.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0671]

The author overturns five arguments of the Pelagians against original sin by the authority and judgments of Catholic teachers who previously shone in the Church: namely, ten distinguished bishops—Irenaeus, Cyprian, Reticius, Olympius, Hilary, Gregory of Nazianzus, Ambrose, Basil, John of Constantinople, and Innocent—as well as the presbyter Jerome, a holy and highly learned man.

## CHAPTER ONE

1. Now I must undertake what I placed third in my plan: with the judgments of bishops who treated the Holy Scriptures with immense glory, and with the Lord’s help, Julian, overthrow your contrivances. I do not do this in order to show that they held a Catholic view of original sin—for I have already done this in the earlier parts of this work, so that I might demonstrate how many and how great men, holy and renowned teachers of the Church, you accuse of the crime of the Manichaeans, and how, when you wish to discredit me in the judgments of the unlearned, you accuse those who defended the Catholic faith against heretics by the name of a detestable heresy.

But now your own arguments, by which you act so that the first birth of human beings may not be believed to be bound by original sin, must be refuted by the utterances of the saints. The Christian people ought to prefer these men to your profane innovations and choose to adhere to them rather than to you.

2. These, certainly, are like the principal points of your arguments—almost frightening arguments—with which you terrify the weak and those less instructed in the Holy Scriptures than would be useful to them against you. For you say:

“By asserting original sin, we say that the devil is the creator of human beings at birth, condemn marriage, deny that all sins are forgiven in Baptism, accuse God of the crime of injustice, and instill despair of perfection.”

You contend that all these consequences follow if we believe that infants are born bound by the sin of the first human being and are therefore under the devil unless they are reborn in Christ.

“For the devil creates,” you say, “if they are created from this wound which the devil inflicted upon human nature when it was first created. And marriage is condemned if it is believed to possess something from which those who are to be condemned are generated. Nor are all sins forgiven in Baptism if some evil remains in baptized married couples from which evil persons are generated.

“How, moreover, is God not unjust when, while forgiving baptized people their own sins, he condemns an infant because, when it was created by him, unknowingly and unwillingly it also drew another’s sins from those parents to whom they had been forgiven?

“Nor can virtue, to which viciousness is understood to be opposed, be believed capable of being perfected, because it is incredible that innate vices can be consumed; and these ought no longer even to be considered vices. For one who cannot be other than he was created does not sin.”

3. If you sought these matters with faithful diligence, and did not attack with faithless audacity those things founded upon the truth and antiquity of the Catholic faith, you would come, nourished by Christ’s grace, to those things that have been hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed to infants (Matt. 11:25).

For “the great abundance of the sweetness of the Lord”—which he certainly did not begrudge, yet hid from those who fear him and perfected for those who hope in him—not in themselves, but in him (Ps. 30:20), would sustain you.

We therefore say what that faith teaches of which it is written: “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint). It teaches that not the devil but the true and truly good God is the creator of human beings, mysteriously bringing forth what is clean even from what is unclean; although no human being is born clean, and therefore, until cleansed by the Holy Spirit, is compelled to remain under an unclean spirit.

Nor is any degree of uncleanness in natures a crime of marriage. For the good proper to marriage is distinguished from any defect of nature.

Nor does the liability of any sin remain which is not removed by the regeneration that takes place in Christ, although weakness remains, against which the reborn person, as he makes progress, fights when it has arisen within him.

Nor is God unjust when he repays what is fitting for sins, whether original or personal. Rather, he would appear more unjust or weak if he imposed upon the children of Adam a heavy yoke—from the day of their birth, as it is written, until the day of their burial, upon the mother of all (Ecclus. 40:1)—under which yoke his image is worn down, or if he imposed that yoke upon the human being or anyone else without any preceding original or personal sin and against his will.

Nor is there reason to despair of the perfection of virtue, through the grace of the one who can change and heal a nature corrupted at its origin.

## CHAPTER II

4. I shall therefore undertake to fulfill my promise. I shall not take up these five arguments of yours, from which you connect all the various things you argue in this question against the Catholic faith, one by one for refutation through the testimonies of the saints. Rather, insofar as each one is struck down and overthrown when I bring forward individual testimonies from the writings of Catholic bishops, so far will one, or two, or several, or all of them be struck down and overthrown, according to the force of what is brought forward.

Such is the passage in the book which blessed Ambrose wrote on Noah’s Ark:

“Through the one Lord Jesus, salvation destined for the nations is declared, for he alone could not be just [Note: [Col. 0674] The printed editions read: “who alone could be just.” We have added the negating particle from an old Floriacensis codex. Otherwise, once it was removed, the sentence would have had to be read with the negation later, after “would err,” as follows: “who was born of a virgin”; or, as we corrected it in Book Four Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, no. 29: “for no other reason than that he was born of a virgin.” Moreover, this testimony of Ambrose is now missing from the cited book On Noah and the Ark.], since every generation would err, unless, born of a virgin, he were in no way held by the privilege of an indebted generation.

“‘Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother bore me in sins’ (Ps. 50:7), says the one who was thought just above others. Whom, then, should I now call just except the one freed from these bonds, whom the bonds of common nature do not hold? All are under sin; from Adam death reigned over all. Let the one just man come into the sight of God, of whom it is no longer said with qualification, ‘He did not sin with his lips’ (Job 1:22), but, ‘He committed no sin’” (1 Pet. 2:22).

Say to him, if you dare, that the devil made himself the creator of human beings who are born through the union of the two sexes, since he excepts only Christ from the bonds of an indebted generation because Christ was born of a virgin, while all others born from Adam are under the obligation of sin—a sin which the devil sowed.

Accuse him of being a condemner of marriage, since he says that the son of a virgin alone was born without sin.

Charge him with denying that virtue can be attained [Note: [Col. 0674] Some manuscripts read “perfected.” This reading fits well with Julian’s statement above, no. 2: “Nor can virtue, to which viciousness is understood to be opposed, be believed capable of being perfected, because it is incredible that innate vices can be consumed.” We have retained “attained,” since that reading is more common and better suits what follows, where it is said that they “think human nature incapable of virtue.”], since he asserts that vices are implanted in the human race at the very beginning of conception.

And say to him what, in the first volume of your work, you seem to yourself to have said against me with sufficient appropriateness and acuteness [Note: [Col. 0674] Ambrosianus, Erasmus, and nearly all the manuscripts read: “with depth and acuteness.”]:

“Nor do those who are said to sin sin at all; for, whoever created them, they necessarily have to live according to what they were created to be, and they cannot oppose their own nature.”

Say all these things to Ambrose, or about Ambrose, which you haughtily, insultingly, shamelessly, and insolently cast at me.

(For perhaps it cannot be said that by these words he also defames the sacrament of Baptism, as though the forgiveness of sins were not complete in it, or makes God unjust because he condemns in children another’s sins which he forgave in their parents. For when he said these things, he was perhaps not speaking about the offspring of baptized people.)

But if holy Ambrose was not among those who make the devil the creator of human beings, or condemn marriage, or regard human nature as incapable of virtue, but rather among those who acknowledge and confess the supreme and supremely good God as the creator of the whole human being—that is, of the whole soul and the whole body—and honor marriage in the goodness proper to its rank, and do not despair that the human being can be perfectly justified, then these three arguments of yours have meanwhile been overthrown by the authority of so great a man [Note: [Col. 0674] The printed editions read “so great.” The manuscripts have “of so great a man.”] and must no longer be brought against us, since we say of original sin what he said—he who neither attributed the creation of human beings to the devil, nor condemned marriage, nor despaired of the perfection of justice in human nature.

## CHAPTER III

5. As for your two remaining arguments, which concern Baptism, we shall soon see what that man thought and how he crushed you beneath the immense weight of his authority [Note: [Col. 0675] Some manuscripts read “crushed” with an alternate spelling.].

For in his book Against the Novatians he says:

“We are all born under sin, and our very birth is in defect, as you find written when David says, ‘For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother bore me in sins.’ Therefore Paul’s flesh was a body of death, as he himself says, ‘Who will free me from this body of death?’ (Rom. 7:24). But Christ’s flesh condemned sin, which he did not experience by being born and which he crucified by dying, so that in our flesh there might be justification through grace, where previously there was a flood of guilt” (Book 1 On Repentance, ch. 3).

Here all your arguments are overthrown at once. If “we are all born under sin, and our very birth is in defect,” why do you object to me on this basis by saying that I make the devil the creator of human beings, when you see me saying what was said by the one who did not say that the devil was the creator of human beings?

If, because the human being’s birth is in defect, David says, “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother bore me in sins,” and this utterance does not accuse the marital union but original sin, why do you call me a condemner of marriage for saying what you would not dare to say about Ambrose?

If, because we are all born under sin and our birth itself is in defect, Paul’s flesh was therefore a body of death, as he himself says, “Who will free me from this body of death?”, do you at last see that in these words he also intended the Apostle himself to be understood?

His inner person, therefore, delighted in the law of God, yet saw another law in his members opposing the law of his mind; and for this reason he called his flesh a body of death. Therefore, in his flesh good did not dwell, because he did not do the good that he wanted, but did the evil that he hated (Rom. 7:15–24).

Here your entire cause has been driven forward, overthrown, crushed, and—like dust that the wind casts from the face of the earth (Ps. 1:4)—cast away from the hearts of those whom you had begun to deceive, if they are willing to consider these things after laying aside their contentious zeal.

For was the Apostle Paul not baptized? Or had any sins been left unforgiven in him—whether original sins, personal sins, sins of ignorance, or sins of knowledge?

Why, then, did he speak in this way, except because what I said in my book, to which you boast that you have replied, is entirely true? This law of sin, which is in the members of this body of death, has both been forgiven through spiritual rebirth and remains in mortal flesh. It has been forgiven because its guilt has been loosed by the sacrament through which the faithful are reborn; yet it remains because it produces desires against which even the faithful struggle.

This is precisely what utterly subverts your heresy. You see and fear it so plainly that you try to escape these apostolic words in no other way than by asserting as forcefully as you can that the person of the Apostle himself is not to be understood there, but that of some Jew still under the law and not yet under grace, against whom the habit of his evil conduct was struggling.

This is as though the force of habit were laid aside in Baptism, rather than baptized people also fighting against it—indeed, with greater strength and intensity, the more earnestly they strive to please the eyes of the one whose grace assists them so that they may not be defeated in such a struggle.

If you had wished to consider this attentively and without obstinacy, you would certainly have found, even in the force of habit itself, how concupiscence is forgiven with respect to guilt while remaining in its activity.

For it is not the case that nothing happens in a human being when he is disturbed by the impulses of his desires, even those to which he does not consent. Yet the Apostle did not call his flesh a body of death because of the force of habit, but for the reason that Ambrose correctly understood: because we are all born under sin, and our birth itself is in defect.

He could not doubt that the guilt of this defect had already been forgiven him in Baptism. Yet, while fighting against its disturbance, he first feared being conquered and subjugated by it; then, although he could not be overcome, he preferred not to fight for a long time but not to have an enemy at all, when he said, “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:24–25).

He knew that by God’s grace we are healed of this concupiscent movement—the same grace by which spiritual rebirth healed us from its original guilt.

This battle, which we have undertaken to wage within ourselves against ourselves [Note: [Col. 0676] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “which we undertake.”], is experienced in themselves, and cannot be denied, by those who most fiercely conquer lust—not by those who most shamelessly praise it.

6. Finally, the most victorious Cyprian also says in his letter On the Lord’s Prayer:

“We ask that the will of God be done in heaven and on earth; and this pertains in both respects to the completion of our safety and salvation. For since we possess a body from the earth and a spirit from heaven, we ourselves are earth and heaven; and in both—that is, in body and spirit—we pray that God’s will may be done.

“For there is a struggle between flesh and spirit, and a daily clash between them as they oppose one another, so that we do not do the things we want: the spirit seeks heavenly and divine things, while the flesh desires earthly and worldly things.

“Therefore, we ask that harmony be brought about between these two by God’s help and assistance, so that, while God’s will is carried out both in spirit and in flesh, the soul that has been reborn through him may be preserved.

“The Apostle Paul openly and plainly declares this in his own words: ‘The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you do not do the things you want’” (Gal. 5:17).

See how this eminent teacher instructs a baptized people—for what Christian does not know that the Lord’s Prayer pertains to the baptized?—so that they may understand that the safety and salvation of human nature are established not by flesh and spirit separating as though they were naturally hostile to one another, as Manichaeus foolishly supposes, but rather by their being healed from the defect of discord and brought into harmony.

For this is what it means to be freed from this body of death: that what is now a body of death may become a body of life, as death itself dies within it—the end of discord, not the end of nature.

Hence the saying will also be fulfilled: “Where, O death, is your contention?” (1 Cor. 15:55).

That this is not completed in the present life is also testified by the Martyr in his letter On Mortality, where he says that the Apostle Paul desired to depart and be with Christ precisely so that he might no longer be subject to any sins or vices of the flesh.

How watchfully does he expound in the Lord’s Prayer that doctrine of yours by which you place your confidence in your own virtue! He teaches that this should rather be requested from the Lord than presumed upon as arising from one’s own powers, so that harmony between flesh and spirit may be produced not by human strength but by divine grace. In this he is entirely consonant with the Apostle, who says: “Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

### 7

Saint Gregory also bears witness to this, saying:

“For when the soul is in labors and distress, when it is pressed by the flesh as by an enemy, then it flees to God and recognizes from whom it must seek help.”

And lest anyone should suppose from these words of Bishop Gregory that the flesh presses hostilely [Note: [Col. 0677] The printed editions read “is pressed”; this is corrected from two Gallican manuscripts.] upon the soul as though evil arose from a contrary nature, according to the madness of the Manichaeans, observe how he himself harmonizes with his brethren and fellow teachers, teaching that the spirit desires against the flesh for no other reason than that, after the most grievous conflict of the two in this life—a conflict in which the life of all the saints labors—both may be recalled to their own Author.

For in the *Apologetic Book* he says:

“I do not yet mention those blows by which we are attacked within ourselves by our own vices and passions, and by which day and night we are pressed by the fiery goads of this body of our humiliation and this body of death, now secretly, now even openly, while the enticements of visible things provoke and irritate us everywhere; this filth, this mire [Note: [Col. 0677] The printed editions read “of this”; the manuscripts, “this.”], to which we are clinging, exhaling through its more capacious veins the stench of its mud; while the law of sin, which is in our members, resists the law of the spirit and strives to lead captive the royal image that is within us, so that whatever has flowed into us through the gift of God and through that first condition of ours may become its spoil. Hence scarcely anyone, perhaps, by governing himself through a long and rigorous [Note: [Col. 0677] The Belgian manuscripts read “distinct.”] philosophy and gradually recalling the nobility of his soul, can draw back and turn toward God the nature of light that is within him, joined as it is to this humble and dark mud. Or, if he acts with God’s favor, he will recall both together, provided that through long and continual meditation he becomes accustomed always to look upward and, with tighter reins, lift up the matter bound to him that drags and weighs him downward.”

(*In the first book of the Apologetic, concerning his flight*.) [Col. 0678]

Recognize, my son Julian, the harmonious Catholic voices, and cease to sound discordantly with them. When blessed Gregory says, “Within ourselves we are attacked by our own vices and passions, and day and night we are pressed by the fiery goads of this body of our humiliation and this body of death,” he is speaking as one baptized and speaking about the baptized. When he says, “The law of sin which is in our members resists the law of the spirit,” he is speaking as one baptized and speaking about the baptized [Note: [Col. 0678] The printed editions read “speaking about one baptized”; the manuscripts more correctly read “about the baptized.”]. This is the struggle of faithful Christians, not of unbelieving Jews.

Believe it, if you do not struggle; acknowledge it, if you do struggle; and in this struggle [Note: [Col. 0678] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “and in this struggle.”] conquer also the rebellious pride of the Pelagian error. Do you now distinguish, do you now perceive, do you now recover your senses: that in Baptism all sins are remitted, and that with the baptized a kind of civil war among inward vices nevertheless remains?

For these vices are not such as should already be called sins, if desire does not draw the spirit toward unlawful acts, conceive, and give birth to sin. Yet they are not outside us. We must labor earnestly to overcome them while we make progress in this contest. They are ours; they are passions; they are vices; they must be restrained, checked, and healed. But while they are being healed, they are hostile. And although, as we advance toward better things, they are diminished more and more, nevertheless, as long as we live here, they do not cease to exist. When the devout soul departs from here, they will perish; when the body rises again, they will not return.

## CHAPTER IV

### 8

Let us therefore return to blessed Ambrose. “Even Paul’s flesh,” he says, “was a body of death, as he himself says: ‘Who will deliver me from this body of death?’”

Ambrose understood it thus; so did Cyprian, so did Gregory—to say nothing for the moment of other teachers endowed with similar authority. To this death it will be said at the end: “Where is your contention, O death?” But this is the grace of those regenerated, not of those generated.

For, as Ambrose adds, “Christ’s flesh condemned sin, which it did not experience in being born, and crucified in dying.” It did not experience it in itself by being born; it crucified it in us by dying.

Therefore the law of sin, resisting the law of the mind, which was present even in the members of so great an apostle, is remitted in Baptism, not ended. From this law of the flesh, resisting the law of the mind, Christ’s body drew nothing, because the Virgin did not conceive from it. From this law of the flesh, resisting the law of the mind, everyone without exception drew that same law through his first birth, because no woman conceived except from it.

And therefore the venerable Hilary did not hesitate to say that all flesh is from sin (above, Book 1, no. 9). But did he thereby deny that it is from God? How can we say that flesh is from flesh and from a human being—do we on that account also deny that it is from God? [Note: [Col. 0678] The printed editions read, “do we on that account also deny that we are generated from God?” The words “are generated” are absent from the manuscripts.]

It is therefore from God, because he creates; from a human being, because he generates; and from sin, because sin corrupts.

But God, who begot for himself the Son coeternal with him, the Word who was in the beginning and through whom he created everything that did not exist, also created that same one as a human being without defect [Note: [Col. 0678] Here some manuscripts, including those of Fleury and Casale, add: “not from a human being without defect.”]—not from human seed, but born through a virgin [Col. 0679]—in whom he regenerates the generated human being and heals the corrupted one: immediately from guilt, gradually from weakness.

Against this weakness the regenerated person, once he has the use of reason, struggles as in an arena, with God looking on and helping, because “power is made perfect in weakness” (1 Cor. XII, 9). Our deficient self, which falls short of righteousness, fights against that aspect of ourselves which advances toward righteousness, so that, as progress gains the victory, the whole may rise toward what is better, rather than, as deficiency gains the victory, the whole decline toward what is worse.

But the little child, in whom there is not yet any use of reason, is by his own will neither in the good nor in the evil, because he turns no thought toward either one [Note: [Col. 0679] There is some variation in the printed editions: Am. and Er. read, “he turns by no thought toward either”; Louvain, “he turns by no thought toward either one.” They are corrected from the Fleury manuscript.]. Rather, both lie dormant and inactive in him: the natural good of reason and the original evil of sin.

But as the years advance and reason awakens, the commandment comes, and sin revives. When it begins to fight against the growing child, then it will become apparent what had lain hidden in the infant: either he conquers and will be condemned [Note: [Col. 0679] The printed editions read, “and will rule,” incorrectly. See below, Book 4, no. 54]; or he is conquered and will be healed.

Yet this does not mean that the evil would have done no harm if the child had departed from this life before it began to appear in him. For the guilt of that evil—not the guilt by which the evil itself is guilty, but the guilt by which it makes guilty the person in whom it is—just as it is contracted through generation, so it is not removed except through regeneration.

This is why infants are baptized: so that they may not only enjoy the good of Christ’s kingdom but also be rescued from the evil of the kingdom of death. This cannot happen except through him who condemned sin in his flesh [Note: [Col. 0679] Erasmus and Louvain read, “condemned sin in his own flesh.” Ambrosius and the manuscripts lack the word “in.” The sentence of Ambrose emphasized here is: “For Christ’s flesh condemned sin.”], which he did not experience in being born and crucified in dying; so that in our flesh there might be justification through grace, where previously there had been defilement through guilt.

### 9

From these words of blessed Ambrose it follows that the devil did not create the human being in goodness but corrupted the human being through malice; that the good of marriage was not removed by the evil of desire; that in the sacrament of Baptism no guilt of any sin is left unforgiven; and that God is not unjust when, by the law of justice, he condemns one who becomes guilty by the law of sin, even if he was born from the one who, because she was reborn, can no longer make his parent guilty.

Moreover, if these things are true, why should the power that is made perfect in weakness be despaired of? For through Christ’s flesh—which condemns sin that it did not experience in being born and crucified in dying—justification through grace is also brought about in our flesh, in which previously there had been defilement through guilt.

Accordingly, these five arguments of yours, by which you chiefly terrify people, will be unable to disturb others—or you yourselves, if you believe Ambrose, Cyprian, Gregory, and the other holy and distinguished Catholic teachers, indeed, even yourselves [Note: [Col. 0679] The old manuscript of Fleury adds here, “for it will also become clear to you yourselves.” Below it reads: “introducing the necessity of fighting—against what, unless against evil?—not against substance, but against a defect of substance.”]—when you teach that the law of sin, which is present in the members of a human being and resists the law of the mind, by which the flesh desires against the spirit, imposes upon even the baptized saints the necessity of fighting.

Against what, unless against evil? Not against substance, but against a defect of substance—an evil not imputed because God’s grace regenerates us, restrained because God’s grace assists us, and healed because God’s grace rewards us.

## CHAPTER V

### 10

But perhaps you will say that the baptized fight rather against what they themselves made for themselves through the evil habit of their former life, and not against what they were born with.

Even if you say this, you unquestionably already see and admit that there is something evil in the human being, something from which not the thing itself, but the guilt contracted from it, is removed in Baptism. Yet because this is insufficient to settle the present question unless it is shown to have been implanted in us from the sin of the first human being, listen to what Saint Ambrose says more explicitly about it elsewhere, in his exposition of the Gospel according to Luke.

He was treating, in various ways that nevertheless did not depart from one rule of faith, the passage where the Lord says that in one house three will be divided against two and two against three [Note: [Col. 0680] Am., Er., and the manuscripts read, “three against two, and two against three.”] (Luke XII, 52). He says:

“They may also be understood as flesh and soul, separated from the odor, touch, and taste of luxury, dividing themselves in one house against the vices that assail them, submitting themselves to the law of God and removing themselves from the law of sin. Although their disagreement, through the transgression of the first human being, turned into nature [Note: [Col. 0680] The printed editions read, “turned itself into nature.” Shortly afterward they read, “turned itself into nature,” and below, “turned itself into nature.” On the authority of the manuscripts, we have removed the word ‘itself’ in these places.], so that they no longer agreed with equal zeal for virtue, nevertheless, through the cross of the Lord the Savior [Note: [Col. 0680] The oldest manuscript of Fleury and several others read, “of the Lord who saves”], once both their hostilities and the law of the commandments had been nullified, they came together in harmony of fellowship, after Christ, descending from heaven as our peace, had made the two one” (Eph. II, 14).

Again, in the same work, when speaking of spiritual and incorruptible food, he says:

“For reason is food for the mind [Note: [Col. 0680] Ambrose, Erasmus, and nearly all the manuscripts read, “For the merciful one is food for the mind”], and a splendid nourishment of sweetness, which does not burden the limbs or turn them into the shameful parts of nature [Note: [Col. 0680] In the Fleury manuscript, by a second hand: “nor turn itself into the shameful parts of nature”], but into ornaments, when the den of lust is changed into a temple of God and the dwelling-place of vices begins to be a sanctuary of virtues.

“This indeed happens [Note: [Col. 0680] The corrected Fleury manuscript reads, “comes about.”] when the flesh, restored to its nature, recognizes the nourisher of its strength and, laying aside the boldness of rebellion, is joined to the will of the soul that governs it [Note: [Col. 0680] Ambrose and several manuscripts read, “of the more moderate soul.” Some others read, “of the soul’s moderation.” Erasmus reads, “of the soul that governs.” A number of manuscripts later agree with Ambrose in reading, “is joined to the will.”]—such as it was when it undertook to inhabit the hidden places of paradise, before, infected by the venom of the destructive serpent, it knew sacrilegious hunger and passed over the memory of the divine commandments, fixed in the senses of the soul, through the zeal of its appetite.

“From this, sin is shown to have flowed, as though body and soul were its parents, while the nature of the body is tempted and the soul complies with its ill health [Note: [Col. 0681] The printed editions read, “the unsound [male sana] soul.” The Fleury manuscript, of the highest quality, reads “of the unsound [male sanae]”—that is, of the very nature of the body.]. Had it restrained the body’s appetite, the origin of sin would have been extinguished at its very beginning. But the soul, ill-delivered [male feta], as though this origin had been infused by a virile movement of the body [Note: [Col. 0681] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “virile [virili].”] and with its own vigor also corrupted, brought it to birth as a burden grievous to others [Note: [Col. 0681] Nearly all manuscripts read “softened” [modefacta] in place of “ill-delivered” [male feta].]” (On Luke, Book 7, nos. 141–142).

### 11

Here, certainly, that teacher Ambrose—so excellently praised by the mouth of your teacher—has declared with the utmost clarity and fullness both what original sin was and from where it came, as well as the source of that first confusion, which was the disobedience of the flesh dissenting from the soul. God’s grace heals this discord through Jesus Christ our Lord.

You see from where the flesh desires against the spirit; you see from where there is a law in the members resisting the law of the mind. You see that the discord of soul and flesh turned into nature, and that through these hostilities our miseries abound—miseries that can be ended only by God’s mercy.

Do not oppose me any longer. For if you still do so, you recognize against whom, or against how many, you are opposing yourself at once. You said of me, “Nothing troubles me more than that I should not be understood.” And in certain places you interpret my meaning according to your own judgment, abusing the somewhat slow minds of people who do not understand you, as though you had chosen not to remain silent rather than been able to answer one work of mine with your four volumes.

Behold Ambrose pouring forth a lucid and transparent river of eloquence: there is nowhere for the reader to stumble or the hearer to grow confused. He says with complete clarity that the Apostle said, “Who will deliver me from this body of death?” because we are all born under sin and birth itself is in a state of defect.

He says with complete clarity that the Lord Christ was without sin because, born of a virgin, he was not at all held by the bonds of an accountable generation and of the common nature, and that he condemned sin which he did not experience in being born.

He says most plainly that the disagreement of flesh and soul turned into nature through the transgression of the first human being. He says most plainly that the flesh, the den of lust and the dwelling-place of vices, is then [Note: [Col. 0681] The printed editions read “thus”; the manuscripts, “then.”] changed into a temple of God and a sanctuary of virtues when, restored to its nature, it recognizes the nourisher of its strength and, laying aside the boldness of rebellion, is joined to the will of the soul that governs it—such as it was when it undertook to inhabit the hidden places of paradise, before it had been infected by the venom of the destructive serpent.

What books you might devise against me—do you still ask? Look at him; dare something against him, the one who anticipated the poisons of your heresy before they were born and prepared these antidotes by which they could be driven out. If these are not enough, listen further.

### 12

In his book *On Isaac and the Soul* he says the same:

“A good driver therefore restrains and turns back bad horses, and urges on good ones. The good horses are four: prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice. The bad horses are anger, desire, fear, and iniquity” (Chapter 8).

Does he say, “A good driver has good horses but does not have bad ones”? No; he says, “He urges on the good ones and restrains and turns back the bad ones.”

Where, then, do these horses come from? Certainly, if we call or think of them as substances, we favor or cling to the madness of the Manichaeans. To prevent that from being the case, we understand these horses in the Catholic manner as our vices [Note: [Col. 0682] The Fleury manuscript reads, “our vices, which are…”], which resist the law of the mind through the law of sin.

These vices will not be separated from us and exist somewhere else; rather, once healed in us, they will exist nowhere. Yet why did they not perish in Baptism? Will you not yet admit that their guilt perished while their weakness remained—not the guilt by which they themselves had been guilty, but the guilt by which they had made us guilty in evil works and had drawn us into them?

Their weakness did not remain in such a way that they were some sort of animals subject to weakness; rather, they are our weakness itself.

Nor should we think that by these bad horses he meant that iniquity which is erased in Baptism. That iniquity belonged to the sins we committed; all those sins have been forgiven and now no longer exist at all. Their guilt remained while they were being committed and passing away.

But he called this law of sin—in which the abiding guilt has been forgiven in the sacred font—“iniquity” because it is iniquitous that the flesh should desire against the spirit, although justice is present in our renewal, since it is just that the spirit should desire against the flesh, so that we may walk by the spirit and not fulfill the desires of the flesh.

This justice of ours, accordingly, is found named among the good horses.

### 13

Listen further to what he says in the book he wrote *On Paradise* (Chapters 11 and 12):

“Perhaps,” he says, “Paul said, ‘Things which it is not lawful for a human being to speak’ (2 Cor. XII, 4), because he was still established in the body; that is, he saw the passions of this body and saw the law of his flesh resisting the law of his mind.”

And again, in the same work:

“When he says ‘the serpent was wiser,’ you understand whom he is speaking about: that is, our adversary, who nevertheless possesses the wisdom of this world. But pleasure and delight are also rightly said to be wise, because the wisdom of the flesh is likewise so called, as you have it: ‘Because the wisdom of this flesh is hostile to God’ (Rom. VIII, 7).

“And those who desire pleasures are clever in seeking out varieties of delight. Therefore, whether you understand it as delight, it is something opposed to the divine commandment and hostile to our senses. Hence Saint Paul [Note: [Col. 0682] The manuscripts read, “hence the saint said,” omitting “Paul”] says, ‘I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin’” (Rom. VII, 23).

What sort of pleasure this teacher means here is obvious, since he added the Apostle’s testimony: “I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin.”

This is that pleasure which you have taken under your protection, although you also condemn its excess. You plainly confess what sort it is, but you defend and praise it when moderated with such elaborate ornamentation of words as though it had established this moderation for itself, rather than the spirit, which desires against its assault.

Against this pleasure that man stood firmly who cried, “I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind.” If this impetuous force that resists were let loose, toward what uncleanness would it incline? Into what precipices would it not drag and hurl a person?

But now, what is more immediately relevant is this: not some Jew according to your view, but, according to blessed Ambrose, the Apostle Paul says of himself, “I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin.”

Again, in another passage of the same work, the same teacher says:

“Paul is attacked, and he sees the law of his flesh resisting the law of his mind and taking him captive in the law of sin. He does not presume upon his conscience but trusts through Christ’s grace that he will be delivered from the body of death. And you suppose that anyone who knows cannot sin?

“Paul says, ‘For I do not do the good that I will, but the evil that I do not will, that I do’ (Rom. VII, 19). And you think that knowledge benefits a human being when it increases the reproach of sin?”

Again, in the same work, that same bishop, referring his words to all of us and diligently pleading a common cause, says:

“For the law of the flesh resists the law of the mind, and we must labor and toil to discipline the body and bring it into servitude, and to sow what is spiritual” (Chapters 12 and 15).

### 14

In another of his books, *On the Sacrament of Regeneration*, or *On Philosophy* [Note: [Col. 0683] This work is not extant], he speaks as follows:

“Blessed, therefore, is the death that rescues us from sin in order to restore us to God. For whoever has died has been justified from sin” (Rom. VI, 7).

“Is anyone,” he says, “justified from sin by the end of nature? Certainly not. For the sinner who dies remains in sin. But the one is justified from sin to whom all sins are forgiven through Baptism.”

Do you have anything to say in response to this? Do you see how the venerable man expressly stated that in Baptism a human being undergoes a blessed death, where all sins are forgiven?

But consider something else; consider what you do not wish to consider:

“We have observed,” he says, “what sort of death is mystical. Let us now consider what sort of burial it ought to be. For it is not enough that vices die unless the luxury of the body withers [Note: [Col. 0683] Am., Er., and several manuscripts read “wither” in the plural.], the whole framework of carnal bonds is dissolved, and every knot of bodily usage is loosened.

“Let no one flatter himself because he has assumed another form, received mystical commandments, and applied his mind to the discipline of continence. We do not do what we wish; rather, we do what we hate. Sin accomplishes many things in us. Often, when we resist, revived pleasures rise again. We must struggle against the flesh.

“Paul struggled against it; therefore he says, ‘I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind and taking me captive in the law of sin.’ Are you stronger than Paul?

“Do not trust your flesh as though it were diligent, nor entrust yourself to it, when the Apostle cries out: ‘For I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. For to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find. For I do not do the good that I will, but the evil that I do not will, that I do. But if I do what I do not will, it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me’” (Rom. VII, 23, 18–20). [Col. 0684]

Julian, however much you may be carried away by stubbornness of spirit, however obstinately you may stand against us in defense of the Pelagian error, you are so surrounded by the evident facts presented through blessed Ambrose and so battered by the clarity of his words that, unless reason, reflection, consideration of religion, piety, and humanity, or the truth that ought to be recognized within yourself recalls you from your obstinate determination, you will show how far a person can advance in human evils—to a point at which he does not wish to remain, but from which he is already ashamed to return.

I imagine that this is how you feel when you read these things. But would that the peace of Christ should prevail in your heart, and that good repentance should carry off the victory from evil shame!

## CHAPTER VI

### 15

But now attend for a little while to how, from this law of sin—whose movement mortality compels even those who practice continence to endure, and upon which chastity within marriage struggles to impose a limit, where the desire of the flesh and the pleasure you praise act against the intention of the will, driving forward their impulses when aroused even if they do not carry the act through, and acting when restrained—attend, then, to how Saint Ambrose declares in that very book of his *On the Sacrament of Regeneration*, or *On Philosophy*, that every human being is generated from this law of sin and therefore bears original sin.

“There is,” he says, “a house that wisdom builds, and a table filled with heavenly sacraments, at which the righteous feast upon divine pleasure, drinking the sweet draught of grace, if he rejoices in the abundant posterity of perpetual merits.

“David, begetting these children, dreaded those births through bodily intercourse, and therefore desired to be cleansed by the irrigation of the sacred font, so that spiritual grace might wash away the carnal and earthly stain.

“‘Behold,’ he says, ‘I was conceived in iniquities, and my mother bore me in sins’” (Ps. L, 7).

“Eve gave birth in evil fashion, so that her childbirth might leave women an inheritance, and so that each person, formed from the pleasure of desire, infused into the generative organs, and coagulated in blood, might be wrapped in swaddling clothes and undergo the contagion of sins before he drew in the gift of the life-giving spirit.”

If you have not been abandoned by whatever human sense you possess, however little, you see what this Ambrose—so often proclaimed, as must repeatedly be said, by the testimony of your teacher—has pronounced about the pleasure of desire, the very pleasure for which you provide the most shameless defense.

Each person, he says, is formed from it, infused into the generative organs by it, and coagulated in blood by it; wrapped in swaddling clothes—not, of course, woolen or linen swaddling clothes, or any of the sort in which infants already born are wrapped, but in the swaddling clothes of a corrupted origin, as though in hereditary garments—he undergoes the contagion of sins before he perceives by breathing the air of this life-giving atmosphere.

Into this atmosphere, like an immense fountain of common and unceasing nourishment, the one who is born is poured after the hidden respiration of his mother’s womb, destined at birth to weep for the guilt he contracted before birth.

Would the first human beings, then, not have blushed at this movement of desire, by which they themselves appeared guilty and their children were foretold to be bound by their parents’ sin [Note: [Col. 0685] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “were declared”]?  Would that, just as they blushed to leave bare those parts of the body in which they felt the disobedience of lust, so you, obedient to the Catholic faith, would blush to praise what ought to be blushed at!

### 16

Observe also what that same teacher wrote about the very covering of fig leaves in his book *On Paradise*:

“What is more serious,” he says, “is that Adam girded himself with this interpretation in the place where he ought rather to have girded himself with the fruit of chastity. For in the loins with which we gird ourselves, certain seeds of generation are said to be located. Therefore Adam was wrongly girded there with useless leaves, where he signified not the future fruit of generation but certain sins” (Chapter 13).

Here, certainly, this holy man frustrated your elaborate and excessively anxious argument, by which you sought to prevent anyone from believing that after the sin Adam and Eve girded their loins with their eyes opened (Gen. III, 7).

For in laboring there with such verbosity, you were going against the judgment of everyone and wished to overwhelm them with the clamor of many words [Note: [Col. 0685] In the manuscripts, “with the clamor of much speech.”]. What is more obvious than that the loins of human beings are covered or girded by girdles or aprons—called in Greek *perizōmata* (περιζώματα)—which the common people also call coverings?

Nor did that man of God, whose eloquence we bring against you, explain this as though it were obscure. Rather, he showed what it signified, something everyone understood:

“For in the loins with which we gird ourselves,” he says, “certain seeds of generation are said to be located. Therefore Adam was wrongly girded there with useless leaves.”

Why wrongly? He continues and says: “Where he signified not the future fruit of generation but certain sins.”

Do you have anything to say in response? Behold the source of that confusion; behold the source of the weaving and girding of leaves; behold the source of original sin in their descendants.

### 17

Saint John, bishop of Constantinople, expressed the entire action of the first human beings in their shame, as far as modesty allowed, clearly in two words, saying:

“But they were covered with fig leaves, concealing the appearance of sin.”

To whom is it not apparent what, or what sort of, appearance of sin had to be covered by those ashamed in the region of the loins—those who before sin were not ashamed of the nakedness of their bodies?

I beg you, understand this. Indeed, allow human beings to understand what they understand together with you, and do not compel us to argue any longer, almost shamelessly, about the shameful parts [Note: [Col. 0685] The Fleury manuscript reads “shamelessly” [impudentes].].

### 18

With good reason, that same blessed John, like the martyr Cyprian also (Epistle 64, to Fidus), commends circumcision of the flesh, prescribed as a sign, as representing Baptism.

“And observe,” he says, “how the Jew does not postpone circumcision because of the threat, since ‘every soul that is not circumcised on the eighth day shall be cut off from his people’” (Gen. XVII, [Col. 0686] 14).

“But you,” he says, “postpone the circumcision not made by hands, which is accomplished in the stripping away of the flesh in the body, even though you hear the Lord himself saying: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he shall not enter the kingdom of heaven’” [Note: [Col. 0686] These words are found in Basil, in Homily 13, which is an exhortation to Baptism.] (John III, 5).

“Do you see how a man endowed with ecclesiastical learning compared circumcision with circumcision and threat with threat? Therefore, not being circumcised on the eighth day is the same as not being baptized in Christ; and perishing from one’s people is the same as not entering the kingdom of heaven.

“And yet you deny that in the Baptism of infants the stripping away of the flesh—that is, circumcision not made by hands—is celebrated, because you insist that they have nothing from which they ought to be stripped. For you do not admit that they are dead in the foreskin of their flesh, by which sin is signified, especially the sin that is drawn in through origin. Through this, our body is a body of sin, which the Apostle says is abolished through the cross of Christ” (Rom. VI, 6).

## CHAPTER VII

### 19

But now I have undertaken to press you with the judgments of the bishops who lived before us and faithfully and memorably expounded these divine utterances.

Let us therefore return to Bishop Ambrose. He does not doubt that human beings—that is, both the souls and bodies of human beings—are God’s work; he honors marriage; he proclaims that all sins are forgiven in the Baptism of Christ; he knows that God is just; and he does not deny that human nature is capable of virtue and perfection through God’s grace.

Yet, although you make these your five arguments, insisting that none of them can be true unless it is false that those who are born contract original sin, he nevertheless sets forth precisely what you are trying to remove through these five arguments in his own sermons wherever it is necessary, so that it may be sufficiently clear to anyone what Catholic truth customarily proclaims and what profane novelty endeavors to overthrow.

Will you perhaps also doubt that Ambrose himself knew and taught that God is the creator of human beings, both of soul and of body? Listen, then, to what he says in his book *On Philosophy* against the philosopher Plato, who asserts that human souls are transformed into animals and thinks that God is the author only of souls, while he decides that bodies are made by lesser gods.

Thus Saint Ambrose says:

“I am astonished at so great a philosopher: how can he enclose the soul, to which he attributes the power of conferring immortality, in owls or little frogs, or clothe it even in the wildness of beasts, when in the *Timaeus* he declared it to be God’s work, made by God among immortal things?

“Yet he asserts that the body does not appear to be the work of the supreme God, because the nature of human flesh differs in nothing from the nature of a beast’s body. If, then, it is worthy to be believed to be God’s work, how is it unworthy to be clothed by God’s work?”

Behold: Ambrose defends not only the soul, as even they do, but also the body—which they deny—to be God’s work, against the Platonists.

20. Or are you going to say that he brings accusation against marriage because he says that what is born from it, having been formed through the pleasure of concupiscence, thereby incurs the contagion of sins? Hear, then, Ambrose’s judgment concerning marriage in his *Apology of the Holy David*:

“Marriage is good, a holy union. Yet those who have wives should be as though they had none: the marriage bed itself is undefiled, and no one ought to defraud the other, except perhaps for a time, so that they may devote themselves to prayer (1 Cor. 7:29, 5). Nevertheless, according to the Apostle, a person is not devoted to prayer during the time when he is engaged in that bodily intercourse.” [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “during the time when he engages in that intercourse.” The reading has been emended on the basis of the manuscripts and the Ambrosian edition.] (Chapter 11.)

Hear also what he says in his book *On Philosophy*:

“Continence is good, a kind of pavement of piety. For it sets firm the footsteps of those slipping along the precipices of this life; a diligent watchwoman, lest anything illicit creep in. But intemperance is the mother of all vices, and it turns even what is lawful into vice. Therefore the Apostle withdraws us not only from fornication, but also teaches a certain moderation within marriage itself and prescribes times for prayer” (1 Cor. 7). “For an intemperate husband, what is he other than a kind of adulterer against his wife?”

Do you see how he wishes marriages themselves, which are truly honorable, to be honorable toward one another? [Note: Thus the principal manuscripts; the printed editions read, “true and honorable.”] Do you see how he says that intemperance turns even what is lawful into vice, while showing that marriage is lawful and refusing to allow intemperance within it to defile what is lawful? [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “and does not wish what is lawful to be defiled by intemperance.”] Do you understand how you ought to agree with us about the disease of desire in which the Apostle did not wish each person to possess his own vessel, like the Gentiles who do not know God (1 Thess. 4:4–5)? For you think that sexual desire is blameworthy only when it is directed outside marriage. What, then, will you say about Ambrose, who calls an intemperate husband a kind of adulterer against his wife?

Do you honor marriage better, by giving desire the most unrestrained freedom within it—lest perhaps, offended, it should seek another advocate for itself? For you did not even wish to touch, at least in words, what I mentioned: that the Apostle grants spouses intercourse by way of concession, where guilt is clearly noted, even though it is forgiven. Nor did you dare, in your response, to reopen what I recalled in its entirety: that spouses are admonished to abstain from that act so that they may devote themselves to prayer (1 Cor. 7:6, 5). I believe you feared that your defense would appear to have betrayed its own cause if, even with you acknowledging it, it became evident that the prayer of married people is also obstructed by the desire whose patronage you are not ashamed to undertake.

Thus, although you wished to answer me on its behalf, you did not dare resist the Apostle, and you could not twist the apostolic testimony into another meaning, as you usually do. Therefore you preferred to remain entirely silent about it. Which of you, then, honors marriage better: you, who discolor its dignity as though it were wholly an irreprehensible whirlpool of carnal concupiscence; or he, who says that marriage is not only lawful but good, and that the union is holy, yet, when the pleasure of desire has ceased, recalls the times for prayer prescribed by the Apostle? He does not want spouses to be devoted to that disease from which original sin is drawn. According to the same Apostle, he wishes those who have wives to be as though they had none; and he does not hesitate to call an intemperate husband an adulterer against his wife. He measures all the good of marriage not by the appetite of the flesh but rather by the faithfulness of chastity; not by the disease of passion but by the covenant of union; not by the pleasure of desire but by the will to propagate.

For he declares that woman was instituted for man only for the purpose of procreation. This is why you thought you had to argue at such length, as though anyone were denying our position. These, then, are his words on the matter in his book *On Paradise*:

“If, therefore,” he says, “woman is the cause of guilt for man, how does she appear to have been added for his good? But if you consider that God cares for the whole universe, you will find that what was the cause of the universe ought to have pleased the Lord more than what was the cause of sin ought to have been condemned.” [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads, “than what was the cause of sin ought not to have been founded.”]

“Therefore, because the propagation of the human race could not proceed from the man alone, the Lord declared that it was not good for man to be alone (Gen. 2:18). For God preferred that there should be more people whom he could save and to whom he could give forgiveness of sins, rather than one Adam alone who would be free from guilt. Finally, because he is the author of both works,” he says, “he came into this world to save sinners. Indeed, he did not allow Cain, guilty of fratricide, to perish before he had begotten sons. Therefore,” he says, “woman had to be added to man for the propagation of the human succession.” (Chapter 10.)

21. Behold, then, my teacher Ambrose—whom you have notably praised [Note: Earlier printed editions read, “wonderfully.”]—confessing and even defending that every human being and the flesh of every human being are God’s work, and that marriage is good insofar as it is marriage. Moreover, I have already demonstrated above that original sin detracts nothing from holy Baptism, when I quoted his words in which he says that “the person whose sins are all forgiven through Baptism is justified from sin” (above, no. 14). “And where does he not proclaim God to be just? Or what Catholic Christian can doubt this, when nearly all the impious also confess it?”

**CHAPTER VIII**

22. The fifth question remains: whether Ambrose considers human nature capable of justification and perfection, and whether he is thereby deterred from this position because he often and in many ways says that every human being is born under sin and that his very origin is in vice. But I have already taught this above, where I recalled that, shortly afterward in the same passage, he said that “sin was condemned by Christ’s flesh: sin which he did not experience in being born, which he crucified in dying, so that in our flesh there might be justification through grace, where previously there had been defilement through guilt” (ibid., no. 5).

There he demonstrated that human nature—even this nature, which is born under sin and whose origin is in vice—is capable of justification, but certainly through grace. That is what is hostile to you, cruel enemies of that same grace. But if this is insufficient, attend again to what he says in his *Exposition of the Prophet Isaiah*:

“Let us see,” he says, “whether after the course of this life there is to be our regeneration, of which it is said, ‘In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his glory’” (Matt. 19:28). “For just as regeneration is spoken of in connection with the washing by which we are renewed after the defilement of sins has been cleansed away, so regeneration seems to be spoken of in connection with that by which, purified from every stain of bodily composition, we are regenerated to eternal life with a pure understanding of the soul.”

The holy and truthful man clearly distinguished the justification of this life, which takes place through the washing of regeneration, from that perfection of the other life, when our bodies too shall have been renewed through immortality. Ambrose, therefore, though he confessed the vice of our inherited origin, did not despair of the perfection of justification. For just as human nature is capable of being formed by God the Creator, so it is capable of being healed by the Redeemer.

23. But you hasten, and by hastening precipitate your presumption. Here you wish the human being to be perfected—and would that it were by God’s gift, rather than by the free, or rather enslaved, choice of his own will. You indeed recognize that you are far from this perfection; but deceit is in your mouth, whether you call yourselves sinners while wishing to be considered just, or whether you profess the perfection of justice, which you certainly do not perceive to exist in yourselves.

Justification in this life is granted to us in three ways: first, through the washing of regeneration, by which all sins are forgiven; next, through the struggle with vices, from whose guilt we have been absolved; and third, when our prayer is heard, in which we say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12). For however courageously we may fight against vices, we are human beings. Yet God’s grace assists us as we fight in this corruptible body, so that there is always a reason for him to hear us when we ask forgiveness.

You do not think that this mercy of God toward us is necessary, because you belong to the number of those about whom it is said in the Psalm, “Those who trust in their own strength” (Ps. 48:7). But how much better do we hear Ambrose, who confesses God’s grace and does not trust in his own strength, saying in his book *On the Flight from the World*:

“We often speak of fleeing this world; and would that our affection were as cautious and concerned as our speech is easy. But what is worse, the enticement of earthly desires frequently creeps in, and the obscurity of vanities occupies the mind, so that we think about and turn over in our minds precisely what we strive to avoid. It is difficult for a human being to guard against this, but impossible to cast it off entirely. Finally, the prophet testifies that this is more a matter of prayer than of achievement, saying, ‘Incline my heart to your testimonies, and not to covetousness’” (Ps. 118:36).

“For our heart and our thoughts are not in our own power. Unexpectedly obscured, they confuse the mind and spirit and draw them elsewhere than you have resolved. They call us back to secular things, insert worldly things, thrust pleasurable things upon us, weave in enticing things; and at the very time when we prepare to lift up our minds, we are often cast down to earthly things by the insertion of empty thoughts.” (Chapter 1.)

If you do not suffer these things, forgive us: we do not believe you. Rather, in these words of holy Ambrose we recognize a kind of mirror—and, if we are making progress, we recognize the common weakness of humanity. But even if we believe you and say, “Pray for us, so that we too may not suffer these things,” we find you so puffed up and so wise in lofty matters that you answer us not only that you do not suffer these things, but that it lies within human power not to suffer them, and that there is no reason to ask God’s help for this.

24. How much better, then, do we repeatedly hear Ambrose confessing God’s grace and not trusting in his own strength. After saying these things, he added:

“Who is so blessed that he always ascends in his heart? But how can this happen without divine assistance? Certainly, in no way. Finally,” he says, “the same Scripture above says: ‘Blessed is the man whose help is from you, O Lord; in his heart are ascents’” (Ps. 83:6).

Likewise, in his book *On the Sacrament of Regeneration*:

“Who is it,” he says, “who uses the flesh for action, except the soul? Therefore, naturally the soul is the ruler and mistress of the flesh; it must subdue and govern the flesh. Thus, supported by the assistance of the Holy Spirit, it says in the Psalm, ‘I will not fear what flesh can do to me’” (Ps. 55:5). “The same soul says in Paul, ‘I chastise my body and bring it into subjection’” (1 Cor. 9:27). “Paul therefore chastises what belongs to him, not what he himself is. For what belongs to him is one thing, and what he himself is is another. He chastises what belongs to him, so that the just person may bring about in himself the death of bodily wantonness.”

When holy Ambrose said these things, was he not struggling with vices? Was he not overcoming vices? Was he not, as an outstanding soldier of Christ, doing battle within himself against an army of varied desires? Was he not chastising his own body? When the works of the devil had been overcome and attacked, was not God’s work—namely, the soul—seeking the peace of justice with God’s work, namely, the flesh, so that, not trusting in its own strength, but, as he says, “supported by the assistance of the Holy Spirit,” it might say, “I will not fear what flesh can do to me”?

Behold how human nature is shown to be capable of justification; behold how power is made perfect in weakness (2 Cor. 12:9).

25. But let us hear on this matter also the most victorious martyr Cyprian in his letter *On Mortality*:

“We are engaged,” he says, “in a struggle with avarice, with impurity, with anger, with ambition; with carnal vices and worldly enticements there is a continual and burdensome contest. The human mind, besieged and surrounded on every side by the devil’s attacks, scarcely confronts each one and scarcely resists. If avarice has been overthrown, lust rises up; if lust has been restrained, ambition follows; if ambition has been despised, anger exasperates and inflates pride; [Note: Lovaniensis reads, “presses hard.” Yet above, in *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book 4, no. 27, as in other books, the reading is “inflates.”] drunkenness entices; envy breaks harmony; jealousy cuts off friendship. You are compelled to curse, which the divine law forbids; you are driven to swear, which is not permitted. The soul suffers so many persecutions every day, the heart is pressed by so many dangers, and yet it is delightful to stand for a long time amid the devil’s swords, when it ought rather to be desired and sought that, with death coming swiftly to our aid, we may hasten to Christ.”

Far be it from us to think that holy Cyprian was avaricious because he struggled with avarice; or impure because he struggled with impurity; or subject to anger because he struggled with anger; or ambitious because he struggled with ambition; or carnal because he struggled with carnal vices; or a lover of this world because he struggled with worldly enticements; or lustful because he struggled with lust; or proud because he struggled with pride; or drunk because he struggled with drunkenness; or envious because he struggled with envy.

Rather, he was none of these precisely because he firmly resisted these evil impulses, which arose partly from our origin and partly from habit, and did not consent to be what they compelled him to be. Yet even in so dangerous and laborious a contest he was not struck by no hostile weapon, since he says in his letter *On Almsgiving*:

“Let no one flatter himself so on the purity and undefiled state of his heart that, relying on his innocence, he thinks no medicine ought to be applied to wounds, since it is written, ‘Who can boast that he has a pure heart? Or who can boast that he is clean from sins?’” (Prov. 20:9).

“And again,” he says, “in his letter John sets forth and says, ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us’” (1 John 1:8). “But if no one can be without sin, and whoever says that he is blameless is either proud or foolish, how necessary and how kind is the divine mercy, which, knowing that certain wounds remain afterward even in those who have been healed, has provided salutary remedies for wounds to be treated and healed again!”

O most illustrious teacher and most glorious witness, thus you taught, thus you admonished, thus you offered yourself to be heard and imitated. [Note: Nearly all manuscripts read “thus you shone forth” (*eminuisti*) in place of “thus you admonished.” The Ambrosian and Erasmus editions print both: “thus you shone forth, or admonished.”] Rightly, after the other struggles with all the desires had ended and the wounds had been healed, you fought for the truth of Christ against the final and greatest desire of this life, and by the abundance of his grace within you, you conquered. Secure is your crown; victorious is your teaching, by which you also conquer those who trust in their own strength. They themselves cry out, “The perfection of virtue comes from us.” But you reply, “No one is strong by his own powers; he is safe through God’s indulgence and mercy.”

26. Hear also the blessed Hilary, concerning where he places the perfection of humanity. When he was speaking about evangelical peace (*On Psalm 118*, on verses 18 and 155), where the Lord says, “My peace I give you” (John 14:27), he says:

“Because the law was a shadow of future goods, by this prefigured sign [Note: Erasmus and Lovaniensis read “signification”; the Ambrosian edition and manuscripts read “significance.”] it taught us that in this dwelling-place of an earthly and mortal body we cannot be clean unless we obtain cleansing through the washing of heavenly mercy, after the transformation of our earthly body at the resurrection has produced a more glorious nature.”

Again, in the same sermon:

“Even though the Apostles had already been cleansed and sanctified by the word of faith, he taught that malice nevertheless remained in them, through the condition of our common origin, saying, ‘Although you are evil, you know how to give good gifts to your children’” (Matt. 7:11).

Do you see how this venerable Catholic teacher does not deny our cleansing even in this life, and yet hopes for a more perfect human nature—that is, the nature of a more perfect cleansing—in the final resurrection?

27. In a certain homily on the book of holy Job [Note: This homily does not survive], observe what he says and how he asserts that the devil’s unceasing warfare against us arises from the fact that he stirs up against us the evils that are in us. He wishes to teach that this is turned to our advantage, since divine mercy turns the devil’s wickedness toward our purification.

“For so great and so wonderful,” he says, “is the goodness of God’s mercy toward us that, through the one by whose envy we lost the nobility of that first and blessed creation in Adam’s offense, we may again deserve to obtain what we lost. Then the devil, in his envy, inflicted harm [Note: The Floriacensis codex reads, “in his envy, conquered.”]; now, when he strives to inflict harm, he is defeated. He moves all the weapons of his power through the weakness of our flesh: when he inflames us to wantonness, when he entices us to drunkenness, when he spurs us to hatred, when he provokes us to avarice, when he prepares us for murder, when he exasperates us to curses. But when, through the firmness of the spirit, the incitements of all these things as they creep in are restrained, we are cleansed from sin through the glory of this victory. For it is said, ‘Or how shall one born of woman be cleansed?’” (Job 25:4).

“For if there were no enemy, there would be no war; and when the war has ceased, there will be no victory. But if victory has not been obtained over the vices that collide against us, there will be no cleansing from vices. For when the pirate of our body has been conquered through these ambushes, we are purified by the contest of the passions struggling against us.” [Note: Three of the five Vatican manuscripts read, “we are purified by the exercise of the passions.”]

“Therefore,” he says, “remembering and recognizing that our very bodies are the material of all vices, through which [Note: Four Vatican manuscripts, together with the Floriacensis manuscript corrected by a second hand, read “through which”; the printed editions read “for which.”] we are polluted and filthy and possess nothing clean, nothing innocent within us, let us rejoice that we have an enemy with whom, in the contest of our own struggle, we may do battle.”

28. In his *Exposition of the First Psalm*, the same teacher does not hesitate to say that our nature—certainly this nature which draws disease from disease—is carried toward sinning, and that, so that we may not sin, we fight against it in a certain way through the religious discipline of faith.

“For there are many,” he says, “who, although separated from impiety through the confession of God, are nevertheless not thereby free from sin, because they do not observe the discipline of the Church: avaricious, drunken, disorderly, insolent, proud, hypocritical” [Note: In Ambrose and Erasmus, instead of “hypocritical,” the reading is “emulous”], “liars, rapacious.”

“And indeed,” he says, “the impulse of our nature drives us toward these vices. But it is useful for us to withdraw from the road toward which we are carried, and not to remain there, applying ourselves without delay to departing from it and turning back. Therefore, ‘Blessed is the man who has not stood in the way of sinners’: nature carries him along this road, but the religious discipline of faith brings him back from it.” (On verse 1.)

Shall we suppose that he was accusing the nature that God created? Certainly not. This Catholic man did not doubt that human nature was God’s work; rather, he accused the vices with which we are born, holding to the apostolic statement: “For we too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3).

Yet if these words I have quoted from Saint Hilary were mine, what would you say against me? With what clamorous noise would you parade the name and charge of the Manichaeans? Now, therefore, lest the bellows of your stomach burst from the undigested crudity of your curses, vomit your slanderous vanities and lying insanities against him, if you dare.

“The impulse of our nature,” he says, “drives us toward these vices.” What nature is this? Is it perhaps the race of darkness introduced by the Manichaean fable? Far from it. A Catholic is speaking; an eminent teacher of the Churches is speaking; Hilary is speaking. It is, then, our nature, corrupted by the transgression of the first human being—not to be separated from any other nature by some division, but itself to be healed. You accuse us of making the devil its author, while you begrudge Christ his role as Savior and insist that his life could be lived here in perfection, entirely without any sin.

29. But hear what the blessed Hilary also teaches you on this subject. When he was expounding the fifty-first Psalm (near the end), he says:

“Hope in the mercy of God is forever and ever. For those very works of justice are not sufficient for the merit of perfect blessedness unless the mercy of God, even in this desire for justice, does not reckon the vices of human changes and movements. Hence the prophet says, ‘Your mercy is better than lives’” [Note: The manuscripts read “lives”; the printed editions read “life.”] (Ps. 62:4).
