Do you see that this man of God belongs to the number of the blessed about whom it was foretold: “Blessed is the man to whom the Lord has not reckoned sin, and there is no deceit in his mouth” (Ps. 31:2)? For he confesses even the sins of the just, asserting that they place their hope in God’s mercy rather than trusting in their own justice. Therefore there is no deceit in his mouth—or rather, in the mouth of all those to whom he bears witness by this truthful humility, or humble truth.

Deceit abounds in your mouth. For where virtue is absent and boastfulness is so great, there is hypocrisy; and where there is hypocrisy, there is certainly deceit. Precisely to the extent that the saints presume upon the mercy of God, which is great, you presume upon your own virtue, which is nonexistent. To the extent that they, assisted by God’s grace, wage war against the vices implanted within them, you wage war against the grace of God itself. Would that, just as it conquers you in its own people, so, by making you its own, it might conquer you in yourselves also.

30. Do you dare to say in your hearts that when people hear you, they are inflamed toward virtue, but when they hear such great and such men as Cyprian, Hilary, Gregory, Ambrose, and the other priests of the Lord, they are crushed by despair and renounce their pursuit of perfection? Do such monstrous thoughts rise into your hearts, and do they not strike your foreheads with shame?

Do you honor the saints of God—Patriarchs, Prophets, and Apostles—by praising nature, while these lights of the Church dishonor them by censuring nature, because they say that, while in this body of death, they fought against the innate evil of concupiscence in order to preserve the good of chastity—an evil that must first be overcome through struggle by God’s grace and afterward healed in the final regeneration?

You understand that it was a Jew who said, “For I do not do the good that I want” (Rom. 7:19). Yet, with this splendid understanding, you neither cast the stains of conduct back as a reproach against nature, nor console yourself for their obscenities by insulting the Apostles and all the saints. And these evils, which you do not commit, Ambrose committed together with his colleagues who held the same view, since he understands the blessed Apostle to have said of himself, “I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want, this I do”; and, “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind” (Rom. 7:19, 23); and other statements of this kind.

Thus, by teaching such things, do these saints—as you charge me—undermine the wall of modesty, while you suffer envy because of your preaching of perfection? Yet, as you write, you console yourself greatly because it is a kind of praise to have displeased one who did not spare the Apostles. If I did not spare the Apostles by saying such things, then Ambrose too did not spare the Apostles, nor did his fellow bishops who held the same view. But if they learned these things from the Apostles and taught them according to the Apostles, why do you attack me alone? Look at them; look again and again at them, laying aside for a little the swelling of your neck.

At last, then, should you console yourself because you displease such men, most confident young man—or should you mourn?

**CHAPTER IX**

31. But let us now gather briefly, as best we can, what we have done throughout this entire book. We proposed to shatter, by the weight of the authority of the saints who were bishops before us and who vigorously defended the Catholic faith—not only by their speech while they lived here but also in writings left to posterity—your arguments, by which you say:

If God creates human beings, they cannot be born with any evil.

If marriage is good, nothing evil arises from it.

If all sins are forgiven in Baptism, those born from the baptized cannot inherit original sin.

If God is just, he cannot condemn the sins of parents in their children, when he forgives the parents their own sins.

If human nature is capable of perfect justice, it cannot possess natural vices.

To this we reply that God is the creator of human beings—that is, of both soul and body; that marriage is good; that through the Baptism of Christ all sins are forgiven; that God is just; and that human nature is capable of perfect justice. Yet, although all these things are true, human beings are born subject to a corrupted origin inherited from the first human being, and therefore go into condemnation unless they are reborn in Christ.

We proved this by the authority of Catholic saints, who both assert what we say about original sin and confess that all five of those propositions are true. Consequently, it does not follow that our position is false because those propositions are true. Such great and such men, according to the Catholic faith spread throughout the whole world from ancient times, affirm both this and those propositions to be true, so that your fragile and somewhat clever novelty is crushed by their sole authority—apart from the fact that they state these things in such a way that truth itself bears witness to speaking through them.

But now your obstinacy must first be restrained by their authority, so that, checked and in a sense wounded by the onset of your presumption, because you do not believe that such men of God could have erred in the Catholic faith to the point of saying anything from which it would follow that God is not the creator of human beings, that marriage should be condemned, that not all sins are forgiven in Baptism, that God is unjust, or that no hope remains for us of perfecting virtue—for it is impious to think any of these things, or even one of them—you may rein in your headlong daring and, as though recovering from madness, begin to recall, consider, and recover the truth in which you were nourished.

32. Blessed Ambrose says that there is one mediator between God and human beings, because he was born from a virgin and did not experience sin in being born, and therefore was not held by the bonds of an indebted generation. But all other human beings are born under sin, and their very origin is in vice, because, formed through the pleasure of concupiscence, they incur the contagion of sins before they draw the breath of life from this air.

He also says that concupiscence itself, like the law of sin in this body of death, so resists the law of the mind that not only all good believers but even the greatness of apostolic virtue has fought against it, so that through Christ’s grace the flesh, subjected to the soul, might be restored to harmony. For these two, which were originally created without sin, were made discordant by the transgression of the first human being.

And who says these things? A man of God, a Catholic, a most ardent defender of Catholic truth against heretics, even to the danger of shedding his blood—praised in the testimony of your own teacher in such a way that it was said that not even an enemy dared criticize his faith or his most pure understanding of the Scriptures.

He asserted, against the error proclaimed by the philosophers of Plato, that God is the creator not only of souls but also of bodies. He proclaimed that the good of marriage was divinely instituted for the propagation of the human race and that its union was made holy by conjugal chastity. He said that no one is justified from sin unless all sins have been forgiven through Baptism. He worshiped the just God as just.

Far from obstructing the perfection of human beings through despair, he hoped for perfection in virtue and justice. Yet he hoped for the perfection to which nothing can be added in another life, which will be fulfilled in the resurrection of the dead. In this life, however, he placed human justice in a kind of military service and warfare, not only against the hostile powers of the air but also against our own desires, through which those external enemies attempt to overthrow or enter us.

In this warfare he says that the flesh itself is a grievous adversary. Its nature would certainly remain in complete harmony with us, as it was created in the beginning, unless, corrupted by the transgression of the first human being, it struggled against us through its own sickness.

In this warfare that holy man urges us to flee the world, and shows how great the difficulty—or rather the impossibility—of that flight is unless God’s grace comes to our aid. He says that vices are dead through the forgiveness of all sins in Baptism, but that we must nevertheless, in a certain way, care for their burial.

In this very work he describes our struggle with dead vices in such a way that we do not do what we want, but do what we hate; that sin often works within us while we resist; that pleasures frequently rise again after having been revived; and that we must struggle against the flesh, against which Paul struggled when he said, “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind.”

He commands us not to trust in our flesh, not to believe in it, when the Apostle cries out, “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh; for to will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find” (Rom. 7:23, 18).

Behold how great a struggle with dead sins that vigorous soldier of Christ and faithful teacher of the Church shows us to have. For how is sin dead when it does many things within us while we resist? What are these many things, except foolish and harmful desires, which plunge those who consent to them into ruin and destruction (1 Tim. 6:9)? To endure these desires and not consent to them is certainly a contest, a conflict, a battle.

Whose battle is it, if not that of good against evil—not of nature against nature, but of nature against vice, already dead but still requiring burial, that is, complete healing?

How, then, do we call this sin dead in Baptism, as this man also does, and how do we confess that it dwells in our members and works many desires while we resist, resisting them by not consenting to them, as this man also confesses? We do so because it is dead with respect to the guilt by which it held us captive, yet, until it is healed through the perfection of burial, it rebels while dead.

Although it is no longer called sin in the sense in which it makes a person guilty, it has become so through the guilt of the first human being, and by rebelling it strives to drag us into guilt, unless the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord assists us. Thus even dead sin may not rebel in such a way that, by conquering, it comes to life again and reigns.

**CHAPTER X**

33. While we labor in this warfare, as long as human life is a time of temptation upon the earth (Job 7:1), we are not therefore without sin simply because what is called sin in this sense works in our members, resisting the law of the mind, even when we do not consent to what is unlawful. For, as far as we are concerned, we would always be without sin until this evil had been healed if we never consented to it for evil.

But in those matters in which we are overcome by that rebellion—though not mortally, yet venially—we contract the condition that makes us say every day, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12). This happens with married people when, for the sake of pleasure alone, they exceed the measure necessary for procreation; and with continent people when they linger with some pleasure in such thoughts, not indeed deciding upon a disgraceful act, but failing to turn the mind away from them as it should, or, if the mind has fallen into them, failing to snatch it away.

To this law of sin—which is also called sin in another sense and which resists the law of the mind, about which blessed Ambrose said much—there also bear witness the saints Cyprian, Hilary, Gregory, and very many others.

Therefore, whoever is born in Adam and must be reborn in Christ, dead in Adam and to be made alive in Christ, is bound by the sin of his origin because he is born from that evil by which the flesh desires against the spirit, not from that good by which the spirit desires against the flesh (Gal. 5:17).

What wonder, then, if a human being born from that evil must be reborn, since the reborn human being struggles against it and would himself remain held by its guilt unless he were liberated by rebirth?

This evil is not the material of God’s creative work, but the wound inflicted by the devil upon that same material. It is not the evil of marriage, but the sin of the first human beings transmitted to their descendants through propagation.

The guilt of this evil too is forgiven through the sanctification of Baptism. But if the just God were to inflict upon infants evils as great as those I cannot now fully describe, when they had drawn no sin from anywhere, he would appear all the more unjust.

Humanity’s perfect capacity for justice is not denied, because the fullest healing from all vices is not despaired of under the omnipotent physician.

For the sake of this Catholic truth, the holy and blessed priests, most eminent in their treatment of the divine Scriptures— Irenaeus, Cyprian, Reticius, Olympius, Hilary, Ambrose, Gregory, Innocent, John, Basil, and, whether you wish it or not, the presbyter Jerome, to say nothing of those who have not yet fallen asleep—bring forward against you their judgment concerning the original sin inherited by the succession of all human beings. No one is rescued from it except the one whom the virgin conceived without the law of sin resisting the law of the mind.

34. Why do you exult and insult me as though you were victorious [Note: [Col. 0697] American, Erasmus, and most manuscripts read: “and insult me, if we were standing before judges, as though you were victorious.”], as though I would not find something to do, some refuge to which I could flee, if I were pressed by the authority of judges, if I were standing with you among learned men, if the trumpet of the true reason which you claim—blown, of course, by you, that great trumpeter—were sounding, and if the weapons of the surrounding audience, favoring you, were resounding? For this is how you place before your eyes our contest in debate: you imagine me, while you argue, having no answer to give, just as it pleases you. Thus the empty and insane imagination of your heart converses with you, as though you were setting me with you before Pelagian judges, who applaud you and permit you to raise your voice like a trumpet and proclaim against the Catholic faith and against the grace of Christ—by which little ones together with adults are delivered from evil—the common error of this recent impiety, shared by you and by them.

Such judges your teacher Pelagius could not find in the Church of God without an adversary standing on the other side. From that judgment he indeed emerged, so far as the view of men was concerned, seemingly acquitted, yet with his doctrine openly condemned by your own party. But I, wherever you may be, wherever you may be able to read this, set you inwardly in your heart before those judges. I do not constitute as your judges men who are my friends and your enemies, who incline toward my side through some favor, who have been alienated from you because of some offense they received from you, and who are therefore opposed to you in this dispute.

Nor have I fabricated in empty thought judges who never existed, or who no longer exist, or whose opinions on the matter under dispute between us are uncertain. Rather, I have expressly named, as was necessary, holy bishops of God, illustrious in the holy Church—not men instructed by Plato, Aristotle, Zeno, or others of that kind, whether Greek or Latin, although some of those bishops were Greek, but all of them instructed in the Sacred Scriptures. I have set forth their opinions, as seemed sufficient, published without any ambiguity, so that in them you may fear not the men themselves, but the One who fashioned them as useful vessels for himself and built them as holy temples.

They judged on this matter at a time when no one can say that they could improperly have opposed or favored anyone. You had not yet come into existence, against whom we might undertake a conflict concerning this question. You did not yet exist to say what you set down in your books: “Because we have lied about you to the multitude”; and that “we frighten people by the name of Coelestians or Pelagians”; and that “by terror we extort assent from people” [Note: [Col. 0698] The manuscripts read thus. The printed editions, however, read: “from everyone.”]. Certainly you yourself said that all judges ought to be free from hatred, friendship, enmity, and anger.

Few such judges could be found; but Ambrose and his colleagues, whom I mentioned together with him, must be believed to have been such. Yet even if they were not such in those cases which, when they were alive, had been brought before them and known to the parties and which they settled by their judgment, they were such in this matter when they delivered their opinions about it. They showed no regard for friendship with us or with you, nor exercised enmity; they were angry neither with us nor with you, nor did they pity either us or you. What they found in the Church, they held; what they learned, they taught; what they received from their fathers, they handed on to their children.

We were not yet conducting anything with you before those judges, yet our case was conducted before them. Neither we nor you had been known to them, yet we recite their judgments, delivered on our behalf against you. We were not yet contending with you, yet when they pronounced judgment, we prevailed. [Note: [Col. 0698] Lovaniensis reads: “we prevail.”]

35. You say that if I were “pressed under the authority of judges”—of the sort you yourself imagine—I would have had nothing to do and nowhere to flee, since I could not find a way to meet your arguments. I certainly would have had something to do; I certainly would have had somewhere to flee. For I would appeal from the darkness of the Pelagians to these brilliant Catholic lights—and that is what I am doing now.

You, then, answer: what will you do? Say where you will flee. I flee from the Pelagians to these men; from these men, where will you flee? Or because you think that “opinions should not be counted but weighed,” and you add—and I too agree that this is true—that “a multitude of blind men contributes nothing toward discovering something,” will you dare to call these men blind as well?

Has the long day so thoroughly mingled the depths with the heights [Note: [Col. 0698] These are words of Lucan, *Pharsalia* 3.138–139.], has darkness so thoroughly been called light and light darkness, that Pelagius, Coelestius, and Julian are men of sight, while Hilary, Gregory, and Ambrose are blind? Yet whatever sort of man you are, since you are nevertheless a man, I seem to see your embarrassment—if, at least, all hope of recovery has not died within you—and in a certain way I hear your voice. You answer: “Far be it from me to dare even to think or say that these men are blind.”

Then weigh their opinions. I do not want them to be numerous, lest you be reluctant to count them; but they are not insignificant, so that you would disdain to weigh them. Indeed, they are so weighty that I see you struggling beneath their burden. Will you also say of these men that I “oppose to you the feeble opinion of a partner, and, as though panic-stricken with fear, name my associates” [Note: [Col. 0699] Two manuscripts read: “associates” rather than “conscious witnesses.”]?

36. You say that “in a case to be judged, once the clamor of the crowds has been removed, concerning every rank of human life—whether priests, administrators, or prefects” [Note: [Col. 0699] All Vatican manuscripts and most Gallican manuscripts read: “private persons.” The editions of American and Erasmus, together with certain other Gallican manuscripts, read: “transgressors.”—“for the examination of such matters, not names alone but prudence must be selected, and the minority honored which reason, learning, and freedom exalt.”

That is indeed as you say. But neither am I troubling you with the numerical strength of any multitude, although, by God’s favor, even the Catholic multitude soundly understands this faith which you oppose. In it, very many people everywhere, wherever and however they can, as they are divinely enabled, refute your empty arguments [Note: [Col. 0699] The Floriacensis manuscript reads: “confound.”].

Therefore, far be from me the arrogance you charge against me: “that I would promise to conduct this case against you, one man for all.” Yet when you do this among the Pelagians, without blushing to say and write that “it is a greater glory for you before God to defend the truth when it has been abandoned,” then those people are greatly abject and truly abandoned, and they depend greatly upon you [Note: [Col. 0699] American, Erasmus, and Belgian manuscripts, together with the Gallican manuscript of Pratellum, read: “are greatly to be marveled at.”], if they do not judge this intolerable arrogance—by which you place yourself even before Pelagius and Coelestius, the teachers of all of you—as though they had already withdrawn and you alone had remained to defend what you consider the truth.

But since you take pleasure not in counting the multitude but in weighing the minority, apart from the Palestinian judges who condemned your heresy in Pelagius, once he had been compelled by fear to condemn the very doctrines of the Pelagians, I have set before you as judges of this case ten bishops who are now dead and one presbyter, who judged this matter while they were alive. If the smallness of your party is considered, they are many; if the multitude of Catholic bishops is considered, they are very few.

Perhaps you will try to remove from their number Pope Innocent and the presbyter Jerome: the former because he condemned Pelagius and Coelestius; the latter because in the East he defended the Catholic faith against Pelagius with pious intention. But read what Pelagius says in praise of the most blessed Pope Innocent [Note: [Col. 0699] In his Profession of Faith addressed to Innocent, Pelagius says: “We desire to be corrected by you, who hold both the faith and the see of Peter.” This is presented below, in the second part of the Appendix.], and see whether you can easily find judges of such a kind.

As for that holy presbyter, who according to the grace given to him labored in the Church so that he greatly assisted Catholic learning in the Latin language through many necessary writings [Col. 0700], Pelagius is not accustomed to boast of him except by saying that he “envied him as a rival.” But I do not want you to think that he should therefore be removed from the number of these judges. For I did not set forth the opinion he held and defended against your error during the time of their enmity, but the opinion he expressed in his writings, free from all party zeal, before your condemnable doctrines had begun to sprout.

37. As for the rest, you have absolutely nothing to say. Were Irenaeus, Cyprian, Reticius, Olympius, Hilary, Gregory, Basil, Ambrose, and John “roused from the plebeian dregs of bench-dwellers,” as you jest in Ciceronian fashion, “to arouse hostility against you”? Were they “soldiers”? Were they “schoolroom students”? Were they “sailors, tavern-keepers, fishmongers, cooks, butchers”? Were they “young men corrupted from among the monks”? Finally, are they “from the crowd of clerics of whatever sort”—those whom you contemptuously dismiss, harried by urban wit, or rather by vanity, “because they cannot judge doctrines according to Aristotle’s Categories”?

As though you, who complain most loudly “that examination and episcopal judgment are being denied you,” could find a council of Peripatetics where a dialectical judgment might be pronounced against original sin concerning substance and the things that exist in a substance.

These are bishops: learned, serious, holy, and most vigorous defenders of the truth against babbling vanities. In their reason, learning, and freedom—the three goods which you attributed to a judge [Note: [Col. 0700] Some manuscripts read: “the good.”]—you cannot find anything to despise. If an episcopal synod were assembled from the whole world, it would be remarkable if so many men of this kind could easily sit there.

For these men did not all live at one time. Rather, God himself distributes his faithful and greatly distinguished stewards throughout the varying ages and distances of times and places, as he wills and judges expedient. Thus you see these men gathered from different periods and regions, from East and West—not into a place to which people must sail, but into a book that can sail to people.

The more desirable these judges would be to you if you held the Catholic faith, the more terrifying they are to you because you attack the Catholic faith. They drank it in as milk; they received it as food; its milk and food they supplied to little ones and adults; and against its enemies—including you, who were not yet born at that time, but by which you are now exposed [Note: [Col. 0700] Three of five Vatican manuscripts read: “refuted.” Two others read: “rebel.”]—they defended it with the utmost clarity and courage.

Through such planters, waterers, builders, shepherds, and nourishers after the Apostles, the holy Church grew. Therefore it was terrified by the profane voices of your novelty; and, cautious and sober in accordance with the apostolic warning—“lest, as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your mind should be corrupted from the purity that is in Christ” (2 Cor. 11:3)—it recoiled from the ambushes of your doctrine as it stealthily crept in against the virginity of the Catholic faith [Note: [Col. 0700] American and the manuscripts read: “of the Catholic faith.” Erasmus and Lovaniensis read: “to the Catholic faith.”]. Like the head of a serpent, it trampled, crushed, and cast it away.

By these words and by so great an authority of the saints [Col. 0701], surely you will either be healed, if God in his mercy grants it—he who sees how greatly I desire this for you—or, if what I abhor should happen, you will persist in the same wisdom that seems to you wisdom but is great folly. Then you will not be seeking judges before whom you may clear your case, but judges before whom you may accuse so many holy, learned, distinguished, and memorable teachers of Catholic truth: Irenaeus, Cyprian, Reticius, Olympius, Hilary, Gregory, Basil, Ambrose, John, Innocent, Jerome [Col. 0702], and all their companions and associates, as well as the whole Church of Christ, in which they shone with great glory in the Lord as they faithfully supplied the household of God with its provisions.

Against this miserable madness—which may God avert from you—I see that my books must answer your books in such a way that the faith also must be defended against you through these men, just as the Gospel itself is defended against the impious, even against those who profess Christ while being his enemies.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0701]

Julian must next be refuted with such method and care that each of his four books receives a separate response in an equal number of books. In this third book, therefore, Augustine first refutes Julian’s first book, aiming to make it clear that, although God is the true and good creator of human beings, and marriage is good and was instituted by him, concupiscence is nevertheless evil—the concupiscence by which the flesh desires against the spirit.

Chastity makes good use of this evil, while continence makes better use of not using it. This evil, however, is not mixed into us from another substance that God did not create, as Manichaeus raves; rather, it arose and was transmitted through Adam’s disobedience, and must be cleansed and healed through Christ’s obedience. The obligation of this evil binds the one who is born to a deserved punishment, while undeserved grace releases the one who is reborn.

Julian’s own statements also show that lust is evil: for he acknowledges remedies against it, wishes it to be restrained by reason, and finally says that those who practice continence wage glorious battles against it.

# CHAPTER ONE

1. Now, since there is no doubt that, if you do not yield to the authority of so many and such great saints—men learned in the Sacred Scriptures and eminent in the Church’s governance for their distinguished memory and praise—and if you do not submit to it, whether you treat them, as you treated me, with the utmost abuse, or treat them more modestly and gently with some partiality toward persons, you will nevertheless say that they too were in error, I must, beloved son Julian, answer you in this way, with the Lord’s help. I must refute your books and arguments so that, if possible, you may understand that you have been wrongly persuaded of what you are trying to persuade others; and so that you may profitably repent of your careless and rash youthful advance and downfall—not merely for your own correction, but also for the benefit of many others, who will recognize and acknowledge how neither vainly nor falsely so many great rulers and teachers of Christian peoples learned and taught this in the Church of God, which you, deceived by a plausible novelty, desired to overthrow.

But if—may the Lord avert this from you—you have a heart so darkened that you cannot understand these things; or if you belong to the number of those whom Truth reproves in the holy Psalms, saying, “He refused to understand so that he might do good” (Ps. 35:4); or if you are among those of whom it is likewise written, “A stubborn servant will not be corrected by words; for even if he understands, he will not obey” (Prov. 29:19), even then this labor, whether mine or that of the other brothers who through Christ’s grace defend the Catholic faith against this error, will not be fruitless.

For there will be many more whom the ancient truth will either instruct, because it has been defended, or correct, if there were not lacking those whom an unfamiliar error, creeping in, either overthrew or disturbed. And, not to make this too long, I will not set down all your words; but, if the Lord helps, I will leave none of your supposedly sharp arguments without solving and demolishing it.

2. Concerning the judges, before whom, you say, “you were therefore unable to conduct your case because no one can deliberate well about doubtful matters unless he brings a heart free from hatred, anger, and friendship,” and whom you say “were not such judges, because they began to hate your case before they knew it,” I already replied in the preceding book (Book 2, §34):

If you were seeking such judges as Sallust defined them—and from whom you derived this statement—then you would certainly yield to holy Ambrose and his fellow bishops. When they pronounced true and tranquil judgments concerning this matter, they had a heart free from hatred or friendship toward you, from anger, or from what you did not include but Sallust did include—mercy on your behalf or against you [Note: [Col. 0702] *On the Conspiracy of Catiline*, in Caesar’s speech.]. At the very least, you would yield to them [Note: [Col. 0702] American and the manuscripts read: “you would believe them.”].

Now it is not enough for you to refuse to have them as judges; you even dare to make them defendants. But I ask you: how could those who condemned your case have begun to hate it before knowing it? They hated it precisely because, without doubt, they knew it. They knew that you said that little ones have no evil at birth which ought to be cleansed through rebirth. They knew that you said God’s grace is given according to our merits, so that grace would no longer be grace (Rom. 11:6), because it would not be given as grace but repaid as a debt. They knew that you said a person can have no sin in this life, so that what the entire Church says in the Lord’s Prayer would not be necessary for him: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12).

They knew these things about you, and they hated them with perfect justice [Note: Some manuscripts add here: “They knew these things about you, and they hated them with perfect justice.” The printed editions then read: “Finally, if by them”; the “if” is absent from the manuscripts.]. Finally, let them know that you have been corrected by them, and they will love you.

For it is not, as you say, that “if anyone says either that human beings possess free choice or that God is the creator of those who are born, he is called a Pelagian and a Coelestian.” Rather, the name of this error is taken by the person who does not attribute to God’s grace the freedom to which we have been called [Note: The manuscripts read: “the freedom in which we have been called.”], who denies that Christ is the liberator of little ones, and who says that no righteous person in this life needs any petition in the Lord’s Prayer on his own account. Such a person receives the name of this error because he shares in its crime.

3. As for the charge of Manichaeism, it is unnecessary here to say what Catholic lights you dare either unknowingly or pretendedly to slander by it. Certainly, as you say, if “the Emperor’s response was given rather on your behalf,” why do you not come forward and voluntarily present this to the civil authorities, showing that you are the people whose faith the Christian ruler approved?

But if you understand God’s law not as it stands but as you wish it to stand, why is it surprising if you do the same with the Emperor’s law? Yet you promise that you will deal with these matters more fully elsewhere. If you do so, what you write will either be exposed as crafty or disregarded as empty [Note: The manuscripts read thus. The printed editions read: “as what you confess.”].

4. How polished and amusing is your congratulation, when you say that “one man has emerged, who wishes it to be understood that the whole burden of the battle rests upon him”—so that you may appear to be David to the Pelagians, while I am Goliath [Note: Three manuscripts read: “a Pelagian.”].

You may appear so if you have entered into this agreement and arrangement with the Pelagians: that if you are defeated, they will dare nothing further. But far be it from me to challenge you to single combat. Wherever you appear, the army of Christ, spread everywhere, defeats you. It defeated Coelestius at Carthage, when I myself was not there; and again at Constantinople [Note: See below, in the second part of the Appendix, concerning the Council of Constantinople held under Atticus in the year 417], so far from the regions of Africa. It defeated Pelagius in Palestine, where, through fear of his condemnation, he condemned your case; for there your heresy completely fell.

And because the one whose figure was David fights against his adversaries through all his soldiers, he cut down your error with the tongue of Pelagius, as with the sword of one who had been struck down and was lying prostrate [Note: American reads: “He fights, and with the tongue of Pelagius he cut down your error as with the sword of one who had been struck down and was lying prostrate.” Erasmus, following the error, changed only “fights” to “attacks.”].

For what you disdain—that “you are called new heretics because you assert that all evil defined as sin consists not in nature but solely in the will”—Pelagius has already severed from you; or rather, through the tongue of Pelagius, the Lord severed it. For, fearing condemnation, Pelagius condemned those who say that infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life.

Therefore, you who deny that there is in a little one an evil that Baptism washes away, tell us by what merit an unbaptized infant is punished with eternal death. But what will you say, unless perhaps you will curse Pelagius? Yet if, while you curse him, he should say to you, “What would you have me do? If Christ says, ‘Unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you will not have life in yourselves’ (John 6:54), should I have said that a little one would have life if he ended this life without that sacrament?”—I think you will regret having cursed the man. Let the whole of this error, then, be a cause of regret to you.

5. Do not use the wretched argument employed by all heretics, whom the laws of Catholic emperors restrain from pernicious license [Col. 0704]. For all such people say what you yourself said: “That part of an argument which introduces terror in debate labors from lack of reason; it wins nothing from the prudent, but extorts blind assent from the fearful.”

You are indeed new heretics, but you have recognized and retained with the others this old saying of nearly all heretics. Do not deceive either yourselves or others, as though you had against us the same sort of argument that we had against the Donatists, whom we compelled by imperial commands to come with us to the Conference. Their madness had occupied all Africa, and they did not permit the truth to be preached by Catholics against their error. Through violent attacks, brigandage, blockades of the roads, robberies, fires, and killings, they laid waste to many things and terrified everyone [Note: American and the Gallican and Vatican manuscripts read: “while committing acts of brigandage.”].

With them we could accomplish nothing before bishops whom we did not share; and what our predecessors had done with them nearly a hundred years earlier was no longer retained in the memory of the peoples. This necessity therefore compelled us, at least after the proceedings of our Conference had been completed, to crush their shamelessness and restrain their audacity.

Your case, however, has now been concluded before a competent judgment of common bishops. So far as the right of examination is concerned, nothing further remains to be done with you except that you peacefully follow the judgment delivered on this matter. If you refuse, you must be restrained from turbulent or crafty agitation.

Rather, you are like the Maximianists, who, wishing to console their smallness at least by the name of a contest, and therefore wishing to seem to be something among those by whom they were despised because they were permitted to enter into examination with us, we dismissed with contempt when they appealed to us, submitted a petition, and issued challenges. They desired to be spoken of in connection with a contest more than they feared being defeated in one. They did not hope for the glory of victory but sought the reputation of a Conference, because they did not possess a multitude.

Therefore, if you think that you are victorious because the kind of examination you desired was not granted to you, the Maximianists preceded you in this empty boasting. Yet the Catholic Church did grant you the judgment it ought to have granted, in which your case was concluded; to them, however, it did not deign to grant any, because they had been separated not from us, as you were, but from the Donatists.

If, then, you see that it does not follow in the case of the Maximianists that those who are not permitted to engage in a particular judgment ought to be considered confident in the truth, stop boasting of these empty claims. Let it be enough for you that the Catholic Church endured you with maternal gentleness and condemned you with judicial severity—or rather, with medicinal necessity.

6. But, so that we do not linger over superfluous matters, I pass over the tumult of your curses and insults, whether those you heaped together at the beginning of your work or those you scarcely ceased scattering throughout all four of its books. Otherwise, to serious men, neither of us would appear a serious debater, but both of us merely frivolous litigants.

Let us now see instead what you bring forward by which, as you promise, you may show that I attribute human beings and marriage to the devil as their author [Col. 0705].

# CHAPTER TWO

7. Certainly you set out to refute my words. By presenting them and pretending to answer them, you try to persuade your readers that “I spoke against myself”: that, while defending myself, I said that “the new heretics call us condemners of marriage and of God’s work,” but afterward I withdrew this by saying that “a human being at birth is possessed in half-ounces by God and by the devil,” or rather, “is wholly possessed by the devil,” with God entirely excluded, as it were, from all his possession, namely, the human being.

Where is your acumen, by which you think you have mastered both Aristotle’s Categories and the other cunning of dialectical art? Do you not notice that what you have objected to me concerning little ones can be objected by an adversary of the truth to both of us concerning any adult who is a worse person?

For I ask you: what answer will you give concerning any extremely wicked person who has not yet been reborn? At least you confess that this person is under the devil unless he is reborn in Christ—is that what you deny? If you deny it, who then are those whom God “delivered from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of the Son of his love”?

But if you confess it, I ask whether, in such a person who remains under the power of darkness, God possesses any authority. If you say, “He does not,” the answer will be made to you: “Then God has been excluded by the devil from his own possession.” If you say, “He does,” the answer will be made to you: “Then God and the devil possess a human being in half-ounces,” and the uninstructed will stir up against you the same sort of envy that you, who wish to be considered learned, tried to stir up against me concerning little ones newly born.

Behold how easily your first argument has been destroyed, because you neglect to observe that human beings are under the devil’s power before they are redeemed by Christ, yet that neither they nor even the devil himself are removed from God’s power.

# CHAPTER THREE

8. Concerning the question of Baptism, about which you complained that you had been made objects of envy among the ignorant through our lies, it is scarcely possible to say how elegantly you have attempted to remove this envy from yourselves by admitting that little ones ought to be baptized. You say that “the grace of Baptism is not to be changed according to causes, because it distributes its gifts according to the capacity produced by circumstances. Therefore Christ, who is the redeemer of his own work,” you say, “continually increases, by unceasing generosity, his benefits toward his image; and those whom he made good by creating, he makes better by renewing and adopting.”

Is this the whole reason why you think no envy should be directed against you concerning the Baptism of little ones? As though any one of us had said that you deny that little ones ought to be baptized.

You do not say that they ought not to be baptized. But, in keeping with the greatness of your wisdom, you say astonishing things: They are baptized in the sacrament of the Savior, but they are not saved; they are redeemed, but they are not liberated; they are washed, but they are not cleansed; they are exorcized and exsufflated, but they are not rescued from the power of the devil.

These are the monstrosities of your opinions, these the unexpected mysteries of your new doctrines, these the paradoxes of the Pelagian heretics, more astonishing than the philosophical doctrines of the Stoics. For you fear being asked: If they are saved, what was sick in them? If they are liberated, what was held in them by the bond of slavery? If they are cleansed, what impurity was hidden in them? If they are rescued, by what merit were they under the devil’s power, since they were not guilty through their own iniquity—unless they carry what you deny, original sin?

And you deny this not so that you may assert that they are saved, liberated, cleansed, and subject to no enemy. For your false testimony offers them no help before the true Judge. Rather, you deny it so that, while they remain in the evil of the old condition, you may pursue a new vanity. For the true opinion is not yours but that of the one who said: “Unless someone is reborn of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

9. Yet you, most excellent lovers of that life which will be eternal with Christ, think that it is no punishment for the image of God to be excluded forever from the kingdom of God [Note: The printed editions read: “you think it is no punishment that the image of God is excluded forever from the kingdom of God.” The manuscripts read: “you think that it is no punishment for the image of God,” and so forth.]. For if you said that this was a small punishment, that would not be the voice of one who loves that kingdom blessedly, but of one who contemptuously rejects it in misery.

But if you admit that what is sufficient for this case is at least a small punishment—which is in fact great, since the image of God is not permitted to enter the kingdom of God—I beg you to open whatever eyes you possess and see by what justice this punishment is inflicted on a little one whom, with closed eyes, you deny to be subject to original sin.

I omit mentioning the evils that nearly all infants suffer in this very transitory life, and how one should explain what is written: “A heavy yoke lies upon the sons of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40:1). Certainly, under a just and omnipotent God, these evils would not be inflicted upon his image if no evil merits were inherited from parents. Nor can it be said that infancy is exercised in virtue through these evils, since it is incapable of such exercise.

But you completely pass over and disregard these evils of little ones—not those you deny that they have, but those which all of us see them enduring. Instead, as a most eloquent man, you roam at will [Note: Most manuscripts read thus. Erasmus and Lovaniensis read: “you wander there,” omitting “but.”] and exercise your intellect and tongue in praising nature.

This nature, fallen into such great and evident miseries, needs Christ as Savior, Liberator, Cleanser, and Redeemer; it does not praise Julian, Coelestius, or Pelagius. You would not admit that this nature is redeemed in little ones except because Coelestius, unable to endure the Christian voice, confessed this in the ecclesiastical proceedings at Carthage.

But I ask you: how can this redemption be understood except as redemption from evil, by the one who redeems Israel from all his iniquities (Ps. 129:8)? For wherever redemption is mentioned, a price is understood. And what is this price except the precious blood of the spotless Lamb, Jesus Christ (1 Pet. 1:18–19)?

But why that price was poured out—why should we ask anyone else? Let the Redeemer himself answer; let the one who made the purchase speak. “This,” he says, “is my blood, which will be poured out for many for the remission of sins” (Matt. 26:28).

Go on, then; go on. As you say, “They are baptized in the sacrament of the Savior, but they are not saved; they are redeemed, but they are not liberated; they are washed, but they are not cleansed; they are exorcized and exsufflated, but they are not rescued from the power of the devil.” So say also: “Blood is poured out for them for the remission of sins, but they are cleansed by the remission of no sin.”

The things you say are astonishing; the things you say are new; the things you say are false. We are stunned by what is astonishing, we avoid what is new, and we refute what is false.

# CHAPTER FOUR

10. Did you not yourself say that “the administration of the body was entrusted to the soul in such a way that the fruit of the work would be shared by both, and that it would experience either the joys of exercised virtue or the punishments of insolence through the affliction of the flesh that it had not governed well here” [Note: One Vatican manuscript reads: “or the punishments of insolence,” which corresponds no less well to the other member, “the joys of exercised virtue.”]?

Answer, then: why is the infant’s soul tortured in this very life by the affliction of the flesh, when its merit, because it has not governed the flesh well, cannot yet be charged against it?

You say that “human nature is endowed at the beginning of birth with the rich gift of innocence.” We certainly admit this insofar as personal sins are concerned. But since you also deny that infants are subject to original sin, answer: by what merit is such innocence sometimes born blind, sometimes deaf?

This defect also prevents faith itself, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Faith comes from hearing” (Rom. 10:17).

And who can tolerate the fact that, as regards the soul itself, the image of God—which, as you assert, is endowed with the rich gift of innocence—is born foolish, if no evil merits pass from parents to little ones? Is anyone among you so foolish as to think that foolishness is no evil, when Scripture says: “Mourn for the dead for seven days, but for a fool mourn all his days” (Ecclus. 22:13)?

Who does not know those whom people commonly call simpletons, who are naturally so foolish that in some of them scarcely more than the senses of animals can be discerned? Yet you do not wish to admit that, from the beginning when the human race deserted God, it carries the guilt of a condemned origin, deserving all these punishments—except where the inscrutable wisdom of the Creator spares it according to the disposition of his hidden plan.

Nor does he withhold the good of his work even from the whole mass of perdition: from the evils of vices he creates, though together with evils, insofar as it is good, a rational and mortal nature, of which no one can be the creator except himself; and within a condemned generation he provides the vessels of mercy with the aid of regeneration.

# CHAPTER FIVE
11. Therefore you think in vain that “there is no sin in infants because sin cannot exist without the will, and there is no will in them.” This is correctly said with regard to each person’s own sin, but not with regard to the contagion of original sin. If this contagion did not exist, infants, being bound by no evil at all, would suffer nothing evil either in body or in soul under the power of so just a God. Yet even this condition took its beginning from the evil will of earlier human beings.[^c0069-1] Thus, unless there is an evil will, there is no origin of anyone’s sin. If you understand this, you will confess simply and truthfully Christ’s grace toward infants, and you will not be forced to say things utterly impious and absurd: either that infants ought not to be baptized—which perhaps you will say later—or that so great a sacrament is a mockery in them, so that they are baptized in the Savior but not saved; redeemed by the Liberator but not liberated; washed in the bath of regeneration but not cleansed; exorcized and exsufflated, yet not rescued from the power of darkness; that their price is the blood poured out for the remission of sins, but that they are cleansed from the remission of no sin. You say all this because you are afraid to say, “Let them not be baptized,” lest not only the faces of men be smeared with spittle upon you, but even your heads be battered by the sandals of little women.

Three others read *For an evil will* instead of *Just as an evil will*. The Floriacensis manuscript reads, “For an evil will …,” and so forth.

12. We certainly say that the reason why one who is born remains under the devil until he is reborn in Christ is the contagion of sin derived from his origin. But you who deny this should at least look at what is plain: why do some infants also suffer from a demon? Unless perhaps you will deny that they are infants, or that they are under the devil; and the Gospel will not remind you, where the Lord perhaps asked what he already knew for your sake, so that the boy’s father might answer that his son had been grievously tormented by a demon from childhood, so grievously that he could not be expelled by Christ’s disciples (Mark 9:16–26).

Look: I do not say that marriage is the reason infants are under the devil, as you falsely accuse me of saying. Marriage has its own order and its own blessing, and its own good, which it could not lose even when sin entered. But explain, if you can, why at least that infant is under the devil who is manifestly tormented by the devil, sometimes even dying from the torment itself. You do not want anyone to undergo punishment for another’s sins, lest it thereby become credible that the contagions of sins can also pass from those who generate to those who are born.

## CHAPTER VI

13. But evidently, as an outstanding dialectician, “you will not let me slip away; rather, you will question me precisely and briefly: Do I regard the infant as guilty because of an action, or because of nature?” And answering for both alternatives, you say: “If because of an action, show what they have done; if because of nature, show who made that nature.”

As though an evil action could make anyone guilty unless nature were guilty. For one who is guilty by an action is a human being; but a human being is a nature. Human beings, therefore, just as adults are guilty through the action of sin, so infants are guilty through the contagion of their ancestors: the former through what they do, the latter through those from whom they derive their origin.

Accordingly, in infants it is good that they are human beings; indeed, they would not exist at all unless the supremely good One had created them. But if they derived no evil from their origin, they would never be born with bodily or other defects. For the God who is the creator of souls is also the creator of bodies, and certainly he does not inflict bodily defects upon undeserving human nature in the very act of creating it.

Nor can it be said of the innumerable infants born with such great variety of defects in soul and body what the Lord said concerning the man born blind: that this had happened neither because of his own sin nor because of his parents’ sin, but so that the works of God might be revealed in him (John 9:3). Many are not healed at all, but die either at some later age or in infancy with the same defects or with whatever defects they possess.[^c0069-2] In some infants who have already been reborn, such evils either remain with which they were born or arise afterward. Far be it from us to say that this happens unjustly. Rather, let us understand from this that their rebirth benefits them for the age to come, while the ordering of this present age is carried out, because of the evil of human pride by which humanity apostatized from God (Sirach 10:14–15), through various human sufferings under a grievous yoke upon the children of Adam, from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all (ibid. 40:1).

[^c0069-2]: **[Col. 0709]** The printed editions read *or in any age*; the manuscripts read *or at whatever age*.

## CHAPTER VII

14. In this work of yours you try to teach how syllogisms are constructed by dialecticians, although no one posed this question to you. The more pleased you are with yourself, the more you displease serious readers. Worse still, you pretend that I say what I do not say, conclude what I do not conclude, grant what I do not grant, and you draw for yourself a conclusion that I reject.

When did I deny that “human nature is praiseworthy” insofar as human beings are human? When did I say that they are guilty for this very reason—that they exist—when plainly they would exist and would not be guilty if no one had sinned? When did I say that fertility ought to be rejected, when it belongs to the blessing of marriage? How could you ask me to grant precisely what I did not say?

15. As for what you claim I assume—“Every commingling of bodies is evil”—nothing could be further from the truth. If I had said that every commingling of bodies is evil, you would have to say that I accused even the mixture of wine and water when our drink is prepared, since there is unquestionably a commingling of bodies there as well, and I would not have excluded it. Nor did I condemn the commingling of the two sexes when it is lawful and marital. Without it, the human race would not be generated, even if no one’s sin had preceded it.

Accordingly, when you add the further statement that I say, “Children are born from the commingling of bodies,” I do say this. But the conclusion you wished to draw as though it were mine is not mine. I do not say, “Therefore the children who proceed from an evil operation are evil,” since I do not call the act of husband and wife, performed for the sake of begetting children, evil, but rather good. It makes good use of the evil of lust, through which human beings—the good work of God—are generated, though not without the evil from which they must be regenerated in order to be liberated.

**[Col. 0710]** 16. Next you weave together another syllogism of yours, since the preceding one is yours as well, not mine.[^c0069-3] You say, therefore, “The cause of the sexes is the commingling of bodies,” and you want me to grant this to you. I grant it. You proceed and add: “If the commingling is always evil, then the condition of the bodies placed in the difference of the sexes is also deformed.”

If this followed, it would not trouble me, since I not only do not call marital commingling—the purpose of which is the procreation of children—evil, but call it good. Moreover, it does not follow that, if the commingling of the two sexes is always evil, the condition of bodies placed in the difference of the sexes is therefore deformed.

Indeed, if human beings were so enslaved to the evil of lust that, with the honor of marriage removed, they all indiscriminately and promiscuously lay together like dogs, the condition of the bodies would not thereby be deformed, since God is its author, even though the commingling of all human males and females would be evil. So too, even now, although adulterous commingling is certainly evil, the work of God in the condition of bodies is good.

You see, then, how dialectically you have said nothing, and this is no fault of the discipline of dialectic, but of how far you have strayed from its path. You use the words of that art so that, inflated by them, you may astonish the uninstructed and make them think you are what you are not. Even if you were what you pretend to be, you would be nothing in the way such matters ought to be argued. But as things stand, you would then have been an inept craftsman, and now you are both inept and uninstructed.

Yet, as though laden with the sharp darts of dialecticians, you enter the contest and brandish leaden daggers, saying: “If the commingling is always evil, then the condition of the bodies placed in the difference of the sexes is also deformed.” You do not see how the conclusion you presented as a necessary argument does not follow. You add: “Since you will not be able to deny this.”

What is it that I cannot deny, thoughtless man? What is it that I cannot deny? This, surely: if you have any sense, you now can do nothing but deny it. For if the commingling of adulterers is evil, it does not follow that the condition of human beings born from them is deformed. The former is the work of human beings acting badly, using good bodily members; the latter is the work of God acting well with evil human beings.

If you say that even in adultery the commingling itself is good because it is natural, but that adulterers use it badly, why are you unwilling to concede that lust may be evil, while married people nevertheless use it well for the purpose of begetting? Can there be a bad use of good things but not a good use of bad things? We find that the Apostle himself made good use of Satan, handing a man over to him for the destruction of the flesh so that his spirit might be saved on the day of the Lord (1 Corinthians 5:5), and handing others over to him so that they might learn not to blaspheme (1 Timothy 1:20).

## CHAPTER VIII

17. You add further, saying, “God cannot be the author of an evil thing.” How can you say this? He himself knows how to speak better than you do, and through the prophet he says that he creates evils (Isaiah 45:7).[^c0069-4]

Furthermore, whatever the status of this addition of yours may be, what does it have to do with me, since I did not grant the proposition to which you attach it? I demonstrated that it does not follow that the condition of bodies is deformed, even if I were to grant that every commingling of bodies, or of the two sexes, is evil.

Let us grant that God is the author of no evil. Does it follow that he is not the author of the condition of bodies, which I have in no way granted to be evil, since nothing I previously conceded compelled me to do so? Your inference therefore remains empty and laughable, when you conclude: “All bodies, therefore, are attributed to an evil author.”

It is much more truly concluded as follows: If even the evil commingling of adulterers does not make the condition of bodies evil—or if the commingling of the two sexes is good even in adulterers, but evil people make bad use of it—then all the more the condition of bodies cannot be evil. Bodies, therefore, are rightly attributed to God as their author.

There is no pit which, fearing that I might turn back as though I were returning to the road, you appear to be trying to lead me toward. But tell me what that road is, and explain your reasoning.

## CHAPTER IX

18. “God,” you say, “the good God through whom all things were made, himself formed the members of our body.” I grant that this is entirely true. You continue and add: “He who had made the bodies also divided the sexes: he divided in appearance what he would join in operation, and he made the difference of the members the cause of their union.” I agree with this as well.

Then you infer: “The commingling of bodies, therefore, comes from him from whom the origin of bodies comes.” Who could deny this? “When you have granted this,” you say, “even if unwillingly, it follows that the fruits of so many good things—bodies, sexes, unions—cannot be evil.”

This too you say truly. The fruit of these good things is the human being, who insofar as he is human is good. But the evil in him, from which he must be healed by the Savior, liberated by the Redeemer,[^c0069-5] washed by the bath, rescued through exorcism, and absolved by the blood poured out for the remission of sins, is not the fruit of bodies, sexes, or unions, but of original and ancient sin.

For if, speaking of the offspring of adulterers, I were to say, “The fruit of so many evils—lust, shame, and crime—cannot be good,” you would rightly answer me that the human being born from adulterers is not the fruit of lust, shame, or crime, whose author is the devil, but of bodies, sexes, and unions, whose author is God. So I rightly say to you that the evil with which a human being is born is not the fruit of bodies, sexes, or unions, whose author is God, but of the first transgression, whose author is the devil.

[^c0069-5]: **[Col. 0711]** Lovaniensis reads *and liberated through redemption*.

19. Far be it from us to say, as you falsely accuse us of saying, that “God makes human beings for the purpose of their being held by the devil by legitimate right.” Although it belongs more to divine than to diabolical power that an unclean generation should be subjected to an unclean ruler unless it is cleansed by regeneration, God does not make human beings so that the devil may in some manner possess a household. Rather, he makes them through that goodness by which he grants all natures their existence, and by which he also causes the devil himself to subsist. If he were to withdraw that goodness from things, they would immediately cease to be.

Just as he does not create cattle in herds and flocks belonging to the impious so that they may be sacrificed to demons, although he knows that the impious will do this, so also, when he sees that generation has become subject to sin, he does not, according to the beautiful order of the ages that he has established, withdraw his goodness from the act of creating it.

## CHAPTER X

20. After this argument by which you deceive yourself and imagine that you have accomplished something, you introduce your customary abuse and then add: “Perhaps I should say that the fact that children born from the commingling of bodies are attributed to God’s work ought to be confirmed by the testimony of Scripture, not by syllogisms.” It is as though anyone who denied this could be a Christian.

Accordingly, you try to demonstrate through the testimonies of Scripture a matter which we readily confess and gladly proclaim, as though it were a point of dispute between us. You labor in vain—not to answer us, but to fill books. Nevertheless, when you said that “to express the faith of the works, the Prophet came close to the danger of impropriety, because he said, ‘The two shall be one flesh’” (Genesis 2:24), this ought to have sufficiently reminded you that nothing shameful would have existed in the works of God if human nature had not first deserved to be confounded by the deformity of its own merit.

## CHAPTER XI

21. You also say, in praise of lust, that “this was restored by God’s gift to Abraham and Sarah, whose bodies were exhausted and dead” (Romans 4:19). And you proclaim in an offensive manner that I should assert, if I can, that something belongs to the work of the devil because I see God sometimes bestowing it as a gift.

But if God were to restore a lame man to life and return him to the living—although, once dead, he could no longer limp—would it therefore seem that God had bestowed lameness as a gift? So, if the vigor of bodies was restored to the man who had previously been in the prime of life, he was restored in accordance with the condition of this body of death. They did not need to be returned to the state in which Adam was before sin, so that without any law in their members resisting the law of the mind they could beget children.

22. Nevertheless, Abraham’s body should also be understood to have been exhausted for this reason: that he was no longer capable of begetting children from every woman who might be able to bear them. The advance of age is said to produce this result: an old man may be able to beget a child from a young woman, while no longer being able to do so from an older woman, even though she might be able to conceive from a young man.

For those who then lived for such a very long time undoubtedly became decrepit later, to the point that they could not be moved to intercourse at all—if this can happen through age to any healthy man. When I had this work in hand, we were told of an old man who was eighty-four years old. He had lived continently with his devout wife for twenty-five years, but had purchased a Lyristria woman for lust. In proportion to the length of human life today, he was certainly more advanced in old age than Abraham had been at one hundred, when Abraham still had another seventy years to live.[^c0069-6]

It is therefore more reasonably believed that God granted his servants the fertility they lacked. Two causes are given for Sarah’s inability to bear children, and her womb is said to have been dead: one was sterility, which had been present in her from youth; the other was age—not simply that she was ninety years old, but that her menstrual function had already ceased.

It is established that when a woman’s monthly discharge has ceased through age, she can no longer conceive, even if she had previously been fertile. Scripture therefore did not wish to omit this detail, so that the glory of the miracle God was about to perform in their offspring might be increased.

When Sarah gave her maidservant to her husband, from whom she wished him to receive children because she herself could not bear them, she was moved not by age but by her sterility. Scripture speaks in this way: “Now Sarah, Abraham’s wife, did not bear him children.” These are her words to her husband: “Behold, God has closed me up, so that I may not bear.”

If we consider the age of both of them at that time, they would have been decrepit had they been people of our era. Abraham was about eighty-five years old, and Sarah was seventy-five. For it is written: “Abraham was eighty-six years old when Hagar bore Ishmael to Abraham” (Genesis 16:1–2, 16). Thus he is found to have had intercourse with the maidservant about a year earlier, when Ishmael was conceived.

What married couples in our time beget children at such an age, unless such a miracle occurs by divine action? Yet they could have done so if Sarah had not been sterile, because he was able to beget a child from Hagar, and she had not yet advanced so far in age that her menstrual function had ceased.

Abraham’s body, therefore, was exhausted so that he could no longer beget a child from Sarah, even if she had been fertile and had nevertheless been approaching the age at which the monthly bleeding ceases. Medical authorities have determined that women from whom it no longer flows at all cannot conceive.

If this were false, Scripture would not have taken care to say, “The menstrual function of Sarah had ceased,” when it had already said above, “Abraham and Sarah were advanced in age” (ibid. 18:11). Thus, in proportion to the length of that period, during which people lived for a much longer span, they could no longer beget children at that age, when Abraham was one hundred and Sarah ninety.

This would have been so even if she had not been sterile and they had intercourse a year earlier, when she perhaps still menstruated and therefore could still have conceived if her husband had been young. At that time, however, she could not conceive because Abraham’s body had been so exhausted by old age that he could not beget a child from a woman of that age. Yet he himself could beget one from a young woman, as he later did from Keturah (ibid. 25:1–2). It may also be said in that case that the gift of fertility continued in him, the gift he had received so that Isaac might be born.

In proportion to the length of our present age, during which human beings live for a much shorter time, married couples are said to be capable of begetting children within the first hundred years of their combined lives. But if the combined years of both spouses exceed the number one hundred, they are firmly declared unable to beget children, even if the woman is fertile and, while still menstruating, could conceive from a young man. It was therefore rightly established that no one should have the legal privilege of children until the combined years of both spouses had been calculated and shown to have passed one hundred.[^c0069-7]

[^c0069-6]: The reference is obscure; *Lyristria* is retained as printed.

[^c0069-7]: **[Col. 0714]** The printed editions read *had not passed one hundred*. The negative particle is absent from the manuscripts. We should therefore understand that childless couples did not possess the legal privilege of children until they had passed that age. By this law they were freed from the penalties imposed on the childless and could receive the whole of one another’s estates by mutual wills, just like those who had children in common. Hence Isidore, *Etymologies* 5, says: “The legal privilege of children is the mutual appointment by childless spouses, in place of offspring, of reciprocal heirs.” Ulpian, *Fragments*, title 16, writes that spouses received the whole estate from one another when they had passed the years fixed by the Papian law—namely, sixty for the husband and fifty for the wife. Augustine, however, seems to have considered the age beyond which they could no longer beget children.

23. It was therefore a miracle of God that Isaac was conceived—not because the parents’ lust was restored, but because fertility was granted. Lust could have existed even in those years; fertility, however, could not, because so many obstacles prevented it.

Although, as we explained above, if lust too had revived when the exhausted senile members were in some manner revived by God’s gift,[^c0069-8] it would necessarily have followed the condition of corruptible flesh, so that it would exist in this body of death, whereas before sin it could not exist in the body of that life, in paradise.

According to the condition of this punitive body, God now grants the gift of fertility to each person, not according to that happiness in which there was nothing in the flesh that lusted against the spirit, and the spirit, lusting against the flesh, had to restrain it. For in human nature before sin there ought to have been peace, not war.

You also labored in vain in that part of your reasoning, as though we could say that “Isaac was begotten without the lust of the flesh or the seed of a man.” We do not say this, and therefore we pass over and disregard everything you argued from it.

## CHAPTER XII

24. You thought you had discovered something with remarkable acuity when you said: “Even if the devil created human beings, they would be evil through no fault of their own; and therefore they would no longer be evil, because no one can be anything except what he was born as, and it is not just to demand from anyone more than he can do.”

We too customarily say such things against the Manichaeans, who do not say that nature is good but corrupted, rather that it is evil without beginning and immutably evil, according to their fables.

According to the Catholic faith, however, human nature was established good, but was corrupted by sin and justly condemned. It is neither strange nor unjust that a condemned root produces condemned offspring, unless the hand of the Creator, which was not absent, is also accompanied by the mercy of the Liberator.[^c0069-9] You begrudge this mercy to the wretched when you say that infants have no evil from which they need to be liberated.

25. But you who oppress miserable infancy with a false defense and attack it with a destructive commendation, why do you not admit so many images of God among infants, who deserve no evil, into the kingdom of God if they are not baptized? Did they themselves fail to do something, so that they should be deprived of the kingdom and punished with so grievous an exile, when they did not do what they were wholly unable to do?

You also assert that they will be deprived of life, because they have not eaten the flesh or drunk the blood of the Son of Man (John 6:54). Hence Pelagius, as I mentioned above, would have left the ecclesiastical judgment condemned if he had not condemned those who say that “infants, even if they are not baptized, possess eternal life.”[^c0069-10]

By what justice, I ask, is the image of God excluded from the kingdom of God and from the life of God, having transgressed the law of God in nothing? Do you not hear how the Apostle condemns certain people, saying that they are alienated from the life of God because of the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their hearts (Ephesians 4:18)?

Will an unbaptized infant be held by this sentence, or will it not? If you say, “It will not,” you will be defeated and punished by evangelical truth, with even Pelagius’s own tongue bearing witness. For where is the life of God except in the kingdom of God, which those who have not been reborn from water and the Spirit cannot enter (John 3:5)?

But if you say, “It will be held,” confess the punishment and state the fault; confess the penalty and state the merit. You find nothing in your doctrine that you can bring forward.

Therefore, at last, if there is any Christian understanding in you, acknowledge even in infants the propagation of death and condemnation, which is to be punished by due justice and liberated freely by God’s grace. In their redemption God’s mercy can be praised; in their destruction God’s truth cannot be accused, because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10).

## CHAPTER XIII

26. You divide, define, and discuss almost medically the genus, species, measure, and excess of lust, asserting that “its genus consists in the vital fire, its species in genital motion, its measure in marital intercourse, and its excess in the intemperance of fornication.”

Yet after this entire supposedly subtle and lengthy discussion, when I ask you briefly and plainly why this vital fire has rooted war in human beings, so that the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit must lust against the flesh (Galatians 5:17); why one who chooses to consent to the vital fire is struck by a mortal wound, I think that the ink of your book itself will blush and turn red.

Behold the vital fire, which does not merely fail to obey the will of our soul, which is the true life of the flesh, but is often aroused against its will by disordered and shameful movements. Unless the spirit lusts against it, this vital fire kills our good life.

**[Col. 0716]** 27. As though concluding after your long discussion, you say: “The origin of lust is therefore rightly defined as existing in the vital fire; when this is gathered together, carnal lust must necessarily be attributed to that through which carnal life was established.”[^c0069-11]

You speak as though you could prove—or as though, whatever your audacity, you would dare to imagine—that in the original constitution of human beings, before deserved condemnation followed upon guilt, this carnal lust either existed in paradise or produced the most shameful battles against the spirit through disordered movements such as we now see.

Then you add: “The appetite of this kind is therefore not a fault in its genus, species, or measure, but in its excess, because its genus and species belong to the Creator’s work, its measure to the choice of moral propriety, and its excess to the vice of the will.”

How neatly these mad words sounded to you—naturally, to a man who does not consider what he is saying![^c0069-12] If the measure of this appetite belongs to the choice of moral propriety, what married man’s moral judgment would want this appetite to be moved except when necessary? And yet he cannot do what he wants.

What continent man’s moral judgment would ever want this appetite to be moved? And yet he cannot do what he wants. Hence the man cries out: “To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find” (Romans 7:18).

Since, then, in the movement itself it has no measure according to the choice of our will, while in its effect it is not itself restrained but must be given measure by the spirit through a vigilant struggle, what are you praising, evil men, instead of crying out to God, “Deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:13)?
