## CHAPTER XIV

28. What does it help you to say that “lust is intercepted by weakness,” as though it were not utterly extinguished by death, when a man who has been overcome and subjugated by it is no longer challenged to a contest, but receives what is owed to the defeated?

This is the more bitter point, the one you do not understand: when we are healthy, this movement is insane.

“Among married couples,” you say, “it is exercised with propriety, or among the chaste it is restrained by virtue.” Is that really so? Have you experienced it in this way? Is this evil—or your good—not restrained by married couples?

When they wish, married couples lie down and attack one another whenever the appetite has been tickled. The appetite is not postponed even for the hour of going to bed; rather, the commingling of bodies appears to be lawful precisely when this natural good of yours has been spontaneously aroused.

If you have led married life in this way, stop bringing your own experiences into the argument, and instead inquire from others how married life ought to be lived or taught.[^c0069-13] Yet I wonder whether you at least restrained adulterous desires, or even recognized that they ought to be restrained.

But if conjugal chastity also restrains this pest—both because of the excessive tumults of lust even within marriage and because of damnable desires, lest anything be done beyond the natural use of the marriage bond[^c0069-14]—what do you mean by saying, “Among married couples it is exercised with propriety,” as though this appetite were always proper in a spouse and nothing were granted to it, at least by way of concession, as the Apostle says (1 Corinthians 7:6)?

How much better you would say, “In the moderation of married couples it is exercised with propriety”! Or did you fear that even there it might be understood to be an evil to which married people impose the bridle of careful moderation?

Finally, now at least, living continently, acknowledge the bad horse in those Ambrosian chariots (see the passage cited above, §12), and do not praise in heart or mouth the one whom you are compelled to restrain by virtue.[^c0069-15]

“The fourth,” you say, “is perpetrated by those who give themselves to wantonness—that is, the excess of that pleasure—and because it arises from insolence, not from nature, it is rightly condemned.”

From whose insolence, I ask, does it arise—from wantonness or from lust? So as not to offend the position you have undertaken, you will answer, “From wantonness.” But all people judge that wantonness is not a sin except because consent is given to lust.

Is there therefore no evil to which one sins by consenting? Yet this evil exists in the flesh when it lusts against the spirit, even if it is not in the spirit that refuses consent and even lusts against the flesh.

Cry out, then, “Deliver us from evil,” and do not add the evil of false praise to this evil.

## CHAPTER XV

29. You eloquently establish conjugal chastity between the wanton and the continent, as though in the middle: “It is indignant that the former have committed what is unlawful, and marvels that the latter have even despised what is lawful; having received the region of the boundary line, it curses the barbarism of those rushing beyond it, venerates the radiance of those shining above it, and with modest hands both comforts those burning with desire and praises those who do not need such a remedy.”[^c0069-16]

I take great pleasure in this most eloquent truth. But I ask you: just as you say—and you say it most eloquently and truthfully—does conjugal chastity praise the continent precisely because they do not need the remedy by which it recognizes that it itself once had need, namely, that according to the Apostle, “if they cannot exercise self-control, let them marry” (1 Corinthians 7:9)?

Why then, when I say that this lust is a disease, do you deny it, even though you confess that it requires a remedy? If you acknowledge the remedy, acknowledge the disease; if you deny the disease, deny the remedy.

I ask you: yield at last to the truth speaking through your own mouth. No one provides a remedy for health.

## CHAPTER XVI

30. You also rightly say that “marriage cannot properly be approved if it is praised by comparison with an evil.” This is true. In its own category marriage is good, but it is good because it preserves fidelity to the marriage bed, because it unites the two sexes for the purpose of receiving offspring, and because it abhors the impiety of separation.

These are the goods of marriage, through which marriage is good. We have very often said that these could have existed even if no one had sinned.

After sin, however, a struggle arising not from happiness but from necessity was added to them, so that marriage itself, by means of its own good, might fight against the evil of lust, allowing it to reach nothing unlawful. Yet lust itself does not cease to incite them, now through milder and now through more violent movements, and they make good use of its evil in the propagation of children.

Who would deny that this is an evil except one who does not listen to the Apostle’s admonition: “But I say this by way of concession, not by command” (1 Corinthians 7:6)? This occurs when married couples have intercourse, overcome not by the desire to receive offspring but by the desire to satisfy carnal pleasure. This is not praised, but forgiven in comparison with a worse evil, with marriage intervening and pleading on their behalf.

Additional textual notes:

- **§13 [Col. 0708].** After *is guilty*, the editors add *of a human being* (*hominis*) from the Floriacensis manuscript; that manuscript, however, later omits *human beings* before “therefore, just as.” The printed editions read “accordingly, infants”; the Floriacensis manuscript reads “accordingly, in infants.” Some editions and most manuscripts read *beginning* rather than *evil* in “because of the evil of human pride.”
- **§16 [Col. 0710].** The printed editions read *purpose* (*causam*) in place of *for the purpose* (*causa*), which the manuscripts have. Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice read: “You seem to use the words of that art for this purpose”; Lovaniensis reads: “You seem to use the words of that art for this.”
- **§18 [Col. 0711].** The Ambrosian edition and the manuscripts read “when you have granted this unwillingly” (*ingratus*) rather than “even if unwillingly” (*ingratis*).
- **§22 [Col. 0712–0713].** Lovaniensis reads “Nevertheless, in order to understand this, [the body] was thus exhausted.” The manuscripts read *dried up* rather than *ceased* of the monthly discharges. Lovaniensis adds *now* after “in proportion to the length of the period,” incorrectly.
- **§24–25 [Col. 0715].** The manuscripts read “you begrudge [it] to the wretched” (*miseris invidetis*); the printed editions read “you wretched people begrudge [it]” (*miseri invidetis*). The Floriacensis manuscript reads *send* (*mittitis*) rather than *admit* (*admittitis*).
- **§26–28 [Col. 0715–0716].** Four Vatican manuscripts read *the spirit* (*spiritum*) rather than *to the spirit* (*spiritui*). The Floriacensis manuscript reads *works* (*opera*) rather than *work* (*operam*) of the Creator; *evil* rather than *evil men*; and *as much as* rather than *except when* in the respective passages. The printed editions read *properly* rather than *what moral judgment*; one manuscript reads “Have you experienced this?” rather than “Is that really so?”
- **§30 [Col. 0717].** Four Vatican manuscripts preserve only the corrupt fragment: “You also rightly say, upon examination [lacuna].”

## CHAPTER XVII
### 31

After this, however, you return somehow to the example of Abraham and Sarah, concerning which I think I have already answered sufficiently. But I do not know what escaped you, which you wanted to add when it later came to mind. It is human; it commonly happens. Let us hear, then, what it is.

You say that “a prophetic event has occurred which is now [Note: [Col. 0718] Am. Er. and manuscripts: *then*.] displayed in the region of Africa: that of a beautiful and holy woman who represented the Church, for whom neither her husband nor her chastity was safe, and that there she was miraculously preserved inviolate.” So that I do not linger uselessly over all your words, you turn to the person to whom you are writing and say:

“Here, most blessed brother Turbanti, dearest fellow priest, God must be entreated that even in this age He may not delay to rescue the Catholic Church, the Bride of His Son—mature, fruitful, chaste, and beautiful—from the defilement of the Manichaeans, who in Africa or from Africa go about as brigands.”

This prayer is rather ours, directed against the Manichaeans, the Donatists, and other heretics, or indeed any enemies of the Christian and Catholic name established in Africa. But against you—since you are a transmarine pestilence for us, to be overcome by Christ our Savior—are we therefore brigands from Africa because we set against you one martyr from here, Cyprian, by whom we prove that we defend the ancient Catholic faith against the vain and profane novelty of your error?

O impiety! Did the Church of God established in Africa lack aid? Did your prayers fail when the most blessed Cyprian proclaimed those very things which you attack? When he said:

“An infant ought much less to be prohibited from Baptism, since one who has just been born has committed no sin, except that, having been born carnally according to Adam, he has contracted the contagion of ancient death in his first birth, so that what is remitted to him is not his own sins but those of another” (*Epistle 64 to Fidus);

when Cyprian had learned and taught these things, did the assistance of your prayers fail, by which Sarah might be preserved inviolate in the region of Africa and the beauty of the Church might be freed from the defilement of the Manichaeans? For, according to your understanding, before the name of Manichaeus had resounded in the Roman lands, they had already deceived Cyprian himself.

Consider what monstrous and frantic things you say against the most ancient Catholic faith, having nothing to say.

### 32

But however much you evade the issue, O Pelagian heresy, which erects new engines against the walls of the most ancient truth and devises new ambushes—the “Punic disputant,” as your defender insults me; the Punic disputant, I say, is not I but the Punic Cyprian. He, a Punic, sacrifices you with this wound and exacts punishment from your criminal doctrine. [Note: [Col. 0719] He imitates Virgil, *Aeneid* 12.946–947:

“Pallas sacrifices you with this wound, Pallas  
and exacts punishment from your criminal blood.”]

What if I had named as many bishops from Africa as I named from other regions of the world? Or what if there had been more Africans among those very men? One is from here; the others are from elsewhere, and by their agreement from East and West you are pierced through. Yet you are blinded by such obstinacy that you do not see that you rather wish to corrupt the Church’s ancient beauty—that is, the ancient faith—as though it were the chastity of the most beautiful old woman Sarah.

For if the Manichaeans have defiled the Church through the holy bishops and renowned teachers of God—Irenaeus, Cyprian, Reticius, Olympius, Hilary, Ambrose, Gregory, Basil, John, Innocent, and Jerome—tell me, Julian, who gave birth to you? Did a chaste woman [Note: [Col. 0719] Louvain: *or rather a chaste woman*.], or rather a prostitute, bring you forth into the light which you have abandoned, through the womb of spiritual grace? Or, in order to defend Pelagian doctrines, are you, at the prompting of a wickedness that is not error but madness, denouncing the inner organs of Christ’s spouse and your mother?

For your new deformity has found nothing to lie about against Sarah’s ancient beauty to such an extent that, in the face of so clear a manifestation of the judgments of so many glorious Catholic bishops—including men who had never even heard the name of Manichaeus—it accuses their agreement of being a Manichaean blasphemy.

### 33

“But from this digression, to which an impulse—not, as you say, of ‘grief,’ but of ‘lost modesty’—had carried you away, you return deliriously to the matters you had begun.” [Note: [Col. 0719] Am. Er. and more manuscripts: *deliberately*. Louvain: *to rave*. But the Victorinus codex and five Vatican manuscripts more aptly read: *deliriously*.] And, introducing testimony from the Apostle (Rom. 4:19), you attempt to confirm what you had said about the dead members of Abraham and Sarah. On this subject, therefore, let what I discussed above, as much as seemed sufficient, now suffice.

But what Christian does not know that “He who first made man from dust fashions all human beings from seed”? Yet He fashions them from seed already corrupted [Note: [Col. 0719] The Floriacensis manuscript reads *violated*.] and condemned, part of which remains in punishment through truth, while part is freed from evil through mercy.

Therefore, as you think and conclude, “the assertion of natural sin is not strangled by any of your snares.” For nature, corrupted by the will of the first transgressor, is not cleansed by your defense, with its empty words, through your novel doctrine; rather, it is cleansed by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.

### Chapter XVIII

### 34

For this reason, I do not think—as you falsely accuse me—that “husbands and wives have generated children without bodily heat.” Nor do I think that “God did not make man, or made him for the devil, or that the devil made him,” because the parents themselves cannot make a human being; rather, God makes him from the parents. [Col. 0720] Nor does the devil withdraw himself from God’s authority—how much less human nature, which God, in condemning it on account of its deserved punishment for sin, subjected to the devil?

Since these things are so, you, even if you are not a worshiper of the devil, as you say I am, are nevertheless shown to be his assistant, however much you may appear to accuse him: you insist that infants ought not to be healed by Christ from that evil by which they are held under the devil, while by unsound teaching you defend them as healthy.

I, however, according to the sound faith, say that “Isaac too was formed from the same pleasure of concupiscence” from which all other human beings were formed, with the one exception of Him through whom we are freed from evil. Nor do I deny that “the hand of divine providence is involved in the generation of sinners.” For it reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly (Wis. 8:1), and nothing defiled enters into it (Wis. 7:25). Therefore, even from things unclean and contaminated it accomplishes whatever it wills, while itself remaining clean and undefiled.

There is no need for you to try, by long circumlocutions, to prove to me what I grant. Instead, answer this, if you can: why would Isaac’s soul have perished from his people (Gen. 17:14) if he had not been circumcised on the eighth day as a sign of Christ’s Baptism? Explain, if you can, by what merit he would have been punished with so great a penalty, unless he were freed from it by that sacrament.

It cannot be denied that God gave life to Sarah’s dead womb for the emission of seed, and to Abraham’s dead body so that he might beget children as young men beget them, so that offspring could be born from those parents in their old age. But as far as his own sins are concerned, even if Isaac had been born of adulterers, he was born innocent. What had he deserved, then, that his soul should perish from his people, unless circumcision came to his aid?

Do not wander through many obscure, perplexing, and superfluous matters. Answer this one clear, simple, and necessary question.

### 35

You introduce the Apostle’s testimony, not according to what he intended by it, but according to what you suppose. Since we are not dealing with that matter now, it would be lengthy and unnecessary to discuss it. Nevertheless, you introduce the passage in which he says:

“How will God judge the world? For if the truth of God has abounded to His glory through my lie, why am I still judged as a sinner?” (Rom. 3:6–7).

Then you add that “through these words the Apostle shows that God has lost the authority to judge if He did not maintain the proper measure in commanding.”

If, then, as you think, “the Apostle said these things so that those who asserted that the sins of mortals contribute to God’s praise might restrain themselves, and that He therefore commanded the impossible in order to prepare an occasion for showing mercy”; and if, as you suppose, “through this apostolic statement it is demonstrated that people are rightly judged because they did not carry out possible commands, but would be unjustly judged if they failed to do what they had been commanded impossibly”—what will you say about Isaac, to whom nothing either possible or impossible was commanded, and yet he would have been struck by the punishment of the destruction of his soul if he had not been circumcised on the eighth day?

Or do you still not finally consider that the command first given in paradise was possible and easy, and that, once it had been despised and violated, all human beings descended from one man possessed that common sin as though in one mass of origin? Hence there is a heavy yoke upon the sons of Adam, from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all (Ecclus. 40:1).

And because no one is freed from this condemned generation in Adam unless he is regenerated in Christ, Isaac would have perished if he had not received the sign of that regeneration. He would not have perished unjustly, since he would have left this life—into which he had entered condemned through a condemned generation—without the sign of regeneration.

Or, if this is not the reason, give another.

God is good; God is just. He can free some without good merits, because He is good; but He cannot condemn anyone without evil merits [Note: [Col. 0721] Here Louvain omits “evil.”], because He is just. An infant eight days old had no evil merit arising from his own sins. Why, then, would he be condemned unless he were circumcised, if he did not derive sin from his origin?

### Chapter XIX

### 36

Proceed to the rest, and pile vanity upon vanity—not, I say, the words of the holy Scriptures which you cite, but the constructions you endeavor to make from them.

You say that “from this it ought to be understood that perfect ignorance is called righteousness,” because God said to Abimelech, who was about to have intercourse with Sarah, not knowing that she was another man’s wife, “I knew that you did this with a pure heart” (Gen. 20:6). And therefore, you say, “the condition of those being born is not harmed by the will of those who beget them, because even if that will were evil, no kind of knowledge of it would reach them.”

Why, then, do you not call them righteous, if perfect ignorance is to be called by the name of righteousness? For nothing is more perfect than the ignorance of infants; therefore, let nothing be called more righteous than they.

Where is what you earlier thought should be asserted: “Infants are born neither righteous nor unrighteous, because they will become so by their actions, but are born merely endowed with the privilege of innocence”? Are these not your own words, when you say:

“A human being is therefore born full of innocence but capable of virtue, destined to merit either praise or blame when intention is added”?

Will you say that virtue is not righteousness? How, then, is an infant not yet full of virtue but capable of it, although he is full of ignorance, which you say is righteousness? Unless you deny that virtue is righteousness.

Will you not at last awaken, struck by this absurdity, and repent of having said it? For the Lord’s words are awake, but you are asleep. He did not say to the king, “I knew that you have a righteous heart,” or “because you have a pure heart,” although it is written, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

Yet you put forward this Abimelech as an example of a sinner. [Note: [Col. 0721] The Floriacensis manuscript reads: “sinners.”] But God says, “I knew that you did this with a pure heart.” He does not say “everything,” or “whatever else,” but “this”—the act in which he had no consciousness of adultery.

### 37

I am nevertheless astonished that, having cited this example, you try to accomplish with it what you cannot accomplish, and that you do not see in it what you refuse to hear. [Note: [Col. 0721] The manuscripts read: “what you do not wish to hear.”]

You try to make people believe that, at Abraham’s prayer, sexual desire was restored to the women, because it is written:

“For God had closed every womb in the house of Abimelech because of Sarah, Abraham’s wife” (Gen. 20:18).

You want this closing to be understood as though God, in anger, had removed sexual desire from those women. Yet these words more likely indicate that their wombs were closed by some illness, so that a woman could neither have intercourse in order to conceive nor give birth after conceiving.

You did not consider, though you are a man unwilling to allow that anyone can be punished by divine judgment for sins not his own but another’s, how it could have happened that Abimelech sinned, even though he himself had not sinned with an adulterous heart, and that God punished whatever slight sin he had committed in the women belonging to him.

You see the contagion of sin passing from the man into the women with whom he had intercourse or over whom he ruled, but you refuse to see it passing from parents into the offspring propagated from their seed.

Consider, then, how unfathomable is the depth of the judgments of God’s wisdom and knowledge (Rom. 11:33), and stop prattling against the mysteries of original sin.

### Chapter XX

### 38

Next you begin to argue about an excess of concupiscence, which you call blameworthy, as though, when a married person makes proper use of it, the horse itself—which is evil—were to be praised rather than its driver. [Note: [Col. 0722] He alludes to Ambrose’s words cited above, no. 12.]

What help, then, do the testimonies from Scripture provide you, by which it is shown how God either prohibits sexual desire or condemns its excess? Consider rather that whatever we shudder at in the shamefulness of any kind of crime committed through the genital members is brought about by the concupiscence of the flesh, unless it is restrained, through the very movements by which it produces an effect even in the bodies of the chaste, carrying them in sleep as far as groaning.

### 39

You say, “For what reason would God seek righteous people in Sodom (Gen. 18:26), if nature made them such?” [Note: [Col. 0722] Lov. reads: “God, unless He made them such,” contrary to the other printed editions and manuscripts.]

You speak as though we were saying that concupiscence of the flesh cannot be restrained by the superior nature of the mind. But we say that it is so great an evil that, when it resists, it is conquered by being fought down, until it is healed by complete treatment just as a wound in the body is healed.

### 40

But if you think that “the Apostle praised sexual desire on this account, because he said that intercourse with a woman is natural,” when he says that certain people, “leaving the natural use of the woman, burned in their desire for one another” (Rom. 1:27), then you are compelled to praise every use of woman. Consequently, you will also praise the adulterous relations committed with women, because there too the use is certainly natural, although it must be condemned because it is not lawful. Hence those who are born from it are called not legitimate but natural children.

The Apostle therefore did not praise the concupiscence of the flesh by that expression. Rather, he called that use natural through which human nature can continue to exist by reproduction.

### 41

You say that “the Sodomites also sinned through the creatures of bread and wine.” Thus you want us to understand that sexual desire is good, but that the people who use it wrongly are blameworthy, just as the creature of bread and wine is good, although sin is committed through its misuse.

You do not understand what you are saying, however, to such an extent that you do not see that the creature of bread and wine does not lust against the spirit. Rather, it is itself lusted after shamefully by those who misuse it, and it enters our body from outside.

For that reason it must be used more sparingly and with greater restraint, lest concupiscence itself—which is an evil within us and our own—be aroused against us more vehemently and more invincibly, as the corruptible body is weighed down by an excessive amount of material.

This, then, is the evil which shows itself to be evil, whether in the person who struggles against it or in the person whom it subjugates. A parent makes good use of it when he chastely begets a child, and God makes good use of it when He providentially creates a human being.

### Chapter XXI

### 42

Now, I beg you, consider; now, I say, lay aside the desire to conquer and consider whether you ought to submit to our judgment or to yours, so that truth may beneficially conquer you.

It is well that you say you will “briefly admonish” me, “so that what you have undertaken throughout the whole book may remain fixed in the reader’s heart.” Then, supplying what this brief admonition is, you say:

“He who keeps the proper measure of natural concupiscence makes good use of a good thing; he who does not keep the proper measure makes bad use of a good thing. But whoever, out of love for holy virginity, has despised even the proper measure itself does not make better use of a good thing; for, relying on his own salvation and strength, he has despised remedies so that he might undertake glorious struggles.”

I answer your words as follows:

He who keeps the proper measure of carnal concupiscence makes good use of an evil thing; he who does not keep the proper measure makes bad use of an evil thing. But whoever, out of love for holy virginity, has despised even the proper measure itself does not make better use of an evil thing; for, relying on divine assistance and gift, he has despised inferior remedies so that he might undertake more glorious struggles. [Note: [Col. 0723] Several manuscripts read *weak remedies*.]

The whole issue between us in this controversy concerns making good use of this thing: whether it is a good or an evil thing.

I would indeed wish that you did not reject the distinguished judges whom, in my earlier books, I showed to have been instructed by sound doctrine and to have delivered judgments on this matter without any partisan zeal. But since, unless you correct yourself, you will undoubtedly prepare an accusation—or, to put it more mildly, a criticism—of them also, I shall use you as judge against yourself, in favor of my position over yours: not somewhere else, but in your own book; not in another passage, but in this very passage.

For you said that “holy virginity, relying on its own salvation and strength, despised remedies so that it might undertake glorious struggles.”

I ask: what remedies did it despise?

You will answer: marriage.

I ask: against what illness are these remedies necessary? A remedy takes its name from *mederi*, that is, from healing or treating.

Thus we both see what the remedy of marriage is. Why do you praise the illness of sexual desire, by which you see that one reaches death unless either the restraint of continence or the remedy of marriage resists it?

I have already dealt with this above, where you most eloquently placed conjugal chastity between those who indulge and those who are continent, saying that it “with modest hands both comforts those who are inflamed and praises those who do not need such a remedy.”

I therefore repeat what I said: hear again what I answered you there briefly and clearly:

“When I say that this concupiscence is an illness, why do you deny it, while nevertheless admitting that a necessary remedy exists for it? If you acknowledge the remedy, acknowledge the illness; if you deny the illness, deny the remedy. I beg you, yield at last to the truth speaking even through your own mouth: no one provides a remedy for health” (above, no. 29).

### 43

What are the “glorious struggles” of holy virgins, as you call them, except that they are not conquered by evil but conquer evil through the good?

I preferred to call their struggles not glorious but more glorious. For conjugal chastity too possesses a palm—although a lesser one—from the subjugation of this evil.

It too wages war against carnal concupiscence, lest it exceed the bounds of the marriage bed. It wages war lest it interrupt the appointed time for prayer agreed upon by the spouses. And if this conjugal chastity has such strength, and is so great a gift of God, that it does what the marriage contract prescribes, it wages an even stronger battle within the marriage bed itself, lest it touch even the body of the spouse beyond what is sufficient for begetting children.

Such chastity does not use women who are menstruating or pregnant, nor women of an age at which it is certain that they can no longer conceive. Nor is it overcome altogether by the desire for intercourse; rather, it relaxes only when the result of procreation is hoped for.

If something takes place between spouses that is not indeed against nature but nevertheless exceeds the limit of the marriage contract, the Apostle finds it pardonable (1 Cor. 7:6), because the boundary of marital intercourse is by no means exceeded. Yet, so that even that boundary may not be exceeded, the evil of concupiscence is resisted.

It is so great an evil that chastity must resist it through struggle lest it cause harm.

### 44

And you, unless I am mistaken, are engaged in this struggle. Because you think that you are fighting faithfully, you are afraid of being defeated.

By whom, I ask you, are you afraid of being defeated? By good or by evil? Or perhaps you are afraid of being defeated by me in such a way that you continue to deny evil and praise as good the thing by which you fear being defeated?

Placed between two adversaries, you are pressed into great difficulties. You want to defeat me by eloquence and lust by continence. But by fighting against it you confess that it is evil; by praising it you abandon the good of truth.

Yet I defeat you—both the conqueror and the praiser of evil—by placing you before a judge who is no one other than yourself.

You want to conquer concupiscence by fighting it, but me by praising it. I answer: “Let the one who praises it be defeated; let the one who fights judge.” [Note: [Col. 0724] Two Vatican manuscripts read *let him conquer*.]

If it is evil, why does he praise it? If it is good, why does he fight it? But if it is neither good nor evil, why does he praise it? Why does he fight it?

As long, therefore, as you are a fighter against sexual desire, you will be a judge on my behalf against yourself.

Or will you perhaps cease fighting against sexual desire lest you be defeated in this struggle that you have with me, saying to yourself, “It is better not to fight than to show by fighting that the thing I praise is evil”?

Do not do this, I beg you. For what am I, whom you so greatly desire to defeat? Let truth defeat you instead, so that you may defeat sexual desire.

For if you cease fighting against it, you are defeated, you will be defeated, and dragged into every impurity. Since that is a dreadful evil, it will not help you even toward what you desire. For even then you are defeated by me—or rather, by the very truth that I proclaim.

But as a praiser of concupiscence and a conqueror of concupiscence, you are defeated even by your own judgment, since you praise the evil whose defeat you glory in.

If, however, you cease fighting so that the tongue of the one who praises will not be defeated by the struggle of the fighter, I shall defeat you as a captive of concupiscence and a deserter of continence—not by my judgment now, but by the judgment of wisdom.

### 45

Our case, then, is finished.

However much you praise the concupiscence of the flesh, as long as you fight against it, you see how truly the Apostle John spoke of it—and of it alone—that it “is not from the Father” (1 John 2:16).

For if, as you say, “he who does not keep its proper measure makes bad use of a good thing,” then it is itself a good thing even in those who use it badly.

What, then, is that thing which is not from the Father? Do you intend to praise it too, however you understand it?

Moreover, if it is itself evil, where will it be? When will it be? Since, according to you, even when someone uses it badly, it will be a good thing; and it will not be evil itself, but the person who makes bad use of a good thing will be evil.

Accordingly, John spoke in vain when he said that the concupiscence of the flesh is not from the Father. For you contend that it is good and therefore from the Father, even when someone uses it badly, because he is making bad use of a good thing.

Nor will you be able to say, “When it is moderate, it is from the Father; when it is immoderate, it is not from the Father,” because even then, according to you, it is a good thing, which an evil person uses badly.

But you will be freed from these difficulties if you believe not your tongue but your struggle.

Continence is from the Father; concupiscence would not be fought down unless it were not from the Father. Therefore, this very thing against which, if you live continently, you fight fiercely is not from the Father.

For you would not fight against it unless it resisted you. Nor would it resist you while you were doing what is given and loved by the Father, if it were from the Father.

### 46

From this evil, and together with this evil, the human being is born—a good work of God, but not without the evil which the origin of generation transmits and the grace of regeneration heals.

Accordingly, I rightly said:

“The good of marriage cannot be accused on account of the original evil drawn from it, just as the evil of adultery and fornication cannot be excused on account of the natural good born from it” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence* 1.1).

I called natural good what you yourself praise together with me; I called original evil that whose movements you oppose together with me, and whose praises you use against me in your struggle.

What you were born as is not evil; rather, evil is what you were born with, and against which you fight spiritually because you have been reborn.

What you were born as belongs to God’s creation and to the fertility of your parents. But that against which you fight because you have been reborn belongs to the transgression which the devil’s cunning sowed, from which Christ’s grace has freed you.

Thus formerly you made good use of this evil in your spouse; now you oppose it within yourself. You are no longer guilty because of it, as you were when born, but you have not been freed from its guilt except by being reborn, so that, redeemed, you may be able to reign with Christ. [Col. 0726]

That is, unless this heresy causes you to perish with the devil. Rather—and this is what we desire—you should confess the evil against which you wage war, so that it may not be separated from you as though it were another nature, but you may be healed completely in every respect and rejoice in perpetual peace. [Note: [Col. 0726] Perhaps: “not separated from you.”]

### 47

I am therefore not “like an apothecary,” as you say, “who promised an animal that would eat itself.” [Note: [Col. 0726] Five Vatican and two Gallican manuscripts read *had eaten itself*.]

But beware lest this bestial movement against which you appear to struggle in your flesh, just as it has perverted you when praised, later consume you when relaxed.

For I did not say, as you falsely accuse me, that “marriage is both a great good and a great evil,” as though the statement itself consumed itself in that fashion. Rather, I said that in one human being there is a good nature and an evil defect.

You yourself certainly acknowledge this in adulterers: you do not disapprove of their nature on account of their defect, nor approve their defect on account of their nature.

I said that marriage is good, from which you were born; but that evil was drawn not from marriage, but from a corrupted origin, against which you wage war because you have been reborn.

### 48

It is ridiculous that you say I am “walking along the roads of Epicurus and cutting all the reins by which desires are restrained.”

What if I were praising bodily pleasure? You do this quite eloquently, which Epicurus did crudely and without refinement—as though you were his opponent merely because he did not know how to express elegantly what you say.

Again, as I understand it, you will have to labor to show yourself both a praiser of pleasure and not an Epicurean. But do not labor; I shall free you from this concern.

You are not an Epicurean because he placed the whole of human good in bodily pleasure, whereas you try to place a large part of human good in virtue—a virtue whose true nature, that is, true piety, you do not know.

For God said to humanity, “Behold, piety is wisdom” (Job 28:28). [Note: [Col. 0726] Five Vatican and three Gallican manuscripts: “The man of God said, ‘Behold, piety,’ etc.”] And from where does wisdom come to humanity unless He gives it, of whom it is written, “The Lord makes the blind wise” (Ps. 145:8), and of whom it is also read, “If anyone lacks wisdom, let him ask God” (James 1:5)?

But if you are not an Epicurean because you have taken from him some portion in praising pleasure, how much less am I, since regarding the pleasure of the flesh I think what Ambrose thinks (*On Paradise*, ch. 12, and the book *On Philosophy* cited above, book 2, nos. 13, 15): namely, that it is hostile to righteousness, and that a human being formed through the pleasure of concupiscence enters into the contagion of sins before being born.

As for our conduct and how we live, it is evident to those with whom we live.

What is at issue now is Catholic doctrine and faith. Do not let the faithlessness of one who has deserted the truth exist in you. For your accusation does not frighten me, like the speech of a censor.

I confess that I teach people what I learned in the Apostolic Letters: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

I confess that in the presence of the people and together with the people of God I beat my breast and truthfully say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12).

Do not insult us on this account. You are heretics precisely because these things displease you. We place our hope in God’s true mercy; you place yours in your false virtue.

You say that God’s grace is given according to our merits—which Pelagius himself would have been condemned for by Catholic bishops, had he not condemned it. [Note: [Col. 0727] See *The Proceedings against Pelagius*, nos. 30, 13.]

We, however, confess that grace is given freely and is therefore called grace, and that all the merits of the saints derive from it, as the Apostle says: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (1 Cor. 15:10). [Note: [Col. 0727] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain editions: “By the grace of God I am what I am.” Thus also the Vulgate. M.]

For this reason you mock us and despise us with uplifted necks. “We have become a reproach to those who abound, and a contempt to the proud” (Ps. 123:4). “You have confounded the plan of the poor, because the Lord is his hope” (Ps. 13:6). [Note: [Col. 0727] Am. Er. and manuscripts: *You have confounded*.]

### 49

Yet in the matter with which we are now concerned, I do not see why you say that I “cut all the reins by which desires are restrained,” since I decree that all desires must be restrained by every virtue according to the grace of God given to human beings.

But I ask you whether these desires which you declare must be restrained, and accuse me of relaxing, are good or evil.

For I suppose they are not the desires of horses or of any animals other than ourselves [Note: [Col. 0727] Thus Am. and the manuscripts. Erasmus and Louvain: “of any animals whatsoever.”], but our desires. Therefore, evil desires exist within us, and we restrain them by living well.

You accuse me of cutting the reins by which not good but evil desires are restrained. [Note: [Col. 0727] The manuscripts omit “not good but.”] One of these is the concupiscence of the flesh, from which and with which infants are born, and on account of which they are reborn.

I say that chaste married people make good use of this evil, while adulterers make bad use of it. You, on the contrary, say that adulterers make bad use of this good, while chaste married people make good use of it. We both say that continence makes better use of not using it; but I say it is an evil, while you say it is a good.

Accordingly, although our conscience is known to God and our conduct also to the human beings among whom we live, we both profess continence. If we practice what we profess, then we certainly both restrain this concupiscence; both fight against its resistance; and, if we make progress, both conquer it.

The difference is this: I say that I restrain evil, while you say that you restrain good. I say that evil resists me; you, that good resists you. I fight against evil; you, against good. I desire to conquer evil; you, good.

From this it may be thought that you are more intent on stimulating this concupiscence by praising it than on restraining it by continence.

### 50

You profess that through continence you undertake glorious struggles. Against what, I ask? What will you say except that you struggle against the concupiscence of the flesh?

But is it a friend or an adversary? You will answer that it is surely an adversary. “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh; for these oppose each other,” as the Apostle testifies (Gal. 5:17).

Perhaps, then, you pretend to praise it if you do not pretend to fight it. For I do not see how you can sincerely do both at once: praise it as a friend and conquer it as an enemy.

We believe one of these claims, but choose which one we are to believe. If you fight sincerely, you do not praise sincerely. But if you speak straightforwardly in your praise, you are playing at war. [Note: [Col. 0728] Several manuscripts: *you conclude in battle*; the Floriacensis manuscript: *you are concluded in battle*.]

Since I am not your enemy—for the evil that dwells in your flesh is your enemy—although I especially desire you both to condemn this evil by sound doctrine and to conquer it by holy living, nevertheless, of these two things, one of which you may be thought to do sincerely and the other to pretend, I would rather you falsely praise concupiscence than falsely conquer it.

For it is more tolerable for your tongue to lie than your life; more tolerable for your opinion to be feigned than your continence.

You are pretending to praise it in order to oppose my opinion, if you are not pretending to be chaste in order to oppose your own concupiscence. Thus it will happen that you will no longer falsely speak against me if you truly wage war against sexual desire.

But whether you pretend to one of these things or to both—which I do not know how you could do sincerely, that is, without any pretense, both fighting against what you praise and praising what you fight against—I nevertheless, believing the more lenient possibility about you, deal with you as though you were a conqueror of sexual desire.

I do not call marriage evil, but say that it makes good use of an evil; whereas you say that one makes good use of a good thing, asserting that the concupiscence of the flesh is good, although by conquering it within yourself you prove it to be evil.

How married people, even those who make good use of it, wage war against it, I have already discussed above.

### Chapter XXII
### 51

Since these things are so, marriage is good insofar as it is marriage, and a human being, whether born from marriage or from adultery, is good insofar as he is a human being; for insofar as he is a human being, he is God’s work. Yet because he is generated with and from that evil which marital chastity uses well, it is necessary for him to be released through regeneration from the bond of that evil.

Why, then, do you ask me “where original evil is found,” when lust itself speaks to you more truly within you—the lust against which you fight—than you yourself do when you praise it? Why do you ask “how man is under the devil, whom God made?” How, then, is he in death, which God did not make?

“You ask,” you say, “what does the devil recognize as his own there, if he himself created neither what was made nor that from which it was made?” Clearly, what was made is man; that from which he was made is human seed. Both are good. The devil created neither of these, but he himself sowed the defect of the seed. He does not recognize there his own good, because that which we both praise is not his; but he recognizes his own evil, against which we both fight. Nor is that rightly praised by either of us against which both of us fight.

Consider carefully how you ask me “among so many good things, whence comes evil in little children,” while remaining silent about what I set down in the same book to which you are replying, and even among the very words to which you are now replying: what the Apostle says, “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so death passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12). [Col. 0729]

You do not want people to hear or read this at this point, where it was especially necessary, lest they recognize their own faith and reject your argument.

### Chapter XXIII

#### 52

You say that I defined the matter as follows: “If a man is born from fornication, he is not guilty; if from marriage, he is not innocent.” This, however, is an excessive and obvious slander. Rather, I defined that a human being, wherever he is born, is—according to the Catholic faith, which the fathers defended with the greatest clarity against you before you were born—innocent with respect to no personal sin, and guilty by original sin. Yet the substance of nature, whose author is God, is good even in great sinners; they are evil on account of their sins, including their own personal sins, which they have added to that evil with which they were born.

[Note: Am. and Er. read, “and that the infant is innocent through personal [sin].” The Louvain editors corrected the text on the authority of the manuscripts.]

Why, then, would I fear being charged, as you say, “with attributing the sins of all parents to all their children”? Even if this were true—not with regard to those already living according to the choice of their own will, but with regard to those being born—nature’s substance would in no way be evil, since its author is God.

[Note: Several manuscripts read “using [the choice]” rather than “living.”] Rather, evil would consist in the defects present in it, against which you too, to use your own words, “conduct glorious battles.”

#### 53

Just as, when adulterers beget children, “a human being is born from the power of the seeds, not from the disgrace of the crimes,” as you say, so, when married people beget children, a human being is born from the power of the seeds, not from the honor of marriage. Or, if in the first case both are involved, then both are involved here as well.

The fruit of marriage, insofar as marriage itself is concerned, is not the generation of human beings—for they can also be born from adulterers—but the orderly reception of children.

Why, then, is “the falsest part of my opinion” the statement that “the good of marriage cannot be accused because of the original evil that is drawn from it,” when married people who used well the evil against which you fight were the means by which you were born, and that evil drawn from them would have held you guilty unless you had been born again?

Thus married people who use the evil well are not to be accused, while children must be regenerated in order to be freed from the evil. For if the good of marriage were nothing other than the good use of something good, it would indeed be astonishing that evil should be drawn from it. But since the good of marriage is the good use of something evil, what is astonishing if from that very evil—of which the goodness of marriage makes good use—there is drawn the evil that is original sin?

What is astonishing is that, although the Apostles were “the good fragrance of Christ,” good was drawn from them and evil was also drawn from them. “To some we are the fragrance of life unto life, and to others the fragrance of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2:15–16), although that fragrance was not the use of evil but of good. They were the good fragrance of Christ precisely because they made good use of Christ’s grace.

What you said, therefore, is false: “If evil is drawn from it, it can be accused and cannot be excused.” Original evil is drawn from it, while good is also drawn from it—namely, the orderly propagation of children. Nor is that evil drawn from it because marriage is good, but because among the goods of marriage there is also the use of evil.

[Col. 0730]

For the marital union was not instituted, as you think, on account of the lust of the flesh, but on account of the good that is made from this evil. Indeed, this good would have come about without this evil if no one had sinned. Now, therefore, it cannot exist without this evil, but it is not for that reason itself evil.

Conversely, no evil can exist without some good, but it is not for that reason good. God’s work is good in nature, yet an evil will cannot exist without it. Accordingly, just as adultery cannot exist without the good of nature, but is not for that reason good, so marriage cannot exist without the evil of lust, but is not for that reason evil.

Therefore, even if it is granted that “every cause of evil is without good,” this has no bearing on marriage, which is not the cause of evil. Marriage did not produce the evil of lust; it found it already present, so that it might use it well.

### Chapter XXIV

#### 54

“That thing does not escape punishment,” you say, “which, by participation in it, also draws other things into guilt.”

If you think this about the lust of the flesh, you are not thinking absurdly. Faithful married people make good use of this evil, and those who are generated from it draw guilt from it; for this reason they too must be regenerated.

That evil does not escape punishment. Its punishment is that, together with those who have been generated, it is punished if they are not regenerated; but in those who have been regenerated, it is consumed when they have been healed in every respect.

“If original evil is also drawn from marriage,” you say, “then the marital union is the cause of evil.” What if someone else were to say: “If an evil will is drawn from nature, then the constitution of nature is the cause of evil”? Would that not be utterly false?

So too with what you yourself have said. Although original evil is not drawn from marriage but from carnal lust—the very evil against which you also fight—married people make good use of that evil if they unite solely for the sake of procreation. And if the sin that passed into all human beings had not occurred beforehand, there would certainly not have been that evil which they used well; yet they would still have united in order to beget children.

#### 55

As for the trees—good and evil—and how greatly you have gone astray, I think I demonstrated sufficiently in the first book of this work (chapter 8, sections 38–41). Since you repeat the same knots that have already been untied, there is no need to dwell on what is superfluous.

You ask “through what means sin is found in little children,” and you enumerate many good things while remaining silent about the evil against which you fight. Yet by remaining silent, you cry out.

“Parents,” you say, “who by their union made the cause of sin, are rightly condemnable; by whose labor it came about that the devil attained dominion over human beings.”

[Col. 0731]

You can say this even to God himself—not, I say, because he creates human beings who draw original sin, since you deny that—but because he nourishes and clothes countless impious people, including those whom he knows will remain in their impiety. If he had not done this, the devil would not have human slaves.

But perhaps you will say that, in feeding them, God has regard only to the good whose author he himself is—namely, that they are human beings. In the same way, then, parents, in begetting children, have regard only to the good that they are human beings, especially since they do not know what sort of people they will become.

Certainly, as you too confess, there would be no sin if no evil will had preceded it. For original sin also—which we affirm and you deny—would certainly not exist unless nature had been corrupted by the evil will of the first human being.

Yet there would also be no evil will if no nature—whether angelic or human—had preceded it. Are you going to call God the cause of sins because his will is the cause of mutable natures?

Therefore, just as it is not charged against God, when he creates, that rational natures turn away from the good, but rather that they are good, so parents who beget children and make good use of the evil of lust should not be charged with the fact that children are born with that evil, but with the fact that they are good.

Nor is it the case, as you think, that “the origin of those who are born is derived from the devil,” insofar as they are human beings, “because the origin of sin is said to be from the devil, without which no human being is born.” For just as the origin of death is from the devil, it does not follow that the origin of mortals is from him.

#### 56

You ask for “a crack among so many defenses of innocence through which sin could have entered,” although the Apostle Paul shows you not a crack but a completely open door, saying,

[Note: Am. and the manuscripts read “cracks.”] “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings.”

Suppressing these words, you state your own: “Because the work of the devil is not permitted to pass through the work of God.” Yet human beings are God’s work, while sin is the devil’s work, and the Apostle says that it passed into all.

You cry out, “If nature is through God, original evil cannot be in it,” as though another person might not more religiously cry out: “If nature is through God, no evil can arise from it, and no evil can exist in it.”

Yet this too is false, because evil can arise only from nature, and it cannot have a place unless it is in nature.

I therefore confess that the one who is born, even though he draws original evil with him, is God’s work, since what is God’s work in him is good. God’s work is good even when accompanied by evil—not only in little children but in persons of every age: substance, form, life, sensation, reason, and all the other goods, even in any evil human being.

Who, then, makes a human being live, except the one “in whom we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28)? He accomplishes this by a hidden work of his beneficence, apart from the obvious nourishment by which we are sustained externally.

[Note: The manuscripts read *beneficientiae* (a variant spelling of “beneficence”).]

Therefore, the one who makes a human being live, even when that person’s conduct is vicious, is the one who makes a human being be born, even when his origin has been corrupted.

### Chapter XXV

#### 57

What is this, then, that you do? After setting out other words from my book, you pretend that I said: “There was another institution of marriage before Adam’s sin, one that could have existed without lust, without bodily movement, and without the necessity of the sexes.”

Remove from marriage the lust by which the flesh desires against the spirit; remove the evil against which you fight by conducting glorious battles through the power of continence; and there is no need to remove anything else if you are asking what sort of marriage could have existed before the sin of the first human beings.

[Col. 0732]

For who has ever imagined any marriage without bodily movement and without the necessity of the sexes? But we say that the warfare which chaste people experience within themselves—whether continent or even married—could in no way have existed in paradise before sin.

Marriage itself, therefore, exists even now; but at that time, in begetting children, it would have made use of no evil, whereas now it makes good use of the evil of lust. Through this evil it has not lost its own goods: the fidelity of chastity, the bond of union, and the propagation of offspring.

Then too the husband would have clung to his wife in order to beget children; yet they would not have had in their flesh the movement of turbulent lust, but only the calm movement of the will by which we command the other members.

[Note: Ambrose has “which we hope for in the other members”; Erasmus and Louvain have “which we observe in the other members.” These readings have been corrected according to the manuscripts.]

#### 58

You accuse me of defining “the little children who have filled the world, for whom Christ died, as the devil’s work, born from disease and guilty from their beginning.”

Little children are not substantially the devil’s work; but through the devil’s work they are guilty in their origin. And therefore Christ died also for little children, as you yourself confess, because the blood that was poured out “for the remission of sins” (Matt. 26:28) also pertains to them.

You make them strangers to that blood when you deny that they draw original sin.

Nor should you be angry that I called lust a disease, since you too have confessed that a remedy was provided for it. The origin of little children, from which they were to be born, was in Adam. When that origin had been corrupted and condemned through sin, Christ established another origin for them, from which they would be reborn.

### Chapter XXVI

#### 59

“If, before sin,” you say, “the source from which human beings were to be born was created by God, while the source by which parents would be moved was created by the devil, then sanctity is undoubtedly attributed to those who are born, and guilt to those who beget.”

What do you mean by “the source by which parents would be moved”? If you mean the pious intention of the will by which each person desires to receive children, then this too was instituted by God. But if you mean the disturbance of lust, for which the choice of the will is sufficient neither to arouse nor to remove it, then it is a wound inflicted upon nature through the transgression persuaded by the devil.

Therefore I rightly said: “The sowing of children would have taken place without this disease in the body of that life, without which it cannot now take place in the body of this death” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, chapter 1).

#### 60

You argue that little children belong to the good of fertility, which was instituted by God’s blessing before the disease of lust, and not to the disease of lust itself, since the latter came upon those who sinned afterward; and therefore, you say, sanctity should be attributed to those who are born and guilt to those who beget.

[Note: The printed editions read “which afterward,” whereas the manuscripts read “if it afterward.”]

[Col. 0733]

You do not consider that through that great sin the whole of nature was changed for the worse, from which the offspring was to be derived.

For in this way you could say that Eve alone, and not the other women, ought to have felt the pains of childbirth, since the blessing by which it was said, “Be fruitful and multiply” (Gen. 1:28)—from which children are procreated—was given before the female sex had been punished by that curse.

But if we say this, the reply will certainly be that, just as nature was changed for the worse through that sin, so also it was changed for the worse through the curse—from which original sin and the heavy yoke upon the sons of Adam are drawn.

#### 61

For the Apostle was not, as you argue, describing a Jew placed under the law who said, “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh”; and, “It is not I who do it, but sin dwelling in me”; and, “Evil lies close at hand for me”; and, “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind.”

Rather, he was describing human nature in this corruptible flesh—not established by God’s work with a defect from the beginning, but wounded through the defect of the first human beings, which came from the choice of the will.

Whose voice is this: “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:18, 20, 23–25)? Is it the voice of Jews? Certainly not, but without doubt the voice of Christians.

These higher statements, from which this one was subsequently expressed, are therefore also the words of Christians. For the one who said, “The grace of God will deliver me from the body of this death through Jesus Christ our Lord,” also said, “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind.”

#### 62

But lest you perhaps think that this is the voice of a catechumen still hoping for the bath of regeneration, after which he would have no law of sin resisting the law of his mind in his members—although you yourself, as you wish us to believe about you, conduct glorious battles after the bath of regeneration against this evil of lust through the good of continence—recall what he writes to the Galatians, certainly baptized people.

[Note: Thus the manuscripts; Erasmus and Louvain read, “if we may believe anything you say about yourself.”]

“I say,” he says, “walk by the Spirit, and you will not fulfill the desires of the flesh.” He does not say, “You shall not have them,” because they could not avoid having them; but he says, “You shall not fulfill them”—that is, you shall not complete their works by the consent of the will.

“For the flesh,” he says, “desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these are opposed to one another, so that you do not do the things you wish” (Gal. 5:16–17).

See whether this is not what he says to the Romans: “For I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I do not wish, that I do.”

Then he adds to the Galatians: “But if you are led by the Spirit, you are no longer under the law” (Gal. 5:18).

See whether this is not what he says to the Romans: “It is no longer I who do it”; and, “I delight in the law of God according to the inner human being”; and, “Let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires” (Rom. 7:15, 20, 22; 6:12).

For if one does not obey the desires that must exist in the flesh of sin and in this body of death, then what the Apostle forbids by saying, “You shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh,” will not be fulfilled.

These are the works of which he speaks in succession: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornications, impurities, licentiousness, the service of idols” (Gal. 5:19–20), and the rest.

[Col. 0734]

If, therefore, the desires of the flesh are not consented to, although they occur as movements, they are nevertheless not completed in works.

Accordingly, when the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, so that we do not do what we wish, neither are the desires of the flesh completed, although they occur, nor are our good works completed, although they occur.

For just as the desire of the flesh is completed when the spirit consents to it for evil works—so that it does not desire against the flesh but together with it—so our good works will be completed when the flesh so consents to the spirit that it itself no longer desires against the spirit.

This is what we want when we desire the perfection of righteousness; this is what we must continually intend to will. But because we cannot complete it in this corruptible flesh, he says to the Romans: “To will lies close at hand for me, but to complete the good I do not find” (Rom. 7:18).

Or, as the Greek manuscripts read: “To will lies close at hand for me, but to complete the good does not”—that is, “completing the good does not lie close at hand for me.”

He does not say “to do,” but “to complete the good.” For “to do good” is not to follow one’s lusts (Ecclus. 18:30); but “to complete the good” is not to desire.

What he says to the Galatians—“You shall not fulfill the desires of the flesh”—is therefore, conversely, what he says to the Romans: “To complete the good I do not find.”

For neither are those desires completed in evil when the consent of our will does not accompany them, nor is our will completed in good so long as the movement of those desires, to which we do not consent, remains.

This very conflict, in which even baptized people struggle as in an arena, when the flesh desires against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh—where the spirit performs a good work by not consenting to evil desire, but does not complete it because it does not remove the evil desires themselves; and where the flesh produces an evil desire, but does not complete it because, since the spirit does not consent, it too does not reach the condemned works—this conflict, then, is shown briefly in the words addressed to the Romans. He says: “Therefore I myself, with my mind, serve the law of God, but with my flesh, the law of sin” (Rom. 7:25).

[Note: Some manuscripts omit “the whole wonderfully”; others retain only “wonderfully.”]

[Note: The Louvain editors deleted the sentence “This we must continually intend to will,” although it appears in all the books. In Ambrose, Erasmus, and three Gallican manuscripts, an inserted gloss was formerly preferred: “Direct this intention—or intend—not to complete the desires of the flesh, and I do not find the good completed; this we must continually intend to will.”]

#### 63

If this, then, is the condition in this body of death—which certainly did not exist in paradise, in that body of life—it is undoubtedly clear enough from where little children draw the obligation of sin when they are born carnally: an obligation that is not dissolved until they are reborn spiritually.

They do not draw it from the work by which God made human nature, but from the wound inflicted upon human nature by its enemy.

The enemy is not, according to the Manichaeans, a being springing from an evil nature that God did not create; he is an angel who was once good through God’s work and became evil through his own work.

[Col. 0735]

By first wounding himself he cast himself down, so that, having been shattered, he might shatter others and inflict, through the evil persuasion of transgression, the wound from which the human race limps—even in those who walk in God’s way.

#### 64

Yet you are angry with me because I said: “This lust, which shameless people shamelessly praise, is a shameful thing” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, section 1).

In your anger you say many things even more shamelessly, exalting yourselves: you claim that you defend, “as though agreeing with the sacred Scriptures and the most certain reason, the proposition that evil is not in nature, in order to incite human beings to the pursuit of virtues; impressing upon them that no summit is so lofty in virtue that a faithful mind cannot reach it with God’s help; and for this reason saying that there is no necessity of evil in the flesh, so that each person, nobly created, may be ashamed to live basely, and thus shame may confront shameful sloth through the commendation of innate nobility.”

You said other things of this sort, which you proclaimed eloquently in your preaching, while lowering us in opposition and saying “that there can be no doubt that the overthrow of holiness, the defilement of chastity, and the corruption of morals belong to—or rather exist within—our doctrines.”

You add that I will not deny this, since, as you say, “I pour the filth of evil conduct into the discredit of nature in order to remove fear from sinners. I console their obscenities by insulting the Apostles and all the saints, because I frequently recall that the Apostle Paul, that golden vessel, said, ‘I do not do the good that I wish, but the evil that I hate, that I do’” (Rom. 7:15), and other things of this sort.

[Note: Here the Louvain editors added “who.”]

#### 65

[Col. 0736]

Yet while praising you and accusing us, you fight against the evil of lust, and by fighting confess what you deny in speech.

You want to appear to have ascended the summit of virtue, so that on that very summit, where you think you have escaped, you fight as though in a fortress against the lust that pursues you; and however high your position may be, you do not cease to battle the enemy within.

Nor are you ashamed to praise the lust which, if it conquers you, will unquestionably destroy you more completely, against the one who seeks you even when you have been destroyed by its victory—especially since at the end of your own book you say that “my intention is not otherwise directed than toward waging war against virtues, swearing allegiance to the sacraments of vices, striving with every trick and fury for the destruction of the city of God, and terrifying those who resist disgrace by despair of attaining chastity; for I falsely claim that the powers of obscene lust are so great that reason cannot govern or restrain it, and that not even the legion of the Apostles could resist it.”

In saying these things about me, you yourself are utterly lying. For I do not wage war against virtues; rather, insofar as I am helped, I wage war against vices, and I proclaim that war must be waged against them.

If you do the same, why do you praise what you fight against? How can I believe that you conquer enemies by virtue when you do not dare to attack them in words?

If we both conquer lust, why do we not both condemn it? If you boast that you conquer it by continence, why do you refuse to condemn it in your judgment?

You say that I falsely claim that the powers of lust are so great that reason cannot govern or restrain it.

Look: I do not say that the powers of lust are so great that human reason, kindled and aided by God, cannot govern or restrain it. But why do you deny that it is evil when, if it is not restrained, it kills?

Look: with whatever voice I possess, I proclaim what you assert that I deny: that the legion of the Apostles resisted lust—certainly lust that resisted them.

[Note: Louvain reads “fighting” rather than “resisting.”]

You accuse us of having done this to the Apostles and, as though indignant at the insult, slander us for it. Why, then, do you adorn with praises both the enemy of those Apostles and your own enemy?

Who could defend the one whom a legion of Apostles resisted, except an enemy of the Apostles?

#### 66

Does lust deserve to have both friendship and war with you, so that you conquer it within yourself while defending it against me?

Your war is hidden; your friendship is visible. From what is visible, you make what is hidden suspect.

What do you want us to believe about the war you wage secretly, when we see your friendship openly? How do you want us to think that you fight against the sting of lust when you fill books with praise of lust?

But look: I overcome my suspicion. I believe that you conquer what you praise; yet I grieve that you praise what you conquer.

From this evil, then, and with this evil—which we too believe you conquer—a human being is generated, whom you deny to be saved through regeneration.

For married people make good use of this evil, which continent people make better use of by not using it. Moreover, if it is evil by which the flesh desires against the spirit—and, as you confess, a legion of Apostles resisted this evil—then married people who use it undoubtedly make good use not of something good but of something evil.

[Note: A Victorinus manuscript reads “that the flesh” rather than “by which the flesh.”]

From this evil, therefore, and with this evil, children are generated and must be regenerated, so that they may be freed from evil.

Their parents too were born guilty of this original evil, even if they were freed from that guilt by being reborn.

What, then, would we expect them to beget—not from the source from which they were reborn, but from the source from which they were born—except what they themselves were when born?

They are therefore guilty, because they too were born guilty; and those who beget from what they were born from could not generate anything other than what they themselves were born from.

But from what they were reborn, they were freed from the guilt with which they were born. Accordingly, those whom parents, freed from guilt, generated are likewise to be freed by the same regeneration.

[Note: Am., Er., two Vatican manuscripts, and several Gallican manuscripts read, “whom they generated, freed from guilt.”]

For they were born guilty from that evil which the reborn use well, so that those who are to be born may be regenerated.

If you do not fight against this evil, believe those who do fight. If you do fight, acknowledge it as your adversary. Do not, by praising the disease, make a friend of the one whom you experience as an enemy when you fight against it.

## Book Four

[Col. 0737]

[Col. 0737]

Augustine replies to the second book of Julian, examining each of his statements, as he did in refuting the first book, passing over in silence only those matters that contain no problem relevant to the question. Here he chiefly proves two things: first, that the virtues of unbelievers are not true virtues; and second, that lust is evil, demonstrating this even from the statements of the pagans, while his adversary provides the occasion. Around the middle of the book he briefly explains in passing how grace is not given according to merits and yet should not be referred to fate, and how what the Apostle says—that God wills all human beings to be saved—is to be understood.

### Chapter I

#### 1

Let us now examine the remaining points from the beginning of your second volume, by which you strive to refute my book. As we have decided, we shall omit those things that do not create problems requiring our attention to solve, lest by lingering over superfluous matters we discourage the reader from the arduous task through the very length of the work.

[Note: Against the manuscripts, the Louvain editors changed “we must devote attention, and” to “we need not devote attention, lest.”]

In the preceding book we dealt sufficiently with the matter so that those who judge rightly might see that, although the true and good God is the creator of human beings, and marriage is good—marriage which he both instituted through the condition and union of the two sexes and blessed with the gift of fertility—nevertheless the lust of the flesh is evil, since through it the flesh desires against the spirit.

We showed that marital chastity makes good use of this evil, while holy continence makes better use of it by not using it. We also showed that this evil has not been mingled with us from some other substance that God did not create, as the Manichaean madness claims, but arose and was transmitted through the disobedience of one human being, and is to be expiated and healed through the obedience of one human being.

Through its obligation, due punishment entangles the one who is born; through undeserved grace, it releases the one who is reborn.

By praising this evil against me, my adversary, you appear to be my opponent; but by conquering it within yourself, you are my witness. If you do not conquer it, you are your own enemy.

Since I therefore think that I answered you sufficiently in your first book, although the whole case was already concluded there, nevertheless, lest we appear unable to answer your other three books, consider also in these how empty your statements have been.

#### 2

You exult over words taken from my book (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, section 3), because “as the Apostle bears witness,” I said that “marital chastity is a gift of God” (1 Cor. 7:7).

You act as though, for that reason, the Apostle praised the evil that you praise—the evil through which the flesh desires against the spirit (Gal. 5:17), the evil of which marital chastity makes good use, as I already demonstrated in the preceding book.

It is therefore no small gift of God that this evil is restrained so that it is not released toward anything unlawful, but serves only the generation of children who are to be regenerated.

Its impulse is not moderated by itself. For it abstains from nothing unlawful if the members serve its desire. Accordingly, it is not the movement itself that is praised—the movement whose motion is restless—but the one who restrains it and uses it well.

#### 3

[Col. 0738]

When faithful married people make good use of this evil, from whose guilt they have been released by the Savior’s gift, then surely those who are born from it are born through the same Creator’s gift—not, as you accuse us, “prepared for the kingdom of the devil,” but rather to be rescued from him and transferred into the kingdom of the Only-Begotten.

For this is, and must be, the intention of pious married people: that generation may prepare the way for regeneration.

If this evil, which parents experience within themselves—the evil against which, to use your own words, “a legion of Apostles resisted” (above, book 3, section 65)—did not pertain to children, they would certainly be born without it.

But now, since they are born with it, why are you surprised that they are reborn because of it, so that they may be released from its obligation—either snatched from this life after being freed from it, or liberated in this life to fight against it, and rewarded as victors at the end?

[Note: At this point the Louvain editors added “they are reborn,” without authority from any ancient books.]

#### 4

Which of us ever supposed that “the use of married people was discovered by the devil”? Who believed that “the intercourse of bodies came about through the evil of transgression,” when without these things marriage could not exist at all?

But the evil which they use well would not exist if no one had sinned. If I said this, bring it against me so that I may clear myself. For if you bring against me what I did not say, when will we ever finish?

#### 5

You think it follows that “the gift of God causes harm if a human being is born with evil,” since “no one is born except by God’s gift.”

Listen, then, and understand: God’s gift harms no one, by which each person exists and lives. But the evil of lust can exist only in one who exists and lives.

Therefore evil can exist in God’s gift, to be healed by another gift of God. Thus, in a human being who exists and lives by God’s gift, there can be an evil contracted through generation and healed through regeneration.
