For certainly no infant would be born with a demon if he were not born; yet it does not follow that his being born is itself the cause of this evil.

He is therefore born by God’s gift, but with a demon by God’s judgment—certainly hidden, but is it therefore unjust?

### Chapter II

#### 6

When I said “even the good of marriage, if it is not possessed, must be requested from the Lord” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, section 3)—and from whom else would it be necessary?—you thought that I was saying that “one must pray for the power to have intercourse.”

But I said that one must ask God for marital chastity itself, in which intercourse is not a free use but a lawful measure.

If a man cannot have intercourse, he should rather not seek a wife. For when the apostolic judgment says, “If he cannot contain himself, let him marry” (1 Cor. 7:9), it intends marriage to be a remedy—which you yourself have confessed—against the disease of lust, although you refuse to confess what you admit when you acknowledge the remedy (above, book 3, sections 29 and 42).

[Col. 0739]

This remedy does not consist in making lust exist when it is absent, but in preventing it, when its movement is unbridled, from snatching a person toward unlawful acts.

This too belongs to the kind of petition expressed in the Lord’s Prayer: “Do not bring us into temptation,” since, as the Apostle James says, “each person is tempted by his own desire” (James 1:14).

The same matter is addressed by the words, “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13). Married people say this concerning this matter so that, while they are free from evil in mind, they may make good use of the evil they have in the flesh. For they know that “good does not dwell in their flesh” (Rom. 7:18), and they ask that afterward, when every corruptibility has been healed, no evil may remain in them for their use.

Why do you triumph as though over a defeated enemy? Conquer within yourself the one whom you praise. For my victory over you is secure, since that evil fights with you.

You will not dare to say that the one who speaks the truth is defeated by the one who speaks falsely. I say that lust, against which you fight, is evil; you say that it is good. But your struggle confesses it to be evil, while your tongue falsely calls it good, adding one lie to another when you assert that I too have called it good.

For I would not call the lust of the flesh good, which the Apostle John said is not from the Father (1 John 2:16). Rather, I said that marital chastity is good, since it resists the evil of lust so that, when it is stirred, it does not snatch a person toward unlawful acts.

7. Yet knowing how empty your argument has been, you say that you “strike at,” as you put it, “the other side of my definition,” and you ask: “If genital heat, the servant of conjugal honor, is restrained from immoderate outbursts both by the zeal of the faithful and by the power of the gift, and is not extinguished by grace but curbed, it is commendable in its kind and in its measure, and is accused only for its excesses.”” In saying this, you do not consider that intercourse between spouses for the sake of generation is therefore a good worthy of praise because by it a permitted limit is set to the evil of desiring. Why should what you admit must be curbed not rather be called evil? Why, I ask, must it be curbed, unless so that it may do no harm, unless so that it may not be released toward the illicit things it desires? And surely the desire for evil is evil, even if one does not consent to it, until we reach the place where it is no longer present. We must therefore consider not what good is made from the concupiscence of the flesh, but what evil the concupiscence itself does. For conjugal chastity curbs a concupiscence that eagerly seeks pleasure, whether from what is illicit or from what is permitted: it restrains it from the illicit and allows it toward the permitted. This is good, but it is not the good of the concupiscence itself; it is the good of the person who makes right use of it. But what concupiscence itself does—burning indifferently toward what is permitted or what is illicit—is plainly evil. Conjugal chastity therefore makes good use of this evil; virginal continence makes better use of it by not using it.

8. “If,” you say, “genital heat could naturally be evil, it ought to be eradicated, not regulated.” Observe how you did not wish to say what you had said above, “curbed,” but preferred “regulated.” You sensed that no one would curb it except one who resisted it; and therefore, by changing the word, you admitted through the very fear of doing so that it is an evil which resists the good. You also call it “genital heat” because you are ashamed to call it lust, or, as divine Scripture commonly calls it, the concupiscence of the flesh.

[Note: Some manuscripts read *Appellasti* (“you called”) rather than *Appellas* (“you call”).]

Speak, then, in this way: “If the concupiscence of the flesh could naturally be evil, it ought to be eradicated, not regulated.” Thus even the slower-witted among those who know Latin can understand what you are saying. But you speak as though all who marry for this reason—that they cannot endure the labor of continence by which one resists this evil—would not prefer to eradicate it if they could, and therefore prefer to make good use of it rather than not use it at all, which would be better. But if, in this body of death, this evil is necessary for married people because the good of generation cannot occur without it, then let the continent eradicate the concupiscence of the flesh. You yourself—you who are speaking and yet do not attend to what you say—eradicate lust from your members. It is not necessary for you either; nor are its desires good, for if you consent or yield to them, you will perish.

9. Furthermore, if there is in you an evil which you resist, attack, and utterly vanquish when you conquer it, then you do not make better use of this evil—the evil of which those in whom you contend that it is good make good use. Here you are plainly either lying or mistaken. Here you are plainly either lying or mistaken.

[Note: Two Vatican manuscripts and three Gallican manuscripts, as well as the margin of the edition of Amerbach, read: “of which evil they do not make use.”]

[Note: The Louvain editors deleted *hoc* (“this”) as superfluous; it nevertheless occurs in almost all the other books and properly refers to “good.”]

For you will surely not say that lust is good in married people but evil in holy virgins or the continent. We already have your position, where you said: “Whoever keeps the measure of natural concupiscence makes good use of the good; whoever does not keep the measure makes bad use of the good; but whoever, out of love for holy virginity, has rejected even the measure itself does not make better use of the good. For,” you say, “in confidence in his salvation and strength he has rejected the remedies, so that he might undertake glorious contests.”

By these words of yours you plainly declare that the concupiscence of the flesh is this same thing in both groups, that is, in married people and in the continent.

[Note: Two manuscripts read *eas* (“them,” feminine) instead of *eos* (“them,” masculine) in the subsequent reference to those who undertake glorious contests.] What married people make good use of, and the continent make better use of by not using, you call good; I call it evil. But in holy virgins and the continent the concupiscence of the flesh reveals itself to be evil, against which you admit that they “undertake glorious contests.” Therefore, plainly, they are not making better use of the good, but of the evil. Married people, then, who use it are likewise not making good use of the good, but of the evil.

Thus the whole controversy—if any controversy remains—comes down to this: whether in those who have vowed continence to God the concupiscence of the flesh about which we are arguing is good or evil. Whichever of these two is found in them will also appear in married people, since married people make good use of what the continent make better use of by not using it.

Gather, then, all the strength of your sharp mind and unblushing face, and dare to answer, if you can, that this is good which, as you confessed in your previous book, “the legion of the Apostles resisted”—reproaching me, of course, because I had said that “the forces of lust are so great that not even the legion of the Apostles resisted it.” Yet this rather serves my case, because against the evil that you call good a legion resisted—not a legion of ordinary saints, but even the Apostles themselves.

Who would believe that so much could be permitted to this evil that it would procure for itself a praiser even from among its own conquerors? Far be it from us to suppose that any of the ancients, whether Apostles or other saints, was such. Yet it is astonishing that there should be even some new heretic who, in inexplicable fashion, professes himself both conqueror and defender of lust: who, while remaining in the Pelagian heresy, attempts to show that he sincerely praises what kills the soul of its own praiser unless it is conquered, and sincerely conquers what destroys his doctrine unless it is praised.

[Note: Amerbach and the manuscripts read, with a slightly different construction, “or any new heretic”; Erasmus and Louvain read “or any saints whatsoever: yet astonishingly, if even any new heretic.”]

10. I ask you: if you possess any human understanding, can sin be evil while the desire for sin is good? What else does this concupiscence do in the flesh of the holy continent except produce desires for sin—desires to which, as you admit, they do not consent, but against which they “undertake glorious contests”? Surely, in that profession of continence, even the desire for marriage cannot be free from evil. What, then, is it doing there, where whatever it does is evil, and where, if one consents to it, it carries the act through? What is this concupiscence doing there, where nothing good is desired through it? What is lust doing there, where nothing good will be pleasing through it?

Let it not be said improperly that it is present in married people. For if they attain the highest degree of conjugal chastity, they do something good through it, although they do nothing for its sake. But in holy virgins and the continent, I ask you, what is it doing? What is this protégé of yours doing, if you are foolish—your adversary, if you are wise?

[Note: Several manuscripts read *si desipis* (“if you are foolish”) rather than *cum desipis* (“when you are foolish”).] What is it doing where it itself does nothing good, and nothing good is done from it? What is it doing in those in whom whatever is desired according to it is evil? What is it doing in those whom it compels to keep watch and fight against it—and if at some time it steals from them any consent, even in dreams, then, when they awaken, to groan and say amid their groaning, “How has my soul been filled with illusions” (Psalm XXXVII, 8)?

[Note: This is an allusion to Virgil, *Aeneid* 10.642.]

For when dreams deceive the senses that sleep, I do not know how even chaste souls slip into shameful consents. If the Most High were to reckon these against them, who would remain chaste?

11. Why, then, is this evil—which you will not call good unless you have become so deaf against every trumpet of truth that you shout that desiring evil is good, something you would not dare say even among the deaf—why, I say, is this evil not eradicated from the flesh of the holy continent? Why is it not “wholly removed by the work of the mind”? For you say that this ought to happen “if it were evil.”

And because this does not happen in married people, where its movement is necessary, you therefore think it good.

[Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read *motus* (“movement”) here and below, rather than *modus* (“measure”).] Yet you see that it does not happen even where no measure of it is necessary, and that to the extent that it is present it does harm—not so as to destroy the standing of the saints, if they do not consent to it, but nevertheless so as to diminish the spiritual delight of holy minds, that delight of which the Apostle says, “I delight in the law of God according to the inner man” (Romans 7:22).

This delight is certainly diminished when the mind of the combatant is occupied—not indeed to fulfill, but certainly to oppose—the pleasure of carnal concupiscence, and so undertakes glorious contests that through those very contests it is drawn away from the delight of intelligible beauty.

But because in this human misery the worse enemy, pride, must be guarded against, this concupiscence is evidently not utterly extinguished in the flesh of the continent saints. While they fight against it, the mind is reminded of its dangers, lest it become secure and be puffed up, until human frailty reaches such perfection of health that no corruption of wantonness and no swelling of pride need be feared.

Thus “power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:9), because even fighting is a sign of weakness. The more easily someone conquers, the less he fights. But who would fight within himself if nothing within himself resisted him? And what resists us from within ourselves except that which is still being treated so that it may be healed within us? Therefore, in ourselves alone, weakness is the reason for fighting; and again, weakness is a warning not to become proud. Consequently, the virtue by which one does not become proud here, where pride is possible, is made perfect in weakness.

[Note: The printed editions incorrectly add *ut* (“so that”) after *potest* (“is possible”).]

12. For this reason, married people make good use of what the continent make better use of by not using it. The evil, therefore, which married people make good use of, and which is present in them so that they may make good use of it, is also present in the continent so that they may make better use of it by not using it.

[Note: The printed editions add *est* (“is”) after “evil.”] For it is present in them so that they may not become exalted.

[Note: The manuscripts read this way. Amerbach and Erasmus read: “For this reason, since married people…”]

Lust is “accused only for its excesses,” but only by one who does not restrain it. In itself, however, it is most rightly accused by its own movements, which are resisted so that it may not go beyond its limits.

Therefore it is not true, as you say, that “modesty contributes nothing to innocence when exercised in relation to something harmful by its very nature.” It does contribute to innocence not to consent to evil. Nor does the thing to which one does not consent thereby cease to be evil; rather, it is undoubtedly evil precisely because not consenting to it is good.

What evil would someone do by consenting to a good concupiscence, when even the person who sows a human being through the marital act—an act not without the evil of concupiscence—does nothing evil, since the human being is God’s good work?

Nor should you call lust “the maker of seeds.” The one who creates a human being’s seed is the one who creates the human being from seed; but it matters from whom it comes. For the hidden and dreadful contagions of this evil are involved. God does not create either seed or human beings from people who are free of this evil—even though some have been freed by regeneration from the guilt of that same evil, just as those who are born from it must be freed.

13. I rightly said—and I do not regret it—of conjugal chastity, concerning which you quoted my words: “When these are shown to be gifts of God, one learns from whom to ask them if they are absent, and to whom to give thanks if they are present.”

For thanks are given, not “for the origin,” as you say, “of concupiscence, whose origin is the first evil of humanity,” but “for its governance,” as you rightly say. You speak of both, “either governance or origin.” Thanks are given for the governance of concupiscence because that which resists is conquered. But what resists a good will is not good. Indeed, who would deny that it is evil except one who lacks the good of the will and therefore refuses to admit that what resists it is evil?

## CHAPTER III

14. You insert other passages from my book, where, after saying that conjugal chastity is a gift of God and teaching this on the testimony of the Apostle, I did not silently pass over the question that then arose: how one should respond when some ungodly people nevertheless appear to live chastely with their spouses (*On Marriage and Concupiscence* 1.4).

“For you are accustomed,” I said, “when denying that the virtues by which people live rightly are gifts of God, and attributing them to nature and human will rather than to God’s grace, to use as an argument that unbelievers sometimes possess them.” In this way you attempt to nullify what we say: that no one lives rightly except by faith through Jesus Christ our Lord, the one mediator between God and human beings. Here you plainly profess yourselves his adversaries.

Let us not go far afield. If I am mistaken, answer this. I said that “a man cannot truthfully be called chaste if he does not preserve faith with his wife for the sake of the true God.” To demonstrate this, shortly afterward I introduced what seemed to me a substantial proof (*ibid.*, chapter 4):

“For since chastity is a virtue, whose contrary vice is unchastity, and since all virtues—even those that operate through the body—dwell in the mind, how can the body rightly be declared chaste when the mind itself commits fornication against the true God?”

Then, lest any of you deny that the minds of unbelievers commit fornication, I added testimony from Holy Scripture, where it is written: “For behold, those who distance themselves from you will perish; you have destroyed everyone who commits fornication away from you” (Psalm 72:27).

But you, who “pursue,” as you say, “what seems sharp to me,” passed over this entire argument as though it had seemed dull to me. Consider, then, which of these points you think must be denied. You readily confess that conjugal chastity is a virtue; you do not deny that all virtues, even those that operate through the body, dwell in the mind. Moreover, only someone who openly professes himself an adversary of the holy Scriptures can deny that the mind of an unbeliever commits fornication against God.

From all this the following conclusion follows: either true chastity can exist in a mind that commits fornication—which you see is absurd—or true chastity cannot exist in the mind of an unbeliever, although when I asserted this you pretended to be deaf.

Therefore, as you slanderously claim, I do not “praise gifts while deliberately condemning the substance.” For the human substance would not be capable of divine gifts unless it were good; and the vices themselves testify to the goodness of its nature. What else is rightly displeasing in a vice except that it detracts from or diminishes what pleases us in nature?

15. When, then, a human being is divinely helped, he is not merely “helped to attain perfection,” as you yourself put it—thereby evidently wishing it to be understood that he begins by himself without grace, while grace completes what he begins. Rather, what the Apostle says is fulfilled: “He who began a good work in us will bring it to completion” (Philippians 1:6).

[Note: Amerbach and all the manuscripts read “in us,” rather than “in you.”]

In the very matter where you wish, as you say, “a human being to be spurred toward something praiseworthy by the impulses of a noble heart,” you do not wish him to glory in the Lord but in free will. Thus you make him give first so that he may be repaid; and in this way grace is no longer grace (Romans 11:35–36), because it is not free.

You call “good” the “nature of human beings, which deserves the assistance of such grace.” I would gladly hear this, if you meant it because human nature is rational. For the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord is not bestowed on stones, wood, or animals. But because human nature is the image of God, it deserves this grace—not, however, in such a way that its good will can precede grace without grace, lest it give even this first, so that it may be repaid, and thus grace is no longer grace, since it is not given freely but rendered as a debt.

[Note: Some manuscripts read *ipsa* (“itself”) rather than *ipsam* (“even this”).]

What, then, did you mean when, according to your manner, you thought that I had called heavenly gifts “the effect of human will,” as though the human will were moved toward good without God’s grace, so that an effect owed to it might be repaid by God?

Had you forgotten that we, together with Scripture, say against you, “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs 8, according to the Septuagint), and that God works in us even the willing? O ungrateful enemies of God’s grace! O enemies of Christ’s grace, Christians only in name!

[Note: Four manuscripts read *est in illis* (“there is in them”) rather than *est illis* (“there is for them”) in the following sentence concerning a good will.]

Does the Church not pray for its enemies? What, I ask, does it pray for? If it prays that the price of their will be repaid to them, what does it pray for them except a great punishment? That would now be against them, not for them. Yet it prays for them. Therefore it is not because they possess a good will, but so that their evil will may be converted into a good one. For “the will is prepared by the Lord,” and, as the Apostle says, “it is God who works in you both the willing” (Philippians 2:13).

16. But you, the fiercest enemies of this grace, set before us examples of ungodly people whom you say are “abounding in virtues while strangers to the faith;

[Note: Some manuscripts read *dicis* (“you say”) rather than *dicitis* (“you say,” plural).] in them there is only the good of nature, although enslaved to superstitions, and by the sole powers of innate freedom they are often found to be merciful, restrained, chaste, and sober.”

In saying this, you have now taken away even what you had attributed to God’s grace—namely, the effect of the will. For you did not say that they wish to be merciful, restrained, chaste, and sober, but are not so because they have not yet obtained through grace the effect of this good will. Rather, if they wished to be so and are so, we already find in them both the will and the effect of the will. What remains for us to reserve to grace, in people whom you said abound in such evident virtues?

How much better it would be—if you take pleasure in praising the ungodly, even though Scripture says, “Whoever declares the ungodly righteous will be cursed among the people and hateful among the nations” (Proverbs 24:24)—to proclaim that they abound in true virtues! How much better, I say, you would confess that these very things are gifts of God, under whose hidden yet just judgment some are born foolish, some extremely slow-witted and, so to speak, leaden in understanding, some forgetful, some sharp or retentive, some endowed with both gifts, understanding sharply and storing what they have learned in the treasury of a most tenacious memory;

[Note: Some manuscripts read *tenacissimo* rather than *tenacissimae*, a difference of inflection in “most tenacious memory.”]

some naturally gentle, others burning with the easiest anger at the slightest causes, others intermediate between these two in their desire for revenge; some eunuchs, others so cold in sexual intercourse that they are scarcely moved at all, others so lustful that they can scarcely be restrained, others between the two, easily moved and easily restrained; some extremely timid, others extremely bold, others neither; some cheerful, others sad, others inclined toward neither of these dispositions.

None of the traits I have mentioned is acquired by deliberate training or choice, but arises by nature. Hence physicians dare to attribute these things to the bodily constitutions. Yet even if this could be established, whether with no question remaining or with the whole matter decided, did each person make his own body? Is what each person suffers, to a greater or lesser degree, from these natural defects to be attributed to his will?

[Note: Amerbach, Erasmus, and some manuscripts read: “But if this too could be established,” rather than “Yet even if this could be established.”]

For while life in this world continues, no one can avoid suffering them altogether, in any way or for any reason. Yet whether someone is afflicted by them greatly or slightly, he may not say to the one who formed him—even though that one is almighty, just, and good—“Why have you made me so?” (Isaiah 45:9; Romans 9:20).

[Note: The printed editions read “whether he is afflicted greatly or slightly”; the source’s masculine singular forms are grammatically defective in context. The allusion is to Horace, *Satires* 1.3.68–69: “For no one is born without faults; that person is best who is burdened by the fewest.”]

And from the grievous yoke that lies upon the children of the first Adam (Sirach 40:1), no one is freed except by the second Adam.

How much more tolerable, then, would it be for you to attribute the “virtues” you say exist in the ungodly to God’s gift rather than merely to their will—even if they themselves do not know this, until, if they belong to the number of the predestined, they receive the Spirit who is from God, so that they may know the things given to them by God (1 Corinthians 2:12)?

17. But far be it from us to say that true virtue exists in anyone unless he is just. And far be it from us to say that anyone is truly just unless he lives by faith: “The just person lives by faith” (Romans 1:17).

Who among those who wish to be regarded as Christians—except the Pelagians alone, or perhaps you alone among them—would call an unbeliever just, call an ungodly person just, or call someone enslaved to the devil just?

[Note: Compare *The City of God* 5.19–20 and 19.23.]

Let him be a Fabricius, a Fabius, a Scipio, or a Regulus—names by which you thought to frighten me, as though we were speaking in the ancient Roman senate. Yet in this matter, even if you appeal to the school of Pythagoras or Plato, where men highly educated and learned, distinguished above other philosophers by a much more excellent philosophy, said that true virtues are those alone which are somehow impressed upon the mind by the form of that eternal and unchangeable substance which is God, even there I shall cry out against you, with the freedom of piety granted by him who called us:

“Nor in these people is there true justice. The just person lives by faith. Faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ. Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:17, 4).

How can those be truly just for whom the humility of the truly just is worthless? The closer they came through understanding, the farther they withdrew through pride. For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks to him; instead, they became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools (Romans 1:21–22).

[Note: The Louvain edition reads *qua* (“by which”) rather than *quia* (“because”).]

How can true justice exist in those in whom true wisdom does not exist? If we grant them wisdom, there will be no reason why we should not say that they reach that kingdom of which it is written, “The desire for wisdom leads to the kingdom” (Wisdom 6:21).

Accordingly, Christ died for nothing if human beings attain true faith, true virtue, true justice, and true wisdom apart from the faith of Christ, by whatever other thing or method.

[Note: The Vatican manuscripts omit “to true faith.”] Just as the Apostle says most truly concerning the law, “If righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21), so it is most truly said: “If righteousness comes through nature and will, then Christ died for nothing. If any kind of righteousness comes through human teachings, then Christ died for nothing.”

By whatever means a person has true justice, by that same means there is also the kingdom of God.

[Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads: “By whatever means a person has true justice.”] For God himself—far be it from us to say otherwise—would be unjust if the truly just person were not admitted to his kingdom, since his kingdom itself is justice, as it is written: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness, peace, and joy” (Romans 14:17).

But if the ungodly do not possess true justice, then plainly they do not possess as true the other virtues that accompany and belong with it, if they have any at all.

[Note: The old Floriacensis manuscript omits the following clause, which is enclosed in brackets in the supplied text: “because when God’s gifts are not referred to their author, those who use them become unjust by that very fact.” Five Vatican manuscripts contain it here. In the printed editions it had been placed earlier, immediately after the words “the other virtues that accompany and belong with it”; after the sentence ended with “become unjust,” there followed: “if they have any, they do not possess them as true.” The same Vatican manuscripts and the Floriacensis manuscript lack the negative particle in that reading.]

Accordingly, even continence or chastity is not a true virtue in the ungodly.

18. But you interpret the Apostle’s statement, “Everyone who competes in the contest exercises self-control in all things” (1 Corinthians 9:25), so badly that you insist that even chorus-flute players (*choraulae*) and similar disgraceful and infamous persons possess continence, such a great virtue, of which it is written that no one can be continent unless God grants it (Wisdom 8:21).

For when these people compete in the contest, they abstain from everything in order to receive a perishable crown; yet they do not abstain from the vain desire for that crown. This vain—and therefore wicked—desire conquers and restrains other wicked desires in them. For this reason they are called continent.

But to inflict the gravest insult upon the Scipios, you bestowed upon actors the continence that you praised in the Scipios with such eloquence. You failed to understand that when the Apostle urged people toward virtue, he took an example from a vicious human passion

[Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads *consuetudine* (“custom”) rather than *affectione* (“passion”).]

just as elsewhere Scripture, when urging people to love wisdom, said that it should be sought like money (Proverbs 2:4).

Should Holy Scripture therefore be said to have praised greed? No. But because it is well known how patiently lovers of money submit to great labors and sufferings, from how many pleasures they abstain, whether from the desire to increase their money or from fear of diminishing it, with what ingenuity they pursue profit and prudently avoid losses, how much they usually fear taking what belongs to others, and how at times they disregard what has been taken from them so as not to lose more by reclaiming it through litigation and lawsuits, we are rightly urged to love wisdom in such a way that we eagerly desire to store it up for ourselves as a treasure; to endure hardships so that it may be acquired for us more and more and not diminished in any respect; to restrain our lusts; to look ahead; and to preserve innocence and generosity.

When we do these things, we possess true virtues because the reason for which we do them is true: that is, this accords with our nature for salvation and true happiness.

19. It was not absurdly that virtue was defined by those who said, “Virtue is a disposition of the soul in agreement with the measure of nature and reason” (Cicero, *On Invention* 2). They spoke truly, but they did not know what is in agreement with the nature of mortals when it is to be liberated and made blessed.

For we would not all naturally desire to be immortal and blessed unless we could be so. But this supreme good cannot be granted to human beings except through Christ, and him crucified—through whose death death is conquered, and through whose wounds our nature is healed.

Therefore the just person lives by the faith of Christ. From this faith he lives wisely, courageously, temperately, and justly, and therefore lives rightly and wisely by all these true virtues, because he lives faithfully.

If, then, virtues are of no benefit to a person for attaining the true blessedness that the true faith in Christ promises us as immortal, they cannot possibly be true virtues.

Would you approve of our calling the virtues of greedy people true when they prudently devise ways of making profits; when, in order to acquire money, they courageously endure many savage and harsh experiences; when they temperately and soberly restrain the various desires by which people live extravagantly; when they abstain from what belongs to others, and often disregard losses of their own—which seems to belong to justice—so that they may not consume more in quarrels and lawsuits?

For when something is done prudently, courageously, temperately, and justly, it is done by all four virtues. According to your argument, these are true virtues if, in determining whether they are true, one looks only at what is done and does not ask why it is done. Therefore, lest you think I am slandering you, I shall now quote your own words:

“The origin of all virtues lies in the rational mind, and all the dispositions through which we are either fruitfully or fruitlessly good are located in our mind: prudence, justice, temperance, and courage. Although the power of these dispositions,” you say, “exists naturally in everyone, it does not hasten toward one end in everyone. Rather, according to the judgment of the will, whose command they obey, they are directed either toward eternal things or toward temporal things. When this happens, they differ not in what they are, nor in what they do, but only in what they deserve. Thus they cannot suffer loss in either their name or their kind, but are enriched by the greatness of the reward they sought, or disappointed by its smallness.”

Where you learned this, I do not know. But now, I think, you see that it follows that the prudence of greedy people is a true virtue, by which they devise kinds of small profits.

[Note: The manuscripts read *locellorum* (“little profits” or “small gains”) rather than *lucellorum* (“profits”).]

The justice of greedy people is true justice, by which, out of fear of serious losses, they sometimes more readily disregard what is theirs than seize anything belonging to another.

The temperance of greedy people is true temperance, by which they restrain their appetite for luxury because it is expensive, and are content with only the food and clothing that are necessary.

And the courage of greedy people is true courage, by which, as Horace says,

> “Through sea, through rocks, through fires they flee poverty.”

(Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.46.)

By this courage, finally, we have learned that some people, during a barbarian invasion, could not be compelled by any tortures of their enemies to betray what they possessed.

[Note: The source’s reference is to Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.46. The preceding discussion also preserves the editorial comparison with the examples of moral traits arising from natural bodily constitutions.]

Thus these virtues, shameful and deformed because of the end toward which they are directed, and therefore in no way genuine and true virtues, nevertheless appear to you so true and beautiful that they “cannot suffer loss in either their name or their kind, but are disappointed only by the smallness of the reward they sought”—that is, by receiving the fruit of earthly advantages rather than heavenly rewards.

Nor will anything else remain than the true justice of Catiline: to win many people through friendship, protect them through compliance, and share with everyone what he possessed. His courage will also be true courage, by which he was able to endure cold, hunger, and thirst; and his true patience will be the fact that he endured hunger, cold, and sleeplessness beyond what anyone could believe (Sallust, *The Conspiracy of Catiline*, chapter 3).

Who could think such things except someone who is out of his mind?

20. But evidently, learned man, you are deceived by the likeness of those vices that appear neighboring and close to the virtues, although they are as far from the virtues as vices are from them.

Just as steadfastness is a virtue opposed by fickleness, obstinacy is nevertheless a vice almost next to it, since it appears to imitate steadfastness. Would that you be free from this vice when you recognize the truth of what I am saying, lest you stubbornly suppose that you must remain in error as though you were cherishing steadfastness.

Thus all virtues have not only vices that are plainly opposed to them, such as rashness opposed to prudence, but also vices that are in some way adjacent and similar—not by truth, but by a deceptive appearance. Thus the vice adjacent to prudence is not rashness or imprudence, but cunning.

[Note: The Louvain edition reads “not by truth” rather than “but not by truth.”]

Yet cunning is a vice, although in Holy Scripture the saying “Be shrewd as serpents” (Matthew 10:16) is taken in a good sense, while in a bad sense it is said that in paradise the serpent was more cunning than all the beasts (Genesis 3:1).

It is not easy to find names for all the vices that we have said are adjacent to the virtues. But even if it cannot be discovered what they should be called, they must be avoided.

21. Know, then, that virtues must be distinguished from vices not by their duties but by their ends. A duty is what ought to be done; an end is that for the sake of which it ought to be done.

When someone does something where he does not appear to sin, if he does not do it for the reason for which he ought to do it, he is shown to be sinning. Since you did not attend to this, you separated ends from duties and said that true virtues should be called duties without ends.

From this such great absurdity follows that you are compelled to call it true justice even when you find greed ruling it. If one considers merely the duty, abstaining from what belongs to another can appear to be a duty of justice. But when the question is asked why it is done, and the answer is, “So that more money may not be lost through lawsuits,” how can this action now be true justice when it serves greed?

These are the kinds of virtues Epicurus introduced as servants of pleasure, since everything they did, they would do either to attain pleasure or to preserve it.

But far be it from us to say that true virtues serve anyone except the one to whom, or for whose sake, we say, “God of virtues, convert us” (Psalm LXXIX, 8).

Consequently, virtues that serve carnal pleasures, or any temporal advantages and profits, cannot possibly be true virtues. Nor are those that wish to serve nothing themselves true virtues. True virtues serve God in human beings, by whom they are given to human beings; they serve God in angels, by whom they are also given to angels.

Whatever good a human being does, if he does not do it for the reason for which true wisdom teaches it ought to be done, is sinful because its end is not right, even if in its performance it appears to be good.

22. Thus some good things can be done by those who do not do them well. For it is good that help be given to a person in danger, especially an innocent person; but if the one who does this acts out of love of human glory more than of God, he does not do a good thing well, because he does not do with a good will what he does. Far be it from us to call good a will that glories in others, or in itself, rather than in the Lord [Note: [Col. 0749] In the earlier printed editions this was followed by: “Nor can its fruit be from the one by whom the good is done unless it has been done with a good will.” But it is a good work of God, by whom good is done even through the wicked. Likewise, below, after “this fruit is to be called,” there was added: “It was uncertain how (or when) a bad tree could not produce good fruits.” These words are entirely absent from the manuscripts.]. Accordingly, this cannot even be called its fruit; for a bad tree does not produce good fruits. Rather, it is the good work of the one who does good even through the wicked.

Therefore it is impossible to say how greatly that opinion deceives you, by which you said that “all virtues are dispositions by which we are either fruitfully or fruitlessly good.” For it is impossible for us to be fruitlessly good; rather, whatever we are fruitlessly, we are not good. “A good tree produces good fruits” (Matt. VII, 17–18). Yet far be it from us to suppose that the good God—by whom the axe is prepared for trees that do not produce good fruit—cuts down good trees and casts them into the fire (ibid. III, 10). In no way, then, are people fruitlessly good; but those who are not good may be less or more evil.

23. Hence I do not see at all how those whom you wished to mention help you—those of whom the Apostle says: “The Gentiles, who do not have the law, are a law to themselves, who have the work of the law written in their hearts” [Col. 0750]. Through these people you attempted to prove that those who are strangers to faith in Christ can nevertheless possess true righteousness, because, as the Apostle testifies, they naturally do what belongs to the law.

Here you expressed more clearly your doctrine, by which you are enemies of the grace of God given through Jesus Christ our Lord, “who takes away the sin of the world” (John I, 17, 29): you introduce a class of people who can please God without faith in Christ, by the law of nature. This is the very reason why the Christian Church detests you most of all.

But what do you want these people to be? Do they possess true virtues and are fruitlessly good because they do not act for God’s sake? Or do they nevertheless please God through these things and receive eternal life as their reward from him? If you say that they are fruitless, what benefit is it to them that, according to the Apostle, their thoughts will defend them on the day when God judges the secrets of human beings (Rom. II, 14–16)? But if those whose thoughts defend them because they have naturally performed the works of the law are not fruitlessly good, and for this reason find an eternal reward with God, then unquestionably they are righteous because they live by faith.

24. For you accepted and explained the testimony that I cited from the Apostle—“Whatever is not from faith is sin”—as it seemed to you, not as it means, but as you wish it to mean. The Apostle was speaking about foods. After saying, “Whoever doubts is condemned if he eats, because it is not from faith,” he wished to establish this particular kind of sin that he was discussing by a general statement, immediately adding: “For whatever is not from faith is sin” (ibid. XIV, 23).

But even if I grant you that this is to be understood only of foods, what will you say about the other testimony that I repeatedly cited? You did not argue from it, because you found no way to twist what is written to the Hebrews into support for your opinion: “Without faith it is impossible to please” [Note: [Col. 0750] The printed editions here read “to please God.” Elsewhere, however, the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, agreeing with the ancient manuscripts, often omit “God,” as below, §§25 and 32; nor did this word occur in the Apostle’s Greek text.]. Surely, when this was said, the whole of human life was being discussed, in which “the righteous person lives by faith.” Yet although without faith it is impossible to please God, virtues without faith please you in such a way that you declare them to be true and declare people good because of them; and then, as though you regretted praising them, you do not hesitate to pronounce them fruitless.

25. Therefore, those who are righteous by natural law either please God and please him by faith—for without faith it is impossible to please him—or they do not. And by what faith do they please him, unless by faith in Christ? For, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles, “In him God has established faith for all, raising him from the dead” (Acts XVII, 31).

Thus they are said to do naturally what belongs to the law without the law, because they came to the Gospel from the Gentiles, not from circumcision, to which the law was given; and they do so naturally because, in order that they might believe, their nature itself was corrected in them by God’s grace. You therefore cannot prove through them what you wish—that unbelievers can possess true virtues. These people are believers.

Or, if they do not have faith in Christ, then certainly they are neither righteous nor pleasing to God, whom it is impossible to please without faith. Their thoughts, however, will defend them on the day of judgment so that they may be punished more tolerably, because they have done, however imperfectly, what belongs to the law naturally, having the work of the law written in their hearts to this extent: that they did not do to others what they would not wish to suffer themselves. Yet even in this they sinned, because, being people without faith, they did not refer these works to the end to which they ought to have referred them.

Fabricius will be punished less than Catiline—not because Fabricius is good, but because Catiline is more evil. Fabricius is less impious than Catiline, not because he possessed true virtues, but because he did not deviate very far from true virtues.

26. Or perhaps you intend to provide for those who displayed Babylonian love toward their earthly fatherland and served, through civic virtue—which was not true but merely resembled it—demons or human glory: Fabricius, Regulus, Fabius, Scipio, Camillus, and others of this kind. Will you assign them, as you do infants who die without Baptism, some place between damnation and the kingdom of heaven, where they are not in misery but in everlasting blessedness—although they did not please God, whom it is impossible to please without faith, and although they possessed faith neither in their works nor in their hearts?

I do not think your ruin can leap forward into such shamelessness. “Then,” you say, “they will be in everlasting damnation, although true righteousness was in them?” O statement driven headlong by even greater shamelessness! It was not in them, I say [Note: [Col. 0751] Amerbach and the manuscripts read “therefore.”], true righteousness, because actions are weighed not by their deeds but by their ends.

27. But with charming and witty elegance, like the refined and urbane man you are, you say: “If it is said that the chastity of unbelievers is not chastity, then by the same logic it will be said that the body of pagans is not a body, that the eyes of pagans have no power of sight, and that the grain growing in the fields of pagans is not grain; and many other things,” you say, “of such absurdity that they can move intelligent people to laughter.”

Your laughter does not move intelligent people to laughter, but rather to tears—just as the laughter of the insane moves healthy minds to tears. Do you deny, contrary to the holy Scriptures, that an unbelieving mind can commit fornication, or do you say that true chastity exists in a mind committing fornication? And you laugh, and you are sane? How, where, by what reasoning could this happen? Certainly neither is that true chastity nor is that true sanity. Certainly, I say, the chastity of a fornication-committing mind is not true chastity, and it is genuine madness for a person to say and laugh at such a disgrace.

We, however, would never say that the body of pagans is not a body, nor anything similar. For it does not follow that, if the virtue of which the wicked person boasts is not true virtue, the body that God has made is not a true body. We can indeed say that the forehead of heretics is not a forehead, if by “forehead” we are understood to mean not the bodily member made by God, but modesty.

What if, in that very book of mine to which you boast that you replied, I had already expressly warned against understanding, in the statement “Whatever is not from faith is sin,” even those things belonging to unbelievers that are gifts of God, whether among the goods of the mind or of the body? There you find those things about which you chatter so foolishly: the body, the eyes, and the other limbs. The grain growing in the fields of pagans also belongs to this category. God is its creator, not the pagans.

Did you not yourself quote, among other things, these words of mine, where I said: “The soul and the body, and whatever natural goods are implanted in the soul and body, are gifts of God even in sinners, since God, not they themselves, made these things. But of the things they do it was said: ‘Whatever is not from faith is sin’” (On Marriage and Concupiscence, book I, §4)?

If you had kept this brief but wholly clear statement of mine in mind, I think you would not have been so shameless as to claim that we could say “that the body of pagans is not a body, that the eyes of pagans have no power of sight, and that the grain growing in the fields of pagans is not grain.”

To repeat my own words to you as though awakening you from sleep—words that may have slipped from your memory when you said these things: “These things too are gifts of God even in sinners, since God, not they themselves, made them. But of the things they do it was said: ‘Whatever is not from faith is sin.’”

When you say and laugh at insane things, you resemble a madman. But when you so fail to notice and so forget the true things I said, which you yourself shortly before recalled and inserted into this very work by which you appear to be answering me, you resemble not the insane but the lethargic.

28. “I am astonished,” you say, “that my exceptionally”—meaning, as you say mockingly, “brilliant”—“genius did not see how much I helped you in this matter also, because I said, ‘Sins are overcome by other sins.’” You immediately add and conclude: “Therefore, by devotion to holiness, which God assists, a person can very easily be without sins. For if,” you say, “sins are overcome by sins, how much more can sins be overcome by virtues?”

It is as though we denied that God’s help would be powerful enough, if he wished, to enable us today to have no evil desires at all against which we might nevertheless fight with the greatest determination. Yet you yourself do not deny that this does not happen. Why it does not happen—who has known the mind of the Lord (Rom. XI, 34)? Still, I know enough when I know that, whatever the reason may be, there is neither iniquity in the just God nor weakness in the almighty God.

There is therefore something in his hidden and profound counsel why, as long as we live in this mortal flesh, there is in us something against which our mind must fight. There is also a reason why we say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. VI, 12).

But let me speak to you as one human being to another, and as one whose earthly dwelling weighs down the sense that considers many things (Wis. IX, 15). Among creatures, insofar as concerns the merits of the kinds of nature established by God, nothing is more excellent than the rational mind. Hence it follows that a good mind takes greater pleasure in itself and is more pleased with itself than with any other creature.

How dangerously—indeed, destructively—it pleases itself when it swells with arrogance and is lifted up by the disease of self-inflation, so long as it does not see, as it will see at the end, that highest and unchangeable good in comparison with which it despises itself and becomes insignificant to itself through love of that good, and is so filled with its Spirit that it places that good before itself not by reason alone but also by eternal love—it would take too long to demonstrate in argument.

One who returns home exhausted by hunger understands this, saying, “I will rise and go to my father” (Luke XV, 18). How, then, do we know that, because this evil of pride will not then be able to assail the mind, and there will be nothing at all against which we must struggle [Note: [Col. 0753] Five Vatican manuscripts read “there will absolutely not be anything.”], when it is satisfied by so great a vision and inflamed by so great a love of the higher good that, by pleasing itself in itself, it cannot fall away from love of that good [Note: [Col. 0753] Amerbach, Erasmus, and several Gallican and Vatican manuscripts read “delight” (delectatione); two other Vatican manuscripts, “refreshment” (refectione).]—how do we know that it was for this reason that we were placed in this condition of weakness, so that we would not live proudly, but live under the daily remission of sins?

For this reason the Apostle Paul himself was not entrusted to his own judgment concerning the evil of pride. Since he had not yet come to such participation in that higher good that he could no longer be exalted there, an angel of Satan, a tormentor, was assigned to him here so that he would not be exalted here, where he could be exalted (II Cor. XII, 7).

29. But whether this is the reason, or another reason that is much more hidden from me, there is nevertheless something I cannot doubt: however much we progress under the burden of this corruptible body, “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I, 8).

For this reason the holy Church too—even in those members of hers where she has neither the stain of crime nor the wrinkle of falsehood (Eph. V, 27)—does not cease to say to God, despite your prideful opposition, “Forgive us our debts.”

But how arrogantly you have spoken from your presumption of virtue—“Therefore, by devotion to holiness, which God assists, a person can very easily be without sins”—is not recognized by anyone who does not know your doctrines.

For you wish devotion to holiness to precede, in the human will and without God’s assistance, that assistance which God ought to give deservedly rather than freely. And you believe that a person can be without sins in this wretched life, so that there is nothing in him for which he should say, “Forgive us our debts.”

Although you seem to have stated this somewhat more cautiously, since you did not say, “A person can be without all sins,” you did not wish to say that this is true of some people either. Rather, as though you yourself had blushed at your excessive presumption, you so moderated your statement that it could be defended both in your language and in ours.

For if the matter is examined among Pelagians, the answer will be that you did not say “some” because you had said that a person could be without all sins. But if it is examined among us, the answer here too will be that you did not say “all” because you wished “any person” to be understood, and any person must necessarily ask forgiveness for certain sins. But since we know what you think, we cannot fail to know how you speak in this way.

30. “If a Gentile,” you say, “covers someone who is naked, is it sin because it is not from faith?” Certainly, insofar as it is not from faith, it is sin—not because the act itself of covering someone who is naked is sin [Note: [Col. 0753] The Floriacensis manuscript reads, “not because the act itself is done through him.”], but because only a wicked person denies that it is sin not to glory in the Lord concerning such a deed.

To make you understand this, although enough has already been said about it, listen a little longer, since the matter is important. Here are the very examples that you yourself supplied: “If a Gentile”—who does not live by faith—“covers someone who is naked, rescues a person in danger, tends the wounds of the sick, spends his wealth on honorable friendship, and cannot be driven even by tortures to give false testimony”—I ask you whether he does these good works well or badly.

If, although the works are good, he nevertheless does them badly, you cannot deny that he sins who does anything badly. But since you do not want him to sin when he does these things, you will certainly say: “He does good things, and he does them well.”

Therefore a bad tree produces good fruits—something Truth says cannot happen. Do not rush to a conclusion; carefully consider what it is appropriate for you to answer.

Do you say that the unbelieving person is a good tree? Then he pleases God, for whatever is good cannot fail to please the good. And what will become of what is written: “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. XI, 6)?

Will you answer: “He is not a good tree insofar as he is an unbeliever, but insofar as he is a human being”? Then of whom did the Lord say, “A bad tree cannot produce good fruits” (Matt. VII, 18), since whoever exists will be either a human being or an angel?

But if a human being is a good tree insofar as he is human, then an angel too is a good tree insofar as he is an angel. These are works of God, who is the creator of good natures. Accordingly, there will be no bad tree of which it was said that it cannot produce good fruits. What unbeliever could reason so unbelievingly?

Therefore no one is a bad tree insofar as he is a human being, which is God’s work; rather, each person is a bad tree insofar as he has an evil will, and he cannot produce good fruits. Consider, then, whether you dare to call an unbelieving will good.

31. Perhaps you will say: “A merciful will is good.” That would rightly be said if mercy were always good, just as the faith of Christ—that is, the faith that works through love (Gal. V, 6)—is always good.

But if even a bad mercy is found, by which the person of the poor is favored in judgment (Exod. XXIII, 3), and on account of which King Saul finally deserved to be condemned by the Lord—even though he acted mercifully—because out of human affection he spared the captive king contrary to the Lord’s command (I Sam. XV), consider more carefully whether mercy may be good only when it belongs to this good faith.

Rather, answer this so that you may see it without any doubt: do you consider an unbelieving mercy good? And if it is a vice to show mercy wrongly, then certainly it is a vice to show mercy unbelievingly.

Moreover, if mercy itself, arising from natural compassion, is a good work, then the person who uses even this good unbelievingly uses it badly, and the one who does this good unbelievingly does it badly. But whoever does anything badly certainly sins.

32. From this it follows that even the good works performed by unbelievers belong not to them but to the one who makes good use of evil things. Their sins, however, belong to them, because they do good things badly: they do them not with a faithful but with an unfaithful—that is, foolish and harmful—will. Such a will, no Christian doubting it, is a bad tree, which can produce only bad fruits, that is, sins.

For, whether you will it or not, “whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV, 23). Therefore God cannot love these trees; and if they remain such, he has determined to cut them down, because without faith it is impossible to please him.

But I linger over this as though you yourself had not already pronounced these trees fruitless. How, then, I ask, are you not either joking in these discussions or raving, when you praise the fruits of fruitless trees?

Such fruits either do not exist, or, if they are bad, they ought not to be praised. Or, if the fruits are good, then the trees are certainly not fruitless; indeed, they are good trees, whose fruits are good, and they must please God, whom good trees cannot fail to please. Thus what is written—“Without faith it is impossible to please”—will be false.

33. But you will answer, “What if not?”—that is, “What if they are merely empty words?” “I,” you say, “called those people fruitlessly good who, because they do the good things they do not for God’s sake, do not receive eternal life from him” [Note: [Col. 0755] The same manuscript reads “fruitless good people.”].

But you will reply: what but empty words? “I,” you say, “called people fruitlessly good who, by doing the good things they do not for God’s sake, do not receive eternal life from him” [Note: [Col. 0755] The same manuscript reads “fruitless good people.”]. Then is the just and good God going to send good people into eternal death? I am already weary of saying how many insane consequences follow you when you think, say, and write such things, and when you censure me as though I were a censor because I do not similarly lose my senses in such matters.

But accept this brief answer, lest, since you are as mistaken as it is possible to be in the matters themselves, I seem to be quarreling with you over words.

Either understand what the Lord says: “If your eye is evil, your whole body will be dark; but if your eye is sound, your whole body will be full of light” (Matt. VI, 23, 22). Recognize that this eye is the intention with which each person does what he does. From this learn that the person who does not perform good works with the intention of good faith—that is, the faith that works through love—has a whole body, as it were, composed of those works as of limbs, dark; that is, full of the blackness of sins.

Or, since you at least concede that the works of unbelievers which seem good to you do not nevertheless lead them to eternal salvation and the kingdom, know that we say that no one can be granted that good, that good will, or that good work without the grace of God given through the one Mediator between God and human beings. Through this alone a person can be brought to God’s eternal gift and kingdom.

Therefore, let everything else that seems to possess some praise among human beings seem to you to be true virtues, seem to be good works, and seem to have been done without any sin. As far as I am concerned, this I know: a good will does not produce them, for an unbelieving and impious will is not good.

Let such wills be called good trees, as you wish. It is enough that before God they are fruitless and therefore not good. Let them be fruitful among human beings, among whom, by your authority, your praise, and, if you wish, your planting, they are also good. Nevertheless, whether you will it or not, I shall establish this: the love of the world, by which someone is a friend of this world, is not from God; and the love of enjoying any creatures without love of the Creator is not from God.

The love of God, by which one reaches God, comes only from God the Father through Jesus Christ with the Holy Spirit. Through this love of the Creator, each person makes good use even of creatures. Without this love of the Creator, no one makes good use of creatures.

This love is therefore necessary for conjugal chastity to be a blessed good, so that when someone uses the flesh of a spouse, the intention is not the pleasure of lust but the will to beget children. But if pleasure prevails and compels something to be done for its own sake rather than for the begetting of children, it is a venial sin on account of Christian marriage [Note: [Col. 0756] Amerbach and Erasmus read “will.”].

CHAPTER IV

34. I did not say what you claim I said by inserting other words from my book: namely, “Therefore children are under the power of the devil because they are born from the union of bodies.”

For it is one thing to say, “those who are born from the union of bodies” [Note: [Col. 0756] Here “those who” is restored from the manuscripts.]; it is another to say, “because they are born from the union of bodies.”

The cause of evil is not that they are born from the union of bodies. For even if human nature had not been corrupted by the sin of the first human beings, children could not be generated except through the union of bodies.

Rather, those who are born from the union of bodies are under the devil before they are reborn through the Spirit, because they are born through that desire by which “the flesh desires against the spirit,” and which compels the spirit to desire against the flesh (Gal. V, 17). This conflict between good and evil would not exist if no one had sinned. Just as there was none before human iniquity, so after weakness [Note: [Col. 0756] In the margin of a certain Gemblacensis codex someone wrote: “Alternatively, ‘health.’”] there will be none.

CHAPTER V

35. You again present other words of mine and argue at length: “Since we are composed of unequal goods, the soul ought to rule the body,” adding that one of these is shared with the gods and the other with beasts. Therefore, you say that what is better—the soul endowed with virtue—ought to rule both the bodily members and the desires well [Note: [Col. 0756] Sallust, in the prologue to Catiline.].

But you do not consider that desires are not ruled in the same way as bodily members. Evil desires are restrained by reason, and we fight against them with the mind. The bodily members, however, are good, and we move them according to the judgment of the will, except for the genital members, although they too are good as works of God.

They are therefore called shameful members because lust has more power in moving them than reason does. Yet we do not allow the arousal itself to carry out what it urges, while we control the other members with an easy command. When does a person use good bodily members badly, except when he consents to the evil desires that dwell within us? Among these, lust is especially shameful; unless it is resisted, it commits dreadful and filthy acts. The only thing that makes good use of this evil is conjugal chastity.

This desire is not evil in beasts because it does not oppose reason, which they lack. Why, then, do you not believe that it could have been divinely granted to human beings placed in paradise before sin that they might beget children through a tranquil movement and union or mingling of the members, without any lust? Or at least that there could have been in them a kind of desire whose movement neither preceded nor exceeded the will?

Is lust insufficient for you because it is pleasing, unless you also approve of such lust as disturbs us even when we are unwilling and resisting? The Pelagians indeed boast of it even in disputes, as though it were some good; but the saints confess it with groans, so that they may be freed from evil.

CHAPTER VI

36. You falsely accuse me of having said, with laughable inconsistency, that some are guilty because of a good work and others holy because of an evil work. I said that unbelieving people turn the good of marriage into evil and sin by using it unbelievingly, and that in this way the faithful turn the evil of concupiscence into the service of righteousness (On Marriage and Concupiscence, book I, §5).

Accordingly, I did not say that some are guilty because of a good work, but because of an evil work by which they make bad use of good things. Nor did I say that others are holy because of an evil work, but because of a good work by which they make good use of evil things.

If you do not wish to understand—or if you pretend not to understand—do not obstruct those who wish and are able to understand.

CHAPTER VII

37. “If some evil could be created,” you say, “it would never pass into good through cleansing.” By the same reasoning you would say that a body created mortal could not become immortal. Yet you would be wrong in both cases.

God did not create evil when he created the human being. Rather, the good that he himself created draws evil from sin, which he did not create; and he heals this evil, which he did not create, in the good that he did create.

38. We do not say that demons instituted marriage, or the seminal union of the two sexes, or that the sexual intercourse of married couples is a work of the devil and the cause of generation. God instituted all these things, and all of them could have existed without the evil of concupiscence if the wound of transgression—which brought about the discord between flesh and spirit—had not been inflicted by the devil.

Do you not look at yourself and blush at your empty verbosity, with which you have told such idle stories? You claim that demons detect married couples in intercourse and, as though they had caught them at their own work, prevent them from begetting children who are to be freed by regeneration.

It is as though, if the devil could do whatever he wished, he would immediately strangle even the adult impious people still under his power whenever he recognized that they were destined to become Christians.

It does not follow, then, that when parents beget children who are to be regenerated, and for this reason have intercourse, demons oppose them threateningly and terrifyingly, as you imagine. Through the wound inflicted by the devil, by which the human race limps, something is begotten while God creates, which is transferred from Adam to Christ.

Even a legion of demons could not have power over the pigs unless Christ permitted it at their request (Matt. VIII, 31–32). He also knows how, from the persecutions of the devil himself—which he permits him to inflict—he raises crowns for martyrs, making good use of every kind of evil [Col. 0758] for the benefit of the good.

But even among those married couples who either do not think about the regeneration of their children or even despise it, marriage is a good work, and the lawful union of the sexes for the purpose of generation is good; the fruit of this work is the orderly reception of children. They nevertheless make bad use of this good and sin in taking pride in offspring that is either impious or destined to be impious.

People polluted by any contagion or commission of sin are, insofar as they are human beings, good. Therefore it is good that they be born, because they are good.

39. Yet adulteries and other acts of sexual misconduct should not be committed so that children may be conceived. You think we can be compelled to this absurdity because we say that marriage produces the good of offspring from the evil of lust. But in no way does that perverse and false conclusion follow from our true and correct position.

The Lord says, “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity” (Luke XVI, 9). It does not follow that we should add further iniquity and commit thefts and robberies so that, through greater generosity, we may feed more poor saints.

Just as friends are to be made from the mammon of iniquity who will receive us into eternal dwellings, so children are to be begotten by married couples from the wound of original sin, children who are to be regenerated into eternal life.

And just as thefts, frauds, and plunderings must not be added so that, through money increased by iniquity, more righteous poor people may be acquired as friends, so adulteries, sexual misconduct, and fornications must not be added to the evil with which we were born [Note: [Col. 0758] The manuscripts read “must not be added,” feminine form.], in order that a more numerous offspring may be born.

For it is one thing to make good use of an evil that was already present, and another to commit an evil that was not present. The former is to make a voluntary good use of the evil drawn from one’s parents; the latter is to heap other evils, already one’s own and voluntary, upon the evil drawn from one’s parents.

There is, moreover, this difference: mammon of iniquity is distributed with praise to those in need, whereas carnal concupiscence is more worthily restrained by the virtue of continence than devoted to the purposes of marriage. For its evil is so great that not to use it is better than to use it well.

CHAPTER VIII

40. You then present other words of mine and say a great deal against them, though in fact you say nothing, repeating certain matters already dealt with in the preceding discussion. If I wished to repeat them as well, what end would there be?

Among other things, you also repeat that statement of yours against the grace of Christ, often made by you without basis: namely, that by the term “grace” we mean that people are made good by a fatal necessity. But those who are not yet able to speak close your mouths and restrain your tongues.

For although you labor with great verbosity to establish and persuade what Pelagius condemned before the judgment of the Palestinian bishops—namely, that God’s grace is given according to our merits—you cannot assert any merits of infants by which those of them who are adopted as God’s children may be distinguished from those who die without receiving this grace.

41. You falsely accuse me of saying that no effort should be expected from the human will, contrary to the Gospel in which the Lord says: “Ask, and you will receive; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you. For everyone who asks receives, and whoever seeks finds, and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matt. VII, 7–8).

There, as I see, you have already begun to place merits preceding grace: asking, seeking, and knocking. You intend that what is owed should be given in return for these merits, so that grace is called grace in vain—as though no grace had preceded and touched the heart so that the blessed good might be sought from God, so that God might be sought, and so that one might knock at God’s door.

In vain, then, would it be written, “His mercy will go before me” (Ps. LVIII, 11); and in vain would he command us to pray for our enemies (Matt. V, 44), if it were not his work to turn hearts that have turned away and become hostile.

42. But you cite apostolic testimony and say that, by him who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4), it is opened to those who knock. Thus, according to your teaching, we are evidently to understand that not all are saved and come to the knowledge of the truth because they themselves do not wish to ask, although God wishes to give; do not wish to seek, although God wishes to show; do not wish to knock, although God wishes to open. But those infants refute this interpretation of yours by their very silence: they neither ask, nor seek, nor knock; indeed, even when they are baptized, they cry out, reject it, and resist. Yet they receive, they find, it is opened to them, and they enter the kingdom of God, where the salvation of eternity is theirs [Note: [Col. 0759] Most manuscripts read, “the eternity of salvation.”] and the knowledge of the truth—while far more infants are not adopted into this grace by him who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

To these he cannot say, “I wanted to, and you did not want to” (Matt. 23:37); for if he had wanted to, who among those who do not yet possess the exercise of their own will could have resisted his all-powerful will? Why, then, do we not understand the statement, “He wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth,” in the same way as we understand what the same apostle said: “Through the justification of one, unto justification of life for all people” (Rom. 5:18)? For all those whom God wills to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth are those to whom, through the justification of one, grace reaches unto justification of life. Otherwise we will be told: If God wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, but they do not come because they themselves do not wish to, why do so many thousands of infants who die without receiving Baptism not come into the kingdom of God, where the knowledge of the truth is certain? Are they perhaps not people, so that they do not belong to what was said, “all people”? Or can anyone say, “God wills it, but they do not,” when they do not yet know how to will or not to will such things—just as those infants who are baptized and die, and through that grace come to the knowledge of the truth that is most certain in the kingdom of God, do not come because they themselves wished to be renewed through Christ’s Baptism?

Since, then, the former are not baptized because they do not wish it, nor the latter baptized because they wish it [Note: [Col. 0759] So the manuscripts. The printed editions, however, read: “because they did not wish it, nor are the latter baptized for that reason because they do not wish it.”], why does God, who wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth, allow so many who offer him no resistance through the exercise of their will not to come into his kingdom, where the knowledge of the truth is certain?

43. Unless perhaps you are going to say that infants should not be counted among those whom God wills all to be saved, because, with regard to the salvation that is to be understood here, they are already saved, bearing no sin at all. In this way an even more intolerable absurdity will follow for you. For by this reasoning you make God more benevolent toward all the most ungodly and criminal people than toward the most innocent and pure, free from every stain of sin. Since he wills all the former to be saved, he also wills them to enter his kingdom—for that is what follows for them if they are saved—but if they do not wish to, they themselves are responsible. Yet he does not wish to add to his kingdom the immense number of infants who die without Baptism, whom, as you suppose, no sins impede, and who, as no one doubts, cannot resist his will with an opposing will.

Thus it turns out that he wills all to be Christians, though many do not wish to be; but he does not will all to be Christians when not one among them does not wish to be. This is contrary to the truth. “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19), and his will concerning their salvation and their introduction into his kingdom is certain. Therefore the statement, “He wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” [Note: [Col. 0760] The Ambrosian, Erasmian, and manuscript witnesses read, “He wills all people to come,” omitting the intervening words.], must be understood in the same way as the statement, “Through the justification of one, unto justification of life for all people.”

44. If you think that this apostolic testimony should be understood in such a way that “all” is taken for “many,” who are justified in Christ—for many others, after all, are not made alive in Christ [Note: [Col. 0760] Several manuscripts lack this sentence; and some, instead of “are not made alive,” read “are not justified.”]—then you will be answered that in the passage where it says, “He wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth,” “all” likewise stands for “many,” whom he wills to come to this grace.

This is understood much more appropriately in light of the fact that no one comes unless he himself wills that person to come. “No one can come to me,” says the Son, “unless the Father who sent me draws him”; and, “No one can come to me unless it has been granted to him by my Father” (John 6:44, 66). Therefore all who are saved and come to the knowledge of the truth are saved and come because he wills it.
