For those who, like infants, do not yet exercise the power of choice are regenerated because he wills it, just as they are generated by his creative will; and those who already exercise the power of choice cannot will unless he wills and assists them—the one by whom the will is prepared (Prov. 8, according to the Septuagint).

45. If you should say to me, “Why, then, does he not convert the wills of all who are unwilling?” [Note: [Col. 0760] The Vatican manuscripts and nearly all the Gallican manuscripts read, “of all who are willing.”] I will answer: Why does he not adopt through the bath of regeneration all infants who are going to die, in whom he as yet finds no wills, and therefore no contrary wills? If you recognize that this is too profound to be discovered by you, then let it be profound for both of us: why, among adults and children alike, God wills to assist one and does not will to assist another. Let us nevertheless hold as certain and immovable that there is no injustice with God (Rom. 9:14), by which he condemns anyone without evil merits, and that there is goodness with God, by which he liberates many without good merits. In those whom he condemns he demonstrates what is owed to all, so that from this those whom he liberates may learn what punishment due to them is remitted and what undeserved grace is bestowed.

46. You do not know how to think about these matters in a way fitting for Christian hearts; rather, according to your own view, you say that such things happen by fate. It is your view, not ours, that “what does not happen by merit happens by fate.” And lest, according to this definition, everything that happens to people without merit happen by fate, you assert merits—good or evil—as strongly as you can, so that fate would follow if you denied merits.

Accordingly, this is said to you: If what is granted to people without any merits must now necessarily happen by fate, and merits must therefore be asserted so that fate does not follow if there are no merits, then infants are baptized by fate and enter the kingdom of God by fate, although they have no good merits; and, again, infants are not baptized by fate and do not enter the kingdom of God by fate, although they have no evil merits. Behold, the little ones who cannot yet speak prove that you, rather, are defenders of fate.

But when we say that there are evil merits arising from a corrupted origin, we say that an infant enters the kingdom of God by grace, because God is good; and that another does not enter by merit, because God is just; and that in neither case is there fate, because God does what he wills. But since we know from him whom we faithfully praise in song for mercy and judgment (Ps. 100:1) that this one is condemned according to judgment and that one is liberated according to mercy, why he condemns or liberates this one rather than that one—who are we to answer God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, “Why did you make me this way?” Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same mass of corrupted and condemned origin, to make one vessel for honor according to mercy and another for dishonor according to judgment (Rom. 9:20–21)?

He therefore does not make both for honor, lest the creature think that it earned this as an unblameworthy nature; nor does he make both for dishonor, so that mercy may exult over judgment (Jas. 2:13) [Note: [Col. 0761] Ambrosian and manuscript witnesses read, “so that mercy may exalt itself over judgment.”]. Thus the condemned person cannot justly complain of punishment imposed as a debt, nor can the one freely liberated boast arrogantly of merit; rather, he humbly gives thanks when, in the one from whom a debt is demanded, he recognizes what is granted to him in the same condition.

47. You claim that I said in another book of mine, “Free choice is denied if grace is commended; and grace is again denied if free choice is commended.” You slander me. I did not say this; rather, because of the difficulty of the question itself, I said that it could seem and be thought that this was being said.

It is not burdensome for me to set down my actual words, so that those who read this may see how you lie in wait for my writings and with what conscience you exploit minds that are either slow or uninformed, so that they may think you are answering because you refuse to remain silent. At the end of the first book I addressed to the holy Pinianus, whose title is *On Grace against Pelagius* [Note: [Col. 0762] Some manuscripts read, “For Grace against Pelagius.” The printed editions read, “On the Grace of God against Pelagius.”], I said:

“This question, in which free choice of the will and the grace of God are discussed, is so difficult to distinguish that when free choice is defended, God’s grace seems to be denied; but when God’s grace is asserted, free choice is thought to be taken away, and so forth” (*On the Grace of Christ*, 52).

But you, an honorable and truthful man, removed the words I spoke and attributed to me what you yourself invented. I said that this question is difficult to distinguish; I did not say that it cannot be distinguished. Much less, then, would I say what you falsely claim that I said: “Free choice is denied if grace is commended, and grace is denied if free choice is commended.”

Restore my words, and your slander will disappear. Put back in their proper places the words “seems” and “is thought,” so that it may become clear by what frauds you argue about so important a matter. I did not say, “Grace is denied,” but “so that grace may seem to be denied.” I did not say, “Free choice is denied or taken away,” but “so that it may be thought to be taken away.”

And you promise that, “when the books themselves begin to be examined, the impiety of my statements will be both stripped bare and pierced through by you.” Who would not expect wisdom from a speaker who has recognized the faith of one who lies? [Note: [Col. 0762] Two Vatican manuscripts omit the negative particle here.]

48. What do you mean when you say, “It has nothing to do with the praise of grace if it gives its own people what sins bestow upon the impious”? You evidently mean conjugal chastity, which you think even the impious possess. Contentious man, true virtue is bestowed through grace—not the virtue that is merely called virtue but is not.

Why, however, do you join chastity and virginity together as though they were of the same kind? Chastity is a matter of the soul; virginity, of the body. Indeed, while the former remains intact in the soul, the latter can be violently taken away from the body; and while the latter remains intact in the body, the former can be corrupted in the soul by a lustful will.

For this reason I did not say, “true marriage, or widowhood, or virginity,” but: “True chastity, whether conjugal, widowed, or virginal, is not to be called such unless it is devoted to the true faith” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, 5).

There can be married women, widows, and virgins who are not chaste, if, with a corrupted will, they commit adultery, or if with an impure spirit they resolve to perpetrate sexual violations. Yet you say that true chastity exists in them even if they fornicate in mind; and the divine pronouncements testify that all the impious do this.

49. Who among us says that “the evil of the conjugal organs is woven into the fabric of marriage,” in which marriage makes good use of concupiscence’s evil for the begetting of children? Concupiscence would not be evil if it moved a person to lawful intercourse solely for the purpose of generation.

But now, since conjugal chastity resists it, it is a boundary against evil, and therefore chastity is good. Hence, contrary to your slanderous way of speaking, “its crime is not made unpunished through religion,” because it is no crime when, through the good of faith, one makes good use of the evil of lust.

Nor can one say here, as you suppose, “Let us do evil so that good may come” (Rom. 3:8), because marriage is not evil in any part of itself. Its evil is not something that marriage has made in the human beings whom parents beget; rather, it found that evil there. In the first married couple, who were born from no parents, the discordant evil of carnal concupiscence arose through sin, and marriage would make good use of it—not through marriage itself, so that marriage might rightly be condemned on that account.

Why, then, do you ask “whether, among Christian married couples, I should call the pleasure of intercourse chastity or unchastity” [Note: [Col. 0763] The Ambrosian, Erasmian, and most manuscripts read “the act of intercourse,” which is less correct.]? I answer: it is not chastity itself that is named, but the good use of that evil; through this good use the evil cannot even be called unchastity. For unchastity is the disgraceful use of that same evil, whereas virginal chastity has no such use at all [Note: [Col. 0763] The printed editions add here, “the use of that same evil.”].

Therefore, while conjugal chastity is preserved, evil is drawn from evil in the process of birth, and this evil is cleansed through rebirth [Note: [Col. 0763] Lovaniensis reads, “which is cleansed.” The other books read, “which may be cleansed.”].

50. “But if,” you say, “because of this evil of lust, offspring born even of Christian married couples is born criminal, it follows that virginal chastity is a bringer of happiness.” And because it is found among the impious, you say, “the unbelievers who are exalted in the virtue of chastity surpass Christians polluted by the stain of lust.”

That is not how matters stand, as you say; you are greatly mistaken. Those who make good use of lust are not polluted by the stain of lust, although they beget people polluted by that stain and therefore in need of rebirth. Nor is virginal chastity found among the impious, although bodily virginity may be found there, because true chastity cannot dwell in a soul that fornicates [Note: [Col. 0763] The printed editions read, “cannot be possessed in a soul that fornicates.”].

Thus the virginal good of the impious is not preferred to the conjugal good of the faithful; rather, married people who make good use of an evil are preferred to virgins who make bad use of a good. Therefore, when faithful married people make good use of the evil of lust, it is not, as you slanderously claim, “among them, because of faith, that the impunity of crime is practiced”; rather, because of faith, true—not false—virtue of chastity exists in them [Note: [Col. 0763] The Ambrosian, Erasmian, and manuscript witnesses read, “true,” feminine, agreeing with “virtue.”].

51. What does it have to do with us that you claim the Manichaeans say, “If someone commits homicide while his conscience is afraid, he is guilty because he was afraid; but if he perpetrates some crime with exultant boldness, as though believing that through faith he is doing what he does wrongly, he escapes guilt”?

I have never heard the Manichaeans say this. But what does it have to do with us, whether they say it or whether you even slander them, since the Catholic faith that we hold—and whose weight we bring to bear upon you—does not say this?

We say that works which seem good are not truly good without faith, because truly good works must please God; and since without faith it is impossible to please him (Heb. 11:6), what is truly a good work cannot exist without faith [Note: [Col. 0763] The Lovaniensis edition alone reads, “truly good.”]. Nevertheless, faith that works through love (Gal. 5:6) does not produce works that are manifestly evil, because love of neighbor does not work evil (Rom. 13:10).

52. “Therefore natural concupiscence is good,” you say—for you are ashamed to say “carnal”—“and when it is kept within its proper limit,” you say, “it is not defiled by any admixture of evil” [Note: [Col. 0764] The printed editions read, “is not disturbed.” The manuscript witnesses have corrected this to “is not defiled.”].

How, I ask you, is it kept within its proper limit? How is it kept there unless it is resisted? And why is it resisted except so that it may not fulfill evil desires? How, then, is it good?

## CHAPTER IX

53. You also come to those words of my book where I said:

“Were not those first married people, whose marriage God blessed when he said, ‘Increase and multiply’ (Gen. 1:28), naked and not ashamed (ibid. 2:25)? Why, then, did shame arise from those members after sin, unless an indecent movement appeared there, which marriage would certainly not have had if human beings had not sinned?” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, 6).

When you saw these words of mine set down in accordance with the Scriptures in such a way that anyone who reads or will read the same passage in the book of Genesis must approve without hesitation what I said, you labored greatly in a lengthy contradiction [Note: [Col. 0764] The printed editions read, “in a lengthy act of contradicting,” less well.], but you did not clarify the matter. You persisted in your perverse opinion, although the very evidence proved that my correct position could not be overturned by you.

In your contradiction I pass over your gestures and flourishes, like those of a man panting, unable to reach the goal toward which he strives, yet pretending to have arrived amid the clouds that, in his confusion, he pours forth [Note: [Col. 0764] The manuscripts read, “which he encounters.”]. But, with the Lord’s help, I grasp and shatter the necessary points of your argument, so that anyone who reads both what you wrote and what we have written may see the whole body of your argument lying defeated—especially since the points you repeat in many forms have often already been refuted by us.

54. Among other things, you say here: “In the fact that after sin the first human beings, ashamed of those members in which lust resides, covered them, I found the basis for persuading people that God had established marriages of air.”

If marriages without lust were therefore “of air,” then, on your authority, bodies will be “of air” when lust no longer exists. Or do you love this lust so much that, just as you place it in those who were previously in paradise before sin, you will also insert it into resurrected bodies?

But I do not say, as you claim I say, “that what is not natural is that without which nature does not exist” [Note: [Col. 0764] Five Vatican manuscripts read, “that what is natural is that without which nature does not exist,” omitting the negative particle found in the other books.]. Rather, I say that a vice is called natural because human nature is not now born without it, although human nature was not established in this way at the beginning. Therefore this evil derives its origin not from that first establishment of nature, but from the evil will of the first human being; nor will it remain, but it will either be condemned or healed.

55. You call my position “a bedbug,” which, “just as it causes annoyance when alive, so when crushed produces an odor”; as though, in your words, “you were ashamed to wear me down by defeating me,” or, “as though overcome, I had fled to swampy places,” so that you shrink from pursuing and destroying me, because, as you claim, the parts of your argument by which I am to be crushed or destroyed—since you are compelled to speak about shameful matters—were driven away from the freedom of speech by your modesty, like some kind of temple-warden.

Why do you not speak freely instead about the good things you praise? Why is there no freedom of speech concerning God’s work, if its unblemished dignity remains and sin did nothing there that would instead provoke shame and restrain freedom of speech?

## CHAPTER X

56. “If,” you say, “there is no marriage without lust, and you generally condemn lust, then you also condemn marriage.”

You might as well say that, because death will be condemned, all mortals must be condemned. But if lust belonged essentially to marriage, then clearly there would be no lust before marriage or apart from marriage.

“It cannot,” you say, “be called a disease without which marriage does not exist, because marriage can exist without sin; but a disease,” you say, “is called sin by the Apostle.”

You are answered: Not every disease is called sin. This disease, however, is the punishment of sin, without which human nature cannot exist while it remains not yet healed in every respect.

But if lust is not evil because the good of marriage does not occur without it, then, conversely, the body is not good because the evil of adultery does not occur without it. This is false; therefore the former is false as well.

Who does not know that the Apostle commanded married people so that each might know how to possess his own vessel—that is, his wife—not in the disease of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God (1 Thess. 4:4–5)? Whoever reads the Apostle on this matter disregards you.

And are you not ashamed—although, bashful as you are, you admit that it is so—to introduce this disease into paradise and assign this lust to married people before sin? Is that why you do not lie hidden in the mud, because you crown yourself with the lust of flesh and blood as though with the rosy flower of paradise, and, as though gladly covered with such a color, both blush and praise it? [Note: [Col. 0765] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “or because you, although bashful,” omitting “admit.”] [Note: [Col. 0765] Lovaniensis reads, “who.” The other books read, “because.”]

## CHAPTER XI

57. What is more, you take such delight in speaking that you try, with unnecessary prolixity, to prove what we confess and teach as though we denied it. For who denies that intercourse would have occurred even if sin had not preceded it?

But it would have occurred through the movement of the will affecting the genital members, just as it affects the other members, not through lustful excitation—or else even through lust itself, so as not to distress you excessively about it, though it would not have been as it is now, but would have served the voluntary command.

Yet you labor so earnestly for the position you have adopted that you are compelled to place in paradise even lust as it now is—not saying that it became such there because of sin, but claiming that it would have remained such without anyone’s sin, so that one would have had to struggle against it in that peace, or, whenever it arose, satisfy it so that there would be no struggle.

O holy delights of paradise! O the forehead of bishops of whatever sort! O the faith of chaste people of whatever sort! [Col. 0766] [Note: [Col. 0766] The Michaelinus manuscript, and several other manuscripts at the margin, read “of armies.” Morel, *Critical Elements*, pp. 216–217, reads “of Christians.”]

## CHAPTER XII

58. But, wishing to show that not everything which is covered must be considered shameful because of sin, you ineffectually mention many things that are naturally covered on our body, as though they were covered after sin in the same way as those people covered the members concerning which there is a dispute between us—members that before sin had been neither shameful nor covered, but which they covered as shameful after sin.

“Balbus,” you say, “argued with Cotta in Cicero carefully and diligently” (*On the Nature of the Gods*, book 2). “For this reason,” you say, “you set down a few passages in order to burden my modesty, since under the instruction of sacred law I did not understand matters to which Gentiles could arrive by the guidance of reason alone.”

You then quote Balbus’s words from Cicero’s book, through which you seek to teach us what the Stoics thought about the differences between male and female among irrational animals, about the genital parts of the body, and about the remarkable lusts involved in the mingling of bodies.

Before you inserted these words, whether Ciceronian or anyone else’s, you cautiously prefaced them by saying that Balbus “touches upon the subject under the pretext of animals and their sexes because, out of regard for propriety, he passed over it in his description of the human being.”

What does “out of regard for propriety” mean? Is propriety confused by the human sexual organs, where God works, as in a superior nature, with greater dignity? The Stoics taught you to discuss hidden matters, but they did not teach you to blush at shameful ones.

You then add “how he depicts the human being himself in his discourse,” as you say, “and how he explains that the nature of the abdomen is subordinate to the stomach, since the abdomen is the receptacle of food and drink; while the lungs and heart draw in breath from outside; and that many things are wonderfully effected in the abdomen, which consists of sinews; and that it is complex and winding, and bars and contains whatever it has received, whether dry or moist” [Note: [Col. 0766] The manuscripts read, “whether it has received something dry or moist.”], “and so forth,” down to the statement, “how the remnants of food are expelled, both by the intestines contracting and by their relaxing.”

Since he could have described these things even in animals, why did he pass from them to the human being, unless because these things are not shameful—just as those things concerning the genitals and sexual natures of animals are not shameful, although in a human being they are shameful? The reason is evidently the same reason why, after sin, the first human beings covered them with fig leaves.

For when, in his description of the human body, he had reached the extremities through which the remnants of food are expelled, Cicero says: “How this happens is not at all difficult to say; but it must nevertheless be passed over, lest the discourse contain anything unpleasant.”

He did not say, “lest the discourse contain anything shameful,” nor, “lest it contain anything that causes confusion,” but “lest it contain anything unpleasant.” For some things provoke horror in the senses because they are deformed; other things provoke shame in the mind even if they are beautiful. The former offend our sense of enjoyment, while the latter arouse lust or are themselves aroused by lust.

59. What help, then, do these matters give you? “Because,” you say, “our maker himself acknowledged no fault in his craft, so as to conceal our vital organs so carefully” [Note: [Col. 0767] [The note appears at the foot of column 767, but the callout number (2) is not printed in the text.] [Col. 0767] The printed editions read “whereas”; so also the Gallic manuscripts. The Vatican manuscripts read “because.”].

Certainly, far be it from us to say that so great an artist acknowledged any fault in his craft. But why he covered these things, you yourself said a little earlier: “so that, when exposed, they might not perish or cause horror.”

But the things which the first married couple covered with fig leaves (Gen. 3:7) certainly neither perished nor caused horror when they were naked and not ashamed (ibid. 2:25). Even now, the vigilance of chastity avoids the sight of those same members in order to prevent desire rather than horror.

Therefore you thought in vain that the testimony of the Stoics should be used to support your adopted position—a position not at all friendly to them, since they assigned no part of the human good to bodily pleasure. In the end, they chose to praise lust in animals rather than in human beings, as you do. In accordance with their opinion, Cicero says in one place that he does not think the good of a ram and the good of Publius Africanus are the same. This opinion should have all the more strongly warned you what you ought to think about human lust.

60. But if you are willing to make use of such writings because some traces of truth are found even in them, I think you ought by now to admit that what you yourself cited has no force against us. Consider now whether what I shall say does not overturn your assertion.

In the third book of *The Republic*, the same Cicero says that the human being is “brought forth into life not by a mother but, as it were, by a stepmother, by nature, with a body naked, fragile, and weak; but with a spirit anxious about troubles, lowly before fears, soft before labors, inclined to lust; yet within him there was, as it were, a divine fire of intellect and mind buried beneath.”

What do you say to this? That author did not attribute this to the conduct of people who live badly, but rather accused nature. He saw the fact but did not know its cause. For he did not know why “a heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam, from the day of their leaving their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all” (Ecclus. 40:1), because, not instructed in the sacred Scriptures, he was ignorant of original sin.

If he had thought rightly about the lust that you defend, he would not have disliked a spirit inclined to lust.

61. But if you defend these things as lesser goods, toward which the mind ought not to incline from higher things—not because lust is a vice, but because it is a lower good—then listen to the clearer statements he makes in that same third book of *The Republic*, when he was discussing the basis of rule.

“Do we not,” he says, “see that dominion has been given by nature itself to the best person, with the greatest advantage to those of lower rank? Why, then, does the mind rule the body, God rule the human being, reason rule lust and anger and the other vicious parts of that same mind?” [Note: [Col. 0767] The Casalensis manuscript reads, “when God rules the human being.”]

Now, at least when this author teaches you, do you confess that the parts of the mind which you defend as good are vicious? Listen further. A little later he says:

“But the distinctions between ruling and serving must also be recognized. For just as the mind is said to rule the body, it is also said to rule lust; but it rules the body as a king rules his citizens or a parent his children, whereas it rules lust as a master rules slaves, because it restrains and breaks it. Thus the dominions of kings, emperors, magistrates, fathers, and peoples preside over citizens and allies as the mind presides over bodies; but masters wear out slaves in the way that the best part of the mind—that is, wisdom—wears out the vicious and weak parts of the same mind, such as lusts, angers, and other disturbances.”

Do you still have anything to babble against us from the authority of secular writers? But if, against the most distinguished interpreters of the divine words among the bishops, you are going to seek support for this error—which may God avert from you—and ask what you should say or how you might resist their holiness, what will Cicero mean to you, unless you insist that he was foolish and delirious in this judgment?

So stop speaking about books of that kind, and do not try to teach us something insultingly from them, lest you be suppressed by the testimony of those by whose authority you vainly think yourself supported.

## CHAPTER XIII

62. But why did you think it worth arguing so vainly about the movement of the woman, a movement of which she too was ashamed? The woman did not cover a visible movement. Rather, when she felt in those same members something more hidden of the kind that the man had felt, both covered what they had both felt when, by seeing one another, each was aroused toward the other; and they were ashamed either each for himself or one for the other.

But while speaking foolishly, you “ask that modest ears forgive you and rather groan than become indignant at your necessity.” Why are you confused about discussing God’s works? Why do you ask to be forgiven? Is not your very request for pardon itself an accusation of lust?

“But if,” you say, “the male member could also move before, then sin introduced nothing new.”

Certainly it could move before, but it was not indecent in such a way as to cause shame [Note: [Col. 0768] The Lovanienses incorrectly corrected this to “it was fitting that it should cause shame.” Immediately afterward, in place of “because,” they used “when,” following Ambrosian and Erasmian usage.], because it was moved by the command of the will, not by flesh lusting against the spirit. In this consisted the new shameful condition, which your novelty impudently defends.

I never generally condemned movement of the genitals, as you claim, “with emphasis.” Rather, I condemned the movement produced by concupiscence, by which the flesh lusts against the spirit. Since your error defends this as good, I do not know how your spirit can lust against it as though against evil.

63. “If,” you say, “this lust was in the fruit of that tree, it is shown to have been made by God, and is thereby itself also defended as good.”

You are answered: Lust was not in the fruit of the tree, and therefore the tree was good. Rather, the evil is the disobedience of lust, which arose, when God withdrew, against the human being’s disobedience committed in connection with the tree.

For far be it from us to say that God would grant to any age of those human beings, at any time, such a benefit from a good tree that they would have in their members an adversary against which chastity would have to fight [Note: [Col. 0768] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “an adversarial thing.”].

64. We know that the apostle John did not condemn this world—that is, heaven and earth and all that substantially exists in it, which was made by the Father through the Son—when he said: “Everything that is in the world is the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the ambition of the age; which is not from the Father, but is from the world” (1 John 2:16).

We know these things; I do not want you to teach us. But when you wished to explain what “lust of the flesh he said was not from the Father,” you said that “luxury” or “licentiousness” was to be understood.

But when I ask you to whom it should yield so as to be licentiousness, or whom it should resist so as not to be licentiousness, your adopted position confronts you face to face. Whether it is still to be praised is for you to decide: to consent to it is licentiousness, while to resist it is continence.

I am amazed if you are deliberating whether you ought rather to condemn it together with licentiousness, which occurs through its consent, or to praise it together with continence, which wages war against it. In that war chastity is the victory of continence, while licentiousness is the victory of concupiscence.

Yet you, as an incorrupt and upright judge, while praising continence and condemning licentiousness, nevertheless take the part of concupiscence—which you may consider why you fear to offend—so completely that you are not ashamed to praise it together with its adversary, nor dare to condemn it together with its victory.

But far be it from any human being of God to hear you as a condemner of licentiousness and thereby approve you as a praiser of concupiscence, and to judge from your speech that what he experiences in himself as evil is good.

Finally, whoever conquers through struggle the concupiscence that you perversely praise will not possess the licentiousness that you rightly condemn. But how do we obey the apostle John if we love the lust of the flesh?

You will reply, “It is not the lust that I praise.” Then what is the one John says is not from the Father? “Licentiousness,” you will say. But we will not be licentious unless we love this concupiscence that you praise.

Therefore, when he said, “Do not love the lust of the flesh,” he wished people not to be licentious. We are forbidden to love this lust of the flesh praised by you when we are forbidden to be licentious; but what we are forbidden to love is not from the Father. Therefore this concupiscence that you praise is not from the Father.

For two good things that are from the Father cannot fight against each other. Continence and concupiscence do fight against each other; answer which of these you would rather be from the Father.

I see what distress you are suffering: you favor concupiscence, but you blush at continence. Let your shame prevail, and through it let your error be conquered. Since, then, continence is from the Father, by which the lust of the flesh is subdued, receive from the Father the continence at which you have blushed with an open face, and conquer the concupiscence that you praised with a perverse mouth.

## CHAPTER XIV
### 65

Moreover, you thought that the pleasure of all the senses should be summoned to your aid, as though the pleasure of the generative organs by itself were not sufficient for so great a patron unless a phalanx of allies came to its assistance. “For it follows,” you think, “that we must acknowledge that the senses of seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling, and touching were bestowed on us not by God but by the devil, if we concede that the concupiscence of the flesh, which we resist through continence, did not exist in paradise before the sin, but arose from that sin which the devil first persuaded the first man to commit.” [Note: [Col. 0769] The Floriacensis manuscript omits “first.”]

Thus you either do not understand, or pretend not to understand, that through every bodily sense [Col. 0770] there is one thing that pertains to the vitality, usefulness, or necessity of sensation, and another that pertains to the lust of sensation.

The vitality of sensation is that by which one person perceives more, another less, within bodily things themselves, according to their measure and nature, what is true, and distinguishes it from what is false to a greater or lesser degree.

The usefulness of sensation is that by which we take counsel for the body and the life we lead, so as to approve or disapprove, take up or reject, seek or avoid something. [Note: Some manuscripts read: “The usefulness of sensation is that which advises the life we lead to reject harmful things and seek useful ones.”]

The necessity of sensation occurs when things we do not want are nevertheless presented to our senses.

But the lust of sensation, which is what we are now discussing, is that which drives us toward sensation—whether our minds consent or resist—by an appetite for carnal pleasure.

This is opposed to the love of wisdom. [Note: Am. and Er., together with the Gallican and Vatican manuscripts, read “the delight of wisdom.”] This is hostile to the virtues. In the part of this evil that concerns the mingling of the two sexes, marriage makes good use of it [Note: Er., Lugd., and Ven. omit “it” (*eam*); Lov. omit “of it” (*ejus*). M.] when spouses beget children through it and do nothing on its account. [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads: “unless they do something on its account.”]

If you had wished, or had been able, to distinguish this from the vitality, usefulness, and necessity of sensation, you would have seen how needlessly you had said so much. For the Lord did not say, “Whoever looks at a woman,” but, “Whoever looks at a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5:28). See how, if you are not stubborn, he briefly and plainly distinguished the sense of sight from the lust of sensation.

God created the former by fashioning the human body; the devil sowed the latter by persuading sin.

### 66

Let pious men, then, praise heaven and earth and all that is in them, and through all these things praise God by contemplating their beauty, not with the heat of lust. Just as a religious man praises the splendor of gold differently from a greedy man: the former with the piety of venerating the Creator, the latter with the lust of possessing the creature.

Certainly the soul is moved toward an affection of piety when a divine song is heard. Yet even there, if the lust of hearing desires the sound rather than the meaning, it is condemned; how much more if it takes pleasure in empty or even shameful little songs?

The remaining three senses are more bodily and, in a certain way, coarser. [Note: Lov. reads “thicker” or “coarser.”] They do not project themselves outward, but perform inwardly whatever belongs to them. Smell is distinguished by the one who smells, taste by the one who tastes, and touch by the one who touches in many different ways. Hot and cold are not the same as smooth and rough, nor are these the same as soft and hard; and what is called light or heavy differs from all of them.

Whenever unpleasant things are avoided in these matters—stenches, bitterness, heat, cold, and whatever is rough, hard, or heavy—the provision made for comfort is not the lust for pleasure. Those things contrary to these, which we conveniently take when they are available, should nevertheless not be desired with lust when they are absent, provided that they contribute nothing to health or to avoiding the discomfort of pain or labor, even if they are taken with some pleasure when at hand. If they are desired, that is not good. In every matter, such an appetite must be subdued and healed.

For who, however strict a chastiser of carnal concupiscence he may be, could enter a place fragrant with incense and cause it not to smell sweet to him, unless he closed his nostrils or, through intense concentration, withdrew himself from bodily sensations? But when he had gone out from there, would he desire that fragrance at home or wherever he went? And if he did desire it, ought he to satisfy that lust rather than restrain it and, through the spirit, lust against the lusting flesh, until he returned to that state of health in which he desired no such thing?

This is a small matter indeed; but “whoever despises small things will gradually fall,” as it is written (Ecclesiasticus 19:1).

### 67

We need the support of food. If what is taken by the mouth is not pleasant, it cannot be taken and is often rejected with nausea; and harmful aversions must be avoided. The weakness of our body therefore needs not only food but also the flavor of food—not to satisfy lust, but to preserve health.

When nature in some way demands the supplementation of what is lacking, this is not called lust but hunger or thirst. But when, after necessity has been supplied, a love of eating troubles the mind, it is already lust; it is already an evil to which one must not yield but must resist.

The poet too distinguished these two things—hunger and the love of eating. After the tossing of the sea, he judged that Aeneas’s shipwrecked and exiled companions needed only as much nourishment as the need for restoration demanded, and wrote:

> After hunger was removed by the feast, and the tables were cleared.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* 1.216.)

[Note: Lov. reads *refectione*, erroneously.]

But when Aeneas himself was received as a guest by King Evander, he judged that more fitting royal banquets should be provided than necessity required. It was not enough for him to say:

> After hunger was removed;

he added:

> and the love of eating was restrained.  
> (*Aeneid* 8.184.)

How much more ought we to distinguish and know what the necessity of restoration demands and what the lust of gluttony demands, since our task is to lust through the spirit against the lusting flesh, to delight in the law of God according to the inner man, and not to cloud the serenity of that delight with any lustful pleasures! For this love of eating must be restrained not by eating but by abstaining.

### 68

Who, with a sober mind, would not prefer—if it were possible—to take dry or liquid nourishment without any biting carnal pleasure, just as we take this airy nourishment, which we draw in and release by breathing the air around us? We take this nourishment continuously through mouth and nostrils, yet it has neither taste nor smell. Nevertheless, without it, even for so brief a time; whereas we can live so long without food and drink, we cannot live without it. We perceive our need of it only as discomfort if our mouths and nostrils are closed, or if, as far as the discomfort itself permits, we briefly restrain the activity of our lungs by an act of will—those lungs by which, like bellows, we draw in and expel the vital breath through alternating motion.

How much happier would it be if, at spacious intervals, as even now—or at still more spacious intervals—we could receive food and drink without any seductive sweetness of flavor, by which we might drive away such great discomfort or danger? [Note: Five Vatican manuscripts read “so much discomfort.”] [Note: An old Floriacensis codex omits the following ten lines, so that immediately after “drive away” it continues: “just as the first human beings are to be believed to have lived in paradise.”]

For if, in the present life, those who take nourishment temperately are called continent and sober, and rightly praised, [Note: The Louvain editions read “are considered worthy of praise.”] and if there are people of this kind who take as much nourishment as nature demands, or less—preferring, if they are mistaken in what accords with necessity, to have taken too little rather than too much—[Note: The manuscripts so read. The editions have “if they are mistaken in what accords with necessity.” Perhaps one should read “if they are mistaken in the measure.”] how much more ought we to believe that there was an honorable moderation in taking nourishment in that state of dignity in which what was necessary for the animal body would be supplied, yet the natural measure would in no way be exceeded—as we must believe the first human beings lived in paradise?

### 69

Although some interpreters of divine Scripture—men who are not contemptible—rather suppose that they had no need of nourishment of this kind, so that the only pleasure or nourishment believed to have existed in paradise was that by which the hearts of the wise are delighted and sustained, I agree with those who understand the words, “He made them male and female, and God blessed them, saying, Increase and multiply, and fill the earth,” as referring to the bodily and visible sexes. Likewise, they understand what follows shortly afterward:

> And God said, “Behold, I have given you every grass bearing seed, which is upon all the earth, and every tree that has in itself the fruit of seed-bearing plants; it shall be food for you, and for all the beasts of the earth, and for all the birds of heaven, and for every creeping serpent upon the earth that has in itself the breath of life; and every green grass for food” (Genesis 1:27–30). [Note: The editions read *reptanti* (“crawling”) for *repenti* (“creeping”).]

They do not understand this otherwise than as meaning that both sexes used bodily the foods by which the other animals also lived, and that from this food they received suitable support—necessary to an animal body, though in a certain immortal mode—so that deprivation would not injure them; while the tree of life kept them from being brought by old age to death.

Yet I could in no way believe that, in a place of such great happiness, the flesh lusted against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, and that they lived in this conflict without inward peace; or that the spirit did not resist carnal desires but performed in shameful servitude whatever lust suggested from any source.

It therefore remains either that there was no carnal concupiscence there, but that life was ordered so that everything necessary was fulfilled through the appropriate functions of the bodily members without any movement of lust—for the fact that the earth is sown by the hands of farmers moved not by lust but by will does not mean that it does not conceive its offspring—or, so that we may not seem excessively offensive to those who defend bodily pleasure in whatever manner, that the lust of the carnal senses existed there in such a way that it was entirely subject to rational will and was present only when through it provision had to be made either for the body’s health or for the propagation of offspring.

It would have been present in such measure that it never withdrew the mind in any respect from the delight of heavenly thoughts; no superfluous or intrusive movement would arise from it; nothing would be done through it except what was beneficial; and nothing at all would be done for its sake.

### 70

But those who fight against it feel most clearly how different its condition now is. It intrudes upon those who see or hear something, even when they see or hear for another reason, so that, even if it derives no pleasure from touch on that account, it may at least steal a pleasurable thought, slipping into what is necessary but has nothing to do with it.

Moreover, within the thoughts themselves, even when nothing seductive is present to the eyes or sounds in the ears, what does it not attempt to stir up with shameful delight, disturbing even what has become faded and dormant through restless memories, and interrupting chaste and holy occupations with a kind of tumultuous, filthy intrusion?

And when we come to the use of necessary pleasure by which we restore our bodies, who could explain in words how it prevents us from perceiving the measure of necessity, conceals and passes beyond the very limit of securing health, and snatches at whatever pleasant things are available? [Note: Am. and Er. read “at whatever things are available”; Lov. read “if any things are available,” omitting “at whatever.” The text has been corrected from the manuscripts.] We think that what is enough is not enough, while we are willingly led by its provocations, imagining that we are still engaged in the business of health when we are instead producing indigestion.

For the regrettable excess of eating bears witness to what evil we have done. [Note: The manuscripts read “the excess to be regretted.” The editions read “the excess in regretting.”] Fearing this, we often eat less than is sufficient to remove hunger. Thus desire does not know where necessity ends. [Note: The editions read “where necessity may end.” Some manuscripts read “where necessity ends.”]

### 71

The pleasure of eating and drinking is tolerable, provided that we remain watchful with as much attention as possible, so that it may more easily fail to fill us than at some point exceed the measure of sufficient nourishment. We fight against this concupiscence both by fasting and by taking nourishment more sparingly. We then make good use of this evil when through it we do only what is conducive to health.

I called this pleasure tolerable because its force is not so great that it breaks us away from and casts us down from thoughts pertaining to wisdom when we are held in them by the mind’s delight. [Note: The editions read “when we are held in them”; the Floriacensis manuscript has the better reading, “when we are held toward them.”] Often, while eating, we not only think about great matters but also discuss them; amid the very bites of food and draughts of drink, we converse no less attentively by listening and speaking; and whatever we wish to learn or recall, we receive with complete concentration when it is read to us.

But that other pleasure for which you contend with me so vigorously—even when one approaches it with a good intention, that is, for the sake of propagating offspring—who, in the very act itself, is able to think about anything else, not to mention wisdom? Is not the whole mind and body devoted to it, and is not its final purpose fulfilled through a kind of submersion of the mind itself?

When it also conquers married people, so that they come together not from the desire to propagate but from the desire for carnal pleasure—something the Apostle testifies that he said by way of concession, not command (1 Corinthians 7:6)—how one emerges from it and, as though into the air, [Note: Er. and Lov. read “into the air” in the singular; Am. reads “in the air”; the manuscripts read “into the airs.”] breathes again after that whirlpool, so that what someone rightly said proves true: repentance is near to pleasure.

Who, then, being a lover of spiritual good and married even solely for the sake of offspring, would not prefer, if possible, to beget children either without this pleasure or without its great force? What holy spouses would prefer in this life, I think we ought to believe concerning that life in paradise, which was far better, if we cannot imagine anything better about it.

### 72

I beg you, let the philosophy of the Gentiles not be more honorable than our Christian philosophy, which is the one true philosophy, since this name signifies the pursuit or love of wisdom.

Consider what Tullius says in the dialogue *Hortensius*. [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads “dialogues.”] These words ought to have pleased you more than those of Balbus, who speaks for the Stoics—words which, although true, concerned the lower part of the human being, namely the body, and could not help you.

See what he says in defense of the vitality of the mind against bodily pleasure:

> “Or are bodily pleasures to be sought, although Plato truly and seriously said that they are the allurements and food of evils? For what disease,” he says, “what disfigurement of complexion and body, what disgraceful loss, what dishonor, is not summoned and drawn forth by pleasure? [Note: The manuscripts read “for pleasure” (*voluptati*).] The greater its movement in each person, the more hostile it is to philosophy. Great bodily pleasure cannot accord with great thought. For when someone is enjoying a pleasure greater than which none can exist, who can attend with the mind, undertake a calculation, or think about anything at all? And what is so great a whirlpool that anyone would wish his senses to be moved day and night, without any interruption, as they are moved in the highest pleasures? [Note: Am. and the manuscripts read “what is so great a whirlpool” (*cujus*); Er. and Lov. read “who” (*quis*).] Who, endowed with a sound mind, would not prefer that nature had given us no pleasures at all?”

This was said by one who had believed nothing about the life of the first human beings, nothing about the happiness of paradise, and nothing about the resurrection of bodies.

Let us meanwhile be ashamed before the true arguments of impious men, [Note: Am. and the manuscripts read “sometimes” (*interdum*) for “meanwhile” (*interim*).] since we have learned, in the true and holy philosophy of true piety, both that the flesh lusts against the spirit and that the spirit lusts against the flesh (Galatians 5:17).

Cicero did not know how this came about; yet he did not favor the concupiscence of the flesh, as you do. Indeed, he vehemently condemned it, which you not only fail to do but angrily attack those who do. Like a timid man in war, fearing to have as an enemy one of the two concupiscences that might defeat the other, you attempt to praise both the concupiscence of the spirit and that of the flesh as though they were waging war against each other. [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads “you attempt to praise both sides.”]

Act rather so that you need not fear, and praise the concupiscence of the spirit against the concupiscence of the flesh, praising it all the more keenly because it fights more chastely. As for the other, which resists the law of the mind, condemn it without fear by that same law of the mind which it resists.

### 73

One thing is the contemplation of beauty, including bodily beauty—whether visible, as in colors and shapes, or audible, as in songs and melodies—which contemplation no rational animal can lack; another thing is the stirring of lust, which must be restrained by reason. [Note: The Belgian, Gallican, and Vatican manuscripts read “must be broken.”]

For the Apostle John said that the concupiscence which lusts against the spirit is not from the Father (1 John 2:16). No one can call it good unless he loves the spirit’s lusting against it.

But if such concupiscence is not present in the movement and ardor of the generative organs, then let the spirit not lust against it, lest by lusting against God’s gift it be found ungrateful. Instead, let whatever it desires be given to it, as to something that comes from the Father. If there is nothing to give, let this rather be requested from the Father—not that he remove or suppress it, but that he fulfill the concupiscence he has bestowed.

If it is foolish to think this way, then why do we compare it with wine and food and imagine that we have said something meaningful by declaring: “Let neither drunkenness condemn wine, nor gluttony condemn food, nor obscenity disgrace concupiscence”? For neither drunkenness, nor gluttony, [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts omit “neither drunkenness nor gluttony.”] nor any obscenity is committed if the concupiscence of the flesh is overcome by the spirit lusting against it.

“You say that its excess is blameworthy.” Yet you do not see—something you could have seen very easily, if you had wished to overcome concupiscence itself rather than me—that, in order that the evil of excess may not occur, one must resist the evil of concupiscence.

There are therefore two evils: one we possess, and the other we commit if we do not resist what we possess. [Note: The following words had intruded into earlier printed editions, perhaps because someone had written them in the margin: “Therefore concupiscence is not evil in animals, because it does not lust against the spirit but rather delights their spirit. For, lacking the concupiscence of wisdom, they do not resist carnal concupiscence; and, being alien from the good of rational life, they possess this good, namely, that in which they delight.” They have been removed on the authority of the very ancient Floriacensis codex and three Vatican manuscripts.]

### 74

We have already said above (section 35) that this is not evil in animals because in them it does not lust against the spirit. They do not possess reason by which they might subjugate their lusts through overcoming them or weary them through struggle.

But who tells you that “sin is always committed by imitating animals”? You worked to refute this proposition—which was not even raised against you—with such verbosity that you collected many superfluous observations, even though medicine too attends to things observed in animals.

Yet lest anyone suppose that carnal concupiscence is therefore not evil in human beings because it is good in an animal, as that nature is delighted by it in which the concupiscence of wisdom cannot exist, it was said that the animal’s concupiscence is good because it delights the animal’s spirit without any opposition, but that it is evil in the human being, in whom it lusts against the spirit. [Note: The editions read “the evil of the human being, by which he lusts,” omitting “in,” which is present in the manuscripts.]

### CHAPTER XV

### 75

You also summoned a crowd of philosophers to your aid, as though, if the natural resourcefulness of animals could not support your position, at least the errors of learned men might assist it.

But who does not see that, in recalling the names of learned men and their differing schools, you sought a display of learning, when anyone who reads what you have written can see that these matters have no bearing at all on the question at issue between us?

Who, I ask, can hear you mention Thales of Miletus, one of the Seven Sages, and then Anaximander, Anaximenes, Anaxagoras, Xenophanes, Parmenides, Leucippus, Democritus, Empedocles, Heraclitus, Melissus, Plato, and the Pythagoreans, each with his own doctrine concerning natural things, without being frightened by the very noise of names and schools piled together, if he is uneducated, as the multitude of people is? Would he not think you some great man because you were able to know these things?

There you have what you seek. For in all these names and doctrines that you have heaped together, you have said absolutely nothing relevant to the matter under discussion.

You announced beforehand that you would say these things, and you wrote:

> “All philosophers, although they discuss different matters in their schools, nevertheless worship idols with the common people. Those who have attempted to devise something concerning natural causes, amid the many vanities of their opinions, have nevertheless, as it were, touched upon certain portions of truth; the following words are textually uncertain: *qui per caliginem vani*; nevertheless, they can rightly be preferred to this doctrine against which we are arguing.” [Note: Belgian manuscripts, three Vatican manuscripts, and two Gallican manuscripts read “amid the many opinions of their vanity.” Am. reads: “some truths, as it were wool-bearing parts, who through the darkness of vanity”; Er. and Lov. read: “some truths, as it were now almost equal, through the darkness of vanity.” The editions are corrected from the old Gallican and Vatican books. The Belgian manuscripts differ only in reading *jam serae* for *lambere*, perhaps through a copyist’s error. One Vatican manuscript has *lambuere*.]

To prove this, you added the names of the natural philosophers and the opinions they held concerning natural causes, which I too have just recalled. Yet you did not mention all of them, whether because you did not wish or were unable to do so. In this matter you deceived the uneducated, without any learned person disputing it. [Note: Lov. reads “without any dispute among the learned.”]

For you had undertaken to demonstrate that “all philosophers who have attempted to devise something concerning natural causes can rightly be preferred to the doctrine against which you were arguing.”

Why, then—to say nothing of many others—when you had mentioned Anaximenes and his pupil Anaxagoras, did you keep silent about another of his pupils, Diogenes, who disagreed with both his teacher and his fellow pupil concerning the nature of things and established a doctrine of his own?

What if he himself held an opinion such that he ought not to be preferred to us, even though you said that all who have philosophized about the nature of things ought to be preferred? And as though to demonstrate this, you foolishly inflated yourself by uselessly recalling the names and doctrines of philosophers.

There: you passed over one whom, whether because of the teacher or the fellow pupil whom you named, you ought to have considered alongside them. Or did you perhaps fear that Diogenes the Cynic would be thought of, or that he would occur to readers because of the same name and bring to mind that he was a better patron of the lust whose practice he was not ashamed to display publicly? From this the sect received its canine name.

You, however, profess to be a defender of lust, but you are ashamed of the position you have undertaken—a shame that did not suit the faithfulness and freedom of its patron.

### 76

But, I beg you, if you were eager to place philosophers before us, why did you not rather mention those who argued most skillfully about morals—that part of philosophy which they call ethics and which we call moral philosophy?

This would have suited you especially, since you consider bodily pleasure to be the good of the human being, though it is inferior to moral excellence of mind.

But who does not see what you had in view? You feared that, in the very question concerning pleasure about which we are disputing, more honorable philosophers would overwhelm you—those whom Cicero, because of their moral excellence, called “consular philosophers”—and especially the Stoics, the most hostile of all to pleasure. You thought it necessary to introduce their testimony, spoken through the person of Balbus in Cicero, a testimony that was true but utterly useless to you (above, section 58). [Note: Am. and all our manuscripts read “whose testimony, spoken through the person of Balbus.”]

You wished to conceal the fact that they consider bodily pleasure no good of the human being. Accordingly, you did not mention the names and doctrines of philosophers concerning moral questions, although that was most relevant if anything about philosophers was to be established.

For they would not have defended you—not Epicurus, who placed the entire good of the human being in bodily pleasure, since you do not hold what he held, but Dinomachus. His doctrine is the one that pleased you. He judged that pleasure should be joined to moral excellence, so that pleasure, like moral excellence, might appear desirable for its own sake (see Cicero, *De finibus* 5 and *Tusculan Disputations* 5).

When you saw that this area, where moral matters are discussed, was hostile to you, you were afraid to touch upon it. [Note: The manuscripts do not have “For”; nor do they begin a new sentence until after “is at issue,” at the words “how great and what kind.”]

For where this controversy is principally situated, you can see how great, what kind, and of what renown among the Gentiles are the philosophers who are preferred to you. Above all there is Plato himself, whom Cicero does not hesitate to call almost the god of philosophers (*On the Nature of the Gods* 2 and *Letters to Atticus* 4.16). You could not pass over even his name when you brought forward or preferred to us the doctrines of philosophers concerning natural rather than moral matters, since he is said to have spoken truly and seriously of bodily pleasures as “the allurements and food of evils” (above, section 72).

### 77

But did you mention what the philosophers you named thought about the condition of the human being? This too belongs to the natural question, and you considered it necessary to mention whatever the case required.

You did not do so, and rightly. For what had they learned, or what had they said, about the first man Adam and his wife, their first transgression, the serpent’s cunning, the nakedness of their bodies before sin without shame, and the shame that immediately followed sin? What had they heard resembling the Apostle’s statement:

> Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death; and so it passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned (Romans 5:12)?

Lacking these Scriptures and this truth, what could they have understood about this matter? [Note: The Gallican and Vatican manuscripts omit “and” (*cum*) in “and with shame immediately after sin.”]

But if you judged that the doctrines of men alien to our sacred Scriptures concerning the condition of the human being should not be included—and you judged correctly—how much less could what you did include assist you: namely, what they thought about the beginnings of this visible world, a matter over which no question is disputed between us?

Rather, your mind is overturned by the vanity of self-display, as though you had learned something great from the books of the philosophers.

### 78

Those philosophers seem not without reason to have approached the Christian faith who did not suppose that this life, so full of deception and misery, had come about except by divine judgment, thereby attributing justice to the Creator by whom this world was made and is governed.

How much better than you, and how much nearer to the truth, did those whom Cicero recalls at the end of the dialogue *Hortensius* think about the generation of human beings—as though led and compelled by the very evidence of things!

After speaking of the many things that we see and lament concerning human vanity and unhappiness, he says:

> “From these errors and hardships of human life it comes about that sometimes those ancient men—whether poets, or interpreters of the divine mind in sacred rites and initiations—who said that we were born to undergo punishment for certain crimes committed in an earlier life, seem to have seen something. And what Aristotle says may be true: that we are afflicted by a punishment like that of those who, once they had fallen into the hands of Etruscan pirates, were killed through an ingeniously devised cruelty. Their living bodies were bound as closely as possible to dead bodies, with face joined to face; so our souls have been joined to our bodies as the living are joined to the dead.”

Did not those who held such views perceive, far better than you, the grievous yoke laid upon the sons of Adam and the power and justice of God—even though they did not see the grace granted through the Mediator for the liberation of human beings?

There: I have found in the writings of those Gentile philosophers something that can rightly be preferred to you. You provoked this by being unable to find anything of the kind in them, yet unwilling to remain silent lest you remind me to find something against you.

### CHAPTER XVI

### 79

What of the fact that you think the Apostle’s testimony supports you, when it is actually against you? You assert that our members—which were certainly naked before sin and did not shame those to whom they belonged—were shameful, not knowing what you are saying.

I should have brought forward the testimony that you yourself cited, where the Apostle says:

> Much more, those parts of our body which seem to be weaker are necessary; and the rest which you yourself cited on our behalf.

You yourself cited these words on our behalf. Yet it is worthwhile to consider how you came to say such things.

“Now, then,” you say, “it is time to show, beyond the testimony of nature, also by the authority of the law, that our members were formed in such a way that some rejoiced in shame and others in freedom. To confirm this,” you say, “let the Teacher of the Gentiles be summoned, who, writing to the Corinthians, says: ‘Our body is not one member but many.’”

Then, after adding the apostolic words in which he magnificently explained the unity and harmony of the members, you say:

> “And because he had named only a few members of the whole body, and, out of regard for decency, did not wish to name the generative organs directly…”

Do you not condemn yourself by these words? Decency, then, required that he not name directly what God had rightly deigned to make; and what had not shamed the Judge himself when he created it shamed the herald when he spoke of it.

When would this be so, unless what God had made honorable by creating it, we had made dishonorable by sinning?

80. You then add an apostolic testimony on this matter, which you recall as written in the following way:

“For much more, those members of our body that seem to be weaker are necessary; and upon those members of the body that we think less honorable we bestow more abundant honor; and our unpresentable members have greater decency, whereas our presentable members have no need of this. But God has so composed the body, giving greater honor to the member that lacked it, so that there might be no division in the body, but that the members might have the same concern for one another” (1 Cor. 12:12, 22–25). [Note: Thus the manuscripts and printed editions; they read *inhonorabilia*, “unhonorable,” rather than *inhonorabiliora*, “less honorable.”] [Note: Thus the manuscripts and printed editions; they read *abundantiorem dando honorem*, “by giving more abundant honor.”]

After these words, you exclaim as though victorious: “Behold a true interpreter of God’s work; behold a faithful herald of his wisdom. ‘Our more unpresentable members,’ he says, ‘are covered with greater decency.’”

You thought that your whole case should certainly be tied to this one word, which you read the Apostle as having said: “our more unpresentable members.” But if you had read “our unhonorable members,” you would in no way have dared to introduce this testimony. For in no way would God—and, what is worse, before sin—have made anything unhonorable in the members of the human body.

Learn, then, what you do not know, because you were unwilling to seek carefully. The Apostle said “unhonorable,” but certain interpreters—including, I think, the one whom you read—being, I believe, ashamed, said “more unpresentable” for what he had called “unhonorable.” This is demonstrated by the words written in the very Greek text from which you translated these apostolic words. For what you have rendered “more unpresentable” is written in Greek as ἀσχήμονα (*aschēmona*). What follows, “have greater decency,” is in Greek εὐσχημοσύνην (*euschēmosynēn*), which, translated fully, means “decency.” Hence it is evident that those things called ἀσχήμονα are called *unhonorable* in Latin.

Finally, for what is added—“whereas our presentable members”—the Greek has εὐσχήμονα (*euschē‌mona*). Hence it is clear that those things called ἀσχήμονα are unhonorable. Indeed, even without any consideration of the Greek words, you ought by that very fact to have been warned that those things requiring the greater honor of a covering are unhonorable, since those that do not require this work are called honorable.

For what else does “our honorable members have no need” mean except “those members that require it are unhonorable”? Honor, therefore, is applied to the unhonorable when they are covered by the very sense of rational nature, which feels shame. Their decency and honor consist in their covering, and this is more abundant in proportion as they are more unhonorable. The Apostle certainly would not have said this if he were describing a body such as human beings had when they were naked and felt no shame.

81. Consider, then, how shamelessly you say that human beings were “originally naked because it belonged to the work of human ingenuity to cover themselves, and that ingenuity was not yet in them.” [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads, “which was not yet theirs,” omitting “in.”] It follows from this that you believe them to have been sluggish before sin, but to have become ingenious through sin.

And how many empty statements you bring together, as though concluding elegantly and cleverly, when you say: “Therefore it was not because they had sinned that they made their genitals diabolical or unhonorable; rather, because they were afraid, they covered those members, which remained in the honor they had possessed at first!”

To this I reply that the members are certainly not diabolical with respect to their substance, form, or quality, which God created. But if those same members remained in the honor they had possessed before, why did the Apostle call them unhonorable? It is good that you yourself have confessed that those members were previously honorable; for you could not think otherwise without holding a blasphemous opinion.

Those things, therefore, that God had made honorable, the Apostle called unhonorable. I ask the reason: if this did not happen through sin, through what did it happen? Who dishonored God’s honorable works, so that the holy Apostle would call them unhonorable? Was it the disposition in which the Creator’s ingenuity is found, or the desire in which the sinner’s punishment is found? Even now, what God does there is honorable; what origin contracts is unhonorable.

And yet, so that there might not be divisions in the body, divine providence has added to natural perception a concern that the members should care for one another. What desire dishonored, shame covers.

82. But you say: “Why did Adam and his wife hide themselves when they heard the voice of God walking in the garden, when those loincloths would have been sufficient” (Gen. 3:8, 7), if they had felt shame at the nakedness of their genitals? [Note: The words “if they had felt shame at the nakedness of their genitals” are absent from the manuscripts.]

What is this that you say, when you do not find anything to say? You do not notice that, with their minds trembling before the face of the Lord, they sought more hidden hiding places. Those coverings placed around their loins concealed, through shame, the movement that was felt there.

If, when they were naked, they felt no shame, it remains that they covered themselves because of shame. There can be no doubt that shame concerns what is unhonorable. Hence it is said there: “They were naked, and they were not ashamed” (Gen. 2:25), so that it might be evident that what they later covered was done because of shame.

But here, when they hid themselves among the trees of the garden, Adam replied: “I heard your voice as you were walking in the garden, and I was afraid because I am naked.” The former was manifest shame; the latter, a hidden conscience, through which manifest shame arose inwardly when he sinned. The former, therefore, was caused by shame; the latter by fear. The former by a desire that ought to be ashamed; the latter by a conscience that ought to be punished. He was like a madman, fleeing by hiding his body from the one who saw the inward things of his heart.

What, then, does the Lord’s statement mean: “Who told you that you are naked, unless you have eaten from the tree from which I commanded you not to eat?” (Gen. 3:10–11). What else does the indication of nakedness after the forbidden food had been tasted mean except that the one whom grace had covered was stripped naked by sin?

For God’s grace was great there, where an earthly and animal body did not possess bestial desire. Therefore, the one who, clothed in grace, had nothing in his naked body of which he should be ashamed, once stripped of grace perceived what he ought to cover.

83. “An opinion must be rejected,” you say, “which supposes that the devil created something either in human members or in the senses of the members.”

Why do you charge us with your own empty extravagances? The devil did not create anything pertaining to human nature. Rather, he violated what God had created well through the persuasion of sin, so that through the wound inflicted by the free will of two human beings the whole human race should limp.

Behold, the misery of the human race surrounds your senses. You are a human being; think that nothing human is foreign to you (Terence, *Heautontimorumenos*, act 1, scene 1, line 25), and in what you do not suffer yourself, sympathize with those who suffer.

Even if you surpass others in whatever earthly happiness, you pass no day without an internal war—if, that is, you try to fulfill what you profess. But in matters you can no longer remember, look at little children: how many and how great are the evils they suffer, amid what vanities, torments, errors, and terrors they grow.

Then, when they have grown, even those serving God are tested: error tests them in order to deceive; labor or pain tests them in order to break them; desire tests them in order to inflame them; grief tests them in order to overthrow them; fever tests them in order to puff them up. Who could quickly enumerate all the things by which the yoke is laid heavily upon the sons of Adam?

The evident misery of the nations compelled philosophers—whether they knew or believed nothing about the first man’s sin—to say that we had been born in order to pay the penalties for crimes committed in an earlier life, and that our souls were joined to corruptible bodies, by the very punishment with which the Etruscan pirates were accustomed to torment their captives, as though the living were joined to the dead.

But the Apostle cuts off the opinion that individual souls are inserted into different bodies according to the merits of their former life. What, then, remains except that the cause of these evils is either God’s injustice or inability, or the punishment of the first and ancient sin?

But since God is neither unjust nor unable, what remains is what you do not wish to confess but are compelled to confess: that the heavy yoke upon the sons of Adam, from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of their burial in the mother of all (Ecclus. 40:1), would not have existed unless the guilt of original sin had preceded it.

# BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0781]

He takes up the third book of Julian and first explains why the Christian multitude detests the new heresy that rejects original sin: evidently because it sees the image of God suffering such great torments in little children and knows that, if they die without the Sacrament of regeneration, they are excluded from the kingdom of God. He proves that the loincloths were assumed by our first parents because of the shame arising from sin. Sin can be the punishment of a preceding sin, as when God hands the ungodly over to a reprobate mind so that they do what is improper. From the same mass of damnation, some sinners are freely elected and predestined, whom he brings to repentance through merciful goodness, while others are made vessels of wrath, whom according to his just judgment he does not bring to repentance. Concupiscence is not worthy of praise because through it human disobedience is punished; rather, it is a vice and remains evil even in those who do not consent to its corrupt movements. How the Apostle’s statement, “that each person should know how to possess his own vessel,” and so forth, is to be understood. That a marriage without intercourse, such as that of Mary with Joseph, is a true marriage. It is futile to argue against sin transmitted from parents by means of Aristotelian categories. He shows how the flesh of Christ differs from the flesh of other human beings subject to sin. Catholics do not favor the Manichaeans when they acknowledge the evil of lust and original sin; rather, they favor the Pelagians when they say that “sins are not born from that which is free from sin.” Throughout, he shows that his opponent strives in vain to extract something in his own favor from his own statements that seem mutually contradictory.

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0781]

1. Since we have responded to your first and second books, the order itself requires that we now examine what your third book contains, and respond to your destructive labors with our salutary labors, insofar as the Lord assists us. We shall retain our established method: we will pass over matters that have no controversy relevant to the issue between us, lest those who wish to know our position spend more labor and time in reading than in gaining instruction.

What need is there, then, for me to say anything against the customary and empty matters that you placed at the beginning of this book—“about the envy that you claim to endure for the sake of truth, and about the small number of people, supposedly wise, whose approval you rejoice to have”?

This is the language of all heretics, both ancient and modern, already dirtied and worn out through constant use. [Note: Erasmus and Louvain read *pertrita*, “worn away.”] Yet even your great pride is forced by necessity to clothe itself in such rags. It is stretched and inflated in such a way that, while eagerly displaying them, it tears them apart still more grotesquely.

Nor is it necessary to refute repeatedly your most slanderous insults, by which you seem to attack me alone by name, while, without naming them, you either madly assault or blindly offend so many and such great lights of the Catholic faith. Hence I think that in my responses to your first two books I answered you in such a way that no one will ask for more.

2.
