You emphasize how “difficult and suited to only a few educated people is knowledge of the holy Scriptures,” evidently so that “God, as the creator of human beings and of the universe, and as just, truthful, and merciful, may likewise be shown to be one who heaps up his gifts upon human beings.” [Note: Most manuscripts read “God, the creator of human beings as of the universe”; others, with Amerbach and Erasmus, read “God, the creator of human beings as of all things”; Louvain reads “God, as the creator of the universe,” omitting “of human beings.”] [Note: The corrected Floriacensis manuscript reads “thus.”] For, as you admit, “there is one excellent reason for good studies: that God may be honored.”

Yet you honor him in such a way as to deny that he delivers little children through Christ Jesus—that is, through the Savior—although you say that they are so washed in his Baptism that they do not attain salvation [Note: The printed editions read “you say”; the manuscripts read “you say” in the plural.], as though they did not need Christ the physician, while Julian, with keen inspection of the vein of human origin, pronounces them healthy.

How much better it would have been if you had learned absolutely nothing, rather than, through that supposed knowledge of the law in which you boast arrogantly—not under the guidance of God’s law, but rather through your own vanity—having reached this impious presumption, hostile to the Christian faith and to your own soul.

3. “Your opinion,” you say, “is so deformed and empty that it attempts to attribute injustice to God, the creation of human beings to the devil, substance to sin, and consciousness without knowledge to little children.”

I answer briefly: Our opinion is not deformed, because it proclaims the Savior of all human beings, including little children, as “beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Ps. 44:3). Nor is it empty, since it does not say without reason, but with sin preceding, that the human being was made like vanity, whose days pass away like a shadow (Ps. 143:4). [Note: Louvain reads “because”; the other printed editions and the manuscripts read “which.”]

It does not attribute injustice to God, but rather justice, because it is not unjust that even a little child should be punished by the many and great evils we see so frequently. It does not attribute the creation of human beings to the devil, but the corruption of human origin. It does not attribute substance to sin [Note: In this place Erasmus adds *deputamus*, “we attribute”; Louvain has *deputat*, “he attributes”; Amerbach, together with some manuscripts, has *deputari*, “to be attributed.” The word is absent from the better manuscripts, with the sense understood as “he attributes.”], but in the first human beings an act, and in their descendants a contagion.

Nor does it attribute consciousness without knowledge to little children, in whom there is neither knowledge nor consciousness. Rather, that one knew what he had done, in whom all sinned, and each individually drew evil from it.

4. But you, who marshal a multitude of uneducated people whom you call “simple,” [Note: The Louvain editors deleted “who.”] who, occupied with other affairs, have acquired nothing of learning but nevertheless took care to come to the Church of Christ by faith alone, so that they would not easily be frightened by obscure questions—yet, believing that God is the true creator of human beings, should also hold without hesitation that he is merciful, truthful, and just [Note: Louvain and Belgian manuscripts read *indubitate*, “without hesitation.”]—and who, maintaining this judgment about the Trinity, embrace and praise whatever they hear that agrees with this opinion, allowing no force of argument to tear it away from them, but detesting every authority and every association attempting to persuade them of the contrary—

if you consider these very words of yours, you make them all the firmer against you.

For there is no other reason why even the Christian multitude detests your innovation [Note: Some manuscripts have “the multitude of Christians.”], from whose supposedly uneducated judgment you appeal to the few of your own whom you wish to appear most wise and learned, except that they think of God as both the creator of human beings and [Note: The coordinating conjunction *et*, “and,” is omitted here in Louvain.] most just. They see their little children suffering such great torments that, under the best and most just Creator, his image could not possibly suffer such evils at that age if original sin did not exist.

Suppose that one of them, carrying his little son, were to address you without envious shouting, and in a place where no one else could hear, saying:

“I possess the mind, understanding, and reason in which I was made in the image of God. I love the kingdom of God so greatly that I judge it a great punishment for a human being never to be able to enter it.”

Would you, then, not as one of the uneducated multitude but as one among the few wisest lovers of that kingdom—more ardent, certainly, because the most fervent fellowship of the few inflames you toward it, and because the colder multitude does not make you grow sluggish—answer that man by saying: “It is not merely a great punishment, but no punishment at all, for the image of God never to be able to enter the kingdom of God”?

I think that you would not dare to say this even to a single man whose force and testimony you did not fear. Whether, therefore, you replied anything or remained silent—which Christian, or at least human, shame would demand of you all the more—he would place his little child before your eyes and say:

“God is just. What evil is there that prevents this innocent image of his from entering his kingdom, if this is not the sin that entered the world through one man?” (Rom. 5:12).

I think that you would have no wisdom by which you could regard yourself as more learned than that uneducated man. But if shamelessness departed from you, you would remain more childish than that infant.

## CHAPTER TWO

5. But now that you have concluded your preface—by dismissing the uneducated after warning them and preparing for yourself the highly learned ears of the few—let us see what argument you undertake.

Something sufficiently clever has occurred to you, it seems, which escaped you in your second book, when you had said much about the shameful members that, after sin, were covered by a covering of fig leaves while rational nature felt shame. You had vainly attempted to refute what I had said: “Why, then, did confusion arise from those members after sin, unless an indecent movement arose there?” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, §5).

What, then, have you thought up that pleased you so much that, even after finishing the volume in which you had discussed this question at such length, you thought it should not be omitted?

You say that it is written, “And they made themselves garments” (Gen. 3:7), and you mention that it has another interpretation, namely, *perizomata*. You claim that “garments may be understood as clothing of the whole body, which is related to the function of modesty.”

Here I am surprised that the interpreter whom you read—if he was not a Pelagian—could have translated the Greek *perizomata* as “garments.” But even here, if shame were present, to whose function you say garments belong, you would never try to persuade us that the first human beings learned these duties of shame from sin as their teacher, and that innocence and shamelessness had previously dwelt together in them as two companions and friends.

When they were naked and were not ashamed, they were, according to your argument, shameless and contrary to the natural sense of modesty. Evidently they were corrected from this depravity by sinning, and a reprobate sense became in them the teacher of shame through transgression. Wickedness made them modest, although justice had made them shameless.

Indeed, your opinion is so indecently shameless and so deformedly naked that, however many leaves of words you sew together, you cannot cover it.

6. You mock me for having learned from painters that Adam and his wife covered their shameful parts, and you order me to hear that celebrated line of Horace:

> Painters and poets  
> Have always had an equal license to dare anything.  
> (*The Art of Poetry*, lines 9–10)

But I learned this not from a painter of empty figures, but from the writer of the divine Scriptures: those first human beings were naked before they sinned, and they were not ashamed.

Far be it from us to suppose that such great innocence was so shameless; there was not yet anything of which they should be ashamed. They sinned, they perceived, they blushed, they covered themselves (Gen. 2:25–3:11). And still you shout: “They perceived nothing indecent or new there.”

No apostle or prophet taught you this utterly incredible shamelessness of yours—not to mention that no painter or poet taught it either. Those very men who, as the elegant saying has it, “have always had an equal license to dare anything,” would be ashamed to imagine anything so ridiculous as what you are not ashamed to argue should be believed.

No painter would dare paint, and no poet sing of, innocence and shamelessness dwelling together as two companions, one excellent and the other most evil, as though agreeing and at peace with each other. Nor would any of them despair so greatly of human perception as to believe that even this gave him an equal license to dare anything; rather, they would recognize it as insane vanity.

7. But when you said, “If support is given to that interpretation which rendered *perizomata*, that is, aprons, I would say that the sides were covered rather than the thighs,” I first regret that you so abuse the ignorance of those who do not know Greek that you have not respected the judgment of those who do.

It has worked out more conveniently, however, that the very word *perizomata*, which is read in the Greek manuscripts, has been adopted by Latin usage as though it were a word of its own language.

Accordingly, when you insisted that a *perizomate* could cover not the thighs but the sides [Note: The printed editions read *perizomata*; the reading has been corrected from Vatican and Gallican manuscripts.], I think you laughed at yourself as well. For what learned or unlearned person does not know what parts of the body *perizomata* cover? The name of this covering is also commonly used and valued in connection with women’s dowries, and it is bound only by a belt that encircles the loins.

Ask, and learn what I do not believe you fail to know.

Even if you do not know it, I do not think you are so far from wishing to distort not human speech but human dress that you would try to raise *perizomata* over their shoulders, or claim that the sides of those human beings were covered in such a way that their genitals and the whole region of their loins and thighs remained naked.

What advantage, then, does this give you rather than me? However much of the upper part of the body may have been covered down toward the lower parts, the law in the members, resisting the law of the mind (Rom. 7:23), was felt in the desire of both and was aroused by each seeing the other. It shamed their disobedient perversity through the novelty of their own disobedience.

The more turbulently it moved, the more shamefully it would become, if the flesh whose appearance provoked it were covered somewhat more extensively.

Whether, therefore, the coverings descended from the loins or from the sides, the shameful parts were covered. They would not be shameful unless the law of sin were enviously resisting the law of the mind [Note: Four Vatican manuscripts have *itidem repugnaret*, “likewise resisted”; a fifth has *ididem*. One Belgian manuscript has *ibidem*, “there.” The Louvain editors think that Augustine is referring to James 4:5: “The spirit that dwells in you desires jealously.”].

But where the matter is clear, we must not add our own sense to the meaning of divine Scripture. This does not arise from human ignorance, but from perverse presumption.

Adam and his wife, who were naked before sin and were not ashamed, covered certain parts of their bodies as soon as they sinned; this is expressed clearly enough by the name *perizomata*. We see what they covered. It is the height of foolishness still to ask what they felt, and the height of shamelessness still to deny it.

For you too, although you contradict this with the utmost obstinacy, judged that nothing else could occur to human perception except that those human beings, ashamed of the movement of desire, wished to cover their genitals. Hence you try to raise the *perizomata* to their sides—either covering the side where you insist that the sinners felt nothing wrong, or exposing shamefully what you agree ought rather to be covered.

## CHAPTER THREE

8. You insert other words from my book, in which I said that “the disobedience of the flesh was most deservedly repaid to the disobedient human being, because it was unjust that his servant—that is, his body—should obey one who had not obeyed his Lord” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, §7).

You try to show that “this disobedience of the flesh is rather praiseworthy if it is the punishment of sin.” And as though it were some person who knowingly afflicts the sinner, you adorn it with the rhetorical grandeur of a tragedy as “the avenger of crime and, in this, God’s minister,” as though it were some great good.

Nor do you consider that by this reasoning you could praise the evil angels, who are certainly nothing other than transgressors and ungodly beings, yet through whom, as Holy Scripture testifies, God inflicts deserved punishments upon sinners. It says: “He sent upon them the fury of his anger, indignation, wrath, and tribulation, a visitation through evil angels” (Ps. 77:49).

Praise them too; praise their prince, Satan, because he too was an avenger of sin when the Apostle handed a man over to him “for the destruction of the flesh” (1 Cor. 5:5).

You are very eloquent against the grace of Christ and well suited to deliver a panegyric to Satan and his angels, through whom God, the judge and avenger of many sinners, repays them according to their works, making those very wicked and damnable spirits the punishments of those who must be punished. He makes good use of both the good and the evil.

So praise the most wicked powers, since through them evil is repaid to the evil. This is why you praise the concupiscence of the flesh: because disobedience is repaid to the disobedience of the sinner.

Praise the wicked king Saul, because he too was a punishment for sinners, as the Lord says: “I gave you a king in my anger” (Hos. 13:11). Praise the demon whom that king suffered (1 Sam. 16:14), because this too was the punishment of a sinner.

Praise the blindness of heart that came upon Israel in part [Note: Louvain has “in Israel.” The word “in” is absent from the other printed editions and manuscripts, as well as from the Apostle’s Greek text.]. Nor is the reason for this omitted [Note: The printed editions read, “Nor is the reason for Israel’s blindness omitted. Why?” The words “for Israel’s blindness” have been removed on the authority of the manuscripts.]. It says: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter” (Rom. 11:25).

Unless perhaps you will also deny that this was a punishment. If you were a lover of the inner light, you would cry out that it was not merely some punishment but a very great one.

That blindness among the Jews was a great evil of unbelief and a great cause of sin, so that they killed Christ. [Note: Erasmus and Louvain read “Now this blindness”; “now” is absent from Amerbach and the manuscripts.] If you deny that this blindness was a punishment, you will show, by refusing to confess it, that you suffer something similar.

But if you contend that it was indeed a punishment, though not the punishment of sin, for the moment you admit that one and the same thing can be both sin and punishment. If this is not the punishment of sin, then the punishment is certainly unjust, and you make God unjust, by whose command or permission it is inflicted, or weak, because he does not avert it, when it is inflicted upon the innocent [Note: The Louvain edition alone has “upon the guilty”; this is incorrect.].

But if you also concede that it is the punishment of sin—lest, by refusing to concede this, you yourself appear blind in heart [Note: Louvain likewise has “lest, by conceding this,” having omitted the negative particle found in the other books.]—then see what you did not wish to see: the question you raised has been resolved.

For just as the devil, his angels, and wicked kings are not only themselves sinners but, through God’s justice, also become the punishments of sins—and are not therefore worthy of praise because a just punishment is inflicted through them upon those who deserve it—so the law in the members that resists the law of the mind does not act justly merely because it becomes the just punishment of one who acted unjustly.

And just as blindness of heart, which God alone—the illuminator—removes, is both a sin, by which God is not believed; a punishment of sin, by which a proud heart is punished with deserved correction; and a cause of sin, when some evil is committed through the error of a blind heart—so the concupiscence of the flesh, against which the good spirit desires, is both a sin, because disobedience against the mind’s dominion is present in it; a punishment of sin, because it was repaid according to the merits of the disobedient; and a cause of sin, through the defection of one who consents or through the contagion of one who is born.

9. Accordingly, all that you said in support of your blind and thoughtless opinion—by which you thought that, simply because we said the concupiscence of the flesh is the punishment of sin, it should not only not be condemned but even praised—has certainly vanished, however long you may have lingered over it in your extended argument [Note: Five manuscripts have “in it” rather than “over it.”].

For when you said, “If lust is the punishment of sin, chastity must be discarded, lest chastity, rebelling against God, be said to weaken the sentence imposed by him,” and the other statements of this kind that you weave together as consequences linked to this absurdity, the very same words could be said, by an entirely similar error, about blindness of heart:

“If blindness of heart is the punishment of sin, instruction must be discarded, lest the illumination of the mind, rebelling against God, be said to weaken the sentence imposed by him.”

If it is absurd to say this, although blindness of heart is the punishment of sin, then what you yourself said is equally absurd, although lust—that is, the disobedience of the flesh—is the punishment of sin.

Knowledge must resist blindness of heart, and self-restraint must resist lust. But the punishment that is neither error nor lust must be endured with patience.

Therefore, when true faith is lived by God’s gift, God himself is present to illuminate the mind, overcome concupiscence, and endure distress. All this is rightly done when it is done for his sake—that is, when he himself is loved freely. Such love cannot exist in us except from him.

Otherwise, when a human being takes great pleasure in himself and trusts in his own virtue, if he is handed over to the desires of his pride, this evil increases all the more in proportion as the other desires have yielded to him, and he has suppressed them while indulging this one as though it were worthy of praise.

10. You say that you read in some of my other works, and vainly attempted to refute, that there are certain sins that are also punishments of sins (*On Nature and Grace*, §25). Set aside your desire to win and attend carefully; you will find that this is entirely true, in accordance with what has been discussed concerning blindness of heart.

What, I ask you, what did you accomplish by recalling the apostolic testimony through which I proved what you read in another argument of mine? The Apostle wrote of certain people: “God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is improper.”

You wanted this to appear to have been said hyperbolically—that is, in a way that exceeds the truth of the matter in order to stir the emotions of those listening. You should not hesitate to show where the Apostle did this.

“When he was attacking the crimes of the ungodly,” you say, “he intensified them by calling them punishments, showing how greatly their shame horrified his breast, the dwelling place of every virtue; and he said that such people seemed to him not so much guilty as condemned.”

On the contrary, just as he himself speaks—not as you pretend that he speaks—he showed them to be both condemned and guilty. He showed them to be guilty not only because of past acts for which they were condemned, but also because of the very thing from which they were condemned.

He shows them guilty where he says: “They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.”

Then he shows that they were condemned because of this guilt. For it follows: “For this reason God handed them over to dishonorable passions.”

You hear the words “for this reason,” and you ask pointlessly how God’s handing them over should be understood, laboring greatly to show that he hands them over by abandoning them.

However he hands them over, it was because of this that he handed them over; because of this that he abandoned them. And you see what followed from his handing them over, however and in whatever manner you understand it.

For the Apostle took care to say how great a punishment it is to be handed over by God to dishonorable passions, whether through abandonment or through any other explicable or inexplicable manner by which the supremely good and ineffably just God brings this about.

“For their women,” he says, “exchanged natural use for that which is against nature. Likewise, the men, abandoning natural use of the woman, burned in their desire for one another, males committing disgraceful acts with males and receiving in themselves the due recompense for their error.”

What could be clearer, more open, or more explicit than this? He says that they received a mutual recompense—obviously condemned people, so that they might commit such great evils. Yet this condemnation is itself also guilt, by which they are more gravely entangled.

Thus these things are both sins and punishments of preceding sins. And what is more remarkable, he says that they ought to have received this mutual recompense.

The Apostle’s preceding words have the same meaning, the words you yourself cited:

“They exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed animals, and serpents. Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity” (Rom. 1:23–24), and the rest that follows.

Here too, plainly and without ambiguity, you see that he indicates the reason for which they were handed over. He said what evil they had previously committed, and added: “Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts.”

This punishment, then, is the punishment of a preceding sin. Yet it is itself also a sin, as he explains in the words that follow.

11. But in arguing against this, you think that you have resolved the question in this way: the Apostle said that they were handed over to their desires.

“For already,” you say, “they were burning with the desires for crimes.” And you add:

“How, then, are they to be thought to have fallen into such acts through the power of the God who handed them over?”

What more, I ask you, was done? Or why would he say, “God handed them over to the desires of their hearts,” if they were already possessed, in some fashion, by the evil desires of their hearts?

But does it follow that, if someone has evil desires of the heart, he already consents to them in order to commit those same evils? Accordingly, it is one thing to have evil desires of the heart and another to be handed over to them—namely, so as to be possessed by them through consenting to them. This happens when a person is handed over to them by divine judgment.

Otherwise it was said in vain: “Do not follow your desires” (Ecclus. 18:30), if a person is already guilty merely because he feels desires that are in turmoil and strive to draw him toward evil, while he does not follow them because he has not been handed over to them, but wages glorious battles against them if he lives in grace.

What do you think of the person who observes what is written [Note: The Louvain edition alone reads “what.”]: “If you grant your soul its desires”—and what else are these than its evil desires?—“it will make you a joy to your enemies and to those who envy you” (Ecclus. 18:30–31) [Note: An old Bigotian manuscript reads “they will make you.”].

Is this person already guilty merely because he has such desires of the soul, which he ought not to grant, lest he become a joy to the devil and his angels, who are our enemies and those who envy us?

[Col. 0790] **12.** When, therefore, a person is said to be handed over to his desires, he becomes guilty because, abandoned by God, he yields to and consents to them; he is conquered, captured, dragged along [Note: [Col. 0790] The Louvain editors think one should read *is handed over*. For thus above: “to be handed over to them; namely, so that by consenting to them he may be possessed by them”; and, “nor does he follow them, if he is not handed over to them.”], and possessed. For “by whatever a person is overcome, by that he is enslaved” (II Peter 2:19); and sin becomes the consequence of sin already committed, as well as its punishment.

Is it not both sin and the punishment of sin where we read: “For the Lord has mingled among them a spirit of error, and they have led Egypt astray in all its works, as a drunken man is led astray” (Isaiah 19:14)? Is it not both sin and the punishment of sin where the Prophet says to God: “Why have you caused us to err from your ways, O Lord? You have hardened our hearts, so that we would not fear you” (ibid. 63:17)? Is it not both sin and the punishment of sin where it is again said to God: “Behold, you were angry, and we sinned; therefore we went astray, and we have all become like the unclean” (ibid. 64:5–6)? Is it not both sin and the punishment of sin where it is read concerning the nations whom Jesus son of Naveh conquered, that “the Lord caused their hearts to be strengthened, so that they might go out to battle against Israel, in order that they might be exterminated” (Joshua 11:20)?

Is it not both sin and the punishment of sin that King Rehoboam did not listen to the people giving him good counsel, since, as Scripture says, “the turning of affairs was from the Lord, so that he might establish his word which he had spoken concerning him by the hand of the prophet” [Note: [Col. 0790] The Louvain edition adds *Ahijah*.] (III Kings 12:15)? Is it not both sin and the punishment of sin in what is written concerning Amaziah, king of Judah, who refused to listen to Joash, king of Israel, giving him good advice not to proceed to battle? For thus we read: “And Amaziah did not listen, because it was from God, in order that he might be handed over into the hands” [Note: [Col. 0790] Here too the Louvain editors added *of the enemies*, although this is absent from all the manuscripts and from the Septuagint.] “of those who had sought the god of Edom” (II Chronicles 25:20).

And we can recall many other examples in which it plainly appears that, by God’s hidden judgment, perversity of heart comes about, so that what is said truthfully is not heard; and that from this there follows sin, so that the sin itself is also the punishment of a preceding sin. For to believe a lie and not to believe the truth is certainly sin. Yet it proceeds from that blindness of heart which, by God’s hidden but nevertheless just judgment, is shown also to be the punishment of sin.

Such too is what the Apostle writes to the Thessalonians: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth, so that they might be saved, and therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie” (II Thessalonians 2:10). Behold: the punishment of sin is itself sin. Both points are clear; the statement is brief, it is explicit, and it was spoken by the one whose other words you have tried in vain to twist into support of your position.

**13.** What, then, is the meaning of your statement that, when people are said to be handed over to their desires, they are to be understood as abandoned through divine patience, not compelled to sin by divine power? It is as though the same Apostle had not placed both patience and power together when he says: “But if God, wishing to show his wrath and to make known his power, endured with much patience the vessels of wrath that were prepared for destruction” (Romans 9:22). Which of these, nevertheless, do you say is meant in what is written: “And if a prophet should err and speak, I, the Lord, have led that prophet astray; and I will stretch out my hand against him, and I will destroy him from the midst of my people Israel” (Ezekiel 14:9)? Is this patience, or power? Choose whichever you wish, or acknowledge both; nevertheless, you see that the prophet’s false utterance is sin and that it is also the punishment of sin.

Or will you say here as well that the words “I, the Lord, have led that prophet astray” are to be understood as “I abandoned him, so that, according to their merits, he might be deceived and err”? Have it as you wish; nevertheless, he was punished for his sin in such a way that, by prophesying falsely, he sinned.

But consider what the Prophet Micaiah saw: the Lord sitting upon his throne, with all the host of heaven standing around him, at his right hand and at his left. And the Lord said: “Who will deceive Ahab, king of Israel, so that he may go up and fall at Ramoth-gilead?” And one said one thing, and another said another. Then a spirit came forth and stood in the presence of the Lord and said: “I will deceive him.” And the Lord said to him: “In what way?” And he said: “I will go forth and be a lying spirit in the mouth of all his prophets.” And he said: “You shall deceive him, and you shall prevail; go forth and do so” (III Kings 22:19–22).

What will you say to this? Certainly the king himself sinned by believing the false prophets. Yet this was also the punishment of sin, with God judging and God sending an evil angel, so that we might understand more clearly how it is said in the Psalm that he “sent the fury of his indignation through evil angels” (Psalm 77:49). But did he do this by erring, or by judging or acting unjustly or rashly? Far from it. Yet it was not said to him without reason: “Your judgments are like a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7). Nor does the Apostle cry out without reason: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways! For who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor? Or who has first given to him, that he should be repaid?” (Romans 11:33–35).

He chooses no one who is worthy, but by choosing makes him worthy [Note: [Col. 0791] Printed editions and some manuscripts read: “He chose no one who was worthy, but by choosing made him worthy.”]; nevertheless, he punishes no one who is unworthy.

## CHAPTER IV

**14.** “The Apostle says,” you object, “‘The goodness of God leads you to repentance.’” It is true; this is established. But it leads the one whom he predestined, although that person, “according to his hardness and impenitent heart,” so far as it depends on him, “stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath and the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will repay each one according to his works” (ibid. 2:4–6).

However much patience he may offer, unless God himself grants it, who practices repentance? Or have you forgotten that the same teacher says: “Lest perhaps God may grant them repentance for acknowledgment of the truth, and they may recover from the snares of the devil” (II Timothy 2:25–26)?

But his judgments are a great abyss. Certainly, if we were to allow those over whom we have authority to perpetrate crimes before our eyes, we would be guilty along with them. Yet how innumerable are the things he allows to happen before his eyes—things which, if he had not wished it, he would certainly not permit in any way—and nevertheless he is just and good.

And while by showing patience he grants a place for repentance, “not wishing anyone to perish” (II Peter 3:9), the Lord knows those who are his (II Timothy 2:19), and “works all things together” [Note: [Col. 0792] Augustine, Erasmus, and some manuscripts read *work together*. See *On Grace and Free Will*, no. 33.] for good, but only for those “who are called according to his purpose.” For not all who are called are called according to his purpose. “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 22:14). Those, therefore, who are chosen are called according to his purpose.

Hence elsewhere he says: “According to the power of God, who saved us and called us with his holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus before eternal ages” (II Timothy 1:8–9).

Finally, here too, after saying, “He works all things together for good for those who are called according to his purpose,” he immediately added: “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Romans 8:28–30).

These are those who are called according to his purpose. They are therefore the chosen, and chosen before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4), by him “who calls into existence the things that do not exist as though they did” (Romans 4:17). They are chosen, however, through the election of grace. Hence the same teacher says concerning Israel: “The remnant has been made through the election of grace” [Note: [Col. 0792] Here the Vatican and Floriacensis manuscripts add *has been saved*. *Saved* is absent from the Greek text of the Apostle.].

And lest they be thought to have been chosen before the foundation of the world on the basis of foreknown works, he continued and added: “But if by grace, then it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (ibid. 11:5–6).

From this number of the chosen and predestined, even those who have led the worst lives are brought to repentance by God’s kindness. Through his patience they have not been taken from this life in the very act of committing their crimes, so that it may be shown both to them and to their fellow heirs how profoundly evil a condition God’s grace can rescue them from.

None of these perishes, at whatever age he may die. For far be it from us to suppose that one predestined to life is permitted to end this life without the sacrament of the Mediator [Note: [Col. 0792] The Floriacensis manuscript reads: “so that those predestined to life may be permitted to end this life.”]. On their account the Lord says: “This is the will of him who sent me, the Father: that I should lose nothing of all that he has given me” (John 6:39).

The other mortals, however, who do not belong to this number—and who are indeed from the same mass from which these too come, but have been made vessels of wrath—are born for the benefit of the chosen. For God does not create any of them rashly or by chance, nor is he ignorant of what good he accomplishes through them. Indeed, he accomplishes this very good by creating human nature in them and by adorning the order of the present world through them.

Yet he brings none of them to that saving and spiritual repentance by which a human being is reconciled to God in Christ, whether he grants them greater patience or patience no less than that granted to others. Although all, from the same mass of perdition and condemnation, according to the hardness of their heart and their impenitent heart, so far as it depends on them, “store up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath,” when each person is repaid according to his works, God nevertheless brings some of them to repentance through his merciful goodness, while according to his just judgment he does not bring others to it.

For he has the power to lead and draw, as the Lord himself says: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 6:44).

But did he bring the sacrilegious and impious King Ahab to repentance? Or did he at least, after Ahab had already been led astray and deceived by a lying spirit, grant him patience and long-suffering? Was what he had been deceived for not immediately completed in him when death seized him (III Kings 22)?

Who would say that he did not sin by believing the lying spirit? Who would say that this sin was not the punishment of sin, coming from God’s judgment upon him to whom he sent—or permitted—the lying spirit? Who says any of these things except one who says what he wishes and does not wish to hear what is true?

**15.** Who, then, would be so foolish that, upon hearing what is sung in the Psalm, “Do not hand me over, O Lord, to the sinner according to my desire” (Psalm 139:9), he would say that the man prayed that God might not be patient toward him—if “God does not hand people over so that evil may be done, except by offering patient goodness while it is being done” [Note: [Col. 0793] This appears to be Julian’s view.]?

What else do we say every day when we pray, “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matthew 6:13), except that we may not be handed over to our desires? “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (James 1:14). Or perhaps we ask God not to show patient goodness toward us? Then we are not invoking his mercy; rather, we are provoking his anger. Who in his right mind could understand this? Indeed, who, even if insane, could say it?

God therefore hands people over to dishonorable passions, so that things may be done which are not fitting; but he hands them over fittingly. And the same acts become both sins and punishments for past sins, as well as merits deserving future punishments: just as he handed Ahab over to the falsehood of the false prophets, and Rehoboam over to false counsel (III Kings 12).

He does these things in marvelous and ineffable ways—he who knows how to work his just judgments not only in human bodies but also in human hearts themselves. He does not create evil desires, but uses them as he wills, since he cannot will anything unjustly.

He hears graciously; he does not hear in anger. And again, he does not hear graciously; he hears in anger. He spares graciously; he does not spare in anger. And again, he does not spare graciously; he spares in anger. Yet in all these things he remains good and just.

“But who is sufficient for these things?” (II Corinthians 2:16)—who, that is, is sufficient to search out and investigate these judgments of his, when the corruptible body weighs heavily upon every human being, even if that person already possesses the pledge of the Holy Spirit?

**16.** But you say that an intelligent and shrewd man would declare lust “just and worthy to be proclaimed with praise, if it punishes by refusing obedience the one who did not obey God.”

If you understood this matter wisely, you would certainly see that there is an injustice by which the lower part of a human being resists the higher and better part. Yet the unjust person is justly punished by the injustice of his flesh, just as an unjust king is punished by the injustice of an evil spirit.

Or are you also preparing to praise the evil spirit? Come, then—what are you waiting for [Note: [Col. 0793] The printed editions read: “Come, why are you waiting?” We have added *then* from the Floriacensis manuscript.]? It is fitting for you, an enemy of God’s gratuitous goodness, to be a praiser of the lying spirit.

Nor will you have difficulty finding what to say: you already have praise prepared for him, if you transfer to him the very words that you used in praising lust, as though they followed from my position, in which I said: “For it was unjust that the servant of his master—that is, the body of the one who had not obeyed his Lord—should obey him” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 7).

You denied this and mocked it as false, as though you wished to show what absurdity would follow if this were so, praising lust as the avenger of sin. Certainly, you do not deny that this lying spirit, because he dragged an impious king to death by deceiving him as he deserved, was an avenger of injustice.

Behold, I say the same thing here: “For it was unjust that the one who had not believed the true God should not be deceived by the false one.” Praise, then, the justice of this spirit’s falsehood also, and say what you said in praise of lust: “Because nothing can be judged more praiseworthy in it, if it avenged an injustice committed” [Note: [Col. 0794] The printed editions read: “if it avenged what had been committed through injustice.” The readings of the Vatican and Gallican manuscripts correct this.], “if it punished the injury done to God, and because it did not share in the sin in such a way as to assume the office of avenging it.”

All these statements, according to your exceedingly sharp reasoning, are properly said also in praise of that unclean spirit [Note: [Col. 0794] Six manuscripts read *in praise of him*.]. Therefore, in a similar case, either restore the tribute of your voice to the lying spirit, or withdraw it from your rebellious lust.

**17.** Why do you flee to the extremely obscure question concerning the soul? In paradise, exaltation certainly began in the mind, and from there came consent to transgress the commandment, because the serpent had said: “You shall be like gods” (Genesis 3:5). But the whole human being completed that sin.

Then the flesh became the flesh of sin, whose vices are healed only through the likeness of sinful flesh. Therefore, so that both soul and flesh alike might be punished, unless what is born is cleansed by being reborn [Note: [Col. 0794] Thus the Floriacensis codex and five Vatican manuscripts. The printed editions read *be corrected*.], either both elements are drawn in a corrupted state from the human being, or one is corrupted in the other, as in a corrupted vessel, within which the hidden justice of the divine law is contained.

Which of these is true I prefer to learn rather than to state, lest I dare to teach what I do not know. Yet I know this: whichever of these alternatives is true, it is the one that the true, ancient, catholic faith—which believes and asserts original sin—has not demonstrated to be false.

Let this faith not be denied. As for what remains hidden concerning the soul, it may either be learned in leisure or, like many other things in this life, remain unknown without injury to salvation. For greater care must be taken—whether concerning little ones or adults—to determine by what help the soul may be healed than by what merit it was corrupted. Yet if its corruption is denied, it will not be healed.

**18.** I could not determine why you said what you did concerning the words of the Apostle: “Their foolish heart was darkened” (Romans 1:21). For you added that “it should be noted that he calls foolishness the cause of all evils.”

That the Apostle said this is not sufficiently clear. But I do not dispute the point with you; rather, I ask why you said it.

Is it perhaps because little children are not properly called foolish, since they cannot yet participate in wisdom, and therefore you wish it to be believed that no evil is present in them? You apparently think this follows if foolishness is the cause of all evils.

But if we need an exceedingly subtle and polished argument to determine whether the first human beings were made proud by foolishness or foolish by pride, then, in view of the matter at issue between us, who does not know that all human beings who become wise first become so from foolishness?

Unless perhaps some of those who proclaim the Mediator were able, by his great and extraordinary grace, to pass into wisdom not from foolishness but from infancy [Note: [Col. 0795] Five Vatican manuscripts and some Gallican manuscripts read: “Unless perhaps someone was able … to pass over.” Augustine is referring to Jeremiah or John the Baptist.].

But if you contend that this can happen by nature without faith in the Mediator, you reveal the hidden poison of your heresy. For it is clear that you accomplish nothing by such extensive defense and praise of nature except that Christ died for nothing (Galatians 2:21). We, however, say that faith in him, “which works through love” (ibid. 5:6), also assists those who are foolish by nature.

There are people born with such great dullness of heart [Note: [Col. 0795] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read *dullness*.] that they seem more like animals than human beings. You cannot claim that the natural stupidity evident in them is any merit, since you say that there is no original sin.

Who, moreover, does not observe every day, from the evidence of human affairs, that a little child first knows nothing, then, as he grows, knows foolish things, and later—if he belongs to the lot of the wise—knows what is right, and thus passes from infancy to wisdom by way of an intermediate foolishness?

Therefore, you see how human nature, which lies in little children, first produces the fruit of foolishness rather than wisdom. You begrudge it a savior through your praises, as though it were healthy; yet you do not wish to see the defect of its root—or, worse, you see it and deny it.

## CHAPTER V [Note: [Col. 0795] In Augustine, Erasmus, and others: “4.”]

**19.** Next you attack me, inserting other words of mine, on the ground “that I contradicted myself, since, after saying that the punishment of disobedience was inflicted upon the disobedient human being in his body, I immediately specified other bodily members, saying that they serve at the command of our will” [Note: [Col. 0795] Some manuscripts read *of our will* rather than *to our will*.] (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 7).

I said this, to be sure, with the genitals excepted—those which I called by the name “body.” Accordingly, the body serves the will in the movement of the other members, but the body does not serve the will in the movements of the genitals.

My words, therefore, are not contradictory to one another, although they allow you to represent them as contradictory, either because you do not understand them or because you prevent others from understanding them.

For if a part of the body could not be called by the name “body,” the Apostle would not say: “The woman does not have authority over her own body, but the man does; likewise, the man does not have authority over his own body, but the woman does” (I Corinthians 7:4). Here he is clearly calling those members “body” by which sex is distinguished and intercourse is carried out.

Who would say that a man does not have authority over his own body if, in these words of the Apostle, you understand the whole body consisting of all its members? Accordingly, following the Apostle, I called even the genital member alone “body.” Human experience recognizes that it is moved not by the will, as the hand or foot is, but by lust. Yet this same experience laughs at you for raising shameless clouds over obvious matters, forcing us to speak longer than necessity requires about shameful things and to speak about them indirectly for the sake of propriety.

But whoever reads my words, which you attempt to refute, and sees the trap you have set for them, will understand what I said about “the body” in that passage. That is sufficient for me.

**20.** But you, who said that I contradicted myself in my own words—a claim that anyone who rereads them after hearing you will see to be utterly false, and who recalls that the Apostle called the genitals “body”—you, then, who marked and attacked in me what you portrayed as mutually conflicting statements, explain how you yourself are consistent with yourself and do not contradict yourself.

At first you said: “When the time comes for children to be conceived, the members created for this work serve entirely at the command of the will; and unless their impediments arise from weakness or excess, they serve the command of the mind” [Note: [Col. 0796] After “they serve the command of the mind,” the editions of Augustine and Erasmus and several manuscripts insert the following: “Although earlier he had said—or you had said—that the genital members serve at the command of the will and are subject to the command of the mind, later he assigned among these bodily parts the same members that require not the command of the will but its consent, by which he is—or you are—most clearly shown to be in conflict with himself—or yourself. Then they continue: ‘Afterward, however, you considered this kind of movement …’ These words are absent from the better manuscripts and were rightly deleted by the Louvain editors.];

but afterward you considered “this kind of movement to belong among those things in our body which, in their proper order and hidden administration, require not the command of the will but its consent” [Note: [Col. 0796] Likewise, in Augustine, Erasmus, and certain ancient codices, after “require not the command of the will but its consent,” the following words had slipped from the margin into the text: “It is more correct to say that the genital members require not the command of the will but its consent, rather than that they are subject to the command of the will or of the mind. Hence it is evident that he was heretical and contradictory to himself, defining the matter first in one way and afterward in another; and although he was ashamed of his earlier statements, he confessed the truth more fully in the later ones, yet through shameless obstinacy or incompetence did not alter what he had previously said wrongly.” The Louvain edition retained the first part of this gloss.].

Here you yielded, at least in part, to manifest truth. But you should have deleted what you had said earlier. For how, according to your earlier position, do “these members,” of which we are speaking, “serve entirely at the command of the will and obey the command of the mind,” if, according to your later position, they “require not the command of the will but its consent, like hunger, thirst, and digestion”?

You worked very hard to find statements that would be directed against yourself rather than against me. But in such a matter you would not have needed to work if you had possessed shame.

For what does it profit you to say that you “feel shame and are prevented by horror from speaking about such matters, but are compelled by necessity,” when you were not ashamed to leave your own position written down, even though, soon afterward, disturbed by manifest truth, you put forward another position against it?

Indeed, even this mention of your shame is excessively shameless. Yet I am pleased by it because it speaks against you. You are a man who is not ashamed to praise lust, while claiming to be ashamed to discuss the movements of lust.

**21.** What great difficulty would it have been to notice that, after saying, “It has been placed within our power for the other members to move,” I immediately added that this is so when we possess a body free from impediments and in good health?

Sleep, when it presses upon us against our will, and weariness are certainly impediments by which the agility of the members is hindered.

Furthermore, when you said that “the members do not follow in the direction we wish, if we wish this in a way that their very constitution does not permit,” you failed to notice that I had previously stated that they are moved “to works appropriate to them.” Accordingly, if we wish to bend them in a direction that their nature does not permit, they do not follow us into works inappropriate to them.

Nevertheless, when we perform voluntary movements with their cooperation, we do not need the assistance of lust. And when we wish to stop moving them, we stop immediately; nor are they excited against our will by the goads [Note: [Col. 0797] The printed editions read *by the goad*. Some manuscripts read *of the goads*.] of lust.

**22.** Certainly, when you say that “the genitals also serve the command of the mind,” you are speaking of some new lust—or perhaps of one that is excessively ancient, such as might also have existed in paradise if no one had sinned.

But what can I do with you on this point, when in your later words you remove this claim as well, saying that they “are not moved at the command of the mind but rather await consent”?

Nevertheless, you should not for that reason compare this lust with hunger or with our other troubles. No one becomes hungry, thirsty, or digestively active whenever he wishes; these are needs for replenishing or emptying the body, needs that must be relieved lest the body be harmed or die.

But is the body harmed or killed if consent is not given to lust? Distinguish, then, between the evils that we endure through patience and those evils that we restrain through continence.

Those too are evils which we are able to experience in this body of death. Yet who could investigate with certainty, or explain as the matter deserves, how great and how tranquil our power would have been over even those movements by which food is taken and digested in the blessedness of paradise?

There, far be it from us to believe that anything existed from which pain could prick or labor weary our senses, whether inwardly or outwardly; or shame confuse them; or heat burn them; or cold constrict them; or horror offend them.

**23.** What shall we say about the fact that you think this most beautiful servant of yours—whom I am ashamed even constantly to mention by way of condemnation, but whom you are not ashamed to praise—is made more commendable because the other parts of the body serve her, so that she may be aroused more ardently: whether the seeing eyes, to desire, or other members, in kisses and embraces?

You even found a way to subordinate human ears to her, and you raised up her very ancient but plainly most glorious title by recalling what Tullius wrote in his discussion of his counsels:

“Pythagoras is said to have advised a flute-player, when drunken young men, excited—as often happens—even by the sound of flutes, were breaking down the doors of a respectable woman, to play a spondee. When she had done this, the slow rhythm and solemnity of the music are said to have calmed their raging wantonness” [Note: [Col. 0798] Boethius, in the preface to his little work *On Music*, where he cites this very passage from Cicero’s *On His Counsels*, reads *had settled down* as *had come to rest*.].

You see, therefore, how much more appropriately I said that this movement is in some sense its own master, since the other senses serve it, so that it may deign either to rise for its task or to rest from its agitation.

I said this because, as you yourself confessed, “one consents to it rather than commands it.” For, as you yourself continue, since “it is excited by other goads or broken and calmed by melody,” this certainly would not happen if it served the human will.

As for women, whom you make immune from this movement, although they may be subject to male desire and may suffer when they do not experience their own, let Joseph be asked how much even they endure of that assault which the dignity and propriety of chaste women resist (Genesis 39).

As an ecclesiastical man, you should rather have been reminded by ecclesiastical music [Note: [Col. 0798] The printed editions read *ecclesiastically, O man*. The manuscripts read *ecclesiastical man*.] than by Pythagorean music of what David’s [Note: [Col. 0798] Augustine, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read *Davidic*.] harp accomplished for Saul when he was tormented by an evil spirit: when David played the harp, Saul was relieved of that affliction (I Kings 16).

You should not, therefore, think that the desire of the flesh is something good merely because it is sometimes restrained by musical sounds.

## CHAPTER VI

**24.** You exclaim: “How worthily Jeremiah, together with the chorus of the prophets and all the saints, would cry out, ‘Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes?’” (Jeremiah 9:1)—so that he might weep over the sins of the foolish people!

If you wished to weep in a salutary way, you would weep over the fact that you are entangled in that error, and with those tears you would cleanse yourself from the same novel plague.

Do you not know—or have you forgotten, or do you refuse to consider—that the holy, one, catholic Church was also signified by the name “paradise”? Why, then, do you wonder if you are expelled from this paradise, since you wish to introduce into that paradise the law which is in our members, resisting the law of the mind—the paradise from which we were expelled by the Lord and to which we cannot return unless we conquer this law in this paradise?

For if it is not this desire that you defend, the desire that resists the law of the mind, no saint exercises any contest against it. Yet you yourself confessed that the saints engage in “glorious battles” against the very desire you defend (above, book 3, no. 42).

It is therefore this desire that resists the law of the mind in the body of this death, from which the Apostle said that he was delivered by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord (Romans 7:23–25).

Do you now at last perceive how greatly the enemies of this grace should be mourned with a fountain of tears, and with what great vigilance of pastoral care they must be avoided, lest they drag others with themselves into destruction?

For you “increase,” through this novelty, the “corruption of the declining age” that exists among all heretics. You are “the ruin of morals,” since you attempt to overthrow the foundations of that very faith upon which morals must be built. You are “the destruction of modesty,” since you are not ashamed to praise what modesty itself resists.

This is what the Church, which is called a virgin, ought rather to hear, so that she may beware of you; and married women, and consecrated virgins, and all Christian chastity ought to hear it.

For, contrary to your accusation, they do not say with the Manichaeans that “there is a necessity of evil in their flesh”—the evil which the Manichaeans falsely claim to be substantial and coeternal with God. Rather, they say with the Apostle: “I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind.” Yet they hold that it remains under the power of the mind; that by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord it must be chastised in this body of death, dissolved in the death of the body, and healed in the resurrection of the body, when death itself is destroyed.

They hold to the holy confession, resisting the desire of the flesh not merely in the outward form of clothing but in mind and body as well: this resistance is possible here, whereas complete freedom from desire is not.

Let them hear this, then, so that, until they are free from it, they may beware of you.

For if you were to ask all the saints—as though in a holy auditorium two people wished to recite—which they would prefer to hear, a critic or a praiser of lust, what do you think all of them would answer: those who labor in continence, those who preserve the modesty of marriage, and all who practice chastity?

Would they really cast the condemnation of lust from their ears and willingly listen to the praise of lust? We must not think that the sense of shame concerning such matters has perished to such an extent [Note: [Col. 0799] This alludes to Persius, *Satires* 5.103–104.] that such disgrace could occur except perhaps in an auditorium of the sort where, while you were reciting, the teacher Caelestius or Pelagius was presiding over his seated disciples.

## CHAPTER VII [Note: [Col. 0799] In Augustine, Erasmus: “5.”]

**25.** From here you proceed to other words of mine, where I said:

“Its movement was therefore indecent because it was disobedient. When the first human beings experienced it in their flesh and were ashamed of their nakedness, they covered those same members with fig leaves, so that at least by the decision of those who felt shame there might be veiled what was not moved by the decision of those who willed it. And because they were ashamed of what pleased them indecently, by covering it they made it something proper” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 7).

After presenting these words of mine, you boastfully recall that you have already destroyed them in the argument of your second book and in the earlier part of this third book, to which I am now replying.

But now, because I said that this “movement” of lust was “indecent because it was disobedient,” you want me to be understood as having said that it “is subject neither to the body nor to the mind, but is always untamed by a savage force.”

I, however, never said that it was a force; I said that it was a vice.

If it is not moved by desire, what is the meaning of chastity’s battle against it through restraint? Where are those “glorious battles” of the saints which you yourself confessed are waged against it?

So far as chastity is concerned, you say what I say: chastity is preserved by conquering, suppressing, restraining, and not permitting its lust to proceed to anything unlawful. But you say that what must be conquered, suppressed, and restrained so that it may not rush toward unlawful things—which it never ceases to desire—is good; I do not.

Let the chaste judge which of us is speaking the truth, as they listen not to your tongue but to their own experience. Let the Apostle judge, saying: “I see another law in my members, resisting the law of my mind.”

### 26

“But the Paterniani,” you say, “who are likewise heretics called Venustiani [Note: [Col. 0800] See the book *On Heresies*, heresy 85], similar to the Manichaeans, say that the devil made the human body from the loins down to the feet, while God placed the upper parts, as it were, upon some kind of base. They add that nothing is required of a human being’s effort except that the soul—which they say dwells in the stomach and head—be kept clean; but if the pubic region is smeared with the filth of every crime, they say that this does not belong to their concern. Thus always,” you say, “in order that they may shamefully serve lust itself, they attach to it the title of a power proper to itself. In affinity with this opinion,” you assert that I wrote in my book: “What was not moved by the will of those who desired was veiled by the judgment of those who felt shame; and although it did not serve the will, lust kindles the body by its own right.”

Will you therefore be able to escape the force of truth because, by slandering us, you impute to us associates in falsehood? [Note: [Col. 0800] Most manuscripts: “imputas” (“you impute”).] For what I wrote in my book—which I wish you had preferred to yield to rather than resist—is very far removed from those Paterniani or Venustiani. For, in accordance with the Catholic faith, I ascribe the whole human being—that is, the whole soul and the whole body—to God, the supreme and true Creator. I say, however, that the devil did not create human nature, or any part of it, but corrupted it; and that we must fight against that devilish wound, which must be healed with God’s help, until we are entirely freed from it. Nor can the soul by which the body lives be kept wholly clean, insofar as a human being is clean in this life, if it consents [Note: [Col. 0800] Some manuscripts read: “the soul by which the body lives, the whole [body], clean,” etc.] to the desires of the flesh for committing crimes and every kind of impurity.

So, as far as this slander of yours is concerned, do you have anything to say against these points? If that is not enough, behold: I condemn and anathematize what you have said the Paterniani or Venustiani believe; I add the Manichaeans as well. Along with the other heretics, I curse, condemn, anathematize, and detest both groups. What more do you seek? Strip away your slanders; fight with strength, not fraud. Answer where that comes from which, unless resisted, permits no chastity to be preserved. It is certainly not nature or substance, according to the Venustiani and Manichaeans. If it is not a vice of nature, what is it?

It rises up—I suppress it; it resists—I restrain it; it fights back—I conquer it. Throughout the whole soul and the whole body I have the God who is the Creator of peace. Who has sown this war within me? Apostle, solve the question and answer: “Through one man sin entered into the world, and through sin death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12). But Julian does not want this. And to this, blessed Apostle, answer: “If anyone announces to you anything beyond what you received, let him be accursed” (Galatians 1:9).

### 27

“But if I connive,” you say, “at the invincible character of the evil of lust, I shall declare myself an advocate of shamefulness. But if I say that I have indeed called this natural thing evil, yet one that can be conquered—that is, one that can be avoided”—then immediately, on the other side, you exult in your own argument. [Col. 0801] “For human beings,” you say, “can avoid every sin, since they can conquer the evil of desire. For if lust is a natural evil and is conquered by love of virtue, then much more,” you say, “all those vices are overcome which arise from the will alone.”

Many times and in many ways we have already answered these arguments of yours. For while we live here, where “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17), no matter how superior we may be in this conflict, and even though we do not present our members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin, obeying its desires (Romans 6:12–13), nevertheless—to say nothing of the bodily senses and of the excesses of pleasure that creep into things we lawfully use—in the very movements and affections of our thought, if we say that we have no sin, “we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

Therefore you exult in vain in another part of your argument—unless perhaps, with sacrilegious presumption, you reject the sentence of the Apostle John. But as for what is now under discussion, I too say that lust is natural, because every human being is born with it; and you say this much more strongly, because you claim that the first human being was created with it. Likewise [Note: [Col. 0801] Printed editions: “Thus.” The manuscripts more correctly read: “Likewise.”], I say—and so do you—that lust must be conquered, and that in order for it to be conquered one must resist and fight against it. I say this so that you may not hear from me what you yourself said to me: that you would “declare yourself an advocate of shamefulness if you denied that lust must be conquered.” Certainly it is not conquered if no war is waged against it.

Since, then, we both say that lust is natural and can be conquered, the question between us is whether we conquer something good or something evil. But see how absurd you are: you wish thus [Note: [Col. 0801] The Floriacensis manuscript reads “et sic”; printed editions read “et sicut,” omitting “qui.”] to conquer lust as an enemy, yet you do not wish to settle the question of its evil character; so that, even if the devil does not conquer you by opposing desire, he may conquer you through the perversity of your argument.

### 28

Are you still not awake enough to understand that what we fight against by virtue is not our nature but a vice? For we do not conquer good with good, but certainly evil with good. Consider what it conquers with and what conquers it. When lust conquers, the devil also conquers; when lust is conquered, the devil also is conquered. Therefore the one whom lust conquers, and by whom it is conquered, is its enemy; but the one with whom it conquers and is conquered is its author.

I beg you, open your eyes and see what is plain. There is no struggle without evil. For whenever there is a struggle, either good fights evil, or evil fights evil; or, if two good things fight against each other, the struggle itself is a great evil. When this occurs in the body—when the elements of which it consists, namely moisture and dryness, heat and cold, although opposed to one another, do not maintain peace and harmony with each other—diseases and illnesses arise. And who would dare say that any of these is not good, since every creature of God is good, and in the hymn of the three young men cold and heat bless the Lord (Daniel 3:67)?

Although these things are opposed to one another, they nevertheless preserve harmony [Col. 0802] for the safety of created things. But when they disagree in our body and attack one another, health is disturbed. And all this, like death itself, descends from the propagation of that sin. For no one would say that, if no one had sinned, we would have suffered such things in the blessedness of paradise.

There are, then, different qualities of bodily things, which are balanced by their opposites so that we may be healthy; and although they are good in different categories, when they disagree they produce ill health. There are also desires of the soul, which are called “of the flesh” because the soul desires according to the flesh when it desires in such a way that the spirit—that is, its better and higher part—ought to resist it.

Finally, these vices do not seek any physicians of the body, but are healed by the grace of Christ as physician: first, so that they may not hold us under guilt; then, so that they may not conquer us in the conflict; finally, so that, healed in every respect, they may leave nothing at all behind.

Therefore, since to desire evil is evil and to desire good is good, and since this war does not cease as long as we live here—when “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh”—who will free me from “this body of death,” except the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord? We shudder at your doctrine as exceedingly hostile to this grace.

### 29

But you, a very brave man—if not an administrator, at least an exhorter, preacher, and herald of nocturnal battles—say that it is “a feeble and effeminate opinion” to believe that in paradise the generative organs could have served at the command of the will. For to you, as to a chaste man, the mind seems more effeminate the more power it has over the body.

But behold: we are not arguing with you about the absence or presence of lust, nor are we attacking the affection that we see you ought to have for it. At least subject it to the rule of the will in that place of blessedness. Remove from there the most obvious struggle, which occurs when the mind resists its movement; remove from there the most shameful peace, which occurs when the mind serves its domination.

Certainly, because you do not see it as being there what you establish it as being there, if reason does not recall you, shame compels you to confess that in its present state it is an original vice. If we serve it, we perish; we resist it so that we may not serve it.

Behold what you praise—and do not fear that you are thereby warning yourself that you ought rather to be called someone who incites human beings to crimes by urging them not to resist desire, which you commend as a natural good. For what helps you that you appear to condemn its excess while approving its movement? It exceeds the permitted limit precisely when its movements are obeyed. Yet it is evil even when it is not obeyed, because one resists evil lest the good of chastity perish if this evil is not resisted.

When you call it naturally good, you cunningly decree that it must always be consented to, lest it be opposed by an improper resistance as though it were a natural good. Thus your other assertion—that a human being is without sin if he wishes—can very easily also be true. For there is no way to do what is not permitted when whatever one desires is permitted, because what one naturally desires is good.

If, then, the pleasures are present, let him enjoy them. [Col. 0803] If they are not present, let him take pleasure, as Epicurus thought, in the thoughts of those pleasures themselves. Then he will be without sin and will deprive himself of no good. Let him not resist the natural movements because of the opinions of any doctrine; rather, as Hortensius says, “let him obey nature when, without a teacher, he has perceived what nature desires” (Cicero’s dialogue entitled *Hortensius*). For what is good cannot desire what is evil, nor should any good be denied to what is good. Let everything that good lust desires therefore be done, lest the one who resists what is good himself become evil.

### 30

“You are not saying this,” you will object, “and it is unjust for you to suspect that I think something other than what I say.” Then do not do what you do not wish to suffer, and say “that we invite people to sweet thefts,” while we quote the Apostle saying: “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Romans 7:18).

For even if they do not accomplish the good they wish, so as not to desire, nevertheless they do good by not following their desires (Ecclesiasticus 18:30). If you think that you teach chastity when you say, “Do not be conquered by good, but conquer good with good,” how much more do we teach it when we say, “Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good” (Romans 12:21)?

See how unjust it is for you not to believe that we seek to conquer what we condemn, while you do not wish it to be believed that you want to enjoy what you praise. How can those who are chaste be enemies of lust if those who are chaste can also be its friends?

Therefore, by denying original sin and begrudging little children the Savior Jesus, you wish to introduce into paradise, before sin, the law of sin opposing the law of the mind. In this work we refute that claim. We do not wish to judge what we neither see in you nor hear from you; it is of no concern to us what the avowed praisers of lust do in secret.

### Chapter VIII  
[Note: [Col. 0803] In the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, chapter 6.]

### 31

But after you had set before me other words of mine—my distinction concerning the marriage and concupiscence of the first human beings, in which I said, “What they afterwards did by propagation is the good of marriage; but what they previously covered in confusion is the evil of concupiscence” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, section 8)—you thought it should be refuted thus: “It cannot be that what is good should not have praise in common with that without which it cannot exist.” You thus wish marriage and lust to have one and the same praise in common. Attend briefly to how this apparently definitive proposition of yours collapses.

First, the universe of things which God created cannot exist without evils; yet evils cannot therefore have praise in common with goods. Next, if “it cannot be that what is good should not have praise in common with that without which it cannot exist,” certainly what is evil cannot fail to have blame in common with that without which it cannot exist. [Note: [Col. 0803] Printed editions read, “thus it cannot be”; “thus” is absent from the manuscripts.] Let us then blame God’s works, just as we blame the evils which cannot exist without them. For no evil exists except in some work of God, nor can it exist anywhere at all without one. Blame, then, lest I send you farther afield, the members of the human body just as you blame adulteries, which cannot exist without those members. If you do not do this, lest you yourself appear manifestly insane, it follows that the good of marriage can fail to have praise in common with lust, without which it now cannot exist, just as any evil can fail to have blame in common with a work of God, without which it can never exist. And just as this definition of yours is false and empty, so are all the things you have linked from it as though by consequence. [Col. 0804]

### 32

Certainly I never said that the “pleasure of the flesh” was “invincible,” as you accuse me of customarily saying. We both say that it ought to be and can be conquered. But you say this as though one good were resisting another good; I say it as though evil were resisting good. You say it is conquered by our own strength; I say it is conquered by the grace of the Savior, so that it may be conquered not by some other corrupt desire but by the love of God—a love that is not poured into our hearts by our own strength, but “through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

### 33

As for “the confusion of those men and their covered private parts,” you recall in vain that you demonstrated something with the Apostle as witness. You call “more honorable” what he calls “dishonorable.” We have therefore already discussed this as much as seemed sufficient [Note: Above, book 4, sections 80–82].

You therefore vainly flee again to Balbus and the writings of the philosophers [Note: Ibid., section 58], as though Balbus could make you speak when you cannot discover what to say about the confusion of the first human beings. If only you would yield, in at least some true opinions, to the writings of the philosophers, you would not hear with deaf ears what they said: that lust is the lure and food of vices, and the vicious part of the soul [Note: Ibid., section 72].

For when Balbus said that the places of digestion in our body are removed from the senses, this is true because what we digest does not attract our senses but offends them. Therefore the part through which such things are expelled is naturally hidden by the other parts projecting on either side. So too it was then, when the naked did not feel shame; but after sin they immediately covered not hidden members, but members plainly exposed.

The more the sight of those members was attracted and moved—not offended by horror but enticed by delight—the more it belonged to the duty of modesty to cover them.

### 34

When I spoke “of limping and reaching the destination” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, section 8), you did not understand me, unless you are acting deceitfully. I did not intend “reaching the destination” to mean the human being born from marital intercourse, as you imagine or pretend that I thought. Rather, I called “reaching the destination” what marriage possesses at the completion of its function, even if no one is born from it.

For sowing belongs to the man, receiving to the woman. This far the spouses can proceed by their own action. To this I plainly said that one cannot arrive without limping—that is, without lust.

But for a fetus to be conceived and born is the work of God, not of human beings. Nevertheless, it is with this purpose and intention that marriage performs even that good which belongs to its own activity.
