But because the fetus itself is born for condemnation unless it is reborn, Christian marriages extend their purpose—not as though they were walking to the end of their activity, but to the end of their will—so that they may beget those who are to be regenerated. For this reason there is in them true chastity, that is, chastity pleasing to God. “Without faith it is impossible to please God” (Hebrews 11:6).

### Chapter IX  
[Note: In the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, chapter 7.]

### 35

You then come to the passage where, on the testimony of the Apostle, we discussed the need for each person to possess his own vessel—that is, his own wife—not “in the disease of desire,” like the Gentiles who do not know God (1 Thessalonians 4:4–5). Explaining this, I said: “It was not marital intercourse—that is, lawful and honorable intercourse—that was prohibited, but that the purpose of this act should be the will to propagate, not the pleasure of the flesh; and although this cannot be done without lust, it should nevertheless be done not for the sake of lust” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, sections 9, 16).

There you exclaim: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God” (Romans 11:13), who, apart from the future recompense of works, wished free will to fulfill in large measure the form of judgment! “For most justly,” you say, “a good person and an evil person are committed to themselves, so that the good person may enjoy himself and the evil person may suffer himself.”

Your exclamation [Note: [Col. 0805] Vatican manuscripts and two Gallican manuscripts read: “your exclamation and declamation.”] has no bearing on the matter by which you feel yourself pressed. Nor does your outcry lighten the weight under which you are being crushed, while you stubbornly hold to your impious doctrine, by which it pleases you that even a good person is committed by divine judgment to himself, lest God’s grace be necessary to him—as though he were capable of directing himself.

But far be it from this to be so. Those who are committed to themselves and directed by themselves are not good, because they are not children of God. “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the children of God” (Romans 8:14). I think you recognize in this sentence the apostolic doctrine by which yours is overturned.

### 36

Nevertheless, you say something against yourself, which I must not pass over in silence. Do you remember how long you argued against the clearest truth drawn forth through the Apostle, asserting that “it is in no way possible for something to be both sin and the punishment of sin”?

What is this, then, that you now praise the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God, having forgotten your great loquacity, because “apart from the future recompense of works, he wished free will to fulfill in large measure the form of judgment”? “Most justly,” as you define it, “a good person and an evil person are committed to themselves, so that the good person may enjoy himself”—that is, in a good work—“and the evil person may suffer himself”—that is, in an evil work.

For that evil person is plainly both guilty of sin, because he does evil, and subject to the punishment of sin, because he suffers evil in himself. Thus free will already fulfills in large measure the form of judgment by which good things are repaid to the good and evil things to the evil: by acting rightly, the good person enjoys himself; by sinning, the evil person suffers himself.

You see, surely, how, while you boastfully brandish your vain and blunted weapons, you have exposed the place by which you could be struck—indeed, you have struck yourself.

Moreover, you boast [Note: [Col. 0806] The Louvain edition adds here: “cause.”] [Col. 0806] that my statements contradict one another because I said—not, as you slanderously claim, that “intercourse of bodies was invented by the devil,” since even if no one had sinned, children could be born only through the intercourse of the two sexes—but I said that “the disobedience of the flesh, which appears in flesh desiring against the spirit, occurred through a wound inflicted by the devil.”

And again, I said that “this law of sin, opposing the law of the mind, was inflicted by God as retribution and therefore is the punishment of sin.” You assert that these statements contradict one another, as though it were impossible for one and the same evil to be inflicted upon sinners both through the devil’s iniquity and through God’s justice.

Even the devil himself is hostile to human beings through his own wickedness, and yet by God’s judgment he is permitted to harm sinners. Nor do the divine Scriptures contradict themselves on this point, because it is written, “God did not make death” (Wisdom 1:13), and it is likewise written, “Life and death are from the Lord God” (Ecclesiasticus 11:14).

The devil, as the deceiver of humanity, is the cause of death; but God inflicted death not as its first author, but as the avenger of sin.

You yourself have resolved this question clearly enough when you said that the evil person was committed to himself so that what is punishment for himself might be both divine judgment and free will. These two things are not opposed to one another: in his own punishment, he himself is both its author, while God is its avenger.

### 37

But you take advantage of slower minds. I do not wish to say that you too do not understand, so that you fail to distinguish these two things and, with malicious cunning or murky blindness, confuse will and pleasure. Because [Note: [Col. 0806] The Floriacensis manuscript reads “ut sicut” (“as”), rather than “et sicut” (“and as”).] these names sound alike to somewhat deaf ears, you trust that you can persuade somewhat deaf hearts that the things themselves are one and the same.

This is why you think—or want it to be thought—that my statements contradict one another, as though I disapprove what I had previously approved, or embrace what I had previously rejected.

Hear, then, my clear position, and understand it—or, if you cannot understand, at least let others understand it—without casting the darkness of clouded argument over the serene clarity of the purest truth.

Just as it is good to make good use of evil things, so it is honorable to make good use of dishonorable things. Hence the Apostle called the members themselves dishonorable, not because of the beauty of the divine work, but because of the foulness of lust (1 Corinthians 12:23).

Those who are chaste are not compelled to commit fornication, because they resist dishonorable lust so that it may not compel them to commit dishonorable acts; nevertheless, without it they cannot honorably beget children. Thus, in chaste spouses, there is both the will to beget offspring and necessity in lust. For what is dishonorable is employed honorably for begetting, when chastity does not love lust but tolerates it in intercourse.

### 38

You are accustomed to recall with pleasure the opinions of secular authors by which you think yourself supported. Consider with an honorable mind, if you can, what the poet Lucan sang about Cato:

[Col. 0807]

> “Father of the city, and husband of the city;
>
> Cultivator of justice, guardian of strict honor,
>
> Good for the commonwealth; and pleasure, once born,
>
> Never crept into any act of Cato or took a share for itself.”  
> (*Pharsalia*, book 2, lines 388–391)

What kind of man Cato was, and whether true virtue and honor were praised in him, is another question. Nevertheless, whatever end he referred his duties toward, he certainly did not beget children without pleasure. Yet “pleasure, once born, never crept into any act of Cato or took a share for itself,” because although he did nothing without pleasure, he did not act for the sake of pleasure. Nor did he possess his vessel in the disease of this desire, although he did not know God—if he was such as he is said to have been.

And you do not wish to understand what the Apostle says: “Let each one of you know how to possess his own vessel, not in the disease of desire, like the Gentiles who do not know God.”

### 39

You distinguish well between the lesser good of marriage and the greater good of continence; but you do not abandon your doctrine, which is exceedingly hostile to grace. For you say “that the Lord honored the glory of continence with freedom of choice, saying, ‘Let the one who can receive it receive it,’” as though this were received not by God’s gift but by the freedom of the will. Yet you are silent about what he had said above: “Not all receive this word, but those to whom it has been given” (Matthew 19:11–12).

See what you are silent about and what you say. I think your conscience pricks you; but it overcomes proper fear by introducing perverse shame, through which it commands that your rash opinion be defended by any means.

You repeatedly condemn only the excess of lust, but you never cease to praise lust itself. You neither observe, feel, nor understand that what temperance is forced to resist, lest it exceed the limit of necessity, is evil.

### 40

Although you have thought that the Apostle’s warning—that no one should possess his vessel in the disease of desire—is to be understood not of marriage but of fornication, you have removed all honor from temperance in marital intercourse. Thus no one would seem to himself to possess his vessel in the disease of desire, however wildly he might rage with lust in his wife’s sexual organs. [Note: After “however wildly he might rage,” the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, along with some manuscripts, add: “If the heretic had understood marital temperance correctly, what he ought to have thought, and what he could have understood from the Apostle’s testimony with sound faith.” The older codices, which lack these words, show that they were transferred here from the margin.]

For if you thought that some limit ought to be observed there, you could also have condemned the excess of desire in that context, and could have said that this was what the Apostle meant by “the disease of desire.” You could also, without impropriety, have denied that the phrase “his own vessel” meant each person’s wife.

The Apostle Peter likewise uses this expression in the same matter, when he advises husbands to give honor to their wives as to a weaker vessel, as fellow heirs of grace, adding: “And see that your prayers are not hindered” (1 Peter 3:7).

His fellow Apostle also prescribes times for marital temperance in prayer, and by way of concession permits intercourse with one’s spouse—not intercourse for the purpose of offspring, but intercourse undertaken for pleasure (1 Corinthians 7:5–6). [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads: “although of spouses, not certainly …”]

Let Christian marriages listen to him, not to you—you who want the desire you defend never to be restrained in them, but whenever it is aroused, to be satisfied in its greed and to reign without fear.

Let the faithful of Christ who are joined in marriage, I say, listen to him, so that by mutual consent they may exercise restraint and devote themselves to prayer. [Col. 0808] And when, because of their lack of restraint, they return to intercourse, let them know that they must also say to God on account of this: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12). For when so great a teacher speaks of something as permitted “by way of concession,” not “by command,” it is certainly forgiven, not ordered.

### Chapter X  
[Note: In the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, chapter 8.]

### 41

But after inserting other words of mine, in which I commended the will of truly pious Christian spouses who beget children in this age so that, for the sake of the other age, they may be reborn in Christ (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, section 9), you recall that you had already destroyed this opinion of mine in your second book. Let those who wish read there what I answered you.

For adulteries are not to be committed even with the intention of begetting those who are to be regenerated, just as thefts are not to be committed even with the intention of feeding the holy poor. Yet what must be done is accomplished not by committing thefts, but by making good use of the mammon of iniquity, so that they may receive us into eternal dwellings (Luke 16:9). Likewise, children are to be begotten not by committing adulteries, but by making good marital use of the evil of lust, with the intention that we may reign eternally with them [Note: Above, book 4, section 39].

### 42

You elegantly praise the position you have undertaken, saying—and saying truly—that “nothing of that kind can be thought of while intercourse is taking place.” It is entirely so. For what can be thought of at the moment when the mind itself by which thought occurs is submerged in that carnal pleasure?

Hence that excellent writer, discussing pleasure, whose words I already set down in the preceding book, said: “The greater each movement is, the more hostile it is to philosophy. Great bodily pleasure cannot harmonize with thought. For who,” he says, “when enjoying a pleasure greater than which none can exist, can attend with his mind, undertake reasoning, or think about anything at all?” (Above, section 72, from Cicero’s *Hortensius*.)

You therefore could not have accused it more gravely while praising it, unless by admitting that in its assault no one can think holy thoughts. Yet certainly a religious mind, making good use of this evil, thinks this: that by intercourse it should endure lust, which it cannot think about while it is enduring it.

It is like a person who thinks about health in order to give himself over to sleep—something he obviously cannot think about while asleep. But when sleep takes possession of his limbs, it does not make them disobedient to the will, because it also removes the will itself from the exercise of this kind of command, turning the soul toward dream-visions, in which future things have often been revealed.

Thus, if there was an alternation of waking and sleeping in paradise, where there was no evil of desiring, the dreams of those sleeping were as blessed as the life of those awake.

### 43

But when you boast and vainly pour forth frothy eloquence, “comparing parents with parricides and asserting that in them lies the cause why children are born under condemnation,” you are carried along as though on wings exulting and applauding your tongue. In this clamor that you yourself create, you do not look toward God.

For why is such a charge [Col. 0809]—or anything like it—not directed rather against the very Creator of human beings than against their parents, since he is certainly the author and creator of every good? Yet he does not cease to create those whom he foreknows will burn in eternal fires; and because he creates them, only goodness is attributed to him. [Note: In Amerbach and the manuscripts: “nor is goodness attributed to him except because he creates them”; except that the Floriacensis manuscript reads, “except insofar as he creates them.”]

And some infants whom he foreknows will become apostates, even though they have been baptized, he does not remove from this life after adopting them into the eternal kingdom. Nor does he thereby grant them the great benefit granted to the one of whom it is written: “He was taken away, lest wickedness change his understanding” (Wisdom 4:11).

Nevertheless, only goodness and justice are attributed to God, by which he does all things well and rightly with the good and the evil. How much more easily can it be understood that parents are to be credited with nothing except that they desire children—children whose future they unquestionably do not know?

### Chapter XI

### 44

As for what you recalled from the Gospel, “It would have been better for that man not to have been born” (Matthew 26:24): was more accomplished by God’s work for him to be born than by the parents’ work? Why did God himself not grant his image what would have been better, since he knew beforehand the evil that would happen to him, which his parents cannot know?

And yet those who understand correctly attribute to God nothing except what should be attributed to the Creator’s kindness. Likewise, without the difficulty of a knotty question, they attribute to the parents the fact that they desired children whose future they did not know. [Note: Two manuscripts read, “that they desired this for their children.”]

I am not saying that little children who die without Christ’s baptism are punished with so great a penalty that it would have been better for them not to be born, since the Lord said this not about sinners generally, but about the most criminal and impious.

For if, concerning Sodom, he wished it to be understood—and certainly did not wish it understood only of Sodom—that “one will be punished more tolerably than another on the day of judgment” (Matthew 10:15; 11:24), who would doubt that unbaptized children, who possess only original sin and are burdened by no personal sins, will suffer the lightest condemnation of all?

What sort and degree that condemnation will be I cannot define. Nevertheless, I do not dare to say that it would be better for them not to exist than to be there.

But you too, who contend that they are free from every condemnation, do not wish to consider with what condemnation you punish them: by alienating so many images of God from the life and kingdom of God, and finally by separating them from pious parents whom you so eloquently urge to beget them.

They suffer these things unjustly if they have no sin at all. If they suffer them justly, then they have original sin.

### 45  
[Note: In the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus, chapter 9.]

Then, after introducing other words of mine in which I recalled how honorably the holy ancient fathers used marriage, you say that “they did not devote themselves to propagation with this intention: to beget children as guilty persons, to be cleansed by baptism, since the baptism by which we are now adopted had not yet been instituted” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, section 9).

You speak truly about baptism. Nevertheless, it should not therefore be believed that before circumcision was given, God’s servants—since they possessed faith in the Mediator who was to come in the flesh—provided no assistance to their little children through any sacrament of his, although [Col. 0810] Scripture may have wished to conceal what that sacrament was for some necessary reason.

For we also read of their sacrifices (Leviticus 12), by which that blood was certainly prefigured which alone takes away the sin [Note: The manuscripts read “sin”; the editions read “sins”] of the world (John 1:29).

Even after the time of the Law had begun, sacrifices were offered more openly for the sins of newborn children. Answer: for what sins?

Consider also that for the fathers who begot them, the soul of a little child was to perish from his people if he was not circumcised on the eighth day (Genesis 17:14). Answer what merit caused him to perish, when you deny that he was subject to original sin.

### Chapter XII
46. Now, concerning Joseph, whose wife, on the testimony of the Gospel, I said Mary was (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, §12), you spend a long time arguing against my position and try to show that “since intercourse was absent, it could in no way have been a marriage.” Accordingly, in your view, when spouses cease to have intercourse, they will no longer be spouses, and that cessation will be a divorce. To prevent this from happening, let the decrepit do, as far as they can, what they did when young, and let them not spare their exhausted [Note: Two manuscripts read *defectis* (“enfeebled”) instead of *effoetis* (“exhausted”).] bodies from this activity, in which even you, while advocating continence, take excessive delight. Let them not think that, as far as the incentives of lust are concerned, they have grown old, so that they may remain spouses.

If this pleases you, that is your concern. But I—since honest human opinion agrees that wives should be taken for the purpose of begetting children, however much weakness may yield to lust—noticed, besides the fidelity that spouses owe one another, lest adultery occur, and besides offspring, for whose begetting the two sexes must be joined, a third good that ought to exist in spouses, especially in those belonging to the people of God. It seemed to me that this was a kind of sacrament, preventing divorce either from a wife who cannot bear children or—as Cato is reported to have done (Plutarch, *Life of Cato*, and Lucan, book 2)—from a husband who does not wish to father more children, so that she might not be handed over to another man for childbearing (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, §11).

For this reason, in the union that I called a marriage according to the Gospel, I said that all three goods of marriage were complete: “fidelity, because there was no adultery; offspring, the Lord Christ himself; sacrament, because there was no divorce.” Therefore, because I said that all of the goods of marriage—that is, this threefold good—were complete in Christ’s parents, I should not for that reason be thought, as you accuse me, to have said this “so that whatever occurred otherwise might seem evil.” For I also say that a marriage can be good in another situation, when offspring cannot be produced except through intercourse. If it could be produced otherwise and the spouses nevertheless had intercourse, they would plainly be yielding to lust and would be making bad use of that evil. But when a human being cannot be born except through the union for which both sexes were instituted, spouses who unite for that reason make good use of that evil. If, however, they seek pleasure from lust as well, they do wrong venially.

47. “As a husband,” you say, “Joseph was regarded by everyone as such.” You want it understood that Scripture called Mary his wife according to this public opinion, not according to the truth. Let us suppose that an evangelist could have done this when reporting either his own words or those of someone else, speaking according to human opinion. But would an angel, speaking privately to one person, have spoken contrary to both his own consciousness and that of the person to whom he spoke, according to opinion rather than truth, when he said to him, “Do not be afraid to take Mary your wife”?

Moreover, why would the genealogies have been traced down to Joseph (Matt. 1:20, 16) if this was not done according to the truth in which the male sex has precedence in marriage? This is what I had set forth in the book to which you are replying (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, §12), but you were entirely afraid to touch upon it.

The evangelist Luke says of the Lord that he “was thought to be the son of Joseph” (Luke 3:23), because he was thought to have been begotten through Joseph’s intercourse. He wished to remove this false opinion, not to deny that Mary was the wife of that man, contrary to the angel’s testimony.

48. Yet you yourself also acknowledge that “she received the name of wife through the fidelity of their betrothal.” This fidelity certainly remained inviolate. For when he saw that she was already a consecrated virgin, endowed with divine fruitfulness, he did not seek another wife; and indeed he would not have sought her either if he had not needed a wife. But he did not therefore judge the bond of marital fidelity to be dissolved because the hope of bodily intercourse had been removed.

You may think whatever you wish about this marriage. We, however, do not say, as you falsely accuse us, “that the first spouses were instituted in such a way that they were spouses without the union of the two sexes.” Rather, the issues debated between us are these: whether, before sin, the flesh lusted against the spirit in paradise; whether this does not now occur in spouses, when the excess of that same concupiscence is restrained even by marital chastity; whether it is not an evil to which one must not consent when it resists, lest it proceed to excess; whether concupiscence is not an evil, to which, when it resists, one must not consent lest it proceed to its own excess; whether a person is not born from and with that very concupiscence, in which you deny that any evil exists [Note: The Vatican and Gallican manuscripts omit “and with that very” (*et cum ipsa*)]; and whether anyone can be freed from an evil implanted in human generation except through regeneration.

In these questions, your impious novelty is strangled by the Catholic truth handed down from ancient times.

### CHAPTER XIII

49. You thought it necessary to pile up testimonies from the sacred Scriptures to prove something about which there is no disagreement between us: “that man is created by God”—something that it would not be permissible to deny even of some little worm. What purpose did this serve except to show that you had searched for fields of words in which you might run about noisily, vainly, and emptily?

But when you also introduced the testimony of holy Job so verbosely, why did it not occur to you what that same man of God said when the subject was human sins [Note: Printed editions read “his” (*ejus*) for *ei*]:  that no one is clean from defilement, “not even an infant whose life upon the earth is but a single day” (Job 14:5, according to the Septuagint)?

Who would deny that mercy is extended to all, great and small, by him from whom comes the salvation both of human beings and of animals, and who makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked (Matt. 5:45), except someone who does not believe that God exists or that he cares for earthly things?

You wished to teach this by the testimony of holy Job, as though we were arguing the contrary, because he said, “You fashioned me from bones and sinews; you granted me life and mercy” (Job 10:11–12). There he may not have been speaking of every human being, but may have been giving thanks concerning himself: although born in the flesh, he had not been abandoned, but the one who created him had granted him mercy so that he might truly live—that is, live justly [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads “so that he might live” (*ut viveret*), omitting *vere* (“truly”).].

Or perhaps, because the life he received by being born was insufficient, he added “and mercy,” lest he remain by nature a child of wrath, like the others, and become one of the vessels of wrath rather than of mercy.

50. How the faithful person is not guilty of the evil that accompanies and inhabits his limbs, while the person born from that evil nevertheless contracts guilt, we have already said I do not know how many times. Regeneration, not generation, has bestowed this benefit upon the faithful. Therefore, the offspring must be freed from that guilt from which the parent was freed.

### CHAPTER XIV

51. But dialectic has taught you something grand [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads “has taught” (*docuerit*).]: “A thing that exists in a subject cannot exist without the thing in which it is subject. Therefore,” you think, “the evil that is in the parent, as in a subject, cannot transmit guilt to another thing, namely the offspring, to which it does not pass.”

You would say this correctly if the evil of concupiscence did not pass from parent to offspring. But since no one is conceived without it, just as no one is born without it, how can you say that it does not pass to the place to which it is transmitted?

It is not Aristotle, whose categories you foolishly profess to understand, but the Apostle who says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through all human beings it passed” (Rom. 5:12).

That dialectic does not deceive you; you simply do not understand it. What you learned there is indeed true: things that exist in a subject, such as qualities, cannot exist without the subject in which they are. Color or shape, for example, exists in a body as its subject. But such things pass by affecting, not by emigrating [Note: The Casalensis manuscript reads “but these pass by affecting”; the Floriacensis, “but from there by affecting.”]. Thus Ethiopians, because they are black, beget black children; yet they do not transfer their color to their children like a garment. Rather, through the quality of their own bodies they affect the body propagated from them.

It is more remarkable when the qualities of bodily things pass into incorporeal things, and yet this happens when we somehow absorb the forms of bodies that we see, store them in memory, and carry them with us wherever we go. Those forms have not withdrawn from their bodies, yet they have passed to us in a remarkable way by affecting our senses.

In the same manner, they pass from spirit to body as they pass from body to spirit. The colors of the rods that Jacob varied passed by affecting the souls of the mother animals, and from there, by passing through the same kind of affection, appeared again in the bodies of their offspring (Gen. 30:37–42).

The distinguished medical authority Soranus writes that something of this kind can also occur in human offspring, and confirms it with an example from history. He relates that the tyrant Dionysius, because he himself was ugly and did not wish to have children like himself, used to place a beautiful picture before his wife during intercourse. By desiring its beauty, he would somehow seize it and transmit it to the offspring she conceived by affecting it [Note: See *Revisions*, book 2, chapter 62.].

God does not create natures in such a way as to remove the laws he has given to the movements of each nature. Thus bodily defects, although they exist in a subject, pass from parents to children—not as though they migrated from their own subject into another subject, which the categories you have read correctly show to be impossible, but, as you do not understand, by affection and contagion.

### CHAPTER XV

52. Why do you labor through elaborate arguments to reach the precipice of impiety, so that “Christ’s flesh, because he was born from Mary, whose virgin flesh, like that of everyone else, had been propagated from Adam, differs in no respect from sinful flesh, and the Apostle must be thought to have said without distinction that he was sent in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. 8:3)? Indeed, you insist that “there is no sinful flesh, lest Christ’s flesh also be sinful.”

What, then, is “the likeness of sinful flesh” if there is no sinful flesh?

You said that “I did not understand this apostolic statement,” but you did not explain it, so that, with you teaching us [Note: Five manuscripts read “teaching” (*docente*) for “teacher” (*doctore*)], we might learn how something can be like a thing that does not exist. If it is madness to say this—and certainly Christ’s flesh is not sinful flesh but is like sinful flesh—what are we left to understand except that, with this one exception, all other human flesh is sinful?

From this it is evident that the concupiscence through which Christ did not wish to be conceived produced the propagation of evil in the human race. Although Mary’s body came from that propagation, it did not transmit it to the body that she conceived without it.

Whoever denies that Christ’s body was called “in the likeness of sinful flesh” because all other human flesh is sinful, and compares Christ’s flesh with the flesh of other human beings at birth in such a way as to assert that both possess equal purity, is found to be a detestable heretic.

53. You think you have discovered something important, and you argue at great length that “even if those being born could receive some evil from their parents, it would be cleansed [Note: Printed editions read “they would be cleansed” (*expiarentur*)] by the hands of God, since he himself forms them in their mothers’ wombs.”

You vigorously prove from many testimonies of Scripture that human beings are formed by God—as though we denied this. Among these testimonies, after quoting words from the book of Ecclesiasticus in which God’s works are said to be hidden (Ecclus. 3:22–23), you immediately added your own words and said: “This statement refutes the vanity of those who think that the depths of nature can be grasped through some investigation.”

Say this to yourself, and do not rashly define anything about the origin of the soul that cannot be grasped either by the most certain reasoning or by unambiguous divine speech. Rather, remember what the very wise mother of the Maccabees said. You also quoted her words to her sons: “I do not know how you appeared in my womb” (2 Macc. 7:22).

She certainly should not be thought to have said this about their bodies, which she did not doubt she had conceived from male seed. Rather, she did not know whether her sons’ souls had been drawn from their father’s soul or had begun to exist in her womb from elsewhere. She was not ashamed to confess her ignorance, so as to avoid rashness.

Why, then, do you complain: “Why are the children not cleansed by the very effect, so that the pollution”—as you say—“of their parents might be expiated by the majesty of the Creator”?

You do not consider that this can also be said of evident bodily defects, with which not a few infants are born [Note: Belgian manuscripts omit “infants” after “are born.”]. Yet no one should doubt that the true and good God is the creator of all bodies. Nevertheless, from the hands of so great a maker there proceed so many things that are not merely defective but even monstrous that some call them “errors of nature.” Since they cannot investigate the divine power at work, or why it does what it does, they are ashamed to admit that they do not know what they do not know.

54. As for the transmission of original sin to all human beings, since it passes through the concupiscence of the flesh, it could not pass into that flesh which the virgin conceived without it.

You wished to set against me, as though prescribing an answer, something from another book of mine, which I wrote to Marcellinus of holy memory: “Adam corrupted in himself all those who would come from his stock.” From what, then, did Adam corrupt them? Certainly not from that source by which Christ came into his mother’s womb.

But I shall state the words in that sentence that bear most directly on the matter, because you did not wish to state them; and immediately it will become clear why you did not. “By the hidden corruption,” I said, “of his carnal concupiscence, he corrupted in himself all those who would come from his stock” (*On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins*, book 1, §10).

Therefore, he did not corrupt the flesh in whose conception that corruption was absent. Christ’s flesh therefore drew mortality from the mortality of his mother’s body, because he found her body mortal; but he did not draw the contagion of original sin [Note: Printed editions read *originale* (“original”)], because he did not encounter the concupiscence of intercourse [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript, corrected by an ancient hand, reads: “because it did not come through the concupiscence of intercourse.”].

If he had taken from his mother not even mortality, but only the substance of flesh, then his flesh could have been neither sinful flesh nor even the likeness of sinful flesh.

55. You compare and equate me with “the error of Apollinaris, who denied that Christ possessed the sense of flesh,” in order to stir up clouds from every direction before the ignorant, lest they attend to the light of truth.

The sense of flesh, without which no human being living in a body ever was, is, or will be, is one thing. The concupiscence by which the flesh lusts against the spirit, without which the first human being existed before sin, is another. Christ the man displayed to us the human nature that Adam had, because just as Adam was created from earth, Christ was created from a woman without such concupiscence.

Yet Christ assumed from her also [Note: The Louvain edition reads “only” (*tantum*)] the weakness of mortality, which had not existed in the flesh of the first human being before sin. Thus he became “the likeness of sinful flesh,” which Adam’s flesh had not then been.

Therefore, in order to provide us an example of suffering, Christ did not possess his own evils but endured those of others. He was in sufferings for us, not in desires.

56. Therefore, those born from Adam must be transferred to Christ through rebirth, lest the images of God perish from the kingdom of God. Whoever says that this can happen without evil possesses neither love nor fear of God.

A human being must be born with this evil from a condemned origin. But far be it from us to “reduce the regenerate,” as you slanderously claim, “under the necessity of sins, while God bestows the gifts of virtues” [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads “under the necessity of crimes” (*sub necessitatem criminum*).].

Although we see another law in our members, opposing the law of our mind, it does not follow that we are under the necessity of sinning. Rather, there is honor worthy of praise in the spirit, aided by a spiritual gift, when it lusts against the concupiscence of the flesh.

But however you turn, however you boast, whatever you gather from every direction, inflate, display, and scatter: whatever the good spirit lusts against is not good.

57. “Nature that is unlike ours,” you say, “could not provide an example.” It certainly could. What else is the point of urging us to imitate the Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the wicked, so that by his example we may love our enemies (Matt. 5:44–45)?

Nevertheless [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads “nevertheless also by nature”; some others, “nevertheless that nature”], the nature of Christ’s humanity was not unlike ours; it was unlike ours in respect of our defect. He was born a human being without defect, which no other human being was.

As regards the life by which we ought to imitate Christ, this too makes a great difference: each of us is a human being, whereas he is also God. A righteous human being who is merely human cannot be as great as a human being who is also God.

You did, however, say something great and true when you quoted the testimony of the Apostle Peter: “He committed no sin” (1 Pet. 2:22). You correctly noted that the apostle judged this sufficient to show that Christ had no sin, since he said that Christ committed no sin. “He taught,” you say, “that one who did not commit sin could not possess it.”

This is entirely true. Certainly even an adult would have committed sin if he had possessed it as a child [Note: The manuscripts read “as a small one”; printed editions read “as a little child.”]. For this reason, no human being except Christ failed to commit sin after reaching maturity: no human being except Christ failed to possess sin from the beginning of infancy.

58. “Remove,” you say, “the cause of the example, and the price that was paid for us will also be removed” [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads, “Remove, you say, the example; the cause and the price will be removed”; two Vatican manuscripts read, “Remove, he says, the cause of the example, and the price will be removed.”]. It is not surprising that you place only an example in Christ, since you attack the aid of grace with which he was filled [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read “with which she was filled.”].

“By hope,” you say, “we flee to the defenses of faith in order to be rid of evil; but we are not rid of what is innate, since virility itself persists after Baptism.”

By “virility” you call the concupiscence of the flesh. It certainly persists, as you cannot deny [Note: Printed editions read impersonally, “as cannot be denied”], against which the spirit ought to lust, lest the already regenerated person be drawn away by his own concupiscence.

The concupiscence that resists in order to draw a person—even if it does not draw him because the spirit lusts and resists against it, and therefore does not conceive and give birth to sin (Jas. 1:14–15)—is not good.

It is this of which the Apostle says: “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh” (Rom. 7:18). If Christ possessed this evil in his own nature, he could not have healed it in ours.

### CHAPTER XVI

[Note: In Ambrosius and Erasmus, chapter 10.]

59. You insert another passage from my book. Because I said that “marital intercourse undertaken with the intention of begetting children is not itself sin, since the good will of the mind leads, rather than follows, the bodily pleasure that accompanies it” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, §13), you reply: “Sins cannot be born from something that is free from sin.” In this way you think you can destroy original sin—the sin destroyed only by the Savior, whom you begrudge to infants.

He destroys it by releasing those who are guilty, not by denying their guilt.

Marital intercourse undertaken with the intention of begetting children is not sin because it makes good use of the law of sin, that is, concupiscence, which exists in the members and resists the law of the mind.

If concupiscence does not hold the parent guilty because the parent has been regenerated, what wonder is it if it holds the person being born guilty because that person has been generated from it? Therefore, in order not to remain guilty, the child too must be regenerated.

If you consider how much this statement of yours—“Sins cannot be born from something that is free from sin”—assists the Manichaeans, you will wish to delete it from your book and from the minds of all who have read it [Note: Several manuscripts read “all human beings who have read your book.”].

If sins are not born from something free from sin, then, according to the Manichaeans, they have another nature of their own from which they are born [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript omits “of their own.”]. I demonstrated in the first volume of this work how much you assist them by other similar statements of yours (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, above, book 1, §§36–44).

The statement just cited has the same force. Do you see that, if we wish to defeat the Manichaeans, we must also overturn certain statements of yours, such as this one, in addition to correcting your own error as Pelagians?

You say, “Sins are not born from something that is free from sin.” But the truth contradicts you, and it overturns both you and the Manichaeans, with whom you share this statement.

The angel whom God first created was something free from sin. The human being whom God first created was something free from sin. Whoever denies that sins were born from things free from sin is either plainly a Manichaean or, through carelessness, an ally of the Manichaeans.

60. Next, after quoting other words of mine, you argue as though I had said: “When lust serves married people in propagating offspring, then lust is honored.”

You tell yourself whatever you wish; I neither said nor meant anything of the kind. For how is lust honored when it serves, if the authority of the mind suppresses it so that it does not proceed to unrestrained excesses?

We therefore did not say that the use of lust always entails guilt. You collect our words as though we had said this and conclude that adulterers sin less than married people: “Lust,” you say, “serves married people so that they may sin, but commands adulterers.”

But since I did not say this, whatever your claim may be, by which you wished to present it as a necessary conclusion, it has nothing to do with me.

I say that using lust is not always sin, because making good use of an evil is not sin. Nor is everything good simply because a good person makes good use of it.

It is written of two people: “An educated son will be wise, but an imprudent servant will be used” (Prov. 10:26, according to the Septuagint). Is it therefore good to be imprudent because a wise person makes good use of the imprudent person?

For this reason the Apostle John does not say, “Do not use the world,” but “Do not love the world,” and there he also mentions “the concupiscence of the flesh” (1 John 2:15–16).

Whoever uses something without loving it uses it as though he were not using it, because he does not use it for the sake of that thing but for the sake of something else that he loves, so that he can use even what he does not love. Hence Paul, his fellow apostle, says: “Those who use this world, as though they did not use it” (1 Cor. 7:31).

What does “as though they did not use it” mean except “let them not love what they use,” because it is the kind of thing that cannot otherwise be used well?

This must be observed even with things in this world that are good in themselves but ought not to be loved. Who could rightly say that money is evil? Yet no one who loves money makes good use of it.

How much more is this true of lust? A wicked spirit desires money, but money itself does not lust against the good spirit, as lust does. Therefore, both the person who denies that lust is evil sins and the person who makes good use of this evil does not sin.

You would therefore argue correctly if you said that, if lust is evil, it binds those spouses whom it serves under greater guilt than the adulterers whom it dominates—provided that we had said that those spouses who, while concupiscence serves them, use it only for the duty of begetting children, employ it for evil purposes just as a murderer uses a servant to commit a crime.

But since we say that the marital duty of begetting children is good, although the one born draws with him the wound of original sin, which can be healed in the regenerate, it follows that good spouses make use of the evil of concupiscence in the same way that a wise person uses an imprudent servant for good works.

61. But you clever people accuse and condemn not the measure or kind of pleasure, but its excess, because, as you say, you know that it can be held within permitted limits by the power of the mind.

Let the power of the mind, if it can, ensure that lust does not become agitated to transgress the limits from whose transgression the mind restrains it. If it cannot do this, then certainly, so that the limits may not be transgressed, one must resist the wicked enemy who attempts to cross them.

“But we affirm,” you say, “that virgins and continent people possess complete contempt for it.” Does this mean that virgins and continent people do not fight against the concupiscence of the flesh?

What is the object against which they conduct those glorious struggles, praised even by you, in order to preserve virginity and continence (above, book 3, §42, and book 4, §9)?

If they fight, then what they fight against is evil [Note: The manuscripts read “this very good” (*ipsum bonum*) for “this good” in the preceding sentence]. And where is this evil except in them? Therefore, it is truly said even by them: “Good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh.”

62. You say that marriage is nothing other than the union of bodies. You later say—and this is true—that propagation cannot occur without mutual desire and the natural act.

Yet do you deny that adulterers too are joined by mutual desire, by the natural act, and by the union of bodies? This, then, is not a definition of marriage.

Marriage is one thing; that without which even marriage cannot propagate children is another. Human beings can be born without marriage, and spouses can exist without the union of bodies. Otherwise they would cease to be spouses—as I shall say nothing else—when they grow old and either cannot unite sexually or, without hope of having children, are ashamed to do so and do not wish to.

You see, therefore, how carelessly you defined marriage by saying that it is nothing other than the union of bodies.

You might perhaps have said more tolerably that marriage does not begin except through the union of bodies, since wives are taken for the purpose of begetting children, and children cannot otherwise be begotten.

But the union of bodies for begetting children would have been different from what it now is if no one had sinned. Far be it from us to suppose that the most honorable happiness of paradise always obeyed agitated lust. Far be it from us to suppose that the peace of mind and body possessed anything for which the nature of the first human being had to fight against itself.

If, then, in paradise there was neither a need to serve lust nor a need to fight against it, either lust was not there, or it was not there in the form it now has.

Now the person who does not wish to serve lust must necessarily resist it; the person who neglects to resist it [Note: The Ambrosian, Erasmian, and manuscript readings have “to fight” (*pugnare*)] must necessarily serve it. One of these is burdensome, though praiseworthy; the other is shameful and pitiable.

Thus in this age one of these two conditions is necessary for the chaste, whereas in paradise both were foreign to the blessed.

63. Again you say that I contradict myself, presenting other words of mine in which, distinguishing the duty of propagation from the desire for carnal pleasure, I said that “it is one thing to have intercourse only with the will to beget children, which has no fault; another to seek the pleasure of the flesh in intercourse, but not outside one’s spouse, which has venial fault” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, §17).

Everyone who sees the truth sees that these two statements provide no basis for showing me to contradict myself.

Still, hear again what should be impressed more forcefully upon the minds of those whom you are trying to deceive.

You slander us by claiming that we offer an excuse to depraved and criminal people, so that when they have committed unspeakable and filthy acts they may say that they acted against their will and therefore have no sin—as though we did not urge, much more vigorously, that one must fight against lust.

If you, while saying that this is good, nevertheless do not want us to believe that your battles against this good grow cold, or at least lukewarm, how much more vigilantly and ardently do we judge that one must fight against evil?

We say that it is against the will that the flesh lusts against the spirit—not that the spirit lusts against the flesh.

Through this concupiscence it becomes good that spouses use the lust of the flesh only for the purpose of begetting children, and thus make good use of an evil. This good use of an evil makes intercourse honorable and truly marital. But intercourse for the sake of pleasure, not offspring, makes it blameworthy, though in a spouse the blame is venial.

What is born even from honorable intercourse nevertheless draws with it something to be cleansed by rebirth, because even in honorable intercourse there is an evil that the goodness of marriage uses well.

What harmed those who were born does not harm those who have been reborn. Consequently, the person born from them is harmed by it if he is not reborn.

64. In the course of your arguments, by which you twist yourself pointlessly against my words, you repeatedly fail to see that you are assisting the Manichaeans.

You think that a child born from marital intercourse does not draw original sin because, as you say, guilt cannot be born from an act that has no fault.

Why, then, was the guilt of the angel and the guilt of the human being born from an act of God that had no fault?

You see how much you support those whose detestation you use to conceal what you think against the firmly established Catholic faith.

If, according to your definition [Note: Three manuscripts read “your definitive statement” (*definitionem tuam*)], guilt cannot be born from a work of God that has no fault, then none of God’s works has any fault. From where, then, was guilt born?

At this point, with your assistance, the Manichaean devises and introduces another nature, as his folly dictates, an evil nature from which guilt might be thought to have been born, since, according to your words, guilt cannot be born from God’s work.

Can the Manichaean be defeated unless you too are defeated along with him?

Both angel and human being are works of God without fault. Yet guilt arose from them when they withdrew from the one who was without guilt by the free will given to them without fault. They became evil not through an admixture of evil, but through the defection of good.

65. You say that I praised continence in the Christian age not so that people might be inflamed toward virginity, but so that the good of marriage instituted by God might be condemned.

Yet, lest you seem to be tormenting me with a malicious suspicion about my mind, as though you wished to test me, you say to me: “If you faithfully invite people to pursue continence, you therefore admit that the virtue of chastity can be preserved by those who desire it, so that whoever wishes may be holy in body and spirit.”

I answer that I do admit this—but not in the way you do. You attribute it to the powers of the mind itself; I attribute it to the will aided by God’s grace.

What, however, is restrained by the authority of the mind so that sin may not occur, except the evil by which a person sins when it prevails? Since we must not say with the Manichaeans that this evil has been mixed into us from an alien nature of evil, it remains for us to acknowledge it in our own nature as a wound requiring healing, whose guilt we already confess to have been healed through regeneration.

66. See how fruitlessly you listed the heretical deceits with which you compare me. Would that you had not increased their number.

You assert that “the apostolic statement condemning heretics who forbid marriage” (1 Tim. 4:3) also “touches me,” as though I said, “After Christ’s coming, marriages are shameful.”

Hear, then, what we say, so that by hearing it repeatedly and in many forms you may not evade the truth by pretending to be deaf.

We do not say that marriages are shameful. Indeed, so that incontinent people may not fall into a damnable crime, they must be supported by the honor of marriage.

But what you say is not taught by Christian doctrine. To use your own words, we do not say that “a human being is sufficient to give laws to the innate impulses within himself.”

We say instead what the Apostle said when speaking about this: “Each person has his own gift from God” (1 Cor. 7:7). And what the Lord said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). And: “Not everyone accepts this word, but only those to whom it has been given” (Matt. 19:11).

He could have said, “Not everyone accepts this word, but only those who wish,” if what you say were true.

I ask, then, by what kind of innate impulses you say that a human being is able to give laws to himself. Are they good or evil?

If they are good, then the flesh lusts against the good spirit [Note: Erasmus and Louvain add “against the spirit,” incorrectly], and two goods oppose each other within the human being. If that were so, the opposition between the two goods could not itself be good.

If they are evil, then admit that evil impulses are innate in the human being, against which chastity fights. And lest you be forced to say with the Manichaeans that a mixture from an alien nature of evil exists within us, acknowledge instead our own original sickness.

Chastity makes good use of the evil of this sickness in marriage. Against the evil of this sickness, the incontinent employ the remedies of marriage, while the continent undertake glorious struggles.

I think that the promise I made when I began responding to everything in which you raised knots of questions is more conveniently fulfilled if I do not exceed the number of your books [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads “from which” (*ex qua*) for “from which time” (*ex quo*)].

Let this, then, be the end of my present book, so that we may refute your last book from another beginning.

## BOOK SIX

[Column 821]

He responds to Book Four of Julian, and to his cavils and calumnies concerning the remaining part of the earlier book *On Marriage and Concupiscence*. He confirms that human beings are born with sin: from the baptism of infants; from the Apostle’s words to the Romans and Corinthians; and from the rite of exorcism and insufflation performed when infants are baptized. He shows that the example of the olive and the wild olive was aptly employed to explain how children who are sinners and in need of regeneration can be born from regenerated and righteous parents. Original sin was voluntary in our first parents; with respect to the act itself it is alien to us, yet through the contagion of propagation it is ours. On account of this sin, the human race is justly worn down by such great miseries from infancy, and infants who die without the grace of regeneration are excluded from the kingdom of God. Through Baptism sanctification is now conferred both upon the soul and upon the body itself, though in this life the corruption of the body is not removed; this corruption also burdens the soul. He explains how concupiscence remains in act but passes away in guilt. He restores to the Catholic understanding the testimonies of the Apostle Paul, which Julian had perversely interpreted. Finally, he interprets according to its legitimate sense the authority of Ezekiel, which Julian had abused.

# CHAPTER ONE

1. I have already replied to your third book; let me reply to the fourth as well. The Lord will be present, so that not only truth but also charity may be shown to you by us. Whoever possesses these two will be neither foolish nor envious. You said much about these vices at the beginning of the book just mentioned. Error must be driven out by truth, and ill will by charity.

Now, in this discussion of yours, when speaking of folly and saying that “it is the mother of all vices,” you brought forward a testimony from Scripture, where we read: “God loves no one except him who dwells with wisdom” (Wisdom 7:28). Consider carefully, then, whether childish vanity can dwell with wisdom—the vanity through which it is necessary that an infant pass from infancy, though he does pass beyond it. Consider also what first fruit is born from the root that you praise, and how great a change in the opposite direction is necessary before he can be loved by God, who loves no one except him who dwells with wisdom. In the case of predestined infants, he consumes what he hates, so that, once freed from vanity, he may love them also as they dwell with wisdom. Yet if the final day should snatch them away from the breast [Note: [Col. 0821] An allusion to Virgil, *Aeneid* 6.426–429.], I wonder whether you dare say that they will dwell with wisdom outside the kingdom of God—a kingdom which, according to you, “the goodness of an inviolate and blameless nature” does not permit them to enter, unless the grace of the true Savior, having redeemed them, frees them from the folly of the false praiser of nature.

I say nothing of those who are naturally foolish, whom Scripture declares to be much more grievously mourned than the dead (Ecclesiasticus 22:13). God’s grace can indeed rescue them also from this great evil through the blood of the Mediator. But how could they have fallen into so great an evil if, by God’s judgment, no penalty were owed to any corrupted origin?

2. You rightly and severely reproved those “who either have neglected to learn what ought to be known or do not fear to condemn what they do not know.” Can you say this of those born without understanding? Yet under a just God you will not find how this could happen to them if children inherit no merits from their parents.

“But by envying you, in a certain midday of discovered truth, without the shadow of ignorance,” as you put it, “we have become insane.” Is it really so? You, who do not envy, do you not see such great evils in infants? God is good; God is just. There is certainly no alien nature of evil which, according to the Manichaeans, is believed to have been mixed into our nature. Whence, then, come such great evils in human beings—not merely in their conduct but in the very dispositions with which they are born—if human origin has not been corrupted and the mass has not been condemned?

Moreover, although you describe a person free from folly and removed from the goads of envy, you describe envy itself in such a way that, in your description, this vice appears both as sin and as the punishment of sin. Is envy not a diabolical sin? Is it not the punishment of sin, since it “immediately torments the very author from whom it arises”? These are your words. Yet with prolonged verbosity you thought that you had argued with the greatest acuity that “one and the same vice cannot be both sin and the punishment of sin.” But perhaps, because you are not envious, you could only with difficulty finally see in another book the envy about which you would say these things, and you contradicted yourself on my behalf because you do not envy me.

# CHAPTER TWO

3. After finishing your preface, in which you also labored, as you usually do, to prove what I proclaim—“that God is the creator of human beings”—you next set out my words. I had said: “The human being who is born from the concupiscence of the flesh is born to the world, not to God; but he is born to God when he is reborn from water and the Spirit” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence* 1.21).

You lie in wait for these words of mine, asserting that I ought thereby to be understood as having said that whatever belongs to the world belongs to the devil, because elsewhere I had said that “those who are born from the union of bodies belong to the devil’s right,” asserting that they are “snatched from the power of darkness when they are regenerated in Christ.”

I therefore answer your calumny. You want me to appear to have called “the world” that which belongs to the devil’s power, as though the devil had made or possessed heaven and earth and everything in them. I do not say this; I detest, refute, and condemn the person who says it.

But in this passage I called “the world” what the Lord meant when he said: “Behold, the prince of the world is coming” (John 14:30). He did not intend the devil to be understood as the prince of heaven and earth and of all things made through the Word—that is, through Christ himself—for it is written: “The world was made through him” (John 1:10). Rather, he meant the world of which it is said: “The world is placed in the evil one” (1 John 5:19); and again: “Everything that is in the world is the concupiscence of the flesh, the concupiscence of the eyes, and the ambition of the age; this is not from the Father but is from the world” (1 John 2:16).

Heaven and earth are, of course, from the Father through the Son; and angels, stars, plants, animals, and human beings are from the Father through the Son, insofar as their substance itself is concerned—the substance by which human beings are human beings. But the devil is the prince of the world, and the world is placed in the evil one: namely, all human beings who are liable to eternal condemnation unless they are freed from it [Note: [Col. 0822] The manuscripts read “and.”], so that they may no longer belong to the prince of sinners, redeemed by that blood which was poured out for the remission of sins.

It is to this world, whose prince is the one about whom he who conquered the world says (John 16:33), “Behold, the prince of the world is coming, and he will find nothing in me,” that the human being is born until he is reborn in him who conquered the world, in whom the prince of the world found nothing.

4. What is the world of which the Savior and conqueror of the world says: “The world cannot hate you, but it hates me because I testify concerning it that its works are evil” (John 7:7)? Are the works of the earth and sea, of heaven and the stars, evil? Surely this world means human beings.

No one is chosen for deliverance from this world except by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, who gave his flesh for the life of the world. He would not have done this unless he had found the world in death.

What is the world of which he said to the Jews: “You are from this world; I am not from this world” (John 8:23)? Finally, what is the world from which Jesus chose his disciples so that they would no longer be of the world, and which itself hated them because they were no longer of it?

The Savior of the world, the light of the world, speaks in this way—this is what he says: “I command you to love one another. If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you. If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own. But because you are not of the world, and I chose you from the world, therefore the world hates you” (John 15:17–19).

If he had not added, “I chose you from the world,” it might be thought that he meant “you are not of the world” in the same way that he had said of himself, “I am not of this world.” For neither was he himself of the world, nor was he chosen from it so that he would not be of the world. What Christian would say this? For even according to the condition in which he graciously became human, the Son of God was not of the world. Why else, except because there was never any sin in him? On account of sin, every human being is born first to the world and not to God; and, in order to be born to God, he who is reborn is chosen from the world so that he may no longer be of the world.

For this reason the prince of the world is cast out by him, as he himself testifies, saying: “Now is the judgment of this world; now the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12:31).

5. Unless perhaps your audacity will go so far as to say that infants are not chosen from the world when they are washed by his Baptism—by him of whom it is said: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.”

If you deny that infants belong to this reconciliation by denying that they are of the world, I do not know with what face you live in the world. But if you acknowledge that, when they pass into the body of Christ, they are chosen from the world, then necessarily they are born to that from which they are chosen in order to be reborn.

They are born through the concupiscence of the flesh; they are reborn through the grace of the Spirit. The former is from the world; the latter comes into the world, so that those who were predestined before the world may be chosen from the world.

After the Apostle had said, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself,” he immediately added how he does this: “Not counting their trespasses against them” (2 Corinthians 5:19).

The whole world, therefore, is guilty through Adam. God does not deny the hand of formation to his work [Note: [Col. 0823] The Am. and Er. editions and seven manuscripts read “to his work”], to the seeds he established, though they have been corrupted by paternal transgression. When the world is reconciled through Christ, it is freed from the world by him who came into the world—not to be chosen from the world, but to choose; not by an election of merits, but of grace, because “the remnant has been saved according to the election of grace” (Romans 11:5).

# CHAPTER THREE

6. Next you set out other words of mine, in which I said: “Regeneration alone remits the guilt of this concupiscence, and therefore generation transmits it.” I immediately added: “Therefore let what has been generated be regenerated, so that, since it cannot be otherwise, what has been transmitted may likewise be remitted” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence* 1.21).

Again and again you vainly try to conceal the fact that you consider Baptism superfluous for infants, saying that “the grace of Christ’s mysteries is rich in many gifts.” Whether you wish it or not, you confess that infants believe in Christ through the hearts and mouths of those who carry them. Therefore the Lord’s sentence also applies to them: “Whoever does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16). On what grounds, and with what justice, if they inherit no original sin?

As for what you say—“By this he approves his own, because, before any obedience of their will, he exalts what he has done in them by increasing his benefits”—if by this he approves these people as his own, then surely those to whom he does not grant this he does not approve as his own. Yet since they too are his for the same reason, namely that he created them, why does he not approve them as his own in the same way?

Here [Note: [Col. 0824] The Am. and Er. editions and most manuscripts read “here.”] you deny nothing concerning fate or the acceptance of persons [Note: [Col. 0824] Three Vatican manuscripts read *garritis*, “you chatter.”]. So now acknowledge grace with us. For what else is it when none of those things is present? In one and the same condition, then, one person is left behind by the judgment of justice, not by fate; another is taken up by the provision of grace, not by merit.

7. You contend altogether in vain that infants are not cleansed from original sin through regeneration. This is not shown by the one who said: “All of us who have been baptized in Christ have been baptized into his death.” By saying “all,” he certainly did not exclude infants.

What is it to be baptized into Christ’s death except to die to sin? Hence, in another passage, he says of Christ himself: “For the one who died has died to sin once for all.” This was said because of the likeness of the flesh of sin; and for this reason the mystery of his cross is great, where our old person was also crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed [Note: [Col. 0824] In the manuscripts, “might be destroyed” rather than “may be destroyed.”].

If, then, infants are baptized in Christ, they are baptized into his death. If they are baptized into his death, they die to sin, having been planted together in the likeness of his death. “For the one who died has died to sin once for all; but the one who lives lives to God.”

And what is it to be planted together in the likeness of his death except what follows: “So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus” (Romans 6:3–11)?

Are we going to say that Jesus died to sin, although he never had any? Far be it from us. Yet it says: “The one who died has died to sin once for all.” His death signified our sin, on account of which death itself occurred. Having died to that death—that is, so as no longer to be mortal—he is said to have died to sin.

What he signified in the likeness of the flesh of sin, we accomplish through his grace in the flesh of sin. Just as he, by dying in the likeness of sin, is proclaimed dead to sin, so whoever has been baptized in him [Note: [Col. 0825] In the printed editions, after “has been baptized” stand the words “the same thing (that is, sin), of which in Christ there is likeness, not reality”; these should be deleted. They were certainly transferred by scribes from the margin into the text, since the oldest manuscripts entirely lack them.], dies to the very thing of which that likeness had existed. And just as there was a true death in his true flesh, so there is true remission in true sins.

# CHAPTER FOUR

8. If this whole passage of the Apostle’s Letter does not correct you from this perversity, you have become exceedingly hardened. Although all the statements he makes in writing to the Romans are connected, since he commends the grace of God through Jesus Christ, we cannot recall and discuss the entire Letter here, for that would be very long. Let us consider, from the chapter before us, the passage in which he says: “God demonstrates his love for us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8–9).

You want this statement to be understood as excluding infants. If I ask you: if they are not to be counted among sinners, how did he die for them who died for sinners? You will answer that he did not die for sinners alone, although he also died for sinners.

But you nowhere read in the divine authorities that Christ died also for those who had absolutely no sin. Consider, however, how forcefully you are pressed by the testimonies. You say that he died also for sinners; I say that he died only for sinners, so that you are compelled to answer that, if infants are bound by no sin, he did not die for infants.

For he says to the Corinthians: “Because one died for all; therefore all died, and he died for all” (2 Corinthians 5:14–15). Here you are in no way permitted to deny that Jesus died only for those who died.

Whom, then, do you understand to be dead in this passage? Those who have departed from the body? Who would be so foolish as to think that? We therefore understand the dead for whom Christ, the one, died, in the same way as he says elsewhere: “And when you were dead in trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made you alive with him” (Colossians 2:13).

Accordingly, “one,” he says, “died for all; therefore all died,” showing that it could not happen that he died except for the dead. From this he proved that all were dead: because one died for all.

I press it upon the one who refuses; I repeat it; I force it upon him: accept it—it is salutary; I do not want you to die. “One died for all; therefore all died.” See that he intended it to follow that all should be understood as dead if he died for all.

Since they were not dead in the body, it remains that all for whom Christ died were dead in sin. No one who does not deny or doubt that he is a Christian can deny or doubt this.

Therefore, if infants inherit no sin, they are not dead. If they are not dead, he did not die for them who died only for the dead. Yet in your first book, when crying out against us, you said that “Christ died also for infants.” You are therefore in no way permitted to deny that they inherit original sin.

From where else did they become dead, if not from that? Or on account of what death of infants did he die who died only for the dead? You confess that he died for infants. Return with me, then, to what I had begun to say concerning Romans [Note: [Col. 0826] The Floriacensis codex, corrected by an ancient hand, reads “what I had begun to say from the Letter to the Romans.”].

9. “God demonstrates,” he says, “his love for us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” “While we were sinners,” he says—that is, while we were dead—“Christ died for us. Much more, therefore, having now been justified by his blood, shall we be saved from wrath through him. For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, shall we be saved in his life.”

This is what is said elsewhere: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19).

Then the passage continues: “And not only this, but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ.” “Not only,” he says, “are we saved, but we also glory.” “Through whom we have now received reconciliation.”

And as though someone might ask why this reconciliation takes place through one Mediator who is human [Note: [Col. 0826] Thus the Gallican and Vatican manuscripts. The printed editions read “of human beings.”], he says: “For this reason, just as through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin death, and so passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.”

What, then, did the Law accomplish? Could it not reconcile? “No,” he says. “For until the Law, sin was in the world.” That is, the Law also could not remove sin. “But sin was not counted where there was no Law.” Sin certainly existed, but it was not counted because it was not known. For through the Law, as he says elsewhere, comes “knowledge of sin” (Romans 3:20).

But death reigned from Adam until Moses, because through Moses—that is, through the Law—the reign of death was not removed. Yet it reigned also over those who had not sinned. Why, then, if they had not sinned? Listen to why: “In the likeness,” he says, “of Adam’s transgression, who is a type of the one to come” [Note: [Col. 0826] Thus the older manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek. The printed editions read “into the likeness.”].

For he gave from himself a type to his descendants, although they had no sins of their own, so that those generated through his carnal concupiscence would die through the contagion of their father’s sin.

“But the gift,” he says, “is not like the transgression. For if by the transgression of the one many died, much more have the grace of God and the gift in the grace of the one human being Jesus Christ abounded in many” [Note: [Col. 0826] Some manuscripts read “unto many,” in accordance with the Greek and the Latin Vulgate reading. The Louvain editors rightly infer that Augustine read “in many,” since he immediately says, “because it abounds in those in whom it abounds.”].

It abounded much more, certainly, because those in whom it abounds die temporarily but will live eternally.

“And the gift,” he says, “is not like what came through the one who sinned. For judgment from one transgression led to condemnation, but grace from many transgressions led to justification.” That one transgression could indeed lead to condemnation; but grace wiped out not only that one, but also the many additional sins.

“For if,” he says, “because of the transgression of the one, death reigned through the one, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ.”

The previous meaning is repeated: they will reign in life much more because they will reign without end, whereas death reigned over them with an end.

“Therefore, just as through the transgression of one the result for all human beings was condemnation, so through the justification of one the result for all human beings is justification of life.” Thus “all” is used there and “all” here, because no one comes to death except through the one, and no one comes to life except through the other.

“For just as through the disobedience of one human being the many were constituted sinners” [Note: [Col. 0827] The manuscripts read “the many are constituted sinners.”], “so through the obedience of one the many will be constituted righteous.”

The Law entered alongside, so that the transgression might abound. But where the transgression abounded, grace abounded still more, so that, just as sin reigned in death [Note: [Col. 0827] The Vatican manuscripts and the Floriacensis read “reigned into death.” The Greek, however, has *en tō thanatō*, “in death.”], so grace might reign through righteousness unto eternal life, through Jesus Christ our Lord.

10. “What then shall we say?” he asks. “Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound?” Far be it from us. For what benefit has grace provided if we must remain in sin?

Finally, he continues and says: “We who died to sin—how shall we live in it?” Attend carefully now, and listen attentively to what follows so that you may understand it. After saying, “We who died to sin—how shall we live in it?” he says: “Or do you not know that all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death?”

Are infants who are baptized present here or not? If they are not here, then what he said is false: “All of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death,” because infants are not baptized into his death. But since the Apostle speaks truly, no one is understood to have been excluded.
