If you think this was said only of adults who already exercise free choice, then the Lord’s sentence—“Unless someone is reborn from water and the Spirit”—frightens you in vain. You have a great shortcut: assert that this too was said only of adults, so that infants are in no way included in this universal statement.

And why do you struggle with the question of Baptism—whether there is eternal life outside the kingdom of God, or whether innocent infants, so many images of God, must be deprived of eternal life and therefore punished with eternal death?

But if you do not dare say this, since the universal sentence was uttered—“Unless someone is reborn from water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God” (John 3:5)—then the same universality constrains you when the Apostle says: “All of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death.”

Therefore infants who are baptized in Christ, since they are baptized into his death, die to sin. For these statements are connected with what was said above: “We who died to sin—how shall we live in it?” For as though someone had asked what it means to die to sin, he says: “Or do you not know that all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death?”

By this he proves what he had said above: “If we died to sin, how shall we live in it?” Those who knew that they had been baptized into Christ’s death, when they were baptized in Christ, would also know that they had died to sin, because to be baptized into Christ’s death is nothing other than to die to sin.

Explaining this more carefully, he adds and says: “Therefore we were buried with him through Baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be so in the likeness of his resurrection [Note: [Col. 0828] Perhaps “but also,” as below in section 13], knowing this: that our old person was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, and that we might no longer serve sin. For whoever has died has been justified from sin.

“But if we died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him, knowing that Christ, having risen from the dead, no longer dies; death shall no longer rule over him. For the one who died has died to sin once for all; but the one who lives lives to God. So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus” (Romans 5:8–6:11).

If, then, infants do not die to sin, they are certainly not baptized into Christ’s death. If they are not baptized into Christ’s death, they are not baptized in Christ. For “all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death.”

But they are baptized in Christ; therefore they die to sin. And what sin, I ask you, except the original sin they inherited?

Let human arguments fall silent [Note: [Col. 0828] The Floriacensis manuscript reads “the argument of human beings.”]. “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” (Psalm 93:11). “He has hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to infants” (Matthew 11:25).

If the Christian faith displeases you, confess it more openly; for you cannot find another Christian faith. One human being leads to death; one leads to life. The former is merely human; the latter is God and human [Note: [Col. 0828] Four manuscripts read “he is both God and human.”].

Through the former, the world became hostile to God; through the latter, the world is reconciled to God, chosen from the world. “For just as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ. And just as we have borne the image of the earthly, let us also bear the image of the one who is from heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:22, 49) [Note: [Col. 0828] The printed editions read “so let us also bear.” “So” is absent from the manuscripts.].

Whoever attempts to overturn these foundations of the Christian faith is himself overturned by them while they stand.

# CHAPTER FIVE [Note: [Col. 0828] In the Am. and Er. editions, 2.]

11. What I said in my book, which you oppose, is entirely true: “For what has been remitted in the parent, so that it may be transmitted in the offspring, happens in marvelous ways, but it does happen; and because the manner itself cannot easily be investigated or explained in speech, it is not believed by unbelievers” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence* 1.21).

You deceitfully lie in wait for these words of mine, as though I had said, “It cannot be understood by any reasoning or explained in any speech,” suppressing what I said: “not easily,” whether “by reasoning” or “in speech.”

“None” is one thing, which you say; “not easily” is another, which I said. What do you appear to be here except a calumniator?

But even if it cannot be investigated by any reasoning or explained in any speech, it remains true that what has been proclaimed and believed from ancient times throughout the whole Church by the true Catholic faith is this: the Church would neither exorcize nor insufflate the children of the faithful if it did not rescue them from the power of darkness and from the prince of death.

I stated this in the book to which you offer what resembles a reply (*On Marriage and Concupiscence* 1.22). But you were afraid to mention it, as though you yourself would have to be insufflated out of the whole world if you wished to contradict that insufflation by which the prince of the world is cast out even from infants.

You vainly twist yourself through empty arguments—not against me, but against our common spiritual mother. She did not give you birth in any other way than she now gives birth, though you no longer want her to give birth. Against her womb you think yourself armed with sufficiently sharp weapons, gathering arguments from God’s justice against God’s justice and from God’s grace against God’s grace.

God’s justice is true only if the heavy yoke laid upon the children of Adam from the day they leave their mother’s womb (Ecclesiasticus 40:1) is not unjust. But how is a heavy yoke not unjust if there is no evil in infants on account of which they are justly oppressed by a heavy yoke?

God’s grace is true only if it does in reality what it says in words. But how does it do this if it insufflates one in whom it knows there is nothing to expel, and washes one in whom it knows there is nothing to cleanse?

12. Would you or any of your followers [Note: [Col. 0829] Five Vatican manuscripts and two Gallican manuscripts read “your like-minded companions.”] seem to have anything to say if, with the holiness of your mind, you could consider how great is the evil of the concupiscence of the flesh—so great that what is born from it must be reborn, and, if it is not reborn, must necessarily be condemned [Note: [Col. 0829] The five Vatican and two Gallican manuscripts omit this sentence, which is enclosed in parentheses.]—and what grace accomplishes when it absolves its guilt, the guilt by which it originally made a human being guilty, when there is a complete remission of sins in him [Note: [Col. 0829] The Floriacensis manuscript, corrected by a second hand, reads “when through it there is remission of sins in him.”]?

The concupiscence itself nevertheless remains, against which the regenerated spirit struggles—either making good use of this evil in the lesser contest, or making no use of it at all in the greater contest.

The sense of this evil is present while it resists and is restrained. But the guilt which is remitted by regeneration alone was not perceived when it was present; so its removal is believed by faith, not perceived by the flesh or by the mind.

That is why you parade yourself amid the obscurity of this matter and fight against a truth that cannot be displayed to the senses of human beings, especially those who are carnal. The more sharply you think you fight, the more faithlessly you fight.

13. But—

“Turn yourselves wholly in every direction,
and summon whatever you possess in courage or skill” [Note: Virgil, *Aeneid* 12.889–890.]:

“All of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death.”

Therefore it is true that we have died to sin in Christ’s death, which was without sin—and consequently both adults and infants. For it is not that they are baptized and infants are not, or that infants are baptized and they are not; rather, “all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death.”

“Therefore we were buried with him through Baptism into death.” This does not exclude infants, since “all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death.”

“So that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been planted together in the likeness of his death, we shall also be so in the likeness of his resurrection.”

Here too are the infants who have been planted together in the likeness of his death. For this applies to all who have been baptized in Christ Jesus.

“Knowing this: that our old person was crucified with him.” Whose old person is this, except that of all who have been baptized in Christ? Let us therefore recognize infants here also, since we do not deny that they too have been baptized in Christ.

And why was our old person crucified with him? “So that,” he says, “the body of sin might be destroyed, so that we might no longer serve sin.” For the sake of this body of sin, “God sent his Son in the likeness of the flesh of sin” (Romans 8:3).

With what impudence, then, do we deny that infants too have a body of sin, when what he says applies to all who have been baptized in Christ?

“For whoever has died has been justified from sin. But if we died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with Christ, knowing that Christ, having risen from the dead, no longer dies; death shall no longer rule over him. For the one who died has died to sin once for all; but the one who lives lives to God. So you also,” he says, “must consider yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus.”

To whom does he say this? Are you awake and paying attention? Surely to those to whom he was saying, “But if we died with Christ.” And who are these except those to whom he had said, “Our old person was crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed”? Except those to whom he had said, “We have been planted together in the likeness of his death”? Except those to whom he had said, “Therefore we were buried with him through Baptism into death”?

And to whom, or concerning whom, had he said this? Read the preceding words, to which all these statements are connected, and you will find: “Or do you not know that all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death?”

When he said this [Note: [Col. 0830] The Gallican manuscripts read “so that this might happen.”], what did he intend to prove? Read a little further above and you will find: “If we died to sin, how shall we live in it?”

Therefore either recognize that infants in Baptism have died to sin and confess that they had original sin to which they could die, or openly say that they were not baptized into Christ’s death when they were baptized in Christ, and accuse the Apostle of falsehood when he says: “All of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death.”

14. I do not abandon these heavenly weapons that conquer the Coelestians; to them I entrust my faith and my speech. The arguments you bring forward are human; these defenses are divine.

“Who understands his transgressions?” (Psalm 18:13). Does it follow that transgressions do not exist because they are not understood? In the same way, who understands the original transgression which is remitted in the regenerated parent, yet passes into the offspring and remains unless the offspring too is regenerated? Does it follow that it is not a transgression?

“One died for all; therefore all died.” With what heart, with what mouth, with what face do you deny that infants are dead, when you do not deny that Christ died for them? If Christ did not die for them, why are they baptized? For “all of us who have been baptized in Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death.”

But if he also died for them—the one who died for all—then they too died with all. And because they died in sin, they also die to sin so that they may live to God when they are reborn from God.

If I cannot explain how a living person generates one who is dead—for a parent who is dead to sin and alive to God nevertheless generates one who is dead in sin, unless the parent too dies to sin through regeneration and lives to God—does this make it false because it cannot be explained in words, or can be explained only with the greatest difficulty?

Deny, if you dare, that one was born dead for whom you do not deny that Christ died. “One died for all; therefore all died” (2 Corinthians 5:14). These are the Apostle’s words, but they are our weapons. If you do not wish to resist them, you understand what must be believed without hesitation, even if you do not understand it.

For the human being who has been born spiritually but generates carnally possesses both kinds of seed: immortal seed, from which he rejoices that he is alive, and mortal seed, from which he generates one who is dead. The death of Christ would in no way be necessary to give life to this one unless he had been born dead.

“One died for all; therefore all died.” Nor do you raise from this death those whom you loudly proclaim not to be dead. Rather, you prevent them from living when, through the machinery of impious arguments, you attack in their parents the faith by which alone they can come alive again.

# CHAPTER VI [Note: [Col. 0831] In Amerbach and Erasmus, chapter 3.]

## 15

But now let us come to your lengthy and laborious argument, by which you have attempted to refute what I thought should be introduced merely because of some slight similarity, in a matter difficult to discern, namely, the olive tree—specifically, that its seed degenerates into the wild olive (On Marriage and Concupiscence, book 1, §21). First you assert “that examples contribute nothing to a matter which cannot be defended on its own.” Why, then, when the Apostle had proposed the question how the dead rise and with what kind of body they come, did he immediately undertake to establish an unknown and untested matter by an example, adding: “Fool! What you sow is not made alive unless it dies” (1 Cor. 15:36), and so forth?

[Note: [Col. 0831] Here the printed editions add “first”; it is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek.]

That example is not altogether irrelevant to the matter under discussion. Wheat is cleansed of its chaff, just as a human being is cleansed of sin; and yet another grows from it together with chaff.

## 16

But what was it that you wanted to say about the crocodile: “that among all animals it alone has, according to Albinus, movable upper jaws; and that fire, although destructive to everything, is a source of amusement to the salamander”? Did you not rather bring these examples against yourselves, since something is found by which the possibility of what was generally denied may be demonstrated?

Since, then, you have generally denied that those who beget can transmit to their offspring what they themselves do not have, if something is found capable of doing this, you are defeated in the same way as the man who had said that animals could move only their lower jaws is unambiguously defeated once the crocodile is found;

[Note: [Col. 0831] Several manuscripts, here and below, read “had said” in the subjunctive.] and the man who had said that no animal could live in fire is unambiguously refuted when the claim made about the salamander is demonstrated.

When, therefore, you define that “things natural cannot, through an accident, be transformed into something else,” if even one person should be found who, having been disfigured by some accident, begets a son with that same defect, so that what was accidental in the parent has become natural in the offspring, surely this definition of yours will be frustrated.

Likewise, when you define that “a parent cannot transmit to his offspring what he himself does not have,” will this definition not also be destroyed when people are shown to have been born with all their limbs intact from parents who had lost some limbs?

We used to hear from our elders—men who said that they knew and had seen this—that Fundanius, an orator of Carthage, although he himself was one-eyed through an accidental defect, fathered a one-eyed son.

[Note: [Col. 0832] The printed editions read “Fundanum”; the Gallican and Vatican manuscripts disagree.]

This example overturns that statement of yours in which you say that “things natural cannot, through an accident, be transformed into something else.” For what was accidental in the father became natural in the son.

As for the other claim, in which you say that “parents cannot transmit to their children what they themselves do not have,” it is overturned by another son of Fundanius, as happens most commonly: although his father was one-eyed, he was born with two eyes. It is also overturned by the countless sighted people born of blind parents. By transmitting to those whom they beget what they themselves do not have, such parents demonstrate that you, rather than your children, are like yourselves—for you, rather than their children, have shown yourselves like them: so blind have you been in your definitions.

# CHAPTER VII

## 17

Certainly, while speaking at length about matters irrelevant to the subject, you said something which reminded me of a point relevant to it, when you stated: “Curiosity is accustomed to admire less whatever it has comprehended; and divine providence has arranged that many things should be produced from the earth, distinguished by innumerable properties.”

And in truth, this is the usefulness of God’s hidden works: lest what is readily available become worthless, and lest what has been comprehended cease to be wonderful. Hence Scripture also says: “As the bones are in the womb of a pregnant woman, so you do not know all the works of God which he makes” (Eccl. 11:5).

Therefore you rightly said that, against curiosity—which is less accustomed to wonder at what it has been able to comprehend—the works of God are incomprehensible. Why, then, do you try by human speculation to overthrow what you are less capable of comprehending in the divine plan?

I certainly did not say—as you falsely accuse me—“that it cannot be comprehended in any way”; I said that “it cannot be comprehended easily.”

[Note: [Col. 0832] The printed editions read “what”; several manuscripts read “what if,” which is preferable.]

Nevertheless, what if, in opposition to the vice of human curiosity, by which things comprehended ordinarily become worthless, God also wished to conceal this matter, as he has concealed many others, so that human conjecture could neither investigate nor comprehend it?

Must you therefore arm yourselves against your mother the Church with your little arguments, like parricidal daggers, so that you may search out the hidden power of her sacrament—by which she conceives infants to be cleansed, even though they are born of parents who have been cleansed—not by handling it, but by tearing it apart, like bones in the womb of a pregnant woman?

If I did not wish to weary the reader with the length of my speech, I could already overwhelm you with a thousand kinds of things whose incomprehensible rationale creeps, as it were, through dark wildernesses contrary to the customary ways of nature. Among these I could point out many seeds that degenerate—not indeed into a wholly dissimilar kind, since the wild olive is not so different from the olive as the vine is—but into a certain, if one may so call it, similar dissimilarity, just as the labrusca is unlike the vine, although it is produced from the seed of the vine.

And why should we not believe that the Creator wished this to occur so that we might also believe that human seed can draw a defect from those who beget, a defect which is not present in those from whom it is begotten? Thus even baptized people, together with their infants, might hasten to his grace, by which human beings are rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into his kingdom—just as your holy father hastened with you, not knowing how ungrateful you would prove to that same grace.

[Note: [Col. 0833] Memorius was Julian’s father.]

## 18

But you, a most acute investigator of nature, discover its limits and establish rules, saying: “By the course of nature it cannot happen that parents are proved to transmit what they are believed to have lacked. If they transmit it,” you say, “then they did not lose it.”

These are Pelagian definitions, which, after reading our work addressed to the memory of Marcellinus, as you mention it (On the Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, book 3, chapters 3, 8, and 9), you ought already to have rejected.

For Pelagius himself first said of faithful parents that “they could not transmit to their descendants what they themselves did not at all possess.” But how false this is is taught by the clearest examples, some of which I gave above; and the following is another that I shall now mention.

What does a circumcised man retain of the foreskin, from whom nevertheless a son is born uncircumcised, and what is no longer in the man is drawn into human seed?

Nor should we believe that the ancient fathers were divinely commanded to circumcise infants on the eighth day for any other reason than to signify the regeneration that takes place in Christ.

[Note: [Col. 0833] Three Vatican manuscripts read “unless to signify”; the Fleury manuscript, “than to signify.” But the addition of either “unless” or “than” distorts the sense of the preceding words, “Nor should we believe for any other reason,” which mean that circumcision was commanded for an infant born of a circumcised man because he derives a foreskin from circumcised seed.] After the seventh day of the week—the day on which he lay in the tomb—he was handed over because of our offenses; on the following day, that is, the eighth day in the sequence of the weeks, he rose because of our justification (Rom. 4:25).

Who, even moderately instructed in the sacred writings, is unaware that the sacrament of circumcision preceded Baptism in figure, when the Apostle says most explicitly of Christ:

“He is the head of every principality and power, in whom you were also circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping away of the body of the flesh, in the circumcision of Christ; having been buried with him in Baptism, in which you also rose through faith in the working of God, who raised him from the dead. And when you were dead in trespasses and in the uncircumcision of your flesh, he made you alive together with him, forgiving us all trespasses” (Col. 2:10–13).

Thus the circumcision made by hand, which was given to Abraham, was a likeness set beforehand of this circumcision not made by hand, which is now performed in Christ.

## 19

[For it cannot be said: “The foreskin is a body, but what is drawn along in origin is a defect; and although the foreskin has been cut away, its power could in no way have been removed from the seed. But this defect, which is not a body but an accident, could not remain in the seed once forgiveness had removed it.”

No one, however clever, can say this, since divine authority refutes it. By that authority this very part of the body was commanded to be cut off for the purpose of cleansing this defect. If the defect were not in the seed, it would in no way reach the infants from whom it must be removed by that bodily circumcision; and if it had not reached them at all, they would in no way need to have it removed by bodily circumcision.

But since an infant has absolutely no personal sin of his own, it remains that nothing else is removed from him except original sin by that remedy without which his soul perishes from his people. Under a just God this would not happen unless there were guilt by which it could happen. Since that guilt is not personal, it remains that it is solely the guilt of a corrupted origin.]

[Note: [Col. 0834] Three Vatican manuscripts and two Gallic manuscripts, among them the very ancient manuscript of Fleury, omit this entire §19, enclosing it in brackets.]

## 20

Behold: the circumcised man transmits to the one born from him what he lacked in himself.

[Note: [Col. 0834] Morel considers that “which he himself lacked” should be read. See *Elementa Critica*, p. 157. M.] What, then, becomes of your statement that “by the course of nature it cannot happen that people are proved to transmit what they are believed to have lacked”?

The foreskin is good; it is not evil, because God made it, just as you argued at great length concerning the wild olive.

You are answered: The wild olive is good in the order of nature, but in the symbolism of the sacred writings it signifies evil—just as wolves, foxes, and the sow washed in the mire, and the dog returning to its vomit. In the order of nature all things are good, just as sheep are good; for God made all things very good (Gen. 1:31). But in the holy books wolves signify evil people, whereas sheep signify good people.

We do not use these comparisons according to what those things are in themselves, but according to what they signify, when we discuss the distinction between good and evil.

So too, since the foreskin is a part of the human body, and the whole body is a good substance, it is naturally good. But it signifies evil figuratively, when the infant is commanded to be circumcised on the eighth day because of Christ, in whom, as the Apostle says, “we were circumcised with a circumcision not made by hand”—which the circumcision made by hand undoubtedly prefigured.

The foreskin, therefore, is not sin, but it signifies sin, especially original sin, because it is through that member that the origin of those who are born is represented; through it we are said to be by nature children of wrath. For that member itself is properly called “nature.”

Accordingly, circumcision of the flesh not only unequivocally overturns that general statement of yours in which you say, “By the course of nature it cannot happen that a parent transmits to his offspring what he himself lacked”; it also does so because the foreskin signifies sin and is found in the one being born, although it was no longer present in the parent. It therefore demonstrates that original sin, which has already been forgiven in baptized parents, remains in infants unless they too are baptized—that is, unless they are cleansed by spiritual circumcision.

And it proves you wrong in denying what is most true. For even in the case of the infant of whom it was said, “His soul shall perish from his people if he is not circumcised on the eighth day” (Gen. 17:14, 12), you cannot find, under a just judge, any reason why he should perish if you deny original sin.

## 21

Let us leave the forests of wild olives and the mountains of African or Italian olive trees; let us not question farmers who, if they happened to answer you one way and me another, could not quickly prove either party wrong, if a tree were planted

[Note: [Col. 0835] The manuscripts read “we can.”]

for the purpose of testing this matter—a tree were planted for the purpose of testing this matter—a tree destined to make shade for its descendants (Virgil, Georgics 2.58).

We have an olive tree—not African, not Italian, but Hebrew—and we rejoice that we, who were wild olives, have been grafted into it.

Circumcision was given to that olive tree, and it settles this question for us without dispute. The offspring draws forth the foreskin which the parent no longer has: he lacked it, yet transmitted it; he had lost it, yet passed it on. And this foreskin signifies sin.

Therefore sin itself can perish in parents and yet pass over to their children.

Let the infant himself also testify, and let him say silently: “My soul will perish from my people if I am not circumcised on the eighth day.” You who both deny original evil and acknowledge a just God, tell me what I have sinned.

[Note: [Col. 0835] The Louvain edition reads, “tell what he has sinned to this crying infant. And since your loquacity”; Erasmus lacks “and,” but with Louvain reads “he has sinned.” The text is corrected from the manuscripts.]

Since your loquacity offers no rational answer to this infant who cries out silently, join your voices instead with ours and with the apostolic voices.

Whether there are other contagions of sins derived from parents, or whether there are any at all, we are free to investigate—whether it is easy, difficult, or impossible to discover. But let us not think it permissible to understand in any other way that through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so passed into all human beings, “in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12), except by believing that all died in the sin of the first man, for whom Christ died, and that all who are baptized in Christ die to sin.

# CHAPTER VIII (a)

## 22

But in other words of mine, which you insert into your argument as though they required refutation, you say that I “have attempted to stir up the common people against you.” I said (The Merits and Forgiveness of Sins, book 1, §22) that “the Christian faith does not doubt”—a faith which, as I know, recent heretics have begun to attack—that those who are washed in the bath of regeneration are redeemed from the power of the devil, whereas those who have not yet been redeemed by such regeneration, including the infant children of the redeemed, remain captive under the power of that same devil unless they too are redeemed by the same grace.

To establish this by apostolic testimony, I said that the benefit of God of which the Apostle speaks pertains “to people of every age”: “He rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son” (Col. 1:13).

If the common people are stirred against you by this statement, should you not rather recognize from this that the Catholic faith has become so widespread and so firmly established among all people that it cannot even escape popular awareness?

For it was necessary that all Christians should know whatever was done with their infants insofar as it concerns the Christian mysteries.

[Note: [Col. 0835–0836] Amerbach and most manuscripts read “whatever was done with their infants,” omitting “in”; three manuscripts read “what they did with their infants,” and one, “what they did when they were with their infants.”]

Why, then, do you say that, “forgetting the singular contest, I have retreated to the common people”? Who promised you my singular contest? Where, when, how, in whose presence, and before what judges?

“When the war was offered,” as you put it, “it was decided to settle it by treaty” (Virgil, Aeneid 12.109), “so that our contest might settle the struggle of all.”

Far be it from me to claim among Catholics what you are not ashamed to claim for yourself among the Pelagians. I am one among many who refute your profane innovations as best we can, according as God has distributed to each of us the measure of faith (Rom. 12:3).

Before I was born into this world, and before I was reborn to God, many Catholic lights anticipated your future darkness by exposing it. I discussed them in my preceding two books with as much clarity as I could.

You have somewhere to withdraw if you still take pleasure in raging against the Catholic faith.

## 23

And do not mock the members of Christ by calling them “craftsmen of the workshops.” Remember that “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1:27).

But what do you mean by saying, “Once you begin to show them these things, they will become more bitter against me”?

Do not lie to them, and they will not become bitter. For I do not, as you falsely accuse me, “assert that those whom I know to have been redeemed by the blood of Christ are the devil’s possession.”

[Note: [Col. 0836] The Fleury manuscript reads: “the devil’s possession, whom Christ redeemed with his blood.”] Nor do I “assign marriages to the devil,” insofar as they are marriages; nor do I “make him the deviser of sexual generation”; nor do I assert that he is “the arouser of men except for illicit acts,” “the fecundator of women,” or “the creator of infants.”

These claims are foreign to me. If you tell them that I have said such things, you will be lying.

[Note: [Col. 0836] The same manuscript reads, “If you tell them that I said these things.”]

And if anyone, believing you, becomes more bitter against me, he may have been deceived, but he has not been instructed.

[Note: [Col. 0836] Amerbach, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read “but not a teacher”; Louvain, “but not more learned.” The better manuscripts read “but not instructed.”]

But those who know both of us, and know the Catholic faith, do not wish to learn anything from you; rather, they are on guard lest you take away what they know.

For many among them learned these things not only before me, but even earlier—things which your new error attacks. Since I did not make them adherents of the truth which you deny, but found them already so, how am I their author of the error which you suppose?

# CHAPTER IX

## 24

“Explain,” you say, “how sin can justly be attributed to a person who neither wished to sin nor was able to do so.”

The perpetration of one’s own sins is one thing; the contagion of the sins of others is another, insofar as each concerns the action of that person’s own life.

For if you did not wish to twist a correct statement into your distorted meaning, you would hear the Apostle briefly explaining this, when he said that there was one in whom all sinned. In that one all died, so that another one might die for all: “One died for all; therefore all died” (2 Cor. 5:14)—all for whom Christ died.

Deny, then, that Christ also died for infants, so that you may remove them from the number of the dead—that is, from the contagion of sins.

“How can it happen,” you ask, “that sin is mingled with the condition of seeds?”

If it could not happen, there would be no basis for calling infants who have not yet emerged from the body dead. For if Christ also died for them, then they too are dead; since if one died for all, then all are dead.

Do you hear, Julian? These are the Apostle’s words, not mine. Why do you ask me “by what manner it happened,” when you see that it happened in some manner—whatever that manner may be—if you believe the Apostle, who could in no way have lied about Christ and those for whom Christ died?

## 25

A perverse person such as you are, though with a different error, can indeed say that God is “always industrious for the gain of his enemy,” as you say we think of infants.

For God does not cease to create, nourish, clothe, and provide life and health to those whom he knows will not remain under the devil for a time, but will burn with him forever, even though they sin with the most obstinate wickedness.

But God does this because he knows how to make good use of both good and evil things. By no art of wickedness can the devil withdraw from the uses of God’s majesty either those whom he oppresses or deceives, or even himself.

Accordingly, those who are rescued from the devil’s power do not belong to the devil; but those who belong to him are under God’s power, just as the devil himself is.

## 26

How foolish, then, is what you think you have said cleverly, as though “the devil and God had made this agreement between themselves: whatever is washed belongs to God, whatever is born the devil claims for himself; yet with this condition,” as you say, “that God, by a power subject to obligation, should make fruitful the intercourse which the devil instituted”?

The devil certainly did not institute intercourse, since it would exist even if no one had sinned. It would, however, exist in such a way that your *suscepta* [reading uncertain] there would either be absent or would not be troubled.

Nor is it by an obligated power, but freely and with the greatest power, that God makes the wombs of women fruitful—even when they are vessels destined to give birth to devilish offspring.

For just as he grants to evil human beings, so also to seeds corrupted in their origin—seeds in which the substance was created good by him—he grants increase, form, life, and health by gratuitous goodness, without compulsion, by unconquerable power, and with irreprehensible truth.

Since both things are under God’s power—both what is washed and what is born—and since not even the devil himself is found to be outside his power, how did you set these two things against each other?

Did you wish birth to be better than washing? Or did you wish washing to be better because birth is also involved in it? For one who has not been born cannot be washed. Or do you weigh both on an equal scale?

If you think birth is better, you do an injury to spiritual rebirth, to which you sacrilegiously prefer carnal generation.

You are rightly thought not to have wished to say “what is reborn,” but “what is washed,” so that, since you wanted our understanding to portray the devil and God as having divided things between themselves, you might make God’s portion inferior by the baseness of your wording.

You could have said, “what is reborn”; you could have said, “what is regenerated”; finally, you could have said, “what is baptized.” For Latin usage has taken this word from the Greek in such a way that it is not ordinarily understood elsewhere than in the sacrament of regeneration.

You wished to say none of these things. Instead, you chose a word by which what you were describing would become contemptible. No reader could prefer someone born to someone reborn, regenerated, or baptized; but you easily thought that someone born could be preferred to someone washed.

If, however, just as heaven is distant from earth, it is so much better to be washed so as to bear the image of the heavenly man than to be born so as to bear the image of the earthly man (1 Cor. 15:49), then your malicious division has already vanished.

For it is not surprising if God claims for himself the image of the heavenly man, which is received through sacred washing, while he allows the image of the earthly man, stained by earthly defilement, to remain under the devil until it is reborn in Christ to receive the image of the heavenly man.

## 27

Moreover, if you weigh washing and birth in an equal judgment, so that infants who have not yet been reborn are not believed to be under the devil lest God and the devil appear to have divided equal portions between themselves—God claiming those who are washed, and the devil claiming those who are born—then, since according to this reasoning washing is worth as much as birth, you persuade people that washing is superfluous, since birth, which is worth just as much, is sufficient.

And yet we give thanks that you do not think this. For you do not admit those who have been born into the kingdom of God unless they are washed; and thus you judge washing to be much better than birth.

Now, then, give yourselves an account, lest you consider it unworthy that those who are not admitted into the kingdom of God should be under him who fell from the kingdom of God, and that those who do not have life should be under him who lost life.

But that infants do not have life unless they have Christ—whom they plainly cannot have unless they have put him on, in the manner in which it is written, “All of you who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3:27)—is attested by the Evangelist John, who says in his Epistle: “The one who has the Son has life; the one who does not have the Son does not have life” (1 John 5:12).

Those who do not have life are therefore rightly understood to be dead—those for whom Christ died so that they might have life. “One died for all; therefore all died.”

He died, as we read in the Letter to the Hebrews, “so that through death he might destroy the one who had the power of death, that is, the devil” (Heb. 2:14).

What, then, is surprising if infants, as long as they are dead, before they begin to have him who died for the dead, are under him who has the power of death?

# CHAPTER X

## 28

You enumerate what the Christian faith truly does not doubt.

[Note: [Col. 0838] Most manuscripts read “true.”] Among these you mention matters which almost all of us also proclaim and which we consider in no way doubtful. To such an extent is this true that even what you say—“Without an act of free will there can be no sin in a human being”—we acknowledge to be true.

For original sin would not itself be sin, transmitted without an act of free will, if the first human being had not sinned by an act of free will, through whom sin entered the world and passed into all people (Rom. 5:12).

But when you say that “one person is not held liable for the sins of others,” it matters how this can rightly be understood.

I am not now discussing the fact that David sinned and that many thousands of people fell because of his sin (2 Sam. 24), nor the fact that, because one person appropriated what had been devoted to destruction contrary to the prohibition, vengeance was inflicted upon people who had not done this and did not know that it had been done (Josh. 7). That is another discussion and need not concern us now, namely, the question of this class of sins or punishments.

The sins of parents are called “others’ sins” in one sense, and in another sense they are found to be our own. They are “others’” by the particular action involved, but they are ours by the contagion of propagation.

If this were false, the heavy yoke upon the children of Adam, from the day they leave their mother’s womb (Sir. 40:1), would in no way be just.

## 29

But when you recall that the Apostle said, “We must all appear before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may receive what belongs to his own body according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10), how do you understand this with respect to infants?

Will they too appear before the tribunal of Christ, or will they not?

If they will not appear, how does this statement help you, since it does not concern those whose case is now under discussion?

But if they will appear, how does each of them receive what he has done, when he has done nothing—unless what is done through the hearts and mouths of those who act on their behalf, whether they believe or do not believe, pertains to them?

For when he said “what belongs to his own body,” he referred to what pertains to each individual who is already living in himself.

How, then, does an infant receive what is good, so as to enter the kingdom of God, if each person receives what he has done—unless what the infant has done through another person, namely believed, pertains to him?

Just as what he has believed pertains to him, so that he receives what is good, that is, obtains the kingdom of God, so also what he has not believed pertains to him, so that he receives the judgment of condemnation. For this too is the sentence of the Gospel: “The one who does not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16).

And when the Apostle says, “We must all appear, so that each may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil,” he wished nothing intermediate to be understood.

[Note: [Col. 0839] The printed editions add “in saying”; it is absent from the manuscripts.]

See, then, how perversely you refuse to allow an infant to receive evil from another’s sin, while you wish him to receive good from another’s righteous act—not just any good, but the kingdom of God.

The action is another’s when he believes through another person, just as the action was another’s when he sinned in another person.

We do not doubt that every sin is cleansed by Baptism; but each person is cleansed by being reborn. Therefore what only regeneration removes, generation does not cease to transmit.

## 30

Certainly, by saying that “desire is not wholly rebellious to the mind,” you undoubtedly confess that it is rebellious. And yet you do not acknowledge the punishment by which you wage war against yourself?

“Let God be called the creator of infants of such a kind as are worthy of the hands of God,” you say, and you add, “that is, innocent.”

Does he not seem to surpass you in piety and praise of God who says that even beautiful and healthy works are fitting for the hands of God?

And yet many people are born deformed, many diseased, many hideous and monstrous. Nevertheless, the whole of that substance, all its parts, and everything that exists and lives substantially within it could have been created only by the good and true God.

[Note: [Col. 0840] The printed editions read “except one good and true God.” The word “one” is absent from the manuscripts.]

## 31

You order me to assert “how the devil dares to claim for himself infants created in Christ, that is, in his power.”

You assert, if you can, how he openly, and not obscurely, claims for himself the infants whom unclean spirits torment.

[Note: [Col. 0840] The manuscripts read the plural “claim,” correctly if what follows were read, “If you say that they have been handed over to them.”]

If you say that they have been handed over to him, we both see the punishment; you explain the merit. We both behold the penalty; you, who say that no evil merits are transmitted from parents, must, while we both acknowledge God to be just, demonstrate, if you can, the guilt in infants that deserves this punishment.

Or do you not recognize that this too belongs to the heavy yoke which lies upon the children of Adam, from the day they leave their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all?

Under this yoke the human race is crushed by various disasters, so that it becomes apparent that the fact that human beings become children of mercy, having first been made children of wrath, is being prepared for the age to come. In this present age, however, from the day of birth until the day of death, even they are crushed under the same heavy yoke.

Indeed, even baptized infants sometimes suffer among the other evils of this life attacks by demons, although they have been rescued from the power of darkness so that they may not be dragged by them into everlasting punishment.

## 32

Again you say what you have already said, and to which I replied (above, book 3, §§8–9), but which I must not pass over now either:

“When God, without infants having merited anything of their own, whether good or evil, grants them the glory of regeneration, by this very act

[Note: [Col. 0840] Five Vatican manuscripts read “the grace of regeneration.”] he teaches that they belong to his care, his right, and his dominion, because his ineffable generosity of grace precedes their will.”

What, then, have those infants offended him whom he likewise creates innocent, clean, and made by him in his image, yet excludes countless numbers from this gift, without their will being preceded by this ineffable generosity of grace, separating so many of his images from his kingdom?

If this will not be evil for them, then such innocent images of God will not love the kingdom of God. But if they will love it, and will love it as much as innocent beings ought to love the kingdom of the one in whose image they were created, will they suffer no evil from this very separation?

Finally, wherever they are and whatever their condition under the judgment of God—who is neither oppressed by fate nor corrupted by partiality—they will not be in the blessedness of that kingdom in which those will be who likewise have deserved neither good nor evil.

But if they had deserved no evil, they would never be deprived, in a common cause, of participation in so great a good.

Therefore, in them—as we have often said—God, according to the Apostle, makes known the riches of his glory to vessels of mercy by means of vessels of wrath (Rom. 9:22–23), so that they may not boast as though on the basis of the merits of their own life, when they recognize that what they see being given to their fellow-partakers of death could most justly have been given to them as well.

[Note: [Col. 0840–0841] After “of their death,” in Amerbach, Erasmus, and some manuscripts, this marginal note passes into the text: “In a remarkable combination of testimonies, the Apostle asserts that infants, along with the rest, are rescued from the power of darkness and are by nature children of wrath, as the others are, because they die to sin when they are baptized into Christ’s death.”]

## 33

If, then, you wish to think rightly, understand also concerning infants what the Apostle says of God the Father: “He rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of his beloved Son” (Col. 1:13); and also the other statement: “For we too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3).

All who die to sin were rescued from the power of darkness and were children of wrath. But all who are baptized into Christ’s death die to sin so that they may live to God. And all who are baptized into Christ are baptized into his death.

Therefore, since infants too are baptized into Christ, they die to sin and are rescued from the power of darkness, where they had been by nature children of wrath.

But when you say, “Where the Apostle says ‘by nature children of wrath,’ it can be understood as ‘simply children of wrath,’” should this not have reminded you that the ancient Catholic faith is being defended against you? For scarcely any Latin manuscript is found—unless you now begin to emend them, or rather to change them into corrupt texts—in which “by nature” is not written.

[Note: [Col. 0841] See Jerome on this passage.]

The ancient translators would certainly have avoided this if this had not also been an antiquity of the faith, against which your novelty has begun to resist.

# CHAPTER XI

## 34

But you are an outstanding man; you do not wish to belong to the common herd. For again you reject the opinion of the common people, after having, by so many arguments with which you had stirred them against me, provoked them more seriously than they had been stirred against you.

But surely, considering what you have argued, you realized that you had not been able, and could not be able, to accomplish anything by such arguments among a people grounded in the truth and antiquity of the Catholic faith.

Accordingly, you once more turn the face of your arrogance toward despising them, and you go through and mock, one by one, the various elements of which they consist—elements which make the multitude of Christians so fiercely hostile to you, and not without reason.

Among these you attack “scholastic auditors,” and you say that they will shout against me, “O the times! O the morals!” (Cicero, First Oration against Catiline and speech 6 against Verres).

And yet you fear the judgment of the common people, among whom you were able to find such loud supporters that they terrify me with Ciceronian expressions: namely, because I “think that the generative part of the body is something other than that from which the whole derives.”

When I answer them, “I do not say this,” he lies. “I blame lust, not the limbs; I point out a defect, not nature.”

Yet this man, who slanders me among you, dares, in the Church of Christ, before the Teacher seated in heaven, to recite a eulogy of lust—a eulogy which, if he were studying with you, none of your teachers would assign him to recite, lest he offend the modesty of all of you.

Will they not turn against you other words of Tully that truly fit the situation, saying: “On this side modesty fights; on your side wantonness; here self-restraint, there lust” (Cicero, Second Oration against Catiline)?

35. You also accuse certain people, as though they were deserters from your doctrine, of having converted to the catholic faith—or returned to it. Yet you indicated that you feared them so much that you did not dare disclose their names, lest perhaps, when they heard from you their false accusations, they might immediately answer you with things that, if not true, would at least be more credible. Whoever these people are, if they are sensible, would not do this, but would spare you in accordance with the Apostle, “not returning reviling for reviling” (1 Peter 3:9). You, however, should at least not disdain to listen to the man who warns you, the very man whose writings you enjoyed invoking with the cry, “O the times, O the customs!” Listen, I say, at least to him: “In proportion as you are removed from disgraceful conduct”—if indeed you are removed from it—“so far should you withdraw from freedom of speech; and do not say about others what, if falsely alleged against you, you would blush to hear.” Let those who read know that you have said such things about these unknown people—things which we know absolutely nothing about in the case of certain persons whom we know to have withdrawn from the Pelagian heretics in their commitment to continence.

[Note: Am. Er. and several manuscripts read *sciunt* (“know”). The better manuscripts, with Lov., read *sciant* (“let them know”). Augustine does not wish those who do not read Julian to learn here through Julian himself of crimes that may falsely have been alleged.]

As for those who are yours, or yours in allegiance, of whatever sort they may be, it is no concern of mine; you deceive them so completely that you claim I define the matter thus: “Even in a diseased body, lust cannot be restrained.” Rather, because I decide that it can and ought to be restrained, I therefore understand it to be evil. Whoever denies that it is evil should consider how he can regard as good that which, whether he wishes it or not, he admits must be restrained. I therefore say that lust can be restrained not only by the old but also by the young; yet I am greatly astonished that the continent are said to be able to praise lust.

36. Who among us says, “This evil which little children inherit originally either can exist, or ever has existed, without the substance in which it is”? Since you pretend that we say this, you seek dialecticians as judges and ridicule the common people, as though I were bringing you before a judge by whom such matters cannot be judged. If you had not learned this, the machinery of the Pelagian doctrine would necessarily have remained without an architect. If you wish to live, do not love “the wisdom of speech,” by which the cross of Christ is emptied of its power (1 Corinthians 1:17).

How qualities, whether good or bad, pass from one substance into other substances—not by migrating, but by affecting them—we have already discussed in the preceding book (above, book 5, §51). If you despise the judgment of the common people, look to those judges whom, in my first two books, I presented to you as endowed with the most splendid authority in the Church of Christ.

## CHAPTER XII

37. What is the meaning of your accusing Zosimus, bishop of the Apostolic See and of blessed memory, of treachery, merely so that you may persist in your perversity? He did not depart from his predecessor Innocent, whose name you were afraid to mention; rather, you chose Zosimus, because at first he dealt more gently with Coelestius.

[Note: Er. and Lov. read “from his predecessor Innocent”; Am. and the manuscripts read “from his predecessor.”] For Zosimus had said that, if anything in your opinions displeased him, he was ready to be corrected, and had promised that he would consent to the letters of Innocent.

38. Remember, too, how mockingly you bring up the disagreement among the Roman people concerning the appointment of a bishop.

[Note: This refers to the schism that arose after Zosimus died toward the end of A.D. 418, when some supported Eulalius against Boniface, who had been canonically elected.]

I ask you whether those people acted of their own will. If you deny this, how do you defend free choice? But if you admit it, how do you call it “God’s vengeance,” and depart from your own doctrine by seeking to be regarded as one divinely avenged?

Or do you at last concede what, with the utmost obstinacy, you had denied: that by God’s hidden judgment something may be found in human wills which is both sin and the punishment of sin? For unless you had understood this within your own position, you would never have said that what human beings did was God’s vengeance. But when something of this sort happened there many years ago concerning the blessed Damasus and Ursicinus, the Roman Church had not yet condemned the Pelagians.

[Note: Am., Er., all the Gallican manuscripts, and all the Vatican manuscripts read *Ursino* (“Ursinus”).]

39. You say that “I myself have also changed my opinions, and that at the beginning of my conversion I held what you hold.” But you are either deceiving or deceived—whether by slandering what I now say, or by failing to understand, or rather by not reading, what I said then. For from the beginning of my conversion I have always held, and still hold, that through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and thus death passed to all human beings, in whom all sinned (Romans 5:12).

[Note: Nearly all manuscripts read *dicit* (“says”) instead of *dicit et docet* (“learns and teaches”).]

There exist books that I wrote while still a layman, soon after my conversion. Although I was not yet instructed in the sacred Scriptures as I later became, even then I held nothing different concerning this matter; and whenever the method of argument required it, I said what the whole Church has learned and taught from ancient times:

The human race had justly fallen into those great and evident miseries in which humanity became like vanity, so that its days pass away like a shadow (Psalm 143:4), and “every living human being is altogether vanity” (Psalm 38:6), because of original sin. From this condition no one delivers us except the one who said, “The truth will set you free” (John 8:32), and, “I am the truth” (John 14:6), and, “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

For nothing but truth delivers from vanity—yet according to grace, not according to debt; through mercy, not through merit. Just as it was a matter of judgment that we should be subjected to vanity, so it is a matter of mercy that we should be freed by the truth; and we must confess that even our good merits are nothing other than God’s gifts.

## CHAPTER XIII

[Note: In Am. and Er., this is numbered “5.”]

40. Let us now examine that slander of yours by which you accuse me of saying that “the baptized are cleansed only in part.” You say that this “appears more clearly in my own words,” and you set out in your argument the passages of mine in which you assert that this can be seen. I am grateful: these, then, are the passages:

“Carnal concupiscence,” I said, “is not to be charged to marriage, but endured. It is not a good that comes from the natural union of marriage, but an evil that has arisen from ancient sin. Because of it, therefore, children of the world, not children of God, are generated even from the just and lawful marriages of the children of God. For those who beget them, if they have already been regenerated, do not beget them from the fact that they are children of God, but from the fact that they are still children of the world. For the Lord’s pronouncement is: ‘The children of this world beget and are begotten’” (Luke 20:34).

“Since, therefore, we are still children of this world, our outward person is being corrupted, and from this condition children of this world are generated.”

[Note: Julian omitted here the words “and they do not become children of God unless they are regenerated.” See *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, §20.]

“Since we are children of God, our inward person is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16).

“Although the outward person itself has been sanctified through the washing [of baptism] and has received the hope of future incorruption, for which reason it is rightly called the temple of God” (1 Corinthians 3:16), “this was said not only because of present sanctification, but especially because of that hope of which it is said: ‘And we ourselves, having the first fruits of the Spirit, groan, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body’” (Romans 8:23).

[Note: Am., Er., and the manuscripts omit “adoption.”]

[Note: In *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, the reading is “but especially because of.”]

“If, therefore, according to the Apostle, the redemption of our body is awaited, then what is awaited is certainly still hoped for and is not yet possessed” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, §§19–20).

These words of mine contain nothing that a baptized person does not acknowledge in himself when, with the Apostle, he says, “We ourselves groan within ourselves.” Hence he also says elsewhere, “Indeed, we groan while we are in this dwelling, being burdened” (2 Corinthians 5:4). To this also belongs what we read in the Book of Wisdom: “For a corruptible body weighs down the soul, and this earthly dwelling burdens the mind with many thoughts” (Wisdom 9:15).

But you, as though you were already dwelling immortally in heaven among the angels, ridicule words of weakness and mortality. And, explaining them not according to my meaning but according to your deceit, you assert that I said “that grace does not make the new person perfect.”

I do not say this. Attend to what I do say. Grace makes the new person perfect, since it also leads him to the full immortality of the body and to complete happiness. Even now it renews the person perfectly insofar as liberation from every sin is concerned, though not insofar as liberation from every evil and from all the corruption of mortality is concerned—the corruption by which the body now weighs down the soul. Hence there is the groaning that the Apostle himself confesses when he says, “We ourselves groan within ourselves.”

Yet one reaches that perfection also, the perfection that is hoped for, through the same Baptism that is received here. Not all children of the world, however, are children of the devil, although all children of the devil are children of the world. There are children of God who are nevertheless still children of the world; and for this reason they are joined in marriage. But they do not beget children of God according to the flesh, because they themselves became children of God not from flesh, nor from blood, nor from the will of man, nor from the will of the flesh, but were born from God (John 1:13).

Sanctification, therefore, is even now conferred upon the body through Baptism; yet its corruption is not now removed, and this corruption itself weighs down the soul. Thus, although bodies are chaste when their members do not serve the desires of sin, and for this reason have begun to belong to the temple of God, there is nevertheless something that grace perfects throughout this entire structure. As long as the flesh desires against the spirit, it arouses evil movements that must be restrained, while the spirit desires against the flesh (Galatians 5:17), so that holiness may persevere.

## CHAPTER XIV

41. Who does not know what you impress upon us through your distinguished teacher: “The reason the flesh is said to desire is that the soul desires carnally”?

[Note: In the editions of Am., Er., and Lov., the following words appearing before this sentence should be deleted: “Therefore you say—or it is said—that the flesh desires because the soul desires carnally. For without the soul the flesh cannot even feel. To desire belongs to a living and sentient nature, without which feeling the members cannot move; that is, they cannot desire by themselves. And what feeling desires even without the members, as in eunuchs?” These words are absent from the better Gallican and Vatican manuscripts.]

There can be no concupiscence of the flesh without the soul. For desiring belongs to a living and sentient nature, so that there is indeed a concupiscence which even the chastity of eunuchs restrains. It is less laborious, certainly, because where it finds no material on which to act, lust rises against it less strongly; nevertheless, it exists and is chastely repressed, lest even an unsuccessful attempt at intercourse should fall into that disgrace for which we know that Calligonus, the eunuch of the younger Valentinian, was punished by an avenging sword after being convicted by the confession of a prostitute.

Nor would the Book of Ecclesiasticus have used this comparison and said, “Seeing with his eyes and groaning, like a eunuch embracing a virgin and sighing” (Ecclesiasticus 30:21), unless eunuchs too were moved by the feelings of carnal desire, although deprived of the bodily acts of the flesh.

The soul, therefore, with its movements according to the spirit, resists other movements that it has according to the flesh; and again, with its movements according to the flesh, it resists other movements that it has according to the spirit. Hence it is said that the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.

For this reason it was also said of the soul itself, “It is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). Indeed, it makes progress in holiness when it increasingly diminishes the carnal desires to which it does not consent.

The Apostle was speaking to people already baptized when he said, “Put to death, therefore, the members that are upon the earth.” There he names fornication, evil desire, and greed (Colossians 3:5). How, then, does a person already baptized put fornication to death, when he no longer commits it and, according to you, “has nothing to put to death”?

How, I ask, does he obey the Apostle who says, “Put fornication to death,” unless he combats its desires, to which he does not consent—desires which, in those who are making good progress and who do not commit fornication at all, neither by consent nor by action, are nevertheless not absent, but diminish daily?

This is what takes place in the temple of God when, with God’s help, what God has commanded is done. The works of the spirit are raised up; the works of the flesh are put to death. “If you live according to the flesh,” he says, “you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.” And so that they might know that they do this only by God’s grace, he immediately adds: “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are children of God” (Romans 8:13–14). Accordingly, all who are led by God’s Spirit put the deeds of the flesh to death by the Spirit.

42. Those who have already been baptized therefore have something to do within themselves—that is, in the temple of God—which is being built in the present age, so that it may be dedicated at the end. It is built after captivity, as the title of the psalm that concerns this matter indicates: namely, after the enemy who had taken captive has been driven out.

[Note: In certain manuscripts and older editions the following gloss was inserted here: “Concerning the Psalm which first proclaims the dedication of the house and afterward its building. But dedication pertains to the head of the house, that is, Christ; building to the whole body of the house, that is, the Church. Therefore dedication comes before building.” The Louvain editors deleted not only this but also the following clause, “as the title of the psalm that concerns this matter indicates,” although it belongs to the context and appears in all manuscripts.]

In the order of the Psalms, something that may seem strange occurs: the psalm of the dedication of the house comes first, and the psalm of its building comes afterward. The psalm of dedication comes first because it sings of that house of which its architect said, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). The later psalm, which speaks of the house being built after captivity, prophesied the Church. It begins:

“Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Psalm 95:1–2).

Let no one, therefore, be so foolish as to think that every baptized person is already perfect simply because it is said, “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (1 Corinthians 3:17), and, “Do you not know that your bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit within you, whom you have from God?” (1 Corinthians 6:19), and elsewhere, “For we are the temple of the living God” (2 Corinthians 6:16), along with other passages of this kind.

The baptized person is already called this; and while the temple is being built, our members that are upon the earth are put to death.

[Note: Lov. adds here, “when.”]

Although we are already dead to sin and live for God, there is nevertheless something in us that must be put to death, so that sin may not reign in our mortal body, making us obey its desires (Romans 6:11–12). Full and perfect remission of sins frees us from these desires so that we are no longer subject to them; yet they remain in us, with which those who are chaste wage their battles.

Among these desires is also the desire from which a married person makes good use while living chastely. When rightly ordered, good arises from evil, though not without evil; and therefore the person is reborn in order to be freed from evil. What God creates and human beings beget is certainly good insofar as it is human; yet it is not without evil because only regeneration frees from the evil that generation draws from the first and greatest sin.

43. You wish it to seem incredible that “in the womb of a baptized woman, whose body is the temple of God, a future human being is formed under the devil unless he is reborn from God”—as though it were not more astonishing that God works even where he does not dwell.

For he does not dwell in a body subjected to sins (Wisdom 1:4), and yet he forms a human being in the womb of a prostitute. For in his purity he reaches everywhere, and nothing defiled enters into him (Wisdom 7:24–25).

What is much more astonishing, he sometimes adopts as a son one whom he forms in the womb of the most impure woman, and sometimes does not will as his son one whom he forms in the womb of his own daughter. The former, by some providence unknown to me, reaches baptism; the latter does not reach it because of sudden death.

Thus God, in whose power all things are, causes one whom he formed in the devil’s dwelling to share in Christ, and does not will in his kingdom one whom he formed in his own temple. Or, if he does will it, why does he not do what he wills? Surely you cannot here say, as you usually do concerning adults, “God wills, but the little child does not will.”

Here there is no immutability of fate, no randomness of fortune, and no distinction of personal status. What remains, then, except the depth of mercy and truth? From this we learn—and grasp something incomprehensible by means of it—that, in relation to the two men, the one through whom sin entered the world and the other who takes away the sin of the world, all children of carnal desire, wherever they are born, belong by merit to the harsh yoke of the children of Adam; while from among them all children of spiritual grace, wherever they are born, reach the gentle yoke of the children of God without merit.

Accordingly, the person formed in the body of another woman, even though that body is the temple of God, bears his own condition. He is constructed there in such a way that he is not himself thereby the temple of God merely because he is being built in the temple of God. For the fact that the mother’s body is the temple of God is a benefit of grace, not of nature; and this grace is conferred not through conception but through regeneration.

If what is conceived in the mother belonged to the mother’s body in such a way that it were reckoned as a part of her, then an infant whose mother had been baptized under the pressure of imminent death, while carrying him in her womb, would not be baptized. But when the infant himself is baptized, he is certainly not considered to have been baptized twice.

Therefore, while he was in the womb, he did not belong to the mother’s body; and yet he was being created in the temple of God, though not as the temple of God.

Thus an unbelieving child was created in a believing woman, and his parents transmitted to him an unbelief that they did not possess when he was born from them, but possessed when they too were similarly born. They therefore transmitted what was no longer in them because of the spiritual seed by which they had been regenerated; but it was present in their carnal seed, by which they begot him.

44. Although the body is sanctified by holy Baptism, it is sanctified for this purpose: that through the remission of sins it should not be subject not only to all past sins, but also to the concupiscence of the flesh that is present within it—to which every human being must be born subject, and to which he will remain subject even in death unless he is reborn.

Where, then, did you hear or read me saying that “people are not renewed through Baptism, but only apparently renewed; not delivered, but only apparently delivered; not saved, but only apparently saved”?

Far be it from me to call empty the grace of that washing in which I was reborn from water and the Spirit, through which I was freed from the guilt of all sins—whether those I had drawn from birth or those I had contracted by living badly. Through it I am delivered so that I may know not to enter into temptation, having been drawn away and enticed by my own concupiscence; and so that I may be heard when I say with my companions, “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12). Through it I shall, as I hope, be delivered eternally, when no law in my members will resist the law of my mind (Romans 7:23).

I therefore do not make God’s grace empty. But you, its enemy, seem to have sought empty boasting so that you could introduce Epicurus into your argument, Epicurus “who denied that the gods have a body, but said that they have something like a body; and denied that they have blood, but said that they have something like blood” (Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, book 3). On this occasion you babbled all the more foolishly, though with the appearance of greater learning, drawing upon philosophical writings irrelevant to the matter at issue between us.

Who among us, however, says that “whatever is done in the present age must be condemned,” when Christ himself did so many good things here, though in order to rescue us from this present evil age?

## CHAPTER XV

45. It is worthwhile to observe how carefully and appropriately you explain the Apostle’s testimony in which he says, “We have been saved in hope,” and so forth, up to “the redemption of our body” (Romans 8:24, 23).

For you say that “that resurrection does not forgive anyone’s sins, but purifies the merits of each person. For it renders to each one,” you say, “according to his works.” Yet you do not say according to what works it will render the kingdom of God to little children.

No sins are indeed forgiven in the kingdom. But if no sins were forgiven in that final judgment, I think the Lord would not have said of a certain sin, “It will not be forgiven, either in this age or in the age to come” (Matthew 12:32). Nor would that thief have hoped for forgiveness when he said, “Remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42).

Since this is a very profound question, judgment about it should not now be rushed. But why does God forgive no sins in the kingdom to his children, except because he finds none to forgive? There can be no sins there where the spirit not only does not consent to the desire of the flesh, but does not even desire against the flesh, because the flesh does not desire against the spirit. That is the ineffable salvation perfected, which does not occur now in Baptism. In Baptism all sins are indeed forgiven, but the evils of carnal desires remain; and after Baptism, if people make progress, the married wage glorious battles against them, while the continent wage even more glorious ones. You yourself admit this (above, book 3, §42), but through some strange misery, whenever you speak for the truth, you do not then listen to yourself.

46. In describing that supreme happiness of the resurrection, you say that “no just person there will make his body livid and subject it to servitude; no one will humble his soul with hard beds and the stench of his limbs.”

Answer, then, why a person does these things here who was freed from every evil in Baptism. Why does he dare to make the temple of God livid? Are his members not certainly members of the temple of God? Why, then, does he either invite God’s presence, obtain his mercy, or appease his anger by the temple’s foul odor rather than its sweet fragrance? Does he discipline, tame, conquer, or suppress no evil in the temple of God, even by making the temple of God itself livid and foul?

Do you not attend? Do you not see that if, in pursuing his body so vehemently, he pursues nothing there that displeases God, then by pursuing the temple in vain he does great injury to God?

Why do you evade the issue? Why do you hesitate to confess it more openly? Surely it is that which this person—whose lividity and foulness you describe—persecutes in his own flesh, concerning which the Apostle said, “I know that nothing good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh” (Romans 7:18). Why do you deny that this voice belongs to the baptized, when you recognize the works of this voice in the lividity of the body and the foulness of the limbs?

For the saints endure such things neither under God’s scourges nor at the hands of enemies; they inflict them upon themselves through continence. And why do they do this except by desiring in the spirit against the concupiscence of the flesh? You evidently understood this yourself.

For when, in describing the happiness of the future life, you added and said, “No one will subject prosperous shamelessness to insults; no one will subject cheeks to slaps; no one will subject backs to lashes; no one will strive to forge virtue out of weakness; neither frugality will struggle with poverty, nor greatness of spirit with sorrows,” why did you not wish to say, “Nor chastity with the concupiscence of the flesh”?

[Note: The editions read, “nor frugality with poverty, nor greatness of spirit with sorrows . . . nor chastity with the concupiscence of the flesh.” Two Vatican manuscripts read, “frugality, greatness of spirit,” and so forth.]

Instead, you hastened to complete the thought and said, “Nor will patience struggle with pain,” mentioning nothing except what bursts in from outside and is endured by courage, not what stirs within and is restrained by chastity.

Or perhaps you accuse us of slowness because we failed to understand that you had already indicated this above when you spoke of the lividity of the body and the labor and foulness of the limbs? For when a courageous person is afflicted not by an enemy but by himself, the enemy who must be overcome is within him.

47. Remember that you have not explained why the Apostle said “awaiting adoption” (Romans 8:23), when the person had already been adopted in the washing of regeneration.
