Again you say “that no one hates his own flesh.” Who denies this? Yet you assert that it must be crushed by the rigor of discipline. Once again, then, you speak for the truth, but do not wish to listen to yourself.

Why is the flesh crushed by the faithful if nothing remains in Baptism that desires against the spirit? Why, I ask, does the temple of God crush itself if there is nothing in it that resists the Spirit of God?

There would not merely be such a thing in us; it would also be gravely harmful, unless the guilt by which it had bound us had been released through the remission of sins. It is therefore released through pardon because it held us in guilt; it is crushed through continence so that it may not prevail in the struggle. The purpose is that it may not harm us until it is healed in such a way that it no longer exists.

Consequently, all sins are forgiven in Baptism: those inherited originally, and those added knowingly or unknowingly. But when the Apostle James says, “Each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own concupiscence; then, when concupiscence has conceived, it gives birth to sin” (James 1:14–15), the words clearly distinguish the offspring from the one giving birth.

Concupiscence is the one giving birth; sin is the offspring. But concupiscence does not give birth unless it has conceived, and it does not conceive unless it has enticed—that is, unless it has obtained the willing assent to commit evil.

The purpose of fighting against it, therefore, is to prevent it from conceiving and giving birth to sin. Since all sins—that is, all the offspring of concupiscence—are forgiven in Baptism, if concupiscence itself was also destroyed there, how do the saints fight against it so that it may not conceive, “with lividity of the body, foulness of the limbs, and crushing of the flesh”—your own words?

How, I ask, do the saints wage war against it with lividity, foulness, and the crushing of the temple of God, if it too was removed by Baptism? It remains, then; and we were not deprived of it by the washing of regeneration, if we did not there lose the perception by which we sense that it remains.

48. Who could be so foolish and shameless, so bold, obstinate, and headstrong, so finally insane and deranged, that, while admitting that sins are evil, he would deny that the concupiscence of sins is evil—even when the spirit desires against it and prevents it from conceiving and giving birth to sins?

How could such a great and serious evil, merely by being present, fail to hold a person in death and drag him into final death, unless its bond were also released in the remission of all sins that takes place in Baptism?

Because of this bond, which is joined to us from the first Adam and can be loosed only in the second Adam, infants are found among the dead—not by that death most familiar to us, which separates the soul from the body, but by the death in which all were held, for whom Christ died.

For we know, as the Apostle says—and this must be repeated by us very frequently—“that one died for all; therefore all died. And he died for all, so that those who live might no longer live for themselves, but for the one who died for all and rose again” (2 Corinthians 5:14–15).

They therefore live for whom the one who lived died, so that they might live. This is expressed more clearly in the following way: They are free from the bond of death, for whom the one “free among the dead” died (Psalm 87:6).

[Note: Four manuscripts read “were freed.”]

Or, more clearly still: They are freed from sin for whom the one who had never been in sin died.

Although he died only once, he dies for each person at the time when that person, whatever his age, is baptized into his death. That is, the death of the one who was without sin benefits a person when, baptized into his death, that person himself dies to sin, having previously been dead in sin.

## CHAPTER XVI

49. You bring forward the Apostle’s testimony in which he says, “Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve images,” and so forth; and after listing these things he concludes that they will not possess the kingdom of God.

[Note: The Floriacensis manuscript adds, “who do such things.”]

But those do such things who, by the movements of the concupiscence that you praise, consent to every evil and shameful act.

When he says, “And such were some of you, but you were washed, but you were sanctified” (1 Corinthians 6:9–11), he said that they had been changed for the better—not so that they would be without it [concupiscence], which cannot happen in this life, but so that they would not obey it, which can happen in a good life; and so that they would recognize that they had been freed from the bond by which they had been subject to them, something that cannot happen except through regeneration.

But you, who think that “if concupiscence were evil, the baptized person would be free from it,” are greatly mistaken. He is free from every sin, not from every evil.

This can be stated more plainly: He is free from the guilt of every evil, not from every evil itself.

Is he free from the corruption of the body? Is it not an evil that weighs down the soul? And was the one who said, “A corruptible body weighs down the soul,” mistaken (Wisdom 9:15)?

Is he free from the evil of ignorance, through which innumerable evils are committed by those who do not know? Is it a small evil through which a person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God?

The Apostle was speaking of baptized people when he said, “The natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God; for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them because they are spiritually discerned” (1 Corinthians 2:14–15).

A little later he says: “And I, brothers, could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal people, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food, for you were not yet able to receive it. Indeed, even now you are not able, for you are still carnal. Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to the human way?”

Consider what evils he says arise from the evil of ignorance. And I think he was not speaking about catechumens. For how could they be infants in Christ unless they had already been reborn?

If you still do not believe this, attend to what he says to them shortly afterward: “Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in you?” (1 Corinthians 3:1–2, 16).

Will you still doubt or deny that they could have been God’s temple, in which God’s Spirit dwelled, unless they had been baptized?

At least consider what he said to them: “Were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Corinthians 1:13).

They therefore had not been free from that great evil of ignorance in the washing of regeneration, where nevertheless they had undoubtedly been freed from all sins. Through this evil of ignorance, the temple of God in which the Spirit of God dwelled was foolish concerning the things that belong to the Spirit of God.

But if they made progress day by day and walked in the way they had reached, this evil would certainly be diminished as sound teaching was added. Let us believe that it can not only be diminished but also be completely removed in this life. Yet this would be after Baptism, not in Baptism.

Who, however, would doubt that concupiscence can be diminished in this life, but cannot be destroyed?

### 50

All the guilt of these evils, therefore, is washed away in its entirety by the sacred font. Thus they are remitted in those who are reborn, and diminished in those who make progress. Ignorance is diminished as truth shines more and more brightly; concupiscence is diminished as charity burns more and more fervently.

None of the good in these two things is from us [Note: Two Vatican manuscripts read: “None of the good things in these two.” The Floriacensis manuscript: “None of these gifts.”]. For we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things granted to us by God (ibid. II, 12). Concupiscence is worse than ignorance in this respect: ignorance without concupiscence sins less; concupiscence without ignorance sins more gravely. And not to know evil is not always evil; but to desire evil is always evil. Even a good thing itself is sometimes profitably unknown, so that it may be known at the proper time. But it is in no way possible for the good of a human being to be desired by carnal concupiscence, since even offspring itself is desired not by the lust of the body but by the will of the mind, although it is not sown without the lust of the body.

We are speaking of that concupiscence by which the flesh desires against the spirit, not of that good desire by which the spirit desires against the flesh (Galatians V, 17), and by which continence is desired, through which concupiscence is conquered. By this concupiscence of the flesh, therefore, no good of a human being is ever desired, if the pleasure of the flesh is not a human good.

But if, as you indicated somewhere, “you approve the school of Dinomachus, joining moral worth and pleasure” (above, book 4, no. 76)—which philosophers of this world who seemed more respectable likewise called the “Scyllaean good,” compounded, that is, from human and beastly nature—if, then, you pursue this monster according to your opinion, it is enough for us that you confess that one pleasure is illicit and another licit. Accordingly, concupiscence is evil when it indiscriminately desires both, unless licit pleasure restrains it from illicit pleasure.

This evil is not placed in Baptism [Note: The printed editions read “punished” (*punitur*). The Vatican manuscripts more correctly read “placed” (*ponitur*), that is, “laid aside.”]; rather, in those who have been baptized and already freed from its obligation through the grace of regeneration, it is healthfully restrained so that it does not drag them toward what is illicit.

But that, at the time of the resurrection, it may not exist at all in the living body, nor cause pain, is the reward of those who faithfully struggled against it; when their sickness has been healed, they will be clothed with most blessed immortality [Note: Here the Amiatine manuscript adds “with sickness healed”; Erasmus and the Louvain edition read “with sickness sound.” Our manuscripts do not contain these words.]. In those, however, who will not rise to life, it will not be absent happily but punitively [Note: The printed editions read “but punitively it will be.” All the Vatican and Gallican manuscripts, however, read “but punitively it will not be”; this reading fits better with what follows: not because anyone will then be cleansed from it—that is, not because its guilt will be removed—but only because the activity of concupiscence, which ordinarily moves pleasantly toward pleasure, will then be turned into torments.], not because anyone will then be cleansed from it, but because then it will not arouse the wicked to delights; rather, it will be turned into torments.

### CHAPTER XVII  
[Note: In the Amiatine and Erasmian editions, chapter 6.]

### 51

Now let us examine that supremely excellent acumen of yours, by which you saw how to refute what I had said: “The concupiscence of the flesh is forgiven in Baptism, not so that it may not exist, but so that it may not be reckoned as sin; although its guilt has already been dissolved, it nevertheless remains” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 28).

Against these words of mine you argue, as the exceedingly acute man you are, as though I had said that concupiscence itself is freed from guilt through Baptism, because I said, “its guilt having already been dissolved”—as though by “its” I meant the guilt by which it itself was guilty, and, when that guilt was dissolved, it remained absolved.

If I had understood the matter in this way, I certainly would not have said that it is evil, but that it had been evil. Thus, according to your marvelous intelligence, whenever you hear that the guilt of murder has been dissolved in someone, you suppose that not the person but the murder itself has been absolved from guilt.

Let anyone understand it in this way—unless he is not ashamed to praise what he is compelled to combat! And how do you boast and exult in refuting this opinion, which is plainly not mine but your own [Note: Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition read: “in refuting this opinion, plainly not mine but yours.”]?

You say things that ought to be said against those who affirm that the concupiscence of the flesh has been sanctified and made faithful through Baptism in those who, though regenerated, still retain it. But this is more appropriately said by you, who proclaim it good: “so that, in addition to its natural goodness,” as you say concerning infants, “the goodness of sanctification may be added,” and the concupiscence of the flesh may be a holy daughter of God.

We, however, who say that it is evil and nevertheless remains in the baptized—although its guilt has been remitted and emptied, not the guilt by which it itself was guilty (for it is not a person), but the guilt by which it originally made the human being guilty—must not say that it is sanctified. Those who are regenerated necessarily have to struggle against it in an inward kind of war as against an enemy, and desire and long to be healed from that plague, if they have not received the grace of God in vain.

### 52

For if you say that no evils remain in the baptized for the reason that the evils themselves might be thought to have been baptized and sanctified, consider what absurdity follows you.

If everything that exists in a person when he is baptized must be thought to be baptized and sanctified, you will say that those things also are baptized and sanctified which must be expelled through the bodily processes from his intestines and bladder. You will say that a human being situated in his mother’s womb is baptized and sanctified, if necessity compels a pregnant woman to receive this Sacrament; and therefore that the one who is born should no longer be baptized.

Finally, you will say that fevers themselves are baptized and sanctified when the sick are baptized; and consequently that even the works of the devil are baptized and sanctified—as though that woman whom Satan had bound in infirmity for eighteen years were baptized before she was healed (Luke XIII, 11).

What shall I say about the evils of the mind itself? Consider how great an evil it is to regard as foolishness the things that belong to the Spirit of God; and yet such were those whom the Apostle fed with milk, not solid food. Will you also say that the great evil of that foolishness, because it had not been removed by Baptism, was baptized and sanctified?

Thus, too, concupiscence, which remains to be opposed and healed, although all sins whatsoever have been forgiven in Baptism, is not only not sanctified; rather, it is emptied so that it may not be able to hold those who have been sanctified subject to eternal death. For those who were fed with milk and not solid food, and were still natural persons, not perceiving the things that belong to the Spirit of God because they were still foolishness to them—if they had departed from the body at that age of the mind, not of the flesh, at which they were called new human beings, little ones in Christ, they would not have been held by any guilt of that foolishness [Note: In the printed editions, the words “at which they were called new human beings” were transposed and placed before “of the mind, not of the flesh, they had departed from the body.” They are restored here to their proper place in accordance with the manuscripts.]. For this benefit had been conferred on them through regeneration: that the guilt of all the evils from which they would later have to be stripped, whether by dying or by making progress, should immediately be dissolved through the forgiveness of all sins—not yet through the healing of all diseases.

Nevertheless, that guilt necessarily holds the one who is generated according to the flesh, since it is remitted only to the one who is regenerated according to the spirit. The human race is freed by the one Mediator between God and human beings from the death of the most just condemnation—not merely from bodily death, but from the death in which those for whom one person died had died. And because he died for all, therefore all died.

### CHAPTER XVIII

### 53

But since you chose to argue at such length about the difference between qualities, because I once used the word “quality,” saying that “concupiscence does not remain substantially, like some body or spirit, but is a certain affection of evil quality, as sickness is” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 28)—do you really not see that this has nothing to do with the matter?

First you say that I “changed my position and confessed, forgetful of my entire book, that lust is a substance.” But when my book is examined and carefully unfolded, you will not find me saying even once that lust is a substance.

Certain philosophers said that it is a vicious part of the mind; and certainly a part of the mind is a substance, because the mind itself is a substance. But I call the very vice by which the mind, or any part of it, is vicious in this way “lust,” so that, when every vice has been healed, the entire substance remains intact.

For those philosophers also seem to me, by a figurative expression, to have called a vicious part of the mind “lust,” the part in which the vice called lust exists, just as “house” is used for those who are in the house.

### 54

Next, by exercising yourself too carelessly with the exceedingly sharp weapons of dialecticians, and by frightening us with excessive boasting, you have mortally wounded your own school.

For when you divided, defined, or even described the differences among qualities, you said, among other things: “The third species of quality is affection and affective quality. Affection is placed among qualities,” you say, “because it is the beginning of qualities; to it also are assigned the passions of either mind or body that approach and depart for a moment. Affective quality,” you say, “arises from greater causes and adheres to all in whom it occurs in such a way that it is separated either with great efforts or not at all.”

You have explained these matters sufficiently for those who know them. But since those who will read our books and are ignorant of this discipline must not be despised, I shall illuminate what I see to be lacking by examples.

With respect to the mind, being afraid is an affection; being timid is an affective quality, just as being angry is one thing and being irascible another; being drunk is one thing and being prone to drunkenness another. The former are affections; the latter, affective qualities.

With respect to the body, being pale is one thing and being pallid another; becoming red is one thing and being ruddy another; and similarly in other cases for which common terms are lacking.

Since, then, you have said that “affective quality arises from greater causes and adheres in such a way that it is separated either by great efforts or not at all,” when the mind is called evil according to this quality—or rather, when the human being is called evil—do you not fear that a good will may either be unable to exist there or be unable to accomplish anything?

Do you not admit that every wretched person, whoever he is or has been, has certainly cried out against such a quality: “To will is present with me, but to accomplish the good I do not find”?

At least here you confess that the necessary groan of these words exists: “Who will free me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans VII, 18, 24–25).

### 55

Therefore, however much you wrap yourself in a dialectical covering before the eyes of the unlearned, you will be stripped bare by manifest truth.

I say that, like an illness arising from a corrupted origin, there is innate in the human being a vice by which the flesh desires against the spirit. Chaste marriages make good use of this evil when they use it for the purpose of procreation; but it is the person who makes good use of the evil who is praised, not the evil itself.

For the evil itself is not innocent; rather, the person who makes his evil serve a good use is innocent of its harm. Just as death, although it is the punishment of the sinner, becomes, when a good use is added to the evil, the martyr’s reward.

In Christian Baptism, those evils of ours of which we were guilty are met by complete newness and complete healing—not those with which we must still struggle so that we may not be guilty of them, since they themselves are in us and are not alien but ours.

After Baptism people also resist the habit of drunkenness—a certainly evil habit that they themselves acquired, rather than drew from birth—so that it may not drag them toward their customary evils. Yet the evil is resisted when, through continence, what is desired through habit is denied to concupiscence.

Hence a widow struggles more intensely than a virgin against this genital concupiscence, which is innate in us through original sin; and a prostitute, when she wishes to be chaste, struggles more intensely than one who has always been chaste. The will will labor all the more to overcome it the greater strength habit has given it.

From this evil of the human being, and together with it, the human being is born. This evil is in itself so great, and has so much obligation toward the condemnation of the human being and separation from the kingdom of God, that even if it is transmitted from regenerated parents, it is dissolved only by regeneration, just as it was in them; by this one remedy the sentence of death is driven from the offspring, just as it was driven from the parents [Note: The following words had been transferred here from the margin: “The affective quality of evil does not pass from substance to substance by migrating from one place to another, but through a certain operative contagion, that is, through the affection of concupiscence, just as diseased offspring are produced from diseased parents.” They are to be deleted from the earlier editions, since the more ancient manuscripts lack them.].

The quality of evil, however, does not migrate from substance into substance as from one place to another, so that it leaves the place where it was and the very same thing that was there becomes elsewhere. Rather, another thing of the same kind arises through a certain operative contagion, as also happens to those born from the diseased bodies of parents.

### 56

What, then, did you intend to say when, as you put it, you were “closing” [Note: Several manuscripts read “applauding.”] Aristotle’s wrestling school, so that from there you might return to the Sacred Scriptures?

For you say: “Concupiscence is therefore a sensation, and an evil quality is not [Note: In the Amiatine and Erasmian editions, after “is not” there was added: “while concupiscence is diminished, sensation is said to be diminished.” Only a few manuscripts contain this, and the Louvain editors deleted it as an inept gloss imported from the margin.]; therefore, when concupiscence is diminished, sensation is diminished.”

Is not the carnal concupiscence diminished more and more every day through the concupiscence of chastity and continence? I should like you to tell me whether someone does not become healthier from the disease of fornication when fornication delights him less and less—even though he has cut off that evil deed from himself by a single conversion and has never committed it since receiving the laver of regeneration.

Likewise, after a habit of drunkenness, someone is baptized and never again becomes completely drunk. I should like you to tell me whether he does not become healthier each day from that disease than he had been, since he desires the flood of drinking less and less than he used to.

“Feeling,” then, is not concupiscence itself; rather, it is the feeling by which we perceive that we have more or less of it. Just as, in bodily passions, feeling is not pain, but the feeling by which pain is felt; nor is feeling disease, but the feeling by which we perceive that we have a disease.

Moreover, if the person who renounces fornication and drunkenness and abstains from such acts immediately becomes good—and certainly becomes good through a good quality—does he not rightly hear, “See, you have become well; do not sin anymore” (John V, 14), and is he not rightly called chaste and sober?

Furthermore, if through the growth of the good desire by which he conquers evil desires for fornication and drinking [Note: The Floriacensis manuscript reads: “if, by growing and conquering the evil desires for fornication and drinking …”], he becomes such as he was not yet at the time of his recent conversion, so that the desires for those sins move him less and less, and so that against those evils he engages not in such great struggles as before but in smaller ones—not because virtues have diminished, but because enemies have diminished; not because the battle has weakened, but because victory has grown—will you hesitate to pronounce him better?

From where, I ask, except from the fact that the good quality has increased and the evil quality diminished? That by which he began to be good has therefore increased; that by which he was evil has diminished. And this he accomplished after Baptism; he did not complete it in Baptism.

Thus, although the full forgiveness of sins was completed there, there nevertheless remained a struggle to be vigilantly and persistently exercised against the hosts of evil desires that are certainly tumultuous within us, so that we might advance toward what is better. Because of this it is also said to the baptized: “Put to death therefore your members that are upon the earth” (Colossians III, 5); and, “If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live” (Romans VIII, 13); and, “Put off the old human being” (Colossians III, 9).

Surely these statements are made with complete agreement in the truth, without any reproach of Baptism.

### 57

If, therefore, you do not wish to be contentious, I think that you now see how correctly the passage is understood which you try to explain otherwise: when the prophet had said, “He who is gracious to all your iniquities”—which occurs, of course, through the remission of all sins—he immediately added, “He who heals all your diseases” (Psalm CII, 3).

He intended those evils to be understood with which, until they are healed, or insofar as they can be in this life, the inward battles of the saints do not cease, while they are diminished more and more. For there is indeed a disease by which the flesh desires against the spirit, even while the virtue of chastity remains unconquered.

If there were no disease, the spirit would not desire against it. The spirit desires against it so that, if it cannot obtain health by ceasing to struggle, it may at least obtain health by refusing to consent.

This thing of which we are now speaking—the thing we perceive resisting us within us—must either be separated as an alien nature or healed as our own. If we say that it must be separated as alien, we favor the Manichaeans. Let us therefore confess that it is ours and must be healed, so that we may avoid both the Manichaeans and the Pelagians.

### CHAPTER XIX  
[Note: In the Amiatine and Erasmian editions, chapter 8.]

### 58

Thus, “the wound inflicted on the human race by the devil compels whatever is born through it to be under the devil, as though he rightly plucked the fruit from his own shrub” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, no. 26).

You set these words from my book before me for refutation, and you lie in wait for them as though I had “called the devil the author of human nature and the creator of the very substance of which the human being consists”—as though you could call a wound in a body a substance.

But if you think that I called the devil the creator of substance because, in the comparison I used, I called it a shrub—for a shrub is unquestionably a substance—why do you reveal or pretend to be so unlearned that you do not think comparisons from substances may be applied to things that are not substances?

Unless perhaps you will also dialectically accuse the Lord himself because he said, “A good tree produces good fruits, and an evil tree produces evil fruits” (Matthew VII, 17). Who would say that malice or goodness, or good or evil works—which he wanted understood as the fruits of those trees—are substances, unless he does not know what he is saying? Who, however, if he knows what he is saying, would deny that trees and their fruits are substances?

We therefore see comparisons taken from things that are substances applied to things that are not substances. But if the good or evil tree is to be understood not as a person's goodness or malice, but as human beings themselves, in whom these qualities are understood to inhere—goodness in a good person and malice in an evil one—so that the trees, that is, the human beings themselves, are substances, certainly no one but an ignoramus would say that their fruits, understood as nothing other than works, are substances [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts read: “certainly no one but an ignoramus would deny that their fruits, understood as nothing other than works, are substances”]; whereas no one but an ignoramus would deny that the fruits of all the trees from which these comparisons are drawn are substances. Accordingly, although the vice that the devil inflicted upon the human race like a wound is in no way a substance, I rightly applied to it a comparison from substance by calling it a shrub, and its vices fruits—those vices, moreover, with which human beings are born, although you deny it, while the truth proves it, and through which they perish from God's eternal kingdom if they are not reborn through liberating truth.

### 59

Accordingly, I called the devil a corrupter, not a creator, of substance. He subjects to himself what he did not create, through what he inflicted, God justly granting him this power. Yet this power does not withdraw from God’s authority either what has been subjected to the devil or the devil himself.

For this reason the second birth was instituted: because the first birth was condemned. Yet even to this condemned birth God’s goodness is extended, so that rational nature may be formed from accursed seed. By this most abundant goodness of his, so great a multitude of wicked human beings is plainly nourished and secretly brought to life.

If this goodness of his operation were withdrawn from the forming and advancing of seeds and from giving life to all living things, not only would those things that are to be begotten fail to occur, but even those already begotten would be reduced entirely to nothing.

Since, then, only foolish impiety would criticize God because human beings, who are condemnable through a vicious will, live by the life-giving power of the one who gives life to all things, why do we think it alien to his works that those who are condemnable through a corrupted origin are born through the creative power of the one who is the creator of all things?

Through the Mediator, those whom he chose before the foundation of the world through the election of grace, not on the basis of works—whether past, present, or future—are regenerated and freed from the condemnation they deserved, by gratuitous mercy, not by anything owed. Otherwise grace is no longer grace (Romans XI, 6).

This is especially evident in infants, whose past works cannot be spoken of, because they did not exist; nor present works, because they perform nothing; nor future works, when they die at that age.

### 60

I did indeed say: “Just as sins that have passed in action remain in guilt, so, conversely, it can happen that concupiscence remains in action and passes away in guilt” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book I, nos. 29–30).

Your error says that this is false, but the truth proves it true. Since you were unable to refute it, you first try to cast dialectical darkness over the unlearned by saying that you “cannot imagine in what dialectic I found the reciprocity of all contraries.”

If I wished to explain this statement of yours and bring it within the understanding of those who have never learned such matters, a full volume would perhaps be required. But for now it is enough that you yourself said that “the reciprocity of all contraries cannot be found in any dialectic.” By this you showed that it can exist for some, though not for all.

Among some of those, then, I found this also. For if you had said that the reciprocity of contraries belongs to none, and thereby showed that the contraries I proposed could not be reciprocals because no such things could exist, I would have had to show that some could exist and then that what I proposed belonged among them.

But you yourself already concede that some exist, since you do not say that there is reciprocity for no contraries, but only that there is not reciprocity for all. Therefore there is reciprocity for some.

Whether this also occurs among those that I proposed remains to be shown: namely, whether, just as it is true that sins that have passed in action remain in guilt, so it is true that concupiscence remains in action and passes away in guilt.

When you wished to show that this could not happen, you said something that I did not say. For I spoke of concupiscence that is in the members, resisting the law of the mind (Romans VII, 23), although its guilt has passed away in the forgiveness of all sins.

The converse example is a sacrifice made to idols: if it is not made thereafter, it has passed away in action but remains in guilt unless it is remitted through pardon. For sacrificing to idols is of such a nature that the act itself passes away when it is performed, while its guilt, after the act has passed, remains to be dissolved by forgiveness.

The concupiscence of the flesh, however, is of such a nature that it remains in the human being who struggles against it through continence, although its guilt—which had been contracted through generation—has already passed away through regeneration.

It remains in action, not by tearing away and enticing the mind, conceiving and giving birth to sins through its consent, but by stirring up evil desires against which the mind resists. For its very movement is an action, although, when the mind does not consent, the result is absent.

There is in the human being an evil apart from this action—that is, apart from this movement—from which this movement arises; and we call this movement “desire.” For there is not always a desire against which we must fight. But if desire is absent when nothing occurs to be desired, whether to the mind thinking or to the bodily senses, it can happen that an evil quality is present without being stirred by any temptation, just as timidity is present in a timid person even when he is not afraid.

When, however, something occurs to be desired and evil desires are not stirred in us even against our will, there is complete health.

This vice could therefore not hold a human being except in guilt, even though he was begotten from chaste spouses through the good use of that same evil. Although the guilt remains while the evil remains, it is dissolved in the forgiveness of all sins through the grace of God, by which we are freed from every evil, when the Lord not only is gracious to all our iniquities but also heals all our diseases [Note: After “heals all our diseases,” the Amiatine and Erasmian editions, together with some manuscripts, immediately add the following passage:

“[The Lord says in the Gospel, ‘Behold, I cast out demons and complete healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected.’ After a long time had passed since this was said, the Lord suffered; he could not have lied. It is therefore understood in this way: the casting out of demons is the remission of sins, because the devil is the father and origin of sins, through the fact that what effects is brought about. And certainly the casting out of demons is the remission of sins, as the cause through which the devil possessed the human soul has been dissolved. The completion of healings occurs as the Church advances day by day, and the daily suffering of corruption, whose guilt has been removed, is diminished through renewal. The third is completed when he showed in himself the resurrection that was to be inaugurated for the Church, by which it might reach the consummation of incorruption and the highest health. He said that he himself was to be perfected: himself the beginning and the end, himself the head and fullness of the body; he himself is perfected in his members.”]

The Louvain editors erased the first part of this addition, which we have enclosed in brackets; they transferred the second part twelve lines later, to the words “the blessedness of incorruptible joys.” We reject both parts on the authority of four Vatican manuscripts and several Gallican manuscripts.]

For remember what the Liberator and Savior himself answered those who had told him to depart from Jerusalem: “Behold,” he said, “I cast out demons and complete healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected” (Luke XIII, 32).

Read the Gospel and see how much later he suffered and rose again. Did he therefore lie? Far from it. Rather, he signified something that is at issue in our present dispute.

The casting out of demons is the remission of sins; the completion of healings is what occurs through progress after Baptism; the third consummation is what he also demonstrated through the immortality of his own flesh: the blessedness of incorruptible joys.

### 61

You, however, offered as an example of the matter under discussion a sacrilegious sacrifice and said: “Whatever belongs to this category can be demonstrated from this one example: if someone once sacrifices to idols, he can, until he obtains forgiveness, be oppressed by the guilt of the impiety committed, and the guilt remains when the action has ended. But it can in no way happen,” you say, “that the action remains and the guilt departs—that is, that he does not cease sacrificing to demons and yet appears free from profanation.”

You speak very truly about a sacrifice offered to idols. The act is performed by the deed itself and will not exist; if it is performed again, it is another act. But the impiety by which these things are done remains until one renounces idols and believes in God.

The sacrifice offered to idols is therefore a passing act, not a remaining vice. The impiety through which the sacrifice was made, however, because it remains even after the sacrifice has been completed, seems similar to the concupiscence through which adultery was committed.

But once the error has been removed—the error by which that impiety was thought to be piety—does anyone take pleasure in sacrificing to idols, or is such a desire stirred in him? Therefore the thing which you thought ought to be put forward as similar is in no way similar.

In no way, I say, is a passing sacrifice similar to the concupiscence that remains: concupiscence that does not cease to trouble a human being who no longer commits, by consenting to it, what he used to commit; who now holds with complete faith and knowledge that such things must not be done; yet is still disturbed by the impulses of illicit desires, against which chastity resists.

Nor does concupiscence come to an end so that it ceases to exist; rather, it is restrained by continence so that it cannot reach the goal toward which it tends.

Therefore, just as an offering to idols, which is no longer present either in action, because it has passed away, or in the will, because the error through which it was performed has been destroyed, nevertheless retains its guilt until that guilt is dissolved in the laver of regeneration through the forgiveness of all sins, so, conversely, although the guilt of evil concupiscence has been dissolved in that same Baptism, concupiscence itself remains until it is healed by the one who, after casting out demons, completes healings through perfected medicine.

### 62

But I ask you: since you yourself also concede that the guilt of a sin committed and completed remains unless it is washed away in the sacred font, tell me what this guilt is and where it remains when the human being has been corrected and is living rightly, but has not yet been freed through the forgiveness of sins.

Is this guilt a subject—that is, a substance, like spirit or body—or does it exist in a subject, as fever or a wound exists in the body, or greed or error in the mind?

You will say that it exists in a subject; for you will certainly not affirm that guilt is a substance. In what subject, then, does it seem to you to exist?

Why should I ask what you will answer, rather than set down your own words? “When the act,” you say, “has passed away, its guilt remains in the conscience of the one who committed the offense until it is forgiven.”

Therefore it exists in a subject—that is, in the mind of the one who remembers that he committed the offense and is troubled by the prick of conscience [Note: The Amiatine manuscript and other manuscripts read “is driven” rather than “is troubled”], until he becomes secure through the remission of the offense.

But what if he forgets that he committed the offense and his conscience is not goaded? Where will that guilt be, which you concede remains after the sin has passed until it is forgiven?

It is certainly not in the body, because it is not among those accidents that occur to the body; it is not in the mind, because forgetfulness has erased its memory—and yet it exists.

Where, then, does it remain when the human being is already living well and committing nothing of that kind, and it cannot be said that the guilt remains of those sins he remembers, while the guilt of those he has forgotten does not remain [Note: The sole Louvain edition reads: “of the sins he remembers, but that of those he has forgotten does not remain.”]?

It remains altogether until it is forgiven. Where, then, does it remain except in the hidden laws of God, which have been written in some manner in the minds of the angels, so that no iniquity is left unpunished unless the blood of the Mediator has expiated it?

By the sign of the cross, the baptismal water is consecrated, so that the guilt may be washed away as though written in a legal bond, in the knowledge of the spiritual powers through which punishment for sins is exacted.

All who are born carnally in the flesh from flesh are born liable to this legal bond. They must be freed from this debt by the blood of the one who was born in the flesh and from flesh, yet not carnally but spiritually.

For he was born of the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary [Note: This should be read, “of the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary,” according to the manuscripts; the alternative reading is “of the Holy Spirit from the virgin Mary.”]—of the Holy Spirit, namely, so that there might not be in him the flesh of sin; but from the virgin Mary, so that there might be in him the likeness of the flesh of sin.

Therefore he did not become liable to that legal bond, and he released those who were liable to it. For iniquity does indeed exist when, in one human being, either the higher faculties shamefully serve the lower, or the lower faculties stubbornly resist the higher, even if they are not permitted to prevail.

If a human being suffered this iniquity outwardly from another human being who opposed him, because it was not in him, he would certainly be punished without that other person. But because it is in him, he will either be punished together with it, or, once he has been freed from its guilt, it will persist in struggle against the spirit in such a way that it will send a human being who is no longer guilty to no torments after death; it will not alienate him from the kingdom of God or cause him to be held by any condemnation.

Nor is it separated from us as though it were an alien nature, so that we might be entirely without it; rather, because it is the sickness of our nature, it is healed in us.

### CHAPTER XX  
[Note: In the Amiatine and Erasmian editions, chapter 8.]

63. Therefore, on account of this defect, as I wrote in that book which you oppose, “human nature is condemned; and for the reason for which it is condemned, for that reason also it is subjected to the condemnable devil; for the devil himself is also an unclean spirit. And certainly that which is spirit is good, while that which is unclean is evil, since spirit is a nature, whereas uncleanness is a defect: of these two, the former is from God, the latter from the devil himself. Therefore he does not hold human beings, whether of mature [Note: [Col. 0861] Most manuscripts read *majores*, “those of greater age.”] or infant age, on account of that by which they are human, but on account of that by which they are unclean” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, §§25–26).

You thought you had to resist these words of mine, which you quoted from my book, by saying: “This condition too ought to have been preserved in the case of an evil human being, as it is preserved in the devil, so that no one might be condemned except on account of the vices of his own will; and therefore there is no original sin. Otherwise, his work”—as you say—“who also created the devil good cannot be approved.”

You do not consider that God did not create the devil from another devil, nor from any angel, even a good one, whose law would nevertheless be warring in his members against the law of the mind, through which and with which every human being is born from a human being. This argument might perhaps help you if, just as a human being begets children, so the devil too were to beget children, and we denied that they were liable to their father’s sin. But now one thing is the devil, who was a murderer from the beginning, because from the beginning—when the human being was established as human—he killed the human being by deceiving the woman, and did not stand fast in the truth through free will (John 8:44), and, falling, cast him down [Note: [Col. 0862] The printed editions add “the human being.”]; and another thing is that through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin, death, and thus passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned (Rom. 5:12). Here it is clearly expressed that, in addition to each person’s own sins, there is an original sin common to all human beings.

64. As for what I said—“If anyone is astonished that God’s creature is subjected to the devil, let him not be astonished; God’s creature is subjected to God’s creature, the lesser to the greater” (*On Marriage and Concupiscence*, book 1, §26)—why did you quote it in such a way that you omitted my following words, in which I showed how I had said “the lesser to the greater,” namely, the human to the angelic? Was it not so that my meaning would be less understood, allowing you to make room for yourself where, as is your habit, you might spread the clouds of Aristotelian categories before the uneducated, in which they would think that you were saying something hidden, while not knowing what you were saying? For your heresy has been reduced to this: your followers lament that dialectical judges cannot be found in the Church from the schools of the Peripatetics or Stoics, by whom you might be acquitted.

For what does it concern, or what does it mean, that you said: “Because ‘greater’ and ‘lesser’ belong to the finite species of quantity”? [Note: [Col. 0862] Vatican and Gallican manuscripts read “the infinite species.”] “But quantity,” you say, “is not only incapable of contraries—which it shares with quality and the other categories—but also has no contrary, which it shares with substance in its definition. Good and evil, however, are contraries.”

You certainly would never say these things if you thought that the readers or hearers of your books would understand what you were saying. Was an unclean human being therefore not to be subjected to an unclean angel because the quantity by which the angel is greater than the human is not only incapable of contraries but also has no contrary—as though a human being would then have been subject to the devil if he were found to be contrary to him; or as though evil things ought not to be subjected to evil things because good things appear contrary to evil things, but evil things do not appear contrary to evil things? What could be imagined more foolish, or said more absurdly?

Is not a servant subject to his master, the good to the good, the evil to the evil, the evil to the good, and the good to the evil? Is not a wife subject to her husband, the good wife to the good husband, the bad wife to the bad husband, the bad wife to the good husband, and the good wife to the bad husband? What, then, does it have to do with the force or rationale by which each thing ought to be subjected to each other, whether this thing or that can or cannot receive or possess a contrary? Yet you plainly would not have poured out these thoughtless claims if you had considered the wisdom contrary to the folly that prompts such suggestions to you.

65. And then, what sort of argument is this of yours? “If,” you say, “a thing that has been properly ordered pertains to God, and a thing that pertains to God is good, then it is good to be subject to the devil, since through this the order established by God is preserved. And it follows,” you say, “that it is evil to rebel against the devil, since by resisting him the order established by God is disturbed.”

You might as well say that farmers resist God and disturb his order by clearing their fields of thorns and thistles, which he ordered to grow for sinners as a punishment (Gen. 3:18).

What is more, by your reasoning one might say: if a thing that has been properly ordered pertains to God, and a thing that pertains to God is good, then it is good for the evil to be in hell [Note: [Col. 0863] Ambrose, Erasmus, and most manuscripts read “for evil people to be in hell.”], since through this the order established by God is preserved.

But why do you add, “And it follows that it is evil to rebel against the devil, since by resisting him the order established by God is disturbed”? Who, after all, rebels against the devil except one who has been freed from his power through the blood of the Mediator? It would therefore have been better not to have an enemy than to conquer one. But because human nature was subjected to the enemy through the merit of sin, the human being is first rescued from his power so that he may be able to fight against him. Then, if life in this flesh is prolonged, he is assisted in his struggle so that he may overcome. Finally, the victor is blessed so that he may reign, saying at the end, “Where is your contention, O death?” (Hos. 13:14), or, as the Apostle says, “Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Cor. 15:55).

## CHAPTER XXI

66. You even thought that some passages from the books of Mani ought to be inserted, with which you might compare my position, although I not only detest and condemn by faith and word the commixture of two natures, namely, good and evil, from which their entire fabulous madness flows, but also, by resisting you yourself as their supporter and refuting you, demonstrate your error.

For when the truth cries out against them that evils have not arisen except from good things, do you not cry out on their behalf and together with them against the truth: “The work of the devil is not permitted to pass through the work of God. The root of evil cannot be placed in the gift of God. The order of things does not permit evil to be produced from good, or injustice from the just. Sins are not born from that which is free from sin. From a work that has no guilt, guilt cannot be born” (*above*, book 1, chapters 8 and 9, and book 5, chapter 16, §§59, 64)?

By all these statements of yours it is established that evils have not arisen from good things, leaving, according to the Manichaeans, only the conclusion that evils have arisen from nothing except evils. How, then, do you accuse anyone under the name of Manichaean as though you were their opponent, when you stand so firmly on their side that they cannot be defeated at all unless you too are defeated together with them?

What we have done in the first book of this work somewhat more fully (chapter 8), and more briefly in the fifth (chapter 16), may suffice here.

67. How much your common heresy assists the Manichaeans I have already often shown, but it must not be omitted here either. The Manichaeans enumerate the evils that they point out in infants [Col. 0864], which Cicero also mentions in his books *On the Republic*, from which I have already translated his very words (*above*, book 4, chapter 12). In recalling these evils, he says that “the human being has been cast into these hardships not by mother Nature, but as though by a stepmother.”

To these are added the many and varied evils [Note: [Col. 0864] Two Vatican manuscripts read “and grave.”] that we see not all infants, but nevertheless very many, undergo, even to attacks by demons. And they conclude by saying: Since God is just and almighty, from where do these evils afflict his image in infants, unless—so they say—the truth of what we assert is established: the commixture of two natures, namely, good and evil?

Catholic truth refutes them by confessing original sin, through which the human race was made a sport for demons and the offspring of mortals was destined for laborious misery. It would not be so if human nature had remained in the condition in which it was first created through free will.

But you, by denying original sin, will certainly be compelled either to say that God is powerless or unjust, under whose authority his image in infants is afflicted with such great evils without any merit of either personal or original sin—for one cannot rightly say that virtue is exercised through these things, as one can rightly say of mature good people, in whom reason is operative—or, since you cannot call God either powerless or unjust, the Manichaeans will establish their wicked error against you concerning the commixture of two mutually hostile substances.

Therefore “no herb of the fuller,” as you say, “cleanses me from the contamination of the Manichaeans” [Note: [Col. 0864] The printed editions read “any”; several manuscripts more correctly read “no.”]. By these insolent words you insult the washing of regeneration, which I received in the bosom of the Catholic mother. But the malicious poison of the ancient dragon has penetrated you so deeply that you both defame Catholics through the horror attached to the name of Manichaean and assist the Manichaeans by the perversity of your doctrine.

## CHAPTER XXII [Note: [Col. 0864] Ambrose and Erasmus number this as chapter 10.]

68. As for that passage from another of my books, where, writing to Marcellinus, I said, “The children of the woman who believed the serpent, so that she might be corrupted by lust, are not freed except through the Son of the Virgin, who believed the angel, so that she might conceive without lust” (*On the Merits and Remission of Sins*, book 1, chapter 28), you quoted and wished it to be understood as though I had said “that the serpent had intercourse with Eve through bodily copulation,” just as the Manichaeans in their madness claim that the prince of darkness had intercourse with that woman and was her father.

I did not say this about the serpent. But do you deny, contrary to the Apostle, that the woman’s mind was corrupted by the serpent? Or do you not hear him when he says, “I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity and chastity that is in Christ” (2 Cor. 11:3)?

From this corruption by the serpent—of the kind that also occurs when evil conversations corrupt good morals (1 Cor. 15:33)—the lust of sinning certainly reached the woman’s mind [Note: [Col. 0864] Most manuscripts read “arose” (*provenit*).]. Then, when the man too had been corrupted by transgression, that lust followed into the flesh [Note: [Col. 0864] The printed editions read, uncertainly, “into the mind of the woman and the man; so that the corruption of transgression thereafter that.” All Vatican and Gallican manuscripts read: “into the woman’s mind; and, when the man too had been corrupted by transgression, then that”—supply “lust.”], from which they blushed and covered their shameful parts [Col. 0865], not because the devil approached through bodily intercourse, but because spiritual grace departed.

69. [Note: [Col. 0865] Ambrose and Erasmus number this as chapter 11.] Therefore, as you boast, you have not “crushed throughout your whole discussion my assertion concerning the evil of carnal concupiscence and original sin,” while the praise of marriage remains—marriage that makes good use of evil, not of what it made, but of what it found.

Nor have you crushed the Manichaeans themselves; rather, you have assisted them, especially you, and all who share in the common error and novelty of the Pelagians, as I have already demonstrated.

As for the testimonies of the Catholic interpreters, Saint Basil of Caesarea and Saint John of Constantinople, whose meaning you said agreed with your opinions, I answered you with fully sufficient and certain truth in the first book of this work (chapters 5 and 6), showing how, by failing to understand certain words of theirs, you fight with remarkable blindness against their doctrine, which is Catholic doctrine.

In the second book as well we dealt sufficiently with the matter to make it clear that there is no, as you insultingly claim, “conspiracy of the lost” (*above*, book 1, chapter 7), but rather the pious and faithful consensus of the holy and learned fathers of the Catholic Church, who resist your heretical novelty on behalf of the most ancient Catholic truth.

Hence the “murmuring of the people,” which you say is “the only thing that we oppose to you,” is not the only consideration, since it rests on the authority of so many teachers; and it is just, because it does not wish you to overturn for them also the salvation of infants, which is so well known to them and is in Christ.

## CHAPTER XXIII

70. As for the apostolic words where he says, “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh,” and the rest up to the point where he says, “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?”—you affirm that I understand “me” differently from the way the entire chapter [Note: [Col. 0865] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “the whole passage.”] ought to be understood. In this you attribute very much to me, without knowing it.

For I was neither the only nor the first person to understand this passage in the way it truly ought to be understood—a way that overthrows your heresy. Indeed, at first I understood it differently, or rather did not understand it; certain writings of mine from that period also testify to this [Note: [Col. 0865] These writings are: the first book *To Simplicianus*, question 1; *Exposition of the Epistle to the Romans*, propositions 41 and 42; *Exposition of the Epistle to the Galatians*, chapter 5. He later followed the better interpretation in *On the Grace of Christ*, §43; the first book *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, §§17–25; the first book of the *Retractions*, chapters 23 and 24; the second book there, chapter 1; and *Against Julian*, book 2, chapter 3 above.].

It did not seem to me that the Apostle could say of himself, “But I am carnal,” since he was spiritual; nor that he was being taken captive under the law of sin, which was in his members (Rom. 7:14, 18–24). For I thought that these things could be said only of those whom the concupiscence of the flesh had so subjugated that they did whatever it compelled them to do; and it is madness to believe this of the Apostle, since an innumerable multitude of holy people also desire in spirit against the flesh so as not to fulfill the desires of the flesh.

But later I yielded to better and more discerning interpreters—or rather, as must be acknowledged, to the truth itself—so that I could see in those words of the Apostle [Col. 0866] the groaning of holy people who struggle against carnal concupiscences. Although they are spiritual in mind, they are still rightly understood to be carnal because of this corruptible body, which weighs down the soul (Wis. 9:15); they will also be spiritual in body when the animal body has been sown and the spiritual body rises (1 Cor. 15:44) [Note: [Col. 0866] Four Vatican manuscripts read “who.” The printed editions shortly thereafter read “when the animal body has been sown and the spiritual body will rise.” The reading has been corrected from Gallican and Vatican manuscripts.].

They are also rightly understood still to be captive under the law of sin in that part of them which is subject to the movements of desires to which they do not consent. This is why I came to understand these words as Hilary, Gregory, Ambrose, and the other holy and renowned teachers of the Church understood them: they believed that the Apostle himself had vigorously fought against the carnal concupiscences that he did not wish to have but nevertheless had, and that he had testified to this very struggle in those words of his (*above*, book 2, chapters 3 and 4).

Against these movements, first to be subdued lest they dominate, and afterward to be healed so that they may be utterly extinguished, you yourself also confessed that the saints wage glorious battles (*above*, book 3, chapter 21).

Let us therefore recognize together the words of those who are fighting, if we are fighting. For in this way we do not live, but Christ lives in us, if we trust in him rather than in ourselves both to undertake the battle against concupiscences and to attain victory until those enemies have been destroyed. For he himself has become for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, so that, as it is written, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:30–31).

71. It is therefore not “contrary,” as you think, for one who says, “I live, yet it is no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2:20), also to say, “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh.”

For insofar as Christ lives in him, he conquers and overcomes that condition in which good does not dwell in his flesh, but evil does. No one’s spirit would rightly desire against his flesh unless the Spirit of Christ dwelled in him.

Far be it from us, then, to say what you falsely accuse us of saying: “The Apostle spoke these words as though he wished it to be understood that he was being dragged, against his will, into some brothel by the hand of pestilential pleasure.” For he says, “It is not I who do it” (Rom. 7:18, 20), showing that the concupiscences of the flesh produce only the impulse of desire, without consent to sin.

72. Why do you vainly attempt to transfer these words “to the pride of the Jews,” as though the Apostle had transformed himself into them, since they despised Christ’s gifts as though they were unnecessary for them? This is what you suppose. Would that you at least understood Christ’s gifts in such a way as to believe that they have some power to conquer concupiscence.

But you say that the Jews despised them because “he would grant forgiveness for sins that they had avoided through the admonition of the law.” As though forgiveness of sins conferred this upon a human being: that the flesh should not desire against the spirit (Gal. 5:17), which is the source of those words, “I know that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh,” and the rest of this kind.

But you do not depart from your doctrine, according to which you think that the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord operates only in the forgiveness of sins, so that it does not help in avoiding sins and overcoming carnal desires by pouring charity into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to us by him (Rom. 5:5).

Nor do you consider that the one who says, “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind,” and cries out that he is freed from this evil only by the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, is neither a Jew nor struggling because he has sinned, but rather struggling so that he may not sin.

73. “The Apostle exaggerates [Note: [Col. 0867] Three manuscripts read this way. Others, with the printed editions, read “exasperates.”],” you say, “the force of habit.” Then answer whether a baptized person does not fight against this force. If you deny it, you contradict the understanding of all Christians; but if he does fight, why do you not recognize in the Apostle’s words the voice of one who is fighting?

“Through the good law,” you say, “and through the holy commandment, the minds of the wicked had become fiercer” [Note: [Col. 0867] Two Vatican manuscripts read: “You say, ‘In place of the good law and in place of the holy commandment the minds of the wicked were fierce.’” Three other Vatican manuscripts read “were ferocious.” Gallican manuscripts read “were fierce.” The printed editions read “were savage.”], “because without the individual will no instruction could inspire virtue.”

O acute interpreter! O outstanding expositor of divine utterances! What do you make of the words that say, “I do not do what I want”; “To will is present with me”; “What I do not want, that I do”; and “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person”? You hear these things and say that, because the will was absent, virtue was absent.

What is more, not only was the will present, but virtue too was present, so that he would not consent to the concupiscence of the flesh, which in its perverse movements served the law of sin [Note: [Col. 0867] Ambrose and several manuscripts read “the law.”]. He did not yield to these movements or present his members as weapons of unrighteousness to sin (Rom. 6:13), yet he felt in his flesh a desire against the spirit, while in turn desiring against it in spirit; and with the truest voice of chastity he said, “Therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin.”

Those words that you quoted, where the Apostle says, “The law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good. Therefore did that which is good become death to me? By no means! But sin, so that it might appear as sin, through that which is good worked death in me, so that through the commandment sin might become exceedingly sinful”—these are rightly understood as having been spoken about his past life, when he had been under the law, not yet under grace.

For he also uses verbs in the past tense, saying, “I did not know sin except through the law”; “I did not know concupiscence”; “It worked in me every concupiscence”; “I was once alive without the law”—namely, when he was not yet able to exercise reason; “When the commandment came, sin revived, but I died”; “Sin, having taken an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me”; and “Through that which is good it worked death in me.”

Through all these statements he is understood to indicate the time when he lived under the law and, not yet assisted by grace, was conquered by carnal concupiscences [Note: [Col. 0867] Thus five Vatican manuscripts and several Gallican manuscripts. The printed editions read “was bound” [Col. 0868].].

But when he says, “The law is spiritual, but I am carnal,” he now shows what he suffered while fighting. For he did not say, “I was carnal” or “I used to be,” but “I am.” And he distinguishes the times still more clearly when he says, “But now it is no longer I who do it, but sin dwelling in me.”

For the movements of evil desires were no longer performed by him, since he did not consent to them in order to commit sins. By the name “sin” he called the concupiscence itself that dwelled in him, because it was made by sin; and if it draws and entices one who consents, it conceives and gives birth to sin.

Everything else up to the passage where he says, “Therefore I myself serve the law of God with my mind, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Rom. 7:7–25), consists of words of one who is already under grace but is still fighting against his concupiscence and does not consent to it so as to sin, yet nevertheless experiences the desires of sin against which he struggles.

74. None of us accuses the substance of the body; none of us accuses the nature of the flesh. You vainly cleanse what we do not accuse. We do not deny that evil concupiscences exist within us, although, if we live rightly, we do not consent to them. They must be disciplined, restrained, attacked, and conquered; nevertheless, they exist, and they are not foreign to us.

Nor are these things good of ours; they are evil. Nor, as Manichaean vanity claimed, will they be separated and remain outside us; rather, as Catholic truth says, they will not remain unhealed.

## CHAPTER XXIV [Note: [Col. 0868] Ambrose and Erasmus number this as chapter 12.]

75. As for those apostolic words against which you resist the most firmly established faith with astonishing shamelessness—or rather, madness—where he says, “Through one human being sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and thus it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Rom. 5:12), you vainly attempt to carve out another new and distorted meaning that departs from the truth, asserting that the expression “in whom all sinned” means “because of which all sinned,” just as it is said, “In which the younger [Note: [Col. 0868] The manuscripts consistently read “the younger.”] corrects his way” (Ps. 118:9).

Thus, you claim, all human beings are not understood to have sinned originally in one human being, as though commonly in the unity of one mass, but rather because that first human being sinned; that is, they sinned when they imitated him, not when they were begotten from him. [Note: [Col. 0868] The Casalensis manuscript reads: “because that first human being sinned, the others sinned; that is…”]

But the expression “in whom,” understood as though it meant “because of which,” does not fit this meaning. For each person sins because he proposes sin to himself, or because of whatever is the cause of his sinning. Who, however, could be so absurd, contrary to all human understanding, as to say: “This man committed murder because Adam in paradise ate from the forbidden tree,” when this man killed another by robbery, thinking nothing of Adam, but doing so in order to take the gold that the other carried?

In the same way, all the other sins that each person commits individually have causes for which they are committed, even if no one thinks about what that first human being committed or proposes it to himself as an example for sinning. Therefore Cain too is not to be said to have sinned because Adam sinned, even though he knew that same father of his. [Col. 0869] For it is known why he killed his brother: not because of what Adam had perpetrated, but because he envied his brother’s goodness.

76. Finally, the testimonies you cited do not support you even in this meaning of yours. It is rightly said, “In which the younger corrects his way.” “Because of what does he correct it?” Because the text continues, “by keeping your words.” He corrects his way for this reason: because he thinks about God’s words as they ought to be thought about, and by thinking about them he keeps them; by keeping them he lives rightly. The very cause of his correcting his way is therefore that he keeps God’s words.

And what blessed Stephen says, “Moses fled because of this word” (Acts 7:29), is rightly understood as “because of this word,” since he heard this, feared this, and thought about this as the reason for fleeing; this was his reason for fleeing.

Has anything been said in these expressions that pertains to imitation, by which one person imitates another without thinking of him at all, so that it could in no way be said that he sinned because the other sinned—since he was neither originally in that other person nor thought of anything concerning him in his own sin?

77. “But,” you say, “if he was speaking of the transmission of sin, he could have said nowhere more appropriately, ‘Therefore sin passed over because all are begotten from the sexual pleasure of married couples’; and he could have added, ‘It passed over in him, from whose diseased flesh it flowed.’”

You do not see that the same thing could be said to you in this way: If the Apostle was speaking of the imitation of sin, he could have said nowhere more appropriately, “Therefore sin passed over because the example of the first human being preceded”; and he could have added, “It passed over in him, in whose imitation all sinned.”

The Apostle would have spoken in one of these two ways in this passage if he had been speaking according to your choice or mine. Since he said neither what you say nor what I say, do you want us to believe that in these words of his sin is to be understood neither as original, according to the Catholics, nor as imitative, according to the Pelagians? I think you do not.

Remove, therefore, these claims that can be made with equal force on either side, and, if you are willing to consider without contention what the Apostle said, observe what he was doing in order to say it. You will find that through one human being there came the wrath of God upon the human race, and through one human being reconciliation with God for those who are freely delivered from the condemnation of the whole race.

The one is the first Adam, made from the earth; the other is the second Adam, made from a woman. In the first case flesh was made through the Word; in the second, the Word itself was made flesh, so that we might live through his death, having died by abandoning him.

“God demonstrates,” he says, “his love for us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him” (Rom. 5:8–9).

78. Concerning this wrath he says, “We too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3).

Concerning this wrath the prophet Jeremiah says, “Cursed be the day on which I was born” (Jer. 20:14).

Concerning this wrath the holy Job says, “May the day perish on which I was born” (Job 3:3).

The same man also says concerning it: “For a human being born of woman is short-lived and full of wrath; like a flower of grass he withers, and he flees like a shadow and does not remain. And have you not cared for him, and have you brought him into your presence for judgment? For who will be clean from defilement? Not even one” [Note: [Col. 0870] Three Vatican manuscripts and several Gallican manuscripts read “Not even an infant.”], “even if his life upon the earth should be but one day” (Job 14:1–5, according to the Septuagint).

Concerning this wrath the book of Ecclesiasticus says, “All flesh grows old like a garment; for the covenant is from of old: ‘You shall surely die’” (Sir. 14:18, 12).

The same book also says: “From a woman sin had its beginning, and because of her we all die” (Sir. 25:33).

And elsewhere: “A great occupation has been created for every human being, and a heavy yoke upon the children of Adam, from the day of their departure from their mother’s womb until the day of burial in the mother of all” (Sir. 40:1).

Concerning this wrath Ecclesiastes says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity. What abundance is there for a human being in all his labor with which he labors under the sun?” (Eccles. 1:2–3) [Note: [Col. 0870] The printed editions read “of a human being.” The manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek, read “for a human being.”]

The apostolic voice concerning this wrath says, “Every creature has been subjected to vanity” (Rom. 8:20).

Concerning this wrath the Psalm laments [Note: [Col. 0870] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read “the Psalmist”]: “Behold, you have made my days old, and my substance is as nothing before you; nevertheless every living human being is altogether vanity” (Ps. 38:6).

Another Psalm also laments: “Their years shall be as nothing. In the morning let it pass away like grass; in the morning let it bloom and pass away; in the evening let it fall, grow hard, and wither. For we have failed in your wrath, and in your indignation we have been troubled. You have set our iniquities before you, our age in the illumination of your face. For all our days have failed, and in your wrath we have failed. Our years shall meditate like a spider” (Ps. 89:5–9).

79. No one is freed [Note: [Col. 0870] The printed editions read “will be freed.”] from this wrath of God unless, through the Mediator, he is reconciled to God. Hence the Mediator himself also says, “Whoever does not believe the Son will not have life, but the wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3:36). He did not say, “It will come,” but “It remains upon him.”

Therefore adults believe and confess through their own heart and mouth, and infants through another’s, so that they may be reconciled to God through the death of his Son, lest the wrath of God remain upon them, whom their corrupted origin also makes guilty.

Speaking of this matter [Note: [Col. 0870] Here “matter” is added from the manuscripts.], the Apostle says: “While we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Much more, now justified by his blood, we shall be saved from wrath through him. For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, we shall be saved by his life. And not only this, but we also glory in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.”

“For this reason, just as through one human being sin entered this world, and through sin, death, and thus passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned.”

It is plainly evident what the Apostle was doing in order to say this. Go further, then, and remove infants from this reconciliation, which takes place through the death of the Son of God, who came into the world without sin; and the wrath of God will remain upon them on account of the one through whom sin entered the world.

What role does imitation play here, I ask you, when you hear: “Judgment indeed came from one transgression to condemnation, but grace came from many transgressions to justification” (Rom. 5:8–12, 16)? From where does grace come from many transgressions to justification, unless, in addition to that one original transgression, it found many others added, which it might together erase?

Otherwise, there would be condemnation from the many transgressions that human beings committed by imitating the one, just as there would be justification from those same many transgressions, once they had been forgiven and the people had drawn breath again into grace.
