But because that one transgression was sufficient to bring condemnation by itself, whereas grace was not sufficient merely to erase that one transgression, but also the many that had been added [Note: [Col. 0871] Four Vatican manuscripts read, “grace indeed was not sufficient only.”], so that justification might take place through the remission of all, it was therefore said: “Judgment came from one transgression to condemnation, but grace came from many transgressions to justification.”

For just as infants do not imitate Christ, since they are not yet able to do so, and yet can belong to his spiritual grace, so without imitating the first human being they are nevertheless bound by contagion from him through carnal generation.

But if you wish them to be alien from the sin of the first human being on the grounds that they did not imitate him by their own will, then by the same reasoning you will alienate them also from the righteousness of Christ, because they did not imitate him by their own will either.

80. But if, when he later said “many,” you do not wish it to be understood as “all,” when earlier he had said “all”—“therefore, thinking that ‘many’ was said so that ‘all’ would not be understood”—you could say the same about Abraham’s offspring, to whom all the nations were promised (Gen. 22:18): that not all nations were promised to him, because elsewhere it is said, “I have made you the father of many nations” (ibid. 17:5). A sound understanding is, rather, that Scripture spoke in this way because some things may be “all” without being “many,” as when we speak of all the Gospels, although they are contained in a small number, namely four. Conversely, some things may be “many” without being “all,” as when we say that many believe in Christ, although not all believe. “For faith is not possessed by all,” says the Apostle (2 Thess. 3:2). But when it is said, “In your offspring all nations shall be blessed,” and, “I have made you the father of many nations,” it has been shown that these same nations are both “all” and “many,” and that the same “many” are “all.” Likewise, when it is said, “Through one sin passed into all,” and later, “Through one man’s disobedience many were constituted sinners” (Rom. 5:12, 18, 19), these “many” are the same as “all.” Similarly, when it is said, “Through one justification unto all men for justification of life,” and again, “Through one man’s obedience many will be constituted righteous” (Rom. 5:18–19), “all” must be understood as the same “many,” not with some excepted—not because all human beings are justified in Christ, but because all who are justified can be justified in no other way than in Christ. Thus we may say that all enter a certain house through one door—not because all human beings enter that same house, but because no one enters except through that door. Therefore, all are brought to death through Adam, and all to life through Christ. “For just as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:22): that is, from the first origin of the human race, no one comes to death except through Adam, and no one comes through Adam except to death; and no one comes to life except through Christ, and no one comes through Christ except to life.

81. But while you wish it to be understood that not all, but only many, were condemned through Adam or liberated through Christ, you are, with horrifying perversity, hostile to the Christian religion. For if some will be saved without Christ, and some justified without Christ, then Christ died for nothing. There was, as you would have it, another way—in nature, in free will, in the natural or written law—by which those who wished could be saved and righteous. And who but an unjust person would prevent righteous images of God from entering the kingdom of God? Perhaps you say: “But it is easier through Christ.” Could one not also say of the law: “There is righteousness through the law, but it is easier through Christ”? Yet the Apostle says, “If righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Gal. 2:21).

There is, therefore, besides the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5), no other name under heaven by which we must be saved (Acts 4:12). For this reason it was said, “In Christ all will be made alive”: because in him God has established faith for all, raising him from the dead (ibid. 17:31). But your doctrine attempts to persuade people that, through the unblemished preaching of nature, the power of free will, and the law—whether natural or given through Moses—it is possible, if necessary, but not actually necessary, to turn to Christ for eternal salvation; since, according to it, the sacrament of his death and resurrection—if indeed you even hold that—provides a more convenient way, not a way without which no other way can exist. Therefore, when Christians consider how greatly they ought to detest you, let them renounce you even while we remain silent. [Note: [Col. 0872] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “they renounce.”]

## CHAPTER XXV

82. As for the prophetic testimony which you wished to make the final and, as it were, strongest support of your case, where we read that it was said through Ezekiel that the proverb would no longer be used in which they said, “The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth have been set on edge” [Note: [Col. 0872] The manuscripts read *obstipuisse*; below, *obstipuerunt*.], and that “the son shall not die for the sin of the father, nor the father for the sin of the son, but the soul that sins shall itself die” [Note: [Col. 0872] Three manuscripts read “the soul that has sinned.”] (Ezek. 18:2–4), you do not understand that this is a promise of the New Testament and of the spiritual inheritance belonging to the age to come. For the grace of the Redeemer effects this: that he erases the father’s bond (Col. 2:14), and that each person gives an account for himself.

Otherwise, who could count how many testimonies there are in the divine Scriptures that bind children because of the sins of their parents? Why did Ham sin, and was vengeance inflicted upon his son Canaan (Gen. 9:22, 24–25)? Why was Solomon’s son punished for Solomon’s sin by the diminution of the kingdom (1 Kings 12)? Why was the punishment for the sins of Ahab, king of Israel, deferred to his descendants (ibid. 21)? Why do we read in the holy Books, “Repaying the sins of the fathers into the bosom of their children after them” (Jer. 32:18), and, “Repaying the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation” (Exod. 20:5)? This number, too, may be understood as referring to the whole. Are these statements false? Who would say so except the most blatant enemy of the divine utterances?

But carnal generation—even that of the people of God belonging to the Old Testament, which “generates into slavery” (Gal. 4:24)—binds children because of the sins of their parents. Spiritual generation [Note: [Col. 0873] The Louvain edition reads “regeneration.”], however, has changed both the inheritance and the threats and promises of punishments and rewards. The Prophets foresaw these things in the Spirit and spoke accordingly. Jeremiah, however, spoke more plainly:

“In those days,” he says, “they shall no longer say, ‘The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the children’s teeth have been set on edge’; but each person shall die in his own sin, and whoever has eaten the sour grape, his own teeth shall be set on edge” [Note: [Col. 0873] The manuscripts read “shall be set on edge,” or “shall be numbed.”] (Jer. 31:29–30).

It is plainly evident that this was prophetically proclaimed in the same manner as the New Testament itself, which had previously been hidden and was afterward revealed through Christ. Finally, lest the things I have mentioned—and many others of the same kind concerning the repayment of parents’ sins upon their children, things certainly written truthfully—move us or appear contrary to this prophecy [Note: [Col. 0873] The printed editions read “lest”; corrected from the manuscripts.], he immediately resolves this most troublesome question by joining these words to it:

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant which I established with their fathers” (Jer. 31:31–32).

In this New Testament, therefore, through the blood of the testator, the father’s bond having been erased [Note: Am. Er. and six manuscripts read “through the blood of the mediator.”], a person begins, by being reborn, not to be liable for his fathers’ debts, to which he had been bound by being born. The Mediator himself says, “Do not call anyone your father on earth” (Matt. 23:9)—understood, of course, in the sense that we have found another birth, by which we do not succeed to the father but live forever with the Father.

## CHAPTER XXVI

83. I think, Julianus, that you perceive—if you are not obstinate—that I have answered all your arguments and refuted everything which, in the four books you composed, you thought and argued should be believed: namely, that original sin does not exist and that the concupiscence of the flesh cannot be blamed without condemning marriage. [Note: [Col. 0873] The Louvain edition omits “you thought and”; Am. and Er. read “you thought,” but omit “and argued.”]

It has been demonstrated that no one is free from the ancient paternal debt except the one who has changed both his inheritance and his father: he finds, by nature, one fellow heir, while he himself is adopted by grace. Likewise, carnal concupiscence does not bring death after death except to the one who has found death in Christ’s death—the death by which he dies to sin—and has escaped the death in which he was born through sin.

“For one died for all; therefore all died” (2 Cor. 5:14); and he died for all [Note: The Louvain editors deleted “and he died for all.” Nevertheless, it is found in the Gallican and Vatican manuscripts.]. No one for whom he did not die will be able to live, for he who is alive died for the dead [Note: So the manuscripts of better quality. The printed editions, however, read, “because one died for the dead.” See above, book 1, chapter 48.].

While denying these things, resisting them, attempting to tear down the defenses of the Catholic faith and to sever the very sinews of the Christian religion and true piety, you dare moreover to say that you have undertaken wars against the impious, when you arm yourself with the weapons of impiety against the mother who spiritually gave birth to you.

You dare to join yourself to the ranks of the holy Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, martyrs, and priests, while the Patriarchs say to you that sacrifices were offered for sins even on behalf of newly born infants (Lev. 12), because “no one is clean from impurity, not even an infant whose life is but one day upon the earth” (Job 14:4–5, according to the Septuagint); while the Prophets say to you, “We were conceived in iniquities” (Ps. 50:7); while the Apostles say to you, “All of us who were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death,” so that we should consider ourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus (Rom. 6:3, 11); while the martyrs say to you that those born carnally according to Adam contract the contagion of the ancient death through their first birth, from which infants are released in Baptism—not from their own sins, but from the sins of another (Cyprian, Letter 64, to Fidus; see above, book 1, chapter 3); while the priests say to you that those formed through carnal pleasure undergo the contagion of sins before they draw the gift of this life (Ambrose, On the Sacrament of Regeneration; see above, book 2, chapter 6).

You presume to associate yourself [Note: [Col. 0874] Am., Er., and the manuscripts read “to be associated.”] with those whose faith you are attempting to defeat. You dare to say that you are victorious over the company of the Manichaeans, though you make the Manichaeans invincible unless you yourself are defeated along with them.

You are deceived, my son—miserably deceived, or rather, detestably deceived. When you have overcome the arrogance by which you are held, then you will be able to hold the truth by which you are overcome.

# [ON GRACE AND FREE WILL]

[Col. 0875]

[Note: [Col. 0873] “FOR THE FOLLOWING BOOK.” See book 2, chapter 66 of the *Retractations*, vol. 1, col. 656, from the words “Because of those who” up to the words “human free will,” where Augustine says that he wrote the book *On Grace and Free Will* for the monks of Hadrumetum. [Note: [Col. 0873] Hadrumetum was a coastal city of Africa and the capital of the province of Byzacena, as Procopius writes in book 6 of *The Buildings of Justinian*. A monastery was inhabited there by those monks for whose benefit Augustine composed the two following books: the former, *On Grace and Free Will*, and the latter, *On Rebuke and Grace*, in the year of Christ 426 or 427. We do not think these books can be placed later than that date, because they are mentioned in the *Retractations*, composed around 427; nor earlier, because they occupy the final place there.]] M.]

TWO LETTERS OF AUGUSTINE TO VALENTINUS AND THE MONKS OF HADRUMETUM WITH HIM, SENT TOGETHER WITH THE FOLLOWING BOOK [Note: [Col. 0875] See the later letter, no. 2.]

## THE FIRST LETTER, NO. CCXIV AMONG THE AUGUSTINIAN LETTERS

To the most beloved lord and brother VALENTINUS, honored among the members of Christ, and to the brothers who are with you, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

Two young men, Cresconius and Felix, came to us, saying that they belonged to your community. They reported to us that your monastery had been disturbed by some disagreement, because certain among you preach grace in such a way as to deny that human beings possess free will; and, what is more serious, say that on the day of judgment God will not repay each person according to his works (Matt. 16:27; Rom. 2:6).

They also indicated that many among you do not hold this view, but acknowledge that free will is assisted by God’s grace, so that we may think and do what is right; and that when the Lord comes to repay each person according to his works, he may find our works good—works which God prepared so that we might walk in them (Eph. 2:10). Those who hold this view hold it rightly.

### 2

Therefore, brothers, I beseech you—as the Apostle beseeched the Corinthians—by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing and that there be no divisions among you (1 Cor. 1:10).

First, the Lord Jesus, as it is written in the Gospel of the apostle John, did not come to judge the world but so that the world might be saved through him (John 3:17). Later, however, as the apostle Paul writes, God will judge the world (Rom. 3:6), when he comes—as the whole Church confesses in the Creed—to judge the living and the dead.

If, then, God’s grace does not exist, how does he save the world? And if free will does not exist, how does he judge the world? Accordingly, understand my book or letter, which the aforementioned men brought with them to us, according to this faith: neither deny God’s grace, nor defend free will in such a way as to separate it from God’s grace, as though without grace we could in any way either think or do anything according to God—which we absolutely cannot do.

For this reason, when the Lord was speaking of the fruit of righteousness, he said to his disciples, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

### 3

You should know, therefore, that the aforementioned letter to Sixtus, a presbyter of the Roman Church [Note: [Col. 0875] Letter 194 among the Augustinian letters.], was written against the new Pelagian heretics. They say that God’s grace is given according to our merits, so that whoever boasts may boast not in the Lord but in himself—that is, in a human being and not in the Lord.

The Apostle forbids this, saying, “Let no one boast in a human being” (1 Cor. 3:21). And elsewhere he says, “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (ibid. 1:31). But those heretics, thinking that they make themselves righteous by themselves, as though God had not given this to them but they had given it to themselves, boast not in the Lord but in themselves.

To such people the Apostle says, “For who makes you different?” (ibid. 4:7). He says this because, from that mass of perdition which was made from Adam, no one distinguishes a human being so as to make him a vessel for honor rather than dishonor except God.

But because a carnal and vainly inflated person, upon hearing “Who makes you different?” might answer either aloud or in thought, “My faith makes me different; my prayer makes me different; my righteousness makes me different,” the Apostle immediately confronts his thoughts and says, “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (ibid. 4:7).

Those who think that they are justified by themselves boast as though they had not received these things; and therefore they boast in themselves, not in the Lord.

### 4

For this reason, in the letter which reached you, I proved through the testimonies of the holy Scriptures—which you can examine there—that our good works, devout prayers, and right faith could in no way exist in us unless we received them from him of whom the apostle James says, “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17).

This was so that no one might say that God’s grace had been given to him because of the merits of his works, or of his prayers, or of his faith, and so that what those heretics say might not be thought true—namely, that God’s grace is given according to our merits. This is utterly false—not because there is no merit, whether the good merit of the devout or the evil merit of the impious; otherwise, how would God judge the world? Rather, God’s mercy and grace convert a human being. Of this the Psalm says, “My God, his mercy will precede me” (Ps. 58:11), so that the impious person may be justified—that is, may be made righteous from being impious—and may begin to possess good merit, which the Lord will crown when the world is judged.

### 5

There was much that I wished to send you, which, once read, would have enabled you to know more carefully and fully the entire case conducted in episcopal councils against those same Pelagian heretics. But the brothers who came to us from your number hastened; through them we did not write a reply to you about these matters, but wrote to you directly.

They brought no letter from your Charity to us. Nevertheless, we received them, since their simplicity sufficiently showed that they could not have fabricated anything for us. They hastened so that they might celebrate Easter among you, in order that, with the Lord’s help, this holy day might find your peace rather than your dissension.

[Col. 0877]

### 6

You will do better—and this I earnestly ask—if you do not hesitate to send me the very man by whom they say they were disturbed. Either he does not understand my book, or perhaps he himself is not understood when he attempts to resolve and untangle a most difficult question, one intelligible to only a few.

This is the question concerning the grace of God, which caused people who did not understand it to think that the apostle Paul was saying, “Let us do evil so that good may come” (Rom. 3:8). Therefore the apostle Peter says in his Second Letter:

“Therefore, beloved, while you await these things, make every effort to be found by him undefiled and unblemished, in peace; and regard the patience of our Lord as salvation, just as our most beloved brother Paul, according to the wisdom given to him, wrote to you, speaking of these things in all his Letters. In them are some things difficult to understand, which the ignorant and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction” (2 Pet. 3:14–16).

### 7

Beware, therefore, of what so great an Apostle says with such terror. And when you perceive that you do not understand something, for the time being believe the divine utterances, because both human free will exists and God’s grace exists, without whose assistance free will can neither turn toward God nor make progress in God.

Pray that what you devoutly believe you may also understand wisely. For free will itself exists for this purpose as well—that is, so that we may understand wisely. If we did not understand and possess wisdom through free will, Scripture would not command us, saying, “Understand, you who are foolish among the people, and become wise at last, you fools” (Ps. 93:8).

By the very fact that we are commanded and ordered to understand and become wise, our obedience is required; and obedience cannot exist without free will. But if this could be done through free will without the assistance of God’s grace—so that we might understand and become wise—then it would not be said to God, “Give me understanding, and I shall learn your commandments” (Ps. 118:125); nor would it be written in the Gospel, “Then he opened their minds so that they might understand the Scriptures” (Luke 24:45); nor would the apostle James say, “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach anyone, and it will be given to him” (James 1:5).

The Lord is powerful, and may he grant both you and us that we may rejoice through the swiftest messengers at news of your peace and devout harmony. I greet you not only in my own name but also in the name of the brothers who are with me, and I ask you to pray for us together and earnestly. May the Lord be with you.

## THE LATER LETTER, NO. CCXV AMONG THE AUGUSTINIAN LETTERS

To the most beloved lord and brother VALENTINUS, honored among the members of Christ, and to the brothers who are with you, AUGUSTINE sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

Your Charity should know that Cresconius, Felix, and another Felix, servants of God who came to us from your community, celebrated Easter with us. We kept them somewhat longer so that they might return to you better instructed against the new Pelagian heretics.

Anyone who thinks that God’s grace—which alone liberates a human being through our Lord Jesus Christ—is given according to certain human merits falls into their error. But anyone who thinks that, when the Lord comes for judgment, a person who by reason of age was already able to use free will will not be judged according to his works is likewise in error.

Only infants, who do not yet have their own works, whether good or evil, will be condemned according to original sin alone, if the grace of the Savior does not come to their aid through the bath of regeneration. All the rest, who, once using free will, have added their own sins to original sin, will receive judgment according not only to the merits of their origin but also to the merits of their own will, unless they are rescued by God’s grace from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of Christ.

The good, too, will obtain a reward according to the merits of their good will; but they have also obtained that good will itself through God’s grace. Thus what is written is fulfilled:

“Wrath and indignation, tribulation and distress upon every soul of a human being who works evil, of the Jew first and also of the Greek; but glory, honor, and peace to everyone who works good, to the Jew first and also to the Greek” (Rom. 2:9–10).

### 2

I did not need to discuss at greater length in this letter that most difficult question—namely, the question of will and grace—because I had already given them another letter, as they were to return rather quickly. I also wrote for you a book [Note: [Col. 0877] The following book, *On Grace and Free Will*.]. If, with the Lord’s help, you read it carefully and understand it keenly, I think that no further disagreements among you on this matter will arise.

They also carry with them other materials which we thought should be sent to you, so that you may learn how the Catholic Church, by God’s mercy, drove back the poisons of the Pelagian heresy. These include what was written to Pope Innocent, bishop of the city of Rome, from the council of the province of Carthage, from the council of Numidia, and somewhat more carefully by five bishops, together with what he himself wrote in reply to those three documents; likewise, what was written to Pope Zosimus concerning the African council, and his reply sent to all the bishops of the entire world; also what we briefly established at the later plenary council of all Africa against that same error; and the book of mine mentioned above, which I have just written to you. We have now read all these things with them and have sent them to you through them.

### 3

We also read with them the book of the blessed martyr Cyprian, *On the Lord’s Prayer*, and showed how he taught that everything pertaining to our morals, by which we live rightly, must be asked from our Father who is in heaven, lest, presuming upon free will, we fall away from divine grace.

There we also demonstrated how that glorious Martyr admonished us to pray even for our enemies who have not yet believed in Christ, so that they may believe. This would certainly be done in vain unless the Church believed that even the evil and unbelieving wills of human beings can be converted to good through God’s grace.

But since they said that this book of Saint Cyprian is also present among you, we did not send it. We also read with them my letter to Sixtus, a presbyter of the Roman Church, which they had brought with them to us, and showed that it was written against those who say that God’s grace is given according to our merits—that is, against those same Pelagians.

### 4

Therefore, as far as we were able, we dealt with these brothers—both yours and ours—so that they might persevere in sound Catholic faith. That faith neither denies free will, whether toward an evil life or a good one, nor grants it so much power that it can accomplish anything without God’s grace: whether turning from evil to good, making persevering progress in the good, or reaching eternal good, where it no longer fears falling away.

You too, beloved, I exhort in this letter with the exhortation of the Apostle to all of us: not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think with sobriety, according as God has apportioned to each the measure of faith (Rom. 12:3).

### 5

Attend to what the Holy Spirit warns through Solomon:

“Make straight paths for your feet, and direct your ways; do not turn aside to the right or to the left, but turn your foot away from the evil way. For the ways that are on the right the Lord knows, but those on the left are crooked. He himself will make your paths straight, and he will lead your journeys forward in peace” (Prov. 4:26–27).

Consider in these words of holy Scripture, brothers, that if free will did not exist, it would not be said, “Make straight paths for your feet, and direct your ways; do not turn aside to the right or to the left.” Yet if this could be done without God’s grace, it would not subsequently be said, “He himself will make your paths straight, and he will lead your journeys forward in peace.”

### 6

Do not, therefore, turn aside to the right or to the left, although the ways on the right are praised and those on the left blamed. This is why he added, “Turn your foot away from the evil way,” that is, from the left. He makes this clear in what follows when he says, “For the ways that are on the right the Lord knows, but those on the left are crooked.”

We ought to walk in the ways that the Lord knows. Concerning them it is written in the Psalm, “The Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the impious will perish” (Ps. 1:6). He does not know this latter way because it is on the left, just as he will say to those placed on the left, “I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12; Luke 13:27).

But what does he not know, since he certainly knows everything, whether human beings’ good or evil deeds? What is “I do not know you” except “I did not make you such”? Likewise, when it is said of the Lord Jesus Christ himself that he did not know sin (2 Cor. 5:21), what does “did not know” mean except “did not make”? Accordingly, what does “The ways that are on the right the Lord knows” mean except that he himself made the ways on the right—that is, the ways of the righteous—which are certainly the good works that God prepared, as the Apostle says, so that we might walk in them (Eph. 2:10)?

He does not know the crooked ways on the left, that is, the ways of the impious, because he himself did not make them for human beings; rather, human beings made them for themselves. For this reason he says, “But I hated the crooked ways of the wicked”; these are the ways on the left.

### 7

But someone answers us: Why, then, did he say, “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left,” when it would rather seem that he should have said, “Keep to the right, and do not turn aside to the left,” if the ways on the right are good?

Why, we may ask, except because the ways on the right are good in such a way that turning toward the right is nevertheless not good? The person who turns to the right is to be understood as the one who wishes to assign to himself, rather than to God, the very good works belonging to the ways on the right.

Therefore, after saying, “For the ways that are on the right the Lord knows, but those on the left are crooked,” as though someone had said to him, “How, then, do you not want us to turn toward the right?” he continued by adding, “He himself will make your paths straight; he will lead your journeys forward in peace.”

Understand, then, what has been commanded you—“Make straight paths for your feet, and direct your ways”—in such a way that you know that, when you do this, it is granted to you by the Lord God that you do it. Then you will not turn toward the right, even though you walk in the ways on the right, because you do not trust in your own strength. Rather, he will be your strength, the one who will make your paths straight and lead your journeys forward in peace.

### 8

Therefore, beloved, whoever says, “My will is sufficient for me to perform good works,” turns toward the right. But those who think that a good life must be abandoned when they hear God’s grace preached in such a way that they believe and understand that grace itself makes human wills good from evil and preserves the wills it has made—and therefore say, “Let us do evil so that good may come” (Rom. 3:8)—turn toward the left.

For this reason he said to you, “Do not turn aside to the right or to the left”: that is, do not defend free will in such a way as to attribute good works to it without God’s grace; nor defend grace in such a way that, as though secure because of it, you love evil works. May God’s grace itself turn this away from you.

Putting before himself the words of such people, the Apostle says, “What shall we say? Shall we continue in sin so that grace may abound?” And he responds, as he ought, to the words of those who are in error and do not understand God’s grace: “By no means! For if we have died to sin, how shall we live in it?” (Rom. 6:1–2).

Nothing could be said more briefly or better. For what more useful thing does God’s grace provide for us in this present evil age than that we die to sin? Therefore the person who wishes to live in sin because of grace is found to be ungrateful to grace itself, through which we die to sin.

But may God, who is rich in mercy, grant you both sound understanding and the ability to remain continually and progressively in the good purpose until the end. Pray earnestly and vigilantly in fraternal peace for this—for you, for us, for all who love you, and for those who hate you. May you live for God. If I deserve anything from you, let brother Florus come to me.

[Col. 0881]

# SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO: ONE BOOK, *ON GRACE AND FREE WILL*, TO VALENTINUS AND THE MONKS WITH HIM

[Note: [Col. 0881] Written in the year of Christ 426 or 427.]

[Note: [Col. 0881] Several excellent copies of this work were collated for the preparation of this new edition: six from the Roman Vatican Library, fourteen Gallican manuscripts, one from the Royal Library, one from the Colbert Library, one from the Sorbonne, another from the Church of Reims, another from the distinguished man Nicolas Manessier, Doctor of Theology in Paris and member of the Sorbonne, two others from the Cistercian abbey, another from Corbie, written, as it appears, more than a thousand years ago, and the remaining copies from the monasteries of Pratellum, Jumièges, Bec, Mont-Saint-Michel, Casale, and Saint-Albinius of Angers. The variant readings of six Belgian codices preserved among the Louvain manuscripts were also examined, and the more celebrated editions of Am., Er., and Lov. were read through.]

[Note: [Col. 0881] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.] (C)

He teaches that care must be taken lest free will be defended by denying grace, or grace by denying free will. For the existence of free will in human beings is established by testimonies from the Scriptures; and the same Scriptures provide divine teachings concerning God’s grace, without which we can do nothing good.

He then proves against the Pelagians that grace is not given according to our merits. He explains how eternal life, which is repaid for good works, is truly grace. He next shows that neither knowledge of the law, nor nature, nor the mere remission of sins is that grace which is given through Jesus Christ our Lord; rather, grace itself causes the law to be fulfilled, nature to be liberated, and sin not to rule.

He defeats the empty refuge of the Pelagians, by which they say that, even if grace is not given according to the merits of good works, it is nevertheless given according to the merits of a good will that precedes it—the will of one who believes and prays.

He addresses the question of why God commands what he himself is going to give, and whether he commands some things that we cannot do. He proves that charity, without which the commandments are not fulfilled, exists in us only from God himself.

He shows that God works in human hearts to incline their wills wherever he wishes—toward good according to his mercy, or toward evil according to their merits—by a judgment that is sometimes manifest and sometimes hidden, but always just.

Finally, he supplies a clear example of gratuitous grace, granted without regard to merits, in those infants who are saved while others, having the same cause as they, perish.

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0881]

### 1

Because of those who so preach and defend human free will that they dare and attempt to remove God’s grace—by which we are called to him, liberated from our evil merits, and enabled to acquire good merits through which we may attain eternal life—we have already discussed and committed much to writing, as much as the Lord has deigned to grant us.

But because there are some who defend God’s grace in such a way as to deny human free will, or who think that, when grace is defended, free will is being denied, I have taken care, compelled by mutual charity, to write something about this to your Charity, brother Valentinus, and to the others who serve God together with you.

I have been informed about you, brothers, by certain people who belong to your congregation and came to us from there, through whom we have also sent these writings, that there are disagreements among you concerning this matter. Therefore, beloved, so that the obscurity of this question may not disturb you, I first urge you to give thanks to God for the things you understand.

Whatever it is that your mind’s attention cannot yet reach, pray to the Lord, while preserving peace and charity among yourselves, that you may understand it. And until he himself leads you to the things you do not yet understand, walk in the way to which you have been able to attain.

The apostle Paul gives this admonition. After saying that he was not yet perfect, he says shortly afterward, “Let all of us who are perfect think this way”—that is, that we are perfect in the sense that we have not yet reached the perfection sufficient for us. He immediately added, “And if you think differently about anything, God will reveal that also to you. Nevertheless, let us walk according to what we have attained” (Phil. 3:12–16).

By walking according to what we have attained, we will be able to reach what we have not yet attained, if God reveals to us anything in which we think differently—provided that we do not abandon the things he has already revealed.

## CHAPTER II
## 2.

But he revealed to us through his holy Scriptures that there is in human beings free choice of the will. How he revealed this, I shall recall to you—not in human language, but in divine language.

First, the divine commandments themselves would not benefit human beings unless they possessed free choice of the will, by which, through fulfilling them, they might attain the promised rewards. They were given for this reason: so that a person would not have the excuse of ignorance. Thus the Lord says in the Gospel concerning the Jews: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15:22). Of what sin does he speak, if not that great one which he knew would be theirs when he said this—that is, the sin by which they were going to kill him? For it is not the case that they had no sin before Christ came to them in the flesh.

The Apostle likewise says: “The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who suppress the truth in unrighteousness, because what can be known of God is manifest in them; for God has manifested it to them. For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are understood and perceived through the things that have been made; and also his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse” (Romans 1:18–20). [Col. 0883] How does he call them “without excuse,” unless he means that excuse with which human pride is accustomed to say, “If I had known, I would have done it; I did not do it because I did not know”? Or, “If I knew, I would do it; I do not do it because I do not know”? This excuse is removed from them when a commandment is given, or knowledge of what it means not to sin is made manifest.

## 3.

But there are people who even try to excuse themselves on God’s account. To them the apostle James says: “Let no one, when he is tempted, say, ‘I am being tempted by God’” [Note: [Col. 0883] More manuscripts read *tentatur*, “is being tempted.” The Greek is *peirazomai*, “I am being tempted.”]. “For God is not susceptible to temptation by evils, and he himself tempts no one. Rather, each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire. Then, when desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin; and sin, when it has been completed, produces death” (James 1:13–15).

To those who wish to excuse themselves on God’s account, the book of Solomon’s Proverbs also replies: “The folly of a man perverts his ways, and in his heart he blames God” (Proverbs 19:3).

And the book of Ecclesiasticus says:

“Do not say, ‘It was because of the Lord that I turned away’; for you must not do what he hates. Do not say, ‘He himself led me astray’; for he has no need of a sinful man. The Lord hates every abomination, and it is not lovable to those who fear him. He himself created human beings from the beginning, and left them in the hand of their own counsel. If you wish, you will keep the commandments, and [keep] good faithfulness in what is pleasing [reading uncertain]. He has set before you fire and water; stretch out your hand toward whichever you wish. Before a human being are life and death, and whichever pleases him will be given to him” (Ecclesiasticus 15:11–18).

Here we see most explicitly that free choice of the human will has been set forth.

## 4.

What of the fact that in so many passages God commands all his commandments to be kept and fulfilled? How does he command this, if there is no free choice? What of that blessed man of whom the Psalm says that “his delight was in the law of the Lord” (Psalm 1:2)? Does this not sufficiently indicate that a person stands in God’s law by his own will?

Furthermore, there are so many commandments that address the will itself by name, such as: “Do not be overcome by evil” (Romans 12:21); and others like it, such as: “Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 31:9); “Do not reject your mother’s instructions” (Proverbs 1:8); “Do not be wise in your own eyes”; “Do not turn away from the discipline of the Lord”; “Do not neglect the law”; “Do not refrain from doing good to the needy”; “Do not devise evil against your friend” (Proverbs 3:7, 11, 27, 29); “Do not attend to the deceitful woman” (Proverbs 5:2); “He refused to understand, that he might do good” (Psalm 35:4); “They refused to accept discipline” (Proverbs 1:29).

What do innumerable such passages in the ancient books of the divine utterances show, except free choice of the human will?

In the new books also—the Gospels and the apostolic writings—what else is shown where it is said: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth” (Matthew 6:19); “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matthew 10:28); “Whoever wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Matthew 16:24); “Peace on earth to people of good will” (Luke 2:14)?

And what the apostle Paul says: “Let him do what he wishes; he is not sinning if he marries” [Note: [Col. 0883] The manuscripts consistently read here and below, “he is not sinning, let him marry,” omitting *si*, “if,” which is also absent from the Greek.]; “but whoever has firmly resolved in his heart, having no necessity but possessing authority over his own will, and has resolved in his heart to preserve his virgin, does well” (1 Corinthians 7:36–37).

He also says: “If I do this willingly, I have a reward” (1 Corinthians 9:17); and elsewhere: “Be sober and righteous, and do not sin” (1 Corinthians 15:34); and again: “So that, just as there is readiness of will, there may also be accomplishment” (2 Corinthians 8:11).

And to Timothy he says: “When they have begun to live luxuriously in Christ, they wish to marry” (1 Timothy 5:11); and elsewhere: “All who wish to live devoutly in Christ Jesus will suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3:12); and to Timothy himself: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you” (1 Timothy 4:14).

And to Philemon: “So that your good deed might not be as though compelled, but voluntary” (Philemon 14).

He also exhorts slaves themselves to serve their masters from the heart, with goodwill (Ephesians 6:6).

Likewise James says: “Therefore, do not go astray, my brothers, and do not hold the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ with partiality” (James 2:1); and: “Do not speak evil of one another” (James 4:11).

Likewise John says in his Epistle: “Do not love the world” (1 John 2:15), and other things of this kind.

Indeed, wherever it is said, “Do not do this,” or “Do not do that,” and wherever the divine admonitions require an act of the will for doing or not doing something [Note: [Col. 0884] The manuscripts read, “where something,” omitting *ad*, “to.” But some of them have *aliquod* instead of *aliquid*.], free choice is sufficiently demonstrated.

Therefore let no one blame God in his heart; let each person blame himself when he sins. Nor, when he performs something according to God, should he remove it from his own will. For when he does something willingly, then the deed should be called good, and then he should hope for the reward of a good deed from him of whom it is said: “He will repay each person according to his works” (Matthew 16:27).

## CHAPTER III

### 5.

For those who know the divine commandments, the excuse that people are accustomed to make on the basis of ignorance is taken away. But even those who do not know God’s law will not be without punishment. “For those who have sinned without the law will perish without the law, and those who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law” (Romans 2:12).

I do not think that the Apostle said this as though he meant that those who do not know the law will suffer something worse for their sins than those who know it. For to perish seems worse than to be judged. But since he was speaking about Gentiles and Jews—because the former are without the law, whereas the latter received the law—who would dare say that Jews who sin under the law will not perish if they have not believed in Christ, since it was said of them that “they will be judged by the law”? No one can be liberated without faith in Christ; and therefore they will be judged in such a way that they perish.

For if the condition of those who do not know God’s law is worse than that of those who know it, how will what the Lord says in the Gospel be true? “The servant who did not know his master’s will, and did things deserving of blows, will receive few blows; but the servant who knew his master’s will, and did things deserving of blows, will receive many blows” (Luke 12:48, 47).

There he shows that the person who knows sins more gravely than the one who does not know. Yet for that reason no one should flee into the darkness of ignorance and seek an excuse there. It is one thing not to have known, another to have been unwilling to know. The will is blamed in the case of the one of whom it is said: “He refused to understand, that he might do good” (Psalm 35:4).

But even that ignorance which belongs not to those who do not wish to know, but to those who are simply ignorant, does not excuse anyone so completely that he will not burn in everlasting fire if he did not believe because he never heard at all what he was to believe [Note: [Col. 0885] The printed editions read *quod*, “what”; the manuscripts read *quid*, “what [he was to believe]”]—although perhaps he may burn less severely. For it was not said without reason: “Pour out your wrath upon the nations that have not known you” (Psalm 78:6); and what the Apostle says: “When he comes in a flame of fire to inflict vengeance on those who do not know God” (2 Thessalonians 1:8).

Nevertheless, so that we may possess knowledge itself, lest anyone say, “I did not know, I did not hear, I did not understand,” the human will is addressed where it is said: “Do not be like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Psalm 31:9). Yet the person concerning whom it is said, “A stubborn servant will not be corrected by words; for if he understands, he will not obey” (Proverbs 29:19), appears worse.

But when a person says, “I cannot do what is commanded, because I am overcome by my desire,” he no longer has an excuse based on ignorance, nor does he blame God in his heart; rather, he recognizes and laments his evil within himself. To him the Apostle says: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21). And surely, when one is told, “Do not be overcome,” his free choice of will is being addressed without doubt. To wish and not to wish belong to one’s own will.

## CHAPTER IV

### 6.

But it must be feared that all these divine testimonies, and whatever others there are—which are undoubtedly very numerous—in defense of free choice may be understood in such a way that no place is left for God’s help and grace in a devout life and good conduct, for which eternal reward is owed. Otherwise the wretched human being may dare, when he lives well and acts well—or rather, when he thinks that he lives and acts well—to glory in himself and not in the Lord, and to place the hope of living rightly in himself. Then he would fulfill the curse of the prophet Jeremiah: “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man, and makes flesh the strength of his arm, and whose heart departs from the Lord” (Jeremiah 17:5).

Understand this prophetic testimony, brothers. Since the prophet did not say, “Cursed is the man who places his hope in himself,” someone might think that the words “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man” were said so that no one should place his hope in another person, but in himself. Therefore, to show that he admonished a person not to place hope even in himself, after saying, “Cursed is the man who places his hope in man,” he immediately added, “and makes flesh the strength of his arm.”

He used “arm” to signify the power of acting. By “flesh” we must understand human weakness. Thus he makes flesh the strength of his arm who thinks that a weak and feeble power—that is, a human power—is sufficient for him to act well, and who does not hope for help from the Lord.

Therefore he added: “and whose heart departs from the Lord.” [Note: [Col. 0886] The printed editions read, “For this reason he added”; the most ancient Corbeiensis codex and some other manuscripts read, “Therefore he added.”] [Col. 0886] Such is the Pelagian heresy—not an ancient one, but one that arose not long ago. Against this heresy, after the dispute had continued for a considerable time, necessity finally brought matters even to the most recent episcopal councils. From there I sent you some things to read—not everything, but at least a portion.

Let us therefore not place our hope in a human being for acting well, making flesh the strength of our arm. Let our heart not depart from the Lord, but let it say to him: “Be my helper; do not abandon me or despise me, O God of my salvation” (Psalm 26:9).

### 7.

Therefore, beloved, just as we proved from the preceding testimonies of the holy Scriptures that free choice of the will exists in human beings for living well and acting rightly, so let us now consider what divine testimonies there are concerning the grace of God, without which we can do nothing good.

First I shall say something about your own profession. This community in which you live continently would not gather you together if you did not despise sexual pleasure within marriage [Note: [Col. 0886] The Corbeiensis manuscript, written nine or ten centuries ago, reads, “in which you live as continent people.”].

When the disciples had said to the Lord as he spoke, “If such is the situation of a man with his wife, it is not expedient to marry,” he answered them: “Not everyone receives this word, but those to whom it has been given” (Matthew 19:10–11).

Did the Apostle not exhort Timothy’s free choice when he said, “Keep yourself chaste” (1 Timothy 5:22)? And in this matter he showed the power of the will when he said: “having no necessity, but possessing authority over his own will, to preserve his virgin.”

And yet: “Not everyone receives this word, but those to whom it has been given.” For those to whom it has not been given either do not wish to do it, or do not fulfill what they wish; but those to whom it has been given wish in such a way that they fulfill what they wish. Thus, for this word—which is not received by everyone—to be received by some is both a gift of God and an exercise of free choice.

### 8.

Concerning conjugal chastity itself, the Apostle indeed says: “Let him do what he wishes; he does not sin if he marries” (1 Corinthians 7:37, 36). Yet even this is a gift of God, since Scripture says: “A wife is joined to a man by the Lord” (Proverbs 19:14).

Therefore the Doctor of the Gentiles, commending in his speech both conjugal chastity, through which adulteries are not committed, and the more perfect continence through which no sexual intercourse is sought, showed that both this and that are gifts of God. Writing to the Corinthians and admonishing married couples not to defraud one another, after admonishing them he added: “I wish that all people were as I myself am”—since he himself was certainly continent from all sexual intercourse—and immediately continued: “But each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that” (1 Corinthians 7:7).

Do the many commandments given in God’s law so that fornication and adultery may not be committed indicate anything other than free choice? They would not be commanded unless a person possessed his own will, by which he might obey the divine commandments.

And yet it is a gift of God, without which the commandments of chastity cannot be kept. Hence that writer says in the Book of Wisdom: “Since I knew that no one can be continent unless God gives it, and this itself was wisdom: to know whose gift it was” (Wisdom 8:21).

But when these holy commandments of chastity are not kept, “each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (James 1:14). If he says, “I wish to keep them, but I am overcome by my desire,” Scripture replies to his free choice—as I said above: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.”

Yet for this to happen, grace helps; unless it helps, the law will be nothing but the power of sin. Desire is increased and receives greater strength through the law’s prohibition, unless the Spirit of grace provides help.

This is what the Doctor of the Gentiles himself says: “The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.” There is the source of the human being’s statement: “I wish to keep the commandment of the law, but I am overcome by the power of my desire.”

And when his will is addressed with the words, “Do not be overcome by evil,” what good does this do him unless it comes about through the assistance of grace? The Apostle himself followed this by adding: after saying, “the power of sin is the law,” he immediately continued, “But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:56–57).

Therefore the victory by which sin is overcome is nothing other than a gift of God, who in this struggle helps free choice.

### 9.

For this reason the heavenly Teacher also says: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matthew 26:41). Therefore let each person who fights against his own desire pray not to enter into temptation—that is, not to be drawn away and enticed by it.

But he does not enter into temptation if by a good will he conquers evil desire. Nevertheless, the free choice of the human will is not sufficient unless the Lord grants victory to the one who prays not to enter into temptation.

What could show God’s grace more clearly than the fact that what is prayed for is received? If our Savior had said only, “Watch, lest you enter into temptation,” he would seem merely to have admonished the human will. But when he added, “and pray,” he showed that God helps so that one does not enter into temptation.

Free choice is addressed in the words: “My son, do not turn away from the discipline of the Lord” (Proverbs 3:11). And the Lord said: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32).

Therefore the human being is helped by grace, so that he is not commanded to will something without purpose [Note: [Col. 0887] The Corbeiensis manuscript reads *enim*, “for.”].

## CHAPTER V

### 10.

When God says, “Turn to me, and I shall turn to you” (Zechariah 1:3), one of these things appears to belong to our will—namely, that we should turn to him—while the other belongs to his grace: that he too should turn to us.

Here the Pelagians may think that their position prevails, according to which they say that God’s grace is given according to our merits. Indeed, in the East—that is, in the province of Palestine, where the city of Jerusalem is located—when Pelagius himself was being heard by the bishops, he did not dare to affirm this.

Among the other charges brought against him, this too was brought forward: that he said God’s grace was given according to our merits. This is so foreign to Catholic doctrine and so hostile to the grace of Christ that, unless he anathematized this charge against himself [Col. 0888] [Note: [Col. 0888] The printed editions have *anathematizasset* and below *anathematizatus* and *anathemasse*. The older manuscripts have *anathemasset*, *anathematus*, and *anathemasse*.], he would have departed from there under anathema [Note: [Col. 0888] See *The Proceedings of Pelagius*, §§30–37.].

But his later books show that he anathematized it deceitfully, since in them he defends absolutely nothing other than that God’s grace is given according to our merits.

Thus they collect from the Scriptures such passages as this one I mentioned shortly before: “Turn to me, and I shall turn to you,” so that grace may be given according to the merit of our turning to God, in which he too turns to us.

Those who think this way do not take into account that, unless our turning to God itself were a gift of God, it would not be said to him: “God of hosts, turn us” (Psalm 79:8); “O God, you will turn us and give us life”; and “Turn us, O God of our salvation” (Psalm 84:7, 5), along with other passages of this kind, which it would take too long to recall.

For what else is coming to Christ than turning to him by believing? And yet he says: “No one can come to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6:66).

### 11.

Likewise, what is written in the Second Book of Chronicles—“The Lord is with you when you are with him; and if you seek him, you will find him; but if you abandon him, he will abandon you” (2 Chronicles 15:2)—certainly manifests the freedom of the will.

But those who say that God’s grace is given according to our merits understand these testimonies in this way: they say that our merit consists in our being with God, and that his grace is given according to this merit, so that he too may be with us. Likewise, they say that our merit consists in seeking him, and that his grace is given according to this merit, so that we may find him.

And in the First Book, where it is said: “And you, Solomon my son, know God, and serve him with a perfect heart and a willing soul; for the Lord searches all hearts and knows every thought of minds. If you seek him, he will be found by you; but if you abandon him, he will reject you forever” (1 Chronicles 28:9), the freedom of the will is declared.

But they place human merit in the words, “If you seek him,” and say that grace is given according to this merit in the words, “He will be found by you” [Note: [Col. 0888] The printed editions had omitted the words “If you seek him; and according to this merit grace is given in the words,” which are restored here from the manuscripts.].

They labor with all their strength to show that God’s grace is given according to our merits—which means that grace is not grace. For when something is repaid according to merit, the payment is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt, as the Apostle says most plainly (Romans 4:4).

### 12.

There was indeed merit in the apostle Paul, but it was evil merit when he was persecuting the Church. Hence he says: “I am not worthy to be called an Apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God.”

Since, then, he possessed this evil merit, good was repaid to him for evil. Therefore he continued by adding: “But by the grace of God I am what I am.”

And to show free choice as well, he immediately added: “and his grace toward me was not in vain, but I labored more than all of them.” This free choice of the human being he also encourages in others, to whom he says: “We entreat you not to receive the grace of God in vain” (2 Corinthians 6:1).

Why would he entreat them in this way if they had received grace in such a manner as to lose their own will?

Yet, lest the will itself be thought capable of doing anything good without God’s grace, immediately after saying, “His grace toward me was not in vain, but I labored more than all of them,” he added: “Not I, however, but the grace of God with me” (1 Corinthians 15:9–10). That is, not I alone, but the grace of God with me. Thus it was neither the grace of God alone nor he alone, but the grace of God with him.

But when he was called from heaven and converted by such a great and efficacious calling (Acts 9), the grace of God was alone, because his merits were great—but evil.

Finally, elsewhere he says to Timothy: “Work together for the Gospel according to the power of God, who saved us and called us with his holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his purpose and grace, which was given to us in Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 1:8–9).

Likewise, recalling his merits, but evil ones, he says: “For we too were once foolish and unbelieving, wandering astray, serving various desires and pleasures, acting in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another.”

What other than punishment was owed for such evil merits? But when God repaid good for evil, through grace—which is not given according to our merits—what follows came to pass. He says:

“But when the goodness and human kindness of God our Savior appeared, not from works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy he saved us, through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior, so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life” (Titus 3:3–7).

## CHAPTER VI

### 13.

By these and similar divine testimonies it is proved that God’s grace is not given according to our merits. For we see that it was given—and see that it is given every day—not merely when no good merits preceded, but even when many evil merits preceded.

But plainly, once grace has been given, our good merits also begin to exist—yet through grace. For if grace withdraws itself, a person falls—not raised up, but hurled headlong by free choice.

Therefore, even when a person begins to have good merits, he ought not to attribute them to himself, but to God, to whom it is said in the Psalm: “Be my helper; do not abandon me” (Psalm 26:9).

By saying, “Do not abandon me,” he shows that, if he is abandoned, he himself is able to do no good on his own. Hence that other passage says: “I said in my abundance, ‘I shall never be moved.’”

He had thought that what abounded in him so greatly that he would not be moved was his own good. But so that it might be shown to him whose it was [Note: [Col. 0889] The printed editions read, “whose that good was”; *good* is absent from most manuscripts]—the thing about which he had begun to glory as though it were his own—when grace abandoned him for a little while [Note: [Col. 0889] The printed editions have “when the grace of God abandoned him.” “Of God” is absent even from most manuscripts.], he says after being admonished: “Lord, by your will you gave strength to my beauty; but you turned your face away from me, and I became troubled” (Psalm 29:7–8).

Therefore it is necessary for a human being not only to be justified by God’s grace when he is ungodly—that is, to be made righteous from ungodliness, when good is repaid to him for evil—but also, once he has been justified by faith, to walk with grace and lean upon it, lest he fall.

For this reason it is written in the Song of Songs concerning the Church herself: “Who is this who ascends, made white, leaning upon her kinsman (*fratruelem*)?” (Song of Songs 8:5).

She has been made white, for she could not be white through herself. And by whom has she been made white, except by him who says through the prophet: “Though your sins be like scarlet, I shall make them white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18)?

When she was made white, she had merited nothing good. Once she has been made white, she walks well; but she must continue steadfastly to lean upon him by whom she was made white.

For this reason Jesus himself, upon whom the one made white leans, said to his disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

### 14.

Let us therefore return to the apostle Paul. We certainly find that he obtained God’s grace without any good merits—indeed, with many evil merits—when good was repaid to him for evil.

Let us see what he says as his passion was already approaching, when he wrote to Timothy: “For I am already being poured out as a sacrifice,” he says, “and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith.”

Here he is certainly recalling his good merits, so that after good merits he may receive the crown—he who after evil merits received grace.

Finally, observe what follows: “There remains for me,” he says, “the crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, will repay me on that day” (2 Timothy 4:6–8).

To whom would the righteous judge repay the crown if the merciful Father had not first given grace? And how would this be a crown of righteousness if grace, which justifies the ungodly, had not preceded it? How would this debt be repaid if that free gift had not first been given?

### 15.

But when the Pelagians say that the only grace not given according to our merits is that by which sins are forgiven, while the grace given at the end—that is, eternal life—is repaid according to our preceding merits, we must answer them.

If they understood our merits in such a way that they recognized that these too are gifts of God, their position would not be rejected [Note: [Col. 0890] The Vatican, Gallican, and Belgian manuscripts read *reproba*, “reprobate/rejected.”]. But since they proclaim human merits in such a way that they say human beings possess them from themselves, the Apostle gives the entirely correct answer: “For who distinguishes you? And what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you glory as though you had not received it?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

To one who thinks in this way it is most truly said: “God crowns his own gifts, not your merits”—if your merits are from yourself, not from him.

For merits of that kind are evil, and God does not crown them [Note: [Col. 0890] The Ambrosian edition has “which are”; Erasmus and Louvain have “which are evil.” The manuscripts add neither *sunt*, “are,” nor *mala*, “evil.”]. But if they are good, they are gifts of God, because, as the apostle James says: “Every good giving and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James 1:17).

Hence John, the forerunner of the Lord, also says: “A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven” (John 3:27)—from heaven, certainly, from which the Holy Spirit also came, when Jesus “ascended on high, led captivity captive, and gave gifts to human beings” (Psalm 67:19; Ephesians 4:8).

Therefore, if your good merits are gifts of God, God does not crown your merits as though they were your merits, but as his gifts.

## CHAPTER VII

### 16.

Let us therefore consider the merits of the apostle Paul himself, concerning which he said that the righteous Judge would repay him with the crown of righteousness [Note: [Col. 0891] The printed editions read, “he said that the righteous Judge would repay him before,” omitting “the crown of righteousness,” which we have restored from the manuscripts.], and let us see whether his merits, as his own—that is, acquired for him from himself—or whether they are gifts of God.

“I have fought,” he says, “the good fight; I have finished the course; I have kept the faith.”

First, these good works would be nothing if good thoughts had not preceded them. Therefore observe what he says about those thoughts. Writing to the Corinthians, he says: “Not that we are sufficient to think anything from ourselves” [Note: [Col. 0891] All the manuscripts read, “to think anything as though from ourselves,” omitting “from ourselves.”], “as though from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5).

Then let us examine each statement individually.

“I have fought,” he says, “the good fight.” I ask by what strength he fought: whether by a strength that came to him from himself, or by one given from above.

But far be it that so great a teacher was ignorant of God’s law [Note: [Col. 0891] The Ambrosian and Erasmus editions, and most manuscripts, read, “that so great a teacher of the Gentiles was ignorant,” etc.], whose voice is heard in Deuteronomy: “Do not say in your heart, ‘My strength and the power of my hand made this great ability for me’; but you shall remember the Lord your God, because he himself gives you strength to acquire ability” (Deuteronomy 8:17–18).

But what benefit is there in a good fight unless victory follows? And who gives victory except the one of whom he himself says: “Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57)?

And in another passage, after recalling the testimony from the Psalm, “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we have been counted as sheep for slaughter,” he added: “But in all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Psalm 43:22; Romans 8:36–37).

Therefore it is not through ourselves, but through him who loved us.

Then he said: “I have finished the course.” But he said this who elsewhere says: “Therefore it is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who has mercy” (Romans 9:16).

This sentence can in no way be twisted so as to say: “It is not of God who has mercy, but of the human being who wills and runs.” Whoever dares to say this openly shows that he contradicts the Apostle.

### 17.

Finally, he said: “I have kept the faith.” But he said this who elsewhere says: “I received mercy so that I might be faithful” (1 Corinthians 7:25).

For he did not say, “I received mercy because I was faithful,” but, “so that I might be faithful.” In this way he showed that faith itself cannot be possessed except through God’s mercy, and that it is a gift of God.

He teaches this most clearly when he says: “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God.” They could have said, “We received grace because we believed” [Note: [Col. 0891] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “because we believe.”], thus attributing faith to themselves and grace to God. For this reason, after the Apostle had said, “through faith,” he added: “and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God.”

Again, lest they say that they had merited such a gift by their works, he immediately added: “not from works, lest anyone should boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9).

He did not deny or nullify good works, since he says that God will repay each person according to his works (Romans 2:6). Rather, works arise from faith, not faith from works. Consequently, the works of righteousness in us come from the one from whom faith itself comes, concerning which it is said: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4).

### 18.

But people who do not understand what the Apostle himself says—“We consider that a person is justified by faith without the works of the law” (Romans 3:28)—have thought that he means faith is sufficient for a person, even if he lives badly and has no good works.

Far be it from the Vessel of Election to have thought this. For when he had said in one place, “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision has any power nor uncircumcision,” he immediately added: “but faith working through love” (Galatians 5:6).

This is the faith that separates God’s faithful from unclean demons. For they too, as the apostle James says, “believe and tremble” (James 2:19), but they do not act well.

Therefore they do not possess that faith by which the righteous person lives—that is, faith that works through love—so that God may repay him with eternal life according to his works.

But because these good works too come to us from God, from whom faith and love also come to us, that same Doctor of the Gentiles therefore called eternal life itself grace.

## CHAPTER VIII

### 19.

And [Note: [Col. 0892] Louvain reads “But”; the Ambrosian and Erasmus editions and the manuscripts read “and.”] from this arises no small question, which must be resolved with the Lord’s help.

If eternal life is repaid for good works, as Scripture says most plainly, “For God will repay each person according to his works” (Matthew 16:27), how is eternal life grace, when grace is not repaid for works but given freely, as the Apostle himself says: “To the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt” [Note: [Col. 0892] Erasmus and several manuscripts read “merit.”] (Romans 4:4)?

And again he says: “The remnant has been saved according to the election of grace.” Then he immediately adds: “But if by grace, then it is no longer from works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Romans 11:5–6).

How, then, is eternal life grace, when it is obtained from works? Or perhaps the Apostle did not call eternal life grace?

On the contrary, he did so in a way that cannot be denied at all; it requires not an acute interpreter, but merely an attentive hearer. For after saying, “The wages of sin is death,” he immediately added: “But the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:23).

20. This question, then, seems to me impossible to resolve in any way unless we understand that our very good works, for which eternal life is rendered, belong to the grace of God, in view of what the Lord Jesus said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). And when the Apostle himself had said, “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves, but is God’s gift—not from works, lest anyone should boast,” he surely saw that people might suppose this to have been said as though good works were not necessary for believers, but faith alone were sufficient for them; and, conversely, that people might become elated over their good works, as though they themselves were sufficient to perform them. Therefore he immediately added: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared beforehand so that we might walk in them” [Col. 0893] (Ephesians 2:8–10).

What does this mean? Having commended God’s grace by saying, “not from works, lest anyone should boast,” why, in explaining why he said this, does he add, “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works”? How, then, is it “not from works, lest anyone should boast”? Listen and understand: “not from works” was said as though they were your works, existing from yourself for yourself, but as works in which God formed you—that is, shaped and created you. For he says, “We are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works”; not the creation by which we became human beings, but that creation of which the one who was already certainly human said, “Create a clean heart in me, O God” (Psalm 50:12); and of which the Apostle says, “Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, there is a new creation; the old things have passed away; behold, they have become new. But all things are from God” (2 Corinthians 5:17–18).

We are therefore fashioned—that is, shaped and created—in good works, which we did not prepare, but which God prepared so that we might walk in them. Therefore, beloved [Note: [Col. 0893] Lov., “Therefore, beloved brothers.” “Brothers” is absent from the manuscripts and from the editions of Am. and Er.], if our good life is nothing other than God’s grace, then without doubt eternal life, which is rendered in return for the good life, is also God’s grace. For this too is given freely, because the life to which it is given was itself given freely. But the life to which it is given is grace alone; whereas this life that is given to it, since it is its reward, is grace in return for grace, as a recompense for righteousness. Thus it is true—indeed, because it is true—that God “will render to each one according to his works.”

## CHAPTER IX

21. Perhaps you are asking whether we have read in the holy Books about “grace in return for grace.” But you have the Gospel according to John, brilliantly illuminated by such great light, where John the Baptist says concerning the Lord Christ: “But we have received from his fullness, and grace in return for grace” (John 1:16).

From his fullness, therefore, we have received according to our measure, as it were our portions, so that we might live well, just as “God has apportioned to each the measure of faith” (Romans 12:3), because “each has his own gift from God, one in this way, another in that” (1 Corinthians 7:7). This itself is grace. But in addition we shall receive grace in return for grace when eternal life is rendered to us, concerning which the Apostle said, “But the grace of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord,” after first saying, “The wages of sin is death.”

It is rightly called wages, because eternal death is rendered as a debt for service in the devil’s army. Although he could have said—and said it correctly—“But the wages of righteousness are eternal life,” he preferred to say, “But the grace of God is eternal life,” so that we might understand from this that God brings us to eternal life not on account of our merits, but on account of his mercy. Concerning this, the man of God says to his soul in the Psalm: “He crowns you with mercy and compassion” (Psalm 102:4).

Is a crown not rendered for good works? Yet because he himself works those good works in the good [Note: [Col. 0893] Four Vatican manuscripts and the very ancient Corbie manuscript read, “works in us”], concerning whom it is said, “For God is the one who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure,” therefore the Psalm says, “He crowns you with mercy and compassion,” because by his mercy we perform the good works for which the crown is rendered. [Col. 0894]

But because he said, “For God is the one who works in you both to will and to work according to his good pleasure,” he should not for that reason be thought to have taken away free choice. If that were so, he would not previously have said, “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling” (Philippians 2:13, 12). For when they are commanded to work, their free choice is being summoned. But they are told to do so with fear and trembling lest, by attributing to themselves what they do well, they become elated over their good works as though they were their own.

It is as though the Apostle were questioned and asked, “Why did you say, ‘with fear and trembling’?” In answer he explained the reason for these words, saying: “For God is the one who works in you.” If you fear and tremble, you do not become elated as though the good works were yours, because God is the one who works in you.

## CHAPTER X

22. Therefore, brothers, you ought indeed, through free choice, not to do evil and to do good; for God’s law commands this of us in the holy Books, both the former and the latter. But let us read and, with the Lord’s help, understand the Apostle when he says: “No flesh will be justified before him by works of the law, for through the law comes knowledge of sin” (Romans 3:20). He said “knowledge,” not “destruction.” When a person recognizes sin, but grace does not help so that the recognized sin may be avoided, then without doubt the law produces wrath. The Apostle himself says this elsewhere—in fact, these are his words: “The law produces wrath.” He said this because God’s wrath is greater against the transgressor who learns sin through the law and nevertheless commits it. Such a person is a transgressor of the law, just as he says elsewhere: “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression” (Romans 4:15).
