For this reason he also says elsewhere, “so that we may serve in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter,” wishing the oldness of the letter to be understood as the law, and what else but grace as the newness of the Spirit? And lest he be thought to have accused or criticized the law, he immediately raised an objection to himself and said: “What shall we say, then? Is the law sin? Certainly not.” Then he added: “But I would not have known sin except through the law”—that is, what he had said: “Through the law comes knowledge of sin.” For he says, “I would not have known covetousness unless the law had said, ‘You shall not covet.’ But sin, taking an occasion through the commandment, produced in me every kind of covetousness; for without the law sin is dead” [Note: [Col. 0894] The editions read, “sin was dead.” The manuscripts read, “sin is dead.” The Greek is νεκρά (“dead”).]

“I was once alive without the law; but when the commandment came, sin revived, and I died. And the commandment that was intended for life was found by me to be for death; for sin, taking an occasion through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me. Thus the law is indeed holy, and the commandment holy and righteous and good. Therefore, did what is good become death to me? Certainly not. But sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good, so that through the commandment the sinner or sin might become exceedingly sinful” [Note: [Col. 0894] Am. and Er. read, “sin beyond measure.” Lov. reads, “sin sinning beyond measure.” The manuscripts, however, read, “the sinner or sin beyond measure,” with a few exceptions omitting the word “or.”] (Romans 7:6–13).

And to the Galatians he says: “Knowing that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, we too have believed in Christ Jesus, so that we might be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no flesh will be justified” [Col. 0895] (Galatians 2:16).

## CHAPTER XI

23. What, then, is the meaning of the most foolish and perverse Pelagians saying that the law is God’s grace, by which we are helped not to sin? What, poor men, is the meaning of their claim, when without any hesitation they contradict so great an Apostle?

He says that through the law sin received strength against the human being, and that through the commandment—although it is holy, righteous, and good—it nevertheless killed the person, and through what is good worked death in him. From this death he would not be freed unless the Spirit gave life to him whom the letter had killed, as he says elsewhere: “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6).

Yet these unteachable people, blind against the light of God and deaf against the voice of God, say that the killing letter gives life, and they contradict the life-giving Spirit.

Therefore, brothers, to admonish you rather in the words of the Apostle himself: “We are debtors, not to the flesh, so that we should live according to the flesh. For if you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” I have said this to deter your free choice from evil and exhort it to good in the Apostle’s words. Nevertheless, when you do not live according to the flesh but put to death the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit, you ought not for that reason to glory in a human being—that is, in yourselves—but in the Lord.

For, so that those to whom he was speaking would not become elated, thinking that they could perform such good works by their own spirit and not by God’s, after saying, “But if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live,” he immediately added: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God” (Romans 8:12–14).

Therefore, when you put to death the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit so that you may live, glorify him, praise him, and give thanks to him, by whose Spirit you are led so that you may be able to do these things and show yourselves to be sons of God. “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are the sons of God.”

## CHAPTER XII

24. Therefore, those who, relying on their own strength, are led by their own spirit with the mere assistance of the law and without the assistance of grace are not sons of God. They are the ones concerning whom the same Apostle says that, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they were not subject to the righteousness of God” (Romans 10:3).

He said this about the Jews, who, presuming upon themselves, rejected grace and for that reason did not believe in Christ. He says that they sought to establish their own righteousness, which is righteousness from the law—not because the law was established by them, but because in the law, which is from God, they had established their own righteousness when they believed that they could fulfill that same law by their own powers.

He says that they were ignorant of God’s righteousness—not the righteousness by which God is righteous, but the righteousness that a human being receives from God. And so that you may know that he called theirs the righteousness that is from the law, and God’s the righteousness that a human being receives from God, listen to what he says elsewhere when speaking about Christ:

“Because of him,” he says, “I have considered everything not only loss but also refuse, in order that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having my own righteousness, which is from the law, but that which is through faith in Christ, which is from God” (Philippians 3:8).

What does “not having my own righteousness, which is from the law” mean, since the law itself was not his but God’s? It means that he called it his own righteousness, even though it was from the law, because by his own will he thought [Note: [Col. 0896] The manuscripts read, “he thought”; the editions, “they thought.”] that he could fulfill the law without the assistance of grace, which comes through faith in Christ [Col. 0896]. Therefore, after saying, “not having my own righteousness, which is from the law,” he immediately added, “but that which is through faith in Christ, which is from God.”

They were ignorant of this righteousness, concerning which he says, “ignorant of God’s righteousness”—that is, the righteousness that is from God. For this is given not by the killing letter but by the life-giving Spirit—and “seeking to establish their own,” the righteousness that he himself called righteousness from the law when he said, “not having my own righteousness, which is from the law.” “They were not subject to the righteousness of God”—that is, they were not subject to the grace of God.

They were under the law, not under grace; and therefore sin ruled over them. A person is not freed from sin by the law, but by grace. For this reason he says elsewhere: “Sin will not rule over you, for you are not under the law but under grace” (Romans 6:14)—not because the law is evil, but because those whom it makes guilty by commanding, without helping, are under it. Grace, on the other hand, helps a person to be a doer of the law; without grace, one who is under the law will merely be a hearer of the law. To such people he says: “You who are being justified by the law have fallen away from grace” (Galatians 5:4).

## CHAPTER XIII

25. Who could be so deaf to the apostolic voices, who could be so foolish—or rather, so insane, without knowing what he is saying—as to dare to claim that the law is grace, when the one who knew what he was saying cries out, “You who are being justified by the law have fallen away from grace”?

But if the law is not grace, because the law cannot help in order that the law itself may be fulfilled, whereas grace can help, will nature perhaps be grace? For the Pelagians have also dared to say that grace is nature, in which we were created in such a way that we possess a rational mind by which we are able to understand, having been made in the image of God so that we might rule over the fish of the sea, the birds of the heavens, and all the animals that crawl upon the earth.

But this is not the grace that the Apostle commends through faith in Jesus Christ. It is certain that we share this nature even with the impious and unbelieving; whereas grace through faith in Jesus Christ belongs only to those who possess that faith. “For faith is not possessed by all” (2 Thessalonians 3:2).

Therefore, just as he most truthfully says to those who wished to be justified by the law and thus fell away from grace, “If righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing” (Galatians 2:21), so it is also most truthfully said to those who think that the grace commended and received by faith in Christ is nature: “If righteousness is through nature, then Christ died for nothing.”

For the law already existed here, and it did not justify; nature also already existed here, and it did not justify. Therefore Christ did not die for nothing: through him the law was to be fulfilled, for he said, “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17); and nature, lost through Adam, was to be restored through him who said that he had come “to seek and to save what was lost” (Matthew 18:11; Luke 19:10). The ancient fathers who loved God had also believed in his coming [Note: [Col. 0896] The manuscripts read “had believed.” The editions read “believed.”]

26. They also say that God’s grace, which is given through faith in Jesus Christ and is neither the law nor nature, serves only to forgive past sins, not to avoid future sins or overcome sins that resist us [Col. 0897]. But if this were true, surely in the Lord’s Prayer, after we had said, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,” we would not add, “and do not lead us into temptation” (Matthew 6:12–13). We say the former so that sins may be forgiven; the latter so that they may be avoided or overcome. We would in no way ask this of the Father who is in heaven if we could accomplish it by the power of the human will.

I remind Your Charity, and strongly exhort you, to read carefully the book that blessed Cyprian wrote on the Lord’s Prayer; and, insofar as the Lord helps you, to understand it and commit it to memory. There you will see how he addresses the free choice of those whom he edifies by composing his discourse, in such a way that he nevertheless shows that those things whose fulfillment is commanded [Note: [Col. 0897] Am., Er., and most manuscripts read, “appear.”] in the law must be requested in prayer. This would of course be utterly pointless if the human will were sufficient to do them without divine assistance.

## CHAPTER XIV

27. But once they have been refuted—since they are not defenders but puffers-up and destroyers of free choice, and since neither knowledge of the divine law, nor nature, nor the mere forgiveness of sins is that grace which is given through Jesus Christ our Lord, but grace itself causes the law to be fulfilled, nature to be set free, and sin not to rule—then they turn to an attempt, by whatever means, to show that God’s grace is given according to our merits.

For they say: “Although it is not given according to the merits of good works, because it is through grace itself that we perform good works, nevertheless it is given according to the merits of a good will. For,” they say, “a good will precedes in the one who prays; and the will of the one who believes preceded it, so that grace follows according to these merits from God who hears.”

28. I have already discussed faith above—that is, the will of the believer (above, §§16–18)—demonstrating to such an extent that it belongs to grace that the Apostle did not say, “I obtained mercy because I was faithful,” but said, “I obtained mercy so that I might be faithful” (1 Corinthians 7:25).

There are also other testimonies, including his saying, “Be wise unto moderation, as God has apportioned to each the measure of faith” (Romans 12:3). And the passage I have already recalled: “You have been saved by grace through faith, and this is not from yourselves, but is God’s gift” (Ephesians 2:8). And what he wrote to the Ephesians: “Peace to the brothers and love with faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Ephesians 6:23). And the passage where he says: “For it has been granted to you for Christ’s sake not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1:29).

Both, therefore, belong to God’s grace: the faith of believers and the endurance of those who suffer, because he says that both have been granted. And especially the passage where he says: “Having the same spirit of faith” (1 Corinthians 4:13). He does not say “knowledge of faith,” but “spirit of faith.” He said this so that we might understand that faith is granted without being requested, so that other things may be granted to the one who requests them through faith.

“For how,” he says, “will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” (Romans 10:14). Therefore the Spirit of grace causes us to have faith, so that through faith we may obtain by prayer the ability to do what we are commanded. For this reason the Apostle constantly places faith before the law, because we cannot do what the law commands unless, by asking through faith, we obtain the ability to do it.

29. For if faith belongs only to free choice and is not given by God, why do we pray for those who do not wish to believe, that they may believe? We would certainly do this in vain unless we rightly believed that almighty God can turn even perverse wills, contrary to faith, toward believing.

Human free choice is summoned when it is said: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Psalm 94:8). But if God could not also remove hardness of heart, he would not say through the prophet: “I will take from them their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh.”

That this was foretold concerning the New Testament the Apostle clearly shows when he says: “You are our letter, written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of fleshy hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:2). Let us not think that this was said so that those who ought to live spiritually might live carnally. Rather, because a stone is without sensation, and the hard heart is compared to it, to what else should an understanding heart be compared than to flesh that feels?

For this is what God says through the prophet Ezekiel: “I will give them,” he says, “another heart, and I will give a new spirit to them; and I will remove the heart of stone from their flesh and give them a heart of flesh, so that they may walk in my commandments, observe my ordinances, and perform them. And they shall be my people, and I shall be their God, says the Lord” (Ezekiel 11:19–20).

Can we then say, except in the most absurd way, that a good merit of a good will preceded in a person so that the heart of stone might be uprooted from him [Note: [Col. 0898] The editions read “pulled away.” The Vatican manuscripts read “uprooted,” correctly; for in Ezekiel the preceding expression is “and I will uproot.”]—when the heart of stone itself signifies nothing other than an exceedingly hard will, wholly inflexible against God? For where a good will precedes, there is no longer a heart of stone.

30. Elsewhere, through the same prophet, God most clearly shows that he does these things not on account of any good merits of theirs but on account of his own name. He says:

“I act,” [Note: [Col. 0898] Am. and Er. and some manuscripts read, “I do not act on your account.”] “O house of Israel, but for the sake of my holy name, which you profaned among the nations to which you entered. And I will sanctify my great name, which was profaned among the nations, which you profaned in their midst; and the nations shall know that I am the Lord, says the Lord God, when I have been sanctified in you before their eyes.

“And I will take you from the nations, and gather you from all the lands, and bring you into your own land. And I will sprinkle clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your uncleannesses and from all your idols, and I will cleanse you [Note: [Col. 0898] Here we have added the word “and” from the manuscripts, which agree with the Greek reading of the Septuagint]. And I will give you a new heart, and I will give a new spirit within you; and the heart of stone shall be removed from your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh, and I will give my spirit within you [Col. 0899]. And I will cause you to walk in my ordinances, observe my judgments, and perform them” (Ezekiel 36:22–27).

Who could be so blind as not to see, or so stony as not to feel, that this grace is not given according to the merits of a good will, when the Lord says and testifies, “I act, O house of Israel, but for the sake of my holy name”? Why did he say, “I act, but for the sake of my holy name,” unless to prevent them from thinking that what is done occurs because of their good merits—the very thing the Pelagians are not ashamed to say?

Moreover, he shows that not only were their good merits absent, but that evil merits preceded, when he says, “but for the sake of my holy name, which you profaned among the nations.” Who does not see that profaning the holy name of the Lord is a dreadful evil? Yet, he says, “for the sake of that very name of mine which you profaned, I will make you good—not for your sake.” And he says, “I will sanctify my great name, which was profaned among the nations, which you profaned in their midst.”

He says that he will sanctify his name, which he had previously called holy. This, then, is what we pray for in the Lord’s Prayer when we say, “Hallowed be your name” (Matthew 6:9): that what is always holy in itself may be sanctified in human beings [Note: [Col. 0899] The older manuscripts omit “in human beings.”]

Finally, the passage continues: “And all the nations shall know that I am the Lord, says the Lord God, when I have been sanctified in you.” Although he is therefore always holy, he is nevertheless sanctified in those to whom he grants his grace by removing from them the heart of stone through which they profaned the name of the Lord.

## CHAPTER XV

31. But lest it be thought that human beings themselves do nothing there through free choice, the Psalm says, “Do not harden your hearts.” And through Ezekiel himself:

“Cast away from yourselves all your impieties which you have committed impiously against me, and make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit, and perform all my commandments. Why will you die, O house of Israel? For I do not desire the death of the one who dies, says the Lord God; turn [Note: [Col. 0899] The Vatican and Gallican manuscripts read, “and turn”; the editions, “but turn.”] and you shall live” (Ezekiel 18:31–32).

Let us remember that the one who says, “Turn and you shall live,” is the one to whom it is said, “Turn us, O God” (Psalms 79:4; 85:5). Let us remember that he says, “Cast away from yourselves all your impieties,” while he himself justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5). Let us remember that he himself says, “Make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit,” while he also says, “I will give you a new heart, and I will give a new spirit within you.”

How, then, does the one who says, “Make for yourselves,” also say, “I will give you”? Why does he command if he himself is going to give? Why does he give if the human being is to make it—unless it is because he gives what he commands, helping the one whom he commands to do it?

Free will is always present in us, but it is not always good. For it is either free from righteousness when it serves sin, and then it is evil; or it is free from sin when it serves righteousness, and then it is good. But God’s grace is always good, and through it the person who previously had an evil will becomes a person of good will.

Through grace also the good will that has already begun to exist is increased and becomes so great that it can fulfill the divine commandments whenever it wills and wills with great and perfect determination. This is the force of what is written: “If you will, you will keep the commandments” (Ecclesiasticus 15, according to the Septuagint), so that the person who wills but cannot may recognize that he does not yet will fully, and may pray to possess as great a will as is sufficient to fulfill the commandments.

In this way he is helped to do what he is commanded. For willing is useful when we are able, and being able is useful when we will. For what good is it if we will what we cannot, or do not will what we can?

## CHAPTER XVI

32. The Pelagians think they know something important when they say, “God would not command what he knew could not be done by a human being.”

Who does not know this? But he commands some things that we cannot do so that we may learn what we ought to ask of him. For this is faith: by praying, it obtains what the law commands.

The very one who said, “If you will, you will keep the commandments,” says somewhat later in the same book of Ecclesiasticus:

“Who will set a guard over my mouth and a prudent seal upon my lips, lest I fall because of it and my tongue destroy me?” (Ecclesiasticus 22:33).

He had certainly already received the commandments: “Restrain your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit” (Psalm 33:14). Since, then, what he said is true—“If you will, you will keep the commandments”—why does he ask that a guard be given to his mouth, like the one who says in the Psalm, “Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth” (Psalm 140:3)?

Why are God’s commandment and his own will not sufficient for him, since, if he wills, he will keep the commandments? How many commandments of God there are against pride! He already knows them; if he wills, he will keep them. Why, then, does he say shortly afterward, “Lord, Father and God of my life, do not give me haughtiness of eyes”?

The law had already said to him, “You shall not covet” (Exodus 20:17). Let him will, then, and do what he is commanded, since, if he wills, he will keep the commandments. Why does he continue and say, “Turn covetousness away from me”?

Against lust God has commanded many things. Let him do them, since, if he wills, he will keep the commandments. What does it mean that he cries out to God, “May the appetite of the belly and sexual intercourse not seize me” (Ecclesiasticus 23:4–6)? If we were saying these things to him in his presence [Note: [Col. 0900] Am. and Er. and most manuscripts read, “If we were saying this to him at present.” Some other manuscripts read, “if this were said to him in the present”], he would rightly answer us: “From this prayer of mine, in which I ask these things from God, understand how I said, ‘If you will, you will keep the commandments.’”

It is certain that we keep the commandments if we will. But because the will is prepared by the Lord, we must ask him to make us will as much as is sufficient for us to do what we do by willing. It is certain that we will when we will; but he makes us will what is good. Concerning him it was said, as I quoted above, “The will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs 8, according to the Septuagint); and it was said, “The steps of a person are directed by the Lord, and he will desire his way” (Psalm 36:23); and it was said, “God is the one who works in you both to will” (Philippians 2:13).

It is certain that we do when we do. But he makes us do, supplying the will with the most effective strength. He said, “I will cause you to walk in my ordinances and observe and perform my judgments.” When he says, “I will cause you to perform,” what else does he say but, “I will remove from you the heart of stone, from which you did not perform, and I will give you a heart of flesh, from which you will perform”?

And what is this but, “I will remove the hard heart, from which you did not perform, and I will give an obedient heart, from which you will perform”?

He makes us do—the one to whom a human being says, “Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth.” For this is to say, “Cause me to set a guard over my mouth.” The one who said, “I set a guard over my mouth” had already received this benefit from God (Psalm 38:2).

## CHAPTER XVII

33. Therefore, whoever wishes to do God’s commandment but cannot already possesses a good will, but it is still small and weak. He will be able when he has a great and strong will.

For when the martyrs performed those great commandments, they certainly did so with a great will—that is, with great love. Concerning this love the Lord himself says: “No one has greater love than this: to lay down his life for his friends” [Note: [Col. 0901] The editions read, “that someone lay down”; “someone” is absent from the manuscripts.] (John 15:13).

Therefore the Apostle says: “Whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.” For “‘You shall not commit adultery,’ ‘You shall not murder,’ ‘You shall not steal,’ ‘You shall not covet,’ and if there is any other commandment, are summed up in this saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Love does no evil to a neighbor; therefore love is the fullness of the law” (Romans 13:8–10).

The apostle Peter did not yet possess this love when, out of fear, he denied the Lord three times (Matthew 26:69–75). For “fear is not in love,” as the evangelist John says in his Epistle; “but perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18).

Nevertheless, although it was small and imperfect, love was not absent when he said to the Lord, “I will lay down my life for you” (John 13:37). For he thought that he could do what he felt himself willing to do.

And who had begun to give him this love, however small, except the one who prepares the will and, by cooperating, perfects what he begins by working? For he works in order that we may will, beginning the work; and he cooperates with those who will, bringing it to completion.

For this reason the Apostle says: “I am confident that the one who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus” [Note: [Col. 0901] The Corbeiensis manuscript reads, “will bring it to completion until the end.” Thus, etc.] (Philippians 1:6).

Therefore, in order that we may will, he works without us; but when we will—and will in such a way that we act—he cooperates with us. Nevertheless, without him, whether working so that we may will or cooperating with us when we will, we have no power at all for good works of piety.

Of him working so that we may will it is said: “For God is the one who works in you both to will.” Of him cooperating with us when we already will and, by willing, act, it is said: “We know that for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8:28).

What does “all things” mean, except even those terrifying and savage sufferings? For that burden of Christ, which is heavy for weakness, becomes light for love. To such people the Lord said that his burden is light (Matthew 11:30)—to one such as Peter was when he suffered for Christ, not to one such as he was when he denied Christ.

[Col. 0902] 34. Commending this love—that is, a will burning with the most ardent divine love—the Apostle says:

“Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written, ‘For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through him who loved us.

“For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angels nor principalities, neither things present nor things to come, neither height nor depth, nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:35–39).

And elsewhere he says: “I show you a still more excellent way. If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love, I have become sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I have prophecy, and know all mysteries, and have all faith, so that I move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions to the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing.

“Love is magnanimous; it is kind. Love does not envy, does not act improperly, is not puffed up, is not dishonored, does not seek its own interests, is not provoked, does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity but rejoices with the truth. It endures all things, believes all things, hopes all things, bears all things. Love never falls away.”

And shortly afterward: “Faith, hope, and love remain—these three; but the greatest of these is love. Pursue love” (1 Corinthians 12:31–14:1).

He also says to the Galatians: “For you were called to freedom, brothers; only do not use freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’” (Galatians 5:13–14).

This is what he says to the Romans: “Whoever loves another has fulfilled the law” (Romans 13:8). He also says to the Colossians: “Above all these things, put on love, which is the bond of perfection” (Colossians 3:14).

And to Timothy: “The end of the commandment is love”; and, describing what kind of love, he adds, “from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (1 Timothy 1:5).

When he says to the Corinthians, “Let all your things be done with love” [Note: [Col. 0902] The particle “with” (cum) is omitted by the Louvain editors and by some manuscripts.] (1 Corinthians 16:14), he sufficiently shows that even the corrections which those being corrected experience as harsh and bitter must be carried out with love.

Therefore, when elsewhere he had said, “Correct the disorderly, encourage the fainthearted, support the weak; be patient toward all,” he immediately added, “See that no one repays anyone evil for evil” (1 Thessalonians 5:14–15). Thus, even when the disorderly are corrected, what is returned is not evil for evil, but rather good.

What of all these things is accomplished except by love?

### 35

And the apostle Peter says: “Above all, maintain perpetual mutual love among yourselves, because love covers a multitude of sins” [Note: The printed editions and some manuscripts read “perpetually”; manuscripts of better quality read “perpetual”] (1 Peter 4:8). The apostle James also says: “If, however, you fulfill the royal law according to the Scriptures, ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself,’ you do well” (James 2:8). The apostle John likewise says: “Whoever loves his brother remains in the light” (1 John 2:10). And elsewhere: “Whoever is not righteous is not from God, nor is the one who does not love his brother; for this is the proclamation that we have heard from the beginning: that we should love one another.” And again elsewhere: “This is his commandment: that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ and love one another” (ibid. 3:10, 23). And again: “We have this commandment from him: that whoever loves God should love his brother also” (ibid. 4:21). A little later he says: “By this we know that we love the children of God, when we love God and do his commandments. For this is the love of God: that we keep his commandments; and his commandments are not burdensome” (ibid. 5:2–3). And in the Second Epistle it is written: “It is not as though I were writing a new commandment to you, but one that we have had from the beginning: that we should love one another” (2 John 5).

### 36

The Lord Jesus himself also says that the whole Law and the Prophets depend upon the two commandments of love: love of God and love of one’s neighbor (Matthew 22:40). Concerning these two commandments, it is written in the Gospel according to Mark:

“One of the scribes who had heard them questioning one another came up; and, seeing that he had answered them well, asked him which commandment was first of all. Jesus answered him: ‘The first of all the commandments is: Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one Lord; and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind. This is the first commandment. The second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. There is no other commandment greater than these’” (Mark 12:28–31).

He also says in the Gospel according to John: “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another, just as I have loved you, so that you also may love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:34–35).

## CHAPTER XVIII

### 37

All these commandments of love—that is, of charity—are so great and so important that whatever a person may suppose he is doing well, if it is done without charity, is in no way done well. These commandments of charity, therefore, would be given to human beings in vain if they did not possess freedom of the will. But since they are given through both the Old and the New Law (although in the New has come the grace that was promised in the Old, while the law without grace is a letter that kills, whereas in grace it is a spirit that gives life), from where does the love of God and neighbor come in human beings, if not from God himself?

For if it comes not from God but from human beings, the Pelagians have won; but if it comes from God, we have defeated the Pelagians. Let the apostle John, therefore, sit as judge between us and say: “Beloved, let us love one another.” When they begin to exalt themselves over these words of John and say, “Why is this commanded us, unless we possess from ourselves the ability to love one another?”, John himself immediately follows, confounding them by saying that “love is from God” (1 John 4:7). It is therefore not from ourselves but from God.

Why, then, was it said, “Let us love one another,” because “love is from God,” unless the command admonished free will to seek God’s gift? This admonition would plainly be without fruit unless it first received some measure of love, so that it might seek what was to be added to it, by which it could fulfill what it was commanded to do. When it is said, “Let us love one another,” there is law; when it is said, “Love is from God,” there is grace. For the wisdom of God carries law and mercy upon its tongue (Proverbs 3:16, according to the Septuagint). Hence it is written in the Psalm: “Indeed, he will give blessing who gave the law” (Psalm 83:8).

### 38

Let no one deceive you, my brothers: we would not love God unless he himself first loved us. John shows this most clearly when he says: “Let us love” [Note: The Vatican and Gallican manuscripts read, “We love”], “because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19). Grace makes us lovers of the law, whereas the law itself without grace makes us nothing but transgressors.

And when the Lord says to his disciples, “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16), he indicates nothing else to us. For if we first loved him, so that he would love us on account of this merit, then we first chose him, so that we might deserve to be chosen by him. But he who is the truth says something else and most clearly contradicts this human vanity: “You did not choose me,” he says. If, then, you did not choose him, surely you did not love him either; for how could they choose one whom they did not love? “But I,” he says, “chose you.”

Did they not themselves afterward choose him and prefer him to all the good things of this world? They chose because they had been chosen; they were not chosen because they had chosen. The merit of those who choose would be nothing unless the grace of God, who chooses them, went before them.

Hence the apostle Paul, blessing the Thessalonians [Note: All the manuscripts read “Colossians”]: “May the Lord,” he says, “make you increase and abound in love for one another and for all” (1 Thessalonians 3:12). He gave this blessing so that we might love one another—the one who had given the law so that we should love one another.

Finally, elsewhere he says to the same people, because without doubt that which he had wished to be in them was already present in some of them: “We ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith is growing abundantly and the love of each one of you for one another is increasing” (2 Thessalonians 1:3). He said this so that they would not exalt themselves as though they possessed from themselves that great good which they had from God. “Because your faith is growing,” he says, “and the love of each one of you for one another is increasing, we ought to give thanks to God for you” [Note: Lovaniensis has “on your behalf.” Other printed editions and the manuscripts read “for you”]; we ought not to praise you as though you possessed this from yourselves.

### 39

And he says to Timothy: “For God did not give us a spirit of fear, but of power and love and self-control” (2 Timothy 1:7). In this testimony of the Apostle, however, we must take care not to suppose that we have not received the spirit of the fear of God, which is undoubtedly a great gift of God. Concerning it the prophet Isaiah says: “The spirit of wisdom and understanding shall rest upon him, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of the Lord” (Isaiah 11:2–3).

This is not the fear by which Peter denied Christ; rather, we have received the spirit of that fear of which Christ himself says: “Fear him who has power to destroy both soul and body in Gehenna; yes, I say to you, fear him.” He said this so that we would not deny him through the fear by which Peter was troubled. He wished this fear to be taken away from us when he first said: “Do not fear those who kill the body and afterward have nothing more that they can do” (Luke 12:5, 4). We have not received the spirit of this fear, but of power, love, and self-control.

Concerning this spirit he himself says to the Romans: “We glory in tribulations, knowing that tribulation produces endurance, endurance produces tested character, and tested character produces hope; but hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:3–5). It is therefore not through ourselves, but through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, that this very love comes about; and this shows it to be God’s gift, so that tribulation does not take endurance away but rather produces it.

To the Ephesians also he says: “Peace to the brothers, and love with faith.” These are great blessings; but let him say from where they come: “from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Ephesians 6:23). Therefore these great blessings are nothing other than gifts of God.

## CHAPTER XIX

### 40

But it is not surprising if light shines in the darkness and the darkness does not comprehend it (John 1:5). In John, the light says: “See what kind of love the Father has given us, that we should be called and should be children of God” (1 John 3:1). But in the Pelagians the darkness says: “Love comes to us from ourselves.”

If they possessed true love—that is, Christian love—they would know from where they possessed it, just as the Apostle knew, when he said: “We have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Corinthians 2:12). John says: “God is love” (1 John 4:16). Yet the Pelagians say that even God himself is possessed by them not from God but from themselves; and although they admit that knowledge of the law comes to us from God, they want charity to come from ourselves.

They do not heed the Apostle when he says: “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Corinthians 8:1). What is more foolish—or rather, what is more insane and more alien to the very holiness of love—than to confess that knowledge, which without love puffs up, is from God, while love, which prevents knowledge from puffing up, is from ourselves?

Again, when the Apostle says that the love of Christ surpasses knowledge (Ephesians 3:19), what is more deranged than to suppose that knowledge, which must be subjected to love, is from God, while love, which surpasses knowledge, is from human beings?

True faith and sound doctrine, however, say that both come from God, because it is written: “From his presence proceed knowledge and understanding” (Proverbs 2, according to the Septuagint); and it is written: “Love is from God” (1 John 4:7). We also read of “the spirit of knowledge and piety” (Isaiah 11:2), and we read of “the spirit of power and love and self-control” (2 Timothy 1:7).

But love is a greater gift than knowledge. For when knowledge is present in a person, love is necessary so that knowledge may not puff him up; but love “does not envy, does not act improperly, is not puffed up” (1 Corinthians 13:4).

## CHAPTER XX

### 41

I think that I have argued sufficiently against those who vehemently attack the grace of God, by which the human will is not removed but changed from evil into good, and, once it has become good, is assisted. I have argued in such a way that it is not so much I as divine Scripture itself that has spoken with you through the clearest testimonies of the truth.

If this divine Scripture is examined carefully, it shows not only that the good wills of human beings—which God himself creates out of evil and, once he has made them good, directs toward good actions and eternal life—are in God’s power, but also that the wills which preserve [Note: Morel judges that one should read “adorn,” *exornant*. See *Elementa Critica*, pp. 91–92] the creature of this world are so subject to God’s power that he causes them to incline wherever and whenever he wishes, either to bestow benefits upon certain people or to inflict punishments upon others, according to his judgment—a judgment indeed most hidden, but without any doubt perfectly just.

For we find that some sins are also punishments for other sins. Such are the vessels of wrath, which the Apostle says were “prepared for destruction” (Romans 9:22). Such is the hardening of Pharaoh, whose cause is also said to be “to show God’s power in him” (Exodus 7:3; 10:1). Such is the flight of the Israelites from the presence of their enemies out of the city of Gai. Fear was produced in their hearts so that they fled, and this happened so that sin might be punished, and punished in the manner in which it was to be punished. Hence the Lord says to Jesus son of Nave: “The children of Israel will not be able to stand before the face of their enemies” [Note: The printed editions read “from the face.” The Corbeiensis manuscripts and two Vatican manuscripts read “before the face”] (Joshua 7:4, 12).

What does “They will not be able to stand” mean? Why did they not stand by free choice, but flee with their wills thrown into confusion by fear, unless it is because God rules even over human wills and, when angry, turns those whom he wishes into terror?

Did not the enemies of the Israelites fight against the people of God, whom Jesus son of Nave was leading, by their own will? And yet Scripture says that it was brought about by the Lord that their hearts were strengthened so that they went out to battle against Israel, in order to destroy them (Joshua 11:20).

Did not the wicked man, the son of Gemini, curse King David by his own will? Yet what does David say, filled with true, profound, and devout wisdom [Note: The Corbeiensis manuscript reads “profound wisdom,” omitting “and devout”]? What does he say to the man who wished to strike the one who was cursing?

“What have I to do with you, sons of Sarvia?” he says. “Leave him, and let him curse, because the Lord has told him to curse David. And who shall say to him, ‘Why have you done this?’”

Then divine Scripture, commending the king’s full judgment as though repeating it from another beginning, says: “And David said to Abessa” [Note: The printed editions read “to Abisai.” The manuscripts read “to Abessa,” as in the Septuagint] “and to all his servants: ‘Behold, my son, who came forth from my body, seeks my life; and now this son of Gemini still more’” [Note: Thus the Gallican, Vatican, and Belgian manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek Septuagint: *kai proséti nûn ho huiòs toû Iemini*—“and now still more the son of Benjamin.” Most printed editions had: “how much more this son of Gemini”]. “Leave him, let him curse, because the Lord has told him to do so, so that the Lord may see my humiliation and repay me good for his cursing on this day” (2 Samuel 16:5–12) [Note: The manuscripts read “he will repay”].

How the Lord could be said to have told this man to curse David—what wise person can understand? He did not say it by commanding him, in which case obedience would have been praised; rather, he inclined the man’s will, already evil through its own fault, toward this sin by his just and hidden judgment. Therefore it is said that the Lord told him.

For if he had obeyed God’s command, he would have deserved praise rather than punishment, as we know that he was later punished for this sin. Nor is the reason hidden why the Lord in this manner told him to curse David—that is, why he directed or permitted his evil heart to enter this sin: “so that the Lord,” he says, “may see my humiliation and repay me good for his cursing on this day.”

Behold how it is proved that God uses even the hearts of the wicked for the praise and assistance of the good. Thus he used Judas, who handed Christ over; thus he used the Jews who crucified Christ. And what great benefits he thereby bestowed upon the peoples who would believe!

He also uses the devil himself, who is supremely evil, but uses him supremely well, to exercise and test the faith and piety of the good—not for himself, who knows everything before it happens, but for us, for whom it was necessary that he deal with us in this way.

Did not Abessalon [Note: The printed editions read “Absalon.” Below, in section 42, they also read “Ahiae Silonitae.” But the manuscripts consistently have “Abessalon” and “Achiae Selonitae,” in accordance with the Septuagint] choose by his own will the counsel that harmed him? Yet he did so because the Lord had heard his father praying that this might happen. Hence Scripture says: “And the Lord commanded that the good counsel of Achitophel be frustrated, so that the Lord might bring all evils upon Abessalon” (2 Samuel 17:14).

It called the counsel “good” because it was temporarily advantageous to the cause: it favored Abessalon against his father, against whom he had rebelled, so that he might overpower him, unless the Lord frustrated the counsel given by Achitophel by acting in Abessalon’s heart so that he rejected that counsel and chose another that was not beneficial to him.

## CHAPTER XXI

### 42

Who would not tremble at these divine judgments, by which God acts even in the hearts of wicked people to bring about whatever he wishes, while nevertheless repaying them according to their merits?

Rehoboam, son of Solomon, rejected the wholesome counsel of the elders, who had advised him not to deal harshly with the people, and instead followed the words of his contemporaries, answering threateningly those whom he ought to have addressed gently. Where did this come from, if not from his own will? Yet on this account the ten tribes of Israel withdrew from him and appointed another king for themselves, Jeroboam, so that the will of the angry God might be fulfilled—something he had also foretold would happen.

For what does Scripture say? “The king did not listen to the people, because the turning was from the Lord, so that he might establish his word which he had spoken by the hand of Ahias the Selonite concerning Jeroboam son of Nabath” (1 Kings 12:3–20). Thus it plainly came about through human will, and yet the turning was from the Lord.

Read the books of Chronicles, and you will find written in the Second Book: “And the Lord stirred up against Joram the spirit of the Philistines and the Arabs who were neighbors of the Ethiopians. They came up into the land of Judah, devastated it, and seized all the property that was found in the king’s house” (2 Chronicles 21:16–17).

Here it is shown that God stirs up enemies to devastate lands which he judges worthy of such punishment. Did the Philistines and Arabs nevertheless come to devastate the land of Judah without their own will? Or did they come by their own will in such a way that it would falsely be written that the Lord stirred up their spirit to do this? On the contrary, both are true: they came by their own will, and yet the Lord stirred up their spirit.

This can also be expressed in the following way: the Lord stirred up their spirit, and yet they came by their own will. For the Almighty acts even upon the movement of human wills in human hearts, so that through them he may accomplish what he himself wishes to accomplish through them—he who does not know how to will anything unjust.

What does the man of God mean when he says to King Amessias [Note: Thus the manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint. The printed editions have “Amasias”]: “Let the army of Israel not go with you, for the Lord is not with Israel, with all the sons of Ephraim. For if you suppose that you will prevail with them, God will turn you to flight before your enemies, because power belongs to God, either to help or to turn to flight” (2 Chronicles 25:7–8)? [Note: We have deleted the conjunction “and,” because it is absent from the manuscripts and the Septuagint.]

How does God’s power help some in battle by giving them confidence, while turning others to flight by putting fear into them, unless it is because he who in heaven and on earth does whatever he wills (Psalm 134:6) also works in human hearts?

We read what Joash, king of Israel, said when he sent a messenger to King Amessias, who wished to fight him. After some other words he said: “Now remain in your house. Why provoke disaster and fall, you and Judah with you?” (2 Kings 14:9–10). Then Scripture added: “Amessias did not listen, because it was from God that he should be delivered into their hands” [Note: Most manuscripts read “into his hand.” The printed editions have “into his hands”; “his” is absent from the manuscripts and the Septuagint], “because they had sought the gods of Edom” (2 Chronicles 25:20).

Behold: God, wishing to punish the sin of idolatry, worked in the heart of one with whom he was justly angry, so that he would not heed wholesome advice but, having rejected it, would go to war, where he would fall together with his army.

Through the prophet Ezekiel God says: “And if the prophet is deceived and speaks, I, the Lord, have deceived that prophet; and I will stretch out my hand against him and destroy him from the midst of my people Israel” (Ezekiel 14:9).

In the Book of Esther it is written that this woman, who was of the people of Israel and had become the foreign wife of King Ahasuerus in the land of captivity, had to intercede for her people, whom the king had ordered to be slaughtered wherever they were in his kingdom. She prayed to the Lord, for great necessity compelled her to dare to enter the king’s presence contrary to his command and contrary to the established order (Esther 3–4).

And see what Scripture says: “He looked upon her like a bull in the violent force of his indignation; the queen was afraid, and her color changed as she fainted, and she bowed over the head of her maidservant who preceded her. But God changed and transformed his indignation into gentleness” (ibid. 5, according to the Septuagint).

It is also written in the Proverbs of Solomon: “As the rush of water, so is the heart of a king in the hand of God; wherever he wills, he will incline it” (Proverbs 21:1).

And in Psalm 104 we read what God did to the Egyptians: “And he turned their heart so that they hated his people, so that they might deal deceitfully with his servants” (Psalm 104:25).

Look also at what is written in the apostolic Letters, in the Epistle of the apostle Paul to the Romans: “Therefore God handed them over to the desires of their hearts, to impurity.” And shortly afterward: “For this reason God handed them over to dishonorable passions.” And shortly afterward: “Since they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a debased mind, to do what is improper” (Romans 1:24, 26, 28).

And in the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians he says of certain people: “Because they did not receive the love of the truth so as to be saved, therefore God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe the lie, so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to wickedness” (2 Thessalonians 2:10–11).

### 43

By these and similar testimonies of the divine words—which it would be too long to recall in their entirety—it is sufficiently clear, as I judge, that God works in human hearts to incline their wills wherever he wishes: toward good, according to his mercy, or toward evil, according to their merits, by his judgment, sometimes manifest and sometimes hidden, but always just.

This must be fixed and immovable in your hearts: “There is no injustice with God” (Romans 9:14). Therefore, when you read in the writings of truth that people are deceived by God, or that their hearts are dulled or hardened, do not doubt that their evil merits came first, so that they might justly suffer these things. Otherwise you will fall into Solomon’s proverb: “The folly of a man perverts his ways, but in his heart he blames God” (Proverbs 19:3).

Grace, however, is not given according to human merits; otherwise grace would no longer be grace (Romans 11:6), because it is called grace precisely because it is given freely.

If God is powerful enough to work even in the hearts of the wicked—whether through angels, good or evil, or by whatever other means—in accordance with their merits, while he himself did not create their wickedness, but it was either originally derived from Adam or increased through their own will, what is surprising if he works through the Holy Spirit in the hearts of his elect to produce good, since he has worked so that those very hearts might become good from evil?

## CHAPTER XXII

### 44

Let people imagine whatever good merits they wish, which they think precede justification by God’s grace. They do not understand that, when they say this, they are doing nothing other than denying grace. But, as I said, let them imagine whatever they wish about adults; concerning infants, at least, the Pelagians find nothing to answer.

Infants have no will involved in receiving grace whose merit they could say preceded it. Moreover, we see them resisting with tears when they are baptized and receive the divine Sacraments. This would be counted against them as a grave sin of impiety if they were already exercising free choice. Yet grace adheres even to those who resist, with no good merit preceding it—plainly; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.

Sometimes this grace is bestowed upon the children of unbelievers, when by God’s hidden providence they come by whatever means into the hands of the godly. Sometimes, however, the children of believers do not obtain it, because some obstacle exists that prevents help from reaching those in danger.

These things take place through God’s hidden providence, whose judgments are inscrutable and whose ways are unsearchable. Consider what the Apostle had foretold when he said this. He was speaking of Jews and Gentiles when he wrote to the Romans—that is, to Gentiles—and said:

“For just as you once did not believe God, but now have obtained mercy through their unbelief, so they also have now not believed through your mercy, so that they too may obtain mercy. For God has enclosed all in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all” (Romans 11:30–33).

When he considered what he had said, marveling at the certain truth but profound depth of his statement—how God had enclosed all in unbelief so that he might have mercy on all, as though he were doing evil in order that good might come—he immediately exclaimed:

“O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and inscrutable his ways!”

Because wicked people do not reflect upon these inscrutable judgments and unsearchable ways, and because they are inclined to criticize but not capable of understanding, they imagined and loudly claimed that the Apostle was saying: “Let us do evil, so that good may come” (Romans 3:8). God forbid that the Apostle should say this.

But people who did not understand thought that this was what he meant when they heard him say: “The law entered so that transgression might increase; but where transgression increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20).

Grace, however, acts so that those who did evil may now do good, not so that they may persist in evil and expect good to be repaid to them. They ought not, therefore, to say: “Let us do evil, so that good may come.” Rather: “We did evil, and good came; now let us do good, so that in the age to come we may receive good for good, we who in this age receive good for evil.”

Hence it is written in the Psalm: “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, Lord” (Psalm 100:1).

At first, therefore, the Son of Man did not come into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him (John 3:17)—this was on account of mercy. Later, however, he will come on account of judgment, to judge the living and the dead. Yet even in the present time salvation does not take place without judgment, though it is hidden. Therefore he says: “For judgment I came into this world: that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

## CHAPTER XXIII

### 45

Refer, then, to God’s hidden judgments the fact that, in one and the same condition—which all infants certainly share, since they inherit evil from Adam—one is helped so that he is baptized while another is not helped and dies in that very bondage; that one who was baptized is left in this life, although God foreknew that he would become impious, while another who was baptized is taken from this life, lest wickedness change his understanding (Wisdom 4:11).

Do not on this account attribute injustice or folly to God, with whom is the fountain of justice and wisdom. Rather, as I exhorted you at the beginning of this discourse, walk according to what you have attained; and “God will reveal this also to you” (Philippians 3:16, 15) [Note: The printed editions insert here, “If you think otherwise,” which was absent from the manuscripts]. If not in this life, certainly in the next, for “nothing is hidden that will not be revealed” (Matthew 10:26).

When, therefore, you hear the Lord saying, “I, the Lord, have deceived that prophet” (Ezekiel 14:9), and the Apostle saying, “He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills” (Romans 9:18), believe that in the one whom he permits to be deceived or hardened there were evil merits [Note: Some manuscripts read “or whom he hardens”]. But in the one upon whom he has mercy, faithfully and without hesitation recognize the grace of God, who does not repay evil with evil but good for evil.

Do not therefore take free choice away from Pharaoh because God says in many places, “I hardened Pharaoh,” or “I have hardened” or “I will harden Pharaoh’s heart” (Exodus 4–14, passim). For this does not mean that Pharaoh himself did not harden his own heart. We also read this about him when the dog-flies were removed from the Egyptians, Scripture saying: “And Pharaoh hardened his heart even at this time and was unwilling to let the people go” (ibid. 8:32).

Thus God hardened him by a just judgment, and Pharaoh himself hardened his heart through free choice.

Be certain, therefore, that your labor will not be in vain if you persevere in your good purpose and continue to the end. For the God who now does not repay those whom he liberates according to their works will then repay each according to his works (Matthew 16:27).

God will indeed repay evil for evil, because he is just; good for evil, because he is good; and good for good, because he is good and just. But he will never repay evil for good, because he is not unjust.

He will therefore repay evil for evil: punishment for injustice. He will repay good for evil: grace for injustice. And he will repay good for good: grace for grace.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### 46

Read this book again and again; and if you understand it, give thanks to God. Where you do not understand, pray that you may understand, for the Lord will give you understanding.

Remember that it is written: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all and does not reproach anyone, and it will be given to him” (James 1:5). This is the wisdom that descends from above, as the apostle James himself says.

Reject from yourselves that other wisdom, and pray that it may not be in you—the wisdom he condemned when he said: “If you have bitter jealousy and contentions among you, this is not the wisdom that descends from above, but earthly, sensual, demonic. For where jealousy and contention are, there is instability and every evil work. But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, compliant, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial, without hypocrisy” (ibid. 3:14–17).

What good, then, will the one lack who asks for this wisdom and obtains it from the Lord? And from this understand grace: if this wisdom came from ourselves, it would not be from above, nor would it need to be sought from God himself, who created us.

Brothers, pray also for us, that we may live temperately, devoutly, and justly in this age, awaiting that blessed hope and the manifestation of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ (Titus 2:12–13), to whom be honor, glory, and kingship with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

---

## [ON CORRECTION AND GRACE]

[Column 0911]

### Note concerning the following book

See Book 2, final chapter, of the *Retractions*, volume 1, column 656, beginning with the words “Again, to the same people” [namely, Valentinus and those monks living in the monastery of Adrumetum. See above, columns 873–874, note (a)] and continuing through the words “Valentinus, most beloved brother.”

Prosper, writing to Augustine, says that the book *On Correction and Grace*, “full of divine authority,” was issued at an opportune time and brought to the knowledge of the Gauls, “because every question” relating to the mystery of divine grace, concerning which “they were to consult” the holy Doctor, “was fully and completely answered there.” After reviewing the book, he says, those who previously followed “the holy and apostolic authority of your teaching” became “far more understanding and much better instructed.”

That same book places the entire economy of divine grace before our eyes, as the distinguished historian of the Pelagian controversy says. Norisius calls it the key by which access is opened to Augustine’s entire doctrine concerning divine grace and free will.

### Letter 216 among Augustine’s letters

### Letter of Valentinus to Augustine, written after the book *On Grace and Free Will* and his earlier letter

To the truly holy Lord, greatly to be revered and preferred above all by us, and honored with devout exultation, the most blessed Pope Augustine: Valentinus, servant of Your Holiness, and the entire congregation which, together with me, places its hope in your prayers, sends greetings in the Lord.

### 1

We received the venerable writings and the book of Your Holiness with such trembling hearts that, just as blessed Elijah, when he stood at the entrance of the cave and the glory of the Lord passed by, veiled his face, so we covered our rebuked eyes, because we were ashamed, in our own judgment, at the rusticity of our brothers; and, because of their disorderly departure, we feared to greet Your Blessedness [Note: Previously, in volume 2, it read *meruimus* (“we deserved”), which is incorrect unless a negative particle is prefixed. Here we follow the very ancient Corbeiensis copy, in which the letter is joined to Augustine’s preceding book].

There is a time for speaking and a time for keeping silent, lest, while writing to you amid doubts and wavering concerning the truth, we should seem to doubt the words of your wisdom, which is like the wisdom of an angel of God.

For we did not need to inquire about Your Blessedness or about your wisdom, which is known to us through the grace of the Lord. We rejoiced so eagerly over the book of Your sweetest Holiness [Note: Elsewhere, “sweetest” is masculine] that, just as the Apostles did not dare ask the Lord, who was dining with them after the resurrection, who he was—for they knew that he was Jesus (John 21:12)—so we neither wished nor dared to ask whether the book belonged to Your Holiness. The very grace of the faithful, which is so generously commended in it, bears witness to us in its most vital words that it is yours, holy lord pope.

### 2

Let us now begin, most blessed lord pope, to explain the sequence of the disturbance itself.

Our dearest brother Florus, a servant of Your Fatherhood, had gone to the region of Uzalis at the prompting of charity. During his stay in his own city, he brought to the monastery gifts from the little works of Your Holiness [Note: Elsewhere, “of the monastery”], while a certain brother Felix—who is known to have come late to Your Holiness after his companions—devoutly took down the same book by dictation [Note: The book, or Letter 194, to Sixtus].

When brother Florus departed from the city of Uzalis for Carthage, the monastery was reached with the same little book. Without showing me the book, they began to read it aloud to the uninstructed brothers. This disturbed the hearts of some who did not understand. For when the Lord also said, “Whoever does not eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood will not have life in himself” (John 6:54), those who understood impiously withdrew—not because of any fault in the Lord who spoke, but because of the hardness of their most impious heart.

3. The aforementioned brothers, who had turned everything upside down, began to disturb the souls of the innocent, while my smallness was utterly unaware of it—so unaware of their murmuring assembly that, unless Brother Florus, returning from Carthage and recognizing their disturbances [Note: [Col. 0913] Another reading: “their repeated disturbances.”], had carefully reported them to me, I would not have known that a secret and, as it were, servile dispute was taking place among them concerning the truth that they did not understand.  

[Note: [Col. 0913] The Corbeiensis manuscripts read *murmurantes*, “murmuring.”]

I proposed, in order to remove their impious questions, that we send to the holy father Bishop Evodius [Note: [Col. 0913] Another reading: “lord.”], so that he himself might write back to us something more certain concerning this sacred book for the sake of the ignorant.

[Note: [Col. 0913] Evodius did indeed write back; and his letter to Valentinus on this very matter was found by Jacques Sirmond in the manuscript of St. Maximin of Trier. From it he transferred this fragment into the *Predestinarian History*, chapter 1: “Honorable brothers have reported to us that I do not know what questions have arisen among you concerning free choice and the justice of God. We praise your zeal, but we do not wish it to be contentious. Contentiousness stirs up disturbance, whereas zeal requires devotion. The man first created—Adam, I mean—possessed the fullest power of free choice. But once free choice itself was wounded, it was weakened. Therefore there is now free choice in man, but wounded. Hence it is said, ‘My strength is weakened through poverty, and the light of my eyes is not with me’ (Ps. 30:11; 37:11). To restore it, the physician Christ the Savior was sent, so that he might save what had perished and heal what had been corrupted.” And later: “Let the saints of God therefore read the sayings of the ancient Fathers, as I have already said, those who possess a devout disposition bestowed by God; and when they do not understand, let them not be quick to condemn, but pray that they may understand.”]

Nor were they willing to receive this response with greater patience. Instead, they hastily undertook a departure that we had not wished for in such circumstances. Brother Florus was almost driven to distraction by their fury, for they raged against him because, as they thought, he had brought them the wounds inflicted by this book; yet the sick were unable to recognize in it the medicine. Accordingly, for the sake of greater authority, we asked the holy presbyter Sabinus to intervene, and his Holiness read the book together with clear interpretations. Even then the wounded soul was not healed.

Out of devotion itself, we gave them the means for their journey, lest we add to their wounds—wounds which the grace of that book could heal, and in which your holy presence shines forth. Once they had departed, rest and peace rejoiced among all the brothers in the Lord. This contention had arisen from the contentiousness of five or more brothers.

4. Yet because joy sometimes arises from sorrow, we are not excessively saddened, since through the ignorant and the curious we have been found worthy to be enlightened by your Holiness’s most gracious admonitions. Indeed, the doubt of the blessed Apostle Thomas, who sought the openings made by the nails (John 20:25), became a confirmation of the universal Church.

We have therefore received, holy father, the medicine of your devout healing together with the grace of your letter, and we have struck our breasts, so that at least in this way our conscience may be healed—a conscience which grace heals and gives life through our free choice, which mercy grants. Yet this is in the present time, when we still sing of mercy together with delay. For when we begin to sing of judgment to the Lord, we shall receive a reward for our work, because “the Lord is merciful and just, compassionate and upright” (Ps. 111:4).

For, as your Holiness teaches us, we must be presented before the tribunal of Christ, “so that each of us may receive what is proper to the body, according to what he has done, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10); because “the Lord will come, and his reward is with him” (Isa. 40:10); because a man will stand, and his work will stand before him; because “the Lord will come like a burning furnace, to set the impious ablaze like straw” (Joel 2:3, 5), and for those who fear the name of the Lord “the sun of righteousness will rise,” when the impious are punished by the judgment of justice (Mal. 4:1–3).

The just man, whose friend you are, holy father, cries out, trembles, and humbly says: “Lord, do not enter into judgment with your servant” (Ps. 142:2). If grace were the rewarder, the just man would not fear the secret judgment of majesty.

This, father, is the faith of your servants Florus—not as these brothers have spoken. At present they have heard from him that the gift of mercy is not given according to our merits, but through the grace of the Redeemer. For concerning that day, who could doubt that grace is far removed, when justice begins to rage?

This is what we cry out, father; this is what, taught by you, we sing—not confidently, but trembling: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath” (Ps. 6:2). This is what we say: “Correct us, Lord, and instruct us in your law, so that you may soothe us from the days of evil” (Ps. 93:12–13).

This we believe, taught by you, venerable father: that the Lord questions the just and the impious; that, with the good and the evil placed at his right and left, he reckons the works of devotion that are to be rewarded and enumerates the stubbornness of impiety that is to be punished. Where will grace be, when works—whether good or evil—are weighed according to their own quality?

5. But why does he not fear to put forward an outright lie?

[Note: [Col. 0913] The Corbie manuscript reads: “But heart [lacuna] to offer.”] We do not deny that free choice has been healed by God’s grace; but we believe and confidently affirm that it makes progress and is assisted through Christ’s daily grace.

What do people mean when they say, “It is in my power to do good”—if only human beings actually did good? O empty boasting of wretched men! Every day their sins accuse them, yet they themselves claim for themselves a naked free choice, without examining their conscience, which cannot be healed except through grace, so that they might say: “Have mercy on me; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you” (Ps. 40:5).

What would those who boast to themselves of free choice—which is not denied when accompanied by God’s help—do if death had already been swallowed up in victory, if our mortal nature had already put on immortality and our corruptible nature had already put on incorruption (1 Cor. 15:53–54)? Behold, the wounds stink, yet medicine is arrogantly demanded.

They do not say with the just man, “Unless the Lord had helped me, my soul would almost have dwelt in hell” (Ps. 93:17). They do not say with the holy man, “Unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain” (Ps. 126:1).

6. But pray, most devout father, that we may now have no concern except for expiating our sin with tears and commending the grace of God. Pray, holy father, that the pit may not close its mouth over us (Ps. 68:16), that we may be saved from those who descend into the pit (Ps. 29:4), and that our soul may not perish with the impious (Ps. 25:9) through our pride, but may be healed through the Lord’s grace.

As you therefore instructed, holy father, our brother Florus, servant of your Holiness, proceeded with all eagerness. His fatigue does not hinder him but benefits him, so that a clarified understanding of the heart may be added to him. We humbly commend him to your Holiness, and at the same time earnestly ask you to commend the ignorant to the Lord in your prayers, so that they may be most gently brought into order.

Pray, lord and sweetest father, that the devil may flee from our community, and that, every storm raised by alien questions having been removed, the ship of our purpose, laden with peaceful passengers—*epibatai* [Note: [Col. 0915] *Epibatai* are marines who serve aboard ships.]—may safely remain within the station of the most secure harbor, while the ship sails across this great and boundless sea; and that, in that harbor where the vessel of life will no longer be subject to fear, it may receive without discrepancy the price of its pleasing merchandise.

We trust that we shall obtain this through the help of your Holiness, by the grace that is in Christ Jesus our Lord. We beg you to deign to greet on our behalf all the sons of your apostolate, our lords the clergy, and the holy men serving in the community of our purpose, so that together with your Beatitude they may deign to pray for us.

May the undivided Trinity of our Lord God preserve your apostolate, which it chose through grace, for us in its Church, and crown you, mindful of us, in the great Church—which is our desire, lord. If, however, your Holiness’s servant, our brother Florus, should suggest anything concerning the rule of the monastery, we beg you, father, to deign to receive it willingly and to instruct us, weak as we are, in every respect.

[Col. 0915]

## One Book of St. Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *On Rebuke and Grace*, addressed to the same Valentinus and with him to the Monks of Hadrumetum

[Note: [Col. 0915] Written in the year of Christ 426 or 427, somewhat after Easter.]

[Note: [Col. 0915] This book, *On Rebuke and Grace*, was collated and corrected against the same manuscripts as the book *On Grace and Free Choice*, mentioned above, cols. 881–882.]

[Note: [Col. 0915] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and the *Confessions*, vol. 1. M.]

(C)

At the beginning he explains what the catholic faith teaches concerning the law, free choice, and grace. He teaches that the grace of God through Jesus Christ is that by which alone human beings are freed from evil and without which they do absolutely no good—not merely because grace itself shows what ought to be done, but because it also grants that they do it with love, God bestowing upon them the inspiration both of a good will and of a good work.

He teaches that the correction of evil people who have not received this grace is neither unjust, since they are evil by their own will, nor useless, although it must be acknowledged that it is only through God that correction becomes beneficial. Perseverance in the good is truly a great gift of God; nevertheless, the correction of one who has not persevered is not for that reason to be neglected. One who, without receiving this gift, has by his own will fallen back into sin is worthy not only of correction but also—if he remains in evil until death—of eternal condemnation.

Why one person receives this gift and another does not is inscrutable. None of the predestined can perish. Accordingly, the perseverance that is not given to all who are here called children of God is given to all who truly are children of God by God’s foreknowledge and predestination.

He responds to the question that arises concerning Adam: how did Adam sin by failing to persevere, when he did not receive perseverance? Augustine shows that Adam was originally given a kind of assistance without which he could not remain in the good if he wished, but not the kind by which he would be made to wish it. Now, however, through Christ, assistance is given not only without which we cannot remain in the good even if we wish, but also such and so great an assistance that we are made to wish it.

He proves that the number of the predestined, for whom this kind of gift is proper, is fixed and can be neither increased nor diminished. Since it is unknown who belongs to that number and who does not, medicinal correction must be applied to all who sin, lest they themselves perish or destroy others. Finally, he concludes that grace does not prohibit correction, nor does correction deny grace.

## CHAPTER ONE

### 1

Having read your letter, dearest brother Valentinus, and that of those who serve God together with you—the letter which your Charity sent through Brother Florus and those who came to us with him—I gave thanks to God, because, through the words you sent back to us, I learned of your peace in the Lord, your agreement in the truth, and your ardor in charity.

But as for what the enemy attempted to overturn among you, through God’s mercy, and through his wondrous goodness turning the enemy’s snares toward the advancement of his servants [Note: [Col. 0917] Some manuscripts read “profit.”], it served rather to ensure that none of you would be destroyed for the worse, but that some would be instructed for the better.

There is therefore no need to go over again everything that we sufficiently discussed and sent to you in a complete book—the book *On Grace and Free Choice*. Your replies indicate how you received it. Nevertheless, do not suppose that one reading could possibly have made it sufficiently known to you.
