If, then, you wish to find it most fruitful, do not be reluctant to make it thoroughly familiar by rereading it, so that you may know most carefully which questions and difficulties divine, not human, authority comes to meet and heal.

[Note: [Col. 0917] The Louvain editors thought “most clearly” should be substituted; the Gallican and Vatican manuscripts, with the older editions, read “most carefully.”] From that authority we must not depart if we wish to arrive where we are making our way.

### 2

The Lord himself not only shows us from what evil we should turn away and what good we should do—something that the written letter of the law alone can accomplish—but he also helps us to turn away from evil and do good (Ps. 36:27), something no one can do without the Spirit of grace.

[Note: [Col. 0917] The most ancient Corbeiensis manuscript reads, “unless the Spirit of grace.” The Casalensis reads, “unless by the Spirit of grace.”]

If grace is absent, the law is present in order to make people guilty and kill them. Hence the Apostle says, “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6).

Whoever uses the law properly learns from it what is evil and what is good; and, not trusting in his own strength, he flees to grace. Through grace he turns away from evil and does good.

But who flees to grace unless “the steps of a man are directed by the Lord, and he wills his way” (Ps. 36:23)? Therefore even the desire for the help of grace is itself the beginning of grace. Concerning this the Psalmist says: “And I said, ‘Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High’” (Ps. 76:11).

We must therefore confess that we possess free choice both for doing evil and for doing good. Yet in doing evil each person is free from righteousness and a servant of sin; whereas in doing good no one can be free unless he has been freed by the one who said, “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free” (John 8:36).

This does not mean that once someone has been freed from the domination of sin, he no longer needs the help of his liberator. Rather, hearing from him, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), he should himself say to him, “Be my helper; do not abandon me” (Ps. 26:9).

I rejoice that I have found this faith—which is unquestionably the true, prophetic, apostolic, and catholic faith—in our brother Florus. Therefore those who failed to understand him must instead be corrected; by God’s favor, I now believe that they have been corrected.

## CHAPTER TWO

### 3

The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord must be understood as that by which alone human beings are freed from evil and without which they do absolutely no good, whether by thinking, willing and loving, or acting. Grace does not merely show them what should be done, so that they may know it; it also grants that they do with love what they know.

The Apostle sought this inspiration of a good will and work for those to whom he said: “We pray to God that you do no evil—not so that we may appear approved, but so that you may do what is good” (2 Cor. 13:7).

Who can hear this and not awaken, and confess that it is from the Lord God that we receive the ability to turn away from evil and do good? For the Apostle does not say, “We warn, teach, exhort, or rebuke”; rather, he says, “We pray to God that you do no evil, but that you do what is good.”

And yet he was also speaking to them and doing all the things I have mentioned: he was warning, teaching, exhorting, and rebuking. But he knew that all these things—which he openly did by planting and watering—were of no avail unless the one who gives the growth secretly heard his prayer on their behalf.

For, as the same teacher of the Gentiles says, “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God, who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7).

### 4

Let those who say, “Why are we preached to and commanded to turn away from evil and do good, if we do not do this ourselves, but God works in us both the willing and the working” (Phil. 2:13), not deceive themselves.

Rather, if they are children of God, let them understand that they are led by the Spirit of God (Rom. 8:14), so that they do what ought to be done; and when they have done it, let them give thanks to the one by whom they do it.

They are led so that they may act, not so that they themselves may do nothing. For this reason what they ought to do is shown to them: so that, when they do it as it ought to be done—that is, with love and delight in righteousness—they may rejoice that they have received the sweetness which the Lord gave, “so that their land might yield its fruit” (Ps. 84:13).

[Note: [Col. 0918] Ambrose, Erasmus, and most manuscripts read “his land.”]

But when they do not act—whether by doing nothing at all or by acting without charity—let them pray that they may receive what they do not yet possess. For what will they have that they will not receive? Or what do they have that they have not received (1 Cor. 4:7)?

## CHAPTER THREE

### 5

“Then,” they say, “let those who preside over us merely command us what we ought to do and pray for us that we may do it; but let them not correct or rebuke us if we do not do it.”

On the contrary, let everything be done. The Apostles, the teachers of the Churches, did everything: they commanded what should be done, rebuked those who did not do it, and prayed that it might be done.

The Apostle commands when he says, “Let all your things be done with charity” (1 Cor. 16:14).

[Note: [Col. 0918] The Gallican and Vatican manuscripts read, as above at col. 902, “with charity.” The printed editions read, “in charity.”]

He rebukes when he says, “There is altogether a fault among you, because you have lawsuits among yourselves. Why do you not rather suffer injustice? Why do you not rather allow yourselves to be defrauded? But you do injustice and defraud—and that against brothers” (1 Cor. 6:7–8).

[Note: [Col. 0918] The manuscripts omit “among you.”]

[Note: [Col. 0918] The printed editions read “against brothers”; all the manuscripts read “brothers,” which must be taken as an accusative according to the Greek.]

“Do you not know that the unjust will not possess the kingdom of God?” (1 Cor. 6:9).

Let us also hear him praying: “May the Lord multiply you and make you abound in charity toward one another and toward all” (1 Thess. 3:12).

He commands that charity be possessed; he rebukes because charity is not possessed; he prays that charity may abound.

O human being, in the command learn what you ought to have; in the rebuke learn that through your own fault you do not have it; in the prayer learn from where you are to receive what you wish to have.

## CHAPTER FOUR

### 6

“But how,” he says, “is something not possessed through my fault when I did not receive it from the one from whom, unless it is given, there is absolutely no other source from which such a great gift can be obtained?”

Bear with me for a little while, my brothers—not against you, whose heart is upright with God, but against those who are earthly-minded; or rather, let me contend against human thoughts themselves on behalf of the truth of heavenly and divine grace.

[Note: [Col. 0919] Ambrose, Erasmus, and eight of the Gallican manuscripts read, “to contend on behalf of the charity of heavenly and divine grace.” The Sorbonicus and Albinensis manuscripts read, “to contend on behalf of heavenly and divine charity.”]

For this is what those say who do not wish to be rebuked by the preachers of this grace for their wicked works:

“Command me what I should do. If I do it, give thanks to God on my behalf, because he gave me the ability to do it. But if I do not do it, I should not be rebuked; rather, he should be entreated to give what he has not given—that is, the faithful love of God and neighbor by which his commands are carried out.

“Pray, then, for me, that I may receive this, and that through it I may sincerely and with a good will do what he commands. I would rightly be rebuked if I did not possess it through my own fault—that is, if I were able to give or take it for myself and did not do so, or if, when he gave it, I refused to receive it.

“But since the will itself is prepared by the Lord (Prov. 8, according to the Septuagint), why do you rebuke me because you see that I do not wish to carry out his commands, rather than entreat him to work in me the willing?”

## CHAPTER FIVE

### 7

To this we reply: Whoever does not carry out the commands of God that are already known to you, and does not wish to be corrected, must be corrected for this reason also—because he does not wish to be corrected.

You do not want your vices to be shown to you; you do not want them to be struck, so that a useful pain may arise in you and you may seek the physician; you do not want yourself to be shown to yourself, so that, when you see how deformed you are, you may desire the one who reforms you and humbly entreat him that you may not remain in that ugliness.

It is your vice that you are evil, and it is a greater vice to refuse correction because you are evil—as though vices ought to be praised or treated with indifference, so that they should neither be praised nor blamed; or as though fear, shame, or pain in the one who is corrected accomplished nothing; or as though, when it healthfully stings, it accomplished anything other than that the Good One should be entreated and should make good, and worthy of praise, those who are corrected while evil.

For the very reason that the one who does not wish to be corrected wants this to be done for him and says, “Pray for me instead,” he must be corrected, so that he too may act on his own behalf.

The pain by which he is displeased with himself, when he feels the sting of correction, awakens him to a greater desire for prayer.

[Note: [Col. 0919] Perhaps “a greater desire.”] Thus, with God’s mercy, and aided by an increase of charity, he may cease doing shameful and lamentable things and begin doing things worthy of praise and thanksgiving.

This is the usefulness of correction. It is applied beneficially, sometimes more and sometimes less, according to the diversity of sins; and it is beneficial when the heavenly physician looks upon the person.

For it accomplishes nothing unless it makes each person repent of his sin. And who gives this except the one who looked upon the Apostle Peter when he was denying the Lord and made him weep (Luke 22:61–62)?

Therefore, after the Apostle Paul had said that those who think differently should be corrected with gentleness, he immediately added: “Lest at some time God grant them repentance for knowing the truth, and they recover from the snare of the devil” (2 Tim. 2:25–26).

### 8

Why do those who do not wish to be corrected say, “Simply command me, and pray for me that I may do what you command”? Why, according to their own perverse reasoning, do they not reject these two things as well and say, “I do not want you either to command me or to pray for me”?

For what human being is shown to have prayed for Peter that God might grant him the repentance by which he wept over having denied the Lord? What human being instructed Paul in the divine commands relating to the Christian faith?

When Paul was heard preaching the Gospel and saying, “For I make known to you, brothers, that the Gospel preached by me is not according to man. For I neither received it from man nor learned it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Gal. 1:11–12), should someone have replied to him:

“Why do you trouble us, so that we should receive and learn from you what you neither received nor learned from a human being? The one who gave it to you is powerful enough to give it to us in the same way”?

If they do not dare to say this, but allow the Gospel to be preached to them by a human being—although it is also possible for God to give it to one person without another—then let them concede that they ought also to be corrected by their superiors, through whom Christian grace is preached.

This does not deny that God can correct whomever he wishes even without any human being’s correction, and by the most hidden and powerful operation of his medicine bring that person to the healing pain of repentance.

Just as we must not cease praying for those whom we wish to correct—even though, without any human being praying for Peter, the Lord looked upon him and made him weep for his sin—so correction must not be neglected, although God makes whomever he wishes corrected even without correction.

Correction benefits a person when the one who makes those whom he wishes advance even without correction has mercy and helps.

But why some are called to be reformed in one way, others in another, and still others in yet another, by diverse and innumerable methods—far be it from us to say that the judgment belongs to the clay rather than to the potter.

## CHAPTER SIX

### 9

“The Apostle,” they say, “said, ‘For who distinguishes you? What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?’ (1 Cor. 4:7). Why, then, are we corrected, rebuked, reproved, and accused? What are we to do, since we did not receive it?”

Those who say this wish to appear free from guilt in the fact that they do not obey God, since obedience itself is certainly his gift. It must be present in the one who possesses charity, which unquestionably comes from God (1 John 4:7), and the Father gives it to his children.

“We did not receive this,” they say. “Why, then, are we corrected as though we could give it to ourselves and refused to do so by our own choice?”

They do not consider that, if they have not yet been regenerated, the first reason why they ought to be displeased when rebuked for being disobedient to God is that God made human beings upright at the beginning of the human creation (Eccl. 7:30), and there is no injustice with God (Rom. 9:14).

Accordingly, the first perversity by which God is not obeyed comes from the human being, because, falling away by his own evil will from the uprightness in which God originally made him, he became perverse.

[Note: [Col. 0921] Six Gallican and three Vatican manuscripts read “who.”]

Or is this perversity not to be corrected in human beings because it does not belong individually to the person who is corrected, but is common to all? On the contrary, let what belongs to all be corrected in each individual. Something does not fail to belong to someone merely because no one is free from it.

These sins are called original and alien because individuals draw them from their parents; but they are also rightly called ours, because in that one man all sinned, as the Apostle says (Rom. 5:12).

Let the damnable origin therefore be corrected, so that from the pain of correction the will to regeneration may arise—provided that the person being corrected is a child of promise, so that, while the sound of correction resounds outwardly and scourges him, God may inwardly work in him, by a hidden inspiration, the willing.

But if someone who has already been regenerated and justified returns by his own will to an evil life, he certainly cannot say, “I did not receive it,” because he lost through his own free choice, turned to evil, the grace of God that he had received.

[Note: [Col. 0921] Four Belgian manuscripts, three Vatican manuscripts, and the Corbie manuscript read “because the grace of God which had been received.”]

If, pierced by correction, he groans beneficially and returns to similar or even better good works, then the usefulness of correction is clearly apparent in him. Yet whether correction through a human being proceeds from charity or not, it benefits the person corrected only through God.

### 10

Can this person, still unwilling to be corrected, say, “What have I done, since I did not receive it?” when it is clear that he received it and lost what he had received through his own fault?

“I can,” he says. “I can certainly still say, when you rebuke me because I have fallen back by my own will from a good life into an evil one, ‘What have I done, since I did not receive it?’ For I received the faith that works through love, but I did not receive perseverance in it to the end.

“Will anyone dare to say that this perseverance is not a gift of God, and that this great good is ours in such a way that, whoever possesses it, the Apostle could not say to him, ‘What do you have that you did not receive?’—because he possesses it as though he had not received it?”

To this we cannot deny that perseverance in the good, advancing all the way to the end, is a great gift of God, and that it comes only from the one of whom it is written: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (James 1:17).

But the correction of one who has not persevered is not for that reason to be neglected, lest God perhaps grant him repentance and he recover from the snare of the devil.

For the Apostle appended this statement to his discussion of the usefulness of correction, saying, as I mentioned above: “Correcting with gentleness those who think differently, lest at some time God grant them repentance” (2 Tim. 2:26, 25).

If we say that this perseverance, so praiseworthy and so blessed, belongs to a human being in such a way that it does not come from God, then first we nullify what the Lord said to Peter: “I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32).

For what did he pray for him except perseverance to the end? If this came from one human being to another, it would not need to be requested from God.

Moreover, when the Apostle says, “We pray to God that you do no evil” (2 Cor. 13:7), he unquestionably prays to God for their perseverance. For the one who abandons the good—which he ought not to abandon—and inclines toward evil, not persevering in the good, certainly does evil.

[Note: [Col. 0922] The printed editions read “which he ought not to abandon,” adding a negative particle absent from the manuscripts. Erasmus attempted to emend the passage by transposing the connective: “the one who abandons the good which he ought not to abandon, and inclines toward evil.”]

In that other passage where he says, “I give thanks to my God in all remembrance of you, always in every prayer of mine making supplication for you all with joy, because of your participation in the Gospel from the first day until now [Note: [Col. 0922] Ambrose, Erasmus, and most manuscripts read “communication.”]; being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus” (Phil. 1:3–6), what else does he promise them from God’s mercy except perseverance in the good to the end?

Likewise, when he says, “Epaphras greets you, who is one of you, a servant of Christ Jesus, always striving for you in his prayers, that you may stand perfect and complete in every will of God” (Col. 4:12), what does “that you may stand” mean except “that you may persevere”?

Hence it is said concerning the devil, “He did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44), because he was there but did not remain. These people, after all, were already standing in the faith.

And when we pray that the one who stands may stand, we are praying for nothing other than perseverance.

Likewise, when the Apostle Jude says, “To him who is able to preserve you without stumbling and to set you before the presence of his glory immaculate in joy” (Jude 24), does he not most clearly show that it is a gift of God to persevere in the good to the end?

For what else does the one who preserves without stumbling give, so that he may set people immaculate in joy before the presence of his glory, except good perseverance?

What else do we read in the Acts of the Apostles? “When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and received the word of the Lord; and as many as had been appointed to eternal life believed” (Acts 13:48).

Who could have been appointed to eternal life except by the gift of perseverance? For “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22). What salvation is this except eternal salvation?

When, in the Lord’s Prayer, we say to God the Father, “Hallowed be your name” (Matt. 6:9), what else are we saying except that his name may be hallowed in us?

But since this has already been accomplished through the bath of regeneration, why is it requested daily by the faithful except so that we may persevere in what has been accomplished in us?

[Note: [Col. 0922] The Albinensis manuscript reads: “except that what has been accomplished in us may persevere in us.”]

The blessed Cyprian also understands it in this way. Explaining the same prayer, he says:

“‘Hallowed be your name’—not that we wish God to be hallowed by our prayers, but that we ask God that his name be hallowed in us. For by whom is God hallowed, when he himself hallows? But because he said, ‘Be holy, for I also am holy’ (Lev. 19:2), we ask and pray for this: that we who have been sanctified in Baptism may persevere in what we have begun to be.”

[Note: [Col. 0922] Nearly all the manuscripts read “just as I am holy,” rather than “for I also am holy.”]

Behold, the most glorious Martyr understands this to be what Christ’s faithful ask daily in these words: that they may persevere in what they began to be. Without anyone’s doubt, whoever asks the Lord to enable him to persevere in the good confesses that such perseverance is his gift.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

### 11

Since these things are so, we nevertheless correct those who, while living well, did not persevere in it—and we correct them justly. For they changed from a good life to an evil one by their own will, and therefore they are worthy of correction.

[Note: [Col. 0923] The printed editions read “they are corrected.” Most manuscripts read “they are worthy of correction,” which refers back to “they are worthy.”]

And if correction does them no good, but they persevere in their ruined life until death, they are also worthy of divine condemnation forever.

Nor will they excuse themselves by saying then, as they say now [Note: [Col. 0923] Some Belgian manuscripts read “as they say here now.”], “Why are we corrected?” They will likewise say, “Why are we condemned, since we did not receive the perseverance by which we might remain in the good, so that we could return from good to evil?”

They will in no way free themselves from just condemnation by this excuse.

For if, as the truth declares, no one is freed from the condemnation brought about through Adam except through faith in Jesus Christ, yet those who can say that they did not hear the Gospel of Christ will not free themselves from that condemnation, since “faith comes from hearing” (Rom. 10:17), how much less will those free themselves who will say, “We did not receive perseverance”?

The excuse of those who say, “We did not receive the opportunity to hear,” appears more just than that of those who say, “We did not receive perseverance.” For it can be said to them: “Human being, in what you had heard and held fast to, you could have persevered if you had wished”—that is, if the same will had remained, or if you had not abandoned by an evil will what you were holding, as he says below, section 17.

But it can in no way be said: “You would have believed what you had not heard if you had wished.”

12. Accordingly, those who have not heard the Gospel; those who, after hearing it and being changed for the better, have not received perseverance; those who, after hearing the Gospel, have not wished to come to Christ—that is, to believe in him—because he himself said, “No one comes to me unless it has been given him by my Father” (John VI, 66); and those who, because of their tender age, could not believe but could be absolved from original guilt only by the washing of regeneration, yet died without receiving it and perished: all these are not separated from that mass which is plainly condemned, since all proceed from one man into condemnation.

They are distinguished, however, not by their own merits but by the grace of the Mediator—that is, freely justified in the blood of the second Adam. Therefore, when we hear, “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. IV, 7), we must understand that no one can be distinguished from that mass of perdition which came through the first Adam except one who possesses this gift—whatever he possesses, he has received through the grace of the Savior.

[Note: [Col. 0923] Am.: “unless he possesses this gift, whatever he possesses that comes through grace,” etc. Er.: “unless he possesses this gift, whoever possesses what comes through grace,” etc. Some manuscripts read *nisi quod* (“except that”); others, *nisi qui* (“except one who”); but all contain the words *hoc bonum habet* (“possesses this good”). Moreover, several of these have *quidquid habet quod gratia* (“whatever he possesses that comes through grace”), while only two have *quisquis habet quod gratia* (“whoever possesses what comes through grace”). One manuscript from Belgium has *quod quidem habet, gratia* (“which indeed he possesses, by grace”). Perhaps the reading should be: “except one who possesses this good, which whoever possesses has received through the grace of the Savior.”]

This apostolic testimony is so weighty that blessed Cyprian, writing to Quirinus, placed it under the heading: “We must glory in nothing, since nothing is ours” (*Book 3 of the Testimonies*, title or chapter 4).

13. Therefore, all who have been separated from that original condemnation by this lavish gift of divine grace undoubtedly have the Gospel arranged to be heard by them; and when they hear it, they believe. In the faith that works through love (Gal. V, 6), they persevere to the end; and if at any time they stray, they are corrected and reformed. Some of them, even if they are not corrected by human beings, return to the way they had abandoned; and some, having received grace at whatever age, are removed from the dangers of this life by a swift death.

For he who fashioned them as vessels of mercy works all these things in them—he who also chose them in his Son, before the foundation of the world, through the election of grace. “But if it is by grace, then it is no longer by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Rom. XI, 6). For they were not called in such a way that they were not chosen; hence it was said, “For many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. XX, 16). Rather, because they were called according to his purpose, they were certainly also chosen through election, as was said, of grace and not of their preceding merits, because grace is their every merit.

14. The Apostle says of such people:

“We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters. And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII, 28–30).

None of these perishes, because all are chosen. They are chosen because they are called according to his purpose; and the purpose is not theirs but God’s. Concerning this he says elsewhere: “So that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not because of works but because of him who calls—it was said to him, ‘The elder shall serve the younger’” (Rom. IX, 11–13). And elsewhere: “Not according to our works,” he says, “but according to his own purpose and grace” (2 Tim. I, 9).

Therefore, when we hear, “Those whom he predestined, he also called,” we must recognize them as called according to his purpose, since he began by saying, “All things work together for good for those who are called according to his purpose.” Then he added, “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters”; and after these words he added, “Those whom he predestined, he also called.” He therefore wishes those whom he called according to his purpose to be understood, lest some who are called but not chosen be thought to belong among them, because of the Lord’s saying, “Many are called, but few are chosen.”

For all who are chosen are undoubtedly also called; but not all who are called are consequently chosen. Those, then, are chosen—as has often been said—who are called according to his purpose, and who are also predestined and foreknown. If any one of these should perish, God would be deceived; but none of them perishes, because God is not deceived. If any one of these should perish, God would be overcome by human fault; but none of them perishes, because God is overcome by nothing.

They are chosen to reign with Christ, not in the manner in which Judas was chosen for the work suited to him. For he was chosen by the one who knows how to use even evil people well, so that through his damnable work the venerable work for which Christ himself had come might be accomplished through his damnable deed. Therefore, when we hear, “Did I not choose you twelve? And one of you is a devil” (John VI, 71), we must understand that the others were chosen through mercy, Judas through judgment: the others to obtain his kingdom, Judas to shed Christ’s blood.

[Note: [Col. 0925] The printed editions read, “therefore he chose them.” The manuscripts, however, do not have *ergo elegit* (“therefore he chose”).]

15. Rightly the voice concerning the kingdom of the chosen follows:

“If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all, how will he not also, with him, freely give us all things? Who shall bring an accusation against God’s chosen? Is it God who justifies? Who is it who condemns? [Note: [Col. 0925] Several manuscripts read: “Who is the one who condemns?”] Christ who died—rather, who also rose again, who is at God’s right hand, who also intercedes for us?”

How great a gift of perseverance to the end they have received, let them also follow and say:

“Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Affliction, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword? As it is written, ‘For your sake we are being put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter.’ But in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through him who loved us. For I am convinced that neither death nor life, neither angel nor principality, neither things present nor things to come, neither power nor height nor depth nor any other creature will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Rom. VIII, 31–39).

16. These people are signified in the passage concerning Timothy. After it had been said that Hymenaeus and Philetus were overthrowing the faith of some, it immediately added: “But God’s firm foundation stands, bearing this seal: ‘The Lord knows those who are his’” (2 Tim. II, 19).

Their faith, which works through love, certainly either does not fail at all, or, if there are some whose faith does fail, it is restored before this life ends; and when the intervening iniquity has been removed, perseverance to the end is credited to them.

But those who will not persevere, and who will fall away from Christian faith and conduct in such a way that the end of this life finds them in that condition, clearly must not be counted among these people even at the time when they live well and devoutly.

[Note: [Col. 0925] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read *isto* (“in that one”).]

For by God’s foreknowledge and predestination they have not been separated from that mass of perdition; and therefore they were not called according to his purpose, and consequently were not chosen. Rather, they belong among those who are called of whom it was said, “Many are called,” not among those of whom it was said, “but few are chosen.”

And yet who would deny that they are chosen when they believe, are baptized, and live according to God? They are certainly called chosen by those who do not know what they will become, but not by the one who knows that they do not possess the perseverance that brings the chosen to blessed life, and who knows that they stand in such a way that he foreknew they would fall.

## CHAPTER VIII

17. If I am asked here why God did not give perseverance to those to whom he gave the love by which they might live as Christians, I answer that I do not know.

For I do not hear the Apostle’s words arrogantly, but recognizing my own smallness: “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. IX, 20); and, “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and how unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. XI, 33).

Therefore, let us give thanks insofar as he deigns to reveal his judgments to us; but insofar as he conceals them, let us not murmur against his purpose. Rather, let us believe that even this is most beneficial for us.

But you, whoever you are who question his grace as an enemy of it, what do you say yourself? It is good that you do not deny yourself to be a Christian and boast that you are a Catholic. If, then, you confess that persevering in the good to the end is God’s gift, why one person receives this gift and another does not, I think you are as ignorant of this as I am, and neither of us can penetrate God’s inscrutable judgments here.

Or, if you say that it belongs to human free will—which you defend not according to God’s grace but against it—for each person to persevere in the good or not to persevere, not because God grants perseverance but because human will produces it, what will you do with the words of the one who says, “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke XXII, 32)?

Will you dare to say that, even though Christ prayed that Peter’s faith would not fail, it would have failed if Peter had wished it to fail—that is, if he had not wished it to persevere to the end? As though Peter could in any way have wished something other than what Christ prayed that he would wish.

For who does not know that Peter’s faith would then have perished if the very will by which he was faithful had failed?

[Note: [Col. 0926] Am. and Er.: “if the will by which he was faithful had failed.”]

And it would have remained if that same will had remained. But because “the will is prepared by the Lord” (Prov. VIII, according to the Septuagint), Christ’s prayer for him could not have been in vain.

When he therefore prayed that Peter’s faith would not fail, what else did he ask except that Peter should possess in faith a completely free, exceedingly strong, unconquerable, and persevering will?

Behold how freedom of will is defended according to God’s grace, not against it. For human will does not obtain grace through freedom; rather, grace obtains freedom, and also grants the will a delightful permanence and an unconquerable strength by which it perseveres.

18. It is indeed astonishing—deeply astonishing—that God does not give perseverance to some of his children whom he has regenerated in Christ and to whom he has given faith, hope, and love, while he forgives such great crimes in alien children and, by imparting grace, makes them his own children. Who would not be astonished at this? Who would not be utterly amazed?

Yet this other matter is no less astonishing and nevertheless true; indeed, it is so evident that even the enemies of God’s grace cannot find a way to deny it. God takes some of the children of his friends—that is, of regenerated and good believers—who depart this life as little ones without Baptism, although he could, if he wished, have procured for them the grace of this washing, since all things are in his power, and excludes them from his kingdom, into which he sends their parents. At the same time, he causes some children of his enemies to come into the hands of Christians and, through this washing, introduces them [Note: [Col. 0927] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read “to be introduced.”] into the kingdom from which their parents are excluded.

[Col. 0927] Yet neither those children possess evil merit nor these good merit, according to their own will. Certainly, God’s judgments here are just and profound; they cannot be censured, nor can they be penetrated.

The same is true of perseverance, which is what we are now discussing. Concerning both matters, then, let us exclaim: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments!”

19. Nor should we be surprised that we cannot investigate his unsearchable ways. To say nothing of countless other things that the Lord God gives to some people and not to others, with whom there is no partiality (Rom. II, 11), and which are not assigned according to the merits of their wills—such as speed, strength, good health, bodily beauty, remarkable intelligence, and minds naturally capable of many arts; or things that come from outside [Note: [Col. 0927] Am., Er., and most manuscripts read *accidunt* (“happen”) rather than *accedunt* (“are added”).], such as wealth, nobility, honors, and other things of this kind, the possession of which lies entirely in God’s power—to say nothing even of the Baptism of little children, concerning which none of these people can say, as they can of those other things, that it does not pertain to the kingdom of God: why is Baptism given to one child and not to another, when both matters lie in God’s power and no one enters the kingdom of God without that sacrament?

But to leave or set aside all these matters, let them look at [Note: [Col. 0927] Some manuscripts read *intueantur* (“let them look”).] the very people under discussion. For we are speaking of those who do not possess perseverance in goodness but, when their good will fails, die after changing from good to evil.

Let them answer, if they can, why God did not snatch them from the dangers of this life while they were living faithfully and devoutly, so that evil might not change their understanding and deceit might not mislead their souls. Was this not in his power, or did he not know that they would later become evil? Surely, nothing could be said more perversely or insanely.

Why, then, did he not do it? Let those who mock us answer when, in matters of this kind, we exclaim, “How inscrutable are his judgments and how unsearchable his ways!” For surely God does give this gift to whomever he wishes; and surely that Scripture does not lie which says of the death of a just person, apparently premature, “He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding or deceit should mislead his soul” (Wis. IV, 11).

Why, then, does God—who is without iniquity or partiality, and in whose power lies the length of time each person remains in this life, which is called a temptation upon the earth (Job VII, 1)—give this great benefit to some and not to others?

Just as they are compelled to confess that it is God’s gift for a person to complete this life before changing from good to evil, although they do not know why it is given to some and not to others, so let them confess with us, on the testimony of the Scriptures, many passages from which I have already cited, that perseverance in goodness is God’s gift; and let them graciously consent to be ignorant with us, without murmuring against God, why it is given to some and not to others.

## CHAPTER IX

20. We should not be troubled that God does not give this perseverance to some of his children. Far be it from being so, if they were among those predestined and called according to his purpose who are truly children of promise.

These people are called children of God while they live devoutly; but because they will live wickedly and die in that same wickedness, God does not call them his children according to his foreknowledge.

There are children of God who are not yet so to us but already are so to God. Concerning them the evangelist John says: “Jesus was about to die for the nation, and not for the nation only, but also to gather into one the scattered children of God” (John XI, 51–52). They were certainly going to become such by believing through the preaching of the Gospel; and yet, before this happened, they were already children of God, written in the unshaken permanence of their Father’s remembrance.

There are, again, some whom we call children of God because they have received grace, even if only temporarily, and yet they are not so to God. Concerning them the same John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John II, 19).

He does not say, “They went out from us, and because they did not remain with us, they are no longer of us.” Rather, he says, “They went out from us, but they were not of us”—that is, “Even when they appeared to be among us, they were not of us.”

And if someone were to say to him, “How do you demonstrate this?”, he replies: “If they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.”

This is the voice of God’s children. John speaks as one appointed to a foremost place among God’s children.

When, therefore, God’s children say of those who did not possess perseverance, “They went out from us, but they were not of us,” and add, “If they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us,” what else do they say except this: “They were not children, even when they were in the profession and name of children”—not because they pretended to righteousness, but because they did not remain in it?

For he does not say, “If they had been of us, they would certainly have held true, rather than false, righteousness with us.” Instead he says, “If they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.” Without doubt, he wanted them to remain in the good.

They were therefore in the good; but because they did not remain in it—that is, because they did not persevere to the end—he says, “They were not of us,” even when they were with us. That is, they were not among the number of children even when they were in the faith of children.

For those who are truly children were foreknown and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, and were called according to his purpose so that they might be chosen. The child of promise does not perish, but the child of perdition does (John XVII, 12).

21. These people therefore belonged to the multitude of the called, but they did not belong to the small number of the chosen.

God did not give perseverance to his predestined children. [Note: [Col. 0928] Lov.: “God therefore did not give perseverance to his children who were not predestined.” The other printed editions and the manuscripts preserve the reading translated above.] For they would have possessed it if they had belonged to that number of children; and what would they possess that they had not received, according to the true apostolic statement (1 Cor. IV, 7)?

Accordingly, such children would have been given to Christ the Son, just as he says to the Father: “So that everything you have given me may not perish but may have eternal life” (John III, 15; VI, 39).

Those, then, are understood to be given to Christ who have been appointed to eternal life. They are the predestined and called according to his purpose, none of whom perishes.

Accordingly, none of them changes from good to evil and ends this life in that condition, because he has been appointed and therefore given to Christ so that he may not perish but have eternal life.

Again, those whom we call his enemies, or the little children of his enemies—those of them whom he will regenerate in such a way that they finish this life in the faith that works through love—are already, before this occurs, his children in that predestination. They have been given to Christ his Son so that they may not perish but have eternal life.

22. Finally, the Savior himself says: “If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples” (John VIII, 31).

Should Judas be counted among these, since he did not remain in his word? Should those people be counted among them of whom the Gospel speaks as follows?

When the Lord had commended the eating of his flesh and the drinking of his blood, the evangelist says:

“He said these things in the synagogue while teaching in Capernaum. Therefore, many of his disciples, when they heard this, said, ‘This is a hard saying; who can hear it?’ But Jesus, knowing in himself that his disciples were murmuring about this, said to them, ‘Does this offend you? Then what if you were to see the Son of Man ascending to where he was before? It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh is of no benefit. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. But there are some among you who do not believe.’ For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who believed and who would betray him. And he said, ‘For this reason I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been given him by my Father.’ From that time many of his disciples turned back and no longer walked with him” (John VI, 60–67).

Were these not also called disciples, since the Gospel speaks of them as such? Yet they were not truly disciples, because they did not remain in his word, according to what he said: “If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples.”

Because they did not possess perseverance, they were not truly disciples of Christ, and likewise were not truly children of God, even when they appeared to be and were called such.

We therefore call those whom we see regenerated and living devoutly both chosen, disciples of Christ, and children of God.

[Note: [Col. 0929] Lov.: “Therefore we call them chosen disciples of Christ.” Other printed editions: “Therefore we call ourselves and chosen disciples of Christ,” omitting the conjunction after *electos* (“chosen”), although we find that conjunction in many manuscripts.]

But they are truly what they are called only if they remain in that for which they are so called. If they do not possess perseverance—that is, if they do not remain in what they began to be—they are not truly called what they are called and are not truly what they are called: for in the sight of the one who knows what they will become—that is, evil from good—they are not this.

23. For this reason, after the Apostle had said, “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God,” knowing that some love God but do not remain in that good to the end, he immediately added, “for those who are called according to his purpose.”

These people remain in their love of God to the end; and if for a time they stray from it, they return, so that they may bring to completion what they began in goodness.

To show what it means to be called according to his purpose, he immediately added the words I cited above:

“For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters; and those whom he predestined, he also called—that is, according to his purpose; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII, 28–30).

All those things have already been done: he foreknew, predestined, called, and justified them. For all have already been foreknown and predestined, and many have already been called and justified.

But what he placed at the end—“he also glorified”—if by this we are to understand that glory of which he says, “When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. III, 4), has not yet occurred.

Although the two expressions “he called” and “he justified” have not yet been fulfilled in all of those concerning whom they were spoken—for many are still to be called and justified until the end of the age—he nevertheless used past-tense words even of future events, as though God had already done what he had eternally appointed to occur.

For this reason the prophet Isaiah also says of him, “Who made the things that are to come” (Isa. XLV, according to the Septuagint).

Therefore, all who in God’s most provident ordering have been foreknown, predestined, called, justified, and glorified—I do not say merely those not yet regenerated, but even those not yet born—are already children of God and cannot perish at all.

These are the people who truly come to Christ, because they come in the manner he himself says: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will never cast out.” And shortly afterward he says: “This is the will of my Father who sent me, that I should lose nothing of everything he has given me” (John VI, 37, 39).

Perseverance in goodness to the end is therefore also given by him. For it is given only to those who will not perish, since those who do not persevere will perish.

24. For such people, who love him, God makes all things work together for good—absolutely all things—so that even if some of them stray and go off course, he causes this very thing to advance them toward good, because they return humbler and more instructed.

For on the very way [Note: [Col. 0930] Am. and most manuscripts read *vita* (“life”) rather than *via* (“way”).] they learn that they must rejoice with trembling, not arrogantly attributing to themselves confidence in their perseverance as though it came from their own strength, nor saying in their prosperity, “I shall never be moved.”

Therefore it is said to them: “Serve the Lord with fear, and rejoice in him with trembling, lest the Lord become angry and you perish from the right way” (Ps. II, 11–12).

For it does not say, “and do not come to the right way,” but, “lest you perish [Note: [Col. 0930] The printed editions read “and you do not”; the manuscripts more correctly read “lest you perish.”] from the right way.” What does this show except that those who are already walking in the right way are warned to serve God in fear—that is, not to be high-minded but to fear (Rom. XI, 20)?

This signifies: “Let them not be arrogant, but humble.” Hence elsewhere he says, “Do not set your mind on high things, but associate with the humble” (Rom. XII, 16).

Let them rejoice in God, but with trembling, glorying in nothing, since nothing is ours; so that “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord” (Jer. IX, 23–24). Let them not perish from the right way on which they have already begun to walk by attributing to themselves the very fact that they are on it.

The Apostle uses the same words when he says: “Work out your own salvation with fear and trembling.” And to show why this should be done with fear and trembling, he says: “For God is the one who works in you both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Phil. II, 12–13).

The person who said in his prosperity, “I shall never be moved,” did not possess this fear and trembling. But because he was a child of promise and not of perdition, he learned what he himself was when God briefly abandoned him:

“Lord,” he said, “in your favor you had established strength for my beauty; you hid your face from me, and I was troubled” (Ps. XXIX, 7–8).

Behold: now more instructed, and for that reason also more humble, he held to the way, seeing and confessing that God, in his favor, had established strength for his beauty. When he attributed this to himself and trusted in himself amid the prosperity God had bestowed, he said, not of the one who had bestowed it, “I shall never be moved.”

He was therefore troubled so that he might discover himself and, learning to think humbly, might understand where hope should be placed—not only for eternal life but also, in this life, for devout conduct and perseverance.

This could also have been the voice of the apostle Peter. In his prosperity he too had said, “I will lay down my life for you” (John XIII, 37), hastily attributing to himself what was later to be granted him by the Lord.

But the Lord turned his face away from him, and he was troubled, so that, fearing to die for the Lord, he denied him three times. Then the Lord turned his face toward him again, and Peter washed away his fault with tears.

For what else does “the Lord looked at him” mean (Luke XXII, 61) except that he turned toward him the face which he had briefly turned away from him?

He had therefore been troubled; but because he learned not to trust in himself, this too advanced him toward good, through the action of him who makes all things work together for good for those who love him. For Peter had been called according to the purpose, so that no one could snatch him from the hand of Christ, to whom he had been given.

25. Therefore, no one should say that the person who strays from the right way ought not to be corrected, but that one should merely ask the Lord to grant him return and perseverance. No prudent and faithful person should say this.

For if this person has been called according to the purpose, then undoubtedly God makes even his correction work together for his good. But since the one who corrects does not know whether he has been called in this way, let him act with love in doing what he knows ought to be done.

He knows that such a person ought to be corrected. God will bring about either mercy or judgment:

[Note: [Col. 0931] Am., Er., and several manuscripts: “with God bringing about either mercy or judgment.” The Louvain editors deleted *ad* (“toward”), although the particle is also absent from the very old Corbie manuscript.]

Mercy, if the person who is corrected has been separated from the mass of perdition by the lavishness of grace and is not among the vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, but among the vessels of mercy that God has prepared for glory (Rom. IX, 22–23); judgment, however, if he belongs among those who are condemned and is not among those predestined.

## CHAPTER X

26. Here [Note: [Col. 0931] The printed editions read “hence”; the manuscripts read “here.”] another question arises—not one to be disregarded, but one that must be undertaken and resolved with the help of the Lord, in whose hand are both we and our words (Wis. VII, 16).

We are asked what we think, with regard to this gift of God that consists in persevering in goodness to the end, about the first human being, who was certainly created upright and without any fault.

I do not say: “If he did not possess perseverance, how was he without fault, when he lacked a gift of God so necessary to him?”

[Note: [Col. 0932] Am., Er., and most manuscripts: “when nevertheless he possessed the necessary gift of God.”]

This question is easily answered: he did not possess perseverance because he did not persevere in the good in which he was without fault. For he began to have fault from the moment he fell; and if he began to have it, then before he began to have it he was certainly without fault.

It is one thing not to have fault, and another not to remain in that goodness in which there is no fault. For precisely because he is not said never to have been without fault, but is said not to have remained without fault, it is undoubtedly shown that he was without fault in the good in which he is blamed for not having remained.

But what must be sought and examined more carefully is how we should answer those who say:

“If he possessed perseverance in that uprightness in which he was created without fault, then he certainly persevered in it; and if he persevered, he certainly did not sin or abandon his uprightness and God. Yet the truth cries out that he sinned and abandoned the good. Therefore, he did not possess perseverance in that good; and if he did not possess it, he certainly did not receive it.

“For how could he both have received perseverance and not have persevered? Further, if he did not possess it because he did not receive it, what fault did he commit by not persevering, when he had not received perseverance?

“For it cannot be said that he did not receive it because he had not been separated from the mass of perdition by the lavishness of grace. For before he sinned, that mass of perdition did not yet exist in the human race; from his sin that corrupted origin was derived.”

27. Therefore, we most beneficially confess what we most rightly believe: that God, the Lord and ruler of all things, created all things very good; foreknew that evil would arise from good; and knew that it belonged more fully to his almighty goodness to do good even from evils [Note: [Col. 0932] Several manuscripts read *bona facere* (“to do good”) rather than *bene facere* (“to do well”).] than not to permit evils to exist.

He therefore ordered the life of angels and human beings in such a way that he might first show what their free will could do, and afterward what could be accomplished by the benefit of his grace and the judgment of his justice.

Some angels, whose prince is the one called the devil, were made deserters from the Lord God through free will. Yet although they deserted his goodness, through which they had been blessed, they could not escape his judgment, by which they were made most miserable.

The others, however, stood in the truth by that same free will, and they merited to know with complete certainty that they would never fall from it.

If we have been able to learn from the holy Scriptures that no holy angels will now fall, how much more sublimely did they themselves know this truth once it had been revealed to them?

To us a blessed life without end and equality with the angels have been promised. From this promise we are certain that, once we have entered that life after the judgment, we will not fall from it. If the angels do not know this concerning themselves, then we shall be not their equals but more blessed than they.

The Truth, however, promised us equality with them (Matt. XXII, 30). It is therefore certain that they know by direct vision what we know by faith: namely, that no holy angel will suffer any future fall.

But the devil and his angels, although they were blessed before they fell and did not know that they would fall into misery, nevertheless still had something that could be added to their blessedness if they had stood in the truth by free will until they received, as the reward of that perseverance, the fullness of supreme blessedness.

That fullness would consist in this: through the great abundance of the love of God given by the Holy Spirit, they would no longer be able to fall at all, and they would know this about themselves with complete certainty.

They did not possess this fullness of blessedness. But because they did not know their future misery, they enjoyed a lesser, yet still genuine, blessedness without any fault.

For if they had known that they would fall and suffer eternal punishment, they could not have been blessed; fear of so great an evil would already have compelled them to be miserable.

28. In the same way, God made the human being with free will. Although he was ignorant of his future fall, he was nevertheless blessed because he perceived that it lay within his power not to die and not to become miserable.

If, in that upright and faultless condition, he had wished to remain through his own free will, he would certainly, without any experience of death or unhappiness, have received—as the merit of this remaining [Note: [Col. 0933] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read *hujusmodi* (“of this kind”).]—the fullness of blessedness by which the holy angels are also blessed.

That is, he would have become unable to fall any further and would have known this with complete certainty.

For even in paradise he could not himself have been blessed—indeed, he would not have been there [Note: [Col. 0933] Two Vatican manuscripts read “be”]—where it would not have been fitting for him to be miserable, if foreknowledge of his fall and fear [Note: [Col. 0933] Some manuscripts read “and fear.”] of so great an evil had made him miserable.

But because through free will he abandoned God, he experienced God’s just judgment, so that he was condemned together with his entire offspring, which was still contained in him and had sinned wholly with him.

All who are liberated from this offspring by God’s grace are certainly liberated from the condemnation by which they are already held bound. Therefore, even if no one were liberated, no one could justly criticize God’s just judgment.

The fact, then, that few are liberated in comparison with those who perish, while many are liberated in their own number, is grace; it is freely done. Thanks must be given for it, lest anyone be exalted as though on the basis of his own merits, but so that every mouth may be stopped (Rom. III, 19), and “the one who boasts may boast in the Lord.”

## CHAPTER XI
29. What, then? Did Adam not have the grace of God? Indeed he did, and a great grace, but one of a different kind. He was among the good things that he had received from the goodness of his Creator; for he had not acquired those good things by his own merits, since he suffered absolutely no evil in them. The saints, however, in this present life—to whom this grace of liberation belongs—are in the midst of evils, from which they cry out to God, “Deliver us from evil” (Matt. 6:13). Adam did not need Christ’s death for those good things; these others are absolved by the blood of that Lamb from both inherited and personal guilt. Adam did not need the help for which these saints appeal when they say: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that is in my members. Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Rom. 7:23–25). For in them “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5:17), and in such a struggle, laboring and endangered, they ask through Christ’s grace that the power to fight and conquer be granted them. Adam, however, tempted and troubled by no such conflict of himself against himself [Note: The old Corbie manuscript reads “of himself” (*de se ipso*); the printed editions, “from himself” (*a se ipso*)], enjoyed his own peace in that place of blessedness.

30. Accordingly, even if these people do not need a happier grace at present, they nevertheless need a more powerful one. And what grace is more powerful than God’s only-begotten Son, equal and coeternal with the Father, who became human for them and was crucified by sinful human beings without any sin of his own [Note: Here “his own” has been restored from the manuscripts], whether original or personal? Although he rose on the third day, never again to die, he nevertheless endured death for mortal beings, granting life to the dead, so that those redeemed by his blood and having received so great and such a pledge might say: “If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all—how will he not also, together with him, graciously give us all things?” (Rom. 8:31–32).

God therefore assumed our nature—that is, the rational soul and human flesh of Christ [Note: Am. Er. and Lov. read “Christ”; some later editions of this work more correctly read “of Christ,” as does the very ancient Corbie manuscript]—by an assumption uniquely marvelous, or marvelously unique, so that the Son of God, without any preceding merits of his own righteousness, should from the beginning at which he began to be human be one person with the Word who is without beginning. No one is so blind with regard to this matter, and so ignorant of the faith, as to dare say that, although the son of man was born of the Holy Spirit and the virgin Mary, he nevertheless merited through free choice, by living well and doing good works without sin, that he should become the Son of God—despite the Gospel’s opposition, which says, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14). For where did this take place, if not in the virgin’s womb, from which Christ’s humanity had its beginning?

Likewise, when the Virgin asked how what was announced to her by the angel would come to pass, the angel replied: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you [Note: Most manuscripts: “will come over you.”], and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore the Holy One who will be born from you will be called the Son of God” (Luke 1:35). “Therefore,” he says—not on account of works, which certainly did not yet exist in one who had not been born, but therefore because the Holy Spirit will come upon you and the power of the Most High will overshadow you: the Holy One who will be born from you will be called the Son of God.

This birth, wholly gratuitous, united humanity to God and flesh to the Word in the unity of one person [Note: Four manuscripts: “into the unity of one person.”]. Good works followed this birth; they did not merit it. There was no reason to fear that, in this ineffable manner, when human nature was assumed by God the Word into the unity of one person, it might sin through the free choice of the will, since the assumption itself was such that human nature, assumed by God in this way, would admit no movement of evil will within itself.

Through this Mediator, God showed that he makes those whom he redeemed by his blood thereafter and forever good, having assumed him in such a way that he would never be evil and would not be made good out of evil, but would always be good [Note: Thus four Vatican manuscripts. Other books read, “lest, having been made out of evil, etc.” In some later editions an additional negative particle is read: “lest, having been made out of evil, he should not always be good.”].

31. The first human being did not possess this grace, by which he would never wish to be evil [Note: Five manuscripts: “by which he would never be evil.”]. But he certainly possessed that grace in which, if he had wished to remain, he would never have been evil; and without it, even with free choice, he could not have been good. Yet through free choice he could abandon it. God therefore did not will even that he should exist without his grace, which he left within Adam’s free choice. For free choice is sufficient for evil, but insufficient for good [Note: Lovaniensis: “is nothing.” Other printed editions and manuscripts: “is insufficient.”], unless it is helped by the omnipotent Good.

If that man had not abandoned this help through free choice, he would always have been good; but he abandoned it, and was abandoned. For the help was of such a kind that he could abandon it whenever he wished. This was the first grace given to the first Adam; but the second Adam possesses a more powerful grace than this [Note: Am. Er. and Lov.: “but this.” Several manuscripts have the more harmonious reading, “but by this.”]. The first grace makes it possible for a person to possess righteousness if he wishes; the second is therefore more powerful [Note: Cistercian manuscripts: “the second, being more powerful,” omitting “therefore”], since it also makes him wish, and wish so greatly, and love with such ardor, that the will of the spirit overcomes the will of the flesh, which desires contrary things [Note: The Casalensis manuscript: “the will of the spirit, which desires contrary things.” Two other manuscripts: “the will of the spirit overcomes the will desiring contrary things.”].

Nor was the first grace a small one, since it displayed even the power of free choice: Adam was helped in such a way that, without this help, he would not remain in the good, but could abandon the help if he wished. The second grace, however, is so much greater that it is little for a human being merely to recover through it the liberty he has lost; indeed, it is little merely not to be able without it either to grasp the good or to remain in the good if he wishes, unless he is also made to wish.

32. At that time, therefore, God had given the human being a good will [Note: Five manuscripts: “a free will.”]; for he had made him upright, and had given him the help [Note: Lov.: “had also given the help”] without which he could not remain in that state if he wished. But, so that he would wish, God left this to his free choice. He could therefore remain if he wished, because the help by which he could do so was not lacking, and without which he could not perseveringly hold to the good that he wished.

But because he did not wish to remain, the fault is certainly his; it would have been his merit had he wished to remain. So acted the holy angels: when others fell through free choice, they themselves stood firm through that same free choice, and merited to receive the reward due to this perseverance—namely, such a fullness of blessedness that they are utterly certain that they will always remain in it [Note: Three Vatican manuscripts: “that this is certain for them.”].

But if this help had been lacking to an angel or to a human being when they were first created—since their nature had not been made such that, without divine help, they could remain if they wished—they would not have fallen through their own fault. The help would have been lacking without which they could not remain.

Now, however, for those who lack such help, this is already the punishment of sin; for those to whom it is given, it is given according to grace, not according to what is owed. And through Jesus Christ our Lord it is given all the more abundantly to those to whom God has chosen to give it, so that it is not merely present, without which we cannot remain even if we wish, but is also of such a kind and so great that we do wish.

Through this grace of God, in receiving the good and holding to it perseveringly, it comes about in us that we not only can do what we wish, but also wish what we can do [Note: All manuscripts read “it happens”; the printed editions read “it is.”]. This was not so in the first human being: one of these two things was present in him, the other was not. He did not need grace in order to receive the good, because he had not yet lost it; but he needed the help of grace in order to remain in it, without which he could not do so at all. He had received the ability to do so if he wished, but he did not possess the will to do what he was able to do; for if he had possessed it, he would have persevered. He could have persevered if he wished [Note: The printed editions add “even if he wished”; most manuscripts omit “even,” while one Vatican manuscript has “Adam” in its place]. But that he should not wish to do so proceeded from free choice, which at that time was so free that it could will either good or evil.

What, then, will be freer than free choice when it cannot be enslaved to sin—the reward of merit that was to come to human beings, as it has come to the holy angels? [Note: Henry Gravius proposed reading “what freedom was to come,” since the relative pronoun does not agree in gender with “free choice”; but the pronoun aptly agrees with the following noun, “reward.” Cicero similarly writes in *On the Laws*, “A provident, sagacious animal, which we call man,” and in his fifth speech against Verres, “That prison which is called the quarries.” Augustine frequently imitates this idiom.] Now, however, after the good has deservedly been lost through sin, what was to have been the reward of merit has become, for those who are liberated, a gift of grace.

## CHAPTER XII

33. Accordingly, we must examine carefully and vigilantly how these pairs differ from one another: to be able not to sin and not to be able to sin; to be able not to die and not to be able to die; to be able not to abandon the good and not to be able to abandon the good.

The first human being was able not to sin, was able not to die, and was able not to abandon the good. Shall we say that he was unable to sin, when he possessed such free choice? Or that he was unable to die, to whom it was said, “If you sin, you will surely die” (Gen. 2:17)? Or that he was unable to abandon the good, when he abandoned it by sinning and therefore died?

The first freedom of the will, therefore, was the ability not to sin; the final freedom will be much greater: the inability to sin. The first immortality was the ability not to die; the final immortality will be much greater: the inability to die. The first was the power of perseverance, the ability not to abandon the good; the final will be the blessedness of perseverance, the inability to abandon the good. Does it follow that, because the final goods will be more excellent and better, the first were either nothing or insignificant?

34. The helps themselves must likewise be distinguished. One kind of help is that without which something does not happen; another is that by which something happens. For without food we cannot live, yet when food is available, it does not make someone live who has wished to die. Food, therefore, is a help without which life does not occur, but not a help by which we are made to live.

Blessedness, however, which a human being does not possess, makes him blessed immediately when it is given. It is a help not only without which something does not happen, but also by which it happens—the reason for which it is given. Accordingly, this help both brings something about and is necessary for it: if blessedness is given to a human being, he immediately becomes blessed; and if it is never given, he will never be blessed. Food, on the other hand, does not necessarily cause a human being to live, although without it he cannot live.

To the first human being, therefore, who had received in the good state in which he had been created the ability not to sin, not to die, and not to abandon that very good, the help of perseverance was given—not a help by which he would persevere, but one without which he could not persevere through free choice. To the saints who, by God’s grace, are predestined for the kingdom of God, the help of perseverance now given is not such a help, but one such that perseverance itself is granted to them—not merely so that without this gift they cannot persevere, but also so that through this gift they cannot be anything but persevering.

For Christ not only said, “Without me you can do nothing,” but also said, “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15:5, 16). By these words he showed that he had given them not only righteousness but also perseverance in it. When Christ appoints them to go, bear fruit, and have their fruit remain, who would dare say, “It will not remain” [Note: The printed editions here omit “who would dare say, ‘It will not remain?’” Nearly all manuscripts contain it]? Who would dare say, “Perhaps it will not remain”?

“For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable” (Rom. 11:29)—but this concerns those who are called according to the purpose. Therefore, with Christ interceding for them that their faith may not fail, it will certainly not fail to the end. Consequently, it will persevere to the end, and the end will find it only as one that remains throughout this life [Note: Am. Er. and manuscripts: “finds it.”].

35. A greater freedom is necessary against the many and great temptations [Note: The Corbeiensis manuscript: “is necessary, amid the many and great temptations”] that did not exist in paradise—a freedom fortified and strengthened by the gift of perseverance, so that this world may be conquered with all its attractions, terrors, and errors. The martyrdoms of the saints have taught this.

Adam [Note: That is, Adam.], when no one was terrifying him, and even while using his free choice against the command of the terrifying God, did not stand firm amid such great happiness and such great ease of not sinning. These others, however, stood firm in the faith—not merely while the world terrified them, but while it raged in order to make them fall—although Adam saw the present goods that he was going to abandon, while they did not see the future goods that they were going to receive.

From where did this come, unless from him who granted them mercy so that they might be faithful (1 Cor. 7:25), from whom they received a spirit not of fear, by which they would yield to their persecutors, but “of power and love and self-control” (2 Tim. 1:7), by which they would overcome everything that threatened, everything that enticed, and everything that tormented them?

To Adam, therefore, a free will was given without any sin, together with which he was created, and he made it serve sin. These others, however, whose will had been the servant of sin, were liberated by the one who said, “If the Son makes you free, then you will be truly free” (John 8:36). Through this grace they receive such great freedom that, although as long as they live here they fight against sinful desires, and although some of these desires creep upon them, on account of which they say daily, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12), they nevertheless no longer serve the sin that leads to death.

Of this sin the apostle John says, “There is sin that leads to death; I do not say that one should pray for that” (1 John 5:16) [Note: The printed editions read “that anyone should pray”; “anyone” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of John]. Since the nature of that sin is not explicitly stated, many and various interpretations are possible. For my part, I say that it is abandoning, until death, the faith that works through love.

They no longer serve this sin—not free by their first creation, as Adam was, but liberated by the grace of God through the second Adam. Through this liberation they possess free choice by which they serve God, not by which they are taken captive by the devil. Having been freed from sin, they have become servants of righteousness (Rom. 6:18), in which they will stand to the end, by the gift of perseverance bestowed on them by the one who foreknew them, predestined them, called them according to his purpose, justified them, and glorified them. For what he promised concerning them, he has already made, though it is still future. Abraham believed him who made the promise, and it was counted to him as righteousness. For he gave glory to God, being fully convinced, as it is written, that what God had promised he was also able to do.

36. He himself therefore makes them good, so that they may do good. He did not promise them to Abraham because he foresaw that they would become good by themselves. For if that were so, what he promised would belong not to him but to them. Abraham, however, did not believe in this way; rather, “he did not weaken in faith,” giving glory to God and being fully convinced that what he had promised he was able to do (Rom. 4:3, 19–21).

He did not say, “He is able to promise what he foresaw”; or, “He is able to display what he foretold”; or, “He is able to foresee what he promised.” Instead he said, “He is able also to do what he promised.” He therefore makes them persevere in the good—the one who makes them good [Note: The very ancient Corbie manuscript has the lacunar reading *f[.....]ci[.....]*; the surviving letters are insufficient to establish the complete wording.].

Those who fall and perish were not among the number of the predestined. Although the Apostle was speaking of all who had been regenerated and were living piously when he said, “Who are you to judge another’s servant?
