Before his own master he stands or falls,” he immediately turned his attention to the predestined and said, “But he will stand.” And lest they claim this for themselves, he added, “For God is able to make him stand” (Rom. 14:4). He therefore gives perseverance—the one who is able to establish those who stand, so that they may stand with the utmost perseverance, or to restore those who have fallen [Note: Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read “those who will have fallen.”]. For “the Lord raises up those who are bowed down” (Ps. 145:8).

37. Thus, in order that the first human being should not receive this gift of God—that is, perseverance in the good—but that it should be left to his choice whether he would persevere or not, his will possessed such powers, having been established without any sin, and nothing within him resisted him by way of desire [Note: The manuscripts read “from himself” (*ex se ipso*); the printed editions, “from herself” (*ex se ipsa*)], that the choice to persevere could rightly be entrusted to him amid such great goodness and such great ease of living well [Note: The printed editions read “and the ease of living well,” omitting “such great”; the phrase is restored from the manuscripts]. God knew beforehand what he would unjustly do, but in knowing it beforehand he did not compel him to do it; at the same time, God knew what he himself would justly do concerning him.

Now, however, after that great freedom was lost through the merit of sin, the weakness that remained had to be assisted by still greater gifts. For it pleased God—especially in order to extinguish human pride and presumption—that no flesh, that is, no human being, should glory before him.

Whence, then, does flesh not glory before him, except because of its own merits? It could indeed have possessed such merits, but it lost them; and through the very means by which it could have possessed them, namely free choice, it lost them. Therefore nothing remains for those who are to be liberated except the grace of the one who liberates. Thus no flesh glories before him.

The unrighteous do not glory, because they have no basis for doing so; nor do the righteous, because they receive from him the basis for glorying and have no glory of their own except him, to whom they say, “You are my glory and the one who lifts up my head” (Ps. 3:4). Accordingly, what is written—“so that no flesh may glory before him”—applies to every human being. But to the righteous belongs the saying, “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord.”

The Apostle makes this perfectly clear. After saying, “so that no flesh may glory before him,” lest the saints think that they had been left without glory, he immediately added: “But from him you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption; so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord’” (1 Cor. 1:29–31). This is why, in this place of miseries, where “human life is a trial upon the earth” (Job 7:1), “power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9). And what power is this, except that the one who glories should glory in the Lord?

38. Accordingly, God did not wish his saints to glory in their own strength even with regard to their perseverance in the good, but in him. He not only gives them the kind of help he gave the first human being, without which they cannot persevere if they wish; he also works in them the will itself. Since they will not persevere unless they both can and will, the possibility and the will to persevere are granted to them by the generosity of divine grace.

Their will is kindled by the Holy Spirit to such an extent that they can because they so will, and they so will because God works in them so that they will. For if, amid the great weakness of this present life—a weakness in which virtue nevertheless had to be perfected in order to restrain pride—their will were left to themselves, so that they would remain in God’s help, without which they could not persevere, if they wished, while God did not work in them so that they would wish, then amid so many and such great temptations their will itself, through its weakness, would succumb. They would therefore be unable to persevere because, weakened by their frailty, they would either not wish to do so or would not wish it with the degree of will necessary for them to be able.

Thus help was given to the weakness of the human will, so that divine grace might direct it unfailingly and inseparably [Note: In B. the reading is “invincibly,” with this note: “Am. and Er. have ‘inseparably,’ wrongly, and the manuscripts disagree.” Most printed editions and manuscripts therefore read “invincibly.” The 1577 Lovaniensis edition likewise says in its note: “Thus all manuscripts correctly read ‘invincibly’ instead of ‘inseparably.’ Augustine does not mean that the elect cannot turn aside from the right path or be overcome by temptation, but that such powerful grace is given to them that, however weak and feeble they may be, they neither turn aside nor are overcome. Thus the meaning is not that the inability to sin must be denied, but only that the outcome is being signified. The following words make this sufficiently clear: ‘and therefore, although weak, it would not fail or be overcome by any adversity.’ And below: ‘he preserved for the weak that, by his gift, they should invincibly will what is good, and invincibly refuse to abandon it.’ Nevertheless, we have removed the word ‘invincibly,’ as favoring new errors.”].

And therefore, although weak, it would not fail or be overcome by any adversity. Thus it came about that the human will, weakened and feeble, persevered in the still limited good through the power of God, whereas the will of the first human being, strong and sound, did not persevere in the greater good, even though it possessed the power of free choice.

The help of God was not lacking to Adam, without which he could not persevere if he wished; yet it was not such help as would cause God to work in him so that he would wish [Note: Several manuscripts read “which” rather than “who.” In the immediately following verse, most manuscripts omit “the man of God.”]. For he was left and permitted, in his great strength, to do what he wished. For the weak, God preserved this: that, by his gift, they should invincibly will what is good, and invincibly refuse to abandon it [Note: Several manuscripts: “so that.”].

When Christ says, “I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32), let us understand that he said this to the one who is built upon the rock [Note: Several manuscripts read “she,” rather than “he.” In the immediately following verse, most manuscripts omit “the man of God.”]. Thus the man of God, not only because he received mercy so that he might be faithful, but also because his faith does not fail, should glory in the Lord.

## CHAPTER XIII

39. I am speaking here of those who are predestined to the kingdom of God, whose number is so certain that no one is added to them and no one is removed from them—not of those who, when he proclaimed and spoke, became more numerous than the number (Ps. 39:6). The latter may be called “called,” but not “elect,” because they were not called according to the purpose.

That the number of the elect is fixed and can neither be increased nor diminished is also indicated by John the Baptist when he says: “Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance, and do not say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3:8–9). He shows that these people will be cut off if they do not produce fruit, yet that the number promised to Abraham will not be lacking.

It is stated still more clearly in the Apocalypse: “Hold fast what you have, so that no one may take your crown” (Rev. 3:11). For if no one else will receive it unless this person loses it, the number is fixed.

40. The fact that these things are also said to saints who will persevere, as though it were uncertain whether they will persevere, should be heard by them in no other way than as instruction to them for whom it is beneficial “not to be haughty, but to fear” (Rom. 11:20). For who among the multitude of the faithful, as long as this mortal life continues, would presume that he is among the predestined?

This must be kept hidden here, where pride must be guarded against so carefully that even an Apostle was struck with such a blow by an angel of Satan lest he be exalted (2 Cor. 12:7). Hence it was said to the Apostles, “If you remain in me” (John 15:7), by the one who certainly knew that they would remain. And through the prophet: “If you are willing and hear me” (Isa. 1:19), although he himself knew in whom he was working the will (Phil. 2:13). Many similar statements are made.

For the sake of this secret, so that no one might become arrogant and so that all—even those who are running well—might fear while it remains hidden who will reach the goal, we must believe that some of the children of perdition, without receiving the gift of persevering to the end, begin to live in the faith that works through love, live faithfully and justly for some time, and afterward fall, without being taken from this life before this happens to them.

If this had happened to none of them, people would retain this most salutary fear—which suppresses the vice of pride—for as long as necessary to reach the grace of Christ by which one lives piously; thereafter they would be secure, never to fall away from him. But such presumption is not beneficial in this place of temptations, where weakness is so great that security can generate pride.

In the end, this too will come to pass; but then what already exists in the angels will also exist in human beings, when no pride can exist. Therefore the number of the saints predestined by God’s grace for the kingdom of God, having also been granted perseverance to the end, will be brought there in its entirety, and there, made wholly complete, will be preserved in supreme blessedness forever, with the mercy of their Savior abiding with them—whether when they are converted, when they struggle, or when they are crowned.

41. Holy Scripture also testifies that even then God’s mercy will be necessary for them, when the holy one [Note: The printed editions read “when holy David”; “David” is absent from the manuscripts] says to his soul concerning the Lord his God [Note: Several manuscripts read “says to his soul concerning the Lord,” omitting “his God”]: “He crowns you with compassion and mercy” (Ps. 103:4).

The apostle James also says, “Judgment without mercy will be for the one who has shown no mercy” (Jas. 2:13). Here he shows that even in that judgment, in which the righteous are crowned and the unrighteous condemned, some are judged with mercy and others without mercy. For this reason the mother of the Maccabees also says to her son, “May I receive you with your brothers in that mercy” (2 Macc. 7:29).

When the just king, as it is written, sits upon the throne, no evil will stand before him. “Who can say, ‘I have made my heart clean’? Or who can say, ‘I am pure from sin’?” (Prov. 20:8–9, according to the Septuagint). Accordingly, even there God’s mercy is necessary, by which the one whom the Lord did not charge with sin is made blessed (Ps. 32:2) [Note: Am. Er. and several manuscripts: “by which it is fashioned”; two manuscripts: “by which it may be fashioned.”].

But then, according to a just judgment, this mercy itself will be bestowed in return for the merits of good works. For when it is said, “Judgment without mercy will be for the one who has shown no mercy,” it is made clear that among those in whom good works of mercy are found, judgment takes place with mercy. Accordingly, mercy itself is also repaid according to the merits of good works.

The situation is not the same now, when, although no good works precede—and indeed many evil works do—the mercy of God comes before a person, so that he may be liberated from the evils he has committed, from those he would have committed had he not been guided by God’s grace [Note: Thus nine manuscripts. The printed editions read “had he not been regenerated”], and from those he would have suffered forever had he not been rescued from the power of darkness and transferred into the kingdom of the Son of God’s love (Col. 1:13).

Nevertheless, since eternal life itself, which is certainly owed in return for good works, is called by so great an Apostle the grace of God (Rom. 6:23), although grace is not repaid for works but given freely, we must confess without any hesitation that eternal life is called grace because it is repaid for merits that grace has bestowed on a human being.

The phrase read in the Gospel, “grace for grace” (John 1:16), can rightly be understood in this way [Note: Am. Er. and several manuscripts: “the grace that is in the Gospel”]: that is, grace in return for those merits that grace itself has bestowed.

42. Those, indeed, who do not belong to this number of the predestined—which God’s grace leads to the kingdom either while they do not yet possess any free choice of their own will, or with a choice of the will that is truly free because it has been liberated by that same grace—those, then, who do not belong to this most certain and most blessed number are judged most justly according to their merits. Either they lie under the sin that they have drawn originally through generation [Note: The printed editions read “through the generation”; “the” is absent from the manuscripts], and depart from this life with that inherited debt, which has not been remitted through regeneration; or, through free choice, they have added further sins. Their choice is free, I say, but not liberated: free with respect to righteousness, yet enslaved to sin. Through it they are rolled about by various harmful desires, some more, some less; but all are evil, and according to this difference they will be judged with different punishments.

Or they receive the grace of God, but are temporary; they do not persevere. They abandon, and are abandoned [Note: Two manuscripts: “but they abandon”]. They have been left to free choice, without receiving the gift of perseverance, by a just and hidden judgment of God.

## CHAPTER XIV

43. Let people therefore allow themselves to be corrected when they sin, and let them not argue against grace on the basis of correction, or against correction on the basis of grace. A just punishment is due for sin, and just correction belongs to that punishment; correction is applied as medicine, even when the sick person’s recovery is uncertain.

If the person who is corrected belongs to the number of the predestined, the correction is a healing medicine for him; but if he does not belong to that number, the correction is a punitive torment for him. Under this uncertainty, correction must nevertheless be administered out of love, since its outcome is unknown; and one must pray for the person to whom it is administered, that he may be healed.

When people either come into or return to the way of righteousness through correction, who brings about salvation in their hearts except the one who gives growth—regardless of who plants or waters, and regardless of who works in fields or among young trees—namely God, whose will to save no human choice can resist [Note: The Lovaniensis edition alone reads “no human being’s choice.”]?

For willing or not willing is so within the power of the one who wills or does not will that it does not impede the divine will or overcome its power. Even concerning those who do what he does not will, he himself does what he wills [Note: The printed editions read “For concerning these things”; “even” is present in the manuscripts.].

[Col. 0943]

44. What is written—“who desires all human beings to be saved” (1 Tim. 2:4)—although not all are saved, can be understood in many ways. We have mentioned some of these elsewhere in our shorter works (*Enchiridion*, ch. 103; *The City of God*, book 22, chapters 1 and 2; above, *Against Julian*, book 4, chapter 8, and elsewhere). Here I shall mention one.

The statement “he desires all human beings to be saved” is made so that “all” may be understood as all the predestined, since every kind of human being is included among them. Thus it was said to the Pharisees, “You tithe every herb” (Luke 11:42), where “every” must mean only every herb that they possessed; for they certainly did not tithe every herb that existed throughout the whole world.

According to this manner of expression it was also said, “Just as I please everyone in everything” (1 Cor. 10:33). Surely the speaker did not please so many of his persecutors as well? Rather, he pleased every kind of person gathered by the Church of Christ, whether those already within it or those who were to be brought into it.

[Col. 0943]

45. Therefore, there can be no doubt that human wills cannot resist the will of God, who in heaven and on earth has done whatever he has willed (Ps. 134:6), and who has also brought about things that are yet to come (Isa. 45, according to the Septuagint), so as to prevent him from doing what he wills—for even with respect to human wills themselves he does what he wills, when he wills it. Unless, perhaps—as I shall mention one example among many—when God wished to give Saul the kingdom, it was in the power of the Israelites to submit to that man or not to submit to him, something that certainly rested on their will, so that they could even resist God.

Yet God accomplished this only through the wills of those people, undoubtedly possessing omnipotent power to incline human hearts wherever it pleased him. For thus it is written: “And Samuel dismissed the people, and each one went to his own place; and Saul went to his house in Gibeah; and valiant men whose hearts God had touched went with Saul. But pestilent men said, ‘How can this man save us?’” [Note: Thus the manuscripts, in accordance with the Septuagint. But the Amerbach and Erasmus editions have: “Can this man save us?” The Louvain edition has: “Can this man possibly save us?”] “And they despised him, and brought him no gifts” (1 Sam. 10:25–27).

Would anyone say that some of those whose hearts the Lord touched so that they would go with Saul would not have gone with him, or that one of the pestilent men went because God had touched his heart so that he would do this?

Likewise, concerning David, whom the Lord established in the kingdom with increasing success, we read: “And David continued to advance and became great, and the Lord was with him” (1 Chron. 11:9). After this had been stated, we read shortly afterward: “And the Spirit clothed Amasai, chief of the thirty” [Note: The manuscripts have, “clothed Samai, chief of the thirty.” The printed editions had, “chief among the thirty.” The word “among” is absent from the Septuagint and the manuscripts.] “and he said: ‘We are yours, O David, and shall be with you, son of Jesse. Peace, peace to you, and peace to your helpers, because God has helped you.’” [Note: Erasmus and the Louvain edition have *filii* (“sons”), incorrectly.]

Could this man have opposed God’s will, rather than doing the will of him who worked in his heart through his Spirit, with which he had been clothed, so that he would will, say, and do this? [Note: Five manuscripts have: “so that he would will to say and do.” The Sorbonne manuscript has: “so that he would will, say, will, and do”; perhaps instead of “will to say, and will to do.”]

[Col. 0944]

Again, a little later the same Scripture says: “All these men of war, setting the battle line with peaceful hearts, came to Hebron to establish David as king over all Israel” (1 Chron. 12:18, 38). These men certainly established David as king by their own will. Who does not see this? Who can deny it? They did what they did with a peaceful heart, not unwillingly or without good intention. Yet it was he who acted in them, who works in human hearts whatever he wills.

For this reason Scripture had already said: “And David continued to advance and became great, and the Lord Almighty was with him.” Thus the Lord Almighty, who was with him, brought these men to establish him as king. And how did he bring them? Did he bind them with any bodily chains? He acted within them; he held their hearts; he moved their hearts; and he drew them by their wills, which he himself had worked in them.

If, then, when God wishes to establish kings on earth, he has human wills more in his power than they have their own wills, who else brings it about that correction is salutary and that a correction takes place in the heart of the person corrected, so that he may be established in the heavenly kingdom?

## CHAPTER XV

46. Therefore, let subjects and brothers be corrected by their superiors with corrections arising from charity, differing according to the diversity of their faults, whether lesser or greater. For even that which is called condemnation—the penalty imposed by episcopal judgment, than which no greater penalty exists in the Church—can, if God wills, turn and contribute to the most salutary correction.

We do not know what the following day may bring; nor should anyone be despaired of before the end of this life. Nor can God be prevented from looking upon someone, granting repentance, and, when the sacrifice of a troubled spirit and a contrite heart has been received, absolving him from guilt, even from a just condemnation, so that the one condemned is not condemned by God himself.

Nevertheless, pastoral necessity requires that, lest dreadful contagion spread among many, the sick sheep be separated from the healthy—perhaps to be healed by that very separation by him for whom nothing is impossible.

Since we do not know who belongs to the number of the predestined and who does not, we ought to be moved by charitable affection so as to desire the salvation of all. This happens when, whenever we encounter individuals with whom we are able to undertake this work, we strive to lead each one to the point where, justified by faith, he may have [Col. 0945] peace with God (Rom. 5:1). The Apostle also preached this peace when he said: “Therefore we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were exhorting through us: we beseech you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God” (2 Cor. 5:20).

For what is it to be reconciled to him except to have peace with him? It was on account of this peace that the Lord Jesus himself also said to his disciples: “Into whatever house you enter, first say, ‘Peace to this house’; and if a son of peace is there, your peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to you” (Luke 10:5–6).

When those who have been foretold announce this peace—their feet are called beautiful, “who announce peace, who announce good things” (Isa. 52:7)—each person begins, in our judgment, to be a son of peace when he obeys and believes this Gospel and, justified by faith, begins to have peace with God. According to God’s predestination, however, he was already a son of peace.

For it was not said, “Upon whom your peace rests, he will become a son of peace,” but: “If a son of peace is there,” he says, “your peace will rest upon that house.” [Note: Thus the manuscripts at this place. The printed editions have: “upon him,” and omit “house.”]

Therefore, even before this peace was announced to him, the son of peace was already there, as God—not the evangelist—knew and foreknew him to be.

Since we do not know who is or is not a son of peace, it is our responsibility to exclude and distinguish no one, but to desire the salvation of all to whom we preach this peace. We need not fear that we shall lose it if the person to whom we preach is not a son of peace, although we do not know this; for it will return to us—that is, this preaching will benefit us, though not him. But if the peace that has been preached rests upon him, it will benefit both him and us.

47. Since, then, God commands us, who do not know which of those to whom we preach this peace will be saved, to desire the salvation of all, and since he himself works this desire in us by pouring out this charity in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5), it can also be understood in this way: God wills all people to be saved because he makes us will this.

In the same way, he sent the Spirit of his Son, crying, “Abba, Father” (Gal. 4:6)—that is, making us cry out. For elsewhere he says of that same Spirit: “We have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:15). We cry out, then, but the Spirit is said to cry out because he causes us to cry out.

If Scripture rightly called the Spirit “crying out,” because he causes us to cry out, then it is also right to call God “willing,” because he causes us to will.

Therefore, since in correcting others we ought to do nothing except ensure that they do not depart from the peace that exists with God, or that those who have departed return to it, let us carry out our work without despair. If the person whom we correct is a son of peace, our peace will rest upon him; but if not, it will return to us.

48. Although, then, even while the faith of some is being overturned, God’s foundation remains firm, because “the Lord knows those who are his,” we must not for that reason become sluggish and negligent in correcting those who ought to be corrected.

For it was not said without reason: “Bad conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15:33); and: “The weak person perishes through your knowledge, [Col. 0946] the brother for whom Christ died” (1 Cor. 8:11). [Note: The manuscripts have “perishes,” rather than “will perish.”]

Let us not argue against these commands and this salutary fear by saying: “Let bad conversations corrupt good morals”; and, “Let the weak person perish—what concern is that of ours?” God’s foundation stands firm, and no one perishes except the son of perdition.

## CHAPTER XVI

Far be it from us, while chattering in this way, to believe that we ought to be secure in such negligence. It is true that no one perishes except the son of perdition; but God says through the prophet Ezekiel: “He indeed will die in his sin, but I will require his blood from the hand of the watchman” (Ezek. 3:18).

49. Therefore, as far as we are concerned—we who cannot distinguish the predestined from the non-predestined, and who for that reason ought to desire the salvation of all—we must apply strict correction medicinally to everyone, lest they perish or cause others to perish. It is God’s task to make this correction useful for those whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.

If at some time we refrain from correcting through fear that someone might perish because of it, why do we not also correct through fear that someone might perish even more because of it? For we do not possess a greater depth of love than the blessed Apostle, who says: “Correct the disorderly, encourage the fainthearted, support the weak, be patient with everyone; see that no one repays anyone evil for evil” (1 Thess. 5:14–15).

This must be understood to mean that evil is then repaid for evil if the person who ought to be corrected is not corrected but is neglected through a wicked concealment of the matter.

He also says: “Those who sin, rebuke before all, so that the others may have fear” (1 Tim. 5:20). This must be understood of sins that are not hidden, lest he be thought to have spoken contrary to the Lord’s judgment. For the Lord says: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him.” Yet he himself carries the severity of correction so far as to say: “If he does not even listen to the Church, let him be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector” (Matt. 18:15, 17).

And who loved the weak more than the one who became weak for all and was crucified for all precisely through that weakness?

Since these things are so, neither grace forbids correction nor correction denies grace. Therefore righteousness must be commanded in such a way that the grace of God—by which what is commanded may be done—is sought in faithful prayer. Both must be done in such a way that just correction is not neglected.

Let all these things be done with charity, because charity neither commits sin nor covers over a multitude of sins.

# [ON THE PREDESTINATION OF THE SAINTS]

## ADMONITION TO THE FOLLOWING TWO BOOKS, ONE ON THE PREDESTINATION OF THE SAINTS, THE OTHER ON THE GIFT OF PERSEVERANCE

### TAKEN FROM THE LOUVAIN EDITION

[Col. 0947]

After certain books written by Augustine against the Pelagians had been brought into Gaul, they offended the minds of many there—not only those of the ordinary body of learned men, but also those of certain presbyters and bishops who were esteemed and commended for their piety and learning. The result was that many who favored Augustine’s teaching, out of respect for their authority, were turned back from the better position, or at least did not dare to profess it publicly.

But certain others, more thoughtful and firmer—among whom Prosper and Hilary were foremost [Note: The Louvain editors call this man Hilary of Arles, but falsely. See the note on Hilary’s letter below, cols. 953–954]—judging that these men were handling the matter incautiously through the influence of Pelagian error, while some were ignorantly slandering a matter they did not understand, courageously opposed them.

Since they could not satisfy them in every respect, they referred the matter to Augustine and asked him to explain more clearly and fully those points in his books—especially *On Correction and Grace*—that offended some of his followers. What these points were may be learned from the two letters that follow.

On this occasion Augustine wrote the following two books: one *On the Predestination of the Saints*, the other *On the Gift of Perseverance*. But those men were not satisfied even by these works; indeed, they became increasingly hostile to Augustine’s teaching and books, ignorantly and maliciously slandering many things in them.

As a result, after Augustine’s death Prosper published various brief defenses against their criticisms. Among other works of this kind are his responses to the Gallic chapters, to the Vincentian objections, to the excerpts of the Genoese, and against the *Collator*.

Although in these works he had very clearly exposed their ignorance and slanders, so that they ought by then to have been ashamed, they later stirred up still greater disturbances and spared neither Prosper nor Hilary. They were therefore compelled to have recourse to the Apostolic See, which at that time was governed by Pope Celestine.

After learning the whole matter from them, Celestine sent a letter to certain bishops of Gaul in which he defended and commended Augustine and his teaching, severely refuted Augustine’s detractors, and instructed the bishops to impose silence upon them.

Yet even then they did not entirely cease. Since the pope had not specifically named the books that they so hatefully disparaged—namely, *On Correction and Grace*, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, and *On the Gift of Perseverance*—but had designated them by their titles, after Celestine’s death they claimed that those books had not been approved and that the author had not been commended on their account, but that the praise had been bestowed upon him for the merits of his earlier writings. Prosper bears witness to this concerning them near the end of his book *Against the Collator*.

Consequently, during the time of Pope Felix IV, a council was held in the city of Orange [Note: Here again the Louvain editors must be corrected: they say that this second Council of Orange was held by order of Pope Leo I.] This was the second council of that place, at which the Catholic and apostolic teaching—also Augustine’s teaching—concerning grace and free will was renewed and reaffirmed, with the canons themselves drawn in many places from Augustine’s books. All this may be found in the second part of the Appendix.

As for the fact that Augustine did not mention these two books in his *Retractations*, this happened because, when he wrote that work, he had already published the two books of the *Retractations*, as he himself testifies below, in Book One and Book Two.

Pope Hormisdas wished it to be recognized especially from Augustine’s books what the Roman—that is, the Catholic—Church professes concerning free will and the grace of God. By the authority of this pope, the African bishops exiled in Sardinia for the faith commend these same books especially in their synodal letter. They say:

“Above all, take care to have the works that he wrote to Prosper and Hilary brought forward for reading by the aforementioned brothers. The blessed Hormisdas, glorious bishop of the Apostolic See, inserted mention of them, with great praise of Catholic teaching, in the letter that he sent in reply to the holy brother and fellow priest Possessor, who had consulted him. His words are these:

‘As for free will and the grace of God, what the Roman—that is, the Catholic—Church follows and maintains can indeed be abundantly recognized in the various books of the blessed Augustine, and especially in those addressed to Prosper and Hilary; nevertheless, the ecclesiastical archives also contain explicit chapters on the subject.’”

## LETTER 225 AMONG THE AUGUSTINIAN LETTERS

[Note: This letter is sent by Prosper to Augustine concerning the remnants of the Pelagian heresy then sprouting in Gaul and the complaints of such men against the teaching on predestination and grace explained in Augustine’s earlier works, especially the book *On Correction and Grace*.]

### To the most blessed pope, ineffably admirable, incomparably worthy of honor, outstanding patron, AUGUSTINE, from PROSPER.

1. I am unknown to you in face, but, if you remember, you have already come to know me to some extent in mind and speech. For through my holy brother the deacon Leontius I sent and received letters. [Note: Four manuscripts have “letter.”] Now also I dare to write to Your Blessedness, not merely, as then, out of a desire to send greetings, but out of devotion to the faith by which the Church lives.

Since your most vigilant diligence keeps watch over all the members of Christ’s body and fights with the power of truth against the snares of heretical teachings, I thought I had no reason to fear being burdensome or intrusive to you in a matter that concerns the salvation of many and therefore your piety. Rather, I believed that I would be guilty if I did not refer to the special patron of the faith matters that I understand to be exceedingly harmful.

2. Many servants of Christ [Note: That is, monks, the most famous of whom was John Cassian, the author of the *Collations*, later refuted by Prosper in his book *Against the Collator*.] who live in the city of Massilia consider contrary to the opinion of the Fathers and to ecclesiastical understanding whatever you have argued in your writings against the Pelagian heretics concerning the calling of the elect according to God’s purpose.

For some time they preferred to blame their own slowness to understand rather than criticize what they had not understood [Col. 0949], and some of them wished to request a clearer and more explicit exposition from Your Blessedness on this matter. [Note: The Louvain editors call this Hilary of Arles, but falsely. See the note on Hilary’s letter below, cols. 953–954.] [Note: Here again the Louvain editors must be corrected: they say that this second Council of Orange was held by order of Pope Leo I.]

It happened, through the arrangement of God’s mercy, that when similar concerns had arisen among certain men in Africa [Note: Monks of Adrumetum], you published the book *On Correction and Grace*, full of divine authority. When it reached our knowledge with unexpected timeliness, we thought that all the complaints of those who resisted would be quieted, because every question on which Your Holiness needed to be consulted had there been answered so fully and decisively, as though you had specifically taken pains to settle the disturbances among us.

After this book of Your Blessedness had been read, those who had previously followed the holy and apostolic authority of your teaching became much more perceptive and better instructed. But those who had been obstructed by the obscurity of their own convictions withdrew more hostile than before.

Their violently abrupt disagreement is to be feared first on their own account, lest the spirit of Pelagian impiety deceive men so distinguished and excellent in their pursuit of every virtue. It is also to be feared for the simpler people, who hold them in great esteem because of their reputation for probity and who may judge it safest to accept what they hear asserted by men whose authority they follow without judgment.

3. Their definition and profession is as follows:

They affirm that every human being sinned when Adam sinned, and that no one is saved through his own works but through the grace of God in regeneration. Nevertheless, they say that reconciliation, which is offered in the sacrament of Christ’s blood, has been set before all human beings without exception, so that whoever wishes to come to faith and Baptism may be saved.

They say that God foreknew before the foundation of the world who would believe and who would remain in that faith, which would afterward be assisted by grace, and that he predestined for his kingdom those whom he foresaw would, once freely called, prove worthy of election and depart from this life with a good end.

Therefore, they say, every human being is admonished by divine commands to believe and to act, so that no one may despair of attaining eternal life, since a reward has been prepared for voluntary devotion.

They maintain, however, that this purpose of God’s calling—in which, either before the beginning of the world or at the very creation of the human race, a distinction between those to be chosen and those to be rejected is said to have been made, so that according to what pleased the Creator some were created as vessels of honor and others as vessels of dishonor—both deprives the fallen of the concern to rise again and offers the saints an occasion for lukewarmness.

For, they say, in either case labor is superfluous: the rejected cannot enter by any effort, and the elect cannot fall away through any negligence. However they conduct themselves, nothing other than what God has determined can happen to them. Nor can one’s course be steady under an uncertain hope, since, if the election of the predestiner has determined otherwise, the effort of the one striving is futile.

Thus, they say, all diligence is removed and virtues are abolished if God’s decree precedes human wills. Under the name of predestination, a kind of fatal necessity is introduced; or else the Lord must be said to be the creator of different natures, if no one can be anything other than what he was made to be.

To set forth more briefly and fully what they think: whatever Your Blessedness opposed in this book from the standpoint of those who contradict you, and whatever you also most powerfully refuted in your books against Julian under this question, is proclaimed by these men with the greatest insistence.

When we bring forward your writings against them, supported by the strongest and most numerous testimonies of the divine Scriptures, and, following the form of your arguments, ourselves establish something by which they may be brought to a conclusion, they defend their obstinacy by antiquity. They assert that the things brought from the Apostle Paul’s Letter to the Romans to demonstrate divine grace preceding the merits of the elect were never understood by any ecclesiastical writer in the sense in which they are now understood.

When we ask them to explain these passages according to whatever meanings they prefer, they profess that they have found nothing satisfactory and demand that these matters be left unspoken, since no one has reached their profundity.

Finally, their obstinacy descends to the point of declaring that our faith is contrary to the edification of those who hear it and therefore, even if it is true, must not be brought forth, because teachings that are pernicious ought not to be received, while matters that cannot be understood may be silenced without danger.

4. Some of these men do not depart so far from the paths of the Pelagians that, when compelled to confess the grace of Christ that precedes all human merits—for if grace is given in response to merits, it is named grace in vain—they nevertheless wish this condition to belong to each human being: before he merits anything, indeed before he exists, the grace of the Creator establishes him as a rational creature possessing free will, so that through the discernment of good and evil, and toward knowledge of God and obedience to his commands, he may direct his will and reach the grace by which we are reborn in Christ through his natural ability—by asking, seeking, and knocking.

Thus, they say, he receives because he asked, finds because he sought, and enters because he knocked; because, having made good use of the good of nature, he has merited, with the help of initial grace, to reach this saving grace.

They define the purpose of calling grace entirely in this way: God has decreed to admit no one into his kingdom except through the sacrament of regeneration, and all human beings universally are called to this gift of salvation—whether through natural law, written law, or evangelical preaching.

Thus, they say, those who wish may become children of God, while those who refuse to believe are without excuse. God’s justice appears in the fact that those who do not believe perish; his goodness appears in the fact that he rejects no one from life but wills all indiscriminately to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.

At this point they produce testimonies in which the exhortation of the divine Scriptures urges human wills to obey—wills that, by free choice, either do what is commanded or neglect it. They think it follows that, since the transgressor is said not to have obeyed because he was unwilling, the believer must likewise be understood to have been devout because he was willing.

They hold that each person has as much ability for good as for evil, and that at the same moment a person can move his mind either toward [Col. 0951] vices or toward virtues. God’s grace supports the one who desires good, while just condemnation receives the one who pursues evil.

5. When, in the midst of these arguments, the innumerable multitude of infants is brought before them—infants who, apart from original sin, under which all human beings are born alike into the condemnation of the first man, have as yet neither wills nor personal actions, and who nevertheless are separated without God’s judgment being absent—some being taken away before they can discern good from evil and, through regeneration, being made heirs of the heavenly kingdom, while others, without Baptism, pass into the debt of everlasting death, they say that such children are lost or saved according to what divine knowledge foresaw they would become in later years if they were preserved until the age of responsible action.

They do not perceive that, according to their own imagining, they make God’s grace—which they wish to be an attendant rather than a precursor of human merits—subject even to those wills that they do not deny were preceded by grace.

They subject God’s election to all sorts of fabricated merits to such an extent that, since past merits do not exist, they invent future merits that will not be future. Thus, in a new form of absurdity among them, things not to be done are foreknown, and things foreknown are not done.

They seem to support this foreknowledge of human merits, according to which the grace of calling operates, with much greater plausibility when they turn to consider those nations that either in past ages were allowed to walk in their own ways (Acts 14:15) or even now perish in the impiety of their ancient ignorance, with no illumination of either the Law or the Gospel shining upon them.

Yet, insofar as a door has been opened and a way made for preachers, the people of the nations who sat in darkness and in the shadow of death have seen a great light (Isa. 9:2; Matt. 4:16); those who once were not a people are now God’s people; and those upon whom mercy was once not shown now receive mercy (Hos. 2:23–24; Rom. 9:25).

They say that the Lord foresaw who would believe and that times and the services of teachers were distributed to each nation in such a way that the belief of good wills would arise.

They say that the statement “God wills all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (1 Tim. 2:4) does not fail, since those are without excuse who could have been instructed by natural understanding in the worship of the one true God but did not hear the Gospel because they would not have received it.

6. They say that our Lord Jesus Christ died for the entire human race, that absolutely no one was excluded from redemption through his blood, even if that person passes through this whole life with a mind utterly alien to Christ, because the sacrament of divine mercy pertains to all human beings. They say that many are not renewed by it because God foreknows that they do not have the will to be renewed.

Thus, as far as God is concerned, eternal life is prepared for all; but, as far as free choice is concerned, it is apprehended by those who freely believe God and receive the help of grace as a reward for their belief.

Those whose contradiction troubles us turned especially toward this preaching of such grace, although previously they held better views, because, if they confessed that all good merits are preceded by grace and are granted by grace so that they can exist, they would necessarily have to concede that God, according to the purpose and counsel of his will, by a hidden judgment and manifest work, creates one vessel for honor and another for dishonor (Rom. 9:21), since no one is justified except by grace and no one is born except in transgression.

But they shrink from confessing this. They fear attributing the merits of the saints to God’s work, and they refuse to accept that the number of the predestined elect can neither be increased nor diminished. They fear that, among unbelievers and negligent people, the exhortations of those who encourage them would then have no place, and that the command to undertake effort and labor would be superfluous, since such striving would be frustrated if election were absent.

They believe, rather, that each person can be called to correction or progress only if he knows that he can become good through his own diligence, and that his freedom is assisted by God’s help if he chooses what God commands.

Thus, since in those who have received the period of free will there are two things that bring about human salvation—namely, God’s grace and human obedience—they wish obedience to precede grace, so that the beginning of salvation should be believed to rest in the one who is saved, not in the one who saves; and so that the human will should obtain divine grace for itself, rather than grace subjecting the human will to itself.

7. Since, through the revelation of God’s mercy and the instruction provided by Your Blessedness, we know this to be utterly perverse, we can indeed remain firm in refusing to believe it, but we are not equal to the authority of those who hold such views. They surpass us greatly in the merits of their lives, and some of them now stand above us by having recently attained the highest priestly office. [Note: [Col. 0951] The manuscripts read *cummi* for *summo* (“highest”).] Apart from a few fearless lovers of perfect grace, scarcely anyone has dared to oppose the disputations of such superior men.

As a result, danger has increased not only for those who listen to them but also for those who are listened to, along with their dignities. Their reverence restrains many in useless silence or leads them to careless agreement; and it seems to the men themselves most salutary that they are criticized by almost no one.

Therefore, since a not inconsiderable vein of Pelagian depravity is nourished in these remnants—if the beginning of salvation is wrongly placed in the human being; if human will is impiously preferred to divine will, so that a person is helped because he willed, rather than wills because he is helped; if someone who is evil by origin is wrongly believed to begin receiving the good not from the highest good but from himself; if God is pleased by anything other than what he himself has given—grant us in this matter, most blessed pope and excellent father, as much diligence in your piety as you can offer with the Lord’s help, so that you may deign to open up with the clearest explanations those points in these questions that are more obscure and difficult to understand.

[Col. 0953]

8. First, since most people do not think that Christian faith is violated by this disagreement, make clear how much danger lies in their conviction. Then explain how free will is not impeded by this grace that works beforehand and cooperates afterward.

Next, clarify whether God’s foreknowledge remains according to his purpose in such a way that the very things that have been purposed are to be understood as foreknown; or whether these matters vary according to kinds of causes and classes of persons, so that, because callings are diverse, God’s purpose seems to exist alone in those who are saved without doing anything, whereas in those who are going to do something good the purpose can stand through foreknowledge.

Or is the truth instead that, although foreknowledge cannot be divided from purpose by any temporal distinction, foreknowledge nevertheless rests upon purpose in a certain order? Just as there is nothing in any undertaking that divine knowledge has not preceded, so there is nothing good that has flowed into our participation without God as its author.

Finally, explain how, through this preaching of God’s purpose—by which those who have been foreordained to eternal life become believers—none of those who ought to be exhorted is hindered, nor given an occasion for negligence if they despair of being predestined.

We also ask you patiently to bear with our ignorance and show how this may be resolved: when the opinions of earlier writers on this subject are reviewed, almost all of them are found to have one and the same view, namely, that they accepted God’s purpose and predestination according to foreknowledge. For this reason, they say, God made some vessels of honor and others of dishonor: he foresaw the end of each person and, under the help of grace, foresaw what that person’s will and action would be.

9. When all these matters, and many others that you are able to see more profoundly as pertaining to this question, have been disentangled and examined, we believe and hope not only that our weakness will be strengthened by the support of your arguments, but also that those who are distinguished by merits and honors yet obscured by the darkness of this opinion will receive the purest light of grace.

Your Blessedness should know that one of them, a man of exceptional authority and spiritual devotion, the holy Hilary, bishop of Arles [Note: Some learned men thought that *Honoratus* should be read instead of *Hilary*, but all the manuscripts examined by us read *Hilary*. This Hilary was formerly a monk of Lérins and became bishop of Arles after Honoratus, who died in the year 428 or at the beginning of 429. Honoratus, who succeeded Patroclus—murdered in 426 according to Prosper’s *Chronicle*—occupied the see of Arles for two years, as Honoratus of Massilia testifies in his *Life of Hilary of Arles*.], is an admirer and follower of your teaching in every other respect, and that he has long wished to discuss by letter with Your Holiness his view concerning the matter over which he raises a complaint.

But since it is uncertain whether he will do this, or with what purpose he will do it, and since, by God’s grace, which provides for the present age, the weariness of us all finds relief in the strength of your charity and knowledge, add instruction to the humble and add rebuke to the proud.

It is necessary and useful to write what has already been written, lest something be considered insignificant because it is not often censured. People think something healthy if it does not hurt, and they do not notice a wound beneath the skin that has grown over it. But they should understand that whatever has a persistent swelling will eventually reach the point of being cut open. [Note: The manuscripts have: “what does not hurt, and they do not feel a wound that has grown over it.”]

May the grace of God and the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ crown you at all times and glorify you forever as you walk from virtue to virtue, most blessed pope, ineffably admirable, incomparably worthy of honor, outstanding patron.

## LETTER 226 AMONG THE AUGUSTINIAN LETTERS

[Note: Namely, Hilary’s letter to Augustine on the same subject.]

To the most blessed lord, greatly desired with all affection, and dearly embraced in Christ as a father, AUGUSTINE, HILARY.

[Note: [Col. 0953] Here Hilary plainly distinguishes himself from Hilary of Arles, who, as Prosper writes in the preceding letter, “was bringing Augustine’s view on predestination into question.” He does so below, no. 10, in these words: “I do not want Your Holiness to think that I am writing these things as though I doubted what you have now published.” He further indicates that he had at some time enjoyed Augustine’s “delights of his presence” and been “nourished by his health-giving breasts.” Then, in no. 9, he indicates that he is a layman; and finally he calls Augustine “father,” while Augustine in turn calls him “son” in the following book, *On the Predestination of the Saints*, no. 1. These details certainly do not fit Hilary, bishop of Arles.]

1. If, when the questions of those who contradict have ceased, the inquiries of earnest students are generally welcome, so that they may learn even those things which could be unknown without danger, I think that the diligence of my report ought to be still more welcome. For while it points out, according to the arguments of certain persons, certain positions contrary to the truth, it seeks, through the counsel of Your Holiness, to provide assistance not so much for itself as for those who are troubled and those who cause trouble, most blessed lord, desired with all affection and greatly embraced in Christ as a father.

2. These, then, are the matters being debated at Massilia, and also in other places in Gaul. They say that it is novel and useless for preaching to maintain that certain people are chosen according to God’s purpose, so that they can neither seize nor retain this election unless the will to believe is granted to them. They think that all force of preaching is excluded if it is said that nothing remains in human beings which preaching might stir up.

They agree that every human being perished in Adam and that no one can be liberated from this condition by his own free choice. But they maintain that it is consistent with the truth, and suitable for preaching, that when the opportunity of attaining salvation is announced to those who have been cast down and will never rise by their own strength, they can be healed of their disease by the merit of whatever they have willed and believed, and that through this they may obtain both an increase of faith itself and the effect of complete healing.

For the rest, they agree that no one is sufficient for himself for beginning any work, much less for completing it. Yet they do not think that a sick person’s frightened and pleading will to be healed should be counted among the works of their healing. For when it is said, “Believe, and you will be saved,” they assert that one of these is required and the other offered, so that, if what is required is supplied, what is offered may subsequently be granted on its account.

Therefore they think that faith must be supplied by the person to whose nature, by the will of the Creator, this has been granted. They do not think that any nature is so corrupted or extinguished that it ought not, or is unable, to will to be healed; and for this reason a person is either healed of his illness or, if he does not will it, punished along with his illness.

Nor, they say, is grace denied if such a will is said to precede—provided that it seeks only the physician and is itself already capable of nothing. For they want those testimonies—such as “as God has apportioned to each the measure of faith” (Romans 12:3), and similar passages—to mean that the one who has begun to will is helped, not that he is also given the will itself. Others who are equally guilty, and who could likewise be liberated if the will to believe, which is granted equally to those who are equally unworthy, were likewise granted to them, are excluded from this gift.

But if, they say, it is maintained that some such will remains in everyone, by which a person can either despise or obey, they think that the question of the elect and the rejected is readily settled by adding to each person the merit of his own will.

3. When they are asked why something is preached to some people or in some places, while it is not preached—or is preached only now—which at one time was not preached to almost everyone, just as it is not now preached to certain nations, they say that this belongs to divine foreknowledge: truth was or is announced at that time, in that place, and to those people when and where it was foreknown that it would be believed.

They claim to establish this not only by the testimony of other Catholics but also by an earlier discussion of Your Holiness, although in that discussion you taught the same grace with no less clarity of truth. Thus, Your Holiness said in the question against Porphyry, concerning the time of the Christian religion: “Christ then wished to appear to human beings, and to have his teaching preached among them, when he knew, and where he knew, that there would be those who would believe in him” (*Letter* 102, question 2, no. 14).

Or there is the passage from the book on the Epistle to the Romans: “You say to me, then, ‘Why does he still find fault? For who resists his will?’” (Romans 9:19; *Explanation of Certain Propositions from the Epistle to the Romans*, proposition 62). “To this inquiry,” you say, “he responds in such a way that we understand that, even among spiritual people—those who do not live according to the earthly human being—the first merits of faith and unbelief can be apparent, namely, how God in his foreknowledge chooses those who will believe and condemns unbelievers: not choosing the former on account of their works, nor condemning the latter on account of their works, but granting the faith of the former so that they may do good works, and hardening the unbelief of the latter by abandoning them, so that they may do evil.”

And again, earlier in the same book: “All are equal before merit, and election cannot be spoken of among things that are altogether equal. But since the Holy Spirit is given only to believers, God does not indeed choose the works which he himself bestows when he gives the Holy Spirit, so that we may do good through love; nevertheless, he chooses faith, because unless each person believes and remains in the will to receive, he does not receive the gift of God, that is, the Holy Spirit, through whom he may do good by the love poured into him.

“Therefore he does not choose, in his foreknowledge, anyone’s works which he himself is going to bestow; rather, in his foreknowledge he chooses faith, so that the one whom he foreknew would believe he might choose to receive the Holy Spirit, and by doing good might also attain eternal life. For the Apostle says: ‘It is the same God who works all things in all’ (1 Corinthians 12:6). But nowhere is it said, ‘God believes all things in all.’ What we believe is ours; what we do is his” (*Explanation of Certain Propositions from the Epistle to the Romans*, propositions 12 and 60).

They testify that they accept and approve the other statements in the same work as being consistent with evangelical truth.

4. They maintain, moreover, that foreknowledge, predestination, or purpose means that God foreknew, predestined, or purposed to choose those who would believe. Nor, they say, can it be said of this faith, “What do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7), since the same nature remained—although corrupted—which had previously been given sound and perfect.

What Your Holiness says, that no one perseveres unless he has received the power of persevering, they interpret to mean that, for those to whom this power is given, it is attributed to their own preceding free choice, though that choice may be sluggish. They say that free choice is granted only for this purpose: that a person may will or refuse to admit the medicine.

For the rest, they testify that they themselves abominate and condemn the view that any strength remains in anyone by which he may advance toward healing. But they do not want this perseverance preached in such a way that it cannot either be obtained through humble supplication or lost through obstinacy. Nor do they want to be led into uncertainty concerning God’s will, since, as far as they think concerns obtaining or losing it, any beginning of the will is evident to them.

They also judge that the testimony you cited, “He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding” (Wisdom 4:11), must be omitted as noncanonical. Accordingly, they understand foreknowledge in this way: people are to be understood as foreknown on account of the faith they would have in the future. They do not think that anyone is given such perseverance that he is not permitted to fall away; rather, they say that a person can defect from it and become weak by his own will.

[Note: [Col. 0955] The old Corbie manuscript refers this to the following sentence in this manner: “And they assert that so useful a practice of exhortation can become weak.”]

5. They maintain that the practice of exhortation is useless if it is said that nothing remains in a human being which correction can stir up. They admit that they say this remains in nature, but in such a way that the very fact that truth is preached to someone who is ignorant must be referred to the benefit of present grace.

For if people are predestined, they say, to either outcome, so that no one can pass from one group to another, what purpose does such persistent external correction serve? If, even though complete faith does not arise from a human being, at least sorrow arising from a contrite awareness of weakness arises, or the danger of death set before him is feared?

For if no one can fear what terrifies him except by a will that is received, then he is not to be blamed for not willing now; rather, the blame lies in and with the one who once willed in such a way that he deserved to incur that condemnation with his descendants, so that he would never will what is right but would always desire what is wrong.

But if some kind of sorrow arises in response to the exhortation of the one who corrects, they say that this very sorrow is the reason why one person is rejected and another accepted. Thus, they say, it is unnecessary to establish separate classes to which nothing can be added or from which nothing can be taken away.

6. Furthermore, they are displeased that grace is divided in the following way: the grace given either to the first human being at that time or now to everyone is said to have been such “that he received perseverance, not such as would make him persevere, but without which he could not persevere through free choice—whereas now the saints, predestined by grace for the kingdom, receive not such assistance of perseverance, but assistance of such a kind that perseverance itself is granted to them; not merely so that they cannot persevere without this gift, but also so that through this gift they can be nothing other than persevering” (*On Correction and Grace*, nos. 29–38 above).

Your Holiness’ words move them so greatly that they say a kind of despair is being presented to human beings. For, they say, if Adam was helped in such a way that he could both stand in righteousness and turn away from righteousness, while the saints are now helped in such a way that they cannot turn away—if indeed they received the perseverance of willing in such a way that they cannot will anything else—and if certain people are abandoned in such a way that they either never approach or, after approaching, depart, then the usefulness of exhortation and warning belonged to that will which possessed the free power both to persist and to desist, not to this will, for which not willing righteousness is joined to an unavoidable necessity—except in the case of those who were created together with those who were condemned along with the entire mass of humanity, so that they might be rescued by grace.

Thus, they want human nature to differ from the first human being only in this respect: grace helped him, while he was willing, with the full strength of his will, without which he could not persevere; but in the case of the present believers, whose powers have been lost and destroyed, grace not only raises those who have been cast down but also supports those who are walking.

For the rest, they maintain that whatever has been given to the predestined can both be lost and retained by their own will. They say that this would be false only if it were true that certain people had received perseverance in such a way that they could be nothing other than persevering.

7. For this reason they likewise do not accept that the number of those to be chosen and those to be rejected is fixed.

[Note: [Col. 0957] Several manuscripts read “do not want.”]

They also accept an interpretation of that statement different from the one drawn from you: namely, that God does not will all human beings to be saved only in the sense that he wills all who will belong to the number of the saints, but that he wills all human beings altogether to be saved, so that no one is excepted.

Nor, they say, should it be feared that some are said to perish against his will. Rather, just as God does not will anyone to sin or abandon righteousness, yet righteousness is continually abandoned against his will and sins are committed, so too he wills all human beings to be saved, yet not all human beings are saved.

[Note: [Col. 0957] Several manuscripts read, “to will them to be saved.”]

They think that the scriptural testimonies you cited concerning Saul and David do not pertain to the question, which concerns exhortation. They refer other passages to the claim that these commend the grace by which each person is helped after the will has arisen, or to the calling that is granted to the unworthy. They testify that they demonstrate this from those passages in your works and in the works of others, which it would take too long to pursue.

8. They do not permit the case of infants to be brought forward as an example for adults. They say that Your Holiness touched upon this subject only to the extent of wanting it to remain uncertain, and preferring that doubt be maintained concerning their punishments. You yourself recalled that this was stated in the third book *On Free Choice* in such a way that it could provide them with this opportunity.

They do the same with books by others that possess authority in the Church. Your Holiness sees that these can greatly assist those who contradict us unless we produce stronger, or at least equally strong, authorities. For your most prudent piety is not unaware how many there are in the Church who are held to a position, or moved away from it, by the authority of names.

In short, after all of us have been wearied, their argument—or rather their complaint—comes down to this. Even those who do not dare to condemn this definition agree in saying: Why was it necessary to trouble the hearts of so many people of lesser understanding with the uncertainty of such a discussion? They say that the Catholic faith had been defended no less usefully without this definition for so many years by so many interpreters, in so many earlier books, both yours and those of others, especially against the Pelagians.

9. My father, I would have preferred to bring these matters, and many other things beyond all limit, to you myself, if I may confess my deepest wishes; or, since I have not deserved that, at least to gather and send over a longer period everything that troubles them, so that I might hear to what extent each objection to this matter ought to be refuted or, if it cannot be refuted, endured.

But since neither outcome has come about as I wished, I preferred to send these matters together as best I could rather than remain completely silent about so great a contradiction on the part of certain people.

Some of the persons involved are of such standing that, according to ecclesiastical custom, laymen must show them the highest reverence. With God’s help we have taken care to observe this, while, when necessary, not remaining silent about what the smallness of our abilities suggested for defending this question.

But now I have offered these points in summary, insofar as the haste of the messenger allowed, as a kind of reminder. It belongs to your holy prudence to discern what must be done, so that the intention of such important and numerous people may be overcome or moderated.

I think it will do little good for you to give an explanation unless authority is also added—authority which contentious minds, however tireless, cannot overstep. Yet I certainly must not remain silent about the fact that, except in this matter, they say that they admire Your Holiness in everything you do and say.

It will be yours to decide how their contradiction in this matter should be endured. Nor should you be surprised that I have added something differently, or some things which I think I did not say in the preceding letter. Their position is now of this kind, apart from what I may perhaps have passed over through haste or forgetfulness.

10. When the books which you are preparing on your entire body of work have been published, I ask that we may be worthy to have them.

[Note: [Col. 0957] He means the books of the *Revisions*.]

Above all, this is so that, by their authority, if there are things in your writings that displease you, we may no longer hesitate, out of respect for your name, to set them aside. We also do not possess the book *On Grace and Free Choice*; since we are confident that it is useful for this question, may we be worthy to receive it.

I do not want Your Holiness to think that I am writing these things as though I doubted what you have now published. Let my punishment be sufficient: exiled from the delights of your presence, where I was nourished by your health-giving breasts, I am tormented not only by your absence but also by the obstinacy of certain people who reject not only what is clear but also criticize what they do not understand.

For the rest, I am so free from this suspicion that I regard as conspicuous my own weakness, by which I endure such people with too little patience. How you judge that these matters should be addressed, as I have said, I leave to your wisdom.

For I have believed that it was my responsibility, out of the charity I owe to Christ and to you, not to remain silent about the things being called into question. Whatever you wish or are able to do in return for that grace which we, the small together with the great, marvel to see in you, we shall receive with the greatest gratitude, as though it had been decreed by an authority most dear and reverend to us.

Since, under pressure from the messenger, I feared that, conscious of my own abilities, I might not be able to send either everything or even these matters in a sufficiently worthy manner, I asked a man distinguished in character, eloquence, and zeal to make known in his letter as much as he could gather.

[Note: [Col. 0959] He seems to mean Prosper, whose letter precedes this one.]

I have taken care to send his letter along with this one. Even apart from this necessity, he is a man who should be considered worthy of Your Holiness’ acquaintance.

The holy deacon Leontius, your devoted servant, sends you many greetings, as do my parents. May the Lord Christ graciously grant to his Church for many years Your Paternity, mindful of me, my lord and father.

And below:

Your Holiness should know that my brother—the chief reason we departed from here—has, with his wife, by mutual agreement, vowed to God a life of perfect continence. Therefore we ask Your Holiness to deign to pray that the Lord may confirm and preserve this very commitment in them.

[Col. 0959]

THE FIRST BOOK OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON THE PREDESTINATION OF THE SAINTS, TO PROSPER AND HILARY

[Note: [Col. 0959] Written after the books of the *Revisions*, in the year of Christ 428 or 429.]

[Note: [Col. 0959] The first book of *On the Predestination of the Saints*, addressed to Prosper and Hilary, has been checked against four Vatican manuscripts and sixteen Gallican manuscripts; against the Regius manuscript; the Noailles manuscript, namely, the one which entered our German library through the gift of the most noble lord, the duke of Noailles; the Colbertine; the Sorbonne; the Sainte-Geneviève; the Reims manuscript of the greater church; the manuscript of Emeric Bigot; the manuscript of Nicolas Manessier; the Metz manuscript of the abbey of Saint Arnulf; the Angers manuscript of Saint Albinus; the manuscript of the abbey of Saint-Evroul; and finally the manuscripts of Gembloux, Bec, Mont-Saint-Michel, Pratelles, and Corbie. It has also been checked against the Louvain variant readings excerpted from four Belgian manuscripts, and against the old editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 0959] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of *Revisions* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C)

In this work the truth of predestination and grace is defended against the Semipelagians—that is, people who had by no means completely withdrawn from the Pelagian heresy, since they wanted the beginning of salvation and of faith to come from ourselves, so that, as though on the basis of this preceding merit, they might obtain the remaining good things as gifts from God.

Augustine shows that the gift of God is not only the increase of faith but also the very beginning of faith. He does not deny that at one time he himself thought otherwise and erred in works written before his episcopate, such as the *Explanation of Certain Propositions from the Epistle to the Romans*, which they cite against him.

But he indicates that he was later convinced, especially by this testimony: “What do you have that you did not receive?” He proves that this testimony must also be understood of faith itself. Faith must be counted among the works by which the Apostle denies that God’s grace is preceded, when he says, “Not from works.”

Grace removes hardness of heart; and all come to Christ who are taught by the Father to come. Those whom he teaches, he teaches through mercy; those whom he does not teach, he does not teach through judgment.

The passage from his own *Letter* 102, question 2, concerning the time of the Christian religion, which the Semipelagians cite, can be properly explained without compromising the doctrine of grace and predestination.

He explains the difference between grace and predestination. Moreover, by predestination God foreknew those things which he himself was going to do.

He is astonished that the opponents of predestination, who are said not to want to be led into uncertainty concerning God’s will, prefer to entrust themselves to their own weakness rather than to the firmness of God’s promise.

He shows that they misuse the authority, “If you believe, you will be saved.” The truth of grace and predestination shines forth in infants who are saved, although they are distinguished by none of their own merits from the others who perish. For they are not distinguished on the basis of foreknown merits which they would have possessed had they lived longer.

The opponents unjustly reject as noncanonical the testimony he cited for this purpose: “He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding,” and so forth.

The Savior himself is a most splendid example of predestination and grace. In him, the human being was assumed by the Word, coeternal with the Father, into the unity of person, so that he might be Savior and the only-begotten Son of God, without acquiring this through any preceding merits of works or faith.

Those who are predestined are called by a certain distinctive calling proper to the elect. They were chosen before the foundation of the world, not because it was foreknown that they would believe and become holy, but so that they might become such through that very election of grace, and so forth.

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0959]

1. We know that the Apostle said in the Epistle to the Philippians, “To write the same things to you is not burdensome for me, and it is safe for you” (Philippians 3:1). Yet, when writing to the Galatians, he perceived that he had done enough among them, since he saw that what was necessary for them had been accomplished through the ministry of his speech: “From now on,” he says, “let no one cause me labor”; or, as most manuscripts read, “let no one trouble me” (Galatians 6:17).

Although I confess that I am distressed that the divine utterances by which God’s grace is preached—which is not grace at all if it is given according to our merits—are not accepted despite being so numerous and so clear, nevertheless I love your zeal and brotherly affection, dearest sons Prosper and Hilary, so greatly that I cannot say how much I love them. And I do not dare to say how much I ought to love you.

For this reason, behold, I am writing back to you. Although I am no longer with you, I am still accomplishing through you what I thought I had sufficiently accomplished.

2. For, having considered your letters, I seem to see that the brothers for whom you exercise pious care must be dealt with in the manner in which the Apostle dealt with those to whom he said, “And if you think differently about anything, God will reveal this also to you.” Your concern is that they should not hold the poetic opinion expressed in the words, “Each man has his own hope” (Virgil, *Aeneid* 11.309), and fall instead into what was said not poetically but prophetically: “Cursed is everyone who places his hope in man” (Jeremiah 17:5).

They are still in darkness concerning the question of the predestination of the saints. But they have grounds for God to reveal this also to them, if they think differently about it, provided that they walk in the way to which they have attained.

For this reason, after the Apostle had said, “If you think differently about anything, God will reveal this also to you,” he added, “Nevertheless, let us walk according to that which we have attained” (Philippians 3:15–16).
