These brothers of ours, for whom your pious charity is concerned, have attained to the point of believing with the Church of Christ that the human race is born subject to the sin of the first human being, and that no one is liberated from this evil except through the righteousness of the second human being.

They have also attained to the point of confessing that human wills are preceded by God’s grace, and of agreeing that no one is sufficient for himself either to begin or to complete any good work.

Their holding fast, therefore, to what they have attained distinguishes them greatly from the error of the Pelagians. Accordingly, if they walk in these things and pray to the one who gives understanding, then, if they think differently about predestination, he himself will reveal this also to them.

Nevertheless, let us also offer them the affection of charity and the ministry of speech, as he grants who is the one we have asked [Note: [Col. 0961] The printed editions read, “the one whom we ask.” The Noailles manuscript reads, “the one whom we have asked.”] to enable us in this letter to say what is suitable [Note: [Col. 0961] The Gallican and Vatican manuscripts read, “what is clear.”] and useful to them.

For how do we know whether our God may perhaps wish to accomplish this through our present service, by which we serve them in the free charity of Christ?

## CHAPTER TWO

3. We must therefore first demonstrate that the faith by which we are Christians is a gift of God—if indeed we can do this more diligently than we have already done in so many and such great volumes.

But now I see that we must answer those who say that the divine testimonies which we have cited concerning this matter mean that we should understand ourselves to possess faith itself from ourselves, while its increase comes from God—as though faith were not given to us by him, but were merely increased in us by him, on account of the merit by which it began from us.

[Note: [Col. 0961] Amerbach, Erasmus, and the manuscripts read *tamen* (“nevertheless”). The Louvain editors conjecturally corrected it to *tantum* (“only”).]

Thus they do not depart from the position which Pelagius himself, as the same proceedings testify, was compelled to condemn at the episcopal judgment in Palestine: “That the grace of God is given according to our merits” [Note: [Col. 0962] See the book *On the Proceedings of Pelagius*, no. 30.].

If what we began to believe does not belong to God’s grace, but only what is added to us on account of this beginning so that we may believe more fully and perfectly, then we give God the beginning of our faith first, so that its completion may be repaid to us, together with anything else we faithfully ask.

4. But against this, why do we not rather hear: “Who first gave to him, that he might be repaid? For from him and through him and in him are all things” (Romans 11:35–36)?

Therefore, the very beginning of our faith—from whom is it, if not from him? For it is not the case that everything else is from him except this; rather, “from him and through him and in him are all things.”

Yet who would say that one who has already begun to believe earns nothing from the one in whom he has believed? Hence it follows that, because he has already merited, the remaining gifts are said to be added by divine repayment; and thus the grace of God is given according to our merits—the very claim which Pelagius condemned in himself in order not to be condemned.

Therefore, whoever wishes to avoid this condemnable opinion in every respect should sincerely understand what the Apostle says: “To you it has been granted for Christ’s sake, not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him” (Philippians 1:29).

[Note: [Col. 0962] Louvain reads, “For both.” The word “for” is absent from the other books.]

He shows that both are gifts of God, because he said that both had been granted. He does not say, “so that you may believe in him more fully and perfectly,” but “so that you may believe in him.”

Nor did he say that he had obtained mercy so that he might be more faithful, but so that he might be faithful (1 Corinthians 7:25). For he knew that he had not first given the beginning of his faith to God, with its increase then repaid to him by God; rather, he was made faithful by the one by whom he was also made an apostle.

For the beginnings of his faith are recorded in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 9), and they are well known through the Church’s customary reading.

[Note: [Col. 0962] The Noailles manuscript reads *celebrata* (“celebrated”). Other manuscripts, together with the printed editions, read *celebri* (“customary,” “well-known”).]

[Note: [Col. 0962] He calls the reading from the Acts of the Apostles customary in the Church because it had already become established practice for it to be solemnly repeated each year at Easter. “The Acts of the Apostles,” he says in Sermon 315, no. 1, “is a book belonging to the canon of Scripture; this book begins to be read on Easter Sunday, as is the custom of the Church.”]

For, having turned away from the faith which he was ravaging and against which he was vehemently hostile, he was suddenly converted to it by a more powerful grace—the one who was to accomplish this very thing having been addressed through the prophet in these words: “When you turn us, you will give us life” (Psalm 84:7).

Thus he was made not only willing to believe from unwillingness, but also, from being a persecutor, willing to suffer persecution in defense of the faith of the one whom he had persecuted.

For it had been granted to him by Christ not only to believe in him but also to suffer for him.

5. Therefore, in commending this grace—which is not given according to any merits but produces every good merit—the Apostle says: “Not that we are sufficient to think anything as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God” (2 Corinthians 3:5).

Let those who think that the beginning of faith comes from ourselves while its completion comes from God pay attention here and weigh these words.

For who does not see that thinking comes before believing? No one believes anything unless he has first thought that it should be believed.

Although certain thoughts concerning the will to believe may fly ahead, however rapidly or swiftly, and although that will immediately follow them so closely as though accompanying them in intimate union, nevertheless everything that is believed must be believed with thought preceding it.

Indeed, believing itself is nothing other than thinking with assent. Not everyone who thinks believes, since many think precisely so that they may not believe. But everyone who believes thinks; by believing he thinks, and by thinking he believes.

Therefore, as far as religion and piety are concerned—which is what the Apostle was discussing—if we are not sufficient to think anything as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God, then surely we are not sufficient to believe anything as from ourselves, since we cannot do so without thought. Our sufficiency, by which we begin to believe, is therefore from God.

Consequently, just as no one is sufficient for himself to begin or complete any good work—as these brothers, as your writings indicate (*Letter of Hilary*, no. 2 above, cols. 0953–0954), agree is true—and just as in every good work, both in beginning and completing it, our sufficiency is from God, so no one is sufficient for himself either to begin or to complete faith. Our sufficiency is from God, because faith does not exist without thought, and we are not sufficient to think anything as from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from God.

6. Beloved brothers, beware of exalting human beings against God when a person says that he does what God promised.

Was not the faith of the nations promised to Abraham? And, giving glory to God, did he not believe with complete conviction that what God had promised he was able also to do (Romans 4:20–21)?

It is God, therefore, who creates the faith of the nations, since he is able to do what he promised.

Moreover, if God works our faith, acting wondrously in our hearts so that we believe, is there any reason to fear that he cannot do the whole work, and therefore that human beings should claim its first parts for themselves in order to deserve to receive its final parts from him?

Consider whether this method does anything other than ensure, in some fashion, that God’s grace is given according to our merits, so that grace is no longer grace.

For in this way it is rendered as something owed, not given freely. It is owed to the believer that the Lord should increase his faith; thus the increased faith becomes the reward of the faith that began. When this is said, it is not considered that this reward is assigned to believers not according to grace but according to debt.

Why, then, should everything not be attributed to human beings, so that the person who was able to establish for himself what he did not possess might himself increase what he established? I cannot see any reason—unless it is because people cannot resist the clearest divine testimonies, by which faith itself, from which the beginning of piety is taken [Note: [Col. 0963] Amerbach and Erasmus read, “from which piety takes its beginning.”], is shown to be a gift of God.

Such is the testimony, “God has apportioned to each the measure of faith” (Romans 12:3), and also, “Peace to the brothers, and love with faith, from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Ephesians 6:23), along with other passages of the same kind.

Thus, unwilling to resist such clear testimonies, yet wishing that what he believes should come from himself, a human being makes a kind of agreement with God, claiming one part of faith for himself and leaving another part to God.

And, what is even more presumptuous, he takes the first part for himself [Note: [Col. 0964] The Evreux manuscript reads, “for himself.”], gives the following part to God, and, in saying that it belongs to both, makes himself first and God second.

## CHAPTER THREE
### 7

That pious and humble teacher did not think in this way—I mean the most blessed Cyprian, who said: “One should glory in nothing, since nothing is ours” (*To Quirinus*, book 3, chapter 4). To demonstrate this, he brought forward the Apostle as a witness, saying: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

This testimony in particular also convicted me, when I was similarly in error, thinking that the faith by which we believe in God was not God’s gift but came from us and was within us, and that through it we obtained from God the gifts by which we might live temperately, justly, and piously in this world. For I did not think that faith was preceded by God’s grace, so that through faith what we profitably requested might be given to us—except insofar as we could not believe unless the proclamation of truth came first. But I considered it our own possession, arising from ourselves, that, once the Gospel had been preached to us, we should assent to it.

Several of my shorter works, written before I became a bishop, sufficiently reveal this error of mine. Among them is the work you mentioned in your letter (*On Hilary’s Letter*, no. 3, above, cols. 955–956), where there is an exposition of certain propositions from the Epistle to the Romans. Finally, when I was revising all my works and committing that revision to writing—having already completed two books of the work before I received your more extensive writings—when I reached this book for revision in the first volume, I spoke of it as follows:

“Likewise,” I said, “in discussing what God chose in one who was not yet born, to whom He said that the elder would serve, and what He rejected in that same elder, likewise not yet born—concerning which, although it was uttered much later, the prophetic testimony is recalled: ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated’ (Rom. 9:13; Mal. 1:3)—I carried my reasoning to the point of saying: ‘Therefore God did not choose, in His foreknowledge, the works of anyone which He Himself was going to give; rather, He chose faith in His foreknowledge, so that He Himself chose the one whom He foreknew would believe in Him, to give him the Holy Spirit, so that by doing good he might also attain eternal life.’

“I had not yet investigated carefully enough, nor had I yet discovered, what the election of grace is—the election of which the same Apostle says: ‘A remnant has been saved through the election of grace’ (Rom. 11:5). Certainly this is not grace if any merits precede it, lest what is given be rendered according to merit rather than according to grace, and thus be repaid as a debt rather than bestowed as a gift.

“Accordingly, what I said immediately afterward—‘For the same Apostle says, “It is the same God who works all things in all people” (1 Cor. 12:6); but nowhere is it said, “God believes all things in all people”’—and then added, ‘Therefore what we believe is ours; but what good we do is His who gives the Holy Spirit to believers’—I certainly would not have said this if I had already known that faith itself is among God’s gifts, which are given in the same Spirit.

“Thus both are ours because of the choice of the will, and yet both are given through the Spirit of faith and love. For it is not love alone, but, as it is written, ‘Love with faith from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ’ (Eph. 6:23).

“And what I said shortly afterward—‘For it is ours to believe and to will; but it is His to give believers and those who will the ability to do good through the Holy Spirit, through whom love is poured into our hearts’—is indeed true, but according to the same principle: both belong to Him, because He prepares the will; and both are ours, because this does not happen unless we will it.

“Accordingly, what I also said afterward—‘For we cannot will unless we are called; and when, after the call, we will, our will and our progress are not sufficient unless God both supplies strength to those who run and brings them to the place to which He calls them’—and then added, ‘It is therefore evident that what we do well belongs not to the one who wills or to the one who runs, but to God who has mercy’ (Rom. 9:16)—is altogether most true.

“But I discussed too little the call itself, which takes place according to God’s purpose. For not all who are called receive such a call, but only the elect.

“Thus what I said shortly afterward—‘For just as, in those whom God chooses, not works but faith begins the merit, so that through God’s gift they may do good; so in those whom He condemns, unbelief and ungodliness begin the merit of punishment, so that through that punishment also they may do evil’—I said most truly; but I did not think it necessary to investigate, nor did I say, that the merit of faith itself is also God’s gift.

“And elsewhere I said: ‘For He has mercy on whom He wills,’ I said, ‘and makes him do good; and whom He hardens (ibid., 18), He leaves him, so that he may do evil.’ But I attributed that mercy to a preceding merit of faith, and that hardening to a preceding iniquity.

“This is indeed true; but it still remained to be investigated whether the merit of faith itself comes from God’s mercy—that is, whether this mercy is bestowed on a person only because he is faithful, or whether it was also bestowed so that he might become faithful. For we read the Apostle saying: ‘I received mercy in order that I might be faithful’ (1 Cor. 7:25); he does not say, ‘because I was faithful.’ Thus mercy is indeed given to the faithful, but it was also given so that he might be faithful.

“Therefore, in another passage in the same book, I said most correctly: ‘Since we are called to believe not on the basis of works but by God’s mercy, and since those who believe are enabled to do good, this mercy should not be begrudged to the Gentiles, although I did not treat with sufficient care the call that takes place according to God’s purpose.’” (*Revisions*, book 1, chapter 23, nos. 3–4).

**[Note: [Col. 0964]** In the manuscripts, *he might choose*.]

[Note: [Col. 0964] At “what therefore” (*quod ergo*), Am., Er., and the manuscripts read *enim* (“for”) instead of *ergo* (“therefore”).]

[Note: [Col. 0965] At “they may do good,” Am., Er., and most manuscripts omit *bene* (“well”).]

[Note: [Col. 0965] At “He leaves him, so that he may do evil,” Am., Er., and most manuscripts read *ut mala* (“so that [he may do] evil things”) for *et male* (“and [he may act] badly”).]

[Note: [Col. 0965] The Vatican and Gallican manuscripts read here and in *Revisions* 1.23 that the merit of faith “comes from God’s mercy” (*de misericordia Dei veniat*). Am. and Er. read *meritum fidei misericordiam Dei praeveniat*, “whether the merit of faith precedes God’s mercy”; Louvain reads *meritum fidei misericordia Dei praeveniat*, “whether God’s mercy precedes the merit of faith.”]

**[Note: [Col. 0965]** Bernard, therefore, in *On Grace and Free Choice*, chapter 1: “God is the author of salvation; free choice is merely receptive.” Compare book 2 of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter 2, and Fulgentius, *On the Incarnation and Grace of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, chapters 22–24.]

### Chapter IV

### 8

You certainly see what I then thought about faith and works, although I was laboring to commend the grace of God. I now see that these brothers of ours hold the same opinion, because they have taken no care to advance along with me in my books as they did to read them. For if they had taken such care, they would have found this question resolved according to the truth of the divine Scriptures in the first of the two books that I wrote to Simplicianus of blessed memory, bishop of the Church of Milan and successor to Saint Ambrose, at the very beginning of my episcopate.

Unless, perhaps, they do not know these books. If that is so, see to it that they come to know them. In the second book of my *Revisions* I first discussed that first book of the two; my statement runs as follows:

“The first two books that I wrote as a bishop,” I said, “are addressed to Simplicianus, bishop of the Church of Milan, who succeeded the most blessed Ambrose. They concern various questions, two of which I brought together in the first book from the Apostle Paul’s Epistle to the Romans.

“The first question concerns the passage: ‘What then shall we say? Is the law sin? Certainly not,’ up to the place where he says: ‘Who will deliver me from this body of death? The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord’ (Rom. 7:7–25). In this passage I explained the Apostle’s words, ‘The law is spiritual, but I am carnal’ (ibid., 14), and the rest, in which the conflict of the flesh against the spirit is shown, as though a person still under the law, not yet established under grace, were being described. Much later I came to understand that these words could also—and this is more probable—belong to the spiritual person.

“The second question in this book extends from the place where he says, ‘And not only this, but Rebecca also, having conceived by one act of intercourse with Isaac our father,’ to the place where he says, ‘Unless the Lord of hosts had left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah’ (Rom. 9:10–29).

“In the resolution of this question there was indeed an effort on behalf of the free choice of the human will; but God’s grace prevailed. [Note: [Col. 0966] The manuscripts read *laboratum est* (“an effort was made”); the editions read *elaboratum est* (“the matter was worked out”).] The only conclusion to which one could arrive was that the Apostle should be understood to have spoken with the clearest truth when he said: ‘For who makes you different? And what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?’ (1 Cor. 4:7).

“And the martyr Cyprian, wishing to demonstrate this very thing, defined the whole matter in the title itself when he said: ‘One should glory in nothing, since nothing is ours’” (*Revisions*, book 2, chapter 1, no. 1).

This is why I said above that I myself had been especially convicted by this apostolic testimony when I thought otherwise about the matter. God revealed this understanding to me in resolving the question when, as I said, I was writing to Bishop Simplicianus.

**[Note: [Col. 0966]** He says that this was revealed to him by God because he understands that what he finally grasped, after more careful consideration of the Apostle’s testimony, should be attributed not to his own intelligence and acumen but to the assistance of divine grace.]

This testimony of the Apostle—where, to restrain human arrogance, he says, “What do you have that you did not receive?”—does not allow any believer to say, “I have faith that I did not receive.” These apostolic words altogether suppress the arrogance of this entire response. [Note: [Col. 0966] The editions read *reprimiturque* (“and is suppressed”); the manuscripts omit *-que* (“and”), reading *reprimitur* (“is suppressed”).]

But one cannot even say: “Although I do not possess perfect faith, I nevertheless possess its beginning, by which I first believed in Christ.” For here too the answer is: “What do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

### Chapter V

**[Col. 0967]**

### 9

But what they think—“This faith cannot be addressed by the words, ‘What do you have that you did not receive?’ because it remained in the same nature, although that nature had been corrupted, which had previously been given sound and perfect” (*On Hilary’s Letter*, no. 4, above, cols. 955–956)—is understood to have no force for their position if one considers why the Apostle said this.

He was acting to prevent anyone from boasting in a human being, because divisions had arisen among the Christian Corinthians, so that one person would say, “I belong to Paul,” another, “I belong to Apollos,” and another, “I belong to Cephas.” From there he proceeded to say: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong; God chose the lowly things of the world and the despised, and things that are not, as though they were, to abolish the things that are, so that no flesh might boast before God.”

Here the Apostle’s intention against human pride is certainly clear enough: no one should boast in a human being, and consequently not in himself either. Finally, after saying, “so that no flesh might boast before God,” to show in what a person ought to boast, he immediately added: “But from Him you are in Christ Jesus, who became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, sanctification, and redemption, so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord’” (1 Cor. 1:12, 27–31).

From there this intention of his proceeds until, rebuking them, he says: “For you are still carnal. Since there is jealousy and strife among you, are you not carnal and walking according to the human standard? For when one says, ‘I belong to Paul,’ and another, ‘I belong to Apollos,’ are you not merely human? What then is Apollos? And what is Paul? Ministers through whom you came to believe, and each as the Lord gave. I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth.”

Do you see that the Apostle is doing nothing except humbling the human being and exalting God alone? For, among those who are planted and watered, he does not even say that the planter and the waterer are anything, but says that God is the one who gives the growth.

**[Note: [Col. 0967]** So the manuscripts. The printed editions have *God* in the nominative.]

Although even the planting that he performs and the watering that the other performs he attributes not to them but to the Lord, saying: “Each according as the Lord gave. I planted, Apollos watered.”

Remaining within this same intention, he proceeds to say: “Therefore let no one boast in a human being” (ibid. 3:2–7, 21). For he had already said: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord.”

After this, and several other matters connected with it, the same intention leads him to say:

“I have applied these things to myself and Apollos for your sake, so that in us you may learn not to go beyond what is written, so that no one may be puffed up in favor of one against another. For who makes you different? And what do you have that you did not receive? But if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (ibid. 4:6–7).

### 10

In this most evident intention of the Apostle, in which he speaks against human pride so that no one may boast in a human being but in the Lord, it is exceedingly absurd, as I judge, to suppose that he is referring to natural gifts of God—whether to the whole and perfect nature as it was given in the first creation, or to whatever remnants belong to corrupted nature.

For are human beings distinguished from one another by these gifts that are common to all human beings? Yet he first said, “Who makes you different?” and then added, “What do you have that you did not receive?”

An arrogant person could indeed say against another: “My faith distinguishes me,” or “My righteousness,” or anything else of that kind. The good teacher meets such thoughts [Note: [Col. 0968] All the manuscripts read *qualibus* (“what kind of”) instead of *talibus* (“such”), referring to “thoughts.”] by saying: “What do you have that you did not receive?” From whom, unless from the one who distinguishes you from another, to whom He did not give what He gave to you? “But if you received it,” he says, “why do you boast as though you had not received it?”

I ask, is he doing anything other than directing the one who boasts to boast in the Lord? Nothing is more contrary to this meaning than for anyone to boast in his own merits as though he himself had produced them and not God’s grace—not the grace that is common to the good and the wicked, but the grace that distinguishes the good from the wicked.

Let grace, then, be attributed to nature, by which we are rational living beings and are distinguished from animals. Let grace also be attributed to nature, by which among human beings the beautiful are distinguished from the deformed, the intelligent from the slow, and so forth, if there is anything of this kind.

But the person whom the Apostle was restraining was not puffed up against an animal, nor against another human being on account of some natural gift that might be present even in the worst person. Rather, he was puffed up because he attributed to himself, and not to God, some good belonging to a good life, when he deserved to hear: “Who makes you different? And what do you have that you did not receive?”

Even if the ability to have faith belongs to nature, does the possession of faith also belong to nature? “For faith is not possessed by all” (2 Thess. 3:2), although the ability to have faith belongs to all.

The Apostle does not say: “What can you have that you did not receive, in order that you might be able to have it”; rather, he says: “What do you have that you did not receive?”

Therefore, the ability to have faith, just as the ability to have love, belongs to human nature; but to have faith, just as to have love, belongs to the grace given to the faithful.

**[Note: [Col. 0968]** Hence Bernard, *On Grace and Free Choice*, chapter 1: “God is the author of salvation; free choice is merely receptive.” Compare book 2 of *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, chapter 2, and Fulgentius, *On the Incarnation and Grace of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, chapters 22–24.]

That nature, therefore, in which the possibility of possessing faith was given to us, does not distinguish one human being from another. Faith itself, however, distinguishes the believer from the unbeliever.

Accordingly, when it is said, “Who makes you different? And what do you have that you did not receive?” whoever dares to say, “I have faith from myself; therefore I did not receive it,” certainly contradicts this most evident truth—not because believing or not believing is not within the choice of the human will, but because in the elect the will is prepared by the Lord (Prov. 8, according to the Septuagint).

Therefore, this also applies to faith itself, which resides in the will: “Who makes you different? And what do you have that you did not receive?”

### Chapter VI

### 11

“Many hear the word of truth, but some believe and others contradict. Therefore some wish to believe, while others do not wish to.”

Who does not know this? Who would deny it? But when the will is prepared for some by the Lord and not prepared for others, we must certainly distinguish what comes [Note: [Col. 0969] The Gallican and Vatican manuscripts read *eveniat* (“happens”) for *veniat* (“comes”).] from His mercy and what comes from His judgment.

“The thing Israel sought,” the Apostle says, “it did not obtain; but the elect obtained it, while the rest were hardened, as it is written: ‘God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes so that they would not see, and ears so that they would not hear, to this very day.’ And David says: ‘Let their table become a snare, a retribution, and a stumbling-block for them; let their eyes be darkened so that they may not see, and keep their back always bent.’”

Here are mercy and judgment: mercy toward the elect who obtained the righteousness of God [Note: [Col. 0969] The editions read *in electione* (“in the election”); the manuscripts more correctly read *in electionem* (“toward the election”), that is, *in electos* (“toward the elect”). The subsequent *in caeteros* (“toward the rest”) is likewise accusative.], but judgment upon the rest who were hardened. And yet the former believed because they willed to; the latter did not believe because they did not will to.

**[Note: [Col. 0969]** The Vatican manuscripts read “those who willed” and below “those who did not will.” Am. and Er. have *because* in the latter place, but *those who* in the former.] Mercy and judgment, therefore, were enacted in the wills themselves.

This election is an election of grace, not of merits. For above he had said: “So also at the present time a remnant has been saved through the election of grace. But if by grace, then not by works; otherwise grace is no longer grace” (Rom. 11:5–10).

The election therefore obtained what it obtained freely. Nothing preceded them that they might first give and that could then be repaid to them. He saved them for nothing.

**[Note: [Col. 0969]** The printed editions have *for He saved them for nothing*. The manuscripts omit *for*, and one of them has *He saves* instead of *He saved*.]

But for the others who were hardened, as the passage does not leave unmentioned, it happened as a retribution.

**[Note: [Col. 0969]** The Noailles manuscript has *as a retribution*.]

“All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24:10). Yet His ways are unsearchable (Rom. 11:33). Unsearchable, therefore, are both the mercy by which He freely delivers and the truth by which He judges justly.

### Chapter VII

### 12

But perhaps they say:

“The Apostle distinguishes faith from works. He says that grace is not from works, but he does not say that it is not from faith.”

That is indeed so. Yet Jesus also says that faith itself is God’s work, and He commands us to perform it. For the Jews said to Him: “What shall we do, so that we may perform the work of God?”

**[Note: [Col. 0969]** Thus all the manuscripts without exception. The printed editions have *the works of God*.]

Jesus answered and said to them: “This is the work of God: that you believe in Him whom He sent” (John 6:28–29).

Thus the Apostle distinguishes faith from works in the same way that, in the two kingdoms of the Hebrews, Judah is distinguished from Israel, although Judah itself is Israel.

He says that a person is justified by faith and not by works (Gal. 2:16) because faith itself is given first, so that by it the other things that are properly called works may be obtained—those in which one lives justly.

For he himself also says: “By grace you have been saved through faith, and this is not from yourselves; it is the gift of God”—that is, even when I said “through faith,” this too is not from yourselves, but faith itself is the gift of God. “Not from works,” he says, “so that no one may boast” (Eph. 2:8–9).

It is often said: “He deserved to believe because he was a good man even before he believed.” This can be said of Cornelius, whose alms were accepted and whose prayers were heard before he believed in Christ (Acts 10:4). Yet he did not give alms or pray without some faith. For how could he call upon one in whom he had not believed (Rom. 10:14)?

But if he could have been saved without the faith of Christ, the apostle Peter would not have been sent to him as an architect to build him up—although, “unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain” (Ps. 126:1).

And we are told: “Faith is from us; the other things pertaining to works of righteousness are from the Lord”—as though faith did not belong to the building; as though, I say, the foundation did not belong to the building.

But if it belongs to the building first and above all, the one who builds faith by preaching labors in vain unless the Lord, by showing mercy, builds it inwardly.

Therefore, whatever good Cornelius did before believing in Christ, while believing, and after believing—

**[Note: [Col. 0970]** The Louvain editors deleted *and while he believed* as superfluous. It is found not only in the earlier editions of Am. and Er., but also in the Vatican manuscripts and several Gallican manuscripts.]

—all of it must be attributed to God, so that no one may boast.

### Chapter VIII

### 13

Accordingly, when the one Teacher and Lord Himself had said what I have recalled above—“This is the work of God: that you believe in Him whom He sent”—shortly afterward, in that same discourse, He said:

“I told you that you have seen me and yet you have not believed. Everything that the Father gives me will come to me.”

What is “will come to me” except “will believe in me”? But for this to happen, the Father gives it.

Again, shortly afterward:

“Do not murmur among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him, and I will raise him up on the last day. It is written in the Prophets: ‘And they shall all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me” (John 6:29, 36–37, 43–45).

What does “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me” mean except: “There is no one who hears from the Father and learns but does come to me”?

For if everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes, then plainly everyone who does not come has not heard from the Father and has not learned. For if he had heard and learned, he would come. No one has heard and learned without coming; rather, as the Truth says, everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes.

This school, in which the Father is heard and teaches so that one may come to the Son, is very far removed from the senses of the flesh. The Son Himself is there, because He is His Word, through whom He teaches in this way. He does not act through the ear of the flesh but through the ear of the heart.

The Spirit of the Father and the Son is also there at the same time. For the Spirit does not fail to teach, nor does He teach separately; we have learned that the works of the Trinity are inseparable.

**[Note: [Col. 0970]** Am. and Er. and some manuscripts have *we say*.]

And it is certainly the Holy Spirit of whom the Apostle says: “But having the same Spirit of faith” (2 Cor. 4:13).

This is attributed especially to the Father because the Only-Begotten is begotten from Him, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from Him. But it would take too long to discuss this more fully. I believe that my work on the Trinity, which is God, in fifteen books has already reached you.

This school, I repeat, in which God is heard and teaches, is very far removed from the senses of the flesh. We see many coming to the Son, because we see many believing in Christ; but where and how they have heard and learned this from the Father, we do not see.

This grace is exceedingly hidden. Yet who can doubt that it is grace? This grace, then, which is secretly bestowed upon human hearts by divine generosity, is rejected by no hardened heart. It is bestowed precisely so that the hardness of the heart may first be removed.

When, therefore, the Father is heard and teaches inwardly so that one may come to the Son, He removes the heart of stone and gives a heart of flesh, as He promised through the prophet (Ezek. 11:19). In this way He makes children of promise and vessels of mercy, which He prepared for glory.

### 14

Why, then, does He not teach everyone to come to Christ, unless because He teaches all whom He teaches through mercy, while those whom He does not teach He does not teach through judgment?

“For He has mercy on whom He wills, and He hardens whom He wills.” But He has mercy by granting good things; He hardens by repaying what is deserved.

Or, if—as some have preferred to distinguish—the following words are those of the person to whom the Apostle is speaking, so that they are understood as his own words, “Therefore He has mercy on whom He wills, and He hardens whom He wills,” and the words that follow—“Why does He still find fault? For who can resist His will?”—was the Apostle’s response, “O man, what you have said is false”?

No.

**[Note: [Col. 0971]** All the manuscripts omit *not*.]

Rather, his response was: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me like this?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay from the same lump?”—and the rest, which you know very well.

Yet, in a certain sense, the Father teaches everyone to come to His Son. For it was not written without purpose in the Prophets: “And they shall all be taught by God.” After presenting this testimony, He then added: “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me.”

Just as we speak correctly when, concerning a teacher of letters who is the only such teacher in a city, we say, “This man teaches everyone here their letters”—not because everyone learns, but because no one who learns letters there learns except from him—so we rightly say, “God teaches everyone to come to Christ,” not because everyone comes, but because no one comes in any other way.

Why He does not teach everyone, the Apostle disclosed as far as he judged it should be disclosed: “Wishing to show His wrath and to make known His power, He endured with much patience the vessels of wrath that had been prepared for destruction, and in order to make known the riches of His glory upon the vessels of mercy, which He prepared for glory” (Rom. 9:18–23).

This is why “the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing, but to those who are being saved it is the power of God” (1 Cor. 1:18).

God teaches all these people to come to Christ. For it is these whom He wills to save and to bring to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4).

**[Note: [Col. 0971]** We add *for*, since all the manuscripts contain it.]

For if He had wished to teach those also to whom the word of the cross is foolishness, so that they might come to Christ, they too would undoubtedly come. The one who says, “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me,” neither deceives nor is deceived.

Far be it, therefore, that anyone who has heard and learned from the Father should not come.

### 15

“Why,” they ask, “does He not teach everyone?”

If we say that it is because those whom He does not teach do not wish to learn, we will be answered: “Then what of the words addressed to Him, ‘O God, by turning us You will make us live’” (Ps. 84:7).

Or if God does not make willing people out of unwilling people, why does the Church, according to the Lord’s command, pray for its persecutors (Matt. 5:44)?

For Saint Cyprian also wished this to be understood by the words we say, “Your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” (Matt. 6:10): that is, just as it is done in those who have already believed and are, as it were, heaven, so also in those who do not believe and therefore are still earth.

What, then, do we pray for those unwilling to believe, except that God may work in them even the willing (Phil. 2:13)?

Concerning the Jews the Apostle certainly says: “Brothers, the good will of my heart and my prayer to God for them is for salvation” (Rom. 10:1).

**[Note: [Col. 0972]** Almost all manuscripts omit *is made*.]

He prays for those who do not believe. For what, except that they may believe? For they cannot otherwise attain salvation.

If, then, the faith of those who pray precedes God’s grace, does the faith of those for whom prayer is offered—that they may believe—also precede God’s grace? After all, the prayer for them is that faith itself may be given to those who do not believe, that is, to those who do not possess faith.

When, therefore, the Gospel is preached, some believe and others do not believe. Those who believe hear and learn inwardly from the Father while the preacher’s voice sounds outwardly; those who do not believe hear outwardly but do not hear or learn inwardly. That is, the gift is given to some and not given to others.

“For no one,” He says, “comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.”

This is stated more clearly later. For after some time, when He was speaking about eating His flesh and drinking His blood, certain of His disciples said: “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?”

Knowing within Himself that His disciples were murmuring about this, Jesus said to them: “Does this offend you?” And shortly afterward:

“The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life. But there are some among you who do not believe.”

Then the Evangelist adds: “For Jesus knew from the beginning who those were who believed and who would betray Him,” and He said:

“That is why I told you that no one can come to me unless it has been granted to him by my Father” (John 6:44–66).

Therefore, to be drawn by the Father to Christ, and to hear and learn from the Father so as to come to Christ, means nothing other than to receive from the Father the gift of believing in Christ.

For the one who said, “No one comes to me unless it has been granted to him by my Father,” was distinguishing not those who hear the Gospel from those who do not hear it, but believers from unbelievers.

### 16

**[Note: [Col. 0972]** In Am. and Er., chapter 9 begins here.]

Faith, therefore—both faith that has begun and faith that has been perfected—is God’s gift. Let no one doubt this gift’s being given to some and not given to others if he does not wish to resist the most evident sacred Scriptures.

But why it is not given to everyone should not trouble the faithful person who believes that all came from one person into condemnation, a condemnation without doubt entirely just, so that there would have been no just accusation against God even if no one had been delivered from it.

Hence it is clear that great is the grace by which many are delivered, and that those who are not delivered recognize in themselves what was owed to them. Thus the one who boasts should boast not in his own merits—which he sees to be equal to those of the condemned—but in the Lord.

**[Note: [Col. 0972]** The printed editions have: “so that those who boast do not boast in their own merits, which they see to be equal to those of the condemned, but boast in the Lord.” The manuscripts have the singular forms *the one who boasts*, *he sees*, and *he should boast*.]

Why, then, He should deliver this person rather than that person—His judgments are unsearchable and His ways inscrutable (Rom. 11:33).

It is better here to hear or say: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Rom. 9:20), than to dare to say, as though we knew what He wished to remain hidden—He who nevertheless could not will anything unjust.

### Chapter IX

### 17

You recall what I said in one of my works against Porphyry, under the title *On the Time of the Christian Religion*. I spoke in such a way as to pass over this more careful and laborious discussion of grace, but not without indicating that I had deliberately declined to explain it at that point and that it could be explained elsewhere or by others.

**[Note: [Col. 0973]** Six manuscripts have *or explained by others*.]

Among other things, in answer to the question proposed—Why did Christ come after so long a time?—I spoke as follows:

“Accordingly, since they do not object to Christ that not everyone follows His teaching—for they themselves understand that this cannot rightly be objected either to the wisdom of the philosophers or even to the divinity of their gods—what will they answer if, setting aside that height of God’s wisdom and knowledge, where perhaps another, far more hidden divine plan lies concealed, and without prejudging any other causes that the wise may be able to investigate, we say this alone, for the sake of brevity in our discussion of the question: Christ wished to appear to human beings and His teaching to be preached among them at the time and in the places where He knew there would be people who would believe in Him?

“For He foreknew that in those times and places where His Gospel was not preached, all such people would have been in His preaching as were—not all, but nevertheless many—in His bodily presence: people who did not wish to believe in Him even after He had raised the dead. Even now we see many like them, although the prophecies of the Prophets concerning Him are being fulfilled with such great clarity. They still refuse to believe and prefer to resist by human cleverness rather than yield to divine authority, so clear and evident, so exalted and so exaltedly proclaimed, as long as the human understanding remains small and weak and cannot approach divine truth.

**[Note: [Col. 0973]** Am. and Er. have *will not be able to approach divine truth*. Louvain has *ought to approach divine truth*. But the Vatican and Gallican manuscripts have neither *ought* nor *will not be able*. These manuscripts seem preferable, even to the Louvain edition, which we followed in volume 2.]

“What wonder is it, then, if Christ knew that the world was so full of unbelievers in earlier ages—

**[Note: [Col. 0973]** Three manuscripts have: “since Christ had not come in earlier ages into a world full of unbelievers.”]

—that He should rightly have been unwilling to appear or to be preached to those whom He foreknew would believe neither His words nor His miracles?

“For it is not incredible that all people at that time were such as we are astonished to find so many having been and still being from His coming to the present day.

“And yet, from the beginning of the human race, sometimes more secretly and sometimes more openly, as seemed divinely appropriate to the times, prophecy about Him did not cease, nor were there lacking those who believed in Him: from Adam to Moses, in the people of Israel itself—which, by a special mystery, was a prophetic nation—and among other nations before He came in the flesh.

“For when certain people are mentioned in the holy Hebrew books, already from the time of Abraham, who were neither of his fleshly descent nor from the people of Israel nor joined to the people of Israel as outsiders, but who nevertheless shared in this mystery, why should we not believe that here and there among the other nations there were others, although we do not read of them being mentioned in those same authoritative writings?

“Thus this salvation of religion, through which alone true salvation is truly promised, was never lacking to anyone who was worthy of it; and to the one to whom it was lacking, there was no worthiness.

“From the beginning of the propagation of the human race to the end, it is preached to some for reward and to others for judgment.

“Accordingly, those to whom it was not announced at all were foreknown not to believe; and those to whom it was announced although they would not believe are displayed as an example to others. But those to whom it is announced because they will believe are prepared for the kingdom of heaven and fellowship with the holy angels” (*Letter 102*, nos. 14–15).

18. Do you see that I wished to speak about Christ’s foreknowledge—without prejudging the hidden counsel of God or other causes—in a way that might seem sufficient to refute the unbelief of the pagans who had raised this question? For what is more certain than that Christ foreknew both when and where there would be people who would believe in him? But whether, when Christ had been preached to them, they would have faith of themselves or would receive it by God’s gift—that is, whether God merely foreknew them or also predestined them—I did not then consider it necessary to ask or discuss.

Accordingly, what I said, “Christ wished to appear to human beings and to have his doctrine preached among them at the time and in the places where he knew there would be those who would believe in him,” may also be expressed in this way: “Christ wished to appear to human beings and to have his doctrine preached among them at the time and in the places where he knew there would be those who had been chosen in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4). But because, if it were expressed in that way, it would make the reader attentive to investigating matters that now, in consequence of the warning provided by the Pelagian error, must necessarily be discussed more fully and laboriously, it seemed to me that what was sufficient at that time should be stated briefly, except—as I said—for the depth of God’s wisdom and knowledge, and without prejudging the other causes that I thought should be discussed not then but on another, more suitable occasion. [Note: [Col. 0974] Here all our manuscripts omit “on another occasion.”]

## CHAPTER X

19. Likewise, when I said, “The salvation of this religion was never lacking to anyone who was worthy, and no one to whom it was lacking was worthy,” if it is examined and the source of each person’s worthiness is sought, some say that it comes from the human will; we, however, say that it comes from divine grace or predestination. The only difference between grace and predestination is that predestination is the preparation for grace, while grace is the gift itself. Thus, what the Apostle says—“not from works, so that no one may boast; for we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works”—is grace; but what follows—“which God prepared beforehand, so that we might walk in them” (Ephesians 2:9–10)—is predestination, which cannot exist without foreknowledge, though foreknowledge can exist without predestination.

For by predestination God foreknew the things that he himself was going to do; hence it is said, “He made the things that were to be” (Isaiah 45, according to the Septuagint). But he can also foreknow things that he himself does not do, such as all sins. For even though there are certain things that are sins in such a way that they are also punishments for sins—hence it is said, “God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is not fitting” (Romans 1:28)—the sin there is not God’s, but his judgment.

Therefore God’s predestination, which concerns what is good, is, as I said, the preparation for grace; grace, however, is the effect of that predestination. When God therefore promised Abraham the faith of the nations in his offspring, saying, “I have appointed you the father of many nations,” from which the Apostle says, “Therefore it is by faith, so that the promise may be firm according to grace for all the offspring” (Genesis 17:4–5), he promised this not on the basis of the power of our will, but on the basis of his own predestination.

For he promised what he himself was going to do, not what human beings were going to do. For even if human beings do good things that pertain to the worship of God, he himself causes them to do what he commands; they do not cause him to do what he has promised. Otherwise, for God’s promises to be fulfilled would depend not on God’s power but on that of human beings, and what was promised by the Lord would be given to Abraham by them.

Abraham, however, did not believe in this way. Rather, he believed, “giving glory to God, because he is able also to do what he has promised” (Romans 4:16–21). He did not say, “He is able to predict”; he did not say, “He is able to foreknow,” for God can also predict and foreknow the acts of others. But he said, “He is able also to do”; and thus the acts are his own, not those of others.

20. Or perhaps God promised Abraham the good works of the nations in his offspring, promising what he himself does, but did not promise the faith of the nations—which human beings produce for themselves—and, in order to promise what he himself does, merely foreknew that human beings would produce that faith?

The Apostle certainly does not speak in this way. God promised Abraham children who would follow the traces of his faith; he says this with complete clarity. But if he promised works of the nations and not faith, then surely, since there are no good works except from faith—“the righteous person lives by faith” (Habakkuk 2:4); “everything that is not from faith is sin” (Romans 14:23); and “without faith it is impossible to please” [Note: [Col. 0975] The printed editions add “God.” “God” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle, and is often omitted by Augustine.] “(Hebrews 11:6)—it is nevertheless within human power for God to fulfill what he promised.

For unless a human being does what belongs to him, without God’s giving it, God will not do what he is to give. That is, unless a human being has faith from himself, God does not fulfill what he promised, namely, that works of righteousness should be given by God. Thus, for God to be able to fulfill his promises, it depends not on God’s power but on that of human beings. But if truth and piety forbid us to believe this, let us believe with Abraham that God is able also to do what he promised.

He promised Abraham children; and they cannot be such if they do not have faith. Therefore he himself gives faith as well.

## CHAPTER XI

21. Since the Apostle says, “Therefore it is by faith, so that the promise may be firm according to grace,” I am amazed that people prefer to entrust themselves to their own weakness rather than to the firmness of God’s promise. “But,” someone says, “God’s will concerning me is uncertain to me.” What then? Is your own will concerning yourself certain to you, and do you not fear the warning, “Let anyone who thinks that he stands take heed lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 10:12)?

Since, therefore, both are uncertain, why does a person not entrust his faith, hope, and love to what is firmer rather than to what is weaker?

22. “But when it is said,” they say, “‘If you believe, you will be saved’ (Romans 10:9), one of these is required and the other is offered. What is required lies within human power; what is offered lies within God’s power” (above, in Hilary’s letter, no. 2, Cols. 947–948).

Why not place both within God’s power—both what he commands and what he offers [Note: [Col. 0976] So the manuscripts read. Lovanienses, however, have: “within God’s power are both what is commanded and what is offered”?]?

For God is asked to give what he commands. Believers ask that their faith be increased; they pray for unbelievers that faith may be given to them. Thus, both in its increase and in its beginning, faith is God’s gift [Note: [Col. 0976] The printed editions read: “so that faith may be a gift both in its increase and in its beginning.” But the manuscripts read: “Thus, both in its increase and in its beginning, faith is God’s gift.”].

The statement “If you believe, you will be saved” is expressed in the same way as: “If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live.” Here too, one of two things is required and the other is offered. “If by the Spirit,” he says, “you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live”: putting to death the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit is required; living is offered.

Are we then to say that putting to death the deeds of the flesh is not God’s gift, or refuse to acknowledge it as God’s gift because we hear it required of us, with the reward of life offered if we do it? God forbid that this should please those who share in and defend grace. That is the damnable error of the Pelagians. The Apostle immediately closed their mouths by adding, “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Romans 8:13–14), lest we believe that we put to death the deeds of the flesh through our own spirit rather than through God’s.

He was speaking of that Spirit of God also where he says, “All these things are worked by one and the same Spirit, distributing to each one individually as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11). Among all these gifts, as you know, he named faith as well.

Therefore, just as putting to death the deeds of the flesh is God’s gift, although it is required of us with the reward of life set before us, so faith is God’s gift, although it too is required of us when it is said, “If you believe, you will be saved,” with the reward of salvation set before us.

These things are commanded to us and are shown to be gifts of God so that it may be understood both that we do them and that God causes us to do them, just as he says most clearly through the prophet Ezekiel. For what could be clearer than his statement, “I will cause you to do them” (Ezekiel 36:27)? Look carefully at the passage of Scripture itself [Note: [Col. 0976] The printed editions add here, “dearest brothers.” This is absent from the manuscripts.], and you will see that God promises that he will cause them to do what he commands to be done. He does not, in fact, remain silent there about their merits, but about their evil merits: he shows that he repays evil with good by causing them thereafter to possess good works, since he himself causes them to perform the divine commandments.

## CHAPTER XII

23. This entire argument by which we defend the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord as truly grace—that is, as given not according to our merits—although it is asserted with the clearest testimony of the divine words, nevertheless encounters some difficulty among those who think that unless they assign something to themselves, which they first give in order to have it repaid to them, they are being restrained from every pursuit of piety. This difficulty arises when dealing with adults who already exercise the power of the will [Note: [Col. 0977] The printed editions read, “it is sometimes laborious.” But the manuscripts read, “it encounters some difficulty,” or “somewhat.” The verb “encounters” refers back to the preceding words, “This entire argument.”].

But when we come to infants, and to the Mediator himself between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), every assertion of preceding human merits that would come before God’s grace collapses. Infants are not distinguished from others by any preceding good merits, so as to belong to the liberator of human beings; nor was he, although himself human, made the liberator of human beings through any preceding human merits.

24. For who could listen to the claim that infants are baptized and leave this life at that infant age because of their future merits, while others who are not baptized die at the same age because their future merits—evil merits—were foreknown, not because God rewards or condemns their good or evil life [Note: [Col. 0977] The printed editions read, “or condemns?” They then begin the following sentence: “But the Apostle indeed fixed no limit.” The text has been corrected on the authority of the manuscripts, whose reading the Lovanienses clearly approve in their notes, where they observe that “life” there refers to no life of infants imagined as future if they had survived.], but no life at all? [The reference is above, in Prosper’s letter, no. 5, Cols. 951–952.]

The Apostle did indeed establish a limit beyond which human beings’—to put it mildly—heedless conjecture ought not to pass. For he says, “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each one may receive according to what he has done through the body, whether good or evil” (2 Corinthians 5:10). He says “has done”; he did not add, “or was going to do.”

But how such a thought entered the minds of these men, so that the future merits of infants—merits that are not future—should be punished or honored, I do not know. Why, moreover, is it said that a person is to be judged according to what he has done through the body, when many things are done by the mind alone, not through the body or any bodily member, and often things so serious that the most just punishment is owed for such thoughts—as, to say nothing of other examples, when the fool says in his heart, “There is no God” (Psalm 13:1)?

What, then, does “according to what he has done through the body” mean except “according to what he has done during the time when he was in the body,” so that by “through the body” we understand “during the time of the body”? After death no one will be in the body except at the final resurrection—not to acquire any merits, but to receive rewards for good merits and suffer punishments for evil ones [Note: [Col. 0977] The printed editions read, “or punishments for evil ones.” The word “or” is absent from the manuscripts.].

In the intervening period between laying aside and receiving the body, souls are either tormented or rest according to what they did during the time of the body. To this time of the body also belongs what the Pelagians deny but the Church of Christ confesses: original sin. When infants die, whether it has been removed by God’s grace or remains through God’s judgment, they pass either by the merit of regeneration from evil to good, or by the merit of their origin from evil to evil.

The Catholic faith knows this; certain heretics also agree with it without any contradiction. But how people could have supposed that anyone is judged not according to the merits he had as long as he was in the body, but according to the merits he would have had if he had lived longer in the body—people whose intelligence your writings show not to be contemptible—I cannot discover, though I am astonished and amazed. Nor would I dare to believe it, were it not that I would not dare disbelieve you.

But I hope that God will be present, so that, once warned, they may quickly see that if sins said to have been going to occur can rightly be punished in the unbaptized by God’s judgment, they can also be forgiven in the baptized by God’s grace. For whoever says that future sins can be punished only when God judges, but cannot be forgiven when God shows mercy, ought to consider how great an insult he inflicts upon God and his grace—as though a future sin could be foreknown but could not be forgiven.

If this is absurd, then infants who, had they lived longer, would have become sinners ought rather, when they die at an early age, to have been helped by the washing in which sins are cleansed.

## CHAPTER XIII

25. If perhaps they say that sins are forgiven to those who repent, and that therefore those who die in infancy are not baptized because it was foreknown that, if they lived, they would not repent, while God foreknew that those who are baptized and die as infants would have repented if they had lived, let them attend and see that, if this is so, then it is no longer original sins that are punished in infants who die without Baptism, but each person’s own future sins, had he lived. Likewise, among those who are baptized, it is not original sins that are washed away, but their own future sins, had they lived, since they could not sin except at a more advanced age [Note: [Col. 0978] The manuscripts read, “since sin could not be committed except at a more advanced age.” Below, where the printed editions have “were foreseen,” the manuscripts perhaps have “were foreseen” with a different reading. Not everything here is entirely coherent, since some words may have entered the text from the margin.].

Thus, some would have been foreseen as going to repent and others as not going to repent; and for that reason some were baptized while others departed this life without Baptism.

If the Pelagians dared to say this [Note: [Col. 0978] The editions of Amerbach and Erasmus read, “if they have heard.” The manuscripts read, “if they heard.”], they would no longer struggle by denying original sin or by seeking for infants outside the kingdom of God some place of their own imagined happiness. They would be especially refuted when they were shown that infants cannot possess eternal life because they have not eaten the flesh or drunk the blood of Christ (John 6:54), and because, in those who have no sin whatsoever, Baptism—which is administered for the remission of sins—would be false.

For they would simply say that there is no original sin, but that infants who depart from the body are baptized or not baptized according to their future merits, had they lived; and that according to their future merits they either receive or do not receive the body and blood of Christ, without which they absolutely cannot have life. They would also say that they are baptized for the true remission of sins, although they derived no sin from Adam, because the sins concerning which God foreknew that they would repent are remitted to them.

In this way they could very easily conduct and win their case, by which they deny that there is original sin and contend that God’s grace is given only according to our merits. But since the future merits of people whose future actions never occur are unquestionably nothing—and this is very easy to see—the Pelagians could not say this; and still less ought these men to have said it.

For I cannot express how deeply I am troubled that those who condemn with us, by Catholic authority, the error of those heretics should fail to see what the Pelagians recognized as utterly false and absurd.

## CHAPTER XIV

26. Cyprian wrote a book *On Mortality*, well and deservedly known to many, indeed almost all, who love ecclesiastical writings. In it he says that death is not merely harmless to the faithful but is also found to be beneficial, because it removes a person from the dangers of sinning and places him in security from sinning.

But what benefit is there if even future sins that have not been committed are punished? Nevertheless, he discusses at great length and very well the dangers of sinning, showing that they are neither absent in this life nor present after it [Note: [Col. 0979] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions have, “he says.”].

There he also cites the testimony from the Book of Wisdom: “He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding.” You said that these brothers rejected this quotation from me as though it had not been taken from a canonical book—as if, even apart from the testimony of this book, the matter itself were not clear, which I wished [Note: [Col. 0979] The printed editions read, “which we wish.” Several manuscripts have, “which I wished.”] to demonstrate from it.

For what Christian would dare deny that a righteous person, if taken prematurely by death, will be in a place of refreshment (Wisdom 4:11, 7)? Whoever said this, what person of sound faith would think he ought to resist it?

Likewise, if someone said that a righteous person who turned away from his righteousness, in which he had lived for a long time, and died in the wickedness in which he had lived—not merely for one year, but for one day—would go from here into the punishments due to the wicked, and that his former righteousness would profit him nothing (Ezekiel 18:24), what believer would contradict this evident truth?

Furthermore, if we were asked whether, had he died at the time when he was righteous, he would have encountered punishment or rest, would we hesitate to answer “rest”? This is the whole reason why it was said—whoever may have said it—“He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding.”

It was said with reference to the dangers of this life, not to the foreknowledge of God, who foreknew what was going to happen, not what was not going to happen: that is, he foreknew that he would grant him an early death so that he might be removed from the uncertainty of temptations, not that he would sin, since he would not remain amid temptation.

For it is of this life that we read in the Book of Job, “Is not human life upon the earth a time of testing?” (Job 7:1, according to the Septuagint). But why some are granted to be taken away from the dangers of this life while they are righteous, whereas others who are righteous are kept amid those same dangers by a longer life until they fall from righteousness—who has known the mind of the Lord? (Romans 11:34)

Yet from this it is also made clear that even those righteous people who preserve good and devout conduct until the maturity of old age and the final day of this life ought to glory not in their own merits but in the Lord. For the one who snatched away the righteous person by the brevity of his life, lest wickedness should change his understanding, himself preserves the righteous person through however long a life, lest wickedness change his understanding.

But why he has kept here the righteous person who would fall, when he could have taken him away before his fall, belongs altogether to his most just yet inscrutable judgments.

27. Since these things are so, the judgment of the Book of Wisdom ought not to have been rejected. It deserved to be read for so many years in the Church of Christ, from the rank of the Church’s readers, and to be heard with reverence for divine authority by all Christians, from bishops down to the least of the faithful laity, penitents, and catechumens.

Certainly, if I were to produce a defense of this judgment from the interpreters of the divine Scriptures who lived before us—a judgment that we are now compelled to defend against the new error of the Pelagians with greater diligence and fullness than usual, namely, that God’s grace is not given according to our merits but is given freely to the one who receives it, because it depends not on the one who wills or runs but on God who shows mercy, while by a just judgment it is not given to the one to whom it is not given, because there is no injustice with God (Romans 9:16, 14)—if, then, I were to draw the defense of this judgment from the Catholic interpreters who preceded us in the exposition of the divine words, these brothers for whom we are now acting would certainly yield to it. Your letter indicates that this is what you mean.

What need, then, is there for us to scrutinize the little works of those who, before this heresy arose, had no need to engage with this difficult question? They would certainly have done so if they had been compelled to answer such claims. As a result, they touched briefly and in passing upon what they thought about God’s grace in certain places in their writings. They lingered instead over what they were arguing against the enemies [Note: [Col. 0980] The printed editions read, “against other enemies.” The manuscripts do not contain “other.”] of the Church, and over exhortations to the various virtues by which God, living and true, is served in pursuit of eternal life and true happiness.

But the frequent practice of prayer plainly showed what they thought the grace of God accomplished. For they would not ask God for what he commands to be done unless it were granted by him that those things should be done [Note: [Col. 0980] So the manuscripts read. The printed editions have, “asked from God.”].

28. But those who wish to be instructed by the judgments of interpreters ought to place this Book of Wisdom, where we read, “He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding,” above all interpreters. For the distinguished interpreters who lived close to the times of the Apostles placed it above themselves as well; when they cited it as a witness, they believed that they were citing nothing other than divine testimony.

Certainly it is known that the blessed Cyprian argued in order to commend the benefit of an earlier death: those who end this life, in which it is possible to sin, are snatched away from the dangers of sins. In the same book he says, among other things:

“Why do you not embrace the prospect of being with Christ, secure in the Lord’s promise, and rejoice that you are called to Christ and freed from the devil?”

And elsewhere:

“Children,” he says, “escape the danger of a slippery age.”

Again, elsewhere:

“Why do we not,” he says, “hasten and run, so that we may see our homeland and greet our parents? A great number of our loved ones awaits us there—parents, brothers, and children. A numerous and abundant crowd longs for us, already secure concerning their own safety but still concerned for ours.”

By these and similar statements, that teacher plainly and sufficiently testifies, in the clearest light of the Catholic faith, that the dangers and temptations of sin must be feared until the laying aside of this body, and that thereafter no one will suffer such things. Even if he had not testified to this, what Christian of any kind would doubt it when considering this matter?

How, then, would it not be of the greatest and highest benefit to a person who had fallen, who was miserably ending this life in the same fall and going into the punishments due to such a life, if he were snatched away by death from this place of temptations before he fell?

29. Accordingly, if excessive and thoughtless contention is set aside, the entire question concerning the one who was taken away lest wickedness should change his understanding has been settled. The Book of Wisdom, which deserved to be read for so many years in the Church of Christ, and in which this statement is also found, ought not to suffer injury because it resists those who are deceived concerning human merits and so advance against God’s manifest grace.

That grace appears especially in infants. When some of them are baptized and others are not, and they reach the end of this life, they sufficiently display both mercy and judgment: gratuitous mercy and deserved judgment.

For if people were judged according to the merits of the life they did not have because they were overtaken by death, but would have had if they had lived, then it would have benefited neither the one who was taken away lest wickedness should change his understanding nor those who die after falling, if they had died earlier. No Christian will dare say this.

Therefore our brothers, who together with us oppose the destruction caused by the Pelagian error in defense of the Catholic faith, ought not to favor so strongly the Pelagian opinion that God’s grace is given according to our merits that they attempt to destroy the thoroughly true and anciently Christian judgment, “He was taken away, lest wickedness should change his understanding”—something the Pelagians themselves cannot dare to do—and to establish a claim that no one, I think, would be found not merely to believe but even to dream: namely, that each of the dead is judged according to what he would have done had he lived longer.

Thus it is plainly evident that what we say is invincible: God’s grace is not given according to our merits. Those clever people who contradict this truth are forced to utter claims that ought to be driven from everyone’s ears and thoughts.

## CHAPTER XV

30. There is also a most splendid light of predestination and grace: the Savior himself, the Mediator himself between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus. What preceding merits of works or faith possessed by his own human nature could have brought it about that he became this?

Let an answer be given, I ask: how did that human being merit to be assumed by the Word, coeternal with the Father, into the unity of person, so that he might be the only-begotten Son of God? What good of his, of whatever kind, preceded this? What did he do, what did he believe, what did he ask, so as to arrive at this ineffable excellence?

Did not that human being, through the action and assumption of the Word, begin to be the only Son of God from the very moment when he began to exist? Did not that woman, full of grace, conceive the only Son of God? Was not the only Son of God born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, not through the desire of the flesh but through God’s singular gift [Note: [Col. 0982] Most manuscripts read, “by God’s gift alone.”]?

Was there any fear that, as his age advanced, that human being would sin by free choice? Or was his will not free—and indeed all the freer because he could not serve sin? Surely all these things, which are uniquely marvelous, and whatever other things may most truly be said to belong uniquely to him, were received by the human nature—that is, by our nature—in him without any preceding merits of its own.

Let this human being answer God, if he dares, and say, “Why not me as well?” And if he hears, “O human being, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9:20), let him not even then restrain himself, but increase his insolence and say, “How do I hear, ‘Who are you, O human being?’ Since I am what I hear—that is, a human being—and he too, of whom I am speaking, is a human being, why should I not be what he is?”

“But,” he says, “that person has such great grace.” Why is the grace different when the nature is common? Certainly, “there is no partiality with God” (Colossians 3:25). Who, I do not say a Christian, but a madman, would say such things?

31. Let us therefore behold in our Head the very source of grace, from which, according to the measure of each person, it spreads through all his members. By that grace any human being becomes a Christian from the beginning of his faith, by which grace that human being became Christ from his beginning. This person too is reborn of the same Spirit from whom that one was born; by the same Spirit forgiveness of sins is effected in us by which it was effected that he had no sin.

God certainly foreknew that he would do these things. This, then, is the predestination of the saints, which shone forth most fully in the Holy One of holy ones. Who can deny it if he rightly understands the words of truth?

For we have learned that the Lord of glory [Note: [Col. 0982] Three manuscripts read, “the Lord of grace.”], insofar as he became human, was predestined [Note: [Col. 0982] Amerbach, Erasmus, and several manuscripts read, “we say.”] to be the Son of God.

The Teacher of the Nations cries out at the beginning of his Epistles: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined as the Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification, by the resurrection of the dead” (Romans 1:1–4).
