Jesus was therefore predestined so that, although according to the flesh he was to be David’s son, he would nevertheless be the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification, because he was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.

This is that singular and ineffable assumption of human nature accomplished by God the Word, so that the Son of God and the son of humanity might simultaneously be truly and properly called the son of humanity because of the human being who was assumed, and the Son of God because of the one who assumed him, the only-begotten God—lest a quaternity rather than a Trinity should be believed.

This exaltation of human nature, so great, lofty, and supreme, was predestined in such a way that it could not be raised any higher; just as the divinity itself, for our sake, had nowhere to lower itself more humbly than to the point at which human nature, with the weakness of the flesh, was assumed even unto the death of the cross.

Therefore, just as that one person was predestined to be our Head, so we, many as we are, were predestined to be his members. Let human merits be silent here, merits that perished through Adam; and let the grace of God reign, which reigns through Jesus Christ our Lord, the only Son of God, the one Lord [Note: [Col. 0983] So all the manuscripts read. The printed editions have, “the only Son of God, our Lord.”].

Whoever finds in our Head the preceding merits of that singular generation should seek in us, his members, the preceding merits of a multiplied regeneration. For that generation was not given to Christ as a recompense, but bestowed as a gift, so that, free from every obligation of sin, he might be born of the Spirit and the Virgin.

Likewise, our rebirth from water and the Spirit was not given to us in recompense for any merit, but bestowed freely. And if faith led us to the washing of regeneration, we ought not therefore to think that we first gave something so that this saving regeneration might be repaid to us. For the one who made us believe in Christ is the one who made Christ, in whom we believe; the one who made the human being Jesus the origin and perfecter of faith is the one who brings about in human beings the beginning and perfection of faith in Jesus.

For this is how he is called, as you know, in the Epistle to the Hebrews (Hebrews 12:2).

## CHAPTER XVI

32. For God calls many of his predestined people as sons, so that he may make them members of his predestined only Son. He does not call them with the calling by which those also were called who refused to come to the wedding (Luke 14:16–20).

By that calling the Jews too were called, for whom Christ crucified is a stumbling block, and the Gentiles, for whom Christ crucified is foolishness. Rather, he calls the predestined with the calling that the Apostle distinguished when he said that to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, he preaches Christ as the power of God and the wisdom of God.

For he says, “But to those who are called” (1 Corinthians 1:23–24), thereby showing that the others were not called. He knew that there is a certain definite calling belonging to those who are called according to the purpose, whom he foreknew and predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son (Romans 8:28–29).

Referring to this calling, he says: “Not from works, but from the one who calls, it was said to him, ‘The elder shall serve the younger’” (Romans 9:12–13). Did he say, “Not from works, but from the one who believes”? Indeed, he also removed this from the human being, so that he might give everything to God.

He therefore said, “but from the one who calls”—not from just any calling, but from that calling by which a person becomes a believer.

### 33

He had this calling in view also when he said: “For the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable.” For there too, observe briefly what was being discussed. For after he had said, “For I do not want you, brothers, to be ignorant of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own estimation: that a partial blindness has happened to Israel [Note: [Col. 0983] The printed editions have *in Israel*. The word *in* is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek text of the Apostle] [Col. 0984], until the fullness of the nations should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved; as it is written: ‘The deliverer will come from Zion, and will turn ungodliness away from Jacob; and this will be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins’”—he immediately added what must be carefully understood: “According to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake; but according to election, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers” (Romans 11:25–29).

What does “According to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake” mean, except that their hostility—in which they killed Christ—plainly benefited the Gospel, as we see? And this shows that it came about by God’s ordering, for he knows how to make good use even of evil—not so that the vessels of wrath may benefit him, but so that, by his making good use of them, they may benefit the vessels of mercy. For what could have been said more plainly than this: “According to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake”?

It is therefore within the power of evil people to sin; but that, by sinning, their wickedness should do this or that is not within their power, but within the power of God, who divides the darkness and orders it, so that even what they do against God’s will fulfills nothing except God’s will.

We read in the Acts of the Apostles that, when the Apostles, having been released by the Jews, came to their own people and reported to them all that the priests and elders had said to them, all raised their voices together to the Lord and said:

“Lord, you are the one who made heaven and earth and the sea and everything that is in them, who through the mouth of our father David, your holy servant, said: ‘Why did the nations rage, and the peoples devise futile things? The kings of the earth stood forth, and the rulers gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ.’ For in truth they gathered together in this city against your holy servant Jesus, whom you anointed—Herod and Pontius Pilate and the people of Israel—to do whatever your hand and your purpose had predestined to take place” (Acts 4:24–28).

Here is what was said: “According to the Gospel, they are enemies for your sake.” For God’s hand and purpose predestined to be done by the hostile Jews as much as was necessary for the Gospel for our sake [Note: Lov. has *for your sake*. A little later the same edition, together with Am. and Er., reads: “there the enemies are to be understood as being for your sake.” But the manuscripts in both places have *for our sake*].

But what is meant by what follows: “According to election, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers”? Are those enemies—the ones who perished in their hostility, and who, by opposing Christ, are still perishing from that very nation—the chosen and beloved? Far from it! Who, even if utterly foolish, would say this?

Rather, although the two terms are mutually contrary—“enemies” and “beloved”—they apply not to the same people, but to the same Jewish nation and to the same carnal seed of Israel: some of them belong to Israel’s stumbling, and others to Israel’s blessing.

For above he explained this meaning more clearly, where he said: “What Israel was seeking, it did not obtain; but election obtained it, while the rest were blinded” (Romans 11:7). Yet in both groups it is the same Israel.

Therefore, wherever we hear “Israel did not obtain it,” or “the rest were blinded,” the enemies for our sake are to be understood; but wherever we hear “election obtained it,” the beloved for the sake of the fathers are to be understood—those fathers to whom these promises were made [Col. 0985]. For the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed (Galatians 3:16). Hence the wild olive of the nations is grafted into this olive tree.

Now, since the election he is speaking of must be understood as according to grace, not according to debt—for “a remnant has been made according to the election of grace” (Romans 11:5) [Note: Some manuscripts have *has been saved*]—this is the election that obtained it, while the others were blinded. According to this election, the Israelites are beloved for the sake of the fathers.

For they were not called with that calling of which it was said, “Many are called” (Matthew 20:16), but with the calling by which the elect are called. Hence here too, after saying, “According to election, they are beloved for the sake of the fathers,” he immediately added the point under discussion: “For the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable”—that is, they are firmly established without change.

All who belong to this calling are taught by God. None of them can say, “I believed in order to be called”; for God’s mercy preceded him, since he was called in such a way that he would believe.

For all who are taught by God come to the Son, because they have heard and learned from the Father through the Son, who says most explicitly: “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me.” But none of these perishes, because of everything the Father has given him he will lose nothing (John 6:45, 39).

Therefore, whoever belongs to that number certainly does not perish; nor did the one who perishes belong to it [Note: Some manuscripts have: *those who perished were not from us*. The printed editions have: *the one who perishes will not be from that number*, or *who may perish*].

For this reason it was said: “They went out from us, but they were not from us; for if they had been from us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19).

### Chapter XVII

#### 34

Let us therefore understand the calling by which people become elect—not that they are chosen because they have believed, but that they are chosen in order that they may believe.

For the Lord himself makes this sufficiently clear where he says: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16). For if they had been chosen because they had believed, then they themselves had first chosen him by believing in him, so that they might deserve to be chosen.

But the one who says, “You did not choose me, but I chose you,” wholly removes this notion. Certainly they too chose him when they believed in him. Therefore he says, “You did not choose me, but I chose you” for no other reason than that they did not choose him so that he might choose them; rather, he chose them so that they might choose him, because his mercy preceded them (Psalm 58:11), according to grace and not according to debt.

Thus he chose them from the world when he was acting in the flesh [Note: All our manuscripts, both Gallican and Vatican, have *when he was acting in the flesh*. The printed editions have *when he was acting in flesh*], but they had already been chosen in him before the foundation of the world.

This is the unchangeable truth of predestination and grace. For what does the Apostle say? “Just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4). If this was said because God foreknew that they would believe, and not because he himself was going to make them believers, then the Son speaks against this foreknowledge when he says, “You did not choose me, but I chose you” [Col. 0986]—although God would rather have foreknown that they themselves were going to choose him, so that they might deserve to be chosen by him [Note: So read the printed editions Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. In B. alone, *you did not choose me* is written with *not* omitted, although above and below it reads, *You did not choose me*. M.].

They were therefore chosen before the foundation of the world by that predestination in which God foreknew his future works. But they were chosen from the world by that calling through which God fulfilled what he predestined.

“For those whom he predestined, he also called”—namely, with the calling according to his purpose. Therefore not others, but those whom he predestined, he also called; and not others, but those whom he thus called, he also justified; and not others, but those whom he predestined, called, and justified, he also glorified (Romans 8:30)—with that end, certainly, which has no end.

God therefore chose the faithful, but in order that they might become so, not because they already were so. The Apostle James says: “Has not God chosen the poor of this world, rich in faith and heirs of the kingdom which God promised to those who love him?” (James 2:5).

By choosing them, therefore, he makes them rich in faith, just as he makes them heirs of the kingdom. For he is rightly said to choose in them what he chooses them in order to bring about in them [Note: The printed editions have *he chose*. Most manuscripts have *he chooses*].

I ask: who could hear the Lord saying, “You did not choose me, but I chose you,” and dare to say that people believe in order to be chosen, when rather they are chosen in order to believe—lest those to whom Christ says, “You did not choose me, but I chose you,” be found to have chosen Christ first, contrary to the sentence of truth?

### Chapter XVIII

#### 35

Who could hear the Apostle saying:

“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and blameless in his presence in love, predestining us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, for himself, according to the good pleasure of his will, in which he graciously favored us in his beloved Son; in whom we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins, according to the riches of his grace, which he made abound toward us [Note: Most manuscripts have *in us*] in all wisdom and prudence, making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in him, in the dispensation [Note: Am. and Er. have *in the arrangement*. The manuscripts have *for the arrangement*; one manuscript from Corbie has *for the dispensation*] of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth, in him; in whom we have also obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose [Note: The printed editions here and in the following passage have *his purpose*. But the manuscripts consistently omit *his* here and below, as do the printed editions below, §38. Augustine adds it in §37 in order to explain the passage: “According to the purpose—not ours, but his.”], who accomplishes everything according to the counsel of his will, so that we may be to the praise of his glory” (Ephesians 1:3–12)?

Who, I ask, could hear these words attentively and intelligently and dare to doubt this truth, so clearly established, which we defend [Note: All the Gallican and Vatican manuscripts have: *to doubt this matter, this truth so clearly established, which we defend*]?

God chose the members of Christ in Christ before the foundation of the world. And how could he choose those who did not yet exist, except by predestining them? He therefore chose us by predestining us.

Would he choose the ungodly and the unclean? For if the question were raised whether he chooses such people [Col. 0987] or rather the holy and blameless, who would seek to know what answer should be given, instead of immediately delivering a judgment in favor of the holy and blameless? [Note: The printed editions have *who is sought*. All our manuscripts have *who would seek?*, apparently expressing hesitation and uncertainty.]

#### 36

“He foreknew,” says the Pelagian, “who would become holy and blameless through the free decision of the will; and therefore, before the foundation of the world, he chose them in that very foreknowledge by which he foreknew that they would become such. He chose,” he says, “before they existed, predestining as sons those whom he foreknew would become holy and blameless. Certainly he did not make them so, nor foresee that he himself would make them so; he merely foresaw that they would become so.”

Let us therefore examine the Apostle’s words and see whether he chose us before the foundation of the world because we were going to be holy and blameless, or in order that we might be so.

“Blessed,” he says, “be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and blameless.”

Therefore not because we were going to be so, but in order that we might be so. Surely it is certain; surely it is clear. For this is why we were going to become such: because he himself chose us, predestining us so that by his grace we might become such.

Thus he blessed us with a spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus, just as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, so that we might be holy and blameless in his presence, in love predestining us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, for himself.

Next, observe what he adds: “according to the good pleasure of his will,” so that in so great a benefit of grace we might not glory in the good pleasure of our own will [Note: The printed editions have *the grace of God, so that we might glory in his good pleasure*. The manuscripts correct this reading].

“In which,” he says, “he graciously favored us in his beloved Son”—that is, in his own will he graciously favored us. The expression “graciously favored” (*gratificavit*) is derived from grace, just as “justified” is derived from justice.

“In whom,” he says, “we have redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of sins according to the riches of his grace, which he made abound toward us in all wisdom and prudence, making known to us the mystery of his will, according to his good pleasure.”

In this mystery of his will he placed the riches of his grace, according to his good pleasure and not according to ours; and ours could not have been good unless he had assisted us, according to his good pleasure, so that it might become good.

After saying, “according to his good pleasure,” he added: “which he purposed in him”—that is, in his beloved Son—“in the dispensation of the fullness of times, to restore all things in Christ, things in heaven and things on earth, in him; in whom we have also obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose, who accomplishes everything according to the counsel of his will, so that we may be to the praise of his glory.”

#### 37

It would take too long to discuss each point individually. But surely you see—surely you see—how clearly and forcefully this grace is defended by the Apostle’s words, against which human merits are exalted, as though a person first gave something so that it might be repaid to him.

God therefore chose us in Christ before the foundation of the world, predestining us for adoption as sons—not because we were going to become holy and [Col. 0988] blameless through ourselves, but he chose and predestined us in order that we might become so.

He did this according to the good pleasure of his will, so that no one might glory in his own will, but in God’s will toward him. He did this according to the riches of his grace, according to his good pleasure, which he purposed in his beloved Son, in whom we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose—not our purpose, but that of him who accomplishes everything, even to the point that he himself works in us even willing (Philippians 2:13).

He works according to the counsel of his will, so that we may be to the praise of his glory. This is why we cry out that no one should glory in a human being (1 Corinthians 3:21), and consequently not in himself; but “whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 1:31), so that we may be to the praise of his glory.

For he himself works according to his purpose, so that we may be to the praise of his glory—holy and blameless, certainly—which is why he called us, predestining us before the foundation of the world.

From this purpose of his comes that distinctive calling of the elect, for whom he works all things together for good, because they are called according to his purpose (Romans 8:28), and “the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable.”

### Chapter XIX

#### 38

But perhaps these people of ours, about whom and for whom we are now speaking, say that the Pelagians are refuted by this apostolic testimony, where he says that we were chosen in Christ and predestined before the foundation of the world so that we might be holy and blameless in his presence in love.

For they themselves think: “After receiving the commandments, we become holy and blameless through ourselves, by the free decision of the will, in his presence in love. Since God foreknew that this would happen,” they say, “he therefore chose and predestined us in Christ before the foundation of the world.”

But the Apostle says that he chose us not because he foreknew that we would become such, but in order that we might become such through that very election of his grace by which he graciously favored us in his beloved Son.

Therefore, when he predestined us, he foreknew his work, by which he makes us holy and blameless. Thus the Pelagian error is rightly convicted by this testimony.

“But we say,” they reply, “that God foreknew nothing concerning us except the faith by which we begin to believe, and that he therefore chose us before the foundation of the world and predestined us so that by his grace and work we might also become holy and blameless.”

Let them hear, then, in this same testimony, where it says: “We have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who accomplishes everything.” He therefore works so that we may begin to believe—the one who accomplishes everything.

The calling of which it was said, “For the gifts and calling of God are irrevocable” (Romans 11:29), and of which it was said, “Not from works, but from him who calls” (Romans 9:12)—although he could have said, “but from one who believes”—and the election signified by the Lord when he said, “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15:16): faith itself does not precede them.

For he did not choose us because we believed, but in order that we might believe, lest we be said to have chosen him first, and the statement “You did not choose me, but I chose you”—which God forbid—be false.

Nor are we called because we believed, but in order that we might believe. Through that calling, which is irrevocable, the very thing is brought about and accomplished: that we believe.

Nor is it necessary to repeat everything we have said at such length about this matter [Col. 0989].

#### 39

Finally, in what follows in this same testimony, the Apostle gives thanks to God for those who believed—not, of course, because the Gospel had been announced to them, but because they believed.

For he says:

“In him you also, having heard the word of truth, the Gospel of your salvation, in him, having believed, were sealed with the Holy Spirit of promise, who is the pledge of our inheritance, for the redemption of the possession, to the praise of his glory. For this reason I too, having heard of your faith in Christ Jesus and toward all the saints, do not cease giving thanks for you” (Ephesians 1:13–16).

Their faith was new and recent, following the preaching of the Gospel to them; and when the Apostle heard of this faith, he gave thanks to God for them.

If he were giving thanks to a human being for something which he either thought that person had not brought about or knew that person had not brought about, it would more truly be called flattery or mockery than thanksgiving.

“Do not be deceived: God is not mocked” [Note: Am. and Er. have *Let us not be deceived: God is not mocked*. Most manuscripts have *Do not be deceived, says the Apostle; God is not mocked*. Following the edition of Lov., we omit *says the Apostle*] (Galatians 6:7).

For even beginning faith is his gift, lest the Apostle’s thanksgiving be rightly judged false or deceptive.

What of this? Does not the beginning of the Thessalonians’ faith appear in the passage where the same Apostle nevertheless gives thanks to God, saying:

“For this reason we too give thanks to God without ceasing, because when you received from us the word of the message of God, you accepted it not as the word of human beings, but, as it truly is, the word of God, which is at work in you who have believed” (1 Thessalonians 2:13)?

Why does he give thanks to God for this? Surely it is vain and empty to give thanks to someone for something that he himself did not do [Note: The printed editions have *if he gives thanks to someone for this, which he himself did not do*. The manuscripts omit the words *for this* and *which*].

But since this is not vain and empty, God himself—whom he thanks for this work—certainly brought it about: when they received from the Apostle the word of the message of God, they accepted it not as the word of human beings, but as it truly is, the word of God.

God therefore works in human hearts through that calling according to his purpose, about which we have spoken at length, so that they do not hear the Gospel fruitlessly, but, after hearing it, are converted and believe, receiving it not as the word of human beings, but as it truly is, the word of God.

### Chapter XX

#### 40

The Apostle also reminds us that the beginning of human faith is God’s gift when he signifies this in his Epistle to the Colossians:

“Persevere in prayer, being watchful in it with thanksgiving, praying also for us that God may open to us a door for the word, to speak the mystery of Christ, for which I am also in chains, so that I may make it known as I ought to speak” (Colossians 4:2–4).

How is the door of the word opened except when the understanding of the hearer is opened so that he may believe, and, once faith has begun, accept what is preached and discussed for the building up of sound doctrine? Otherwise, with the heart closed through unbelief, he disapproves and rejects what is said.

Hence he also says to the Corinthians:

“I will remain in Ephesus until Pentecost, for a great and evident door has been opened to me, and there are many adversaries” (1 Corinthians 16:8–9).

What else can be understood here except that, when the Gospel was first preached there through him, many believed, while many adversaries [Col. 0990] of that same faith arose, in accordance with the Lord’s saying: “No one comes to me unless it has been given to him by my Father” (John 6:66); and, “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of heaven, but to them it has not been given” (Matthew 13:11)?

The door, therefore, has been opened in those to whom it has been given; but the many adversaries are among those to whom it has not been given.

#### 41

Likewise, in the second Epistle to the same people, the same Apostle says:

“When I came to Troas for the Gospel of Christ, and a door had been opened to me in the Lord, I had no rest in my spirit because I did not find Titus my brother; but, saying farewell to them, I departed for Macedonia.”

To whom did he say farewell except to those who had believed, in whose hearts the door had been opened to the one preaching the Gospel?

But observe what he adds:

“But thanks be to God, who always makes us triumph in Christ and manifests through us the fragrance of the knowledge of himself in every place; for we are the good fragrance of Christ to God, both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing: to some, a fragrance of death unto death; to others, a fragrance of life unto life.”

See why the most zealous soldier and unconquered defender of grace gives thanks. See why he gives thanks: because the Apostles are the good fragrance of Christ to God, both among those who are being saved through his grace and among those who are perishing through his judgment.

But so that those who understand these matters poorly may not be too indignant [Note: The printed editions have *so that indignation may be lessened toward those who understand these matters poorly*. The particle *toward* is absent from the manuscripts], he himself adds the reminder: “And who is sufficient for these things?” (2 Corinthians 2:12–16).

But let us return to the opening of the door by which the Apostle signified the beginning of the hearers’ faith. What else does “praying also for us that God may open to us a door for the word” mean except the clearest demonstration that even the beginning of faith is God’s gift?

For no one would ask him for it in prayer unless he believed that it was granted by him.

This gift of heavenly grace had descended upon that seller of purple cloth whose understanding, as Scripture says in the Acts of the Apostles, God had opened, and she attended to what was being said by Paul (Acts 16:14).

She was called in such a way that she would believe.

For God does what he wills in human hearts, either by helping or by judging, so that even through them what his hand and purpose predestined to take place may be fulfilled (Acts 4:28).

#### 42

Therefore they also said in vain that the point which we proved from the testimony of the Books of Kings and Chronicles—that, whenever God wills something to be done which ought to be done only by willing human beings, their hearts are inclined so that they will it (1 Kings 10:26; 1 Chronicles 12:18), by him who in a marvelous and ineffable manner works even willing in us—does not pertain to the matter under discussion (above, in the Epistle of Hilary, §7).

What else is it to say nothing and yet contradict us? Unless, perhaps, they gave you some reason why this seemed so to them, which you preferred to leave unmentioned in your letter. But I do not know what that reason could be.

Perhaps it is because we showed that God had worked this in human hearts and had brought about the wills of those whom he pleased, so that Saul or David might be established as king. For this reason they do not think that these examples fit the present matter, since temporal kingship in this age is not the same as reigning [Col. 0991] with God eternally; and consequently they suppose that God inclines people’s wills in order to establish earthly kingdoms, but does not incline the wills of those whom he chooses in order to obtain the heavenly kingdom.

But I think that the following passages were spoken concerning the kingdom of heaven, not an earthly kingdom:

“Incline my heart to your testimonies” (Psalm 118:36);

“By the Lord a man’s steps are directed, and he wills his way” (Psalm 36:23);

“The will is prepared by the Lord” (Proverbs 8, according to the Septuagint);

“May the Lord our God be with us, as he was with our fathers; may he not abandon us or turn us away from himself; may he incline our hearts toward himself, so that we may walk in all his ways” (1 Kings 8:57–58);

“I will give them a heart to know me and ears that hear” (Baruch 2:31);

“I will give them another heart, and I will give them a new spirit” (Ezekiel 11:19).

Let them also hear this:

“I will put my spirit in you, and I will make you walk in my statutes, observe my judgments, and carry them out” (Ezekiel 36:27).

Let them hear:

“The steps of a man are directed by the Lord; but how can a mortal understand his ways?” (Proverbs 20:24) [Note: In this verse all the manuscripts have *are corrected* instead of *are directed*];

“Every person seems righteous in his own eyes, but the Lord directs hearts” (Proverbs 21:2);

“As many as had been appointed to eternal life believed” (Acts 13:48).

Let them hear these passages, and all the others I have not mentioned, by which it is shown that God also prepares and turns human wills toward the kingdom of heaven and eternal life.

Consider, then, what it means to believe that God works human wills in order to establish earthly kingdoms, while human beings work their own wills in order to attain the kingdom of heaven.

### Chapter XXI

#### 43

We have said much, and perhaps long ago we were able to persuade you of what we want; yet we still speak to such good minds as though they were dull [Note: The manuscripts have *dull* with a doubled consonant], for whom even what is excessive is not enough.

But they should pardon us, for a new question compelled us to do this. In our earlier short works, we had dealt with sufficiently suitable [Col. 0992] testimonies to establish that faith too is God’s gift. Yet an objection was found: those testimonies, it was said, serve to show that the increase of faith is God’s gift, but that the beginning of faith—the point at which a person first believes in Christ—comes from the person himself and is not God’s gift.

On this view, God demands that, once this beginning has preceded, the remaining things—which are God’s gifts—follow as though they were received on account of this merit; and none of them is given freely, although God’s grace, which is gratuitous and nothing else, is proclaimed in them [Note: A certain learned man thinks one should read *and that none of them is given freely* with an additional *not*, as though the following sentence would then naturally result: “although in them ...” But the ancient manuscripts, as many as we have been able to consult, agree with the printed editions in reading *and that none of them is given freely*, so that the sense of the following sentence is: “although in them ...” The learned man is moved by the fact that the Semi-Pelagians, except for the beginning of good will or faith, assign all good works to the gratuitous grace of God, as may be seen in Cassian, *Collation* 13, chapters 13 and 17; and also in Hilary above, in Epistle 226 to Augustine, §2, where he says, “For no work, whether begun ...” Augustine, however, argues that this implication is contained in their position, whether they wish it or not: the other gifts of God follow the beginning of faith as though that beginning were a preceding merit, and none of them is therefore given freely. Following Augustine, Pope Boniface II, in his letter to Caesarius confirming the decrees of the Second Council of Orange, writes: “Those, however, who, with faith preceding, wish to attribute the remaining things, as you indicate, to grace, are constrained by their own profession to ascribe faith itself even more to the gift of grace. For if nothing good exists without faith, while faith itself is denied to come from grace, then, God forbid, no good thing will be attributable to grace.” We present Boniface’s letter in full in the second part of the Appendix.].

You see how absurd this is. For that reason we persisted, as far as we could, in showing that even the beginning of faith is God’s gift [Note: Here we follow Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. B. has *we established*.].

Even if we have pursued this at greater length than those for whose sake we did so might have wished, we are prepared to be criticized by them for it—provided that, although at much greater length than they wished, and even with the weariness and irritation of those who understand, they acknowledge that we have done what we did: namely, that we have taught that the beginning of faith, just like continence, patience, justice, piety, and the other virtues about which there is no dispute between us, is God’s gift.

Let this therefore be the end of this volume, lest excessive length offend.

[Col. 0991] **The first part of the tenth volume ends.**
